markscheme: (a) $8i=8e^{\frac{\pi}{2}i}$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $z^3=8e^{\left(\frac{\pi}{2}+2k\pi\right)i}$, so $z=2e^{\left(\frac{\pi}{6}+\frac{2k\pi}{3}\right)i}$ [M1] $z=2e^{\frac{\pi}{6}i}$ [A1] $z=2e^{\frac{5\pi}{6}i}$ [A1] $z=2e^{-\frac{\pi}{2}i}$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) $\sqrt3+i$ and $-\sqrt3+i$ [A1] $-2i$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $(\sqrt3+i)+(-\sqrt3+i)+(-2i)=0$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: The solutions of $z^n=w$ have equal modulus $|w|^{1/n}$ and arguments spaced by $\dfrac{2\pi}{n}$. Bring the arguments back into the stated interval at the end.

subtopic: Exact value of cos 15 degrees from a complex quotient
statement: Let $w=\dfrac{1+\sqrt3\,\mathrm i}{1+\mathrm i}$. (a) Write $w$ in the form $a+b\mathrm i$, with $a$ and $b$ in exact form. [3] (b) Write $1+\sqrt3\,\mathrm i$ and $1+\mathrm i$ in modulus-argument form, and hence show that $w=\sqrt2\left(\cos\dfrac\pi{12}+\mathrm i\sin\dfrac\pi{12}\right)$. [3] (c) Hence find the exact value of $\cos\dfrac\pi{12}$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{(1+\sqrt3\mathrm i)(1-\mathrm i)}{2}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{1+\sqrt3+(\sqrt3-1)\mathrm i}2$ [A1][A1] [3 marks] (b) $1+\sqrt3\mathrm i=2\operatorname{cis}\dfrac\pi3$ and $1+\mathrm i=\sqrt2\operatorname{cis}\dfrac\pi4$ [A1][A1] divide moduli, subtract arguments, $\dfrac\pi3-\dfrac\pi4=\dfrac\pi{12}$ [AG] [A1] [3 marks] (c) equate real parts: $\sqrt2\cos\dfrac\pi{12}=\dfrac{1+\sqrt3}2$ [M1] $\cos\dfrac\pi{12}=\dfrac{\sqrt2+\sqrt6}4$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Rationalize the denominator by multiplying by the conjugate, and separately divide in polar form. Equate the two expressions for $w$.

subtopic: A point moving on a circle described by a complex function
statement: A point $P$ moves in the Argand plane so that at time $t$ seconds its position is $z(t)=(3+2i)+4e^{i(0.8t-\frac{\pi}{6})}$. (a) Write down the centre and the radius of the circle on which $P$ moves, and find the time for one complete revolution, correct to three significant figures. [3] (b) Find the position of $P$ when $t=2$, in the form $a+bi$ with $a$, $b$ correct to three significant figures. [3] (c) Find the first time, in seconds, at which the imaginary part of $z(t)$ equals $4$. Give your answer to three significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) centre $3+2i$ [A1]; radius $4$ [A1]; period $\dfrac{2\pi}{0.8}=7.85$ s [A1] [3 marks] (b) $z(2)=3+2i+4e^{i(1.6-0.5236)}$ [M1]; real part $4.90$ [A1]; imaginary part $5.52$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $2+4\sin\left(0.8t-\frac\pi6\right)=4$ [M1]; $\sin\left(0.8t-\frac\pi6\right)=\frac12$, so $0.8t-\frac\pi6=\frac\pi6$ [A1]; $t=1.31$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The imaginary part of $e^{i\theta}$ is $\sin\theta$.

subtopic: Cube roots of unity
statement: Let $\omega=\mathrm{e}^{2\pi\mathrm{i}/3}$. (a) Show that $1+\omega+\omega^2=0$. [2] (b) Hence show that $(1-\omega)(1-\omega^2)=3$. [2] (c) Show that $\left(1+\omega^2\right)^6=1$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\omega^3=\mathrm{e}^{2\pi\mathrm{i}}=1$ and $\omega\neq1$, and $\omega^3-1=(\omega-1)(\omega^2+\omega+1)=0$ [M1] so $\omega^2+\omega+1=0$ [A1][AG] [2 marks] (b) $(1-\omega)(1-\omega^2)=1-\omega-\omega^2+\omega^3$ [M1] $=1-(\omega+\omega^2)+1=1+1+1=3$ [A1][AG] [2 marks] (c) $1+\omega^2=-\omega$ [A1] $(-\omega)^6=\omega^6=(\omega^3)^2=1$ [A1][AG] [2 marks]
tips: The cube roots of unity satisfy $\omega^3=1$ and $1+\omega+\omega^2=0$; nearly every simplification uses these two facts. Reduce powers of $\omega$ by taking multiples of $3$ in the exponent.

subtopic: Intersection of a circle and a ray in the complex plane
statement: Consider the locus $|z-2-2\mathrm i|=2$ and the half-line $\arg z=\dfrac\pi4$. (a) Describe each of the two loci geometrically. [2] (b) Write $z=t(1+\mathrm i)$ with $t>0$, and find the values of $z$ that lie on both loci, in exact form. [4]
markscheme: (a) circle with centre $(2,2)$ and radius $2$ [A1] half-line from the origin at $45^\circ$ to the positive real axis, along $y=x$ with $x>0$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $|(t-2)(1+\mathrm i)|=2$ [M1] $\sqrt2|t-2|=2$ [A1] $t=2\pm\sqrt2$, both positive [A1] $z=(2\pm\sqrt2)(1+\mathrm i)$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Points on the ray $\arg z=\pi/4$ have the form $t(1+\mathrm i)$ with $t>0$. Substitute into the equation of the circle.

subtopic: Impedance of a series RLC circuit
statement: In a series circuit a resistor has resistance $R=30\ \Omega$, an inductor has reactance $X_L=40\ \Omega$ and a capacitor has reactance $X_C=16\ \Omega$. The impedance is the complex number $Z=R+i(X_L-X_C)$. The supply voltage has amplitude $V_0=120$ V. (a) Write $Z$ in the form $a+bi$. [1] (b) Find the modulus $|Z|$ and the argument $\arg Z$ in radians, to 3 significant figures. [3] (c) The current amplitude is $I_0=\dfrac{V_0}{|Z|}$. Find $I_0$ in amperes. [2] (d) The current lags the voltage by the angle $\arg Z$. State this angle in radians. [1] (e) The capacitor is replaced by one with a different reactance $X_C$ so that the current amplitude is as large as possible. Find this value of $X_C$ and the maximum current amplitude. [2]
markscheme: (a) $Z=30+24i$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $|Z|=\sqrt{30^2+24^2}$ [M1] $=38.4\ \Omega$ [A1] $\arg Z=\arctan\dfrac{24}{30}=0.675$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $I_0=\dfrac{120}{38.42}$ [M1] $=3.12$ A [A1] [2 marks] (d) $0.675$ rad [A1] [1 mark] (e) $|Z|$ is smallest when the imaginary part is zero, so $X_C=40\ \Omega$ [A1] $I_0=\dfrac{120}{30}=4$ A [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Impedance combines resistance (real part) and net reactance (imaginary part), so its modulus is smallest when the imaginary part vanishes. Keep extra digits in $|Z|$ before dividing.

subtopic: Impedance of an alternating-current circuit
statement: This question investigates a circuit using complex impedance. A resistor of $R=30$ ohms, an inductor of $L=0.2$ henry and a capacitor of $C=100\,\mu$F ($=10^{-4}$ F) are driven by a source of angular frequency $\omega$ rad/s. Their impedances are $R$, $i\omega L$ and $\dfrac{1}{i\omega C}=-\dfrac{i}{\omega C}$ respectively. (a) For $\omega=150$, find the impedances of the inductor and of the capacitor in the form $bi$. [3] (b) The three components are connected in series. Find the total impedance $Z$ in the form $a+bi$, and find $|Z|$ and $\arg Z$. [4] (c) The source has peak voltage $120$ V. Find the peak current and state whether the current leads or lags the voltage. [3] (d) Show that the impedance of the series circuit is real when $\omega=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}$, and calculate this resonant frequency. [3] (e) At resonance find $|Z|$ and the peak current. Comment on how the current compares with part (c). [3] (f) The inductor-resistor branch $Z_1=R+i\omega L$ and the capacitor branch $Z_2=-\dfrac{i}{\omega C}$ are connected in parallel, with $\omega=150$. Find the total impedance $Z_p=\dfrac{Z_1Z_2}{Z_1+Z_2}$ in the form $a+bi$. [4] (g) Find the power factor $\cos\varphi$ of the series circuit, where $\varphi=\arg Z$. [2]
markscheme: (a) Inductor: $i(150)(0.2)=30i$ [A1]; capacitor: $-\dfrac{i}{150\times10^{-4}}=-66.67i$ [M1][A1] [3 marks] (b) $Z=30+30i-66.67i=30.0-36.67i$ [A1]; $|Z|=47.376$ [A1]; $\arg Z=-0.885$ rad [M1][A1] [4 marks] (c) $I=\dfrac{V}{|Z|}=2.533$ A [M1][A1]; $\arg Z<0$ so the circuit is capacitive and the current leads the voltage by $0.885$ rad [A1] [3 marks] (d) Imaginary part $\omega L-\dfrac{1}{\omega C}=0$ [M1]; $\omega^2=\dfrac{1}{LC}$ [AG]; $\omega_0=223.61$ rad/s [A1] [3 marks] (e) $Z=R=30$ so $|Z|=30$ [A1]; $I=\dfrac{120}{30}=4$ A [A1]; larger than 2.533 A because the reactances cancel [R1] [3 marks] (f) $Z_1=30+30i$, $Z_2=-66.67i$ [A1]; $Z_1Z_2=2000.00-2000.00i$ [M1]; $Z_1+Z_2=30.0-36.67i$ [A1]; $Z_p=59.406+5.941i$ [A1] [4 marks] (g) $\cos\varphi=\dfrac{R}{|Z|}=\dfrac{30}{47.376}=0.633$ [M1][A1] [2 marks]
tips: Impedances in series add; the reactance of an inductor is positive imaginary and of a capacitor is negative imaginary. Resonance occurs when the imaginary parts cancel.

subtopic: Quadratic with complex coefficients
statement: (a) Find the square roots of $5-12\mathrm{i}$, giving your answers in the form $a+b\mathrm{i}$ where $a,b\in\mathbb{Z}$. [4] (b) Hence solve the equation $z^2-2(1+\mathrm{i})z-5+14\mathrm{i}=0$. [3]
markscheme: (a) Let $(a+b\mathrm{i})^2=5-12\mathrm{i}$. Then $a^2-b^2=5$ and $2ab=-12$ [M1] [A1] Substitute $b=-\dfrac6a$: $a^4-5a^2-36=0$ [M1] $(a^2-9)(a^2+4)=0$, so $a=\pm3$ and the square roots are $3-2\mathrm{i}$ and $-3+2\mathrm{i}$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) Complete the square: $\big(z-(1+\mathrm{i})\big)^2=(1+\mathrm{i})^2+5-14\mathrm{i}=5-12\mathrm{i}$ [M1] [A1] $z=1+\mathrm{i}\pm(3-2\mathrm{i})$, so $z=4-\mathrm{i}$ or $z=-2+3\mathrm{i}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: To find $\sqrt{a+b\mathrm{i}}$, equate real and imaginary parts of $(x+y\mathrm{i})^2$ and solve; reject only real-number extraneous roots such as $a^2=-4$. Completing the square is neater than the formula when the linear coefficient is even.

subtopic: Roots of a complex number
statement: (a) Write $-8$ in the form $r(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)$, where $r>0$ and $0<\theta\le\pi$. [1] (b) Solve the equation $z^{3}=-8$, giving the three solutions in the form $r\left(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta\right)$ with $-\pi<\theta\le\pi$. [3] (c) Write the three solutions in the form $a+bi$. [1] (d) The three solutions are represented as points in the complex plane. Show that they are the vertices of an equilateral triangle with side length $2\sqrt3$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $-8=8(\cos\pi+i\sin\pi)$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $z=2\left(\cos\dfrac{\pi+2k\pi}{3}+i\sin\dfrac{\pi+2k\pi}{3}\right)$, $k=0,1,2$ [M1] $z=2\left(\cos\dfrac\pi3+i\sin\dfrac\pi3\right)$ [A1] $z=2(\cos\pi+i\sin\pi)$ and $z=2\left(\cos\left(-\dfrac\pi3\right)+i\sin\left(-\dfrac\pi3\right)\right)$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $1+\sqrt3\,i$, $-2$, $1-\sqrt3\,i$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) $|(1+\sqrt3i)-(-2)|=|3+\sqrt3i|=\sqrt{12}=2\sqrt3$ and $|(1+\sqrt3i)-(1-\sqrt3i)|=|2\sqrt3i|=2\sqrt3$ [M1] by the symmetry in the real axis the third side $|(1-\sqrt3i)-(-2)|$ is also $2\sqrt3$, so all sides are equal [R1] [2 marks]
tips: The cube roots of a complex number are equally spaced around a circle, separated by $\frac{2\pi}{3}$ in argument, so they always form an equilateral triangle. Divide the argument by $3$ and add multiples of $\frac{2\pi}{3}$.

subtopic: Complex roots of a quadratic equation
statement: Consider the equation $z^2-6z+25=0$, $z\in\mathbb{C}$. (a) Solve the equation. [3] (b) Write the root with positive imaginary part in the form $re^{i\theta}$, giving $\theta$ to 3 significant figures. [3] (c) Show that the sum of the roots is $6$ and the product is $25$, and explain how these relate to the coefficients. [3]
markscheme: (a) $z=\dfrac{6\pm\sqrt{36-100}}{2}$ [M1]; $=\dfrac{6\pm8i}{2}$ [A1]; $z=3\pm4i$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $r=5$ [A1]; $\theta=\arctan\dfrac43$ [M1] $=0.927$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Sum $=(3+4i)+(3-4i)=6$ [A1]; product $=9+16=25$ [A1]; for $z^2+bz+c$, sum $=-b$ and product $=c$ [R1] [3 marks]
tips: Complex roots of a polynomial with real coefficients occur in conjugate pairs; their sum and product are real.

subtopic: Triangle area from three complex numbers
statement: Three points in the complex plane represent the complex numbers $z_1=1+i$, $z_2=4+i$ and $z_3=2+5i$. (a) Find $|z_2-z_1|$ and $|z_3-z_1|$. [2] (b) Find the area of the triangle with vertices $z_1$, $z_2$ and $z_3$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $z_2-z_1=3$ so $|z_2-z_1|=3$ [A1]; $z_3-z_1=1+4i$ so $|z_3-z_1|=\sqrt{17}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Base $z_1z_2$ is horizontal with length $3$ [A1]; height $=5-1=4$ [A1]; area $=\dfrac12\times3\times4=6$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The distance between the points representing $z_1$ and $z_2$ is $|z_2-z_1|$.

subtopic: Polar and Cartesian forms with products and quotients
statement: Let $z=-3+5i$ and $w=4e^{0.6i}$. Give moduli and arguments correct to 3 significant figures, with arguments in radians in the interval $(-\pi,\pi]$. (a) Find the modulus and the argument of $z$. [3] (b) Find the modulus and argument of $zw$ and of $\dfrac{z}{w}$. [4] (c) Write $w$ in the form $a+bi$, giving $a$ and $b$ to 3 significant figures. [2]
tips: Multiply moduli and add arguments for a product; divide moduli and subtract arguments for a quotient. Work in radian mode.

subtopic: Square root of a complex number
statement: Let $w=5-12i$. (a) Find real numbers $a$ and $b$ such that $(a+bi)^{2}=w$, by equating real and imaginary parts. [4] (b) Hence solve $z^{2}-3z+(1+3i)=0$. [3] (c) Explain why the two solutions are not complex conjugates of each other. [1]
markscheme: (a) $a^{2}-b^{2}=5$ and $2ab=-12$ [M1][A1]; $b=-\dfrac6a$ so $a^{4}-5a^{2}-36=0$ [M1]; $a=\pm3$, so $3-2i$ or $-3+2i$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) Discriminant $9-4(1+3i)=5-12i$ [A1]; $z=\dfrac{3\pm(3-2i)}{2}$ [M1]; $z=3-i$ or $z=i$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) The coefficients of the quadratic are not all real, so the conjugate root theorem does not apply [R1] [1 mark]
tips: If $(a+bi)^{2}=x+yi$ then $a^{2}-b^{2}=x$ and $2ab=y$.

subtopic: Modulus and argument with a calculator
statement: Let $z_1=2+3\mathrm i$ and $z_2=-1+4\mathrm i$. (a) Find $|z_1+z_2|$ and $\arg(z_1+z_2)$. [3] (b) Find $\arg\left(\dfrac{z_1}{z_2}\right)$ using $\arg z_1-\arg z_2$, giving the answer in $(-\pi,\pi]$. [3] (c) Find the smallest positive integer $n$ for which $z_1^n$ has a negative real part and a positive imaginary part. [3]
markscheme: (a) $z_1+z_2=1+7\mathrm i$ [A1] $|z_1+z_2|=\sqrt{50}=7.071$ [A1] argument $=1.429$ rad [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\arg z_1=0.9828$ [A1] $\arg z_2=\pi-\arctan4=1.816$ [A1] difference $-0.8330$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\arg z_1^n=n\times0.9828$ [M1] need argument in $\left(\dfrac\pi2,\pi\right)$ [M1] $n=2$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Use the calculator in radian mode. When subtracting arguments, adjust by $2\pi$ to bring the result into $(-\pi,\pi]$.

subtopic: Gain and phase shift of an electronic filter
statement: An electronic filter multiplies the complex amplitude of an input signal by the complex number $H=1.2-0.9i$. The gain of the filter is $|H|$ and its phase shift is $\arg H$. (a) Find the gain and the phase shift, in radians, to 3 significant figures. [3] (b) An input signal has complex amplitude $8e^{0.4i}$. Find the output signal in the form $re^{i\theta}$, with $r$ and $\theta$ to 3 significant figures. [2] (c) Identical filters are connected one after another, with the input signal of part (b). Find the smallest number of filters for which the output amplitude exceeds $100$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $|H|=\sqrt{1.2^2+0.9^2}$ [M1] gain $=1.5$ [A1] phase shift $=\arctan\left(\dfrac{-0.9}{1.2}\right)=-0.644$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Multiply moduli, add arguments [M1] $12e^{-0.244i}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $8(1.5)^n>100$ [M1] $n=7$ (since $8(1.5)^6=91.1$ and $8(1.5)^7=137$) [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Multiplying by $H$ scales the amplitude by $|H|$ and shifts the phase by $\arg H$. Several filters in series multiply gains, giving a power of $|H|$.

subtopic: Exact powers using modulus-argument form
statement: Let $z=-1+\sqrt3\,i$. (a) Find $|z|$ and $\arg z$, giving $\arg z$ in radians in the interval $(-\pi,\pi]$. [3] (b) Write $z$ in the form $re^{i\theta}$ and hence find $z^{6}$ exactly. [3] (c) Find $z^{-3}$ in Cartesian form. [2]
tips: Use $(re^{i\theta})^{n}=r^{n}e^{in\theta}$, then evaluate the exponential using $e^{i\theta}=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$.

subtopic: Complex number and its reciprocal
statement: Let $z$ be a complex number such that $z+\dfrac1z=1$. (a) Show that $z^2-z+1=0$ and solve for $z$ in the form $r\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta}$. [4] (b) Hence find the value of $z^3+\dfrac1{z^3}$. [2]
markscheme: (a) multiply by $z$ [M1] $z^2-z+1=0$ [A1] $z=\dfrac{1\pm\sqrt3\mathrm i}2$ [A1] $z=\mathrm e^{\pm\mathrm i\pi/3}$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $z^3=\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\pi}=-1$ [M1] $-1+(-1)=-2$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A real value of $z+\frac1z$ with modulus at most $2$ forces $|z|=1$; then $z^n+z^{-n}=2\cos n\theta$.

subtopic: Fifth roots of unity and an exact cosine sum
statement: Let $\omega=e^{\frac{2\pi}{5}i}$. (a) Solve $z^5=1$, giving all five solutions as powers of $\omega$. [2] (b) Show that the sum of the five solutions is zero. [2] (c) Hence show that $\cos\dfrac{2\pi}{5}+\cos\dfrac{4\pi}{5}=-\dfrac12$. [3] (d) Use your GDC to verify the result in part (c) numerically. [1] (e) The five solutions are the vertices of a regular pentagon. Find the length of one side of this pentagon, to 3 significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) $z=e^{\frac{2k\pi}{5}i}$ for $k=0,1,2,3,4$ [M1] so the solutions are $1,\ \omega,\ \omega^2,\ \omega^3,\ \omega^4$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $z^5-1=0$ has no $z^4$ term, so the sum of the roots is $0$ [M1] [A1] (alternatively $1+\omega+\dots+\omega^4=\dfrac{1-\omega^5}{1-\omega}=0$) [2 marks] (c) $\omega+\omega^4=2\cos\dfrac{2\pi}{5}$ and $\omega^2+\omega^3=2\cos\dfrac{4\pi}{5}$ since these are conjugate pairs [A1] taking real parts of $1+\omega+\omega^2+\omega^3+\omega^4=0$ [M1] $1+2\cos\dfrac{2\pi}{5}+2\cos\dfrac{4\pi}{5}=0$, so the sum is $-\dfrac12$ [AG] [3 marks] (d) $0.309-0.809=-0.500$ [A1] [1 mark] (e) Side $=|\omega-1|$ [M1] $=2\sin\dfrac{\pi}{5}=1.18$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Roots of unity sum to zero, and conjugate pairs add to twice their real part, which is how exact trigonometric values often arise. The distance between two points on the unit circle separated by angle $\theta$ is $2\sin\frac{\theta}{2}$.

subtopic: Powers of complex numbers using polar form
statement: (a) Find $(1+i)^{8}$. [3] (b) Find $\left(\sqrt3-i\right)^{6}$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $1+i=\sqrt2\left(\cos\dfrac\pi4+i\sin\dfrac\pi4\right)$ [A1] $(1+i)^8=(\sqrt2)^8\left(\cos2\pi+i\sin2\pi\right)$ [M1] $=16$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\sqrt3-i=2\left(\cos\left(-\dfrac\pi6\right)+i\sin\left(-\dfrac\pi6\right)\right)$ [A1] $\left(\sqrt3-i\right)^6=2^6\left(\cos(-\pi)+i\sin(-\pi)\right)$ [M1] $=-64$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Convert to modulus-argument form before raising to a power: the modulus is raised to the power and the argument is multiplied by it. Use $\cos$ and $\sin$ of exact angles to finish.

subtopic: Arithmetic with complex numbers in Cartesian form
statement: Let $z=2 - 5 i$ and $w=3 + i$. (a) Find $zw$. [2] (b) Find $\dfrac zw$ in the form $a+b\mathrm i$. [3] (c) Find $|z|$ and $|w|$ and verify that $|zw|=|z||w|$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $(2 - 5 i)(3 + i)$ expanded [M1] $=11 - 13 i$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) multiply by the conjugate $\overline w=3 - i$ [M1] $\dfrac{1 - 17 i}{10}$ [A1] $=\frac{1}{10} - \frac{17 i}{10}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $|z|=\sqrt{29}$, $|w|=\sqrt{10}$ [A1] $|zw|=\sqrt{290}$ [M1] both products equal $\sqrt{290}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Divide by multiplying numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator. The modulus of a product is the product of the moduli.

subtopic: Quadratic equations with complex roots
statement: (a) Solve the equation $z^2-4z+13=0$, giving the solutions in the form $a+bi$. [3] (b) Let $\alpha$ be the solution with positive imaginary part. Find $\alpha^2$ in the form $a+bi$. [2] (c) Write down the exact value of $\arg\alpha$, in radians. [1]
markscheme: (a) $z=\dfrac{4\pm\sqrt{16-52}}{2}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{4\pm\sqrt{-36}}{2}$ [A1] $z=2\pm3i$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\alpha^2=(2+3i)^2=4+12i+9i^2$ [M1] $=-5+12i$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\arg\alpha=\arctan\dfrac32$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: The discriminant is negative, so the roots are complex conjugates; use $\sqrt{-36}=6i$. The argument of a number in the first quadrant is $\arctan\frac{\text{Im}}{\text{Re}}$.

subtopic: Solving equations for a complex number
statement: (a) Solve $z^2+4z+13=0$, giving the roots in the form $a+b\mathrm i$. [3] (b) Find the complex number $z=x+y\mathrm i$ satisfying $2z+3\overline z=10-\mathrm i$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $z=\dfrac{-4\pm\sqrt{16-52}}2$ [M1] $=\dfrac{-4\pm6\mathrm i}2$ [A1] $z=-2\pm3\mathrm i$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $2x+2y\mathrm i+3x-3y\mathrm i=5x-y\mathrm i$ [M1][A1] $5x=10$ and $-y=-1$ [M1] $z=2+\mathrm i$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Write $z=x+y\mathrm i$ and equate real and imaginary parts when conjugates appear.

subtopic: Echoes modeled as a complex geometric series
statement: A sound produces a signal represented by the complex number $1$. Each successive echo has its amplitude multiplied by $0.9$ and its phase advanced by $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ relative to the previous one, so the echoes are represented by $1,w,w^2,\dots$ where $w=0.9e^{\frac{\pi}{6}i}$. The total signal after $n$ terms is $S_n=1+w+\dots+w^{n-1}$. (a) Write $w$ and $w^2$ in the form $a+bi$, with $a$ and $b$ to 3 significant figures. [2] (b) Explain why the series converges, and find $S_\infty$ in the form $a+bi$, with $a$ and $b$ to 3 significant figures. [4] (c) Find $|S_\infty|$ to 3 significant figures. [1] (d) Show that $\left|S_\infty-S_n\right|=\dfrac{0.9^n}{|1-w|}$ and hence find the smallest $n$ for which $\left|S_\infty-S_n\right|<0.01$. [4]
tips: A complex geometric series converges when $|w|<1$ and its sum is $\frac{1}{1-w}$, exactly as in the real case. The remainder after $n$ terms is $\frac{w^n}{1-w}$; use moduli to compare it with the tolerance.

subtopic: Quartic equation solved as a quadratic in z squared
statement: Consider the equation $z^4-2z^2+4=0$, where $z\in\mathbb C$. (a) Solve the equation for $z^2$, and write each value in the form $r\operatorname{cis}\theta$. [3] (b) Hence find the four solutions for $z$ in the form $a+b\mathrm i$, with $a$ and $b$ exact. [4]
markscheme: (a) $z^2=\dfrac{2\pm\sqrt{4-16}}2$ [M1] $=1\pm\sqrt3\mathrm i$ [A1] $=2\operatorname{cis}\left(\pm\dfrac\pi3\right)$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $z=\sqrt2\operatorname{cis}\left(\pm\dfrac\pi6\right)$ [M1][A1] and the negatives of these [M1] $z=\pm\left(\dfrac{\sqrt6}2\pm\dfrac{\sqrt2}2\mathrm i\right)$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Treat $z^2$ as the unknown. The square roots of a complex number come in pairs differing by a sign.

subtopic: Adding sinusoidal voltages with phasors
statement: Two alternating voltages in a circuit are given by $V_1=12\sin(100\pi t)$ and $V_2=9\sin\left(100\pi t+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$, where $t$ is in seconds. Each voltage can be written as the imaginary part of $Ae^{i(100\pi t+\phi)}$. (a) Write down the complex numbers $z_1=12e^{i\cdot0}$ and $z_2$ that represent the amplitude and phase of $V_1$ and $V_2$, giving $z_2$ in Cartesian form $a+bi$. [2] (b) Find $z_1+z_2$ in the form $re^{i\theta}$, where $r>0$ and $-\pi<\theta\le\pi$. [3] (c) Hence write the total voltage $V_1+V_2$ in the form $R\sin(100\pi t+\alpha)$. [2]
tips: Phasor addition works only because both voltages have the same frequency; add the complex amplitudes, then convert back. Make sure your GDC is in radian mode for the argument.

subtopic: A pair of simultaneous equations with complex coefficients
statement: Solve the simultaneous equations $z+2iw=4+2i$ and $(2-i)z+w=1$, where $z,w\in\mathbb{C}$. (a) Eliminate $w$ to show that $\left(1-2i(2-i)\right)z=4+2i-2i$ and find $z$. [3] (b) Hence find $z$ and $w$ in the form $a+bi$, using your calculator for the arithmetic. [4]
tips: Treat $i$ as a constant when eliminating; rationalize denominators using the conjugate.

subtopic: Loci in the complex plane
statement: The complex number $z=x+y\mathrm{i}$ satisfies $|z-4|=2|z-1|$. (a) Show that the locus of $z$ is a circle, and state its centre and radius. [4] (b) Find the complex number $z$ that satisfies this equation and has argument $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $|z-4|^2=4|z-1|^2$ [M1] $(x-4)^2+y^2=4\left[(x-1)^2+y^2\right]$ [A1] $x^2-8x+16+y^2=4x^2-8x+4+4y^2$ [A1] so $3x^2+3y^2=12$, i.e. $x^2+y^2=4$: a circle with centre $(0,0)$ and radius $2$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $|z|=2$ and $\arg z=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$, so $z=2\operatorname{cis}\dfrac{\pi}4$ [M1] $z=\sqrt2+\sqrt2\,\mathrm{i}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: To find a locus, write $z=x+y\mathrm{i}$ and square both sides so that the moduli become sums of squares. Interpret the final equation geometrically before continuing.

subtopic: Quadratic with complex roots in Euler form
statement: Consider the equation $z^{2}-4z+8=0$ where $z\in\mathbb{C}$. (a) Solve the equation, giving the roots in the form $a+bi$. [3] (b) Write the root with positive imaginary part in the form $re^{i\theta}$, where $r>0$ and $\theta$ is exact. [3] (c) Write down the other root in the form $re^{i\theta}$, and state the sum of the two roots. [2]
markscheme: (a) $z=\dfrac{4\pm\sqrt{16-32}}{2}$ [M1]; $\sqrt{-16}=4i$ [A1]; $z=2\pm2i$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $r=\sqrt{4+4}=2\sqrt2$ [A1]; $\theta=\arctan\dfrac{2}{2}=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ [M1]; $2\sqrt2e^{i\pi/4}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $2\sqrt2e^{-i\pi/4}$ [A1]; sum $=4$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Complex roots of a real quadratic come in conjugate pairs, so the second root has the same modulus and the negative argument.

subtopic: Conjugates and dividing by a complex number
statement: Let $z=4-3i$. (a) Write down $z^*$, the complex conjugate of $z$. [1] (b) Find $zz^*$. [2] (c) Find real numbers $a$ and $b$ such that $(a+bi)(1+2i)=z$. [3]
tips: Multiplying a complex number by its conjugate always gives a real number, the squared modulus. Use the same trick to remove $i$ from a denominator.

subtopic: Cartesian operations on complex numbers
statement: Let $z=3+4i$ and $w=1-2i$. (a) Find $zw$ in the form $a+bi$. [2] (b) Find $\dfrac zw$ in the form $a+bi$. [3] (c) Find $|z|$ and $\arg z$ (to 3 significant figures, in radians). [3]
markscheme: (a) $zw=(3 + 4 i)(1 - 2 i)$ [M1] $=11 - 2 i$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Multiply numerator and denominator by $\bar w=1 + 2 i$ [M1]; denominator $=5$ [A1]; $\dfrac zw=-1 + 2 i$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $|z|=\sqrt{9+16}=5$ [A1]; $\arg z=$ angle in the correct quadrant (use the reference angle $\arctan\left|\dfrac{4}{3}\right|$) [M1] $=0.927$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Multiply by the conjugate of the denominator to realize it; check the quadrant for the argument.

subtopic: Roots of a complex number
statement: (a) Solve the equation $z^3=8\mathrm{i}$, giving the roots in the form $r\operatorname{cis}\theta$ where $r>0$ and $-\pi<\theta\le\pi$. [5] (b) The roots are represented by points on an complex plane. Find the exact area of the triangle formed by these three points. [2]
markscheme: (a) $8\mathrm{i}=8\operatorname{cis}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}+2k\pi\right)$ [M1] $|z|=\sqrt[3]{8}=2$ [A1] $\arg z=\dfrac{\pi}{6}+\dfrac{2k\pi}{3}$ [M1] Roots: $2\operatorname{cis}\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ and $2\operatorname{cis}\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$ [A1] $2\operatorname{cis}\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$ [A1] [5 marks] (b) The points are $(\sqrt3,1)$, $(-\sqrt3,1)$, $(0,-2)$ [M1] Base $2\sqrt3$, height $3$: area $=\dfrac12\times2\sqrt3\times3=3\sqrt3$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Include the $2k\pi$ when writing the number in polar form, then divide the argument by $n$ to get $n$ evenly spaced roots. Roots of $z^n=w$ lie on a circle and form a regular polygon.

subtopic: Square on the Argand diagram
statement: In the complex plane, the points $A$ and $B$ represent the complex numbers $1+i$ and $5+3i$. Multiplying a complex number by $i$ rotates it by $90^{\circ}$ anticlockwise about the origin. The points $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$ are the vertices of a square in that order, going anticlockwise. (a) Find $B-A$, and hence find the complex number represented by $C$. [3] (b) Find the complex number represented by $D$, and the area of the square. [3] (c) Find the complex number at the center of the square and the radius of the circle passing through all four vertices. [2]
markscheme: (a) $B-A=4+2i$ [A1]; $C=B+i(B-A)$ [M1]; $C=5+3i+4i-2=3+7i$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $D=A+i(B-A)=1+i+4i-2=-1+5i$ [A1]; side length $\sqrt{16+4}=\sqrt{20}$ [M1]; area $=20$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) center $=\dfrac{A+C}{2}=2+4i$ [A1]; radius $=\dfrac{\sqrt{20}\,\sqrt2}{2}=\sqrt{10}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Going around a square anticlockwise, each side vector is the previous one multiplied by $i$.

subtopic: Loci in the complex plane
statement: (a) Describe geometrically the locus of points $z$ satisfying $|z-2+\mathrm i|=3$. [2] (b) Find the Cartesian equation of the locus $|z-1|=|z+3\mathrm i|$. [3] (c) Find the least value of $|z|$ for $z$ on the circle in part (a). [3]
markscheme: (a) $|z-(2-\mathrm i)|=3$ [M1] a circle with centre $(2,-1)$ and radius $3$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $(x-1)^2+y^2=x^2+(y+3)^2$ [M1] $-2x+1=6y+9$ [A1] $x+3y+4=0$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) distance from origin to centre $=\sqrt{4+1}=\sqrt5$ [M1][A1] since $\sqrt5<3$ the origin is inside the circle, so the least value is $3-\sqrt5$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: $|z-a|$ is the distance from $z$ to $a$. Equal distances to two points give a perpendicular bisector.

subtopic: Complex impedance in an AC circuit
statement: In an alternating-current circuit, the impedance of a component is a complex number $Z=R+iX$ ohms. Two components have impedances $Z_1=3+4i$ and $Z_2=6-8i$. (a) When the components are connected in series, the total impedance is $Z_1+Z_2$. Find the total impedance and its magnitude, to three significant figures. [2] (b) When the components are connected in parallel, the total impedance is $Z=\dfrac{Z_1Z_2}{Z_1+Z_2}$. Find $Z$ in the form $\dfrac{a+bi}{c}$, where $a,b,c\in\mathbb{Z}$. [3] (c) Find the phase angle, $\arg(Z_1+Z_2)$, in radians, correct to three significant figures. [2]
tips: For a parallel combination multiply the numerator first: here the imaginary parts cancel and give a real product. The argument of a number with positive real part is $\arctan(\text{Im}/\text{Re})$, which is negative when the imaginary part is negative.

subtopic: Exact product and quotient in Euler form
statement: Let $z=-2+2\sqrt3\,i$ and $w=2e^{i\pi/6}$. (a) Find $|z|$ and $\arg z$ exactly, and write $z$ in the form $re^{i\theta}$. [3] (b) Find $zw$ in the form $re^{i\theta}$ and then in the form $a+bi$ with exact values. [3] (c) Find $\dfrac{z}{w}$ in the form $a+bi$. [2]
tips: Use $\tan\theta=\sqrt3$ for the reference angle $\frac{\pi}{3}$, then place it in the correct quadrant.

subtopic: Drone flight path using complex numbers
statement: A drone leaves a launch point at the origin of a complex plane, where the real axis points east and the imaginary axis points north, with distances in km. It flies $5$ km in the direction making an angle of $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ with the positive real axis. It then turns $90^\circ$ anticlockwise and flies a further $3$ km. (a) Write the first displacement as a complex number in the form $a+bi$, to 3 significant figures. [1] (b) Find the second displacement as a complex number in the form $a+bi$, to 3 significant figures. [2] (c) Find the drone's final position as a complex number, to 3 significant figures. [1] (d) Find the final distance of the drone from the launch point, to 3 significant figures. [2] (e) Find the bearing of the drone from the launch point, to the nearest degree. [2]
markscheme: (a) $5e^{\frac{\pi}{6}i}=4.33+2.50i$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) New direction is $\dfrac{\pi}{6}+\dfrac{\pi}{2}=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ [M1] $3e^{\frac{2\pi}{3}i}=-1.50+2.60i$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $2.83+5.10i$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) $\sqrt{2.830^2+5.098^2}$ [M1] $=5.83$ km [A1] [2 marks] (e) Angle from east $=\arctan\dfrac{5.098}{2.830}=61.0^\circ$ [M1] bearing $=90^\circ-61.0^\circ=29^\circ$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A turn through an angle corresponds to multiplying by $e^{i\theta}$, equivalently adding $\theta$ to the argument. Bearings are measured clockwise from north, so subtract the angle from the east axis from $90^\circ$.

subtopic: Simultaneous equations in two complex unknowns
statement: The complex numbers $z$ and $w$ satisfy $z+2w=4+3i$ and $iz-w=1+2i$. (a) Show that $(1+2i)z=6+7i$. [3] (b) Hence find $z$ and $w$ in the form $a+bi$. [4]
markscheme: (a) From the second equation $w=iz-1-2i$ [M1]; substitute: $z+2iz-2-4i=4+3i$ [A1]; $(1+2i)z=6+7i$ [AG] [3 marks] (b) $z=\dfrac{(6+7i)(1-2i)}{5}$ [M1]; $=\dfrac{20-5i}{5}=4-i$ [A1]; $w=i(4-i)-1-2i$ [M1]; $w=2i$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator to divide complex numbers.

subtopic: Adding two complex numbers given in exponential form
statement: Let $z_1=3e^{i\pi/4}$ and $z_2=2e^{-i\pi/3}$. (a) Write $z_1$ and $z_2$ in the form $a+bi$. [2] (b) Find $z_1+z_2$ in Cartesian form, and its modulus and argument. [4] (c) Find $z_1z_2$ and $\dfrac{z_1}{z_2}$ in exponential form. [2] (d) Explain why $|z_1+z_2|\neq|z_1|+|z_2|$ here. [1]
markscheme: (a) $z_1=2.121+2.121i$ [A1]; $z_2=1.000-1.732i$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $z_1+z_2=3.121+0.389i$ [M1][A1]; modulus $=3.146$ [A1]; argument $=0.124$ rad [A1] [4 marks] (c) $z_1z_2=6e^{i(\pi/4-\pi/3)}=6e^{-i\pi/12}$ [A1]; $\dfrac{z_1}{z_2}=1.5e^{i7\pi/12}$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) Modulus of the sum $3.146<5$; the numbers point in different directions (the triangle inequality is strict) [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Add in Cartesian form; multiply or divide in exponential form. The modulus of a sum is not the sum of moduli unless the arguments are equal.

subtopic: Rotation and scaling by multiplying by a complex number
statement: The tip of a robot arm is at the point $P$ represented by $z=3.2+1.5i$, with distances in meters. A command rotates the arm about the origin by $35^{\circ}$ anticlockwise and extends its length by a factor of $1.4$. (a) Write down the complex number $m$ that you multiply $z$ by to carry out this command, in modulus-argument form. [2] (b) Find the new position $mz$ in the form $a+bi$, with $a$ and $b$ correct to three significant figures. [3] (c) Verify that the new distance from the origin is $1.4$ times the original distance, giving both distances to three significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) modulus $1.4$ [A1]; argument $35^{\circ}$, so $m=1.4\left(\cos35^{\circ}+i\sin35^{\circ}\right)$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Use $mz$ [M1]; $a=2.47$ [A1]; $b=4.29$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $|z|=3.53$ [A1]; $|mz|=4.95$ [A1]; $1.4\times3.53\approx4.95$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Multiplying by $re^{i\theta}$ scales by $r$ and rotates anticlockwise by $\theta$.

subtopic: Equation involving a complex number and its conjugate
statement: Find the complex number $z$ that satisfies $z+2z^{*}=9-4i$, where $z^{*}$ is the complex conjugate of $z$. (a) Let $z=x+iy$ and write two real equations for $x$ and $y$. [2] (b) Solve for $z$ and find $\arg z$ in radians, correct to three significant figures. [3]
tips: Equate real parts and imaginary parts separately.

subtopic: Proof that the modulus of a product is the product of moduli
statement: Let $z_1=a+b\mathrm i$ and $z_2=c+d\mathrm i$, where $a,b,c,d\in\mathbb R$. (a) Show that $|z_1z_2|^2=(a^2+b^2)(c^2+d^2)$, and hence that $|z_1z_2|=|z_1||z_2|$. [4] (b) Use the result to show that $\left|\dfrac1z\right|=\dfrac1{|z|}$ for $z\ne0$. [2] (c) Hence find $\left|\dfrac{(3+4\mathrm i)^5}{(1-\sqrt3\mathrm i)^3}\right|$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $z_1z_2=(ac-bd)+(ad+bc)\mathrm i$ [M1] $|z_1z_2|^2=(ac-bd)^2+(ad+bc)^2$ [A1] $=a^2c^2+b^2d^2+a^2d^2+b^2c^2=(a^2+b^2)(c^2+d^2)$ [A1] take square roots (both sides non-negative) [R1] [4 marks] (b) $|z|\left|\dfrac1z\right|=\left|z\times\dfrac1z\right|=|1|=1$ [M1] so $\left|\dfrac1z\right|=\dfrac1{|z|}$ [AG] [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\dfrac{5^5}{2^3}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{3125}8$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Expand the product in Cartesian form, then compare with the product of the two sums of squares.

subtopic: Multiplication by a complex number as a rotation and enlargement
statement: A triangle has vertices at the points $1,\ 3$ and $3+2\mathrm i$ in the complex plane. Each vertex $z$ is mapped to $w=(1+\mathrm i)z$. (a) Describe the transformation as a rotation followed by an enlargement, giving the angle and the scale factor. [2] (b) Find the images of the three vertices. [3] (c) Find the area of the original triangle, and use the scale factor to find the area of the image. [3]
markscheme: (a) $1+\mathrm i=\sqrt2\operatorname{cis}\dfrac\pi4$ [M1] rotation of $\dfrac\pi4$ anticlockwise about the origin, enlargement with scale factor $\sqrt2$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $1+\mathrm i$ [A1] $3+3\mathrm i$ [A1] $(3+2\mathrm i)(1+\mathrm i)=1+5\mathrm i$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) base $2$, height $2$, area $=2$ [A1] area scale factor $(\sqrt2)^2=2$ [M1] image area $=4$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Multiplying by $r\operatorname{cis}\theta$ rotates by $\theta$ and enlarges lengths by $r$, so areas are multiplied by $r^2$.

subtopic: De Moivre's theorem: powers
statement: (a) Write $\sqrt3+\mathrm{i}$ in the form $r\operatorname{cis}\theta$. [2] (b) Use de Moivre's theorem to show that $\left(\sqrt3+\mathrm{i}\right)^9$ is purely imaginary, and find its value. [3] (c) Find the smallest positive integer $m$ for which $\left(\sqrt3+\mathrm{i}\right)^m$ is real. [1]
markscheme: (a) $r=2$ [A1] $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$, so $\sqrt3+\mathrm{i}=2\operatorname{cis}\dfrac{\pi}6$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\left(\sqrt3+\mathrm{i}\right)^9=2^9\operatorname{cis}\dfrac{9\pi}6$ [M1] $=512\operatorname{cis}\dfrac{3\pi}2=512(0-\mathrm{i})$ [A1] $=-512\mathrm{i}$, purely imaginary [A1] [3 marks] (c) Real when $\sin\dfrac{m\pi}6=0$, so $m=6$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: With de Moivre's theorem, the modulus is raised to the power and the argument is multiplied. Reduce the resulting angle to a standard one before evaluating cosine and sine.

subtopic: Circle and ray in the Argand plane
statement: Let $S$ be the set of points $z$ satisfying $|z-(2+3i)|=5$ in the complex plane. (a) Write down the centre and radius of the circle described by $S$. [2] (b) Find the two complex numbers in $S$ that are real. [3] (c) Find the complex number in $S$ with argument $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$. [3]
tips: A point with argument $\frac\pi4$ in the first quadrant has equal real and imaginary parts.

subtopic: Quotient of two complex numbers and its powers
statement: Let $z_1=\sqrt3+i$ and $z_2=1-i$. (a) Write $z_1$ and $z_2$ in the form $re^{i\theta}$. [3] (b) Hence write $\dfrac{z_1}{z_2}$ in the form $re^{i\theta}$. [2] (c) Find the smallest positive integer $n$ for which $\left(\dfrac{z_1}{z_2}\right)^n$ is purely imaginary, and find the value of $\left(\dfrac{z_1}{z_2}\right)^n$ for this $n$. [5]
markscheme: (a) $z_1=2e^{\frac{\pi}{6}i}$ [A1] $|z_2|=\sqrt2$ [A1] $z_2=\sqrt2\,e^{-\frac{\pi}{4}i}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Divide moduli, subtract arguments [M1] $\dfrac{z_1}{z_2}=\sqrt2\,e^{\frac{5\pi}{12}i}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\left(\dfrac{z_1}{z_2}\right)^n=2^{n/2}e^{\frac{5n\pi}{12}i}$, purely imaginary when $\dfrac{5n\pi}{12}=\dfrac{\pi}{2}+k\pi$ [M1] $5n=6+12k$ [A1] $n$ must be an integer, so test $k=0,1,2$: $\dfrac65,\ \dfrac{18}{5},\ 6$ [M1] $n=6$ [A1] value $=2^3e^{\frac{5\pi}{2}i}=8i$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: A number is purely imaginary when its argument is $\frac{\pi}{2}$ plus a multiple of $\pi$. Turn that into an equation for $n$ and look for the first integer solution.

subtopic: Square root of a complex number
statement: Find the two square roots of $5+12\mathrm i$ in the form $a+b\mathrm i$ with $a,b\in\mathbb Z$. [4]
markscheme: $(a+b\mathrm i)^2=a^2-b^2+2ab\mathrm i$ [M1] $a^2-b^2=5$ and $ab=6$ [A1] $a=3$, $b=2$ [A1] roots $\pm(3+2\mathrm i)$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Equate real and imaginary parts of $(a+b\mathrm i)^2$ and look for integer solutions of $ab=6$.

subtopic: Using conjugate roots to factorize a cubic
statement: The polynomial $p(z)=z^3-5z^2+9z-5$ has real coefficients and $z=2+i$ is a root of $p(z)=0$. (a) Write down a second non-real root. [1] (b) Hence find a quadratic factor of $p(z)$ with real coefficients. [2] (c) Find all three roots of $p(z)=0$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $2-i$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\left(z-(2+i)\right)\left(z-(2-i)\right)=(z-2)^2-i^2$ [M1] $=z^2-4z+5$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Divide (or compare coefficients): $p(z)=(z^2-4z+5)(z-1)$ [M1] [A1] Roots: $z=1$, $z=2+i$, $z=2-i$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Non-real roots of a polynomial with real coefficients come in conjugate pairs, so a quadratic factor with real coefficients is $z^2-(\text{sum})z+(\text{product})$.

subtopic: Roots of unity and regular polygons
statement: In this question you will investigate the geometry of the $n$th roots of unity. Let $n \ge 2$ be an integer and let $\omega = e^{\frac{2\pi i}{n}}$. (a) Show that the solutions of $z^n = 1$ are $1, \omega, \omega^2, \ldots, \omega^{n-1}$, and explain why these points are the vertices of a regular $n$-sided polygon inscribed in the unit circle. [3] (b) Show that $1 + \omega + \omega^2 + \cdots + \omega^{n-1} = 0$. [2] (c) Hence show that $\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\cos\frac{2\pi k}{n} = 0$. [2] (d) By factorizing $z^n - 1$ in two ways, show that $$1 + z + z^2 + \cdots + z^{n-1} = \prod_{k=1}^{n-1}\left(z - \omega^k\right).$$ [2] (e) Show that $\left|1-\omega^k\right| = 2\sin\dfrac{k\pi}{n}$ for $k = 1, 2, \ldots, n-1$. [4] (f) The vertex $P_0$ of the polygon is at $1$ and the other vertices are $P_k$ at $\omega^k$. Use parts (d) and (e) to show that the product of the distances $P_0P_1 \times P_0P_2 \times \cdots \times P_0P_{n-1}$ is equal to $n$. [3] (g) Hence show that $\displaystyle\prod_{k=1}^{n-1}\sin\frac{k\pi}{n} = \frac{n}{2^{n-1}}$, and verify this result directly for $n=3$ and $n=4$. [4] (h) (i) For a regular hexagon ($n=6$), find the sum of the squares of the distances from $P_0$ to each of the other five vertices. (ii) Show that, for any $n$, $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\left|1-\omega^k\right|^2 = 2n$. [5]
markscheme: (a) Let $z=e^{i\theta}$ ($|z|=1$ since $|z|^n=1$); then $e^{in\theta}=1$ so $n\theta=2\pi k$ [M1] giving $z=e^{\frac{2\pi i k}{n}}=\omega^k$, $k=0,1,\ldots,n-1$, which are $n$ distinct roots [A1] All have modulus $1$ and consecutive arguments differ by $\frac{2\pi}{n}$, so they are equally spaced on the unit circle and form a regular $n$-gon [R1] [3 marks] (b) Geometric series: $\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\omega^k=\frac{1-\omega^n}{1-\omega}$ [M1] $=0$ since $\omega^n=1$ and $\omega\ne 1$ [A1][AG] [2 marks] (c) Taking real parts of (b) [M1] with $\operatorname{Re}\left(\omega^k\right)=\cos\frac{2\pi k}{n}$ [A1] gives $\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\cos\frac{2\pi k}{n}=0$ [AG] [2 marks] (d) The roots of $z^n-1$ are $\omega^k$, so $z^n-1=\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}\left(z-\omega^k\right)=(z-1)\prod_{k=1}^{n-1}\left(z-\omega^k\right)$ [M1] Also $z^n-1=(z-1)\left(1+z+\cdots+z^{n-1}\right)$; comparing (polynomial identity) gives the result [A1][AG] [2 marks] (e) With $\theta=\frac{2\pi k}{n}$: $1-\omega^k=(1-\cos\theta)-i\sin\theta$ [M1] $\left|1-\omega^k\right|^2=(1-\cos\theta)^2+\sin^2\theta=2-2\cos\theta$ [A1] $=4\sin^2\frac{\theta}{2}=4\sin^2\frac{k\pi}{n}$ [A1] Since $0<\frac{k\pi}{n}<\pi$, $\sin\frac{k\pi}{n}>0$, so $\left|1-\omega^k\right|=2\sin\frac{k\pi}{n}$ [R1][AG] [4 marks] (f) Substituting $z=1$ in (d) (valid as it is a polynomial identity): $\prod_{k=1}^{n-1}\left(1-\omega^k\right)=n$ [M1][A1] Taking moduli, $\prod_{k=1}^{n-1}P_0P_k=\prod_{k=1}^{n-1}\left|1-\omega^k\right|=n$ [R1][AG] [3 marks] (g) Using (e): $2^{n-1}\prod_{k=1}^{n-1}\sin\frac{k\pi}{n}=n$, so the product is $\frac{n}{2^{n-1}}$ [A1] $n=3$: $\sin\frac{\pi}{3}\sin\frac{2\pi}{3}=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{2}=\frac34=\frac{3}{2^2}$ [A1][A1] $n=4$: $\sin\frac{\pi}{4}\sin\frac{\pi}{2}\sin\frac{3\pi}{4}=\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\cdot1\cdot\frac{\sqrt2}{2}=\frac12=\frac{4}{2^3}$ [A1] [4 marks] (h)(i) Distances are $2\sin\frac{k\pi}{6}$: $1,\sqrt3,2,\sqrt3,1$, so the sum of squares is $1+3+4+3+1=12$ [A1] (ii) $\left|1-\omega^k\right|^2=2-2\cos\frac{2\pi k}{n}$ [M1] so the sum is $2(n-1)-2\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\cos\frac{2\pi k}{n}$ [M1] From (c), $\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\cos\frac{2\pi k}{n}=-1$ (removing the $k=0$ term) [A1] so the sum is $2(n-1)+2=2n$ [A1][AG] [5 marks] Total [25 marks]
tips: Keep the identity in (d) as a polynomial identity so you may substitute z = 1 afterwards.

subtopic: Region defined by a modulus and an argument
statement: The region $R$ in the complex plane is the set of points $z$ with $|z|\le2$ and $\dfrac\pi6\le\arg z\le\dfrac\pi2$. (a) Find the area of $R$. [2] (b) Find the perimeter of $R$. [2] (c) Determine whether the point $1.5+0.5\mathrm i$ lies in $R$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $R$ is a sector of radius $2$ and angle $\dfrac\pi2-\dfrac\pi6=\dfrac\pi3$ [M1] area $=\dfrac12\times4\times\dfrac\pi3=\dfrac{2\pi}3$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) arc length $2\times\dfrac\pi3$ [M1] perimeter $=2+2+\dfrac{2\pi}3=4+\dfrac{2\pi}3$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\arg=\arctan\dfrac13=0.322$ [M1] this is less than $\dfrac\pi6=0.524$, so it is not in $R$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The modulus condition gives a disc of radius 2 and the argument condition cuts a wedge from it. Together they form a sector.

subtopic: Locus of points equidistant from two complex numbers
statement: A complex number $z=x+iy$ satisfies $|z-2|=|z+2i|$. (a) Show that the point $(x,y)$ lies on the line $y=-x$. [3] (b) Find the complex numbers $z$ that satisfy both $|z-2|=|z+2i|$ and $|z|=2\sqrt2$. [3]
tips: Squaring both modulus expressions removes the square roots; the quadratic terms cancel, leaving a straight line (the perpendicular bisector of the two points $2$ and $-2i$).

subtopic: Division of complex numbers and polar form
statement: Let $z=-2+6i$ and $w=2+i$. (a) Find $zw$ in the form $a+bi$. [2] (b) Find $\dfrac zw$ in the form $a+bi$. [3] (c) Find $|z|$ and $\arg z$ (to 3 significant figures, in radians). [3]
markscheme: (a) $zw=(-2 + 6 i)(2 + i)$ [M1] $=-10 + 10 i$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Multiply numerator and denominator by $\bar w=2 - i$ [M1]; denominator $=5$ [A1]; $\dfrac zw=\frac{2}{5} + \frac{14 i}{5}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $|z|=\sqrt{4+36}=2 \sqrt{10}$ [A1]; $\arg z=$ angle in the correct quadrant (use the reference angle $\arctan\left|\dfrac{6}{-2}\right|$) [M1] $=1.893$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: For $z$ in the second quadrant the argument is $\pi-\arctan|b/a|$; a calculator's arctan alone may be wrong.

subtopic: De Moivre and multiple angle identities
statement: (a) Use de Moivre's theorem and the binomial expansion of $(\cos\theta+\mathrm i\sin\theta)^3$ to show that $\sin3\theta=3\sin\theta-4\sin^3\theta$. [5] (b) Hence solve $\sin3\theta=\sin\theta$ for $0\le\theta\le\pi$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $(\cos\theta+\mathrm i\sin\theta)^3=\cos3\theta+\mathrm i\sin3\theta$ [M1] binomial expansion: imaginary part $3\cos^2\theta\sin\theta-\sin^3\theta$ [M1][A1] $\sin3\theta=3(1-\sin^2\theta)\sin\theta-\sin^3\theta$ [M1] $=3\sin\theta-4\sin^3\theta$ [A1] [5 marks] (b) $2\sin\theta-4\sin^3\theta=0$ [M1] $2\sin\theta\left(1-2\sin^2\theta\right)=0$ [A1] $\sin\theta=0$: $\theta=0,\pi$ [A1] $\sin\theta=\pm\dfrac1{\sqrt2}$: $\theta=\dfrac\pi4,\dfrac{3\pi}4$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Equate imaginary parts after expanding. Replace $\cos^2\theta$ by $1-\sin^2\theta$ to leave powers of sine only.

subtopic: Quartic with real coefficients from two complex roots
statement: A quartic polynomial $p(z)=z^{4}+az^{3}+bz^{2}+cz+d$ has real coefficients, and two of its roots are $1+i$ and $2-i$. (a) Write down the other two roots. [1] (b) Express $p(z)$ as a product of two quadratic factors with real coefficients. [3] (c) Hence find $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$. [3] (d) Use your calculator to evaluate $p(2.5)$. [1]
tips: Non-real roots of a polynomial with real coefficients come in conjugate pairs; each pair gives a real quadratic factor $z^{2}-2\operatorname{Re}(\alpha)z+|\alpha|^{2}$.

subtopic: Roots of unity and their sum
statement: Let $\omega=\mathrm e^{2\pi\mathrm i/5}$. (a) Write down the five roots of $z^5=1$ in terms of $\omega$. [2] (b) Show that $1+\omega+\omega^2+\omega^3+\omega^4=0$. [3] (c) Hence show that $\cos\dfrac{2\pi}5+\cos\dfrac{4\pi}5=-\dfrac12$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $1,\ \omega,\ \omega^2,\ \omega^3,\ \omega^4$ [A1][A1] [2 marks] (b) $z^5-1=(z-1)\left(z^4+z^3+z^2+z+1\right)$ [M1] $\omega\ne1$ is a root of $z^5-1$ so $\omega^4+\omega^3+\omega^2+\omega+1=0$ [R1] [A1] [3 marks] (c) taking real parts: $1+\cos\dfrac{2\pi}5+\cos\dfrac{4\pi}5+\cos\dfrac{6\pi}5+\cos\dfrac{8\pi}5=0$ [M1] $\cos\dfrac{6\pi}5=\cos\dfrac{4\pi}5$ and $\cos\dfrac{8\pi}5=\cos\dfrac{2\pi}5$ [M1][A1] $2\left(\cos\dfrac{2\pi}5+\cos\dfrac{4\pi}5\right)=-1$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Factorize $z^n-1$ to see that the non-trivial roots sum with $1$ to zero. Real parts then give cosine identities.

subtopic: Complex conjugate roots of a real cubic
statement: The cubic equation $z^3+az^2+bz-5=0$, where $a,b\in\mathbb{R}$, has a root $1+2\mathrm{i}$. (a) Write down another complex root. [1] (b) Find the third root. [2] (c) Find the values of $a$ and $b$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $1-2\mathrm{i}$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Product of roots $=-(-5)=5$ [M1] $(1+2\mathrm{i})(1-2\mathrm{i})r=5r=5$, so the third root is $r=1$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $(z-1)\left(z^2-2z+5\right)$ [M1] $=z^3-3z^2+7z-5$ [A1] $a=-3$, $b=7$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Non-real roots of a polynomial with real coefficients come in conjugate pairs. Use the sum and product of roots, or multiply out the factors, to recover the coefficients.

subtopic: Cubic with a real root and a conjugate pair
statement: Let $p(z)=z^3-9z^2+33z-65$. (a) Show that $z=5$ is a root of $p(z)=0$. [1] (b) Find the other two roots of $p(z)=0$. [3] (c) The three roots are represented in the complex plane. Find the area of the triangle whose vertices are the three roots. [2] (d) Verify that the sum and product of the three roots agree with the coefficients of $p(z)$. [2]
tips: The conjugate pair is symmetric about the real axis, so the triangle has a vertical side. For a cubic $z^3+bz^2+cz+d$, the roots sum to $-b$ and multiply to $-d$.

subtopic: Damped oscillator with complex characteristic roots
statement: The motion of a mass on a damped spring satisfies the characteristic equation $2s^2+cs+50=0$, where $c>0$ is the damping constant. The motion oscillates only if the equation has non-real roots. (a) Find the range of values of $c$ for which the motion oscillates. [3] (b) For $c=8$, solve the equation, giving the roots in the form $a+bi$ with exact values. [2] (c) For $c=8$, the displacement is proportional to $e^{-2t}\cos(bt)$ where $b$ is the imaginary part found in part (b). Find the period of the oscillation, in seconds, to 3 significant figures. [2] (d) Find the factor by which the amplitude is multiplied during one period, to 3 significant figures. [2]
tips: The sign of the discriminant decides whether roots are real. For $e^{at}\cos(bt)$ the period is $\frac{2\pi}{b}$ and the amplitude changes by $e^{a\times\text{period}}$ each cycle.

subtopic: Impedance of two components in parallel
statement: Two components in an AC circuit have impedances $Z_1=6+8i$ ohms and $Z_2=12-5i$ ohms. When they are connected in parallel, the combined impedance $Z$ satisfies $\dfrac1Z=\dfrac1{Z_1}+\dfrac1{Z_2}$. (a) Show that $Z=\dfrac{Z_1Z_2}{Z_1+Z_2}$. [2] (b) Find $Z$ in the form $a+bi$, with $a$ and $b$ to 3 significant figures. [3] (c) Find $|Z|$ and $\arg Z$, each to 3 significant figures. [2] (d) The supply voltage has amplitude $100$ V. Find the amplitude of the total current, given that current amplitude equals voltage amplitude divided by $|Z|$. [2]
tips: For parallel components add reciprocals, which leads to product over sum. Use the conjugate of the denominator to divide complex numbers, or the complex-number mode of your GDC.

subtopic: Locus of points with a ratio of distances
statement: The complex number $z=x+y\mathrm i$ satisfies $|z-3\mathrm i|=2|z|$. Show that the locus is a circle and find its centre and radius. [5]
tips: Square both sides to remove the moduli, then complete the square.

subtopic: Arithmetic with complex numbers in Cartesian form
statement: Let $z=3 + 2 i$ and $w=1 - i$. (a) Find $zw$. [2] (b) Find $\dfrac zw$ in the form $a+b\mathrm i$. [3] (c) Find $|z|$ and $|w|$ and verify that $|zw|=|z||w|$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $(3 + 2 i)(1 - i)$ expanded [M1] $=5 - i$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) multiply by the conjugate $\overline w=1 + i$ [M1] $\dfrac{1 + 5 i}{2}$ [A1] $=\frac{1}{2} + \frac{5 i}{2}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $|z|=\sqrt{13}$, $|w|=\sqrt{2}$ [A1] $|zw|=\sqrt{26}$ [M1] both products equal $\sqrt{26}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Divide by multiplying numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator. The modulus of a product is the product of the moduli.

subtopic: Adding two voltages with phasors
statement: Two alternating voltages in a circuit, in volts, are $V_1=4\cos(\omega t)$ and $V_2=4\cos\left(\omega t+\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)$. A voltage $R\cos(\omega t+\varphi)$ is represented by the complex number $Re^{i\varphi}$. (a) Write down the complex numbers representing $V_1$ and $V_2$. [1] (b) Find the complex number representing $V_1+V_2$ in the form $a+bi$. [2] (c) Hence write $V_1+V_2$ in the form $R\cos(\omega t+\varphi)$ with $R>0$ and $0<\varphi<\pi$. [3] (d) State the maximum value of $V_1+V_2$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $4$ and $4e^{\frac{2\pi}{3}i}$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $4+4\left(-\dfrac12+\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}i\right)$ [M1] $=2+2\sqrt3\,i$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $R=\sqrt{4+12}=4$ [A1] $\varphi=\arctan\sqrt3=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ [A1] $V_1+V_2=4\cos\left(\omega t+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $4$ volts [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Waves of the same frequency add by adding their phasors, which are complex numbers. Convert the sum back to modulus-argument form to read off amplitude and phase.

subtopic: Quartic with two conjugate pairs of roots
statement: The polynomial $p(z)=z^4-6z^3+15z^2-18z+10$ has real coefficients and $z=1+i$ is a root of $p(z)=0$. (a) Write down a second root. [1] (b) Find a quadratic factor of $p(z)$ with real coefficients. [2] (c) Hence find the other two roots of $p(z)=0$. [4] (d) Find the sum of the squares of the moduli of the four roots. [2]
markscheme: (a) $1-i$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\left(z-1-i\right)\left(z-1+i\right)=(z-1)^2+1$ [M1] $=z^2-2z+2$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $p(z)=(z^2-2z+2)(z^2+az+5)$ with constant term $10$ [M1] compare $z^3$ coefficients: $a-2=-6$, so $a=-4$ [A1] $z^2-4z+5=0$ [M1] $z=2\pm i$ [A1] [4 marks] (d) $|1\pm i|^2=2$ each and $|2\pm i|^2=5$ each [M1] total $=2+2+5+5=14$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Divide out the known real quadratic factor, either by long division or by comparing coefficients. For $|z|^2$ with $z=a+bi$ use $a^2+b^2$.

subtopic: Equations involving the conjugate
statement: (a) Find the complex number $z$ that satisfies $2z+3z^*=10+i$, where $z^*$ is the complex conjugate of $z$. [4] (b) Solve $(2+i)z=3-4i$, giving $z$ in the form $a+bi$. [3]
markscheme: (a) let $z=x+iy$, so $z^*=x-iy$ [M1] $2x+2iy+3x-3iy=5x-iy$ [A1] equate real and imaginary parts: $5x=10$ and $-y=1$ [M1] $z=2-i$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $z=\dfrac{3-4i}{2+i}\times\dfrac{2-i}{2-i}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{6-3i-8i+4i^2}{5}$ [A1] $=\dfrac{2-11i}{5}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: For equations with $z^*$ write $z=x+iy$ and equate the real and imaginary parts separately. Always check your answer by substituting back into the original equation.

subtopic: Arithmetic of complex numbers in Cartesian form
statement: Let $z=2+3i$ and $w=1-i$. (a) Find $zw$ in the form $a+bi$. [2] (b) Find $\dfrac{z}{w}$ in the form $a+bi$. [2] (c) Write down $|z|$. [1]
tips: To divide complex numbers multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator. Remember $i^2=-1$ when expanding.

subtopic: Argument locus and region
statement: (a) State the locus of $z$ with $\arg(z-1)=\dfrac\pi4$. [2] (b) Find the Cartesian equation of this half-line, including any restriction on $x$. [3] (c) Find the complex number where this half-line meets the circle $|z|=\sqrt5$. [3]
markscheme: (a) a half-line starting at $1$ (not including $1$) [A1] making angle $\dfrac\pi4$ with the positive real direction [A1] [2 marks] (b) $z-1=(x-1)+y\mathrm i$ [M1] $y=x-1$ [A1] with $x>1$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $x^2+(x-1)^2=5$ [M1] $x^2-x-2=0$ so $x=2$ ($x>1$) [A1] $z=2+\mathrm i$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: An argument locus is a half-line from the point (excluded). Use $x>$ constant to keep only the correct half.

subtopic: Multiplying and dividing in modulus-argument form
statement: Let $z=4\left(\cos\dfrac\pi3+i\sin\dfrac\pi3\right)$ and $w=2\left(\cos\dfrac\pi6+i\sin\dfrac\pi6\right)$. (a) Write $zw$ and $\dfrac zw$ in modulus-argument form. [4] (b) Hence write $zw$ and $\dfrac zw$ in the form $a+bi$. [3] (c) Write $z$ in the form $a+bi$ and verify that $|z|^2=z\bar z$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $|zw|=8$, $\arg(zw)=\dfrac\pi3+\dfrac\pi6=\dfrac\pi2$ [M1][A1]; $|z/w|=2$, $\arg=\dfrac\pi3-\dfrac\pi6=\dfrac\pi6$ [A1][A1] [4 marks] (b) $zw=8\left(\cos\dfrac\pi2+i\sin\dfrac\pi2\right)=8i$ [A1]; $\dfrac zw=2\left(\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}+\dfrac i2\right)$ [M1] $=\sqrt3+i$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $z=4\left(\dfrac12+\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}i\right)=2+2\sqrt3i$ [A1]; $z\bar z=4+12=16$ [M1]; $|z|^2=16$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Multiplying complex numbers multiplies the moduli and adds the arguments; dividing divides the moduli and subtracts the arguments.

subtopic: Vertices of a square using rotation by 90 degrees
statement: In the complex plane, $A$ is the point $1+\mathrm i$ and $B$ is the point $4+2\mathrm i$. The points $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ are the vertices of a square, taken in anticlockwise order. (a) Find the complex number representing $\overrightarrow{AB}$, and explain how $\overrightarrow{BC}$ is obtained from it. [2] (b) Find $C$ and $D$, and the area of the square. [4] (c) The square could instead lie on the other side of $AB$. Find the two corresponding vertices in this case. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\overrightarrow{AB}=3+\mathrm i$ [A1] $\overrightarrow{BC}=\mathrm i\times\overrightarrow{AB}$, a rotation by $90^\circ$ anticlockwise [R1] [2 marks] (b) $\overrightarrow{BC}=\mathrm i(3+\mathrm i)=-1+3\mathrm i$ [A1] $C=3+5\mathrm i$ [A1] $D=A+\overrightarrow{BC}=4\mathrm i$ [A1] area $=|AB|^2=10$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) multiply $\overrightarrow{AB}$ by $-\mathrm i$: $-\mathrm i(3+\mathrm i)=1-3\mathrm i$ [M1] $C=5-\mathrm i$ and $D=2-2\mathrm i$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Multiplying by $\mathrm i$ rotates a vector by $90^\circ$ anticlockwise, and multiplying by $-\mathrm i$ rotates it clockwise.

subtopic: Sum of squared distances between vertices of a regular polygon
statement: The vertices of a regular $n$-gon inscribed in the unit circle are $1,\omega,\omega^2,\ldots,\omega^{n-1}$, where $\omega=\operatorname{cis}\dfrac{2\pi}n$ and $n\ge3$. (a) Show that $|1-\operatorname{cis}\theta|^2=2-2\cos\theta$. [2] (b) Explain why $1+\omega+\cdots+\omega^{n-1}=0$, and deduce that $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\cos\dfrac{2\pi k}n=-1$. [3] (c) Hence show that the sum of the squares of the distances from the vertex $1$ to the other $n-1$ vertices is $2n$. [3] (d) Verify the result for $n=6$ by finding the distances from the vertex $1$ to the other five vertices. [2] (e) By symmetry, the same result holds for every vertex. Find the sum of the squares of the lengths of all $\dbinom n2$ chords joining pairs of vertices. [2]
markscheme: (a) $(1-\cos\theta)^2+\sin^2\theta$ [M1] $=2-2\cos\theta$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) geometric series with ratio $\omega\ne1$ and $\omega^n=1$, so the sum is $\dfrac{1-\omega^n}{1-\omega}=0$ [M1][R1] real parts give $1+\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\cos\dfrac{2\pi k}n=0$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) distance squared to $\omega^k$ is $2-2\cos\dfrac{2\pi k}n$ [A1] sum $=2(n-1)-2\sum\cos\dfrac{2\pi k}n$ [M1] $=2(n-1)+2=2n$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) distances $1,\ \sqrt3,\ 2,\ \sqrt3,\ 1$ [A1] squares sum to $1+3+4+3+1=12=2\times6$ [A1] [2 marks] (e) summing over all $n$ vertices counts each chord twice: $\dfrac{n\times2n}2$ [M1] $=n^2$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A regular polygon's vertices are the $n$th roots of unity, whose sum is zero. Use the cosine form of the distance formula.

subtopic: Modulus and argument of 1 + e^(i theta)
statement: Let $\theta$ be a real number with $-\pi<\theta<\pi$. (a) Show that $1+e^{\mathrm i\theta}=2\cos\dfrac\theta2\,e^{\mathrm i\theta/2}$. [3] (b) Hence write down the modulus and argument of $1+e^{\mathrm i\theta}$. [2] (c) Find the modulus and argument of $1+\operatorname{cis}\dfrac{5\pi}6$, giving the modulus exactly. [3]
markscheme: (a) factor out $e^{\mathrm i\theta/2}$: $e^{\mathrm i\theta/2}\left(e^{-\mathrm i\theta/2}+e^{\mathrm i\theta/2}\right)$ [M1][A1] $=2\cos\dfrac\theta2\,e^{\mathrm i\theta/2}$ [AG] [A1] [3 marks] (b) modulus $2\cos\dfrac\theta2$ [A1] argument $\dfrac\theta2$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\theta=\dfrac{5\pi}6$, argument $\dfrac{5\pi}{12}$ [A1] modulus $2\cos\dfrac{5\pi}{12}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{\sqrt6-\sqrt2}2$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Pull out half of the angle, so that the exponentials combine into a cosine. The factor is positive only for $|\theta|<\pi$, which is why the modulus is $2\cos(\theta/2)$.

subtopic: Rotation and an equilateral triangle in the complex plane
statement: The points $A$ and $B$ represent the complex numbers $a=1+\mathrm i$ and $b=4+2\mathrm i$ in the complex plane. The point $C$ is such that triangle $ABC$ is equilateral, with $C$ above the line $AB$ in the sense of anticlockwise orientation $A\to B\to C$. (a) Find $b-a$ and its modulus. [2] (b) Show that $c=a+\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\pi/3}(b-a)$ and find $c$ in the form $x+y\mathrm i$. [5]
markscheme: (a) $b-a=3+\mathrm i$ [A1] $|b-a|=\sqrt{10}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) rotate $AB$ about $A$ by $\dfrac\pi3$ anticlockwise [M1] $c=a+\left(\dfrac12+\dfrac{\sqrt3}2\mathrm i\right)(3+\mathrm i)$ [A1] product $=\dfrac{3-\sqrt3}2+\dfrac{1+3\sqrt3}2\mathrm i$ [M1][A1] $c=\dfrac{5-\sqrt3}2+\dfrac{3+3\sqrt3}2\mathrm i$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: Multiplying by $\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\alpha}$ rotates a vector anticlockwise by $\alpha$ without changing its length.

subtopic: Square root of a complex number by equating parts
statement: Let $(x+yi)^2=5+12i$, where $x$ and $y$ are real. (a) Show that $x^2-y^2=5$ and $xy=6$. [2] (b) Hence find the two square roots of $5+12i$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $(x+yi)^2=x^2-y^2+2xyi$ [M1] equating real and imaginary parts: $x^2-y^2=5$ and $2xy=12$, so $xy=6$ [AG] [2 marks] (b) $y=\dfrac6x$ so $x^2-\dfrac{36}{x^2}=5$, giving $x^4-5x^2-36=0$ [M1] $(x^2-9)(x^2+4)=0$ [A1] $x^2=9$ since $x$ is real [R1] $x=3,\ y=2$ or $x=-3,\ y=-2$, so the roots are $\pm(3+2i)$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Whenever two complex numbers are equal, both their real parts and their imaginary parts must match. Substitute one equation into the other to get a quadratic in $x^2$.

subtopic: Euler form and powers of a complex number
statement: Let $z=4-3i$. (a) Find the modulus of $z$ and its argument in radians, correct to three significant figures. [2] (b) Write $z$ in the form $re^{i\theta}$, with the values from part (a). [1] (c) Find $z^{3}$ in the form $a+bi$, where $a,b\in\mathbb{Z}$. [2] (d) Hence verify that $|z^3|=125$. [1]
tips: The argument of $4-3i$ is negative because the point lies in the fourth quadrant. Expanding the cube directly in two steps (square first) is quick and avoids binomial errors.

subtopic: Cubic equation with a real root and complex conjugate roots
statement: Consider the equation $z^3-5z^2+17z-13=0$, where $z\in\mathbb{C}$. (a) Show that $z=1$ is a root. [1] (b) Find the other two roots, in the form $a+bi$. [4] (c) The three roots are represented as points in the complex plane as the vertices of a triangle. Find the area of the triangle. [2]
markscheme: (a) $1-5+17-13=0$ [AG] [1 mark] (b) $(z-1)$ is a factor, so $z^3-5z^2+17z-13=(z-1)(z^2-4z+13)$ [M1][A1] $z^2-4z+13=0$ gives $z=\dfrac{4\pm\sqrt{16-52}}{2}$ [M1] $z=2\pm3i$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) vertices $(1,0)$, $(2,3)$ and $(2,-3)$ [M1] base $=6$ (vertical side at $x=2$), height $=1$, so area $=\dfrac12\times6\times1=3$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A cubic with real coefficients has either one or three real roots; non-real roots appear as conjugate pairs. Sketch the three points: the conjugate pair is symmetric about the real axis, which makes the area easy.

subtopic: Polar form, products and quotients
statement: Let $z=1+\sqrt3\,\mathrm{i}$ and $w=\sqrt3-\mathrm{i}$. (a) Write $z$ and $w$ in the form $r\operatorname{cis}\theta$, where $r>0$ and $-\pi<\theta\le\pi$. [2] (b) Hence find $zw$ and $\dfrac zw$ in the form $r\operatorname{cis}\theta$. [3] (c) Find the smallest positive integer $n$ for which $(zw)^n$ is a positive real number. [2]
markscheme: (a) $z=2\operatorname{cis}\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ [A1] $w=2\operatorname{cis}\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Multiply moduli and add arguments [M1] $zw=4\operatorname{cis}\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ [A1] $\dfrac zw=\operatorname{cis}\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $(zw)^n=4^n\operatorname{cis}\dfrac{n\pi}{6}$ [M1] Positive real requires $\dfrac{n\pi}6=2k\pi$, so smallest $n=12$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Convert to modulus-argument form before multiplying or dividing: moduli multiply or divide, arguments add or subtract. "Positive real" means the argument must be a multiple of $2\pi$, not just of $\pi$.

subtopic: Sum of cosines using a geometric series of complex exponentials
statement: This question uses complex exponentials to sum trigonometric series. Let $\theta\ne2m\pi$ and $S=\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathrm e^{\mathrm ik\theta}$. (a) Show that $S=\dfrac{\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta}\left(\mathrm e^{\mathrm in\theta}-1\right)}{\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta}-1}$. [3] (b) By writing $\mathrm e^{\mathrm ia}-1=\mathrm e^{\mathrm ia/2}\times2\mathrm i\sin\dfrac a2$, show that $S=\dfrac{\sin\frac{n\theta}2}{\sin\frac\theta2}\mathrm e^{\mathrm i(n+1)\theta/2}$. [4] (c) Hence deduce that $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^n\cos k\theta=\dfrac{\sin\frac{n\theta}2\cos\frac{(n+1)\theta}2}{\sin\frac\theta2}$, and write down the corresponding formula for $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^n\sin k\theta$. [3] (d) Verify the formula for $n=4$ and $\theta=\dfrac{2\pi}5$, where the sum equals $-1$. [3] (e) Show that $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^6\cos\dfrac{k\pi}3=0$, and explain this using the geometry of the complex plane. [2]
markscheme: (a) geometric series with first term $\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta}$ [A1] common ratio $\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta}\ne1$ [A1] $S_n=\dfrac{a(r^n-1)}{r-1}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\mathrm e^{\mathrm in\theta}-1=\mathrm e^{\mathrm in\theta/2}\,2\mathrm i\sin\dfrac{n\theta}2$ [M1][A1] $\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta}-1=\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta/2}\,2\mathrm i\sin\dfrac\theta2$ [A1] combine the exponentials: $\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta+\mathrm in\theta/2-\mathrm i\theta/2}=\mathrm e^{\mathrm i(n+1)\theta/2}$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) real part of $S$ [M1] $\sum\cos k\theta=\dfrac{\sin\frac{n\theta}2\cos\frac{(n+1)\theta}2}{\sin\frac\theta2}$ [A1] imaginary part: $\dfrac{\sin\frac{n\theta}2\sin\frac{(n+1)\theta}2}{\sin\frac\theta2}$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $\sin\dfrac{4\pi}5=\sin\dfrac\pi5$ [M1] $\cos\dfrac{5\pi}5=\cos\pi=-1$ [A1] $\dfrac{\sin\frac{4\pi}5(-1)}{\sin\frac\pi5}=-1$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) $n=6$, $\theta=\dfrac\pi3$: $\sin\dfrac{6\pi}6=\sin\pi=0$ [A1] the six points $\mathrm e^{\mathrm ik\pi/3}$ are the sixth roots of unity, symmetric about the origin, so their sum is $0$ [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Sum $\mathrm e^{\mathrm ik\theta}$ as a geometric series, then factor half-angle terms so that sines appear. The real and imaginary parts separate the cosine and sine sums.

subtopic: Real and imaginary quotients with an unknown parameter
statement: Let $w=\dfrac{a+2\mathrm i}{1-\mathrm i}$, where $a$ is a real number. (a) Write $w$ in the form $x+y\mathrm i$, with $x,y$ in terms of $a$. [2] (b) Find the value of $a$ for which $w$ is real, and the value for which $w$ is purely imaginary. [2] (c) For $a=0$, find the modulus and argument of $w$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{(a+2\mathrm i)(1+\mathrm i)}2$ [M1] $=\dfrac{a-2}2+\dfrac{a+2}2\mathrm i$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) real: $a+2=0$ so $a=-2$ [A1] purely imaginary: $a-2=0$ so $a=2$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $w=-1+\mathrm i$ [A1] modulus $\sqrt2$ [A1] argument $\dfrac{3\pi}4$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator to separate real and imaginary parts.

subtopic: Three-phase and six-phase supplies using roots of unity
statement: This question investigates how alternating voltages combine, using complex numbers. A voltage $A\cos(\omega t+\varphi)$ is represented by the complex number $Ae^{i\varphi}$ (a phasor), and voltages of the same frequency add by adding their phasors. Let $\zeta=e^{\frac{2\pi}{3}i}$. A three-phase supply has three voltages $V_A=A\cos(\omega t)$, $V_B=A\cos\left(\omega t-\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)$ and $V_C=A\cos\left(\omega t-\dfrac{4\pi}{3}\right)$, where $A>0$. (a) Write $\zeta$ in the form $a+bi$ and show that $\zeta^3=1$. [2] (b) (i) Show that $1+\zeta+\zeta^2=0$. [2] (ii) Hence show that $V_A+V_B+V_C=0$ for all $t$. [3] (c) The line voltage is $V_A-V_B$. Show that $V_A-V_B=\sqrt3A\cos\left(\omega t+\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$. [4] (d) For $A=325$ V, find the amplitude of the line voltage to 3 significant figures. [1] (e) Phase $C$ fails, so only $V_A+V_B$ remains. Show that $V_A+V_B=A\cos\left(\omega t-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$, and show that this equals $-V_C$. [3] A six-phase supply uses the voltages $A\cos\left(\omega t+\dfrac{k\pi}{3}\right)$ for $k=0,1,2,3,4,5$, with phasors $z^k$ where $z=e^{\frac{\pi}{3}i}$. Let $S_m=1+z+\dots+z^{m-1}$. (f) (i) Write down an expression for $S_4$ as a quotient, using the formula for the sum of a geometric series. [1] (ii) Show that $S_4=\sqrt3\,i$. [4] (g) Hence show that $\cos\theta+\cos\left(\theta+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)+\cos\left(\theta+\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)+\cos(\theta+\pi)=-\sqrt3\sin\theta$. [3] (h) (i) Show that $\left|1-z^m\right|=2\sin\dfrac{m\pi}{6}$ for $m=1,2,\dots,5$. [3] (ii) The first $m$ phase voltages of the six-phase supply with $A=10$ V are added together. Find all values of $m$, with $1\le m\le5$, for which the amplitude of the sum exceeds $15$ V. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\zeta=-\dfrac12+\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}i$ [A1] $\zeta^3=e^{2\pi i}=1$ [A1] [2 marks] (b)(i) $\zeta^2=e^{\frac{4\pi}{3}i}=-\dfrac12-\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}i$ [A1] $1+\zeta+\zeta^2=1-\dfrac12-\dfrac12+\left(\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}-\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)i=0$ [A1] [2 marks] (ii) Phasors of $V_A,V_B,V_C$ are $A,\ A\zeta^{-1}=A\zeta^2,\ A\zeta^{-2}=A\zeta$ [M1] their sum is $A(1+\zeta+\zeta^2)=0$ [A1] so the sum of the voltages, the real part of $e^{i\omega t}$ times the sum of phasors, is $0$ for all $t$ [R1] [3 marks] (c) Phasor of $V_A-V_B$ is $A(1-\zeta^2)$ [M1] $=A\left(\dfrac32+\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}i\right)$ [A1] modulus $A\sqrt{\dfrac94+\dfrac34}=\sqrt3A$ and argument $\arctan\dfrac{\sqrt3/2}{3/2}=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ [A1] so $V_A-V_B=\sqrt3A\cos\left(\omega t+\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$ [AG] [4 marks] (d) $325\sqrt3=563$ V [A1] [1 mark] (e) Phasor of $V_A+V_B$ is $A(1+\zeta^2)=A\left(\dfrac12-\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}i\right)$ [M1] $=Ae^{-\frac{\pi}{3}i}$, so $V_A+V_B=A\cos\left(\omega t-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$ [A1] From (b), $V_A+V_B=-V_C=-A\cos\left(\omega t-\dfrac{4\pi}{3}\right)=A\cos\left(\omega t-\dfrac{4\pi}{3}+\pi\right)=A\cos\left(\omega t-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$ [R1] [3 marks] (f)(i) $S_4=\dfrac{1-z^4}{1-z}$ [A1] [1 mark] (ii) $z^4=e^{\frac{4\pi}{3}i}=-\dfrac12-\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}i$, so $1-z^4=\dfrac32+\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}i$ [M1] [A1] $1-z=\dfrac12-\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}i$, which has modulus $1$; multiply numerator and denominator by $\dfrac12+\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}i$ [M1] $S_4=\left(\dfrac32+\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}i\right)\left(\dfrac12+\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}i\right)=\dfrac34-\dfrac34+\left(\dfrac{3\sqrt3}{4}+\dfrac{\sqrt3}{4}\right)i=\sqrt3\,i$ [AG] [4 marks] (g) The sum equals $\mathrm{Re}\left(e^{i\theta}S_4\right)$ [M1] $=\mathrm{Re}\left(\sqrt3\,i(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)\right)$ [A1] $=-\sqrt3\sin\theta$ [A1] [3 marks] (h)(i) $\left|1-z^m\right|$ is the distance between the points $1$ and $z^m=e^{i m\pi/3}$ on the unit circle; with the origin they form an isosceles triangle with equal sides $1$ and apex angle $\dfrac{m\pi}{3}$ [M1] splitting it into two right-angled triangles gives base $=2\times1\times\sin\dfrac{m\pi}{6}$ [A1] and $\sin\dfrac{m\pi}{6}>0$ for $m=1,\dots,5$, so $\left|1-z^m\right|=2\sin\dfrac{m\pi}{6}$ [R1] [3 marks] (ii) $|1-z|=2\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}=1$, so $|S_m|=2\sin\dfrac{m\pi}{6}$ and the amplitude is $20\sin\dfrac{m\pi}{6}$ [M1] require $\sin\dfrac{m\pi}{6}>0.75$ [A1] $m=2$ ($17.3$ V), $m=3$ ($20$ V), $m=4$ ($17.3$ V) [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Part (b) is the key idea: the three phasors are the cube roots of unity scaled by $A$, so they cancel exactly. In (f) and (h) a geometric series of phasors gives a closed form whose modulus can be found with $|1-e^{i\varphi}|=2\sin\frac{\varphi}{2}$.

subtopic: Solving z squared equals the conjugate of z
statement: Consider the equation $z^2=z^*$, where $z\in\mathbb C$ and $z^*$ is the complex conjugate of $z$. (a) By taking moduli, show that either $z=0$ or $|z|=1$. [3] (b) When $|z|=1$, show that $z^3=1$, and hence find all the solutions of $z^2=z^*$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $|z|^2=|z^*|=|z|$ [M1] so $|z|(|z|-1)=0$ [A1] hence $z=0$ or $|z|=1$ [AG] [A1] [3 marks] (b) $z^*=\dfrac1z$ since $zz^*=|z|^2=1$ [M1] so $z^2=\dfrac1z$ and $z^3=1$ [A1] $z=1$ or $z=\operatorname{cis}\left(\pm\dfrac{2\pi}3\right)=-\dfrac12\pm\dfrac{\sqrt3}2\mathrm i$ [A1] with $z=0$ the solutions are $0,\ 1,\ -\dfrac12\pm\dfrac{\sqrt3}2\mathrm i$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: For a number of modulus 1, the conjugate equals the reciprocal, because $zz^*=|z|^2$.

subtopic: An equation involving a complex number and its conjugate
statement: Consider the equation $z^2=\overline z$ where $z\in\mathbb C$. (a) By taking moduli, show that $|z|=0$ or $|z|=1$. [3] (b) Multiply both sides by $z$ to show that if $z\ne0$ then $z^3=1$, and hence find all solutions. [4]
markscheme: (a) $|z|^2=|\overline z|=|z|$ [M1] $|z|(|z|-1)=0$ [A1] so $|z|=0$ or $|z|=1$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $z^3=z\overline z=|z|^2=1$ [M1][A1] $z=1$ or $z=-\dfrac12\pm\dfrac{\sqrt3}2\mathrm i$ [A1] together with $z=0$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Taking the modulus of both sides and using $z\overline z=|z|^2$ turns the equation into one about cube roots of unity.

subtopic: Fifth roots of a complex number using GDC
statement: Let $w=3+4\mathrm{i}$. (a) Write $w$ in the form $r\operatorname{cis}\theta$, where $r>0$ and $0<\theta<\dfrac{\pi}2$, giving $\theta$ to three significant figures. [2] (b) Find all solutions of $z^5=w$, giving each in the form $r\operatorname{cis}\theta$ where $-\pi<\theta\le\pi$. Give $r$ and $\theta$ to three significant figures. [3] (c) Write down the sum of the five solutions, justifying your answer. [2]
markscheme: (a) $r=5$ [A1] $\theta=\arctan\dfrac43=0.927$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $|z|=5^{1/5}=1.38$ [M1] $\arg z=\dfrac{0.9273+2k\pi}{5}$ [A1] Roots: $1.38\operatorname{cis}0.185$, $1.38\operatorname{cis}1.44$, $1.38\operatorname{cis}2.70$, $1.38\operatorname{cis}(-2.33)$, $1.38\operatorname{cis}(-1.07)$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) The coefficient of $z^4$ in $z^5-w=0$ is zero [R1] so the sum of roots is $0$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Remember the five arguments are evenly spaced by $\frac{2\pi}{5}$ and must be adjusted into the requested interval. By symmetry, the roots of $z^n=w$ always sum to zero for $n\ge2$.

subtopic: The map w = (z - 1)/(z + 1) and the unit circle
statement: For $z\in\mathbb C$ with $z\ne-1$, define $w=\dfrac{z-1}{z+1}$. (a) Let $z=\cos\theta+\mathrm i\sin\theta$ with $-\pi<\theta<\pi$. Show that $w=\mathrm i\tan\dfrac\theta2$. [4] (b) Deduce that $w$ traces the whole imaginary axis as $z$ goes around the unit circle (excluding $z=-1$). [2] (c) Let $z=x+y\mathrm i$. Show that $\operatorname{Re}(w)=\dfrac{x^2+y^2-1}{(x+1)^2+y^2}$. [3] (d) Hence describe the image of the region $|z|<1$ under the map, with a reason. [2] (e) Verify the result of part (a) for $z=\mathrm i$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $w=\dfrac{e^{\mathrm i\theta}-1}{e^{\mathrm i\theta}+1}$ [M1] multiply top and bottom by $e^{-\mathrm i\theta/2}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{e^{\mathrm i\theta/2}-e^{-\mathrm i\theta/2}}{e^{\mathrm i\theta/2}+e^{-\mathrm i\theta/2}}=\dfrac{2\mathrm i\sin(\theta/2)}{2\cos(\theta/2)}$ [A1] $=\mathrm i\tan\dfrac\theta2$ [AG] [A1] [4 marks] (b) $\tan\dfrac\theta2$ takes every real value for $-\pi<\theta<\pi$ [R1] so $w=\mathrm iy$ takes every pure imaginary value [R1] [2 marks] (c) $w=\dfrac{(z-1)(z^*+1)}{|z+1|^2}$ [M1] numerator $=|z|^2+z-z^*-1$ [A1] $z-z^*$ is imaginary, so real part is $\dfrac{x^2+y^2-1}{(x+1)^2+y^2}$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) the denominator is positive and the numerator is negative when $|z|<1$, so $\operatorname{Re}(w)<0$ [R1] the open unit disc maps into the left half-plane [A1] [2 marks] (e) $\dfrac{\mathrm i-1}{\mathrm i+1}=\mathrm i=\mathrm i\tan\dfrac\pi4$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Write $z=e^{\mathrm i\theta}$ and use half-angles so that numerator and denominator become $\sin$ and $\cos$ of $\theta/2$.

subtopic: Complex roots of a quadratic with modulus and argument
statement: Consider the equation $z^2-5z+9=0$. (a) Solve the equation, giving the solutions in the form $a+bi$ with exact values of $a$ and $b$. [2] (b) Show that both solutions have modulus $3$. [2] (c) Let $\alpha$ be the solution with positive imaginary part. Find $\arg\alpha$, correct to 3 significant figures. [1] (d) Find $\alpha^5$ in the form $x+yi$, giving $x$ and $y$ to 4 significant figures. [3]
tips: A negative discriminant gives a conjugate pair, which automatically share the same modulus. For powers, use $\alpha=re^{i\theta}$ and keep the unrounded argument in your calculator.

subtopic: Sixth roots of 64 forming a regular hexagon
statement: The solutions of $z^6=64$ are represented in the complex plane as the vertices of a polygon. (a) Find the six solutions in the form $re^{i\theta}$ with $-\pi<\theta\le\pi$. [3] (b) Find the area of the polygon, giving your answer to 3 significant figures. [3] (c) Show that the distance between two adjacent vertices is $2$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $z=64^{1/6}e^{i\frac{2k\pi}{6}}$ [M1] modulus $2$ [A1] $z=2e^{0i},\ 2e^{\pm\frac{\pi}{3}i},\ 2e^{\pm\frac{2\pi}{3}i},\ 2e^{\pi i}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) The polygon is made of six identical triangles with two sides $2$ and included angle $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ [M1] area of each $=\dfrac12(2)(2)\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\sqrt3$ [A1] total $=6\sqrt3=10.4$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Cosine rule: $d^2=2^2+2^2-2(2)(2)\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ [M1] $=8-4=4$ [A1] $d=2$ [AG] [3 marks]
tips: The $n$th roots of a number lie on a circle and are equally spaced by $\frac{2\pi}{n}$. A regular polygon splits into $n$ congruent triangles meeting at the centre.

subtopic: Modulus-argument form and products in polar form
statement: Let $z=1 - \sqrt{3} i$. (a) Find $|z|$ and $\arg z$. [3] (b) Write $z$ in the form $r\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta}$. [1] (c) Find $z^6$ in Cartesian form. [3]
markscheme: (a) $|z|=\sqrt{4}=2$ [A1] quadrant check [M1] $\arg z=-\frac{\pi}{3}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $z=2\mathrm e^{- \frac{\pi}{3}\mathrm i}$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $z^6=64\mathrm e^{- 2 \pi\mathrm i}$ [M1][A1] $=64$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Find the modulus from Pythagoras and the argument from the quadrant. For powers use de Moivre: $\left(r\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta}\right)^n=r^n\mathrm e^{\mathrm in\theta}$.

subtopic: Cubic with a complex root
statement: The polynomial $z^3+az^2+bz+c$ has real coefficients $a,b,c$ and has roots $2$ and $1+\mathrm i$. (a) Write down the third root. [1] (b) Find $a$, $b$ and $c$. [4]
tips: A real polynomial of degree three with one non-real root must also have its conjugate as a root. Multiply the linear factors.

subtopic: A cubic with a complex root
statement: The cubic $p(z)=z^3-5z^2+17z-13$ has $z=1$ as a root. (a) Show that $z=1$ is a root. [1] (b) Factorize $p(z)$ completely over $\mathbb{C}$. [4] (c) Plot the three roots on an Argand diagram (describe their positions) and find the area of the triangle they form. [2]
markscheme: (a) $1-5+17-13=0$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $p(z)=(z-1)(z^2-4z+13)$ [M1][A1]; roots of the quadratic $z=\dfrac{4\pm\sqrt{16-52}}{2}=2\pm3i$ [M1][A1] [4 marks] (c) $(1,0)$, $(2,3)$, $(2,-3)$ [A1]; base $6$ (vertical) and height $1$: area $=\dfrac12(6)(1)=3$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Conjugate roots are mirror images in the real axis, so the triangle formed by a cubic's roots is isosceles.

subtopic: Solving z + 1/z = 1 and a high power
statement: The complex number $z$ satisfies $z+\dfrac1z=1$. (a) Show that $z^2-z+1=0$, and find the two possible values of $z$ in the form $r\operatorname{cis}\theta$. [3] (b) Show that $z^3=-1$ for both values. [2] (c) Hence find $z^{2025}$. [2]
markscheme: (a) multiply by $z$: $z^2+1=z$ [M1] $z=\dfrac{1\pm\sqrt3\mathrm i}2$ [A1] $z=\operatorname{cis}\left(\pm\dfrac\pi3\right)$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $z^3+1=(z+1)(z^2-z+1)=0$ [M1] since $z\ne-1$ ($z=-1$ gives $-2\ne1$), $z^3=-1$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $2025=3\times675$ [M1] $z^{2025}=(-1)^{675}=-1$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Multiply through by $z$ to get a quadratic. The factorization of $z^3+1$ links the quadratic to the cube.
