markscheme: (a) base is a square of side $12-2x$ and height $x$ [M1] $V=x(12-2x)^2$ [A1] $0<x<6$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $V=4x^3-48x^2+144x$ [M1] $\dfrac{dV}{dx}=12x^2-96x+144=12(x-2)(x-6)$ [A1] $x=2$ (since $x<6$) [A1] check the sign change from positive to negative or $V''(2)=24\cdot2-96<0$ [R1] [4 marks] (c) $V=2\times8^2=128\text{ cm}^3$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Express the volume in one variable, state the allowed domain, differentiate, and justify that the stationary point is a maximum.

subtopic: Rate of change of the distance between two ships
statement: Ship $A$ is $60$ km west of a lighthouse and sails east at $20$ km/h. At the same time, ship $B$ is $80$ km south of the lighthouse and sails north at $15$ km/h. Let $s$ be the distance between the ships after $t$ hours. (a) Show that $s^2=(60-20t)^2+(80-15t)^2$. [2] (b) Find the rate of change of $s$ when $t=1$. [4] (c) State what the sign of your answer means. [1]
markscheme: (a) $A$ is $60-20t$ km from the lighthouse along the east-west line [A1] $B$ is $80-15t$ km along the north-south line, and the two lines are perpendicular so Pythagoras applies [A1] [2 marks] (b) $2s\dfrac{ds}{dt}=-40(60-20t)-30(80-15t)$ [M1][A1] at $t=1$: $s=\sqrt{40^2+65^2}=76.3$ [A1] $\dfrac{ds}{dt}=\dfrac{-1600-1950}{2\times76.3}=-23.3$ km/h [A1] [4 marks] (c) the ships are getting closer [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Differentiate the equation for $s^2$ implicitly with respect to $t$. A negative rate means the distance is decreasing.

subtopic: Tangent to y = ln x passing through the origin
statement: Consider the curve $y=\ln x$. (a) Find the equation of the tangent to the curve at the point where $x=a$. [2] (b) Find the value of $a$ for which the tangent passes through the origin, and write down the equation of that tangent. [3] (c) Hence state the number of solutions of $\ln x=kx$ when $k=\dfrac1e$. [1]
markscheme: (a) gradient $\dfrac1a$ [A1] $y-\ln a=\dfrac1a(x-a)$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $0-\ln a=\dfrac1a(0-a)=-1$ [M1] $\ln a=1$ so $a=e$ [A1] $y=\dfrac xe$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) exactly one solution, $x=e$, since the line is tangent to the curve [R1] [1 mark]
tips: A line through the origin has the form $y=kx$. Substitute the origin into the tangent equation to find the point of tangency.

subtopic: Logistic growth model: rate of change and maximum growth rate
statement: The number of bacteria $P$, in thousands, in a culture $t$ hours after the start of an experiment is modeled by $P=\dfrac{200}{1+9e^{-0.5t}}$, for $t\ge0$. (a) Find the initial number of bacteria in the culture. [1] (b) Write down the value that $P$ approaches as $t\to\infty$. [1] (c) Show that $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=0.5P\left(1-\dfrac{P}{200}\right)$. [4] (d) Use your GDC to find the maximum rate of increase of $P$, and the time at which this occurs. [3] (e) Find the number of bacteria, in thousands, at the time found in part (d). [1]
markscheme: (a) $P(0)=\dfrac{200}{10}=20$ thousand [A1] [1 mark] (b) $P\to200$ thousand [A1] [1 mark] (c) $P=200\left(1+9e^{-0.5t}\right)^{-1}$, so $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=\dfrac{900e^{-0.5t}}{\left(1+9e^{-0.5t}\right)^2}$ [M1][A1] $1-\dfrac{P}{200}=1-\dfrac{1}{1+9e^{-0.5t}}=\dfrac{9e^{-0.5t}}{1+9e^{-0.5t}}$ [M1] $0.5P\left(1-\dfrac P{200}\right)=0.5\cdot\dfrac{200}{1+9e^{-0.5t}}\cdot\dfrac{9e^{-0.5t}}{1+9e^{-0.5t}}=\dfrac{900e^{-0.5t}}{\left(1+9e^{-0.5t}\right)^2}$ [A1][AG] [4 marks] (d) Graphing $\dfrac{dP}{dt}$ and finding its maximum [M1] $t=4.39$ hours [A1] Maximum rate $=25.0$ thousand bacteria per hour [A1] [3 marks] (e) $P=100$ thousand [A1] [1 mark]
tips: For the chain rule write the denominator as a negative power first. The maximum rate of increase occurs at the point of inflexion of $P$, which is where $P$ is half of its limiting value.

subtopic: Differentiating logarithmic and inverse trigonometric functions
statement: (a) Show that $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln\left(\sec x+\tan x\right)=\sec x$. [3] (b) Show that $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x\arcsin x+\sqrt{1-x^2}\right)=\arcsin x$, for $-1<x<1$. [3] (c) Hence find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac12}\arcsin x\,dx$. [2]
markscheme: (a) Chain rule [M1] $\dfrac{\sec x\tan x+\sec^2x}{\sec x+\tan x}$ [A1] $=\dfrac{\sec x\left(\tan x+\sec x\right)}{\sec x+\tan x}=\sec x$ [A1][AG] [3 marks] (b) Product rule on $x\arcsin x$ [M1] $\arcsin x+\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}$ [A1] and $\dfrac{d}{dx}\sqrt{1-x^2}=-\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}$, so the sum is $\arcsin x$ [A1][AG] [3 marks] (c) $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac12}\arcsin x\,dx=\left[x\arcsin x+\sqrt{1-x^2}\right]_0^{\frac12}$ [M1] $=\left(\dfrac\pi{12}+\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)-1$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: In a "show that" differentiation, aim for the target expression and factor to cancel. A result of the form "derivative of $F$ equals $f$" immediately gives you $\int f=F$, which is what part (c) uses.

subtopic: Related rates: expanding sphere
statement: A spherical balloon is inflated so that its volume increases at a constant rate of $100\text{ cm}^3\text{s}^{-1}$. The volume of a sphere is $V=\dfrac43\pi r^3$. (a) Find $\dfrac{dV}{dr}$. [1] (b) Find the rate at which the radius is increasing when $r=5$ cm. [3] (c) Find the rate at which the surface area $S=4\pi r^2$ is increasing at that instant. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{dV}{dr}=4\pi r^2$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\dfrac{dr}{dt}=\dfrac{dV}{dt}\div\dfrac{dV}{dr}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{100}{4\pi\times25}$ [A1] $=\dfrac1\pi\text{ cm s}^{-1}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\dfrac{dS}{dt}=\dfrac{dS}{dr}\times\dfrac{dr}{dt}$ [M1] $=8\pi\times5\times\dfrac1\pi$ [A1] $=40\text{ cm}^2\text{s}^{-1}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Use the chain rule: $\dfrac{dr}{dt}=\dfrac{dV/dt}{dV/dr}$. Relate each rate to $\dfrac{dr}{dt}$.

subtopic: L'Hopital's rule with a parameter
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{e^{ax}-1-bx}{x^2}$ where $a$ and $b$ are constants and $x\ne0$. (a) Given that $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}f(x)$ exists and is finite, show that $b=a$. [3] (b) Hence find the limit in terms of $a$. [3]
markscheme: (a) the denominator tends to $0$, so the numerator must tend to $0$ as well [R1] by l'Hôpital, $\dfrac{ae^{ax}-b}{2x}$ must also be $\dfrac00$ [M1] so $a-b=0$, $b=a$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\dfrac{ae^{ax}-a}{2x}$ [M1] $\dfrac{a^2e^{ax}}{2}$ [A1] limit $=\dfrac{a^2}2$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: For the limit of a quotient to be finite when the denominator tends to zero, the numerator must also tend to zero.

subtopic: Stationary points of a product with an exponential
statement: Let $f(x)=x^2e^{-x}$, for $x\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Find $f'(x)$. [2] (b) Hence find the coordinates of the stationary points of the graph of $f$. [2] (c) Find $f''(x)$ and use it to determine the nature of each stationary point. [3]
markscheme: (a) Product rule [M1] $f'(x)=2xe^{-x}-x^2e^{-x}=(2x-x^2)e^{-x}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $f'(x)=0$: $x(2-x)e^{-x}=0$, and $e^{-x}\ne0$ [M1] Stationary points $(0,0)$ and $\left(2,4e^{-2}\right)$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $f''(x)=(2-2x)e^{-x}-(2x-x^2)e^{-x}=\left(x^2-4x+2\right)e^{-x}$ [A1] $f''(0)=2>0$ and $f''(2)=-2e^{-2}<0$ [M1] $(0,0)$ is a local minimum and $\left(2,4e^{-2}\right)$ is a local maximum [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Factor $e^{-x}$ out of $f'$ so that setting it to zero is immediate; an exponential is never zero. When finding $f''$, differentiate the factored form $(2x-x^2)e^{-x}$ again with the product rule.

subtopic: Minimum average cost occurs where marginal cost equals average cost
statement: The total cost of producing $x$ items is $C(x)=x^3-6x^2+20x+32$ dollars, for $x>0$. The average cost is $A(x)=\dfrac{C(x)}x$ and the marginal cost is $C'(x)$. (a) Show that $A'(x)=\dfrac{C'(x)-A(x)}x$. [2] (b) Hence explain why, at the minimum of the average cost, the marginal cost equals the average cost. [1] (c) Show that the average cost is minimized at $x=4$, and find the minimum average cost. [4]
tips: Use the quotient rule on $C(x)/x$. Setting the derivative to zero links the three quantities.

subtopic: Stationary points of a function with an exponential factor
statement: Let $f(x)=x^2e^{-x}$ for $x\in\mathbb R$. (a) Show that $f'(x)=x(2-x)e^{-x}$. [3] (b) Find the coordinates of the stationary points, and determine their nature using the sign of $f'$. [4] (c) Find the range of $f$ when the domain is restricted to $x\ge0$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $f'(x)=2xe^{-x}-x^2e^{-x}$ [M1][A1] $=x(2-x)e^{-x}$ [A1] [AG] [3 marks] (b) $f'(x)=0$ at $x=0$ and $x=2$ [A1] $f(0)=0$ and $f(2)=0.5413$ [A1] $f'$ changes from negative to positive at $x=0$, so $(0,0)$ is a minimum [A1] $f'$ changes from positive to negative at $x=2$, so $(2,4e^{-2})$ is a maximum [A1] [4 marks] (c) as $x\to\infty$, $f(x)\to0$, and $f(0)=0$ is the least value [A1] range $0\le y\le4e^{-2}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A stationary point is a maximum if $f'$ changes from positive to negative. Since the exponential factor is always positive, the sign of $f'$ comes from $x(2-x)$.

subtopic: Curve sketching: stationary points and asymptote of a rational function
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{2x}{x^2+1}$. (a) Show that $f'(x)=\dfrac{2(1-x^2)}{(x^2+1)^2}$. [3] (b) Find the coordinates of the stationary points and determine their nature. [4] (c) Write down the equation of the horizontal asymptote and the range of $f$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $f'(x)=\dfrac{2(x^2+1)-2x\times2x}{(x^2+1)^2}$ [M1][A1] $=\dfrac{2-2x^2}{(x^2+1)^2}$ [A1] [AG] [3 marks] (b) $1-x^2=0$ gives $x=\pm1$ [A1] $f(1)=1$ and $f(-1)=-1$ [A1] $f'$ changes from $+$ to $-$ at $x=1$: a maximum [A1] and from $-$ to $+$ at $x=-1$: a minimum [A1] [4 marks] (c) $y=0$ [A1] range $-1\le y\le1$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The sign of $f'$ depends only on $1-x^2$ since the denominator is positive. As $x\to\pm\infty$ the numerator grows more slowly than the denominator.

subtopic: Tangent and normal to a curve
statement: Consider the curve $y=\sqrt{4 x + 1}$ for $x>-\frac14$. (a) Find the value of $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ at the point where $x=2$. [3] (b) Find the equation of the tangent at this point. [2] (c) Find the equation of the normal at this point. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{4 x + 1}}$ [M1][A1] at $x=2$: $\frac{2}{3}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $y_0=3$ so $y-3=\frac{2}{3}(x-2)$ [M1] $y=\frac{2 x}{3} + \frac{5}{3}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) normal gradient $=-\dfrac1{\frac{2}{3}}=-\frac{3}{2}$ [M1] $y=6 - \frac{3 x}{2}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The tangent has gradient $f'(a)$; the normal has gradient $-1/f'(a)$. Both pass through the point on the curve.

subtopic: Minimum of a function with a logarithm
statement: Let $f(x)=x-2\ln x$ for $x>0$. (a) Find $f'(x)$ and the value of $x$ at which $f'(x)=0$. [3] (b) Show that this is a minimum and find the minimum value of $f$. [3] (c) Hence show that $x>2\ln x$ for all $x>0$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $f'(x)=1-\dfrac2x$ [A1] $1-\dfrac2x=0$ [M1] $x=2$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $f''(x)=\dfrac2{x^2}>0$ for all $x>0$, so a minimum [R1] $f(2)=2-2\ln2$ [M1] $=0.614\dots$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) the minimum value is $2-2\ln2=2(1-0.693\dots)>0$ [M1] so $f(x)>0$ for all $x>0$, i.e. $x>2\ln x$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: At a minimum $f''>0$. A positive global minimum shows the function is positive everywhere.

subtopic: Point where the gradient of a cubic is least
statement: The curve $C$ has equation $y=x^3-6x^2+9x$. (a) Find the gradient function $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ and its minimum value. [3] (b) Find the coordinates of the point on $C$ where the gradient is least, and show that it is a point of inflection. [3]
markscheme: (a) $3x^2-12x+9$ [A1] minimum at $x=2$ [M1] $12-24+9=-3$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $y=8-24+18=2$, so the point is $(2,2)$ [A1] $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=6x-12$ [M1] it changes sign at $x=2$, so inflection [R1] [3 marks]
tips: The gradient is least where its own derivative, the second derivative of $y$, is zero.

subtopic: Logarithmic differentiation of x raised to sin x
statement: Let $y=x^{\sin x}$ for $x>0$. (a) Show that $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=x^{\sin x}\left(\cos x\ln x+\dfrac{\sin x}x\right)$. [4] (b) Find the equation of the tangent to the curve at $x=\dfrac\pi2$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\ln y=\sin x\ln x$ [M1] $\dfrac1y\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\cos x\ln x+\dfrac{\sin x}x$ [M1][A1] multiply by $y=x^{\sin x}$ [AG] [A1] [4 marks] (b) $y=\dfrac\pi2$ at $x=\dfrac\pi2$ [A1] gradient $=\dfrac\pi2\left(0+\dfrac{1}{\pi/2}\right)=1$ [A1] $y-\dfrac\pi2=x-\dfrac\pi2$, so $y=x$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Take natural logarithms of both sides, then differentiate implicitly using the product rule on the right-hand side.

subtopic: Optimization: cylinder of fixed volume
statement: A closed cylindrical can has volume $500\text{ cm}^3$. Let the radius be $r$ cm and the height $h$ cm. (a) Express $h$ in terms of $r$ and show that the total surface area is $A=2\pi r^2+\dfrac{1000}{r}$. [3] (b) Find the value of $r$ that minimizes $A$, giving your answer to three significant figures. [4] (c) Find the minimum surface area and show that the corresponding height equals the diameter. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\pi r^2h=500$ so $h=\dfrac{500}{\pi r^2}$ [A1] $A=2\pi r^2+2\pi rh$ [M1] $=2\pi r^2+\dfrac{1000}{r}$ [A1] [AG] [3 marks] (b) $\dfrac{dA}{dr}=4\pi r-\dfrac{1000}{r^2}$ [A1] set to zero: $r^3=\dfrac{250}{\pi}$ [M1] $r=4.30$ [A1] $\dfrac{d^2A}{dr^2}=4\pi+\dfrac{2000}{r^3}>0$ so a minimum [R1] [4 marks] (c) $A=348.7\text{ cm}^2$ [A1] $h=\dfrac{500}{\pi r^2}$ and $r^3=\dfrac{250}{\pi}$ gives $h=\dfrac{2r^3}{r^2}=2r$ [M1][A1] [3 marks]
tips: Eliminate $h$ using the volume constraint, differentiate the surface area with respect to $r$, and confirm a minimum with the second derivative.

subtopic: L'Hopital's rule: limits at infinity
statement: Evaluate each limit. (a) $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to\infty}\dfrac{\ln x}{\sqrt x}$. [3] (b) $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to\infty}\dfrac{x^2}{e^{3x}}$. [3] (c) $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0^+}x\ln x$ (write as a quotient first). [3]
markscheme: (a) form $\dfrac\infty\infty$ [R1] $\dfrac{1/x}{\frac1{2\sqrt x}}=\dfrac2{\sqrt x}$ [M1] limit $=0$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) form $\dfrac\infty\infty$ [R1] $\dfrac{2x}{3e^{3x}}$ then $\dfrac{2}{9e^{3x}}$ [M1] limit $=0$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $x\ln x=\dfrac{\ln x}{1/x}$, form $\dfrac{-\infty}{\infty}$ [M1] $\dfrac{1/x}{-1/x^2}=-x$ [A1] limit $=0$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Exponentials beat powers and powers beat logarithms. For $0\cdot\infty$ products, rewrite as a quotient before using l'Hôpital.

subtopic: Differentiation from first principles
statement: (a) Use differentiation from first principles to show that the derivative of $f(x)=\sqrt x$ is $f'(x)=\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt x}$, for $x>0$. [4] (b) The tangent to the graph of $y=\sqrt x$ at the point $Q$ is parallel to the line $y=\dfrac x4$. Find the coordinates of $Q$. [2] (c) Find the equation of the tangent at $Q$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $f'(x)=\displaystyle\lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{\sqrt{x+h}-\sqrt x}{h}$ [M1] Multiplying numerator and denominator by $\sqrt{x+h}+\sqrt x$ [M1] $=\displaystyle\lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{h}{h\left(\sqrt{x+h}+\sqrt x\right)}=\lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x+h}+\sqrt x}$ [A1] $=\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt x}$ [A1][AG] [4 marks] (b) $\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt x}=\dfrac14$ [M1] $\sqrt x=2$, so $Q=(4,2)$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $y-2=\dfrac14(x-4)$, that is $y=\dfrac x4+1$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: To rationalize a difference of square roots, multiply by the conjugate; the factor $h$ then cancels. Show the limit step explicitly, since first-principles questions award marks for it.

subtopic: Tangent, normal and a triangle area for y = x ln x
statement: Let $f(x)=x\ln x$, for $x>0$. The point $P$ on the graph of $f$ has $x$-coordinate $e$. (a) Find $f'(x)$ and hence the gradient of the tangent to the graph at $P$. [2] (b) Find the equation of the tangent and the equation of the normal to the graph at $P$. [3] (c) The tangent and the normal meet the $x$-axis at $A$ and $B$ respectively. Find the exact area of triangle $PAB$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $f'(x)=\ln x+1$ [M1] At $x=e$: gradient $=2$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $P=(e,e)$; tangent: $y-e=2(x-e)$, that is $y=2x-e$ [A1] Normal gradient $-\dfrac12$ [M1] Normal: $y-e=-\dfrac12(x-e)$, that is $y=-\dfrac x2+\dfrac{3e}{2}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $A=\left(\dfrac e2,0\right)$ and $B=(3e,0)$ [A1] Area $=\dfrac12\times\left(3e-\dfrac e2\right)\times e$ [M1] $=\dfrac{5e^2}{4}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Find the $y$-coordinate of $P$ from the function itself, not from the derivative. The height of the triangle is the $y$-coordinate of $P$ because the base lies on the $x$-axis.

subtopic: Tangent and normal to a curve
statement: Consider the curve $y=- 3 x + e^{2 x}$ (a) Find the value of $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ at the point where $x=0$. [3] (b) Find the equation of the tangent at this point. [2] (c) Find the equation of the normal at this point. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=2 e^{2 x} - 3$ [M1][A1] at $x=0$: $-1$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $y_0=1$ so $y-1=-1(x-0)$ [M1] $y=1 - x$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) normal gradient $=-\dfrac1{-1}=1$ [M1] $y=x + 1$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The tangent has gradient $f'(a)$; the normal has gradient $-1/f'(a)$. Both pass through the point on the curve.

subtopic: Related rates for water filling a cone
statement: Water is poured at a constant rate of $20\ \text{cm}^3\,\text{s}^{-1}$ into a container in the shape of an inverted right circular cone with its vertex pointing downward. When the depth of water is $h$ cm, the radius of the circular surface of the water is $\dfrac h2$ cm. (a) Show that the volume $V$ of water in the cone is $V=\dfrac{\pi h^3}{12}$. [2] (b) Find the exact rate of increase of $h$ at the instant when $h=10$. [3] (c) At this instant, find the rate of increase of the area of the circular surface of the water. [3]
markscheme: (a) $V=\dfrac13\pi r^2h$ with $r=\dfrac h2$ [M1] $V=\dfrac13\pi\cdot\dfrac{h^2}{4}\cdot h=\dfrac{\pi h^3}{12}$ [A1][AG] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac{dV}{dh}=\dfrac{\pi h^2}{4}$ [M1] $\dfrac{dV}{dt}=\dfrac{dV}{dh}\times\dfrac{dh}{dt}$, so $20=25\pi\dfrac{dh}{dt}$ at $h=10$ [M1] $\dfrac{dh}{dt}=\dfrac{4}{5\pi}\ \text{cm s}^{-1}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $A=\pi r^2=\dfrac{\pi h^2}{4}$, so $\dfrac{dA}{dh}=\dfrac{\pi h}{2}$ [A1] $\dfrac{dA}{dt}=\dfrac{dA}{dh}\times\dfrac{dh}{dt}$ [M1] $=5\pi\times\dfrac{4}{5\pi}=4\ \text{cm}^2\,\text{s}^{-1}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Express the quantity you differentiate in terms of a single variable (here $h$) before applying the chain rule. Substitute the numerical value of $h$ only after differentiating.

subtopic: Wire cut to form a square and a circle with minimum total area
statement: A wire of length $100$ cm is cut into two pieces. One piece is bent into a square of side $a$ cm, and the other into a circle of radius $r$ cm. (a) Express $r$ in terms of $a$, and show that the total area is $A=a^2+\dfrac{(100-4a)^2}{4\pi}$. [3] (b) Find the value of $a$ that minimizes the total area, and the minimum area. [5] (c) Find the total area when the whole wire is used for the square, and when it is used for the circle, and comment. [3]
markscheme: (a) $4a+2\pi r=100$ [M1] $r=\dfrac{100-4a}{2\pi}$ [A1] $A=a^2+\pi r^2=a^2+\dfrac{(100-4a)^2}{4\pi}$ [AG] [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\dfrac{dA}{da}=2a-\dfrac{2(100-4a)}{\pi}$ [M1][A1] $=0$ gives $a\pi=100-4a$, so $a=\dfrac{100}{\pi+4}=14.0$ [A1] $A=350\text{ cm}^2$ [A1] $\dfrac{d^2A}{da^2}=2+\dfrac8\pi>0$, so a minimum [R1] [5 marks] (c) all square: $25^2=625$ [A1] all circle: $\pi\left(\dfrac{50}\pi\right)^2=796$ [A1] the minimum $350$ lies below both, so the greatest area occurs at an extreme and the stationary point is a minimum [R1] [3 marks]
tips: Eliminate $r$ using the length of wire, then differentiate the area as a function of $a$ only.

subtopic: Minimum distance from a point to a curve
statement: The point $A$ has coordinates $(4,0)$. The point $P(x,y)$ lies on the curve $y=\sqrt x$, for $x\ge0$. Let $D$ be the distance $AP$. (a) Show that $D^2=x^2-7x+16$. [2] (b) Find the value of $x$ for which $D^2$ is a minimum. [3] (c) Justify that this value gives a minimum. [1] (d) Find the exact minimum distance from $A$ to the curve. [2]
markscheme: (a) $D^2=(x-4)^2+\left(\sqrt x\right)^2$ [M1] $=x^2-8x+16+x=x^2-7x+16$ [A1][AG] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac{d\left(D^2\right)}{dx}=2x-7$ [A1] Setting equal to zero [M1] $x=\dfrac72$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\dfrac{d^2\left(D^2\right)}{dx^2}=2>0$, so the stationary point is a minimum [R1] [1 mark] (d) $D^2=\dfrac{49}{4}-\dfrac{49}{2}+16$ [M1] $=\dfrac{15}{4}$, so $D=\dfrac{\sqrt{15}}{2}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Minimizing $D^2$ gives the same $x$ as minimizing $D$ and avoids differentiating a square root. Remember to take the square root at the end to get the distance itself.

subtopic: Window of maximum area for a fixed perimeter
statement: A window is a rectangle of width $2r$ and height $h$ metres, with a semicircle of radius $r$ metres on top of the rectangle's upper side. The perimeter of the whole window (the base, two vertical sides and the semicircular arc) is $12$ m. (a) Show that $h=6-\left(1+\dfrac\pi2\right)r$, and that the area of the window is $A=12r-\left(2+\dfrac\pi2\right)r^2$. [4] (b) Find the value of $r$ that maximizes $A$, and show that $h=r$ for this value. [4] (c) Find the maximum area to three significant figures, with a reason why it is a maximum. [2]
markscheme: (a) perimeter $2r+2h+\pi r=12$ [M1] $h=6-\left(1+\dfrac\pi2\right)r$ [AG] [A1] $A=2rh+\dfrac12\pi r^2$ [M1] $=12r-(2+\pi)r^2+\dfrac\pi2r^2=12r-\left(2+\dfrac\pi2\right)r^2$ [AG] [A1] [4 marks] (b) $\dfrac{dA}{dr}=12-(4+\pi)r$ [A1] $=0$ at $r=\dfrac{12}{4+\pi}=1.68$ [A1] $h=6-\dfrac{(2+\pi)r}2$ [M1] $=\dfrac{12-(2+\pi)r}{2}=\dfrac{(4+\pi)r-(2+\pi)r}2=r$ [AG] [A1] [4 marks] (c) $A=12r-\dfrac{4+\pi}2r^2=6r=10.1\text{ m}^2$ [A1] $\dfrac{d^2A}{dr^2}=-(4+\pi)<0$ [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Write the perimeter condition to eliminate $h$, then maximize a quadratic in $r$ by differentiating.

subtopic: Second derivative, stationary point and point of inflexion
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{\ln x}{x}$, for $x>0$. (a) Show that $f'(x)=\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x^2}$. [2] (b) Find the coordinates of the stationary point of the graph of $f$. [2] (c) Show that $f''(x)=\dfrac{2\ln x-3}{x^3}$. [3] (d) Hence determine the nature of the stationary point. [1] (e) Find the exact coordinates of the point of inflexion, justifying that it is a point of inflexion. [3]
markscheme: (a) Quotient rule [M1] $f'(x)=\dfrac{\frac1x\cdot x-\ln x\cdot1}{x^2}=\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x^2}$ [A1][AG] [2 marks] (b) $f'(x)=0$ gives $\ln x=1$ [M1] $\left(e,\dfrac1e\right)$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $f'(x)=(1-\ln x)x^{-2}$ [M1] $f''(x)=-\dfrac1x\cdot x^{-2}-2(1-\ln x)x^{-3}$ [A1] $=\dfrac{-1-2+2\ln x}{x^3}=\dfrac{2\ln x-3}{x^3}$ [A1][AG] [3 marks] (d) $f''(e)=\dfrac{2-3}{e^3}<0$, so the point is a local maximum [A1] [1 mark] (e) $f''(x)=0$ gives $\ln x=\dfrac32$, so $x=e^{\frac32}$ [M1] $f''$ changes sign from negative to positive as $x$ increases through $e^{\frac32}$ (because $x^3>0$ and $2\ln x-3$ changes sign) [R1] Point of inflexion $\left(e^{\frac32},\ \dfrac32e^{-\frac32}\right)$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A zero second derivative is not enough for a point of inflexion; you must show the sign of $f''$ changes. Using the product form with negative powers is often less error-prone than a second quotient rule.

subtopic: Stationary points and their nature
statement: Let $f(x)=x^3-6x^2+9x+2$. (a) Find $f'(x)$ and solve $f'(x)=0$. [3] (b) Use the second derivative to determine the nature of each stationary point. [3] (c) Find the coordinates of the stationary points. [2]
tips: Set $f'(x)=0$ for stationary points; $f''<0$ gives a maximum and $f''>0$ a minimum.

subtopic: Optimization of a can with fixed volume
statement: A closed cylindrical can has radius $r$ cm and height $h$ cm. Its volume is $500\ \text{cm}^3$. (a) Show that the total surface area $A$ of the can satisfies $A=2\pi r^2+\dfrac{1000}{r}$. [2] (b) Find the value of $r$ that minimizes $A$. [3] (c) Justify that this value of $r$ gives a minimum. [2] (d) Find the minimum surface area, correct to three significant figures. [1] (e) Show that for the can with minimum surface area, $h=2r$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\pi r^2h=500$, so $h=\dfrac{500}{\pi r^2}$ [M1] $A=2\pi r^2+2\pi rh=2\pi r^2+\dfrac{1000}{r}$ [A1][AG] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac{dA}{dr}=4\pi r-\dfrac{1000}{r^2}$ [A1] Setting equal to zero: $r^3=\dfrac{250}{\pi}$ [M1] $r=4.30$ cm [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\dfrac{d^2A}{dr^2}=4\pi+\dfrac{2000}{r^3}$ [A1] which is positive for $r>0$, so the stationary point is a minimum [R1] [2 marks] (d) $A_{\min}=349\ \text{cm}^2$ [A1] [1 mark] (e) $h=\dfrac{500}{\pi r^2}=\dfrac{2\pi r^3}{\pi r^2}$ using $250=\pi r^3$ [M1] $=2r$ [A1][AG] [2 marks]
tips: Eliminate $h$ using the volume constraint before differentiating. Use the unrounded value of $r$ when calculating the minimum area.

subtopic: Related rates: sliding ladder
statement: A ladder of length $5$ m leans against a vertical wall. The foot of the ladder slides away from the wall at a constant speed of $0.4\text{ m s}^{-1}$. Let $x$ be the distance of the foot from the wall and $y$ the height of the top of the ladder. (a) Write an equation connecting $x$ and $y$. [1] (b) Find $\dfrac{dy}{dt}$ at the instant when $x=3$ m. [4] (c) Explain the sign of your answer. [1]
markscheme: (a) $x^2+y^2=25$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $2x\dfrac{dx}{dt}+2y\dfrac{dy}{dt}=0$ [M1][A1] $y=4$ when $x=3$ [A1] $\dfrac{dy}{dt}=-\dfrac{3\times0.4}{4}=-0.3\text{ m s}^{-1}$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) negative because the top of the ladder is moving down [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Differentiate the constraint with respect to time $t$ using implicit differentiation, and substitute values only after differentiating.

subtopic: Linear approximation using the tangent line
statement: Let $f(x)=\sqrt x$. (a) Find the equation of the tangent to the graph of $f$ at $x=25$. [3] (b) Use the tangent to estimate $\sqrt{26}$. [1] (c) Using the sign of $f''(x)$, state whether $5.1$ is an overestimate or an underestimate, and give a reason. [2]
markscheme: (a) $f'(x)=\dfrac1{2\sqrt x}$ [A1] $f'(25)=\dfrac1{10}$ [A1] $y=5+\dfrac{x-25}{10}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $5+\dfrac1{10}=5.1$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $f''(x)=-\dfrac14x^{-3/2}<0$, so the graph is concave down [A1] the tangent lies above the curve, so $5.1$ is an overestimate [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Near $x=a$, $f(x)\approx f(a)+f'(a)(x-a)$. A concave-down curve lies below its tangent lines.

subtopic: Logarithmic differentiation
statement: Let $f(x)=x^x$ for $x>0$. (a) By taking natural logarithms of $y=x^x$, show that $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=x^x(1+\ln x)$. [4] (b) Find the value of $x$ at which $f$ has its minimum, and the minimum value. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\ln y=x\ln x$ [M1] $\dfrac1y\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\ln x+x\times\dfrac1x$ [M1][A1] $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=x^x(1+\ln x)$ [A1] [AG] [4 marks] (b) $1+\ln x=0$ [M1] $x=e^{-1}$ [A1] minimum value $=\left(e^{-1}\right)^{e^{-1}}=e^{-1/e}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: When the variable appears in both base and exponent, take $\ln$ of both sides and differentiate implicitly.

subtopic: Curve sketching: a rational function with oblique asymptote
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{x^2}{x-2}$ for $x\ne2$. (a) Write down the equation of the vertical asymptote, and show that $f(x)=x+2+\dfrac4{x-2}$. Hence state the equation of the oblique asymptote. [3] (b) Show that $f'(x)=\dfrac{x(x-4)}{(x-2)^2}$. [3] (c) Find the coordinates of the local maximum and local minimum. [3] (d) Hence state the range of $f$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $x=2$ [A1] polynomial division: $x^2=(x-2)(x+2)+4$ [M1] oblique asymptote $y=x+2$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $f'(x)=\dfrac{2x(x-2)-x^2}{(x-2)^2}$ [M1][A1] $=\dfrac{x^2-4x}{(x-2)^2}=\dfrac{x(x-4)}{(x-2)^2}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $f'(x)=0$ at $x=0$ and $x=4$ [A1] $f(0)=0$ is a maximum (sign of $f'$ changes from $+$ to $-$) [A1] $f(4)=8$ is a minimum [A1] [3 marks] (d) $y\le0$ or $y\ge8$ [A1][A1] [2 marks]
tips: Divide to find the oblique asymptote. The range has a gap because the local maximum lies below the local minimum.

subtopic: Product rule with an exponential
statement: Let $f(x)=x^2e^{3x}$. (a) Find $f'(x)$, giving your answer in factorized form. [3] (b) Hence find the $x$-coordinates of the stationary points of the graph of $f$. [2] (c) Find the gradient of the tangent at $x=1$, giving the exact value. [2]
tips: Product rule: $(uv)'=u'v+uv'$. Factorizing makes the stationary points easy to read.

subtopic: Slope field gradients and a straight-line solution
statement: The slope field of the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=y-x$ has, at each point $(x,y)$, a short segment whose gradient equals $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ there. (a) Find the gradient of the slope segment at each of the points $(0,1)$, $(2,2)$ and $(3,0)$. [3] (b) Show that the line $y=x+1$ is a solution curve of the differential equation, and describe the slope segments along this line. [3] (c) Explain why any solution curve that crosses the line $y=x$ must have a horizontal tangent at the crossing point. [1]
markscheme: (a) $(0,1)$: $1-0=1$ [A1] $(2,2)$: $2-2=0$ [A1] $(3,0)$: $0-3=-3$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) for $y=x+1$, $\frac{dy}{dx}=1$ [M1] and $y-x=1$, so the equation is satisfied [A1] along this line every slope segment has gradient $1$, so the segments are parallel to the line itself [R1] [3 marks] (c) on $y=x$ we have $y-x=0$, so $\frac{dy}{dx}=0$ and the tangent is horizontal [R1] [1 mark]
tips: To check that a given curve is a solution, differentiate it and substitute both $y$ and $dy/dx$ into the differential equation. Slope segments are determined only by the point $(x,y)$.

subtopic: Logistic growth and harvesting
statement: This question investigates models for the population of fish in a lake. Let $P$ be the number of fish, in thousands, $t$ years after the lake was first stocked with $2000$ fish. (a) In model A, $\dfrac{dP}{dt} = 0.4P$. (i) Solve this differential equation to find $P$ in terms of $t$. (ii) Find the number of fish predicted by model A after $10$ years. (iii) State one reason why model A is unrealistic in the long term. [4] In model B, $\dfrac{dP}{dt} = 0.4P\left(1 - \dfrac{P}{20}\right)$. (b) (i) Find the equilibrium values of $P$ for model B. (ii) Find the value of $P$ for which the population grows fastest, and the maximum rate of growth. [5] (c) Show that $P = \dfrac{20}{1 + 9e^{-0.4t}}$ satisfies the differential equation in model B and the initial condition. [5] (d) Using model B, find the time taken for the population to reach $15\,000$ fish. [3] (e) A fishing company proposes to harvest fish at a constant rate of $h$ thousand fish per year, so that $\dfrac{dP}{dt} = 0.4P\left(1 - \dfrac{P}{20}\right) - h$. (i) For $h = 1.5$, find the equilibrium values of $P$ and determine whether each is stable or unstable. (ii) Find the largest value of $h$ for which the population can be maintained at a constant level. [6] (f) Use Euler's method with a step length of $0.5$ to estimate $P(1)$ for model B (without harvesting). Compare your answer with the exact value from part (c) and explain the difference. [4]
markscheme: (a)(i) $\displaystyle\int\frac{dP}{P}=\int0.4\,dt\Rightarrow\ln P=0.4t+c$ [M1] $P=2e^{0.4t}$ [A1] (ii) $P(10)=2e^{4}=109.196\ldots$, so about $109\,000$ fish [A1] (iii) e.g. it predicts unlimited growth, but the lake has limited food/space [R1] [4 marks] (b)(i) $P=0$ and $P=20$ [A1][A1] (ii) $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=0.4P-0.02P^2$ is a quadratic in $P$, maximized where $0.4-0.04P=0$ [M1] $P=10$ (i.e. $10\,000$ fish) [A1] maximum rate $=0.4\times10\times0.5=2$ thousand fish per year [A1] [5 marks] (c) $P(0)=\dfrac{20}{1+9}=2$ [A1] $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=\dfrac{20\times9\times0.4e^{-0.4t}}{\left(1+9e^{-0.4t}\right)^2}=\dfrac{72e^{-0.4t}}{\left(1+9e^{-0.4t}\right)^2}$ [M1][A1] $1-\dfrac{P}{20}=1-\dfrac{1}{1+9e^{-0.4t}}=\dfrac{9e^{-0.4t}}{1+9e^{-0.4t}}$ [A1] so $0.4P\left(1-\dfrac{P}{20}\right)=0.4\cdot\dfrac{20}{1+9e^{-0.4t}}\cdot\dfrac{9e^{-0.4t}}{1+9e^{-0.4t}}=\dfrac{72e^{-0.4t}}{\left(1+9e^{-0.4t}\right)^2}=\dfrac{dP}{dt}$ [A1][AG] [5 marks] (d) $\dfrac{20}{1+9e^{-0.4t}}=15$ [M1] $e^{-0.4t}=\dfrac{1}{27}$ [A1] $t=\dfrac{\ln27}{0.4}=8.24$ years [A1] [3 marks] (e)(i) $0.4P-0.02P^2-1.5=0\Rightarrow P^2-20P+75=0$ [M1] $P=5$ or $P=15$ [A1] Let $f(P)=0.4P\left(1-\frac{P}{20}\right)-1.5$: $f(P)<0$ for $P<5$, $f(P)>0$ for $5<P<15$, $f(P)<0$ for $P>15$ (or $f'(5)=0.2>0$, $f'(15)=-0.2<0$) [R1] so $P=15$ is stable and $P=5$ is unstable [A1] (ii) An equilibrium exists only if $h\le$ the maximum of $0.4P\left(1-\frac{P}{20}\right)$ [M1] so $h_{\max}=2$, i.e. $2000$ fish per year [A1] [6 marks] (f) $P_{n+1}=P_n+0.5\times0.4P_n\left(1-\frac{P_n}{20}\right)$ [M1] $P(0.5)\approx2+0.5\times0.72=2.36$ [A1] $P(1)\approx2.36+0.5\times0.832608=2.78$ [A1] Exact value $\dfrac{20}{1+9e^{-0.4}}=2.84$; Euler underestimates because the solution curve is concave up for $P<10$, so the tangent lies below the curve [R1] [4 marks] Total [27 marks]
tips: For stability, check the sign of dP/dt on either side of each equilibrium.

subtopic: Exponential growth from a separable equation
statement: A culture of bacteria has population $y$ (in thousands) at time $t$ hours, and grows at a rate proportional to its size. (a) Solve the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dt}=0.3y$ with $y(0)=50$, giving $y$ in terms of $t$. [4] (b) Find the exact time at which $y=200$. [3]
tips: Separate the variables, integrate both sides, then use the initial value to find the constant.

subtopic: Euler's method with a product gradient
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=xy$ with $y(1)=2$. (a) Use Euler's method with step size $h=0.5$ to approximate $y(2.5)$. Show each step. [5] (b) State, with a reason, how the accuracy of the approximation could be improved. [1]
markscheme: (a) $y_{n+1}=y_n+h f(x_n,y_n)$ [M1]: $y_{1}=2+0.5\cdot f(1,2)=3$, $y_{2}=3+0.5\cdot f(1.5,3)=5.25$, $y_{3}=5.25+0.5\cdot f(2,5.25)=10.5$ [A1][A1][A1]; so $y(2.5)\approx10.5$ [A1] [5 marks] (b) Use a smaller step size $h$ (more steps), because the local error of Euler's method decreases with $h$ [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Evaluate the gradient at the current point $(x_n,y_n)$, not at the new point.

subtopic: Step size, error and stability of Euler's method for logistic growth
statement: This question investigates how the step size affects the accuracy and stability of Euler's method. The population $P$ (in thousands) of algae in a pond satisfies $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=0.5P\left(1-\dfrac{P}{50}\right)$, where $t$ is in days and $P(0)=5$. (a) Find the equilibrium values of $P$, and state, with a reason, whether $P$ is increasing or decreasing when $0<P<50$. [3] (b) Use Euler's method with step size $h=1$ to estimate $P(1)$, $P(2)$ and $P(3)$. [4] (c) The exact solution is $P(t)=\dfrac{50}{1+9e^{-0.5t}}$. Show that it satisfies the initial condition, find $P(3)$ to 4 significant figures, and find the error in your estimate of $P(3)$ from part (b). [4] (d) Use a GDC spreadsheet with step sizes $h=0.5$, $0.25$ and $0.125$ to estimate $P(3)$ to 4 significant figures, and describe how the error changes as $h$ is halved. [4] (e) Now take $h=3$. Find the estimates $P_1$, $P_2$, $P_3$ and $P_4$ at $t=3,6,9,12$, and show that Euler's method produces a value greater than the carrying capacity $50$. [4] (f) For general $h$, Euler's method gives $P_{n+1}=g(P_n)$, where $g(P)=P+0.5hP\left(1-\dfrac P{50}\right)$. (i) Show that $g(50)=50$. (ii) Find $g'(50)$ in terms of $h$. (iii) Given that the iteration settles to $P=50$ only if $|g'(50)|<1$, find the range of values of $h$ for which this happens. [5] (g) Take $h=4.2$. Find $P_1$, $P_2$, $P_3$ and $P_4$ to 4 significant figures, describe what happens, and refer to your answer to part (f). [3]
tips: In (f) the derivative of the update function at a fixed point controls whether small errors shrink or grow. In (d) and (g) keep unrounded values in your spreadsheet and round only for the final answer.

subtopic: Mixing in a single tank
statement: A tank contains $200$ liters of pure water. Brine containing $0.15$ kg of salt per liter flows in at $4$ liters per minute. The well-mixed solution flows out at $4$ liters per minute. Let $x$ kg be the mass of salt in the tank after $t$ minutes. (a) Show that $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=0.6-\dfrac{x}{50}$. [2] (b) Solve the differential equation with $x=0$ when $t=0$, to find $x$ in terms of $t$. [4] (c) Find the time when the mass of salt is $20$ kg, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (d) Use Euler's method with step size $h=10$ minutes to estimate $x$ at $t=20$, and compare with the exact value from part (b) correct to 3 significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) rate in $=4\times0.15=0.6$ kg per minute [A1]; rate out $=4\times\dfrac{x}{200}=\dfrac{x}{50}$ [AG] [2 marks] (b) $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{dx}{30-x}=\int\dfrac{1}{50}\,dt$ [M1]; $-\ln(30-x)=\dfrac{t}{50}+c$ [A1]; $x=0$ at $t=0$ gives $c=-\ln30$ [A1]; $x=30\left(1-e^{-t/50}\right)$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) $30\left(1-e^{-t/50}\right)=20$ [M1]; $t=50\ln3=54.9$ minutes [A1] [2 marks] (d) $x(10)\approx0+10(0.6)=6$ [A1]; $x(20)\approx6+10(0.6-0.12)=10.8$ [A1]; exact $=9.89$, so Euler overestimates by $0.91$ kg [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Rewrite $0.6-\frac{x}{50}$ as $\frac{30-x}{50}$ before separating the variables.

subtopic: Rabbit and fox populations: equilibrium and Euler step
statement: The numbers of rabbits $x$ and foxes $y$ in a reserve at time $t$ months are modeled by $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=0.6x-0.03xy$ and $\dfrac{dy}{dt}=0.01xy-0.4y$. (a) Show that $(x,y)=(40,20)$ is an equilibrium point of the system. [3] (b) Find $\dfrac{dx}{dt}$ and $\dfrac{dy}{dt}$ when $x=80$ and $y=10$, and interpret your answers. [3] (c) Use Euler's method with step size $h=0.5$ to estimate $x$ and $y$ at $t=0.5$, given $x=50$ and $y=10$ at $t=0$. [3] (d) The solution curves in the $xy$-plane are closed loops. Explain what this implies for the two populations. [1]
markscheme: (a) equilibrium requires $\frac{dx}{dt}=0$ and $\frac{dy}{dt}=0$ [M1] $x(0.6-0.03y)=40\left(0.6-0.6\right)=0$ [A1] $y(0.01x-0.4)=20\left(0.4-0.4\right)=0$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\frac{dx}{dt}=48-24=24$ [A1] $\frac{dy}{dt}=10(0.8-0.4)=4$ [A1] both populations are increasing at that moment [R1] [3 marks] (c) at $(50,10)$: $\frac{dx}{dt}=30-15=15$ and $\frac{dy}{dt}=10(0.5-0.4)=1$ [M1] $x=50+0.5(15)=57.5$ [A1] $y=10+0.5(1)=10.5$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) closed loops mean both populations rise and fall periodically, with the predator cycle lagging behind the prey cycle [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Euler's method for a system updates both variables using the rates at the same starting point. At an equilibrium both derivatives are zero.

subtopic: Euler's method and concavity
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=x+y^2$ with $y=1$ when $x=0$. (a) Use Euler's method with step size $h=0.1$ to find an approximation for $y$ when $x=0.2$. [3] (b) Continue the method to estimate $y$ when $x=0.3$, giving your answer to 3 significant figures. [2] (c) Show that $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=1+2y(x+y^2)$, and hence explain why the Euler estimates are less than the true values of $y$ for $x\geq 0$. (Assume $y>0$.) [3]
markscheme: (a) $y_1=1+0.1(0+1^2)=1.1$ [M1] [A1] $y_2=1.1+0.1(0.1+1.1^2)=1.231$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $y_3=1.231+0.1(0.2+1.231^2)$ [M1] $=1.4025\ldots\approx 1.40$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=1+2y\dfrac{dy}{dx}=1+2y(x+y^2)$ [A1] For $x\ge0$, $y>0$ this is positive, so the solution curve is concave up [R1] Each Euler step follows the tangent line, which lies below a concave-up curve, so each estimate is an underestimate [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Write each Euler step as $y_{n+1}=y_n+h\,f(x_n,y_n)$ and keep full calculator accuracy until the last step. Link the sign of the second derivative to the geometry of tangent lines.

subtopic: Fish population with constant harvesting
statement: A fish population $P$ in a lake, $t$ years after monitoring began, is modeled with harvesting by $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=0.5P\left(1-\dfrac{P}{800}\right)-40$. (a) Use your GDC to find the equilibrium values of $P$, giving your answers to 3 significant figures. [3] (b) Determine the stability of each equilibrium. [3] (c) Without harvesting, the maximum growth rate is $100$ fish per year. Deduce what happens to the population if the harvesting rate is increased to $120$ fish per year. [2] (d) Find $\dfrac{dP}{dt}$ when $P=50$, and interpret the result. [2]
markscheme: (a) $0.5P\left(1-\frac{P}{800}\right)-40=0$ [M1] $P=90.2$ [A1] $P=710$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) test the sign of $\frac{dP}{dt}$ on each side of the equilibria [M1] for $90.2<P<710$ it is positive (for example $P=400$ gives $60$), and for $P>710$ it is negative, so $P=710$ is stable [A1] for $P<90.2$ it is negative, so $P=90.2$ is unstable [A1] [3 marks] (c) the growth term has maximum $0.5(400)(0.5)=100$ at $P=400$ [M1] since $100<120$, $\frac{dP}{dt}<0$ for every $P$ and the population collapses to zero [A1] [2 marks] (d) $0.5(50)\left(1-\frac{50}{800}\right)-40=-16.6$ fish per year [A1] this is below the unstable equilibrium $90.2$, so the population keeps falling toward extinction [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A stable equilibrium attracts nearby solutions, an unstable one repels them. Check the sign of the derivative in each region between and beyond the equilibria.

subtopic: Coupled linear system: eigenvalues and saddle
statement: Consider the coupled system $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=x+2y,\quad \dfrac{dy}{dt}=3x+2y$. (a) Write the system in the form $\dfrac{d\mathbf{x}}{dt}=A\mathbf{x}$ and find the eigenvalues of $A$. [3] (b) Find an eigenvector corresponding to each eigenvalue. [3] (c) Write down the general solution of the system. [2] (d) Classify the equilibrium point at the origin, justifying your answer. [2]
markscheme: (a) $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&2\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\det(A-\lambda I)=(1-\lambda)(2-\lambda)-6=\lambda^2-3\lambda-4=0$ [M1] $\lambda=4$ or $\lambda=-1$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) For $\lambda=4$: $-3a+2b=0$ [M1] eigenvector $\begin{pmatrix}2\\3\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] For $\lambda=-1$: $a+b=0$, eigenvector $\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] (any non-zero multiples) [3 marks] (c) $\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\end{pmatrix}=c_1\begin{pmatrix}2\\3\end{pmatrix}e^{4t}$ [A1] $+\,c_2\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix}e^{-t}$ [A1] (follow through from (b)) [2 marks] (d) Saddle point (unstable) [A1] because the eigenvalues are real with opposite signs [R1] [2 marks]
tips: For a $2\times2$ system, solve $\det(A-\lambda I)=0$ and then find each eigenvector from $(A-\lambda I)\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$. The signs of the eigenvalues classify the equilibrium.

subtopic: A separable differential equation
statement: Solve $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=2xy$ with $y>0$ and $y=3$ when $x=0$. (a) Separate the variables and integrate. [3] (b) Use the initial condition to find the particular solution for $y$. [3]
tips: Write all $y$ terms with $dy$ and all $x$ terms with $dx$ before integrating.

subtopic: Predator-prey model: equilibrium, Euler and linearization
statement: The populations (in hundreds) of a prey species $x$ and its predator $y$ at time $t$ years are modelled by $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=0.4x-0.02xy,\quad \dfrac{dy}{dt}=0.01xy-0.3y$, for $x,y\ge 0$. (a) Find the coordinates of the equilibrium point at which both populations are non-zero. [3] (b) Find $\dfrac{dx}{dt}$ and $\dfrac{dy}{dt}$ when $x=40$ and $y=15$. [2] (c) Given that $x=40$ and $y=15$ when $t=0$, use Euler's method with step size $h=0.5$ to estimate the populations when $t=1$. Give your answers to 3 significant figures. [4] (d) Near the equilibrium point, let $u=x-30$ and $v=y-20$. The system can be approximated by $\dfrac{du}{dt}=-0.6v,\quad \dfrac{dv}{dt}=0.2u$. Find the eigenvalues of the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&-0.6\\0.2&0\end{pmatrix}$. [2] (e) Hence describe the long-term behavior of the populations near the equilibrium point, and find the approximate time between successive peaks of the prey population. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\frac{dx}{dt}=0$: $x(0.4-0.02y)=0$ [M1] $y=20$ [A1] $\frac{dy}{dt}=0$: $y(0.01x-0.3)=0$, so $x=30$; equilibrium $(30,20)$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\frac{dx}{dt}=16-12=4$ [A1] $\frac{dy}{dt}=6-4.5=1.5$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Step 1: $x_1=40+0.5(4)=42$, $y_1=15+0.5(1.5)=15.75$ [M1] [A1] Step 2: $\frac{dx}{dt}=0.4(42)-0.02(42)(15.75)=3.57$, $\frac{dy}{dt}=0.01(42)(15.75)-0.3(15.75)=1.89$ [M1] $x_2=43.785\approx 43.8$, $y_2=16.695\approx 16.7$ [A1] [4 marks] (d) $\lambda^2+0.12=0$ [M1] $\lambda=\pm i\sqrt{0.12}=\pm0.346i$ [A1] [2 marks] (e) Purely imaginary eigenvalues, so the equilibrium is a center [A1] The populations follow closed orbits, oscillating periodically rather than converging or diverging [R1] Period $=\frac{2\pi}{0.3464}=18.1$ years [A1] [3 marks]
tips: In coupled-system questions, set both rates to zero to find equilibria. Purely imaginary eigenvalues give a center, and the period of oscillation is $2\pi$ divided by the imaginary part.

subtopic: Euler's method with two steps on a linear equation
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=2x+y$ with $y=1$ when $x=0$. (a) Use Euler's method with step size $h=0.5$ to estimate $y$ when $x=1$. Show each step. [4] (b) The exact solution is $y=3e^x-2x-2$. Find the exact value of $y(1)$ and show that your estimate in part (a) is an underestimate. [2]
tips: Write the iteration formula $y_{n+1}=y_n+h\,f(x_n,y_n)$ explicitly and update both $x$ and $y$ at each step. For (b), compare using a simple bound on $e$.

subtopic: Newton's law of cooling for a metal block
statement: A metal block is removed from a furnace and left to cool in a room at $20^\circ$C. Its temperature $T^\circ$C after $t$ minutes is observed. (a) Show that the temperature $T$ satisfies $\dfrac{dT}{dt}=-k(T-20)$ for some constant $k>0$, and solve the equation to show that $T=20+Ae^{-kt}$. [4] (b) Given that $T=180$ at $t=0$ and $T=120$ at $t=10$, find $A$ and $k$. [3] (c) Find the time at which the temperature is 45$^\circ$C. [2] (d) Find $\dfrac{dT}{dt}$ at the time found in part (c), and interpret the sign. [2]
markscheme: (a) Newton's law of cooling: the rate is proportional to the difference from the surroundings [R1]; separate: $\int\dfrac{dT}{T-20}=-\int k\,dt$ [M1]; $\ln|T-20|=-kt+c$ [A1]; $T=20+Ae^{-kt}$ [AG] [4 marks] (b) $A=160$ [A1]; $120=20+160e^{-10k}$ [M1]; $k=0.0470$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $45=20+160e^{-0.0470t}$ [M1]; $t=39.5$ minutes [A1] [2 marks] (d) $\dfrac{dT}{dt}=-0.0470(45-20)=-1.175$ [A1]; the negative sign means the temperature is falling [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Use the observation at $t=10$ to find $k$ before solving for the time.

subtopic: Euler's method: accuracy and numerical stability
statement: This question investigates the accuracy and stability of Euler's method. Euler's method with step size $h$ for $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=f(x,y)$ uses $y_{n+1}=y_n+h\,f(x_n,y_n)$, with $x_n=nh$. Throughout, $y_0=1$. (a) Solve $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=y$ with $y(0)=1$ exactly. [2] (b) For $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=y$, show that $y_n=(1+h)^n$. [3] (c) With $h=0.25$, find Euler's estimate for $y(1)$ and its absolute error. [3] (d) Now take $h=\dfrac1n$, so that the estimate of $y(1)$ is $\left(1+\dfrac1n\right)^n$. Let $E_n=e-\left(1+\dfrac1n\right)^n$. Complete the table of values of $E_n$ and $nE_n$ for $n=10,100,1000$ (3 significant figures). [3] (e) Hence suggest the limit of $nE_n$ as $n\to\infty$, and state what this suggests about how the error depends on $h$. [2] (f) Now consider $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-5y$ with $y(0)=1$. Show that $y_n=(1-5h)^n$. [2] (g) Find $y_n$ in terms of $n$ for $h=0.1$, $h=0.3$ and $h=0.5$, and describe how each sequence behaves as $n$ increases. [3] (h) Hence find the set of values of $h>0$ for which $y_n\to0$ as $n\to\infty$. [3] (i) For $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-ky$ with $k>0$, find in terms of $k$ the values of $h$ for which $y_n\to0$, and the values of $h$ for which the signs of $y_n$ alternate. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\int\frac1y\,dy=\int dx$, $\ln y=x+C$ [M1] $y=e^{x}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $y_{n+1}=y_n+hy_n=(1+h)y_n$ [A1] This is a geometric sequence with common ratio $1+h$ [M1] and $y_0=1$, so $y_n=(1+h)^n$ [A1][AG] [3 marks] (c) $y_4=1.25^4=2.44140625\approx2.44$ [A1] Error $=e-2.4414$ [M1] $=0.277$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $n=10$: $E_n=0.125$, $nE_n=1.25$ [A1] $n=100$: $E_n=0.0135$, $nE_n=1.35$ [A1] $n=1000$: $E_n=0.00136$, $nE_n=1.36$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) The limit appears to be $\frac e2\approx1.36$ [A1] So $E_n\approx\frac{e}{2n}=\frac e2h$: the error is approximately proportional to $h$, so halving $h$ roughly halves the error [A1] [2 marks] (f) $y_{n+1}=y_n-5hy_n=(1-5h)y_n$ [M1] geometric with ratio $1-5h$ and $y_0=1$, so $y_n=(1-5h)^n$ [A1][AG] [2 marks] (g) $h=0.1$: $y_n=0.5^n$, decreases to $0$ smoothly [A1] $h=0.3$: $y_n=(-0.5)^n$, alternates in sign while tending to $0$ [A1] $h=0.5$: $y_n=(-1.5)^n$, alternates in sign with growing magnitude (diverges) [A1] [3 marks] (h) Require $|1-5h|<1$ [M1] $-1<1-5h<1$ [A1] $0<h<0.4$ [A1] [3 marks] (i) $y_n=(1-kh)^n$, tends to $0$ iff $|1-kh|<1$ [M1] $0<h<\frac2k$ [A1] Signs alternate iff $1-kh<0$, i.e. $h>\frac1k$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: For a linear equation Euler's method produces a geometric sequence, so convergence depends on the size of the common ratio. Always link numerical behavior back to the exact solution, which here decays to zero.

subtopic: Three steps of Euler's method
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=x+y$ with $y(0)=1$. (a) Use Euler's method with step size $h=0.1$ to approximate $y(0.3)$. Show each step. [5] (b) State, with a reason, how the accuracy of the approximation could be improved. [1]
markscheme: (a) $y_{n+1}=y_n+h f(x_n,y_n)$ [M1]: $y_{1}=1+0.1\cdot f(0,1)=1.1$, $y_{2}=1.1+0.1\cdot f(0.1,1.1)=1.22$, $y_{3}=1.22+0.1\cdot f(0.2,1.22)=1.362$ [A1][A1][A1]; so $y(0.3)\approx1.362$ [A1] [5 marks] (b) Use a smaller step size $h$ (more steps), because the local error of Euler's method decreases with $h$ [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Write each step on its own line: new $y$ = old $y$ + $h\times$ (gradient at the old point).

subtopic: Spread of information in a population
statement: In a town of $1000$ people, the number $N$ who have heard a news story satisfies $\dfrac{dN}{dt}=k(1000-N)$, where $t$ is in hours, and $N=100$ at $t=0$. After $5$ hours, $N=400$. (a) Solve the differential equation to show that $N=1000-900e^{-kt}$. [3] (b) Find $k$ to three significant figures. [2] (c) Find the time at which $900$ people have heard the story, to three significant figures. [2]
tips: The rate is proportional to the number of people who have not yet heard the story.

subtopic: Mixing problem: salt in a tank
statement: A tank contains 200 liters of pure water. Brine containing $0.5$ kg of salt per liter flows in at $4$ liters per minute. The well-mixed solution flows out at $4$ liters per minute, so the volume stays at 200 liters. Let $S$ kg be the mass of salt in the tank after $t$ minutes. (a) Show that $\dfrac{dS}{dt}=2-\dfrac{S}{50}$. [3] (b) Solve the differential equation with $S=0$ when $t=0$, giving $S$ in terms of $t$. [4] (c) Find the time taken for the tank to contain $60$ kg of salt, to 3 significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) Rate of salt in $=0.5\times4=2$ kg/min [A1] Concentration in the tank $=\frac{S}{200}$ kg/L [M1] Rate out $=4\times\frac{S}{200}=\frac{S}{50}$, so $\frac{dS}{dt}=2-\frac{S}{50}$ [A1][AG] [3 marks] (b) $\frac{dS}{dt}=\frac{100-S}{50}$, so $\int\frac{50}{100-S}\,dS=\int dt$ [M1] $-50\ln(100-S)=t+c$ [A1] $t=0,S=0$: $c=-50\ln100$ [M1] $S=100\left(1-e^{-t/50}\right)$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) $60=100(1-e^{-t/50})$, $e^{-t/50}=0.4$ [M1] $t=50\ln2.5=45.8$ minutes [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Model inflow minus outflow, and remember that the outflow depends on the current concentration $S/V$. Factor the right-hand side before separating.

subtopic: Spiral sink and period of oscillation for coupled populations
statement: The deviations $x$ and $y$ (in hundreds) of a prey population and a predator population from their equilibrium values are modeled by $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=-0.2x+0.8y$ and $\dfrac{dy}{dt}=-0.8x-0.2y$, where $t$ is in years. (a) Use your GDC to find the eigenvalues of the matrix of the system. [2] (b) Classify the equilibrium at the origin and describe the phase portrait. [2] (c) Find the period of the oscillations. [2] (d) Use Euler's method with step size $h=0.1$ to estimate $x$ and $y$ at $t=0.1$, given $x=10$ and $y=5$ at $t=0$. [2] (e) Find the factor by which the amplitude of the oscillations decreases over one period. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\lambda=-0.2\pm0.8i$ [A1][A1] [2 marks] (b) the real part is negative and the eigenvalues are complex, so the origin is a stable spiral (spiral sink) [A1] trajectories spiral inward toward the origin [A1] [2 marks] (c) period $=\frac{2\pi}{0.8}$ [M1] $=7.85$ years [A1] [2 marks] (d) $\frac{dx}{dt}=-2+4=2$, $\frac{dy}{dt}=-8-1=-9$ [M1] $x\approx10.2$, $y\approx4.1$ [A1] [2 marks] (e) factor $=e^{-0.2\times7.854}$ [M1] $=0.208$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: For $\lambda=p\pm qi$ the real part $p$ controls growth or decay and the imaginary part $q$ gives the angular frequency, so the period is $2\pi/q$. Over one period the amplitude is multiplied by $e^{p\times\text{period}}$.

subtopic: Newton's law of cooling with exact time
statement: A cup of coffee at $80^\circ\mathrm{C}$ is placed in a room at a constant temperature of $20^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Its temperature $T$ at time $t$ minutes satisfies $\dfrac{dT}{dt}=-k(T-20)$, where $k>0$ is a constant. (a) Solve the differential equation to show that $T=20+Ae^{-kt}$, and find $A$. [4] (b) After $10$ minutes the temperature is $50^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Show that $k=\dfrac{\ln2}{10}$. [2] (c) Find the exact time at which the coffee reaches $35^\circ\mathrm{C}$. [2]
tips: The temperature difference $T-20$ decays exponentially, so work with that difference. Use $\ln\frac12=-\ln2$ and $\ln\frac14=-2\ln2$ to keep answers exact.

subtopic: Euler estimate for a logistic model
statement: The number $P$ of users of a service (in hundreds) is modeled by $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=0.25P\left(1-\dfrac{P}{2000}\right)$ with $t$ in months and $P(0)=300$. (a) Find the equilibrium populations and state which is stable. [3] (b) Find the population at which the growth rate is greatest, and the value of that greatest growth rate. [3] (c) Use Euler's method with step size $h=2$ to estimate the population after $6$ units of time. [4] (d) The exact solution gives $P(6)=883.2$. Find the percentage error of the Euler estimate. [2]
markscheme: (a) $rP(1-P/K)=0$ gives $P=0$ or $P=2000$ [A1][A1]; $P=2000$ is stable (growth rate positive below, negative above) [A1] [3 marks] (b) Maximum of $f(P)=rP(1-P/K)$ at $P=\dfrac K2=1000$ [M1][A1]; $f=125$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Table: $t=0$: $P=300.000$; $t=2$: $P=427.500$; $t=4$: $P=595.561$; $t=6$: $P=804.668$ [M1][A1][A1]; estimate $804.7$ [A1] [4 marks] (d) $\dfrac{|804.67-883.23|}{883.23}\times100=8.90\%$ [M1][A1] [2 marks]
tips: Use a table with columns $t_n$, $P_n$ and $f(P_n)$ to keep the Euler steps organized.

subtopic: Coupled linear system for two connected compartments
statement: This question models the amounts of a chemical, $x$ and $y$ milligrams, in two connected compartments at time $t$ hours. The amounts satisfy $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=-2x+y$ and $\dfrac{dy}{dt}=x-2y$, with $x=10$ and $y=0$ at $t=0$. (a) Write the system in the form $\dfrac{d\mathbf{v}}{dt}=A\mathbf{v}$, stating $A$. [1] (b) Find the eigenvalues of $A$. [3] (c) Find an eigenvector for each eigenvalue. [2] (d) Find the solution for $x$ and $y$ in terms of $t$. [4] (e) Find the maximum amount of the chemical in the second compartment and the time at which it occurs, correct to 3 significant figures. [3] (f) Use Euler's method with $h=0.1$ to estimate $x$ and $y$ at $t=0.1$. [2] (g) Describe the long-term behavior of the system and classify the equilibrium at the origin. [2]
markscheme: (a) $A=\begin{pmatrix} -2 & 1 \\ 1 & -2 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $(-2-\lambda)^{2}-1=0$ [M1]; $\lambda^{2}+4\lambda+3=0$ [A1]; $\lambda=-1$ and $\lambda=-3$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\lambda=-1$: $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; $\lambda=-3$: $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $\mathbf{v}=\alpha e^{-t}\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}+\beta e^{-3t}\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1]; $\alpha+\beta=10$ and $\alpha-\beta=0$ [A1]; $\alpha=\beta=5$ [A1]; $x=5e^{-t}+5e^{-3t}$ and $y=5e^{-t}-5e^{-3t}$ [A1] [4 marks] (e) $\dfrac{dy}{dt}=-5e^{-t}+15e^{-3t}=0$ [M1]; $e^{2t}=3$ so $t=0.549$ hours [A1]; $y=1.92$ mg [A1] [3 marks] (f) $x\approx10+0.1(-20)=8$ [A1]; $y\approx0+0.1(10)=1$ [A1] [2 marks] (g) both eigenvalues are negative, so $x,y\to0$ [A1]; the origin is a stable node [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Eigenvalues give the decay rates and the eigenvectors give the directions. Both being negative means every solution decays to the origin.

subtopic: Separable equation with circular solution curves
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-\dfrac{x}{y}$, where $y>0$, with $y=4$ when $x=0$. (a) By separating the variables, show that $x^2+y^2=C$ for some constant $C$. [3] (b) Find $y$ in terms of $x$ for the given initial condition. [2] (c) Find the value of $y$ when $x=2$, giving your answer in the form $a\sqrt b$. [1] (d) Describe the shape of the solution curve. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\int y\,dy=-\int x\,dx$ [M1] $\frac{y^2}{2}=-\frac{x^2}{2}+k$ [A1] $x^2+y^2=C$ where $C=2k$ [AG] [3 marks] (b) $16=C$ [A1] $y=\sqrt{16-x^2}$ (positive root since $y>0$) [A1] [2 marks] (c) $y=\sqrt{12}=2\sqrt3$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) the upper half of a circle with centre the origin and radius $4$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Multiply both sides to collect all $y$ terms with $dy$ and all $x$ terms with $dx$ before integrating. Use $y>0$ to choose the positive square root.

subtopic: Cooling of a drink in a refrigerator
statement: A bottle at $25^\circ$C is placed in a refrigerator kept at $4^\circ$C. After $6$ minutes it is $15^\circ$C. Let $T^\circ$C be its temperature after $t$ minutes. (a) Show that the temperature $T$ satisfies $\dfrac{dT}{dt}=-k(T-4)$ for some constant $k>0$, and solve the equation to show that $T=4+Ae^{-kt}$. [4] (b) Given that $T=25$ at $t=0$ and $T=15$ at $t=6$, find $A$ and $k$. [3] (c) Find the time at which the temperature is 8$^\circ$C. [2] (d) Find $\dfrac{dT}{dt}$ at the time found in part (c), and interpret the sign. [2]
markscheme: (a) Newton's law of cooling: the rate is proportional to the difference from the surroundings [R1]; separate: $\int\dfrac{dT}{T-4}=-\int k\,dt$ [M1]; $\ln|T-4|=-kt+c$ [A1]; $T=4+Ae^{-kt}$ [AG] [4 marks] (b) $A=21$ [A1]; $15=4+21e^{-6k}$ [M1]; $k=0.1078$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $8=4+21e^{-0.1078t}$ [M1]; $t=15.4$ minutes [A1] [2 marks] (d) $\dfrac{dT}{dt}=-0.1078(8-4)=-0.431$ [A1]; the negative sign means the temperature is falling [R1] [2 marks]
tips: The constant $A$ is the initial temperature difference, $T(0)-T_{\text{room}}$.

subtopic: Logistic solution for the spread of a rumor
statement: A rumor spreads through a school of $1200$ students. The number $N$ of students who have heard the rumor $t$ days after it started satisfies $\dfrac{dN}{dt}=0.08N\left(1-\dfrac{N}{1200}\right)$ with $N(0)=150$. The solution is $N(t)=\dfrac{1200}{1+7e^{-0.08t}}$. (a) Verify that $N(0)=150$ and find the limit of $N$ as $t\to\infty$. [2] (b) Find the time at which $600$ students have heard the rumor. [2] (c) Use the differential equation to find the maximum rate at which the rumor spreads, and state when it occurs. [2] (d) Find the time at which $1000$ students have heard the rumor. [2]
tips: Rearrange the given solution to isolate the exponential term and take logarithms. The logistic growth rate is greatest when the population is half the carrying capacity.

subtopic: Two-compartment drug model: coupled system
statement: This question investigates how a drug moves from the gut into the bloodstream. After an oral dose, let $x(t)$ mg be the amount of drug in the gut and $y(t)$ mg the amount in the blood, where $t$ is the time in hours. The model is $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=-0.5x,\quad \dfrac{dy}{dt}=0.5x-0.2y$, with $x(0)=100$ and $y(0)=0$. (a) Use Euler's method with step size $h=0.5$ to estimate $x(1)$ and $y(1)$. [4] (b) Write the system in the form $\dfrac{d\mathbf{x}}{dt}=A\mathbf{x}$ and find the eigenvalues of $A$. [3] (c) Find an eigenvector for each eigenvalue. [3] (d) Hence find $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ for the given initial conditions. [4] (e) Hence find the exact amounts at $t=1$ and the percentage error in the Euler estimate of $x(1)$ from part (a). [3] (f) Find the time at which the amount of drug in the blood is greatest. [4] (g) Hence find the maximum amount of drug in the blood. [2] (h) Describe the long-term behavior of the system and the nature of the equilibrium at the origin. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\frac{dx}{dt}=-50$, $\frac{dy}{dt}=50$ at $t=0$, so $x(0.5)\approx75$, $y(0.5)\approx25$ [M1] [A1] At $(75,25)$: $\frac{dx}{dt}=-37.5$, $\frac{dy}{dt}=37.5-5=32.5$ [M1] $x(1)\approx56.25$, $y(1)\approx41.25$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $A=\begin{pmatrix}-0.5&0\\0.5&-0.2\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\det(A-\lambda I)=(-0.5-\lambda)(-0.2-\lambda)=0$ [M1] $\lambda=-0.5$ or $\lambda=-0.2$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\lambda=-0.5$: $0.5a+0.3b=0$ [M1] eigenvector $\begin{pmatrix}3\\-5\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\lambda=-0.2$: $-0.3a=0$, so $\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] (non-zero multiples accepted) [3 marks] (d) $\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\end{pmatrix}=c_1\begin{pmatrix}3\\-5\end{pmatrix}e^{-0.5t}+c_2\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\end{pmatrix}e^{-0.2t}$ [A1] $t=0$: $3c_1=100$ and $-5c_1+c_2=0$ [M1] $c_1=\frac{100}{3}$, $c_2=\frac{500}{3}$ [A1] $x=100e^{-0.5t}$, $y=\frac{500}{3}\left(e^{-0.2t}-e^{-0.5t}\right)$ [A1] [4 marks] (e) $x(1)=100e^{-0.5}=60.65$ [A1] $y(1)=\frac{500}{3}(e^{-0.2}-e^{-0.5})=35.4$ [A1] Percentage error $=\frac{60.65-56.25}{60.65}\times100=7.26\%$ [A1] [3 marks] (f) $\frac{dy}{dt}=0$ gives $0.5x=0.2y$, so $y=2.5x$ [M1] $\frac{500}{3}\left(e^{-0.2t}-e^{-0.5t}\right)=250e^{-0.5t}$ [M1] $e^{0.3t}-1=1.5$, so $e^{0.3t}=2.5$ [A1] $t=\frac{\ln2.5}{0.3}=3.05$ hours [A1] [4 marks] (g) $y_{\max}=2.5x(3.054)=250e^{-0.5(3.054)}$ [M1] $=54.3$ mg [A1] [2 marks] (h) Both eigenvalues negative, so $(0,0)$ is a stable node (all trajectories tend to the origin) [A1] Trajectories approach tangent to the eigenvector $\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\end{pmatrix}$ of the slower eigenvalue $-0.2$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Make each 'hence' part use the previous one: the eigenvector solution gives exact values for comparison with Euler, and the maximum occurs where $dy/dt=0$. Keep unrounded values in the final calculation.

subtopic: Separable model for the thickness of pond ice
statement: Ice forms on a pond. Its thickness $h$ cm at time $t$ days satisfies $\dfrac{dh}{dt}=\dfrac{0.6}{h}$, with $h=1$ when $t=0$. (a) Show that $h^2=1.2t+1$. [4] (b) Find the time taken for the ice to reach a thickness of $4$ cm. [2] (c) Find the thickness of the ice after $30$ days. [1] (d) State one limitation of this model for large values of $t$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\int h\,dh=\int0.6\,dt$ [M1] $\frac{h^2}{2}=0.6t+c$ [A1] $h(0)=1$ gives $c=\frac12$ [A1] $h^2=1.2t+1$ [AG] [4 marks] (b) $16=1.2t+1$ [M1] $t=12.5$ days [A1] [2 marks] (c) $h=\sqrt{37}=6.08$ cm [A1] [1 mark] (d) the model predicts that the thickness grows without bound, whereas in reality it is limited by air temperature and insulation by the ice [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Separate $h$ and $t$, integrate both sides, and use the initial condition to find the single constant. Comment on what the model predicts as $t\to\infty$.

subtopic: Separation of variables with a nonlinear right-hand side
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-2xy^2$, with $y=1$ when $x=0$. (a) Solve the differential equation, giving $y$ in terms of $x$. [4] (b) Write down the maximum value of $y$ and the equation of the horizontal asymptote of the solution curve. [2] (c) Find the positive value of $x$ for which $y=\dfrac15$. [1]
tips: After integrating, use the initial condition immediately to find the constant, then rearrange to make $y$ the subject. Check your answer by testing it at $x=0$.

subtopic: Predator-prey model: linearization, Euler's method and a conserved quantity
statement: This question investigates a predator-prey model. The numbers of rabbits $x$ and foxes $y$ (in hundreds) in a region at time $t$ months satisfy $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=0.8x-0.04xy$ and $\dfrac{dy}{dt}=0.02xy-0.6y$. (a) Find the two equilibrium points of the system. [3] (b) Starting from $x=40$, $y=15$ at $t=0$, use Euler's method with step size $h=0.1$ to estimate $x$ and $y$ at $t=0.2$. [4] (c) Near the equilibrium point with $x,y>0$, let $x=30+u$ and $y=20+w$, where $u$ and $w$ are small. Show that, ignoring the term in $uw$, $\dfrac{du}{dt}=-1.2w$ and $\dfrac{dw}{dt}=0.4u$. [4] (d) Write the linearized system in matrix form, find its eigenvalues, and hence find the period of small oscillations about the equilibrium, to 3 significant figures. [3] (e) Interpret the eigenvalues found in (d) in the context of the populations. [2] (f) Continue Euler's method with $h=0.1$ using a GDC spreadsheet to estimate $x$ and $y$ at $t=5$, to 3 significant figures. [2] (g) Show that $V(x,y)=0.02x-0.6\ln x+0.04y-0.8\ln y$ satisfies $\dfrac{dV}{dt}=0$ along any solution of the system. [4] (h) Find $V$ at $t=0$ and, using the Euler estimates, at $t=10$ ($100$ steps, where $x=48.7$ and $y=17.2$). Hence comment on the accuracy of Euler's method for this system. [3]
markscheme: (a) set $x(0.8-0.04y)=0$ and $y(0.02x-0.6)=0$ [M1] $(0,0)$ [A1] $(30,20)$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $x_{n+1}=x_n+0.1x_n(0.8-0.04y_n)$, $y_{n+1}=y_n+0.1y_n(0.02x_n-0.6)$ [M1] step 1: $x_1=40+0.1(8)=40.8$, $y_1=15+0.1(3)=15.3$ [A1] step 2: $\frac{dx}{dt}=40.8(0.8-0.612)=7.6704$ and $\frac{dy}{dt}=15.3(0.816-0.6)=3.3048$ so $x(0.2)\approx41.6$ [A1] $y(0.2)\approx15.6$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) $\frac{du}{dt}=\frac{dx}{dt}=(30+u)\left(0.8-0.04(20+w)\right)$ [M1] $=(30+u)(-0.04w)$ [A1] $=-1.2w-0.04uw\approx-1.2w$ [A1] $\frac{dw}{dt}=(20+w)\left(0.02(30+u)-0.6\right)=(20+w)(0.02u)=0.4u+0.02uw\approx0.4u$ [AG] [4 marks] (d) $\begin{pmatrix} u' \\ w' \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1.2 \\ 0.4 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} u \\ w \end{pmatrix}$, so $\lambda^2+0.48=0$ [M1] $\lambda=\pm0.693i$ [A1] period $=\frac{2\pi}{0.693}=9.07$ months [A1] [3 marks] (e) the eigenvalues are purely imaginary, so the equilibrium is a centre and the populations oscillate periodically [A1] with a period of about $9.07$ months, and with small oscillations that neither grow nor decay [A1] [2 marks] (f) $x(5)\approx17.5$ [A1] $y(5)\approx21.5$ [A1] [2 marks] (g) $\frac{dV}{dt}=\left(0.02-\frac{0.6}{x}\right)\frac{dx}{dt}+\left(0.04-\frac{0.8}{y}\right)\frac{dy}{dt}$ [M1] first term $=\left(0.02x-0.6\right)(0.8-0.04y)$ [A1] second term $=\left(0.04y-0.8\right)\left(0.02x-0.6\right)$ [A1] sum $=\left(0.02x-0.6\right)\left[(0.8-0.04y)+(0.04y-0.8)\right]=0$ [A1] [4 marks] (h) $V(40,15)=-2.98$ [A1] $V(48.7,17.2)=-2.94$ [A1] $V$ should stay constant, but the Euler estimate has drifted upward, so Euler's method is accumulating error (the numerical solution spirals outward) and is unreliable over long times with this step size [R1] [3 marks]
tips: In (c) factor the right-hand sides around the equilibrium so that one factor is the small quantity $u$ or $w$. In (g) apply the chain rule and look for cancellation between the two terms.

subtopic: Euler's method with a GDC
statement: Consider $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=y-x^{2}$ with $y=1$ when $x=0$. The exact solution is $y=x^{2}+2x+2-e^{x}$. (a) Use Euler's method with step size $h=0.2$ to estimate $y$ at $x=0.2$, $0.4$ and $1.0$ (five steps in total), to four significant figures. [4] (b) Find the exact value of $y$ at $x=1$ and the percentage error in the Euler estimate, to three significant figures. [3] (c) State whether the Euler estimate is an overestimate or an underestimate and suggest how to improve accuracy. [2]
tips: At each step, compute the gradient $f(x_n,y_n)$ and move a step $h$ along the tangent.

subtopic: Saddle point from a coupled linear system
statement: The deviations $x$ and $y$ of two interacting quantities from an equilibrium are modeled by $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=x+2y$, $\dfrac{dy}{dt}=2x-2y$. (a) Use your GDC to find the eigenvalues of the matrix of the system. [2] (b) Find an eigenvector for each eigenvalue. [2] (c) State the general solution and classify the equilibrium point at the origin. [2] (d) Given that $x=3$ and $y=4$ when $t=0$, find the particular solution. [3] (e) Describe the long-term behavior of the ratio $\dfrac yx$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $A=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & -2 \end{pmatrix}$, $\lambda^2+\lambda-6=0$ [M1] $\lambda=2$ and $\lambda=-3$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\lambda=2$: $-x+2y=0$ gives $\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\lambda=-3$: $4x+2y=0$ gives $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\mathbf x=c_1e^{2t}\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}+c_2e^{-3t}\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] the eigenvalues have opposite signs, so the origin is a saddle point [A1] [2 marks] (d) $2c_1+c_2=3$ and $c_1-2c_2=4$ [M1] $c_1=2$, $c_2=-1$ [A1] $x=4e^{2t}-e^{-3t}$, $y=2e^{2t}+2e^{-3t}$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) as $t\to\infty$ the $e^{2t}$ terms dominate, so $\frac yx\to\frac12$ (the solution approaches the line in the direction $\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$) [A1] [1 mark]
tips: With eigenvalues of opposite sign, only trajectories starting along the eigenvector for the negative eigenvalue approach the origin. In (d) set up two simultaneous equations from the initial condition.

subtopic: Euler's method compared with the exact solution
statement: Consider $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=x+y$ with $y=1$ when $x=0$. Use Euler's method with step size $h=0.1$, and keep every value exact (no rounding) at each step. (a) Use Euler's method to estimate $y$ at $x=0.1$, $0.2$, $0.3$ and $0.4$. [4] (b) Show that $y=2e^{x}-x-1$ satisfies the differential equation and the initial condition. [3] (c) Find the exact solution at $x=0.4$ correct to 4 decimal places, and the percentage error of the Euler estimate, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (d) Explain why Euler's method gives an underestimate here. [1]
markscheme: (a) $y_{n+1}=y_n+0.1(x_n+y_n)$ [M1]; $y(0.1)\approx1.1$ [A1]; $y(0.2)\approx1.22$ and $y(0.3)\approx1.362$ [A1]; $y(0.4)\approx1.5282$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $y(0)=2-0-1=1$ [A1]; $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=2e^{x}-1$ [M1]; $x+y=x+2e^{x}-x-1=2e^{x}-1$ [AG] [3 marks] (c) $2e^{0.4}-1.4=1.5836$ [A1]; $\dfrac{1.5836-1.5282}{1.5836}\times100=3.50\%$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) the solution is concave up ($y''=2e^{x}>0$), so each tangent line lies below the curve [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Each step uses the gradient at the start of the step: $y_{n+1}=y_n+h\,f(x_n, y_n)$.

subtopic: A harvested population
statement: A fish population $P$ (in thousands) satisfies $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=0.3P-60$ for $P\ge0$, where $t$ is in years and $60$ thousand fish are harvested per year. (a) Find the equilibrium population and state whether it is stable. [3] (b) It can be shown that $P=200+(P_0-200)e^{0.3t}$ for initial population $P_0$. Find the population after $5$ years when $P_0=250$, to three significant figures. [2] (c) When $P_0=150$, find the time at which the population reaches $0$, to three significant figures. [3]
tips: At an equilibrium the rate of change is zero; here the equilibrium is unstable because the growth term exceeds the harvest above it.

subtopic: Epidemic model: Euler's method and threshold
statement: In an outbreak, $S$ and $I$ denote the numbers of susceptible and infected people at time $t$ days. The model is $\dfrac{dS}{dt}=-0.002SI,\quad \dfrac{dI}{dt}=0.002SI-0.4I$. Initially $S=500$ and $I=10$. (a) Find the initial values of $\dfrac{dS}{dt}$ and $\dfrac{dI}{dt}$. [2] (b) Use Euler's method with step size $0.5$ to estimate $S$ and $I$ when $t=1$. Give your answers to 3 significant figures. [4] (c) Show that $I$ is increasing if and only if $S>200$, assuming $I>0$. [2] (d) Since $\dfrac{dS}{dt}<0$ whenever $S>0$ and $I>0$, explain why $I$ eventually decreases, and state the value of $S$ when $I$ is greatest. [2]
tips: Factor the rate equation for $I$ to read off its sign. In Euler's method with two coupled equations, update both variables using the values from the previous step.

subtopic: Exponential decay from a differential equation
statement: The number $N$ of bacteria in a culture satisfies $\dfrac{dN}{dt}=-0.1N$, where $t$ is in hours, and $N=500$ when $t=0$. (a) Solve the differential equation to find $N$ as a function of $t$. [3] (b) Find the exact time for the number of bacteria to halve. [2] (c) State the rate of change of $N$ at $t=0$ and interpret it. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\int\dfrac{dN}{N}=\int-0.1\,dt$ [M1]; $\ln N=-0.1t+C$ [A1]; $N=500e^{-0.1t}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $e^{-0.1t}=\dfrac12$ [M1]; $t=10\ln2$ hours [A1] [2 marks] (c) $-50$ bacteria per hour: the culture is initially decreasing by $50$ per hour [A1] [1 mark]
tips: The solution of $\frac{dN}{dt}=kN$ is $N=N_0e^{kt}$.

subtopic: Logistic growth: Euler's method and maximum growth rate
statement: A population $P$ of fish in a lake (measured in hundreds) is modelled by $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=0.2P\left(1-\dfrac{P}{500}\right)$, where $t$ is in years and $P(0)=100$. (a) Use Euler's method with a step size of $1$ year to estimate $P$ at $t=1$, $t=2$ and $t=3$. Give your answers to 3 significant figures. [4] (b) Find the values of $P$ for which the population is in equilibrium. [2] (c) Find the value of $P$ at which the population grows fastest, and the maximum rate of growth. [3]
tips: Euler's method: $P_{n+1}=P_n+h\,\frac{dP}{dt}$ evaluated at $P_n$. For part (c) the growth rate is itself a quadratic in $P$, so no differentiation of the model is needed.

subtopic: Terminal velocity of a parachutist from a separable equation
statement: The velocity $v$ m s$^{-1}$ of a parachutist falling after opening the parachute satisfies $\dfrac{dv}{dt}=9.8-0.2v$, where $t$ is in seconds and $v(0)=0$. (a) Find the terminal velocity. [1] (b) Solve the differential equation to show that $v=49\left(1-e^{-0.2t}\right)$. [4] (c) Find the time taken to reach a velocity of $40$ m s$^{-1}$. [2] (d) Find the distance fallen in the first $10$ seconds. [2]
tips: Terminal velocity is an equilibrium solution, found by setting the derivative to zero. Integrate $\frac{1}{a-bv}$ with a factor $-\frac1b$.

subtopic: Equilibrium solutions of a logistic model
statement: A population $P$ (in thousands) satisfies $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=0.2P\left(1-\dfrac{P}{500}\right)$ for $P\ge0$. (a) Find the equilibrium values of $P$. [2] (b) Determine the sign of $\dfrac{dP}{dt}$ for $0<P<500$ and for $P>500$, and hence state which equilibrium is stable. [3] (c) Find the value of $P$ at which the population grows fastest and the maximum rate. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=0$ [M1]; $P=0$ and $P=500$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) positive for $0<P<500$ [A1]; negative for $P>500$ [A1]; $P=500$ is stable (populations move toward it) [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=0.2P-0.0004P^{2}$ is a downward parabola with maximum at $P=250$ [M1][A1]; maximum rate $=0.2\times250\times0.5=25$ thousand per unit time [A1] [3 marks]
tips: At an equilibrium the rate of change is zero.

subtopic: Salt concentration in a stirred tank
statement: A tank holds $200$ L of pure water. A salt solution containing $0.5$ g of salt per liter flows into the tank at $10$ L per minute, and the well-stirred mixture flows out at $10$ L per minute, so the volume stays constant. Let $Q$ grams be the amount of salt in the tank at time $t$ minutes. (a) Show that $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=5-\dfrac{Q}{20}$. [2] (b) Solve the differential equation with $Q(0)=0$ to show that $Q=100\left(1-e^{-t/20}\right)$. [4] (c) Find the time at which the tank contains $90$ g of salt. [2]
markscheme: (a) salt in: $0.5\times10=5$ g per minute [A1] salt out: $10\times\frac{Q}{200}=\frac{Q}{20}$ g per minute, so $\frac{dQ}{dt}=5-\frac{Q}{20}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\int\frac{dQ}{5-\frac{Q}{20}}=\int dt$ [M1] $-20\ln\left(5-\frac{Q}{20}\right)=t+c$ [A1] $5-\frac{Q}{20}=Ae^{-t/20}$ [A1] $Q(0)=0$ gives $A=5$, so $Q=100\left(1-e^{-t/20}\right)$ [AG] [4 marks] (c) $90=100\left(1-e^{-t/20}\right)$ so $e^{-t/20}=0.1$ [M1] $t=20\ln10=46.1$ minutes [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Rate of change equals rate in minus rate out, with the outflow concentration equal to $Q$ divided by the volume. The salt amount cannot exceed $100$ g here, so the bracket $5-\frac{Q}{20}$ stays positive.

subtopic: Coupled linear systems and phase portraits
statement: Two adjoining rooms are heated and then the heating is switched off. Let $x$ and $y$ be the amounts, in $^\circ\text{C}$, by which the temperatures of room $1$ and room $2$ exceed the outdoor temperature, $t$ hours after the heating is switched off. The temperatures are modeled by $$\frac{dx}{dt}=-0.3x+0.1y,\qquad \frac{dy}{dt}=0.2x-0.4y.$$ Initially $x=12$ and $y=3$. (a) Write the system in the form $\dfrac{d\mathbf{X}}{dt}=A\mathbf{X}$, where $\mathbf{X}=\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\end{pmatrix}$. [1] (b) Find the eigenvalues of $A$ and a corresponding eigenvector for each. [5] (c) Hence find expressions for $x$ and $y$ in terms of $t$. [4] (d) Describe, in words, the phase portrait of this system, including the type of equilibrium at the origin and the direction from which trajectories approach the origin as $t\to\infty$. Interpret this in context. [3] (e) Use Euler's method with a step length of $0.5$ hours to estimate the values of $x$ and $y$ when $t=1$. Compare your answers with the values given by part (c). [4]
markscheme: (a) $A=\begin{pmatrix}-0.3&0.1\\0.2&-0.4\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\det(A-\lambda I)=(-0.3-\lambda)(-0.4-\lambda)-0.02=0$ [M1] $\lambda^2+0.7\lambda+0.1=0$ [A1] $\lambda=-0.2,\ -0.5$ [A1] $\lambda=-0.2$: $-0.1x+0.1y=0\Rightarrow\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\lambda=-0.5$: $0.2x+0.1y=0\Rightarrow\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [5 marks] (c) $\mathbf{X}=c_1e^{-0.2t}\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}+c_2e^{-0.5t}\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $c_1+c_2=12$, $c_1-2c_2=3$ [M1] $c_1=9,\ c_2=3$ [A1] $x=9e^{-0.2t}+3e^{-0.5t}$, $y=9e^{-0.2t}-6e^{-0.5t}$ [A1] [4 marks] (d) both eigenvalues are real and negative, so the origin is a stable node (sink); all trajectories move towards the origin [A1] as $t\to\infty$ the $e^{-0.5t}$ term decays faster, so trajectories approach the origin tangent to the line $y=x$ (except those on the line $y=-2x$) [R1] in context, both rooms cool towards the outdoor temperature and their temperature excesses become approximately equal [R1] [3 marks] (e) $x_1=12+0.5(-3.6+0.3)=10.35$, $y_1=3+0.5(2.4-1.2)=3.6$ [M1][A1] $x_2=8.98$ ($8.9775$), $y_2=3.92$ ($3.915$) [A1] exact values: $x(1)=9.19$, $y(1)=3.73$; Euler underestimates $x$ and overestimates $y$ because the step length is large relative to the rate of change [R1] [4 marks]
tips: In a coupled linear system the eigenvector of the eigenvalue closest to zero gives the long-term direction of approach. Lay out Euler's method as a table so each new value uses both previous x and y.

subtopic: Pollutant exchange between two lakes
statement: Pollutant moves between two connected lakes. Let $x$ and $y$ be the masses in kg of the pollutant in Lake 1 and Lake 2 at time $t$ years, where $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=-0.5x+0.2y$ and $\dfrac{dy}{dt}=0.5x-0.5y$. (a) Write the system in the form $\dfrac{d\mathbf x}{dt}=A\mathbf x$, stating the matrix $A$. [1] (b) Use your GDC to find the eigenvalues of $A$ to 3 significant figures. [2] (c) Find an eigenvector for each eigenvalue, with first component $1$. [2] (d) Initially $x=100$ and $y=0$. Find the particular solution. [3] (e) Find the time at which Lake 2 contains the greatest mass of pollutant, and that mass. [2]
markscheme: (a) $A=\begin{pmatrix} -0.5 & 0.2 \\ 0.5 & -0.5 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\lambda=-0.184$ [A1] $\lambda=-0.816$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\lambda=-0.184$: $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1.58 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\lambda=-0.816$: $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1.58 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $c_1+c_2=100$ and $1.58\left(c_1-c_2\right)=0$ [M1] $c_1=c_2=50$ [A1] $x=50e^{-0.184t}+50e^{-0.816t}$, $y=79.1\left(e^{-0.184t}-e^{-0.816t}\right)$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) maximum of $y$ on the GDC (or $\frac{dy}{dt}=0$) [M1] $t=2.36$ years, $y=39.7$ kg [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Eigenvectors can be scaled, so the first-component-1 form just keeps answers comparable. Both eigenvalues are negative, so the pollutant decays to zero in both lakes.
