subtopic: Eigenvalues of a coupled linear system
statement: Two quantities $x$ and $y$ vary with time $t$ according to $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=x + 2y$ and $\dfrac{dy}{dt}=3x$. (a) Write the system in the form $\dfrac{d\mathbf{X}}{dt}=A\mathbf{X}$, stating $A$. [1] (b) Find the eigenvalues of $A$. [3] (c) Find an eigenvector corresponding to $\lambda=-2$. [2] (d) Classify the equilibrium point at the origin and describe the long-term behavior of the solutions. [2]
markscheme: (a) $A=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\det(A-\lambda I)=0$ [M1]; $\lambda^2-(1)\lambda+(-6)=0$ [A1]; eigenvalues $\lambda=-2$ and $\lambda=3$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Solve $(A-(-2)I)\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$ [M1]: $\mathbf{v}=\begin{pmatrix} -2 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$ (or any multiple) [A1] [2 marks] (d) The origin is a saddle point (unstable) [A1] because the eigenvalues have opposite signs [R1] [2 marks]
tips: The characteristic polynomial of a $2\times2$ matrix is $\lambda^2-(\text{trace})\lambda+\det$; a negative determinant always gives real eigenvalues of opposite sign (a saddle).

subtopic: Separation of variables with initial condition
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=2xy$, where $y>0$. (a) Find the general solution, giving $y$ in terms of $x$. [3] (b) Given that $y=3$ when $x=0$, find the value of $y$ when $x=1$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\int\frac{1}{y}\,dy=\int 2x\,dx$ [M1] $\ln y=x^2+C$ [A1] $y=Ae^{x^2}$, where $A=e^{C}>0$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $3=Ae^{0}$, so $A=3$ [A1] $y=3e^{x^2}$, so when $x=1$, $y=3e$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Separate the variables first, then integrate each side; a single constant of integration is enough. Remember $y>0$ lets you write $\ln y$ without modulus signs.

subtopic: Salt concentration in a stirred tank
statement: A tank holds $200$ liters of water containing $10$ kg of salt. Brine containing $0.5$ kg of salt per liter flows in at $4$ liters per minute, and the well-mixed solution flows out at $4$ liters per minute. (a) Show that the mass $S$ kg of salt in the tank satisfies $\dfrac{dS}{dt}=2-0.02S$. [2] (b) Solve the differential equation with the initial condition to find $S$ as a function of $t$. [4] (c) Find the time at which the mass of salt first reaches 90 kg, and state the long-term mass of salt. [3]
markscheme: (a) Salt in: $0.5\times4=2$ kg per minute [A1]; salt out: concentration $\dfrac{S}{200}$ times $4$ $=0.02S$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Separate: $\int\dfrac{dS}{2-0.02S}=\int dt$ [M1]; $-\dfrac{1}{0.02}\ln|2-0.02S|=t+c$ [A1]; $S=100+Ae^{-0.02t}$ [A1]; $S(0)=10$ gives $A=-90$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) $100+(-90)e^{-0.02t}=90$ [M1]; $t=109.9$ minutes [A1]; long-term $100$ kg [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The volume stays constant, so the outflow concentration is $S/V$; the long-term value balances inflow and outflow of salt.

subtopic: Eigenvalues and node classification for a coupled system
statement: A system of two interacting quantities is modeled by $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=4x+y$, $\dfrac{dy}{dt}=2x+3y$. (a) Write the system in the form $\dfrac{d\mathbf x}{dt}=A\mathbf x$ and find the eigenvalues of $A$. [3] (b) Find an eigenvector corresponding to each eigenvalue. [2] (c) Write down the general solution of the system. [1] (d) Describe the behavior of solutions as $t\to\infty$ and classify the equilibrium point at the origin. [2]
markscheme: (a) $A=\begin{pmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\det(A-\lambda I)=(4-\lambda)(3-\lambda)-2=\lambda^2-7\lambda+10=0$ [M1] $\lambda=5$ and $\lambda=2$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\lambda=5$: $-x+y=0$ gives $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\lambda=2$: $2x+y=0$ gives $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\mathbf x=c_1e^{5t}\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}+c_2e^{2t}\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) both eigenvalues are positive, so solutions grow without bound (except at the origin) [R1] the origin is an unstable node [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Any non-zero multiple of an eigenvector is acceptable. Both eigenvalues real and positive means every trajectory moves away from the origin.

subtopic: Logistic growth of a population
statement: A population $P$ satisfies $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=0.1P\left(1-\dfrac{P}{800}\right)$ with $P(0)=100$ and $t$ in years. It can be shown that $P(t)=\dfrac{800}{1+7e^{-0.1t}}$. (a) Find $P(20)$, to three significant figures. [2] (b) Find the time when the population reaches $400$, to three significant figures. [3] (c) Find the rate of growth at the time found in part (b), and explain why it is the maximum rate. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{800}{1+7e^{-2}}$ [M1]; $411$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $1+7e^{-0.1t}=2$ [M1]; $e^{-0.1t}=\dfrac17$ [A1]; $t=19.5$ years [A1] [3 marks] (c) $0.1\times400\times\left(1-\dfrac{400}{800}\right)=20$ per year [A1][M1]; the growth rate $0.1P(1-P/800)$ is greatest at $P=400$, the midpoint of $0$ and $800$ [R1] [3 marks]
tips: The logistic growth rate is greatest when $P$ is half of the carrying capacity.

subtopic: Logistic growth with Euler's method and the exact solution
statement: A population $P$ of fish in a lake is modeled by $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=0.4P\left(1-\dfrac{P}{500}\right)$, where $t$ is in years and $P(0)=50$. (a) Find the equilibrium populations and state which is stable. [3] (b) Find the population at which the growth rate is greatest, and the value of that greatest growth rate. [3] (c) Use Euler's method with step size $h=1$ to estimate the population after $4$ units of time. [4] (d) The exact solution gives $P(4)=177.5$. Find the percentage error of the Euler estimate. [2]
tips: The growth rate is a parabola in $P$ with its maximum halfway between the two equilibria.

subtopic: Classifying the equilibrium of a coupled linear system
statement: Two systems of differential equations are $\dfrac{d\mathbf{x}}{dt}=A\mathbf{x}$ with $A=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ and $\dfrac{d\mathbf{x}}{dt}=B\mathbf{x}$ with $B=\begin{pmatrix} -2 & 1 \\ 1 & -2 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find the eigenvalues of $A$. [3] (b) Classify the equilibrium point at the origin for system $A$. [2] (c) Find the eigenvalues of $B$ and classify the equilibrium at the origin for system $B$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $(1-\lambda)(2-\lambda)-6=0$ [M1]; $\lambda^{2}-3\lambda-4=0$ [A1]; $\lambda=4,\ -1$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) eigenvalues of opposite sign [R1]; a saddle point (unstable) [A1] [2 marks] (c) $(\lambda+2)^{2}-1=0$ [M1]; $\lambda=-1,\ -3$ [A1]; both negative, so a stable node [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Opposite-sign real eigenvalues give a saddle; two negative real eigenvalues give a stable node.

subtopic: Equilibria and maximum growth rate of a deer herd
statement: The size $P$ of a deer herd on an island, $t$ years after it was introduced, is modeled by $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=0.2P\left(1-\dfrac{P}{500}\right)$. (a) Find the equilibrium populations. [2] (b) Find the rate of change of the population when $P=100$. [2] (c) Find the population at which the herd grows fastest, and the maximum growth rate. [2]
markscheme: (a) $0.2P\left(1-\frac{P}{500}\right)=0$ [M1] $P=0$ or $P=500$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $0.2(100)\left(1-0.2\right)$ [M1] $=16$ deer per year [A1] [2 marks] (c) the growth rate is a quadratic in $P$ with roots $0$ and $500$, so it is greatest at $P=250$ [M1] rate $=0.2(250)(0.5)=25$ deer per year [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Equilibria occur where the derivative is zero. The logistic growth rate is largest at half the carrying capacity.

subtopic: A separable equation with an implicit solution
statement: A curve passes through the point $(0,2)$ and satisfies $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{x+1}{y}$ with $y>0$. (a) Separate the variables and integrate to show that $y^{2}=(x+1)^{2}+C$. [3] (b) Find $C$ and then the value of $y$ when $x=2$, as an exact value. [3]
tips: Integrate $y\,dy$ and $(x+1)\,dx$ separately and combine the constants.

subtopic: Euler's method for a drug infusion model
statement: A drug is infused into a patient's bloodstream at a constant rate. The concentration $C$ in mg L$^{-1}$ at time $t$ hours satisfies $\dfrac{dC}{dt}=12-0.5C$, with $C=0$ when $t=0$. (a) Use Euler's method with step size $h=0.5$ to complete a table of values of $t$ and $C$ from $t=0$ to $t=2$, and state the estimate of $C(2)$. [4] (b) The exact solution is $C=24\left(1-e^{-0.5t}\right)$. Find the exact value of $C(2)$ to 4 significant figures and the percentage error in the Euler estimate, to 3 significant figures. [3] (c) State one way to reduce the error in the estimate. [1]
tips: On the GDC you can build the table in a spreadsheet by repeating the Euler formula. Percentage error is relative to the exact value.

subtopic: Exact time from an exponential model
statement: The mass $y$ grams of a mold colony grows at a rate proportional to its mass. (a) Solve the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dt}=0.2y$ with $y(0)=8$, giving $y$ in terms of $t$. [4] (b) Find the exact time at which $y=40$. [3]
tips: Leave the answer in terms of $\ln$ when asked for an exact value.

subtopic: Separable differential equation with an initial condition
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=3x^{2}y$, with $y=2$ when $x=0$. (a) Solve the differential equation, giving $y$ in terms of $x$. [4] (b) Find the exact value of $y$ when $x=1$. [1] (c) State the equation of the horizontal asymptote of the solution curve as $x\to-\infty$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{1}{y}\,dy=\int3x^{2}\,dx$ [M1]; $\ln y=x^{3}+c$ [A1]; $y=2$ at $x=0$ so $c=\ln2$ [A1]; $y=2e^{x^{3}}$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $2e$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $x^{3}\to-\infty$ so $e^{x^{3}}\to0$ [M1]; $y=0$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Separate the variables so each side involves one variable only, integrate, then use the initial condition.

subtopic: The effect of step size in Euler's method
statement: Consider $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=y$ with $y=1$ when $x=0$. The exact solution is $y=e^{x}$, so $y(1)=e=2.71828$. (a) Use Euler's method with step size $h=0.5$ to estimate $y(1)$. [2] (b) Use Euler's method with step size $h=0.25$ to estimate $y(1)$, to five significant figures. [2] (c) Find the error in each estimate (exact value minus estimate) and describe how halving the step size $h$ affects the error, to three significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) $y_1=1+0.5(1)=1.5$ [A1]; $y_2=1.5+0.5(1.5)=2.25$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) each step multiplies by $1.25$ [M1]; $1.25^{4}=2.4414$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) error with $h=0.5$: $0.468$ [A1]; error with $h=0.25$: $0.277$ [A1]; halving $h$ reduces the error by a factor of about $1.7$ (roughly in proportion to $h$ for small $h$) [R1] [3 marks]
tips: Euler's method is first-order accurate: the error is roughly proportional to the step size.

subtopic: Coupled system with complex eigenvalues: spiral
statement: Consider the coupled system $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=-x+2y,\quad \dfrac{dy}{dt}=-2x-y$. (a) Find the eigenvalues of the matrix of coefficients. [3] (b) Classify the equilibrium point at the origin. [2] (c) By considering the point $(1,0)$, determine whether trajectories rotate clockwise or anticlockwise about the origin. [2] (d) Use Euler's method with step size $h=0.1$, starting at $(x,y)=(1,0)$ when $t=0$, to estimate $(x,y)$ when $t=0.2$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\det\begin{pmatrix}-1-\lambda&2\\-2&-1-\lambda\end{pmatrix}=(\lambda+1)^2+4=0$ [M1] $\lambda+1=\pm2i$ [A1] $\lambda=-1\pm2i$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Stable spiral (spiral sink) [A1] The real part is negative so trajectories approach the origin, and the imaginary part gives rotation [R1] [2 marks] (c) At $(1,0)$: $\frac{dx}{dt}=-1$, $\frac{dy}{dt}=-2$ [M1] The point moves downwards below the $x$-axis, so the rotation is clockwise [A1] [2 marks] (d) Step 1: $x_1=1+0.1(-1)=0.9$, $y_1=0+0.1(-2)=-0.2$ [M1] [A1] Step 2: rates $-0.9+2(-0.2)=-1.3$ and $-2(0.9)-(-0.2)=-1.6$, giving $(0.77,\,-0.36)$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Complex eigenvalues $a\pm bi$ give spirals if $a\neq0$: stable when $a<0$ and unstable when $a>0$. Evaluate the vector field at a single test point to find the direction of rotation.

subtopic: Newton's law of cooling
statement: A cup of tea is cooling in a room with constant temperature $20^\circ$C. Its temperature $T^\circ$C after $t$ minutes satisfies $\dfrac{dT}{dt}=-k(T-20)$, where $k>0$. Initially $T=90$, and after 10 minutes $T=60$. (a) Solve the differential equation to show that $T=20+70e^{-kt}$. [4] (b) Find the value of $k$. [2] (c) Find the time taken for the tea to cool to $30^\circ$C, giving your answer to 3 significant figures. [2] (d) Find the rate at which the temperature is changing when $T=50$. [2]
tips: Use the unrounded value of $k$ in later parts, or store it on your calculator. A negative rate of change means the temperature is falling.

subtopic: Linear first-order equation with integrating factor e^x
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}+y=x$, where $y=1$ when $x=0$. (a) Write down an integrating factor for this differential equation. [1] (b) Hence find $y$ in terms of $x$. [6]
markscheme: (a) Integrating factor $=e^{\int 1\,dx}=e^{x}$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(ye^{x}\right)=xe^{x}$ [M1] $ye^{x}=\int xe^{x}\,dx$. By parts: $\int xe^{x}\,dx=xe^{x}-e^{x}$ [M1][A1] $ye^{x}=xe^{x}-e^{x}+C$ [A1] Using $y=1$ when $x=0$: $1=-1+C$, so $C=2$ [M1] $y=x-1+2e^{-x}$ [A1] [6 marks]
tips: Once multiplied by the integrating factor, the left side is the derivative of $ye^{x}$. Integration by parts on $xe^{x}$ is expected, so choose $u=x$ and $dv=e^{x}dx$.

subtopic: First-order linear equation with an integrating factor
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}+\dfrac{2}{x}y=x^2$, for $x>0$. (a) Find the integrating factor for this differential equation, simplifying your answer. [2] (b) Hence find the solution of the differential equation given that $y=2$ when $x=1$. Give your answer in the form $y=f(x)$. [4]
markscheme: (a) Integrating factor $=e^{\int \frac{2}{x}dx}=e^{2\ln x}$ [M1] $=x^2$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x^2y\right)=x^2\cdot x^2=x^4$ [M1] $x^2y=\dfrac{x^5}{5}+C$ [A1] Substituting $x=1,\ y=2$: $2=\dfrac15+C$, so $C=\dfrac95$ [M1] $y=\dfrac{x^5+9}{5x^2}$ [A1] Accept $y=\dfrac{x^3}{5}+\dfrac{9}{5x^2}$. [4 marks]
tips: Because $x>0$ you may write $e^{2\ln x}=x^2$ with no modulus signs. Multiply the whole equation by the integrating factor so that the left side becomes a single product derivative.

subtopic: Population with constant harvesting
statement: A fish farm models its stock of fish by $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=0.05P-30$, where $P$ is the number of fish and $t$ is the time in years since the start of harvesting. Initially there are $500$ fish. (a) Show that $P=600-100e^{0.05t}$. [4] (b) Find the number of fish after $10$ years. Give your answer to the nearest whole number. [1] (c) Show that the stock of fish is exhausted after $20\ln 6$ years, and evaluate this time to three significant figures. [3]
tips: Factor the right-hand side as $0.05(P-600)$ to see the equilibrium value $600$. Since the initial population is below $600$, the stock decreases and eventually reaches zero.

subtopic: Euler method with GDC and convexity
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\sqrt{x+y}$, where $y=2$ when $x=1$. (a) Use Euler's method with step length $0.1$ to find an estimate for $y(1.5)$. Give your answer to three significant figures. [4] (b) Show that $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\dfrac{1+\frac{dy}{dx}}{2\sqrt{x+y}}$. [2] (c) Hence state, with a reason, whether your estimate in part (a) is greater than or less than the true value of $y(1.5)$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $y_{n+1}=y_n+0.1\sqrt{x_n+y_n}$ [M1] $$\begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline x & y \\ \hline 1.0 & 2 \\ \hline 1.1 & 2.1732 \\ \hline 1.2 & 2.3541 \\ \hline 1.3 & 2.5426 \\ \hline 1.4 & 2.7387 \\ \hline 1.5 & 2.9421 \\ \hline \end{array}$$ [A1][A1] $y(1.5)\approx 2.94$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=(x+y)^{1/2}$ [M1] $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\dfrac12(x+y)^{-1/2}\left(1+\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)=\dfrac{1+\frac{dy}{dx}}{2\sqrt{x+y}}$ [A1] [AG] [2 marks] (c) $\dfrac{dy}{dx}>0$, so $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}>0$ and the solution is concave up [R1] The tangent lines lie below the curve, so the estimate is less than the true value [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Use the table or sequence feature of your GDC to avoid arithmetic slips, and do not round intermediate values. Convexity of the solution tells you the direction of the Euler error without solving the equation.

subtopic: Newton warming law with two data points
statement: A bottle of water at $4^\circ$C is placed in a room kept at $24^\circ$C. The temperature $T$ of the water, in degrees Celsius, $t$ minutes after the bottle is placed in the room satisfies $\dfrac{dT}{dt}=-k(T-24)$, where $k>0$. (a) Show that $T=24-20e^{-kt}$. [3] After 10 minutes the temperature of the water is $10^\circ$C. (b) Find the value of $k$. [2] (c) Find the time taken for the water to reach $20^\circ$C. Give your answer in minutes to three significant figures. [2]
tips: Keep $k$ unrounded in your calculator memory for part (c). The constant $24$ is the long-term temperature, so the solution tends to $24$ from below.

subtopic: Separable differential equation with an initial condition
statement: Given that $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac xy$ and $y=3$ when $x=4$, with $y>0$: (a) Find $y$ in terms of $x$. [5] (b) State the domain of the solution. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\int y\,dy=\int x\,dx$ [M1] $\dfrac{y^2}2=\dfrac{x^2}2+c$ [A1] $9=16+k$ so $k=-7$ in $y^2=x^2+k$ [M1][A1] $y=\sqrt{x^2-7}$ [A1] [5 marks] (b) $x>\sqrt7$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Separate the variables, integrate both sides, then use the initial condition to find the constant.

subtopic: Homogeneous equations by substitution
statement: Consider the differential equation $$x^2\frac{dy}{dx}=y^2+3xy+x^2,\quad x>0,$$ with $y=0$ when $x=1$. (a) Use the substitution $y=vx$ to show that $x\dfrac{dv}{dx}=(v+1)^2$. [3] (b) Hence find $y$ in terms of $x$. [6] (c) Write down the equation of the vertical asymptote of the graph of the solution. [1] (d) Find the exact value of $y$ when $x=\sqrt{e}$. [2] (e) Find the value of $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ when $x=\sqrt{e}$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=v+x\dfrac{dv}{dx}$ [A1] Dividing the equation by $x^2$: $v+x\dfrac{dv}{dx}=v^2+3v+1$ [M1] $x\dfrac{dv}{dx}=v^2+2v+1=(v+1)^2$ [A1][AG] [3 marks] (b) Separating variables: $\displaystyle\int\frac{1}{(v+1)^2}\,dv=\int\frac{1}{x}\,dx$ [M1] $-\dfrac{1}{v+1}$ [A1] $=\ln x+C$ [A1] When $x=1$, $v=0$: $-1=0+C$ [M1] $C=-1$ [A1] $v+1=\dfrac{1}{1-\ln x}$, so $v=\dfrac{\ln x}{1-\ln x}$ and $y=\dfrac{x\ln x}{1-\ln x}$ [A1] [6 marks] (c) $x=e$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) $\ln\sqrt{e}=\dfrac{1}{2}$ [M1] $y=\dfrac{\sqrt{e}\cdot\frac{1}{2}}{\frac{1}{2}}=\sqrt{e}$ [A1] [2 marks] (e) Substituting $x=y=\sqrt{e}$ into the differential equation: $e\dfrac{dy}{dx}=e+3e+e$ [M1] $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=5$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Once you have the solution, the original differential equation is often the quickest way to find a gradient: substitute $x$ and $y$ directly rather than differentiating your answer. Keep the constant of integration on the $\ln x$ side and find it before rearranging.

subtopic: Linear equation with a tan x coefficient and a maximum value
statement: The function $y(x)$ satisfies $\dfrac{dy}{dx}+y\tan x=\sec x$, for $0\le x<\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, where $y=2$ when $x=0$. (a) Show that an integrating factor for this differential equation is $\sec x$. [2] (b) Hence show that $y=\sin x+2\cos x$. [4] (c) Find the exact maximum value of $y$ on the given domain. [2]
markscheme: (a) Integrating factor $=e^{\int\tan x\,dx}=e^{\ln|\sec x|}$ [M1] $=\sec x$ since $\sec x>0$ on the domain [A1] [AG] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(y\sec x\right)=\sec^2 x$ [M1] $y\sec x=\tan x+C$ [A1] Using $y=2$ when $x=0$: $C=2$ [M1] $y=\sin x+2\cos x$ [A1] [AG] [4 marks] (c) $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\cos x-2\sin x=0$ gives $\tan x=\dfrac12$, which lies in the domain [M1] Then $\sin x=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt5}$ and $\cos x=\dfrac{2}{\sqrt5}$, so $y_{\max}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt5}+\dfrac{4}{\sqrt5}=\sqrt5$ [A1] Alternatively write $y=\sqrt5\sin(x+\alpha)$. [2 marks]
tips: Multiplying the whole equation by $\sec x$ gives $\sec x\,y'+\sec x\tan x\,y$, which is the derivative of $y\sec x$. In (c), check that the stationary point lies inside the stated domain.

subtopic: Second-order chemical reaction rate
statement: In a chemical reaction the concentration $x$ mol/L of a product after $t$ minutes satisfies $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=0.015(4-x)^2$, where $x=0$ when $t=0$ and $x<4$. (a) Show that $x=4-\dfrac{1}{0.25+0.015t}$. [4] (b) Find the concentration after $20$ minutes. [1] (c) Find the time taken for the concentration to reach $3.5$ mol/L. Give your answer to three significant figures. [2] (d) Write down the limiting value of $x$ as $t\to\infty$. [1]
tips: Integrating $(4-x)^{-2}$ gives $(4-x)^{-1}$ with a positive sign, as $\frac{d}{dx}(4-x)^{-1}=(4-x)^{-2}$. Check your answer against the initial condition and the limiting behavior.

subtopic: Homogeneous equation whose solution is a circle
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{y^2-x^2}{2xy}$, where $x>0$, $y>0$ and $y=1$ when $x=1$. (a) Use the substitution $y=vx$ to show that $x\dfrac{dv}{dx}=-\dfrac{1+v^2}{2v}$. [3] (b) Hence show that $x^2+y^2=2x$. [4] (c) Hence find $y$ in terms of $x$, and state the set of values of $x$ for which the solution is defined (the endpoints are excluded). [2]
markscheme: (a) $y=vx$ gives $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=v+x\dfrac{dv}{dx}$ [M1] $v+x\dfrac{dv}{dx}=\dfrac{v^2x^2-x^2}{2vx^2}=\dfrac{v^2-1}{2v}$ [M1] $x\dfrac{dv}{dx}=\dfrac{v^2-1}{2v}-v=\dfrac{v^2-1-2v^2}{2v}=-\dfrac{1+v^2}{2v}$ [A1] [AG] [3 marks] (b) $\int\dfrac{2v}{1+v^2}\,dv=-\int\dfrac1x\,dx$ [M1] $\ln(1+v^2)=-\ln x+C$ [A1] Using $v=1$ when $x=1$: $C=\ln 2$ [M1] $x(1+v^2)=2$, so $x+\dfrac{y^2}{x}=2$, hence $x^2+y^2=2x$ [A1] [AG] [4 marks] (c) $y=\sqrt{2x-x^2}$ (positive root since $y>0$) [A1] Defined for the open interval $0<x<2$, since $x>0$ is given and $y>0$ excludes $x=2$ where $y=0$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: After substituting $y=vx$ every $x$ cancels from the right-hand side, which is the test of a homogeneous equation. Separate the variables $v$ and $x$ before integrating. Complete the square if you want to recognize the final curve.

subtopic: Separable differential equation with a trigonometric factor
statement: A function $y(x)$ satisfies $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=y\cos x$ with $y(0)=2$. (a) Find $y$ in terms of $x$. [4] (b) Find the maximum value of $y$ and the least positive value of $x$ at which it occurs. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\int\dfrac{dy}y=\int\cos x\,dx$ [M1] $\ln y=\sin x+c$ [A1] $y=A\mathrm e^{\sin x}$ [A1] $y(0)=2$ gives $A=2$, $y=2\mathrm e^{\sin x}$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) maximum when $\sin x=1$ [M1] $y=2\mathrm e$ at $x=\dfrac\pi2$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Separate to $\dfrac1y\,dy=\cos x\,dx$ and integrate; exponentiate and absorb the constant into $A$.

subtopic: Separable equation modelling a draining tank
statement: Water drains from a tank. The depth of water $h$ centimeters at time $t$ minutes satisfies $\dfrac{dh}{dt}=-0.2\sqrt{h}$, where $h=25$ when $t=0$. (a) Solve the differential equation to show that $h=(5-0.1t)^2$. [4] (b) Find the time at which the tank is empty. [1] (c) Find the rate of change of the depth when $t=20$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\int h^{-\frac12}\,dh=\int-0.2\,dt$ [M1] $2\sqrt h=-0.2t+c$ [A1] When $t=0$, $h=25$: $c=10$ [M1] $\sqrt h=5-0.1t$, so $h=(5-0.1t)^2$ [A1][AG] [4 marks] (b) $h=0$ when $5-0.1t=0$, so $t=50$ minutes [A1] [1 mark] (c) When $t=20$, $\sqrt h=3$, so $\dfrac{dh}{dt}=-0.2\times3=-0.6$ cm per minute [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Write the square root as a power of $h$ before integrating. In part (c) you do not need to differentiate the solution; use the differential equation directly.

subtopic: Growth rate proportional to the square root of the population
statement: The size $N$ of a colony at time $t$ hours satisfies $\dfrac{dN}{dt}=k\sqrt N$, where $k>0$. At $t=0$, $N=400$, and at $t=4$, $N=900$. (a) Show that $\sqrt N=20+\dfrac{kt}2$. [3] (b) Find $k$, and the time when the colony reaches $2500$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\int N^{-1/2}\,dN=\int k\,dt$ [M1] $2\sqrt N=kt+c$ [A1] $c=40$ so $\sqrt N=20+\dfrac{kt}2$ [AG] [A1] [3 marks] (b) $30=20+2k$ so $k=5$ [A1] $\sqrt N=20+2.5t$ [M1] $50=20+2.5t$ so $t=12$ hours [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Use the power rule to integrate $N^{-1/2}$. The two data points fix the two constants.

subtopic: Mixing problem with brine entering a tank
statement: A tank contains $100$ liters of pure water. Brine containing $0.2$ kg of salt per liter flows into the tank at $5$ liters per minute. The solution is kept well mixed and flows out of the tank at $5$ liters per minute. Let $S$ kg be the mass of salt in the tank after $t$ minutes. (a) Show that $\dfrac{dS}{dt}=1-\dfrac{S}{20}$. [2] (b) Solve this differential equation to find $S$ in terms of $t$. [4] (c) Find the exact time at which the concentration of salt in the tank first reaches $0.1$ kg per liter. [2]
markscheme: (a) Rate of salt in $=0.2\times 5=1$ kg per minute [A1] Rate of salt out $=\dfrac{S}{100}\times 5=\dfrac{S}{20}$ kg per minute [A1] $\dfrac{dS}{dt}=1-\dfrac{S}{20}$ [AG] [2 marks] (b) $\int\dfrac{1}{20-S}\,dS=\int\dfrac{1}{20}\,dt$ [M1] $-\ln(20-S)=\dfrac{t}{20}+C$ [A1] Using $S=0$ when $t=0$: $C=-\ln 20$ [M1] $S=20\left(1-e^{-t/20}\right)$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) Concentration $0.1$ means $S=10$ [M1] $e^{-t/20}=\dfrac12$, so $t=20\ln 2$ minutes [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The volume stays at $100$ liters because inflow and outflow rates are equal, so the concentration is simply $S/100$. Note that $S<20$ throughout, so $20-S>0$ and no modulus is needed.

subtopic: Separable equation with a quotient involving x squared plus one
statement: Solve $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{xy}{x^2+1}$ given that $y=3$ when $x=0$. Find $y$ in terms of $x$. [5]
markscheme: $\int\dfrac{dy}y=\int\dfrac{x}{x^2+1}\,dx$ [M1] $\ln|y|=\dfrac12\ln(x^2+1)+c$ [A1] $y=A\sqrt{x^2+1}$ [A1] $A=3$ [M1] $y=3\sqrt{x^2+1}$, valid for all real $x$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: The $x$ integral is of the form $f'(x)/f(x)$. Take exponentials and combine the constant into one multiplier.

subtopic: The logistic differential equation
statement: This question investigates the logistic model $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=0.2P\left(1-\dfrac P{1000}\right)$ for a population $P$ with $P(0)=100$. (a) Find the values of $P$ for which the population is in equilibrium. [1] (b) Show that $\dfrac{1}{P\left(1-\frac P{1000}\right)}=\dfrac1P+\dfrac1{1000-P}$. [2] (c) Hence solve the differential equation to show that $P=\dfrac{1000}{1+9\mathrm e^{-0.2t}}$. [6] (d) Find the time at which the population first reaches $500$. [2] (e) Show that the rate of growth $\dfrac{dP}{dt}$ is greatest when $P=500$ and find this greatest rate. [3] (f) State the limit of $P$ as $t\to\infty$ and interpret it. [1]
markscheme: (a) $P=0$ and $P=1000$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\dfrac{1000}{P(1000-P)}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{(1000-P)+P}{P(1000-P)}=\dfrac1P+\dfrac1{1000-P}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\int\left(\dfrac1P+\dfrac1{1000-P}\right)dP=\int0.2\,dt$ [M1] $\ln P-\ln(1000-P)=0.2t+c$ [A1] $\dfrac P{1000-P}=A\mathrm e^{0.2t}$ [A1] $P(0)=100$ gives $A=\dfrac19$ [A1] solve for $P$: $P=\dfrac{1000}{1+9\mathrm e^{-0.2t}}$ [M1][A1] [6 marks] (d) $1+9\mathrm e^{-0.2t}=2$ [M1] $t=5\ln9=10.99$ [A1] [2 marks] (e) $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=0.2P-\dfrac{0.2P^2}{1000}$, a downward parabola in $P$ [M1] maximum at $P=500$ [A1] rate $=0.2\times500\times0.5=50$ [A1] [3 marks] (f) $P\to1000$, the carrying capacity of the environment [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Separate the variables and use partial fractions. The logistic curve is S-shaped with its steepest growth at half the carrying capacity.

subtopic: Salt in a tank: constant and increasing volume
statement: A tank initially contains $200$ litres of pure water. Brine containing $0.3$ kg of salt per litre flows into the tank at $4$ litres per minute. The mixture is kept uniform by stirring. Let $x$ kg be the mass of salt in the tank after $t$ minutes. (a) The mixture leaves the tank at $4$ litres per minute, so the volume stays at $200$ litres. Show that $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=1.2-\dfrac x{50}$, and solve this equation to find $x$ in terms of $t$. [5] (b) Find the time taken for the mass of salt to reach $30$ kg, giving your answer to three significant figures. [2] (c) Now suppose that the mixture leaves at $3$ litres per minute instead, so the volume after $t$ minutes is $(200+t)$ litres. Show that $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=1.2-\dfrac{3x}{200+t}$, and solve this equation to find $x$ in terms of $t$. [6] (d) For the model in part (c), find the mass of salt and the concentration of salt in kg per litre when $t=100$, to three significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) rate in $=0.3\times4=1.2$ and rate out $=\dfrac x{200}\times4=\dfrac x{50}$ [M1][A1] separate variables: $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{dx}{1.2-x/50}=\int dt$ [M1] $-50\ln\left|1.2-\dfrac x{50}\right|=t+C$ and $x(0)=0$ gives the solution $x=60\left(1-e^{-t/50}\right)$ [A1][A1] [5 marks] (b) $60\left(1-e^{-t/50}\right)=30$ so $e^{-t/50}=\dfrac12$ [M1] $t=50\ln2=34.7$ minutes [A1] [2 marks] (c) rate out $=\dfrac{x}{200+t}\times3$ [A1] integrating factor $e^{\int\frac3{200+t}dt}=(200+t)^3$ [M1][A1] $\dfrac d{dt}\left[(200+t)^3x\right]=1.2(200+t)^3$ [M1] $(200+t)^3x=0.3(200+t)^4+C$ [A1] $x(0)=0$ gives $C=-0.3\times200^4$, so $x=0.3(200+t)-\dfrac{0.3\times200^4}{(200+t)^3}$ [A1] [6 marks] (d) $x(100)=90-\dfrac{4.8\times10^8}{300^3}=72.2$ kg [A1] concentration $=\dfrac{72.2}{300}=0.241$ kg per litre [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Mass of salt changes at the rate of (salt in) minus (salt out), and the concentration is the mass divided by the current volume. In part (c) the coefficient of $x$ depends on $t$, so use an integrating factor.

subtopic: Slope field described in words, isoclines and a particular solution
statement: Consider a slope field for the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=x-2y$. At each point $(x,y)$ the short line segment has gradient equal to $x-2y$. (a) Find the gradient of the line segment at (i) the point $(2,1)$; (ii) the point $(0,3)$. [2] (b) Describe the set of points at which the line segments are horizontal. [2] (c) Show that $y=\dfrac{x}{2}-\dfrac14$ is a solution of the differential equation. [3] (d) Find the solution of the differential equation whose graph passes through the origin. Give your answer in the form $y=f(x)$. [5] (e) Write down the equation of the straight line to which the solution curve in part (d) gets closer and closer as $x\to\infty$. [1]
markscheme: (a) (i) $2-2(1)=0$ [A1] (ii) $0-2(3)=-6$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Horizontal segments occur where $x-2y=0$ [M1] that is, at all points on the straight line $y=\dfrac{x}{2}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) If $y=\dfrac{x}{2}-\dfrac14$ then $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac12$ [A1] $x-2y=x-x+\dfrac12=\dfrac12$ [M1] so the differential equation is satisfied for all $x$ [R1] [3 marks] (d) Write as $\dfrac{dy}{dx}+2y=x$; integrating factor $e^{\int2\,dx}=e^{2x}$ [A1] $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(e^{2x}y\right)=xe^{2x}$ [M1] Integration by parts: $\int xe^{2x}dx=\dfrac{x}{2}e^{2x}-\int\dfrac12e^{2x}dx$ [M1] $e^{2x}y=\dfrac{x}{2}e^{2x}-\dfrac14e^{2x}+C$ [A1] Using $y=0$ when $x=0$: $C=\dfrac14$, so $y=\dfrac{x}{2}-\dfrac14+\dfrac14e^{-2x}$ [A1] [5 marks] (e) $y=\dfrac{x}{2}-\dfrac14$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Every segment is found by substituting coordinates into the right-hand side; no solving is needed. To test a proposed solution, differentiate it and substitute both $y$ and $y'$ into the equation.

subtopic: Population with constant harvesting
statement: A fish population $P$ satisfies $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=0.1P-50$, where $t$ is in years, with $P(0)=400$. (a) Find the equilibrium population and explain why it is unstable. [2] (b) Solve the differential equation to show that $P=500-100\mathrm e^{0.1t}$. [4] (c) Find the time at which the population dies out. [2]
markscheme: (a) $0.1P-50=0$ gives $P=500$ [A1] below $500$ the rate is negative and above it is positive, so the population moves away from $500$ [R1] [2 marks] (b) $\int\dfrac{dP}{0.1P-50}=\int dt$ [M1] $10\ln|0.1P-50|=t+c$ [A1] $0.1P-50=A\mathrm e^{0.1t}$ with $A=-10$ [A1] $P=500-100\mathrm e^{0.1t}$ [A1] [AG] [4 marks] (c) $500=100\mathrm e^{0.1t}$ [M1] $t=10\ln5=16.1$ years [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Separate the variables and integrate with a logarithm. Constant harvesting makes the equilibrium unstable.

subtopic: Euler's method recursion and error analysis
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=3-y$, where $y=0$ when $x=0$. (a) Euler's method with step size $h$ is used to approximate the solution. Show that $y_{n+1}=(1-h)y_n+3h$. [2] (b) Use Euler's method with $h=0.5$ to estimate the value of $y$ when $x=2$. [3] (c) Solve the differential equation, and hence find the value of $y$ when $x=2$, giving your answer to four significant figures. [4] (d) Find the percentage error in your estimate from part (b). [2] (e) State one change that would reduce the error in the estimate. [1]
tips: Writing the Euler recursion in simplified form saves effort when there are several steps. Here the DE is simple enough to check your numerical answer against the exact solution.

subtopic: A dissolving sugar cube with a surface-area rate law
statement: A sugar cube dissolves so that its volume $V$ cm$^3$ at time $t$ minutes satisfies $\dfrac{dV}{dt}=-0.5V^{2/3}$. Initially $V=27$. (a) Show that $V^{1/3}=3-\dfrac t6$. [4] (b) Find the time at which the volume has reduced to one eighth of its initial value. [2] (c) Find the time at which the cube has completely dissolved. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\int V^{-2/3}\,dV=-\int0.5\,dt$ [M1] $3V^{1/3}=-0.5t+c$ [A1] $c=3\times3=9$ [M1] $V^{1/3}=3-\dfrac t6$ [AG] [A1] [4 marks] (b) $V=\dfrac{27}8$ so $V^{1/3}=\dfrac32$ [M1] $t=6\left(3-\dfrac32\right)=9$ minutes [A1] [2 marks] (c) $V=0$ when $t=18$ minutes [A1] [1 mark]
tips: The right-hand side is a power of $V$, so separate and integrate with a power rule. Note that the cube dissolves in a finite time.

subtopic: A curve whose normal always passes through the origin
statement: A curve passes through the point $(3,4)$. At every point $(x,y)$ on the curve, the normal to the curve passes through the origin. (a) Show that the curve satisfies $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-\dfrac xy$. [2] (b) Solve the differential equation to find the equation of the curve, and describe the curve. [4]
markscheme: (a) the normal has the gradient of the line from the origin to $(x,y)$, which is $\dfrac yx$ [M1] the tangent gradient is the negative reciprocal, $-\dfrac xy$ [AG] [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\int y\,dy=-\int x\,dx$ [M1] $y^2=-x^2+c$ [A1] $c=25$ so $x^2+y^2=25$ [A1] a circle with centre at the origin and radius $5$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: The normal and tangent are perpendicular. Use the fact that the line from the origin to the point has gradient $y/x$.

subtopic: Euler's method with a convexity argument
statement: A curve satisfies the differential equation $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=\ln(x+y)$, where $y=1$ when $x=1$. (a) Use Euler's method with a step length of $h=0.25$ to find an approximation for the value of $y$ when $x=2$. Give each intermediate value of $y$ to four significant figures. [4] (b) Show that $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2y}{\mathrm{d}x^2}=\dfrac{1+\ln(x+y)}{x+y}$. [2] (c) Given that $x+y>1$ for $x\ge 1$ on the solution curve, explain why your answer to part (a) is an underestimate of the true value of $y$ at $x=2$. [2] (d) State how the accuracy of the approximation could be improved. [1]
markscheme: (a) $y_{n+1}=y_n+0.25\ln(x_n+y_n)$ [M1] $y(1.25)\approx 1+0.25\ln 2=1.173$ [A1] $y(1.5)\approx 1.173+0.25\ln(2.423)=1.395$ [A1] $y(1.75)\approx 1.660$, $y(2)\approx 1.967$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2y}{\mathrm{d}x^2}=\dfrac{1}{x+y}\left(1+\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}\right)$ [M1] $=\dfrac{1+\ln(x+y)}{x+y}$ [AG] [A1] [2 marks] (c) If $x+y>1$ then $\ln(x+y)>0$ and $x+y>0$, so $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2y}{\mathrm{d}x^2}>0$ [R1] The solution curve is concave up, so each tangent line segment used by Euler's method lies below the curve and the estimate is too small [R1] [2 marks] (d) Use a smaller step length $h$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Euler's method follows tangent lines, so it underestimates on a concave-up curve and overestimates on a concave-down curve. Carry full calculator precision between steps.

subtopic: Euler method compared with an exact solution
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=2y-x$, where $y=1$ when $x=0$. (a) Use Euler's method with step length $0.1$ to find an estimate for $y(0.5)$. Give your answer to four significant figures. [4] (b) Show that the exact solution is $y=\dfrac{x}{2}+\dfrac14+\dfrac34e^{2x}$. [5] (c) Find the percentage error of your estimate in part (a), to three significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) $y_{n+1}=y_n+0.1(2y_n-x_n)$ [M1] $$\begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline x & y \\ \hline 0 & 1 \\ \hline 0.1 & 1.2 \\ \hline 0.2 & 1.43 \\ \hline 0.3 & 1.696 \\ \hline 0.4 & 2.0052 \\ \hline 0.5 & 2.36624 \\ \hline \end{array}$$ [A1][A1] $y(0.5)\approx 2.366$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $\dfrac{dy}{dx}-2y=-x$, integrating factor $e^{-2x}$ [M1] $ye^{-2x}=-\int xe^{-2x}\,dx$. By parts [M1] $\int xe^{-2x}\,dx=-\dfrac{x}{2}e^{-2x}-\dfrac14e^{-2x}$ [A1] $ye^{-2x}=\dfrac{x}{2}e^{-2x}+\dfrac14e^{-2x}+C$, so $y=\dfrac x2+\dfrac14+Ce^{2x}$ [A1] Using $y=1$ when $x=0$: $1=\dfrac14+C$, so $C=\dfrac34$ [M1] $y=\dfrac x2+\dfrac14+\dfrac34e^{2x}$ [AG] [5 marks] (c) Exact $y(0.5)=\dfrac14+\dfrac14+\dfrac34e=2.5387$ [M1] Percentage error $=\dfrac{2.5387-2.36624}{2.5387}\times100=6.79\%$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Enter the recursion in your GDC as a sequence in $(x_n,y_n)$ so that you can read off each row. The Euler estimate is below the exact value here because the solution is concave up.

subtopic: Newton's law of cooling as a separable equation
statement: The temperature $T$ degrees Celsius of a cup of coffee $t$ minutes after it is poured satisfies $\dfrac{dT}{dt}=-k(T-20)$, where $k>0$ is a constant and the room temperature is $20^\circ$C. When the coffee is poured, its temperature is $90^\circ$C. (a) By solving the differential equation, show that $T=20+70e^{-kt}$. [4] (b) After $10$ minutes the temperature of the coffee is $60^\circ$C. Find the value of $k$. [2] (c) Find the time taken for the coffee to cool to $30^\circ$C, giving your answer in minutes to one decimal place. [2]
tips: Because $T-20>0$ throughout, you may write $\ln(T-20)$ without modulus signs. Use the unrounded value of $k$ (store it in your GDC) in part (c).

subtopic: Separable equation needing integration by parts
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=xe^{x-y}$, where $y=0$ when $x=0$. (a) Solve the differential equation, giving $y$ in terms of $x$. [7] (b) Find the value of $y$ when $x=1$. [1] (c) Show that the solution in part (a) is defined for all real $x$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=xe^{x}e^{-y}$, so $\int e^{y}\,\mathrm{d}y=\int xe^{x}\,\mathrm{d}x$ [M1] $e^{y}=\ldots$ on the left [A1] Integration by parts: $\int xe^{x}\,\mathrm{d}x=xe^{x}-e^{x}+C$ [M1] [A1] $e^{y}=xe^{x}-e^{x}+C$ Using $y=0$, $x=0$: $1=-1+C$ [M1] $C=2$ [A1] $y=\ln\left((x-1)e^{x}+2\right)$ [A1] [7 marks] (b) $y=\ln 2$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) Let $f(x)=(x-1)e^{x}+2$, so $f'(x)=xe^{x}$ [M1] $f'(x)<0$ for $x<0$ and $f'(x)>0$ for $x>0$, so the minimum value is $f(0)=1>0$, hence $f(x)>0$ for all $x$ and $\ln f(x)$ is defined [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Separate so that every $y$ is on one side with $\mathrm{d}y$ and every $x$ is on the other with $\mathrm{d}x$. Remember to include the constant of integration before applying the initial condition.

subtopic: Separable equation whose solution has a restricted domain
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=e^{x+y}$, with $y=0$ when $x=0$. (a) Show that $-e^{-y}=e^x+C$ for a constant $C$, and find $C$. [3] (b) Find $y$ in terms of $x$, and state the largest set of values of $x$ for which the solution is defined. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=e^xe^y$ so $\int e^{-y}\,dy=\int e^x\,dx$ [M1] $-e^{-y}=e^x+C$ [AG] [A1] $-1=1+C$ so $C=-2$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $e^{-y}=2-e^x$ [A1] $y=-\ln\left(2-e^x\right)$ [A1] $2-e^x>0$ so $x<\ln2$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Write $e^{x+y}=e^xe^y$ and separate the variables. The logarithm in the final answer needs a positive argument.

subtopic: Separable equation with an exponential in y
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=x\,e^{-y}$, where $y=0$ when $x=0$. (a) Solve the differential equation, giving $y$ in terms of $x$. [5] (b) Find the exact value of $y$ when $x=2$. [1]
markscheme: (a) Separating variables: $\int e^{y}\,dy=\int x\,dx$ [M1] $e^{y}=\dfrac{x^2}{2}+C$ [A1][A1] Using $y=0$ when $x=0$: $1=C$ [M1] $y=\ln\left(1+\dfrac{x^2}{2}\right)$ [A1] [5 marks] (b) $y=\ln 3$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Move all the $y$ terms to one side before integrating. Apply the initial condition before taking the logarithm, as it keeps the arithmetic simple.

subtopic: Separable equation with a trigonometric squared term
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=2y\sin^2 x$, where $y>0$ and $y=2$ when $x=0$. (a) Find $y$ in terms of $x$. [6] (b) Explain why $y$ is a non-decreasing function of $x$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\int\dfrac{1}{y}\,dy=\int 2\sin^2 x\,dx$ [M1] Using $2\sin^2 x=1-\cos 2x$ [M1] $\ln y=x-\dfrac{1}{2}\sin 2x+C$ [A1][A1] Using $y=2$ when $x=0$: $C=\ln 2$ [M1] $y=2e^{\,x-\frac{1}{2}\sin 2x}$ [A1] [6 marks] (b) $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=2y\sin^2 x\ge 0$ because $y>0$ and $\sin^2 x\ge 0$ [R1] [1 mark]
tips: A squared trigonometric function must be rewritten with a double-angle identity before it can be integrated. Do not forget the factor $\frac12$ when integrating $\cos 2x$.

subtopic: Isoclines and a solution curve that is also an isocline
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=y-x$. (a) An isocline is the set of all points $(x,y)$ at which solution curves have the same gradient $m$. Describe the isocline for gradient $m$ in terms of its equation, and describe what the isoclines look like as $m$ varies. [2] (b) Show that the line $y=x+1$ is a solution curve of the differential equation, and that it is also an isocline. [3] (c) Find the solution of the differential equation for which $y=3$ when $x=0$. [5]
markscheme: (a) Isocline: $y-x=m$, that is $y=x+m$ [M1] These are parallel straight lines with gradient $1$ and $y$-intercept $m$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) For $y=x+1$: $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=1$ [M1] and $y-x=1$, so the equation is satisfied [A1] The isocline for $m=1$ is $y-x=1$, which is the line $y=x+1$ itself, and the gradient of this line is $1=m$, so the solution curve through it follows the isocline [R1] [3 marks] (c) Write as $\dfrac{dy}{dx}-y=-x$ with integrating factor $e^{-x}$ [M1] $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(ye^{-x}\right)=-xe^{-x}$ [A1] $ye^{-x}=xe^{-x}+e^{-x}+C$ [M1][A1] Using $y=3$ when $x=0$: $3=1+C$, so $C=2$ and $y=x+1+2e^{x}$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: An isocline is a curve of constant slope, found by setting $\frac{dy}{dx}=m$ in the equation. In (c) the coefficient of $y$ is $-1$, so the integrating factor is $e^{-x}$.

subtopic: Integrating factor with a variable coefficient
statement: Solve $x\dfrac{dy}{dx}-2y=x^3$ for $x>0$, given that $y=0$ when $x=1$. [6]
markscheme: divide by $x$: $\dfrac{dy}{dx}-\dfrac2xy=x^2$ [M1] integrating factor $\mathrm e^{-2\ln x}=x^{-2}$ [M1][A1] $\dfrac d{dx}\left(\dfrac y{x^2}\right)=1$ [A1] $\dfrac y{x^2}=x+c$ with $c=-1$ [A1] $y=x^3-x^2$ [A1] [6 marks]
tips: Put the equation in the standard form $y'+P(x)y=Q(x)$ before finding the integrating factor.

subtopic: Euler's method for a non-separable equation
statement: A function satisfies $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=x^2+y^2$ with $y(0)=1$. (a) Use Euler's method with $h=0.1$ to estimate $y(0.2)$. [4] (b) Explain why the actual value of $y(0.2)$ is likely to be larger than your estimate. [1]
markscheme: (a) $y_1=1+0.1(0+1)=1.100$ [A1] $y_2=y_1+0.1\left(0.1^2+y_1^2\right)$ [M1] $=1.1+0.1(0.01+1.21)$ [A1] $=1.222$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $y''$ is positive ($y$ is convex), so the tangent line lies below the curve and Euler's method underestimates [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Euler's method follows tangent lines; for a convex solution the tangent lines are below the curve.

subtopic: Homogeneous equation using y = vx
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{x^2+y^2}{xy}$, for $x>0,\ y>0$, where $y=2$ when $x=1$. (a) Use the substitution $y=vx$ to show that $x\dfrac{dv}{dx}=\dfrac{1}{v}$. [3] (b) Hence solve the differential equation, giving $y$ in terms of $x$. [5]
markscheme: (a) $y=vx$ so $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=v+x\dfrac{dv}{dx}$ [A1] $v+x\dfrac{dv}{dx}=\dfrac{x^2+v^2x^2}{x\cdot vx}=\dfrac{1+v^2}{v}$ [M1] $x\dfrac{dv}{dx}=\dfrac{1+v^2}{v}-v=\dfrac{1}{v}$ [A1][AG] [3 marks] (b) $\int v\,dv=\int\dfrac{1}{x}\,dx$ [M1] $\dfrac{v^2}{2}=\ln x+C$ [A1] When $x=1$, $v=2$: $2=C$ [M1] $v^2=2\ln x+4$ [A1] $y=x\sqrt{2\ln x+4}$ (positive root since $y>0$) [A1] [5 marks]
tips: After the substitution the new equation must be separable; if $v$ and $x$ do not separate, recheck the algebra. Substitute back $v=y/x$ at the end and choose the sign of the root from the initial condition.

subtopic: Homogeneous differential equation using y = vx
statement: Consider $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{x+y}x$ for $x>0$, with $y=0$ when $x=1$. (a) Use the substitution $y=vx$ to show that $x\dfrac{dv}{dx}=1$. [3] (b) Hence solve the differential equation. [4]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=v+x\dfrac{dv}{dx}$ [M1] $v+x\dfrac{dv}{dx}=1+v$ [A1] $x\dfrac{dv}{dx}=1$ [A1] [AG] [3 marks] (b) $\int dv=\int\dfrac1x\,dx$ [M1] $v=\ln x+c$ [A1] $y=x\ln x+cx$ [A1] $y(1)=0$ gives $c=0$, $y=x\ln x$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: For a homogeneous equation substitute $y=vx$, use the product rule for $dy/dx$, and separate $v$ and $x$.

subtopic: Integrating factor with a trigonometric coefficient
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}+y\tan x=\sin 2x$, for $0\le x<\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, where $y=0$ when $x=0$. (a) Show that an integrating factor for this differential equation is $\sec x$. [3] (b) Hence show that $y=2\cos x-2\cos^2x$. [4] (c) Find the maximum value of $y$ for $0\le x<\dfrac{\pi}{2}$. [3]
markscheme: (a) Integrating factor $=e^{\int\tan x\,dx}$ [M1] $\int\tan x\,dx=-\ln(\cos x)=\ln(\sec x)$ [A1] so the integrating factor is $\sec x$ [A1][AG] [3 marks] (b) $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(y\sec x\right)=\sin2x\sec x$ [M1] $=\dfrac{2\sin x\cos x}{\cos x}=2\sin x$ [A1] $y\sec x=-2\cos x+C$ [A1] When $x=0$, $y=0$: $0=-2+C$, so $C=2$, giving $y=2\cos x-2\cos^2x$ [A1][AG] [4 marks] (c) $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-2\sin x+4\sin x\cos x$ [A1] Setting $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$: $2\sin x(2\cos x-1)=0$, so $\cos x=\dfrac12$ (since $\sin x=0$ gives the minimum $y=0$) [M1] $y=2\cdot\dfrac12-2\cdot\dfrac14=\dfrac12$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Use $\sin 2x=2\sin x\cos x$ so that the $\cos x$ cancels after multiplying by $\sec x$. For the maximum, you can also treat $y$ as a quadratic in $\cos x$.

subtopic: Isoclines of a slope field and a solution curve
statement: The differential equation $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=y-x^2$ defines a slope field: at each point $(x,y)$ the short line segment has gradient $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}$. (a) Show that the points where the segments have gradient $m$ lie on the curve $y=x^2+m$, and write down the equation of the curve along which all segments are horizontal. [2] (b) The solution curve passes through the point $(1,1)$. Show that this point is a local maximum of the solution curve. [3] (c) Show that $y=x^2+2x+2$ is a solution of the differential equation. [2] (d) By considering the gradient of the slope field at points on the curve $y=x^2+2x+2$, explain why this solution curve is increasing for $x>-1$ and decreasing for $x<-1$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $y-x^2=m$ gives $y=x^2+m$ [A1] Horizontal segments: $m=0$, so $y=x^2$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) At $(1,1)$: $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=1-1=0$, so the point is stationary [A1] $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2y}{\mathrm{d}x^2}=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}-2x$ [M1] $=0-2=-2<0$, so it is a local maximum [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=2x+2$ [M1] $y-x^2=2x+2$, which equals $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}$ [AG] [A1] [2 marks] (d) On this curve the gradient of the slope field is $y-x^2=2x+2$ [M1] This is positive for $x>-1$ and negative for $x<-1$, so the curve increases then decreases (minimum at $x=-1$) [R1] [2 marks]
tips: The isocline for gradient $m$ is found by setting $\mathrm{d}y/\mathrm{d}x=m$. To classify a stationary point on a solution curve, differentiate the equation implicitly to get $\mathrm{d}^2y/\mathrm{d}x^2$.

subtopic: Bernoulli-type equation solved by the substitution u = 1/y
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}+\dfrac{y}{x}=xy^2$, where $x>0$, $y>0$ and $y=\dfrac12$ when $x=1$. (a) Use the substitution $u=\dfrac1y$ to show that $\dfrac{du}{dx}-\dfrac{u}{x}=-x$. [3] (b) Find an integrating factor for this equation and hence show that $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac ux\right)=-1$, and find the general solution for $u$. [4] (c) Find $y$ in terms of $x$. [3] (d) State the set of values of $x$ for which this solution is positive. [1]
markscheme: (a) $y=\dfrac1u$ gives $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-\dfrac{1}{u^2}\dfrac{du}{dx}$ [M1] $-\dfrac{1}{u^2}\dfrac{du}{dx}+\dfrac{1}{xu}=\dfrac{x}{u^2}$ [M1] Multiplying by $-u^2$: $\dfrac{du}{dx}-\dfrac ux=-x$ [A1] [AG] [3 marks] (b) Integrating factor $=e^{-\int\frac1x\,dx}$ [M1] $=e^{-\ln x}=\dfrac1x$ [A1] $\dfrac1x\dfrac{du}{dx}-\dfrac{u}{x^2}=-1$, so $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac ux\right)=-1$ [A1] $\dfrac ux=-x+C$, so $u=Cx-x^2$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) $y=\dfrac12$ when $x=1$ gives $u=2$, so $2=C-1$ and $C=3$ [M1] $u=3x-x^2$ [A1] $y=\dfrac{1}{3x-x^2}$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $y>0$ when $0<x<3$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: When a substitution is given, differentiate it carefully using the chain rule: $\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{1}{u^2}\frac{du}{dx}$. Remember to check where the final formula is defined and positive.

subtopic: First-order linear equation using an integrating factor
statement: Solve $\dfrac{dy}{dx}+2y=\mathrm e^{-x}$ given that $y=3$ when $x=0$. [6]
markscheme: integrating factor $\mathrm e^{\int2\,dx}=\mathrm e^{2x}$ [M1][A1] $\dfrac d{dx}\left(y\mathrm e^{2x}\right)=\mathrm e^{x}$ [M1] $y\mathrm e^{2x}=\mathrm e^x+c$ [A1] $y=\mathrm e^{-x}+c\mathrm e^{-2x}$ and $3=1+c$ [M1] $y=\mathrm e^{-x}+2\mathrm e^{-2x}$ [A1] [6 marks]
tips: Multiply by $\mathrm e^{\int P\,dx}$ so the left side becomes a single derivative.

subtopic: Recognizing a product derivative with a 1/x coefficient
statement: Consider the differential equation $x\dfrac{dy}{dx}+y=\ln x$, where $x>0$ and $y=0$ when $x=1$. (a) Show that the differential equation can be written as $\dfrac{d}{dx}(xy)=\ln x$. [2] (b) Hence find $y$ in terms of $x$. [5]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{d}{dx}(xy)=x\dfrac{dy}{dx}+y$ by the product rule [M1] $=\ln x$ [A1] [AG] [2 marks] (b) $xy=\int\ln x\,dx$ [M1] $=x\ln x-x+C$ [A1][A1] Using $y=0$ when $x=1$: $0=-1+C$, so $C=1$ [M1] $y=\ln x-1+\dfrac1x$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: Look for the product rule hiding on the left side before reaching for an integrating factor. You may need to recall that $\int \ln x\,dx=x\ln x-x+C$.

subtopic: Drug elimination with a second dose
statement: The amount $A$ mg of a drug in a patient's body satisfies $\dfrac{dA}{dt}=-kA$, where $t$ is the time in hours and $k>0$. The drug has a half-life of $6$ hours. A first dose gives $A=200$ at $t=0$. (a) Show that $k=\dfrac{\ln 2}{6}$. [3] A second dose of $150$ mg is taken at $t=4$, which increases the amount in the body by exactly $150$ mg. (b) Find the amount of the drug in the body immediately before the second dose is taken. [2] (c) Find the amount of the drug in the body at $t=10$. [2] (d) Find the time at which the amount of the drug first falls to $50$ mg. Give your answer to three significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) $A=200e^{-kt}$ [M1] Half-life: $100=200e^{-6k}$ [M1] $e^{-6k}=\dfrac12$ so $-6k=-\ln 2$ and $k=\dfrac{\ln 2}{6}$ [A1] [AG] [3 marks] (b) $A(4)=200e^{-4k}$ [M1] $=126$ mg [A1] [2 marks] (c) Amount just after second dose $=126+150=276$ [M1] After a further $6$ hours (one half-life): $\dfrac{276}{2}=138$ mg [A1] [2 marks] (d) $276e^{-ks}=50$ where $s=t-4$ [M1] $s=\dfrac{\ln 5.52}{k}=14.8$ [M1] $t=18.8$ hours [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Restart the exponential decay from the new amount after the second dose, measuring time from $t=4$. Use the unrounded value of $A(4)$ in later parts to avoid a rounding error in your final answer.

subtopic: Euler's method for dy/dx = x + y
statement: Consider $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=x+y$ with $y=1$ when $x=0$. Euler's method with step size $h=0.1$ is used. (a) Use Euler's method $y_{n+1}=y_n+hf(x_n,y_n)$ to find $y_1$ and $y_2$. [3] (b) Continue to estimate $y$ at $x=0.5$. [2] (c) The exact solution is $y=2\mathrm e^x-x-1$. Find the percentage error in your estimate at $x=0.5$. [3]
tips: Each Euler step moves along the tangent: $y_{n+1}=y_n+h\,f(x_n,y_n)$. Smaller steps reduce the error.

subtopic: Newton's law of cooling
statement: A cup of coffee at $90^\circ$C is placed in a room at $20^\circ$C. Its temperature $T$ satisfies $\dfrac{dT}{dt}=-k(T-20)$, where $t$ is in minutes. After $10$ minutes its temperature is $50^\circ$C. (a) Show that $T=20+70\mathrm e^{-kt}$. [4] (b) Find the value of $k$. [2] (c) Find the time for the coffee to cool to $30^\circ$C. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\int\dfrac{dT}{T-20}=-\int k\,dt$ [M1] $\ln(T-20)=-kt+c$ [A1] $T-20=A\mathrm e^{-kt}$ [A1] $T(0)=90$ gives $A=70$ [A1] [AG] [4 marks] (b) $30=70\mathrm e^{-10k}$ [M1] $k=0.0847$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $10=70\mathrm e^{-kt}$ [M1] $t=23.0$ minutes [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The rate is proportional to the difference from room temperature, so separate $T-20$ from $t$.

subtopic: Falling body with a resistance proportional to speed
statement: A body falls from rest, and its speed $v$ m/s after $t$ seconds satisfies $\dfrac{dv}{dt}=9.8-0.4v$. (a) Find the terminal speed. [2] (b) Solve the differential equation to show that $v=24.5\left(1-e^{-0.4t}\right)$. [4] (c) Find the time taken to reach $90\%$ of the terminal speed. [2]
tips: The equation is separable. Factor the right-hand side as a multiple of $24.5-v$ to integrate easily.

subtopic: Orthogonal trajectories of a family of parabolas
statement: A family of curves is given by $y=cx^2$, where $c$ is a constant. (a) Show that every curve in the family satisfies $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{2y}x$. [2] (b) Write down the differential equation satisfied by the curves that cross every member of the family at right angles, and solve it. [5] (c) Find the member of the perpendicular family that passes through $(2,1)$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=2cx$ [M1] and $c=\dfrac y{x^2}$, so $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{2y}x$ [AG] [A1] [2 marks] (b) perpendicular gradient $-\dfrac x{2y}$ so $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-\dfrac x{2y}$ [M1][A1] $\int2y\,dy=-\int x\,dx$ [M1] $y^2=-\dfrac{x^2}2+k$ [A1] $x^2+2y^2=K$ [A1] [5 marks] (c) $4+2=6$, so $x^2+2y^2=6$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Two curves are perpendicular where their gradients multiply to $-1$. The perpendicular family satisfies the negative reciprocal gradient equation.

subtopic: Homogeneous equation leading to an implicit solution
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{x+y}{x-y}$, for $x>0$, where $y=0$ when $x=1$. (a) Use the substitution $y=vx$ to show that $x\dfrac{dv}{dx}=\dfrac{1+v^2}{1-v}$. [3] (b) Hence show that the solution of the differential equation satisfies $\arctan\left(\dfrac{y}{x}\right)=\dfrac12\ln\left(x^2+y^2\right)$. [6]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=v+x\dfrac{dv}{dx}$ [A1] $v+x\dfrac{dv}{dx}=\dfrac{x+vx}{x-vx}=\dfrac{1+v}{1-v}$ [M1] $x\dfrac{dv}{dx}=\dfrac{1+v}{1-v}-v=\dfrac{1+v^2}{1-v}$ [A1][AG] [3 marks] (b) $\int\dfrac{1-v}{1+v^2}\,dv=\int\dfrac1x\,dx$ [M1] $\int\left(\dfrac{1}{1+v^2}-\dfrac{v}{1+v^2}\right)dv$ [A1] $\arctan v-\dfrac12\ln\left(1+v^2\right)=\ln x+C$ [A1] When $x=1$, $v=0$: $C=0$ [M1] $\arctan\dfrac{y}{x}=\ln x+\dfrac12\ln\left(1+\dfrac{y^2}{x^2}\right)$ [A1] $=\dfrac12\ln x^2+\dfrac12\ln\dfrac{x^2+y^2}{x^2}=\dfrac12\ln\left(x^2+y^2\right)$ [A1][AG] [6 marks]
tips: Split the numerator before integrating so you can recognize an arctangent and a logarithm. When converting back, write $\ln x$ as $\tfrac12\ln x^2$ so the logarithms combine.

subtopic: Homogeneous equation involving tan(y/x)
statement: Let $y$ be the solution of $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=\dfrac{y}{x}+\tan\left(\dfrac{y}{x}\right)$, for $0<x\le 1$, where $y=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ when $x=1$. (a) Use the substitution $y=vx$ to show that $x\dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}=\tan v$. [2] (b) Solve the differential equation to find $y$ in terms of $x$. [5] (c) Find the exact value of $y$ when $x=\dfrac{1}{2}$. [1] (d) Show that the solution curve has a vertical tangent at the point $\left(1,\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $y=vx$ gives $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=v+x\dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}$ [M1] $v+x\dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}=v+\tan v$, so $x\dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}=\tan v$ [AG] [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\int\cot v\,\mathrm{d}v=\int\dfrac{1}{x}\,\mathrm{d}x$ [M1] $\ln(\sin v)=\ln x+C$ [A1] [A1] Using $x=1$, $v=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$: $\ln 1=\ln 1+C$, so $C=0$ [M1] $\sin v=x$, so $y=x\arcsin x$ [A1] [5 marks] (c) $y=\dfrac{1}{2}\arcsin\dfrac{1}{2}=\dfrac{\pi}{12}$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=v+\tan v$ where $v=\arcsin x$ [M1] As $x\to 1$, $v\to\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and $\tan v\to\infty$, so the gradient is unbounded: vertical tangent [R1] [2 marks]
tips: After substituting $y=vx$ the equation must separate in $v$ and $x$; do not forget the product rule when finding $\mathrm{d}y/\mathrm{d}x$. Replace $v$ by $y/x$ at the end.

subtopic: Heating towards a steady state
statement: The temperature $T$ $^\circ$C of a pan on a hot plate at time $t$ minutes satisfies $\dfrac{dT}{dt}=-0.1(T-20)+2$, where $20^\circ$C is the room temperature. Initially $T=25$. (a) Show that the differential equation can be written $\dfrac{dT}{dt}=-0.1(T-40)$, and state the steady-state temperature. [2] (b) Solve the differential equation to show that $T=40-15e^{-0.1t}$. [3] (c) Find the time taken for the pan to reach $35^\circ$C, to three significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) $-0.1T+2+2=-0.1T+4=-0.1(T-40)$ [M1] steady-state temperature $40^\circ$C [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\int\dfrac{dT}{T-40}=-0.1\int dt$ [M1] $T-40=Ae^{-0.1t}$ [A1] $A=-15$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $15e^{-0.1t}=5$ [M1] $t=10\ln3=11.0$ minutes [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Combine the constants so that the equation has the form $dT/dt=-k(T-T_s)$ with steady state $T_s$.

subtopic: Logistic model of a fish population
statement: The number of fish, $P$, in a lake $t$ years after stocking is modeled by $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}P}{\mathrm{d}t}=0.15P\left(1-\dfrac{P}{1200}\right)$. (a) Find the rate of growth of the population when $P=300$. [2] (b) Show that the rate of growth is greatest when $P=600$, and find this greatest rate. [3] The solution of the differential equation can be written as $P=\dfrac{1200}{1+Ae^{-0.15t}}$, where $A$ is a constant. The initial population is 200 fish. (c) Find the value of $A$. [2] (d) Find the time taken for the population to reach 900 fish. [3] (e) Describe what happens to the population in the long term. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}P}{\mathrm{d}t}=0.15\times 300\times\left(1-\dfrac{300}{1200}\right)$ [M1] $=33.75$ fish per year [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}P}{\mathrm{d}t}=0.15P-\dfrac{0.15}{1200}P^2$, a quadratic in $P$ with negative leading coefficient [R1] Maximum at $P=\dfrac{0.15}{2\times 0.15/1200}=600$ [AG] [M1] Greatest rate $=0.15\times 600\times 0.5=45$ fish per year [A1] [3 marks] (c) $200=\dfrac{1200}{1+A}$ [M1] $A=5$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $900=\dfrac{1200}{1+5e^{-0.15t}}$ [M1] $e^{-0.15t}=\dfrac{1}{15}$ [A1] $t=\dfrac{\ln 15}{0.15}=18.1$ years [A1] [3 marks] (e) $P\to 1200$ as $t\to\infty$: the population approaches the carrying capacity of 1200 fish [A1] [1 mark]
tips: In a logistic model the growth rate is largest at half the carrying capacity. Treat $\mathrm{d}P/\mathrm{d}t$ as a quadratic in $P$ when maximizing it.

subtopic: Exponential decay of a radioactive isotope
statement: The mass, $m$ mg, of a radioactive isotope at time $t$ days satisfies $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}m}{\mathrm{d}t}=-km$, where $k>0$. Initially the mass is 120 mg and the half-life of the isotope is 8 days. (a) Solve the differential equation to show that $m=120e^{-kt}$. [3] (b) Find the exact value of $k$. [2] (c) Find the time taken for the mass to fall to 15 percent of its initial value. [2] (d) Find the rate at which the mass is decreasing when $t=10$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\int\dfrac{1}{m}\,\mathrm{d}m=\int -k\,\mathrm{d}t$ [M1] $\ln m=-kt+C$ [A1] Using $m=120$ when $t=0$: $m=120e^{-kt}$ [AG] [A1] [3 marks] (b) $60=120e^{-8k}$ [M1] $k=\dfrac{\ln 2}{8}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $18=120e^{-kt}$, so $e^{-kt}=0.15$ [M1] $t=\dfrac{8\ln(1/0.15)}{\ln 2}=21.9$ days [A1] [2 marks] (d) $m(10)=120e^{-10k}=50.45\ldots$ [M1] $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}m}{\mathrm{d}t}=-km=-\dfrac{\ln 2}{8}\times 50.45\ldots=-4.37$, so the mass decreases at $4.37$ mg per day [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Half-life gives $k$ directly through $\tfrac12=e^{-kT}$. Keep $k$ exact until the final calculation to avoid rounding errors.

subtopic: Logistic growth with partial fractions
statement: The size $P$ of a population of birds on an island, $t$ years after observation begins, satisfies the logistic differential equation $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=0.1P\left(1-\dfrac{P}{200}\right)$, where $P=50$ when $t=0$. (a) Express $\dfrac{1}{P(200-P)}$ in partial fractions. [2] (b) Hence show that $P=\dfrac{200}{1+3e^{-t/10}}$. [5] (c) Find the exact time at which the population reaches $100$. [2] (d) Find the maximum rate of growth of the population, and the population size when this occurs. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{1}{P(200-P)}=\dfrac{A}{P}+\dfrac{B}{200-P}$ so $1=A(200-P)+BP$ [M1] $\dfrac{1}{P(200-P)}=\dfrac{1}{200}\left(\dfrac1P+\dfrac{1}{200-P}\right)$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=\dfrac{P(200-P)}{2000}$ so $\int\dfrac{1}{P(200-P)}\,dP=\int\dfrac{1}{2000}\,dt$ [M1] $\ln P-\ln(200-P)=\dfrac{t}{10}+C$ [A1] Using $P=50$ when $t=0$: $C=\ln\dfrac13$ [M1] $\dfrac{P}{200-P}=\dfrac13e^{t/10}$ [A1] $3P=e^{t/10}(200-P)$, so $P\left(3+e^{t/10}\right)=200e^{t/10}$ [M1] $P=\dfrac{200}{1+3e^{-t/10}}$ [AG] [5 marks] (c) $100=\dfrac{200}{1+3e^{-t/10}}$ so $3e^{-t/10}=1$ [M1] $t=10\ln 3$ years [A1] [2 marks] (d) $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=\dfrac{P(200-P)}{2000}$ is a quadratic in $P$ with maximum at $P=100$ [M1] Maximum rate $=\dfrac{100\times100}{2000}=5$ birds per year [A1] Population size $100$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: In part (d) work with $dP/dt$ as a function of $P$, not of $t$. The growth rate of a logistic model is greatest when the population is half of the limiting value.

subtopic: Separable equation with inverse tangent solutions
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{1+y^2}{1+x^2}$, with $y=1$ when $x=0$. (a) Show that $\arctan y=\arctan x+C$ for some constant $C$, and find $C$. [4] (b) Show that $y=\dfrac{1+x}{1-x}$, for $-1<x<1$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\int\dfrac{dy}{1+y^2}=\int\dfrac{dx}{1+x^2}$ [M1][A1] $\arctan y=\arctan x+C$ [AG] $\arctan1=\arctan0+C$ [M1] $C=\dfrac\pi4$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $y=\tan\left(\arctan x+\dfrac\pi4\right)$ [M1] $=\dfrac{x+1}{1-x\times1}$ using the compound angle formula for tangent [M1][A1] [3 marks]
tips: Both sides integrate to inverse tangents. Take the tangent of both sides and apply the compound angle formula.

subtopic: Separable equation with an inverse tangent
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=2x\left(1+y^2\right)$, where $y=1$ when $x=0$. (a) Solve the differential equation, giving $y$ in terms of $x$. [5] (b) The graph of the solution has vertical asymptotes. Find the exact value of the smallest positive $x$-coordinate at which an asymptote occurs. [2]
markscheme: (a) Separating variables: $\int\dfrac{1}{1+y^2}\,dy=\int 2x\,dx$ [M1] $\arctan y=x^2+C$ [A1][A1] Using $y=1$ when $x=0$: $\dfrac{\pi}{4}=C$ [M1] $y=\tan\left(x^2+\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$ [A1] [5 marks] (b) $y$ is undefined when $x^2+\dfrac{\pi}{4}=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ [M1] $x^2=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$, so $x=\dfrac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Do not forget the constant of integration until you have used the initial condition; it fixes the phase of the tangent. In part (b), the first asymptote comes from the first time the argument of the tangent reaches $\pi/2$.

subtopic: Separable equation needing partial fractions
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=y(4-y)$, where $0<y<4$ and $y=1$ when $x=0$. (a) Show that $y=\dfrac{4}{1+3e^{-4x}}$. [6] (b) Write down the limiting value of $y$ as $x\to\infty$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\int\dfrac{1}{y(4-y)}\,dy=\int1\,dx$ [M1] $\dfrac{1}{y(4-y)}=\dfrac14\left(\dfrac1y+\dfrac1{4-y}\right)$ [A1] $\dfrac14\ln y-\dfrac14\ln(4-y)=x+C$ [A1] Using $y=1$ at $x=0$: $C=\dfrac14\ln\dfrac13$, so $\ln\dfrac{y}{4-y}=4x+\ln\dfrac13$ [M1] $\dfrac{y}{4-y}=\dfrac{e^{4x}}{3}$, so $3y=4e^{4x}-ye^{4x}$ and $y=\dfrac{4e^{4x}}{3+e^{4x}}$ [M1] $y=\dfrac{4}{1+3e^{-4x}}$ [A1][AG] [6 marks] (b) $y\to4$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Partial fractions is the key step for any equation of the form $y'=y(a-y)$. Because $0<y<4$ both logarithm arguments are positive, so no modulus signs are needed.

subtopic: Separable equation with partial fractions in x
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{y}{(x+1)(x+3)}$, where $x>-1$, $y>0$ and $y=\sqrt{3}$ when $x=0$. (a) Express $\dfrac{1}{(x+1)(x+3)}$ in partial fractions. [2] (b) Hence show that $y=3\sqrt{\dfrac{x+1}{x+3}}$. [5] (c) Write down the value that $y$ approaches as $x\to\infty$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{1}{(x+1)(x+3)}=\dfrac{A}{x+1}+\dfrac{B}{x+3}$ so $1=A(x+3)+B(x+1)$ [M1] $\dfrac{1}{(x+1)(x+3)}=\dfrac{1}{2(x+1)}-\dfrac{1}{2(x+3)}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\int\dfrac{1}{y}\,dy=\int\left(\dfrac{1}{2(x+1)}-\dfrac{1}{2(x+3)}\right)dx$ [M1] $\ln y=\dfrac{1}{2}\ln(x+1)-\dfrac{1}{2}\ln(x+3)+C$ [A1][A1] Using $y=\sqrt3$ when $x=0$: $\dfrac12\ln 3=-\dfrac12\ln 3+C$, so $C=\ln 3$ [M1] $\ln y=\ln 3+\dfrac12\ln\dfrac{x+1}{x+3}$ [A1] $y=3\sqrt{\dfrac{x+1}{x+3}}$ [AG] [5 marks] (c) $y\to 3$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Partial fractions turn an awkward integral into two logarithms. Combine the logarithms only at the end, once the constant has been found.

subtopic: Separable equation with inverse tangents
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{1+y^2}{1+x^2}$, with $y=1$ when $x=0$. (a) Solve the differential equation, giving your answer in the form $y=\tan(\dots)$. [4] (b) Show that $y=\dfrac{1+x}{1-x}$. [3] (c) State the largest interval of the form $x<c$ on which this solution is valid, with $c$ a positive constant, and give a reason. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{dy}{1+y^2}=\int\dfrac{dx}{1+x^2}$ [M1] $\arctan y=\arctan x+C$ [A1] $x=0$, $y=1$: $C=\dfrac\pi4$ [M1] $y=\tan\left(\arctan x+\dfrac\pi4\right)$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $y=\dfrac{\tan(\arctan x)+\tan\frac\pi4}{1-\tan(\arctan x)\tan\frac\pi4}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{x+1}{1-x\cdot1}$ [A1] $=\dfrac{1+x}{1-x}$ [AG] [A1] [3 marks] (c) $c=1$ [A1] at $x=1$ the denominator is zero, so $y$ is undefined (and $y\to\infty$ as $x\to1^-$) [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Both sides integrate to inverse tangent functions. For part (b), use the compound angle formula for $\tan(A+B)$ with $A=\arctan x$.

subtopic: Euler's method and exact solution comparison
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=2x-y$, where $y=1$ when $x=0$. (a) Use Euler's method with a step size of $h=0.25$ to estimate the value of $y$ when $x=1$. Show each step of your working. [4] (b) The exact solution of the differential equation is $y=2x-2+3e^{-x}$. Show that this function satisfies both the differential equation and the initial condition. [3] (c) Find the percentage error in your estimate from part (a). [2]
tips: Keep several extra decimal places in the intermediate Euler values and round only at the end. For a percentage error, divide by the exact value, not by the estimate.

subtopic: Substitution u = x + y in a differential equation
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=(x+y)^2$, with $y=0$ when $x=0$. (a) Let $u=x+y$. Show that $\dfrac{du}{dx}=1+u^2$. [2] (b) Hence find $y$ in terms of $x$, for $-\dfrac\pi2<x<\dfrac\pi2$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{du}{dx}=1+\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ [M1] $=1+u^2$ [AG] [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\int\dfrac{du}{1+u^2}=\int dx$ [M1] $\arctan u=x+c$ [A1] $u=0$ at $x=0$ so $c=0$ [M1] $u=\tan x$ so $y=\tan x-x$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: The substitution turns the equation into a separable equation in $u$ and $x$.

subtopic: Loan balance with continuous interest and repayments
statement: The balance $A$ dollars of a loan at time $t$ years satisfies $\dfrac{dA}{dt}=0.05A-2000$, with $A=30\,000$ when $t=0$. (a) Explain the meaning of each of the two terms on the right-hand side. [2] (b) Solve the differential equation to show that $A=40\,000-10\,000e^{0.05t}$. [4] (c) Find, in years to three significant figures, when the loan is fully repaid. [2]
markscheme: (a) $0.05A$: interest is added continuously at $5\%$ of the balance [A1] $-2000$: repayments at a constant rate of $\$2000$ per year [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\int\dfrac{dA}{0.05A-2000}=\int dt$ [M1] $20\ln|0.05A-2000|=t+c$ [A1] $0.05A-2000=-500e^{0.05t}$ using $t=0$ [M1] $A=40\,000-10\,000e^{0.05t}$ [AG] [A1] [4 marks] (c) $40\,000=10\,000e^{0.05t}$ [M1] $t=20\ln4=27.7$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The equation separates after factoring out $0.05$. The loan is repaid when the balance reaches zero.

subtopic: Euler method by hand and sign of the second derivative
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=xy$, where $y=1$ when $x=0$. (a) Use Euler's method with step length $h=0.2$ to find an approximation for $y(0.6)$. [3] (b) Solve the differential equation to show that $y=e^{x^2/2}$. [4] (c) Show that $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=(1+x^2)y$, and hence explain why your answer to part (a) is an underestimate of $y(0.6)$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $y_{n+1}=y_n+0.2\,x_ny_n$ [M1] $y(0.2)\approx 1+0.2(0)(1)=1$, $y(0.4)\approx 1+0.2(0.2)(1)=1.04$ [A1] $y(0.6)\approx 1.04+0.2(0.4)(1.04)=1.1232$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\int\dfrac1y\,dy=\int x\,dx$ [M1] $\ln y=\dfrac{x^2}{2}+C$ [A1] Using $y=1$ when $x=0$: $C=0$ [M1] $y=e^{x^2/2}$ [A1] [AG] [4 marks] (c) $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=y+x\dfrac{dy}{dx}=y+x^2y=(1+x^2)y$ [M1] This is positive, so the solution curve is concave up, the tangent lines used by Euler's method lie below the curve and the estimate is an underestimate [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Write the recursion $y_{n+1}=y_n+h\,f(x_n,y_n)$ and keep exact decimals at each step. The sign of $y''$ tells you which side of the curve the tangent lines lie on.

subtopic: Homogeneous equation with an exponential of y/x
statement: A curve $y=y(x)$ satisfies $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{y}{x}+e^{y/x}$, where $0<x<e$ and $y=0$ when $x=1$. (a) Use the substitution $u=\dfrac{y}{x}$ to show that $x\dfrac{du}{dx}=e^{u}$. [2] (b) Hence find $y$ in terms of $x$. [5]
markscheme: (a) $y=ux$ gives $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=u+x\dfrac{du}{dx}$ [M1] $u+x\dfrac{du}{dx}=u+e^{u}$, so $x\dfrac{du}{dx}=e^{u}$ [A1] [AG] [2 marks] (b) $\int e^{-u}\,du=\int\dfrac1x\,dx$ [M1] $-e^{-u}=\ln x+C$ [A1] Using $u=0$ when $x=1$: $-1=C$ [M1] $e^{-u}=1-\ln x$ [A1] $u=-\ln(1-\ln x)$, so $y=-x\ln(1-\ln x)$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: The substitution is given in the question, so use it exactly as stated. The condition $x<e$ guarantees that $1-\ln x>0$ so the logarithm in the answer exists.

subtopic: First-order linear equation with a trigonometric integrating factor
statement: The function $y$ satisfies $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}+y\tan x=\cos x$, for $-\dfrac{\pi}{2}<x<\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, where $y=2$ when $x=0$. (a) Show that an integrating factor for this equation is $\sec x$. [2] (b) Solve the differential equation, giving $y$ in terms of $x$. [4] (c) Find the exact value of $y$ when $x=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$. [1] (d) Show that at any stationary point of the curve, $(x+2)\tan x=1$. [2]
markscheme: (a) Integrating factor $=e^{\int \tan x\,\mathrm{d}x}=e^{-\ln(\cos x)}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{1}{\cos x}=\sec x$ [AG] (valid since $\cos x>0$) [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(y\sec x\right)=\cos x\sec x=1$ [M1] $y\sec x=x+C$ [A1] Using $y=2$ when $x=0$: $2=C$ [M1] $y=(x+2)\cos x$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) $y=\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}+2\right)\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\dfrac{\pi}{6}+1$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=\cos x-(x+2)\sin x$ [M1] Setting to zero and dividing by $\cos x\neq 0$: $1=(x+2)\tan x$ [AG] [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Write the equation in the form $y'+P(x)y=Q(x)$, multiply by $e^{\int P\,\mathrm{d}x}$ and recognize the left side as a product derivative. For part (d) you can differentiate the solution or use the original equation with $y'=0$.

subtopic: First-order linear equation with a repeated exponential
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}+2y=e^{-2x}$, with $y=3$ when $x=0$. (a) Find the integrating factor and use it to show that $\dfrac d{dx}\left(ye^{2x}\right)=1$. [3] (b) Hence solve the differential equation. [3]
markscheme: (a) integrating factor $e^{\int2\,dx}=e^{2x}$ [A1] multiply the equation by $e^{2x}$ [M1] $\dfrac d{dx}\left(ye^{2x}\right)=e^{2x}e^{-2x}=1$ [AG] [A1] [3 marks] (b) $ye^{2x}=x+C$ [M1] $C=3$ [A1] $y=(x+3)e^{-2x}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: After multiplying by the integrating factor, the left side is a product derivative and the right side simplifies.

subtopic: Drug concentration modelled with an integrating factor
statement: After an injection, the concentration $C$ mg/L of a drug in the blood at time $t$ hours satisfies $\dfrac{dC}{dt}+0.4C=5e^{-0.1t}$, where $C=0$ when $t=0$. (a) Show that $e^{0.4t}$ is an integrating factor for this differential equation. [1] (b) Hence show that $C=\dfrac{50}{3}\left(e^{-0.1t}-e^{-0.4t}\right)$. [4] (c) Find the maximum concentration of the drug and the time at which it occurs. [3] (d) The drug is effective when the concentration exceeds $5$ mg/L. Find, to the nearest tenth of an hour, how long the drug is effective. [2]
markscheme: (a) $e^{\int0.4\,dt}=e^{0.4t}$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(Ce^{0.4t}\right)=5e^{0.3t}$ [M1] $Ce^{0.4t}=\dfrac{5}{0.3}e^{0.3t}+K=\dfrac{50}{3}e^{0.3t}+K$ [A1] When $t=0$, $C=0$: $K=-\dfrac{50}{3}$ [M1] $C=\dfrac{50}{3}\left(e^{-0.1t}-e^{-0.4t}\right)$ [A1][AG] [4 marks] (c) Sketch or differentiate: $\dfrac{dC}{dt}=0$ gives $e^{0.3t}=4$ [M1] $t=\dfrac{\ln4}{0.3}=4.62$ hours [A1] $C_{\max}=7.87$ mg/L [A1] [3 marks] (d) Solving $\dfrac{50}{3}\left(e^{-0.1t}-e^{-0.4t}\right)=5$ with a GDC gives $t=1.413$ and $t=11.74$ [M1] Duration $=11.74-1.413=10.3$ hours [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Rewrite the equation in the form $y'+P(x)y=Q(x)$ first, then multiply by the integrating factor. In part (d) look at the graph of $C$ against $t$; there are two intersections with $C=5$.

subtopic: Mixing in a tank whose volume increases
statement: A tank initially contains $100$ L of solution with $20$ g of dissolved salt. A solution containing $2$ g of salt per liter flows in at $3$ L/min, and the well-mixed solution flows out at $1$ L/min. Let $S$ grams be the amount of salt at time $t$ minutes. (a) Show that the volume of liquid in the tank is $V=100+2t$ liters, and that $\dfrac{dS}{dt}=6-\dfrac S{100+2t}$. [3] (b) Find the integrating factor, and show that $\dfrac d{dt}\left(S\sqrt{100+2t}\right)=6\sqrt{100+2t}$. [3] (c) Solve the differential equation to show that $S=2(100+2t)-\dfrac{1800}{\sqrt{100+2t}}$. [4] (d) Find the amount of salt and the concentration in g/L when $t=50$. [2] (e) Show that the concentration is $2-\dfrac{1800}{(100+2t)^{3/2}}$, and find when it first reaches $1.5$ g/L. [3]
markscheme: (a) volume increases at $3-1=2$ L/min [A1] salt in: $3\times2=6$ g/min [A1] salt out: $1\times\dfrac S{100+2t}$ g/min, giving the equation [A1] [3 marks] (b) integrating factor $e^{\int\frac{dt}{100+2t}}=e^{\frac12\ln(100+2t)}$ [M1][A1] $=\sqrt{100+2t}$ and multiply through [A1] [3 marks] (c) $S\sqrt{100+2t}=\int6\sqrt{100+2t}\,dt=2(100+2t)^{3/2}+C$ [M1][A1] $S=2(100+2t)+\dfrac C{\sqrt{100+2t}}$ [A1] $20=200+\dfrac C{10}$ so $C=-1800$ [A1] [4 marks] (d) $S=400-\dfrac{1800}{\sqrt{200}}=273$ g [A1] concentration $\dfrac{273}{200}=1.36$ g/L [A1] [2 marks] (e) divide $S$ by $V=100+2t$ [A1] $\dfrac{1800}{V^{3/2}}=0.5$ so $V=3600^{2/3}=235$ [M1] $t=\dfrac{235-100}2=67.4$ minutes [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The volume changes with time, so the outflow of salt depends on $t$ through $S/V$. Use an integrating factor for the resulting linear equation.

subtopic: Quotient rule and stationary points of a rational function
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{2x}{x^{2}+1}$, for $x\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Show that $f'(x)=\dfrac{2-2x^{2}}{\left(x^{2}+1\right)^{2}}$. [3] (b) Find the coordinates of the stationary points of the graph of $f$. [3] (c) Find the equation of the tangent to the graph of $f$ at the origin. [2]
tips: Write down $u$, $v$, $u'$ and $v'$ before applying the quotient rule. A fraction is zero only when its numerator is zero, so you can ignore the denominator when finding stationary points.

subtopic: Optimization: open box
statement: A square sheet of metal of side $60$ cm has a square of side $x$ cm cut from each corner. The sides are then folded up to form an open box with a square base. (a) Show that the volume of the box is $V=x(60-2x)^2$ cm$^3$, and state the possible values of $x$. [2] (b) Find $\dfrac{dV}{dx}$. [3] (c) Find the value of $x$ that gives the maximum volume, justifying that it is a maximum. [3] (d) Find the maximum volume. [1]
markscheme: (a) Base has side $60-2x$ and height $x$, so $V=x(60-2x)^2$ [A1][AG] $0<x<30$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $V=4x^3-240x^2+3600x$ [A1] $\dfrac{dV}{dx}=12x^2-480x+3600$ [M1] [A1] (accept $(60-2x)^2-4x(60-2x)$ unexpanded) [3 marks] (c) $12(x^2-40x+300)=0$, $(x-10)(x-30)=0$ [M1] $x=10$ (reject $x=30$ as outside the domain) [A1] $\dfrac{d^2V}{dx^2}=24x-480=-240<0$, so a maximum [R1] [3 marks] (d) $V=10\times40^2=16\,000$ cm$^3$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: State the domain from the geometry of the problem, and reject any stationary point outside it. Justify the maximum with $V''$ or a sign change.

subtopic: Minimum surface area of a cylindrical can
statement: A closed cylindrical can has radius $r$ cm, height $h$ cm and volume $500$ cm$^3$. (a) Show that the total surface area is $A=2\pi r^2+\dfrac{1000}{r}$. [3] (b) Use your calculator to find the value of $r$ that minimizes $A$, and the minimum area. [3] (c) Find the height at this radius and show that $h\approx2r$. [2] (d) Show algebraically that the minimum occurs when $h=2r$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\pi r^2h=500$ so $h=\dfrac{500}{\pi r^2}$ [M1]; $A=2\pi r^2+2\pi rh$ [A1]; $=2\pi r^2+\dfrac{1000}{r}$ [AG] [3 marks] (b) Differentiate or use the minimum function [M1]; $r=4.30$ [A1]; $A_{min}=348.7$ cm$^2$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $h=8.60$ [A1]; $\dfrac{h}{r}=2.000\approx2$ [R1] [2 marks] (d) $\dfrac{dA}{dr}=4\pi r-\dfrac{1000}{r^2}=0$ [M1] gives $4\pi r^3=1000=2\pi r^2h$ [A1] so $h=2r$ [AG] [3 marks]
tips: Eliminate $h$ using the volume first so that $A$ depends on one variable; the optimum shape of a closed can has height equal to its diameter.

subtopic: Optimization of cost
statement: A company designs a closed cylindrical water tank with volume $2.5\ \text{m}^3$. The tank has radius $r$ meters and height $h$ meters. The material for the top and the base costs USD $30$ per $\text{m}^2$ and the material for the curved surface costs USD $20$ per $\text{m}^2$. (a) Show that $h=\dfrac{2.5}{\pi r^2}$. [1] (b) Show that the total cost of the material, USD $C$, is given by $C=60\pi r^2+\dfrac{100}{r}$. [3] (c) Find $\dfrac{dC}{dr}$. [2] (d) Find the value of $r$ that minimizes the cost, and the minimum cost. [4] (e) Use the second derivative to justify that this value of $r$ gives a minimum. [2] (f) Find the height of the tank with minimum cost. [1]
