markscheme: (a) $V=\pi r^2h=2.5\Rightarrow h=\dfrac{2.5}{\pi r^2}$ [A1][AG] [1 mark] (b) cost of top and base $=30\times2\pi r^2=60\pi r^2$ [A1] curved surface cost $=20\times2\pi rh$ [M1] $=40\pi r\times\dfrac{2.5}{\pi r^2}=\dfrac{100}{r}$ [A1] so $C=60\pi r^2+\dfrac{100}{r}$ [AG] [3 marks] (c) $\dfrac{dC}{dr}=120\pi r-\dfrac{100}{r^2}$ [A1][A1] [2 marks] (d) $120\pi r-\dfrac{100}{r^2}=0$ [M1] $r^3=\dfrac{100}{120\pi}$ [A1] $r=0.643$ m ($0.642524\ldots$) [A1] minimum cost USD $233$ ($233.454\ldots$) [A1] [4 marks] (e) $\dfrac{d^2C}{dr^2}=120\pi+\dfrac{200}{r^3}$ [A1] which is positive for $r>0$ (e.g. $1130$ at $r=0.643$), so a minimum [R1] [2 marks] (f) $h=\dfrac{2.5}{\pi(0.642524\ldots)^2}=1.93$ m [A1] [1 mark]
tips: In 'show that' parts every step must be written out, ending with the given expression. Use the unrounded value of r when computing the minimum cost and the height.

subtopic: Linear approximation to a square root
statement: Let $f(x)=\sqrt{x}$. The tangent to the graph at $x=25$ is used to approximate $f$ near $25$. (a) Find the equation of the tangent at $x=25$. [3] (b) Use the tangent to estimate $\sqrt{26}$, and find the percentage error compared with the calculator value, to two significant figures. [3] (c) State whether the tangent estimate is an overestimate or an underestimate, and explain using the concavity of $f$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $f'(x)=\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt x}$, so $f'(25)=\dfrac1{10}$ [A1]; $f(25)=5$ [A1]; $y=5+\dfrac{x-25}{10}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) estimate $5.1$ [A1]; calculator $5.0990$ [A1]; $\dfrac{5.1-5.0990}{5.0990}\times100=0.019\%$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) overestimate [A1]; $f''(x)<0$, so the curve lies below its tangent lines [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Near $x=a$, $f(x)\approx f(a)+f'(a)(x-a)$.

subtopic: Second derivative and points of inflection with a Gaussian factor
statement: Let $f(x)=xe^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2}}$, for $x\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Show that $f'(x)=\left(1-x^{2}\right)e^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2}}$. [3] (b) Show that $f''(x)=\left(x^{3}-3x\right)e^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2}}$. [3] (c) Find the $x$-coordinates of the points of inflection of the graph of $f$, justifying that the concavity changes. [3] (d) Find the coordinates of the local maximum point. [2]
markscheme: (a) product rule with $u=x$ and $v=e^{-x^{2}/2}$ [M1] $f'(x)=e^{-x^{2}/2}+x\left(-x\right)e^{-x^{2}/2}$ [A1] $=\left(1-x^{2}\right)e^{-x^{2}/2}$ [AG] [3 marks] (b) $f''(x)=-2xe^{-x^{2}/2}+\left(1-x^{2}\right)\left(-x\right)e^{-x^{2}/2}$ [M1][A1] $=\left(x^{3}-3x\right)e^{-x^{2}/2}$ [AG] [3 marks] (c) $f''(x)=0$ gives $x\left(x^{2}-3\right)=0$ [M1] $x=0,\ \pm\sqrt3$ [A1] each root is simple so the sign of $f''$ changes at each [R1] [3 marks] (d) $f'(x)=0$ gives $x=\pm1$ and $f''(1)=-2e^{-1/2}<0$ [M1] local maximum at $\left(1,e^{-1/2}\right)$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The exponential factor is never zero, so factorize it out and solve the polynomial factor. A zero of $f''$ is a point of inflection only if $f''$ changes sign there.

subtopic: Differentiating sums, products and composite functions
statement: (a) Differentiate $y=4x^{3}-\dfrac{6}{x^{2}}+\sqrt{x}$. [3] (b) Differentiate $y=x^{2}\ln x$ for $x>0$. [3] (c) Differentiate $y=(2x^{2}+1)^{5}$ and find the gradient at $x=1$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $y=4x^{3}-6x^{-2}+x^{1/2}$ [M1]; $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=12x^{2}+12x^{-3}+\dfrac12x^{-1/2}$ [A1][A1] [3 marks] (b) product rule [M1]; $2x\ln x+x^{2}\cdot\dfrac1x$ [A1]; $2x\ln x+x$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) chain rule: $5(2x^{2}+1)^{4}\times4x$ [M1][A1]; gradient $20\times81=1620$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Rewrite roots and reciprocals as powers of $x$ before differentiating.

subtopic: Maximizing the volume of an open box
statement: An open box is made from a rectangular metal sheet of length 48 cm and width 30 cm by cutting a square of side $x$ cm from each corner and folding up the sides. (a) Show that the volume of the box is $V=4x^{3}-156x^{2}+1440x$. [2] (b) State the possible values of $x$. [1] (c) Use calculus to find the value of $x$ that gives the maximum volume, justifying that it is a maximum. [4] (d) Find the maximum volume. [1]
tips: State the domain from the geometry: each cut must leave positive length and width. Reject any stationary point outside the domain and justify the maximum with $V''$.

subtopic: Concavity and points of inflection
statement: Let $f(x)=x^4-8x^3+18x^2$, for $x\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Show that $f'(x)=4x(x-3)^2$. [3] (b) Write down the $x$-coordinates of the stationary points of the graph of $f$. [1] (c) Find $f''(x)$, and hence show that the point at $x=0$ is a local minimum. [3] (d) Show that the stationary point at $x=3$ is neither a local maximum nor a local minimum. [2] (e) Find the coordinates of the points of inflection of the graph of $f$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $f'(x)=4x^3-24x^2+36x$ [A1] $=4x(x^2-6x+9)$ [M1] $=4x(x-3)^2$ [A1][AG] [3 marks] (b) $x=0$ and $x=3$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $f''(x)=12x^2-48x+36$ [A1] $f''(0)=36>0$ [M1] so a local minimum [R1] [3 marks] (d) $f'(x)=4x(x-3)^2\ge0$ for $x>0$, so $f'$ does not change sign at $x=3$ [M1] therefore it is not a local extremum [R1] [2 marks] (e) $f''(x)=12(x-1)(x-3)=0$ [M1] $x=1$ or $x=3$, with $f''$ changing sign at each [A1] $(1,11)$ and $(3,27)$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A point where $f''=0$ is an inflection only if $f''$ changes sign. At $x=3$ the tangent is horizontal and the curve crosses it, which is a stationary point of inflection.

subtopic: Quotient rule with logarithms
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{\ln x}{x^2}$, for $x>0$. (a) Show that $f'(x)=\dfrac{1-2\ln x}{x^3}$. [3] (b) Find the exact coordinates of the stationary point of the graph of $f$. [3] (c) Show that this stationary point is a local maximum. [2]
markscheme: (a) Quotient rule: $f'(x)=\dfrac{x^2\cdot\frac1x-\ln x\cdot2x}{x^4}$ [M1] [A1] $=\dfrac{x-2x\ln x}{x^4}=\dfrac{1-2\ln x}{x^3}$ [A1][AG] [3 marks] (b) $1-2\ln x=0$ [M1] $x=e^{1/2}=\sqrt e$ [A1] $y=\dfrac{\frac12}{e}=\dfrac1{2e}$, so the point is $\left(\sqrt e,\dfrac1{2e}\right)$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) For $x<\sqrt e$, $\ln x<\frac12$ so $f'(x)>0$; for $x>\sqrt e$, $f'(x)<0$ [M1] $f'$ changes from positive to negative, so a local maximum [R1] [2 marks]
tips: The denominator $x^3$ is positive for $x>0$, so the sign of $f'$ is the sign of $1-2\ln x$. A sign change of $f'$ is a valid way to classify the point.

subtopic: Tangent parallel to a given line
statement: Let $f(x)=x^3-3x^2+2x+1$. (a) Find $f'(x)$. [2] (b) Find the coordinates of the two points on the graph of $f$ at which the tangent is parallel to the line $y=2x+5$. [3] (c) Find the equation of the tangent to the graph of $f$ at the point with $x=2$. [2]
tips: Parallel lines have equal gradients, so set $f'(x)$ equal to the gradient of the given line. Remember to substitute back into $f$ to get the $y$-coordinates.

subtopic: Investigating the function ln x over x
statement: Consider $f(x)=\dfrac{\ln x}{x}$ for $x>0$. (a) Find the $x$-intercept and the sign of $f(x)$ for $0<x<1$. [2] (b) Show that $f'(x)=\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x^{2}}$. [3] (c) Find the exact coordinates of the stationary point and show that it is a maximum. [4] (d) Given that $f''(x)=\dfrac{2\ln x-3}{x^{3}}$, find the exact $x$-coordinate of the point of inflection. [2] (e) Describe the behavior of $f$ as $x\to0^{+}$ and as $x\to\infty$, and write down the equations of any asymptotes. [3] (f) Use the maximum to explain which is larger, $\pi^{e}$ or $e^{\pi}$, by comparing $f(e)$ and $f(\pi)$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\ln x=0$ gives $x=1$ [A1]; $f(x)<0$ for $0<x<1$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) quotient rule: $\dfrac{\frac1x\cdot x-\ln x\cdot1}{x^{2}}$ [M1][A1]; $=\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x^{2}}$ [AG] [3 marks] (c) $1-\ln x=0$ gives $x=e$ [A1]; $f(e)=\dfrac1e$ [A1]; $f'>0$ for $x<e$ and $f'<0$ for $x>e$ [M1]; so a maximum [A1] [4 marks] (d) $2\ln x=3$ [M1]; $x=e^{3/2}$ [A1] [2 marks] (e) as $x\to0^{+}$, $f\to-\infty$ and $x=0$ is a vertical asymptote [A1][A1]; as $x\to\infty$, $f\to0^{+}$ and $y=0$ is a horizontal asymptote [A1] [3 marks] (f) $f(\pi)<f(e)$ since the maximum is at $x=e$ [R1]; $\dfrac{\ln\pi}{\pi}<\dfrac{\ln e}{e}$ gives $e\ln\pi<\pi$ [M1]; so $\pi^{e}<e^{\pi}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The function has a single maximum at $x=e$; compare values of $f$ either side of it.

subtopic: Closest point on a logarithmic curve to a given point
statement: The point $P$ has coordinates $(5,0)$. The point $Q(x,\ln x)$ lies on the curve $y=\ln x$, for $x>0$. Let $D$ be the distance $PQ$. (a) Show that $D^{2}=(x-5)^{2}+(\ln x)^{2}$. [1] (b) Find the value of $x$ for which $PQ$ is a minimum, to three significant figures. [3] (c) Find the minimum value of $PQ$, to three significant figures. [2] (d) Show that, at this minimum, the line $PQ$ is perpendicular to the tangent to the curve at $Q$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $D^{2}=(x-5)^{2}+(\ln x-0)^{2}$ [AG] [1 mark] (b) minimizing $D^{2}$ is equivalent to minimizing $D$ [M1] solve $\dfrac{d\left(D^{2}\right)}{dx}=2(x-5)+\dfrac{2\ln x}{x}=0$ with the GDC (or find the minimum of the graph) [M1] $x=4.67$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $D^{2}=2.484\ldots$ [M1] $PQ=1.58$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) gradient of the tangent $=\dfrac1x=0.2141\ldots$ [A1] gradient of $PQ=\dfrac{\ln x}{x-5}=-4.670\ldots$ [A1] product $=-1$, so perpendicular [R1] [3 marks]
tips: Minimizing $D^{2}$ gives the same $x$ as minimizing $D$ and avoids a square root. Use the unrounded value of $x$ from your GDC when checking perpendicularity in part (d).

subtopic: Logistic model: rate of change and maximum rate
statement: The total number of units $S$ of a product sold $t$ weeks after launch is modelled by $S(t)=\dfrac{1000}{1+49e^{-0.4t}}$, for $t\ge0$. (a) Find the number of units sold at launch, and the value that $S$ approaches as $t$ becomes large. [2] (b) Find the rate of sales, $\dfrac{dS}{dt}$, when $t=5$. [3] (c) Find the time at which the rate of sales is greatest, and the greatest rate of sales. [3]
markscheme: (a) $S(0)=\frac{1000}{50}=20$ [A1] As $t\to\infty$, $e^{-0.4t}\to0$ so $S\to1000$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Attempt to differentiate or use GDC derivative at $t=5$ [M1] $\dfrac{dS}{dt}=\dfrac{19600e^{-0.4t}}{(1+49e^{-0.4t})^2}$ [A1] $=45.5$ units per week [A1] [3 marks] (c) Maximum of $\frac{dS}{dt}$ found using GDC (or solve $\frac{d^2S}{dt^2}=0$) [M1] $t=9.73$ weeks [A1] Greatest rate $=100$ units per week [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Use the GDC to differentiate numerically or to find the maximum of the derivative graph. For a logistic model the fastest growth occurs at half the carrying capacity.

subtopic: Tangent, normal and gradient conditions for a logarithmic curve
statement: Let $f(x)=\ln\left(x^{2}+3\right)$. (a) Find $f'(x)$. [2] (b) Find the equation of the tangent to the graph of $f$ at $x=1$, in the form $y=mx+c$ with $m$ and $c$ correct to three significant figures. [2] (c) The normal to the graph at $x=1$ meets the $x$-axis at the point $P$. Find the $x$-coordinate of $P$, to three significant figures. [2] (d) Find the values of $x$ for which the gradient of the graph is $0.3$. [2]
tips: The derivative of $\ln u$ is $u'/u$. In part (d) rearrange into a quadratic equation, or use your GDC to find the intersections of $y=f'(x)$ with $y=0.3$.

subtopic: Product rule and stationary points
statement: Let $f(x)=x^2e^{2x}$, for $x\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Find $f'(x)$. [3] (b) Find the exact coordinates of the stationary points of the graph of $f$. [3] (c) Given that $f''(x)=(4x^2+8x+2)e^{2x}$, determine the nature of each stationary point. [2]
tips: Factor $f'(x)$ before solving: the exponential factor is never zero, so only the polynomial factor gives stationary points. Use the sign of $f''$ to decide the nature.

subtopic: Rate of change of a periodic model
statement: The temperature $T^\circ$C in a greenhouse $t$ hours after 06:00 is modelled by $T(t)=22+5\sin(0.5t)$, for $0\le t\le12$. (a) Find the rate of change of temperature at $t=3$. [2] (b) Find the values of $t$ for which $T'(t)=0$. [3] (c) Write down the greatest rate at which the temperature rises. [1]
markscheme: (a) $T'(t)=2.5\cos(0.5t)$ [M1] $T'(3)=0.177^\circ$C per hour [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\cos(0.5t)=0$ [M1] $0.5t=\frac\pi2$ or $\frac{3\pi}2$ [A1] $t=3.14$ or $t=9.42$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $2.5^\circ$C per hour [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Make sure your calculator is in radian mode for the trigonometric model. Stationary points of $T$ occur where the rate of change is zero.

subtopic: Stationary points of a quartic on an interval
statement: Let $f(x)=x^{4}-8x^{2}+3$ for $-3\le x\le3$. (a) Use your GDC to find the coordinates of the stationary points. [3] (b) Classify each stationary point using $f''(x)=12x^{2}-16$. [2] (c) Find the range of $f$ on the given domain. [3]
tips: Check the end points of the domain as well as the stationary points when finding the range.

subtopic: Drug concentration, maximum and fastest decrease
statement: The concentration of a drug in a patient's blood, in mg per liter, is modeled by $C(t)=20te^{-0.5t}$, where $t\ge0$ is the time in hours after the drug is taken. (a) Find $C'(t)$. [3] (b) Find the maximum concentration and the time at which it occurs. [3] (c) Find the rate of change of the concentration when $t=1$, to three significant figures. [1] (d) Find the time at which the concentration is decreasing at its greatest rate. [2]
markscheme: (a) product rule [M1] $C'(t)=20e^{-0.5t}+20t\left(-0.5\right)e^{-0.5t}$ [A1] $=20e^{-0.5t}(1-0.5t)$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $C'(t)=0$ gives $t=2$ [M1][A1] $C(2)=40e^{-1}=14.7$ mg/L [A1] [3 marks] (c) $C'(1)=10e^{-0.5}=6.07$ mg L$^{-1}$ h$^{-1}$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) the rate of decrease is greatest where $C'$ is a minimum, so find the minimum of $C'(t)$ with the GDC (or solve $C''(t)=0$) [M1] $t=4$ hours [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The fastest decrease of $C$ corresponds to the minimum of $C'$, which is a point of inflection of $C$. Use your GDC to find the minimum of the derivative graph.

subtopic: Stationary points and inflection of a cubic
statement: A curve has equation $y=f(x)$ where $f(x)=x^{3} - 6 x^{2} + 9 x + 2$. (a) Find $f'(x)$ and solve $f'(x)=0$. [3] (b) Find $f''(x)$ and use it to determine the nature of each stationary point. [3] (c) Find the coordinates of the stationary points. [2] (d) Find the coordinates of the point of inflection. [2]
markscheme: (a) $f'(x)=3 x^{2} - 12 x + 9$ [A1]; $f'(x)=0$ gives $x=1$ and $x=3$ [M1][A1] [3 marks] (b) $f''(x)=6 \left(x - 2\right)$ [A1]; at $x=1$, $f''=-6$ so a local maximum; at $x=3$, $f''=6$ so a local minimum [M1][A1] [3 marks] (c) $(1,6)$; $(3,2)$ [A1][A1] [2 marks] (d) $f''(x)=0$ gives $x=2$ [M1]; point $(2,4)$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A point of inflection occurs where $f''$ changes sign, not merely where it is zero; here $f''$ is linear so it does change sign.

subtopic: Nature of stationary points using the second derivative
statement: Consider the function $f(x)=2 x^{3} - 9 x^{2} - 24 x + 10$. (a) Find $f'(x)$ and solve $f'(x)=0$. [3] (b) Find $f''(x)$ and use it to determine the nature of each stationary point. [3] (c) Find the coordinates of the stationary points. [2] (d) Find the coordinates of the point of inflection. [2]
markscheme: (a) $f'(x)=6 x^{2} - 18 x - 24$ [A1]; $f'(x)=0$ gives $x=-1$ and $x=4$ [M1][A1] [3 marks] (b) $f''(x)=6 \left(2 x - 3\right)$ [A1]; at $x=-1$, $f''=-30$ so a local maximum; at $x=4$, $f''=30$ so a local minimum [M1][A1] [3 marks] (c) $(-1,23)$; $(4,-102)$ [A1][A1] [2 marks] (d) $f''(x)=0$ gives $x=\frac{3}{2}$ [M1]; point $(\frac{3}{2},- \frac{79}{2})$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: If $f''(c)<0$ at a stationary point the curve is concave down, so it is a local maximum.

subtopic: Particle kinematics with a cubic displacement
statement: A particle moves along a straight line. Its displacement from a fixed point $O$ is $s=2t^{3}-15t^{2}+36t$ meters, for $0\le t\le5$, where $t$ is in seconds. (a) Find expressions for the velocity $v$ and the acceleration $a$ at time $t$. [2] (b) Find the times when the particle is momentarily at rest. [2] (c) Find the total distance traveled by the particle in the first 5 seconds. [3] (d) Find the minimum velocity of the particle during the first 5 seconds. [2]
tips: Distance is not the same as displacement: split the journey at each time when $v=0$ and add the absolute changes. A minimum of $v$ occurs where $a=0$ with $a'>0$.

subtopic: Maximum volume of an open box without a calculator
statement: A square sheet of cardboard of side $12$ cm has a square of side $x$ cm cut from each corner, and the sides are folded up to form an open box. (a) Show that the volume of the box is $V=x(12-2x)^2$. [2] (b) Find $\dfrac{dV}{dx}$ and the value of $x$ for which $V$ is a maximum. [4] (c) Use the second derivative to verify that this value gives a maximum, and find the maximum volume. [3]
markscheme: (a) Base is a square of side $12-2x$ [A1]; height $x$ so $V=x(12-2x)^2$ [AG] [2 marks] (b) $V=4 x^{3} - 48 x^{2} + 144 x$, $\dfrac{dV}{dx}=12 x^{2} - 96 x + 144$ [A1]; $=0$ gives $x=2$ or $x=6$ [M1][A1]; reject $x=6$ as the base would vanish [R1] [4 marks] (c) $\dfrac{d^2V}{dx^2}=24 x - 96$, which is negative at $x=2$ [A1][R1]; $V_{max}=128$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The domain is $0<x<L/2$; reject any stationary value outside it, and confirm the maximum with the second derivative.

subtopic: Minimizing average cost
statement: The cost in dollars of producing $x$ items per day is $C(x)=500+8x+0.02x^2$. The average cost per item is $A(x)=\dfrac{C(x)}{x}$. (a) Write down an expression for $A(x)$. [1] (b) Find $A'(x)$. [2] (c) Find the number of items per day that minimizes the average cost, and the minimum average cost per item. [3] (d) Find the marginal cost $C'(x)$ at the value of $x$ found in part (c), and comment on its value compared with the minimum average cost. [2]
tips: Differentiate each term of $A(x)$ separately, using $500x^{-1}$ for the first term. At the minimum average cost, the marginal cost equals the average cost.

subtopic: Closest point on a parabola to a given point
statement: Let $P(x,\,y)$ be a point on the curve $y=x^{2}$ and let $A$ be the point $(0,3)$. (a) Show that $AP^{2}=x^{2}+(x^{2}-3)^{2}$. [1] (b) Use your GDC to find the values of $x$ for which $AP$ is a minimum, to three significant figures. [3] (c) Find the minimum distance $AP$ as an exact value and to three significant figures. [2]
tips: Minimize the squared distance, which has the same minimizing $x$ as the distance.

subtopic: Tangent and normal to a trigonometric curve
statement: Let $f(x)=3\cos(2x)+4x$, for $0\le x\le\pi$. (a) Find $f'(x)$. [2] (b) Find the equation of the tangent to the graph of $f$ at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$, giving your answer in the form $y=mx+c$. [3] (c) Find the $x$-intercept of this tangent. [1] (d) Find the equation of the normal to the graph of $f$ at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $f'(x)=-6\sin(2x)+4$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (b) $f\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)=3\cos\dfrac{\pi}{2}+\pi=\pi$ [A1] $f'\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)=-6+4=-2$ and $y-\pi=-2\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$ [M1] $y=-2x+\dfrac{3\pi}{2}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $x=\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) normal gradient $=\dfrac12$ [M1] $y-\pi=\dfrac12\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Use radians throughout. The normal gradient is the negative reciprocal of the tangent gradient.

subtopic: Tangent to a quotient at a given point
statement: The function $f$ is defined by $f(x)=\frac{e^{2 x}}{x + 1}$, for $x>-1$. (a) Find $f'(x)$. [3] (b) Find the equation of the tangent to the curve at $x=0$. [3] (c) Find the equation of the normal at $x=0$ and the coordinates of the point where the normal meets the $x$-axis. [3]
markscheme: (a) Using the quotient rule [M1][A1]: $f'(x)=\frac{\left(2 x + 1\right) e^{2 x}}{x^{2} + 2 x + 1}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $f(0)=1$ [A1]; $f'(0)=1$ [A1]; $y-1=1(x-0)$ so $y=x + 1$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Normal gradient $=-\dfrac{1}{1}=-1$ [A1]; $y=1 - x$ [A1]; at $y=0$, $x=1$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: For a quotient $u/v$ use $(u'v-uv')/v^2$; evaluate each part at $x=0$ separately.

subtopic: Tangent and normal to a square root curve
statement: Let $y=\sqrt{x}$ and let $P$ be the point on the curve where $x=4$. (a) Find the gradient of the curve at $P$. [2] (b) Find the equation of the tangent at $P$ in the form $y=mx+c$. [2] (c) Find the equation of the normal at $P$ and the point where it meets the $x$-axis. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt x}$ [M1]; $\dfrac14$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $y-2=\dfrac14(x-4)$ [M1]; $y=\dfrac14x+1$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) normal gradient $-4$ [A1]; $y-2=-4(x-4)$ so $y=-4x+18$ [A1]; $\left(\dfrac92,\ 0\right)$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The normal is perpendicular to the tangent: its gradient is the negative reciprocal.

subtopic: Minimizing a sum with a reciprocal
statement: For $x>0$, let $S(x)=x+\dfrac{16}{x}$. (a) Find $S'(x)$ and the value of $x$ for which $S'(x)=0$. [3] (b) Show that this gives a minimum and find the minimum value of $S$. [3]
tips: Use the second derivative test, remembering that $x>0$.

subtopic: Area of a triangle formed by a tangent and the axes
statement: Let $f(x)=x^2e^{-x}$ for $x\geq0$. The tangent to the curve at the point $P$ where $x=3$ meets the $x$-axis at $A$ and the $y$-axis at $B$. The origin is $O$. (a) Find $f'(x)$. [2] (b) Find the equation of the tangent at $P$. [3] (c) Find the coordinates of $A$ and $B$. [2] (d) Find the area of triangle $OAB$. [2] (e) Use your calculator to find the values of $x$ for which the gradient of the curve is $-0.05$. [3]
tips: The tangent at a point has gradient $f'(a)$; intercepts come from setting $x=0$ and $y=0$ in its equation.

subtopic: Quotient rule and a tangent line
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{2x+1}{x-3}$ for $x\ne3$. (a) Use the quotient rule to show that $f'(x)=-\dfrac{7}{(x-3)^{2}}$. [3] (b) Explain why $f$ has no stationary points. [1] (c) Find the equation of the tangent at the point where $x=4$. [3]
tips: For $\dfrac{u}{v}$ the derivative is $\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^{2}}$.

subtopic: Rate of cooling of a liquid
statement: The temperature $T$ in $^\circ$C of a liquid $t$ minutes after it is poured into a cup is modeled by $T(t)=20+65e^{-0.08t}$ for $t\geq0$. (a) Write down the initial temperature and the temperature that the liquid approaches in the long run. [2] (b) Find $\dfrac{dT}{dt}$ and the rate at which the liquid is cooling when $t=10$. [3] (c) Find the time at which the liquid is cooling at exactly $1.5^\circ$C per minute. [2] (d) Find the time at which the temperature is $55^\circ$C and the rate of change at that time. [3] (e) Show that $\dfrac{dT}{dt}=-0.08(T-20)$ and explain what this says about the cooling rate. [2]
markscheme: (a) $T(0)=85$ [A1]; $T\to20$ as $t\to\infty$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $T'(t)=-5.2e^{-0.08t}$ [A1][A1]; at $t=10$: $-2.337$ $^\circ$C per minute [A1] [3 marks] (c) $-5.2e^{-0.08t}=-1.5$ [M1]; $t=15.54$ minutes [A1] [2 marks] (d) $20+65e^{-0.08t}=55$ [M1]; $t=7.74$ [A1]; $T'=-2.800$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) $\dfrac{dT}{dt}=-5.2e^{-0.08t}=-0.08\left(65e^{-0.08t}\right)=-0.08(T-20)$ [AG]; the rate is proportional to the temperature difference from the surroundings [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Differentiate $e^{-0.08t}$ using the chain rule; the cooling rate is largest at the start and decreases as the liquid nears room temperature.

subtopic: Marginal cost, average cost and profit
statement: This question investigates the costs of producing $q$ items per day in a small factory. The total daily cost in dollars is $C(q)=0.01q^3-0.9q^2+30q+400$ for $0<q\leq80$. (a) Find the marginal cost $C'(q)$. [2] (b) Find the value of $q$ at which the marginal cost is least, and the least marginal cost. [3] (c) The average cost per item is $A(q)=\dfrac{C(q)}{q}$. Write down an expression for $A(q)$. [1] (d) Use your calculator to find the value of $q$ that minimizes the average cost, and the minimum average cost. [3] (e) Show that when $A(q)$ is a minimum, $C'(q)=A(q)$. [3] (f) Verify numerically that the marginal cost and the average cost agree at the value of $q$ from part (d). [2] (g) The revenue is $R(q)=45q-0.02q^2$. Find $P(q)=R(q)-C(q)$ and use your calculator to find the production level that maximizes the daily profit, and the maximum profit. [4] (h) Show that at the profit-maximizing level marginal revenue equals marginal cost, and state the sign of $P''$ there. [2]
tips: Average cost is minimized where marginal cost equals average cost; profit is maximized where marginal revenue equals marginal cost. Check endpoints of the domain when optimizing on a closed interval.

subtopic: Minimizing trip cost with a speed limit
statement: A delivery truck makes a 400 km trip at a constant speed of $v$ km h$^{-1}$. The driver is paid \$45 per hour. The fuel cost for the whole trip is \$$0.018v^{2}$. Let \$$C$ be the total cost of the trip. (a) Show that $C(v)=\dfrac{18\,000}{v}+0.018v^{2}$. [2] (b) Find $\dfrac{dC}{dv}$. [2] (c) Find the speed that minimizes the cost, and the minimum cost, to three significant figures. [3] (d) The speed limit on the route is $70$ km h$^{-1}$. Find the minimum possible cost of the trip, to the nearest cent, justifying your answer. [2]
markscheme: (a) time $=\dfrac{400}{v}$ hours [M1] wages $=45\times\dfrac{400}{v}=\dfrac{18000}{v}$, so $C=\dfrac{18000}{v}+0.018v^{2}$ [AG] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac{dC}{dv}=-\dfrac{18000}{v^{2}}+0.036v$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (c) solve $\dfrac{dC}{dv}=0$ [M1] $v=79.4$ km h$^{-1}$ [A1] $C=\$340$ ($340.18$) [A1] [3 marks] (d) $C'(v)<0$ for $0<v<79.4$, so $C$ decreases up to the limit and the least cost is at $v=70$ [R1] $C(70)=\$345.34$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A constrained optimization problem may have its minimum at the boundary rather than at the stationary point. Check the sign of $C'$ on the allowed interval.

subtopic: Investigating the family x e^(-kx) as a drug concentration model
statement: This question investigates the family of functions $f(x)=xe^{-kx}$, for $x\ge0$ and $k>0$, which can model the concentration of a drug in the bloodstream. (a) Show that $f'(x)=(1-kx)e^{-kx}$. [2] (b) Find, in terms of $k$, the coordinates of the local maximum point of the graph of $f$, and justify that it is a maximum. [4] (c) Show that $f''(x)=k(kx-2)e^{-kx}$, and hence show that the graph of $f$ has exactly one point of inflection. Find its coordinates in terms of $k$. [5] (d) The concentration of a drug, in mg per liter, $t$ hours after it is taken is $C(t)=40te^{-0.5t}$. (i) Find the maximum concentration and the time at which it occurs. [2] (ii) Find the length of time for which the concentration exceeds 20 mg per liter, to three significant figures. [3] (e) Show that the tangent to the graph of $f$ at the point of inflection meets the $x$-axis at $x=\dfrac{4}{k}$. [4] (f) For the drug in part (d), use the result of part (e) to estimate when the drug is cleared from the blood. Find the actual concentration at that time, and comment on the estimate. [3] (g) A different drug has concentration $C(t)=Ate^{-kt}$. Its concentration is greatest at $t=3$ hours, where it equals 30 mg per liter. Find $k$ and $A$. [4]
markscheme: (a) product rule with $u=x$ and $v=e^{-kx}$ [M1] $f'(x)=e^{-kx}-kxe^{-kx}=(1-kx)e^{-kx}$ [AG] [2 marks] (b) $f'(x)=0$ and $e^{-kx}>0$ so $1-kx=0$ [M1] $x=\dfrac1k$ [A1] $f\!\left(\dfrac1k\right)=\dfrac{1}{ek}$, so $\left(\dfrac1k,\dfrac{1}{ek}\right)$ [A1] $f'>0$ for $x<\dfrac1k$ and $f'<0$ for $x>\dfrac1k$, so a maximum [R1] [4 marks] (c) $f''(x)=-ke^{-kx}+(1-kx)(-k)e^{-kx}$ [M1] $=k(kx-2)e^{-kx}$ [AG] $f''(x)=0$ gives $x=\dfrac2k$ [A1] $f''$ changes from negative to positive at $x=\dfrac2k$, so exactly one point of inflection [R1] $\left(\dfrac2k,\dfrac{2}{ke^{2}}\right)$ [A1] [5 marks] (d)(i) $C=40f$ with $k=0.5$: maximum at $t=2$ hours [A1] $C(2)=29.4$ mg/L [A1] (ii) solve $40te^{-0.5t}=20$ with the GDC [M1] $t=0.715$ and $t=4.31$ [A1] duration $=3.59$ hours [A1] [5 marks] (e) $f'\!\left(\dfrac2k\right)=(1-2)e^{-2}=-e^{-2}$ [A1] tangent: $y-\dfrac{2}{k}e^{-2}=-e^{-2}\left(x-\dfrac2k\right)$ [M1][A1] $y=0$ gives $x-\dfrac2k=\dfrac2k$, so $x=\dfrac4k$ [AG] [4 marks] (f) with $k=0.5$ the estimate is $t=8$ hours [A1] $C(8)=40(8)e^{-4}=5.86$ mg/L [A1] this is about $20\%$ of the maximum concentration, so the drug is not fully cleared and the estimate is too early [R1] [3 marks] (g) maximum at $t=\dfrac1k=3$, so $k=\dfrac13$ [M1][A1] $C(3)=3Ae^{-1}=30$ [M1] $A=10e=27.2$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Part (b) of this question is the key result: for the family $xe^{-kx}$ the maximum is at $x=1/k$. Reuse the results for general $k$ in parts (d), (f) and (g) rather than recomputing from scratch.

subtopic: Tangent and normal to a rational curve
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{x}{1+x^{2}}$ and let $A$ be the point on the graph where $x=2$. (a) Use the quotient rule to find $f'(x)$ and show that $f'(2)=-0.12$. [3] (b) Find the equation of the tangent at $A$ and the $x$-coordinate where it meets the $x$-axis, to three significant figures. [3] (c) Find the $x$-coordinate where the normal at $A$ meets the $x$-axis, to four significant figures. [3]
tips: The normal has gradient equal to the negative reciprocal of the tangent gradient.

subtopic: Largest window with a semicircular top
statement: A window is made from a rectangle of width $2r$ meters and height $h$ meters, with a semicircle of radius $r$ on top. The total length of the frame (the perimeter) is $12$ m. (a) Show that $h=6-r-\dfrac{\pi r}{2}$. [2] (b) Show that the area of the window is $A=12r-2r^2-\dfrac{\pi r^2}{2}$. [3] (c) Find the value of $r$ that maximizes $A$, and the maximum area. [3] (d) Find the corresponding height $h$ and state the ratio $h:r$. [2]
markscheme: (a) Perimeter $=2h+2r+\pi r=12$ [M1] (bottom side, two vertical sides and semicircular arc); rearranging gives $h=6-r-\dfrac{\pi r}2$ [AG] [2 marks] (b) $A=2rh+\dfrac12\pi r^2$ [M1]; $=2r\left(6-r-\dfrac{\pi r}{2}\right)+\dfrac{\pi r^2}{2}$ [A1]; $=12r-2r^2-\pi r^2+\dfrac{\pi r^2}{2}=12r-2r^2-\dfrac{\pi r^2}{2}$ [AG] [3 marks] (c) $\dfrac{dA}{dr}=12-4r-\pi r=0$ [M1]; $r=\dfrac{12}{4+\pi}=1.680$ [A1]; $A_{max}=10.08$ m$^2$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $h=1.680$ [A1]; $h=r$, ratio $1:1$ [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Write the perimeter equation in terms of $r$ and $h$, solve for $h$, and substitute into the area; the optimal window has height of the rectangle equal to the radius.

subtopic: Profit and break-even points
statement: A bakery sells $x$ dozen cakes per day. Revenue is $R(x)=40x-0.5x^2$ dollars and the cost is $C(x)=80+12x$ dollars. (a) Find an expression for the profit $P(x)$ in dollars. [2] (b) Find $\dfrac{dP}{dx}$ and hence the value of $x$ that maximizes the profit. [3] (c) Find the maximum profit. [1] (d) Use your calculator to find the values of $x$ between which the company makes a profit. [2]
tips: Break-even happens at the two values of $x$ where profit is zero.

subtopic: Points of inflection of a cubic
statement: Let $f(x)=x^{3}-6x^{2}+9x$. (a) Find $f'(x)$ and the coordinates of the stationary points. [4] (b) Find $f''(x)$ and classify the stationary points. [2] (c) Find the coordinates of the point of inflection. [2]
tips: A point of inflection occurs where $f''$ changes sign.

subtopic: Stationary point of a product with an exponential
statement: Let $f(x)=xe^{-2x}$ for $x\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Find $f'(x)$. [2] (b) Find the exact coordinates of the stationary point. [2] (c) Use the sign of $f'(x)$ either side of the stationary point to show that it is a maximum. [2]
markscheme: (a) product rule [M1]; $f'(x)=e^{-2x}-2xe^{-2x}=(1-2x)e^{-2x}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $1-2x=0$ [M1]; $\left(\dfrac12,\ \dfrac{1}{2e}\right)$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $f'>0$ for $x<\frac12$ and $f'<0$ for $x>\frac12$ [M1]; so a maximum [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The factor $e^{-2x}$ is never zero, so $f'(x)=0$ only when $1-2x=0$.

subtopic: A lifeguard running then swimming
statement: A lifeguard is on a straight beach and a swimmer is in trouble $30$ m from the shore, at a point whose nearest point on the shore is $80$ m along the beach from the lifeguard. The lifeguard runs along the beach a distance $s$ m at $6$ m/s and then swims in a straight line to the swimmer at $1.5$ m/s. (a) Show that the total time in seconds is $T(s)=\dfrac{s}{6}+\dfrac{\sqrt{900+(80-s)^{2}}}{1.5}$. [2] (b) Use your GDC to find the value of $s$ that minimizes the time, and the minimum time, each to three significant figures. [3] (c) Find the time if the lifeguard only swims from the start (that is, $s=0$) and compare it with the minimum. [2]
markscheme: (a) running time $\dfrac{s}{6}$ [A1]; swimming distance $\sqrt{30^{2}+(80-s)^{2}}$ at $1.5$ m/s [A1] [2 marks] (b) minimum of $T(s)$ for $0\le s\le80$ [M1]; $s=72.3$ m [A1]; $T=32.7$ s [A1] [3 marks] (c) $T(0)=57.0$ s [A1]; the best strategy is $24.3$ s quicker [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The best strategy runs most of the way along the beach because running is much faster than swimming.

subtopic: Tangent and normal to an exponential curve
statement: Let $y=x^2e^{-x}$. (a) Find the exact value of $y$ when $x=1$. [1] (b) Find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$. [3] (c) Find the equation of the tangent to the curve at the point where $x=1$. [2] (d) Find the equation of the normal to the curve at the point where $x=1$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $y=e^{-1}$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Product rule [M1] $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=2xe^{-x}-x^2e^{-x}$ [A1] $=(2x-x^2)e^{-x}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Gradient $=e^{-1}$ [A1] $y-e^{-1}=e^{-1}(x-1)$, so $y=\dfrac xe$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) Normal gradient $=-e$ [A1] $y-e^{-1}=-e(x-1)$, so $y=-ex+e+e^{-1}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The normal gradient is the negative reciprocal of the tangent gradient. Keep answers exact when no calculator is allowed.

subtopic: Chain rule, tangent, normal and stationary point
statement: Let $f(x)=(2x-1)^{4}$. (a) Find $f'(x)$. [2] (b) Find the equation of the tangent to the graph of $f$ at the point where $x=1$, in the form $y=mx+c$. [3] (c) Find the equation of the normal at the same point, in the form $ax+by+d=0$ with integer coefficients. [2] (d) Find the coordinates of the stationary point of the graph of $f$ and determine its nature. [3]
markscheme: (a) chain rule [M1]; $f'(x)=8(2x-1)^{3}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $f(1)=1$ and $f'(1)=8$ [A1]; $y-1=8(x-1)$ [M1]; $y=8x-7$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) gradient $-\dfrac18$ so $y-1=-\dfrac18(x-1)$ [M1]; $x+8y-9=0$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $8(2x-1)^{3}=0$ so $x=\dfrac12$ [M1]; $\left(\dfrac12, 0\right)$ [A1]; $f'$ changes from negative to positive, so it is a minimum [R1] [3 marks]
tips: The normal has gradient equal to the negative reciprocal of the tangent's gradient.

subtopic: Drug concentration in the bloodstream
statement: The concentration $C$ (mg/L) of a drug in the blood $t$ hours after an injection is $C(t)=20te^{-0.5t}$ for $t\ge0$. (a) Find the time at which the concentration is greatest and the maximum concentration, to three significant figures. [3] (b) Find the rate of change of the concentration at $t=1$, to three significant figures, and state whether the concentration is increasing. [2] (c) Use your GDC to find the times between which the concentration exceeds $10$ mg/L. [3]
markscheme: (a) $C'(t)=20(1-0.5t)e^{-0.5t}$ [A1]; $t=2$ hours [A1]; $C(2)=14.7$ mg/L [A1] [3 marks] (b) $C'(1)=20(0.5)e^{-0.5}=6.07$ mg/L per hour [A1]; positive, so increasing [A1] [2 marks] (c) solve $20te^{-0.5t}=10$ [M1]; $t=0.715$ and $t=4.31$ [A1]; the concentration exceeds $10$ mg/L for $0.715<t<4.31$ hours [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A maximum occurs where $C'(t)=0$ and $C'$ changes from positive to negative.

subtopic: Tangent and normal using the product rule
statement: The function $f$ is defined by $f(x)=x^{2} e^{x}$. (a) Find $f'(x)$. [3] (b) Find the equation of the tangent to the curve at $x=1$. [3] (c) Find the equation of the normal at $x=1$ and the coordinates of the point where the normal meets the $x$-axis. [3]
markscheme: (a) Using the product rule [M1][A1]: $f'(x)=x \left(x + 2\right) e^{x}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $f(1)=e$ [A1]; $f'(1)=3 e$ [A1]; $y-e=3 e(x-1)$ so $y=3 e x - 2 e$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Normal gradient $=-\dfrac{1}{3 e}=-\frac{1}{3 e}$ [A1]; $y=-\frac{x}{3 e} + \frac{1}{3 e} + e$ [A1]; at $y=0$, $x=1 + 3 e^{2}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Apply $(uv)'=u'v+uv'$ and simplify before substituting; the normal gradient is the negative reciprocal of the tangent gradient.

subtopic: Optimizing a cylindrical can
statement: This question investigates the design of a closed cylindrical can with volume $500$ cm$^{3}$. The can has radius $r$ cm and height $h$ cm. (a) Show that the total surface area is $A=2\pi r^{2}+\dfrac{1000}{r}$. [3] (b) Find $\dfrac{dA}{dr}$ and hence find the value of $r$ that gives a stationary point, correct to 3 significant figures. [3] (c) Show that this value of $r$ gives a minimum, and find the minimum surface area, correct to 3 significant figures. [3] (d) Show that, for this can, $h=2r$. [2] (e) Metal for the curved side costs $0.004$ dollars per cm$^{2}$ and for the top and base costs $0.007$ dollars per cm$^{2}$. Show that the cost is $C=0.014\pi r^{2}+\dfrac{4}{r}$ dollars, and find the radius that minimizes $C$, correct to 3 significant figures. [5]
tips: Use $V=\pi r^{2}h$ to eliminate $h$ before differentiating. Check the second derivative to confirm a minimum.

subtopic: Differentiating powers and finding a tangent
statement: Let $f(x)=3\sqrt x-\dfrac4{x^2}+5$, for $x>0$. (a) Find $f'(x)$. [3] (b) Find the gradient of the graph of $f$ at the point where $x=4$. [1] (c) Find the equation of the tangent to the graph of $f$ at the point where $x=4$, in the form $y=mx+c$. [3]
tips: Rewrite roots and reciprocals as powers of $x$ before differentiating. Evaluate $f(4)$ separately to obtain the point of tangency.

subtopic: Binomial model with exact answers
statement: A fair coin is tossed six times and $X$ is the number of heads. (a) State the distribution of $X$, the number of successes in 6 trials. [1] (b) Find $P(X=2)$, giving your answer as a fraction in its simplest form. [2] (c) Find the probability of at least one success. [2] (d) Write down $E(X)$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)$. [2]
tips: With $p=\tfrac12$ every outcome with $k$ heads has probability $1/2^6$, so $P(X=k)=\binom6k/64$.

subtopic: Normal distribution: finding mean and standard deviation from percentiles
statement: The random variable $X$ is normally distributed with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$. It is known that $P(X<42)=0.1$ and $P(X>71)=0.2$. (a) Find the values of $\mu$ and $\sigma$. [5] (b) Find $P(X>65)$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{42-\mu}{\sigma}=-1.2816$ [A1] $\dfrac{71-\mu}{\sigma}=0.8416$ [A1] Attempt to solve the simultaneous equations (e.g. subtract) [M1] $\sigma=\dfrac{29}{2.1232}=13.7$ [A1] $\mu=59.5$ [A1] [5 marks] (b) $X\sim\mathrm{N}(59.5,\,13.7^2)$ [M1] $P(X>65)=0.344$ [A1] (using unrounded values from part (a); accept $0.343$ to $0.344$) [2 marks]
tips: Convert each percentile to a $z$-value with the inverse normal function; the lower percentile gives a negative $z$. Use unrounded values of $\mu$ and $\sigma$ in later parts.

subtopic: Normal distribution: symmetry and conditional probability without a calculator
statement: Let $X$ follow a normal distribution with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$. Two tail probabilities are known: $P(X<8)=0.15$ and $P(X>18)=0.15$. (a) Show that $\mu=13$. [2] (b) Find $P(8<X<18)$. [2] (c) Find $P(X<13\mid X<18)$, giving your answer as a fraction in its simplest form. [3] Two independent observations of $X$ are made. (d) Find the probability that exactly one of them lies between 8 and 18. [2]
markscheme: (a) The normal distribution is symmetric about $\mu$ and the two tail probabilities are equal, so 8 and 18 are equidistant from $\mu$ [R1] $\mu=\dfrac{8+18}{2}=13$ [AG] [A1] [2 marks] (b) $P(8<X<18)=1-0.15-0.15$ [M1] $=0.7$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $P(X<13\mid X<18)=\dfrac{P(X<13)}{P(X<18)}$ [M1] $P(X<13)=0.5$ [A1] $P(X<18)=1-0.15=0.85$, so the probability is $\dfrac{0.5}{0.85}=\dfrac{10}{17}$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $2\times0.7\times0.3$ [M1] $=0.42$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Without a calculator, use the symmetry of the normal curve about the mean and the fact that $P(X<\mu)=0.5$. In a conditional probability, check that the event in the numerator is contained in the event in the denominator.

subtopic: A triangular density function and its variance
statement: A continuous random variable $X$ has probability density function $f(x)=k(1-|x|)$ for $-1\le x\le1$, and $f(x)=0$ otherwise. (a) Find $k$. [3] (b) Explain why $E(X)=0$. [1] (c) Find $\operatorname{Var}(X)$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $2\displaystyle\int_0^1k(1-x)\,dx$ by symmetry [M1] $=2k\left[x-\dfrac{x^2}2\right]_0^1=k$ [A1] so $k=1$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) the density is symmetric about $x=0$ [R1] [1 mark] (c) $\operatorname{Var}(X)=E(X^2)=2\displaystyle\int_0^1x^2(1-x)\,dx$ [M1] $=2\left[\dfrac{x^3}3-\dfrac{x^4}4\right]_0^1$ [A1] $=\dfrac16$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Split the integral at 0, or use the symmetry of the graph about the $y$-axis to double the integral from 0 to 1.

subtopic: Normal probabilities and percentiles
statement: The time taken by customers to complete an online form is modeled. The quantity $X$ is normally distributed with mean $45$ seconds and standard deviation $6$ seconds. (a) Find $P(X<40)$. [1] (b) Find $P(40<X<55)$. [2] (c) Find the value $q$ such that $P(X<q)=0.25$. [2] (d) Find the probability that a value is more than 55 seconds, given that it is more than 40 seconds. [3]
markscheme: (a) $P(X<40)=0.202$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) normal cdf between the limits [M1] $=0.750$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $q$ from inverse normal [M1] $q=40.95$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $P(X>55\mid X>40)=\dfrac{P(X>55)}{P(X>40)}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{0.04779}{0.7977}$ [A1] $=0.0599$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Define the normal distribution on your calculator, then use cdf for probabilities and inverse normal for percentiles. A conditional probability with $X>b$ inside $X>a$ is a ratio of two tail areas.

subtopic: Finding n and p of a binomial from its mean and variance
statement: The random variable $X$ follows a binomial distribution with mean $6$ and variance $4.2$. (a) Find the parameters $n$ and $p$. [4] (b) Find $P(X=6)$ and $P(X\ge8)$. [3]
tips: Divide the variance by the mean to isolate $1-p$. Then use binomial pdf and cdf on your calculator.

subtopic: Delivery times: conditional normal probability and percentiles
statement: The delivery time $X$ minutes of a meal is normally distributed with mean $32$ and standard deviation $6$. (a) Find the probability that a delivery takes more than $40$ minutes. [2] (b) Given that a delivery takes more than $35$ minutes, find the probability that it takes more than $40$ minutes. [3] (c) Find the time that is exceeded by $10\%$ of deliveries. [2] (d) Twelve deliveries are made independently. Find the probability that exactly two take more than $40$ minutes. [2]
tips: For a conditional probability with a threshold inside another, the numerator is the smaller event: $P(X>40\text{ and }X>35)=P(X>40)$. Use the unrounded value of $P(X>40)$ in part (d).

subtopic: Binomial probabilities, mean, variance and mode
statement: The random variable $X$ is binomially distributed with $n=15$ and $p=0.35$. (a) Find $\mathrm{E}(X)$ and $\mathrm{Var}(X)$. [2] (b) Find $P(X=5)$. [1] (c) Find $P(X\ge8)$. [2] (d) Write down the mode of $X$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\mathrm{E}(X)=15\times0.35=5.25$ [A1] $\mathrm{Var}(X)=15\times0.35\times0.65=3.41$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $P(X=5)=0.212$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $P(X\ge8)=1-P(X\le7)$ [M1] $=0.113$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) Mode $=5$ [A1] (since $P(X=5)=0.212$ is the largest probability, compared with $P(X=4)=0.179$ and $P(X=6)=0.191$) [1 mark]
tips: For 'at least' probabilities use the complement, $1-P(X\le k-1)$, taking care with the boundary value. The mode is the value with the largest probability; check its neighbors on your GDC.

subtopic: The exponential distribution and its memoryless property
statement: The lifetime $X$ (in years) of a component has probability density function $f(x)=\lambda e^{-\lambda x}$ for $x\ge0$, where $\lambda>0$, and $f(x)=0$ otherwise. (a) Show that $f$ is a valid probability density function. [2] (b) Use integration by parts to show that $E(X)=\dfrac1\lambda$. [4] (c) Find the median of $X$ in terms of $\lambda$. [3] (d) Show that $P(X>s+t\mid X>s)=P(X>t)$ for $s,t>0$. [3] (e) The mean lifetime is $2$ years. Given that a component has already lasted $1$ year, find the probability that it lasts more than $3$ years in total. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\displaystyle\int_0^b\lambda e^{-\lambda x}dx=1-e^{-\lambda b}$ [M1] as $b\to\infty$ this tends to $1$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $E(X)=\displaystyle\int_0^\infty\lambda xe^{-\lambda x}dx$, with $u=x$, $v'=\lambda e^{-\lambda x}$ [M1] $=\left[-xe^{-\lambda x}\right]_0^\infty+\displaystyle\int_0^\infty e^{-\lambda x}dx$ [A1] the first term is $0$ since $xe^{-\lambda x}\to0$ [R1] $=\dfrac1\lambda$ [AG] [A1] [4 marks] (c) $P(X\le m)=1-e^{-\lambda m}$ [A1] $1-e^{-\lambda m}=\dfrac12$ [M1] $m=\dfrac{\ln2}\lambda$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $P(X>a)=e^{-\lambda a}$ [A1] $\dfrac{P(X>s+t)}{P(X>s)}=\dfrac{e^{-\lambda(s+t)}}{e^{-\lambda s}}$ [M1] $=e^{-\lambda t}=P(X>t)$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) $\lambda=0.5$ [A1] by the result above, $P(X>2)=e^{-1}=0.368$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: For the mean, differentiate $x$ and integrate $\lambda e^{-\lambda x}$. For the conditional probability, use $P(A\mid B)=P(A\cap B)/P(B)$, noting $X>s+t$ implies $X>s$.

subtopic: Normal probability feeding a binomial model
statement: The mass of a packet of rice is normally distributed with mean $250$ g and standard deviation $4$ g. A packet is underweight if its mass is less than $243$ g. (a) Find the probability that a randomly chosen packet is underweight, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (b) An inspector takes a random sample of $20$ packets. Using the unrounded probability from part (a), find the probability that at most $2$ packets are underweight, correct to 3 significant figures. [3] (c) A batch of $500$ packets is produced. Estimate the number of underweight packets, to the nearest whole number. [2] (d) The inspector rejects a batch if a sample of $20$ contains more than $2$ underweight packets. Find the probability that a batch is rejected, correct to 3 significant figures. [1]
tips: Use the normal distribution to get the success probability, then the binomial distribution for the sample.

subtopic: Defective items in a batch of 25
statement: Each item produced by a machine is independently defective with probability $0.08$. A batch contains $25$ items and $X$ is the number of defective items in a batch. (a) Find $P(X=2)$ and $P(X\ge4)$, to three significant figures. [3] (b) Find the mean and standard deviation of $X$. [2] (c) Find the most likely number of defective items in a batch, justifying your answer using your GDC. [2]
markscheme: (a) $X\sim B(25,\,0.08)$ [A1]; $P(X=2)=0.282$ [A1]; $P(X\ge4)=1-P(X\le3)=0.135$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) mean $=25\times0.08=2$ [A1]; standard deviation $=\sqrt{25\times0.08\times0.92}=1.36$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $P(X=1)=0.270$, $P(X=2)=0.282$, $P(X=3)=0.188$ [A1]; the greatest probability is at $X=2$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Use the binomial pdf for exact values and the cdf for cumulative probabilities.

subtopic: Infinite discrete distribution with geometric probabilities
statement: The discrete random variable $X$ takes the values $1,2,3,\ldots$ with $P(X=x)=k\left(\dfrac13\right)^x$. (a) Use the sum to infinity of a geometric series to show that $k=2$. [3] (b) Find $P(X\ge3)$. [3] (c) Find the probability that $X$ is even. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\displaystyle\sum_{x=1}^\infty k\left(\dfrac13\right)^x$ is geometric with $u_1=\dfrac k3$, $r=\dfrac13$ [M1] $S_\infty=\dfrac{k/3}{2/3}=\dfrac k2$ [A1] $\dfrac k2=1$ so $k=2$ [AG] [A1] [3 marks] (b) $P(X\ge3)=2\left(\dfrac1{27}+\dfrac1{81}+\cdots\right)$ [M1] $=\dfrac{2/27}{2/3}$ [A1] $=\dfrac19$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $P(X=2)+P(X=4)+\cdots=2\left(\dfrac19+\dfrac1{81}+\cdots\right)$ [M1] common ratio $\dfrac19$ [A1] $=2\times\dfrac{1/9}{8/9}=\dfrac14$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The probabilities form an infinite geometric series with ratio $\tfrac13$. For even values of $x$ the ratio becomes $\tfrac19$.

subtopic: Normal then binomial
statement: The masses of apples from an orchard are normally distributed with mean $150$ g and standard deviation $12$ g. An apple is classified as premium if its mass is greater than $165$ g. (a) Find the probability that a randomly chosen apple is premium. [2] A box contains 12 apples chosen at random. (b) Find the probability that the box contains at least 3 premium apples. [3] (c) The heaviest $5\%$ of apples are rejected as oversized. Find the least mass of a rejected apple. [2] (d) Find the expected number of premium apples in the box. [1]
markscheme: (a) $M\sim N(150,12^2)$ [M1] $P(M>165)=0.106$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Let $Y$ be the number of premium apples: $Y\sim B(12,0.10565)$ [M1] $P(Y\ge3)=1-P(Y\le2)$ [M1] $=0.126$ [A1] Use the unrounded value of $p$ from part (a); accept $0.127$ if $p=0.106$ was used. [3 marks] (c) $P(M>w)=0.05$, so $P(M<w)=0.95$ [M1] $w=169.7$ g [A1] Accept $170$. [2 marks] (d) $12\times0.10565=1.27$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Store the unrounded probability from the normal calculation and reuse it as the binomial parameter. Link the two distributions explicitly by writing $Y\sim B(12,p)$.

subtopic: Normal model for cereal box masses
statement: The mass, $X$ grams, of cereal in a box is normally distributed with mean $502$ and standard deviation $4.5$. (a) Find the probability that a randomly chosen box contains less than $495$ g. [2] (b) Find the probability that a randomly chosen box contains between $498$ g and $510$ g. [2] (c) Find the mass that is exceeded by $5\%$ of boxes. Give your answer to three significant figures. [2] (d) A delivery contains $500$ boxes. Find the expected number of boxes that contain less than $495$ g, to the nearest whole number. [1]
tips: Use normal cdf for probabilities and inverse normal for a given probability. A mass exceeded by $5\%$ of boxes is the $95$th percentile. Expected number $=n\times p$.

subtopic: Distribution of the larger of two dice
statement: Two fair six-sided dice are rolled, and $M$ is the larger of the two scores (equal to the common score if they are equal). (a) Show that $P(M=m)=\dfrac{2m-1}{36}$ for $m=1,2,\ldots,6$. [3] (b) Find $E(M)$ as an exact fraction and the standard deviation of $M$ to three significant figures. [4]
markscheme: (a) $P(M\le m)=\left(\dfrac m6\right)^2$ [M1] $P(M=m)=\dfrac{m^2-(m-1)^2}{36}$ [A1] $=\dfrac{2m-1}{36}$ [AG] [A1] [3 marks] (b) $E(M)=\dfrac{1\times1+2\times3+\cdots+6\times11}{36}=\dfrac{161}{36}$ [M1][A1] $\operatorname{Var}(M)=\dfrac{2555}{1296}$ [M1] standard deviation $=1.40$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: The larger score is at most $m$ only if both dice show at most $m$.

subtopic: Trials until the first success
statement: A treatment works for a patient with probability $0.35$, independently for each patient. Patients are treated one at a time. (a) Find the probability that the first patient helped by the treatment is the fourth patient treated. [2] (b) Find the probability that none of the first five patients is helped. [2] (c) Given that none of the first two patients was helped, find the probability that none of the first five is helped, and explain why this is $0.65^3$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $0.65^3\times0.35$ [M1] $=0.0961$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $0.65^5$ [M1] $=0.116$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\dfrac{P(\text{none of first }5)}{P(\text{none of first }2)}=\dfrac{0.65^5}{0.65^2}$ [M1] $=0.275$ [A1] the later patients are independent of the earlier ones, so only the next three matter [R1] [3 marks]
tips: For the first success on trial $k$ you need $k-1$ failures followed by a success. Independence means earlier results do not affect later ones.

subtopic: From the binomial to the Poisson: faults in cable and hypothesis tests
statement: This question investigates how the Poisson distribution arises from the binomial distribution and uses it to test a claim about the rate of faults in a cable. Faults occur randomly along a cable at a mean rate of $\lambda$ per kilometer. Consider one kilometer of cable divided into $n$ equal sections. Each section independently contains a fault with probability $\frac{\lambda}{n}$, so the number of faults $X$ in the kilometer is modeled by $X\sim\mathrm{B}\left(n,\frac{\lambda}{n}\right)$. (a) For $\lambda=2$, find $P(X=0)$ when $n=10$, $n=100$ and $n=1000$. Give each answer to three significant figures. [3] (b) Write down $\mathrm{e}^{-2}$ to three significant figures and state the Poisson distribution that $X$ approaches as $n$ becomes large. [2] (c) For $X\sim\mathrm{B}(n,p)$, show that $\dfrac{P(X=k+1)}{P(X=k)}=\dfrac{n-k}{k+1}\times\dfrac{p}{1-p}$. Hence show that, when $p=\dfrac{\lambda}{n}$, this ratio tends to $\dfrac{\lambda}{k+1}$ as $n\to\infty$. [3] (d) For $X\sim\mathrm{Po}(4.6)$, use the ratio $\dfrac{P(X=k+1)}{P(X=k)}=\dfrac{4.6}{k+1}$ with $P(X=0)=\mathrm{e}^{-4.6}$ to find $P(X=4)$ and $P(X=5)$, and hence write down the mode of $X$. [4] A cable manufacturer claims that a new process has reduced the mean number of faults below the previous rate of $1.2$ per kilometer. A $5$ km length of cable made by the new process has $3$ faults. (e) Test the claim at the $5\%$ significance level, stating your hypotheses, the distribution used, the $p$-value and your conclusion. [4] (f) Find the critical region for this test on a $5$ km length, and the actual probability of a Type I error. [4] (g) Suppose the true mean rate is in fact $0.5$ faults per kilometer. Find the probability that the test in part (f) correctly rejects the null hypothesis. [3] The test is now applied to a length of $L$ km, where $L$ is a whole number, using the largest critical region $X\le c$ whose probability under the null hypothesis does not exceed $5\%$. (h) Find the smallest $L$ for which the probability of rejecting the null hypothesis is at least $0.8$ when the true rate is $0.5$ per kilometer. [2] (i) Find the power of the test for $L=12$, and comment on your answer in relation to part (h). [3]
markscheme: (a) $P(X=0)=\left(1-\frac2n\right)^n$ [M1] $n=10$: $0.107$; $n=100$: $0.133$; $n=1000$: $0.135$ [A1][A1] [3 marks] (b) $\mathrm{e}^{-2}=0.135$ [A1] $X\to\mathrm{Po}(2)$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\dfrac{P(X=k+1)}{P(X=k)}=\dfrac{\binom n{k+1}p^{k+1}(1-p)^{n-k-1}}{\binom nkp^k(1-p)^{n-k}}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{n-k}{k+1}\times\dfrac{p}{1-p}$ [A1] With $p=\frac{\lambda}{n}$: ratio $=\dfrac{n-k}{k+1}\times\dfrac{\lambda}{n-\lambda}\to\dfrac{\lambda}{k+1}$ since $\dfrac{n-k}{n-\lambda}\to1$ [R1] [3 marks] (d) $P(X=1)=4.6\mathrm{e}^{-4.6}=0.0462$, $P(X=2)=0.1063$, $P(X=3)=0.1631$ [M1] $P(X=4)=\dfrac{4.6}{4}\times0.1631=0.188$ [A1] $P(X=5)=\dfrac{4.6}{5}\times0.1875=0.173$ [A1] Mode is $4$, since the ratio $\frac{4.6}{k+1}>1$ for $k\le3$ and $<1$ for $k\ge4$ [A1] [4 marks] (e) $\mathrm{H}_0:\lambda=1.2$ per km, $\mathrm{H}_1:\lambda<1.2$ per km [A1] Under $\mathrm{H}_0$, $X\sim\mathrm{Po}(6)$ for $5$ km [M1] $p$-value $=P(X\le3)=0.151$ [A1] $0.151>0.05$ so do not reject $\mathrm{H}_0$; there is insufficient evidence that the new process reduces the fault rate [A1] [4 marks] (f) $P(X\le2)=0.0620>0.05$ [M1] and $P(X\le1)=0.0174\le0.05$ [A1] Critical region $X\le1$ [A1] Probability of Type I error $=0.0174$ [A1] [4 marks] (g) Under the true rate, $X\sim\mathrm{Po}(2.5)$ [M1] $P(X\le1)$ [M1] $=0.287$ [A1] [3 marks] (h) Evaluate the power for increasing $L$ (critical region $c$ from $\mathrm{Po}(1.2L)$, power from $\mathrm{Po}(0.5L)$): $L=10$ gives $0.762$ [M1] $L=11$ gives $0.809$, so smallest $L=11$ [A1] [2 marks] (i) For $L=12$: under $\mathrm{H}_0$, $X\sim\mathrm{Po}(14.4)$ and the critical region is $X\le7$ [A1] Power $=P(X\le7)$ with $X\sim\mathrm{Po}(6)=0.744$, which is below $0.8$ [A1] Because the distribution is discrete the actual significance level drops for $L=12$ ($0.0253$ compared with $0.0487$ for $L=11$), so the power is not increasing steadily with $L$ [R1] [3 marks]
tips: In part (c), write each binomial coefficient out and cancel; the limit uses $\frac{n-k}{n-\lambda}\to1$. For tests with a Poisson distribution, always rescale the mean to the length of cable examined. In (h) and (i), remember that a discrete test cannot use the full $5\%$, so the power can move up and down as $L$ changes.

subtopic: Discrete random variable: unknown probabilities, mean and variance
statement: A fair-looking game assigns scores to a spinner. The probability distribution of a discrete random variable $X$ is given by $P(X=x)=kx$ for $x=1,2,3,4$, where $k$ is a constant. (a) Find the value of $k$. [2] (b) Find $P(X\ge3)$. [1] (c) Find $E(X)$. [2] (d) Find $\operatorname{Var}(X)$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\sum P(X=x)=1$ [M1] gives $k=\frac{1}{10}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $P(X\ge3)=P(3)+P(4)=\frac{7}{10}$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $E(X)=\sum xP(X=x)$ [M1] $=3$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $E(X^2)=10$ [A1] $\operatorname{Var}(X)=E(X^2)-[E(X)]^2$ [M1] $=1$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The probabilities must sum to $1$. Use $\operatorname{Var}(X)=E(X^2)-[E(X)]^2$.

subtopic: Normal and binomial distributions
statement: The masses of bags of rice filled by a machine are normally distributed with mean $1012$ grams and standard deviation $6$ grams. (a) Find the probability that a randomly chosen bag has a mass of less than $1000$ grams. [2] (b) Ten bags are chosen at random. Find the probability that at least two of them have a mass of less than $1000$ grams. [3] (c) Find the mass $m$ such that $95\%$ of bags have a mass greater than $m$ grams. [2]
tips: Recognize when a normal probability becomes the success probability of a binomial model, and carry the unrounded value forward. For at least two, use $1-P(Y\le 1)$.

subtopic: Normal probabilities from given standard normal values
statement: The mass, $X$ grams, of a loaf of bread is normally distributed with mean $750$ and standard deviation $20$. You are given that $P(Z\le1)=0.8413$ and $P(Z\le1.5)=0.9332$, where $Z\sim\mathrm{N}(0,1)$. (a) Find $P(X<730)$. [2] (b) Find $P(730<X<780)$. [3] (c) Find the value of $c$ such that $P(X>c)=0.1587$. [2]
tips: Standardize with $z=\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$ and use the symmetry $P(Z<-a)=1-P(Z<a)$. In part (c) recognize the tail probability $0.1587$ as $P(Z>1)$.

subtopic: Median, mode and conditional probability of a discrete variable
statement: The probability distribution of a discrete random variable $X$ is given by: $P(X=1)=0.15$, $P(X=2)=0.25$, $P(X=3)=0.30$, $P(X=4)=0.20$, $P(X=5)=0.10$. (a) Find the mode of $X$ and the median of $X$. [3] (b) Find $E(X)$. [2] (c) Find $P(X\ge2\mid X\le4)$. [3]
tips: The median is the smallest value at which the cumulative probability reaches $0.5$ or more.

subtopic: Normal distribution: symmetry and conditional probability without a calculator
statement: The mass $M$ kg of a parcel is normally distributed with mean $40$ and $P(M<30)=0.15$. (a) Find $P(M>50)$. [1] (b) Find $P(30<M<50)$. [2] (c) Find $P(M<40\mid M<50)$. [3]
tips: A conditional probability $P(A\mid B)$ with $A\subset B$ is $P(A)/P(B)$. Use symmetry to read off the tail probabilities.

subtopic: Binomial parameters from the mean and variance
statement: A random variable $X$ has a binomial distribution with mean $12$ and variance $7.2$. (a) Find the probability of success $p$ and the number of trials $n$. [4] (b) Write down the standard deviation of $X$ to three significant figures. [1]
tips: Divide the variance by the mean to find $1-p$.

subtopic: Normal probabilities and percentiles
statement: The heights of adult women in a town are normally distributed with mean $172$ cm and standard deviation $6.5$ cm. (a) Find the probability that a randomly chosen woman has a height between $160$ cm and $180$ cm. [2] (b) Find the probability that a randomly chosen woman is taller than $185$ cm. [1] (c) The tallest $10\%$ of women are at least $h$ cm tall. Find $h$, correct to the nearest cm. [2] (d) In a random sample of 200 women, find the expected number who are taller than $185$ cm. [2]
tips: Identify the distribution and the required probability before using the calculator; for inverse normal, make sure you are using the area to the left. Expected frequency is $n\times$ probability.

subtopic: Normal, Poisson and binomial models
statement: A machine fills bags of coffee labeled $500$ g. The mass, $X$ grams, of coffee in a bag is normally distributed with mean $502$ g and standard deviation $4.5$ g. (a) Find the probability that a randomly chosen bag contains less than $500$ g. [2] (b) Find the mass exceeded by $90\%$ of bags. [2] (c) The manufacturer adjusts the mean, keeping the standard deviation unchanged, so that only $2\%$ of bags contain less than $500$ g. Find the new mean. [3] (d) Before the adjustment, $12$ bags are chosen at random. Find the probability that at most $2$ of them contain less than $500$ g. [3] (e) The number of customer complaints received per week follows a Poisson distribution with mean $1.8$. (i) Find the probability of exactly $3$ complaints in a week. (ii) Find the probability of more than $10$ complaints in a period of $4$ weeks. [4]
tips: When scaling a Poisson distribution to a longer period, multiply the mean (1.8 × 4 = 7.2). Carry the unrounded normal probability into the binomial part to avoid accuracy penalties.

subtopic: Linear combinations of independent normal masses
statement: A shipping company packs parcels. The mass of a large box is normally distributed with mean $12.4$ kg and standard deviation $0.8$ kg, and the mass of a crate is normally distributed with mean $9.6$ kg and standard deviation $1.1$ kg. All masses are independent. (a) Find the mean and variance of the total mass $W$ of four boxes and one crate. [3] (b) Find $P(W>64.2)$. [2] (c) Find the probability that a randomly chosen box is heavier than a randomly chosen crate. [3]
tips: The variance of a sum of independent variables is the sum of the variances; for a sum of four boxes use $4\sigma^2$, not $(4\sigma)^2$.

subtopic: Binomial probabilities with a calculator
statement: Each seed planted in a nursery germinates with probability $0.4$, independently of the others. Fifteen seeds are planted. Let $X$ be the number of successes, so that $X\sim B(15,0.4)$. (a) Find $P(X=6)$. [2] (b) Find $P(X\le4)$. [2] (c) Find $P(X\ge9)$. [2] (d) Find the mean and the standard deviation of $X$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $P(X=6)=\binom{15}{6}0.4^{6}(1-0.4)^{9}$ [M1] $=0.207$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $P(X\le4)$ using binomial cdf [M1] $=0.217$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $P(X\ge9)=1-P(X\le8)$ [M1] $=0.0950$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) mean $=15\times0.4=6.000$ [A1] standard deviation $=\sqrt{15\times0.4\times0.6000}=1.90$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: State $X\sim B(n,p)$ and use the binomial pdf and cdf functions. For 'at least', use the complement of the cdf.

subtopic: Linear combinations of independent random variables
statement: The random variable $X$ has $E(X)=5$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=4$. (a) Let $Y=3X-2$. Find $E(Y)$ and $\operatorname{Var}(Y)$. [2] Let $X_1$ and $X_2$ be two independent observations of $X$. (b) Find $E(2X_1-X_2)$ and $\operatorname{Var}(2X_1-X_2)$. [3] (c) Find $E(X^2)$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $E(Y)=3(5)-2=13$ [A1] $\operatorname{Var}(Y)=3^2\times4=36$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $E(2X_1-X_2)=2(5)-5=5$ [A1] $\operatorname{Var}(2X_1-X_2)=2^2\operatorname{Var}(X_1)+(-1)^2\operatorname{Var}(X_2)$ [M1] $=16+4=20$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $E(X^2)=\operatorname{Var}(X)+[E(X)]^2=4+25=29$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: The variance of a linear combination of independent variables uses the squares of the coefficients and ignores constants, so subtraction still adds variances. Rearrange $\operatorname{Var}(X)=E(X^2)-[E(X)]^2$ for $E(X^2)$.

subtopic: Normal probabilities and percentiles
statement: The masses of bags of rice filled by a machine are recorded. The quantity $X$ is normally distributed with mean $500$ g and standard deviation $12$ g. (a) Find $P(X<490)$. [1] (b) Find $P(490<X<520)$. [2] (c) Find the value $q$ such that $P(X<q)=0.9$. [2] (d) Find the probability that a value is more than 520 g, given that it is more than 490 g. [3]
markscheme: (a) $P(X<490)=0.202$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) normal cdf between the limits [M1] $=0.750$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $q$ from inverse normal [M1] $q=515.4$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $P(X>520\mid X>490)=\dfrac{P(X>520)}{P(X>490)}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{0.04779}{0.7977}$ [A1] $=0.0599$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Define the normal distribution on your calculator, then use cdf for probabilities and inverse normal for percentiles. A conditional probability with $X>b$ inside $X>a$ is a ratio of two tail areas.

subtopic: Inverse normal to set a mean
statement: A machine fills bottles with water. The volume of water in a bottle, $V$ ml, is normally distributed with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $4$ ml. The machine is set so that $2\%$ of bottles contain less than $500$ ml. (a) Find the value of $\mu$, correct to one decimal place. [3] (b) Given that $\mu=508.2$, find the probability that a randomly chosen bottle contains more than $510$ ml. [2] (c) Five bottles are chosen at random. Find the probability that at least one contains less than $500$ ml. [2]
tips: Standardize using the inverse normal function so that $\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$ equals the $z$-value from the tail area, then solve for the unknown. In part (c), use the exact probability $0.02$ from the stem.

subtopic: Finding n and p from the mean and variance of a binomial
statement: The random variable $X$ is binomially distributed, $X\sim\mathrm{B}(n,p)$, with $\mathrm{E}(X)=6$ and $\mathrm{Var}(X)=4.2$. (a) Show that $1-p=0.7$. [2] (b) Find the values of $p$ and $n$. [2] (c) Find $\mathrm{E}(3X-2)$ and $\mathrm{Var}(3X-2)$. [3] (d) Write down an expression for $P(X=0)$. [1]
tips: Dividing the variance by the mean eliminates $n$ and leaves $1-p$. For a linear transformation $aX+b$, the mean is $a\mathrm{E}(X)+b$ but the variance is $a^2\mathrm{Var}(X)$ with no effect from $b$.

subtopic: Finding a Poisson mean from a probability
statement: The number of faults $X$ in a roll of cable is modeled by a Poisson distribution with mean $\lambda$. It is known that $P(X=0)=0.15$. (a) Show that $\lambda=\ln\dfrac{20}{3}$ and write down its value correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (b) Find $P(X\ge3)$. [2] (c) Two independent rolls are inspected. Find the probability that the total number of faults is exactly $4$. [2] (d) Find the smallest integer $k$ such that $P(X\le k)\ge0.99$. [2]
tips: Use the exact value of $\lambda=-\ln0.15$ in later parts. For sums of independent Poisson variables, add the means.

subtopic: Continuous random variable with an exponential pdf
statement: The time $T$ minutes spent waiting for a bus has probability density function $f(t)=ke^{-t/4}$ for $t\ge0$, and $f(t)=0$ otherwise. (a) Show that $k=\dfrac14$. [3] (b) Find $P(T>6)$. [2] (c) Find $E(T)$. [2] (d) Find the median waiting time. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\displaystyle\int_0^\infty ke^{-t/4}\,dt=1$ [M1] $\left[-4ke^{-t/4}\right]_0^\infty=4k$ [A1] $4k=1$ so $k=\dfrac14$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\displaystyle\int_6^\infty\dfrac14e^{-t/4}\,dt=e^{-1.5}$ [M1] $=0.223$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\displaystyle\int_0^\infty \dfrac t4e^{-t/4}\,dt$ [M1] $=4$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $\displaystyle\int_0^m\dfrac14e^{-t/4}\,dt=\dfrac12$ gives $1-e^{-m/4}=\dfrac12$ [M1][A1] $m=4\ln2=2.77$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The area under $f$ must equal $1$. Use integration (or your calculator) over $[0,\infty)$; the median satisfies $P(T\le m)=0.5$.

subtopic: Comparing the lengths of two independent parts
statement: Part $A$ has length $L_A\sim N(12.4,\,0.3^{2})$ and part $B$ has length $L_B\sim N(12.1,\,0.4^{2})$, both in cm and independent of each other. A pair is chosen, one of each part. (a) State the distribution of $D=L_A-L_B$. [3] (b) Find the probability that part $B$ is longer than part $A$, to three significant figures. [2] (c) Find the probability that the two parts differ in length by less than $0.5$ cm, to three significant figures. [2]
tips: The variances of independent variables add, even when the variables are subtracted.

subtopic: Discrete random variable with an unknown constant
statement: A discrete random variable $X$ has probability distribution $P(X=x)=k(x+1)$ for $x=1, 2, 3, 4$, where $k$ is a constant. (a) Find the value of $k$. [2] (b) Find $E(X)$. [2] (c) Find $\mathrm{Var}(X)$. [3] (d) Find $P(X\ge3)$. [1]
tips: Probabilities sum to $1$; $\mathrm{Var}(X)=E(X^{2})-[E(X)]^{2}$.

subtopic: Binomial probabilities with a calculator
statement: A factory makes light bulbs, and each bulb is faulty with probability $0.15$ independently. A box contains 20 bulbs. Let $X$ be the number of successes, so that $X\sim B(20,0.15)$. (a) Find $P(X=3)$. [2] (b) Find $P(X\le2)$. [2] (c) Find $P(X\ge5)$. [2] (d) Find the mean and the standard deviation of $X$. [2]
tips: State $X\sim B(n,p)$ and use the binomial pdf and cdf functions. For 'at least', use the complement of the cdf.

subtopic: Continuous random variable with a trigonometric pdf
statement: The continuous random variable $X$ has probability density function $f(x)=k\sin x$ for $0\le x\le\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, and $f(x)=0$ otherwise. (a) Show that $k=1$. [2] (b) Find $E(X)$. [3] (c) Find the exact value of the median of $X$. [3] (d) Find $\operatorname{Var}(X)$, correct to three significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}k\sin x\,dx=k[-\cos x]_0^{\pi/2}$ [M1] $=k(0+1)=k=1$ [AG] [A1] [2 marks] (b) $E(X)=\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}x\sin x\,dx$ [M1] Integration by parts or GDC: $[\sin x-x\cos x]_0^{\pi/2}$ [A1] $=1$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Median $m$: $\displaystyle\int_0^m\sin x\,dx=\dfrac12$ [M1] $1-\cos m=\dfrac12$, so $\cos m=\dfrac12$ [A1] $m=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $E(X^2)=\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}x^2\sin x\,dx=\pi-2$ [A1] $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\pi-2-1=\pi-3=0.142$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The median $m$ satisfies $\int_{-\infty}^m f(x)\,dx=\tfrac12$. Use your calculator to check integrals by parts, but write the setup so that method marks are secure.

subtopic: Normal distribution: finding mean and standard deviation from two percentiles
statement: The waiting time $W$ minutes at a clinic is normally distributed with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$. It is known that $20\%$ of patients wait less than 30 minutes and $10\%$ of patients wait more than 50 minutes. (a) Find the value of $\mu$ and of $\sigma$. [4] (b) Find $P(35<W<45)$. [2] Six patients are chosen at random. (c) Find the probability that at least two of them wait between 35 and 45 minutes. [3]
markscheme: (a) $P(W<30)=0.2$ gives $\dfrac{30-\mu}{\sigma}=-0.8416$ and $P(W<50)=0.9$ gives $\dfrac{50-\mu}{\sigma}=1.2816$ [M1] Subtracting: $\dfrac{20}{\sigma}=2.1232$ [M1] $\sigma=9.42$ [A1] $\mu=37.9$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) Using the GDC with $W\sim N(37.93,\ 9.42^2)$ [M1] $P(35<W<45)=0.396$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Let $Y$ be the number in this range, $Y\sim B(6,\ 0.3956)$ [M1] $P(Y\ge2)=1-P(Y\le1)$ [M1] $=0.760$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Convert each given probability to a $z$-value with inverse normal, then solve the two simultaneous equations. Keep unrounded values in your calculator for later parts.

subtopic: Expectation and variance without a calculator
statement: A discrete random variable $X$ has probability distribution given by the table. $$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c|}x & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 5 \\ \hline P(X=x) & 2k & 3k & 3k & k & k \end{array}$$ (a) Find the value of $k$. [2] (b) Find $E(X)$. [2] (c) Find $\operatorname{Var}(X)$. [3] (d) Find $P(X>E(X))$. [2]
tips: Compute $E(X^2)$ separately from $[E(X)]^2$ to avoid errors in the variance.

subtopic: Expected value and fair price of a game
statement: A raffle ticket wins nothing with probability $\frac58$, a $\$4$ prize with probability $\frac14$ and a $\$24$ prize with probability $\frac18$. (a) Find the expected gain of a player per game (the prize minus the stake of $\$6$). [3] (b) Find the stake that would make the game fair. [1]
markscheme: (a) expected prize $=\sum\text{prize}\times\text{probability}$ [M1] $=4$ [A1] expected gain $=4-6=-2$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) a fair game has expected gain $0$, so the stake is $\$4$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: A game is fair when the expected prize equals the stake. Compute $E=\sum xP(x)$.

subtopic: Sum of independent Poisson random variables and conditional probability
statement: The number of customers arriving at counter A in a $10$-minute period is $X\sim\mathrm{Po}(2.5)$ and the number arriving at counter B in the same period is $Y\sim\mathrm{Po}(3.1)$. The variables $X$ and $Y$ are independent. Let $S=X+Y$. (a) State the distribution of $S$ and find $P(S\ge8)$. [3] (b) Find $P(X=2\mid S=5)$. [4] (c) Find the probability that, over three independent $10$-minute periods, the total number of customers arriving at the two counters is at most $15$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $S\sim\mathrm{Po}(5.6)$ [A1] $P(S\ge8)=1-P(S\le7)$ [M1] $=0.203$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $P(X=2\mid S=5)=\dfrac{P(X=2)\,P(Y=3)}{P(S=5)}$ [M1] [M1] $=\dfrac{0.2565\times0.2237}{0.1697}$ [A1] $=0.338$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) Total over three periods $\sim\mathrm{Po}(16.8)$ [M1] $P(\le15)=0.390$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The sum of independent Poisson variables is Poisson with the means added. For the conditional probability, write the event $\{X=2\}\cap\{S=5\}$ as $\{X=2\}\cap\{Y=3\}$ and use independence.

subtopic: Expected profit with uniformly distributed demand
statement: The weekly demand $X$ (in units) for a product is uniformly distributed on $[0,4]$. A shop buys $3$ units each week at a cost of $2$ per unit and sells each unit it can at $5$. Unsold units have no value, and demand beyond $3$ units is lost. (a) Write down the number of units sold when $X\le3$ and when $X>3$. [1] (b) Find the expected number of units sold. [3] (c) Hence find the expected weekly profit. [2]
markscheme: (a) $X$ units when $X\le3$, and $3$ units when $X>3$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\displaystyle\int_0^3x\times\dfrac14\,dx=\dfrac98$ [M1][A1] $+\ 3\times P(X>3)=3\times\dfrac14$, giving $\dfrac98+\dfrac34=\dfrac{15}8$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $5\times\dfrac{15}8-3\times2$ [M1] $=\dfrac{27}8=3.375$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Split the possible demands into those below the stock level (where sales equal demand) and those above it (where sales equal the stock).

subtopic: How many trials are needed to be nearly certain of a success
statement: In each independent attempt, a salesperson makes a sale with probability $0.1$. Let $n$ be the number of attempts. (a) Write an inequality for $n$ so that the probability of at least one sale in $n$ attempts exceeds $0.95$. [2] (b) Find the smallest whole number $n$ that satisfies the inequality. [3] (c) Verify your answer by evaluating the probability for $n=28$ and $n=29$, to three significant figures. [2]
tips: Use the complement: at least one sale is $1$ minus the probability of no sales.

subtopic: Finding the mean and standard deviation of a normal variable
statement: The random variable $X$ is normally distributed with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$. It is known that $P(X<30)=0.2$ and $P(X>48)=0.1$. (a) Write down two equations in $\mu$ and $\sigma$ that are satisfied. [3] (b) Find the value of $\mu$ and the value of $\sigma$. [3] (c) Hence find $P(X>40)$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $z$-value for $0.2$ is $-0.8416$ [A1] and for $0.9$ is $1.2816$ [A1] $\dfrac{30-\mu}{\sigma}=-0.8416$ and $\dfrac{48-\mu}{\sigma}=1.2816$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Subtract the equations: $18=2.1232\sigma$ [M1] $\sigma=8.48$ [A1] $\mu=37.1$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $P(X>40)=0.368$ [M1][A1] Accept $0.368$ from unrounded values. [2 marks]
tips: Convert each probability to a standardized value with the inverse normal function and form simultaneous equations. Take care that $P(X>48)=0.1$ corresponds to a left-tail area of $0.9$.

subtopic: Bottle fill volumes: probability and a cut-off
statement: The volume of liquid in a bottle is normally distributed with mean $500.4$ mL and standard deviation $1.8$ mL. (a) Find the probability that a bottle contains less than $498$ mL, to three significant figures. [2] (b) The lowest $5\%$ of bottles are rejected. Find the volume below which a bottle is rejected, to one decimal place. [2] (c) The mean can be changed but the standard deviation stays $1.8$ mL. Find the smallest mean, to one decimal place, so that at most $2\%$ of bottles contain less than $500$ mL. [3]
tips: Use the inverse normal function to find the value with a given lower-tail probability.

subtopic: Defective microchips and how many to inspect
statement: Each microchip produced by a factory is defective independently with probability $0.025$. (a) In a batch of $40$ chips, find the probability that exactly two are defective. [2] (b) Find the probability that a batch of $40$ chips contains at least one defective chip. [2] (c) Find the smallest number of chips $n$ such that the probability of at least one defective chip in the sample exceeds $0.95$. [3] (d) Given that a batch of $40$ chips contains at least one defective chip, find the probability that it contains exactly one. [2]
tips: At least one is best found with the complement $1-P(X=0)$. For (c) take logarithms (dividing by $\ln0.975$, which is negative, reverses the inequality) or test values on your GDC table. In (d) the condition reduces the sample space, so divide by $P(X\ge1)$.

subtopic: Poisson distribution with exact answers
statement: The random variable $X$ has a Poisson distribution with mean $4$. (a) Show that $P(X\le1)=5e^{-4}$. [2] (b) Find $P(X=2\mid X\ge1)$, giving your answer in terms of $e$. [3] (c) Find $\mathrm{E}(2X+1)$ and $\mathrm{Var}(2X+1)$. [2]
tips: For a Poisson distribution the mean and variance are equal, which gives $\mathrm{Var}(X)=4$. In a conditional probability where the condition contains the event, the numerator is just the probability of the event.

subtopic: Continuous random variable with a quadratic pdf
statement: The continuous random variable $X$ has probability density function $f(x)=kx^2$ for $0\le x\le3$, and $f(x)=0$ otherwise. (a) Find the value of $k$. [2] (b) Find $E(X)$. [2] (c) Find $\operatorname{Var}(X)$. [3] (d) Find the exact value of the median. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\displaystyle\int_0^3kx^2\,dx=1$ [M1] $9k=1$ so $k=\frac{1}{9}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\displaystyle\int_0^3x\cdot\frac{1}{9}x^2\,dx$ [M1] $=\frac{9}{4}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $E(X^2)=\displaystyle\int_0^3\frac{1}{9}x^4\,dx=\frac{27}{5}$ [M1][A1] $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\frac{27}{5}-\left(\frac{9}{4}\right)^2=\frac{27}{80}$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $\displaystyle\int_0^m\frac{1}{9}x^2\,dx=\dfrac12$ [M1] $\dfrac{m^3}{27}=\dfrac12$ [A1] $m=\frac{3 \cdot 2^{\frac{2}{3}}}{2}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Integrate the pdf over its support to find $k$. The median $m$ satisfies $\int_{\text{lower}}^{m}f(x)\,dx=\tfrac12$.

subtopic: Poisson fit to goals per match
statement: This question tests whether the number of goals scored per match in a football league can be modeled by a Poisson distribution. The numbers of goals in $100$ matches were recorded, and no match had more than $5$ goals. $$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c|c}\text{Goals in a match} & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5\\\hline\text{Number of matches} & 11 & 28 & 30 & 18 & 9 & 4\end{array}$$ (a) Find the mean number of goals per match. [2] (b) Using a Poisson distribution with mean $1.98$, find the expected number of matches with $0$, $1$, $2$ and $3$ goals, and with $4$ or more goals, correct to 2 decimal places. [4] (c) State suitable hypotheses for a $\chi^{2}$ goodness-of-fit test, and the number of degrees of freedom when the categories $0$, $1$, $2$, $3$ and $4$ or more are used and the mean is estimated from the data. [3] (d) Observed frequencies for the five categories are $11$, $28$, $30$, $18$, $13$. Find the $\chi^{2}$ statistic and the $p$-value, correct to 3 significant figures. [3] (e) State the conclusion at the $5\%$ significance level, in context. [2] (f) Explain why matches with $4$ goals and $5$ goals were combined into a single category. [1]
