subtopic: Different transformations mapping sine onto cosine
statement: Consider the graphs of $y=\sin x$ and $y=\cos x$. (a) Show that $\cos x=\sin\left(x+\dfrac\pi2\right)$, and describe the translation that maps $y=\sin x$ onto $y=\cos x$. [2] (b) Describe a translation followed by a reflection that maps $y=\sin x$ onto $y=\cos x$. [3] (c) Describe a reflection followed by a translation that maps $y=\sin x$ onto $y=\cos x$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\sin\left(x+\dfrac\pi2\right)=\sin x\cos\dfrac\pi2+\cos x\sin\dfrac\pi2=\cos x$ [M1] translation by $\dfrac\pi2$ to the left [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\cos x=-\sin\left(x-\dfrac\pi2\right)$ [M1] translation $\dfrac\pi2$ to the right [A1] reflection in the $x$-axis [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\cos x=\sin\left(\dfrac\pi2-x\right)=\sin\left(-\left(x-\dfrac\pi2\right)\right)$ [M1] reflection in the $y$-axis [A1] translation $\dfrac\pi2$ to the right [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Use the identity $\sin(\pi/2-x)=\cos x$ and check the order of the two transformations carefully.

subtopic: Reciprocal function with stretch and translation
statement: The graph of $y=\dfrac1x$ is transformed onto the graph of $y=g(x)$, where $g(x)=\dfrac{2}{x-1}+3$, $x\ne1$. (a) Describe a sequence of transformations that maps $y=\dfrac1x$ onto $y=g(x)$. [3] (b) Write down the equations of the asymptotes of the graph of $g$. [2] (c) Find the coordinates of the axis intercepts of the graph of $g$. [3] (d) Solve $g(x)=x$, giving exact answers. [3]
markscheme: (a) Vertical stretch with scale factor $2$ [A1] Translation $1$ unit to the right [A1] Translation $3$ units up [A1] [3 marks] (b) $x=1$ [A1] $y=3$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $y$-intercept: $g(0)=-2+3=1$, so $(0,1)$ [A1] $x$-intercept: $\dfrac{2}{x-1}=-3$ [M1] $x=\frac13$, so $\left(\frac13,0\right)$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $2+3(x-1)=x(x-1)$ [M1] $x^2-4x+1=0$ [A1] $x=2\pm\sqrt3$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The asymptotes of $y=\frac1x$ are the axes; after the translation they move to $x=1$ and $y=3$. For part (d), multiply through by $(x-1)$ and use the quadratic formula.

subtopic: Finding the parameters of a sine model from extreme points
statement: A sound wave is modeled by $y=a\sin(bx+c)+d$ with $a>0$, $b>0$ and $0\le c<2\pi$. Its first maximum for $x\ge0$ is at $(0.5,\,7)$ and the next minimum is at $(1.25,\,-1)$, where $x$ is in milliseconds. (a) Find $a$ and $d$. [2] (b) Find $b$. [2] (c) Find $c$, correct to three significant figures. [3] (d) Use your GDC to find the first time after $x=0$ at which $y=5$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $a=\dfrac{7-(-1)}{2}=4$ [A1]; $d=\dfrac{7+(-1)}{2}=3$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Half a period is $1.25-0.5=0.75$ so period $1.5$ [M1]; $b=\dfrac{2\pi}{1.5}=\dfrac{4\pi}{3}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $b(0.5)+c=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ [M1]; $c=\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\dfrac{2\pi}{3}=-\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ [A1]; add $2\pi$ so $c=\dfrac{11\pi}{6}=5.76$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) Solve $4\sin\left(\frac{4\pi}{3}x+\frac{11\pi}{6}\right)+3=5$ [M1]; $x=0.25$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A maximum occurs where the sine argument equals $\frac{\pi}{2}$ (plus multiples of $2\pi$).

subtopic: Daylight hours modeled by a transformed cosine
statement: The number of hours of daylight, $D$, in a northern city on day $t$ of the year, where $t=1$ is January 1, is modeled by $D(t)=a\cos\big(b(t-c)\big)+d$, where $a>0$ and $b>0$. The longest day has $15.2$ hours of daylight and occurs on day $172$. The shortest day has $8.8$ hours of daylight. The model has period $365$ days. (a) Find the values of $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$. [4] (b) Find the length of time, in days, during which the city has more than $14$ hours of daylight. Give your answer to three significant figures. [4]
tips: The maximum is at $t=c$ for a cosine model, so the horizontal shift is read directly from the day of the maximum. In part (b) the required length of time is the difference between the two crossing times.

subtopic: Logistic fish population and a time delay translation
statement: The population of fish in a lake, $P$, is modeled by $P(t)=\dfrac{1200}{1+7\mathrm{e}^{-0.45t}}$, where $t$ is the time in years since the lake was stocked. (a) Find the number of fish in the lake when it was stocked. [2] (b) State the value that the population approaches in the long term. [1] (c) Find the time at which the population first reaches $600$ fish. [3] (d) Using your GDC, find the greatest rate at which the population grows, and the time at which this occurs. [2] A second lake is stocked three years after the first and its population is modeled by $Q(t)=P(t-3)$, $t\ge3$. (e) Describe the transformation that maps the graph of $P$ onto the graph of $Q$. [1] (f) Find the time at which the population of the second lake first reaches $600$ fish. [2]
markscheme: (a) $P(0)=\dfrac{1200}{1+7}$ [M1] $=150$ fish [A1] [2 marks] (b) $1200$ fish [A1] [1 mark] (c) $\dfrac{1200}{1+7\mathrm{e}^{-0.45t}}=600$ [M1] $7\mathrm{e}^{-0.45t}=1$ [A1] $t=4.32$ years [A1] [3 marks] (d) Greatest rate is $135$ fish per year [A1] at $t=4.32$ years [A1] [2 marks] (e) Horizontal translation by $3$ units to the right (vector $\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$) [A1] [1 mark] (f) $t-3=4.32$ [M1] $t=7.32$ years [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A logistic curve grows fastest when the population is half of its limiting value, which is also the inflection point. A horizontal translation of $3$ units to the right delays every event by $3$ years.

subtopic: Amplitude, period and maximum of a sine transformation
statement: Let $g(x)=4\sin\left(2x-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)+1$, for $x\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Write down the amplitude and the period of $g$. [2] (b) Write down the range of $g$. [1] (c) Find the smallest positive value of $x$ at which $g$ takes its maximum value. [2]
markscheme: (a) Amplitude $4$ [A1] period $\dfrac{2\pi}{2}=\pi$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $-3\le g(x)\le 5$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) Maximum when $2x-\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\dfrac{\pi}{2}+2\pi n$ [M1] $x=\dfrac{5\pi}{12}+\pi n$; the smallest positive value is $x=\dfrac{5\pi}{12}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The value $b$ in $\sin(bx-c)$ changes the period to $2\pi/b$ and the phase shift to $c/b$, not $c$. When asked for the smallest positive value, check that the value with $n=-1$ is negative.

subtopic: Ferris wheel height with a phase shifted second wheel
statement: A Ferris wheel has radius $25$ m and its axle is $27$ m above the ground. One revolution takes $8$ minutes. A rider boards at the lowest point at time $t=0$ minutes. The height of the rider above the ground is modeled by $h(t)=a\cos(bt)+d$. (a) Find the values of $a$, $b$ and $d$. [3] (b) Find the height of the rider at $t=3$. [2] (c) Find the times during the first revolution, $0\le t\le8$, at which the rider is at least $40$ m above the ground. [4] (d) Find the percentage of each revolution for which the rider is at least $40$ m above the ground. [2] A second wheel is modeled by $g(t)=h(t-2)+5$. (e) Describe the transformation that maps the graph of $h$ onto the graph of $g$ and write down the maximum height reached on the second wheel. [2]
markscheme: (a) $a=-25$ [A1] $b=\dfrac{2\pi}{8}=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ [A1] $d=27$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $h(3)=-25\cos\left(\frac{3\pi}{4}\right)+27$ [M1] $=44.7$ m [A1] [2 marks] (c) Solve $-25\cos\left(\frac{\pi t}{4}\right)+27=40$ [M1] $t=2.70$ [A1] and $t=5.30$ [A1] The rider is at least $40$ m high for $2.70\le t\le5.30$ [A1] [4 marks] (d) $\dfrac{5.30-2.70}{8}\times100$ [M1] $=32.6\%$ [A1] [2 marks] (e) Translation by $\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 5 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] Maximum height $=52+5=57$ m [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The rider starts at the bottom, so the cosine is reflected: $a$ is negative. Set your calculator to radians. In (d) the fraction of the cycle is the length of the interval divided by the period.

subtopic: Graph of y = 1/f(x) for a quadratic
statement: Let $f(x)=x^2-4x+3$, for $x\in\mathbb{R}$, and let $g(x)=\dfrac{1}{f(x)}$. (a) Write down the equations of the vertical asymptotes of the graph of $y=g(x)$. [2] (b) The graph of $y=f(x)$ has a minimum point. Find the coordinates of the corresponding local extremum of $y=g(x)$, stating whether it is a maximum or a minimum, and write down the equation of the horizontal asymptote of $y=g(x)$. [3] (c) Find the range of $g$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $f(x)=(x-1)(x-3)$ [M1] $x=1$ and $x=3$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $f(x)=(x-2)^2-1$ so the minimum point is $(2,-1)$ [M1] $g(2)=-1$ so the extremum is $(2,-1)$, a local maximum because $f<0$ nearby and the reciprocal reverses the order [A1] horizontal asymptote $y=0$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $f(x)\in[-1,0)$ for $1<x<3$ so $g\in(-\infty,-1]$ [M1] $f(x)\in(0,\infty)$ for $x<1$ or $x>3$ so $g\in(0,\infty)$ [A1] range is $g(x)\le -1$ or $g(x)>0$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The graph of $1/f$ has a vertical asymptote at every zero of $f$, and a minimum of $f$ becomes a maximum of $1/f$ when $f$ is negative there. Use the range of $f$ on each interval to find the range of the reciprocal.

subtopic: The normal density as a transformation of the standard curve
statement: The standard normal density is $\phi(z)=\dfrac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-z^2/2}$. The density of $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ is $f(x)=\dfrac1\sigma\phi\left(\dfrac{x-\mu}\sigma\right)$. (a) Describe the sequence of transformations that maps the graph of $y=\phi(x)$ onto the graph of $y=f(x)$. [3] (b) Find the maximum value of $f$ when $\sigma=2$, correct to three significant figures. [2] (c) Explain why the total area under the graph of $f$ is $1$ for every $\mu$ and $\sigma$. [2]
markscheme: (a) horizontal stretch with scale factor $\sigma$ [A1] translation $\mu$ to the right [A1] vertical stretch with scale factor $\dfrac1\sigma$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\dfrac1{2\sqrt{2\pi}}$ [M1] $=0.199$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) the horizontal stretch by $\sigma$ multiplies the area by $\sigma$ [R1] the vertical stretch by $\dfrac1\sigma$ cancels this, and the translation leaves the area unchanged [R1] [2 marks]
tips: A horizontal stretch scales area by the same factor as a vertical stretch does, so a pair of reciprocal stretches leaves the area unchanged.

subtopic: Finding the parameters of a transformation from points
statement: Let $f(x)=x^3-3x$. The graph of $g(x)=af(x-b)+c$ is obtained from $y=f(x)$ by a vertical stretch, a horizontal translation and a vertical translation. The graph of $g$ passes through $(0,7)$, $(1,3)$, $(2,-1)$ and $b=1$. (a) Write $g(0)$, $g(1)$ and $g(2)$ in terms of $a$ and $c$. [3] (b) Hence find $a$ and $c$. [2] (c) Find the coordinates of the local maximum and local minimum of the graph of $g$. [3] (d) Use your calculator to solve $g(x)=10$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $g(0)=af(-1)+c=2a+c$ [A1]; $g(1)=af(0)+c=c$ [A1]; $g(2)=af(1)+c=-2a+c$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) From $g(1)=c$: $c=3$ [A1]; $2a+3=7$ so $a=2$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $f$ has a local maximum $(-1,2)$ and a local minimum $(1,-2)$ [A1]; image points: $(0,2(2)+3)=(0,7)$ and $(2,2(-2)+3)=(2,-1)$ [A1][A1] [3 marks] (d) Solve on the GDC [M1]: $x=3.151$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Substitute the given points into $g(x)=af(x-b)+c$ using the known values of $f$; the turning points of $f$ move with the same transformation.

subtopic: Transformations of the square root function
statement: Let $f(x)=\sqrt{4-2x}+1$. (a) Describe a sequence of four transformations that maps the graph of $y=\sqrt x$ onto the graph of $y=f(x)$. [4] (b) Write down the domain and range of $f$. [2] (c) Find $f^{-1}(x)$, and state its domain. [3]
markscheme: (a) horizontal stretch with scale factor $\dfrac12$, giving $\sqrt{2x}$ [A1] reflection in the $y$-axis, giving $\sqrt{-2x}$ [A1] translation by $2$ to the right, giving $\sqrt{-2(x-2)}=\sqrt{4-2x}$ [A1] translation by $1$ upward [A1] [4 marks] (b) domain $x\le2$ [A1] range $f(x)\ge1$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $(y-1)^2=4-2x$ [M1] $f^{-1}(x)=2-\dfrac{(x-1)^2}2$ [A1] domain $x\ge1$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Factor the expression under the root as $-2(x-2)$ to read off the stretch, reflection and translation.

subtopic: Composite functions and when two composites are equal
statement: Let $f(x)=x+2$ and $g(x)=x^2-3$, for $x\in\mathbb R$. (a) Find $(f\circ g)(x)$. [2] (b) Find $(g\circ f)(x)$. [2] (c) Solve $(f\circ g)(x)=(g\circ f)(x)$. [2] (d) Find the range of $g\circ f$. [2]
tips: $f\circ g$ means apply $g$ first. In general $f\circ g\ne g\circ f$; the equation in part (c) is linear because the $x^2$ terms cancel. For the range, use the completed-square form.

subtopic: Domain, range and key points under stretches and translations
statement: The function $f$ has domain $-2\le x\le6$ and range $1\le f(x)\le5$. The graph of $y=f(x)$ has a maximum point at $(4,5)$ and a minimum point at $(-2,1)$. (a) Find the domain and the range of $g(x)=f(x-3)+2$. [2] (b) Find the domain and the range of $h(x)=-3f(2x)$. [3] (c) Write down the coordinates of the maximum point and of the minimum point of the graph of $y=h(x)$. [2]
markscheme: (a) Domain $1\le x\le9$ [A1] Range $3\le g(x)\le7$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $-2\le2x\le6$ so domain $-1\le x\le3$ [A1] $-15\le h(x)\le-3$ [A1][A1] [3 marks] (c) The minimum of $h$ comes from the maximum of $f$: $(2,-15)$ [A1] The maximum of $h$ comes from the minimum of $f$: $\left(-1,-3\right)$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A negative vertical stretch turns maxima into minima, so swap their roles before transforming. Divide the domain by the horizontal stretch factor, not multiply.

subtopic: Inverse of a transformed function
statement: The function $f$ is one-to-one, and $g(x)=f(2x+1)-3$. (a) Show that $g^{-1}(x)=\dfrac{f^{-1}(x+3)-1}2$. [3] (b) Given that $f(x)=x^3$, find $g^{-1}(5)$, and verify your answer by calculating $g$ of it. [3]
tips: Undo the operations in the reverse order: add 3, apply $f^{-1}$, subtract 1, divide by 2.

subtopic: Building a sinusoidal equation from stretches and a translation
statement: The graph of $y=\sin x$ is transformed by a vertical stretch with scale factor $4$ and a horizontal stretch with scale factor $\frac13$, in either order, followed by a translation by the vector $\begin{pmatrix} \frac{\pi}{6} \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$. The resulting graph is $y=g(x)$. (a) Show that $g(x)=4\sin\left(3\left(x-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)\right)+1$. [3] (b) Write down the period, the maximum value and the minimum value of $g$. [3] (c) Find the smallest positive value of $x$ for which $g(x)=-1$. [3]
markscheme: (a) After the two stretches the equation is $y=4\sin(3x)$ [A1] Translation right by $\frac{\pi}{6}$: replace $x$ by $x-\frac{\pi}{6}$ [M1] Translation up by $1$: add $1$ to obtain $g(x)=4\sin\left(3\left(x-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)\right)+1$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Period $=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ [A1] Maximum $=4+1=5$ [A1] Minimum $=-4+1=-3$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $4\sin\left(3\left(x-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)\right)+1=-1$ so $\sin\left(3\left(x-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)\right)=-\frac12$ [M1] $3\left(x-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)=-\frac{\pi}{6}$ [A1] $x=\frac{\pi}{6}-\frac{\pi}{18}=\frac{\pi}{9}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A horizontal stretch with scale factor $\frac13$ multiplies the period by $\frac13$ and puts a $3$ inside the sine. Factor out the $3$ so that the translation is visible as $x-\frac{\pi}{6}$. In part (c), check that the next solution further left is negative.

subtopic: Reciprocal model for time to complete a job
statement: A team of $n$ workers completes a job in $T(n)=\dfrac{480}{n}+30$ minutes, where $30$ minutes is the setup time and $n\ge1$. (a) Find $T(6)$. [1] (b) Describe the transformations that map the graph of $y=\dfrac1n$ onto the graph of $y=T(n)$. [2] (c) Write down the equations of the asymptotes of the graph of $T$ and interpret the horizontal asymptote in this context. [2] (d) Find the smallest number of workers needed to complete the job in at most $90$ minutes. [2] (e) Find an expression for $n$ in terms of $T$. [2] (f) Find the smallest whole number of workers needed to complete the job in $75$ minutes or less. [2]
markscheme: (a) $T(6)=\frac{480}{6}+30=110$ minutes [A1] [1 mark] (b) Vertical stretch with scale factor $480$ [A1] Translation up by $30$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $n=0$ and $T=30$ [A1] Even with very many workers the job still takes at least $30$ minutes because of the setup time [A1] [2 marks] (d) $\dfrac{480}{n}+30\le90$ so $\dfrac{480}{n}\le60$ [M1] $n\ge8$, so $8$ workers [A1] [2 marks] (e) $T-30=\dfrac{480}{n}$ [M1] $n=\dfrac{480}{T-30}$ [A1] [2 marks] (f) $n\ge\dfrac{480}{75-30}=10.67$ [M1] $11$ workers [A1] [2 marks]
tips: In a model such as $\frac ab+c$, the constant $c$ is the horizontal asymptote and gives the lowest possible value. Always round the number of workers up when a time limit must be met.

subtopic: Graphs of y=|ln x| and y=ln|x| and an equation with a modulus
statement: Let $g(x)=\ln|x|$ and $h(x)=|\ln x|$, where $h$ is defined for $x>0$. (a) For the graph of $g$, write down its domain, its line of symmetry, and its $x$-intercepts. [3] (b) Solve $h(x)=2$. [2] (c) Solve the equation $|\ln x|=\ln x+\ln4$. [4]
markscheme: (a) domain: $x\in\mathbb{R},\ x\neq0$ [A1] symmetric about the $y$-axis (since $g(-x)=g(x)$) [A1] $x$-intercepts $(1,0)$ and $(-1,0)$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\ln x=2$ or $\ln x=-2$ [M1] $x=e^2$ or $x=e^{-2}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) consider cases by the sign of $\ln x$ [M1] if $x\ge1$: $\ln x=\ln x+\ln4$ is impossible [R1] if $0<x<1$: $-\ln x=\ln x+\ln4\Rightarrow2\ln x=-\ln4$ [M1] $x=\dfrac12$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Remember that $|\ln x|$ equals $\ln x$ when $x\ge1$ and $-\ln x$ when $0<x<1$. Always check each case against its own condition.

subtopic: Reflections and stretches of an exponential graph
statement: Let $f(x)=2^x$. (a) The graph of $y=g(x)$ is obtained from $y=f(x)$ by a reflection in the $y$-axis followed by a translation $3$ units up. Find $g(x)$ and the equation of its horizontal asymptote. [3] (b) The graph of $y=h(x)$ is obtained from $y=f(x)$ by a horizontal stretch with scale factor $\dfrac13$. Show that $h(x)=8^x$. [2] (c) Show that the graph of $y=2^{x+3}$ can be obtained by a vertical stretch of $y=2^x$, and state the scale factor. [2]
markscheme: (a) $g(x)=2^{-x}+3$ [M1][A1] asymptote $y=3$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $h(x)=f(3x)=2^{3x}$ [M1] $=8^x$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $2^{x+3}=8\times2^x$ [M1] vertical stretch with scale factor $8$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A horizontal translation of an exponential graph is equivalent to a vertical stretch.

subtopic: Reflection in the lines y = c and x = c
statement: Let $f(x)=x^2+2x$. (a) The graph of $y=f(x)$ is reflected in the line $y=3$. Find the equation of the image in the form $y=\ldots$ [2] (b) The graph of $y=f(x)$ is reflected in the line $x=2$. Find the equation of the image, giving your answer in the form $y=ax^2+bx+c$. [3] (c) Show that the two image graphs found in parts (a) and (b) do not intersect. [2]
markscheme: (a) Reflection in $y=3$ maps $y$ to $6-y$ [M1] $y=6-x^2-2x$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Reflection in $x=2$ replaces $x$ by $4-x$ [M1] $y=(4-x)^2+2(4-x)$ [A1] $y=x^2-10x+24$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $6-x^2-2x=x^2-10x+24$ so $2x^2-8x+18=0$, i.e. $x^2-4x+9=0$ [M1] discriminant $=16-36=-20<0$, so there are no real solutions and the graphs do not intersect [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Reflection in $y=c$ sends $y$ to $2c-y$, and reflection in $x=c$ sends $x$ to $2c-x$. To show two graphs never meet, form an equation and use the discriminant.

subtopic: Transformations of a cubic and its turning points
statement: Let $f(x)=x^3-3x^2$, for $x\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Find the coordinates of the stationary points of the graph of $f$. [3] Let $g(x)=2-f(x+1)$. (b) Find the coordinates of the stationary points of the graph of $g$, and state whether each is a local maximum or a local minimum. [4] (c) Find the values of $k$ for which the equation $g(x)=k$ has exactly one real solution. [2]
markscheme: (a) $f'(x)=3x^2-6x$ [A1] $3x(x-2)=0$ [M1] stationary points $(0,\,0)$ and $(2,\,-4)$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $f(x+1)$: translate left by $1$; then $2-f$: reflect in the $x$-axis and translate up by $2$ [M1] $(-1,\,2)$ [A1] $(1,\,6)$ [A1] $f$ has a local maximum at $(0,0)$ and a local minimum at $(2,-4)$, so the reflection gives a local minimum at $(-1,2)$ and a local maximum at $(1,6)$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) $g$ has a negative leading coefficient, and its local minimum value ($2$) is below its local maximum value ($6$) [M1] exactly one solution when $k<2$ or $k>6$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Transform the turning points of $f$ rather than differentiating $g$ again, and remember that a reflection in the $x$-axis swaps maxima and minima. For (c), picture the cubic's shape: it has three solutions only for $k$ between the two turning-point values.

subtopic: A sum of a function and its translated copy
statement: Let $f(x)=x^2$ and $h(x)=f(x)+f(x-2)$. (a) Show that $h(x)=2(x-1)^2+2$. [2] (b) State the coordinates of the vertex of the graph of $h$, and describe the transformations that map $y=x^2$ onto $y=h(x)$. [3] (c) Explain, using symmetry, why the vertex of $h$ lies at $x=1$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $h(x)=x^2+(x-2)^2=2x^2-4x+4$ [M1] $=2(x-1)^2+2$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) vertex $(1,2)$ [A1] vertical stretch with scale factor $2$ [A1] translation $1$ to the right and $2$ up [A1] [3 marks] (c) the two parabolas have vertices at $x=0$ and $x=2$, and $h$ is symmetric about the midpoint $x=1$ [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Expand both squares, collect like terms and complete the square.

subtopic: Reflection in the y-axis of a quadratic and where the graphs meet
statement: Let $f(x)=x^2+2x$. (a) Write $f(x)$ in the form $(x+p)^2+q$ and write down the coordinates of the vertex of the graph of $f$. [3] The graph of $g$ is obtained by reflecting the graph of $f$ in the $y$-axis and then translating it by the vector $\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$. (b) Show that $g(x)=x^2-2x+3$. [2] (c) Find the coordinates of the vertex of the graph of $g$. [2] (d) Find the coordinates of the point where the graphs of $f$ and $g$ intersect. [3]
markscheme: (a) $x^2+2x=(x+1)^2-1$ [M1] [A1] Vertex $(-1,-1)$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Reflection in the $y$-axis: $f(-x)=(-x)^2+2(-x)=x^2-2x$ [M1] Translation up by $3$: $g(x)=x^2-2x+3$ [AG] [2 marks] (c) $g(x)=(x-1)^2+2$ [M1] Vertex $(1,2)$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $x^2+2x=x^2-2x+3$ [M1] $x=\frac34$ [A1] $y=\frac{9}{16}+\frac32=\frac{33}{16}$, so the point is $\left(\frac34,\frac{33}{16}\right)$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Reflection in the $y$-axis replaces $x$ with $-x$. The vertex moves from $(-1,-1)$ to $(1,-1)$ and then up by $3$. At the intersection the $x^2$ terms cancel, leaving a linear equation.

subtopic: Reciprocal function in transformed form
statement: The graph of $y=\dfrac1x$ is transformed to the graph of $y=g(x)$ where $g(x)=\dfrac{2x+1}{x-1}$. (a) Show that $g(x)=2+\dfrac{3}{x-1}$. [2] (b) Describe the transformations from $y=\dfrac1x$ to $y=g(x)$. [3] (c) Write down the equations of the asymptotes and find the axes intercepts of the graph of $g$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $2x+1=2(x-1)+3$ [M1]; $g(x)=2+\dfrac{3}{x-1}$ [AG] [2 marks] (b) vertical stretch scale factor $3$ [A1]; translation $1$ unit to the right [A1]; translation $2$ units up [A1] [3 marks] (c) asymptotes $x=1$ and $y=2$ [A1]; $x$-intercept $\left(-\dfrac12, 0\right)$ [A1]; $y$-intercept $(0, -1)$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Divide the numerator by $x-1$ to reveal the stretch and translations.

subtopic: Reciprocal function transformations
statement: Let $g(x)=\dfrac1{x-2}+3$, for $x\neq2$. The graph of $g$ is obtained from the graph of $f(x)=\dfrac1x$ by a single transformation. (a) Describe this transformation. [1] (b) Write down the equations of the asymptotes of the graph of $g$. [2] (c) Find the coordinates of the axis intercepts of the graph of $g$. [3] (d) Solve $|g(x)|=1$. [3]
markscheme: (a) Translation by $\begin{pmatrix}2\\3\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $x=2$ [A1] $y=3$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $g(0)=-\frac12+3=\frac52$, so $\left(0,\frac52\right)$ [A1] $\frac1{x-2}=-3$ [M1] $x=\frac53$, so $\left(\frac53,0\right)$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $g(x)=1$ or $g(x)=-1$ [M1] $\frac1{x-2}=-2$ gives $x=\frac32$ [A1] $\frac1{x-2}=-4$ gives $x=\frac74$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A translation by $(p,q)$ moves vertical asymptotes by $p$ and horizontal asymptotes by $q$. For modulus equations, split into the two cases $g(x)=\pm c$.

subtopic: Relationships between families of exponential and logarithmic graphs
statement: Many graphs of exponential and logarithmic functions are related by simple transformations of $y=2^x$ and $y=\log_2x$. (a) Show that the horizontal translation $y=2^{x+3}$ is also a vertical stretch of $y=2^x$, and state the scale factor. [2] (b) Show that $y=\log_4x$ is a vertical stretch of $y=\log_2x$ and state the scale factor. Show also that $y=\log_2(8x)$ is a vertical translation of $y=\log_2x$. [3] (c) Describe the transformations that map $y=2^x$ onto $y=2^{3-x}$. [3] (d) Let $g(x)=2^x+2^{-x}$. Show that $g$ is even, and show that its minimum value is $2$, occurring at $x=0$. [4] (e) Explain why the graph of $y=g(x)$ lies above the graph of $y=2^x$ for all $x$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $2^{x+3}=2^3\times2^x=8\times2^x$ [M1] vertical stretch with scale factor $8$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\log_4x=\dfrac{\log_2x}{\log_24}=\dfrac12\log_2x$ [M1] scale factor $\dfrac12$ [A1] $\log_2(8x)=3+\log_2x$, a translation $3$ up [A1] [3 marks] (c) $2^{3-x}=2^{-(x-3)}$ [M1] reflection in the $y$-axis [A1] translation $3$ to the right [A1] [3 marks] (d) $g(-x)=2^{-x}+2^x=g(x)$ [A1] for $u=2^x>0$: $u+\dfrac1u-2=\dfrac{(u-1)^2}u\ge0$ [M1][A1] equality when $u=1$, that is $x=0$, so the minimum is $2$ [A1] [4 marks] (e) $g(x)-2^x=2^{-x}>0$ [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Use the laws of exponents and logarithms to turn one type of change into another. For the last part, treat $u=2^x$ as a positive variable.

subtopic: Reflection and translation of a logarithm graph
statement: The graph of $y=\ln x$ is reflected in the $y$-axis and then translated by $\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$ to give the graph of $y=g(x)$. (a) Find $g(x)$. [2] (b) State the domain of $g$ and the equation of the vertical asymptote. [2] (c) Find the exact $x$-intercept of the graph of $g$. [2]
markscheme: (a) Reflection: $y=\ln(-x)$ [A1]; translation: $g(x)=\ln(-(x-2))-1=\ln(2-x)-1$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) domain $x<2$ [A1]; $x=2$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\ln(2-x)=1$ [M1]; $x=2-e$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A reflection in the $y$-axis replaces $x$ by $-x$; a translation right by $2$ replaces $x$ by $x-2$.

subtopic: Transformations of an exponential graph
statement: The graph of $y=e^x$ is transformed by a horizontal stretch of scale factor $\dfrac12$, then a translation $\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ -4 \end{pmatrix}$, then a reflection in the $y$-axis. (a) Find the equation of the final graph. [3] (b) Write down the equation of the horizontal asymptote and the $y$-intercept. [2] (c) Find the exact $x$-intercept. [2]
markscheme: (a) Horizontal stretch: $y=e^{2x}$ [A1]; translation: $y=e^{2x}-4$ [A1]; reflection: $y=e^{-2x}-4$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $y=-4$ [A1]; $(0,-3)$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $e^{-2x}=4$ [M1]; $x=-\dfrac12\ln4=-\ln2$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A horizontal stretch of scale factor $k$ replaces $x$ by $x/k$.

subtopic: Composite transformations checked with a graphing calculator
statement: Let $f(x)=x^3-3x$ and let $g(x)=2f(x-1)+4$. (a) Find the coordinates of the local maximum and minimum of $f$. [3] (b) Hence find the coordinates of the local maximum and minimum of $g$. [3] (c) Use your calculator to find the $x$-intercepts of $g$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $f'(x)=3x^2-3=0$ so $x=\pm1$ [M1] maximum $(-1,2)$ [A1] minimum $(1,-2)$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) translate $1$ right, stretch vertically by $2$, translate up $4$ [M1] maximum $(0,8)$ [A1] minimum $(2,0)$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) solve $2\left[(x-1)^3-3(x-1)\right]+4=0$ [M1] $x=-1$ [A1] $x=2$ (a repeated root, where the graph touches the axis at the local minimum) [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Track key points through each transformation in order: horizontal shift, vertical stretch, vertical shift.

subtopic: Exponential graph: reflection, translation and intercepts
statement: Let $g(x)=9\left(3^{-x}\right)-2$, for $x\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Show that $g(x)=3^{-(x-2)}-2$. [2] (b) The graph of $y=3^x$ is mapped onto the graph of $y=g(x)$ by a reflection followed by a translation. Describe both transformations. [2] (c) Write down the equation of the horizontal asymptote of the graph of $y=g(x)$, and find the exact $x$-intercept. [3]
markscheme: (a) $9=3^2$ [M1] $9\left(3^{-x}\right)=3^{2-x}=3^{-(x-2)}$ so $g(x)=3^{-(x-2)}-2$ [A1] [AG] [2 marks] (b) Reflection in the $y$-axis [A1] translation by $\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $y=-2$ [A1] $3^{2-x}=2$ [M1] $2-x=\log_3 2$ so $x=2-\log_3 2$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Write the constant factor as a power of the base to turn a vertical stretch into a horizontal translation. An exponential graph's asymptote moves only with the vertical translation.

subtopic: Stopping distance model, inverse and wet road stretch
statement: The stopping distance, $s$ meters, of a car traveling at $v$ kilometers per hour on a dry road is modeled by $s(v)=0.0065v^2+0.18v$, $v\ge0$. (a) Find the stopping distance at $80$ km/h. [1] (b) Find the speed for which the stopping distance is $100$ m. [2] (c) Explain why the restriction $v\ge0$ is needed for $s$ to have an inverse function. [1] (d) Find an expression for $s^{-1}(x)$. [3] (e) Use your expression to verify your answer to part (b). [1] On a wet road the stopping distance is modeled by $w(v)=1.5s(v)$. (f) Find the speed on a wet road for which the stopping distance is $60$ m. [2]
markscheme: (a) $s(80)=56.0$ m [A1] [1 mark] (b) Solve $0.0065v^2+0.18v=100$ [M1] $v=111$ km/h [A1] [2 marks] (c) The vertex is at $v=-13.8$, so $s$ is increasing for $v\ge0$ and is one-to-one there; without the restriction it would fail the horizontal line test [R1] [1 mark] (d) $0.0065v^2+0.18v-x=0$ [M1] $v=\dfrac{-0.18\pm\sqrt{0.0324+0.026x}}{0.013}$ [A1] reject the negative root because $v\ge0$, so $s^{-1}(x)=\dfrac{-0.18+\sqrt{0.0324+0.026x}}{0.013}$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) $s^{-1}(100)=111$ [A1] [1 mark] (f) $1.5s(v)=60$ so $s(v)=40$ [M1] $v=s^{-1}(40)=65.8$ km/h [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A quadratic only has an inverse on a domain where it is one-to-one, so choose the branch on the side of the vertex that matches the context. A stretch by $1.5$ of $s$ means the same speed gives a stopping distance $1.5$ times as large, so solve $s(v)=\frac{60}{1.5}$.

subtopic: Transformations of a sine function
statement: Let $g(x)=3\sin\left(2\left(x-\dfrac\pi6\right)\right)-1$, for $0\le x\le\pi$. (a) Write down the amplitude, the period and the range of $g$. [3] (b) The graph of $y=\sin x$ is transformed onto the graph of $y=g(x)$ by four transformations, applied in this order: a horizontal stretch, a horizontal translation, a vertical stretch, a vertical translation. Describe each fully. [4] (c) Solve $g(x)=0.5$ for $0\le x\le\pi$. [4]
markscheme: (a) Amplitude $=3$ [A1] period $=\pi$ [A1] range $-4\le g(x)\le2$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Horizontal stretch with scale factor $\frac12$ [A1] translation by $\begin{pmatrix}\frac\pi6\\0\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] vertical stretch with scale factor $3$ [A1] translation by $\begin{pmatrix}0\\-1\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) $\sin\left(2x-\frac\pi3\right)=\frac12$ [M1] Let $\theta=2x-\frac\pi3\in\left[-\frac\pi3,\frac{5\pi}3\right]$; $\theta=\frac\pi6$ or $\frac{5\pi}6$ [A1] $x=\frac{\theta+\pi/3}2$ [M1] $x=\frac\pi4$ or $x=\frac{7\pi}{12}$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Convert the interval for $x$ into an interval for the angle before listing solutions, so no solutions are missed or invented. In $a\sin(b(x-c))+d$, $c$ is a horizontal translation and $d$ a vertical one.

subtopic: Sine and cosine graphs related by a translation
statement: (a) Show that $\cos\left(2x-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)=\sin\left(2x+\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$. [2] (b) Hence describe a single transformation that maps the graph of $y=\sin 2x$ onto the graph of $y=\cos\left(2x-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$. [3] (c) The same image can be obtained by a translation to the right. Find the smallest positive distance of such a translation. [1]
markscheme: (a) Use $\cos\theta=\sin\left(\theta+\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$ [M1] $\cos\left(2x-\dfrac\pi3\right)=\sin\left(2x-\dfrac\pi3+\dfrac\pi2\right)=\sin\left(2x+\dfrac\pi6\right)$ [A1] [AG] [2 marks] (b) $\sin\left(2x+\dfrac\pi6\right)=\sin\left(2\left(x+\dfrac\pi{12}\right)\right)$ [M1] translation [A1] by $\begin{pmatrix} -\frac{\pi}{12} \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) The period of $\sin2x$ is $\pi$ so a translation right by $\pi-\dfrac\pi{12}=\dfrac{11\pi}{12}$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Factor out the coefficient of $x$ so that the horizontal shift can be read off: $\sin(2x+c)=\sin\left(2\left(x+\tfrac c2\right)\right)$. Shifts that differ by a whole number of periods give the same graph.

subtopic: Projectile path shifted by a translation
statement: A ball is thrown from a point above level ground. Its height $h$ meters above the ground, when it is a horizontal distance $x$ meters from the origin, is modeled by $h(x)=-0.04x^2+1.2x+1.5$, $x\ge0$. (a) Write down the initial height of the ball. [1] (b) Find the maximum height reached by the ball and the value of $x$ at which it occurs. [3] (c) Find the horizontal distance from the origin at which the ball hits the ground. [2] Another throw is modeled by $g(x)=h(x-3)+2$. (d) Describe the transformation that maps the graph of $h$ onto the graph of $g$. [2] (e) Find the maximum height reached by the second ball and the horizontal distance from the origin at which it hits the ground. [2]
markscheme: (a) $h(0)=1.5$ m [A1] [1 mark] (b) Use GDC or $x=-\dfrac{1.2}{2(-0.04)}=15$ [M1] [A1] Maximum height $h(15)=10.5$ m [A1] [3 marks] (c) Solve $-0.04x^2+1.2x+1.5=0$ [M1] $x=31.2$ m [A1] [2 marks] (d) Translation by the vector $\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1][A1] [2 marks] (e) Maximum height $10.5+2=12.5$ m [A1] Lands at $x=35.7$ m [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Reject the negative root in part (c) because $x\ge0$. For the translated graph, add the translation to the vertex and to the positive root, or solve $g(x)=0$ directly.

subtopic: Composite transformations of a quadratic
statement: Let $f(x)=x^2-4x+3$ and $g(x)=f(2x-1)$. (a) Show that $g(x)=4x^2-12x+8$. [2] (b) Hence find the zeros of $g$. [2] (c) The graph of $g$ is obtained from the graph of $f$ by two transformations. Describe each fully. [3] (d) Find the coordinates of the vertex of the graph of $g$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $g(x)=(2x-1)^2-4(2x-1)+3$ [M1] $=4x^2-4x+1-8x+4+3=4x^2-12x+8$ [A1][AG] [2 marks] (b) $4(x-1)(x-2)=0$ [M1] $x=1$ or $x=2$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $g(x)=f(2(x-\frac12))$ [M1] horizontal stretch with scale factor $\frac12$ [A1] then translation by $\begin{pmatrix}\frac12\\0\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] (accept: translation by $\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix}$ followed by horizontal stretch with scale factor $\frac12$) [3 marks] (d) $x=\frac{12}8=\frac32$ [A1] $g\left(\frac32\right)=-1$, so $\left(\frac32,-1\right)$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Replacing $x$ by $2x-1$ stretches horizontally and shifts. The zeros of $g$ are the zeros of $f$ transformed: $x=1,3$ become $x=1,2$.

subtopic: Vertex form, horizontal stretch and translation
statement: Let $f(x)=x^2-6x+5$. (a) Write $f(x)$ in the form $(x-h)^2+k$. [2] The graph of $y=f(x)$ is transformed by a horizontal stretch with scale factor $\dfrac12$, giving the graph of $y=p(x)$. (b) Write down $p(x)$ in the form $(ax-b)^2+c$. [1] The graph of $y=p(x)$ is then translated by the vector $\begin{pmatrix}0\\k\end{pmatrix}$ to give the graph of $y=q(x)$. The graph of $q$ passes through the point $(1,3)$. (c) Find the value of $k$. [2] (d) Write down the coordinates of the vertex of the graph of $q$. [1]
tips: A horizontal stretch with scale factor $\frac12$ replaces $x$ by $2x$, not $x/2$. Complete the square first so that the effect on the vertex is easy to read.

subtopic: Describing the sine graph transformation to 3 sin(2x - pi/3) + 1
statement: The graph of $y=\sin x$ is transformed to the graph of $y=g(x)$, where $g(x)=3\sin\left(2x-\dfrac\pi3\right)+1$. (a) Describe a sequence of four transformations that maps $y=\sin x$ onto $y=g(x)$. [4] (b) The point $\left(\dfrac\pi2,1\right)$ lies on the graph of $y=\sin x$. Find the coordinates of its image on the graph of $y=g(x)$. [2] (c) Write down the range and the period of $g$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $g(x)=3\sin\left(2\left(x-\dfrac\pi6\right)\right)+1$. Horizontal stretch with scale factor $\dfrac12$ [A1] translation $\dfrac\pi6$ to the right [A1] vertical stretch with scale factor 3 [A1] translation $1$ unit up [A1] (any equivalent valid sequence is accepted, for example a translation $\dfrac\pi3$ to the right applied before the horizontal stretch, or the vertical transformations applied first) [4 marks] (b) $x$: $\dfrac\pi2\to\dfrac\pi4\to\dfrac{5\pi}{12}$, $y$: $1\to3\to4$ [M1] image $\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{12},4\right)$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) range $-2\le y\le4$ [A1] period $\pi$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Factor the coefficient of $x$ out of the bracket to see the true horizontal translation: $2x-\dfrac\pi3=2\left(x-\dfrac\pi6\right)$. Check your image point by substituting it into $g$.

subtopic: Logarithmic function with a horizontal stretch and shift
statement: Let $f(x)=\ln x$ and $g(x)=\ln(3x-6)+1$. (a) Write $g(x)$ in the form $\ln(x-2)+c$, giving the exact value of $c$, and describe the transformation from $f$ to $g$. [3] (b) State the domain of $g$ and the equation of its vertical asymptote. [2] (c) Find the exact solution of $g(x)=3$ and the $x$-intercept of $g$, correct to 3 significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) $g(x)=\ln3+\ln(x-2)+1$ [M1]; $c=1+\ln3$ [A1]; translation $\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1+\ln3 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) domain $x>2$ [A1]; asymptote $x=2$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $3x-6=e^{2}$ [M1]; $x=\dfrac{6+e^{2}}{3}$ [A1]; $x$-intercept: $3x-6=e^{-1}$ gives $x=2.12$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Use $\ln(ab)=\ln a+\ln b$ to separate the factor $3$ from $(x-2)$.

subtopic: A rational function as a translated reciprocal
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{3x+5}{x+1}$ for $x\ne-1$. (a) Show that $f(x)=3+\dfrac{2}{x+1}$. [2] (b) Describe a sequence of transformations that maps the graph of $y=\dfrac1x$ to the graph of $y=f(x)$. [3] (c) Write down the equations of the asymptotes of the graph of $f$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $3x+5=3(x+1)+2$ [M1]; so $f(x)=3+\dfrac{2}{x+1}$ [AG] [2 marks] (b) Vertical stretch factor $2$ [A1]; translation $\begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; translation $\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $x=-1$ [A1]; $y=3$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Divide the numerator by the denominator to rewrite the function in terms of $\frac{1}{x+1}$.

subtopic: Sinusoidal tide model from transformations of cosine
statement: The depth of water in a harbor, $h$ meters, at $t$ hours after midnight is modeled by $h(t)=a\cos(bt)+d$, for $t\ge 0$, where $a,b,d>0$. The maximum depth is $5.4$ m, the minimum depth is $0.6$ m, and the time between consecutive high tides is $12$ hours. There is a high tide at midnight ($t=0$). (a) Find the value of $a$, of $d$ and of $b$ (exact form or to 3 s.f.). [4] (b) Find the depth of the water at $t=5$. [1] A boat can enter the harbor only when the depth is greater than $4$ m. (c) Find the total time, in hours, during the first $24$ hours after midnight for which the boat can enter the harbor. [3]
markscheme: (a) $a=\dfrac{5.4-0.6}{2}=2.4$ [A1] $d=\dfrac{5.4+0.6}{2}=3$ [A1] $b=\dfrac{2\pi}{12}$ [M1] $b=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ ($0.524$) [A1] [4 marks] (b) $h(5)=2.4\cos\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right)+3=0.922$ m ($0.92153\ldots$) [A1] [1 mark] (c) Solve $2.4\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{6}\right)+3=4$ using the GDC [M1] first interval $0\le t<2.18$ ($2.1792\ldots$) and, by symmetry, $9.82<t<14.18$, then $21.8<t\le 24$ [A1] Total time $=4\times 2.1792\ldots=8.72$ hours ($8.7168\ldots$) [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Match the amplitude, vertical shift and period to the maximum, minimum and time between peaks before using a GDC. In part (c) use the symmetry and periodicity of the cosine curve to avoid missing the interval that straddles $t=12$.

subtopic: Even and odd extensions and symmetry of transformed graphs
statement: This question investigates how transformations affect the symmetry of the graph of $f(x)=x^3-x$. (a) Show that $f$ is an odd function and describe the symmetry of its graph. [3] (b) The graph of $g(x)=f(x-a)$ is a translation of the graph of $f$. Show that $g$ has rotational symmetry about the point $(a,0)$. [3] (c) Find $a$ such that the graph of $y=f(x-a)+c$ has $(2,3)$ as its centre of symmetry, and state $c$. [2] (d) Find the coordinates of the local maximum and minimum of $y=f(x-2)+3$, and verify that they are symmetric about $(2,3)$. [4] (e) Show that the graph of $y=|f(x)|$ is symmetric about the line $x=0$ whenever $f$ is odd or even, and verify this for $f(x)=x^3-x$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $f(-x)=-x^3+x=-f(x)$ [M1][A1] rotational symmetry of order $2$ about the origin [A1] [3 marks] (b) $g(a+h)=f(h)$ and $g(a-h)=f(-h)=-f(h)$ [M1][A1] so $g(a+h)+g(a-h)=0$: point symmetry about $(a,0)$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) centre of symmetry of $f$ is $(0,0)$, moved to $(a,c)$ [M1] $a=2$, $c=3$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $f'(x)=3x^2-1$ so $x=\pm\dfrac1{\sqrt3}$ [M1] $f\left(-\dfrac1{\sqrt3}\right)=\dfrac2{3\sqrt3}$ and $f\left(\dfrac1{\sqrt3}\right)=-\dfrac2{3\sqrt3}$ [A1] new maximum $\left(2-\dfrac1{\sqrt3},3+\dfrac2{3\sqrt3}\right)$ [A1] new minimum $\left(2+\dfrac1{\sqrt3},3-\dfrac2{3\sqrt3}\right)$, the midpoint of the two points is $(2,3)$ [A1] [4 marks] (e) $|f(-x)|=|f(x)|$ when $f$ is odd or even [M1] for $f(x)=x^3-x$, $|f(-x)|=|-f(x)|=|f(x)|$ [A1] so the graph of $|f|$ is symmetric about the $y$-axis [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A translation moves the centre of symmetry with it. Symmetry statements follow from $f(a+h)\pm f(a-h)$.

subtopic: Exponential function, its inverse and the graph of the inverse
statement: Let $f(x)=3+e^{x-1}$, for $x\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Describe the single transformation that maps the graph of $y=e^x$ onto the graph of $y=f(x)$. [2] (b) Write down the equation of the horizontal asymptote of the graph of $y=f(x)$ and the range of $f$. [2] (c) Find an expression for $f^{-1}(x)$ and state its domain. [4] (d) Find the exact $x$-intercept of the graph of $y=f^{-1}(x)$. [2]
markscheme: (a) Translation [M1] by $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $y=3$ [A1] range $f(x)>3$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $x=3+e^{y-1}$ [M1] $e^{y-1}=x-3$ [M1] $f^{-1}(x)=1+\ln(x-3)$ [A1] domain $x>3$ [A1] [4 marks] (d) $1+\ln(x-3)=0$ [M1] $x=3+e^{-1}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The domain of $f^{-1}$ is the range of $f$. For part (d), set $f^{-1}(x)=0$ directly; there is no need to sketch anything.

subtopic: Splitting a polynomial into even and odd parts
statement: Any function $f$ can be written as $f=E+O$, where $E(x)=\dfrac{f(x)+f(-x)}2$ and $O(x)=\dfrac{f(x)-f(-x)}2$. (a) Show that $E$ is even and $O$ is odd. [2] (b) Find $E(x)$ and $O(x)$ for $f(x)=x^3+2x^2-5x+1$. [3] (c) Find $E(x)$ and $O(x)$ for $f(x)=e^x$. [2]
tips: For a polynomial, the even part contains the even powers of $x$ and the odd part contains the odd powers.

subtopic: Reciprocal-squared graph: sequence of four transformations
statement: Let $g(x)=\dfrac{8}{(2x+4)^2}-3$, for $x\in\mathbb{R}$, $x\ne-2$. (a) The graph of $y=\dfrac{1}{x^2}$ is mapped onto the graph of $y=g(x)$ by the following sequence of four transformations: a horizontal stretch, a horizontal translation, a vertical stretch, and a vertical translation. Find the scale factor of each stretch and describe each translation. [4] (b) Write down the equations of the asymptotes of the graph of $y=g(x)$. [2] (c) Solve $g(x)=0$, giving your answers in exact form. [2]
markscheme: (a) $g(x)=\dfrac{8}{\big(2(x+2)\big)^2}-3$. Horizontal stretch with scale factor $\dfrac12$ gives $y=\dfrac{1}{(2x)^2}$ [A1] translation $2$ units to the left gives $y=\dfrac{1}{(2x+4)^2}$ [A1] vertical stretch with scale factor $8$ [A1] translation $3$ units down [A1] [4 marks] (b) $x=-2$ [A1] $y=-3$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\dfrac{8}{(2x+4)^2}=3$ [M1] $(2x+4)^2=\dfrac83$ so $2x+4=\pm\sqrt{\tfrac83}$ and $x=-2\pm\sqrt{\tfrac23}=-2\pm\dfrac{\sqrt6}{3}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Factor $2$ out of the bracket first: $2x+4=2(x+2)$. The factor $2$ then gives the horizontal stretch and the $+2$ gives the horizontal translation.

subtopic: Parabolic cable reflected to form an arch
statement: The shape of a bridge cable between two towers is modeled by $f(x)=0.02x^2-1.6x+32$, where $x$ meters is the horizontal distance from the left tower and $0\le x\le80$, and $f(x)$ is the height of the cable in meters above the lowest point of the road. (a) Show that $f(x)=0.02(x-40)^2$. [2] (b) Write down the height of the cable at each tower and the coordinates of its lowest point. [2] A decorative arch has the shape of the graph of $g(x)=-f(x)+40$, $0\le x\le80$. (c) Describe the sequence of two transformations that maps the graph of $f$ onto the graph of $g$. [2] (d) Write $g(x)$ in the form $-0.02(x-h)^2+k$. [1] (e) Find the horizontal width of the arch at heights of at least $30$ m. [3]
markscheme: (a) $0.02(x-40)^2=0.02\left(x^2-80x+1600\right)$ [M1] $=0.02x^2-1.6x+32$ [AG] [2 marks] (b) Height $32$ m at both towers [A1] Lowest point $(40,0)$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Reflection in the $x$-axis [A1] Translation up by $40$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $g(x)=-0.02(x-40)^2+40$ [A1] [1 mark] (e) $-0.02(x-40)^2+40\ge30$ so $(x-40)^2\le500$ [M1] $40-\sqrt{500}\le x\le40+\sqrt{500}$ [A1] Width $=2\sqrt{500}=44.7$ m [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Once a quadratic is in vertex form the transformations from $y=x^2$ can be read off directly. For (e), solve $g(x)=30$ and use the symmetry of the parabola about $x=40$.

subtopic: Effect of stretches on turning points
statement: Let $f(x)=xe^{-x/3}$ for $x\geq0$ and let $g(x)=2f\left(\dfrac x2\right)$. (a) Use your calculator to find the maximum point of $f$. [2] (b) Describe the transformations from $y=f(x)$ to $y=g(x)$. [2] (c) Write down the maximum point of $g$. [2] (d) Find the zero(s) of $g$ and the equation of the horizontal asymptote. [2] (e) Solve $g(x)=1$. [3]
markscheme: (a) Maximum at $x=3.00$, $y=1.104$ [A1][A1] (exact: $(3,3e^{-1})$) [2 marks] (b) Horizontal stretch scale factor $2$ [A1]; vertical stretch scale factor $2$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $(2\times3.00,2\times1.104)=(6.00,2.207)$ [A1][A1] [2 marks] (d) $g(0)=0$, the only zero [A1]; $y=0$ as $x\to\infty$ [A1] [2 marks] (e) Solve on the GDC [M1]: $x=1.227$, $x=16.999$ [A1][A1] [3 marks]
tips: A horizontal stretch of scale factor $a$ multiplies $x$-coordinates by $a$; a vertical stretch of scale factor $b$ multiplies $y$-coordinates by $b$.

subtopic: Asymptotes and image points of a function with known properties
statement: The function $f$ is defined for $x\ne 2$. Its graph has vertical asymptote $x=2$, and $f(x)\to-3$ as $x\to\pm\infty$. The graph of $y=f(x)$ passes through the point $(4,1)$. (a) The function $g$ is defined by $g(x)=-2f(x+1)+5$. Write down the equations of the asymptotes of the graph of $y=g(x)$, and the coordinates of the image of $(4,1)$ on the graph of $y=g(x)$. [4] (b) The function $h$ is defined by $h(x)=f(2-x)$. Write down the equations of the asymptotes of the graph of $y=h(x)$, and the coordinates of the image of $(4,1)$ on the graph of $y=h(x)$. [3] (c) Write down the equation of the horizontal asymptote of the graph of $y=\dfrac{1}{f(x)}$. [1]
markscheme: (a) Translation $1$ unit left, vertical stretch with scale factor $2$, reflection in the $x$-axis, translation $5$ units up [M1] vertical asymptote $x=1$ [A1] horizontal asymptote $y=-2(-3)+5=11$ [A1] image of $(4,1)$ is $(3,\ 3)$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $h(x)=f(-(x-2))$: reflection in the $y$-axis then translation $2$ units right; vertical asymptote $2-x=2$ so $x=0$ [A1] horizontal asymptote $y=-3$ [A1] image of $(4,1)$ is $(-2,\ 1)$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $y=-\dfrac13$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: A horizontal asymptote is affected only by changes outside the brackets, and a vertical asymptote only by changes inside. For $f(2-x)$ solve $2-x=4$ to find the new $x$-coordinate.

subtopic: Transformations of an absolute value function
statement: Let $f(x)=|x-2|$. The graph of $y=f(x)$ is transformed to give $g(x)=f(x+1)-3$. (a) Write down $g(x)$ and the coordinates of its vertex. [2] (b) Find the $x$-intercepts and $y$-intercept of the graph of $g$. [3] (c) Use your GDC to solve $g(x)\le0$. [2]
tips: A translation by $\begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ -3 \end{pmatrix}$ replaces $x$ by $x+1$ and $y$ by $y+3$.

subtopic: Discount coupon and voucher as composite functions
statement: An online store offers two discounts. A coupon takes $15\%$ off the price, so $c(x)=0.85x$. A voucher takes \$20 off the price, so $v(x)=x-20$. Here $x$ is the price in dollars and $x>20$. (a) Find $(c\circ v)(x)$ and $(v\circ c)(x)$, giving each in the form $ax+b$. [2] (b) A jacket has a price of \$140. Find the final price when the voucher is applied first and when the coupon is applied first. [2] (c) Show that the difference between the two expressions in part (a) is the same for every price. [2] (d) A customer applies the coupon first and then the voucher and pays \$55. Find the original price of the item, to the nearest cent. [2]
tips: $c\circ v$ means apply $v$ first. The order of discounts matters because a percentage discount applied after the voucher also reduces the amount taken off by the voucher.

subtopic: Transforming key points of a graph
statement: The graph of $y=f(x)$ has a local maximum at $(2,5)$, a local minimum at $(6,-1)$ and passes through the origin. (a) Find the coordinates of the local maximum on the graph of $y=f(x-3)+2$. [2] (b) Find the coordinates of the local minimum on the graph of $y=2f\left(\dfrac x2\right)$. [3] (c) Find the coordinates of the images of the origin and the local maximum under $y=-f(x)$. [2]
markscheme: (a) horizontal translation $3$ right and vertical translation $2$ up [M1] $(5,7)$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) horizontal stretch by factor $2$ [M1] vertical stretch by factor $2$ [M1] $(12,-2)$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) reflection in the $x$-axis [M1] $(0,0)$ and $(2,-5)$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: For $y=af(b(x-c))+d$: the horizontal stretch is $1/b$ and the translations are $c$ and $d$; apply stretches before translations to each coordinate.

subtopic: Order of horizontal stretch and translation
statement: Let $f(x)=x^2$. (a) Find the equation of the graph obtained from $y=f(x)$ by (i) a horizontal stretch with scale factor $2$, followed by a translation by $\begin{pmatrix}3\\0\end{pmatrix}$; [2] (ii) the translation by $\begin{pmatrix}3\\0\end{pmatrix}$, followed by a horizontal stretch with scale factor $2$. [2] (b) Find the coordinates of the point where the two graphs found in part (a) intersect. [3]
markscheme: (a)(i) After the stretch: $y=\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)^2$ [M1] After the translation: $y=\left(\dfrac{x-3}{2}\right)^2$ [A1] [2 marks] (ii) After the translation: $y=(x-3)^2$ [M1] After the stretch: $y=\left(\dfrac{x}{2}-3\right)^2=\left(\dfrac{x-6}{2}\right)^2$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\left(\dfrac{x-3}{2}\right)^2=\left(\dfrac{x-6}{2}\right)^2\Rightarrow (x-3)^2=(x-6)^2$ [M1] $-6x+9=-12x+36$, so $x=\dfrac{9}{2}$ [A1] $y=\left(\dfrac{3/2}{2}\right)^2=\dfrac{9}{16}$, so the point is $\left(\dfrac{9}{2},\dfrac{9}{16}\right)$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A horizontal stretch replaces $x$ by $x/2$, so the order of transformations changes the result: if the translation comes first, the stretch also scales the translation distance. Substitute step by step rather than combining the two moves mentally.

subtopic: Piecewise taxi fare after a price rise
statement: A taxi fare, in dollars, for a journey of $d$ kilometers is $f(d)=\begin{cases}4+2.5d, & 0\le d\le8\\ 24+1.8(d-8), & d>8\end{cases}$. (a) Find $f(5)$ and $f(12)$. [2] The company raises all fares by $10\%$ and adds a fixed booking fee of \$2, giving a new fare function $g(d)=1.1f(d)+2$. (b) Show that $g(d)=6.4+2.75d$ for $0\le d\le8$, and find a similar expression for $g(d)$ when $d>8$. [3] (c) Find the distance for which the new fare is \$40. [2] (d) Find $g^{-1}(x)$ for $x>28.4$ and interpret what it represents. [3]
tips: Check which piece applies by comparing with the fare at the break point, $g(8)=28.4$. A vertical stretch by $1.1$ and a translation up by $2$ apply to every piece of a piecewise function.

subtopic: Areas under transformed graphs
statement: For a continuous function $f$, $\displaystyle\int_1^4f(x)\,dx=6$. (a) Find $\displaystyle\int_3^63f(x-2)\,dx$. [2] (b) Find $\displaystyle\int_{1}^{4}\left(f(x)+2\right)dx$. [2] (c) Find $\displaystyle\int_{1/2}^{2}f(2x)\,dx$. [2]
markscheme: (a) the graph is shifted $2$ to the right, so the limits $3$ to $6$ correspond to $1$ to $4$ [M1] $3\times6=18$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $6+2\times3$ [M1] $=12$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) let $u=2x$: $\dfrac12\int_1^4f(u)\,du$ [M1] $=3$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A horizontal stretch by factor $1/2$ halves the area, a vertical stretch by $3$ triples it, and translations leave it unchanged.

subtopic: Sequence of transformations from a square root to a reflected form
statement: Let $f(x)=\sqrt{x}$ for $x\ge 0$, and let $g(x)=2\sqrt{4-x}+1$. (a) The graph of $y=f(x)$ is mapped onto the graph of $y=g(x)$ by a vertical stretch, followed by a reflection in the $y$-axis, followed by a translation. Find the scale factor of the stretch and the translation vector. [4] (b) Write down the domain and the range of $g$. [2]
markscheme: (a) Vertical stretch with scale factor $2$ [A1] gives $y=2\sqrt{x}$, then reflection in the $y$-axis gives $y=2\sqrt{-x}$ [A1] $4-x=-(x-4)$ so replace $x$ by $x-4$ [M1] translation by $\begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ (4 units right, 1 unit up) [A1] [4 marks] (b) $x\le 4$ [A1] $g(x)\ge 1$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Rewrite $4-x$ as $-(x-4)$ so the reflection and the translation can be read off separately. The translation is to the right even though the bracket contains $-4$. The stretch and the reflection can be done in either order, but the translation must come last.

subtopic: Reflections of a logarithmic graph
statement: Let $f(x)=\ln(x+3)$ for $x>-3$. The graph of $g$ is the reflection of the graph of $f$ in the $y$-axis, and the graph of $h$ is the reflection of $f$ in the $x$-axis. (a) Write down expressions for $g(x)$ and $h(x)$, and state the domain of $g$. [3] (b) Find the equations of the vertical asymptotes of $g$ and of $h$. [2] (c) Find the $x$-intercepts of $f$, $g$ and $h$. [3] (d) Use your calculator to find the points where $y=g(x)$ meets the line $y=0.5x-0.2$. [3]
tips: Reflection in the $y$-axis replaces $x$ by $-x$ (the domain reverses); reflection in the $x$-axis negates the function.

subtopic: The modulus transformation of a graph
statement: Let $f(x)=x^2-4x+3$. (a) Find the zeros and the vertex of $f$. [3] (b) Consider the graph of $y=|f(x)|$. Find the coordinates of its local maximum point, and the number of solutions of $|f(x)|=\dfrac12$. [3] (c) Find the range of $y=|f(x)|$ and solve $|f(x)|=1$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $(x-1)(x-3)=0$ so $x=1,3$ [A1] vertex at $x=2$, $f(2)=-1$, $(2,-1)$ [A1][A1] [3 marks] (b) the part below the $x$-axis is reflected: local maximum $(2,1)$ [A1] the horizontal line $y=\dfrac12$ cuts the graph at $4$ points [M1][A1] [3 marks] (c) range $y\ge0$ [A1] $x^2-4x+3=1$ gives $x=2\pm\sqrt2$ [A1] $x^2-4x+3=-1$ gives $x=2$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: $|f|$ reflects the negative part of the graph upward. Equations $|f(x)|=k$ split into $f(x)=k$ and $f(x)=-k$.

subtopic: Tidal depth modeled by a cosine function
statement: At a harbor entrance, the depth of water, $d$ meters, $t$ hours after midnight is modeled by $d(t)=a\cos\big(b(t-c)\big)+k$, where $a>0$, $b>0$ and $0\le c<12.4$. High tide has depth $7.8$ m and occurs at $t=2$. Low tide has depth $3.2$ m. Successive high tides are $12.4$ hours apart. (a) Find the values of $a$, $k$ and $c$. [3] (b) Show that $b=0.507$, correct to three significant figures. [1] In the rest of this question use $b=\dfrac{2\pi}{12.4}$. (c) Find the depth of water at $t=5$. [2] (d) Boats can enter the harbor only when the depth is at least $4.5$ m. Find the first time after $t=2$ at which boats can no longer enter. [2] (e) Find the number of hours in each cycle of $12.4$ hours during which the depth is less than $4.5$ m. [2]
markscheme: (a) $a=\frac{7.8-3.2}{2}=2.3$ [A1] $k=\frac{7.8+3.2}{2}=5.5$ [A1] $c=2$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $b=\dfrac{2\pi}{12.4}=0.507$ [AG] [1 mark] (c) $d(5)=2.3\cos\left(\frac{2\pi}{12.4}\times3\right)+5.5$ [M1] $=5.62$ m [A1] [2 marks] (d) Solve $2.3\cos\left(\frac{2\pi}{12.4}(t-2)\right)+5.5=4.5$ [M1] $t=5.99$ hours [A1] [2 marks] (e) The depth is below $4.5$ from $t=5.99$ to $t=10.41$ [M1] Duration $=4.42$ hours [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Amplitude is half the difference between maximum and minimum; the midline is their mean. Use your GDC to solve the equation, in radians, and take the first solution after the maximum. By symmetry the depth is below $4.5$ over an interval centered on the low tide.

subtopic: Daylight hours modeled by a sine curve
statement: The number of hours of daylight, $D$, in a northern city on day $t$ of the year ($t=1$ is 1 January) is modeled by $D(t)=2.4\sin\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{365}(t-80.75)\right)+12$. (a) Write down the maximum number of hours of daylight and the value of $t$ at which it occurs. [2] (b) Find the number of hours of daylight on day $100$. Give your answer to three significant figures. [1] (c) Find the number of days, to the nearest whole number, for which $D(t)>13$ during the year. [4] A second city further north has daylight modeled by $E(t)=1.5D(t)-6$. (d) Describe the sequence of transformations that maps the graph of $D$ onto the graph of $E$. [2] (e) Find the maximum and the minimum number of hours of daylight in the second city. [2]
markscheme: (a) Maximum $=12+2.4=14.4$ hours [A1] at $t=80.75+\frac{365}{4}=172$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $D(100)=12.8$ hours [A1] [1 mark] (c) Solve $D(t)=13$ [M1] $t=105.7$ [A1] and $t=238.3$ [A1] Number of days $=238.3-105.7=132.6\approx133$ [A1] [4 marks] (d) Vertical stretch with scale factor $1.5$ [A1] Translation down by $6$ [A1] [2 marks] (e) Maximum $1.5(14.4)-6=15.6$ hours [A1] Minimum $1.5(9.6)-6=8.4$ hours [A1] [2 marks]
tips: For a sine model the maximum occurs when the sine equals $1$, a quarter period after the horizontal shift. For part (c) the interval between the two solutions of $D(t)=13$ gives the length of time above $13$ hours. Apply the stretch before the translation.

subtopic: Equation involving |2cos x - 1| and number of solutions
statement: Consider $f(x)=|2\cos x-1|$, for $0\le x\le 2\pi$. (a) Solve the equation $f(x)=1$. [4] (b) Find all values of $k\ge 0$ for which the equation $f(x)=k$ has exactly two solutions. [2]
markscheme: (a) $2\cos x-1=1$ or $2\cos x-1=-1$ [M1] $\cos x=1$ gives $x=0,\ 2\pi$ [A1] $\cos x=0$ gives $x=\dfrac\pi2,\ \dfrac{3\pi}2$ [A1] four solutions: $0,\ \dfrac{\pi}{2},\ \dfrac{3\pi}{2},\ 2\pi$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $2\cos x-1$ takes values from $-3$ to $1$ so $f$ takes values from $0$ to $3$; for $1<k<3$ only $2\cos x-1=-k$ is possible, giving two solutions [A1] $k=0$ gives $\cos x=\dfrac12$, two solutions [A1] (for $0<k\le1$ there are four solutions and for $k=3$ only one) [2 marks]
tips: Split $|g(x)|=k$ into two cases, then count solutions of each case across the whole domain. Check the extreme values of $k$ separately, since a solution at an endpoint or a repeated root changes the count.

subtopic: Translating an exponential graph by a vector
statement: The graph of $y=3^x$ is translated by the vector $\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -4 \end{pmatrix}$ to give the graph of $y=f(x)$. (a) Write down an expression for $f(x)$. [1] (b) Write down the equation of the horizontal asymptote of the graph of $f$. [1] (c) Find the exact $y$-intercept of the graph of $f$. [2] (d) Find the exact $x$-intercept of the graph of $f$, in terms of a logarithm to base $3$. [2]
tips: A translation by $\begin{pmatrix} a \\ b \end{pmatrix}$ replaces $x$ by $x-a$ and adds $b$. The horizontal asymptote shifts vertically with the graph. To solve $3^{x-2}=4$ take $\log_3$ of both sides.

subtopic: Transformations that give the same graph
statement: For some functions, a vertical stretch produces the same graph as a horizontal stretch or a translation. (a) Show that a vertical stretch of the graph of $y=x^3$ with scale factor $8$ gives the same graph as a horizontal stretch with scale factor $\dfrac12$. [2] (b) Find the horizontal stretch that gives the same graph as the vertical stretch of $y=\sqrt x$ with scale factor $3$. [2] (c) Find the horizontal translation that gives the same graph as the vertical stretch of $y=e^x$ with scale factor $5$. [2] (d) Explain why no horizontal translation of $y=x^2$ gives the same graph as a vertical stretch of $y=x^2$ with scale factor $4$. [1]
markscheme: (a) vertical stretch: $y=8x^3$ [A1] horizontal stretch with scale factor $\dfrac12$: $y=(2x)^3=8x^3$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $y=3\sqrt x=\sqrt{9x}$ [M1] horizontal stretch with scale factor $\dfrac19$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $5e^x=e^{x+\ln5}$ [M1] translation by $\ln5$ to the left [A1] [2 marks] (d) a translation moves the vertex, but the vertex of the stretched graph stays at the origin [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Rewrite the stretched equation in a form that looks like a horizontal change. Powers, roots and exponentials each have an identity that allows this.

subtopic: Evaluating a transformed function from given values
statement: The function $f$ has the values $f(0)=3$, $f(1)=5$, $f(2)=4$, $f(3)=-1$ and $f(6)=7$. A new function is $g(x)=2f(3x)+1$. (a) Find $g(0)$ and $g(1)$. [2] (b) Find $g(2)$ and the value of $x$ for which $g(x)=11$. [3] (c) Describe the transformations from $y=f(x)$ to $y=g(x)$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $g(0)=2f(0)+1=7$ [A1]; $g(1)=2f(3)+1=-1$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $g(2)=2f(6)+1=15$ [A1]; $2f(3x)+1=11$ so $f(3x)=5$ [M1]; $3x=1$ so $x=\dfrac13$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Horizontal stretch factor $\dfrac13$ [A1]; vertical stretch factor $2$ [A1]; translation $\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A point $(a,b)$ on $y=f(x)$ moves to $\left(\frac{a}{3},\,2b+1\right)$ on $y=g(x)$.

subtopic: Why the order of transformations matters
statement: The graph of $y=x^2$ is transformed by the following three transformations: $T_1$ is a horizontal stretch with scale factor $2$ (away from the $y$-axis); $T_2$ is a reflection in the $x$-axis; $T_3$ is a translation by the vector $\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) The transformations are applied in the order $T_1$, then $T_2$, then $T_3$. Find the equation of the image graph. [3] (b) Write down the coordinates of the vertex of this image graph. [1] (c) The transformations are now applied in the order $T_3$, then $T_1$, then $T_2$. Find the equation of the new image graph. [3] (d) Write down the coordinates of the vertex of the new graph. [1] (e) Find the $x$-coordinate of the point where the two image graphs intersect. [3]
tips: Apply each transformation to the equation obtained so far. A horizontal stretch replaces $x$ by $\frac x2$, which also stretches a translation applied earlier, so the vertex ends up at a different place. Write $\left(\frac x2-3\right)^2=\frac{(x-6)^2}{4}$ before equating.

subtopic: Log function: transformations, intercept and inverse
statement: Let $g(x)=3\ln(x+2)-1$, for $x>-2$. (a) Write down the equation of the vertical asymptote of the graph of $g$. [1] (b) Find the $x$-intercept of the graph of $g$. [2] (c) Describe a sequence of three transformations that maps the graph of $y=\ln x$ onto the graph of $y=g(x)$. [3] (d) Find $g^{-1}(x)$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $x=-2$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $3\ln(x+2)=1$ [M1] $x=e^{1/3}-2=-0.604$ ($-0.60438\ldots$) [A1] [2 marks] (c) Translation by $\begin{pmatrix}-2\\0\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] vertical stretch with scale factor $3$ [A1] translation by $\begin{pmatrix}0\\-1\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] (the stated order must be valid; equivalent sequences are accepted) [3 marks] (d) $x=3\ln(y+2)-1$ [M1] $\ln(y+2)=\dfrac{x+1}{3}$ [A1] $g^{-1}(x)=e^{(x+1)/3}-2$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: When describing a sequence of transformations, the order matters: the vertical stretch must be done before the final translation by $-1$. To find an inverse, swap $x$ and $y$ and then undo the operations in reverse order.

subtopic: Completing the square and describing transformations
statement: Let $g(x)=2x^{2}-12x+19$. (a) Write $g(x)$ in the form $a(x-h)^{2}+k$. [3] (b) Describe a sequence of transformations that maps the graph of $y=x^{2}$ to the graph of $y=g(x)$. [3] (c) Write down the coordinates of the vertex and the range of $g$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $2(x^{2}-6x)+19$ [M1]; $2(x-3)^{2}-18+19$ [A1]; $2(x-3)^{2}+1$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Vertical stretch factor $2$ [A1]; translation $\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; translation $\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $(3,1)$ [A1]; $g(x)\ge1$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Taking out the factor $2$ before completing the square gives the vertical stretch directly.

subtopic: Transformations of a quadratic graph
statement: The graph of $y=x^2$ is transformed by a translation $\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}$, followed by a vertical stretch with scale factor $2$ about the $x$-axis, followed by a reflection in the $x$-axis. (a) Find the equation of the resulting graph in the form $y=a(x-h)^2+k$. [4] (b) Write down the coordinates of the vertex and state whether it is a maximum or minimum. [2] (c) Find the $x$-intercepts of the resulting graph, in exact form. [3]
markscheme: (a) Translation: $y=(x-3)^2-2$ [M1][A1]; stretch: $y=2(x-3)^2-4$ [A1]; reflection: $y=-2(x-3)^2+4$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) Vertex $(3,4)$ [A1]; maximum, since the parabola opens downward [A1] [2 marks] (c) $-2(x-3)^2+4=0$ [M1]; $(x-3)^2=2$ [A1]; $x=3\pm\sqrt2$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Apply the transformations in the order stated; a vertical stretch multiplies the whole expression (including constants) by the scale factor.

subtopic: Stretches of a sine curve
statement: The graph of $y=\sin x$ is transformed to the graph of $y=3\sin\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)+1$ for $0\le x\le4\pi$. (a) Describe the two stretches and the translation in the transformation. [3] (b) Write down the amplitude, the period and the range of the new function. [3] (c) Find the exact values of $x$ in $0\le x\le4\pi$ where $y=\dfrac52$. [2]
markscheme: (a) Vertical stretch factor $3$ [A1]; horizontal stretch factor $2$ [A1]; translation $\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) amplitude $3$ [A1]; period $4\pi$ [A1]; range $-2\le y\le4$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\sin\dfrac{x}{2}=\dfrac12$ [M1]; $x=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ or $x=\dfrac{5\pi}{3}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Replacing $x$ by $\frac{x}{b}$ stretches horizontally by the factor $b$.

subtopic: Fitting a logarithmic function with a vertical asymptote
statement: The graph of $g(x)=a\ln(x-b)+c$ has vertical asymptote $x=1.5$ and passes through the points $(2.5,\,4)$ and $(3.5,\,7)$. (a) Write down the value of $b$. [1] (b) Find the value of $c$ and the exact value of $a$. [4] (c) Solve $g(x)=0$. [2]
tips: The vertical asymptote of $a\ln(x-b)+c$ is at $x=b$. Choose a point where $x-b=1$ first, since $\ln 1=0$ isolates $c$ immediately.

subtopic: Choosing a translation that makes a function even
statement: Let $f(x)=x^2+bx+c$. (a) Find the value of $b$ for which $g(x)=f(x+2)$ is an even function. [3] (b) State the equation of the axis of symmetry of the graph of $y=f(x)$ for this value of $b$, and explain your answer. [2]
markscheme: (a) $g(x)=x^2+(4+b)x+4+2b+c$ [M1][A1] even requires $4+b=0$, so $b=-4$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $x=2$ [A1] $g$ is even, so its graph is symmetric about the $y$-axis; $f$ is $g$ translated $2$ units to the right [R1] [2 marks]
tips: The graph of $y=f(x+2)$ is the graph of $y=f(x)$ moved 2 units to the left.

subtopic: Cubic road profile and its translated copy
statement: The height, $f(x)$ meters, of a road above sea level is modeled by $f(x)=0.1x^3-1.2x^2+3.6x+2$, where $x$ is the horizontal distance in hundreds of meters from the start, $0\le x\le12$. (a) Use your GDC to find the coordinates of the local maximum point and the local minimum point of the graph of $f$. [2] A second road follows the profile $g(x)=f(x-3)-1.5$. (b) Write down the coordinates of the local maximum point and the local minimum point of the graph of $g$. [2] (c) Find the values of $x$ for which $g(x)=2$. [3] (d) Write down the domain of $g$ and find its range. [3]
markscheme: (a) Local maximum $(2,5.2)$ [A1] Local minimum $(6,2)$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) The graph is translated by $\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ -1.5 \end{pmatrix}$, so the local maximum is $(5,3.7)$ [A1] and the local minimum is $(9,0.5)$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Solve $g(x)=2$ [M1] $x=3.49$ [A1] $x=7.08$ and $x=10.4$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) Domain $3\le x\le15$ [A1] $g(3)=f(0)-1.5=0.5$ and $g(15)=f(12)-1.5=43.7$ [M1] Range $0.5\le g(x)\le43.7$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A translation moves stationary points by the same vector. When the domain is limited, check the end points of the interval as well as the turning points before stating the range.

subtopic: Graphs of |f(x)| and f(|x|)
statement: Let $f(x)=x^2-2x-3$. Consider the graphs of $y=|f(x)|$ and $y=f(|x|)$. (a) Find the zeros of $f$ and the vertex of $y=f(x)$. [3] (b) Describe how the graph of $y=|f(x)|$ is obtained from that of $y=f(x)$, and write down its range and the greatest value of $|f(x)|$ on $-2\leq x\leq4$. [3] (c) Use your calculator to solve $|f(x)|=2$. [3] (d) Describe the graph of $y=f(|x|)$ and use your calculator to solve $f(|x|)=2$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $(x-3)(x+1)=0$ so $x=-1,3$ [A1][A1]; vertex $(1,-4)$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Reflect the part below the $x$-axis in the $x$-axis [A1]; range $y\geq0$ [A1]; greatest value on the interval is $5$ (at $x=-2$ and $x=4$) [A1] [3 marks] (c) Intersections [M1]: $x=-1.449$, $x=-0.414$, $x=2.414$, $x=3.449$ [A2] [3 marks] (d) Reflect the part with $x\geq0$ in the $y$-axis (symmetric in the $y$-axis) [A1]; solutions $x=-3.449$, $x=3.449$ [A1][A1] [3 marks]
tips: $|f(x)|$ reflects negative $y$-values upward; $f(|x|)$ copies the right half of the graph onto the left.

subtopic: Currency exchange with a fixed fee and its inverse
statement: A currency bureau converts $x$ US dollars into $E(x)$ euros using $E(x)=0.92(x-5)$, $x>5$, where the \$5 is a fixed fee. (a) Find the number of euros received for \$250. [1] (b) Find an expression for $E^{-1}(x)$ and explain what it represents. [3] (c) Find the number of dollars needed to receive 300 euros, to the nearest cent. [2]
markscheme: (a) $E(250)=0.92(245)=225.4$ euros [A1] [1 mark] (b) $y=0.92(x-5)$ so $x=\dfrac{y}{0.92}+5$ [M1] $E^{-1}(x)=\dfrac{x}{0.92}+5$ [A1] It gives the number of dollars needed to receive $x$ euros [R1] [3 marks] (c) $E^{-1}(300)=\dfrac{300}{0.92}+5$ [M1] $=331.09$ dollars [A1] [2 marks]
tips: To find an inverse, swap the roles of input and output and rearrange; the inverse reverses the order of operations, so the fee is added back last.

subtopic: Exact rotation matrix through 60 degrees
statement: Let $\mathbf{R}$ be the matrix of an anticlockwise rotation through $60^\circ$ about the origin. (a) Write down $\mathbf{R}$, giving exact values for each entry. [2] (b) Find the exact coordinates of the image of $A(4,2)$ under this rotation. [2] (c) Find $\mathbf{R}^3$, and hence describe the single transformation represented by $\mathbf{R}^3$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{R}=\begin{pmatrix}\cos60^\circ&-\sin60^\circ\\ \sin60^\circ&\cos60^\circ\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $=\begin{pmatrix}\tfrac12&-\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\\ \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}&\tfrac12\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\mathbf{R}\begin{pmatrix}4\\2\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}2-\sqrt3\\2\sqrt3+1\end{pmatrix}$ [M1] Image is $(2-\sqrt3,\ 2\sqrt3+1)$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Three rotations of $60^\circ$ give a rotation of $180^\circ$, so $\mathbf{R}^3=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] This is a rotation through $180^\circ$ about the origin (equivalently an enlargement with scale factor $-1$ and centre the origin) [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Learn the exact values of $\sin$ and $\cos$ at $30^\circ$, $45^\circ$ and $60^\circ$; they appear constantly in rotation matrices. Repeating a rotation just adds the angles, which is faster than multiplying matrices out.

subtopic: Identifying a reflection matrix and a composite rotation
statement: The matrix $\mathbf{M}=\begin{pmatrix} 0.6 & 0.8 \\ 0.8 & -0.6 \end{pmatrix}$ represents a transformation of the plane. (a) Show that $\mathbf{M}^2=\mathbf{I}$. [2] (b) Find $\det\mathbf{M}$. [1] (c) Find the equation of the line of invariant points of $\mathbf{M}$. [3] The matrix $\mathbf{M}$ has the form $\begin{pmatrix} \cos2\theta & \sin2\theta \\ \sin2\theta & -\cos2\theta \end{pmatrix}$ for a reflection in a line through the origin at angle $\theta$ to the positive $x$-axis, where $0^\circ<\theta<90^\circ$. (d) Find $\theta$, correct to 3 significant figures, and show that your value is consistent with your answer to part (c). [2] The reflection $\mathbf{M}$ is followed by a reflection $\mathbf{N}$ in the $y$-axis. (e) Show that the combined transformation is a rotation about the origin, and find its angle, correct to 1 decimal place, and direction. [4]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{M}^2=\begin{pmatrix} 0.36+0.64 & 0.48-0.48 \\ 0.48-0.48 & 0.64+0.36 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}=\mathbf{I}$ [AG] [2 marks] (b) $\det\mathbf{M}=(0.6)(-0.6)-(0.8)(0.8)=-1$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $\mathbf{M}\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{v}$ gives $0.6x+0.8y=x$ [M1] so $-0.4x+0.8y=0$ [A1] $y=0.5x$ (the second equation $0.8x-1.6y=0$ is the same line) [A1] [3 marks] (d) $\cos2\theta=0.6$ gives $2\theta=53.13^\circ$, so $\theta=26.6^\circ$ [M1] $\tan26.565^\circ=0.5$, which matches the gradient found in part (c) [A1] [2 marks] (e) $\mathbf{NM}=\begin{pmatrix} -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 0.6 & 0.8 \\ 0.8 & -0.6 \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} -0.6 & -0.8 \\ 0.8 & -0.6 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1] This has the form $\begin{pmatrix} \cos\varphi & -\sin\varphi \\ \sin\varphi & \cos\varphi \end{pmatrix}$ with $\cos\varphi=-0.6$ and $\sin\varphi=0.8$ (and $\det=1$), so it is a rotation [R1] $\varphi=180^\circ-53.13^\circ=126.9^\circ$ anticlockwise [A1] [4 marks]
tips: The matrix $\begin{pmatrix} c & s \\ s & -c \end{pmatrix}$ with $c^2+s^2=1$ is always a reflection, and the product of two reflections is a rotation (determinant $+1$). For the rotation angle, use both the cosine and the sine to choose the correct quadrant.

subtopic: Composite stretch, reflection and enlargement
statement: A transformation of the plane is made in three stages: $S$: a horizontal stretch (parallel to the $x$-axis) with scale factor $3$; $R$: a reflection in the $x$-axis; $E$: an enlargement with centre the origin and scale factor $2$. (a) Write down the matrix of each of $S$, $R$ and $E$. [3] (b) Find the single matrix $\mathbf{T}$ that represents $S$, followed by $R$, followed by $E$. [2] (c) The parabola with equation $y=x^2$ is transformed by $\mathbf{T}$. Find the equation of the image curve. [3] (d) A region of area $5$ square units is transformed by $\mathbf{T}$. Find the area of its image. [2]
markscheme: (a) $S=\begin{pmatrix}3&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $R=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $E=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\mathbf{T}=ERS$ [M1] $\mathbf{T}=\begin{pmatrix}6&0\\0&-2\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) A point $(x,y)$ maps to $(X,Y)=(6x,-2y)$, so $x=\dfrac X6$ and $y=-\dfrac Y2$ [M1] Substituting into $y=x^2$: $-\dfrac Y2=\dfrac{X^2}{36}$ [M1] The image curve is $y=-\dfrac{x^2}{18}$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $\det\mathbf{T}=-12$, so the area scale factor is $12$ [M1] Image area $=12\times5=60$ square units [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The matrix for 'first S, then R, then E' is the product written right to left, $\mathbf{ERS}$. For the image of a curve, express the old coordinates in terms of the new ones and substitute into the original equation.

subtopic: Order of composite reflection and rotation
statement: Let $A$ be a reflection in the $y$-axis and let $B$ be a clockwise rotation through $90^\circ$ about the origin. (a) Write down the matrices $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$. [2] (b) Find the matrix of the transformation '$A$ followed by $B$', and describe the single transformation it represents. [3] (c) Find the matrix of the transformation '$B$ followed by $A$', and describe the single transformation it represents. [3] (d) State whether $\mathbf{AB}=\mathbf{BA}$, and give a reason. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\mathbf{B}=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) '$A$ then $B$' is $\mathbf{BA}=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] Reflection in the line $y=x$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) '$B$ then $A$' is $\mathbf{AB}=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] Reflection in the line $y=-x$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $\mathbf{AB}\neq\mathbf{BA}$ because the two products are different matrices (the order of transformations matters) [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Matrix multiplication is not commutative, so always decide which transformation is applied first before multiplying. Testing the image of a simple point such as $(1,0)$ quickly confirms the geometric description.

subtopic: Reflection matrix in a line through the origin
statement: The matrix of a reflection in the line $y=x\tan\theta$ is $\begin{pmatrix} \cos2\theta & \sin2\theta \\ \sin2\theta & -\cos2\theta \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find the matrix of the reflection in the line $y=\sqrt3x$. [3] (b) Show that the point $(1,\sqrt3)$ on the line is invariant. [2] (c) Find the determinant of the matrix and its square, and explain their values. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\tan\theta=\sqrt3$ so $\theta=60^\circ$ [A1]; $2\theta=120^\circ$ [M1]; $\begin{pmatrix} -\frac12 & \frac{\sqrt3}{2} \\ \frac{\sqrt3}{2} & \frac12 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $-\dfrac12+\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\sqrt3=1$ [A1]; $\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}+\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}=\sqrt3$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\det=-\dfrac14-\dfrac34=-1$ [A1]; square $=I$ [A1]; a reflection reverses orientation and applying it twice returns every point [R1] [3 marks]
tips: Points on the line of reflection are invariant; a reflection matrix squared is the identity.

subtopic: Finding a transformation matrix from two image points
statement: A linear transformation with matrix $M$ maps the point $(1,2)$ to $(4,7)$ and the point $(3,1)$ to $(7,6)$. (a) Write down a matrix equation for $M$ using the two points as columns. [2] (b) Use your GDC to find $M$. [3] (c) Find the area of the image of a triangle of area $6$, and the image of the point $(2,-1)$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $M\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 4 & 7 \\ 7 & 6 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1][A1] [2 marks] (b) $M=\begin{pmatrix} 4 & 7 \\ 7 & 6 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}^{-1}$ [M1]; $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}^{-1}=-\dfrac15\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -3 \\ -2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; $M=\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\det M=5$ [A1]; area $30$ [A1]; image $(3,-1)$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: If the two given points are written as the columns of a matrix $P$ and their images as the columns of $Q$, then $MP=Q$.

subtopic: Unknown parameter from the area of an image triangle
statement: The matrix $\mathbf{M}=\begin{pmatrix} a & 2 \\ 1 & a \end{pmatrix}$ represents a transformation of the plane, where $a$ is a real constant. Triangle $ABC$ has vertices $A(1,\,0)$, $B(4,\,0)$ and $C(1,\,3)$. (a) Find an expression for $\det\mathbf{M}$ in terms of $a$. [1] (b) Find the area of triangle $ABC$. [2] The image of triangle $ABC$ under $\mathbf{M}$ has area $22.5$ square units. (c) Find the possible values of $a$. [3] (d) Given that $a>0$, find the exact distance between $A'$ and $C'$, the images of $A$ and $C$. [3]
