statement: In triangle $ABC$, the bisector of angle $A$ meets $BC$ at $D$. (a) By applying the sine rule in triangles $ABD$ and $ACD$, show that $\dfrac{BD}{DC}=\dfrac{AB}{AC}$. [4] (b) Given $AB=7$ cm, $AC=5$ cm and angle $A=60^\circ$, find $BC$, $BD$ and $DC$. [4]
markscheme: (a) in $ABD$: $\dfrac{BD}{\sin(A/2)}=\dfrac{AB}{\sin\angle ADB}$ [M1] in $ACD$: $\dfrac{DC}{\sin(A/2)}=\dfrac{AC}{\sin\angle ADC}$ [M1] $\angle ADB+\angle ADC=180^\circ$, so the sines are equal [R1] divide: $\dfrac{BD}{DC}=\dfrac{AB}{AC}$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $BC^2=49+25-70\cos60^\circ=39$ [M1] $BC=6.24$ [A1] $BD=\dfrac7{12}\times6.24=3.64$ cm [A1] $DC=2.60$ cm [A1] [4 marks]
tips: The two angles at $D$ on the line $BC$ add to $180^\circ$, so their sines are equal. Use this to compare the two sine rule equations.

subtopic: Proof of the sine rule
statement: In triangle $ABC$, the sides opposite $A$, $B$, $C$ have lengths $a$, $b$, $c$. (a) Let $CH$ be the perpendicular from $C$ to the line $AB$, with length $h$, in the case where angles $A$ and $B$ are both acute. Show that $h=b\sin A$ and $h=a\sin B$, and deduce that $\dfrac a{\sin A}=\dfrac b{\sin B}$. [3] (b) Explain why the result still holds if angle $A$ is obtuse. [2]
markscheme: (a) in right-angled triangle $ACH$, $h=b\sin A$ [A1] in right-angled triangle $BCH$, $h=a\sin B$ [A1] so $b\sin A=a\sin B$, giving $\dfrac a{\sin A}=\dfrac b{\sin B}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) the perpendicular meets $AB$ extended, so the angle in the right-angled triangle is $180^\circ-A$ [M1] $\sin(180^\circ-A)=\sin A$, so $h=b\sin A$ is unchanged [R1] [2 marks]
tips: The perpendicular height can be expressed in two ways using the two right-angled triangles. Equate them.

subtopic: Bearings forming a right-angled triangle
statement: A boat leaves a harbor $H$ and sails $12$ km on a bearing of $035^\circ$ to a buoy $B$. It then sails $9$ km on a bearing of $125^\circ$ to a point $C$. (a) Show that angle $HBC=90^\circ$. [2] (b) Find the distance $HC$. [2] (c) Find the bearing of $C$ from $H$, to the nearest tenth of a degree. [3]
markscheme: (a) The bearing of $H$ from $B$ is $035^\circ+180^\circ=215^\circ$ [M1] The bearing of $C$ from $B$ is $125^\circ$, and $215^\circ-125^\circ=90^\circ$, so angle $HBC=90^\circ$ [AG] [A1] [2 marks] (b) $HC=\sqrt{12^2+9^2}$ [M1] $=15$ km [A1] [2 marks] (c) Angle $BHC=\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{9}{12}\right)=36.87^\circ$ [M1] $C$ lies clockwise from $B$ as seen from $H$, so the bearing is $35^\circ+36.87^\circ$ [M1] $=71.9^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Use alternate (back) bearings by adding or subtracting $180^\circ$. A quick sketch with a north line at each point prevents sign errors.

subtopic: Angles of elevation of a tower from two points
statement: From a point $A$ on level ground the angle of elevation of the top $T$ of a vertical tower is $25^\circ$. From a point $B$, $50$ m closer to the tower and in line with it and $A$, the angle of elevation is $40^\circ$. (a) Show that angle $ATB=15^\circ$. [2] (b) Use the sine rule in triangle $ATB$ to find $BT$. [3] (c) Find the height of the tower. [2]
markscheme: (a) exterior angle of triangle $ATB$ at $B$ is $40^\circ$ [M1] $\angle ATB=40^\circ-25^\circ=15^\circ$ [A1] [AG] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac{BT}{\sin25^\circ}=\dfrac{50}{\sin15^\circ}$ [M1][A1] $BT=81.64$ m [A1] [3 marks] (c) $h=BT\sin40^\circ$ [M1] $=52.5$ m [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Use the exterior angle theorem to find the angle at the top, then the sine rule to get a side, then a right triangle for the height.

subtopic: Cosine rule with 4, 5, 6 triangle and double angle
statement: In triangle $ABC$, $BC=4$, $CA=5$ and $AB=6$. (a) Use the cosine rule to show that $\cos A=\dfrac34$. [2] (b) Find the value of $\cos C$. [2] (c) Show that $\cos C=2\cos^2A-1$, and hence explain why angle $C$ is twice angle $A$. [3] (d) Find the exact area of triangle $ABC$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\cos A=\dfrac{5^2+6^2-4^2}{2(5)(6)}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{45}{60}=\dfrac34$ [AG] [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\cos C=\dfrac{4^2+5^2-6^2}{2(4)(5)}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{5}{40}=\dfrac18$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $2\cos^2A-1=2\left(\dfrac{9}{16}\right)-1=\dfrac18=\cos C$ [AG] [M1] Since $\cos C=\cos2A$ [A1] and since $\cos A>0$ means $0<2A<\pi$, while $0<C<\pi$, and cosine is one-to-one on $(0,\pi)$, $C=2A$ [R1] [3 marks] (d) $\sin A=\sqrt{1-\dfrac{9}{16}}=\dfrac{\sqrt7}{4}$ [M1] Area $=\tfrac12(5)(6)\dfrac{\sqrt7}{4}=\dfrac{15\sqrt7}{4}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Label the triangle carefully so that each angle is opposite the matching side in the cosine rule. Use $\sin^2A+\cos^2A=1$ to get an exact sine without a calculator.

subtopic: Trigonometry in a square-based pyramid
statement: A pyramid $VABCD$ has a horizontal square base $ABCD$ of side $8$ cm. The vertex $V$ is vertically above the centre $M$ of the base, with $VM=10$ cm. (a) Find the length of $AC$ and of $AM$. [2] (b) Find the length of the slant edge $VA$ and the angle between $VA$ and the base. [4] (c) Find the angle between the face $VAB$ and the base. [3]
markscheme: (a) $AC=8\sqrt2=11.31$ cm [A1] $AM=5.657$ cm [A1] [2 marks] (b) $VA=\sqrt{10^2+32.00}=11.49$ cm [M1][A1] $\tan\theta=\dfrac{10}{5.657}$ [M1] $\theta=60.5^\circ$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) let $N$ be the midpoint of $AB$, $MN=4$ [A1] $\tan\phi=\dfrac{10}4$ [M1] $\phi=68.2^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Draw right triangles using the vertical height. The angle between a face and the base is measured along a line perpendicular to their common edge.

subtopic: Resultant velocity of an aircraft in a crosswind
statement: An aircraft flies at an airspeed of $400$ km/h on a heading of $060^\circ$. The wind blows from a bearing of $330^\circ$ (that is, towards $150^\circ$) at $60$ km/h. (a) Show that the angle between the aircraft's heading and the direction towards which the wind blows is $90^\circ$. [1] (b) Find the aircraft's ground speed. [2] (c) Find the bearing of the aircraft's actual path, to the nearest degree. [3]
markscheme: (a) $150^\circ-60^\circ=90^\circ$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\sqrt{400^2+60^2}$ [M1] $=404$ km/h [A1] [2 marks] (c) the path is turned from the heading towards the wind direction by $\arctan\dfrac{60}{400}=8.53^\circ$ [M1][A1] bearing $=60^\circ+8.53^\circ\approx069^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Add the velocity vectors as the sides of a right-angled triangle. The wind pushes the aircraft towards the direction it blows to.

subtopic: Sprinkler sector: radians, area and perimeter
statement: A garden sprinkler waters a sector of a circle of radius $7.5$ m, with central angle $110^\circ$. (a) Write $110^\circ$ in radians, correct to 3 significant figures. [1] (b) Find the area watered. [2] (c) Find the length of fencing needed to enclose the sector, that is, the perimeter of the sector. [2]
markscheme: (a) $110\times\dfrac{\pi}{180}=1.92$ radians [A1] [1 mark] (b) Area $=\tfrac12(7.5)^2\left(\dfrac{11\pi}{18}\right)$ [M1] $=54.0\text{ m}^2$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Arc length $=7.5\times1.9199=14.399$ [M1] Perimeter $=2(7.5)+14.399=29.4$ m [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Do not round the angle until the end of a calculation; store the unrounded value on your GDC. Remember the perimeter includes both straight radii.

subtopic: Wedge: angles between lines and planes
statement: A solid wedge has a horizontal rectangular base $ABCD$ with $AB=6$ m and $AD=8$ m. The point $E$ is $5$ m vertically above $D$, and the point $F$ is $5$ m vertically above $C$. The top face $ABFE$ is a sloping rectangle, the face $DCFE$ is a vertical rectangle, and the triangles $ADE$ and $BCF$ are vertical triangular ends. (a) Find $AC$. [2] (b) Find the exact length of $AF$. [2] (c) Find the angle between $AF$ and the base $ABCD$. [2] (d) Find the angle between the sloping face $ABFE$ and the base $ABCD$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $AC=\sqrt{6^2+8^2}$ [M1] $=10$ m [A1] [2 marks] (b) $AF=\sqrt{AC^2+CF^2}=\sqrt{100+25}$ [M1] $=\sqrt{125}=5\sqrt5$ m [A1] [2 marks] (c) The angle is $\angle FAC$, so $\tan\angle FAC=\dfrac{5}{10}$ [M1] $=26.6^\circ$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) The faces meet along $AB$. $AD\perp AB$ and $AE$ lies in the sloping face, with $DE\perp AD$, so the angle is $\angle EAD$ with $\tan\angle EAD=\dfrac58$ [M1] $=32.0^\circ$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: For the angle between two planes, find a line in each plane perpendicular to their common edge. Check that the triangle you pick for the angle is right-angled.

subtopic: Area of a quadrilateral split by a diagonal
statement: In quadrilateral $ABCD$, $AB=5$ cm, $BC=7$ cm, $CD=6$ cm, $DA=4$ cm and angle $ABC=60^\circ$. (a) Find the length of the diagonal $AC$. [3] (b) Find angle $ADC$. [3] (c) Find the area of the quadrilateral. [2]
markscheme: (a) $AC^2=5^2+7^2-2\times5\times7\cos60^\circ$ [M1] $=39$ [A1] $AC=6.24$ cm [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\cos D=\dfrac{6^2+4^2-39}{2\times6\times4}$ [M1][A1] $D=74.3^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\dfrac12\times5\times7\sin60^\circ+\dfrac12\times6\times4\sin74.3^\circ$ [M1] $=26.7\text{ cm}^2$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Split the quadrilateral into two triangles along the diagonal. Use the cosine rule to find the diagonal and then the unknown angle.

subtopic: Area of a regular polygon inscribed in a circle
statement: A regular $n$-gon is inscribed in a circle of radius $r$. (a) Show that the area of the polygon is $\dfrac n2r^2\sin\dfrac{2\pi}n$. [2] (b) Find the area, as a multiple of $r^2$ to four significant figures, for $n=6$, $n=12$ and $n=100$. [3] (c) Explain why the area approaches $\pi r^2$ as $n$ becomes large. [1]
markscheme: (a) the polygon is made of $n$ isosceles triangles with sides $r,r$ and included angle $\dfrac{2\pi}n$ [M1] each has area $\dfrac12r^2\sin\dfrac{2\pi}n$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $n=6$: $2.598r^2$ [A1] $n=12$: $3.000r^2$ [A1] $n=100$: $3.140r^2$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) for small angles $\sin x\approx x$, so the area tends to $\dfrac n2r^2\times\dfrac{2\pi}n=\pi r^2$ [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Each triangle has two sides equal to the radius and an included angle of a $n$th of a full turn.

subtopic: Diagonals and angles in a cuboid
statement: A cuboid $ABCDEFGH$ has a horizontal rectangular base $ABCD$ with $AB=4$ cm and $AD=3$ cm. The vertical edges $AE$, $BF$, $CG$ and $DH$ each have length $12$ cm, with $E$, $F$, $G$, $H$ directly above $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ respectively. (a) Show that the space diagonal $AG=13$ cm. [2] (b) Find the exact value of the sine of the angle between $AG$ and the base $ABCD$. [2] (c) Find the exact value of $\cos\angle AGE$, where $E$ is directly above $A$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $AC=\sqrt{4^2+3^2}=5$ [M1] $AG=\sqrt{5^2+12^2}=13$ cm [AG] [A1] [2 marks] (b) The angle between $AG$ and the base is $\angle GAC$, in the right-angled triangle $ACG$ with $CG=12$ [M1] $\sin\angle GAC=\dfrac{CG}{AG}=\dfrac{12}{13}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $EG=\sqrt{4^2+3^2}=5$ and $AE\perp EG$, so triangle $AEG$ is right-angled at $E$ [M1] $\cos\angle AGE=\dfrac{EG}{AG}=\dfrac{5}{13}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: In 3D problems, identify a right-angled triangle that contains the required angle and write down its sides before using any ratio. The angle between a line and a plane is measured to its projection onto the plane.

subtopic: The space diagonal of a cuboid
statement: A cuboid $ABCDEFGH$ has base $ABCD$ with $AB=6$ cm, $BC=4$ cm and height $AE=3$ cm. (a) Find the length of the diagonal $AG$. [3] (b) Find the angle between $AG$ and the base $ABCD$. [3] (c) Find the angle between $AG$ and the edge $AB$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $AC=\sqrt{36+16}$ [M1] $AG=\sqrt{36+16+9}$ [A1] $=7.810$ cm [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\tan\theta=\dfrac{CG}{AC}=\dfrac3{\sqrt{52}}$ [M1][A1] $\theta=22.6^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\cos\alpha=\dfrac{\overrightarrow{AG}\cdot\overrightarrow{AB}}{|AG||AB|}=\dfrac6{7.810}$ [M1][A1] $\alpha=39.8^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Find the base diagonal first, then use Pythagoras again. The angle with an edge uses the scalar product or a right triangle.

subtopic: Ambiguous case: peg positions for a rope
statement: A straight wall starts at a point $A$. A post $B$ is $18$ m from $A$, and the line $AB$ makes an angle of $38^\circ$ with the wall. A rope of length $13$ m is fixed at $B$, and its other end $C$ is pegged to the wall. (a) Find the two possible sizes of angle $ACB$. [4] (b) Hence find the two possible distances $AC$. [3] (c) Find the shortest rope length for which it is possible to reach the wall. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{\sin\angle ACB}{18}=\dfrac{\sin38^\circ}{13}$ [M1] $\sin\angle ACB=0.8525$ [A1] $\angle ACB=58.5^\circ$ [A1] or $\angle ACB=180^\circ-58.5^\circ=121.5^\circ$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) For $58.5^\circ$: $\angle ABC=180^\circ-38^\circ-58.5^\circ=83.5^\circ$ and $AC=\dfrac{13\sin83.52^\circ}{\sin38^\circ}=21.0$ m [M1] [A1] For $121.5^\circ$: $\angle ABC=20.5^\circ$ and $AC=\dfrac{13\sin20.48^\circ}{\sin38^\circ}=7.39$ m [A1] [3 marks] (c) The shortest rope is the perpendicular distance $18\sin38^\circ=11.1$ m [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Test for a second solution whenever you use the sine rule to find an angle: the obtuse supplement is valid if the angle sum is still below $180^\circ$. Keep full calculator precision to avoid drift in the second length.

subtopic: Segment area equal to triangle area
statement: The sector $OAB$ of a circle has centre $O$, radius $10$ cm and angle $AOB=\theta$ radians, where $0<\theta<\pi$. (a) Show that the area of the segment bounded by chord $AB$ and arc $AB$ is $50(\theta-\sin\theta)\text{ cm}^2$. [2] (b) The area of the segment equals the area of triangle $OAB$. Show that $\theta=2\sin\theta$. [2] (c) Solve $\theta=2\sin\theta$ for $0<\theta<\pi$. [2] (d) Hence find the length of arc $AB$. [1]
markscheme: (a) Segment $=$ sector $-$ triangle $OAB$ [M1] $=\tfrac12(10^2)\theta-\tfrac12(10^2)\sin\theta=50(\theta-\sin\theta)$ [AG] [A1] [2 marks] (b) Triangle area $=50\sin\theta$ [M1] $50(\theta-\sin\theta)=50\sin\theta\Rightarrow\theta=2\sin\theta$ [AG] [A1] [2 marks] (c) Attempt to solve graphically or with GDC (note $\theta=0$ is excluded) [M1] $\theta=1.90$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $10\times1.8955=19.0$ cm [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Use the unrounded value of $\theta$ from your calculator in later parts. The equation has no algebraic solution, so a GDC intersection is expected.

subtopic: Composite solid: cone with hemisphere
statement: A frozen dessert is made in the shape of a cone with a hemisphere on top. The cone has base radius $3$ cm and perpendicular height $10$ cm, and the hemisphere has radius $3$ cm with its flat face joined exactly to the base of the cone. (a) Find the total volume of the dessert. [3] (b) Find the total outer surface area of the dessert. [3] (c) The outer surface is coated with chocolate costing \$0.004 per $\text{cm}^2$. Find the cost of the chocolate, to the nearest cent. [2]
markscheme: (a) Cone: $\tfrac13\pi(3^2)(10)=30\pi$ [M1] Hemisphere: $\tfrac23\pi(3^3)=18\pi$ [M1] Total $=48\pi=151\text{ cm}^3$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Slant height $=\sqrt{3^2+10^2}=\sqrt{109}$ [M1] Curved cone surface $=\pi(3)\sqrt{109}$ and hemisphere surface $=2\pi(3^2)=18\pi$ [M1] Total $=18\pi+3\pi\sqrt{109}=155\text{ cm}^2$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Cost $=154.95\times0.004$ [M1] $=\$0.62$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The flat face where the two solids join is not part of the outer surface. Keep unrounded values in your GDC until the final cost.

subtopic: Length of a median using the cosine rule
statement: In triangle $ABC$, $BC=a$, $CA=b$, $AB=c$, and $M$ is the midpoint of $BC$ with $AM=m$. (a) By applying the cosine rule to triangles $ABM$ and $ACM$, show that $4m^2=2b^2+2c^2-a^2$. [4] (b) Find the exact length of the median from $A$ in the triangle with $a=8$, $b=7$, $c=5$. [2]
markscheme: (a) in $ABM$: $c^2=m^2+\dfrac{a^2}4-am\cos\theta$ with $\theta=\angle AMB$ [M1] in $ACM$: $b^2=m^2+\dfrac{a^2}4+am\cos\theta$, since $\angle AMC=180^\circ-\theta$ [M1][A1] add: $b^2+c^2=2m^2+\dfrac{a^2}2$, which gives $4m^2=2b^2+2c^2-a^2$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $4m^2=98+50-64=84$ [M1] $m=\sqrt{21}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Since $\cos(180^\circ-\theta)=-\cos\theta$, adding the two equations eliminates the cosine of the angle at $M$.

subtopic: Triangle sides to angle and area
statement: Triangle $PQR$ has $PQ=9$ cm, $QR=11$ cm and $PR=16$ cm. (a) Find the size of the largest angle of the triangle. [3] (b) Find the area of the triangle. [2] (c) Find the shortest distance from $Q$ to the line $PR$. [2]
markscheme: (a) Largest angle is $Q$, opposite the longest side [M1] $\cos Q=\dfrac{9^2+11^2-16^2}{2(9)(11)}=-\dfrac{3}{11}$ [A1] $Q=106^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Area $=\tfrac12(9)(11)\sin Q$ [M1] $=47.6\text{ cm}^2$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\tfrac12(16)h=47.62$ [M1] $h=5.95$ cm [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The largest angle is opposite the longest side. Use unrounded values from earlier parts and remember that the shortest distance is the perpendicular height.

subtopic: Radian measure, arc length and sector area
statement: A sector of a circle has radius $3$ cm and angle $210^\circ$. (a) Convert $210^\circ$ to radians, giving your answer as a multiple of $\pi$. [1] (b) Find the arc length of the sector. [2] (c) Find the area of the sector. [2]
markscheme: (a) $210\times\dfrac{\pi}{180}=\dfrac{7\pi}{6}$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $s=3\times\dfrac{7\pi}{6}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{7\pi}{2}$ cm [A1] [2 marks] (c) $A=\tfrac12(3^2)\dfrac{7\pi}{6}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{21\pi}{4}\text{ cm}^2$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The formulas $s=r\theta$ and $A=\tfrac12r^2\theta$ require $\theta$ in radians, so convert first.

subtopic: How closely a chord approximates its arc
statement: A chord of a circle of radius $r$ subtends an angle $\theta$ radians at the centre. (a) Show that the length of the chord is $2r\sin\dfrac\theta2$. [2] (b) Find the percentage by which the chord is shorter than the arc when $\theta=0.2$, to two significant figures. [3] (c) Find the largest value of $\theta$ for which the chord is within $1\%$ of the arc length, to three significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) the radii and the chord form an isosceles triangle [M1] splitting it into two right-angled triangles gives half the chord $=r\sin\dfrac\theta2$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) arc $=0.2r$ and chord $=2r\sin0.1=0.19967r$ [M1][A1] percentage $=\dfrac{0.2-0.19967}{0.2}\times100=0.17\%$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) solve $1-\dfrac{\sin(\theta/2)}{\theta/2}=0.01$ on the calculator [M1] $\theta=0.491$ radians [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A right-angled triangle formed by half the chord, the radius and the perpendicular from the centre gives the chord formula.

subtopic: Exact trigonometric values in radians
statement: (a) Write down the exact values of $\sin\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$, $\cos\dfrac{5\pi}{4}$ and $\tan\dfrac{11\pi}{6}$. [3] (b) Hence find the exact value of $\sin\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\times\tan\dfrac{11\pi}{6}$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\sin\dfrac{2\pi}{3}=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ [A1] $\cos\dfrac{5\pi}{4}=-\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$ [A1] $\tan\dfrac{11\pi}{6}=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\left(=-\dfrac{\sqrt3}{3}\right)$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\times\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt3}{3}\right)$ [M1] $=-\dfrac12$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Use a reference angle in the correct quadrant and decide the sign with the unit circle. Rationalizing denominators makes products like the one in (b) quicker to simplify.

subtopic: Closest approach of a boat to a lighthouse
statement: A boat leaves a harbor $H$ and sails in a straight line on a bearing of $050^\circ$. A lighthouse $L$ is $8$ km from $H$ on a bearing of $090^\circ$. (a) Show that the angle between the boat's path and the line $HL$ is $40^\circ$. [1] (b) Find the shortest distance between the boat's path and the lighthouse. [2] (c) Find how far the boat has sailed from $H$ when it is closest to the lighthouse. [2]
markscheme: (a) $90^\circ-50^\circ=40^\circ$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $8\sin40^\circ$ [M1] $=5.14$ km [A1] [2 marks] (c) $8\cos40^\circ$ [M1] $=6.13$ km [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The closest point on a straight path is the foot of the perpendicular from the lighthouse, which forms a right-angled triangle with $H$.

subtopic: Sliding ladder and its midpoint
statement: A ladder of length $6$ m rests with its top on a vertical wall and its foot on horizontal ground. The ladder makes an angle $\theta$ with the ground. (a) When $\theta=60^\circ$, find the exact height of the top of the ladder and the exact distance of its foot from the wall. [2] (b) The foot is pulled away from the wall until the top of the ladder is at a height of $3\sqrt2$ m. Find the exact distance the foot has moved. [3] (c) Let $M$ be the midpoint of the ladder and $O$ the point where the wall meets the ground. By taking $O$ as the origin, show that $OM$ has the same length for every value of $\theta$, and state this length. [3]
markscheme: (a) Height $=6\sin60^\circ=3\sqrt3$ m [A1] Distance of foot $=6\cos60^\circ=3$ m [A1] [2 marks] (b) $6\sin\theta=3\sqrt2$, so $\sin\theta=\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$ and $\theta=45^\circ$ [M1] Foot distance $=6\cos45^\circ=3\sqrt2$ [A1] Distance moved $=3\sqrt2-3$ m [A1] [3 marks] (c) The foot is at $(6\cos\theta,0)$ and the top at $(0,6\sin\theta)$, so $M=(3\cos\theta,3\sin\theta)$ [M1] $OM^2=9\cos^2\theta+9\sin^2\theta=9$ [A1] So $OM=3$ m for every $\theta$ [R1] [3 marks]
tips: Place the corner at the origin and write coordinates using $6\cos\theta$ and $6\sin\theta$. The identity $\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1$ turns the midpoint problem into a one-line proof.

subtopic: Height from two angles of elevation on opposite sides
statement: A vertical tower stands on level ground between two points $A$ and $B$, which are $100$ m apart and in line with the base of the tower. The angle of elevation of the top of the tower is $30^\circ$ from $A$ and $40^\circ$ from $B$. (a) Show that the height $h$ of the tower satisfies $h\left(\dfrac1{\tan30^\circ}+\dfrac1{\tan40^\circ}\right)=100$. [2] (b) Find the height of the tower, to three significant figures. [2] (c) Find the distance of $A$ from the base of the tower. [1]
markscheme: (a) distance from $A$ to the base is $\dfrac h{\tan30^\circ}$ [A1] distance from $B$ is $\dfrac h{\tan40^\circ}$, and the two distances add to $100$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $h=\dfrac{100}{1.732+1.192}$ [M1] $=34.2$ m [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\dfrac{34.2}{\tan30^\circ}=59.2$ m [A1] [1 mark]
tips: The two horizontal distances to the base add up to the total distance between $A$ and $B$.

subtopic: Radian conversion, arc length and sector area
statement: A sector of a circle has radius $6$ cm and a central angle of $150^\circ$. (a) Write the angle $150^\circ$ in radians, in terms of $\pi$. [1] (b) Find the exact length of the arc of the sector. [2] (c) Find the exact area of the sector. [2]
markscheme: (a) $150\times\dfrac{\pi}{180}=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Arc length $=r\theta=6\times\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$ [M1] $=5\pi$ cm [A1] [2 marks] (c) Area $=\tfrac12r^2\theta=\tfrac12(36)\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right)$ [M1] $=15\pi\text{ cm}^2$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The formulas $s=r\theta$ and $A=\tfrac12r^2\theta$ only work when $\theta$ is in radians, so convert first. Leave $\pi$ in your answer when an exact value is requested.

subtopic: Cosine rule leading to a quadratic in x
statement: In triangle $ABC$, $AB=x$ cm, $AC=(x+3)$ cm, $BC=7$ cm and angle $BAC=60^\circ$. (a) Show that $x^2+3x-40=0$. [3] (b) Hence find the value of $x$. [2] (c) Find the exact area of triangle $ABC$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $7^2=x^2+(x+3)^2-2x(x+3)\cos60^\circ$ [M1] $49=x^2+x^2+6x+9-x(x+3)$ [A1] $49=x^2+3x+9$, so $x^2+3x-40=0$ [AG] [A1] [3 marks] (b) $(x+8)(x-5)=0$ [M1] $x=5$ (reject $x=-8$ since a length is positive) [A1] [2 marks] (c) $AC=8$, so area $=\tfrac12(5)(8)\sin60^\circ$ [M1] $=10\sqrt3\text{ cm}^2$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Substitute $\cos60^\circ=\tfrac12$ before expanding, and always reject any root that gives a negative length.

subtopic: Angle between two faces of a regular tetrahedron
statement: A regular tetrahedron $ABCD$ has all edges of length $1$. The point $M$ is the midpoint of $AB$. (a) Show that $CM=DM=\dfrac{\sqrt3}2$. [2] (b) Both $CM$ and $DM$ are perpendicular to $AB$. Hence find the angle between the faces $ABC$ and $ABD$, correct to the nearest tenth of a degree. [4]
markscheme: (a) $CM$ is the height of equilateral triangle $ABC$ [M1] $\sqrt{1-\left(\dfrac12\right)^2}=\dfrac{\sqrt3}2$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) the angle between the faces is angle $CMD$ [R1] $\cos CMD=\dfrac{\frac34+\frac34-1}{2\times\frac34}$ [M1] $=\dfrac13$ [A1] $CMD=70.5^\circ$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: The angle between two planes is measured between lines perpendicular to their common edge, drawn in each plane through the same point.

subtopic: Cosine rule, sine rule and area of a triangle
statement: In triangle $ABC$, $BC=7.2$ cm, $AC=5.4$ cm and angle $ACB=68^\circ$. (a) Find $AB$. [3] (b) Find the size of angle $BAC$. [3] (c) Find the area of the triangle. [2]
tips: Use the cosine rule when two sides and the included angle are known. The area is $\frac12ab\sin C$.

subtopic: Bearings and the cosine rule
statement: A ship sails $12$ km on a bearing of $040^\circ$ from port $P$ to a point $Q$. It then sails $9$ km on a bearing of $170^\circ$ to a point $R$. (a) Show that angle $PQR=50^\circ$. [2] (b) Find the distance $PR$. [3] (c) Find the bearing of $R$ from $P$. [3]
markscheme: (a) the bearing of $P$ from $Q$ is $040^\circ+180^\circ=220^\circ$ [M1] angle $PQR=220^\circ-170^\circ=50^\circ$ [A1] [AG] [2 marks] (b) $PR^2=12^2+9^2-2(12)(9)\cos50^\circ$ [M1][A1] $PR=9.282$ km [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\dfrac{\sin\angle RPQ}{9}=\dfrac{\sin50^\circ}{9.282}$ [M1] $\angle RPQ=48.0^\circ$ [A1] bearing $=040^\circ+48.0^\circ=88.0^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Draw a diagram with north lines at each point. Co-interior and back-bearing angles give the angle in the triangle.

subtopic: The parallelogram law and a diagonal length
statement: In parallelogram $ABCD$, $AB=6$, $AD=9$ and diagonal $AC=11$. (a) Use the cosine rule in triangles $ABC$ and $ABD$, noting that angle $ABC$ and angle $BAD$ are supplementary, to show that $AC^2+BD^2=2\left(AB^2+AD^2\right)$. [4] (b) Find the length of the diagonal $BD$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $AC^2=AB^2+BC^2-2AB\cdot BC\cos B$ and $BD^2=AB^2+AD^2-2AB\cdot AD\cos A$ [M1][A1] $\cos A=-\cos B$ and $BC=AD$ [M1] adding: $AC^2+BD^2=2AB^2+2AD^2$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $BD^2=2(36+81)-121=113$ [M1] $BD=10.6$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Adjacent angles of a parallelogram sum to $180^\circ$, so their cosines are opposite. Add the two cosine rule equations to cancel the cosine terms.

subtopic: Overlap of two circles
statement: Two circles have centres $C_1$ and $C_2$ with $C_1C_2=7$ cm. The first circle has radius $5$ cm and the second has radius $3$ cm. The circles intersect at points $X$ and $Y$. Let $\alpha=\angle XC_1C_2$ and $\beta=\angle XC_2C_1$. (a) Show that $\cos\alpha=\dfrac{13}{14}$ and find $\alpha$ in radians. [3] (b) Find $\beta$ in radians. [2] (c) Find the area of the region common to both circles. [4]
markscheme: (a) Cosine rule in triangle $XC_1C_2$: $3^2=5^2+7^2-2(5)(7)\cos\alpha$ [M1] $\cos\alpha=\dfrac{65}{70}=\dfrac{13}{14}$ [AG] [A1] $\alpha=0.380$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $5^2=3^2+7^2-2(3)(7)\cos\beta$ [M1] $\cos\beta=\dfrac{33}{42}=\dfrac{11}{14}$, $\beta=0.667$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Common area $=$ segment of circle 1 (angle $2\alpha$) $+$ segment of circle 2 (angle $2\beta$) [M1] $\left(\tfrac12\cdot25(2\alpha-\sin2\alpha)\right)+\left(\tfrac12\cdot9(2\beta-\sin2\beta)\right)$ [M1] Substituting $\alpha=0.38025$, $\beta=0.66695$ [A1] $=2.52\text{ cm}^2$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: The common region is the union of two circular segments, one from each circle, sharing the chord $XY$. Use the double angle $2\alpha$ at each centre.

subtopic: Overlapping circles: common region
statement: Two circles each have radius $2$. Their centers $A$ and $B$ are $2$ units apart. The circles intersect at points $P$ and $Q$. (a) Show that angle $PAQ=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$. [2] (b) Find the length of the minor arc $PQ$ of the circle with center $A$. [2] (c) Find the exact area of the segment cut off from that circle by the chord $PQ$. [3] (d) Hence find the exact area of the region common to both circles. [2] (e) Find the perimeter of the region common to both circles. [1]
markscheme: (a) $AP=AB=BP=2$, so triangle $ABP$ is equilateral and $\angle PAB=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ [M1] By symmetry $\angle PAQ=2\times\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ [AG] [A1] [2 marks] (b) Arc $=r\theta=2\times\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{4\pi}{3}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Sector area $=\tfrac12(4)\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)=\dfrac{4\pi}{3}$ [M1] Triangle $APQ=\tfrac12(4)\sin\dfrac{2\pi}{3}=\sqrt3$ [M1] Segment $=\dfrac{4\pi}{3}-\sqrt3$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) The common region is two identical segments [M1] Area $=\dfrac{8\pi}{3}-2\sqrt3$ [A1] [2 marks] (e) Perimeter $=2\times\dfrac{4\pi}{3}=\dfrac{8\pi}{3}$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Spot the equilateral triangle formed by the two centers and an intersection point. The common region of two equal circles is made of two identical segments.

subtopic: The cone of greatest volume made from a circular sector
statement: A cone is made from a sector of a circle of radius $1$ by joining the two straight edges of the sector. The sector has angle $\theta$ radians, and the cone has base radius $r$ and height $h$. (a) Show that $\theta=2\pi r$ and $h=\sqrt{1-r^2}$. [3] (b) Show that the volume of the cone is $V=\dfrac\pi3r^2\sqrt{1-r^2}$, for $0<r<1$. [1] (c) By considering $W=V^2$ as a function of $w=r^2$, find the value of $r$ that maximizes $V$. [5] (d) Justify that this value gives a maximum. [2] (e) Find the angle $\theta$ of the sector, in radians and degrees to the nearest degree, and the maximum volume to three significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) the arc of the sector becomes the circumference of the base: $\theta\times1=2\pi r$ [M1][A1] the slant height is $1$, so $h=\sqrt{1-r^2}$ by Pythagoras [A1] [3 marks] (b) $V=\dfrac13\pi r^2h$ [AG] [A1] [1 mark] (c) $W=\dfrac{\pi^2}9w^2(1-w)$ [A1] $\dfrac{dW}{dw}=\dfrac{\pi^2}9(2w-3w^2)$ [M1][A1] $=0$ at $w=\dfrac23$ [A1] $r=\sqrt{\dfrac23}$ [A1] [5 marks] (d) $\dfrac{dW}{dw}>0$ for $w<\dfrac23$ and $<0$ for $w>\dfrac23$ [M1] so $W$, and hence $V$, has a maximum [R1] [2 marks] (e) $\theta=2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac23}=5.13$ rad [A1] $=294^\circ$ [A1] $V=\dfrac{2\pi}{9\sqrt3}=0.403$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Maximizing $V^2$ is simpler than maximizing $V$, and it has its maximum at the same value of $r$ since $V>0$.

subtopic: Largest sphere inside a cone
statement: A solid right circular cone has base radius $5$ cm and height $12$ cm. The largest possible sphere is placed inside the cone, so that it touches the base and the curved surface of the cone. (a) Find the slant height of the cone. [1] (b) Find the radius of the sphere. [4] (c) Find the volume of the sphere, in cm$^3$, to three significant figures. [2] (d) Find the percentage of the volume of the cone that is occupied by the sphere, to three significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\sqrt{5^2+12^2}=13$ cm [A1] [1 mark] (b) a vertical cross-section through the axis is an isosceles triangle with sides $13$, $13$, $10$ and the sphere's cross-section is its inscribed circle [M1] area of the triangle $=\dfrac12\times10\times12=60$ [A1] semi-perimeter $=\dfrac{13+13+10}2=18$ [A1] area $=r\times$ semi-perimeter so $r=\dfrac{60}{18}=\dfrac{10}3$ cm [A1] [4 marks] (c) $\dfrac43\pi\left(\dfrac{10}3\right)^3$ [M1] $=155$ cm$^3$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) volume of cone $=\dfrac13\pi\times25\times12=100\pi$ [A1] $\dfrac{4000\pi/81}{100\pi}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{40}{81}=49.4\%$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Take a cross-section through the axis of the cone: the sphere becomes a circle tangent to all three sides of an isosceles triangle. The area of a triangle equals the inradius times the semi-perimeter.

subtopic: Triangle area gives two possible angles
statement: In triangle $ABC$, $AB=8$ cm, $AC=11$ cm and the area of the triangle is $30\text{ cm}^2$. Angle $BAC$ may be acute or obtuse. (a) Show that $\sin\angle BAC=\dfrac{15}{22}$. [2] (b) Find the two possible lengths of $BC$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $30=\tfrac12(8)(11)\sin A$ [M1] $\sin A=\dfrac{30}{44}=\dfrac{15}{22}$ [AG] [A1] [2 marks] (b) $A=43.0^\circ$ or $A=137.0^\circ$ [A1] Cosine rule: $BC^2=8^2+11^2-2(8)(11)\cos A$ [M1] Acute: $BC=7.50$ cm [A1] Obtuse: $BC=17.7$ cm [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Both $A$ and $180^\circ-A$ have the same sine, so there are two triangles. Use the cosine rule for each, keeping unrounded angles.

subtopic: Cosine rule, sine rule and sectors
statement: A park is in the shape of a triangle $PQR$, where $PQ=85\ \mathrm{m}$, $QR=120\ \mathrm{m}$ and $\angle PQR=52^\circ$. (a) Find $PR$. [3] (b) Find $\angle QPR$. [2] (c) A sprinkler at $Q$ waters the region of the park within $40\ \mathrm{m}$ of $Q$. This region is a sector of a circle with center $Q$, bounded by the sides $QP$ and $QR$. Find the area of the park that is not watered by the sprinkler. [3]
markscheme: (a) $PR^2=85^2+120^2-2(85)(120)\cos 52^\circ$ [M1][A1] $PR=95.2\ \mathrm{m}$ ($95.2129\ldots$) [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\dfrac{\sin\angle QPR}{120}=\dfrac{\sin 52^\circ}{95.2129\ldots}$ or $\cos\angle QPR=\dfrac{85^2+95.2129\ldots^2-120^2}{2(85)(95.2129\ldots)}$ [M1] $\angle QPR=83.3^\circ$ ($83.2926\ldots$) [A1] [2 marks] (c) Area of triangle $=\dfrac{1}{2}(85)(120)\sin 52^\circ=4018.85\ldots$ and area of sector $=\dfrac{52}{360}\pi(40)^2=726.056\ldots$ [A1][A1] Area not watered $=4018.85\ldots-726.056\ldots=3290\ \mathrm{m^2}$ ($3292.79\ldots$) [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Use the unrounded value of $PR$ in later parts. Before using the sine rule to find an angle, check whether the angle could be obtuse; the cosine rule avoids that ambiguity.

subtopic: Cone formed from a sector
statement: A sector of a circle of radius $12$ cm and angle $\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$ radians is cut out of paper. The two straight edges are joined together to form a cone (with no overlap). (a) Find the arc length of the sector. [1] (b) Find the radius of the base of the cone. [2] (c) Show that the height of the cone is $\sqrt{119}$ cm. [2] (d) Find the exact volume of the cone. [2]
markscheme: (a) $12\times\dfrac{5\pi}{6}=10\pi$ cm [A1] [1 mark] (b) Arc length equals base circumference: $2\pi r=10\pi$ [M1] $r=5$ cm [A1] [2 marks] (c) Slant height $=12$ cm [M1] $h=\sqrt{12^2-5^2}=\sqrt{119}$ [AG] [A1] [2 marks] (d) $V=\tfrac13\pi(5^2)\sqrt{119}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{25\pi\sqrt{119}}{3}\text{ cm}^3$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The arc length of the sector becomes the circumference of the base, and the radius of the sector becomes the slant height of the cone.

subtopic: Region between a circle and its inscribed equilateral triangle
statement: An equilateral triangle is inscribed in a circle of radius $6$ cm, with its vertices on the circle. (a) Show that the side of the triangle is $6\sqrt3$ cm. [2] (b) Find the exact area of the triangle. [2] (c) Find the exact area of the region inside the circle but outside the triangle, and its value to three significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) central angle between adjacent vertices is $120^\circ$ [A1] cosine rule: $s^2=36+36-72\cos120^\circ=108$, so $s=6\sqrt3$ [AG] [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac12(6\sqrt3)^2\sin60^\circ$ [M1] $=27\sqrt3$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $36\pi-27\sqrt3$ [A1] $=66.3\text{ cm}^2$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The triangle's vertices divide the circle into three arcs of equal central angle $120^\circ$.

subtopic: Right pyramid: edges and face angles
statement: A right pyramid $VABCD$ has a horizontal square base $ABCD$ of side $8$ cm. The vertex $V$ is vertically above the centre $O$ of the base and $VO=6$ cm. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$. (a) Find the length of $VA$. [2] (b) Find the angle between $VA$ and the base $ABCD$. [2] (c) Find the angle between the face $VBC$ and the base $ABCD$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $AC=\sqrt{8^2+8^2}=8\sqrt2$, so $AO=4\sqrt2$ [A1] $VA=\sqrt{(4\sqrt2)^2+6^2}=\sqrt{68}=8.25$ cm [A1] [2 marks] (b) Required angle is $\angle VAO$ [M1] $\tan\angle VAO=\dfrac{6}{4\sqrt2}$, so $\angle VAO=46.7^\circ$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Required angle is $\angle VMO$ (since $OM\perp BC$ and $VM\perp BC$) [M1] $OM=4$ [A1] $\tan\angle VMO=\dfrac64$, so $\angle VMO=56.3^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Identify the right-angled triangle that contains the required angle, and state it. The angle between a plane face and the base is measured along a line perpendicular to their line of intersection.

subtopic: Distances between two cities on the same line of latitude
statement: Model the Earth as a sphere of radius $6371$ km. Two cities lie on the $40^\circ$N line of latitude, and their longitudes differ by $30^\circ$. (a) Find the radius of the circle of latitude $40^\circ$N. [2] (b) Find the distance between the cities along the line of latitude. [2] (c) Find the length of the straight line segment joining the two cities, through the Earth. [3]
markscheme: (a) radius $=6371\cos40^\circ$ [M1] $=4880$ km [A1] [2 marks] (b) arc length $=4880\times\dfrac\pi6$ [M1] $=2560$ km [A1] [2 marks] (c) chord of the circle of latitude with central angle $30^\circ$ [M1] $2\times4880\sin15^\circ$ [A1] $=2530$ km [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A circle of latitude has a smaller radius than the Earth. Use arc length $r\theta$ and chord length $2r\sin(\theta/2)$ in this circle.

subtopic: Exact value of sin 75 degrees and the sine rule
statement: In triangle $ABC$, angle $A=60^\circ$, angle $B=45^\circ$ and $BC=\sqrt6$. (a) Show that $\sin75^\circ=\dfrac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}{4}$. [3] (b) Find the exact length of $AC$. [2] (c) Find the exact length of $AB$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\sin75^\circ=\sin(45^\circ+30^\circ)=\sin45^\circ\cos30^\circ+\cos45^\circ\sin30^\circ$ [M1] $=\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}+\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\cdot\dfrac12$ [A1] $=\dfrac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}{4}$ [AG] [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\dfrac{AC}{\sin45^\circ}=\dfrac{\sqrt6}{\sin60^\circ}$ [M1] $AC=\dfrac{\sqrt6\cdot\frac{\sqrt2}{2}}{\frac{\sqrt3}{2}}=\sqrt6\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt2}{\sqrt3}=2$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Angle $C=75^\circ$ and $\dfrac{AB}{\sin75^\circ}=\dfrac{\sqrt6}{\sin60^\circ}$ [M1] $AB=\dfrac{\sqrt6(\sqrt6+\sqrt2)}{4}\cdot\dfrac{2}{\sqrt3}=\dfrac{6+2\sqrt3}{2\sqrt3}$ [A1] $=\sqrt3+1$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Split $75^\circ$ as $45^\circ+30^\circ$ and use a compound angle formula. Rationalize denominators at each step to keep the surds under control.

subtopic: Space diagonals of a cube
statement: $ABCDEFGH$ is a cube of side $2$, where $ABCD$ is the horizontal base, $E,F,G,H$ lie directly above $A,B,C,D$ respectively, so $G$ is opposite to $A$ and $H$ is opposite to $B$. The diagonals $AG$ and $BH$ intersect at the centre $O$ of the cube. (a) Find the exact length of $AG$. [2] (b) Find the exact value of $\sin\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between $AG$ and the base $ABCD$. [3] (c) Show that $\cos\angle AOB=\dfrac13$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $AG=\sqrt{2^2+2^2+2^2}$ [M1] $=2\sqrt3$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Required angle is $\angle GAC$, where $C$ is directly below $G$ [M1] $CG=2$ [A1] $\sin\theta=\dfrac{2}{2\sqrt3}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\ \left(=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{3}\right)$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $AO=BO=\tfrac12(2\sqrt3)=\sqrt3$ [A1] Cosine rule in triangle $AOB$ with $AB=2$: $\cos\angle AOB=\dfrac{3+3-4}{2\sqrt3\cdot\sqrt3}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{2}{6}$ [A1] $=\dfrac13$ [AG] [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Draw a sketch of the cube and mark the relevant right angles. For part (c), $O$ is the midpoint of both diagonals, so $AO=BO$.

subtopic: Cosine rule with bearings
statement: Two ships leave port $P$ at the same time. Ship $A$ travels on a bearing of $060^\circ$ at $40\text{ km h}^{-1}$ and ship $B$ travels on a bearing of $140^\circ$ at $30\text{ km h}^{-1}$. After $2$ hours the ships are at points $A$ and $B$ respectively. (a) Write down the size of angle $APB$. [1] (b) Find the distance $AB$ in km. [3] (c) Find the bearing of $B$ from $A$, giving your answer to the nearest degree. [4]
markscheme: (a) $140^\circ-60^\circ=80^\circ$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $PA=80$ km, $PB=60$ km [A1] $AB^2=80^2+60^2-2(80)(60)\cos80^\circ$ [M1] $AB=91.3$ km [A1] [3 marks] (c) Sine rule: $\dfrac{\sin\angle PAB}{60}=\dfrac{\sin80^\circ}{91.285}$ [M1] $\angle PAB=40.3^\circ$ [A1] The bearing of $P$ from $A$ is $240^\circ$ [M1] Bearing of $B$ from $A$ is $240^\circ-40.3^\circ=199.7^\circ\approx200^\circ$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Draw a quick sketch with a north line at each point. For the bearing from $A$ to $B$, start from the back bearing $A\to P$ and adjust by the angle at $A$.

subtopic: Angles of elevation from two points
statement: A vertical tower $PQ$ stands on level ground with $Q$ at its base and $P$ at its top. Points $A$ and $B$ are on the ground with $AB=120$ m, angle $QAB=64^\circ$ and angle $QBA=48^\circ$. The angle of elevation of $P$ from $A$ is $26^\circ$. (a) Find the length $AQ$. [3] (b) Find the height of the tower. [2] (c) Find the angle of elevation of $P$ from $B$. [3]
markscheme: (a) Angle $AQB=180^\circ-64^\circ-48^\circ=68^\circ$ [A1] $\dfrac{AQ}{\sin48^\circ}=\dfrac{120}{\sin68^\circ}$ [M1] $AQ=96.2$ m [A1] [3 marks] (b) $PQ=AQ\tan26^\circ$ [M1] $=96.18\times0.4877=46.9$ m [A1] [2 marks] (c) $BQ=\dfrac{120\sin64^\circ}{\sin68^\circ}=116.3$ m [A1] $\tan\theta=\dfrac{46.91}{116.33}$ [M1] $\theta=22.0^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Keep unrounded values in your calculator between parts. The ground triangle is not right-angled, so use the sine rule there and ordinary trigonometry in the vertical triangles.

subtopic: Ambiguous case with exact values
statement: In triangle $ABC$, $AB=8$, $AC=5$ and angle $ABC=30^\circ$. (a) Show that $\sin C=\dfrac45$. [2] (b) Find the two possible exact values of $\cos C$. [2] (c) Hence find the two possible exact values of $BC$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{\sin C}{8}=\dfrac{\sin30^\circ}{5}$ [M1] $\sin C=\dfrac{8\times\frac12}{5}=\dfrac45$ [AG] [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\cos^2C=1-\dfrac{16}{25}=\dfrac{9}{25}$ [M1] $\cos C=\dfrac35$ or $\cos C=-\dfrac35$ (angle $C$ may be acute or obtuse) [A1] [2 marks] (c) $A=180^\circ-30^\circ-C=150^\circ-C$, so $\sin A=\sin150^\circ\cos C-\cos150^\circ\sin C=\tfrac12\cos C+\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\cdot\dfrac45$ [M1] Sine rule: $\dfrac{BC}{\sin A}=\dfrac{5}{\sin30^\circ}$ gives $BC=10\sin A$ [M1] When $\cos C=\dfrac35$: $BC=10\left(\dfrac{3}{10}+\dfrac{2\sqrt3}{5}\right)=3+4\sqrt3$ [A1] When $\cos C=-\dfrac35$: $BC=10\left(-\dfrac{3}{10}+\dfrac{2\sqrt3}{5}\right)=4\sqrt3-3$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: The ambiguous case arises when the side opposite the given angle is shorter than the other given side. Write $\sin A$ as $\sin(150^\circ-C)$ and expand with the compound angle formula to stay exact.

subtopic: Cosine rule with exact values
statement: In triangle $ABC$, $AB=4$ cm, $AC=2\sqrt3$ cm and angle $BAC=30^\circ$. (a) Use the cosine rule to find the length of $BC$. [3] (b) Find the area of triangle $ABC$. [2] (c) Hence show that angle $ACB=90^\circ$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $BC^2=4^2+(2\sqrt3)^2-2(4)(2\sqrt3)\cos30^\circ$ [M1] $=16+12-16\sqrt3\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ [A1] $=28-24=4$, so $BC=2$ cm [A1] [3 marks] (b) Area $=\tfrac12(4)(2\sqrt3)\sin30^\circ$ [M1] $=2\sqrt3\text{ cm}^2$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $BC^2+AC^2=4+12=16$ [M1] $=AB^2$, so by the converse of Pythagoras' theorem angle $ACB=90^\circ$ [A1] Accept $\sin C=1$ from the area formula in (b). [2 marks]
tips: Know the exact values of $\sin$ and $\cos$ at $30^\circ$, $45^\circ$ and $60^\circ$. Simplify surds fully and check your answer by looking for special triangles.

subtopic: A cyclic quadrilateral
statement: The quadrilateral $ABCD$ is cyclic with $AB=5$, $BC=7$, $CD=6$ and $DA=4$ (in cm). (a) Let $AC=x$. Use the cosine rule in triangles $ABC$ and $ADC$ and the fact that $\angle ABC+\angle ADC=180^\circ$ to show that $\dfrac{74-x^2}{70}=-\dfrac{52-x^2}{48}$. [4] (b) Solve for $x$, giving the answer to three significant figures. [3] (c) Find the area of the quadrilateral. [3]
tips: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary, so their cosines are negatives and their sines are equal.

subtopic: Common tangent of two touching circles
statement: Two circles with centres $O_1$ and $O_2$ and radii $9$ and $4$ touch externally. A line touches the larger circle at $P$ and the smaller circle at $Q$ (a common external tangent). (a) Show that $O_1O_2=13$ and that the length of $PQ$ is $12$. [4] (b) Find the area of the quadrilateral $O_1PQO_2$. [2]
markscheme: (a) circles touch externally, so $O_1O_2=9+4=13$ [A1] the radii $O_1P$ and $O_2Q$ are perpendicular to the tangent, hence parallel [R1] draw from $O_2$ a line parallel to $PQ$ to form a right-angled triangle with hypotenuse $13$ and one side $9-4=5$ [M1] $PQ=\sqrt{13^2-5^2}=12$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) it is a trapezium with parallel sides $9$ and $4$ and height $12$ [M1] area $=\dfrac{9+4}2\times12=78$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The radii to the points of tangency are perpendicular to the tangent line. Drop a perpendicular from the smaller centre to the larger radius.

subtopic: Triangle in the coordinate plane: midpoints, bisectors and area
statement: The vertices of a triangle are $A(1,2)$, $B(7,4)$ and $C(3,8)$. (a) Find the midpoint $M$ of $BC$ and the gradient of $AM$. [3] (b) Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of $AB$. [3] (c) Find the area of the triangle. [2]
markscheme: (a) $M=\left(\dfrac{7+3}2,\dfrac{4+8}2\right)=(5,6)$ [A1] gradient $=\dfrac{6-2}{5-1}$ [M1] $=1$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) midpoint $(4,3)$ [A1] gradient of $AB=\dfrac13$ so perpendicular gradient $-3$ [M1] $y-3=-3(x-4)$, i.e. $y=-3x+15$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\dfrac12\left|1(4-8)+7(8-2)+3(2-4)\right|$ [M1] $=\dfrac12|-4+42-6|=16$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The perpendicular bisector passes through the midpoint with gradient the negative reciprocal. The shoelace formula gives the area from coordinates.

subtopic: Region inside an equilateral triangle outside three equal sectors
statement: An equilateral triangle $ABC$ has side length $6$ cm. Three circular arcs of radius $3$ cm, one centred at each vertex, lie inside the triangle and neighbouring arcs meet at the midpoints of the sides. The region $R$ lies inside the triangle but outside the three sectors. (a) Find the exact area of the triangle. [2] (b) Find the exact total area of the three sectors. [3] (c) Hence find the exact area of $R$. [2] (d) Find the exact perimeter of $R$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac12\times6\times6\times\sin\dfrac\pi3$ [M1] $=9\sqrt3$ cm$^2$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) each sector has angle $\dfrac\pi3$ and radius $3$ [M1] area of one sector $=\dfrac12\times3^2\times\dfrac\pi3=\dfrac{3\pi}2$ [A1] three sectors: $\dfrac{9\pi}2$ cm$^2$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $9\sqrt3-\dfrac{9\pi}2$ cm$^2$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (d) the boundary of $R$ is the three arcs, each of length $3\times\dfrac\pi3=\pi$ [M1] perimeter $=3\pi$ cm [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Every angle of an equilateral triangle is $\dfrac\pi3$. The arcs meet at the midpoints of the sides because each has radius half of the side length.

subtopic: Kite string and angle of elevation
statement: A kite is flown on a straight string of length $80$ m, held $1.4$ m above level ground. Assume the string is taut and straight. (a) The string makes an angle of $35^\circ$ with the horizontal. Find the height of the kite above the ground. [2] (b) The wind changes and the kite rises to a height of $60$ m above the ground, with the same string length. Find the new angle the string makes with the horizontal. [3]
markscheme: (a) Height above hand $=80\sin35^\circ=45.89$ [M1] Height above ground $=45.89+1.4=47.3$ m [A1] [2 marks] (b) Height above hand $=60-1.4=58.6$ [M1] $\sin\theta=\dfrac{58.6}{80}$ [M1] $\theta=47.1^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Remember to add (or subtract) the height of the hand when moving between the height above the hand and the height above the ground. Draw a right-angled triangle with the string as hypotenuse.

subtopic: Pythagoras with an unknown side and a double angle
statement: A right-angled triangular flower bed has perpendicular sides of length $x$ m and $(x+7)$ m, and a hypotenuse of length $(x+8)$ m. (a) Show that $x^2-2x-15=0$. [3] (b) Hence find $x$. [1] (c) Let $\theta$ be the smallest angle of the triangle. Find the exact value of $\cos2\theta$. [2]
tips: Expand each bracket carefully before collecting terms. The smallest angle is opposite the shortest side.

subtopic: Sector perimeter and area equations
statement: A sector of a circle has radius $r$ cm and angle $\theta$ radians, where $0<\theta<2\pi$. The perimeter of the sector is $20$ cm and its area is $24\text{ cm}^2$. (a) Show that $r^2-10r+24=0$. [3] (b) Find the two possible pairs of values of $r$ and $\theta$. [3]
markscheme: (a) Arc length $=r\theta$, so perimeter $2r+r\theta=20$, giving $r\theta=20-2r$ [M1] Area $=\tfrac12r^2\theta=\tfrac12r(r\theta)=\tfrac12r(20-2r)$ [M1] $=10r-r^2=24$, so $r^2-10r+24=0$ [AG] [A1] [3 marks] (b) $(r-4)(r-6)=0$ [M1] $r=4,\ \theta=\dfrac{20-8}{4}=3$ [A1] $r=6,\ \theta=\dfrac{20-12}{6}=\dfrac43$ [A1] Both satisfy $0<\theta<2\pi$. [3 marks]
tips: Express the arc length as $r\theta$ and eliminate $\theta$ using the perimeter condition. Always check that each solution satisfies the stated restriction on $\theta$.

subtopic: Area and perimeter of a segment
statement: $O$ is the centre of a circle of radius $4$ cm. Points $A$ and $B$ lie on the circle such that angle $AOB=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$. The minor segment is the region bounded by the chord $AB$ and the minor arc $AB$. (a) Write down the length of the minor arc $AB$. [1] (b) Find the exact area of the segment. [3] (c) Find the exact perimeter of the segment. [2]
markscheme: (a) $s=4\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\dfrac{4\pi}{3}$ cm [A1] [1 mark] (b) Sector area $=\tfrac12(4^2)\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\dfrac{8\pi}{3}$ [M1] Triangle area $=\tfrac12(4^2)\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}=4\sqrt3$ [M1] Segment area $=\dfrac{8\pi}{3}-4\sqrt3\text{ cm}^2$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Triangle $OAB$ is isosceles with apex angle $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$, hence equilateral, so $AB=4$ (or cosine rule) [M1] Perimeter $=4+\dfrac{4\pi}{3}$ cm [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Segment area is sector area minus triangle area. The chord is not the arc: do not forget it when you are asked for a perimeter.

subtopic: Proof of the cosine rule using coordinates
statement: In triangle $ABC$, place $A$ at the origin and $B$ at $(c,0)$, with $C$ above the $x$-axis and $AC=b$. (a) Write down the coordinates of $C$ in terms of $b$ and angle $A$, and hence show that $a^2=b^2+c^2-2bc\cos A$. [4] (b) Use the rule to find angle $A$ in the triangle with $a=7$, $b=5$ and $c=8$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $C=(b\cos A,\ b\sin A)$ [A1] $a^2=BC^2=(b\cos A-c)^2+(b\sin A)^2$ [M1] $=b^2\cos^2A-2bc\cos A+c^2+b^2\sin^2A$ [A1] $=b^2+c^2-2bc\cos A$ using $\sin^2A+\cos^2A=1$ [AG] [A1] [4 marks] (b) $\cos A=\dfrac{25+64-49}{2\times5\times8}=\dfrac12$ [M1] $A=60^\circ$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Use the distance formula between $B$ and $C$, then simplify with the Pythagorean identity.

subtopic: Exact values in a triangle with a 30 degree angle
statement: In triangle $ABC$, angle $B=30^\circ$, $AB=6$ and $BC=4\sqrt3$. (a) Find $AC$ exactly. [3] (b) Use the sine rule to find angle $A$. [3] (c) Find the exact area of the triangle. [1]
markscheme: (a) $AC^2=6^2+\left(4\sqrt3\right)^2-2(6)\left(4\sqrt3\right)\cos30^\circ$ [M1] $=36+48-48\sqrt3\times\dfrac{\sqrt3}2=84-72$ [A1] $AC^2=12$ so $AC=2\sqrt3$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\dfrac{\sin A}{4\sqrt3}=\dfrac{\sin30^\circ}{2\sqrt3}$ [M1] $\sin A=1$ [A1] $A=90^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\dfrac12(6)(2\sqrt3)=6\sqrt3$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Compute $\cos30^\circ=\frac{\sqrt3}2$ exactly; a right angle appears when $\sin A=1$.

subtopic: Optimizing a sector with a restricted angle
statement: A piece of wire of length $40$ cm is bent to form the boundary of a sector of a circle of radius $r$ cm and angle $\theta$ radians. (a) Show that the area $A\text{ cm}^2$ of the sector is $A=20r-r^2$. [3] (b) Ignoring any restriction on $\theta$, find the value of $r$ for which $A$ is greatest, and the greatest value of $A$. [3] (c) It is now required that $\theta\le\dfrac32$. Find the greatest possible area of the sector, giving your answer as an exact fraction. [4]
markscheme: (a) Perimeter: $2r+r\theta=40$, so $r\theta=40-2r$ [M1] $A=\tfrac12r^2\theta=\tfrac12r(40-2r)$ [M1] $=20r-r^2$ [AG] [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\dfrac{dA}{dr}=20-2r=0$ [M1] $r=10$ [A1] $A=200-100=100\text{ cm}^2$ (a maximum since $\dfrac{d^2A}{dr^2}=-2<0$) [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\theta=\dfrac{40-2r}{r}\le\dfrac32$ [M1] $80-4r\le3r$, so $r\ge\dfrac{80}{7}$ [A1] When $r=10$, $\theta=2>\dfrac32$, so the unrestricted maximum is not allowed; $A$ is decreasing for $r>10$, so the maximum occurs at $r=\dfrac{80}{7}$ [R1] $A=20\left(\dfrac{80}{7}\right)-\left(\dfrac{80}{7}\right)^2=\dfrac{11200-6400}{49}=\dfrac{4800}{49}\text{ cm}^2$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: When a constraint rules out the stationary point, the optimum lies at the boundary of the allowed interval. State clearly why the function is monotonic on that interval.

subtopic: Hexagonal prism
statement: A prism has a base that is a regular hexagon of side $6$ cm and a height of $10$ cm. (a) Find the area of the hexagonal base by dividing it into equilateral triangles, to three significant figures. [3] (b) Find the volume of the prism. [2] (c) Find the length of the longest diagonal of the hexagonal base, and hence the length of the longest straight line between two vertices of the prism, to three significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) six equilateral triangles [R1]; $6\times\dfrac12(6)(6)\sin60^{\circ}$ [M1]; $93.5$ cm$^{2}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $93.53\times10$ [M1]; $935$ cm$^{3}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) base diagonal $12$ cm [A1]; $\sqrt{12^{2}+10^{2}}$ [M1]; $15.6$ cm [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The longest diagonal of a regular hexagon passes through its centre and equals twice the side.

subtopic: Plane section of a sphere
statement: A sphere has centre $O$ and radius $13$ cm. A plane cuts the sphere in a circle. The perpendicular distance from $O$ to the plane is $5$ cm. (a) Find the radius of the circle of intersection. [2] (b) Find the area of this circle, giving your answer in terms of $\pi$. [1] (c) Find the volume of the sphere, giving your answer in terms of $\pi$. [2]
markscheme: (a) The radius of the circle, $r$, satisfies $r^2+5^2=13^2$ [M1] $r=12\ \text{cm}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $A=\pi(12)^2=144\pi\ \text{cm}^2$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $V=\tfrac43\pi(13)^3$ [M1] $=\dfrac{8788\pi}{3}\ \text{cm}^3$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A right-angled triangle always links the sphere's radius, the distance from the centre to the plane and the radius of the circular section. Leave answers in terms of $\pi$ when the question asks.

subtopic: Capacity of a rectangular fish tank in liters
statement: A fish tank is a cuboid with interior base $50$ cm by $40$ cm and interior height $30$ cm. Note that $1000\ \mathrm{cm}^3=1$ liter. (a) Find the capacity of the tank in liters. [2] (b) The tank is filled with water to $\dfrac34$ of its height. Find the volume of water in liters. [2] (c) A solid ornament of volume $3$ liters is placed on the bottom of the tank and is completely covered by the water. Find the rise in the water level, in cm. [2]
markscheme: (a) $50\times40\times30=60000\ \mathrm{cm}^3$ [M1] $=60$ liters [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac34\times60$ [M1] $=45$ liters [A1] [2 marks] (c) Volume of ornament $=3000\ \mathrm{cm}^3$, base area $=2000\ \mathrm{cm}^2$ [M1] Rise $=\dfrac{3000}{2000}=1.5$ cm [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Convert units at the start: $1000\ \mathrm{cm}^3=1$ liter. A submerged object raises the water level by its volume divided by the base area of the tank.

subtopic: Minimizing the surface area of a closed 500 mL can
statement: A closed cylindrical can has base radius $r$ cm, height $h$ cm and volume $500\ \mathrm{cm}^3$. (a) Show that $h=\dfrac{500}{\pi r^2}$. [1] (b) Hence show that the total surface area $A\ \mathrm{cm}^2$ of the can is given by $A=2\pi r^2+\dfrac{1000}{r}$. [2] (c) Find $\dfrac{dA}{dr}$, and hence find the value of $r$ that minimizes $A$. Give your answer correct to three significant figures. [4] (d) Find the minimum surface area, and the corresponding height of the can, each correct to three significant figures. Write down the ratio $h:r$. [3] (e) The metal costs \$0.012 per $\mathrm{cm}^2$. Find the minimum cost of the metal for one can, to the nearest cent. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\pi r^2h=500$, so $h=\dfrac{500}{\pi r^2}$ [AG] [1 mark] (b) $A=2\pi r^2+2\pi rh$ [M1] $=2\pi r^2+2\pi r\cdot\dfrac{500}{\pi r^2}=2\pi r^2+\dfrac{1000}{r}$ [AG] [2 marks] (c) $\dfrac{dA}{dr}=4\pi r-\dfrac{1000}{r^2}$ [M1][A1] Setting $=0$: $r^3=\dfrac{250}{\pi}$ [M1] $r=4.30$ cm [A1] [4 marks] (d) $A_{\min}=349\ \mathrm{cm}^2$ [A1] $h=8.60$ cm [A1] $h:r=2:1$ (the height equals the diameter) [A1] [3 marks] (e) $349\times0.012=\$4.18$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Eliminate $h$ first so that $A$ is a function of one variable. You can also confirm the minimum by sketching $A(r)$ on your GDC.

subtopic: Melting a large sphere into small spheres
statement: A jeweler melts a solid gold sphere of radius $3$ cm and uses all of the gold to make identical small spherical beads, each of radius $1$ cm. Assume no gold is lost. (a) Find the volume of the large sphere, in terms of $\pi$. [2] (b) Find the volume of one bead, in terms of $\pi$. [1] (c) Hence find the number of beads that can be made. [2] (d) Find the total surface area of the $27$ beads as a multiple of the surface area of the large sphere. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac43\pi(3)^3$ [M1] $=36\pi\ \mathrm{cm}^3$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac43\pi$ $\mathrm{cm}^3$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $36\pi\div\dfrac43\pi$ [M1] $=27$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) Surface area of one bead $=4\pi(1)^2=4\pi$, so total $=108\pi$ [M1] Surface area of the large sphere $=4\pi(3)^2=36\pi$ [A1] Ratio $=\dfrac{108\pi}{36\pi}=3$, so three times as large [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Compare volumes, not radii, when one shape is recast into another. The surface area scales with the square of the radius while the volume scales with the cube.

subtopic: Filling a conical funnel
statement: A funnel is an inverted cone with its vertex at the bottom, height $16$ cm and radius $8$ cm at the top. Water is poured in at a constant rate of $10$ cm$^{3}$ per second. When the depth of water is $h$ cm, the surface of the water has radius $\dfrac{h}{2}$ cm. (a) Show that the volume of water is $V=\dfrac{\pi h^{3}}{12}$. [2] (b) Find the time for the water depth to reach $8$ cm, to three significant figures. [3] (c) Find the depth of water after $20$ seconds, to three significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) $V=\dfrac13\pi\left(\dfrac h2\right)^{2}h$ [M1]; $=\dfrac{\pi h^{3}}{12}$ [AG] [2 marks] (b) $V=\dfrac{\pi\times512}{12}=134.0$ [A1]; time $=\dfrac{134.0}{10}$ [M1]; $13.4$ s [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\dfrac{\pi h^{3}}{12}=200$ [M1]; $h=9.14$ cm [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The cross-section of the water is similar to the whole funnel, so its radius is half its depth.

subtopic: Angles between faces of a rectangular pyramid
statement: A right pyramid has a rectangular base of length $12$ cm and width $8$ cm. The vertex is $9$ cm vertically above the centre of the base. (a) Find the angle between a triangular face containing a $12$ cm base edge and the base, correct to the nearest tenth of a degree. [3] (b) Find the angle between a triangular face containing an $8$ cm base edge and the base, correct to the nearest tenth of a degree. [2] (c) Find the volume of the pyramid. [2]
markscheme: (a) The perpendicular distance from the centre of the base to a $12$ cm edge is half the width, $4$ cm [A1] $\tan\alpha=\dfrac94$ [M1] $\alpha=66.0^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) The perpendicular distance from the centre to an $8$ cm edge is $6$ cm, so $\tan\beta=\dfrac96$ [M1] $\beta=56.3^\circ$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $V=\tfrac13\times12\times8\times9$ [M1] $=288\ \text{cm}^3$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The angle between a face and the base is measured along a line perpendicular to the shared edge, so use the distance from the centre to the edge, not to the corner. The longer base edge is closer to the centre, which gives the steeper face.

subtopic: Cylinder with a conical cavity
statement: A solid metal cylinder has radius $6$ cm and height $10$ cm. A conical cavity is drilled out of the top: the cone has the same circular top face as the cylinder, and its apex is at the center of the bottom face. (a) Find the exact volume of metal remaining. [3] (b) Find the exact slant height of the cone. [1] (c) Find the exact total surface area of the remaining solid, including the surface of the cavity. [3]
markscheme: (a) cylinder $=\pi\times36\times10=360\pi$ [A1]; cone $=\dfrac13\pi\times36\times10=120\pi$ [A1]; remaining $=240\pi$ cm$^{3}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\sqrt{6^{2}+10^{2}}=\sqrt{136}=2\sqrt{34}$ cm [A1] [1 mark] (c) curved surface of cylinder $=2\pi\times6\times10=120\pi$ and bottom face $=36\pi$ [A1]; inside cone surface $=\pi\times6\times2\sqrt{34}=12\sqrt{34}\,\pi$ [A1]; total $=\left(156+12\sqrt{34}\right)\pi$ cm$^{2}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The top face of the cylinder disappears completely because the cone's base covers it.

subtopic: Submerging steel balls in a cylindrical container of water
statement: A cylindrical glass container has internal radius $6$ cm and internal height $15$ cm. It contains water to a depth of $10$ cm. A solid steel ball of radius $4.5$ cm is lowered into the water and rests on the bottom of the container. (a) Find the volume of the ball, correct to three significant figures. [2] (b) Find the rise in the water level, correct to three significant figures. [3] (c) Show that the ball is completely under water. [2] (d) A second identical ball is added. Find the volume of water that overflows, correct to three significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac43\pi(4.5)^3$ [M1] $=382\ \mathrm{cm}^3$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Volume displaced $=$ volume of ball [R1] $\pi(6)^2\times\text{rise}=382$ [M1] rise $=3.37$ cm [A1] [3 marks] (c) New depth $=10+3.37=13.4$ cm [M1] $13.4>9$ (the diameter of the ball), so the ball is completely covered [R1] [2 marks] (d) Total rise would be $2(3.37)=6.75$ cm, giving depth $16.8$ cm [M1] This exceeds $15$ cm by $1.75$ cm [A1] Overflow $=\pi(6)^2(1.75)=198\ \mathrm{cm}^3$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: An object that is completely submerged displaces its own volume of water. Treat the rise in level as a thin cylinder with the same base as the container.

subtopic: Triangular prism tent: cross-section, volume and canvas
statement: A tent has the shape of a triangular prism lying on one of its rectangular faces. Its two ends are isosceles triangles with equal sides $1.8$ m and an angle of $80^\circ$ between the equal sides. The tent is $3.2$ m long. (a) Find the area of one triangular end of the tent, correct to three significant figures. [2] (b) Find the volume of air inside the tent, correct to three significant figures. [2] (c) Find the width of the ground sheet, that is, the side opposite the $80^\circ$ angle, correct to three significant figures. [3] (d) The tent is made from two sloping rectangular sides, two triangular ends and a rectangular ground sheet. Find the total area of material, correct to three significant figures. [3]
tips: The area of a triangle with two sides and the included angle is $\frac12ab\sin C$. The cosine rule gives the third side of the end triangle.

subtopic: Scale model of a water tower: lengths, volumes and areas
statement: A water tower has a cylindrical tank of radius $4.5$ m and height $10$ m. A museum builds a scale model of the tank, which is also a cylinder, with radius $18$ cm and height $40$ cm. (a) Find the volume of the real tank in cubic meters, and give the capacity in liters, to three significant figures. Note that $1\ \mathrm{m}^3=1000$ liters. [3] (b) Find the volume of the model in $\mathrm{cm}^3$. [2] (c) Show that the model is built to a scale of $1:25$, and show that the ratio of the volume of the real tank to the volume of the model is $25^3$. [3] (d) The curved surface of the model required $0.15$ liters of paint. Assuming the same coverage, find the amount of paint needed for the curved surface of the real tank. [2]
markscheme: (a) Volume $=\pi(4.5)^2(10)$ [M1] $=636\ \mathrm{m}^3$ [A1] Capacity $=636000$ liters [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\pi(18)^2(40)$ [M1] $=40700\ \mathrm{cm}^3$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $450\div18=25$ and $1000\div40=25$, so both dimensions have scale factor $25$ [R1] Real volume in $\mathrm{cm}^3=636000000$ [M1] $\dfrac{636000000}{40700}=15625=25^3$ [AG] [3 marks] (d) Area scale factor $=25^2=625$ [M1] $0.15\times625=93.75\approx93.8$ liters [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Lengths scale by $k$, areas by $k^2$ and volumes by $k^3$. Convert to the same units before comparing the volumes.

subtopic: Diagonals and angles inside a rectangular room
statement: A room is a cuboid $ABCDEFGH$. The floor $ABCD$ is a horizontal rectangle with $AB=8$ m and $BC=6$ m. The vertical edges $AE$, $BF$, $CG$ and $DH$ each have length $3.5$ m, so that $EFGH$ is the ceiling directly above the floor. A cable runs in a straight line from corner $A$ on the floor to corner $G$ on the ceiling. (a) Find the length of $AC$. [2] (b) Find the length of the cable $AG$, correct to three significant figures. [2] (c) Find the angle between the cable $AG$ and the floor, correct to the nearest $0.1^\circ$. [2] (d) Find the angle between the cable $AG$ and the edge $AB$, correct to the nearest $0.1^\circ$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\sqrt{8^2+6^2}$ [M1] $=10$ m [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\sqrt{10^2+3.5^2}$ [M1] $=10.6$ m [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\tan\theta=\dfrac{3.5}{10}$ [M1] $\theta=19.3^\circ$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $AB$ is perpendicular to the plane $BCGF$, so angle $ABG=90^\circ$ [R1] $\cos\phi=\dfrac{8}{10.6}$ [M1] $\phi=41.0^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The angle between a line and a plane uses the projection of the line on the plane. For the angle with an edge, find a triangle with a right angle at the end of that edge.

subtopic: Sphere inscribed in a cylinder: volume and surface ratios
statement: A solid sphere of radius $r$ fits exactly inside a closed cylinder, so that the sphere touches the curved wall and both circular ends of the cylinder. (a) Write down the height of the cylinder in terms of $r$, and show that the volume of the cylinder is $2\pi r^3$. [2] (b) Show that the volume of the sphere is $\dfrac23$ of the volume of the cylinder. [2] (c) Show that the area of the curved surface of the cylinder equals the surface area of the sphere. [2] (d) The volume of the sphere is $288\pi\ \mathrm{cm}^3$. Find the radius and the volume of the cylinder. [2]
markscheme: (a) Height $=2r$ [A1] $V=\pi r^2(2r)=2\pi r^3$ [AG] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac{\frac43\pi r^3}{2\pi r^3}$ [M1] $=\dfrac23$ [AG] [2 marks] (c) Curved area of cylinder $=2\pi r(2r)=4\pi r^2$ [M1] which equals the surface area of the sphere $4\pi r^2$ [AG] [2 marks] (d) $\dfrac43\pi r^3=288\pi\Rightarrow r^3=216$, so $r=6$ cm [A1] Cylinder volume $=2\pi(6)^3=432\pi\ \mathrm{cm}^3$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: For "show that" questions, write each algebraic step; do not substitute numbers. Use the fact that the sphere's diameter equals both the cylinder's height and its base diameter.

subtopic: Packing six cylindrical cans in a cuboid box: wasted space
statement: Six identical cylindrical cans of radius $3.3$ cm and height $12.2$ cm are packed upright in a cuboid box in two rows of three. Each can touches its neighbors and the sides of the box, and the box has no spare height. (a) Write down the length and width of the base of the box. [2] (b) Find the volume of the box, correct to three significant figures. [2] (c) Find the total volume of the six cans, correct to three significant figures. [2] (d) Find the percentage of the volume of the box that is empty, correct to three significant figures. [3]
tips: The diameter of a can sets the spacing in each row. Use unrounded volumes in the final percentage.

subtopic: Conical sand pile with a given angle of repose
statement: Sand is poured onto flat ground and forms a cone with base radius $2.4$ m. The sloping surface of the pile makes an angle of $35^\circ$ with the ground. (a) Find the height of the pile, in meters, correct to three significant figures. [2] (b) Find the volume of sand in the pile, in $\mathrm{m}^3$, correct to three significant figures. [2] (c) The sand has a density of $1600\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$. Find the mass of the pile, in tonnes. Note that $1$ tonne $=1000$ kg. [2] (d) A tarpaulin is used to cover the whole sloping surface of the pile. Find the least area of tarpaulin needed, in $\mathrm{m}^2$, correct to three significant figures. [3]
tips: Draw the right-angled triangle formed by the height, radius and slant height of the cone. Use unrounded values from your calculator in later parts to avoid accumulated rounding error.

subtopic: Longest rod in a cuboid cabinet and its angle with the base
statement: A storage cabinet is a cuboid with a rectangular base measuring $30$ cm by $40$ cm and an interior height of $120$ cm. A thin metal rod is to be placed inside the cabinet with one end at a bottom corner and the other end at the opposite top corner. (a) Find the length of a diagonal of the base. [2] (b) Find the length of the longest rod that fits in the cabinet. [2] (c) The rod makes an angle $\theta$ with the base of the cabinet. Find the exact value of $\tan\theta$, and hence write down the value of $\sin\theta$. [3]
tips: Break a 3D problem into two right-angled triangles: first the base diagonal, then the space diagonal. For the angle, draw the right-angled triangle formed by the rod, the base diagonal and the vertical edge.

subtopic: Right pyramid on a rectangular base: edges and face angles
statement: $VABCD$ is a right pyramid with a horizontal rectangular base $ABCD$, where $AB=12$ cm and $BC=9$ cm. The apex $V$ is vertically above the centre $O$ of the base, and $VO=10$ cm. (a) Show that $AC=15$ cm and find the length of $VA$, correct to three significant figures. [3] (b) Find the angle between the edge $VA$ and the base, correct to the nearest $0.1^\circ$. [2] (c) Find the angle between the face $VAB$ and the base, and the angle between the face $VBC$ and the base, each correct to the nearest $0.1^\circ$. [4] (d) Find the angle $\angle AVC$, correct to the nearest $0.1^\circ$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $AC=\sqrt{12^2+9^2}=15$ [AG] $AO=7.5$ [A1] $VA=\sqrt{10^2+7.5^2}=12.5$ cm [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\tan\theta=\dfrac{10}{7.5}$ [M1] $\theta=53.1^\circ$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Distance from $O$ to $AB$ is $4.5$ and from $O$ to $BC$ is $6$ [M1][A1] Face $VAB$: $\tan^{-1}\dfrac{10}{4.5}=65.8^\circ$ [A1] Face $VBC$: $\tan^{-1}\dfrac{10}{6}=59.0^\circ$ [A1] [4 marks] (d) $\cos\angle AVC=\dfrac{12.5^2+12.5^2-15^2}{2(12.5)(12.5)}$ [M1][A1] $\angle AVC=73.7^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The perpendicular distance from the centre to each base edge differs for the two pairs of faces, so the two face angles are not equal. For $\angle AVC$ use the cosine rule in triangle $AVC$.

subtopic: Ice cream cone topped with a hemisphere of ice cream
statement: An ice cream cone is a hollow cone with a circular opening of radius $3.2$ cm and slant height $11.5$ cm. The cone is filled to the brim with ice cream, and a hemisphere of ice cream of the same radius sits on top. (a) Find the vertical height of the cone, correct to three significant figures. [2] (b) Find the volume of ice cream inside the cone, correct to three significant figures. [2] (c) Find the volume of the hemisphere of ice cream, correct to three significant figures. [2] (d) The ice cream has density $0.55\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$. Find the total mass of ice cream, in grams, correct to three significant figures. [2] (e) The outside of the cone is covered with a paper wrapper (the curved surface only). Find the area of the wrapper, correct to three significant figures. [2]
tips: Use the vertical height in the volume formula and the slant height in the curved surface area. Keep full calculator values until the final line of each part.

subtopic: Largest cylinder and cone inside a sphere: 3D optimization
statement: This question investigates the largest solid cylinder, and the largest solid cone, that can be cut from a solid sphere of radius $10$ cm. All lengths are in centimeters. A cylinder is cut so that its axis passes through the centre $O$ of the sphere and both of its circular ends lie on the surface of the sphere. Let the cylinder have half-height $y$ (so its height is $2y$) and base radius $x$, where $0<y<10$. (a) Show that $x^2=100-y^2$, and hence that the volume of the cylinder is $V=2\pi y\left(100-y^2\right)$. [3] (b) Calculate $V$, correct to three significant figures, for $y=2,\ 4,\ 6$ and $8$. Hence comment on how $V$ changes as $y$ increases from $2$ to $8$. [3] (c) Use your GDC to sketch the graph of $V$ against $y$ for $0<y<10$. Write down the maximum value of $V$ and the value of $y$ at which it occurs, each correct to three significant figures. [3] (d) Differentiate $V$ with respect to $y$. Hence show that the maximum volume occurs when $y=\dfrac{10}{\sqrt3}$, and show that this is a maximum. [4] (e) Find the maximum volume of the cylinder as a percentage of the volume of the sphere, correct to three significant figures. Show that for a sphere of any radius $R$ this percentage is the same, and state its exact value. [3] (f) Now a cone is cut from the same sphere. Its apex is at the top of the sphere, its axis is vertical through $O$, and its circular base lies in a horizontal plane at distance $y$ below $O$, with its rim on the sphere, where $0\leq y<10$. Show that the volume of the cone is $V_c=\dfrac{\pi}{3}\left(100-y^2\right)(10+y)$. [3] (g) Find the value of $y$ for which the volume of the cone is a maximum, and find that maximum volume correct to three significant figures. Hence find which of the two solids, the largest cylinder or the largest cone, wastes less of the sphere, and state the percentage of the sphere wasted in each case. [5]
markscheme: (a) A rim point of the cylinder is on the sphere, so $x^2+y^2=10^2$ [M1][A1] $V=\pi x^2(2y)=2\pi y(100-y^2)$ [AG] [3 marks] (b) $y=2$: $1210$; $y=4$: $2110$; $y=6$: $2410$; $y=8$: $1810$ (in $\mathrm{cm}^3$) [A2] $V$ increases to a maximum near $y=6$ and then decreases [A1] [3 marks] (c) Correct shape of graph with a single maximum [A1] $y=5.77$ [A1] $V_{\max}=2420\ \mathrm{cm}^3$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $\dfrac{dV}{dy}=2\pi\left(100-3y^2\right)$ [M1][A1] Set $\dfrac{dV}{dy}=0$: $y^2=\dfrac{100}{3}$, so $y=\dfrac{10}{\sqrt3}$ [M1] $\dfrac{d^2V}{dy^2}=-12\pi y<0$ for $y>0$, so a maximum [R1] [4 marks] (e) Sphere volume $=\dfrac43\pi(10)^3=4190$; percentage $=\dfrac{2420}{4190}\times100=57.7\%$ [M1][A1] For radius $R$: $V_{\max}=2\pi\dfrac{R}{\sqrt3}\cdot\dfrac{2R^2}{3}=\dfrac{4\pi R^3}{3\sqrt3}$, so the ratio to $\dfrac43\pi R^3$ is $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}$ ($\approx57.7\%$) [A1] [3 marks] (f) Height of cone $=10+y$ [A1] Base radius squared $=100-y^2$ [A1] $V_c=\dfrac13\pi\left(100-y^2\right)(10+y)$ [AG] [3 marks] (g) $\dfrac{dV_c}{dy}=\dfrac\pi3\left(100-20y-3y^2\right)$ [M1][A1] Setting $=0$: $(10-3y)(10+y)=0$, so $y=\dfrac{10}{3}$ (as $y\ge0$) [A1] $V_{c,\max}=1240\ \mathrm{cm}^3$ [A1] Waste: cylinder $42.3\%$, cone $70.4\%$, so the cylinder wastes less [A1] [5 marks]
tips: In Paper 3 questions, each part builds on the last: reuse the results you have shown. Sketch the graph on your GDC to check your calculus answer for the maximum, and quote exact values before rounding.

subtopic: A wedge-shaped ramp
statement: A ramp is a right triangular prism. Its horizontal base is a rectangle $3.5$ m by $1.2$ m, its vertical back face is a rectangle $0.6$ m by $1.2$ m and the sloping face joins the front edge of the base to the top edge of the back face. (The slope rises $0.6$ m over $3.5$ m of horizontal distance.) (a) Find the angle that the sloping face makes with the horizontal. [2] (b) Find the length of the sloping face and its area. [3] (c) Find the volume of concrete needed to make the ramp. [2] (d) Concrete costs \$145 per cubic meter. Find the cost of the concrete, to the nearest dollar. [2]
tips: The volume of a prism is cross-section area times length; here the cross-section is a right triangle.

subtopic: Cylinder with a hemispherical cap
statement: A solid is made of a cylinder of radius $3$ cm and height $8$ cm, with a hemisphere of radius $3$ cm attached on top. Give all answers in terms of $\pi$. (a) Find the volume of the solid. [3] (b) Find the total surface area of the solid, including the flat base. [3]
markscheme: (a) cylinder $\pi(9)(8)=72\pi$ [A1]; hemisphere $\dfrac23\pi(27)=18\pi$ [A1]; total $90\pi$ cm$^{3}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) base $9\pi$ [A1]; curved cylinder $2\pi(3)(8)=48\pi$ [A1]; hemisphere $2\pi(9)=18\pi$, total $75\pi$ cm$^{2}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The flat top of the cylinder is covered by the hemisphere, so it is not part of the surface.

subtopic: Frustum of a cone using similar cones
statement: A solid cone has base radius $10$ cm and vertical height $24$ cm. It is cut by a plane parallel to its base at a height of $15$ cm above the base, forming a smaller cone at the top and a frustum below. (a) Find the height and the base radius of the smaller cone. [2] (b) Find the volume of the smaller cone, correct to three significant figures. [2] (c) Find the volume of the frustum, correct to three significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) Height of small cone $=24-15=9$ cm [A1] The cones are similar with ratio $\tfrac{9}{24}=\tfrac38$, so radius $=10\times\tfrac38=3.75$ cm [A1] [2 marks] (b) $V=\tfrac13\pi(3.75)^2(9)$ [M1] $=42.1875\pi=133\ \text{cm}^3$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Volume of whole cone $=\tfrac13\pi(10)^2(24)=800\pi$ [A1] Frustum $=800\pi-42.1875\pi$ [M1] $=757.8125\pi=2380\ \text{cm}^3$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Similar solids have linear ratio $k$, so lengths scale by $k$ and volumes by $k^3$. Subtracting the small cone from the whole cone is the quickest route to the frustum.

subtopic: Grain silo: cylinder with a hemispherical roof
statement: A grain silo is modeled as a cylinder of radius $3$ m and height $10$ m, topped by a hemisphere of radius $3$ m. The base of the cylinder sits flat on the ground. (a) Find the total volume of the silo, in terms of $\pi$. [3] (b) The curved outside surface of the silo (cylinder wall and hemisphere roof) is to be painted. Find the area to be painted, in terms of $\pi$. [3] (c) A second silo is a plain cylinder with the same radius and the same volume as the first. Find its height. [2]
markscheme: (a) Cylinder $=\pi(3)^2(10)=90\pi$ [A1] Hemisphere $=\dfrac12\cdot\dfrac43\pi(3)^3=18\pi$ [A1] Total $=108\pi\ \mathrm{m}^3$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Cylinder wall $=2\pi(3)(10)=60\pi$ [A1] Hemisphere $=2\pi(3)^2=18\pi$ [A1] Total $=78\pi\ \mathrm{m}^2$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\pi(3)^2h=108\pi$ [M1] $h=12$ m [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Treat each piece separately and add. Remember that the curved surface of a hemisphere is half of $4\pi r^2$, and that the circular base is not painted here.

subtopic: Exact volume and surface area of a cylindrical tin
statement: A cylindrical tin of olive oil has radius $5$ cm and height $12$ cm. (a) Find the volume of the tin. Give your answer in terms of $\pi$. [2] (b) Find the total outer surface area of the tin, including both circular ends. Give your answer in terms of $\pi$. [2] (c) The tin is filled with oil to $\dfrac34$ of its height. Find the volume of oil, in terms of $\pi$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $V=\pi\times5^2\times12$ [M1] $=300\pi\ \mathrm{cm}^3$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $2\pi(5)^2+2\pi(5)(12)$ [M1] $=50\pi+120\pi=170\pi\ \mathrm{cm}^2$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\dfrac34\times300\pi$ [M1] $=225\pi\ \mathrm{cm}^3$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Keep the answer in terms of $\pi$ when asked; do not use your calculator on a Paper 1 question like this. A cylinder has two circular ends and one curved face.

subtopic: Cylinder with hemispherical top: volume and area
statement: A storage silo is made from a cylinder of radius $2.5$ m and height $h$ m with a hemisphere of radius $2.5$ m attached to the top. (a) Find the volume of the hemisphere, correct to three significant figures. [2] (b) The silo must have a total volume of $180\ \text{m}^3$. Find the value of $h$, correct to three significant figures.
