markscheme: (a) $\mathrm{H}_0:p=0.4$, $\mathrm{H}_1:p<0.4$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Under $\mathrm{H}_0$, $X\sim\mathrm{B}(20,0.4)$ [M1] $P(X\le3)=0.0160$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $P(X\le4)=0.0510$ [A1] which is greater than $0.05$, so $X\le3$ is the largest critical region [R1] [2 marks] (d) Concluding that fewer than $40\%$ of visitors click when in fact $40\%$ do [A1] [1 mark] (e) Type II error means accepting $\mathrm{H}_0$ when it is false, i.e. $X\ge4$ [M1] With $X\sim\mathrm{B}(20,0.2)$ [M1] $P(X\ge4)=1-P(X\le3)=0.589$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A Type I error is rejecting a true $\mathrm{H}_0$, and its probability is the probability of landing in the critical region when $p=p_0$. A Type II error uses the true (alternative) value of $p$ and the acceptance region.

subtopic: Correlation, regression and chi-squared
statement: A teacher investigates whether the time students spend revising is related to their test scores. Eight students recorded the number of hours, $x$, they spent revising and their test score, $y$ (out of $100$). $$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline x & 2 & 3 & 5 & 6 & 8 & 9 & 11 & 12 \\ \hline y & 48 & 50 & 59 & 61 & 70 & 68 & 80 & 84 \\ \hline\end{array}$$ (a) Calculate Pearson's product-moment correlation coefficient, $r$, and interpret its value. [3] (b) Find the equation of the regression line of $y$ on $x$. [2] (c) (i) Use your regression line to estimate the score of a student who revised for $7$ hours. (ii) Explain why it would not be appropriate to use the line to estimate the score of a student who revised for $20$ hours. [3] (d) Test, at the $1\%$ significance level, whether there is positive correlation between $x$ and $y$ in the population. State your hypotheses, the $p$-value and your conclusion. [5] (e) (i) Calculate Spearman's rank correlation coefficient, $r_s$, for the data. (ii) Explain why $r_s$ is slightly smaller than $1$ even though $y$ generally increases with $x$. [4] The teacher then surveys $100$ students about their main revision method and whether they passed the test. $$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|}\hline \text{Method} & \text{Pass} & \text{Fail} \\ \hline \text{Flashcards} & 18 & 12 \\ \hline \text{Past papers} & 27 & 8 \\ \hline \text{Re-reading notes} & 15 & 20 \\ \hline\end{array}$$ (f) Perform a $\chi^2$ test for independence at the $5\%$ significance level. State your hypotheses, the expected frequencies, the number of degrees of freedom, the $\chi^2$ statistic, the $p$-value and your conclusion. [7] (g) State, with a reason, whether your conclusion to part (f) would change at the $1\%$ significance level. [1]
markscheme: (a) $r=0.990$ (to 3 s.f.) [A2] very strong positive linear correlation [R1] [3 marks] (b) $y=3.55x+40.1$ (more precisely $y=3.554x+40.12$) [A1][A1] [2 marks] (c)(i) $y=3.554\times7+40.12\approx65.0$ [A1] (ii) $20$ hours is outside the range of the data ($2\le x\le12$), so this is extrapolation [R1]; also the line predicts about $111$, which exceeds the maximum score of $100$ [R1] [3 marks] (d) $H_0:\ \rho=0$; $H_1:\ \rho>0$ [A1][A1] $p$-value $=1.26\times10^{-6}$ (from $t=17.1$ with $6$ degrees of freedom) [A1] since $p<0.01$ [R1] reject $H_0$: there is evidence of positive correlation between revision time and score [A1] [5 marks] (e)(i) ranks of $x$: $1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8$; ranks of $y$: $1,2,3,4,6,5,7,8$ [M1] $\sum d^2=2$, $r_s=1-\dfrac{6\times2}{8\times63}=0.976$ [A1][A1] (ii) the relationship is not perfectly monotonic: the student with $x=9$ scored less than the student with $x=8$ [R1] [4 marks] (f) $H_0$: pass/fail is independent of revision method; $H_1$: pass/fail is not independent of revision method [A1] Expected frequencies: Flashcards $18, 12$; Past papers $21, 14$; Re-reading $21, 14$ [A1] degrees of freedom $=(3-1)(2-1)=2$ [A1] $\chi^2=8.57$ [A1] $p$-value $=0.0138$ [A1] since $0.0138<0.05$ [R1] reject $H_0$: there is evidence that the result depends on the revision method [A1] [7 marks] (g) Yes: $0.0138>0.01$, so at the $1\%$ level $H_0$ would not be rejected [R1] [1 mark] Total [25 marks]
tips: State hypotheses in terms of the population parameter (ρ), not the sample value r.

subtopic: Chi-squared goodness of fit: equal preference
statement: A cafe owner suspects that customers are not equally likely to choose each of four pastries. Over one morning, $120$ customers each choose one pastry: croissant $36$, muffin $24$, scone $32$, danish $28$. A chi-squared goodness of fit test is carried out at the $5\%$ significance level to test whether the four pastries are equally popular. (a) State the null and alternative hypotheses. [1] (b) Write down the expected frequency for each pastry and the number of degrees of freedom. [2] (c) Calculate the value of $\chi^2_{\mathrm{calc}}$. [2] (d) The critical value at the $5\%$ level is $7.815$. State the conclusion of the test, giving a reason. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\mathrm{H}_0$: the four pastries are equally popular (choices follow a uniform distribution); $\mathrm{H}_1$: they are not equally popular [A1] [1 mark] (b) Expected frequency $=\dfrac{120}{4}=30$ for each pastry [A1] Degrees of freedom $=4-1=3$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\chi^2=\dfrac{6^2+(-6)^2+2^2+(-2)^2}{30}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{80}{30}=\dfrac{8}{3}\approx2.67$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $2.67<7.815$ [R1] Do not reject $\mathrm{H}_0$: there is insufficient evidence that the pastries are not equally popular [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Under a uniform null hypothesis every expected frequency is the total divided by the number of categories. Compare the calculated statistic with the critical value, and word the conclusion in terms of the original claim.

subtopic: Poisson model investigation: dispersion, goodness of fit and rate test
statement: This question investigates whether the number of arrivals at a mountain hut check-in desk can be modelled by a Poisson distribution, and then uses the model to test a claim about the arrival rate. The number of hikers arriving in each of $200$ consecutive five-minute intervals was recorded. Number of arrivals: $0,\ 1,\ 2,\ 3,\ 4,\ 5,\ 6,\ 7$; number of intervals: $20,\ 46,\ 47,\ 38,\ 25,\ 13,\ 7,\ 4$. (a) Show that the sample mean is $2.445$, and find the unbiased estimate of the population variance. [4] (b) Comment on whether the relationship between your two answers is consistent with a Poisson model. [1] (c) Assuming that the number of arrivals in a five-minute interval is $\mathrm{Po}(2.445)$, find the expected number of intervals with $0,\ 1,\ 2,\ 3,\ 4,\ 5$ and at least $6$ arrivals. [3] (d) A $\chi^2$ goodness of fit test of the Poisson model is carried out at the $5\%$ level. State the hypotheses, and explain why the categories for $6$ and $7$ arrivals are combined, and find the degrees of freedom. [3] (e) Find $\chi^2_{\mathrm{calc}}$ and the $p$-value, and state your conclusion. [5] (f) Let $Y$ be the total number of arrivals in all $200$ intervals. If arrivals in each interval are independent with $\mathrm{Po}(\lambda)$, show that $Y\sim\mathrm{Po}(200\lambda)$. [2] (g) A manager claims that the mean number of arrivals per five-minute interval is $2.2$, but a ranger believes it is higher. Using $Y$ and the data above, carry out a test at the $5\%$ level: state the hypotheses, find the $p$-value and state the conclusion. [5] (h) Use a normal approximation with continuity correction to estimate the $p$-value in part (g), and comment on the accuracy of the approximation. [4]
markscheme: (a) Total arrivals $=0(20)+1(46)+2(47)+3(38)+4(25)+5(13)+6(7)+7(4)=489$ [M1] $\bar x=\dfrac{489}{200}=2.445$ [AG] Unbiased variance estimate $s_{n-1}^2=2.78$ [M1][A1] [4 marks] (b) For a Poisson distribution the mean equals the variance; $2.78$ is close to $2.445$, so the data are broadly consistent with a Poisson model [R1] [1 mark] (c) $200\times P(X=k)$ with $X\sim\mathrm{Po}(2.445)$ [M1] Expected: $17.3,\ 42.4,\ 51.8,\ 42.3,\ 25.8,\ 12.6$ [A1] at least $6$: $7.69$ (the remainder) [A1] [3 marks] (d) $\mathrm{H}_0$: the number of arrivals follows a Poisson distribution; $\mathrm{H}_1$: it does not [A1] The expected frequency for $7$ arrivals alone is below $5$ so $6$ and $7$ are combined into a single category [R1] There are $7$ categories and $1$ parameter ($\lambda$) was estimated from the data, so $\nu=7-1-1=5$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) Observed: $20,46,47,38,25,13,11$ against expected values above [M1] $\chi^2_{\mathrm{calc}}=3.05$ [A1] $p=0.692$ [A1] $0.692>0.05$ [R1] Do not reject $\mathrm{H}_0$: the Poisson model is a reasonable fit [A1] [5 marks] (f) The sum of independent Poisson random variables is Poisson [M1] with mean equal to the sum of the means, $200\lambda$ [AG] [2 marks] (g) $\mathrm{H}_0:\lambda=2.2$, $\mathrm{H}_1:\lambda>2.2$ [A1] Under $\mathrm{H}_0$, $Y\sim\mathrm{Po}(440)$ [A1] $p$-value $=P(Y\ge489)=1-P(Y\le488)$ [M1] $=0.0113$ [A1] $0.0113<0.05$: reject $\mathrm{H}_0$, sufficient evidence that the mean number of arrivals per interval exceeds $2.2$ [A1] [5 marks] (h) $Y\approx\mathrm{N}(440,440)$ [M1] $P(Y\ge489)\approx P(Y>488.5)$ [M1] $z=\dfrac{488.5-440}{\sqrt{440}}=2.31$, $p\approx0.0104$ [A1] Close to the exact value $0.0113$, so the approximation is reasonably accurate (slightly underestimates the tail) [R1] [4 marks]
tips: Expected frequencies must be at least $5$ for a valid $\chi^2$ test, so merge sparse categories and subtract one extra degree of freedom for each parameter estimated from the data. In part (g), do not forget to scale the Poisson mean to the whole recording period.

subtopic: Chi-squared independence test for a 2 by 2 table, gym classes
statement: A gym surveys $180$ members. Of the $80$ members on a monthly contract, $48$ regularly attend group classes and $32$ do not. Of the $100$ members on an annual contract, $36$ regularly attend group classes and $64$ do not. A $\chi^2$ test for independence is carried out at the $1\%$ significance level. Do not apply a continuity correction. (a) State the null and alternative hypotheses. [1] (b) Find the expected number of monthly-contract members who regularly attend classes. [2] (c) Write down the degrees of freedom. [1] (d) Find the value of $\chi^2_{\mathrm{calc}}$ and the $p$-value. [3] (e) State the conclusion of the test. [2] (f) Give a brief description of the association found, using the data. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\mathrm{H}_0$: attending classes is independent of contract type; $\mathrm{H}_1$: attending classes depends on contract type [A1] [1 mark] (b) Total attending $=48+36=84$ [M1] Expected $=\dfrac{80\times84}{180}=37.3$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $(2-1)(2-1)=1$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) $\chi^2_{\mathrm{calc}}=10.3$ [M1][A1] $p=0.00134$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) $0.00134<0.01$ [R1] Reject $\mathrm{H}_0$: sufficient evidence of an association between contract type and class attendance [A1] [2 marks] (f) $\dfrac{48}{80}=60\%$ of monthly members attend classes compared with $\dfrac{36}{100}=36\%$ of annual members, so monthly members are more likely to attend [A1] [1 mark]
tips: A $2\times2$ table has one degree of freedom. After rejecting independence, compare row percentages to describe the direction of the association rather than just saying a link exists.

subtopic: Critical region for a one-tailed z-test
statement: The masses of cereal boxes are normally distributed with known standard deviation $6$ g. A sample of $36$ boxes is used to test $H_0:\ \mu=50$ against $H_1:\ \mu>50$ at the $5\%$ significance level. You may use $z=1.645$ as the value with $5\%$ of the standard normal distribution above it. (a) Find the standard deviation of the sample mean $\bar X$. [1] (b) Find the critical value of $\bar x$ and state the critical region. [3] (c) The sample mean is $\bar x=51.5$. State the conclusion. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{6}{\sqrt{36}}=1$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\bar x>50+1.645\times1$ [M1][A1]; critical region $\bar x>51.645$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $51.5<51.645$ is not in the critical region [M1]; do not reject $H_0$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The critical region for a one-tailed test is $\bar x>\mu_0+z\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}$.

subtopic: One-sample t-test: p-value and critical sample mean, tablet battery
statement: A manufacturer states that the battery of its tablet lasts $60$ hours on average. A reviewer believes the true mean is higher. She tests $15$ tablets chosen at random. The battery lives are assumed normally distributed, with sample mean $62.9$ hours and unbiased standard deviation estimate $s=5.2$ hours. (a) Find the estimated standard error of the sample mean. [1] (b) State hypotheses for the reviewer's test. [1] (c) Find the value of the test statistic and the $p$-value. [3] (d) State the conclusion at the $5\%$ significance level. [2] (e) Find the least value of the sample mean, correct to $2$ decimal places, that would lead to the rejection of $\mathrm{H}_0$ at the $5\%$ level, assuming the sample standard deviation is again $5.2$ hours. [3] (f) A colleague suggests treating $5.2$ as the known population standard deviation and using a $z$-test. State the corresponding critical sample mean and explain why it is smaller than your answer to part (e). [2]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{5.2}{\sqrt{15}}=1.34$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\mathrm{H}_0:\mu=60$, $\mathrm{H}_1:\mu>60$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $t=\dfrac{62.9-60}{1.3426}=2.16$ [M1] [A1] $p=0.0243$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $0.0243<0.05$ [R1] Reject $\mathrm{H}_0$: sufficient evidence that the mean battery life exceeds $60$ hours [A1] [2 marks] (e) Critical $t$ with $14$ degrees of freedom and upper tail $0.05$: $1.761$ [M1] $\bar x=60+1.761\times1.3426$ [M1] $\bar x\ge62.36$ [A1] [3 marks] (f) $60+1.645\times1.3426=62.21$ [A1] The $t$-distribution has heavier tails than the normal distribution (to allow for estimating $\sigma$), so the $t$ critical value is larger and a bigger sample mean is needed [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Use the inverse $t$ function on your GDC with $n-1$ degrees of freedom to find a critical value, then convert it back to a sample mean using the standard error. With small samples, the $t$ critical value is noticeably larger than the $z$ critical value.

subtopic: Chi-squared test of independence
statement: A school asks $80$ Year 12 students and $80$ Year 13 students for their main revision method: online resources, textbook or a mixture of both. The results are in this contingency table. $$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}\text{ } & \text{Online} & \text{Textbook} & \text{Mixture}\\\hline\text{Year 12} & 34 & 22 & 24\\\text{Year 13} & 20 & 38 & 22\end{array}$$ A $\chi^{2}$ test of independence is carried out at the $5\%$ significance level. (a) State the null and alternative hypotheses. [1] (b) Find the number of degrees of freedom and the expected frequency for Year 12 students who prefer a textbook. [3] (c) Use your GDC to find the $\chi^{2}$ statistic and the $p$-value, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (d) State the conclusion in context, with a reason. [2]
markscheme: (a) $H_0$: revision method is independent of year group; $H_1$: revision method is not independent of year group [A1] [1 mark] (b) $df=(2-1)(3-1)=2$ [A1]; $\dfrac{80\times60}{160}$ [M1]; $30$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\chi^{2}=7.98$ [A1]; $p=0.0185$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $0.0185<0.05$ so reject $H_0$ [A1]; there is evidence that revision method depends on year group [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Expected frequency is row total times column total divided by the grand total.

subtopic: Paired t-test on running times
statement: Eight runners complete a $5$ km run before and after a training program. Their times in minutes are given as pairs (before, after): $(34,31)$, $(41,38)$, $(29,30)$, $(38,33)$, $(45,41)$, $(36,32)$, $(40,37)$, $(33,31)$. Assume the differences are normally distributed. Test at the $5\%$ level whether the program reduces mean running time. (a) State the hypotheses in terms of the mean difference $\mu_d$ (before minus after). [1] (b) Find the mean and standard deviation $s_{n-1}$ of the differences, and the $p$-value of the paired $t$-test. [4] (c) State the conclusion in context. [2]
markscheme: (a) $H_0:\ \mu_d=0$, $H_1:\ \mu_d>0$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) differences $3,3,-1,5,4,4,3,2$ [A1]; $\bar d=2.875$ [A1]; $s_{n-1}=1.81$ [A1]; $p=0.00140$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) $p<0.05$ so reject $H_0$ [A1]; there is evidence the program reduces the mean time [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A paired test works with the differences, so it is a one-sample $t$-test on the differences.

subtopic: One-sample t-test, one-tailed
statement: A machine is set to fill bottles with $50.0$ cl of juice. An inspector suspects that the machine underfills. The volumes, in cl, of a random sample of $10$ bottles are: $48.2,\ 51.5,\ 49.8,\ 47.9,\ 50.6,\ 46.8,\ 49.1,\ 48.5,\ 50.2,\ 47.4$. (a) Find the sample mean and the unbiased estimate of the population standard deviation. [2] (b) State suitable null and alternative hypotheses. [1] (c) Perform a $t$-test and find the $p$-value. [2] (d) Using a $5\%$ significance level, state the conclusion of the test in context. [2] (e) State one assumption needed for the test to be valid. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\bar x=49.0$ [A1] $s_{n-1}=1.51$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\mathrm{H}_0:\mu=50$, $\mathrm{H}_1:\mu<50$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) One-sample $t$-test with $9$ degrees of freedom, $t=-2.10$ [M1] $p=0.0325$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $0.0325<0.05$ [R1] Reject $\mathrm{H}_0$: there is sufficient evidence at the $5\%$ level that the machine underfills (mean volume is less than $50$ cl) [A1] [2 marks] (e) The volumes are (approximately) normally distributed [A1] [1 mark]
tips: The alternative hypothesis is one-tailed here because the inspector suspects underfilling, not just a difference. Always finish with a conclusion in the context of the question.

subtopic: One-tailed z-test with known standard deviation
statement: A machine fills bags of flour. The mass of a bag is normally distributed with mean $250$ g and known standard deviation $6$ g. After servicing, the operator suspects the mean mass has decreased. A random sample of $36$ bags has mean mass $248.2$ g. (a) State suitable hypotheses. [2] (b) Calculate the test statistic $z$. [2] (c) The critical value of $z$ for a one-tailed test at the $5\%$ level is $-1.645$. State the conclusion. [2] (d) Find the critical region for the sample mean $\bar X$. [2] (e) Explain what a Type I error would mean in this context. [1]
markscheme: (a) $H_0:\mu=250$ [A1]; $H_1:\mu<250$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $z=\dfrac{\bar x-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n}=\dfrac{248.2-250}{6/\sqrt{36}}$ [M1] $=-1.80$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Reject $H_0$ since $-1.80<-1.645$ [A1]; there is evidence that the mean has decreased [R1] [2 marks] (d) $\bar X<250-1.645\times\dfrac{6}{\sqrt{36}}$ [M1] $=248.355$ so $\bar X<248.355$ [A1] [2 marks] (e) Concluding that the mean has decreased when it has not [R1] [1 mark]
tips: The standard error of the sample mean is $\sigma/\sqrt n$; the critical value for a lower-tail test is negative.

subtopic: Binomial test for a proportion
statement: A seed supplier claims that $85\%$ of its tomato seeds germinate. A gardener suspects the germination rate is lower. She plants $40$ seeds and $29$ of them germinate. Let $X$ be the number of seeds out of $40$ that germinate, and let $p$ be the true probability that a seed germinates. (a) State suitable null and alternative hypotheses for a test of the supplier's claim. [1] (b) Find the $p$-value for the test. [2] (c) State the conclusion of the test at the $5\%$ significance level, giving a reason. [2] (d) Find the critical region for this test at the $5\%$ significance level. [2]
markscheme: (a) $H_0: p=0.85$, $H_1: p<0.85$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $X\sim B(40,\,0.85)$ under $H_0$; $p$-value $=P(X\le29)$ [M1] $=0.0299$ ($0.0299208\ldots$) [A1] [2 marks] (c) $0.0299<0.05$ [R1] reject $H_0$: there is sufficient evidence that the germination rate is lower than $85\%$ [A1] Note: do not award [A1] without [R1] [2 marks] (d) $P(X\le29)=0.0299<0.05$ and $P(X\le30)=0.0672>0.05$ [M1] critical region $X\le29$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: For a one-tailed 'lower' test the p-value is P(X ≤ observed), not P(X = observed). To find the critical region, list cumulative probabilities until they first exceed the significance level.

subtopic: Chi-squared test for independence with a contingency table
statement: Students at two schools, P and Q, were asked how they usually travel to school. The results are given in the table. $$\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|}\hline &\text{Walk}&\text{Bus}&\text{Car}\\\hline \text{School P}&30&45&25\\\hline \text{School Q}&50&40&30\\\hline\end{array}$$ A $\chi^2$ test for independence is carried out at the $5\%$ significance level. (a) State the null hypothesis. [1] (b) Show that the expected number of School P students who travel by bus is $38.6$, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (c) Write down the number of degrees of freedom. [1] (d) Find the $\chi^2$ statistic and the $p$-value. [3] (e) State the conclusion of the test. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\mathrm{H}_0$: the method of travel is independent of the school [A1] [1 mark] (b) Row total $=100$, column total $=85$, grand total $=220$ [M1] $E=\dfrac{100\times85}{220}=38.6$ [A1][AG] [2 marks] (c) $(2-1)(3-1)=2$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) $\chi^2=\sum\dfrac{(O-E)^2}{E}$ [M1] $\chi^2=3.96$ [A1] $p=0.138$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) $0.138>0.05$, so do not reject $\mathrm{H}_0$; there is insufficient evidence that travel method depends on school [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Expected frequency is row total times column total divided by grand total. Degrees of freedom for an $r\times c$ table are $(r-1)(c-1)$.

subtopic: Chi-squared independence, age group and transport mode
statement: A city survey asks $300$ residents about their age group and their main mode of transport. The observed frequencies are: young (under $30$): bus $42$, bicycle $31$, car $17$; middle-aged: bus $38$, bicycle $44$, car $28$; older (over $60$): bus $20$, bicycle $35$, car $45$. A $\chi^2$ test for independence is carried out at the $5\%$ significance level. (a) State the null and alternative hypotheses. [1] (b) Show that the expected frequency of older residents who travel mainly by car is $30$. [2] (c) State the number of degrees of freedom. [1] (d) Find the value of $\chi^2_{\mathrm{calc}}$ and the $p$-value. [3] (e) State the conclusion of the test. [2] (f) Identify the cell that contributes most to $\chi^2_{\mathrm{calc}}$ and describe what this suggests. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\mathrm{H}_0$: age group and transport mode are independent; $\mathrm{H}_1$: they are not independent (associated) [A1] [1 mark] (b) Older residents: $20+35+45=100$; car users: $17+28+45=90$ [M1] Expected $=\dfrac{100\times90}{300}=30$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $(3-1)(3-1)=4$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) Matrix $\chi^2$ test [M1] $\chi^2_{\mathrm{calc}}=22.7$ [A1] $p=0.000147$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) $0.000147<0.05$ [R1] Reject $\mathrm{H}_0$: there is sufficient evidence that transport mode depends on age group [A1] [2 marks] (f) Older residents who use a car: contribution $\dfrac{(45-30)^2}{30}=7.5$ [A1] Many more older residents travel mainly by car than expected if mode were independent of age [A1] [2 marks]
tips: On the GDC, enter the observed values as a matrix and the calculator returns both the statistic and the expected matrix. When commenting on a large contribution, compare observed with expected to say which direction the association goes.

subtopic: Testing a Poisson mean
statement: An insurer has found that the number of claims per week has a Poisson distribution with mean $2.4$. Over the next $12$ weeks, $38$ claims are received. Test at the $5\%$ level whether the weekly rate has increased. (a) State the hypotheses and the distribution of the total number of claims $Y$ in $12$ weeks under $H_0$. [2] (b) Calculate $P(Y\ge38)$, to three significant figures. [2] (c) State the conclusion, and find the smallest total number of claims in $12$ weeks that would lead to rejecting $H_0$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $H_0:\ \lambda=2.4$ per week, $H_1:\ \lambda>2.4$ [A1]; $Y\sim\mathrm{Po}(28.8)$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $1-P(Y\le37)$ [M1]; $0.0573$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $0.0573>0.05$, do not reject $H_0$ [A1]; $P(Y\ge39)=0.0403$ [M1]; reject for $Y\ge39$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Scale the weekly mean to the length of the period, then use the upper tail of the Poisson distribution.

subtopic: Chi-squared test of independence for a 2 by 2 table
statement: One hundred people were asked whether they prefer tea or coffee. The observed counts are given as (group, prefers tea, prefers coffee): Students: $30$ and $20$; Teachers: $15$ and $35$. A test of independence between group and drink is carried out at the $5\%$ level, with critical value $3.84$. (a) State the hypotheses and find the expected frequency for each of the four cells. [3] (b) Show that $\chi^{2}=\dfrac{100}{11}$. [3] (c) State the degrees of freedom and the conclusion. [2]
markscheme: (a) $H_0$: group and drink preference are independent; $H_1$: they are not [A1]; tea total $45$ and coffee total $55$ [A1]; expected: students $22.5$ and $27.5$, teachers $22.5$ and $27.5$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) each $(O-E)^{2}=7.5^{2}=56.25$ [A1]; $56.25\left(\dfrac{2}{22.5}+\dfrac{2}{27.5}\right)$ [M1]; $\dfrac{100}{11}$ [AG] [3 marks] (c) $(2-1)(2-1)=1$ [A1]; $9.09>3.84$ so reject $H_0$; group and drink preference are associated [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Expected frequency $=\dfrac{\text{row total}\times\text{column total}}{\text{grand total}}$.

subtopic: Goodness of fit to a Poisson model with combining cells
statement: The number of cars passing a checkpoint in each of $100$ one-minute intervals is recorded. $$\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline \text{Cars}&0&1&2&3&4&5&6\text{ or more}\\\hline \text{Frequency}&10&28&26&19&10&5&2\\\hline\end{array}$$ A $\chi^2$ goodness of fit test is used at the $5\%$ significance level to test whether the number of cars per minute follows a Poisson distribution with mean $2$. (a) State the null hypothesis. [1] (b) Find the expected frequency for $2$ cars, correct to 3 significant figures. [1] (c) The expected frequencies for $5$ cars and for $6$ or more cars are $3.61$ and $1.66$. Explain why these two categories must be combined, and write down the observed and expected frequencies of the combined category. [3] (d) Write down the number of degrees of freedom. [1] (e) Find the $\chi^2$ statistic and the $p$-value. [2] (f) State the conclusion of the test. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\mathrm{H}_0$: the number of cars per minute follows $\mathrm{Po}(2)$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $100\times P(X=2)=100\times\dfrac{e^{-2}2^2}{2!}=27.1$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) Expected frequencies below $5$ make the $\chi^2$ approximation unreliable [R1] Combined category is '$5$ or more' with observed frequency $5+2=7$ [A1] and expected frequency $3.61+1.66=5.27$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) There are $6$ categories after combining, so $\nu=6-1=5$ [A1] [1 mark] (e) $\chi^2=1.72$ [A1] $p=0.886$ [A1] [2 marks] (f) $0.886>0.05$, so do not reject $\mathrm{H}_0$; the Poisson model with mean $2$ is a reasonable fit [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Check every expected frequency before you run the test and combine neighboring categories if any is below $5$; the degrees of freedom are based on the number of categories after combining.

subtopic: Chi-squared tests
statement: A city transport department surveyed $250$ randomly selected commuters about their main mode of transport. The results are shown below. $$\begin{array}{l|ccc|c} & \text{Car} & \text{Bus} & \text{Bicycle} & \text{Total}\\\hline \text{Under }30 & 38 & 42 & 30 & 110\\ 30\text{ and over} & 72 & 44 & 24 & 140\\\hline \text{Total} & 110 & 86 & 54 & 250\end{array}$$ A $\chi^2$ test for independence is carried out at the $5\%$ significance level. (a) State the null and alternative hypotheses. [1] (b) Show that the expected frequency of commuters under $30$ who travel by car is $48.4$. [2] (c) Write down the number of degrees of freedom. [1] (d) Find the $\chi^2$ statistic and the $p$-value. [2] (e) State the conclusion of the test, giving a reason. [2] A previous city report claimed that commuters use car, bus and bicycle in the ratio $45\%:35\%:20\%$. (f) Using the column totals, carry out a $\chi^2$ goodness of fit test at the $5\%$ significance level to test this claim. State your hypotheses, the expected frequencies, the $p$-value and your conclusion. [5]
markscheme: (a) $H_0$: mode of transport is independent of age group; $H_1$: mode of transport is not independent of age group [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\dfrac{110\times110}{250}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{12100}{250}$ [A1] $=48.4$ [AG] [2 marks] (c) $(2-1)(3-1)=2$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) using GDC: $\chi^2_{calc}=7.73$ ($7.73363\ldots$) [A1] $p=0.0209$ ($0.0209248\ldots$) [A1] [2 marks] (e) $0.0209<0.05$ [R1] reject $H_0$: there is evidence that mode of transport depends on age group [A1] Note: do not award [A1] without [R1] [2 marks] (f) $H_0$: the proportions are $45\%,35\%,20\%$; $H_1$: the proportions are not as claimed [A1] expected frequencies $112.5,\ 87.5,\ 50$ [A1] using GDC with $2$ degrees of freedom [M1] $p=0.818$ ($\chi^2_{calc}=0.401$) [A1] $0.818>0.05$ so do not reject $H_0$: insufficient evidence to doubt the report's ratio [R1] [5 marks]
tips: Write hypotheses in context, using the words 'independent' or the claimed proportions. Always compare the p-value with the significance level explicitly before stating the conclusion.

subtopic: One-tailed binomial test and critical region
statement: Historically, $30\%$ of patients with a certain condition recover within a week. A new treatment is given to $25$ randomly chosen patients, and $13$ recover within a week. Let $p$ be the probability that a patient given the new treatment recovers within a week. A test at the $5\%$ significance level is carried out to see whether the treatment improves the recovery rate. (a) State the null and alternative hypotheses. [1] (b) Find the $p$-value of the test. [3] (c) State the conclusion of the test in context. [2] (d) Find the critical region for the test, and the actual significance level of the test. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\mathrm{H}_0:p=0.3$, $\mathrm{H}_1:p>0.3$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Under $\mathrm{H}_0$, $X\sim\mathrm{B}(25,0.3)$ [M1] $p$-value $=P(X\ge13)=1-P(X\le12)$ [M1] $=0.0175$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $0.0175<0.05$ [R1] Reject $\mathrm{H}_0$; there is sufficient evidence that the treatment improves the recovery rate [A1] [2 marks] (d) $P(X\ge12)=0.0442\le0.05$ but $P(X\ge11)=0.0978>0.05$ [M1] Critical region is $X\ge12$ [A1] Actual significance level $=0.0442$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: For an upper-tailed binomial test the $p$-value is $P(X\ge x_{\text{obs}})$, so use $1-P(X\le x_{\text{obs}}-1)$. The critical region contains the largest set of extreme values whose probability does not exceed the significance level.

subtopic: Poisson test for the rate of customer calls
statement: A help desk receives calls at an average rate of $12$ per hour. After a website improvement the manager wants to test whether the rate has decreased. In a random half hour period, $2$ calls are received. (a) State the hypotheses in terms of the mean number of events. [2] (b) State the distribution of the number of events $X$ over the observation period under $H_0$. [1] (c) Find the $p$-value for the observation of 2 events and state the conclusion at the $5\%$ level. [3] (d) Find the critical region for the test at the $5\%$ level and the actual probability of a Type I error. [3]
markscheme: (a) $H_0:\lambda=12$ per hour [A1]; $H_1:\lambda<12$ per hour [A1] [2 marks] (b) $X\sim\text{Po}(6)$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $P(X\leq2)=0.0620$ [M1][A1]; do not reject $H_0$ as $p>0.05$ [R1] [3 marks] (d) Critical region $X\leq1$ [A1][M1]; $P(\text{Type I})=0.0174$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Convert the rate to the observation period before testing; for a lower-tail test $p=P(X\leq\text{observed})$.

subtopic: One-sample t-test on battery life
statement: A manufacturer claims that the mean life of a battery is $48$ hours. A consumer group tests ten batteries to see whether the claim is too high. The sample values are: 44.2, 47.1, 45.8, 49.5, 43.9, 46.7, 48.3, 45.1, 44.8, 47.6. (a) State suitable null and alternative hypotheses, defining any symbols. [2] (b) Find the sample mean and the unbiased estimate of the population standard deviation. [2] (c) Perform a $t$-test, stating the degrees of freedom, the $p$-value and your conclusion at the $5\%$ significance level. State any assumption. [5] (d) Find a $95\%$ confidence interval for the population mean battery life. [2]
markscheme: (a) $H_0:\mu=48$ [A1]; $H_1:\mu<48$ [A1] where $\mu$ is the population mean [2 marks] (b) $\bar x=46.300$ [A1], $s_{n-1}=1.851$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $df=9$ [A1]; $t=-2.904$ [M1]; $p=0.009$ [A1]; reject $H_0$ since $p<0.05$ [R1]; the population is normally distributed [A1] [5 marks] (d) (44.976, 47.624) [M1][A1] [2 marks]
tips: Use the sample standard deviation $s_{n-1}$ (the unbiased estimate) in the $t$ statistic; for a one-tailed test the $p$-value comes from one tail only.

subtopic: Chi-squared goodness of fit by hand
statement: A genetics model predicts that the offspring of a certain cross of plants have four types of seed in the ratio $9:3:3:1$. In an experiment, $160$ offspring are observed with $84$, $36$, $28$ and $12$ plants of the four types respectively. A $\chi^2$ goodness of fit test is carried out at the $5\%$ significance level. (a) Find the expected frequencies under the model. [2] (b) Show that the value of the $\chi^2$ statistic is $\dfrac{32}{15}$. [3] (c) Write down the number of degrees of freedom. Given that the critical value at the $5\%$ level is $7.815$, state the conclusion of the test, giving a reason. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{9}{16}\times160=90$ [M1] Expected frequencies $90,\ 30,\ 30,\ 10$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\chi^2=\dfrac{(84-90)^2}{90}+\dfrac{(36-30)^2}{30}+\dfrac{(28-30)^2}{30}+\dfrac{(12-10)^2}{10}$ [M1] $=\dfrac25+\dfrac65+\dfrac2{15}+\dfrac25$ [A1] $=\dfrac{32}{15}$ [A1][AG] [3 marks] (c) $\nu=4-1=3$ [A1] $\dfrac{32}{15}=2.13<7.815$ [R1] Do not reject $\mathrm{H}_0$; the data are consistent with the $9:3:3:1$ ratio [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Use the ratio to split the total into expected counts: divide $160$ by $9+3+3+1=16$ first. Simplify each fraction before adding so the arithmetic stays manageable without a calculator.

subtopic: Stating hypotheses and reaching a conclusion
statement: A bakery claims that the mean mass of its loaves is $800$ g. An inspector suspects the mean mass is lower and tests a random sample of loaves, obtaining a $p$-value of $0.032$. (a) State the null and alternative hypotheses in terms of the population mean mass $\mu$. [2] (b) State the conclusion at the $5\%$ significance level, in context. [2] (c) State whether the conclusion changes at the $1\%$ level, and explain what a $p$-value of $0.032$ means. [2]
markscheme: (a) $H_0:\ \mu=800$ [A1]; $H_1:\ \mu<800$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $0.032<0.05$ so reject $H_0$ [M1]; there is sufficient evidence that the mean mass is less than $800$ g [A1] [2 marks] (c) $0.032>0.01$ so do not reject $H_0$ at $1\%$ [A1]; $p=0.032$ is the probability of results at least this extreme if $H_0$ is true [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Reject $H_0$ when the $p$-value is smaller than the significance level.

subtopic: Type I and Type II errors for a binomial test
statement: A coin is tossed $10$ times to test $H_0:\ p=0.5$ against $H_1:\ p\ne0.5$, where $p$ is the probability of heads. The null hypothesis is rejected if the number of heads $X$ satisfies $X\le1$ or $X\ge9$. (a) Describe a Type I error in this context. [1] (b) Find the probability of a Type I error as an exact fraction. [3] (c) Describe a Type II error and explain why it is more likely when the true value of $p$ is $0.55$ than when it is $0.9$. [2]
markscheme: (a) Concluding the coin is biased when it is actually fair [A1] [1 mark] (b) $P(X\le1)=\dfrac{1+10}{1024}$ [A1]; $P(X\ge9)=\dfrac{11}{1024}$ [A1]; total $\dfrac{22}{1024}=\dfrac{11}{512}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Failing to reject $H_0$ when the coin is actually biased [A1]; a coin with $p=0.55$ gives results similar to a fair coin, so it rarely falls in the critical region [R1] [2 marks]
tips: A Type I error rejects a true null hypothesis; a Type II error accepts a false one.

subtopic: Chi-squared test of independence with a 2 by 3 table
statement: A school survey asks $200$ students how they usually travel to school (walk, cycle or bus) and records whether each student is male or female. The results are: male: walk $36$, cycle $24$, bus $40$; female: walk $24$, cycle $36$, bus $40$. A chi-squared test for independence is carried out at the $5\%$ significance level. (a) State the null hypothesis. [1] (b) Show that the expected number of male students who cycle is $30$ under the null hypothesis. [2] (c) State the number of degrees of freedom. [1] (d) Given that the other expected frequencies are $30,\ 40,\ 30,\ 30,\ 40$ for male walk, male bus, female walk, female cycle and female bus respectively, show that $\chi^2_{\mathrm{calc}}=4.8$. [3] (e) The critical value is $5.991$. State the conclusion of the test, giving a reason. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\mathrm{H}_0$: the method of travel is independent of gender [A1] [1 mark] (b) Cyclists: $24+36=60$; males: $36+24+40=100$ [M1] Expected $=\dfrac{100\times60}{200}=30$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $(2-1)(3-1)=2$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) Differences between observed and expected are $\pm6$ for walk and cycle, and $0$ for bus [M1] $\chi^2=\dfrac{36}{30}\times4+0$ [M1] $=4.8$ [AG] [3 marks] (e) $4.8<5.991$ [R1] Do not reject $\mathrm{H}_0$: insufficient evidence that the method of travel depends on gender [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Expected frequency is (row total times column total) divided by the grand total, and the degrees of freedom are (rows minus 1)(columns minus 1). Cells whose observed and expected values agree contribute nothing to the statistic.

subtopic: Two-sample t-test comparing battery lives
statement: A company compares the lives, in minutes, of batteries from two brands. Random samples gave the following. Brand A ($9$ batteries): $312$, $298$, $325$, $301$, $318$, $290$, $309$, $322$, $305$. Brand B ($10$ batteries): $289$, $301$, $284$, $296$, $278$, $292$, $299$, $287$, $281$, $294$. Assume both populations are normally distributed with equal variances. Use a significance level of $5\%$. (a) State suitable hypotheses to test whether Brand A has a longer mean battery life than Brand B. [2] (b) Find the sample mean and the unbiased estimate of the standard deviation for each brand, correct to 3 significant figures. [3] (c) Use your GDC to carry out a pooled two-sample $t$-test and find the $t$-statistic, the number of degrees of freedom and the $p$-value. [3] (d) State the conclusion of the test, in context. [2] (e) Find a $95\%$ confidence interval for $\mu_A-\mu_B$, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (f) State two assumptions made in this test, and explain why the confidence interval supports the conclusion. [2]
markscheme: (a) $H_0$: $\mu_A=\mu_B$ [A1]; $H_1$: $\mu_A>\mu_B$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Brand A: $\bar x=309$, $s=11.6$ [A1]; Brand B: $\bar y=290$ [A1]; $s=7.67$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) two-sample pooled $t$-test [M1]; $t=4.21$ and $df=17$ [A1]; $p=0.000296$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $p<0.05$ so reject $H_0$ [A1]; there is sufficient evidence that Brand A batteries last longer on average [A1] [2 marks] (e) pooled two-sample interval on the GDC [M1]; $(9.37, 28.2)$ minutes [A1] [2 marks] (f) normal populations and equal variances (and independent random samples) [A1]; the interval contains only positive values, so $\mu_A>\mu_B$ [R1] [2 marks]
tips: A pooled test assumes equal variances. For a one-sided test, use the one-tailed $p$-value.

subtopic: t-test for the mean mass of cereal boxes
statement: A factory is supposed to fill cereal boxes with a mean mass of $500$ g. An inspector weighs nine randomly chosen boxes (in grams) and wishes to test whether the mean differs from $500$ g. The sample values are: 497.5, 502.1, 495.3, 499.8, 496.4, 503.2, 498.1, 494.9, 500.6. (a) State suitable null and alternative hypotheses, defining any symbols. [2] (b) Find the sample mean and the unbiased estimate of the population standard deviation. [2] (c) Perform a $t$-test, stating the degrees of freedom, the $p$-value and your conclusion at the $5\%$ significance level. State any assumption. [5] (d) Find a $95\%$ confidence interval for the population mean mass in grams. [2]
markscheme: (a) $H_0:\mu=500$ [A1]; $H_1:\mu\neq500$ [A1] where $\mu$ is the population mean [2 marks] (b) $\bar x=498.656$ [A1], $s_{n-1}=2.952$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $df=8$ [A1]; $t=-1.366$ [M1]; $p=0.209$ [A1]; do not reject $H_0$ since $p>0.05$ [R1]; the population is normally distributed [A1] [5 marks] (d) (496.387, 500.924) [M1][A1] [2 marks]
tips: For a two-sided test double the one-tail probability, or compare $|t|$ with the critical value from both tails.

subtopic: One-tailed binomial test for a proportion
statement: A store claims that $30\%$ of its customers buy an advertised product. After a new advertisement, a random sample of $40$ customers shows that $18$ bought it. Test at the $5\%$ level whether the proportion $p$ has increased. (a) State the hypotheses and the distribution of the number of buyers $X$ under $H_0$. [2] (b) Calculate the $p$-value, to three significant figures. [2] (c) State the conclusion in context, and explain what a Type I error would mean here. [3]
markscheme: (a) $H_0:\ p=0.3$, $H_1:\ p>0.3$ [A1]; $X\sim B(40,\,0.3)$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $P(X\ge18)=1-P(X\le17)$ [M1]; $0.0320$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $0.0320<0.05$ so reject $H_0$ [A1]; evidence that the proportion has increased [A1]; concluding the advertisement worked when it actually had no effect [R1] [3 marks]
tips: The $p$-value is the probability, under $H_0$, of a result at least as extreme as the one observed.

subtopic: Testing a fair die without a calculator
statement: A die is rolled $120$ times. The frequencies of the scores $1$ to $6$ are recorded. $$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\text{Category} & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6 \\ \hline \text{Observed} & 16 & 25 & 18 & 22 & 14 & 25 \end{array}$$ (a) State the null and alternative hypotheses. [2] (b) Find the expected frequencies. [2] (c) Calculate the $\chi^2$ test statistic. [3] (d) The critical value of $\chi^2$ at the $5\%$ level for $5$ degrees of freedom is $11.07$. State the conclusion. [2]
markscheme: (a) $H_0$: the data follow the stated distribution [A1]; $H_1$: they do not [A1] [2 marks] (b) Expected $=n\times p$: 20, 20, 20, 20, 20, 20 [M1][A1] [2 marks] (c) $\chi^2=\sum\dfrac{(O-E)^2}{E}$ [M1]; $\dfrac{(16-20)^2}{20} + \dfrac{(25-20)^2}{20} + \dfrac{(18-20)^2}{20} + \dfrac{(22-20)^2}{20} + \dfrac{(14-20)^2}{20} + \dfrac{(25-20)^2}{20}$ [A1] $=5.5$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) Do not reject $H_0$ since $5.5<11.07$ [A1]; the data are consistent with the distribution [R1] [2 marks]
tips: The degrees of freedom are the number of categories minus one, because the total is fixed.

subtopic: Two-tailed binomial test: critical regions and power, website clicks
statement: The probability that a visitor to a website clicks on an advertisement has been $0.4$. After the page layout is changed, the web manager wants to test, at the $5\%$ significance level, whether the probability $p$ has changed in either direction. She will observe $30$ independent visitors and let $X$ be the number who click. Each tail of the critical region should have probability as close as possible to, but not more than, $2.5\%$. (a) State the null and alternative hypotheses. [1] (b) Find the lower and upper parts of the critical region, showing the probabilities that justify your choice. [6] (c) State the critical region and the actual significance level of the test. [2] (d) In the sample, $17$ visitors click. State the conclusion of the test. [2] (e) Find the power of the test if the true value of $p$ is $0.6$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\mathrm{H}_0:p=0.4$, $\mathrm{H}_1:p\ne0.4$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Under $\mathrm{H}_0$, $X\sim\mathrm{B}(30,0.4)$ [M1] Lower tail: $P(X\le6)=0.0172\le0.025$ [A1] and $P(X\le7)=0.0435>0.025$ [A1] Upper tail: $P(X\ge18)=0.0212\le0.025$ [A1] and $P(X\ge17)=0.0481>0.025$ [A1] Lower part: $X\le6$; upper part: $X\ge18$ [A1] [6 marks] (c) Critical region: $X\le6$ or $X\ge18$ [A1] Actual significance level $=0.0172+0.0212=0.0384$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $17$ is not in the critical region [R1] Do not reject $\mathrm{H}_0$: insufficient evidence that the click probability has changed [A1] [2 marks] (e) Power $=P(X\le6)+P(X\ge18)$ with $X\sim\mathrm{B}(30,0.6)$ [M1] $=0.0000092+0.5785$ [M1] $=0.578$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: For a two-tailed test with a discrete distribution, find each tail separately and take the largest tail not exceeding half the significance level. The actual significance level is the sum of the two tail probabilities, which is less than $5\%$.

subtopic: One-sample t-test with confidence interval, nitrate level
statement: A regulator states that the mean nitrate concentration in a river should be $12.0$ mg per litre. An environmental scientist takes eight independent water samples and measures the nitrate concentration, in mg per litre: $12.4,\ 11.8,\ 13.1,\ 12.9,\ 11.5,\ 12.2,\ 13.4,\ 12.7$. Assume that concentrations are normally distributed. (a) Find the sample mean and the unbiased estimate of the population standard deviation. [2] (b) State suitable hypotheses to test whether the mean concentration differs from $12.0$ mg per litre. [1] (c) Find the $p$-value for a $t$-test. [2] (d) State the conclusion at the $5\%$ significance level. [2] (e) Find a $95\%$ confidence interval for the mean concentration and explain how it is consistent with your answer to part (d). [2]
markscheme: (a) $\bar x=12.5$ [A1] $s_{n-1}=0.650$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\mathrm{H}_0:\mu=12.0$, $\mathrm{H}_1:\mu\ne12.0$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) Two-tailed one-sample $t$-test with $7$ degrees of freedom, $t=2.17$ [M1] $p=0.0661$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $0.0661>0.05$ [R1] Do not reject $\mathrm{H}_0$: insufficient evidence that the mean nitrate concentration differs from $12.0$ mg per litre [A1] [2 marks] (e) $(11.96,\ 13.04)$ [A1] The interval contains $12.0$, consistent with not rejecting $\mathrm{H}_0$ at the $5\%$ level [R1] [2 marks]
tips: A two-sided $5\%$ test and a $95\%$ confidence interval always agree about whether the hypothesized mean is plausible. Use the $t$ option on your GDC because the population standard deviation is estimated from the sample.

subtopic: Chi-squared goodness of fit: testing a die
statement: A die is rolled $130$ times with the results shown. $$\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline \text{Score}&1&2&3&4&5&6\\\hline \text{Frequency}&18&25&14&22&31&20\\\hline\end{array}$$ A $\chi^2$ goodness of fit test at the $5\%$ significance level is used to test whether the die is fair. (a) State the null hypothesis. [1] (b) Find the expected frequency for each score, correct to 3 significant figures. [1] (c) Find the value of the $\chi^2$ statistic. [2] (d) Write down the number of degrees of freedom and the $p$-value. [2] (e) State the conclusion of the test. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\mathrm{H}_0$: the die is fair (scores are uniformly distributed) [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\dfrac{130}{6}=21.7$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $\chi^2=\sum\dfrac{(O-E)^2}{E}$ [M1] $\chi^2=8.00$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $\nu=5$ [A1] $p=0.156$ [A1] [2 marks] (e) $0.156>0.05$ (equivalently $8.00<11.07$), so do not reject $\mathrm{H}_0$; there is insufficient evidence that the die is unfair [A1] [1 mark]
tips: For a goodness of fit test with no estimated parameters, degrees of freedom are the number of categories minus one. Not rejecting $\mathrm{H}_0$ does not prove the die is fair.

subtopic: One-sample t-test on battery life
statement: A manufacturer claims the mean life of its batteries is $23$ hours. The lives of a random sample of nine batteries are: 22.1, 23.4, 21.8, 24.0, 22.7, 21.5, 23.1, 22.2, 22.9 hours. Assume the lives are normally distributed. Test at the $5\%$ significance level whether the mean life is less than claimed. (a) State the hypotheses and find the sample mean and the unbiased estimate of the standard deviation. [3] (b) Use your GDC to find the $t$-statistic and the $p$-value, to three significant figures. [3] (c) State the conclusion in context. [2]
markscheme: (a) $H_0:\ \mu=23$, $H_1:\ \mu<23$ [A1]; $\bar x=22.6$ [A1]; $s_{n-1}=0.806$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) one-sample $t$-test with $df=8$ [M1]; $t=-1.36$ [A1]; $p=0.105$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $0.105>0.05$ so do not reject $H_0$ [A1]; there is not enough evidence that the mean battery life is below $23$ hours [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A one-tailed test with $H_1:\mu<\mu_0$ gives a $p$-value from the lower tail of the $t$-distribution.

subtopic: Integration by parts
statement: (a) Find $\displaystyle\int x e^{2 x}\,dx$. [4] (b) Hence find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}x e^{2 x}\,dx$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $u=x$, $\dfrac{dv}{dx}=\mathrm e^{2x}$ so $v=\dfrac12\mathrm e^{2x}$ [M1][A1] $\int x\mathrm e^{2x}dx=\dfrac x2\mathrm e^{2x}-\dfrac12\int\mathrm e^{2x}dx$ [M1] $=\dfrac{x}{2}\mathrm e^{2x}-\dfrac14\mathrm e^{2x}+c$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $\left[\dfrac{\mathrm e^{2x}(2x-1)}4\right]_0^1=\dfrac{\mathrm e^2}4+\dfrac14$ [M1] value $\frac{1}{4} + \frac{e^{2}}{4}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Choose $u$ as the factor that simplifies on differentiation ($x$) and $dv$ as the factor that integrates easily.

subtopic: Area of a region bounded by a curve, a line and the x-axis
statement: Let $R$ be the region enclosed by the curve $y=\ln x$, the line $y=2-x$ and the $x$-axis. (a) Find the coordinates of the point $A$ where the curve $y=\ln x$ meets the line $y=2-x$. [2] (b) Find the area of $R$. [4] (c) Write down an integral with respect to $y$ that gives the area of $R$. [2]
markscheme: (a) Solving $\ln x=2-x$ using a GDC [M1] $A=(1.56,\ 0.443)$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $R$ lies under the curve from $x=1$ to $x=a$, where $a=1.557$ is the $x$-coordinate of $A$, and under the line from $x=a$ to $x=2$ [A1] Area $=\displaystyle\int_1^{1.557}\ln x\,dx+\int_{1.557}^{2}(2-x)\,dx$ [M1] $=0.1324+0.0981$ [A1] $=0.231$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) $x$ ranges from $e^y$ (the curve) to $2-y$ (the line) for $0\le y\le0.443$ [A1] Area $=\displaystyle\int_0^{0.443}\left(2-y-e^y\right)dy$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Sketch the curve and line first: the $x$-axis forms the lower boundary, and the upper boundary changes at the intersection point. Store the intersection value in your GDC so it is used without rounding error.

subtopic: Volume of revolution evaluated with a calculator
statement: The region between the curve $y=1+\sin x$, the $x$-axis and the lines $x=0$ and $x=\pi$ is rotated through $2\pi$ about the $x$-axis. (a) Write down an integral for the volume of the solid. [2] (b) Find the volume, and verify it exactly by expanding the square. [4]
markscheme: (a) $V=\pi\displaystyle\int_0^\pi(1+\sin x)^2dx$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (b) $V=27.37$ [A1] expand: $1+2\sin x+\sin^2x$ with $\sin^2x=\dfrac{1-\cos2x}2$ [M1] integral $=\pi+4+\dfrac\pi2$ [A1] $V=\pi\left(\dfrac{3\pi}2+4\right)=27.37$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Square the function before integrating and use $\sin^2x=\frac12(1-\cos2x)$ for an exact evaluation.

subtopic: Finding a function from its derivative
statement: (a) The gradient of a curve is $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=6x^2-4x+1$ and the curve passes through $(1,5)$. Find $y$ in terms of $x$. [4] (b) A different curve has $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac3{2x+1}$ for $x>-\dfrac12$ and passes through $(0,2)$. Find $y$. [3]
tips: Integrate to get a constant of integration, then use the given point to find it.

subtopic: Integrating an improper rational function by division
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{x^2+1}{x+1}$. (a) Show that $f(x)=x-1+\dfrac2{x+1}$. [2] (b) Hence find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_0^1f(x)\,dx$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $x^2+1=(x+1)(x-1)+2$ [M1] divide by $x+1$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\left[\dfrac{x^2}2-x+2\ln(x+1)\right]_0^1$ [M1][A1] $=2\ln2-\dfrac12$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: When the degree of the numerator is at least the degree of the denominator, divide first.

subtopic: Area under a curve found analytically and checked with a calculator
statement: Let $f(x)=x\mathrm e^{-x/2}$ for $x\ge0$. (a) Use integration by parts to show that $\displaystyle\int_0^6f(x)\,dx=4-16\mathrm e^{-3}$. [5] (b) Verify the value with your calculator. [1]
markscheme: (a) $u=x$, $v=-2\mathrm e^{-x/2}$ [M1][A1] $\int f=-2x\mathrm e^{-x/2}+2\int\mathrm e^{-x/2}dx$ [M1] $=-2x\mathrm e^{-x/2}-4\mathrm e^{-x/2}$ [A1] limits: $(-12\mathrm e^{-3}-4\mathrm e^{-3})-(-4)=4-16\mathrm e^{-3}$ [A1] [5 marks] (b) $4-16\mathrm e^{-3}=3.2034$ agrees with numerical integration $3.2034$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Take $u=x$ so the derivative is constant. Numerical integration on the calculator is a good independent check.

subtopic: Circle, ellipse, sphere and ellipsoid by integration
statement: The curve $x^2+y^2=1$ with $y\ge0$ is the upper unit semicircle. (a) Use the substitution $x=\sin\theta$ to show that $\displaystyle\int_0^1\sqrt{1-x^2}\,dx=\dfrac\pi4$. [4] (b) Hence show that the ellipse $\dfrac{x^2}{a^2}+\dfrac{y^2}{b^2}=1$ has area $\pi ab$. [3] (c) The upper semicircle of radius $r$ is rotated through $360^\circ$ about the $x$-axis. Show that the volume of the sphere is $\dfrac43\pi r^3$. [3] (d) The upper half of the ellipse $\dfrac{x^2}{a^2}+\dfrac{y^2}{b^2}=1$ is rotated through $360^\circ$ about the $x$-axis. Find the volume of the ellipsoid. [3] (e) Verify that the ellipsoid volume reduces to the sphere volume when $a=b=r$, and find the ratio of the volume of the ellipsoid to that of a sphere of radius $a$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $dx=\cos\theta\,d\theta$, limits $0$ to $\dfrac\pi2$ [M1][A1] $\sqrt{1-\sin^2\theta}=\cos\theta$ so the integral is $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos^2\theta\,d\theta$ [A1] $=\left[\dfrac\theta2+\dfrac{\sin2\theta}4\right]_0^{\pi/2}=\dfrac\pi4$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) area $=4\displaystyle\int_0^ab\sqrt{1-\dfrac{x^2}{a^2}}\,dx$ [M1] let $x=au$: $4ab\displaystyle\int_0^1\sqrt{1-u^2}\,du$ [A1] $=4ab\times\dfrac\pi4=\pi ab$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $V=\pi\displaystyle\int_{-r}^r\left(r^2-x^2\right)dx$ [M1] $=\pi\left[r^2x-\dfrac{x^3}3\right]_{-r}^r$ [A1] $=\pi\left(\dfrac{4r^3}3\right)=\dfrac43\pi r^3$ [AG] [A1] [3 marks] (d) $V=\pi\displaystyle\int_{-a}^ab^2\left(1-\dfrac{x^2}{a^2}\right)dx$ [M1] $=\pi b^2\left[x-\dfrac{x^3}{3a^2}\right]_{-a}^a$ [A1] $=\dfrac43\pi ab^2$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) $\dfrac43\pi r\times r^2=\dfrac43\pi r^3$ [A1] ratio $=\dfrac{\frac43\pi ab^2}{\frac43\pi a^3}=\dfrac{b^2}{a^2}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Use $x=\sin\theta$ for $\sqrt{1-x^2}$, and scale the ellipse to the unit circle by writing $x=au$.

subtopic: Integration by substitution
statement: (a) Use the substitution $u=1+e^{2x}$ to find $\displaystyle\int \frac{e^{2 x}}{e^{2 x} + 1}\,dx$. [4] (b) Hence evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\ln{\left(2 \right)}}\frac{e^{2 x}}{e^{2 x} + 1}\,dx$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $u=1+\mathrm e^{2x}$, $du=2\mathrm e^{2x}dx$ [M1] $\int\dfrac{\mathrm e^{2x}}{1+\mathrm e^{2x}}dx=\dfrac12\int\dfrac{du}u$ [A1] $=\dfrac12\ln u$ [A1] $=\dfrac12\ln\left(1+\mathrm e^{2x}\right)+c$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $\dfrac12\ln\left(1+4\right)-\dfrac12\ln2$ [M1][A1] so the value is $-\frac{\ln{\left(2 \right)}}{2} + \frac{\ln{\left(5 \right)}}{2}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The numerator is half the derivative of the denominator, so the integral is a logarithm.

subtopic: Volume of revolution about the x-axis
statement: The region bounded by the curve $y=x^2$, the $x$-axis and the line $x=2$ is rotated through $360^\circ$ about the $x$-axis. (a) Write down an integral for the volume of the solid generated. [2] (b) Find the exact volume. [2]
markscheme: (a) $V=\pi\displaystyle\int_0^2y^2\,dx$ [M1] $=\pi\displaystyle\int_0^2x^4\,dx$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\pi\left[\dfrac{x^5}5\right]_0^2$ [M1] $=\frac{32 \pi}{5}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Volume about the $x$-axis is $\pi\int y^2\,dx$.

subtopic: Root mean square value of a sinusoidal quantity
statement: The root mean square (RMS) value of a function $f$ over $[0,T]$ is $\sqrt{\dfrac1T\displaystyle\int_0^Tf(t)^2\,dt}$. Let $f(t)=A\sin\omega t$ with $A,\omega>0$, and $T=\dfrac{2\pi}\omega$. (a) Use $\cos2\theta=1-2\sin^2\theta$ to show that $\displaystyle\int_0^T\sin^2\omega t\,dt=\dfrac T2$. [3] (b) Hence show that the RMS value of $f$ is $\dfrac A{\sqrt2}$. [2] (c) A mains voltage has an RMS value of $230$ V. Find its peak value to three significant figures. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\sin^2\omega t=\dfrac{1-\cos2\omega t}2$ [M1] $\left[\dfrac t2-\dfrac{\sin2\omega t}{4\omega}\right]_0^T$ [A1] $\sin(2\omega T)=\sin4\pi=0$ so the value is $\dfrac T2$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\sqrt{\dfrac1T\times A^2\times\dfrac T2}$ [M1] $=\dfrac A{\sqrt2}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $A=230\sqrt2=325$ V [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Squaring the function and averaging over a full period gives half of the square of the amplitude.

subtopic: Integration using partial fractions
statement: (a) Express $\dfrac{4}{x^{2} - 4}$ in partial fractions. [3] (b) Hence find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_{3}^{4}\frac{4}{x^{2} - 4}\,dx$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac4{x^2-4}=\dfrac A{x-2}+\dfrac B{x+2}$ [M1] $4=A(x+2)+B(x-2)$ [A1] $A=1$, $B=-1$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\left[\ln(x-2)-\ln(x+2)\right]_3^4=\ln\dfrac13-\ln\dfrac15$ [M1][A1] value $\ln{\left(\frac{5}{3} \right)}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Factorize the denominator as a difference of squares before splitting.

subtopic: Completing the square before integrating
statement: (a) Write $x^2+2x+5$ in the form $(x+a)^2+b$. [1] (b) Hence find $\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1}\dfrac1{x^2+2x+5}\,dx$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $(x+1)^2+4$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\int\dfrac{dx}{(x+1)^2+4}$ [M1] $=\dfrac12\arctan\dfrac{x+1}2$ [A1] $\dfrac12\left(\arctan1-\arctan0\right)$ [M1] $=\dfrac\pi8$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: A quadratic with no real roots in the denominator is handled by completing the square, giving an arctangent.

subtopic: Orthogonality of sine functions and the root mean square of a sum
statement: Let $m$ and $n$ be positive integers. (a) Use the compound angle formulae to show that $2\sin A\sin B=\cos(A-B)-\cos(A+B)$. [2] (b) Hence show that $\displaystyle\int_0^{2\pi}\sin mx\sin nx\,dx=0$ when $m\ne n$. [4] (c) Show that $\displaystyle\int_0^{2\pi}\sin^2mx\,dx=\pi$. [2] (d) Hence find $\displaystyle\int_0^{2\pi}\left(3\sin x+2\sin3x\right)^2dx$. [3] (e) Find the RMS value of $3\sin x+2\sin3x$ over $[0,2\pi]$, to three significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\cos(A-B)=\cos A\cos B+\sin A\sin B$ and $\cos(A+B)=\cos A\cos B-\sin A\sin B$ [M1] subtract [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac12\displaystyle\int_0^{2\pi}\left[\cos(m-n)x-\cos(m+n)x\right]dx$ [M1] $=\dfrac12\left[\dfrac{\sin(m-n)x}{m-n}-\dfrac{\sin(m+n)x}{m+n}\right]_0^{2\pi}$ [A1] $m-n$ and $m+n$ are non-zero integers [R1] $\sin2\pi k=0$ so the integral is $0$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) $\dfrac12\displaystyle\int_0^{2\pi}(1-\cos2mx)\,dx$ [M1] $=\dfrac12\times2\pi=\pi$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) expand: $9\sin^2x+12\sin x\sin3x+4\sin^23x$ [M1] the cross term integrates to $0$ [A1] $9\pi+4\pi=13\pi$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) $\sqrt{\dfrac{13\pi}{2\pi}}$ [M1] $=\sqrt{6.5}=2.55$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Convert products of sines into sums of cosines, which integrate to zero over complete periods unless the frequencies match.

subtopic: Mean value of a function
statement: The temperature $T$ degrees Celsius in a greenhouse $t$ hours after midnight is modeled by $T(t)=15+6\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{12}-\dfrac\pi2\right)$ for $0\le t\le24$. (a) Find the mean temperature over the first $6$ hours using $\dfrac16\displaystyle\int_0^6T(t)\,dt$. [4] (b) State the mean temperature over a full $24$ hours and explain why it differs from your answer to (a). [2]
markscheme: (a) $\displaystyle\int_0^6T\,dt=67.08$ [M1][A1] mean $=\dfrac16\times67.08$ [M1] $=11.18$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $15$ [A1] over a full period the sine term averages to zero, while the first $6$ hours cover only the cooler part of the cycle [R1] [2 marks]
tips: The mean value of $f$ on $[a,b]$ is $\dfrac1{b-a}\int_a^bf(x)\,dx$. A sinusoid averages to its midline over whole periods.

subtopic: Evaluating a definite integral using a symmetry substitution
statement: Let $I=\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\dfrac{\sin x}{\sin x+\cos x}\,dx$ and $J=\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x+\cos x}\,dx$. (a) Show that $I+J=\dfrac\pi2$. [2] (b) By using the substitution $u=\dfrac\pi2-x$ in $I$, show that $I=J$. [3] (c) Hence find the value of $I$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $I+J=\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\dfrac{\sin x+\cos x}{\sin x+\cos x}\,dx$ [M1] $=\dfrac\pi2$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $du=-dx$, limits $\dfrac\pi2\to0$ [M1] $\sin\left(\dfrac\pi2-u\right)=\cos u$ and $\cos\left(\dfrac\pi2-u\right)=\sin u$ [A1] $I=\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\dfrac{\cos u}{\cos u+\sin u}du=J$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $2I=\dfrac\pi2$ so $I=\dfrac\pi4$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Add the two integrals to get an integrand of 1. The substitution $u=\pi/2-x$ swaps sine and cosine.

subtopic: Finding an unknown limit of integration
statement: Find the value of $k$ in each case. (a) $\displaystyle\int_0^k(2x+1)\,dx=12$, where $k>0$. [3] (b) $\displaystyle\int_1^k\dfrac1x\,dx=2$. [2] (c) $\displaystyle\int_0^k\sin x\,dx=\dfrac12$, where $0<k<\pi$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\left[x^2+x\right]_0^k=k^2+k$ [M1] $k^2+k-12=0$ [A1] $k=3$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\ln k=2$ [M1] $k=e^2$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $1-\cos k=\dfrac12$ [M1] $k=\dfrac\pi3$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Evaluate each integral in terms of $k$, then solve the resulting equation. Check that your answer lies in any stated range.

subtopic: Using a derivative to integrate x times sec squared x
statement: Consider the function $g(x)=x\tan x$. (a) Show that $g'(x)=\tan x+x\sec^2x$. [1] (b) Hence show that $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/4}x\sec^2x\,dx=\dfrac\pi4-\dfrac12\ln2$. [4]
markscheme: (a) product rule [AG] [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/4}\left(\tan x+x\sec^2x\right)dx=\left[x\tan x\right]_0^{\pi/4}=\dfrac\pi4$ [M1][A1] $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/4}\tan x\,dx=\left[-\ln\cos x\right]_0^{\pi/4}=\dfrac12\ln2$ [A1] subtract: $\dfrac\pi4-\dfrac12\ln2$ [AG] [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Integrate the derivative of $x\tan x$, then subtract the integral that you can already do.

subtopic: Integral of a modulus function
statement: Find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_0^3\left|x^2-4\right|\,dx$. Split the integral where the expression inside the modulus changes sign, and evaluate. [5]
markscheme: $x^2-4=0$ at $x=2$ in the interval [A1] $\displaystyle\int_0^2(4-x^2)dx+\int_2^3(x^2-4)dx$ [M1] $=\left[4x-\dfrac{x^3}3\right]_0^2=\dfrac{16}3$ [A1] $\left[\dfrac{x^3}3-4x\right]_2^3=\dfrac73$ [A1] total $\dfrac{23}3$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: The modulus makes the integrand non-negative, so on $[0,2]$ where $x^2-4<0$ use $4-x^2$.

subtopic: Integration by parts
statement: (a) Find $\displaystyle\int x^{2} \sin{\left(x \right)}\,dx$. [4] (b) Hence find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi}x^{2} \sin{\left(x \right)}\,dx$. [2]
markscheme: (a) first: $u=x^2$, $v=-\cos x$: $-x^2\cos x+\int2x\cos x\,dx$ [M1][A1] second: $u=2x$, $v=\sin x$: $2x\sin x-\int2\sin x\,dx$ [M1] $\int x^2\sin x\,dx=-x^2\cos x+2x\sin x+2\cos x+c$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $\left[-x^2\cos x+2x\sin x+2\cos x\right]_0^\pi=\left(\pi^2-2\right)-(2)$ [M1] value $-4 + \pi^{2}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Apply integration by parts twice; each application lowers the power of $x$ by one.

subtopic: Integration by parts
statement: (a) Find $\displaystyle\int x \ln{\left(x \right)}\,dx$. [4] (b) Hence find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_{1}^{e}x \ln{\left(x \right)}\,dx$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $u=\ln x$, $\dfrac{dv}{dx}=x$ so $\dfrac{du}{dx}=\dfrac1x$, $v=\dfrac{x^2}2$ [M1][A1] $\int x\ln x\,dx=\dfrac{x^2}2\ln x-\int\dfrac x2\,dx$ [M1] $=\dfrac{x^2}2\ln x-\dfrac{x^2}4+c$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $\left[\dfrac{x^2}{2}\ln x-\dfrac{x^2}{4}\right]_1^{\mathrm e}=\left(\dfrac{\mathrm e^2}2-\dfrac{\mathrm e^2}4\right)-\left(0-\dfrac14\right)$ [M1] value $\frac{1}{4} + \frac{e^{2}}{4}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: When a logarithm appears, differentiate it: let $u=\ln x$.

subtopic: Odd power of cosine by substitution
statement: Find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac\pi2}\cos^3x\,dx$. [5]
markscheme: $\cos^3x=\cos x\left(1-\sin^2x\right)$ [M1] Let $u=\sin x$, $du=\cos x\,dx$ [A1] Limits: $x=0\to u=0$ and $x=\dfrac\pi2\to u=1$ [A1] $\displaystyle\int_0^1\left(1-u^2\right)du=\left[u-\dfrac{u^3}{3}\right]_0^1$ [A1] $=\dfrac23$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: For an odd power of sine or cosine, split off one factor and convert the rest with $\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1$. The remaining single factor becomes $du$.

subtopic: A solid of revolution with finite volume and an unbounded area
statement: The region under $y=\dfrac1x$ for $x\ge1$ is rotated about the $x$-axis. Let $V(b)$ be the volume of the solid for $1\le x\le b$. (a) Find $V(b)$ and show that $V(b)\to\pi$ as $b\to\infty$. [4] (b) Show that the area under the curve $y=\dfrac1x$ for $1\le x\le b$ tends to infinity as $b\to\infty$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $V(b)=\pi\displaystyle\int_1^b\dfrac1{x^2}dx$ [M1] $=\pi\left[-\dfrac1x\right]_1^b=\pi\left(1-\dfrac1b\right)$ [A1] as $b\to\infty$, $\dfrac1b\to0$ [M1] so $V\to\pi$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $\displaystyle\int_1^b\dfrac1x\,dx=\ln b$ [A1] which grows without bound as $b\to\infty$ [R1] [2 marks]
tips: The volume integral involves $1/x^2$, which converges, while the area integral involves $1/x$, which diverges.

subtopic: Integration by substitution
statement: (a) Use the substitution $u=x+1$ to show that $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x+1}}\,dx=\dfrac23(x+1)^{3/2}-2(x+1)^{1/2}+c$. [4] (b) Hence evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^3\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x+1}}\,dx$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $x=u-1$, $dx=du$ [M1] $\int\dfrac{u-1}{\sqrt u}du=\int\left(u^{1/2}-u^{-1/2}\right)du$ [M1][A1] $=\dfrac23u^{3/2}-2u^{1/2}+c$ [A1] [AG] [4 marks] (b) $\left[\dfrac23(x+1)^{3/2}-2(x+1)^{1/2}\right]_0^3$ [M1] $=\left(\dfrac{16}3-4\right)-\left(\dfrac23-2\right)$ [A1] $=\frac{8}{3}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: When the integrand contains a square root of a linear expression, substitute for the linear expression and rewrite $x$ in terms of $u$.

subtopic: Volumes of revolution about the y-axis and the x-axis
statement: The region $R$ is bounded by the curve $y=e^{\frac x2}$, the $y$-axis and the line $y=3$. (a) Show that the curve can be written as $x=2\ln y$. [1] (b) The region $R$ is rotated through $360^\circ$ about the $y$-axis. Find the volume of the solid formed. [3] (c) The region $R$ is rotated through $360^\circ$ about the $x$-axis. Find the volume of the solid formed. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\ln y=\dfrac x2$, so $x=2\ln y$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $V=\pi\displaystyle\int x^2\,dy$ [M1] $=\pi\displaystyle\int_1^3\left(2\ln y\right)^2dy$ [A1] $=12.9$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $R$ lies between $y=e^{\frac x2}$ and $y=3$, for $0\le x\le2\ln3$ [A1] $V=\pi\displaystyle\int_0^{2\ln3}\left(9-e^x\right)dx$ [M1] $=37.0$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: For rotation about the $y$-axis you need $x$ in terms of $y$, and the limits are $y$-values. For rotation about the $x$-axis a region between two curves gives a washer: subtract the squares, not the square of the difference.

subtopic: Repeated integration by parts of e^x cos x
statement: Let $I=\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac\pi2}e^x\cos x\,dx$. (a) By using integration by parts twice, show that $2I=e^{\frac\pi2}-1$. [5] (b) Hence find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac\pi2}e^x\sin x\,dx$. [2]
markscheme: (a) First application, $u=\cos x$, $\dfrac{dv}{dx}=e^x$: $I=\left[e^x\cos x\right]_0^{\frac\pi2}+\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac\pi2}e^x\sin x\,dx$ [M1] $=-1+J$, where $J=\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac\pi2}e^x\sin x\,dx$ [A1] Second application, $u=\sin x$, $\dfrac{dv}{dx}=e^x$: $J=\left[e^x\sin x\right]_0^{\frac\pi2}-\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac\pi2}e^x\cos x\,dx$ [M1] $=e^{\frac\pi2}-I$ [A1] So $I=-1+e^{\frac\pi2}-I$, giving $2I=e^{\frac\pi2}-1$ [A1][AG] [5 marks] (b) $J=e^{\frac\pi2}-I$ [M1] $=e^{\frac\pi2}-\dfrac{e^{\frac\pi2}-1}{2}=\dfrac{e^{\frac\pi2}+1}{2}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: When the original integral reappears after two rounds of parts, treat it as an unknown and solve an equation. Be consistent in your choice of $u$ and $dv$ in both applications, otherwise you will undo the first step.

subtopic: Area between sine and cosine curves
statement: The curves $y=\sin x$ and $y=\cos x$ for $0\le x\le\dfrac\pi2$ intersect at one point, and $R$ is the region enclosed by the two curves, the $y$-axis and the line $x=\dfrac\pi2$. (a) Find the $x$-coordinate of the point of intersection. [2] (b) Find the exact area of $R$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $\tan x=1$ [M1] $x=\dfrac\pi4$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/4}(\cos x-\sin x)dx+\int_{\pi/4}^{\pi/2}(\sin x-\cos x)dx$ [M1][A1] $=\left[\sin x+\cos x\right]_0^{\pi/4}+\left[-\cos x-\sin x\right]_{\pi/4}^{\pi/2}$ [A1] $=2\left(\sqrt2-1\right)$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: The upper and lower curves swap at the intersection, so split the area into two integrals.

subtopic: Definite integral by substitution with an exponential
statement: Find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_0^{\ln2}\dfrac{e^x}{\left(1+e^x\right)^2}\,dx$. Use the substitution $u=1+e^x$ to evaluate the integral. [5]
markscheme: $du=e^x\,dx$ [A1] limits $u=2$ to $u=3$ [A1] $\displaystyle\int_2^3u^{-2}\,du$ [M1] $=\left[-\dfrac1u\right]_2^3$ [A1] $=-\dfrac13+\dfrac12=\dfrac16$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: The numerator is the derivative of the inner expression $1+e^x$. Change the limits along with the variable.

subtopic: Definite integral by substitution
statement: Use the substitution $u=x^2-1$ to find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_1^{\sqrt5}x\sqrt{x^2-1}\,dx$. [5]
markscheme: $du=2x\,dx$, so $x\,dx=\dfrac12du$ [M1] When $x=1$, $u=0$; when $x=\sqrt5$, $u=4$ [A1] $\displaystyle\int_0^4\dfrac12u^{\frac12}\,du$ [A1] $=\left[\dfrac13u^{\frac32}\right]_0^4$ [A1] $=\dfrac13\times8=\dfrac83$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: Change the limits when you change variable, so you never have to return to $x$. Check that all of the $x$ in the integrand is absorbed by $du=2x\,dx$.

subtopic: Integration using partial fractions
statement: (a) Express $\dfrac{1}{x \left(x + 2\right)}$ in partial fractions. [3] (b) Hence find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{x \left(x + 2\right)}\,dx$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac1{x(x+2)}=\dfrac Ax+\dfrac B{x+2}$ [M1] $1=A(x+2)+Bx$ [A1] $A=\dfrac12$, $B=-\dfrac12$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\dfrac12\left[\ln x-\ln(x+2)\right]_1^2=\dfrac12\left(\ln\dfrac12-\ln\dfrac13\right)$ [M1][A1] value $-\frac{\ln{\left(2 \right)}}{2} + \frac{\ln{\left(3 \right)}}{2}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Cover-up: substitute the root of each linear factor to find the constants.

subtopic: Area between two curves
statement: The curves $y=x^2$ and $y=4x-x^2$ intersect at the origin and at another point $P$. (a) Find the coordinates of $P$. [2] (b) Find the area of the region enclosed by the two curves. [4]
markscheme: (a) $x^2=4x-x^2$ [M1] $2x(x-2)=0$ so $x=2$ and $P=(2,4)$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\displaystyle\int_0^2\left(4x-x^2-x^2\right)dx$ [M1][A1] $=\left[2x^2-\dfrac{2x^3}3\right]_0^2$ [A1] $=\frac{8}{3}$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: The area between curves is the integral of (upper curve minus lower curve) between the intersection points.

subtopic: Integral of 1/(x ln x)
statement: Consider the integral $\displaystyle\int\dfrac1{x\ln x}\,dx$ for $x>1$. (a) Use the substitution $u=\ln x$ to find the integral. [3] (b) Hence find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_e^{e^2}\dfrac1{x\ln x}\,dx$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $du=\dfrac{dx}x$ [M1] $\int\dfrac{du}u$ [A1] $=\ln|\ln x|+C$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\ln(\ln e^2)-\ln(\ln e)$ [M1] $=\ln2-\ln1=\ln2$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The integrand has the form $f'(x)/f(x)$ when $f(x)=\ln x$, after separating the factor of $1/x$.

subtopic: Volume of revolution of a region between two curves
statement: The curves $y=x$ and $y=x^2$ enclose a region $R$ between their points of intersection. (a) Find the coordinates of the two points of intersection. [2] (b) Write down an integral for the volume obtained when $R$ is rotated through $2\pi$ about the $x$-axis. [2] (c) Evaluate the volume, and check with your calculator. [2]
markscheme: (a) $x=x^2$ [M1] $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) outer radius $y=x$, inner radius $y=x^2$ [M1] $V=\pi\displaystyle\int_0^1\left(x^2-x^4\right)dx$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\pi\left(\dfrac13-\dfrac15\right)=\dfrac{2\pi}{15}$ [A1] $=0.4189$, matching numerical integration [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A region between two curves rotated about the $x$-axis gives a solid with a hole: subtract the squares of the radii.

subtopic: Partial fractions integrated over a definite interval
statement: (a) Find constants $A$ and $B$ such that $\dfrac{3x+5}{(x+1)(x+3)}\equiv\dfrac{A}{x+1}+\dfrac{B}{x+3}$. [3] (b) Hence show that $\displaystyle\int_0^1\dfrac{3x+5}{(x+1)(x+3)}\,dx=\ln\dfrac{32}{9}$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $3x+5\equiv A(x+3)+B(x+1)$ [M1] Substituting $x=-1$: $2=2A$, so $A=1$ [A1] Substituting $x=-3$: $-4=-2B$, so $B=2$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\displaystyle\int_0^1\left(\dfrac1{x+1}+\dfrac2{x+3}\right)dx=\left[\ln(x+1)+2\ln(x+3)\right]_0^1$ [A1] $=\ln2+2\ln4-2\ln3$ [M1] $=\ln2+\ln16-\ln9=\ln\dfrac{32}{9}$ [A1][AG] [3 marks]
tips: Substituting the roots of the denominator is the fastest way to find the constants. When combining logarithms, convert multiples into powers first: $2\ln4=\ln16$.

subtopic: Integrating powers of sine and cosine
statement: (a) Use a double angle identity to find $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/4}\cos^22x\,dx$. [4] (b) Use the substitution $u=\cos x$ to evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^\pi\sin^3x\,dx$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $\cos^22x=\dfrac{1+\cos4x}2$ [M1][A1] $\left[\dfrac x2+\dfrac{\sin4x}8\right]_0^{\pi/4}$ [A1] $=\dfrac\pi8$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $\sin^3x=\sin x\left(1-\cos^2x\right)$ [M1] $-\int\left(1-u^2\right)du$ with limits $u=1$ to $-1$ [A1] $=\left[-u+\dfrac{u^3}3\right]_1^{-1}$ [M1] $=\dfrac43$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Even powers need a double angle identity; odd powers can be split to leave one factor for the substitution.

subtopic: Integration by parts with an inverse tangent
statement: Let $I=\displaystyle\int_0^1x\arctan x\,dx$. (a) Use integration by parts to show that $I=\dfrac\pi8-\dfrac12\displaystyle\int_0^1\dfrac{x^2}{1+x^2}\,dx$. [4] (b) Hence find the exact value of $I$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $u=\arctan x$, $dv=x\,dx$ so $du=\dfrac{dx}{1+x^2}$, $v=\dfrac{x^2}2$ [M1][A1] $I=\left[\dfrac{x^2}2\arctan x\right]_0^1-\dfrac12\int_0^1\dfrac{x^2}{1+x^2}dx$ [A1] first term $=\dfrac\pi8$ [AG] [A1] [4 marks] (b) $\dfrac{x^2}{1+x^2}=1-\dfrac1{1+x^2}$ [M1] $\int_0^1=1-\dfrac\pi4$ [A1] $I=\dfrac\pi8-\dfrac12\left(1-\dfrac\pi4\right)=\dfrac\pi4-\dfrac12$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Choose $u=\arctan x$ because its derivative is a simple rational function. Rewrite the new integrand using polynomial division.

subtopic: Area between a curve and a line
statement: Let $f(x)=\mathrm e^x$ for $0\le x\le1$. The line $y=1$ and the curve $y=f(x)$ and the line $x=1$ bound a region $R$. (a) Write down an integral for the area of $R$. [1] (b) Find the exact area. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\displaystyle\int_0^1\left(\mathrm e^x-1\right)dx$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\left[\mathrm e^x-x\right]_0^1$ [M1][A1] $=(\mathrm e-1)-1=\mathrm e-2$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The region lies between the curve and the horizontal line; integrate the difference of the two functions.

subtopic: Splitting a rational integrand into two standard forms
statement: Find $\displaystyle\int_0^1\dfrac{3x+1}{x^2+1}\,dx$, giving the answer in exact form. Write the integrand as a sum of two terms and integrate each. [5]
markscheme: $\dfrac{3x}{x^2+1}+\dfrac1{x^2+1}$ [M1] $\dfrac32\ln\left(x^2+1\right)$ [A1] $\arctan x$ [A1] limits: $\dfrac32\ln2+\dfrac\pi4$ [M1][A1] [5 marks]
tips: The first term has its numerator proportional to the derivative of the denominator, and the second is a standard arctangent integral.

subtopic: Area between curves found with a calculator
statement: The curve $y=2+\sin x$ and the line $y=\dfrac x2$ for $x\ge0$ intersect at the point with $x=p$ (the first such intersection). (a) Find the value of $p$. [2] (b) Find the area of the region bounded by the curve, the line and the $y$-axis. [3]
markscheme: (a) solve $2+\sin x=\dfrac x2$ on the calculator [M1] $p=3.430$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\displaystyle\int_0^{p}\left(2+\sin x-\dfrac x2\right)dx$ [M1][A1] $=5.877$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Find the intersection with the solver, then integrate (curve minus line) from $0$ to $p$.

subtopic: Volume of revolution using a double-angle identity
statement: Let $y=\sin x+\cos x$, for $0\le x\le\dfrac\pi2$. The region between the graph of $y$ and the $x$-axis is rotated through $360^\circ$ about the $x$-axis. (a) Show that $y^2=1+\sin2x$. [2] (b) Hence find the exact volume of the solid formed. [4]
markscheme: (a) $y^2=\sin^2x+2\sin x\cos x+\cos^2x$ [M1] $=1+\sin2x$ [A1][AG] [2 marks] (b) $V=\pi\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac\pi2}\left(1+\sin2x\right)dx$ [M1] $=\pi\left[x-\dfrac12\cos2x\right]_0^{\frac\pi2}$ [A1] $=\pi\left[\left(\dfrac\pi2+\dfrac12\right)-\left(0-\dfrac12\right)\right]$ [M1] $=\pi\left(\dfrac\pi2+1\right)$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Square the function before integrating, and use $\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1$ and $2\sin x\cos x=\sin2x$ to avoid integrating a square directly. Keep the factor of $\pi$ outside the integral.

subtopic: Integration using partial fractions
statement: (a) Express $\dfrac{3 x + 5}{\left(x + 1\right) \left(x + 3\right)}$ in partial fractions. [3] (b) Hence find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}\frac{3 x + 5}{\left(x + 1\right) \left(x + 3\right)}\,dx$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{3x+5}{(x+1)(x+3)}=\dfrac A{x+1}+\dfrac B{x+3}$ [M1] $3x+5=A(x+3)+B(x+1)$ gives $A=1$ [A1] $B=2$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\left[\ln(x+1)+2\ln(x+3)\right]_0^1$ [M1][A1] value $\ln{\left(\frac{32}{9} \right)}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Write the fraction over the common denominator and equate numerators, substituting convenient values of $x$.

subtopic: Integration by substitution
statement: (a) Use the substitution $u=x^2+1$ to find $\displaystyle\int x \left(x^{2} + 1\right)^{3}\,dx$. [4] (b) Hence evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}x \left(x^{2} + 1\right)^{3}\,dx$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $u=x^2+1$, $\dfrac{du}{dx}=2x$ [M1] $\int x(x^2+1)^3dx=\dfrac12\int u^3\,du$ [A1] $=\dfrac{u^4}8$ [A1] $=\dfrac{(x^2+1)^4}8+c$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) limits in $x$: $\dfrac{2^4}{8}-\dfrac18$ [M1][A1] so the value is $\frac{15}{8}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Spot that the derivative of the inner function ($2x$) appears, up to a constant factor, outside it.

subtopic: Integral with an arcsine and an algebraic part
statement: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^{1/2}\dfrac{1+x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\,dx$, giving the exact value. Split the integrand and integrate each part. [5]
markscheme: $\dfrac1{\sqrt{1-x^2}}+\dfrac x{\sqrt{1-x^2}}$ [M1] $\arcsin x$ [A1] $-\sqrt{1-x^2}$ [A1] limits $\dfrac\pi6+\left(1-\dfrac{\sqrt3}2\right)$ [M1] $=1+\dfrac\pi6-\dfrac{\sqrt3}2$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: One part is a standard inverse sine integral. The other is of the form $f'(x)f(x)^{-1/2}$ and integrates by the reverse chain rule.

subtopic: Volume of revolution about the y-axis
statement: The region bounded by the curve $y=x^2$, the $y$-axis and the line $y=4$ is rotated through $360^\circ$ about the $y$-axis. (a) Write down an integral for the volume in terms of $y$. [2] (b) Find the exact volume, and verify it using the formula for the volume of a paraboloid $V=\dfrac12\pi r^2h$ with $r=2$, $h=4$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $V=\pi\displaystyle\int_0^4x^2\,dy$ [M1] with $x^2=y$: $\pi\displaystyle\int_0^4y\,dy$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\pi\left[\dfrac{y^2}2\right]_0^4$ [M1] $=8 \pi$ [A1] $\dfrac12\pi\times4\times4=8\pi$ agrees [A1] [3 marks]
tips: For rotation about the $y$-axis, express $x^2$ as a function of $y$ and integrate with respect to $y$.

subtopic: Reduction formula and a series for 1/e
statement: This question investigates $J_n=\displaystyle\int_0^1x^n\mathrm e^x\,dx$ for integers $n\ge0$. (a) Find $J_0$, and show that $J_n=\mathrm e-nJ_{n-1}$ for $n\ge1$.
