[4] (b) Hence find $J_1$, $J_2$ and $J_3$ exactly. [3] (c) Show that $0<J_n<\dfrac{\mathrm e}{n+1}$, and deduce that $\dfrac{J_n}{n!}\to0$ as $n\to\infty$. [3] (d) Let $a_n=\dfrac{(-1)^nJ_n}{n!}$. Show that $a_n-a_{n-1}=\dfrac{(-1)^n\mathrm e}{n!}$, and hence that $a_n=\mathrm e\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^n\dfrac{(-1)^k}{k!}-1$. [4] (e) Hence deduce that $\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^\infty\dfrac{(-1)^k}{k!}=\dfrac1{\mathrm e}$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $J_0=\mathrm e-1$ [A1] by parts with $u=x^n$, $v=\mathrm e^x$: $J_n=\left[x^n\mathrm e^x\right]_0^1-n\displaystyle\int_0^1x^{n-1}\mathrm e^x\,dx$ [M1][A1] $=\mathrm e-nJ_{n-1}$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $J_1=\mathrm e-(\mathrm e-1)=1$ [A1] $J_2=\mathrm e-2$ [A1] $J_3=\mathrm e-3(\mathrm e-2)=6-2\mathrm e$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) for $0<x<1$, $0<x^n\mathrm e^x<\mathrm ex^n$ [M1] integrate: $J_n<\dfrac{\mathrm e}{n+1}$ [A1] $0<\dfrac{J_n}{n!}<\dfrac{\mathrm e}{(n+1)!}\to0$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $a_n-a_{n-1}=\dfrac{(-1)^n\left(J_n+nJ_{n-1}\right)}{n!}$ [M1] using $J_n+nJ_{n-1}=\mathrm e$ [A1] telescoping: $a_n=a_0+\mathrm e\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^n\dfrac{(-1)^k}{k!}$ [M1] with $a_0=\mathrm e-1$ [A1] [4 marks] (e) as $n\to\infty$, $a_n\to0$ by part (c) [M1] so $\mathrm e\sum\dfrac{(-1)^k}{k!}=1$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The recurrence comes from one application of integration by parts. Dividing by $n!$ and alternating the sign makes it telescope.

subtopic: Integration by substitution
statement: (a) Use the substitution $u=\cos x$ to find $\displaystyle\int \sin{\left(x \right)} \cos^{2}{\left(x \right)}\,dx$. [4] (b) Hence evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\sin{\left(x \right)} \cos^{2}{\left(x \right)}\,dx$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $u=\cos x$, $du=-\sin x\,dx$ [M1] $\int\sin x\cos^2x\,dx=-\int u^2\,du$ [A1] $=-\dfrac{u^3}3$ [A1] $=-\dfrac{\cos^3x}3+c$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $\left[-\dfrac{\cos^3x}{3}\right]_0^{\pi/2}=0-\left(-\dfrac13\right)$ [M1][A1] so the value is $\frac{1}{3}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Choose $u$ as the function whose derivative (apart from sign) is the remaining factor.

subtopic: Integration by parts: a cyclic integral
statement: Let $I=\displaystyle\int\mathrm e^x\cos x\,dx$. (a) Use integration by parts twice to show that $I=\mathrm e^x\cos x+\mathrm e^x\sin x-I$. [4] (b) Hence find $I$ and evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\mathrm e^x\cos x\,dx$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $u=\cos x$, $v=\mathrm e^x$: $I=\mathrm e^x\cos x+\int\mathrm e^x\sin x\,dx$ [M1][A1] second application: $\int\mathrm e^x\sin x\,dx=\mathrm e^x\sin x-\int\mathrm e^x\cos x\,dx$ [M1] so $I=\mathrm e^x\cos x+\mathrm e^x\sin x-I$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $2I=\mathrm e^x(\sin x+\cos x)$ so $I=\dfrac{\mathrm e^x(\sin x+\cos x)}2+c$ [A1] limits: $\dfrac{\mathrm e^{\pi/2}}2-\dfrac12$ [M1] $=\dfrac{\mathrm e^{\pi/2}-1}2$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: When parts reproduces the original integral, treat it as an algebraic equation for $I$.

subtopic: Integrating the natural logarithm
statement: (a) Use integration by parts with $u=\ln x$ and $\dfrac{dv}{dx}=1$ to find $\displaystyle\int\ln x\,dx$. [3] (b) Find the exact area of the region bounded by $y=\ln x$, the $x$-axis and the line $x=\mathrm e$. [2] (c) Find the exact area of the region bounded by $y=\ln x$, the line $y=1$ and the line $x=1$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\int\ln x\,dx=x\ln x-\int x\cdot\dfrac1x\,dx$ [M1][A1] $=x\ln x-x+c$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\left[x\ln x-x\right]_1^{\mathrm e}=(\mathrm e-\mathrm e)-(0-1)$ [M1] $=1$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) the curve lies below $y=1$ for $1\le x\le\mathrm e$ [R1] area $=\displaystyle\int_1^{\mathrm e}(1-\ln x)\,dx$ [M1] $=(\mathrm e-1)-1=\mathrm e-2$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Treat $\ln x$ as $\ln x\times1$ to apply parts. For area between a curve and a horizontal line, subtract the lower function from the upper one.

subtopic: Integrals giving inverse trigonometric functions
statement: (a) Find $\displaystyle\int_0^1\dfrac1{4+x^2}\,dx$. [3] (b) Find $\displaystyle\int_0^{3/2}\dfrac1{\sqrt{9-4x^2}}\,dx$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $\int\dfrac1{a^2+x^2}dx=\dfrac1a\arctan\dfrac xa$ with $a=2$ [M1][A1] $\dfrac12\arctan\dfrac12-0=\dfrac12\arctan\dfrac12$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\sqrt{9-4x^2}=2\sqrt{\dfrac94-x^2}$ [M1] $\dfrac12\arcsin\dfrac{2x}3$ [A1] $\dfrac12\left[\arcsin\dfrac{2x}3\right]_0^{3/2}=\dfrac12\arcsin1$ [M1] $=\dfrac\pi4$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Recognize the forms $\dfrac1{a^2+x^2}$ and $\dfrac1{\sqrt{a^2-x^2}}$ from the formula booklet; adjust by a constant factor when the coefficient of $x^2$ is not $1$.

subtopic: Reduction formula for the integral of sin^n
statement: This question investigates $I_n=\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^nx\,dx$ for integers $n\ge0$. (a) Find $I_0$ and $I_1$. [2] (b) Use integration by parts with $u=\sin^{n-1}x$ and $\dfrac{dv}{dx}=\sin x$ to show that $I_n=\dfrac{n-1}nI_{n-2}$ for $n\ge2$. [5] (c) Hence find $I_2$, $I_3$, $I_4$ and $I_5$. [3] (d) Show that $I_{2n}=\dfrac\pi2\times\dfrac{1\cdot3\cdot5\cdots(2n-1)}{2\cdot4\cdot6\cdots2n}$. [3] (e) The region under $y=\sin^2x$ for $0\le x\le\dfrac\pi2$ is rotated through $2\pi$ about the $x$-axis. Find the exact volume. [3]
markscheme: (a) $I_0=\dfrac\pi2$ [A1] $I_1=\left[-\cos x\right]_0^{\pi/2}=1$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $I_n=\left[-\sin^{n-1}x\cos x\right]_0^{\pi/2}+(n-1)\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^{n-2}x\cos^2x\,dx$ [M1][A1] the bracket is $0$ [A1] $\cos^2x=1-\sin^2x$ gives $I_n=(n-1)\left(I_{n-2}-I_n\right)$ [M1] $nI_n=(n-1)I_{n-2}$, so $I_n=\dfrac{n-1}nI_{n-2}$ [A1] [5 marks] (c) $I_2=\dfrac12\cdot\dfrac\pi2=\dfrac\pi4$ [A1] $I_3=\dfrac23$ [A1] $I_4=\dfrac34\cdot\dfrac\pi4=\dfrac{3\pi}{16}$, $I_5=\dfrac45\cdot\dfrac23=\dfrac8{15}$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) repeated use of the recurrence: $I_{2n}=\dfrac{2n-1}{2n}\cdot\dfrac{2n-3}{2n-2}\cdots\dfrac12I_0$ [M1][A1] with $I_0=\dfrac\pi2$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) $V=\pi\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^4x\,dx$ [M1] $=\pi I_4$ [A1] $=\dfrac{3\pi^2}{16}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The boundary term vanishes at both limits. Substituting $\cos^2x=1-\sin^2x$ returns $I_n$ on the right-hand side, giving an equation to solve for $I_n$.

subtopic: Reduction formulae
statement: This question investigates the family of integrals $$I_n = \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \sin^n x \, dx, \qquad n \in \mathbb{N}.$$ (a) Find the exact values of $I_0$ and $I_1$. [2] (b) By writing $\sin^n x = \sin^{n-1}x \sin x$ and using integration by parts, show that $I_n = \dfrac{n-1}{n} I_{n-2}$ for $n \ge 2$. [6] (c) Hence find the exact values of $I_2$, $I_3$, $I_4$ and $I_5$. [3] (d) Show that $n I_n I_{n-1} = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$ for all $n \ge 1$. [4] (e) Explain why $I_{n+1} \le I_n \le I_{n-1}$ for $n \ge 1$. [2] (f) Using parts (b) and (e), show that $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{I_n}{I_{n-1}} = 1$. [3] (g) Use parts (d) and (f) to show that $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty} n I_n^2 = \frac{\pi}{2}$. Hence write down an approximation for $I_n$ when $n$ is large, and use it to estimate $I_{100}$ to three significant figures. [5]
markscheme: (a) $I_0=\int_0^{\pi/2}1\,dx=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ [A1] $I_1=\left[-\cos x\right]_0^{\pi/2}=1$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Let $u=\sin^{n-1}x$, $\dfrac{dv}{dx}=\sin x$ [M1] so $\dfrac{du}{dx}=(n-1)\sin^{n-2}x\cos x$, $v=-\cos x$ [A1] $I_n=\left[-\sin^{n-1}x\cos x\right]_0^{\pi/2}+(n-1)\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^{n-2}x\cos^2x\,dx$ [A1] The boundary term is $0$ at both limits (as $n\ge2$) [R1] Using $\cos^2x=1-\sin^2x$: $I_n=(n-1)\left(I_{n-2}-I_n\right)$ [M1] so $nI_n=(n-1)I_{n-2}$, i.e. $I_n=\dfrac{n-1}{n}I_{n-2}$ [A1][AG] [6 marks] (c) $I_2=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$, $I_3=\dfrac23$ [A1] $I_4=\dfrac34\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{4}=\dfrac{3\pi}{16}$ [A1] $I_5=\dfrac45\cdot\dfrac23=\dfrac{8}{15}$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) For $n=1$: $1\cdot I_1I_0=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ [A1] For $n\ge2$: $nI_nI_{n-1}=n\cdot\dfrac{n-1}{n}I_{n-2}I_{n-1}$ [M1] $=(n-1)I_{n-1}I_{n-2}$ [A1] so the quantity $nI_nI_{n-1}$ does not depend on $n$; by induction it equals $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ for all $n\ge1$ [R1] [4 marks] (e) For $0\le x\le\frac{\pi}{2}$, $0\le\sin x\le1$, so $\sin^{n+1}x\le\sin^nx\le\sin^{n-1}x$ [R1] Integrating an inequality over $\left[0,\frac{\pi}{2}\right]$ preserves it [R1] [2 marks] (f) Dividing by $I_{n-1}>0$: $\dfrac{I_{n+1}}{I_{n-1}}\le\dfrac{I_n}{I_{n-1}}\le1$ [M1] By (b), $\dfrac{I_{n+1}}{I_{n-1}}=\dfrac{n}{n+1}\to1$ [A1] so by the squeeze principle $\dfrac{I_n}{I_{n-1}}\to1$ [R1] [3 marks] (g) $nI_n^2=\left(nI_nI_{n-1}\right)\cdot\dfrac{I_n}{I_{n-1}}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\cdot\dfrac{I_n}{I_{n-1}}$ [A1] $\to\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ by (f) [R1] So $I_n\approx\sqrt{\dfrac{\pi}{2n}}$ [A1] $I_{100}\approx\sqrt{\dfrac{\pi}{200}}\approx0.125$ [A1] [5 marks] Total [25 marks]
tips: In (b) the boundary term vanishes because sin 0 = 0 and cos(π/2) = 0.

subtopic: Completing the square and an arctangent integral
statement: (a) Write $x^2+2x+5$ in the form $(x+p)^2+q$. [1] (b) Hence find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1}\dfrac{1}{x^2+2x+5}\,dx$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $x^2+2x+5=(x+1)^2+4$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{1}{(x+1)^2+4}\,dx$ is of the form $\int\dfrac{1}{u^2+a^2}\,du$ with $a=2$ [M1] $=\dfrac12\arctan\left(\dfrac{x+1}{2}\right)$ [A1] $=\dfrac12\left[\arctan1-\arctan0\right]$ [M1] $=\dfrac\pi8$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: A quadratic with no real roots in the denominator usually signals an arctangent. The formula booklet gives $\int\frac{1}{a^2+x^2}dx=\frac1a\arctan\frac xa+C$; do not forget the factor $\frac1a$.

subtopic: Partial fractions and logarithmic integrals
statement: (a) Express $\dfrac{5x-1}{x^2-1}$ in partial fractions. [2] (b) Hence show that $\displaystyle\int_{2}^{4}\frac{5x-1}{x^2-1}\,dx=\ln\left(\frac{125}{3}\right)$. [5]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{5x-1}{(x-1)(x+1)}=\dfrac{A}{x-1}+\dfrac{B}{x+1}$, so $5x-1=A(x+1)+B(x-1)$ [M1] $A=2,\ B=3$, giving $\dfrac{2}{x-1}+\dfrac{3}{x+1}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\displaystyle\int\left(\frac{2}{x-1}+\frac{3}{x+1}\right)dx=2\ln(x-1)+3\ln(x+1)$ [A1][A1] Substituting limits: $(2\ln 3+3\ln 5)-(2\ln 1+3\ln 3)$ [M1] $=3\ln 5-\ln 3$ [A1] $=\ln 125-\ln 3=\ln\left(\dfrac{125}{3}\right)$ [A1][AG] [5 marks]
tips: Find partial fraction constants quickly by substituting $x=1$ and $x=-1$. In a show that question every log law you use must be visible, so write $3\ln 5=\ln 125$ explicitly.

subtopic: Integration by parts with a logarithm
statement: Find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_1^ex^2\ln x\,dx$. Give your answer in the form $\dfrac{ae^3+b}{c}$, where $a,b,c\in\mathbb{Z}^+$. [5]
markscheme: Integration by parts with $u=\ln x$, $\dfrac{dv}{dx}=x^2$ [M1] $\displaystyle\int x^2\ln x\,dx=\dfrac{x^3}{3}\ln x-\int\dfrac{x^2}{3}\,dx$ [A1] $=\left[\dfrac{x^3}{3}\ln x-\dfrac{x^3}{9}\right]_1^e$ [A1] $=\left(\dfrac{e^3}{3}-\dfrac{e^3}{9}\right)-\left(0-\dfrac19\right)$ [A1] $=\dfrac{2e^3+1}{9}$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: For $\ln x$ times a power of $x$, choose $u=\ln x$ since it simplifies on differentiation. Remember $\ln1=0$ when evaluating the lower limit.

subtopic: Integral of tan cubed using an identity and substitution
statement: Consider $\displaystyle\int\tan^3x\,dx$. (a) Use $\tan^2x=\sec^2x-1$ to show that $\displaystyle\int\tan^3x\,dx=\dfrac12\tan^2x+\ln|\cos x|+C$. [4] (b) Hence find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/4}\tan^3x\,dx$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\tan^3x=\tan x\left(\sec^2x-1\right)=\tan x\sec^2x-\tan x$ [M1] $\int\tan x\sec^2x\,dx=\dfrac12\tan^2x$ using $u=\tan x$ [A1] $\int\tan x\,dx=-\ln|\cos x|$ [A1] so the integral is $\dfrac12\tan^2x+\ln|\cos x|+C$ [AG] [A1] [4 marks] (b) $\left[\dfrac12\tan^2x+\ln\cos x\right]_0^{\pi/4}$ [M1] $\dfrac12+\ln\dfrac{\sqrt2}2$ [A1] $=\dfrac12-\dfrac12\ln2$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Split off a factor $\sec^2x$, so that the remaining $\tan x$ is the derivative-friendly substitution variable.

subtopic: Reduction formula for powers of sine and a limit
statement: This question investigates the integrals $I_n=\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac\pi2}\sin^nx\,dx$, where $n\in\mathbb{N}$. (a) Find the exact values of $I_0$ and $I_1$. [2] (b) For $n\ge2$, use integration by parts to show that $nI_n=(n-1)I_{n-2}$. [6] (c) Hence find the exact values of $I_4$ and $I_5$. [3] (d) Hence, using the substitution $u=\dfrac\pi2-x$, find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac\pi2}\cos^6x\,dx$. [3] (e) Show that $I_{n+1}\le I_n$ for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$. [2] (f) Use the result of part (b) to show that $(n+1)I_{n+1}I_n=\dfrac\pi2$ for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$. [4] (g) Hence show that $\dfrac{\pi}{2(n+1)}\le I_n^2\le\dfrac{\pi}{2n}$ for $n\ge1$, and deduce the value of $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}nI_n^2$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $I_0=\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac\pi2}1\,dx=\dfrac\pi2$ [A1] $I_1=\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac\pi2}\sin x\,dx=\left[-\cos x\right]_0^{\frac\pi2}=1$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $I_n=\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac\pi2}\sin^{n-1}x\,\sin x\,dx$ [A1] Using parts with $u=\sin^{n-1}x$ and $\dfrac{dv}{dx}=\sin x$ [M1] $I_n=\left[-\sin^{n-1}x\cos x\right]_0^{\frac\pi2}+(n-1)\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac\pi2}\sin^{n-2}x\cos^2x\,dx$ [A1] The boundary term is $0$ for $n\ge2$ [A1] Using $\cos^2x=1-\sin^2x$: $I_n=(n-1)\left(I_{n-2}-I_n\right)$ [M1] $nI_n=(n-1)I_{n-2}$ [A1][AG] [6 marks] (c) $I_2=\dfrac12I_0=\dfrac\pi4$ and $I_3=\dfrac23I_1=\dfrac23$ [M1] $I_4=\dfrac34\cdot\dfrac\pi4=\dfrac{3\pi}{16}$ [A1] $I_5=\dfrac45\cdot\dfrac23=\dfrac8{15}$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $I_6=\dfrac56I_4=\dfrac{5\pi}{32}$ [M1][A1] With $u=\dfrac\pi2-x$: $\cos x=\sin u$ and the limits swap and $dx=-du$, so $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac\pi2}\cos^6x\,dx=\int_0^{\frac\pi2}\sin^6u\,du=I_6$, hence the value is $\dfrac{5\pi}{32}$ [R1] [3 marks] (e) For $0\le x\le\dfrac\pi2$, $0\le\sin x\le1$, so $\sin^{n+1}x\le\sin^nx$ [R1] Integrating over $\left[0,\dfrac\pi2\right]$ preserves the inequality, so $I_{n+1}\le I_n$ [R1] [2 marks] (f) Applying (b) with $n$ replaced by $n+1$: $(n+1)I_{n+1}=nI_{n-1}$ for $n\ge1$ [M1] Multiplying by $I_n$: $(n+1)I_{n+1}I_n=nI_nI_{n-1}$ [A1] so the quantity $(n+1)I_{n+1}I_n$ does not change as $n$ increases [R1] For $n=0$ it equals $I_1I_0=\dfrac\pi2$, hence it equals $\dfrac\pi2$ for all $n$ [A1] [4 marks] (g) For $n\ge1$, (e) gives $I_{n+1}\le I_n\le I_{n-1}$; multiplying by $I_n>0$: $I_nI_{n+1}\le I_n^2\le I_nI_{n-1}$ [M1] By (f): $I_nI_{n+1}=\dfrac{\pi}{2(n+1)}$ and $I_nI_{n-1}=\dfrac{\pi}{2n}$, which gives the stated inequality [A1] Multiplying by $n$: $\dfrac{n\pi}{2(n+1)}\le nI_n^2\le\dfrac\pi2$ [M1] As $n\to\infty$ the lower bound tends to $\dfrac\pi2$, so by the squeeze principle $nI_n^2\to\dfrac\pi2$ [R1] [4 marks]
tips: In reduction-formula questions, always integrate by parts so that the original integral reappears on the right-hand side, then solve for it. In the later parts, look for a quantity that is unchanged from one index to the next; that usually signals a telescoping argument.

subtopic: Integration by reverse chain rule
statement: Find the following. (a) $\displaystyle\int2xe^{x^{2}}\,dx$ [2] (b) $\displaystyle\int\cos(3x)\,dx$ [2] (c) $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}\dfrac{x}{x^{2}+1}\,dx$, giving an exact answer. [3]
markscheme: (a) recognize $\dfrac{d}{dx}e^{x^{2}}=2xe^{x^{2}}$ [M1]; $e^{x^{2}}+C$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac13\sin(3x)+C$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (c) numerator is half the derivative of the denominator [M1]; $\left[\dfrac12\ln(x^{2}+1)\right]_0^1$ [A1]; $\dfrac12\ln2$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: If the integrand is of the form $kf'(x)g(f(x))$, try the reverse of the chain rule.

subtopic: Velocity and displacement from a quadratic acceleration
statement: A toy train moves along a straight track. Its acceleration at time $t$ seconds is $a=6t-4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, for $t\ge0$. When $t=0$ the train is at the starting point $s=0$ with velocity $3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. (a) Find an expression for the velocity $v$ at time $t$. [3] (b) Find the displacement from the starting point when $t=2$. [2] (c) Find the displacement of the train between $t=1$ and $t=3$. [2] (d) Show that the train never changes direction, and state what this tells you about the distance traveled in part (c). [2]
markscheme: (a) $v=\displaystyle\int(6t-4)\,\mathrm{d}t=3t^2-4t+c$ [M1][A1] $v(0)=3$ gives $c=3$ so $v=3t^2-4t+3$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $s=\displaystyle\int v\,\mathrm{d}t=t^3-2t^2+3t$ (with $s(0)=0$) [M1] $s(2)=8-8+6=6\ \mathrm{m}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $s(3)-s(1)=(27-18+9)-(1-2+3)$ [M1] $=18-2=16\ \mathrm{m}$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) The discriminant of $3t^2-4t+3$ is $16-36=-20<0$ and the leading coefficient is positive, so $v>0$ for all $t$ [R1] The train never reverses, so the distance traveled between $t=1$ and $t=3$ equals the displacement, $16\ \mathrm{m}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Integrate acceleration to get velocity, using the initial velocity to find the constant, and integrate again for displacement. Distance equals displacement when the velocity never changes sign.

subtopic: Exact area under a polynomial-exponential curve
statement: The function $f$ is defined by $f(x)=3 x^{2} + e^{x}$. (a) Find $\int f(x)\,dx$. [2] (b) Hence find the exact area of the region bounded by the curve, the $x$-axis and the lines $x=0$ and $x=2$. [3] (c) The curve passes through $(0,1)$. State, giving a reason, whether the region lies entirely above the $x$-axis. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\int f(x)\,dx=x^{3} + e^{x}+c$ [A1][A1] (A1 for each correct term/part) [2 marks] (b) $\left[x^{3} + e^{x}\right]_{0}^{2}$ [M1]; $=e^{2} + 8-(1)$ [A1]; $=7 + e^{2}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $f(x)>0$ on the interval, so the definite integral equals the area [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Integrate term by term: $\int e^x\,dx=e^x$; substitute the limits upper minus lower.

subtopic: Net signed area versus total area for a cubic
statement: The height of a hiking trail above a reference level is modeled by $f(x)=x^3-4x$, where $x$ is the horizontal distance in hundreds of meters, for $-2\le x\le3$. (a) Find the values of $x$ for which $f(x)=0$. [2] (b) Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{-2}^{3}f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x$. [2] (c) Find the total area of the regions enclosed between the graph of $f$ and the $x$-axis for $-2\le x\le3$. [3] (d) Explain why your answers to parts (b) and (c) are different. [1]
markscheme: (a) $x(x-2)(x+2)=0$ [M1] $x=-2,\ 0,\ 2$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\displaystyle\int_{-2}^{3}(x^3-4x)\,\mathrm{d}x=6.25$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (c) $\displaystyle\int_{-2}^{0}f\,\mathrm{d}x=4$, $\ \displaystyle\int_0^2f\,\mathrm{d}x=-4$, $\ \displaystyle\int_2^3f\,\mathrm{d}x=6.25$ [M1][A1] Total area $=4+4+6.25=14.25$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) In part (b) the regions below the $x$-axis count as negative and cancel part of the regions above, whereas in part (c) all areas are counted as positive [R1] [1 mark]
tips: A definite integral gives signed area. To find the area enclosed by a curve and the axis, split at each zero and take the absolute value of each part, or integrate $|f(x)|$ on your GDC.

subtopic: Exact volume of revolution about the x-axis
statement: The region is bounded by the curve $y=x + 1$, the $x$-axis and the lines $x=0$ and $x=3$. (a) Write down an integral for the volume of the solid formed when the region between the curve, the $x$-axis, $x=0$ and $x=3$ is rotated through $360^\circ$ about the $x$-axis. [2] (b) Find the exact volume. [3]
markscheme: (a) $V=\pi\int_{0}^{3}y^2\,dx=\pi\int_{0}^{3}\left(x + 1\right)^2dx$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (b) $y^2=x^{2} + 2 x + 1$ [A1]; integrate [M1]; $V=21 \pi$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Square $y$ before integrating; the factor $\pi$ stays outside.

subtopic: Integrating a power function with a negative index
statement: A curve $C$ has gradient function $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=12x^3-\dfrac{6}{x^2}+5$ for $x>0$, and passes through the point $(1,\,10)$. (a) Find $\displaystyle\int\left(12x^3-\dfrac{6}{x^2}+5\right)\mathrm{d}x$. [3] (b) Find the equation of $C$. [2] (c) Find the value of $y$ on $C$ when $x=2$. [1]
tips: Write $\dfrac{1}{x^2}$ as $x^{-2}$ before integrating: the integral of $-6x^{-2}$ is $+6x^{-1}$. Do not forget the constant of integration, then use the given point to find it.

subtopic: Volume of a solid of revolution of an exponential-quadratic
statement: The region bounded by $y=\frac{x}{4} + 2 e^{- \frac{x}{3}}$, the axes and $x=5$ is rotated through $360^\circ$ about the $x$-axis (units are centimeters). (a) Write down an integral for the volume of the solid formed by rotating the region about the $x$-axis. [2] (b) Use your calculator to evaluate the volume, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (c) Find the radius of the solid at its widest point and the position at which it occurs. [3]
markscheme: (a) $V=\pi\int_{0}^{5}\left(\frac{x}{4} + 2 e^{- \frac{x}{3}}\right)^2dx$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (b) $V=40.39$ (units$^3$) [M1][A1] $\approx40.4$ [2 marks] (c) Use the maximum function [M1]; widest radius $2.000$ at $x=0.000$ [A1][A1] [3 marks]
tips: Include the factor $\pi$; squaring $f$ first helps when entering it into the GDC.

subtopic: Finding a function from its derivative
statement: A function $f$ has derivative $f'(x)=6x^{2}-\dfrac{4}{x}+e^{2x}$ for $x>0$, and $f(1)=\dfrac{e^{2}}{2}$. (a) Find $f(x)$ including the constant of integration. [3] (b) Use $f(1)=\dfrac{e^{2}}{2}$ to find $C$. [2]
tips: Integrate each term, then substitute the given point to find the constant.

subtopic: Accumulated change from a rate of flow
statement: Water flows into a reservoir at a rate of $R(t)=40e^{-0.2t}+5t$ thousand liters per hour, where $t$ is the number of hours after midnight, for $0\leq t\leq12$. (a) Find the rate of flow at $t=0$ and at $t=10$. [2] (b) Find the total volume that enters the reservoir during the first $10$ hours, to the nearest thousand liters. [3] (c) Find the time at which the total volume that has entered first reaches $300$ thousand liters. [3] (d) Show that $R$ has a minimum value for $t>0$ and find the time at which it occurs. [3]
tips: The area under a rate-of-flow graph gives the total change; use the GDC definite integral and equation solver with the upper limit as the unknown.

subtopic: Area enclosed by a parabola and a line
statement: The curves $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$ have equations $f(x)=-x^{2} + 6 x$ and $g(x)=2 x$. (a) Find the $x$-coordinates of the points of intersection of the two curves. [2] (b) Find the exact area of the region enclosed by the two curves. [4]
tips: The region between two curves has area $\int(\text{upper}-\text{lower})\,dx$ between the intersection points.

subtopic: Definite integral with a reciprocal term
statement: The function $f$ is defined by $f(x)=4 x + \frac{3}{x}$ for $x>0$. (a) Find $\int f(x)\,dx$. [2] (b) Hence find the exact area of the region bounded by the curve, the $x$-axis and the lines $x=1$ and $x=3$. [3] (c) The curve passes through $(1,7)$. State, giving a reason, whether the region lies entirely above the $x$-axis. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\int f(x)\,dx=2 x^{2} + 3 \log{\left(x \right)}+c$ [A1][A1] (A1 for each correct term/part) [2 marks] (b) $\left[2 x^{2} + 3 \log{\left(x \right)}\right]_{1}^{3}$ [M1]; $=3 \log{\left(3 \right)} + 18-(2)$ [A1]; $=\log{\left(27 \right)} + 16$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $f(x)>0$ on the interval, so the definite integral equals the area [R1] [1 mark]
tips: $\int\dfrac1x\,dx=\ln|x|$; for exact answers leave $\ln$ terms unevaluated.

subtopic: Integrating sine and cosine of a linear argument
statement: (a) Find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/6}6\cos3x\,\mathrm{d}x$. [3] (b) Find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_{\pi/4}^{\pi/2}8\sin2x\,\mathrm{d}x$. [3] (c) Find $\displaystyle\int10\cos\left(\dfrac x2\right)\mathrm{d}x$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\displaystyle\int6\cos3x\,\mathrm{d}x=2\sin3x$ [A1] $\left[2\sin3x\right]_0^{\pi/6}=2\sin\dfrac\pi2-2\sin0$ [M1] $=2$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\displaystyle\int8\sin2x\,\mathrm{d}x=-4\cos2x$ [A1] $\left[-4\cos2x\right]_{\pi/4}^{\pi/2}=-4\cos\pi+4\cos\dfrac\pi2$ [M1] $=4+0=4$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $20\sin\left(\dfrac x2\right)$ [A1] $+\,c$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: For $\int\cos(kx)\,\mathrm{d}x$ divide by $k$ (and for $\int\sin(kx)\,\mathrm{d}x$ divide by $-k$). Angles must be in radians for calculus, and the constant $c$ is needed in an indefinite integral.

subtopic: Trapezoidal rule and volumes of revolution
statement: A glass vase is modeled by rotating the curve $r(x)=4+2\sin\left(\dfrac{x}{5}\right)$, for $0\le x\le20$, through $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis. Here $x$ cm is the height above the base of the vase and $r$ cm is the internal radius at that height. (a) Find the maximum internal radius of the vase and the height at which it occurs. [2] (b) Use the trapezoidal rule with $4$ intervals of equal width to estimate $\displaystyle\int_0^{20}r(x)\,dx$. [3] (c) Find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_0^{20}r(x)\,dx$ using your GDC, and hence the percentage error of your estimate in part (b). [2] (d) (i) Write down an integral that gives the internal volume of the vase. (ii) Find the internal volume of the vase. [3] (e) Water is poured into the vase until it holds $500\ \text{cm}^3$. Find the depth of the water. [3]
markscheme: (a) maximum radius $6$ cm [A1] at height $x=\dfrac{5\pi}{2}=7.85$ cm [A1] [2 marks] (b) $r(0)=4$, $r(5)=5.683$, $r(10)=5.819$, $r(15)=4.282$, $r(20)=2.486$ [A1] $\dfrac{5}{2}\left[4+2(5.683+5.819+4.282)+2.486\right]$ [M1] $=95.1$ ($95.1348\ldots$) [A1] [3 marks] (c) $96.5$ ($96.5364\ldots$) [A1] percentage error $=\left|\dfrac{95.1348-96.5364}{96.5364}\right|\times100\%=1.45\%$ [A1] [2 marks] (d)(i) $V=\pi\displaystyle\int_0^{20}\left(4+2\sin\frac{x}{5}\right)^2dx$ [A1][A1] (ii) $V=1530\ \text{cm}^3$ ($1531.03\ldots$) [A1] [3 marks] (e) $\pi\displaystyle\int_0^{k}\left(4+2\sin\frac{x}{5}\right)^2dx=500$ [M1] solving using GDC [M1] $k=6.10$ cm ($6.10213\ldots$) [A1] [3 marks]
tips: For a volume of revolution remember to square the radius and multiply by pi. When the upper limit is unknown, set up the integral equal to the volume and solve graphically or with the GDC solver.

subtopic: Mean value of a periodic temperature function
statement: The temperature in a greenhouse is modeled by $T(t)=18-6\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{12}\right)$ degrees Celsius, where $t$ is the number of hours after midnight, for $0\le t\le24$. The mean value of $T$ over $a\le t\le b$ is $\dfrac{1}{b-a}\int_a^bT(t)\,dt$. (a) Find the lowest and highest temperatures predicted by the model and the times at which they occur. [3] (b) Use your GDC to find the mean temperature over the whole day. [2] (c) Find the mean temperature between 8 am and 4 pm ($8\le t\le16$), to three significant figures, and explain why it is higher than the daily mean. [3]
markscheme: (a) lowest $12^{\circ}$C at $t=0$ and $t=24$ [A1]; highest $24^{\circ}$C [A1]; at $t=12$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\dfrac{1}{24}\int_0^{24}T\,dt$ [M1]; $18^{\circ}$C [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\dfrac18\int_8^{16}T\,dt$ [M1]; $23.0^{\circ}$C [A1]; this interval is centered on the warmest time of day [R1] [3 marks]
tips: The mean value of a function over an interval is its integral divided by the length of the interval.

subtopic: Exact definite integrals of exponential and reciprocal functions
statement: (a) Find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_0^{\ln2}4\mathrm{e}^{2x}\,\mathrm{d}x$. [3] (b) Find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_1^{\mathrm{e}^2}\left(\dfrac3x+2\right)\mathrm{d}x$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\displaystyle\int4\mathrm{e}^{2x}\,\mathrm{d}x=2\mathrm{e}^{2x}$ [A1] $\left[2\mathrm{e}^{2x}\right]_0^{\ln2}=2\mathrm{e}^{2\ln2}-2$ [M1] $=2(4)-2=6$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\displaystyle\int\left(\dfrac3x+2\right)\mathrm{d}x=3\ln x+2x$ [A1] $\left[3\ln x+2x\right]_1^{\mathrm{e}^2}=(6+2\mathrm{e}^2)-(0+2)$ [M1] $=4+2\mathrm{e}^2$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Use $\mathrm{e}^{\ln a}=a$ and $\ln\mathrm{e}^2=2$, $\ln1=0$ to keep answers exact. The integral of $\mathrm{e}^{kx}$ is $\dfrac1k\mathrm{e}^{kx}$.

subtopic: Signed integral versus total area
statement: Let $f(x)=(x+1)(x-2)(x-4)$. The graph of $f$ crosses the $x$-axis at $x=-1$, $x=2$ and $x=4$. (a) Use your GDC to evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{-1}^2f(x)\,dx$ and $\displaystyle\int_2^4f(x)\,dx$. [2] (b) Find the total area enclosed between the graph of $f$ and the $x$-axis for $-1\le x\le4$. [3] (c) Find $\displaystyle\int_{-1}^4f(x)\,dx$, and explain why it differs from the area found in part (b). [2]
markscheme: (a) $\int_{-1}^2f(x)\,dx=15.75$ [A1] $\int_2^4f(x)\,dx=-5.33$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) The graph lies above the axis on $(-1,2)$ and below it on $(2,4)$ [M1] Area $=15.75+|-5.33|$ [M1] $=21.1$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $15.75-5.33=10.4$ [A1] Integration counts regions below the axis as negative, so the two regions partly cancel [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Split the interval at every $x$-intercept when finding area. A definite integral gives a signed quantity, so negative regions reduce its value.

subtopic: Indefinite integration and finding a function
statement: (a) Find $\displaystyle\int\left(6x^2-\frac4x+e^{2x}\right)dx$. [3] (b) Given that $g'(x)=4x-3$ and $g(2)=5$, find $g(x)$. [3]
tips: Do not forget the constant of integration in indefinite integrals. For $\int e^{ax}dx$ divide by the coefficient $a$.

subtopic: Area between a parabola and a line
statement: The curve $y=x^{2}$ and the line $y=2x$ enclose a region. (a) Find the $x$-coordinates of the points of intersection. [2] (b) Find the area of the region. [3]
tips: On $0\le x\le2$ the line is above the parabola.

subtopic: Displacement and total distance with a change of direction
statement: A drone moves along a straight corridor. Its velocity at time $t$ seconds is $v(t)=4\mathrm{e}^{-0.3t}-1.5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ for $0\le t\le8$. Positive velocity means moving away from the start of the corridor. (a) Find the time at which the drone is instantaneously at rest, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (b) Find the acceleration of the drone when $t=2$. [2] (c) Find the displacement of the drone during the $8$ seconds, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (d) Find the total distance traveled by the drone during the $8$ seconds, correct to 3 significant figures. [3] (e) The drone starts at $s=3$ meters from the start of the corridor. Find the position of the drone when $t=8$, and the greatest value of $s$ during the $8$ seconds, correct to 3 significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) $4\mathrm{e}^{-0.3t}-1.5=0$ [M1] $t=3.27$ s [A1] [2 marks] (b) $a(t)=-1.2\mathrm{e}^{-0.3t}$ [M1] $a(2)=-0.659\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\displaystyle\int_0^8v\,\mathrm{d}t$ [M1] $=0.124\ \mathrm{m}$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) The velocity changes sign at $t=3.269$ [M1] Distance $=\displaystyle\int_0^{3.269}v\,\mathrm{d}t+\left|\int_{3.269}^{8}v\,\mathrm{d}t\right|$ $=3.429+3.305$ [A1] $=6.73\ \mathrm{m}$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) $s(8)=3+0.124=3.12\ \mathrm{m}$ [A1] The greatest value of $s$ occurs when $v=0$, at $t=3.269$ [M1] $s=3+3.429=6.43\ \mathrm{m}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The total distance requires splitting the integral where the velocity changes sign (or integrating $|v|$ on the GDC). Displacement, distance and position are different quantities: position adds the starting value $s(0)$.

subtopic: Area between an exponential curve and a line
statement: The graph of $y=xe^{-x}$ and the line $y=0.1x$ meet at the origin and at a second point $P$. (a) Find the $x$-coordinate of $P$ exactly. [2] (b) Use your GDC to find the area enclosed between the curve and the line, to three significant figures. [3] (c) State the coordinates of $P$ to three significant figures. [1]
markscheme: (a) $xe^{-x}=0.1x$, so $e^{-x}=0.1$ [M1]; $x=\ln10$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) area $=\int_0^{\ln10}\left(xe^{-x}-0.1x\right)dx$ [M1]; curve is above the line [R1]; $0.405$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $(2.30,\,0.230)$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: The curve $y=xe^{-x}$ is above the line between the two intersection points; check one value of $x$.

subtopic: Area between two curves using GDC
statement: The curves $y=e^x$ and $y=4-x^2$ intersect at two points, and the region $R$ is bounded by the two curves. (a) Find the $x$-coordinates of the two points of intersection. [2] (b) Find the area of $R$. [3] (c) Find the greatest vertical distance between the two curves within the region $R$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $e^x=4-x^2$ solved on GDC: $x=-1.96$ [A1] and $x=1.06$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\displaystyle\int_{-1.96}^{1.06}\left(4-x^2-e^x\right)dx$ [M1] [A1] $=6.43$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Distance $d(x)=4-x^2-e^x$ [M1] Maximum of $d$ from GDC (or solve $-2x-e^x=0$): $x=-0.352$ [A1] Greatest distance $=3.17$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: State which curve is above the other before setting up the integral, and use unrounded intersection values from your calculator. The greatest vertical gap occurs where the gradients are equal.

subtopic: Trapezoidal rule and exact area
statement: The depth $d$ meters of a river at distance $x$ meters from one bank was measured across its width, giving the following table. $\begin{array}{c|cccccc} x & 0&1&2&3&4&5\\ \hline d & 0&1.2&1.8&1.8&1.2&0\end{array}$ (a) Use the trapezoidal rule with five strips to estimate the area of the cross-section of the river. [3] (b) The depth is modeled by $d(x)=-0.3x^2+1.5x$. Use the model to find the area of the cross-section. [2] (c) Find the percentage error in the estimate from part (a), relative to the value in part (b). [2] (d) Explain why the trapezoidal rule gives an underestimate for this model. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\frac12\cdot1\left[0+0+2(1.2+1.8+1.8+1.2)\right]$ [M1] [A1] $=6.0$ m$^2$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\displaystyle\int_0^5(-0.3x^2+1.5x)\,dx$ [M1] $=6.25$ m$^2$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\frac{6.25-6.0}{6.25}\times100$ [M1] $=4\%$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) The graph of $d$ is concave down, so each trapezoid lies below the curve [R1] [1 mark]
tips: The trapezoidal rule uses $\frac h2[\text{first}+\text{last}+2(\text{sum of the rest})]$. For a concave-down curve the chords lie below the curve, giving an underestimate.

subtopic: Area under a concentration curve in pharmacology
statement: The concentration of a medicine in a patient's blood, in milligrams per liter, is modeled by $C(t)=8t\mathrm{e}^{-0.5t}$, where $t$ is the time in hours after the dose and $t\ge0$. (a) Find the maximum concentration and the time at which it occurs, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (b) Find $\displaystyle\int_0^{12}C(t)\,\mathrm{d}t$, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (c) State what this integral represents, including its units. [1] (d) The dose is considered effective if the area under the concentration curve over the first $12$ hours is at least $30$. State whether the dose is effective, with a reason. [2]
markscheme: (a) Using the GDC maximum function [M1] maximum concentration $5.89$ mg/L at $t=2.00$ hours [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\displaystyle\int_0^{12}8t\mathrm{e}^{-0.5t}\,\mathrm{d}t=31.4$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (c) The area under the concentration curve (total exposure to the medicine) over the first $12$ hours, in $\mathrm{mg\,h\,L^{-1}}$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) $31.4\ge30$ [R1] so the dose is effective [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The unit of an integral is the product of the units of the integrand and the variable, here $(\mathrm{mg/L})\times\mathrm{h}$. Use the GDC maximum function to answer part (a) without differentiating.

subtopic: Consumer and producer surplus
statement: A market has demand curve $D(q)=100e^{-0.02q}$ (the price in dollars consumers will pay for the $q$th unit) and supply curve $S(q)=10+0.5q$ (the price in dollars at which producers will supply the $q$th unit), for $q\ge0$. The market equilibrium is at the quantity $q^{*}$ where $D(q^{*})=S(q^{*})$, with equilibrium price $p^{*}=D(q^{*})$. (a) Use your GDC to find $q^{*}$ and $p^{*}$, to three significant figures. [3] (b) The consumer surplus is the area between the demand curve and the horizontal line $p=p^{*}$ for $0\le q\le q^{*}$. Write down an integral for it and find its value, to the nearest dollar. [3] (c) The producer surplus is the area between the line $p=p^{*}$ and the supply curve for $0\le q\le q^{*}$. Find its value as an integral and, since the supply curve is straight, as the area of a triangle, to the nearest dollar. [4] (d) Find the total surplus, and the percentage of it that goes to consumers, to three significant figures. [2] (e) Use the trapezoidal rule with $4$ equal strips to estimate the consumer surplus, to the nearest dollar, and find the percentage error. [4] (f) Explain why the trapezoidal estimate is an overestimate for this convex decreasing demand curve. [2]
markscheme: (a) solve $100e^{-0.02q}=10+0.5q$ [M1]; $q^{*}=51.5$ [A1]; $p^{*}=35.7$ dollars [A1] [3 marks] (b) $CS=\int_0^{q^{*}}\left(D(q)-p^{*}\right)dq$ [M1][A1]; \$1,375 [A1] [3 marks] (c) $PS=\int_0^{q^{*}}\left(p^{*}-S(q)\right)dq$ [M1]; the triangle has base $q^{*}$ and height $p^{*}-10=25.73$ [A1]; $\dfrac12\times51.46\times25.73$ [A1]; \$662 [A1] [4 marks] (d) total $=\$2037$ [A1]; $\dfrac{1375}{2037}\times100=67.5\%$ [A1] [2 marks] (e) strip width $=\dfrac{q^{*}}{4}=12.86$ [A1]; trapezoidal estimate \$1,393 [A1][A1]; error $=\dfrac{1393-1375}{1375}\times100=1.29\%$ [A1] [4 marks] (f) the demand curve is convex (curves upward) [R1]; so each chord lies above the curve [R1] [2 marks]
tips: The surpluses are areas of regions bounded by the demand and supply curves and the equilibrium price line.

subtopic: Volume of revolution of a reciprocal curve
statement: The region bounded by the curve $y=\dfrac{1}{x}$, the $x$-axis and the lines $x=1$ and $x=3$ is rotated through $360^{\circ}$ about the $x$-axis. (a) Write down an integral for the volume of the solid. [2] (b) Find the exact volume. [2]
tips: The volume of revolution about the $x$-axis is $\pi\int y^{2}\,dx$.

subtopic: Antiderivative with a condition and a definite integral
statement: A function $f$ satisfies $f'(x)=3x^{2}-4x+1$ and $f(2)=5$. (a) Find $f(x)$. [4] (b) Find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_{1}^{3}f'(x)\,dx$. [2] (c) Solve $f'(x)=0$. [2]
tips: Do not forget the constant of integration; use the given point to find it.

subtopic: Integrating linear functions of x
statement: (a) Find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_0^1(2x+1)^4\,dx$. [3] (b) Find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/6}\cos3x\,dx$. [3] (c) Find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_1^2\frac1{3x-2}\,dx$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\left[\frac{(2x+1)^5}{10}\right]_0^1$ [M1] [A1] $=\frac{243-1}{10}=\frac{121}5$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\left[\frac13\sin3x\right]_0^{\pi/6}$ [M1] [A1] $=\frac13\sin\frac\pi2-0=\frac13$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\left[\frac13\ln(3x-2)\right]_1^2$ [M1] $=\frac13\ln4$ (accept $\frac23\ln2$) [A1] [2 marks]
tips: For $\int f(ax+b)\,dx$, integrate $f$ and divide by $a$. Substitute the limits exactly and simplify values such as $\sin\frac\pi2$.

subtopic: An exact definite integral
statement: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{1}^{4}\left(\sqrt{x}+\dfrac{2}{x^{2}}\right)dx$, giving an exact value. (a) Find an antiderivative of $\sqrt{x}+\dfrac{2}{x^{2}}$. [2] (b) Hence evaluate the integral. [3]
markscheme: (a) $x^{1/2}+2x^{-2}$ [M1]; $\dfrac23x^{3/2}-\dfrac2x$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) upper limit: $\dfrac{16}{3}-\dfrac12$ [A1]; lower limit: $\dfrac23-2$ [A1]; difference $\dfrac{37}{6}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Rewrite $\frac{2}{x^{2}}$ as $2x^{-2}$ before integrating.

subtopic: Volume of revolution using the GDC
statement: The region bounded by $y=e^{x/2}$, the $x$-axis, the $y$-axis and the line $x=2$ is rotated through $360^{\circ}$ about the $x$-axis. (a) Write down an integral for the volume. [2] (b) Find the volume to three significant figures. [2] (c) Find the exact volume. [2]
markscheme: (a) $V=\pi\int_0^2\left(e^{x/2}\right)^{2}dx$ [M1]; $\pi\int_0^2e^{x}\,dx$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) evaluate using the GDC [M1]; $20.1$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\pi\left[e^{x}\right]_0^2$ [M1]; $\pi(e^{2}-1)$ [A1] [2 marks]

subtopic: Finding a function from its derivative and a point
statement: The gradient function of a curve is $f'(x)=6 x^{2} - 4 x + 2 e^{2 x}$ and the curve passes through $(0,5)$. Find $f(x)$. [4]
tips: Do not forget the constant of integration; use the given point to find it.

subtopic: Total rainfall from a rate of rainfall
statement: During a storm, rain falls at a rate of $R(t)=4\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{12}\right)$ mm per hour, for $0\le t\le12$ hours. (a) Find the greatest rate of rainfall and the time at which it occurs. [2] (b) Find the total rainfall during the $12$ hours, to three significant figures. [3] (c) Find the time by which half of the total rainfall has fallen. [2]
markscheme: (a) $4$ mm/h [A1]; at $t=6$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\int_0^{12}4\sin\left(\frac{\pi t}{12}\right)dt$ [M1]; $\dfrac{96}{\pi}$ [A1]; $30.6$ mm [A1] [3 marks] (c) by symmetry about $t=6$ [R1]; $t=6$ hours [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The total change is the integral of the rate of change over the interval.

subtopic: Exact volumes of revolution about the x-axis
statement: The inside of a decorative bowl is formed by rotating the curve $y=\sqrt{x+1}$, for $0\le x\le3$, through $360^\circ$ about the $x$-axis, where $x$ and $y$ are in centimeters. (a) Write down an integral for the volume $V$ of the solid formed. [2] (b) Find the exact value of $V$. [3] (c) A second solid is formed by rotating the curve $y=\dfrac2x$, for $1\le x\le4$, through $360^\circ$ about the $x$-axis. Find the exact volume of this solid. [3]
markscheme: (a) $V=\pi\displaystyle\int_0^3\left(\sqrt{x+1}\right)^2\mathrm{d}x$ [M1] $=\pi\displaystyle\int_0^3(x+1)\,\mathrm{d}x$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\pi\left[\dfrac{x^2}{2}+x\right]_0^3$ [M1] $=\pi\left(\dfrac92+3\right)$ [A1] $=\dfrac{15\pi}{2}\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\pi\displaystyle\int_1^4\dfrac{4}{x^2}\,\mathrm{d}x=4\pi\left[-\dfrac1x\right]_1^4$ [M1] $=4\pi\left(-\dfrac14+1\right)$ [A1] $=3\pi\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The volume formula is $V=\pi\int y^2\,\mathrm{d}x$, so square the function first (the square root disappears here). For $\int x^{-2}\,\mathrm{d}x$ use $-x^{-1}$.

subtopic: Total cost from a marginal cost function
statement: A factory's marginal cost, in dollars per unit, when $x$ units have been produced is $\mathrm{MC}(x)=0.002x^2-0.6x+60$, for $0\le x\le300$. (a) Find the increase in total cost when production rises from $100$ units to $200$ units, correct to the nearest dollar. [2] (b) The fixed cost, which is the total cost when $x=0$, is \$5000. Find an expression for the total cost $C(x)$. [3] (c) Find the total cost of producing $150$ units. [1] (d) Find the production level at which the marginal cost is least, and the least marginal cost. [2]
tips: Total cost is the integral of marginal cost plus the fixed cost. In part (d), the marginal cost is itself a function, so minimize it by differentiating it (or use the GDC minimum function).

subtopic: Area of a metal plate between an exponential and a parabola
statement: A metal plate is cut so that its upper edge follows the curve $y=6-x^2$ and its lower edge follows the curve $y=\mathrm{e}^{0.5x}$, where $x$ and $y$ are in centimeters. The two edges meet at two points. (a) Find the $x$-coordinates of the two points where the edges meet, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (b) Find the area of the plate, correct to 3 significant figures. [3] (c) The plate is coated at a cost of \$0.35 per square centimeter. Use the unrounded area to find the cost of coating one face of the plate, to the nearest cent. [2]
markscheme: (a) Solve $6-x^2=\mathrm{e}^{0.5x}$ on the GDC [M1] $x=-2.39$ and $x=1.86$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Area $=\displaystyle\int_{-2.3868}^{1.8612}\left(6-x^2-\mathrm{e}^{0.5x}\right)\mathrm{d}x$ [M1][A1] $=14.3\ \mathrm{cm}^2$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $14.3408\times0.35$ [M1] $=\$5.02$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Store the intersection points in your GDC's memory and reuse the unrounded values as the limits. Area between curves is the integral of the upper curve minus the lower curve.

subtopic: Volume of a vase by rotation and the trapezoidal rule
statement: A vase is modeled by rotating the region under the curve $y=1+\sqrt{x}$, for $0\le x\le9$, through $360^{\circ}$ about the $x$-axis. Here $x$ cm is the height above the base and $y$ cm is the radius of the vase at that height. (a) Write down the radius of the vase at its base and at its top. [2] (b) Show that the volume of the vase is $\dfrac{171\pi}{2}$ cm$^{3}$ and find its value correct to 3 significant figures. [5] (c) Use the trapezoidal rule with $3$ equal strips to estimate $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{9}\left(1+\sqrt{x}\right)^{2}dx$, and hence an estimate of the volume, correct to 3 significant figures. [4] (d) State, with a reason, whether the trapezoidal estimate is an underestimate or an overestimate. [2] (e) Water is poured into the vase at a constant rate of $20$ cm$^{3}$ per second. Find the time to fill the vase, correct to 3 significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) base: $y=1$ cm [A1]; top: $y=1+3=4$ cm [A1] [2 marks] (b) $V=\pi\displaystyle\int_{0}^{9}\left(1+\sqrt{x}\right)^{2}dx$ [M1]; $=\pi\displaystyle\int_{0}^{9}\left(1+2x^{1/2}+x\right)dx$ [A1]; $=\pi\left[x+\dfrac43x^{3/2}+\dfrac{x^{2}}{2}\right]_{0}^{9}$ [A1]; $=\pi(9+36+40.5)$ [A1]; $\dfrac{171\pi}{2}=269$ cm$^{3}$ [AG] [5 marks] (c) $h=3$ and values $1,\ 7.464,\ 11.899,\ 16$ [A1][A1]; $\dfrac32\left(1+2\times7.464+2\times11.899+16\right)=83.6$ [M1]; volume $\approx263$ cm$^{3}$ [A1] [4 marks] (d) underestimate [A1]; the function $\left(1+\sqrt{x}\right)^{2}$ is concave, so the chords lie below the curve [R1] [2 marks] (e) $\dfrac{85.5\pi}{20}$ [M1]; $13.4$ seconds [A1] [2 marks]
tips: For rotation about the $x$-axis, $V=\pi\int y^{2}\,dx$. A concave integrand makes the trapezoidal rule underestimate.

subtopic: Accuracy of the trapezoidal rule for the integral of 1/x
statement: This question investigates how accurately the trapezoidal rule approximates $I=\displaystyle\int_1^2\dfrac1x\,\mathrm{d}x$ and how the error behaves as the number of strips increases. Let $T_n$ be the trapezoidal rule estimate of $I$ using $n$ equal strips, and let $E_n=T_n-I$. (a) Find the exact value of $I$ and write it correct to 5 significant figures. [2] (b) Show that $T_4=0.69702$, correct to 5 significant figures, stating the function values used. [3] (c) Use your GDC to find $T_8$ correct to 5 significant figures, and find $E_4$ and $E_8$ correct to 3 significant figures. [4] (d) Find $\dfrac{E_4}{E_8}$, and hence suggest how $E_n$ depends on $n$. [2] (e) Show that the trapezoidal rule overestimates $I$ for every $n$, by considering the second derivative of $\dfrac1x$. [3] (f) Assume $E_n\approx\dfrac{c}{n^2}$ for some constant $c$. Use $E_4$ to find $c$, correct to 3 significant figures, and hence estimate the least number of strips needed for $E_n<1\times10^{-5}$. [4] (g) Consider the combination $\mathrm{R}=\dfrac{4T_8-T_4}{3}$. Find $\mathrm{R}$ correct to 5 significant figures and its error $\mathrm{R}-I$ correct to 3 significant figures, using unrounded values, and comment on its accuracy compared with $T_8$. [4] (h) The region under the curve $y=\dfrac1x$ for $1\le x\le2$ is rotated through $360^\circ$ about the $x$-axis. (i) Find the exact volume $V$ of the solid formed. (ii) Use the trapezoidal rule with $4$ strips to estimate $\displaystyle\int_1^2\dfrac1{x^2}\,\mathrm{d}x$ and hence estimate $V$, correct to 4 significant figures. (iii) Find the percentage error in your estimate of $V$, correct to 3 significant figures. [8]
markscheme: (a) $I=\left[\ln x\right]_1^2=\ln2$ [M1] $=0.69315$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $h=0.25$ and $f(1)=1$, $f(1.25)=0.8$, $f(1.5)=0.6667$, $f(1.75)=0.5714$, $f(2)=0.5$ [M1] $T_4=\dfrac{0.25}{2}\left[1+0.5+2(0.8+0.6667+0.5714)\right]$ [A1] $=0.69702$ [AG] [3 marks] (c) $T_8=\dfrac{0.125}{2}\left[f(1)+f(2)+2\left(f(1.125)+\dots+f(1.875)\right)\right]$ [M1] $=0.69412$ [A1] $E_4=0.69702-0.693147=0.00388$ [A1] $E_8=0.000975$ [A1] [4 marks] (d) $\dfrac{E_4}{E_8}=3.98\approx4$ [A1] Doubling $n$ divides the error by about $4$, so $E_n$ is approximately proportional to $\dfrac{1}{n^2}$ [R1] [2 marks] (e) $f(x)=x^{-1}$, $f'(x)=-x^{-2}$, $f''(x)=2x^{-3}$ [A1] $f''(x)>0$ for $1\le x\le2$ so the graph is concave up [R1] each chord lies above the curve, so each trapezium has area greater than the area under the curve, giving $T_n>I$ [R1] [3 marks] (f) $c=E_4\times4^2=0.0620$ [A1] $\dfrac{c}{n^2}<10^{-5}$ [M1] $n^2>6200$ so $n>78.8$ [A1] least $n=79$ [A1] [4 marks] (g) $\mathrm{R}=\dfrac{4(0.69412)-0.69702}{3}$ [M1] $=0.69315$ [A1] $\mathrm{R}-I=7.35\times10^{-6}$ [A1] This error (about $7\times10^{-6}$) is roughly $130$ times smaller than $E_8\approx9.75\times10^{-4}$, so $\mathrm{R}$ is much more accurate than $T_8$ [R1] [4 marks] (h) (i) $V=\pi\displaystyle\int_1^2\dfrac{1}{x^2}\,\mathrm{d}x=\pi\left[-\dfrac1x\right]_1^2$ [M1] $=\pi\left(-\dfrac12+1\right)$ [A1] $=\dfrac\pi2$ [A1] (ii) For $y=x^{-2}$: $\dfrac{0.25}{2}\left[1+0.25+2(0.64+0.4444+0.3265)\right]$ [M1] $=0.50899$ [A1] $V\approx\pi\times0.50899=1.599$ [A1] (iii) $\dfrac{1.5991-1.5708}{1.5708}\times100=1.80\%$ [M1][A1] [8 marks]
tips: In the final parts, remember the volume integral uses $\pi y^2$, so the trapezoidal rule must be applied to $y^2=\dfrac1{x^2}$, not to $\dfrac1x$. The $\dfrac{1}{n^2}$ pattern in part (d) is the key to part (f).

subtopic: Mean value over an interval
statement: The temperature $T^\circ$C inside a warehouse $t$ hours after midnight is modeled by $T(t)=15+8\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi(t-9)}{12}\right)$. The mean temperature between $t=a$ and $t=b$ is defined as $\dfrac1{b-a}\displaystyle\int_a^bT(t)\,dt$. (a) Find $\displaystyle\int_6^{18}T(t)\,dt$. [2] (b) Hence find the mean temperature between 06:00 and 18:00. [2] (c) Find the time at which the temperature first reaches $20^\circ$C, to the nearest minute. [2] (d) Write down the maximum temperature and the time at which it occurs. [1]
markscheme: (a) Use of definite integral on GDC [M1] $223$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\frac{223.2}{12}$ [M1] $18.6^\circ$C [A1] [2 marks] (c) $15+8\sin\left(\frac{\pi(t-9)}{12}\right)=20$ solved on GDC [M1] $t=11.58$, i.e. 11:35 [A1] [2 marks] (d) $23^\circ$C at $t=15$ (15:00) [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Use the stated definition of the mean value and check that the integral is evaluated in radians. For the time in minutes, convert $0.58$ hours to minutes.

subtopic: Temperature found by integrating a rate of change
statement: A metal rod is heated so that its temperature $T\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ changes at the rate $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}T}{\mathrm{d}t}=3\mathrm{e}^{-t/2}$, where $t$ is the time in minutes after heating starts. The initial temperature is $10\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. (a) Find an expression for $T$ in terms of $t$. [3] (b) Find the temperature after $4$ minutes, correct to 3 significant figures. [1] (c) Find the temperature that the rod approaches in the long run, with a reason. [2] (d) Find the time at which the temperature reaches $14\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, correct to 3 significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) $T=\displaystyle\int3\mathrm{e}^{-t/2}\,\mathrm{d}t=-6\mathrm{e}^{-t/2}+c$ [M1][A1] $T(0)=10$ gives $c=16$, so $T=16-6\mathrm{e}^{-t/2}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $T(4)=16-6\mathrm{e}^{-2}=15.2\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) As $t\to\infty$, $\mathrm{e}^{-t/2}\to0$ [R1] so $T\to16\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $16-6\mathrm{e}^{-t/2}=14$ [M1] $t=2\ln3=2.20$ minutes [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Integrating $\mathrm{e}^{-t/2}$ gives $-2\mathrm{e}^{-t/2}$, so the factor $3$ becomes $-6$. Use the initial condition to find the constant before answering later parts.

subtopic: Accumulation from a rate of flow
statement: Water flows into a tank at a rate $R(t)=12e^{-0.2t}$ liters per minute, where $t$ is the time in minutes since the flow began. The tank initially contains $30$ liters. (a) Show that the volume $V$ liters in the tank after $T$ minutes is $V=90-60e^{-0.2T}$. [3] (b) Find the time at which the tank contains $70$ liters. [3] (c) Find the value that the volume approaches in the long term, and explain your answer. [2]
tips: The amount accumulated is the integral of the rate, plus the initial amount. Check that your formula gives the initial volume at $T=0$.

subtopic: Area between a parabola and a line
statement: The graphs of $y=x^{2}+1$ and $y=5-x$ intersect at two points. (a) Find the $x$-coordinates of the intersection points, correct to 3 significant figures. [3] (b) Find the area of the region enclosed by the two graphs, correct to 3 significant figures. [3]
tips: Subtract the lower curve from the upper curve and integrate between the intersection points.

subtopic: Total cost from a marginal cost function
statement: The marginal cost, in dollars per unit, of producing the $x$th unit is $M(x)=0.03x^{2}-4x+200$. (a) Find the additional cost of increasing production from $100$ to $200$ units. [3] (b) Find the average additional cost per unit over this increase. [1] (c) Find the value of $x$ at which the marginal cost is smallest, and the smallest marginal cost. [3]
tips: The accumulated change in cost is the integral of the marginal cost.

subtopic: Area between an exponential and a line using a GDC
statement: The graphs of $f(x)=e^{\frac{x}{2}}$ and $g(x)=3 x - 1$ enclose a finite region. (a) Use your calculator to find the $x$-coordinates of the points where the two graphs intersect. [2] (b) Find the area of the region enclosed by the two graphs. [3] (c) Explain why it is not enough to evaluate $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx-\int_a^b g(x)\,dx$ without checking which function is greater. [1]
markscheme: (a) Solve $f(x)=g(x)$ [M1]: $x=0.841$ and $x=5.470$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Area $=\int_{0.841}^{5.470}|f(x)-g(x)|\,dx$ [M1][A1]; $=11.417$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) If the graphs swap order, the signed integrals partly cancel; the area uses upper minus lower on each section [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Sketch both graphs first so that you know which one is on top between the intersection points.

subtopic: Volume of revolution of a region between two parabolas
statement: The region $R$ is enclosed by the curves $y=x^2+1$ and $y=7-x^2$. The region is rotated through $360^\circ$ about the $x$-axis to form a solid, where $x$ and $y$ are in centimeters. (a) Show that the curves intersect at $x=\pm\sqrt3$. [2] (b) Write down an integral for the volume of the solid. [3] (c) Find the volume of the solid, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (d) Show that the exact volume is $64\sqrt3\,\pi\ \mathrm{cm^3}$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $x^2+1=7-x^2$ [M1] $2x^2=6$, so $x=\pm\sqrt3$ [AG] [2 marks] (b) The upper curve is $y=7-x^2$ and the lower curve is $y=x^2+1$ [M1] $V=\pi\displaystyle\int_{-\sqrt3}^{\sqrt3}\left[\left(7-x^2\right)^2-\left(x^2+1\right)^2\right]\mathrm{d}x$ [M1][A1] [3 marks] (c) $V=348\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (d) $\left(7-x^2\right)^2-\left(x^2+1\right)^2=48-16x^2$ [M1] $V=\pi\left[48x-\dfrac{16x^3}{3}\right]_{-\sqrt3}^{\sqrt3}=2\pi\left(48\sqrt3-16\sqrt3\right)$ [M1] $=64\sqrt3\,\pi$ [AG] [3 marks]
tips: For a region between two curves rotated about the $x$-axis, subtract the squares of the functions, not the square of the difference: $V=\pi\int(y_{\text{upper}}^2-y_{\text{lower}}^2)\,\mathrm{d}x$. Using symmetry, the integral from $-\sqrt3$ to $\sqrt3$ is twice the integral from $0$ to $\sqrt3$.

subtopic: Reverse chain rule integrals
statement: (a) Find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_0^1xe^{x^2}\,dx$. [3] (b) Find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_0^2\frac{3x}{x^2+1}\,dx$. [3]
markscheme: (a) Recognize $\frac{d}{dx}e^{x^2}=2xe^{x^2}$ (or substitute $u=x^2$) [M1] $\left[\frac12e^{x^2}\right]_0^1$ [A1] $=\frac{e-1}{2}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Integrand is $\frac32\cdot\frac{2x}{x^2+1}$ [M1] $\left[\frac32\ln(x^2+1)\right]_0^2$ [A1] $=\frac32\ln5$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Look for an integrand of the form $f'(g(x))\,g'(x)$ or $\frac{g'(x)}{g(x)}$, and adjust constant factors. Check by differentiating your answer.

subtopic: Volume of a vase using a GDC
statement: A vase is modeled by rotating the curve $y=\sqrt{x} e^{- \frac{x}{4}} + 0.5$, for $0\leq x\leq6$ (units in decimeters), about the $x$-axis. (a) Write down an integral for the volume of the solid formed by rotating the region about the $x$-axis. [2] (b) Use your calculator to evaluate the volume, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (c) Find the radius of the solid at its widest point and the position at which it occurs. [3]
markscheme: (a) $V=\pi\int_{0}^{6}\left(\sqrt{x} e^{- \frac{x}{4}} + 0.5\right)^2dx$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (b) $V=28.33$ (units$^3$) [M1][A1] $\approx28.3$ [2 marks] (c) Use the maximum function [M1]; widest radius $1.358$ at $x=2.000$ [A1][A1] [3 marks]
tips: Use the exact function (not a rounded copy) in the GDC integral; $V=\pi\int y^2dx$.

subtopic: Water pumped into a tank at a sinusoidal rate
statement: Water is pumped into a storage tank at a rate $r(t)=12+8\sin(0.4t)$ cubic meters per hour, where $t$ is the time in hours and $0\le t\le10$. (a) Find the volume of water pumped in during the first $10$ hours, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (b) The tank initially contains $50\ \mathrm{m^3}$ of water. Find the volume in the tank after $10$ hours. [1] (c) Find the first time at which the rate of pumping is exactly $15\ \mathrm{m^3\,h^{-1}}$, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (d) Find the mean rate of pumping over the first $10$ hours. [1]
tips: Use your GDC's numerical integration with the angle in radians (check the mode). For (c), solve the equation numerically or rearrange to $\sin(0.4t)=0.375$ and take the first solution.

subtopic: Integrals with a parameter
statement: (a) Given that $k>0$ and $\displaystyle\int_0^k\frac1{2x+1}\,dx=\ln3$, find the value of $k$. [4] (b) Find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_0^{\ln2}\left(e^x+e^{-x}\right)dx$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\left[\frac12\ln(2x+1)\right]_0^k$ [A1] $=\frac12\ln(2k+1)$ [M1] $\frac12\ln(2k+1)=\ln3$, so $2k+1=9$ [M1] $k=4$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $\left[e^x-e^{-x}\right]_0^{\ln2}$ [A1] $=\left(2-\frac12\right)-(1-1)$ [M1] $=\frac32$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Take care with $\int e^{-x}\,dx=-e^{-x}$. When a log equation appears, use $a\ln b=\ln b^a$ before removing logarithms.

subtopic: Area between a curve and a line
statement: The region $R$ is enclosed by the graphs of $y=\sqrt x$ and $y=\dfrac x2$. (a) Find the $x$-coordinates of the points where the graphs intersect. [2] (b) Find the exact area of $R$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $\sqrt x=\frac x2$, so $x=\frac{x^2}4$ [M1] $x=0$ and $x=4$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\displaystyle\int_0^4\left(\sqrt x-\frac x2\right)dx$ [M1] $=\left[\frac23x^{3/2}-\frac{x^2}4\right]_0^4$ [A1] [A1] $=\frac{16}3-4=\frac43$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: The upper curve minus the lower curve gives the integrand. Check which is larger by testing a point between the intersections, such as $x=1$.

subtopic: Exact area enclosed between a parabola and a line
statement: A garden bed is bounded by the curve $y=x^2$ and the straight path $y=2x+3$, where $x$ and $y$ are in meters. (a) Find the $x$-coordinates of the two points where the path meets the curve. [2] (b) Find the exact area of the garden bed. [4]
tips: Area between curves is $\int(\text{upper}-\text{lower})\,\mathrm{d}x$. Be careful with signs when substituting the lower limit $x=-1$.

subtopic: Volume of a vase from a rotated sinusoidal profile
statement: The outer surface of a vase is formed by rotating the curve $y=2+\sin(0.5x)$, for $0\le x\le8$, through $360^\circ$ about the $x$-axis, where $x$ and $y$ are in centimeters. (a) Write down an integral for the volume of the vase. [2] (b) Find the volume of the vase, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (c) Find the greatest diameter of the vase. [2]
markscheme: (a) $V=\pi\displaystyle\int_0^8\left(2+\sin(0.5x)\right)^2\mathrm{d}x$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (b) $V=153\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ [A1][A1] [2 marks] (c) The greatest radius occurs when $\sin(0.5x)=1$, which is at $x=\pi$ (within the interval) [M1] greatest radius $=3$, so the greatest diameter is $6\ \mathrm{cm}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Remember to square the whole expression $2+\sin(0.5x)$ and include the factor $\pi$. For the greatest radius, use the maximum value of the sine function, but check that it occurs inside the interval.

subtopic: Reservoir volume from a net rate of change
statement: The volume of water $V$ in a reservoir, in millions of liters, changes at a rate $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}V}{\mathrm{d}t}=6+3\sin(0.5t)-1.2t$, where $t$ is the time in days and $0\le t\le12$. Initially $V=120$. (a) Find the value of $t$ at which $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}V}{\mathrm{d}t}=0$, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (b) Justify that $V$ is greatest at this value of $t$. [2] (c) Find the greatest volume of water in the reservoir, correct to 3 significant figures. [3] (d) Find the time at which the volume first returns to $120$ million liters after reaching its greatest value, correct to 3 significant figures. [3] (e) A warning is issued if the volume falls below $110$ million liters. Find the volume at $t=12$ and the time at which the warning is first issued. Give your answers correct to 3 significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) Solve $6+3\sin(0.5t)-1.2t=0$ on the GDC [M1] $t=5.71$ days [A1] [2 marks] (b) The rate is positive before $t=5.71$ (for example at $t=5$ it is $1.80$) and negative after (for example at $t=6$ it is $-0.777$) [R1] so $V$ increases and then decreases, giving a maximum at $t=5.71$ [R1] [2 marks] (c) $V=120+\displaystyle\int_0^{5.7085}\left(6+3\sin(0.5t)-1.2t\right)\mathrm{d}t$ [M1][A1] $=146$ million liters [A1] [3 marks] (d) $\displaystyle\int_0^{t}\left(6+3\sin(0.5u)-1.2u\right)\mathrm{d}u=0$ with $t>5.71$ [M1][A1] $t=10.5$ days [A1] [3 marks] (e) $V(12)=120+\displaystyle\int_0^{12}\left(6+3\sin(0.5t)-1.2t\right)\mathrm{d}t=106$ million liters [A1] Solve $V=110$ for $t>5.71$ [M1] $t=11.6$ days [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The reservoir volume is $V(t)=V(0)+\int_0^t\frac{\mathrm{d}V}{\mathrm{d}u}\,\mathrm{d}u$. A maximum of $V$ occurs where its derivative changes sign from positive to negative, so show the sign change rather than only solving for zero.

subtopic: Trapezoidal rule from tabulated rainfall rates
statement: The rate of rainfall, $r$ millimeters per hour, is recorded at hourly intervals. $t$ (hours): 0, 1, 2, 3, 4; $r$: 0, 4, 6, 5, 2. (a) Use the trapezoidal rule with $4$ strips to estimate $\displaystyle\int_0^4 r\,\mathrm{d}t$. [3] (b) State what this integral represents, including units. [1] (c) The graph of $r$ against $t$ is concave down for $0\le t\le4$. State, with a reason, whether your estimate in part (a) is an overestimate or an underestimate. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac12(1)\left[0+2+2(4+6+5)\right]$ [M1][A1] $=16$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) The total rainfall in the $4$ hours, in millimeters [A1] [1 mark] (c) The estimate is an underestimate [A1] because on a concave-down graph the chords lie below the curve, so the trapezia have smaller area than the region under the curve [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Trapezoidal rule: $\dfrac h2\left[\text{first}+\text{last}+2(\text{sum of the others})\right]$. For a concave-down curve the trapezoidal rule underestimates, and for a concave-up curve it overestimates.

subtopic: Cumulative drug dose with an unknown upper limit
statement: A drug is absorbed into the bloodstream at a rate $r(t)=20\mathrm{e}^{-0.25t}$ milligrams per hour, where $t$ is the time in hours after the drug is taken. (a) Find the amount of drug absorbed during the first $2$ hours, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (b) Find the time $k$ at which a total of $50$ mg has been absorbed, correct to 3 significant figures. [3] (c) Show that the total amount absorbed over all time cannot exceed $80$ mg. [2] (d) Find the time at which the rate of absorption first falls below $1$ mg per hour, correct to 3 significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\displaystyle\int_0^2 20\mathrm{e}^{-0.25t}\,\mathrm{d}t=80\left(1-\mathrm{e}^{-0.5}\right)$ [M1] $=31.5$ mg [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\displaystyle\int_0^k20\mathrm{e}^{-0.25t}\,\mathrm{d}t=80\left(1-\mathrm{e}^{-0.25k}\right)=50$ [M1] $\mathrm{e}^{-0.25k}=0.375$ [A1] $k=3.92$ hours [A1] [3 marks] (c) The amount absorbed by time $k$ is $80\left(1-\mathrm{e}^{-0.25k}\right)$ [M1] and $\mathrm{e}^{-0.25k}>0$, so the amount is always less than $80$ mg (it approaches $80$ as $k\to\infty$) [R1] [2 marks] (d) $20\mathrm{e}^{-0.25t}<1$ [M1] $t>4\ln20=12.0$ hours [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The amount absorbed up to time $k$ is the definite integral $\int_0^k r(t)\,\mathrm{d}t$. Setting it equal to a target value gives an equation in $k$ that you can solve algebraically or with your GDC solver.

subtopic: Trapezoidal rule for the area of a curved lawn
statement: The curved edge of a lawn is modeled by $y=\sqrt x$ for $1\le x\le5$, where $x$ and $y$ are in meters. The lawn lies between this edge and the $x$-axis. (a) Use the trapezoidal rule with $4$ equal strips to estimate the area of the lawn, correct to 4 significant figures. [3] (b) Use your GDC to find the exact area of the lawn, correct to 4 significant figures. [1] (c) Explain, using the shape of the curve, why the trapezoidal rule gives an underestimate. [2] (d) Find the percentage error in your estimate from part (a), correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (e) Using your GDC, find the least number of strips for which the trapezoidal rule has a percentage error of less than $0.1\%$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $h=1$: $\dfrac12(1)\left[\sqrt1+\sqrt5+2\left(\sqrt2+\sqrt3+\sqrt4\right)\right]$ [M1][A1] $=6.764\ \mathrm{m^2}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\displaystyle\int_1^5\sqrt x\,\mathrm{d}x=6.787\ \mathrm{m^2}$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) The curve $y=\sqrt x$ is concave down (second derivative $-\dfrac14x^{-3/2}<0$) [R1] so each chord lies below the curve and the trapezia have less area than the region under the curve [R1] [2 marks] (d) $\dfrac{6.7869-6.7643}{6.7869}\times100$ [M1] $=0.333\%$ [A1] [2 marks] (e) Calculating the trapezoidal estimate for increasing $n$: $n=7$ gives an error of about $0.11\%$ and $n=8$ gives $0.084\%$ [M1] so the least number of strips is $8$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Percentage error is $\dfrac{|\text{exact}-\text{approximate}|}{\text{exact}}\times100$. Keep full calculator accuracy in part (d) rather than the rounded values.

subtopic: Trapezoidal rule from tabulated depth readings
statement: The depth $d$ meters of a river is measured at distances $x$ meters from one bank: $x=0,2,4,6,8,10$ with $d=0,3.2,5.9,7.4,6.8,3.1$ . (a) Use the trapezoidal rule with 5 intervals to estimate the cross-sectional area of the river. [3] (b) The river flows at an average speed of $0.8$ m/s. Estimate the volume of water passing per second. [2] (c) State, with a reason, whether the estimate is likely to be an underestimate or overestimate if the depth profile is concave down between readings. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{h}{2}\left(y_0+2(y_1+\dots+y_4)+y_5\right)$ with $h=2$ [M1][A1]; $=49.7$ m$^2$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Flow $=0.8\times49.7$ [M1] $=39.76$ m$^3$/s [A1] [2 marks] (c) Underestimate [A1]; the chords of a concave-down curve lie below the curve, so the trapezia have less area [R1] [2 marks]
tips: The trapezoidal rule adds $h/2$ times (first + last + twice the rest); concavity tells you whether it overestimates or underestimates.

subtopic: Net signed area and total area
statement: Let $f(x)=x^{2}-2x$ for $0\le x\le3$. (a) Find $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{3}f(x)\,dx$ and explain what a value of $0$ means for the signed area. [3] (b) Find the total area enclosed between the graph of $f$ and the $x$-axis for $0\le x\le3$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\left[\dfrac{x^{3}}{3}-x^{2}\right]_0^3=9-9=0$ [M1][A1]; the area below the axis cancels the area above it [R1] [3 marks] (b) $f(x)=0$ at $x=0,2$ [A1]; $\left|\int_0^2f\right|=\dfrac43$ and $\int_2^3f=\dfrac43$ [M1]; total $\dfrac83$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: To find a total area, split the integral where the curve crosses the $x$-axis and add the absolute values.

subtopic: Trigonometric acceleration: velocity never changes sign, distance equals displacement
statement: A particle starts at the origin $O$ and moves along a straight line. Its acceleration at time $t$ seconds is $a=8\sin2t\ \text{m s}^{-2}$, and its initial velocity is $0$. (a) Find an expression for the velocity $v$. [3] (b) Hence show that the particle never moves in the negative direction. [2] (c) Find the distance traveled by the particle during the first $\pi$ seconds. [3]
markscheme: (a) $v=\displaystyle\int8\sin2t\,dt=-4\cos2t+c$ [M1][A1] $v(0)=0$ gives $c=4$, so $v=4-4\cos2t$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $v=4(1-\cos2t)$ [M1] Since $\cos2t\le1$, $v\ge0$ for all $t$, so the particle never moves in the negative direction [R1] [2 marks] (c) $s=\displaystyle\int(4-4\cos2t)\,dt=4t-2\sin2t$ with $s(0)=0$ [M1][A1] Since $v\ge0$, distance equals displacement: $s(\pi)=4\pi$ m [A1] [3 marks]
tips: If the velocity never changes sign, the distance traveled equals the magnitude of the displacement, so no splitting of the interval is needed. Use the initial condition immediately after each integration.

subtopic: Simple harmonic style displacement: acceleration relation and maximum speed via amplitude
statement: Consider a particle on a straight line whose displacement from a fixed point $O$ at time $t$ seconds is $s=3\sin2t+4\cos2t$ meters. (a) Find an expression for the velocity of the particle. [2] (b) Show that the acceleration $a$ satisfies $a=-4s$. [2] (c) Find the maximum speed of the particle. [3]
markscheme: (a) $v=\dfrac{ds}{dt}=6\cos2t-8\sin2t$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (b) $a=\dfrac{dv}{dt}=-12\sin2t-16\cos2t$ [M1][A1] $=-4(3\sin2t+4\cos2t)=-4s$ [AG] [2 marks] (c) Write $6\cos2t-8\sin2t=R\cos(2t+\alpha)$ with $R=\sqrt{6^2+8^2}$ [M1] $R=10$ [A1] The maximum speed is $10\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Combining a sine and a cosine of the same angle into a single cosine gives the amplitude immediately, which is the maximum value of $|v|$. Differentiate twice and compare with $s$ for the acceleration relation.

subtopic: Resistive acceleration using a = v dv/ds and a = dv/dt
statement: A particle moves in a straight line with $s$ meters its displacement from the origin $O$ at time $t$ seconds. The velocity of the particle is $v\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ and its acceleration is $a=-\dfrac12v^2$. When $t=0$, $s=0$ and $v=8$. (a) By using $a=v\dfrac{dv}{ds}$, show that $v=8e^{-\frac s2}$. [4] (b) Find the displacement of the particle when $v=2$. Give your answer in the form $k\ln2$. [2] (c) By using $a=\dfrac{dv}{dt}$, show that $v=\dfrac{8}{4t+1}$. [3] (d) Find an expression for $s$ in terms of $t$, and hence verify your answer to part (b). [3]
markscheme: (a) $v\dfrac{dv}{ds}=-\dfrac12v^2$, so $\dfrac{dv}{ds}=-\dfrac12v$ [M1] $\displaystyle\int\dfrac1v\,dv=\int-\dfrac12\,ds$ [M1] $\ln v=-\dfrac s2+c$ [A1] Using $v=8$ when $s=0$: $v=8e^{-\frac s2}$ [A1][AG] [4 marks] (b) $2=8e^{-\frac s2}$, so $e^{-\frac s2}=\dfrac14$ [M1] $s=2\ln4=4\ln2$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\dfrac{dv}{dt}=-\dfrac12v^2$, so $\displaystyle\int v^{-2}\,dv=\int-\dfrac12\,dt$ [M1] $-\dfrac1v=-\dfrac t2+c$ and $v=8$ at $t=0$ gives $c=-\dfrac18$ [A1] $\dfrac1v=\dfrac t2+\dfrac18=\dfrac{4t+1}{8}$, so $v=\dfrac{8}{4t+1}$ [A1][AG] [3 marks] (d) $s=\displaystyle\int\dfrac{8}{4t+1}\,dt=2\ln(4t+1)+c$ [M1] $s=0$ when $t=0$ gives $c=0$, so $s=2\ln(4t+1)$ [A1] $v=2$ when $4t+1=4$, so $t=\dfrac34$ and $s=2\ln4=4\ln2$, which agrees with part (b) [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Choose the form of acceleration that matches the variables you are given: $v\,dv/ds$ when the variable is displacement, $dv/dt$ when it is time. Always use the initial values to find the constants of integration.

subtopic: Position from velocity vector of a kayak on a lagoon
statement: A kayak moves on a calm lagoon. Relative to a buoy at the origin $O$, the velocity of the kayak at time $t$ seconds is $\mathbf v(t)=\begin{pmatrix} 3\cos(0.5t) \\ 2\sin(0.5t) \end{pmatrix}$ m s$^{-1}$, and the kayak is at the point $(0,-4)$ when $t=0$. (a) Find the position vector $\mathbf r(t)$ of the kayak. [3] (b) Find the speed of the kayak at $t=2$. [2] (c) Find the first time at which the speed of the kayak is $2.5$ m s$^{-1}$. [3] (d) Find the magnitude of the acceleration of the kayak at $t=2$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $x=6\sin(0.5t)+C_1$ and $y=-4\cos(0.5t)+C_2$ [M1][A1] using $\mathbf r(0)=\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ -4 \end{pmatrix}$: $C_1=0$, $C_2=0$, so $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix} 6\sin(0.5t) \\ -4\cos(0.5t) \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\sqrt{(3\cos1)^2+(2\sin1)^2}$ [M1] $=2.34$ m s$^{-1}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $9\cos^2(0.5t)+4\sin^2(0.5t)=6.25$ [M1] equivalent to $4+5\cos^2(0.5t)=6.25$, so $\cos(0.5t)=0.671$ [A1] $t=1.67$ s [A1] [3 marks] (d) $\mathbf a=\begin{pmatrix} -1.5\sin(0.5t) \\ \cos(0.5t) \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $|\mathbf a(2)|=1.37$ m s$^{-2}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Integrate each component and use the initial position vector to fix both constants. Speed is the magnitude of the velocity vector; set its square equal to $2.5^2$ and solve on your GDC.

subtopic: Velocity and displacement from acceleration
statement: A particle moves in a straight line. Its acceleration at time $t$ seconds is $a=6t-4$ m s$^{-2}$. When $t=0$ the velocity is $-4$ m s$^{-1}$ and the displacement from the origin is $1$ m. (a) Find an expression for the velocity $v$ at time $t$. [3] (b) Find the displacement $s$ at time $t$, given that $s=1$ when $t=0$. [3] (c) Find the velocity and the displacement when $t=3$. [2] (d) Find the time(s), for $t>0$, at which the particle is momentarily at rest. [2]
tips: Integrate once for velocity and again for displacement, using each initial condition to find its constant.

subtopic: Velocity from acceleration and checking the particle never rests
statement: A particle moves in a straight line. Its acceleration at time $t$ seconds, for $t\ge0$, is $a=6t-4\ \text{m s}^{-2}$. When $t=0$ the velocity is $3\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ and the displacement is $s=0$. (a) Find an expression for the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$. [2] (b) Show that the particle never changes direction. [2] (c) Find the displacement of the particle when $t=2$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $v=\displaystyle\int(6t-4)\,dt=3t^2-4t+c$ [M1] $v(0)=3$, so $v=3t^2-4t+3$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Discriminant of $3t^2-4t+3$ is $16-36=-20<0$ [M1] so $v\ne0$ for all $t$ (and $v(0)>0$, so $v>0$): the particle never changes direction [R1] [2 marks] (c) $s=t^3-2t^2+3t$ [M1] $s(2)=8-8+6=6$ m [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A particle can only change direction when its velocity changes sign, so look for real roots of $v=0$. The discriminant is a quick way to rule them out.

subtopic: Logarithmic displacement of a barge after engine cut
statement: After its engine is cut, a cargo barge drifts along a straight canal with velocity $v(t)=\dfrac{1}{2t+1}$ m s$^{-1}$, $t\ge0$. Let $s(t)$ be the distance in meters from the point where the engine is cut, so $s(0)=0$. (a) Find the acceleration of the barge as a function of $t$, and its value at $t=0$. [2] (b) Find an expression for $s(t)$. [3] (c) Find the exact time at which $s=\ln3$. [2]
tips: The reverse chain rule for $\dfrac{1}{ax+b}$ gives $\dfrac1a\ln|ax+b|$; do not forget the $\frac12$. Use $2\ln3=\ln9$ to solve exactly.

subtopic: Velocity and displacement from a linear acceleration
statement: A particle moves on a straight line with acceleration $a=6t-4$ m/s$^{2}$ at time $t$ seconds. When $t=0$, its velocity is $3$ m/s and its displacement is $0$ m. (a) Find the velocity as a function of $t$. [2] (b) Find the displacement as a function of $t$. [2] (c) Find the velocity and the displacement at $t=2$. [2]
tips: Integrate once for velocity and again for displacement, using each initial condition.

subtopic: Piecewise velocity described in words: areas under a velocity-time graph
statement: A particle moves in a straight line during the first $16$ seconds of its motion. Its velocity $v\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ at time $t$ seconds is as follows. For $0\le t\le4$, the velocity increases at a constant rate from $0$ to $8$. For $4\le t\le10$, the velocity is constant and equal to $8$. For $10\le t\le16$, the velocity decreases at a constant rate from $8$ to $-4$. (a) Write down the acceleration of the particle in each of the three time intervals. [3] (b) Find the time at which the particle is instantaneously at rest after $t=10$. [2] (c) Find the displacement of the particle from its starting position at $t=16$. [3] (d) Find the total distance traveled by the particle in the $16$ seconds. [2] (e) Find the average speed of the particle over the $16$ seconds. [1]
markscheme: (a) $2\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ for $0<t<4$, $0\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ for $4<t<10$, and $-2\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ for $10<t<16$ [A1][A1][A1] [3 marks] (b) For $10\le t\le16$: $v=8-2(t-10)=28-2t$ [M1] $v=0$ at $t=14$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Displacement is the signed area under the graph [M1] $\dfrac12(4)(8)+6(8)+\dfrac12(4)(8)-\dfrac12(2)(4)$ [A1] $=16+48+16-4=76$ m [A1] [3 marks] (d) Distance is the total unsigned area [M1] $16+48+16+4=84$ m [A1] [2 marks] (e) Average speed $=\dfrac{84}{16}=\dfrac{21}{4}=5.25\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Areas below the time axis count as negative for displacement but positive for distance. Average speed uses total distance, not displacement.

subtopic: Two particles moving on the same line: meeting time
statement: Two particles $A$ and $B$ move along the same straight line, with displacements $s_A$ and $s_B$ meters from a point $O$ at time $t$ seconds, for $0\le t\le6$. Particle $A$ starts at $O$, and has velocity $v_A=6t-t^2\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. Particle $B$ starts at the point with $s=30$ and moves toward $O$ with constant speed $2\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. (a) Find the maximum velocity of $A$. [2] (b) Show that $s_A=3t^2-\dfrac{t^3}{3}$. [2] (c) Find the time at which the two particles meet, and their displacement from $O$ at that time. [3] (d) Find the velocity of $A$ when the particles meet. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{dv_A}{dt}=6-2t=0$ gives $t=3$ [M1] $v_A(3)=9\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $s_A=\displaystyle\int\left(6t-t^2\right)dt=3t^2-\dfrac{t^3}{3}+c$ and $s_A(0)=0$ gives $c=0$ [M1][A1][AG] [2 marks] (c) $s_B=30-2t$ [A1] Solving $3t^2-\dfrac{t^3}{3}=30-2t$ with a GDC [M1] $t=3.55$ s, with displacement $22.9$ m [A1] [3 marks] (d) $v_A=6(3.55)-(3.55)^2=8.70\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: For a meeting problem write both displacements from the same origin and set them equal. $B$ moves toward $O$, so its displacement decreases: use a negative velocity.

subtopic: Particle with an oscillating displacement
statement: The displacement of a particle from a fixed point is $s(t)=2 t e^{- \frac{t}{2}} \sin{\left(t \right)} + 1$ meters at time $t$ seconds (radians for the sine). (a) Find the velocity and acceleration when $t=2$. [3] (b) Find the times in the interval $0<t<6$ at which the particle is at rest. [2] (c) Find the total distance traveled in the first 6 seconds. [3] (d) Find the greatest speed of the particle in the interval $0\leq t\leq6$ and when it occurs. [3]
markscheme: (a) $v=s'(t)=\left(-t \sin{\left(t \right)} + 2 t \cos{\left(t \right)} + 2 \sin{\left(t \right)}\right) e^{- \frac{t}{2}}$ [A1]; $a=v'(t)=\frac{\left(-3 t \sin{\left(t \right)} - 4 t \cos{\left(t \right)} - 4 \sin{\left(t \right)} + 8 \cos{\left(t \right)}\right) e^{- \frac{t}{2}}}{2}$ [A1]; $v(2)=-0.612$, $a(2)=-1.673$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Solve $v=0$ on the GDC [M1]: $t=1.669$, $t=4.444$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Distance $=\int_0^{6}|v|\,dt$ [M1][A1]; $=4.575$ m [A1] [3 marks] (d) Maximize $|v|$ on the interval (check endpoints) [M1]; greatest speed $1.372$ m s$^{-1}$ [A1] at $t=2.872$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Set the calculator to radian mode; solve $v=0$ numerically and integrate $|v|$ for the distance.

subtopic: Trapezoidal rule for distance from speed readings
statement: A GPS unit records the speed of a car, in m s$^{-1}$, every $5$ seconds as it accelerates onto a motorway. Time $t$ (s): 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25. Speed: 0, 4.2, 9.8, 13.1, 14.6, 15.0. (a) Use the trapezoidal rule with $5$ intervals to estimate the distance traveled in the $25$ seconds. [3] (b) Find the average acceleration during the first $10$ seconds. [1] (c) The increases in speed over successive $5$ second intervals are $4.2$, $5.6$, $3.3$, $1.5$ and $0.4$. Explain why it is not certain that your estimate in part (a) is an underestimate. [2] (d) Suggest one way to obtain a more accurate estimate of the distance. [1]
