markscheme: (a) $\frac52\left[0+15.0+2(4.2+9.8+13.1+14.6)\right]$ [M1][A1] $=246$ m [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\frac{9.8-0}{10}=0.98$ m s$^{-2}$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) the speed curve is concave up at first (increases are growing) where trapezoids overestimate [R1] and concave down later (increases are shrinking) where trapezoids underestimate, so the errors partly cancel and the overall sign cannot be determined [R1] [2 marks] (d) use more frequent readings (smaller intervals) [R1] [1 mark]
tips: The trapezoidal rule overestimates where the curve is concave up and underestimates where it is concave down. Growing differences between readings indicate concave up.

subtopic: Vector position with Pythagorean speed: speed, distance and velocity parallel to a given direction
statement: A particle moves in a plane. Its position vector relative to the origin $O$ at time $t\ge0$ seconds is $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix} \dfrac13t^3-t \\ t^2 \end{pmatrix}$ meters. (a) Find the velocity vector $\mathbf v(t)$, and hence the velocity and the speed of the particle when $t=2$. [3] (b) Show that the speed of the particle at time $t$ is $t^2+1$. [2] (c) Find the distance traveled by the particle between $t=0$ and $t=3$. [2] (d) Find the exact value of $t$ at which the particle is moving in the direction of the vector $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf v=\begin{pmatrix} t^2-1 \\ 2t \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\mathbf v(2)=\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] Speed $=\sqrt{9+16}=5\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $|\mathbf v|^2=(t^2-1)^2+(2t)^2=t^4+2t^2+1$ [M1] $=(t^2+1)^2$, so speed $=t^2+1$ since $t^2+1>0$ [A1][AG] [2 marks] (c) Distance $=\displaystyle\int_0^3(t^2+1)\,dt$ [M1] $=\left[\dfrac{t^3}{3}+t\right]_0^3=12$ m [A1] [2 marks] (d) The components must be equal and positive: $t^2-1=2t$ [M1] $t^2-2t-1=0$ [A1] $t=1+\sqrt2$ (the root $1-\sqrt2$ is negative and rejected) [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Speed is the magnitude of the velocity vector, and the distance traveled along a path is the integral of speed. For motion in a given direction, set the components of velocity in proportion and make sure both point the correct way.

subtopic: Plane motion with trigonometric component: velocity direction, distance along path and acceleration magnitude
statement: In a plane, a particle has position vector $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix} t^2-4t \\ 3\sin2t \end{pmatrix}$ meters relative to the origin at time $t\ge0$ seconds, where $2t$ is in radians. (a) Find the velocity vector $\mathbf v(t)$. The particle first moves parallel to the $y$-axis at time $t=T$; find $T$ and the velocity of the particle at this time. [4] (b) Find the distance traveled by the particle along its path from $t=0$ to $t=3$. [3] (c) Find the magnitude of the acceleration of the particle when $t=1.5$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf v=\begin{pmatrix} 2t-4 \\ 6\cos2t \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] Moving parallel to the $y$-axis requires $2t-4=0$ [M1] $T=2$ [A1] $\mathbf v(2)=\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ -3.92 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) Distance $=\displaystyle\int_0^3|\mathbf v|\,dt$ [M1] $=\displaystyle\int_0^3\sqrt{(2t-4)^2+36\cos^22t}\,dt$ [A1] $=12.8$ m [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\mathbf a=\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -12\sin2t \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] At $t=1.5$: $\mathbf a=\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -1.69 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $|\mathbf a|=2.62\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Set the calculator to radians for trigonometric functions of time. Path length is the integral of speed, not the magnitude of the displacement between the endpoints.

subtopic: Boat slowing after the engine is switched off
statement: After the engine of a boat is switched off, its velocity is modeled by $v=12e^{-0.15t}$ m s$^{-1}$, where $t$ is the time in seconds after switch-off. (a) Find an expression for the displacement from the start after $t$ seconds. [3] (b) Find the distance traveled in the first $3$ seconds. [2] (c) Show that the boat can never travel further than 80 m, and find how long it takes to travel 60 m. [4] (d) Find the acceleration when $t=0$ and when $t=5$. [3]
tips: Find the limit of the displacement first to decide which target distances are reachable.

subtopic: Energy and motion for a particle with a = -omega^2 s
statement: This question investigates a particle moving on a straight line with displacement $s=A\cos\omega t$ meters, where $A>0$ and $\omega>0$ are constants. (a) Show that the acceleration satisfies $a=-\omega^2s$. [3] (b) Show that $v^2=\omega^2\left(A^2-s^2\right)$. [3] (c) The particle has mass $m$ kg. Show that $\dfrac12mv^2+\dfrac12m\omega^2s^2$ is constant. [3] (d) Given $A=3$ and $\omega=2$, find the maximum speed, the maximum acceleration and the speed when $s=1.5$. [4] (e) Find the average speed over one complete oscillation, and compare it with the maximum speed. [3]
markscheme: (a) $v=-A\omega\sin\omega t$ [A1] $a=-A\omega^2\cos\omega t$ [A1] $=-\omega^2s$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $v^2=A^2\omega^2\sin^2\omega t$ [M1] $=A^2\omega^2\left(1-\cos^2\omega t\right)$ [A1] $=\omega^2\left(A^2-s^2\right)$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) substitute $v^2$ [M1] $\dfrac12m\omega^2\left(A^2-s^2\right)+\dfrac12m\omega^2s^2$ [A1] $=\dfrac12m\omega^2A^2$, constant [A1] [3 marks] (d) max speed $=A\omega=6$ m s$^{-1}$ [A1] max $|a|=A\omega^2=12$ m s$^{-2}$ [A1] $v^2=4\left(9-2.25\right)=27$ [M1] $v=3\sqrt3=5.20$ m s$^{-1}$ [A1] [4 marks] (e) distance in one period $=4A=12$ m [A1] period $=\dfrac{2\pi}\omega=\pi$ s [A1] average speed $=\dfrac{12}\pi=3.82$ m s$^{-1}$, which is $\dfrac2\pi$ of the maximum speed [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Differentiate twice for the acceleration, and eliminate $t$ using $\sin^2+\cos^2=1$ to relate $v$ and $s$.

subtopic: A cubic displacement function
statement: The displacement of a particle from the origin is $s=t^3-6t^2+9t$ meters, for $t\ge0$ seconds. (a) Find the velocity and acceleration as functions of $t$. [2] (b) Find the times at which the particle is at rest and its displacement at those times. [3] (c) Find the total distance travelled in the first $4$ seconds. [4]
tips: At rest means $v=0$. Add up the lengths of each stage between turning points.

subtopic: A skydiver approaching terminal velocity
statement: The velocity of a skydiver falling toward the ground is $v(t)=50\left(1-e^{-0.2t}\right)$ m/s, where $t$ is the time in seconds after jumping, measured downward. (a) Find the acceleration as a function of $t$ and its value at $t=0$. [3] (b) State the terminal velocity predicted by the model and explain what happens to the acceleration in the long run. [2] (c) Find the time at which the skydiver reaches $90\%$ of terminal velocity, to three significant figures. [3] (d) Find the distance fallen in the first $10$ seconds, to three significant figures. [3] (e) Find the exact distance fallen in time $T$ and use it to find the distance fallen when the speed reaches $90\%$ of terminal velocity, to three significant figures. [4] (f) The parachute opens after the skydiver has fallen $1500$ m. Use your GDC to find the time at which this happens, to three significant figures. [3]
tips: Displacement is the integral of velocity from $0$ to $T$; the acceleration tends to zero as the velocity approaches its limit.

subtopic: Acceleration given as an exponential: terminal velocity and displacement from rest
statement: A particle starts from rest at the origin $O$ and moves along a straight line with acceleration $a=12e^{-2t}\ \text{m s}^{-2}$, where $t$ is the time in seconds. (a) Find an expression for the velocity $v$ at time $t$. [3] (b) Find the value that $v$ approaches as $t\to\infty$, giving a reason. [1] (c) Show that the displacement from $O$ is $s=6t+3e^{-2t}-3$. [3] (d) Find the exact time at which the velocity is $3\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, and the exact displacement of the particle at that time. [3]
markscheme: (a) $v=\displaystyle\int12e^{-2t}\,dt=-6e^{-2t}+c$ [M1][A1] $v(0)=0$ gives $c=6$, so $v=6-6e^{-2t}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) As $t\to\infty$, $e^{-2t}\to0$, so $v\to6\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $s=\displaystyle\int(6-6e^{-2t})\,dt=6t+3e^{-2t}+k$ [M1][A1] $s(0)=0$ gives $3+k=0$, so $k=-3$ [A1] $s=6t+3e^{-2t}-3$ [AG] [3 marks] (d) $6-6e^{-2t}=3$ gives $e^{-2t}=\dfrac12$ [M1] $t=\dfrac12\ln2$ [A1] $s=3\ln2+\dfrac32-3=3\ln2-\dfrac32$ m [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Use the initial conditions after each integration to find the constants. A velocity that approaches a finite limit is a terminal velocity, found by letting $t\to\infty$.

subtopic: Sinusoidal velocity of a vehicle on an undulating road
statement: A vehicle travels along a straight, undulating road. Its velocity is modeled by $v(t)=15+8\sin(0.4t)$ m s$^{-1}$ for $0\le t\le20$, where $t$ is in seconds and the argument of the sine is in radians. (a) Write down the minimum and maximum speeds of the vehicle according to the model. [2] (b) Find the distance traveled by the vehicle in the $20$ seconds. [3] (c) Find the acceleration of the vehicle at $t=5$. [2] (d) Find the first time at which the acceleration is zero. [2]
tips: Make sure your GDC is in radian mode. The extreme values of $a+b\sin(ct)$ are $a\pm b$.

subtopic: Quadratic regression model for cyclist speed
statement: A cyclist sets off from traffic lights and then eases off. The cyclist's speed $v$ in m s$^{-1}$ was recorded each second. Time $t$ (s): 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Speed $v$: 0.0, 3.1, 5.2, 6.4, 6.8, 6.3. (a) Use your GDC to find the quadratic regression model $v=at^2+bt+c$, giving $a$, $b$ and $c$ to three significant figures. [2] (b) Use the model to find the maximum speed and the time at which it occurs. [2] (c) Use the model, with unrounded coefficients, to estimate the distance traveled in the first $5$ seconds. [2] (d) Find the time at which the model predicts the cyclist's speed is zero again, and comment on the validity of the model beyond this time. [2]
markscheme: (a) $a=-0.443$, $b=3.47$ [A1] $c=0.0286$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $t=-\frac{b}{2a}=3.91$ s [A1] $v=6.81$ m s$^{-1}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\int_0^5\left(at^2+bt+c\right)dt$ [M1] $=25.0$ m [A1] [2 marks] (d) $v=0$ gives $t=7.83$ s [A1] for $t>7.83$ the model gives negative speeds (for example $v(10)=-9.6$), which is not meaningful for a cyclist moving forward, so the model is only valid for $0\le t\le7.83$ [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Store the unrounded regression coefficients on your GDC and use them in later parts. Always comment on what the model predicts outside the data range.

subtopic: Distance traveled with velocity of the form t times exponential
statement: A remotely operated submarine moves in a straight line. Its velocity at time $t$ minutes, $t\ge0$, is modeled by $v=20te^{-0.3t}$ meters per minute. (a) Find the greatest speed of the submarine and the time at which it occurs. [3] (b) Find the distance traveled in the first $10$ minutes. [2] (c) Find the time at which the submarine has traveled $100$ meters. [2] (d) Find the distance traveled between $t=10$ and $t=30$. [2]
markscheme: (a) Maximize $v$ using the GDC (or solve $\dfrac{dv}{dt}=20e^{-0.3t}(1-0.3t)=0$) [M1] $t=3.33$ minutes [A1] Greatest speed $=24.5$ m min$^{-1}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\int_0^{10}20te^{-0.3t}\,dt$ [M1] $=178$ m [A1] [2 marks] (c) Solve $\int_0^T20te^{-0.3t}\,dt=100$ [M1] $T=5.08$ minutes [A1] [2 marks] (d) $\int_{10}^{30}20te^{-0.3t}\,dt$ [M1] $=44.0$ m [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Since $v\ge0$, distance equals the integral of $v$, so no splitting is needed. Use the GDC's solver on an integral equation for part (c) and give 3 significant figures.

subtopic: Greatest speed on a closed interval
statement: A particle moves along a straight line so that its displacement from a fixed point at time $t$ seconds is $s(t)=t^3-9t^2+15t+4$ meters, for $0\le t\le5$. (a) Find an expression for the velocity $v(t)$. [1] (b) Find the values of $t$ at which the particle is instantaneously at rest. [2] (c) Find the greatest speed of the particle during the time interval $0\le t\le5$. [3] (d) Find the acceleration of the particle at $t=2$. [1] (e) State the time interval during which the particle is moving in the negative direction. [1]
markscheme: (a) $v(t)=3t^2-18t+15$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $3(t-1)(t-5)=0$ [M1] $t=1$ and $t=5$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $v(t)=3(t-3)^2-12$, so the minimum velocity is $-12$ at $t=3$ [A1] Compare with the endpoint $v(0)=15$ [M1] Greatest speed is $15$ m s$^{-1}$ (at $t=0$) [A1] [3 marks] (d) $a(t)=6t-18$, so $a(2)=-6$ m s$^{-2}$ [A1] [1 mark] (e) $1<t<5$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Speed is the magnitude of velocity, so a large negative velocity can still be a large speed. On a closed interval, always compare turning-point values with endpoint values.

subtopic: Stopping distance of a decelerating vehicle
statement: A vehicle enters a gravel runway with velocity $v=25e^{-0.3t}$ m s$^{-1}$, where $t$ is the time in seconds after entering. (a) Find an expression for the displacement from the start after $t$ seconds. [3] (b) Find the distance traveled in the first $3$ seconds. [2] (c) Show that the vehicle can never travel further than 83.33 m, and find how long it takes to travel 50 m. [4] (d) Find the acceleration when $t=0$ and when $t=5$. [3]
tips: Because the velocity never reaches zero, the displacement approaches a finite limit; use $e^{-kt}\to0$.

subtopic: Acceleration that decays with time
statement: A rocket sled starts with velocity $1$ m/s at $t=0$ and has acceleration $a=2e^{-0.2t}$ m/s$^{2}$, with $t$ in seconds. (a) Show that $v=11-10e^{-0.2t}$. [3] (b) State the limiting velocity as $t\to\infty$. [1] (c) Find the time at which the velocity reaches $10$ m/s, to three significant figures. [2]
tips: As $t\to\infty$, the exponential term tends to $0$.

subtopic: Acceleration proportional to displacement: v dv/ds, amplitude, verification and time to reach a position
statement: A particle moves along a straight line. Its acceleration is $a=-9s\ \text{m s}^{-2}$, where $s$ meters is its displacement from a fixed point $O$. At $t=0$ seconds the particle is at $O$ with velocity $12\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ in the positive direction. (a) Use $a=v\dfrac{dv}{ds}$ to show that $v^2=144-9s^2$. [4] (b) Find the greatest displacement of the particle from $O$. [2] (c) Verify that $s=4\sin3t$ satisfies the acceleration relation and both initial conditions. [3] (d) Find the first time at which the particle is at $s=2$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $v\dfrac{dv}{ds}=-9s$ [M1] $\displaystyle\int v\,dv=\int-9s\,ds$ [A1] $\dfrac{v^2}{2}=-\dfrac{9s^2}{2}+c$ [A1] $s=0,\ v=12$ gives $c=72$, so $v^2=144-9s^2$ [A1][AG] [4 marks] (b) $v=0$: $9s^2=144$ [M1] $s=4$ m [A1] [2 marks] (c) $v=12\cos3t$ and $a=-36\sin3t=-9(4\sin3t)=-9s$ [A1][A1] $s(0)=0$ and $v(0)=12$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $4\sin3t=2$ gives $\sin3t=\dfrac12$ [M1] First positive solution $3t=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$, so $t=\dfrac{\pi}{18}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Acceleration proportional to negative displacement produces oscillation, and the greatest displacement is where the velocity is zero. To verify a proposed solution, differentiate it twice and check the initial values too.

subtopic: Speed as a function of displacement in simple harmonic motion
statement: A particle moves along a line with displacement $x=A\cos\omega t$ from its centre of oscillation, where $A,\omega>0$. (a) Show that the acceleration is $-\omega^2x$. [2] (b) Using $a=v\dfrac{dv}{dx}$, show that $v^2=\omega^2\left(A^2-x^2\right)$. [3] (c) The amplitude is $0.5$ m and the period is $2$ s. Find the maximum speed and the speed when $x=0.3$ m, each to three significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) $v=-A\omega\sin\omega t$ [A1] $a=-A\omega^2\cos\omega t=-\omega^2x$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $v\dfrac{dv}{dx}=-\omega^2x$ [M1] $\dfrac{v^2}2=-\dfrac{\omega^2x^2}2+C$ [A1] $v=0$ when $x=A$, so $C=\dfrac{\omega^2A^2}2$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\omega=\dfrac{2\pi}2=\pi$ [A1] maximum speed $A\omega=1.57$ m/s [A1] $v=\pi\sqrt{0.25-0.09}=1.26$ m/s [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The relation $a=v\,dv/dx$ turns an equation in $x$ and $a$ into one in $x$ and $v$ that can be integrated directly.

subtopic: Speed and distance with a velocity of the form exponential minus constant
statement: A diver moves along a vertical line. Her velocity at time $t$ seconds is modeled by $v=10e^{-0.4t}-4$ m s$^{-1}$ for $0\le t\le6$, where positive velocity means moving upward. At $t=0$ her displacement from her starting position is $0$. (a) Find her acceleration when $t=1$. [2] (b) Find the time when she is momentarily at rest. [2] (c) Find the total distance she travels during the $6$ seconds. [3] (d) Find her displacement from her starting position when $t=6$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $a=\dfrac{dv}{dt}=-4e^{-0.4t}$ [M1] $a(1)=-4e^{-0.4}=-2.68$ m s$^{-2}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $10e^{-0.4t}=4$ [M1] $t=\dfrac{\ln2.5}{0.4}=2.29$ s [A1] [2 marks] (c) Distance $=\int_0^6|v|\,dt$ [M1] $\int_0^{2.29}v\,dt=5.84$ and $\left|\int_{2.29}^6v\,dt\right|=7.11$ [A1] Distance $=12.9$ m [A1] [3 marks] (d) Displacement $=\int_0^6v\,dt$ [M1] $=-1.27$ m (that is, $1.27$ m below the start) [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Use the GDC to integrate $|v|$ directly, or integrate each side of the rest time. Keep the sign for displacement and the absolute value for distance.

subtopic: Greatest speed and total distance
statement: A cart moves along a track for $0\le t\le6$ seconds with velocity $v=t(6-t)$ m/s. (a) Find the time at which the velocity is greatest and the greatest velocity. [3] (b) Find the total distance traveled in the $6$ seconds. [3]
tips: The velocity is never negative on this interval, so distance equals displacement.

subtopic: Acceleration as a function of displacement
statement: A particle moves along a straight line. Its acceleration is $a=-4s$ where $s$ meters is its displacement from the origin. When $s=0$ its speed is $6$ m s$^{-1}$. (a) Use $a=v\dfrac{dv}{ds}$ to show that $v^2=36-4s^2$. [4] (b) Find the greatest distance of the particle from the origin. [2] (c) Find the speed when $s=2$ m. [2]
tips: When acceleration is given in terms of displacement, use $a=v\frac{dv}{ds}$ and separate the variables.

subtopic: Projectile with parametric position: maximum height, range and clearing a fence
statement: A ball is hit from a point above horizontal ground. Its position at time $t$ seconds after being hit, in meters relative to the point on the ground directly below the hitting point, is $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix} 18t \\ 1.2+14t-4.9t^2 \end{pmatrix}$, for $t\ge0$ until the ball lands. The first component is horizontal distance and the second is height above the ground. (a) Find the maximum height of the ball above the ground. [3] (b) Find the time at which the ball lands and the horizontal distance it has then traveled. [3] (c) A vertical fence of height $6$ m stands at a horizontal distance of $45$ m from the hitting point, in the path of the ball. Determine whether the ball passes over the fence. [3]
markscheme: (a) Vertical velocity $14-9.8t=0$ [M1] $t=1.43$ [A1] Maximum height $=1.2+14(1.4286)-4.9(1.4286)^2=11.2$ m [A1] [3 marks] (b) Solve $1.2+14t-4.9t^2=0$ [M1] $t=2.94$ s [A1] Horizontal distance $=18(2.9404)=52.9$ m [A1] [3 marks] (c) $18t=45$ gives $t=2.5$ [A1] Height $=1.2+35-30.625=5.575$ m [A1] Since $5.575<6$ the ball hits the fence and does not pass over it [R1] [3 marks]
tips: Find the time at which the ball reaches the fence from the horizontal component, then substitute into the vertical component. Use the GDC to solve the quadratic for landing time and keep full accuracy until the end.

subtopic: Inverse-square acceleration: v dv/ds with initial condition, greatest displacement and return speed
statement: A particle moves along a straight line away from the origin $O$. When its displacement from $O$ is $s$ meters, $s>0$, its acceleration is $a=-\dfrac{16}{s^2}\ \text{m s}^{-2}$. When $s=2$, the velocity of the particle is $2\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. (a) Use $a=v\dfrac{dv}{ds}$ to show that $v^2=\dfrac{32}{s}-12$. [4] (b) Find the greatest value of $s$ reached by the particle. [2] (c) Find the speed of the particle when $s=1$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $v\dfrac{dv}{ds}=-\dfrac{16}{s^2}$ [M1] $\displaystyle\int v\,dv=\int-16s^{-2}\,ds$ [M1] $\dfrac{v^2}{2}=\dfrac{16}{s}+c$ [A1] $s=2,\ v=2$: $2=8+c$, so $c=-6$ [A1] $v^2=\dfrac{32}{s}-12$ [AG] [4 marks] (b) $v=0$: $\dfrac{32}{s}=12$ [M1] $s=\dfrac83$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $v^2=32-12=20$, speed $=2\sqrt5\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: When acceleration is given in terms of position, separate variables using $a=v\frac{dv}{ds}$ and integrate both sides with respect to their own variable. The velocity is zero at the greatest displacement.

subtopic: Velocity with an exponential model
statement: A particle moves along a line with velocity $v=6e^{-t/2}$ m s$^{-1}$, $t\geq0$. (a) Find the acceleration at time $t$ and its value at $t=0$. [2] (b) Find the exact distance traveled between $t=0$ and $t=2\ln2$. [3] (c) Find the limit of the displacement as $t\to\infty$. [2]
tips: $e^{-t/2}$ decreases but never reaches zero, so the particle never stops in finite time, yet its total displacement is finite.

subtopic: Projectile motion of a balloon from a launcher
statement: A water-balloon launcher fires a balloon from a point $1.5$ m above level ground. Relative to the point on the ground directly below the launch point, the position of the balloon at time $t$ seconds is $\mathbf r(t)=\begin{pmatrix} 12t \\ 1.5+9t-4.9t^2 \end{pmatrix}$ meters, where the first component is horizontal and the second is vertical. (a) Find the velocity vector of the balloon and its initial speed. [2] (b) Find the maximum height reached by the balloon. [3] (c) Find the horizontal distance from the launch point at which the balloon hits the ground. [3] (d) Find the speed of the balloon just before impact. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf v=\begin{pmatrix} 12 \\ 9-9.8t \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] initial speed $\sqrt{12^2+9^2}=15$ m s$^{-1}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) maximum height when vertical velocity is zero: $9-9.8t=0$ [M1] $t=0.918$ s [A1] height $=1.5+9(0.918)-4.9(0.918)^2=5.63$ m [A1] [3 marks] (c) $1.5+9t-4.9t^2=0$ [M1] $t=1.99$ s (positive root) [A1] horizontal distance $=12\times1.9905=23.9$ m [A1] [3 marks] (d) vertical velocity $=9-9.8(1.9905)=-10.5$ [A1] speed $=\sqrt{12^2+10.5^2}=15.9$ m s$^{-1}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Treat horizontal and vertical components separately. Keep unrounded values from earlier parts to avoid accumulating rounding error in later parts.

subtopic: Closest approach of a survey drone to a radio mast
statement: A survey drone flies in a horizontal plane. Relative to a ground station $O$, its position in meters at time $t$ seconds is $\mathbf r(t)=\begin{pmatrix} 4t \\ 30-2t \end{pmatrix}$ for $0\le t\le30$. A radio mast stands at the point $M(60,10)$. (a) Find the velocity of the drone and its speed. [2] (b) Show that the square of the distance $d$ between the drone and the mast is $d^2=20t^2-560t+4000$. [3] (c) Find the minimum distance between the drone and the mast, and the time at which it occurs. [3] (d) The drone's camera photographs the mast clearly only when $d\le10$ m. Find the length of time for which this is true. [3]
tips: Minimizing $d^2$ gives the same time as minimizing $d$ and avoids the square root. In (d) solve the quadratic inequality using the roots of $d^2=100$.

subtopic: Maximum displacement and distance for a particle
statement: A particle moves on a straight line with displacement $s=5te^{-0.5t}$ meters at time $t$ seconds, for $0\le t\le6$. (a) Find $v=\dfrac{ds}{dt}$ and the time at which the particle changes direction. [3] (b) Find the maximum displacement, and the displacement at $t=6$, to three significant figures. [2] (c) Find the total distance traveled in the $6$ seconds, to three significant figures. [3]
tips: A change of direction occurs where the velocity is zero and changes sign.

subtopic: Sprinter velocity model and time for 100 m
statement: In a $100$ m race a sprinter's velocity is modeled by $v(t)=12\left(1-e^{-0.8t}\right)$ m s$^{-1}$, where $t$ is the time in seconds after the starting gun. (a) Find the initial acceleration of the sprinter. [2] (b) Find the distance covered in the first $10$ seconds. [2] (c) Find the time the sprinter takes to complete the $100$ m. [3] (d) State the maximum speed predicted by the model. [1]
tips: For part (c) either find $s(t)$ analytically and solve, or use a graph of $\int_0^x v\,dt$ on your GDC and find where it equals $100$. The limiting velocity comes from $e^{-0.8t}\to0$.

subtopic: A particle with exponentially decaying velocity
statement: A boat slows after its engine is switched off, with velocity $v=10e^{-0.5t}$ m/s at time $t$ seconds after the engine stops. (a) Find the acceleration at $t=0$ and explain the sign. [2] (b) Find the exact distance the boat travels in the first $4$ seconds. [3] (c) State the limit of the distance traveled as $t\to\infty$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $a=-5e^{-0.5t}$, so $a(0)=-5$ m/s$^{2}$ [A1]; negative because the boat is slowing down [R1] [2 marks] (b) $\int_0^410e^{-0.5t}dt$ [M1]; $\left[-20e^{-0.5t}\right]_0^4$ [A1]; $20-20e^{-2}$ m [A1] [3 marks] (c) $20$ m [A1] [1 mark]
tips: The limit of $e^{-0.5t}$ as $t\to\infty$ is $0$.

subtopic: Average speed and average velocity from a velocity function
statement: A particle moves in a line with velocity $v=t^2-4t+3$ m/s for $0\le t\le4$. (a) Find the times at which the particle changes direction. [2] (b) Find the total distance travelled and the average speed over the $4$ seconds. [4] (c) Find the average velocity over the same interval. [2]
markscheme: (a) $(t-1)(t-3)=0$ [M1] $t=1$ and $t=3$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\displaystyle\int_0^1v\,dt=\dfrac43$, $\displaystyle\int_1^3v\,dt=-\dfrac43$, $\displaystyle\int_3^4v\,dt=\dfrac43$ [M1][A1] distance $=4$ m [A1] average speed $=\dfrac44=1$ m/s [A1] [4 marks] (c) displacement $=\dfrac43-\dfrac43+\dfrac43=\dfrac43$ [M1] average velocity $=\dfrac13$ m/s [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Average speed uses the total distance travelled, which needs $|v|$, while average velocity uses the displacement.

subtopic: Maximum speed on a closed interval with endpoint check and total distance
statement: A particle moves along a straight line. Its velocity is $v=t^2-6t+5\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ for $0\le t\le6$, where $t$ is in seconds. At $t=0$ the particle is at the origin. (a) Find the time at which the velocity is least, and state the least value of $v$. [3] (b) Find the greatest speed of the particle during the six seconds, justifying your answer. [3] (c) Find the exact total distance traveled by the particle in the six seconds. [4]
markscheme: (a) $a=\dfrac{dv}{dt}=2t-6=0$ [M1] $t=3$ [A1] $v(3)=9-18+5=-4\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Speed is $|v|$. The least velocity is $-4$, which has speed $4$ [M1] At the endpoints $v(0)=5$ and $v(6)=5$ [A1] Since $v$ is a quadratic with least value $-4$ at $t=3$, on $0\le t\le6$ we have $-4\le v\le5$, so the greatest speed is $5\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ [R1] [3 marks] (c) $v=(t-1)(t-5)=0$ at $t=1,\ 5$ [A1] $s=\displaystyle\int(t^2-6t+5)\,dt=\dfrac{t^3}{3}-3t^2+5t$ [M1] $s(1)=\dfrac73,\ s(5)=-\dfrac{25}{3},\ s(6)=-6$ [A1] Distance $=\dfrac73+\dfrac{32}{3}+\dfrac73=\dfrac{46}{3}$ m [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Maximum speed on a closed interval can occur at an endpoint rather than at the stationary point of the velocity. Compare $|v|$ at the turning point of $v$ and at both ends.

subtopic: Displacement with a product of polynomial and exponential: rest, zero acceleration and exact maximum speed
statement: A bead slides along a straight wire. Its displacement from a fixed point $O$ at time $t\ge0$ seconds is $s=t^2e^{-t}$ meters. (a) Show that the velocity is $v=t(2-t)e^{-t}$. [2] (b) Find the displacement of the particle at the time $t>0$ when it is instantaneously at rest. [2] (c) Show that the acceleration is $a=(t^2-4t+2)e^{-t}$, and hence find the exact times at which the acceleration is zero. [4] (d) Find the exact maximum speed of the particle for $t\ge0$, justifying that it is the maximum. [4]
markscheme: (a) $v=2te^{-t}-t^2e^{-t}$ [M1] $=t(2-t)e^{-t}$ [AG] [A1] [2 marks] (b) $v=0$ with $t>0$ gives $t=2$ [A1] $s=4e^{-2}$ m [A1] [2 marks] (c) $a=(2-2t)e^{-t}-(2t-t^2)e^{-t}$ [M1] $=(t^2-4t+2)e^{-t}$ [AG] [A1] $t^2-4t+2=0$ [M1] $t=2\pm\sqrt2$ [A1] [4 marks] (d) The speed is greatest where $a=0$, so evaluate $v$ at $t=2\pm\sqrt2$ [M1] $v(2-\sqrt2)=2(\sqrt2-1)e^{\sqrt2-2}\approx0.461$ [A1] $v(2+\sqrt2)=-2(\sqrt2+1)e^{-2-\sqrt2}\approx-0.159$, so the speed there is about $0.159$ [A1] Also $v=0$ at $t=0$ and $v\to0$ as $t\to\infty$, so the maximum speed is $2(\sqrt2-1)e^{\sqrt2-2}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ [R1] [4 marks]
tips: Candidates for maximum speed are the zeros of acceleration, but compare $|v|$ at each one and check the behavior at $t=0$ and as $t\to\infty$. Factorize the velocity before differentiating again to keep the algebra manageable.

subtopic: Piecewise velocity of a lift over three stages
statement: A lift in a tall building travels upward from the ground floor. Its velocity, in m s$^{-1}$, at time $t$ seconds is $v(t)=0.8t$ for $0\le t\le5$; $v(t)=4$ for $5<t\le20$; and $v(t)=4-0.8(t-20)$ for $20<t\le25$. (a) Find the acceleration of the lift in each of the three stages. [3] (b) Find the distance traveled in each stage, and hence the total height of the journey. [5] (c) Find the average speed of the lift over the $25$ seconds. [1]
tips: Treat each piece of a piecewise velocity separately, with its own limits of integration. Check that the pieces agree at the boundaries, $v(5)=4$ and $v(20)=4$.

subtopic: Oscillating acceleration and direction changes
statement: A particle moves in a straight line. Its acceleration at time $t$ seconds is $a(t)=4\cos2t$ m s$^{-2}$. When $t=0$ its velocity is $1$ m s$^{-1}$ and its displacement from the origin is $0$ m. (a) Find an expression for the velocity $v(t)$. [2] (b) Show that the displacement is $s(t)=t+1-\cos2t$. [2] (c) Find the first time $t>0$ at which the particle is instantaneously at rest. [3] (d) Find the total distance traveled by the particle between $t=0$ and $t=\pi$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $v(t)=\int4\cos2t\,dt=2\sin2t+C$ [M1] $v(0)=1$ so $v(t)=2\sin2t+1$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $s(t)=\int(2\sin2t+1)\,dt=-\cos2t+t+C$ [M1] $s(0)=0$ gives $C=1$, so $s(t)=t+1-\cos2t$ [A1][AG] [2 marks] (c) $2\sin2t+1=0$, so $\sin2t=-\frac12$ [M1] $2t=\frac{7\pi}6$ [A1] $t=\frac{7\pi}{12}=1.83$ s [A1] [3 marks] (d) $v<0$ for $\frac{7\pi}{12}<t<\frac{11\pi}{12}$, so the particle changes direction at these times [M1] $s\left(\frac{7\pi}{12}\right)=3.699$, $s\left(\frac{11\pi}{12}\right)=3.014$, $s(\pi)=3.142$ [A1] Distance $=3.699+(3.699-3.014)+(3.142-3.014)$ [A1] $=4.51$ m [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Find the times at which the velocity changes sign and evaluate the displacement at each of them. The total distance is the sum of the magnitudes of the displacements between these times.

subtopic: Velocity, displacement and distance
statement: A particle $P$ moves along a straight line. Its velocity, $v\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, at time $t$ seconds is given by $$v(t)=10te^{-0.5t}-2,\quad 0\le t\le 10.$$ At $t=0$, $P$ is at a fixed point $O$ on the line. (a) Write down the initial velocity of $P$. [1] (b) Find the values of $t$ for which $P$ is at rest. [3] (c) Find the maximum velocity of $P$ and the time at which it occurs. [2] (d) Find the acceleration of $P$ when $t=3$. [2] (e) Find the total distance traveled by $P$ in the first $10$ seconds. [3] (f) Find the displacement of $P$ from $O$ when $t=10$. [2] (g) Find the greatest distance of $P$ from $O$ during the first $10$ seconds. [2]
markscheme: (a) $-2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Solving $10te^{-0.5t}-2=0$ [M1] $t=0.224$ ($0.223665\ldots$) [A1] $t=7.15$ ($7.15430\ldots$) [A1] [3 marks] (c) $v'(t)=0$ when $t=2$ (or use of GDC) [M1] Maximum velocity $20e^{-1}-2=5.36\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ ($5.35758\ldots$) at $t=2$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $a(t)=10e^{-0.5t}-5te^{-0.5t}$ [M1] $a(3)=-1.12\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ ($-1.11565\ldots$) [A1] [2 marks] (e) $\displaystyle\int_0^{10}|v(t)|\,dt$ [M1][A1] $=23.2\ \mathrm{m}$ ($23.1936\ldots$) [A1] Award [M1] for an integral of $|v|$ or for splitting the integral at both values from part (b). [3 marks] (f) $\displaystyle\int_0^{10}v(t)\,dt$ [M1] $=18.4\ \mathrm{m}$ ($18.3828\ldots$) [A1] [2 marks] (g) The greatest distance occurs when $v$ changes sign from positive to negative, at $t=7.15430\ldots$ [M1] $\displaystyle\int_0^{7.15430\ldots}v(t)\,dt=20.6\ \mathrm{m}$ ($20.5731\ldots$) [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Distance traveled uses $\int|v|\,dt$, while displacement uses $\int v\,dt$; mixing them up is the most common error. The particle is furthest from $O$ at a time when $v$ changes sign, or at an endpoint, so compare candidate displacements.

subtopic: Direction changes and total distance for t cos t velocity
statement: A particle moves along a straight line with velocity $v(t)=t\cos t$ m s$^{-1}$ for $0\le t\le8$, where $t$ is in seconds and the argument of cosine is in radians. At $t=0$ the particle is at the origin. (a) Find the times at which the particle changes direction. [3] (b) Find the displacement of the particle from the origin at $t=8$. [2] (c) Find the total distance traveled by the particle in the $8$ seconds. [3] (d) Find the acceleration at $t=2$, and state whether the particle is speeding up or slowing down at that instant. [2]
markscheme: (a) $t\cos t=0$ [M1] $t=\frac{\pi}{2}=1.57$ [A1] $t=\frac{3\pi}{2}=4.71$ and $t=\frac{5\pi}{2}=7.85$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\int_0^8t\cos t\,dt$ [M1] $=6.77$ m [A1] [2 marks] (c) displacements at the turning points: $s\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)=0.571$, $s\left(\frac{3\pi}{2}\right)=-5.71$, $s\left(\frac{5\pi}{2}\right)=6.85$ [A1] distance $=0.571+6.28+12.57+0.0847$ [M1] $=19.5$ m [A1] [3 marks] (d) $a=\cos t-t\sin t$, so $a(2)=-2.23$ m s$^{-2}$ [A1] $v(2)=2\cos2=-0.832<0$; $v$ and $a$ have the same sign, so the particle is speeding up [R1] [2 marks]
tips: For total distance, integrate the speed or split the interval at every sign change of $v$ and add the absolute values. Use your GDC to evaluate each integral.

subtopic: Velocity and acceleration vectors of a line-marking robot
statement: A line-marking robot moves on a flat sports field. Its position relative to a fixed origin, in meters, is $\mathbf r(t)=\begin{pmatrix} t^2 \\ t^3-3t \end{pmatrix}$ for $t\ge0$ seconds. (a) Find the velocity vector $\mathbf v(t)$. [2] (b) Find the time at which the robot is moving parallel to the $x$-axis, and its speed at that time. [3] (c) Find the magnitude of the robot's acceleration at that time. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf v=\begin{pmatrix} 2t \\ 3t^2-3 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (b) parallel to the $x$-axis means the $y$-component of velocity is zero: $3t^2-3=0$ [M1] $t=1$ (since $t\ge0$) [A1] $\mathbf v=\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$ so speed $=2$ m s$^{-1}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\mathbf a=\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 6t \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] at $t=1$: $\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 6 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] magnitude $=\sqrt{4+36}=\sqrt{40}=2\sqrt{10}$ m s$^{-2}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Differentiate each component separately. Moving parallel to an axis means the other component of velocity is zero (and the first is not).

subtopic: Amplitude and phase of oscillating motion from initial conditions
statement: A particle oscillates with displacement $s=A\sin(2t+\varphi)$, where $A>0$ and $0<\varphi<\dfrac\pi2$. At $t=0$, $s=1$ and the velocity is $\sqrt3$. (a) Show that $A\sin\varphi=1$ and $2A\cos\varphi=\sqrt3$. [2] (b) Find $\varphi$ and $A$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $s(0)=A\sin\varphi=1$ [A1] $v=2A\cos(2t+\varphi)$, so $v(0)=2A\cos\varphi=\sqrt3$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\tan\varphi=\dfrac2{\sqrt3}$ [M1] $\varphi=0.857$ [A1] $A=\sqrt{1+\dfrac34}=\dfrac{\sqrt7}2=1.32$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Use the displacement and velocity at $t=0$ to form two equations in $A\sin\varphi$ and $A\cos\varphi$, then divide.

subtopic: Intervals where a trolley is speeding up
statement: A trolley moves along a straight rail with velocity $v(t)=t^2-6t+5$ m s$^{-1}$ for $0\le t\le6$. (a) Find the times at which the trolley is momentarily at rest. [2] (b) Find the acceleration $a(t)$ and the time at which the acceleration is zero. [2] (c) Determine the time intervals during which the speed of the trolley is increasing. Justify your answer. [3]
markscheme: (a) $(t-1)(t-5)=0$ [M1] $t=1$ and $t=5$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $a=2t-6$ [A1] $a=0$ at $t=3$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) speed increases when $v$ and $a$ have the same sign [M1] for $1<t<3$: $v<0$ and $a<0$ [A1] for $5<t\le6$: $v>0$ and $a>0$ [A1] (for $0\le t<1$ and $3<t<5$ the signs differ, so the trolley is slowing) [3 marks]
tips: Speed increases when velocity and acceleration have the same sign, and decreases when they have opposite signs. Test the sign of each between the critical times $1$, $3$ and $5$.

subtopic: Exponentially decaying velocity of a sled on ice
statement: A sled slides in a straight line across ice after being pushed. Its velocity is $v(t)=6e^{-2t}$ m s$^{-1}$ for $t\ge0$, and it starts at the origin. (a) Find the acceleration of the sled as a function of $t$. [2] (b) Find an expression for the displacement $s(t)$ of the sled. [3] (c) State the limiting value of $s(t)$ as $t\to\infty$. [1] (d) Find the exact time at which the sled has traveled $2.25$ m. [2]
tips: The negative exponent gives a factor $-2$ on differentiating and $-\frac12$ on integrating. Take logarithms to solve for $t$ in an exact answer.

subtopic: Distance traveled with a velocity involving a logarithm
statement: A particle moves in a straight line. Its velocity at time $t$ seconds, for $1\le t\le e^2$, is $v=\ln t-1$ m s$^{-1}$. (a) Find the exact time at which the particle is instantaneously at rest. [2] (b) Find the acceleration of the particle at this time. [2] (c) Show that the displacement of the particle between $t=1$ and $t=e^2$ is $2$ m. [4] (d) Find the exact total distance traveled by the particle between $t=1$ and $t=e^2$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $\ln t-1=0$ [M1] $t=e$ s [A1] [2 marks] (b) $a=\dfrac{dv}{dt}=\dfrac1t$ [M1] At $t=e$: $a=\dfrac1e$ m s$^{-2}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\int\ln t\,dt$ by parts (with $u=\ln t$, $dv=dt$) [M1] $=t\ln t-t$ [A1] so $\int(\ln t-1)\,dt=t\ln t-2t$ [A1] $\big[t\ln t-2t\big]_1^{e^2}=(2e^2-2e^2)-(0-2)$ [M1] $=2$ m [AG] [4 marks] (d) The particle changes direction at $t=e$, so distance $=\left|\int_1^e v\,dt\right|+\left|\int_e^{e^2} v\,dt\right|$ [M1] $\int_1^e v\,dt=(e-2e)-(0-2)=2-e$ [A1] $\int_e^{e^2} v\,dt=(2e^2-2e^2)-(e-2e)=e$ [A1] Distance $=(e-2)+e=2e-2$ m [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Integrating $\ln t$ needs integration by parts; remember it as $t\ln t-t$. The displacement of $2$ is not the distance: part (d) needs the sign change at $t=e$.

subtopic: Estimating distance from tabulated velocities
statement: The velocity $v$ m s$^{-1}$ of a cyclist at time $t$ seconds is recorded in the table. $\begin{array}{c|ccccc} t&0&2&4&6&8\\ \hline v&0&3.2&5.1&4.4&1.8\end{array}$ The cyclist moves in a straight line in the positive direction. (a) Use the trapezoidal rule with four strips to estimate the distance traveled in the first 8 seconds. [3] (b) Find the average acceleration between $t=2$ and $t=6$. [2] (c) Given that the graph of $v$ against $t$ is concave down for $0\le t\le8$, state whether your answer to part (a) is an overestimate or underestimate, giving a reason. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\frac22\left[0+1.8+2(3.2+5.1+4.4)\right]$ [M1] [A1] $=27.2$ m [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\frac{4.4-3.2}{6-2}$ [M1] $=0.3$ m s$^{-2}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Underestimate [A1] The chords of a concave-down curve lie below the curve, so the trapezoids have less area than the region under the curve [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Distance is the area under the velocity-time graph (when $v\ge0$), and average acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the change in time.

subtopic: Speed profile and distance of a delivery drone
statement: A delivery drone flies in a straight line between two rooftops. Its speed in m s$^{-1}$ is modeled by $v(t)=0.4t(12-t)$ for $0\le t\le12$, where $t$ is the time in seconds after takeoff. (a) Find the maximum speed of the drone and the time at which it occurs. [2] (b) Find the distance between the two rooftops. [2] (c) Find the average speed of the drone for the whole journey. [1] (d) Find the two times at which the speed of the drone is exactly $10$ m s$^{-1}$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $v$ is a quadratic symmetric about $t=6$, so maximum at $t=6$ s [M1] $v(6)=14.4$ m s$^{-1}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\int_0^{12}0.4t(12-t)\,dt$ [M1] $=115.2$ m (115 m to 3 s.f.) [A1] [2 marks] (c) average speed $=\frac{115.2}{12}=9.6$ m s$^{-1}$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) $0.4t(12-t)=10$ [M1] $t=2.68$ s and $t=9.32$ s [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Use your GDC for the definite integral and for solving $v(t)=10$ (two intersection points with a horizontal line). Average speed is total distance divided by total time.

subtopic: Velocity with an exponential factor: acceleration, integration by parts and limiting displacement
statement: A particle moves in a straight line. Its velocity $v\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ at time $t$ seconds, $t\ge0$, is $v=6te^{-0.5t}$. At $t=0$ the particle is at the origin $O$ with displacement $s=0$. (a) Find an expression for the acceleration $a$ at time $t$, and hence find the time at which $a=0$. [3] (b) Find the maximum speed of the particle. [1] (c) Use integration by parts to show that the displacement is $s=24-12(t+2)e^{-0.5t}$. [4] (d) Find the distance traveled by the particle in the first $5$ seconds. [1] (e) Find the value that $s$ approaches as $t\to\infty$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $a=\dfrac{dv}{dt}=6e^{-0.5t}-3te^{-0.5t}$ [M1][A1] $a=3e^{-0.5t}(2-t)=0$ gives $t=2$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $v(2)=12e^{-1}=4.41\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $s=\displaystyle\int6te^{-0.5t}\,dt$; parts with $u=t$, $\dfrac{dv}{dt}=e^{-0.5t}$ [M1] $=6\left[-2te^{-0.5t}+2\displaystyle\int e^{-0.5t}\,dt\right]$ [A1] $=-12te^{-0.5t}-24e^{-0.5t}+C$ [A1] $s=0$ when $t=0$: $C=24$, so $s=24-12(t+2)e^{-0.5t}$ [A1][AG] [4 marks] (d) Since $v\ge0$ for $t\ge0$ the distance equals $s(5)=24-84e^{-2.5}=17.1$ m [A1] [1 mark] (e) $(t+2)e^{-0.5t}\to0$, so $s\to24$ m [A1] [1 mark]
tips: For the maximum speed, set the acceleration to zero and check that the velocity there is a maximum, not a minimum. When the velocity never changes sign, the distance traveled equals the displacement.

subtopic: Distance covered in a speed-time trapezium
statement: A train starts from rest and accelerates uniformly for $20$ s to a speed $V$ m/s. It travels at this constant speed, and then decelerates uniformly to rest in $30$ s. The total time is $150$ s and the total distance is $3000$ m. (a) Find $V$. [4] (b) Find the acceleration in the first $20$ s and the deceleration in the last $30$ s. [2]
markscheme: (a) the speed-time graph is a trapezium with parallel sides $150$ and $150-20-30=100$ [A1] area $=\dfrac12(150+100)V$ [M1] $125V=3000$ [A1] $V=24$ m/s [A1] [4 marks] (b) $\dfrac{24}{20}=1.2$ m/s$^2$ [A1] $\dfrac{24}{30}=0.8$ m/s$^2$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The area under a speed-time graph is the distance travelled. The graph has the shape of a trapezium.

subtopic: Displacement from a given velocity and starting position
statement: A particle moves on a straight line with velocity $v=3t^{2}-12$ m/s at time $t$ seconds. When $t=0$, its displacement is $s=5$ m. (a) Find an expression for the displacement $s$ in terms of $t$. [3] (b) Find the time at which the particle is momentarily at rest, for $t>0$, and its displacement then. [3] (c) Find the displacement when $t=3$. [1]
tips: Integrate the velocity to get displacement and use the initial position to find the constant.

subtopic: Projectile motion with a position vector
statement: A ball is thrown from a point $2$ m above the ground. Its position (in meters) $t$ seconds later is $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix} 15t \\ 2+12t-4.9t^2 \end{pmatrix}$, where the second component is the height. (a) Find the initial speed of the ball. [3] (b) Find the time at which the ball hits the ground and the horizontal distance travelled. [4] (c) Find the speed of the ball just before it lands. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf v=\begin{pmatrix} 15 \\ 12-9.8t \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] at $t=0$: $\begin{pmatrix} 15 \\ 12 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] speed $=\sqrt{369}=19.2$ m s$^{-1}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $2+12t-4.9t^2=0$ [M1] $t=2.606$ s [A1] horizontal distance $=15\times2.606$ [M1] $=39.1$ m [A1] [4 marks] (c) vertical velocity $=12-9.8\times2.606=-13.54$ [M1][A1] speed $=\sqrt{15^2+(-13.54)^2}=20.2$ m s$^{-1}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Separate the horizontal and vertical components. The ball lands when the height is zero; take the positive root.

subtopic: Total time and distance for a bouncing ball
statement: A ball is dropped from rest at a height $H=10$ m and bounces repeatedly. After each impact it rebounds with $e=0.8$ times its speed just before the impact. Take $g=10$ m/s$^2$ and ignore air resistance. (a) Show that the ball first hits the ground at $t_0=\sqrt{\dfrac{2H}g}$ with speed $v_0=gt_0$. [2] (b) Show that the ball rises and falls after the $n$th impact in a time $2e^nt_0$. [3] (c) Show that the total time until the ball comes to rest is $t_0\dfrac{1+e}{1-e}$, and evaluate it. [4] (d) Show that the greatest height after the $n$th impact is $e^{2n}H$, and find the total distance travelled by the ball. [4] (e) Find the number of impacts after which the greatest height first falls below $1$ cm. [2]
markscheme: (a) $H=\dfrac12gt_0^2$ [M1] $v_0=gt_0$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) speed after the $n$th impact is $e^nv_0$ [A1] rising time $\dfrac{e^nv_0}g=e^nt_0$ [M1] falling time is equal, so total $2e^nt_0$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $T=t_0+2t_0\left(e+e^2+\cdots\right)$ [M1] sum of the geometric series $\dfrac e{1-e}$ [A1] $T=t_0\left(1+\dfrac{2e}{1-e}\right)=t_0\dfrac{1+e}{1-e}$ [AG] [A1] $t_0=\sqrt2$ so $T=9\sqrt2=12.7$ s [A1] [4 marks] (d) $h_n=\dfrac{(e^nv_0)^2}{2g}=e^{2n}H$ [M1][A1] $D=H+2H\left(e^2+e^4+\cdots\right)=H\dfrac{1+e^2}{1-e^2}$ [M1] $=10\times\dfrac{1.64}{0.36}=45.6$ m [A1] [4 marks] (e) $10\times0.8^{2n}<0.01$ so $n>\dfrac{\ln0.001}{2\ln0.8}=15.5$ [M1] $n=16$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Use the constant acceleration formulas for each flight. The times and heights form geometric sequences.

subtopic: Trigonometric velocity of a float in a wave tank
statement: A float in a wave tank moves along a vertical guide rail. Its upward velocity is $v(t)=4\cos(2t)$ cm s$^{-1}$, where $t$ is in seconds and angles are in radians. At $t=0$ the float is $1$ cm above the rail's zero mark. (a) Find the acceleration of the float at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$. [2] (b) Find the first time $t>0$ at which the float is momentarily at rest. [2] (c) Find an expression for the height $s(t)$ of the float above the zero mark. [2] (d) Hence find the height of the float when it first comes to rest. [1]
markscheme: (a) $a=-8\sin(2t)$ [A1] $a\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=-8\sin\frac{\pi}{2}=-8$ cm s$^{-2}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\cos(2t)=0$ [M1] $2t=\frac{\pi}{2}$ so $t=\frac{\pi}{4}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $s=2\sin(2t)+C$ [M1] $s(0)=1$ so $s=2\sin(2t)+1$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $s\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=2+1=3$ cm [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Remember the factor of $2$ from the chain rule when differentiating and the factor $\frac12$ when integrating $\cos(2t)$. Work in radians throughout.

subtopic: Velocity-time graph described in words: areas and gradients
statement: A train travels along a straight track. During the motion its velocity-time graph consists of three straight line segments. From $t=0$ to $t=4$ seconds the velocity increases uniformly from $0$ to $12$ m s$^{-1}$. From $t=4$ to $t=10$ the velocity stays constant at $12$ m s$^{-1}$. From $t=10$ the velocity decreases uniformly until the train comes to rest at $t=19$. (a) Write down the acceleration of the train during the first $4$ seconds. [1] (b) Find the total distance traveled by the train. [3] (c) Find the magnitude of the deceleration during the final stage. [2] (d) Find the velocity of the train at $t=15$. [2] (e) Find the time at which the train has traveled exactly half of its total distance. [3]
markscheme: (a) $a=\dfrac{12-0}{4}=3$ m s$^{-2}$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Distance = area under the graph: $\tfrac12(4)(12)=24$, $12\times6=72$, $\tfrac12(9)(12)=54$ [M1] [A1] Total $=24+72+54=150$ m [A1] [3 marks] (c) Gradient $=\dfrac{0-12}{19-10}$ [M1] Deceleration $=\dfrac43$ m s$^{-2}$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $v(15)=12-\dfrac43(15-10)$ [M1] $=\dfrac{16}{3}$ m s$^{-1}$ [A1] [2 marks] (e) Half the distance is $75$ m. After $4$ s the train has gone $24$ m and after $10$ s it has gone $96$ m, so the time lies in the constant-velocity stage [M1] $24+12(t-4)=75$ [M1] $t=\dfrac{33}{4}=8.25$ s [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Read each segment of a described graph as a gradient (acceleration) or an area (distance). Before setting up an equation, decide which segment the required time falls in.

subtopic: Velocity requiring a substitution to integrate, then acceleration by the chain rule
statement: On a straight track, at time $t\ge0$ seconds, a particle has velocity $v=3t\sqrt{t^2+16}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. When $t=0$ the displacement of the particle from a fixed point $O$ is $0$. (a) Use the substitution $u=t^2+16$ to show that the displacement is $s=(t^2+16)^{\frac32}-64$. [4] (b) Hence find the displacement when $t=3$. [1] (c) Find the acceleration of the particle when $t=3$. [3]
tips: A product of $t$ and a function of $t^2+16$ signals the substitution $u=t^2+16$. For the acceleration, differentiate with the product rule and the chain rule, then substitute the value of $t$.

subtopic: Two particles on the same line
statement: Particles $A$ and $B$ move on the same straight line. Their displacements from a fixed point $O$ at time $t$ seconds are $s_A=t^2-4t+3$ and $s_B=\dfrac12t^2-t+1$, in meters, for $t\geq0$. (a) Find the initial positions of $A$ and $B$ and their initial velocities. [3] (b) Find the times at which the particles are at the same position. [3] (c) Find the speeds of the two particles at the first of these times. [3] (d) Find the maximum distance between the particles in the interval between their meetings, and describe their relative motion. [3]
tips: Two particles meet when their displacements are equal; relative velocity is the difference of the velocities.

subtopic: Vector position with quadratic components: parallel to an axis and exact minimum speed
statement: A drone moves in a horizontal plane. Its position vector relative to the origin at time $t\ge0$ seconds is $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix} 2t^2-3t \\ 8t-t^2 \end{pmatrix}$ meters. (a) Find the velocity vector and the acceleration vector at time $t$. [2] (b) The drone is moving parallel to the $y$-axis at time $t=T$. Find $T$ and the position vector of the drone at this time. [3] (c) Show that the square of the speed of the drone is $20t^2-56t+73$. [2] (d) Find the exact minimum speed of the drone. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf v=\begin{pmatrix} 4t-3 \\ 8-2t \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\mathbf a=\begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $x$-component of velocity is zero: $4t-3=0$ [M1] $T=\dfrac34$ [A1] $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix} -\dfrac98 \\ \dfrac{87}{16} \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $|\mathbf v|^2=(4t-3)^2+(8-2t)^2$ [M1] $=16t^2-24t+9+64-32t+4t^2=20t^2-56t+73$ [A1][AG] [2 marks] (d) Minimum of $20t^2-56t+73$ at $t=\dfrac{56}{40}=\dfrac75$ [M1][A1] Minimum $|\mathbf v|^2=\dfrac{169}{5}$, so minimum speed $=\dfrac{13}{\sqrt5}=\dfrac{13\sqrt5}{5}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Moving parallel to an axis means the other velocity component is zero. For a minimum speed, minimize the squared speed, which is a quadratic here, rather than differentiating a square root.

subtopic: Average velocity versus instantaneous velocity of a cable car
statement: A cable car moves along a straight cable. The distance traveled from the lower station is $s(t)=0.05t^3-0.6t^2+2.4t$ meters for $0\le t\le10$, where $t$ is in seconds. (a) Find $v(t)$ and show that $v(t)\ge0$ for all $t$. [4] (b) Find the average velocity over the $10$ seconds. [2] (c) Find the times at which the instantaneous velocity equals the average velocity. [3] (d) The cable car stops momentarily at one instant. Find this time and explain why the distance traveled in the $10$ seconds equals the final displacement. [2]
markscheme: (a) $v=0.15t^2-1.2t+2.4$ [M1][A1] discriminant $=1.44-4(0.15)(2.4)=0$ [M1] so $v=0.15(t-4)^2\ge0$ [R1] [4 marks] (b) $s(10)=50-60+24=14$ [M1] average velocity $=\frac{14}{10}=1.4$ m s$^{-1}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $0.15(t-4)^2=1.4$ [M1] $t=4\pm\sqrt{\frac{28}{3}}$ [A1] $t=0.945$ s and $t=7.06$ s [A1] [3 marks] (d) $t=4$ s [A1] the velocity is never negative, so the car never reverses and distance equals displacement ($14$ m) [R1] [2 marks]
tips: A quadratic with a zero discriminant touches the axis without crossing it, so the velocity never changes sign. Check by sketching $v(t)$ on your GDC.

subtopic: Simple harmonic motion with a sinusoidal displacement
statement: A particle moves on a straight line with displacement $s=2\sin3t$ meters at time $t$ seconds. (a) Find the velocity and acceleration. [2] (b) Find the maximum speed and the first positive time at which it is attained. [3] (c) Show that $a=-9s$ and explain what this means about the motion. [2]
markscheme: (a) $v=6\cos3t$ [A1] $a=-18\sin3t$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) maximum $|v|=6$ m s$^{-1}$ [A1] when $\cos3t=\pm1$ [M1] $t=\dfrac\pi3$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $a=-18\sin3t=-9(2\sin3t)=-9s$ [A1] the acceleration is proportional to the displacement and opposite in direction, so the motion is simple harmonic [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Differentiate twice. SHM has acceleration proportional to minus the displacement.

subtopic: Maximum velocity and distance for a test-track cart
statement: A cart on a straight test track has velocity $v(t)=12t-3t^2$ m s$^{-1}$ for $t\ge0$, and $s(0)=0$. (a) Find the maximum velocity of the cart and the time at which it occurs. [3] (b) Find an expression for the displacement $s(t)$. [2] (c) Find the time at which the cart comes to rest after $t=0$. [1] (d) Find the total distance traveled by the cart in the first $5$ seconds. [3]
tips: Check where the velocity changes sign before finding distance; the cart reverses at $t=4$, so distance is not simply $s(5)$.

subtopic: Intervals where speed is increasing from the signs of velocity and acceleration
statement: The velocity of a particle on a straight path at time $t\ge0$ seconds is $v=t^2-5t+4\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. (a) Find the times at which the particle is instantaneously at rest. [2] (b) Find the acceleration of the particle at time $t$. [1] (c) Find all values of $t\ge0$ for which the speed of the particle is increasing. [4]
markscheme: (a) $(t-1)(t-4)=0$ [M1] $t=1,\ t=4$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $a=2t-5$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) The speed is increasing when $v$ and $a$ have the same sign [R1] $v>0$ for $0\le t<1$ and $t>4$; $v<0$ for $1<t<4$; $a<0$ for $t<2.5$ and $a>0$ for $t>2.5$ [M1] Both negative: $1<t<\dfrac52$ [A1] Both positive: $t>4$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Speed increases when velocity and acceleration have the same sign, and decreases when their signs differ. Build a sign table using the zeros of $v$ and $a$ to avoid missing an interval.

subtopic: Distance and speed from a displacement function
statement: A particle moves in a straight line so that its displacement from the origin at time $t$ seconds is $s(t)=t^{3} - \frac{15 t^{2}}{2} + 12 t + 3$ meters. (a) Find the velocity and acceleration when $t=2$. [3] (b) Find the times in the interval $0<t<6$ at which the particle is at rest. [2] (c) Find the total distance traveled in the first 6 seconds. [3] (d) Find the greatest speed of the particle in the interval $0\leq t\leq6$ and when it occurs. [3]
markscheme: (a) $v=s'(t)=3 t^{2} - 15 t + 12$ [A1]; $a=v'(t)=6 t - 15$ [A1]; $v(2)=-6.000$, $a(2)=-3.000$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Solve $v=0$ on the GDC [M1]: $t=1.000$, $t=4.000$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Distance $=\int_0^{6}|v|\,dt$ [M1][A1]; $=45.000$ m [A1] [3 marks] (d) Maximize $|v|$ on the interval (check endpoints) [M1]; greatest speed $30.000$ m s$^{-1}$ [A1] at $t=6.000$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Total distance needs $|v|$: integrate on each interval where $v$ keeps one sign, or use the GDC integral of $|v|$.

subtopic: Motion in the plane: position vector and speed
statement: A particle moves in a plane with position vector $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix} t^2-4t \\ 3t+1 \end{pmatrix}$ meters at time $t\ge0$ seconds. (a) Find the velocity vector and the speed at $t=3$. [3] (b) Find the minimum speed of the particle and the time at which it occurs. [3] (c) Find the acceleration and state its direction. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf v=\begin{pmatrix} 2t-4 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] at $t=3$: $\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] speed $=\sqrt{13}=3.606$ m s$^{-1}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) speed$^2=(2t-4)^2+9$ [M1] minimized when $t=2$ [A1] minimum speed $=3$ m s$^{-1}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\mathbf a=\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] constant, in the positive $x$ direction [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Differentiate each component. The speed is the magnitude of the velocity; minimize its square.

subtopic: Sinusoidal velocity with a constant offset: times at rest, total distance, displacement and greatest speed
statement: A particle moves along a straight line, starting at the origin $O$ at $t=0$. Its velocity at time $t$ seconds is $v=3\sin(0.9t)-1.2\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, for $0\le t\le10$. (a) Find the times at which the particle is instantaneously at rest. [3] (b) Find the total distance traveled by the particle in the ten seconds. [3] (c) Find the displacement of the particle from $O$ when $t=10$. [2] (d) Find the greatest speed of the particle during the ten seconds, and the time at which it first occurs. [3]
markscheme: (a) Solve $3\sin(0.9t)-1.2=0$ on the GDC [M1] $t=0.457$ and $t=3.03$ [A1] and $t=7.44$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Distance $=\displaystyle\int_0^{10}|v|\,dt$ [M1] using the turning times from part (a) as breakpoints (or the GDC absolute value) [A1] $=17.7$ m [A1] [3 marks] (c) $s(10)=\displaystyle\int_0^{10}v\,dt$ [M1] $=-5.63$ m [A1] [2 marks] (d) The velocity is least when $\sin(0.9t)=-1$, giving $v=-4.2$; the greatest positive velocity is only $1.8$, so the greatest speed is $4.2\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ [M1][A1] This occurs when $0.9t=\dfrac{3\pi}{2}$, so $t=5.24$ s [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Use the GDC graph of $v$ to see how many times it crosses the axis before choosing breakpoints. For greatest speed compare the most negative and the most positive velocities, since speed is $|v|$.

subtopic: Oscillating motion from a trigonometric acceleration: total distance
statement: A bead slides along a straight wire. Its acceleration at time $t$ seconds is $a=-4\sin 2t$ m s$^{-2}$, for $0\le t\le\pi$. When $t=0$ the bead is at the origin $O$ and its velocity is $3$ m s$^{-1}$. (a) Show that $v=2\cos 2t+1$. [3] (b) Find the times at which the particle is instantaneously at rest. [3] (c) Find an expression for the displacement $s$ of the particle from $O$ at time $t$. [2] (d) Find the exact total distance traveled by the particle during the interval $0\le t\le\pi$. [5]
markscheme: (a) $v=\int-4\sin2t\,dt=2\cos2t+c$ [M1] $v(0)=3$ gives $c=1$ [A1] $v=2\cos2t+1$ [A1] [AG] [3 marks] (b) $\cos2t=-\dfrac12$ [M1] $2t=\dfrac{2\pi}3$ or $\dfrac{4\pi}3$ (for $0\le2t\le2\pi$) [A1] $t=\dfrac\pi3$ and $t=\dfrac{2\pi}3$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $s=\int(2\cos2t+1)\,dt=\sin2t+t+k$ [M1] $s(0)=0$ so $s=\sin2t+t$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) The direction changes at $t=\tfrac\pi3$ and $t=\tfrac{2\pi}3$, so find $s$ at $0,\tfrac\pi3,\tfrac{2\pi}3,\pi$ [M1] $s\left(\tfrac\pi3\right)=\dfrac{\sqrt3}2+\dfrac\pi3$ [A1] $s\left(\tfrac{2\pi}3\right)=\dfrac{2\pi}3-\dfrac{\sqrt3}2$ and $s(\pi)=\pi$ [A1] Distance $=\left(\dfrac{\sqrt3}2+\dfrac\pi3\right)+\left(\sqrt3-\dfrac\pi3\right)+\left(\dfrac\pi3+\dfrac{\sqrt3}2\right)$ [M1] $=2\sqrt3+\dfrac\pi3$ m [A1] [5 marks]
tips: List the angles $2t$ over the full interval $[0,2\pi]$ before halving them, or you will miss a rest time. Add the three leg lengths as positive quantities.

subtopic: Velocity with exponential and linear terms: direction change and return to start
statement: A particle moves in a straight line. Its velocity $v\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ at time $t$ seconds, for $0\le t\le6$, is $v=5e^{-0.4t}-t$. When $t=0$ the particle is at the origin $O$, with displacement $s=0$. (a) Find the time $T$ at which the particle is first instantaneously at rest. [2] (b) Find the acceleration of the particle at time $T$. [2] (c) Find an expression for the displacement $s$ at time $t$, and hence find the displacement when $t=6$. [3] (d) Find the total distance traveled by the particle in the $6$ seconds. [3] (e) Find the value of $t$, for $t>0$, at which the particle returns to $O$. [2]
markscheme: (a) Solving $5e^{-0.4t}-t=0$ with a GDC [M1] $T=2.13$ s [A1] [2 marks] (b) $a=\dfrac{dv}{dt}=-2e^{-0.4t}-1$ [M1] $a(T)=-1.85\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $s=\displaystyle\int\left(5e^{-0.4t}-t\right)dt=-12.5e^{-0.4t}-\dfrac{t^2}{2}+c$ and $s(0)=0$ gives $c=12.5$ [M1] $s=12.5\left(1-e^{-0.4t}\right)-\dfrac{t^2}{2}$ [A1] $s(6)=-6.63$ m [A1] [3 marks] (d) $v$ is positive for $t<T$ and negative after, since $v$ is decreasing, so $s(T)=4.90$ m [A1] Distance $=s(T)+\left(s(T)-s(6)\right)$ [M1] $=4.90+(4.90+6.63)=16.4$ m [A1] [3 marks] (e) Solving $s=0$ for $t>0$ using a GDC [M1] $t=4.58$ s [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Use your GDC to find the root of $v$ and store it, since $T$ is needed for both the acceleration and the distance. The particle turns around at $T$, so the distance is not simply $|s(6)|$.

subtopic: Velocity with a reciprocal term: times at rest, total distance and final displacement on the GDC
statement: A particle moves along a straight line. Its velocity at time $t$ seconds is $v=t-6+\dfrac{8}{t+1}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, for $0\le t\le6$. (a) Show that the particle is at rest when $t^2-5t+2=0$. [2] (b) Hence find the times at which the particle is at rest. [2] (c) Find the total distance traveled by the particle in the six seconds. [2] (d) Find the displacement of the particle from its starting position at $t=6$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $t-6+\dfrac{8}{t+1}=0$ gives $(t-6)(t+1)+8=0$ [M1] $t^2-5t-6+8=t^2-5t+2=0$ [AG] [A1] [2 marks] (b) $t=\dfrac{5\pm\sqrt{17}}{2}$, so $t=0.438$ and $t=4.56$ [A1][A1] [2 marks] (c) Distance $=\displaystyle\int_0^6|v|\,dt$ [M1] $=4.79$ m [A1] [2 marks] (d) Displacement $=\displaystyle\int_0^6v\,dt$ [M1] $=-2.43$ m [A1] [2 marks]
tips: On a calculator paper, enter $|v|$ into the integral for total distance rather than splitting by hand, but know the difference between $\int|v|\,dt$ and $\int v\,dt$. A negative displacement means the final position is on the negative side of the start.

subtopic: Constant acceleration between two points
statement: A car passes post $A$ and, with constant acceleration, passes post $B$ $100$ m further on, $4$ seconds later, at a speed of $30$ m/s. (a) Find the speed of the car at $A$. [3] (b) Find the acceleration of the car. [2]
tips: For constant acceleration, the average velocity over an interval equals the mean of the initial and final velocities.

subtopic: Velocity, rest and distance
statement: A camera drone moves along a straight horizontal cable. Its velocity, $v$ meters per second, $t$ seconds after it is switched on, is given by $v(t)=8\sin(0.3t)-2$, for $0\le t\le15$. (a) Find the acceleration of the drone when $t=4$. [2] (b) Find the values of $t$ when the drone is instantaneously at rest. [2] (c) Find the total distance traveled by the drone in the first $15$ seconds. [2]
markscheme: (a) $a=v'(t)=2.4\cos(0.3t)$ or using GDC derivative [M1] $a(4)=0.870\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ ($0.869658\ldots$) [A1] [2 marks] (b) $8\sin(0.3t)-2=0$ [M1] $t=0.842,\ 9.63$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\displaystyle\int_0^{15}\left|8\sin(0.3t)-2\right|\,dt$ [M1] $=65.8$ m ($65.8419\ldots$) [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Distance requires the integral of the absolute value of velocity; integrating v alone gives displacement (here only 2.29 m). Check the interval for every root of v = 0 before integrating.

subtopic: Speed and displacement for an exponential-type velocity
statement: A particle moves in a straight line with velocity $v(t)=4te^{-0.5t}$ m s$^{-1}$, for $t\ge0$. At $t=0$ its displacement from the origin is $0$. (a) Find the time at which the acceleration is zero, and the particle's greatest speed. [4] (b) Find the displacement of the particle at $t=6$. [2] (c) Explain why the distance traveled in the first 6 seconds equals the displacement at $t=6$. [1] (d) The displacement is given by $s(t)=16-8(t+2)e^{-0.5t}$. Find the time at which the particle is 12 m from the origin. [2]
markscheme: (a) $a(t)=4e^{-0.5t}(1-0.5t)$ [M1] [A1] $a=0$ at $t=2$ [A1] Greatest speed $v(2)=\frac8e=2.94$ m s$^{-1}$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $\displaystyle\int_0^64te^{-0.5t}\,dt$ [M1] $=12.8$ m [A1] [2 marks] (c) $v(t)\ge0$ for $t\ge0$, so the particle never changes direction [R1] [1 mark] (d) $16-8(t+2)e^{-0.5t}=12$ solved on GDC [M1] $t=5.39$ s [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Maximum speed occurs where acceleration is zero (check it is a maximum). If the velocity never changes sign, distance traveled equals the magnitude of the displacement.

subtopic: Average speed for a journey with two different speeds
statement: A car travels from $A$ to $B$ at a constant speed of $60$ km/h and returns along the same road at a constant speed of $40$ km/h. (a) Find the average speed for the whole journey. [3] (b) Explain why the average speed is not $50$ km/h. [1]
markscheme: (a) let the distance be $d$: time $\dfrac d{60}+\dfrac d{40}=\dfrac{5d}{120}$ [M1][A1] average speed $=\dfrac{2d}{5d/120}=48$ km/h [A1] [3 marks] (b) more time is spent travelling at the slower speed, so the average is weighted towards $40$ [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Average speed is total distance divided by total time, not the mean of the two speeds.

subtopic: Constant acceleration formulae from integration, applied to braking
statement: A particle moves in a straight line with constant acceleration $a$. At time $t=0$ it has displacement $0$ and velocity $u$. (a) By integrating, show that $v=u+at$ and $s=ut+\dfrac12at^2$. [3] (b) Eliminate $t$ to show that $v^2=u^2+2as$. [2] (c) A car travelling at $20$ m/s brakes with constant deceleration $4$ m/s$^2$. Find the time taken to stop and the stopping distance. [3]
markscheme: (a) $v=\int a\,dt=at+C$ and $v=u$ at $t=0$, so $v=u+at$ [M1][A1] $s=\int(u+at)dt=ut+\dfrac12at^2$ using $s=0$ at $t=0$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $t=\dfrac{v-u}a$ substituted into $s=ut+\dfrac12at^2$ [M1] $2as=v^2-u^2$ [AG] [A1] [2 marks] (c) $0=20-4t$ so $t=5$ s [A1] $0=400-8s$ [M1] $s=50$ m [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Integrate acceleration to get velocity, then velocity to get displacement. For the braking problem, set the final velocity to zero.

subtopic: Projectile from a cliff: time of flight, impact speed and angle, minimum speed
statement: A stone is thrown from the top of a cliff that is $10$ m above the sea. Its position, in meters, $t$ seconds after it is thrown, relative to the point at sea level directly below the throwing point, is $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix} 25t\cos40^\circ \\ 10+25t\sin40^\circ-4.9t^2 \end{pmatrix}$, where the first component is horizontal. (a) Find the time at which the stone hits the sea and its horizontal distance from the base of the cliff at that time. [4] (b) Find the speed of the stone when it hits the sea, and the angle below the horizontal at which it is moving. [4] (c) Find the minimum speed of the stone during its flight, and the time at which it occurs. [2]
markscheme: (a) Solve $10+25t\sin40^\circ-4.9t^2=0$ [M1] $t=3.81$ s [A1] Horizontal distance $=25(3.8145)\cos40^\circ$ [M1] $=73.1$ m [A1] [4 marks] (b) $\mathbf v=\begin{pmatrix} 25\cos40^\circ \\ 25\sin40^\circ-9.8t \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] At $t=3.8145$: $\mathbf v=\begin{pmatrix} 19.15 \\ -21.31 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] Speed $=\sqrt{19.15^2+21.31^2}=28.7\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ [A1] Angle $=\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{21.31}{19.15}\right)=48.1^\circ$ below the horizontal [A1] [4 marks] (c) The horizontal component is constant, so the speed is least when the vertical component is zero, at $t=\dfrac{25\sin40^\circ}{9.8}=1.64$ s [M1] Minimum speed $=25\cos40^\circ=19.2\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Horizontal velocity is constant in projectile motion, and the vertical velocity is the derivative of the vertical position. The speed is smallest when the vertical velocity component is zero, at the highest point.

subtopic: Oscillating particle: velocity, acceleration and total distance
statement: A particle moves along a straight line. Its displacement from a fixed point $O$ at time $t$ seconds, $t\ge0$, is $s=3\sin t+4\cos t$ meters. (a) Find expressions for the velocity $v$ and the acceleration $a$ of the particle. [2] (b) Show that $a=-s$. [1] (c) Find the first time at which the particle is instantaneously at rest. [3] (d) Find the total distance traveled by the particle in the first $2$ seconds. [3]
markscheme: (a) $v=3\cos t-4\sin t$ [A1] $a=-3\sin t-4\cos t$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $a=-\left(3\sin t+4\cos t\right)=-s$ [A1][AG] [1 mark] (c) $v=0$ gives $3\cos t=4\sin t$, so $\tan t=\dfrac34$ [M1][A1] $t=0.644$ s [A1] [3 marks] (d) The velocity changes sign at $t=0.6435$ (the next zero is at $t=0.6435+\pi>2$) [M1] $s(0)=4$, $s(0.6435)=5$, $s(2)=1.063$ [A1] Distance $=(5-4)+(5-1.063)=4.94$ m [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Set the GDC to radians for trigonometric motion. Distance requires splitting at every time the velocity is zero within the interval; compare the sign of $v$ at the endpoints.

subtopic: Vertical throw from a height: maximum height, time to hit the ground and impact speed
statement: A ball is thrown vertically upward from a point $1.5$ m above horizontal ground. Its height above the ground at time $t$ seconds is $s=1.5+12t-4.9t^2$ meters, until it hits the ground. (a) Find an expression for the velocity of the ball at time $t$. [1] (b) Find the maximum height of the ball above the ground. [3] (c) Find the time at which the ball hits the ground. [2] (d) Find the speed of the ball when it hits the ground. [2]
tips: The maximum height occurs when the velocity is zero. Discard the negative root of the quadratic and remember that speed is the magnitude of the velocity, so give a positive value.

subtopic: Braking distance with a reaction time and impact speed
statement: A car travels at $20$ m s$^{-1}$ along a straight road. The driver sees an obstacle $58$ m ahead. After a reaction time of $0.5$ s, during which the speed is unchanged, the driver applies the brakes, giving a constant deceleration of $4$ m s$^{-2}$. (a) Find the distance travelled by the car during the reaction time. [1] (b) Show that the car does not stop before reaching the obstacle. [3] (c) Find the speed of the car when it reaches the obstacle. [3]
markscheme: (a) $20\times0.5=10$ m [A1] [1 mark] (b) braking distance until stopped: $v^2=u^2+2as$ gives $0=400-2\times4\times s$ so $s=50$ m [M1][A1] total $=10+50=60>58$, so the car does not stop in time [R1] [3 marks] (c) distance available for braking $=58-10=48$ m [A1] $v^2=400-2\times4\times48=16$ [M1] $v=4$ m s$^{-1}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The car travels at constant speed during the reaction time, so the braking only starts after $10$ m. Use a constant-acceleration formula that links speeds and distance without time.

subtopic: Drone ascent with linear velocity and maximum height
statement: A drone climbs vertically from a launch platform. Its upward velocity at time $t$ seconds is $v(t)=12-4t$ m s$^{-1}$ for $0\le t\le5$, and at $t=0$ the drone is $10$ m above the ground. (a) Write down the acceleration of the drone. [1] (b) Find the time at which the drone is momentarily at rest. [1] (c) Find an expression for the height $h(t)$ of the drone above the ground. [2] (d) Find the maximum height reached by the drone. [2]
tips: The maximum height of a body moving up and then down occurs when the velocity is zero. Use the initial height to fix the constant of integration.

subtopic: Acceleration from velocity as a function of displacement using v dv/ds
statement: The velocity $v\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ of a particle moving along a straight line, when its displacement from a fixed point $O$ is $s$ meters, is given by $v=4-s^2$. (a) Use $a=v\dfrac{dv}{ds}$ to show that the acceleration is $a=2s^3-8s$. [3] (b) Find the acceleration of the particle when $s=1$. [1] (c) Find all values of $s$ for which the acceleration is zero. [2]
tips: When velocity is given in terms of displacement, the chain rule gives $a=v\frac{dv}{ds}$ directly, with no need to introduce time. Factorize fully when asked for zeros.

subtopic: Finding a parameter from total distance for a tunnel cart
statement: A tunnel-inspection cart moves along a straight track with velocity $v(t)=kt(6-t)$ m s$^{-1}$ for $0\le t\le6$, where $k$ is a positive constant. The cart travels a total distance of $54$ m in these $6$ seconds. (a) Find the value of $k$. [3] (b) Find the maximum speed of the cart. [2] (c) Find the acceleration at $t=5$ and state what it tells you about the motion at that instant. [2] (d) Find the length of time for which the speed of the cart is at least $10$ m s$^{-1}$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\int_0^6kt(6-t)\,dt=k\left[3t^2-\frac{t^3}{3}\right]_0^6$ [M1] $=36k$ [A1] $36k=54$ so $k=1.5$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) maximum at $t=3$ (symmetry) [M1] $v(3)=1.5(3)(3)=13.5$ m s$^{-1}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $a=1.5(6-2t)=9-3t$ so $a(5)=-6$ m s$^{-2}$ [A1] velocity is positive and acceleration negative, so the cart is slowing down [R1] [2 marks] (d) $1.5t(6-t)\ge10$ [M1] $1.47\le t\le4.53$ [A1] duration $=3.06$ s [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Because $v\ge0$ on the interval, the total distance equals the definite integral of $v$. For a parameter problem, write the integral in terms of $k$ first.

subtopic: Exponentially decaying velocity
statement: A skater glides along a straight line so that her displacement from the starting point after $t$ seconds is $s(t)=50\left(1-e^{-0.2t}\right)$ meters, for $t\ge0$. (a) Find an expression for her velocity at time $t$. [2] (b) Find her acceleration at time $t$, and state its value at $t=0$. [1] (c) Find the limiting value of $s(t)$ as $t\to\infty$, and explain what it represents. [2] (d) Find the time after which her speed is less than $1$ m s$^{-1}$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $v(t)=\frac{ds}{dt}$ [M1] $=10e^{-0.2t}$ m s$^{-1}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $a(t)=-2e^{-0.2t}$, so $a(0)=-2$ m s$^{-2}$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $e^{-0.2t}\to0$, so $s\to50$ [M1] the skater approaches, but never passes, a point 50 m from the start [A1] [2 marks] (d) $10e^{-0.2t}=1$ [M1] $t=5\ln10=11.5$ s [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Velocity is the derivative of displacement and acceleration is the derivative of velocity. A limit as $t\to\infty$ tells you about the long-term position.

subtopic: Constant acceleration from integration: velocity, displacement and greatest displacement
statement: A particle moves along a straight line with constant acceleration $-4\ \text{m s}^{-2}$. At $t=0$ seconds its velocity is $10\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ and its displacement from a fixed point $O$ is $3$ m. (a) Find an expression for the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$. [2] (b) Show that the displacement $s$ meters at time $t$ is $s=3+10t-2t^2$. [2] (c) Find the greatest displacement of the particle from $O$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $v=\int -4\,dt=-4t+c$ [M1] $v(0)=10$ gives $v=10-4t$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $s=\int(10-4t)\,dt=10t-2t^2+k$ [M1] $s(0)=3$ so $k=3$ [A1] $s=3+10t-2t^2$ [AG] [2 marks] (c) Greatest displacement occurs when $v=0$ [M1] $10-4t=0$ so $t=2.5$ [A1] $s=3+25-12.5=15.5$ m [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The constant-acceleration formulas are just the result of integrating a constant twice, so use integration and the initial conditions. A turning point of the displacement occurs where the velocity is zero.

subtopic: Displacement versus total distance
statement: A particle moves in a straight line with velocity $v=t^2-6t+8$ m s$^{-1}$ for $0\leq t\leq5$. (a) Find the times at which the particle changes direction in the interval given. [2] (b) Find the displacement of the particle between $t=0$ and $t=5$. [2] (c) Find the total distance traveled in this time. [3]
markscheme: (a) $v=0$: $t=2$, $t=4$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (b) $\int_0^{5}v\,dt=\frac{20}{3}$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (c) Split the integral at the direction changes [M1]: $\frac{20}{3}$, $-\frac{4}{3}$, $\frac{4}{3}$ [A1]; total distance $=\frac{28}{3}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Distance is the integral of $|v|$; split the interval where the velocity changes sign and add the absolute values.

subtopic: Range, height and trajectory of a projectile at a general angle
statement: A projectile is launched from the ground at speed $V$ at an angle $\alpha$ above the horizontal, with $0<\alpha<\dfrac\pi2$. Take the acceleration due to gravity as $g$ and ignore air resistance. (a) Show that the position at time $t$ is $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}Vt\cos\alpha\\ Vt\sin\alpha-\dfrac12gt^2\end{pmatrix}$, and that the range is $R=\dfrac{V^2\sin2\alpha}g$. [5] (b) Find the value of $\alpha$ that gives the greatest range, and state that range. [2] (c) Show that angles $\alpha$ and $90^\circ-\alpha$ give the same range. [2] (d) With $V=20$ m/s and $g=10$ m/s$^2$, find the two angles, to the nearest tenth of a degree, that give a range of $30$ m. [3] (e) Show that the greatest height is $H=\dfrac{V^2\sin^2\alpha}{2g}$, and that $\dfrac HR=\dfrac{\tan\alpha}4$. [3]
markscheme: (a) acceleration $\begin{pmatrix}0\\ -g\end{pmatrix}$, integrate twice with initial velocity $\begin{pmatrix}V\cos\alpha\\ V\sin\alpha\end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1] landing when $Vt\sin\alpha-\dfrac12gt^2=0$, $t=\dfrac{2V\sin\alpha}g$ [M1] $R=V\cos\alpha\times\dfrac{2V\sin\alpha}g$ [M1] $=\dfrac{V^2\sin2\alpha}g$ [AG] [A1] [5 marks] (b) $\sin2\alpha=1$ so $\alpha=45^\circ$ [A1] $R_{\max}=\dfrac{V^2}g$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\sin\left(2(90^\circ-\alpha)\right)=\sin(180^\circ-2\alpha)$ [M1] $=\sin2\alpha$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $40\sin2\alpha=30$ [M1] $2\alpha=48.6^\circ$ or $131.4^\circ$ [A1] $\alpha=24.3^\circ$ or $65.7^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) vertical velocity zero at $t=\dfrac{V\sin\alpha}g$ [M1] $H=\dfrac{V^2\sin^2\alpha}{2g}$ [A1] $\dfrac HR=\dfrac{\sin^2\alpha}{4\sin\alpha\cos\alpha}=\dfrac{\tan\alpha}4$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Resolve the initial velocity into horizontal and vertical components. The horizontal speed is constant and the vertical motion has acceleration $-g$.

subtopic: Overtaking of two trams on a straight track
statement: Two trams, A and B, travel in the same direction along a straight track. Measured from a depot, the displacement of tram A at time $t$ seconds is $s_A=0.4t^2$ m and the displacement of tram B is $s_B=25+6t$ m, for $t\ge0$. (a) Find the velocity of each tram at time $t$. [2] (b) Find the time at which tram A overtakes tram B. [3] (c) Find the speed of tram A at this moment. [1] (d) Find the greatest distance by which tram B is ahead of tram A before A overtakes B. [3]
tips: The gap between two moving objects is greatest or least when their velocities are equal (gap derivative is zero). Use the positive root only for the overtaking time.

subtopic: Velocity, rest, displacement and distance
statement: A particle moves in a straight line. Its velocity at time $t$ seconds is $v(t)=3t^2-12t+9$ m s$^{-1}$, for $t\ge0$. At $t=0$ the particle is at the origin. (a) Find the times at which the particle is instantaneously at rest. [2] (b) Find the acceleration of the particle at $t=2$. [2] (c) Find an expression for the displacement $s(t)$ of the particle from the origin. [2] (d) Find the total distance traveled by the particle in the first 4 seconds. [3]
tips: Total distance needs the position at every time the velocity changes sign, not just at the endpoints. Displacement and distance are different quantities.

subtopic: Two particles with exponential and quadratic displacements: rest, meeting and greatest separation
statement: Two particles $A$ and $B$ move along the same straight line.
