Their displacements from a fixed point $O$, in meters, at time $t$ seconds, $t\ge0$, are $s_A=5te^{-0.2t}$ and $s_B=\dfrac{t^2}{4}$. (a) Show that $A$ is instantaneously at rest when $t=5$, and find the displacement of $A$ at this time. [4] (b) Find the time $t>0$ at which the particles meet. [2] (c) Find the greatest distance between the particles for $0\le t\le t_m$, where $t_m$ is the time found in part (b). [3] (d) Find the velocity of each particle at time $t_m$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $v_A=5e^{-0.2t}-te^{-0.2t}$ [M1][A1] $=(5-t)e^{-0.2t}$, which is zero when $t=5$ since $e^{-0.2t}>0$ [A1] $s_A(5)=25e^{-1}=9.20$ m [A1] [4 marks] (b) Solve $5te^{-0.2t}=\dfrac{t^2}{4}$ for $t>0$ using the GDC [M1] $t=6.01$ s [A1] [2 marks] (c) Distance apart $d=s_A-s_B$ (since $s_A\ge s_B$ on this interval) [M1] Maximum of $d$ on the GDC occurs at $t=2.69$ [A1] Greatest distance $=6.04$ m [A1] [3 marks] (d) $v_A(6.01)=-0.304\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ [A1] $v_B=\dfrac t2=3.01\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Use the GDC to solve equations that cannot be rearranged, and report answers to 3 significant figures. When maximizing the gap between two particles, define the distance as one function and find its maximum on the correct interval.

subtopic: Velocity and displacement from acceleration, direction changes
statement: A cyclist rides along a straight path. Her acceleration at time $t$ seconds is $a=12-6t$ m s$^{-2}$, for $0\le t\le 4$. At $t=0$ she is at the origin $O$ with velocity $-9$ m s$^{-1}$. (a) Find an expression for her velocity $v$ at time $t$. [3] (b) Find the times at which she is instantaneously at rest. [2] (c) Find the total distance she travels in the first $4$ seconds. [4]
tips: Whenever the velocity changes sign, total distance needs separate pieces; find the displacement at each turning time and add the absolute changes. Check that $s(3)=0$ makes sense with $v$'s factorized form.

subtopic: Stopping distance of a braking tram
statement: A tram travelling at $15$ m s$^{-1}$ applies its brakes at $t=0$ and decelerates at a constant $2.5$ m s$^{-2}$ until it stops. Take the direction of travel as positive and $s=0$ at the point where braking begins. (a) Find an expression for the velocity $v(t)$ of the tram while braking. [2] (b) Find the time taken for the tram to stop. [1] (c) Find the distance the tram travels while braking. [2]
tips: Deceleration means a negative acceleration when the direction of travel is taken as positive. The tram stops when $v=0$.

subtopic: Particle with a sinusoidal velocity
statement: The velocity of a particle moving on a straight line is $v=5\sin(0.8t)-1$ m s$^{-1}$ for $0\leq t\leq8$, where $t$ is in seconds. Use radians. (a) Find the times at which the particle is at rest in this interval. [3] (b) Find the displacement of the particle from its starting point at $t=8$. [2] (c) Find the total distance traveled in the 8 seconds. [3] (d) Find the greatest magnitude of the acceleration and the first time it occurs. [3] (e) State the period of the motion of the velocity and the first time after $t=0$ at which the velocity is again $-1$ m s$^{-1}$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $5\sin(0.8t)=1$ [M1]; $t=0.252$ [A1]; $t=3.675$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\int_0^8v\,dt$ [M1] $=-7.957$ m [A1] [2 marks] (c) Split at the rest times: $\int|v|\,dt$ [M1][A1] $=25.605$ m [A1] [3 marks] (d) $a=4\cos(0.8t)$ [A1]; greatest magnitude $4$ m s$^{-2}$ [A1] at $t=0$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) Period $=\dfrac{2\pi}{0.8}=7.854$ s [A1]; $5\sin(0.8t)-1=-1$ gives $\sin(0.8t)=0$ [M1]; first positive time $t=3.927$ s [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A velocity that is sinusoidal has an acceleration that is its derivative; remember the chain-rule factor $0.8$ when differentiating.

subtopic: Position and velocity from a vector acceleration
statement: A particle has acceleration $\mathbf a=\begin{pmatrix}6t\\ -4\end{pmatrix}$ m/s$^2$. At $t=0$ its position is $\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 2\end{pmatrix}$ m and its velocity is $\begin{pmatrix}0\\ 5\end{pmatrix}$ m/s. (a) Find the velocity and position vectors at time $t$. [4] (b) Find the time at which the particle is moving parallel to the $x$-axis, and its position and speed then. [4]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf v=\begin{pmatrix}3t^2\\ 5-4t\end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1] $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}1+t^3\\ 2+5t-2t^2\end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1] [4 marks] (b) $5-4t=0$ so $t=1.25$ [A1] position $(2.95,\ 5.13)$ [A1][A1] speed $=3\times1.25^2=4.69$ m/s [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Integrate each component of the acceleration separately, using the initial conditions for the constants. Motion parallel to the $x$-axis means the $y$-component of velocity is zero.

subtopic: Velocity inversely proportional to displacement
statement: A particle moves along the positive $x$-axis with velocity $v=\dfrac2x$ m/s at displacement $x$ m. At $t=0$, $x=1$. (a) Show that $x=\sqrt{4t+1}$. [4] (b) Show that the acceleration is $-\dfrac4{x^3}$, and find its value when $t=2$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=\dfrac2x$ so $\int x\,dx=\int2\,dt$ [M1] $\dfrac{x^2}2=2t+C$ [A1] $C=\dfrac12$ [A1] $x^2=4t+1$ [AG] [A1] [4 marks] (b) $a=v\dfrac{dv}{dx}=\dfrac2x\times\left(-\dfrac2{x^2}\right)=-\dfrac4{x^3}$ [M1][A1] $x=3$ so $a=-\dfrac4{27}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Separate the variables $x$ and $t$. Use $a=v\,dv/dx$ to find the acceleration directly as a function of $x$.

subtopic: Acceleration proportional to velocity: v dv/ds and dv/dt, never reaching the limit
statement: A particle moves along a straight line with acceleration $a=-0.5v\ \text{m s}^{-2}$, where $v\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ is its velocity. At $t=0$ seconds the particle is at the origin $O$ with $v=8$. Let $s$ meters be the displacement from $O$. (a) Use $a=v\dfrac{dv}{ds}$ to show that $v=8-0.5s$. [4] (b) Hence find the value of $s$ at which $v=0$. [1] (c) By using $a=\dfrac{dv}{dt}$, find $v$ in terms of $t$. [3] (d) Find $s$ in terms of $t$, and hence explain why the particle never actually reaches the position found in part (b). [3]
markscheme: (a) $v\dfrac{dv}{ds}=-0.5v$ [M1] Since $v\ne0$, $\dfrac{dv}{ds}=-0.5$ [A1] $v=-0.5s+c$ [M1] $s=0,\ v=8$ gives $c=8$, so $v=8-0.5s$ [A1][AG] [4 marks] (b) $8-0.5s=0$ gives $s=16$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $\dfrac{dv}{dt}=-0.5v$, so $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{1}{v}\,dv=\int -0.5\,dt$ [M1] $\ln v=-0.5t+c$ [A1] $v=8e^{-0.5t}$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $s=\displaystyle\int 8e^{-0.5t}\,dt=-16e^{-0.5t}+k$ [M1] $s(0)=0$ gives $s=16-16e^{-0.5t}$ [A1] Since $e^{-0.5t}>0$ for all $t$, $s<16$ always, so $s=16$ is approached but never reached [R1] [3 marks]
tips: In part (a) you may divide by $v$ because the particle is moving. A particle can approach a limiting position as $t\to\infty$ without ever getting there, so check the time-based formula when a question asks whether a position is reached.

subtopic: Elliptical path: velocity, speed function, extreme speeds and acceleration
statement: A particle moves in a plane so that its position vector at time $t$ seconds is $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix} 4\cos t \\ 3\sin t \end{pmatrix}$ meters relative to the origin, for $0\le t\le\pi$. (a) Find the velocity vector of the particle. [2] (b) Show that the speed of the particle is $\sqrt{9+7\sin^2t}$. [3] (c) Find the minimum and maximum speeds of the particle, and the values of $t$ at which they occur. [3] (d) Show that the acceleration vector satisfies $\mathbf a=-\mathbf r$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf v=\begin{pmatrix} -4\sin t \\ 3\cos t \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (b) $|\mathbf v|^2=16\sin^2t+9\cos^2t$ [M1] $=9\sin^2t+9\cos^2t+7\sin^2t$ [A1] $=9+7\sin^2t$ using $\sin^2t+\cos^2t=1$ [A1] so speed $=\sqrt{9+7\sin^2t}$ [AG] [3 marks] (c) $0\le\sin^2t\le1$ [M1] Minimum speed $3\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ at $t=0$ and $t=\pi$ [A1] Maximum speed $4\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $\mathbf a=\begin{pmatrix} -4\cos t \\ -3\sin t \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=-\begin{pmatrix} 4\cos t \\ 3\sin t \end{pmatrix}=-\mathbf r$ [A1] [AG] [2 marks]
tips: To find extreme speeds, rewrite the squared speed so that a single trigonometric term remains, then use its range. Remember that acceleration is the derivative of velocity, so differentiate componentwise twice.

subtopic: Velocity and displacement from an exponential acceleration
statement: A particle moves in a straight line. Its acceleration at time $t$ seconds is $a=4e^{-0.5t}$ m s$^{-2}$ for $t\ge0$, and it starts from rest. (a) Find an expression for the velocity $v$ in terms of $t$. [3] (b) Write down the limiting value of the velocity as $t\to\infty$. [1] (c) Find the time at which the velocity first reaches $7$ m s$^{-1}$, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (d) Find the distance traveled in the first $5$ seconds, correct to 3 significant figures. [3]
tips: Integrate acceleration to get velocity and use the initial condition. Since $v\ge0$, distance equals displacement here.

subtopic: Vertical velocity of a passenger on a Ferris wheel
statement: A Ferris wheel completes one revolution every $40$ seconds. The height of a passenger above the ground, in meters, is modeled by $h(t)=11-10\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{20}\right)$, where $t$ is the time in seconds after the passenger boards at the lowest point and the argument of cosine is in radians. (a) Find an expression for the vertical velocity $v(t)=h'(t)$. [2] (b) Write down the maximum vertical speed and find the height of the passenger when it first occurs. [3] (c) Find the vertical velocity of the passenger at the first time the passenger is $16$ m above the ground. [3] (d) During one complete revolution, find the total time for which the vertical speed of the passenger exceeds $1$ m s$^{-1}$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $v=\frac{\pi}{2}\sin\left(\frac{\pi t}{20}\right)$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (b) maximum vertical speed $\frac{\pi}{2}=1.57$ m s$^{-1}$ [A1] occurs when $\sin\left(\frac{\pi t}{20}\right)=1$, i.e. $t=10$ [M1] $h(10)=11$ m [A1] [3 marks] (c) $11-10\cos\left(\frac{\pi t}{20}\right)=16$ so $\cos\left(\frac{\pi t}{20}\right)=-0.5$ [M1] $\frac{\pi t}{20}=\frac{2\pi}{3}$ so $t=13.3$ s [A1] $v=\frac{\pi}{2}\sin\frac{2\pi}{3}=1.36$ m s$^{-1}$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $\left|\sin\left(\frac{\pi t}{20}\right)\right|>\frac{2}{\pi}$ [M1] $4.39<t<15.6$ and $24.4<t<35.6$ [A1] total time $=2(11.2)=22.4$ s [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The speed condition $|v|>1$ gives two intervals in one revolution because the vertical speed is large both when rising and when descending. Use the symmetry of the sine curve or the GDC to find all four boundaries.

subtopic: Speed from a vector velocity
statement: A drone moves in a horizontal plane. At time $t$ seconds its velocity is $\mathbf{v}=\begin{pmatrix} 3t \\ 4-2t \end{pmatrix}$ m/s and at $t=0$ its position vector is $\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$ m. (a) Find the position vector of the drone at $t=2$. [3] (b) Show that the speed squared is $13t^{2}-16t+16$. [2] (c) Find the time at which the speed is least and the least speed, to three significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{r}=\begin{pmatrix} 2+1.5t^{2} \\ -1+4t-t^{2} \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1]; at $t=2$: $\begin{pmatrix} 8 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $(3t)^{2}+(4-2t)^{2}$ [M1]; $=13t^{2}-16t+16$ [AG] [2 marks] (c) minimum of $13t^{2}-16t+16$ at $t=\dfrac{16}{26}$ [M1]; $t=0.615$ s [A1]; least speed $3.33$ m/s [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Speed is the magnitude of the velocity vector; minimize its square for convenience.

subtopic: Displacement from velocity and total distance with direction changes
statement: A particle moves along a straight line. Its velocity $v\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ at time $t$ seconds, for $t\ge0$, is given by $v=3t^2-12t+9$. When $t=0$ the particle is $2$ m from a fixed point $O$, with displacement $s=2$. (a) Find the times at which the particle is instantaneously at rest. [2] (b) Find an expression for the displacement $s$ of the particle at time $t$. [3] (c) Find the total distance traveled by the particle in the first $4$ seconds. [3]
markscheme: (a) $3t^2-12t+9=3(t-1)(t-3)=0$ [M1] $t=1$ and $t=3$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $s=\displaystyle\int\left(3t^2-12t+9\right)dt$ [M1] $s=t^3-6t^2+9t+c$ [A1] $s=0+c=2$, so $s=t^3-6t^2+9t+2$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) The particle changes direction at $t=1$ and $t=3$ [M1] $s(0)=2,\ s(1)=6,\ s(3)=2,\ s(4)=6$ [A1] Total distance $=4+4+4=12$ m [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Total distance is not the same as displacement: split the time interval at each instant when the velocity is zero and add the absolute changes in $s$. Use $s(0)$ to fix the constant of integration.

subtopic: A particle with sinusoidal velocity
statement: A particle moves on a straight line with velocity $v=4\sin(2t)$ m/s at time $t$ seconds. (a) Find the acceleration at time $t$ and the acceleration at $t=0$. [2] (b) Find the displacement of the particle between $t=0$ and $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$. [3] (c) State the greatest speed of the particle. [1]
tips: The derivative of $\sin(2t)$ is $2\cos(2t)$.

subtopic: Velocity involving an exponential: distance and maximum speed
statement: A particle moves in a straight line with velocity $v=t\mathrm e^{-t/2}$ m s$^{-1}$ for $t\ge0$. (a) Find the time at which the speed is greatest, and the greatest speed. [4] (b) Find the distance travelled in the first $6$ seconds. [2] (c) Find the acceleration at $t=4$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{dv}{dt}=\mathrm e^{-t/2}\left(1-\dfrac t2\right)$ [M1][A1] $t=2$ [A1] $v=0.7358$ m s$^{-1}$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $\displaystyle\int_0^6t\mathrm e^{-t/2}\,dt$ [M1] $=3.203$ m [A1] [2 marks] (c) $a=\mathrm e^{-2}\left(1-2\right)$ [M1] $=-0.135$ m s$^{-2}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The maximum of $v$ is where its derivative (the acceleration) is zero. The velocity never changes sign here, so distance equals the integral.

subtopic: Return to origin with a two-term trigonometric velocity
statement: A particle moves along a straight line with velocity $v(t)=3\sin t-2\sin(2t)$ m s$^{-1}$ for $t\ge0$, where the argument is in radians. At $t=0$ the particle is at the origin. (a) Find an expression for the displacement $s(t)$. [3] (b) Use your GDC to find all times in $0<t\le2\pi$ at which the particle is at the origin. [2] (c) The particle initially moves in the negative direction. Find the greatest distance it reaches from the origin in the negative direction before it turns back. [3] (d) Find the total distance traveled in the interval $0\le t\le\frac{\pi}{3}$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $s=-3\cos t+\cos(2t)+C$ [M1][A1] $s(0)=0$ gives $-3+1+C=0$ so $C=2$ and $s=2-3\cos t+\cos(2t)$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) graph $s=0$ for $0<t\le2\pi$: $t=1.05$ and $t=5.24$ [A1] and $t=6.28$ [A1] (these are $\frac{\pi}{3}$, $\frac{5\pi}{3}$ and $2\pi$) [2 marks] (c) $v=0$ with $t>0$: $3\sin t=2\sin(2t)$ solved on the GDC gives $t=0.723$ s [M1][A1] $s(0.723)=-0.125$, so the greatest distance in the negative direction is $0.125$ m [A1] [3 marks] (d) the particle moves to $s=-0.125$ at $t=0.723$ and then returns to $s=0$ at $t=\frac{\pi}{3}$ [M1] distance $=0.125+0.125=0.25$ m [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Look for sign changes of $v$ to find turning points, then evaluate $s$ there. Part (d) needs the distance out and the distance back, not just the net displacement.

subtopic: Two particles in the plane: velocities, no collision and minimum distance between them
statement: Two particles $A$ and $B$ move in a plane. Relative to the origin, their position vectors at time $t\ge0$ seconds are $\mathbf r_A=\begin{pmatrix} 1+2t \\ 4-t \end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf r_B=\begin{pmatrix} 8-t \\ 1+t \end{pmatrix}$, in meters. (a) Find the speed of each particle. [2] (b) Show that the particles never collide. [2] (c) Show that the square of the distance between the particles at time $t$ is $13t^2-54t+58$. [2] (d) Find the minimum distance between the particles and the time at which it occurs. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf v_A=\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$, speed $\sqrt5=2.24\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ [A1] $\mathbf v_B=\begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$, speed $\sqrt2=1.41\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Equal $x$: $1+2t=8-t$ gives $t=\dfrac73$; equal $y$: $4-t=1+t$ gives $t=\dfrac32$ [M1] The times differ, so the particles are never at the same point at the same time [R1] [2 marks] (c) $\mathbf r_B-\mathbf r_A=\begin{pmatrix} 7-3t \\ 2t-3 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $d^2=(7-3t)^2+(2t-3)^2=13t^2-54t+58$ [A1][AG] [2 marks] (d) Minimum of $\sqrt{13t^2-54t+58}$ found on the GDC (or at $t=\dfrac{54}{26}$) [M1] $t=2.08$ s [A1] Minimum distance $=1.39$ m [A1] [3 marks]
tips: To show two moving points never collide, find the times that match each coordinate separately and show they disagree. Minimizing the squared distance gives the same time as minimizing the distance.

subtopic: Cubic velocity of a metro train leaving a station
statement: A metro train leaves a station and accelerates along a straight track. For $0\le t\le30$ its acceleration is $a(t)=0.12t-0.004t^2$ m s$^{-2}$, where $t$ is in seconds. The train starts from rest at $s=0$. (a) Show that the acceleration is zero when $t=30$, and find the maximum acceleration. [3] (b) Find an expression for the velocity $v(t)$. [2] (c) Find the speed of the train at $t=30$, in m s$^{-1}$. [2] (d) Find the distance covered by the train in the $30$ seconds. [2]
tips: The speed keeps increasing while the acceleration is positive, so the maximum speed occurs when $a=0$, here at $t=30$. A quadratic with known roots is symmetric about the midpoint of its roots.

subtopic: Integrating acceleration with two initial conditions
statement: A particle moves along a straight line with acceleration $a(t)=6t-4$ m s$^{-2}$ for $t\ge0$. At $t=0$ the particle has velocity $5$ m s$^{-1}$ and displacement $2$ m from the origin. (a) Find an expression for the velocity $v(t)$. [2] (b) Find an expression for the displacement $s(t)$. [2] (c) Show that the particle never comes to rest. [3] (d) Find the displacement of the particle when $t=3$. [1]
tips: Each integration introduces a constant that must be found from the matching initial condition. To show a quadratic is never zero, use the discriminant.

subtopic: Velocity from exponential acceleration, limiting velocity and least displacement
statement: A particle moves along a straight line. Its acceleration at time $t$ seconds is $a=12e^{-2t}$ m s$^{-2}$, for $t\ge0$. When $t=0$ the particle is at the origin $O$ and its velocity is $-2$ m s$^{-1}$. (a) Show that the velocity of the particle is $v=4-6e^{-2t}$. [3] (b) Find the exact time at which the particle is instantaneously at rest. [2] (c) Write down the limiting value of $v$ as $t\to\infty$. [1] (d) Show that the least displacement of the particle from $O$ is $2\ln\left(\tfrac32\right)-1$ meters. [5]
markscheme: (a) $v=\int12e^{-2t}\,dt=-6e^{-2t}+c$ [M1] $v(0)=-2$: $-6+c=-2$ so $c=4$ [A1] $v=4-6e^{-2t}$ [A1] [AG] [3 marks] (b) $4-6e^{-2t}=0$ so $e^{-2t}=\dfrac23$ [M1] $t=\dfrac12\ln\dfrac32$ s [A1] [2 marks] (c) As $t\to\infty$, $e^{-2t}\to0$ so $v\to4$ m s$^{-1}$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) $s=\int v\,dt=4t+3e^{-2t}+k$ and $s(0)=0$ gives $k=-3$ [M1] [A1] Since $a>0$ for all $t$, $v$ is increasing, so $v<0$ before $t=\tfrac12\ln\tfrac32$ and $v>0$ after; the displacement is least at that time [R1] $s=4\left(\tfrac12\ln\tfrac32\right)+3\cdot\dfrac23-3$ [M1] $=2\ln\dfrac32-1$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: In a "show that" integration problem the constant of integration is usually the point of the mark. To justify a least value, say why the sign of $v$ changes only once.

subtopic: Particle with changing acceleration
statement: A particle $P$ moves along a straight line. At time $t$ seconds its acceleration is $a=12-6t$ m s$^{-2}$. When $t=0$, $v=-9$ m s$^{-1}$ and $s=2$ m. (a) Find an expression for the velocity $v$ at time $t$. [3] (b) Find the displacement $s$ at time $t$, given that $s=2$ when $t=0$. [3] (c) Find the velocity and the displacement when $t=3$. [2] (d) Find the time(s), for $t>0$, at which the particle is momentarily at rest. [2]
tips: Velocity is the integral of acceleration; momentarily at rest means $v=0$ (take the positive root of the quadratic).

subtopic: Displacement and distance travelled from a velocity function
statement: A particle moves along a straight line with velocity $v=t^2-6t+8$ m s$^{-1}$ for $t\ge0$. At $t=0$ its displacement from the origin is $2$ m. (a) Find the times at which the particle is instantaneously at rest. [2] (b) Find an expression for the displacement $s$ at time $t$. [3] (c) Find the total distance travelled in the first $4$ seconds. [4]
markscheme: (a) $(t-2)(t-4)=0$ [M1] $t=2$ and $t=4$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $s=\dfrac{t^3}3-3t^2+8t+c$ [M1][A1] $c=2$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $s(0)=2$, $s(2)=\dfrac83-12+16+2=\dfrac{26}3$, $s(4)=\dfrac{64}3-48+32+2=\dfrac{22}3$ [A1][A1] the particle changes direction at $t=2$ [R1] distance $=\left(\dfrac{26}3-2\right)+\left(\dfrac{26}3-\dfrac{22}3\right)=\dfrac{20}3+\dfrac43=8$ m [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Distance travelled is not the same as displacement: split the interval at the times when the velocity changes sign.

subtopic: Three-dimensional velocity vector of an inspection drone
statement: A drone flies a short inspection route. Relative to a landing pad at the origin $O$, with the third coordinate as height, its velocity in m s$^{-1}$ at time $t$ seconds is $\mathbf v(t)=\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 4 \\ 2-0.4t \end{pmatrix}$, and its initial position is $\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1.5 \end{pmatrix}$ m. (a) Find the initial speed of the drone. [2] (b) Find the time at which the drone reaches the ground. [3] (c) Find the horizontal distance traveled by the drone between $t=0$ and the time it reaches the ground. [2] (d) Find the greatest height reached by the drone. [2]
markscheme: (a) speed $=\sqrt{3^2+4^2+2^2}$ [M1] $=\sqrt{29}=5.39$ m s$^{-1}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) height $z=1.5+2t-0.2t^2$ [M1][A1] $z=0$ gives $t=10.7$ s [A1] [3 marks] (c) horizontal speed $=\sqrt{3^2+4^2}=5$ m s$^{-1}$ (constant) [M1] distance $=5\times10.70=53.5$ m [A1] [2 marks] (d) greatest height when $2-0.4t=0$, i.e. $t=5$ [M1] $z=1.5+10-5=6.5$ m [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Horizontal motion uses only the first two components of the velocity vector, and height uses the third. Use the positive root of the quadratic for the landing time.

subtopic: Direction changes in a quadratic velocity
statement: A particle moves on a straight line with velocity $v=t^{2}-5t+4$ m/s for $0\le t\le5$ seconds. (a) Find the times at which the particle changes direction. [2] (b) Use your GDC to find the displacement over the $5$ seconds, to three significant figures. [2] (c) Find the total distance traveled over the $5$ seconds, to three significant figures. [3]
tips: For total distance, integrate the absolute value of the velocity (or split at the times when $v=0$).

subtopic: Braking at a constant deceleration
statement: A train traveling at $25$ m/s brakes with constant deceleration and comes to rest after traveling $60$ m. (a) Write down expressions for the velocity and the displacement during braking in terms of the deceleration $k$ m/s$^{2}$ and time $t$ s. [2] (b) Find the time taken to stop and the deceleration, to three significant figures. [4] (c) Find the distance needed to stop from $30$ m/s with the same deceleration, to three significant figures. [2]
tips: Constant acceleration means $v$ is linear in $t$; set $v=0$ to find the stopping time.

subtopic: Acceleration depending on velocity squared: separation of variables with arctan, stopping time and distance
statement: A particle travels on a straight track with acceleration $a=-(1+v^2)\ \text{m s}^{-2}$, where $v\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ is its velocity at time $t$ seconds. At $t=0$ the particle is at the origin $O$ with $v=1$. Let $s$ meters be its displacement from $O$. (a) By using $a=\dfrac{dv}{dt}$, show that $v=\tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}-t\right)$ for as long as $v>0$. [4] (b) Find the exact time at which the particle first comes to rest. [1] (c) By using $a=v\dfrac{dv}{ds}$, find an expression for $s$ in terms of $v$, and hence find the exact distance the particle travels before coming to rest. [4] (d) Verify your answer to part (c) by integrating the velocity found in part (a). [3]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{dv}{dt}=-(1+v^2)$ so $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{1}{1+v^2}\,dv=\int-1\,dt$ [M1] $\arctan v=-t+c$ [A1] $v(0)=1$ gives $c=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ [A1] $v=\tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}-t\right)$ [A1][AG] [4 marks] (b) $v=0$ when $\dfrac{\pi}{4}-t=0$, so $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $v\dfrac{dv}{ds}=-(1+v^2)$ so $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{v}{1+v^2}\,dv=\int-1\,ds$ [M1] $\dfrac12\ln(1+v^2)=-s+c$ [A1] $s=0,\ v=1$ gives $c=\dfrac12\ln2$, so $s=\dfrac12\ln\dfrac{2}{1+v^2}$ [A1] At rest, $v=0$: $s=\dfrac12\ln2$ m [A1] [4 marks] (d) $s=\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/4}\tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}-t\right)dt$ [M1] $=\left[\ln\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}-t\right)\right]_0^{\pi/4}$ [A1] $=\ln1-\ln\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}=\dfrac12\ln2$ m [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Choose the form of acceleration that matches the variables in the equation: $\frac{dv}{dt}$ gives velocity against time, while $v\frac{dv}{ds}$ gives velocity against position. Recognize $\frac{1}{1+v^2}$ as the derivative of arctan, and $\frac{v}{1+v^2}$ as a logarithmic derivative.

subtopic: Uniform circular motion in vector form
statement: A particle moves so that its position vector at time $t$ seconds is $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}3\cos2t\\ 3\sin2t\end{pmatrix}$ meters. (a) Find the velocity and the speed of the particle. [3] (b) Show that the acceleration is $-4\mathbf r$, and find its magnitude. [3] (c) Show that the velocity and acceleration are perpendicular at every time, and describe the path. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf v=\begin{pmatrix}-6\sin2t\\ 6\cos2t\end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1] speed $=\sqrt{36\sin^22t+36\cos^22t}=6$ m/s [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\mathbf a=\begin{pmatrix}-12\cos2t\\ -12\sin2t\end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1] $=-4\mathbf r$, magnitude $4\times3=12$ m/s$^2$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf a=72\sin2t\cos2t-72\cos2t\sin2t=0$ [A1] the distance from the origin is always $3$, so the path is a circle of radius $3$ centered at the origin [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Differentiate each component. Constant speed does not mean zero acceleration, because the direction of velocity changes.

subtopic: A ball thrown upward
statement: A ball is thrown vertically upward from a height of $1.5$ m with an initial speed of $14$ m/s. Its height at time $t$ seconds is $h=1.5+14t-4.9t^{2}$ meters (upward positive), until it hits the ground. (a) Find the maximum height reached and the time at which it occurs, to three significant figures. [3] (b) Find the time at which the ball hits the ground, to three significant figures. [2] (c) Find the speed of the ball on impact, to three significant figures, and state its direction. [3]
tips: Velocity is the derivative of height; the ball is at its highest point when its velocity is zero.

subtopic: Trigonometric displacement with exact total distance over a full period
statement: The displacement of a particle from a fixed point $O$ on a line is $s=t-2\sin t$ meters at time $t$ seconds, for $0\le t\le2\pi$. (a) Find the exact values of $t$ for which the particle is instantaneously at rest. [4] (b) Find the exact displacement of the particle at each of these times. [2] (c) Find the exact total distance traveled by the particle during the first $2\pi$ seconds. [3]
markscheme: (a) $v=\dfrac{ds}{dt}=1-2\cos t$ [M1][A1] $1-2\cos t=0$ gives $\cos t=\dfrac12$ [M1] $t=\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{3}$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $s\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)=\dfrac{\pi}{3}-\sqrt3$ [A1] $s\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{3}\right)=\dfrac{5\pi}{3}+\sqrt3$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $s(0)=0$ and $s(2\pi)=2\pi$. Sum the absolute changes between the turning points: [M1] $\left(\sqrt3-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)+\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{3}+2\sqrt3\right)+\left(\sqrt3-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$ [A1] $=4\sqrt3+\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ m [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Split the journey at every time when $v=0$ and add the absolute values of the changes in displacement. Check the sign of each change: here the first and last legs are in the negative direction relative to the previous point, so a sketch of $s$ values on a number line helps.

subtopic: Maximum acceleration of a particle
statement: A particle moves in a line with velocity $v=-t^3+9t^2-15t$ m/s for $0\le t\le8$. (a) Find the acceleration as a function of $t$. [2] (b) Find the maximum acceleration and the time at which it occurs. [3] (c) Find the times at which the particle is instantaneously at rest. [2]
tips: Acceleration is the derivative of velocity. Its maximum is found by differentiating again.

subtopic: Acceleration inversely proportional to time for a model rocket
statement: A model rocket launches vertically from ground level at $t=0$ from rest. For $0\le t\le9$ its upward acceleration is $a(t)=\dfrac{50}{t+1}$ m s$^{-2}$, where $t$ is in seconds. (a) Show that the velocity is $v(t)=50\ln(t+1)$. [3] (b) Find the velocity at $t=9$. [1] (c) Use your GDC to find the distance traveled between $t=0$ and $t=9$. [2] (d) Find the exact time at which the velocity is $100$ m s$^{-1}$. [2] (e) Find the acceleration when $t=9$. [1]
tips: Since the velocity function is given in part (a), later parts can be done even if you were unable to show it. Use the numerical integration facility of your GDC for (c).

subtopic: Two particles from the same origin: meeting, separation and distance
statement: Two particles $A$ and $B$ start from the origin $O$ at time $t=0$ and move along the same straight line. For $0\le t\le8$, the velocity of $A$ is $v_A=6t-t^2$ and the velocity of $B$ is $v_B=2t$, where $t$ is in seconds and velocities are in m s$^{-1}$. (a) Find the time at which $B$ catches up with $A$. [4] (b) Find the greatest distance by which $A$ is ahead of $B$ before $B$ catches up with $A$. [4] (c) Find the total distance travelled by $A$ in the time interval $0\le t\le8$. Give your answer to three significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) $s_A=3t^2-\dfrac{t^3}3$ [M1][A1] $s_B=t^2$ [A1] equal when $2t^2=\dfrac{t^3}3$ so $t=6$ (since $t\ne0$) [A1] [4 marks] (b) $d=s_A-s_B=2t^2-\dfrac{t^3}3$ [M1] $\dfrac{dd}{dt}=4t-t^2=0$ gives $t=4$ [A1] $d(4)=32-\dfrac{64}3$ [A1] $=\dfrac{32}3$ m [A1] [4 marks] (c) $v_A=t(6-t)$ is negative for $t>6$, so $A$ reverses at $t=6$ [R1] $s_A(6)=36$ and $s_A(8)=\dfrac{64}3$ [A1] distance $=36+\left(36-\dfrac{64}3\right)=\dfrac{152}3=50.7$ m [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Both particles start at the same point, so they are together when their displacements are equal. The distance travelled by $A$ in part (c) must be split at the time when its velocity changes sign.

subtopic: Greatest speed from a logarithmic displacement
statement: A particle moves on a straight line with displacement $s=\ln(t^{2}+1)$ meters at time $t\ge0$ seconds. (a) Find the velocity $v$ as a function of $t$. [2] (b) Show that the speed is greatest when $t=1$ and find the greatest speed. [4] (c) Find the acceleration at $t=1$ and explain what this means. [2]
markscheme: (a) chain rule [M1]; $v=\dfrac{2t}{t^{2}+1}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac{dv}{dt}=\dfrac{2(t^{2}+1)-2t(2t)}{(t^{2}+1)^{2}}=\dfrac{2(1-t^{2})}{(t^{2}+1)^{2}}$ [M1][A1]; zero at $t=1$ with $v'$ changing from positive to negative [R1]; greatest speed $v(1)=1$ m/s [A1] [4 marks] (c) $a(1)=0$ [A1]; the velocity is momentarily constant at its maximum [R1] [2 marks]
tips: The acceleration is zero where the velocity has a maximum or minimum.

subtopic: Total time for which the speed exceeds a given value
statement: A particle moves in a line with velocity $v=(t-1)(t-5)$ m/s for $0\le t\le7$. (a) Solve $v=3$ and $v=-3$. [3] (b) Find the total time in $0\le t\le7$ for which the speed exceeds $3$ m/s. [3]
tips: A speed greater than 3 means either $v>3$ or $v<-3$. Sketch $v$ against $t$ to find the intervals.

subtopic: A particle approaching its starting point forever
statement: The displacement of a particle from the origin is $s=te^{-t}$ meters at time $t\ge0$ seconds. (a) Find the time at which the particle is furthest from the origin, and that greatest displacement. [4] (b) Explain why $s\to0$ as $t\to\infty$, and find the total distance travelled by the particle. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{ds}{dt}=(1-t)e^{-t}$ [M1][A1] $=0$ at $t=1$ [A1] $s=e^{-1}$ m [A1] [4 marks] (b) $te^{-t}\to0$ as $t\to\infty$ [R1] the particle moves out $e^{-1}$ and then back $e^{-1}$ [M1] total distance $=\dfrac2e=0.736$ m [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The particle moves away until the velocity is zero, then returns, never quite reaching the origin.

subtopic: Total distance for a cubic velocity
statement: The velocity of a particle on a straight line is $v=(t-1)(t-2)(t-4)$ m s$^{-1}$, for $0\leq t\leq5$. (a) Find the times at which the particle changes direction in the interval given. [2] (b) Find the displacement of the particle between $t=0$ and $t=5$. [2] (c) Find the total distance traveled in this time. [3]
markscheme: (a) $v=0$: $t=1$, $t=2$, $t=4$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (b) $\int_0^{5}v\,dt=-\frac{5}{12}$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (c) Split the integral at the direction changes [M1]: $-\frac{37}{12}$, $\frac{5}{12}$, $-\frac{8}{3}$, $\frac{59}{12}$ [A1]; total distance $=\frac{133}{12}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Sketch $v$ first: the sign pattern tells you on which intervals the particle moves forward or backward.

subtopic: Gradient, midpoint and distance
statement: Points $A(-2,1)$ and $B(4,4)$ are given. (a) Find the gradient of the line $AB$ and its equation in the form $y=mx+c$. [3] (b) Find the midpoint $M$ and the exact length of $AB$. [3] (c) Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of $AB$. [3] (d) Determine whether the point $P(1,1)$ lies on the perpendicular bisector. [1]
markscheme: (a) $m=\dfrac{4-1}{4--2}=\frac{1}{2}$ [M1][A1]; $y=\frac{1}{2}x+2$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $M=(1,\frac{5}{2})$ [A1]; $AB=\sqrt{(4--2)^2+(4-1)^2}$ [M1] $=3 \sqrt{5}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Gradient $-\dfrac1m=-2$ [A1]; through $M$: $y-\frac{5}{2}=-2(x-1)$ [M1]; $y=-2x+\frac{9}{2}$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) At $x=1$: $y=\frac{5}{2}$, which does not equal $1$, so $P$ does not lie on it [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Use the midpoint as a point on the bisector and the negative reciprocal of the gradient as its gradient.

subtopic: Line through two points and a perpendicular line
statement: The points $A(2, -3)$ and $B(6, 5)$ lie on a line $L_1$. (a) Find the gradient of $L_1$ and its equation in the form $y=mx+c$. [3] (b) The line $L_2$ is perpendicular to $L_1$ and passes through $P(1, 4)$. Find its equation in the form $ax+by=d$ with integer coefficients. [3] (c) Find the coordinates of the point where $L_1$ and $L_2$ intersect. [3]
tips: Perpendicular gradients multiply to $-1$. Substitute $y=2x-7$ into the second equation to intersect.

subtopic: Distance between two parallel straight roads
statement: Two straight roads have equations $L_1: 4x-3y=6$ and $L_2: 4x-3y=21$, where each unit represents $100$ m. (a) Show that the point $P(0,-2)$ lies on $L_1$. [1] (b) Find the equation of the line through $P$ that is perpendicular to $L_1$, in the form $y=mx+c$. [2] (c) Find the coordinates of the point $Q$ where this perpendicular meets $L_2$. [2] (d) Find the shortest distance between the two roads, in meters. [2]
markscheme: (a) $4(0)-3(-2)=6$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) gradient of $L_1=\dfrac43$, so perpendicular gradient $=-\dfrac34$ [M1] $y=-\dfrac34x-2$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $4x-3\left(-\dfrac34x-2\right)=21$ [M1] $Q=(2.4,\,-3.8)$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $PQ=\sqrt{2.4^2+1.8^2}=3$ units [M1] $=300$ m [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The shortest distance between parallel lines is measured along a common perpendicular. Convert to meters at the end using the scale.

subtopic: Linear depreciation of a delivery van
statement: The value $V$ dollars of a delivery van $t$ years after it was bought is modeled by $V=18000-1500t$. (a) Find the value of the van after $4$ years. [1] (b) Find when the value of the van is \$6000. [2] (c) State what the number $1500$ represents in this model. [1]
markscheme: (a) $18000-1500\times4=12000$, so \$12 000 [A1] [1 mark] (b) $18000-1500t=6000$ [M1] $t=8$ years [A1] [2 marks] (c) the van loses \$1500 of value each year [A1] [1 mark]
tips: The gradient of a linear model is the constant rate of change, so give it with units and a direction (increase or decrease).

subtopic: Two burning candles: intersecting linear height models
statement: Candle $A$ is $24$ cm tall and burns down at a constant rate of $1.6$ cm per hour. Candle $B$ is $18$ cm tall and burns down at $0.9$ cm per hour. Both are lit at the same time. Let $t$ be the time in hours after lighting. (a) Write down the heights $h_A$ and $h_B$ of the candles at time $t$. [2] (b) Find the time at which the candles have the same height, and find that height. Give your answers to three significant figures. [3] (c) Find the time at which candle $A$ is completely burned, and the height of candle $B$ at that time. [2] (d) State the domain of $h_A$ in this model. [1]
tips: Write each height as starting height minus rate times time. A height cannot be negative, so the domain ends where the candle reaches zero.

subtopic: Filling a tank at two different rates
statement: A tank is filled by a pump. For the first $10$ minutes the pump delivers $20$ L per minute. After that, a second pump is switched on and the tank fills at $35$ L per minute. Let $V$ liters be the volume in the tank after $t$ minutes; the tank is empty at $t=0$. (a) Write down $V(t)$ for $0\le t\le10$ and for $t>10$. [3] (b) Find the time needed to reach $600$ L, in minutes and seconds, to the nearest second. [3] (c) Find the average rate of filling, in liters per minute, over the first $15$ minutes. [2]
tips: The gradient of each piece is the filling rate during that period.

subtopic: Shortest pipe from a farm to a straight pipeline
statement: A main pipeline runs along the straight line $3x-2y=12$, where $x$ and $y$ are measured in kilometers. A farm is at $F(5,8)$. A branch pipe is to be laid in a straight line from $F$ to the closest point $P$ on the main pipeline. (a) Find the equation of the line through $F$ perpendicular to the main pipeline, in the form $ax+by=c$. [3] (b) Find the coordinates of $P$. [3] (c) Find the length of the branch pipe, giving an exact value. [2] (d) Laying the pipe costs \$4800 per kilometer. Find the cost, correct to three significant figures. [1]
markscheme: (a) gradient of main pipeline $=\dfrac32$ [A1] perpendicular gradient $=-\dfrac23$ [A1] $y-8=-\dfrac23(x-5)$, so $2x+3y=34$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) solve $3x-2y=12$ and $2x+3y=34$ simultaneously [M1] $x=8$ [A1] $y=6$, so $P=(8,6)$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $FP=\sqrt{(8-5)^2+(6-8)^2}$ [M1] $=\sqrt{13}$ km [A1] [2 marks] (d) $4800\times\sqrt{13}=\$17\,300$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: The closest point on a line is the foot of the perpendicular from the point. Use the simultaneous equation solver on your GDC to find where two lines meet.

subtopic: Temperature conversion function
statement: The temperature in degrees Fahrenheit $F$ is related to the temperature in degrees Celsius $C$ by $F=1.8C+32$. (a) Find the value of $F$ when water boils at $C=100$. [1] (b) Find the value of $C$ when $F=50$. [2] (c) Find the temperature at which $F$ and $C$ have the same numerical value. [2] (d) Write $C$ in terms of $F$. [2]
tips: Set $F=C=x$ to find where the two scales agree.

subtopic: Used car prices against age: regression and model limits
statement: The asking prices $P$ (in thousands of dollars) of eight used cars of the same model, aged $a$ years, are: a: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8; P: 21.4, 19.8, 18.9, 16.7, 15.6, 13.4, 12.9, 10.8. (a) Find the equation of the regression line of $P$ on $a$. Give the coefficients to three significant figures. [2] (b) Write down the value of $r$ and describe the correlation. [2] (c) Interpret the gradient and the intercept of the line in this context. [2] (d) Use the unrounded regression line to estimate the price of a car aged $5.5$ years, to three significant figures. [2] (e) Find the age at which the model predicts a price of zero, and comment on the validity of the model at that age. [2]
markscheme: (a) $P=-1.50a+23.0$ [A1][A1] [2 marks] (b) $r=-0.996$ [A1] very strong negative linear correlation [A1] [2 marks] (c) gradient: the price falls by about \$1500 for each extra year of age [A1] intercept: a new car (age $0$) is modeled as costing about \$23 000 [A1] [2 marks] (d) $P=-1.5036\times5.5+22.954$ [M1] $=14.7$ thousand dollars [A1] [2 marks] (e) $a=\dfrac{22.954}{1.5036}=15.3$ years [A1] this is outside the data range ($1$ to $8$ years) and real car prices do not reach zero linearly, so the model is not valid there [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Always interpret the gradient with units (thousands of dollars per year). Use unrounded coefficients stored in your GDC for estimates, then round only the final answer.

subtopic: Two tanks: intersecting linear models
statement: Tank $A$ contains $120$ liters of water and is being filled at a constant rate of $8$ liters per minute. Tank $B$ contains $450$ liters and is being emptied at a constant rate of $12$ liters per minute. Let $t$ be the time in minutes from the start. (a) Find the time at which the two tanks contain the same volume, and find this volume. [3] (b) Find the time at which tank $B$ becomes empty. [1] (c) Find the time at which tank $A$ contains twice as much water as tank $B$, correct to three significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) $V_A=120+8t$ and $V_B=450-12t$ [A1] Equating: $120+8t=450-12t$ [M1] $t=16.5$ minutes, and the volume is $120+8(16.5)=252$ liters [A1] [3 marks] (b) $450-12t=0$, so $t=37.5$ minutes [A1] [1 mark] (c) $120+8t=2(450-12t)$ [M1] $32t=780$ [A1] $t=24.4$ minutes (this is before $37.5$, so tank $B$ still contains water) [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Write each volume as a linear function of time, then set up an equation matching the condition. Check that your solution lies in the time interval where both models make sense.

subtopic: Comparing three phone plans
statement: Plan $A$ costs \$18 per month plus \$4 per gigabyte (GB) of data used. Plan $B$ costs \$30 per month plus \$2.50 per GB. Plan $C$ costs \$55 per month with unlimited data. Let $g$ be the data used in a month, in GB. (a) Write down expressions for the monthly costs of plans $A$ and $B$, and find the value of $g$ at which they cost the same. [3] (b) Find the usage above which plan $C$ is cheaper than plan $A$, and the usage above which it is cheaper than plan $B$. Hence state, with a reason, the usage above which plan $C$ is the cheapest of the three plans. [3] (c) State the best plan for a customer who uses $4$ GB, $9$ GB and $12$ GB respectively. [2]
markscheme: (a) $A=18+4g$, $B=30+2.5g$ [A1]; $18+4g=30+2.5g$ [M1]; $g=8$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $18+4g>55$ gives $g>9.25$ [A1]; $30+2.5g>55$ gives $g>10$ [A1]; plan $B$ is cheaper than $A$ for $g>8$, so $C$ is cheapest for $g>10$ [R1] [3 marks] (c) $4$ GB: plan $A$ [A1]; $9$ GB: plan $B$; $12$ GB: plan $C$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Plot all three cost lines on your GDC; the cheapest plan is the lowest line at each usage.

subtopic: Acid mixture from two linear equations
statement: A chemist mixes $x$ litres of a $20\%$ acid solution with $y$ litres of a $50\%$ acid solution to make $40$ litres of a $38\%$ acid solution. (a) Write down two equations connecting $x$ and $y$. [2] (b) Solve the equations to find $x$ and $y$. [2] (c) The $20\%$ solution costs \$4.50 per litre and the $50\%$ solution costs \$9.00 per litre. Find the total cost of the mixture and the cost per litre of the mixture. [2]
tips: One equation tracks total volume and the other tracks the amount of pure acid. Two straight lines in the $xy$-plane meet at the solution.

subtopic: Distance from a point to a line using a perpendicular
statement: The line $L$ has equation $3x-4y=12$. The point $P$ is $(1,\,4)$. (a) Find the gradient of $L$ and of the line through $P$ perpendicular to $L$. [2] (b) Find the equation of the line through $P$ perpendicular to $L$, and the coordinates of the point $F$ where it meets $L$. [4] (c) Hence find the shortest distance from $P$ to $L$. [2]
markscheme: (a) gradient of $L$ is $\dfrac34$ [A1]; perpendicular gradient $-\dfrac43$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $y-4=-\dfrac43(x-1)$ so $4x+3y=16$ [M1][A1]; solve with $3x-4y=12$ [M1]; $F=(4,0)$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) $PF=\sqrt{(4-1)^{2}+(0-4)^{2}}$ [M1]; $5$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The shortest distance from a point to a line is measured along the perpendicular from the point to the line.

subtopic: Intersection of lines and area of a triangle
statement: The lines $l_1$: $y=2x-1$, $l_2$: $y=-x+8$ and $l_3$: the $x$-axis form a triangle. (a) Find the coordinates of the three vertices of the triangle. [4] (b) Find the area of the triangle. [3] (c) Show that the lines $l_1$ and $l_2$ are not perpendicular. [1]
markscheme: (a) $l_1\cap l_2$: $2x-1=-x+8$ [M1] gives $(3,5)$ [A1]; $l_1\cap l_3$: $\left(\dfrac12,0\right)$ [A1]; $l_2\cap l_3$: $(8,0)$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) Base on the $x$-axis $=8-\dfrac12=\dfrac{15}{2}$ [A1]; height $5$ [A1]; area $=\dfrac12\cdot\dfrac{15}{2}\cdot5=\dfrac{75}{4}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Gradients $2$ and $-1$: product $-2\neq-1$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Use the $x$-axis as the base of the triangle, since two vertices lie on it; the height is the $y$-coordinate of the third vertex.

subtopic: Collinear points and the equation of a line
statement: The points $A(-2,1)$, $B(2,7)$ and $C(k,16)$ lie on a straight line. (a) Find the gradient of $AB$. [1] (b) Find the value of $k$. [2] (c) Find the equation of the line in the form $y=mx+c$. [2]
tips: Points are collinear exactly when any two of the pairs give the same gradient. Check your equation by substituting point $B$.

subtopic: Piecewise linear electricity tariff
statement: An electricity company charges a fixed fee of $9.50$ dollars per month plus $0.14$ dollars per unit for the first $120$ units used, and $0.21$ dollars per unit for every unit above $120$. Let $C$ dollars be the monthly bill for $u$ units. Round money to the nearest cent. (a) Find the bill for a month in which $95$ units are used, and for a month in which $200$ units are used. [3] (b) Show that, for $u>120$, $C=0.21u+1.1$. [2] (c) A customer's bill must not exceed $61.40$ dollars. Find the greatest whole number of units that can be used. [3]
tips: Remember the two rates apply to different portions of the units used.

subtopic: Boiling point of water against altitude (linear regression)
statement: The boiling point $B$ (in $^\circ$C) of water was measured at different altitudes $h$ km above sea level. h: 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3; B: 100.0, 98.4, 96.7, 95.1, 93.5, 91.8, 90.1. (a) Find the equation of the regression line of $B$ on $h$, giving the coefficients correct to three significant figures. [2] (b) Write down the value of $r$ and describe the correlation. [2] (c) Interpret the gradient of the line in this context. [1] (d) Estimate the boiling point at an altitude of $2.2$ km. [1] (e) A hiker uses the model to estimate the boiling point at $30$ km above sea level. Calculate this estimate and give a reason why it is unreliable. [2]
markscheme: (a) $a=-3.29$ [A1] $b=100$ [A1] so $B=-3.29h+100$ [2 marks] (b) $r=-1.00$ [A1] very strong negative linear correlation [A1] [2 marks] (c) the boiling point falls by about $3.29\,^\circ$C for each extra kilometer of altitude [A1] [1 mark] (d) $B=92.8\,^\circ$C [A1] [1 mark] (e) $B\approx1.2$ to $1.3\,^\circ$C (using unrounded coefficients $1.24$) [A1] $30$ km is far outside the data range $0$ to $3$ km, so this is extrapolation (and the boiling point of water cannot keep falling linearly) [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Use your GDC regression for both the line and $r$. When estimating far outside the range of the data, say that it is extrapolation and therefore unreliable.

subtopic: A piecewise linear tax model
statement: In a country the tax $T$ (in dollars) on an annual income $I$ is: $T=0$ for $I\leq10\,000$; $T=0.2(I-10\,000)$ for $10\,000<I\leq40\,000$; $T=6000+0.4(I-40\,000)$ for $I>40\,000$. (a) Find the tax on an income of \$28\,000 and on an income of \$65\,000. [3] (b) Find the gradient of each of the three pieces and interpret the last. [2] (c) A person pays \$9500 in tax. Find their income. [2] (d) Find the average tax rate (tax divided by income) for the income \$65\,000, as a percentage to 3 significant figures. [2]
tips: Identify the correct piece from the size of the output (tax) before solving for the input.

subtopic: Perpendicular bisector and a point equidistant from two towns
statement: Two villages are at $A(1,6)$ and $B(7,2)$, with units in kilometers. A charging station is to be built on the straight road with equation $y=x-1$, at the same distance from both villages. (a) Find the midpoint of $AB$ and the gradient of $AB$. [2] (b) Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of $AB$ in the form $y=mx+c$. [2] (c) Find the coordinates of the charging station. [2] (d) Find the distance from the charging station to each village. [1]
markscheme: (a) midpoint $M=(4,4)$ [A1] gradient $=\dfrac{2-6}{7-1}=-\dfrac23$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) perpendicular gradient $=\dfrac32$ [M1] $y-4=\dfrac32(x-4)$, so $y=\dfrac32x-2$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\dfrac32x-2=x-1$ [M1] $x=2$, $y=1$, so $(2,1)$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $\sqrt{(2-1)^2+(1-6)^2}=\sqrt{26}$ km [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Every point on the perpendicular bisector of $AB$ is equidistant from $A$ and $B$. Check by confirming the distances to $A$ and $B$ are both $\sqrt{26}$.

subtopic: Break-even point and minimum sales for a target profit
statement: A baker sells cakes for \$30 each. The monthly costs are a fixed \$450 plus \$12 for each cake made. Let $n$ be the number of cakes made and sold in a month. (a) Write down expressions for the monthly cost $C$ and the monthly revenue $R$ in dollars. [2] (b) Find the number of cakes that must be sold to break even. [2] (c) The baker wants a monthly profit of at least \$500. Find the least number of cakes that must be sold. [3]
tips: Break-even occurs where revenue equals cost. For a minimum number of items, solve the inequality and round up to the next whole number.

subtopic: Two simultaneous equations from ticket sales
statement: At a theater, all adult tickets cost $\$a$ each and all child tickets cost $\$c$ each. A group buys $5$ adult tickets and $3$ child tickets for a total of $\$64$. A second group buys $2$ adult tickets and $4$ child tickets for a total of $\$41$. (a) Write down two equations in $a$ and $c$. [2] (b) Solve the equations to find the price of an adult ticket and of a child ticket. [2] (c) A third group buys $4$ adult tickets and $6$ child tickets. Find the total cost. [1] (d) The line $5a+3c=64$ is plotted with $a$ on the horizontal axis and $c$ on the vertical axis. Write down its gradient, and interpret it in context. [2]
markscheme: (a) $5a+3c=64$ [A1] $2a+4c=41$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Solving, e.g. by GDC [M1] $a=9.50$ and $c=5.50$ (adult \$9.50, child \$5.50) [A1] [2 marks] (c) $4(9.5)+6(5.5)=38+33=\$71$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) Gradient $=-\dfrac53$ [A1] Each \$1 increase in the adult price must be matched by a decrease of $\$\tfrac53$ in the child price to keep the first group's total at \$64 [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Define your variables clearly and write one equation per piece of information. For the gradient, rearrange to $c=-\tfrac53a+\tfrac{64}{3}$.

subtopic: Two linear models and their intersection
statement: Plan $A$ for mobile data costs $C_A=12+0.8g$ dollars for $g$ gigabytes. Plan $B$ costs $C_B=4+1.3g$ dollars. (a) Find the cost of each plan for $g=10$. [2] (b) Find the value of $g$ for which the two plans cost the same, and that common cost. [3] (c) State which plan is cheaper for $g=25$ and explain the situation in terms of gradients. [2] (d) Find the range of $g$ for which plan $B$ is cheaper than plan $A$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $C_A=20$ [A1]; $C_B=17$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $12+0.8g=4+1.3g$ [M1]; $g=16$ [A1]; cost $24.80$ dollars [A1] [3 marks] (c) Plan $A$ is cheaper ($32$ against $36.50$) [A1]; plan $A$ has the smaller gradient (rate per gigabyte) [R1] [2 marks] (d) $g<16$ [A1] (since $B$ has the smaller fixed fee) [R1] [2 marks]
tips: At the intersection both models give the same value; compare gradients to see which wins beyond it.

subtopic: Town population: continuous piecewise linear growth
statement: The population $P$ of a town, $t$ years after 1 January 2015, is modeled by $P=12500+340t$ for $0\le t\le8$. After $t=8$ the population grows at a faster constant rate of $520$ people per year, and the model has no sudden jump at $t=8$. (a) Find $P$ when $t=8$. [1] (b) Find an expression for $P$ for $t>8$ in the form $P=pt+q$. [2] (c) Find when the population reaches $20000$, correct to three significant figures. [3] (d) Give one reason why a linear model may not be suitable for long-term prediction. [1]
markscheme: (a) $12500+340\times8=15220$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $P=15220+520(t-8)$ [M1] $=520t+11060$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $520t+11060=20000$ [M1] $t=17.2$ years [A1] $17.2>8$, so the second piece is the correct one to use [R1] [3 marks] (d) real populations are limited by resources and space or change their growth rate, so constant growth cannot continue indefinitely [R1] [1 mark]
tips: For a continuous piecewise model, anchor the second piece at the value from the first piece at the breakpoint. Always check that the solution lies in the domain of the piece you used.

subtopic: Hiking trail elevation profile (three-piece linear function)
statement: The elevation $E$ meters of a hiking trail at horizontal distance $x$ km from the start is modeled by three straight sections. From $x=0$ to $x=3$ the trail rises uniformly from $200$ m to $650$ m. From $x=3$ to $x=5$ it is level. From $x=5$ to $x=9$ it descends uniformly to $250$ m. (a) Find the gradient of the first section, in meters per kilometer. [1] (b) Write down the equation of $E$ for each of the three sections, with their domains. [3] (c) Find both distances from the start at which the elevation is $400$ m. [3] (d) Find the elevation at $x=7$. [1]
tips: Find each gradient from the endpoints of its section, and match every equation to its own domain. A given elevation may occur on more than one section.

subtopic: Ship, buoy and lighthouse on a coordinate grid
statement: On a chart, a ship is at $S(-12,5)$ and a lighthouse is at $L(9,-15)$, where each unit represents $1$ km. A buoy $B$ is placed at the midpoint of $SL$. (a) Find the coordinates of $B$. [2] (b) Find the distance $SL$. [2] (c) The ship sails directly to the lighthouse at a constant speed of $18$ km/h. Find the time taken, to the nearest minute. [2]
tips: Midpoint: average the coordinates. Distance: use Pythagoras on the coordinate differences. Convert hours to minutes by multiplying by $60$.

subtopic: Intersecting drone flight paths
statement: Two drones fly over a region, with coordinates in kilometers. Drone $A$ flies in a straight line from $A_1(0,2)$ to $A_2(10,8)$. Drone $B$ flies in a straight line from $B_1(2,10)$ to $B_2(9,3)$. (a) Find the equation of each flight path in the form $y=mx+c$. [4] (b) Find the coordinates of the point where the two lines intersect. [2] (c) Show that this point lies on both flight paths. [2] (d) Find the distance from $A_1$ to the intersection point, correct to three significant figures. [2]
tips: Two infinite lines always meet (unless parallel), but flight paths are segments, so check that the intersection lies within both $x$-ranges.

subtopic: Piecewise linear taxi fare model
statement: A taxi company charges a fare of $F$ dollars for a journey of $d$ km, modeled by $F(d)=4+2.5d$ for $0\le d\le6$ and $F(d)=19+1.5(d-6)$ for $d>6$. (a) Find the fare for a journey of (i) $4$ km; (ii) $10$ km. [3] (b) A passenger pays \$31. Find the length of the journey. [2] (c) State the meaning of the number $1.5$ in this model. [1]
markscheme: (a) (i) $4+2.5\times4=14$, so \$14 [A1] (ii) $19+1.5(10-6)$ [M1] $=25$, so \$25 [A1] [3 marks] (b) $19+1.5(d-6)=31$ [M1] $d=14$ km [A1] [2 marks] (c) each additional kilometer beyond $6$ km costs \$1.50 [A1] [1 mark]
tips: For a piecewise function, first decide which piece applies to the input. A fare above $F(6)=19$ must come from the second piece.

subtopic: Parallel line through a point with intercepts
statement: The line $L_1$ has equation $2x+3y=12$. (a) Find the gradient of $L_1$. [2] (b) The line $L_2$ is parallel to $L_1$ and passes through the point $(3,-1)$. Find the equation of $L_2$ in the form $y=mx+c$. [2] (c) Find the $x$-intercept of $L_2$. [2]
tips: Parallel lines share the same gradient. For an $x$-intercept, set $y=0$ and solve for $x$.

subtopic: Largest rectangle under a straight line
statement: The line $L$ has equation $y=-0.75x+6$, where $x$ and $y$ are in meters. It meets the $x$-axis at $A$ and the $y$-axis at $B$. A rectangular flower bed has one corner at the origin $O$, two sides along the axes, and the opposite corner $P(x,y)$ on $L$, where $0<x<8$. (a) Find the coordinates of $A$ and $B$. [2] (b) Find the area of triangle $OAB$. [1] (c) Show that the area of the flower bed is $A=x(6-0.75x)$. [2] (d) Use your GDC to find the maximum area of the flower bed, and the dimensions that give it. [3]
markscheme: (a) $A=(8,0)$ [A1] $B=(0,6)$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac12\times8\times6=24$ m$^2$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $y=6-0.75x$ on $L$ [M1] $A=xy=x(6-0.75x)$ [AG] [2 marks] (d) maximum found using the GDC [M1] $x=4$ m, $y=3$ m [A1] maximum area $=12$ m$^2$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Express both side lengths using the single variable $x$ before maximizing. Check that your answer is half the triangle area, which is a known property of this configuration.

subtopic: Right-angled triangle and circle through its vertices
statement: The triangle $ABC$ has vertices $A(1,2)$, $B(5,4)$ and $C(3,8)$. (a) Show that $AB$ is perpendicular to $BC$. [3] (b) Find the area of triangle $ABC$. [3] (c) Since angle $ABC$ is a right angle, $AC$ is a diameter of the circle through $A$, $B$ and $C$. Find the coordinates of the centre and the radius of this circle. [3]
markscheme: (a) gradient $AB=\dfrac{4-2}{5-1}=\dfrac12$ [A1] gradient $BC=\dfrac{8-4}{3-5}=-2$ [A1] $\dfrac12\times(-2)=-1$, so perpendicular [R1] [3 marks] (b) $AB=\sqrt{20}$ and $BC=\sqrt{20}$ [A1][A1] area $=\dfrac12\times\sqrt{20}\times\sqrt{20}=10$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) centre is midpoint of $AC$: $(2,5)$ [A1] $AC=\sqrt{4+36}=\sqrt{40}$ [M1] radius $=\dfrac{\sqrt{40}}{2}=\sqrt{10}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Two lines are perpendicular when the product of their gradients is $-1$. In a right-angled triangle the two perpendicular sides serve as base and height for the area.

subtopic: Line through two points and the perpendicular bisector
statement: The points $A(1,2)$ and $B(5,10)$ lie on a straight line. (a) Find the gradient of the line $AB$ and its equation in the form $y=mx+c$. [3] (b) Find the midpoint $M$ and the exact length of $AB$. [3] (c) Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of $AB$. [3] (d) Determine whether the point $P(2,6)$ lies on the perpendicular bisector. [1]
markscheme: (a) $m=\dfrac{10-2}{5-1}=2$ [M1][A1]; $y=2x$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $M=(3,6)$ [A1]; $AB=\sqrt{(5-1)^2+(10-2)^2}$ [M1] $=4 \sqrt{5}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Gradient $-\dfrac1m=-\frac{1}{2}$ [A1]; through $M$: $y-6=-\frac{1}{2}(x-3)$ [M1]; $y=-\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{15}{2}$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) At $x=2$: $y=\frac{13}{2}$, which does not equal $6$, so $P$ does not lie on it [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Perpendicular gradients multiply to $-1$; the perpendicular bisector passes through the midpoint.

subtopic: Two cyclists approaching on a straight road
statement: A straight road is $39$ km long between towns $P$ and $Q$. Anna leaves $P$ at 9:00 am and cycles towards $Q$ at $22$ km/h. Ben leaves $Q$ at 9:30 am and cycles towards $P$ at $18$ km/h. Let $t$ be the time in hours after 9:00 am, and let $x$ km be the distance of a cyclist from $P$. (a) Write down $x$ as a linear function of $t$ for Anna, and for Ben (valid for $t\ge0.5$). [3] (b) Find the time at which they meet, and their distance from $P$ at that time. [3]
tips: Each cyclist's position is a linear function of time; they meet when the positions are equal.

subtopic: A line through points with an unknown coordinate
statement: The line $l_1$ has equation $y=2x+1$. The points $A(k,\,3)$ and $B(5,\,k+1)$ lie on a line $l_2$ that is perpendicular to $l_1$. (a) Write down the gradient of $l_2$. [1] (b) Find the gradient of $AB$ in terms of $k$ and hence find $k$. [4] (c) Find the equation of $l_2$ in the form $y=mx+c$, and the point where $l_2$ meets $l_1$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $-\dfrac12$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) gradient $=\dfrac{(k+1)-3}{5-k}=\dfrac{k-2}{5-k}$ [A1]; $\dfrac{k-2}{5-k}=-\dfrac12$ [M1]; $2k-4=k-5$ [A1]; $k=-1$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) $A(-1,3)$ and gradient $-\dfrac12$ so $y=-\dfrac12x+\dfrac52$ [M1][A1]; $2x+1=-\dfrac12x+\dfrac52$ [M1]; $\left(\dfrac35,\ \dfrac{11}{5}\right)$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Perpendicular lines have gradients whose product is $-1$.

subtopic: Income tax bands as a piecewise linear function
statement: In a country, the income tax $T$ thousand dollars on an annual income of $I$ thousand dollars is calculated as follows: no tax on the first $11.6$; $18\%$ on the part of income between $11.6$ and $46.8$; $35\%$ on any part of income above $46.8$. (a) Find the tax on an income of $30$ thousand dollars, correct to three significant figures. [2] (b) Show that, for $I>46.8$, the tax can be written as $T=0.35I-10.044$. [3] (c) A person pays $9.5$ thousand dollars in tax. Find the person's income, correct to three significant figures. [2] (d) Find the average tax rate, as a percentage of income, for an income of $62.5$ thousand dollars. Give your answer to three significant figures. [1]
tips: Marginal rates apply only to the income inside each band. Calculate the tax at each band boundary first, then extend with the next rate.

subtopic: Gradient and elevation of a mountain road
statement: A straight section of a mountain road rises from point $A$ at an elevation of $120$ m to point $B$ at an elevation of $300$ m. The horizontal distance between $A$ and $B$ is $2400$ m. (a) Find the gradient of the road, giving your answer as a percentage. [2] (b) Find the angle of elevation of the road, correct to three significant figures. [2] (c) A rest area lies $1000$ m horizontally from $A$ along the road. Find its elevation. [2]
tips: Gradient is vertical change over horizontal change, and the angle of elevation comes from the inverse tangent. Make sure your GDC is in degree mode.

subtopic: Line through two points: equation, intercepts and midpoint
statement: The points $A(-2,\,5)$ and $B(4,\,-1)$ lie on a straight line $l$. (a) Find the gradient of $l$ and its equation in the form $y=mx+c$. [3] (b) Write down the coordinates of the points where $l$ meets the axes. [2] (c) Find the midpoint of $AB$ and the length of $AB$. [3]
tips: Use $m=\frac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}$, then substitute one point to find the intercept.

subtopic: A linear cost model
statement: A taxi company charges a fixed fee plus a rate per kilometer. A $5$ km journey costs \$14 and a $12$ km journey costs \$28. (a) Find the cost per kilometer and the fixed fee. [3] (b) Write down a model $C=md+c$ and find the cost of a $20$ km journey. [2] (c) A passenger pays \$60. Find the distance traveled. [2]
markscheme: (a) Rate $=\dfrac{28-14}{12-5}=2$ dollars per km [M1][A1]; fixed fee $=14-2(5)=4$ dollars [A1] [3 marks] (b) $C=2d+4$ [A1]; $C(20)=44$ dollars [A1] [2 marks] (c) $60=2d+4$ [M1] so $d=28$ km [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A linear model has a constant rate of change: gradient $=$ change in cost over change in distance.

subtopic: Taxi fare as a linear model
statement: A taxi fare consists of a fixed charge plus a charge per kilometer. A $4$ km trip costs \$11 and a $10$ km trip costs \$20. (a) Find the charge per kilometer and the fixed charge. [3] (b) Write down the fare $F$ dollars for a trip of $d$ km, and find the distance of a trip costing \$32. [2] (c) Interpret the value of the gradient and the value of the $F$-intercept in this context. [2]
markscheme: (a) gradient $\dfrac{20-11}{10-4}=1.5$ [A1]; $11=1.5\times4+c$ [M1]; fixed charge \$5 [A1] [3 marks] (b) $F=5+1.5d$ [A1]; $d=18$ km [A1] [2 marks] (c) Each extra kilometer adds \$1.50 [A1]; the fixed charge, the fare for a trip of zero distance, is \$5 [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The gradient is the rate of change of the fare with distance; the intercept is the value when the distance is zero.

subtopic: Gym membership plans compared (intersection of linear costs)
statement: Gym $X$ charges a joining fee of \$90 plus \$28 per month. Gym $Y$ has no joining fee but charges \$41 per month. Let $m$ be the number of months of membership. (a) Write down expressions for the total cost of each gym after $m$ months. [2] (b) Find the value of $m$ for which the total costs are equal. Give your answer to three significant figures. [2] (c) Find which gym is cheaper for $12$ months of membership, and by how much. [2] (d) Find the greatest whole number of months for which gym $Y$ is cheaper than gym $X$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $C_X=90+28m$ [A1] $C_Y=41m$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $90+28m=41m$ [M1] $m=6.92$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $C_X=90+28\times12=426$ and $C_Y=41\times12=492$ [M1] gym $X$ is cheaper by \$66 [A1] [2 marks] (d) $Y$ is cheaper when $m<6.92$, so $6$ months [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Equal cost means the two linear expressions meet at the intersection point; your GDC can solve this directly. Remember that $m$ must be a whole number in part (d).

subtopic: Parallel and perpendicular lines with a parameter
statement: The line $l_1$ has equation $3x-ky=12$ and the line $l_2$ has equation $y=\dfrac{x}{2}+4$. (a) Find the value of $k$ for which $l_1$ is parallel to $l_2$. [3] (b) Find the value of $k$ for which $l_1$ is perpendicular to $l_2$. [2] (c) For $k=6$, find the distance between the two parallel lines (to 3 significant figures). [3]
markscheme: (a) $l_1$: $y=\dfrac3kx-\dfrac{12}{k}$ [A1]; $\dfrac3k=\dfrac12$ [M1]; $k=6$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\dfrac3k\times\dfrac12=-1$ [M1]; $k=-\dfrac32$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Point on $l_2$: $(0,4)$; $l_1$: $3x-6y-12=0$ [A1]; distance $=\dfrac{|0-24-12|}{\sqrt{9+36}}$ [M1]; $=\dfrac{36}{\sqrt{45}}=5.37$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Rewrite each line as $y=mx+c$; parallel lines share a gradient and perpendicular gradients multiply to $-1$.

subtopic: Spring extension against mass (regression and prediction)
statement: A spring is stretched by hanging different masses $m$ grams from it. The extension $e$ cm is measured. m: 50, 100, 150, 200, 250; e: 2.1, 4.3, 6.2, 8.5, 10.4. (a) Find the equation of the regression line of $e$ on $m$, in the form $e=am+b$. [2] (b) Write down the value of $r$ to four decimal places and comment. [2] (c) By rearranging your equation from part (a), estimate the mass that gives an extension of $7.0$ cm. Give your answer to three significant figures. [2] (d) The line is used to predict the extension for a mass of $2000$ g. Give a reason why this prediction is unreliable. [1]
markscheme: (a) $a=0.0416$ [A1] $b=0.0600$ [A1] so $e=0.0416m+0.06$ [2 marks] (b) $r=0.9996$ [A1] very strong positive linear correlation, so a linear model is appropriate in the measured range [A1] [2 marks] (c) $7.0=0.0416m+0.06$ [M1] $m=167$ g [A1] [2 marks] (d) $2000$ g is far outside the data range, and a real spring stops obeying a linear law beyond its elastic limit [R1] [1 mark]
tips: State the correlation strength and direction, not only the value of $r$. Rearranging the line to estimate $m$ is acceptable here because $r$ is very close to $1$.

subtopic: Tank filling then draining (piecewise linear volume)
statement: A tank holds $120$ litres of water at time $t=0$ minutes. For the first $15$ minutes it is filled at a constant rate of $40$ litres per minute. At $t=15$ the filling stops and a drain is opened, which empties the tank at a constant rate of $25$ litres per minute until the tank is empty. Let $V$ litres be the volume of water at time $t$ minutes. (a) Find $V$ when $t=15$. [1] (b) Write $V$ as a piecewise linear function of $t$, until the tank is empty, stating the domain of each piece. [3] (c) Find the time at which the tank becomes empty. [2] (d) Find the two times at which the tank contains $500$ litres. [3]
tips: Write the second piece starting from the value at the breakpoint, $V(15)=720$, so that the function is continuous. A level reached twice must be checked in each piece.

subtopic: Midpoint, distance and gradient of a segment
statement: Two radio masts stand at the points $P(-3,2)$ and $Q(5,-4)$ on a map grid, where each unit represents $1$ km. (a) Find the coordinates of the midpoint of $PQ$. [1] (b) Find the distance between the masts. [2] (c) Find the gradient of the line $PQ$. [2]
tips: Subtract coordinates in the same order in the numerator and the denominator when finding a gradient. Distance is the square root of the sum of squared differences.

subtopic: Modeling delivery costs with a regression line
statement: A delivery company records the cost $c$ (in dollars) of eight deliveries over different distances $d$ (in km). The values are given as pairs $(d,c)$: $(2,9.1)$, $(5,12.6)$, $(8,15.4)$, $(12,20.8)$, $(15,24.9)$, $(20,30.3)$, $(24,36.0)$, $(30,42.1)$. (a) Find the equation of the regression line of $c$ on $d$, and the correlation coefficient $r$. Give coefficients to three significant figures and $r$ to four decimal places. [3] (b) Interpret the gradient and the $c$-intercept in this context. [2] (c) Use the line to estimate the cost of an $18$ km delivery and the distance that can be covered for \$50. Give the cost to three significant figures and the distance to the nearest kilometer. [3] (d) A competitor charges $c=3+1.5d$. Using the rounded line $c=1.20d+6.48$, find the distance at which the two companies cost the same, to three significant figures, and state which company is cheaper for longer distances. [3] (e) A ninth delivery of $40$ km costs \$70. When this point is added, the regression line changes to $c=1.49d+3.27$ and $r=0.9796$. Comment on this point and its effect on the line. [2] (f) Give one reason why the original line may not be reliable for a $100$ km delivery. [1]
markscheme: (a) $c=1.20d+6.48$ [A1][A1]; $r=0.9993$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Each extra kilometer adds about \$1.20 to the cost [A1]; about \$6.48 is charged even for a trip of zero distance (a fixed charge) [A1] [2 marks] (c) $c(18)=28.1$ dollars [A1]; $d=\dfrac{50-6.48}{1.20}$ [M1]; $36$ km [A1] [3 marks] (d) $3+1.5d=6.48+1.20d$ [M1]; $d=11.6$ km [A1]; the regression-line company is cheaper beyond this distance since its gradient is smaller [A1] [3 marks] (e) The point is an outlier, well above the pattern of the other points [A1]; it increases the gradient from $1.20$ to $1.49$ and lowers the correlation [A1] [2 marks] (f) $100$ km is far outside the data range, so the linear trend may not continue (extrapolation) [R1] [1 mark]
tips: The gradient of a cost line is the cost per unit distance and the intercept is the fixed charge.

subtopic: Two vehicles with linear distance-time graphs
statement: Car $A$ leaves a town $O$ at 9:00 and travels along a straight road at a constant $72$ km/h. Car $B$ is already $30$ km from $O$ at 9:00 on the same road, traveling in the same direction at a constant $54$ km/h. (a) Write down models $d_A$ and $d_B$ for the distance from $O$ at time $t$ hours after 9:00. [2] (b) Find the time at which $A$ overtakes $B$, to the nearest minute. [3] (c) Find how far from $O$ the overtaking happens. [1] (d) When car $A$ is $15$ km ahead of car $B$, find the time. [2]
tips: The gradient of a distance-time graph is the speed; the intersection of two graphs is where the distances are equal.

subtopic: Parallel and perpendicular lines and a distance
statement: The line $L_1$ has equation $2x-3y=12$. (a) Find the equation of the line $L_2$ that is parallel to $L_1$ and passes through $P(3,-4)$, giving your answer in the form $ax+by=c$. [2] (b) Find the equation of the line $L_3$ that is perpendicular to $L_1$ and passes through $P$, in the form $ax+by=c$. [3] (c) Find the coordinates of the point $Q$ where $L_1$ and $L_3$ intersect. [3] (d) Find the exact distance $PQ$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $L_2$ has the form $2x-3y=k$ [M1] $k=2(3)-3(-4)=18$, so $L_2:\ 2x-3y=18$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) The gradient of $L_1$ is $\dfrac23$, so the gradient of $L_3$ is $-\dfrac32$ [A1] $y+4=-\dfrac32(x-3)$ [M1] $3x+2y=1$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Solve $2x-3y=12$ and $3x+2y=1$ [M1] $x=\dfrac{27}{13}$ [A1] $y=-\dfrac{34}{13}$, so $Q=\left(\dfrac{27}{13},-\dfrac{34}{13}\right)$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $PQ=\sqrt{\left(3-\dfrac{27}{13}\right)^2+\left(-4+\dfrac{34}{13}\right)^2}=\dfrac{\sqrt{12^2+18^2}}{13}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{6\sqrt{13}}{13}$ (equivalently $\dfrac{6}{\sqrt{13}}$) [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Lines parallel to $ax+by=c$ share the same $a$ and $b$; perpendicular lines swap them and change one sign. For an exact distance, keep fractions with a common denominator before taking the square root.

subtopic: Least squares regression line and minimizing squared residuals
statement: This question investigates why the least squares regression line is the best-fitting line. A technician calibrates a pressure sensor by applying five known pressures $x$ (in bars) and recording the output voltage $y$ (in volts). x: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5; y: 2.9, 5.2, 6.8, 9.3, 10.8. (a) Use your GDC to find the equation of the regression line of $y$ on $x$ in the form $y=ax+b$, and write down the value of $r$ correct to three significant figures. [2] (b) For this line, find the residual (observed value minus predicted value) at each of the five data points, and show that the residuals sum to zero. [3] (c) Hence find $S$, the sum of the squares of the residuals. [2] (d) Another technician proposes the line $y=2x+0.9$. Find the sum of squared residuals for this line and comment on your answer. [3] (e) Write down $\bar x$ and $\bar y$, and show that the line in part (a) passes through the point $(\bar x,\bar y)$. [2] (f) Consider lines through $(\bar x,\bar y)$ of the form $y-\bar y=m(x-\bar x)$. (i) Show that the sum of squared residuals is $S(m)=39.82-39.8m+10m^2$. [4] (ii) Use differentiation to find the value of $m$ that minimizes $S(m)$, and comment on your result. [3] (g) The technician now assumes that the output is zero when the pressure is zero, so the model is $y=mx$. Show that the sum of squared residuals $S(m)=\sum(y_i-mx_i)^2$ is minimized when $m=\dfrac{\sum x_iy_i}{\sum x_i^2}$, and find this value of $m$ to three significant figures. [5] (h) Find the sum of squared residuals for the line in part (g) and state what this tells you about the model $y=mx$ compared with the regression line. [2]
markscheme: (a) $y=1.99x+1.03$ [A1] $r=0.997$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) predicted values $3.02,\ 5.01,\ 7.00,\ 8.99,\ 10.98$ [M1] residuals $-0.12,\ 0.19,\ -0.20,\ 0.31,\ -0.18$ [A1] sum $=0$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $S=0.0144+0.0361+0.04+0.0961+0.0324$ [M1] $=0.219$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) predicted $2.9,\ 4.9,\ 6.9,\ 8.9,\ 10.9$, residuals $0,\ 0.3,\ -0.1,\ 0.4,\ -0.1$ [M1] $S=0+0.09+0.01+0.16+0.01=0.27$ [A1] larger than $0.219$, consistent with the regression line minimizing $S$ [R1] [3 marks] (e) $\bar x=3$ and $\bar y=7$ [A1] $1.99\times3+1.03=7$ [A1] [2 marks] (f) (i) residual at each point is $(y_i-\bar y)-m(x_i-\bar x)$, so $S(m)=\sum(y_i-\bar y)^2-2m\sum(x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)+m^2\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2$ [M1] $\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2=10$ [A1] $\sum(x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)=19.9$ [A1] $\sum(y_i-\bar y)^2=39.82$, giving $S(m)=39.82-39.8m+10m^2$ [AG] (ii) $S'(m)=20m-39.8$ [A1] $20m-39.8=0$ [M1] $m=1.99$, which is the gradient found in part (a) [A1] [7 marks] (g) $S'(m)=-2\sum x_i(y_i-mx_i)$ [M1] $S'(m)=0$ gives $\sum x_iy_i=m\sum x_i^2$ [AG] $\sum x_iy_i=124.9$ [A1] $\sum x_i^2=55$ [A1] $m=\dfrac{124.9}{55}=2.27$ [A1] [5 marks] (h) $S=\sum y_i^2-\dfrac{(\sum x_iy_i)^2}{\sum x_i^2}=284.82-283.637=1.18$ [A1] this is much larger than $0.219$, so forcing the line through the origin gives a clearly worse fit than the regression line with its intercept [R1] [2 marks]
tips: In part (f), expanding the squared residual and using the three sums turns the problem into minimizing a simple quadratic in $m$. In part (g), differentiate $S(m)$ term by term and set the derivative to zero; compare sums of squared residuals to decide which model fits better.

subtopic: A runner and a cyclist
statement: A runner leaves a town at time $t=0$ hours and runs along a straight road at a constant speed of $8$ km h$^{-1}$. A cyclist leaves the same town $0.6$ hours later and follows the same road at a constant speed of $20$ km h$^{-1}$. Let $d$ km be the distance of each from the town after $t$ hours. (a) Write down $d$ in terms of $t$ for the runner, and for the cyclist when $t\ge0.6$. [2] (b) Find the time at which the cyclist catches the runner and the distance from the town at that time. [3] (c) Find the time, in minutes after the cyclist starts, at which the cyclist is $4$ km ahead of the runner. [3]
markscheme: (a) runner: $d=8t$ [A1]; cyclist: $d=20(t-0.6)$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $8t=20t-12$ [M1]; $t=1$ hour [A1]; $d=8$ km [A1] [3 marks] (c) $20(t-0.6)-8t=4$ [M1]; $t=\dfrac43$ hours [A1]; $\dfrac43-0.6=0.7333$ hours, which is $44$ minutes after the cyclist starts [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The cyclist's distance is zero until $t=0.6$, so use $t-0.6$ for the time spent cycling.

subtopic: Triangle formed by a line and the axes
statement: The line $3x+4y=24$ meets the $x$-axis at $A$ and the $y$-axis at $B$. $O$ is the origin. (a) Find the coordinates of $A$ and $B$. [2] (b) Find the area of triangle $OAB$ and the length $AB$. [3] (c) Use the area to find the perpendicular distance from $O$ to the line $AB$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $A=(8,0)$ [A1]; $B=(0,6)$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) area $=\dfrac12\times8\times6=24$ [A1]; $AB=\sqrt{64+36}$ [M1]; $10$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\dfrac12\times10\times h=24$ [M1]; $h=4.8$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The area of a triangle can be found using different base and height pairs.

subtopic: Triangle on coordinate axes with lines
statement: The vertices of triangle $ABC$ are $A(1,2)$, $B(7,4)$ and $C(3,9)$. (a) Find the lengths of the three sides, to 3 significant figures. [3] (b) Find the equation of the line $AB$ and the perpendicular distance from $C$ to $AB$. [4] (c) Find the area of the triangle. [2] (d) Find the coordinates of the midpoint of each side and the gradient of the line joining the midpoints of $AC$ and $BC$. Comment. [3]
markscheme: (a) $AB=6.325$, $BC=6.403$, $CA=7.280$ [A1][A1][A1] [3 marks] (b) $m=\dfrac13$, $y=\dfrac13x+\dfrac53$ [A1]; $x-3y+5=0$ [M1]; distance $=\dfrac{|3-27+5|}{\sqrt{10}}=6.008$ [M1][A1] [4 marks] (c) $\dfrac12\times6.325\times6.008=19.0$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (d) Midpoints $(2,5.5)$, $(4,3)$, $(5,6.5)$ [A1]; midpoints of $AC$ and $BC$: $(2,5.5)$ and $(5,6.5)$: gradient $\dfrac{1}{3}$ [A1]; parallel to $AB$ (midpoint theorem) [R1] [3 marks]
tips: The perpendicular distance from a point to a line uses the line in the form $ax+by+c=0$.

subtopic: Perpendicular line, foot of perpendicular and shortest distance
statement: The line $L_1$ has equation $3x-4y=8$. (a) Write down the gradient of $L_1$. [1] (b) The line $L_2$ is perpendicular to $L_1$ and passes through $P(7,-3)$. Find the equation of $L_2$ in the form $4x+3y=k$. [3] (c) The lines $L_1$ and $L_2$ intersect at the point $F$. Find the coordinates of $F$. [3] (d) Find the shortest distance from $P$ to $L_1$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $y=\dfrac34x-2$, so gradient $=\dfrac34$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) perpendicular gradient $=-\dfrac43$ [A1] $y+3=-\dfrac43(x-7)$ [M1] $4x+3y=19$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) eliminate a variable, e.g. $9x-12y=24$ and $16x+12y=76$ [M1] $25x=100$, so $x=4$ [A1] $y=1$, so $F=(4,1)$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $PF=\sqrt{(7-4)^2+(-3-1)^2}$ [M1] $=5$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The shortest distance from a point to a line is measured along the perpendicular, so it equals the distance from the point to the foot of the perpendicular. Check $F$ lies on both lines.

subtopic: Regression of x on y: estimating dose from reaction time
