statement: Use Maclaurin series to evaluate each limit. (a) $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin x-x\cos x}{x^3}$ [3] (b) $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\frac{e^x-\cos x-x}{x^2}$ [3]
markscheme: (a) $\sin x-x\cos x=\left(x-\dfrac{x^3}{6}+\cdots\right)-x\left(1-\dfrac{x^2}{2}+\cdots\right)$ [M1] $=\dfrac{x^3}{3}+\cdots$ [A1] so the limit is $\dfrac13$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $e^x-\cos x-x=\left(1+x+\dfrac{x^2}{2}+\cdots\right)-\left(1-\dfrac{x^2}{2}+\cdots\right)-x$ [M1] $=x^2+\cdots$ [A1] so the limit is $1$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Expand the numerator far enough that a nonzero term survives, then divide through by the lowest power of $x$. If the leading terms cancel, include one more term of each series.

subtopic: Limit of a ratio of two series with cancelling leading terms
statement: Find $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\ln(1+x)-x+\frac{1}{2}x^2}{x-\sin x}$, using Maclaurin series. [5]
markscheme: $\ln(1+x)-x+\dfrac12x^2=\left(x-\dfrac{x^2}{2}+\dfrac{x^3}{3}-\cdots\right)-x+\dfrac12x^2$ [M1] $=\dfrac{x^3}{3}-\dfrac{x^4}{4}+\cdots$ [A1] $x-\sin x=\dfrac{x^3}{6}-\dfrac{x^5}{120}+\cdots$ [A1] divide numerator and denominator by $x^3$ [M1] limit $=\dfrac{1/3}{1/6}=2$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: Both numerator and denominator start at $x^3$, so you must keep terms up to $x^3$ in each series. Applying L'Hopital's rule here would need three rounds of differentiation, which is far slower.

subtopic: Stretch followed by rotation as a composite matrix
statement: Let $\mathbf{S}=\begin{pmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ be a horizontal stretch and $\mathbf{R}=\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ a rotation through $90^\circ$ anticlockwise about the origin. (a) Find the matrix $\mathbf{M}$ that represents the stretch followed by the rotation. [2] (b) Find the image of the point $(2,1)$ under $\mathbf{M}$. [2] (c) A triangle of area $4\ \mathrm{cm}^2$ is transformed by $\mathbf{M}$. Find the area of its image. [2] (d) Find $\mathbf{M}^{-1}$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{M}=\mathbf{R}\mathbf{S}$ (stretch applied first) [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 3 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 3 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 6 \end{pmatrix}$, so the image is $(-1,6)$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\det\mathbf{M}=3$ [M1] area $=3\times4=12\ \mathrm{cm}^2$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $\mathbf{M}^{-1}=\dfrac13\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -3 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix} 0 & \frac13 \\ -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The first transformation applied is the matrix written closest to the point, so 'S then R' is $\mathbf{RS}$. The determinant of a transformation matrix is the area scale factor.

subtopic: Markov chains and eigenvectors
statement: A bike-share scheme has three docking stations, $A$, $B$ and $C$. Bikes are moved by customers during the day and every bike is docked at one of the stations each night. Records show that, from one night to the next: of the bikes at $A$, $50\%$ stay at $A$, $10\%$ move to $B$ and $40\%$ move to $C$; of the bikes at $B$, $20\%$ move to $A$, $60\%$ stay at $B$ and $20\%$ move to $C$; of the bikes at $C$, $30\%$ move to $A$, $10\%$ move to $B$ and $60\%$ stay at $C$. On the first night there are $200$ bikes at $A$, $150$ at $B$ and $150$ at $C$. Let $\mathbf{s}_n$ be the column vector giving the numbers of bikes at $A$, $B$, $C$ after $n$ days, so that $\mathbf{s}_0 = \begin{pmatrix}200\\150\\150\end{pmatrix}$. (a) Write down the transition matrix $T$ such that $\mathbf{s}_{n+1} = T\mathbf{s}_n$. [2] (b) Find $\mathbf{s}_1$ and $\mathbf{s}_3$. [3] (c) Find the probability that a bike that is at $B$ tonight will be at $A$ two nights later. [2] (d) (i) Verify that $\begin{pmatrix}1\\-3\\2\end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\-1\end{pmatrix}$ are eigenvectors of $T$, and state the corresponding eigenvalues. (ii) Show that $\begin{pmatrix}7\\4\\9\end{pmatrix}$ is an eigenvector of $T$ with eigenvalue $1$. [5] (e) By writing $\mathbf{s}_0$ as a linear combination of the three eigenvectors, find an expression for $\mathbf{s}_n$, and hence show that the number of bikes at $A$ after $n$ days is $$175 - \frac{50}{3}(0.5)^n + \frac{125}{3}(0.2)^n.$$ [6] (f) Write down the long-term number of bikes at each station. [2] (g) Find the first day on which the number of bikes at $B$ is within $1$ of its long-term value. [3] (h) The company wants at least $120$ bikes to be at $B$ in the long term. Assuming the same transition probabilities, find the minimum number of extra bikes that should be added to the scheme. [2]
markscheme: (a) $T=\begin{pmatrix}0.5&0.2&0.3\\0.1&0.6&0.1\\0.4&0.2&0.6\end{pmatrix}$ [A2] (award [A1] for the transpose or one column incorrect) [2 marks] (b) $\mathbf{s}_1=T\mathbf{s}_0=\begin{pmatrix}175\\125\\200\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\mathbf{s}_3=T^3\mathbf{s}_0$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix}173.25\\106.25\\220.5\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $T^2=\begin{pmatrix}0.39&0.28&0.35\\0.15&0.40&0.15\\0.46&0.32&0.50\end{pmatrix}$ [M1] the required entry (row $A$, column $B$) is $0.28$ [A1] [2 marks] (d)(i) $T\begin{pmatrix}1\\-3\\2\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0.5\\-1.5\\1\end{pmatrix}=0.5\begin{pmatrix}1\\-3\\2\end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1] $T\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\-1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0.2\\0\\-0.2\end{pmatrix}=0.2\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\-1\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] (ii) $T\begin{pmatrix}7\\4\\9\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}3.5+0.8+2.7\\0.7+2.4+0.9\\2.8+0.8+5.4\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}7\\4\\9\end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1][AG] [5 marks] (e) $\mathbf{s}_0=a\begin{pmatrix}7\\4\\9\end{pmatrix}+b\begin{pmatrix}1\\-3\\2\end{pmatrix}+c\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\-1\end{pmatrix}$ [M1] Adding the three equations gives $20a=500$, so $a=25$; then $4a-3b=150\Rightarrow b=-\dfrac{50}{3}$; $7a+b+c=200\Rightarrow c=\dfrac{125}{3}$ [A1][A1][A1] $\mathbf{s}_n=T^n\mathbf{s}_0=25\begin{pmatrix}7\\4\\9\end{pmatrix}-\dfrac{50}{3}(0.5)^n\begin{pmatrix}1\\-3\\2\end{pmatrix}+\dfrac{125}{3}(0.2)^n\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\-1\end{pmatrix}$ [M1] First component: $175-\dfrac{50}{3}(0.5)^n+\dfrac{125}{3}(0.2)^n$ [A1][AG] [6 marks] (f) As $n\to\infty$, $(0.5)^n\to0$ and $(0.2)^n\to0$: $A=175$, $B=100$, $C=225$ [A2] [2 marks] (g) $B_n=100+50(0.5)^n$ [A1] $50(0.5)^n<1\Rightarrow n>\dfrac{\ln 50}{\ln 2}=5.64$ [M1] so after $6$ days [A1] [3 marks] (h) Long-term proportion at $B$ is $\dfrac{4}{20}=0.2$, so the total must be at least $\dfrac{120}{0.2}=600$ [M1] i.e. $100$ extra bikes [A1] [2 marks] Total [25 marks]
tips: Columns of a transition matrix (used as T s_n) sum to 1; eigenvectors for eigenvalues other than 1 have components summing to 0.

subtopic: Markov chain with an absorbing state
statement: A machine is in one of three states each week: working (state $1$), under repair (state $2$) or scrapped (state $3$). The transition matrix is $$\mathbf{T}=\begin{pmatrix}0.5&0.2&0\\0.3&0.6&0\\0.2&0.2&1\end{pmatrix},$$ where the entry in row $i$ and column $j$ is the probability of moving from state $j$ to state $i$. The machine is working at the start of week $0$, so $\mathbf{s}_0=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\0\end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{s}_n=\mathbf{T}^n\mathbf{s}_0$. (a) Explain why state $3$ is called an absorbing state. [1] (b) Find the probability that the machine has been scrapped after $4$ weeks. [2] (c) Find the smallest value of $n$ for which the probability that the machine has been scrapped is greater than $0.95$. [3] (d) Use your graphic display calculator to find $\mathbf{T}^{40}\mathbf{s}_0$, and write down what this suggests about the long-term behaviour of the machine. [2]
markscheme: (a) Once in state $3$ the probability of staying there is $1$ (the third column is $(0,0,1)^T$), so the machine can never leave [R1] [1 mark] (b) Third entry of $\mathbf{T}^4\mathbf{s}_0$ [M1] $0.590$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Probability scrapped after $13$ weeks is $0.945$ and after $14$ weeks is $0.956$ [M1][A1] $n=14$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $\mathbf{T}^{40}\mathbf{s}_0\approx\begin{pmatrix}0.0000532\\0.0000798\\1.00\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] The machine is eventually scrapped with probability tending to $1$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: An absorbing state has a column with a $1$ on the leading diagonal. Use the table feature of your GDC to test successive values of $n$ and show the two values either side of your answer.

subtopic: Two-state Markov chain and its eigenvalues
statement: Each day a commuter either drives (D) or cycles (C). The transition matrix, with rows and columns in the order D, C, is $T=\begin{pmatrix} 0.9 & 0.1 \\ 0.2 & 0.8 \end{pmatrix}$, where each entry is the probability of moving from the row state to the column state. (a) Show that $1$ is an eigenvalue of $T$ and find the other eigenvalue. [3] (b) Find the steady state probability vector. [3] (c) Explain why $T^{n}$ approaches a matrix with identical rows as $n\to\infty$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\lambda^{2}-1.7\lambda+0.7=0$ [M1]; $(\lambda-1)(\lambda-0.7)=0$ [A1]; eigenvalues $1$ and $0.7$ [AG] [3 marks] (b) $\pi=(p,q)$ with $0.9p+0.2q=p$ [M1]; $p=2q$ with $p+q=1$ [A1]; $\pi=\left(\dfrac{2}{3},\dfrac{1}{3}\right)$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) the eigenvalue $0.7$ has $0.7^{n}\to0$ [R1]; only the eigenvalue $1$ component remains, which gives $\left(\frac{2}{3},\frac{1}{3}\right)$ in every row [R1] [2 marks]
tips: A steady state is a vector $\pi$ with $\pi T=\pi$ whose entries sum to $1$.

subtopic: Revenue from sales data using matrix multiplication
statement: Three cafes sell bagels, wraps and cookies. The numbers sold in a day are given by the matrix $\mathbf{Q}=\begin{pmatrix} 120 & 80 & 200 \\ 90 & 110 & 150 \\ 60 & 140 & 180 \end{pmatrix}$, where each row is a cafe and the columns are bagels, wraps and cookies. The prices are \$1.50 for a bagel, \$2.25 for a wrap and \$0.80 for a cookie. (a) Write the prices as a column matrix $\mathbf{p}$ and find $\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{p}$. [3] (b) State which cafe has the highest daily revenue and its value. [1] (c) All prices increase by $8\%$. Find the new total daily revenue of the three cafes, to the nearest dollar. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{p}=\begin{pmatrix} 1.50 \\ 2.25 \\ 0.80 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{p}$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix} 520 \\ 502.5 \\ 549 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Cafe 3, with \$549 [A1] [1 mark] (c) Total now $=520+502.5+549=1571.5$ [M1] $1571.5\times1.08=1697.22$, so \$1697 [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Make sure the matrix dimensions are compatible: a $3\times3$ matrix times a $3\times1$ column gives a $3\times1$ column. Rows of the product correspond to the rows of the first matrix.

subtopic: Market share with a change of transition matrix after a promotion
statement: Three coffee chains $X$, $Y$ and $Z$ share a market. For the first three months the monthly switching is given by $\mathbf{T}_1=\begin{pmatrix} 0.7 & 0.2 & 0.1 \\ 0.2 & 0.6 & 0.2 \\ 0.1 & 0.2 & 0.7 \end{pmatrix}$. After a promotion by chain $Z$, the matrix becomes $\mathbf{T}_2=\begin{pmatrix} 0.8 & 0.15 & 0.05 \\ 0.1 & 0.7 & 0.15 \\ 0.1 & 0.15 & 0.8 \end{pmatrix}$ for all later months. Initially the market shares are $\begin{pmatrix} 0.5 \\ 0.3 \\ 0.2 \end{pmatrix}$ for $X$, $Y$, $Z$. (a) Find the market shares after $3$ months, to 3 significant figures. [3] (b) Find the market shares $4$ months after the promotion starts, to 3 significant figures. [3] (c) Find the long-term market shares under $\mathbf{T}_2$, to 3 significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{T}_1^3\begin{pmatrix} 0.5 \\ 0.3 \\ 0.2 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $X=0.367$ [A1] $Y=0.331,\ Z=0.302$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\mathbf{T}_2^4\begin{pmatrix} 0.367 \\ 0.331 \\ 0.302 \end{pmatrix}$ (using unrounded values) [M1] $X=0.337$ [A1] $Y=0.298,\ Z=0.365$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\mathbf{T}_2\mathbf{s}=\mathbf{s}$ with sum $1$ [M1] $X=0.319$ [A1] $Y=0.298,\ Z=0.383$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Apply each matrix in the correct order: the first matrix acts for its months, then the new one takes over from the resulting vector. The long-term shares do not depend on the starting shares.

subtopic: Linear system for a diet plan solved in matrix form
statement: A dietitian mixes three foods $A$, $B$ and $C$. Per $100$ g, food $A$ has $12$ g protein, $30$ g carbohydrate and $5$ g fat; food $B$ has $20$ g protein, $10$ g carbohydrate and $8$ g fat; food $C$ has $5$ g protein, $45$ g carbohydrate and $2$ g fat. A meal must contain exactly $63$ g protein, $110$ g carbohydrate and $25.5$ g fat. Let $x$, $y$ and $z$ be the amounts of $A$, $B$ and $C$ in units of $100$ g. (a) Write the requirements as a matrix equation $\mathbf{M}\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{t}$. [2] (b) Solve for $x$, $y$ and $z$. [2] (c) The foods cost \$0.90, \$1.20 and \$0.70 per $100$ g respectively. Find the cost of the meal. [2] (d) Find $\det\mathbf{M}$ and explain why there is a unique solution for any target amounts. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{M}=\begin{pmatrix} 12 & 20 & 5 \\ 30 & 10 & 45 \\ 5 & 8 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\mathbf{v}=\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{pmatrix}$, $\mathbf{t}=\begin{pmatrix} 63 \\ 110 \\ 25.5 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{M}^{-1}\mathbf{t}$ [M1] $x=1.5,\ y=2,\ z=1$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $0.90(1.5)+1.20(2)+0.70(1)$ [M1] $=\$4.45$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $\det\mathbf{M}=170\neq0$, so $\mathbf{M}$ is invertible and $\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{M}^{-1}\mathbf{t}$ is unique for any $\mathbf{t}$ [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Entries must line up: each row is one nutrient and each column one food. Enter the matrices into your GDC and use the inverse or the simultaneous-equation solver.

subtopic: Two lakes exchanging a pollutant (discrete model)
statement: Two connected lakes $P$ and $Q$ hold pollutant masses $p_n$ and $q_n$ (in kg) at the start of week $n$. Each week $15\%$ of the pollutant in $P$ moves to $Q$, and $20\%$ of the pollutant in $Q$ moves to $P$. Initially $p_0=120$ and $q_0=40$. (a) Write down the transition matrix $T$ such that $\begin{pmatrix} p_{n+1} \\ q_{n+1} \end{pmatrix}=T\begin{pmatrix} p_n \\ q_n \end{pmatrix}$. [2] (b) Find the masses of pollutant in each lake after 4 weeks. [3] (c) Show that the total mass of pollutant is constant. [1] (d) Find the eigenvalues of $T$ and the eigenvector for $\lambda=1$. [3] (e) Find the long-run mass in each lake. [2] (f) Show that the deviation from the long-run state decays by a factor of $0.65$ each week, and find after how many weeks the mass in $P$ is within $1$ kg of its long-run value. [3]
markscheme: (a) $T=\begin{pmatrix} 0.85 & 0.20 \\ 0.15 & 0.80 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1][A1] [2 marks] (b) $T^4\begin{pmatrix}120\\40\end{pmatrix}$ [M1]; $p_4=96.53$ [A1]; $q_4=63.47$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Each column of $T$ sums to $1$, so $p_{n+1}+q_{n+1}=p_n+q_n$ [R1] [1 mark] (d) $\lambda=1$ and $\lambda=0.65$ [A1][A1]; eigenvector $\begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) Total $=160$ kg shared in ratio $4:3$ [M1]: $p\to91.43$, $q\to68.57$ kg [A1] [2 marks] (f) Second eigenvalue $0.65$ [A1]; $|p_n-91.43|=|28.57|(0.65)^n<1$ [M1]; $n=8$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The second eigenvalue controls how quickly the system approaches the steady state; the first (equal to 1) reflects conservation of total mass.

subtopic: Enlargement and rotation matrix for a logo
statement: A logo is transformed by an enlargement with scale factor $1.5$ and centre the origin, followed by an anticlockwise rotation of $40^\circ$ about the origin. The composite transformation has matrix $\mathbf{N}$. (a) Find $\mathbf{N}$, giving entries to 3 significant figures. [2] (b) A triangle in the logo has area $6\ \mathrm{cm}^2$. Find the area of its image. [2] (c) A point on the transformed logo has coordinates $(5,2)$. Find the coordinates of the original point, to 3 significant figures. [3] (d) Find $\mathbf{N}^9$ in the form $k\mathbf{I}$, giving $k$ to 3 significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{N}=1.5\begin{pmatrix} \cos40^\circ & -\sin40^\circ \\ \sin40^\circ & \cos40^\circ \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix} 1.15 & -0.964 \\ 0.964 & 1.15 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\det\mathbf{N}=1.5^2=2.25$ [M1] area $=2.25\times6=13.5\ \mathrm{cm}^2$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\mathbf{N}^{-1}\begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix} 3.41 \\ -1.12 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [A1] [3 marks] (d) Nine rotations of $40^\circ$ total $360^\circ$, which is the identity [M1] $\mathbf{N}^9=1.5^9\mathbf{I}=38.4\,\mathbf{I}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: An enlargement about the origin and a rotation about the origin commute, and the composite determinant is the square of the scale factor. To find an original point, multiply by the inverse matrix.

subtopic: Absorbing Markov chain for student progression
statement: A university tracks first-year students (Y1), second-year students (Y2), graduates (G) and withdrawals (W). Each year: a Y1 student repeats the year with probability $0.1$, moves to Y2 with probability $0.8$ and withdraws with probability $0.1$; a Y2 student repeats with probability $0.05$, graduates with probability $0.85$ and withdraws with probability $0.1$; graduates and withdrawals remain in their states. The state vector is ordered Y1, Y2, G, W. (a) Write down the transition matrix $\mathbf{T}$, with columns giving the probabilities of moving from each state. [2] (b) A cohort of $1000$ first-year students begins. Find the expected number of students in each state after $3$ years, to the nearest whole number. [3] (c) Find the long-term proportion of the cohort who graduate, to 3 significant figures. [2] (d) Show that the exact probability that a Y1 student eventually graduates is $\dfrac{136}{171}$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{T}=\begin{pmatrix} 0.1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0.8 & 0.05 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0.85 & 1 & 0 \\ 0.1 & 0.1 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\mathbf{T}^3\begin{pmatrix} 1000 \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $Y1=1$, $Y2=14$ [A1] $G=782$, $W=203$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) A high power of $\mathbf{T}$ applied to the initial vector [M1] graduate proportion $=0.795$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) Probability a Y1 student eventually reaches Y2: $p=0.8+0.1p$, so $p=\dfrac{0.8}{0.9}=\dfrac89$ [M1] probability a Y2 student eventually graduates: $q=0.85+0.05q$, so $q=\dfrac{0.85}{0.95}=\dfrac{17}{19}$ [M1] $\dfrac89\times\dfrac{17}{19}=\dfrac{136}{171}$ [AG] [3 marks]
tips: Absorbing states have a $1$ on the diagonal and zeros elsewhere in their column. To find eventual probabilities, either take a very high power on your GDC or solve a first-step equation such as $p=0.8+0.1p$.

subtopic: Patterns in powers of a matrix
statement: Let $B=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find $B^{2}$ and $B^{3}$. [3] (b) Write down a general expression for $B^{n}$ for a positive integer $n$ based on the pattern, and use it to find $B^{50}$. [2] (c) Describe the effect of $B$ on the point $(x,y)$ and state $\det B$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $B^{2}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1]; $B^{3}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $B^{n}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & n \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; $B^{50}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 50 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $(x,y)\to(x+y,\ y)$, a horizontal shear [A1]; $\det B=1$, so areas are unchanged [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Multiply the matrix by itself repeatedly and look for how the entries change.

subtopic: Matrix equation with an inverse
statement: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ -1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 4 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find $A^{2}$ and $\det A$. [3] (b) Find $A^{-1}$. [2] (c) Solve $AX=B$ for the matrix $X$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $A^{2}=\begin{pmatrix} 3 & 5 \\ -5 & 8 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1][A1]; $\det A=7$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\dfrac{1}{7}\begin{pmatrix} 3 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (c) $X=A^{-1}B$ [M1]; $\dfrac17\begin{pmatrix} 3 & 12-2 \\ 1 & 4+4 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; $X=\dfrac17\begin{pmatrix} 3 & 10 \\ 1 & 8 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: To solve $AX=B$, multiply on the left by $A^{-1}$: the order matters in matrix multiplication.

subtopic: Inverse of a 2 by 2 matrix and solving a system
statement: The matrix $A=\begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 5 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find $\det A$. [1] (b) Find $A^{-1}$. [2] (c) Hence solve $A\mathbf{x}=\begin{pmatrix} 7 \\ 12 \end{pmatrix}$, where $\mathbf{x}=\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix}$. [3] (d) State the value of $k$ for which the matrix $A$ with its entry $2$ replaced by $k$ is singular. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\det A=3(2)-(1)(5)=1$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $A^{-1}=\dfrac{1}{1}\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -5 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -5 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\mathbf{x}=A^{-1}\mathbf{b}$ [M1]; $x=2$ [A1]; $y=1$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) Singular when $\det=0$: $3k-(1)(5)=0$ [M1]; $k=\frac{5}{3}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: For a $2\times2$ matrix, swap the diagonal entries, negate the off-diagonal entries and divide by the determinant.

subtopic: Steady state of a robot moving between rooms
statement: A cleaning robot moves between rooms $A$, $B$ and $C$ once per hour. From $A$ it stays with probability $0.2$, moves to $B$ with probability $0.5$ and to $C$ with probability $0.3$. From $B$ it moves to $A$ with probability $0.4$, stays with probability $0.4$ and moves to $C$ with probability $0.2$. From $C$ it moves to $A$ with probability $0.3$, to $B$ with probability $0.3$ and stays with probability $0.4$. (a) Write down the transition matrix $\mathbf{T}$, whose columns give the probabilities of moving from each room, and find the exact steady state probabilities. [4] (b) The robot starts in room $A$. Find the probability that it is in room $C$ after $3$ moves, to 3 significant figures. [2] (c) Over a long period of $200$ hours, find the expected number of hours the robot spends in room $B$, to 3 significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{T}=\begin{pmatrix} 0.2 & 0.4 & 0.3 \\ 0.5 & 0.4 & 0.3 \\ 0.3 & 0.2 & 0.4 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\mathbf{T}\mathbf{s}=\mathbf{s}$ with $a+b+c=1$ [M1] solving [A1] $\mathbf{s}=\dfrac{1}{97}\begin{pmatrix} 30 \\ 39 \\ 28 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $\mathbf{T}^3\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] probability $=0.289$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $200\times\dfrac{39}{97}$ [M1] $=80.4$ hours [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Each column of $\mathbf{T}$ lists where the robot goes from one room, so columns sum to $1$. The expected time in a state over a long run is the steady-state probability times the number of periods.

subtopic: Eigenvalue with an unknown matrix entry
statement: The matrix $\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix}k&2\\3&1\end{pmatrix}$ has an eigenvalue $4$, where $k\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Find the value of $k$. [3] (b) Find the other eigenvalue of $\mathbf{A}$. [2] (c) Find an eigenvector for each eigenvalue. [3] (d) Hence find $\mathbf{A}^5\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\det(\mathbf{A}-4\mathbf{I})=(k-4)(1-4)-6=0$ [M1] $-3k+12-6=0$ [A1] $k=2$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Trace $=3$, so the sum of the eigenvalues is $3$ [M1] Other eigenvalue $=-1$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) For $\lambda=4$: $\begin{pmatrix}-2&2\\3&-3\end{pmatrix}$ gives $\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] For $\lambda=-1$: $\begin{pmatrix}3&2\\3&2\end{pmatrix}$ [M1] gives $\begin{pmatrix}2\\-3\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}$ is an eigenvector for $\lambda=4$, so $\mathbf{A}^5\mathbf{v}=4^5\mathbf{v}$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix}1024\\1024\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: If $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue then $\det(\mathbf{A}-\lambda\mathbf{I})=0$, which gives an equation for any unknown entry. If $\mathbf{v}$ is an eigenvector, then $\mathbf{A}^n\mathbf{v}=\lambda^n\mathbf{v}$.

subtopic: Markov chain with three states
statement: Three phone brands $X$, $Y$ and $Z$ compete in a market. Each month customers may switch brands. The transition matrix is $$\mathbf{T}=\begin{pmatrix}0.8&0.2&0.1\\0.1&0.7&0.3\\0.1&0.1&0.6\end{pmatrix},$$ where the entry in row $i$ and column $j$ is the proportion of customers of brand $j$ this month who use brand $i$ next month, with the brands in the order $X,Y,Z$. Currently $60\%$ of customers use $X$, $10\%$ use $Y$ and $30\%$ use $Z$. (a) Find the proportion of customers using brand $Z$ after $4$ months. [3] (b) Find the long-term proportion of customers using each brand. [4] (c) Find the number of months after which the proportion using brand $X$ first lies within $0.01$ of its long-term value. [3]
markscheme: (a) Use of $\mathbf{T}^4\begin{pmatrix}0.6\\0.1\\0.3\end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $\begin{pmatrix}0.463\\0.331\\0.206\end{pmatrix}$ (approximately) [A1] Proportion using $Z$ is $0.206$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Solve $\mathbf{T}\mathbf{s}=\mathbf{s}$ with $x+y+z=1$ [M1] $-0.2x+0.2y+0.1z=0$ and $0.1x-0.3y+0.3z=0$ (or equivalent) [A1] $x=0.45$, $y=0.35$ [A1] $z=0.2$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) Proportions of $X$ after $4$ and $5$ months are $0.4627$ and $0.4570$ [M1] $|0.4627-0.45|=0.0127>0.01$ [A1] $|0.4570-0.45|=0.0070<0.01$, so $5$ months [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A steady state satisfies $\mathbf{T}\mathbf{s}=\mathbf{s}$ and its entries sum to $1$. For 'first within' questions use a table of values from your GDC and compare consecutive terms.

subtopic: Three-state Markov chain for weather
statement: The weather in a town each day is sunny, cloudy or rainy. The transition matrix $T$ (columns = today's weather in the order sunny, cloudy, rainy) is $T=\begin{pmatrix} 0.7 & 0.3 & 0.2 \\ 0.2 & 0.5 & 0.3 \\ 0.1 & 0.2 & 0.5 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Verify that $T$ is a valid transition matrix and state what the $(2,1)$ entry represents. [2] (b) Find the distribution after 5 steps, starting from $\mathbf{p}_0=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$. [3] (c) Find the steady state vector. [3] (d) Explain why the long-run distribution does not depend on the starting distribution. [1] (e) Find the smallest $n$ such that the probability of being in the first state after $n$ steps (starting from the first state) is within $0.01$ of its long-run value. [3]
markscheme: (a) Each column sums to $1$ [A1]; the $(2,1)$ entry is the probability of moving from sunny to cloudy in one step [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\mathbf{p}_{5}=T^{5}\mathbf{p}_0$ [M1]; $=\begin{pmatrix} 0.4737 \\ 0.3131 \\ 0.2133 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1][A1] [3 marks] (c) Solve $T\mathbf{s}=\mathbf{s}$ with sum $1$ (eigenvector for $\lambda=1$) [M1]; $\mathbf{s}=\begin{pmatrix} 0.4634 \\ 0.3171 \\ 0.2195 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1][A1] [3 marks] (d) All entries of some power of $T$ are positive (a regular chain), so $T^n$ converges to a matrix with identical columns equal to $\mathbf{s}$ [R1] [1 mark] (e) Compute $T^n\mathbf{e}_1$ for increasing $n$ [M1]; $n=6$ [A1][A1] [3 marks]
tips: Each column of a transition matrix sums to 1; a steady state is the eigenvector for the eigenvalue 1, scaled to sum to 1.

subtopic: Eigenvalues, eigenvectors and a matrix power
statement: The matrix $A=\begin{pmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find the eigenvalues of $A$. [3] (b) Find an eigenvector for each eigenvalue. [3] (c) Write $A=PDP^{-1}$ and use it to find $A^{3}$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\det(A-\lambda I)=\lambda^2-(7)\lambda+(10)=0$ [M1][A1]; $\lambda=2$ or $5$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) For $\lambda=2$: $\mathbf{v}_1=\begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1]; for $\lambda=5$: $\mathbf{v}_2=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] (any non-zero multiples) [3 marks] (c) $P=\begin{pmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$, $D=\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; $A^{3}=PD^{3}P^{-1}$ [M1]; $A^{3}=\begin{pmatrix} 86 & 39 \\ 78 & 47 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Find eigenvalues from the characteristic polynomial, then each eigenvector from $(A-\lambda I)\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$; powers use $A^n=PD^nP^{-1}$.

subtopic: Working backward with an inverse transition matrix
statement: Customers of two streaming services $X$ and $Y$ switch each month according to $T=\begin{pmatrix} 0.8 & 0.3 \\ 0.2 & 0.7 \end{pmatrix}$, where the columns give the current service in the order $X$, $Y$. After one month, $50$ thousand customers use each service. (a) Find $\det T$ and $T^{-1}$. [3] (b) Find how many thousand customers used each service the month before. [2] (c) Verify your answer by applying $T$ to your result. [2]
tips: To go back one step, multiply by the inverse of the transition matrix.

subtopic: Fibonacci numbers from powers of a matrix
statement: Let $F=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$. It can be shown that $F^{n}=\begin{pmatrix} f_{n+1} & f_n \\ f_n & f_{n-1} \end{pmatrix}$ where $f_n$ is the $n$th Fibonacci number, so that $f_1=1$, $f_2=1$, $f_3=2$ and $f_{n+1}=f_n+f_{n-1}$. (a) Find $F^{2}$ and $F^{3}$, and verify that the entries are consistent with the formula. [2] (b) Use your calculator to find $F^{20}$, and write down $f_{20}$. [3] (c) Calculate $\dfrac{f_{20}}{f_{19}}$ to six significant figures and compare it with $\dfrac{1+\sqrt5}{2}$. [3] (d) Find the eigenvalues of $F$ exactly, and explain how one of them relates to the ratio in part (c). [3]
markscheme: (a) $F^{2}=\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; $F^{3}=\begin{pmatrix} 3 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $F^{20}=\begin{pmatrix} 10946 & 6765 \\ 6765 & 4181 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1][A1]; $f_{20}=6765$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $f_{19}=4181$ [A1]; $\dfrac{6765}{4181}=1.61803$ [A1]; this agrees with $\dfrac{1+\sqrt5}{2}=1.61803$ to the accuracy shown [A1] [3 marks] (d) $\lambda^{2}-\lambda-1=0$ [M1]; $\lambda=\dfrac{1\pm\sqrt5}{2}$ [A1]; the dominant eigenvalue is the limit of the ratio of consecutive terms [R1] [3 marks]
tips: The ratio of consecutive Fibonacci numbers tends to the dominant eigenvalue of $F$.

subtopic: Rate of convergence to a steady state
statement: The weather in a town is either sunny or rainy each day. The transition matrix is $\mathbf{T}=\begin{pmatrix}0.7&0.4\\0.3&0.6\end{pmatrix}$, where the entry in row $i$ and column $j$ is the probability of moving from state $j$ (sunny, rainy) to state $i$ on the next day. Today is sunny. (a) Find the steady state probability vector. [3] (b) Find the smallest number of days after which the probability that it is sunny is within $0.001$ of its steady state value. [3] (c) The eigenvalues of $\mathbf{T}$ are $1$ and $\lambda$. Find $\lambda$, and explain why the probabilities converge to the steady state. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{T}\mathbf{s}=\mathbf{s}$ gives $0.3a=0.4b$ [M1] With $a+b=1$: $a=\frac47\approx0.571$ [A1] $b=\frac37\approx0.429$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Probability sunny after $n$ days from $\mathbf{T}^n\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix}$ [M1] After $5$ days: $0.57247$, difference from $0.571429$ is $0.00104>0.001$ [A1] After $6$ days: difference is $0.00031<0.001$, so $6$ days [A1] [3 marks] (c) Trace $=1.3$, so $\lambda=0.3$ [A1] Since $|\lambda|<1$, the term $\lambda^n$ tends to $0$, so the probabilities approach the steady state [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Compare the difference from the steady state value for consecutive days, and show both so that the smallest $n$ is clear. The second eigenvalue controls how fast the chain converges.

subtopic: Using the inverse matrix to solve linear equations
statement: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -3 \\ 1 & 4 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find $\det A$. [1] (b) Find $A^{-1}$. [2] (c) Hence solve $A\mathbf{x}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 13 \end{pmatrix}$, where $\mathbf{x}=\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix}$. [3] (d) State the value of $k$ for which the matrix $A$ with its entry $4$ replaced by $k$ is singular. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\det A=2(4)-(-3)(1)=11$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $A^{-1}=\dfrac{1}{11}\begin{pmatrix} 4 & 3 \\ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix} \frac{4}{11} & \frac{3}{11} \\ - \frac{1}{11} & \frac{2}{11} \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\mathbf{x}=A^{-1}\mathbf{b}$ [M1]; $x=\frac{43}{11}$ [A1]; $y=\frac{25}{11}$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) Singular when $\det=0$: $2k-(-3)(1)=0$ [M1]; $k=-\frac{3}{2}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ gives $\mathbf{x}=A^{-1}\mathbf{b}$; multiply the inverse on the left.

subtopic: Solving a pair of linear equations with an inverse matrix
statement: Consider the system $2x+y=7$ and $3x+2y=12$. (a) Write the system in the form $\mathbf{M}\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix}=\mathbf{c}$. [1] (b) Find $\det\mathbf{M}$ and $\mathbf{M}^{-1}$. [3] (c) Hence solve the system. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 3 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 7 \\ 12 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\det\mathbf{M}=4-3=1$ [M1] $\mathbf{M}^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -3 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -3 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 7 \\ 12 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $x=2,\ y=3$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Multiply by the inverse on the left of both sides: $\mathbf{M}^{-1}\mathbf{M}\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{M}^{-1}\mathbf{c}$. Check the answer by substituting into the original equations.

subtopic: Three equations in three unknowns with a parameter
statement: Consider the system $x+y+z=6$, $x+2y+3z=14$ and $x+3y+az=b$, where $a,b\in\mathbb{R}$. This is written $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 3 & a \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 6 \\ 14 \\ b \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Show that the determinant of the coefficient matrix is $a-5$, and state the condition on $a$ for the system to have a unique solution. [3] (b) For $a=5$, find the value of $b$ for which the system has solutions. [3] (c) For this value of $b$, find the general solution in terms of $z$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\det=1(2a-9)-1(a-3)+1(3-2)$ [M1] $=2a-9-a+3+1=a-5$ [AG]; unique solution when $a\neq5$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) With $a=5$: (equation 3) $-2\times$(equation 2) $+$ (equation 1) gives $0=b-28+6$ [M1] $0=b-22$ [A1] solutions exist only if $b=22$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) (equation 2) $-$ (equation 1): $y+2z=8$ [M1] $y=8-2z$ [A1] $x=6-y-z=z-2$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: When the determinant is zero the equations are dependent, so the system is either inconsistent or has infinitely many solutions. Combine equations to eliminate all variables and see whether the leftover statement is true.

subtopic: Characteristic equation and the inverse
statement: Let $\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix}4&2\\1&3\end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{A}$. [3] (b) Show that $\mathbf{A}^2=7\mathbf{A}-10\mathbf{I}$. [2] (c) Hence show that $\mathbf{A}^{-1}=\dfrac{1}{10}\left(7\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{A}\right)$, and write down $\mathbf{A}^{-1}$ as a matrix. [2] (d) Express $\mathbf{A}^3$ in the form $p\mathbf{A}+q\mathbf{I}$, where $p,q\in\mathbb{Z}$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $(4-\lambda)(3-\lambda)-2=0$ [M1] $\lambda^2-7\lambda+10=0$ [A1] $\lambda=2$ or $\lambda=5$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\mathbf{A}^2=\begin{pmatrix}18&14\\7&11\end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $7\mathbf{A}-10\mathbf{I}=\begin{pmatrix}18&14\\7&11\end{pmatrix}$ [A1][AG] [2 marks] (c) $\mathbf{A}^2-7\mathbf{A}=-10\mathbf{I}$, so $\mathbf{A}(7\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{A})=10\mathbf{I}$ [M1] $\mathbf{A}^{-1}=\dfrac{1}{10}\begin{pmatrix}3&-2\\-1&4\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $\mathbf{A}^3=7\mathbf{A}^2-10\mathbf{A}=7(7\mathbf{A}-10\mathbf{I})-10\mathbf{A}$ [M1] $=39\mathbf{A}-70\mathbf{I}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A $2\times2$ matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation, which gives a quick route to inverses and higher powers. Check by multiplying $\mathbf{A}$ by your inverse.

subtopic: Singular matrix condition and inverse with a parameter
statement: Let $\mathbf{M}=\begin{pmatrix} k & 2 \\ 3 & k+1 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find the values of $k$ for which $\mathbf{M}$ has no inverse. [3] (b) For $k=1$, find $\mathbf{M}^{-1}$. [3] (c) For $k=1$, solve $\mathbf{M}\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 6 \end{pmatrix}$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\det\mathbf{M}=k(k+1)-6=0$ [M1] $k^2+k-6=0$ [A1] $(k+3)(k-2)=0$, so $k=2$ or $k=-3$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\mathbf{M}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$, $\det\mathbf{M}=-4$ [M1] $\mathbf{M}^{-1}=-\dfrac14\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -2 \\ -3 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $=\begin{pmatrix} -\frac12 & \frac12 \\ \frac34 & -\frac14 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix}=\mathbf{M}^{-1}\begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 6 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $x=1,\ y=\dfrac32$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A square matrix has no inverse exactly when its determinant is zero. Verify part (c) by multiplying $\mathbf{M}$ by your answer.

subtopic: Closed form for a recurrence using eigenvalues
statement: A sequence is defined by $a_0=1$, $a_1=2$ and $a_{n+1}=a_n+6a_{n-1}$ for $n\ge1$. (a) Find the matrix $\mathbf{M}$ such that $\begin{pmatrix} a_{n+1} \\ a_n \end{pmatrix}=\mathbf{M}\begin{pmatrix} a_n \\ a_{n-1} \end{pmatrix}$. [1] (b) Find the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{M}$. [3] (c) Find an eigenvector for each eigenvalue. [3] (d) Write $\begin{pmatrix} a_1 \\ a_0 \end{pmatrix}$ as a linear combination of the two eigenvectors found in part (c). [2] (e) Hence show that $a_n=\dfrac45\,3^n+\dfrac15(-2)^n$. [2] (f) Verify the formula for $n=2$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{M}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 6 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\lambda^2-\lambda-6=0$ [M1] $(\lambda-3)(\lambda+2)=0$ [A1] $\lambda=3,\ \lambda=-2$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\lambda=3$: $-2x+6y=0$ [M1] $\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\lambda=-2$: $\begin{pmatrix} -2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}=\alpha\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}+\beta\begin{pmatrix} -2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ gives $3\alpha-2\beta=2$ and $\alpha+\beta=1$ [M1] $\alpha=\dfrac45,\ \beta=\dfrac15$ [A1] [2 marks] (e) $\begin{pmatrix} a_{n+1} \\ a_n \end{pmatrix}=\mathbf{M}^n\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}=\alpha3^n\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}+\beta(-2)^n\begin{pmatrix} -2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] second component: $a_n=\dfrac45\,3^n+\dfrac15(-2)^n$ [AG] [2 marks] (f) $a_2=a_1+6a_0=8$ and $\dfrac45(9)+\dfrac15(4)=\dfrac{40}{5}=8$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Writing a recurrence as a matrix power lets you use diagonalization: express the starting vector in terms of eigenvectors and each component then scales by $\lambda^n$. Always check the closed form against the first few terms.

subtopic: Two-stage population projection with a Leslie matrix
statement: A gecko population is modeled by $\begin{pmatrix} J_{n+1} \\ A_{n+1} \end{pmatrix}=\mathbf{L}\begin{pmatrix} J_n \\ A_n \end{pmatrix}$ where $J_n$ and $A_n$ are the numbers of juveniles and adults after $n$ years and $\mathbf{L}=\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 2.4 \\ 0.5 & 0.9 \end{pmatrix}$. Currently there are $200$ juveniles and $300$ adults. (a) Find the population of each stage after $3$ years, to the nearest whole number. [3] (b) Find the dominant eigenvalue of $\mathbf{L}$ to 3 significant figures and interpret it. [3] (c) Find the proportion of the population that is juvenile in the long term, as a percentage to 3 significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{L}^3\begin{pmatrix} 200 \\ 300 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $J_3=1663$ [A1] $A_3=1068$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\lambda^2-0.9\lambda-1.2=0$ [M1] $\lambda=1.63$ [A1] In the long term the population is multiplied by about $1.63$ each year, an annual growth of about $63\%$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Eigenvector satisfies $-\lambda J+2.4A=0$ so $J:A=2.4:1.634$ [M1] juvenile proportion $=\dfrac{2.4}{2.4+1.634}$ [A1] $=59.5\%$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The dominant eigenvalue of a projection matrix is the long-term growth factor, and its eigenvector gives the long-term stage proportions. Normalize the eigenvector so its entries add to $1$.

subtopic: Coding and decoding with a 2 by 2 matrix
statement: A message is encoded by splitting it into pairs of numbers and multiplying each pair, written as a column, by $K=\begin{pmatrix} 3 & 2 \\ 4 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$. A pair is encoded as $\begin{pmatrix} 23 \\ 32 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find $K^{-1}$. [2] (b) Decode the pair. [2] (c) Explain why a matrix with determinant $0$ cannot be used as an encoding matrix. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\det K=1$ [A1]; $K^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix} 3 & -2 \\ -4 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $K^{-1}\begin{pmatrix} 23 \\ 32 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1]; $\begin{pmatrix} 69-64 \\ -92+96 \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) It has no inverse, so the original pair could not be recovered uniquely [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Decoding multiplies the encoded column by the inverse of the encoding matrix.

subtopic: General two-state Markov chain from long-term data
statement: A two-state Markov chain has transition matrix $\mathbf{T}=\begin{pmatrix}1-a&b\\a&1-b\end{pmatrix}$, where $0<a<1$ and $0<b<1$, and the entry in row $i$ and column $j$ is the probability of moving from state $j$ to state $i$. (a) Show that $1$ is an eigenvalue of $\mathbf{T}$. [2] (b) Find the other eigenvalue of $\mathbf{T}$ in terms of $a$ and $b$. [2] It is given that the other eigenvalue is $0.5$ and that the long-term probability of being in state $1$ is $0.4$. (c) Find the value of $a$ and the value of $b$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $\det(\mathbf{T}-\mathbf{I})=(-a)(-b)-ba$ [M1] $=0$, so $1$ is an eigenvalue [A1][AG] [2 marks] (b) Sum of eigenvalues equals the trace $=2-a-b$ [M1] Other eigenvalue $=1-a-b$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $1-a-b=0.5$, so $a+b=0.5$ [M1] The steady state $(0.4,0.6)^T$ satisfies $\mathbf{T}\mathbf{s}=\mathbf{s}$, so $0.4(1-a)+0.6b=0.4$ [M1] Hence $-0.4a+0.6b=0$, so $a=1.5b$ [A1] $a=0.3$ and $b=0.2$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: The long-term vector is an eigenvector for eigenvalue $1$, and the trace gives the sum of the eigenvalues. Write both conditions as equations in $a$ and $b$ and solve them simultaneously.

subtopic: Complex eigenvalues of a rotation-enlargement matrix
statement: Let $\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -2 \\ 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Show that the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{A}$ are $2\pm2i$. [3] (b) Write each eigenvalue in the form $re^{i\theta}$. [2] (c) The matrix $\mathbf{A}$ represents an enlargement with centre the origin followed by a rotation about the origin. State the scale factor and the angle of rotation, and hence find $\mathbf{A}^8$. [3] (d) Find the image of the point $(1,0)$ under $\mathbf{A}^3$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\det(\mathbf{A}-\lambda\mathbf{I})=(2-\lambda)^2+4=0$ [M1] $\lambda^2-4\lambda+8=0$ [A1] $\lambda=\dfrac{4\pm\sqrt{16-32}}{2}=2\pm2i$ [AG] [3 marks] (b) $2+2i=2\sqrt2\,e^{\frac{\pi}{4}i}$ [A1] $2-2i=2\sqrt2\,e^{-\frac{\pi}{4}i}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Scale factor $2\sqrt2$ and rotation $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ ($45^\circ$) anticlockwise [A1] $\mathbf{A}^8$ has scale factor $\left(2\sqrt2\right)^8=4096$ and rotation $8\times45^\circ=360^\circ$ [M1] $\mathbf{A}^8=4096\mathbf{I}$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $\mathbf{A}(1,0)=(2,2)$, $\mathbf{A}^2(1,0)=(0,8)$ [M1] $\mathbf{A}^3(1,0)=(-16,16)$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A matrix of the form $\begin{pmatrix} a & -b \\ b & a \end{pmatrix}$ acts like the complex number $a+bi$: its modulus is the scale factor and its argument the rotation angle. This explains why its eigenvalues are complex.

subtopic: Population projection with a Leslie matrix
statement: A population of animals is split into three age groups: young, adult and old. Each year, a young animal produces no offspring, each adult produces $1.5$ young and each old animal produces $1.2$ young. Of the young, $60\%$ survive to become adults the next year; of the adults, $50\%$ survive to become old; no old animals survive the following year. The numbers in the groups, in order (young, adult, old), are written as a column vector $\mathbf{x}_n$ for year $n$, and $\mathbf{x}_{n+1}=L\mathbf{x}_n$. In year $0$ the vector is $\mathbf{x}_0=(200,\,150,\,80)^{T}$. (a) Write down the matrix $L$. [2] (b) Find the numbers in each age group in year $1$ and year $3$. [3] (c) Find the total population in year $10$, correct to the nearest whole number, using $L^{10}\mathbf{x}_0$. [2] (d) Find the ratio of the total population in year $11$ to the total in year $10$, correct to three significant figures, and state what it suggests about the long-term yearly growth. [2]
tips: Compute powers of $L$ with your calculator; the ratio of successive totals settles to the long-term growth factor.

subtopic: Long-term ratio from an eigenvector of a 2 by 2 matrix
statement: Two interacting groups have sizes $x_n$ and $y_n$ at the end of year $n$, with $\begin{pmatrix} x_{n+1} \\ y_{n+1} \end{pmatrix}=A\begin{pmatrix} x_n \\ y_n \end{pmatrix}$ and $A=\begin{pmatrix} 1.1 & 0.2 \\ 0.3 & 0.9 \end{pmatrix}$. Initially $x_0=500$ and $y_0=300$. (a) Find $x_2$ and $y_2$. [3] (b) Use your GDC to find the eigenvalues of $A$, correct to four significant figures. [2] (c) State the long-term yearly percentage growth of each group, and find the long-term ratio $x_n:y_n$ to three significant figures using the eigenvector for the larger eigenvalue. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\begin{pmatrix} x_1 \\ y_1 \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 610 \\ 420 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; $A\begin{pmatrix} 610 \\ 420 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1]; $x_2=755$, $y_2=561$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $1.265$ [A1]; $0.7354$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Dominant eigenvalue $1.265$ so growth $26.5\%$ per year [A1]; eigenvector $(0.772,\,0.635)^{T}$ [A1]; $x_n:y_n\approx1.22:1$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: In the long run the vector tends to point along the eigenvector with the largest eigenvalue, and each year it is multiplied by that eigenvalue.

subtopic: Diagonalization of a 2 by 2 matrix
statement: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find the eigenvalues of $A$. [3] (b) Find an eigenvector for each eigenvalue. [2] (c) Write $A=PDP^{-1}$, stating $P$ and $D$, and use it to find $A^{3}$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $\det(A-\lambda I)=(4-\lambda)(3-\lambda)-2$ [M1]; $\lambda^{2}-7\lambda+10=0$ [A1]; $\lambda=5$ and $\lambda=2$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\lambda=5$: $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; $\lambda=2$: $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $P=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -2 \end{pmatrix}$ and $D=\begin{pmatrix} 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; $A^{3}=PD^{3}P^{-1}$ [M1]; $P^{-1}=-\dfrac{1}{3}\begin{pmatrix} -2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; $A^{3}=\begin{pmatrix} 86 & 39 \\ 78 & 47 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Eigenvalues come from $\det(A-\lambda I)=0$. Then $A^{n}=PD^{n}P^{-1}$, where the columns of $P$ are eigenvectors.

subtopic: Powers of a triangular matrix by diagonalization
statement: Let $\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Write down the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{A}$. [1] (b) Find a corresponding eigenvector for each eigenvalue. [3] (c) Hence find an expression for $\mathbf{A}^n$ in terms of $n$. [3] (d) Write down the top-right entry of $\mathbf{A}^5$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $3$ and $2$ (the diagonal entries of a triangular matrix) [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\lambda=3$: $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\lambda=2$: $(\mathbf{A}-2\mathbf{I})\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$ gives $x+y=0$ [M1] $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\mathbf{P}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$, $\mathbf{P}^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\mathbf{A}^n=\mathbf{P}\begin{pmatrix} 3^n & 0 \\ 0 & 2^n \end{pmatrix}\mathbf{P}^{-1}$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix} 3^n & 3^n-2^n \\ 0 & 2^n \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $3^5-2^5=211$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Use $\mathbf{A}^n=\mathbf{P}\mathbf{D}^n\mathbf{P}^{-1}$, raising only the diagonal entries to the power $n$. Test your formula with $n=1$, which must return $\mathbf{A}$.

subtopic: Powers of a matrix by diagonalisation
statement: Let $\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix}7&-3\\10&-4\end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{A}$. [3] (b) Find an eigenvector corresponding to each eigenvalue. [3] (c) Hence find an expression for $\mathbf{A}^n$ in terms of $n$, where $n\in\mathbb{Z}^+$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $\det(\mathbf{A}-\lambda\mathbf{I})=(7-\lambda)(-4-\lambda)+30=0$ [M1] $\lambda^2-3\lambda+2=0$ [A1] $\lambda=1$ or $\lambda=2$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) For $\lambda=1$: $6x-3y=0$ [M1] giving $\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] For $\lambda=2$: $5x-3y=0$, giving $\begin{pmatrix}3\\5\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\mathbf{P}=\begin{pmatrix}1&3\\2&5\end{pmatrix}$, $\mathbf{D}^n=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&2^n\end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{A}^n=\mathbf{P}\mathbf{D}^n\mathbf{P}^{-1}$ [M1] $\mathbf{P}^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}-5&3\\2&-1\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] Attempt to multiply the three matrices [M1] $\mathbf{A}^n=\begin{pmatrix}6\times2^n-5&3-3\times2^n\\10\times2^n-10&6-5\times2^n\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: After finding $\mathbf{A}^n=\mathbf{P}\mathbf{D}^n\mathbf{P}^{-1}$, test your formula with $n=1$, which must give $\mathbf{A}$. Remember that $\mathbf{P}^{-1}$ for a $2\times2$ matrix swaps the leading diagonal, negates the other entries and divides by the determinant.

subtopic: Three-state Markov chain for weather
statement: The weather each day is Sunny (S), Cloudy (C) or Rainy (R). The transition matrix $T$ below gives the probability of moving from the state in the row to the state in the column, in the order S, C, R, from one day to the next. $$T=\begin{pmatrix} 0.6 & 0.3 & 0.1 \\ 0.2 & 0.5 & 0.3 \\ 0.1 & 0.4 & 0.5 \end{pmatrix}$$ (a) Today is Sunny. Find the probability that it is Rainy in two days' time. [3] (b) Find the steady state probabilities of S, C and R, correct to 3 significant figures. [3] (c) In a year of $365$ days, estimate the number of rainy days, to the nearest day, assuming the chain has reached its steady state. [2] (d) State one reason why a Markov chain might not be a good model of real weather. [1]
markscheme: (a) required entry of $T^{2}$ [M1]; $0.6\times0.1+0.3\times0.3+0.1\times0.5$ [A1]; $=0.2$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) solve $\pi T=\pi$ with $\pi_S+\pi_C+\pi_R=1$ [M1]; $\pi_S=\dfrac{13}{46}=0.283$ [A1]; $\pi_C=0.413$ and $\pi_R=0.304$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $365\times\dfrac{14}{46}$ [M1]; $111$ days [A1] [2 marks] (d) e.g. tomorrow's weather depends on more than today's weather, or the probabilities change with season [R1] [1 mark]
tips: The steady state is the left eigenvector for eigenvalue $1$, normalized so the entries sum to $1$.

subtopic: Matrix products, inverse and a singular sum
statement: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 3 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 4 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find $AB$. [2] (b) Find $A^{-1}$ and hence solve $A\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ 8 \end{pmatrix}$. [3] (c) Find the values of $k$ for which $A+kB$ is singular. Give your answers in exact form. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\begin{pmatrix} 2+4 & -1 \\ 3+8 & -2 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1]; $AB=\begin{pmatrix} 6 & -1 \\ 11 & -2 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\det A=1$, $A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -3 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; $\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix}=A^{-1}\begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ 8 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1]; $x=2$, $y=1$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $A+kB=\begin{pmatrix} 2+k & 1 \\ 3+4k & 2-k \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; $\det=(2+k)(2-k)-(3+4k)=1-4k-k^{2}=0$ [M1]; $k=-2\pm\sqrt5$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A matrix is singular when its determinant is zero. Expand $(2+k)(2-k)$ carefully.

subtopic: Finding a parameter from a given eigenvector
statement: Let $\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix} k & 2 \\ 3 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$. Given that $\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ is an eigenvector of $\mathbf{A}$, (a) find the value of $k$ and the corresponding eigenvalue. [3] (b) Find the other eigenvalue of $\mathbf{A}$. [2] (c) Find an eigenvector corresponding to the other eigenvalue. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{A}\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 2k+2 \\ 7 \end{pmatrix}=\lambda\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $\lambda=7$ [A1] $2k+2=14$, so $k=6$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) The sum of the eigenvalues equals the trace: $6+1=7$ [M1] other eigenvalue $=7-7=0$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $(\mathbf{A}-0\mathbf{I})\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$ gives $6x+2y=0$ [M1] $\mathbf{v}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -3 \end{pmatrix}$ (or any multiple) [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Use $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}=\lambda\mathbf{v}$ directly, since the second component immediately gives $\lambda$. The eigenvalues of a $2\times2$ matrix add to the trace and multiply to the determinant.

subtopic: Sales, prices and profit with matrices
statement: A company sells three products in three towns. The matrix $S$ gives the numbers of units sold, with rows for the towns (Alder, Birch, Cedar) and columns for the products (X, Y, Z): $S=\begin{pmatrix} 120 & 80 & 45 \\ 95 & 110 & 60 \\ 150 & 70 & 30 \end{pmatrix}$. The selling prices in dollars are $4.50$, $7.25$ and $12$ per unit of X, Y and Z. The costs in dollars are $2.80$, $4.90$ and $8.30$ per unit of X, Y and Z. (a) Write the selling prices as a column matrix $\mathbf{p}$ and find $S\mathbf{p}$. State what each entry of $S\mathbf{p}$ represents. [3] (b) Find the total profit from all three towns. [3] (c) The prices of all three products are reduced by $10\%$ with the costs and the numbers sold unchanged. Find the new total profit. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{p}=\begin{pmatrix} 4.5 \\ 7.25 \\ 12 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; $S\mathbf{p}=\begin{pmatrix} 1660 \\ 1945 \\ 1542.5 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; each entry is the total revenue, in dollars, from one town [A1] [3 marks] (b) profit per unit is $\mathbf{p}-\mathbf{c}$ with $\mathbf{c}=(2.8, 4.9, 8.3)^{T}$ [M1]; $S(\mathbf{p}-\mathbf{c})=\begin{pmatrix} 558.5 \\ 642 \\ 530.5 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; total $=1731$ dollars [A1] [3 marks] (c) new prices $0.9\mathbf{p}$ [M1]; total profit $=1216.25$ dollars [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Rows of $S$ are towns, so $S\mathbf{p}$ gives one revenue per town. Profit per unit is price minus cost.

subtopic: Matrix products for costs and orders
statement: Two bakeries order flour (F), sugar (S) and butter (B) in kilograms. Bakery 1 orders $20$, $10$, $5$ of F, S, B and bakery 2 orders $30$, $5$, $15$. The price per kilogram, in dollars, is $1.20$ for F, $2.00$ for S and $8.00$ for B. (a) Write the orders as a $2\times3$ matrix $Q$ and the prices as a $3\times1$ matrix $P$. [2] (b) Find $QP$ and state what its entries represent. [3] (c) Prices rise by $10\%$. Write down a matrix expression for the new total costs and evaluate it. [2]
markscheme: (a) $Q=\begin{pmatrix} 20 & 10 & 5 \\ 30 & 5 & 15 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; $P=\begin{pmatrix} 1.2 \\ 2 \\ 8 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $QP=\begin{pmatrix} 24+20+40 \\ 36+10+120 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1]; $\begin{pmatrix} 84 \\ 166 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; total cost in dollars for each bakery [A1] [3 marks] (c) $1.1\,QP$ [M1]; $\begin{pmatrix} 92.4 \\ 182.6 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Each entry of $QP$ is a row of $Q$ (quantities) multiplied by the column of prices.

subtopic: Invariant points and eigenvalues of a transformation
statement: A transformation is given by $\begin{pmatrix} x' \\ y' \end{pmatrix}=\mathbf{M}\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix}$ where $\mathbf{M}=\begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find $\det\mathbf{M}$. [1] (b) Show that the invariant points of the transformation lie on a line and find its equation. [3] (c) Find the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{M}$ and explain the connection to part (b). [3] (d) A triangle of area $5$ is transformed by $\mathbf{M}$. Find the area of the image triangle. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\det\mathbf{M}=6-2=4$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Invariant: $3x+y=x$ and $2x+2y=y$ [M1] both reduce to $2x+y=0$ [A1] so the invariant points lie on the line $y=-2x$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\lambda^2-5\lambda+4=0$ [M1] $\lambda=1$ or $\lambda=4$ [A1] Invariant points satisfy $\mathbf{M}\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{v}$, so they are eigenvectors with eigenvalue $1$ [R1] [3 marks] (d) $4\times5=20$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: A point is invariant when $\mathbf{M}\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{v}$, so invariant points form the set of eigenvectors with eigenvalue $1$ (together with the origin). Area scales by the absolute value of the determinant.

subtopic: Eigenvalues, eigenvectors and diagonalisation of a 2x2 matrix
statement: Let $\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix}4&1\\2&3\end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{A}$. [3] (b) Find an eigenvector corresponding to each eigenvalue. [3] (c) Write down a matrix $\mathbf{P}$ and a diagonal matrix $\mathbf{D}$ such that $\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{P}\mathbf{D}\mathbf{P}^{-1}$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\det(\mathbf{A}-\lambda\mathbf{I})=(4-\lambda)(3-\lambda)-2=0$ [M1] $\lambda^2-7\lambda+10=0$ [A1] $\lambda=2$ or $\lambda=5$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) For $\lambda=5$: $\begin{pmatrix}-1&1\\2&-2\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\end{pmatrix}=\mathbf{0}$ [M1] giving $\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] For $\lambda=2$: $2x+y=0$, giving $\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] (any non-zero multiples) [3 marks] (c) $\mathbf{P}=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-2\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\mathbf{D}=\begin{pmatrix}5&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix}$ (with the same order as the columns of $\mathbf{P}$) [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The columns of $\mathbf{P}$ are eigenvectors and the diagonal of $\mathbf{D}$ holds the matching eigenvalues in the same order. Check an eigenvector by multiplying it by $\mathbf{A}$.

subtopic: Expected profit from a two-state machine
statement: A machine is either working ($W$) or broken ($B$) at the start of each day. A working machine breaks during the day with probability $0.05$. A broken machine is repaired by the next day with probability $0.6$. The transition matrix has columns for today's state and rows for tomorrow's state, in the order $W$, $B$. A working day earns a profit of \$500 and a day with the machine broken has a profit of $-200$ dollars (a loss of \$200). The machine is working on day $1$. (a) Write down the transition matrix $T$. [2] (b) Find the probability that the machine is working on day $3$, and the expected profit on day $3$. [3] (c) Find the long-run proportion of days on which the machine is working, and the long-run expected profit per day, to the nearest cent. [3]
markscheme: (a) $T=\begin{pmatrix} 0.95 & 0.6 \\ 0.05 & 0.4 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1][A1] [2 marks] (b) $T^{2}\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 0.9325 \\ 0.0675 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1]; $P(W)=0.9325$ [A1]; expected profit $500(0.9325)-200(0.0675)=\$452.75$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $0.05s_W=0.6s_B$ with $s_W+s_B=1$ [M1]; $s_W=\dfrac{12}{13}$ [A1]; $500\times\dfrac{12}{13}-200\times\dfrac{1}{13}=\$446.15$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Expected profit on a day is the profit for each state multiplied by the probability of that state.

subtopic: Markov chains and eigenvalues
statement: A bike-share scheme has three docking stations: Harbor ($H$), Market ($M$) and University ($U$). Each bike is returned to one of the stations at the end of every day. Data show that: of the bikes at $H$ at the start of a day, $60\%$ end the day at $H$, $30\%$ at $M$ and $10\%$ at $U$; of the bikes at $M$, $20\%$ end at $H$, $50\%$ at $M$ and $30\%$ at $U$; of the bikes at $U$, $25\%$ end at $H$, $25\%$ at $M$ and $50\%$ at $U$. The scheme has $300$ bikes. At the start of day $1$ there are $150$ bikes at $H$, $90$ at $M$ and $60$ at $U$. (a) Write down the transition matrix $T$, with columns representing the station at the start of a day, in the order $H, M, U$. [2] (b) Find the expected number of bikes at each station at the end of day $3$. [3] (c) By solving a system of equations, find the long-term expected number of bikes at each station. [4] (d) Given that $1$ is an eigenvalue of $T$, use the trace and determinant of $T$ to find the other eigenvalues. [3] (e) (i) Find the smallest value of $n$ for which, at the end of day $n$, the expected number of bikes at every station is within $1$ bike of its long-term value. (ii) With reference to your answer to part (d), explain why the distribution settles down so quickly. [3]
markscheme: (a) $T=\begin{pmatrix}0.6&0.2&0.25\\0.3&0.5&0.25\\0.1&0.3&0.5\end{pmatrix}$ [A1][A1] Note: award [A1] for one correct column structure and [A1] for all correct [2 marks] (b) $T^3\begin{pmatrix}150\\90\\60\end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix}109.11\\107.49\\83.4\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] so about $109$ at $H$, $107$ at $M$ and $83$ at $U$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $T\mathbf{s}=\mathbf{s}$ with $h+m+u=300$ [M1] e.g. $-0.4h+0.2m+0.25u=0$, $0.3h-0.5m+0.25u=0$, $h+m+u=300$ [A1] solving (using GDC) [M1] $h=m=107.14\ldots\approx107$, $u=85.71\ldots\approx86$ (exactly $\frac{5}{14},\frac{5}{14},\frac{4}{14}$ of $300$) [A1] [4 marks] (d) $\text{tr}(T)=1.6$ so $\lambda_2+\lambda_3=0.6$; $\det T=0.09$ so $\lambda_2\lambda_3=0.09$ [M1][A1] $\lambda^2-0.6\lambda+0.09=0\Rightarrow\lambda_2=\lambda_3=0.3$ [A1] [3 marks] (e)(i) end of day $3$: $U$ has $83.4$, which differs from $85.71$ by $2.31$; end of day $4$: $\begin{pmatrix}107.81\\107.33\\84.86\end{pmatrix}$, all within $1$ [M1] $n=4$ [A1] (ii) the other eigenvalues are $0.3$, and $0.3^n\to0$ rapidly, so the non-steady-state part of the distribution decays very quickly [R1] [3 marks]
tips: Check that each column of a column-stochastic matrix sums to 1 before doing anything else. The size of the second-largest eigenvalue controls how fast a Markov chain approaches its steady state.

subtopic: Bike sharing between three stations
statement: A city has three bike stations $A$, $B$ and $C$. Each evening, bikes are rebalanced according to a transition matrix $T$ (columns give the station a bike starts at, rows give where it is next, in order $A$, $B$, $C$): $T=\begin{pmatrix} 0.6 & 0.2 & 0.1 \\ 0.3 & 0.5 & 0.2 \\ 0.1 & 0.3 & 0.7 \end{pmatrix}$. There are $600$ bikes, and on Monday morning $300$, $200$ and $100$ are at stations $A$, $B$ and $C$ respectively. (a) Explain why each column of $T$ sums to $1$. [1] (b) Find the expected number of bikes at each station after three evenings of rebalancing. [3] (c) Find the long-term expected number of bikes at each station, to the nearest bike. [3] (d) Station $C$ has parking for $230$ bikes. State whether it will be over capacity in the long term, and give a reason. [1]
markscheme: (a) Every bike at a station must end up at some station [R1] [1 mark] (b) $T^{3}\begin{pmatrix} 300 \\ 200 \\ 100 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1]; $A$: $178.6$, $B$: $201.4$, $C$: $220$ [A1][A1] [3 marks] (c) Solve $T\mathbf{s}=\mathbf{s}$ with $s_A+s_B+s_C=1$ [M1]; $\mathbf{s}=\left(\frac{9}{34},\ \frac{11}{34},\ \frac{14}{34}\right)$ [A1]; $159$, $194$, $247$ bikes [A1] [3 marks] (d) Yes, since $247>230$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: The long-term vector satisfies $T\mathbf{s}=\mathbf{s}$; scale its entries so that they add to the total number of bikes.

subtopic: Eigen-decomposition of a subscription Markov chain
statement: This question investigates how quickly a Markov chain approaches its steady state, using eigenvalues and eigenvectors. A streaming service has three tiers: Free (F), Standard (S) and Premium (P). Each month the proportions of subscribers in each tier are given by $\mathbf{x}_{n+1}=\mathbf{T}\mathbf{x}_n$ where $\mathbf{x}_n=\begin{pmatrix} f_n \\ s_n \\ p_n \end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{T}=\begin{pmatrix} 0.5 & 0.3 & 0.2 \\ 0.3 & 0.5 & 0.2 \\ 0.2 & 0.2 & 0.6 \end{pmatrix}$, with the entry in row $i$ and column $j$ the proportion of tier $j$ subscribers who are in tier $i$ the next month. Initially $\mathbf{x}_0=\begin{pmatrix} 0.7 \\ 0.2 \\ 0.1 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Show that every column of $\mathbf{T}$ sums to $1$, and show that $\begin{pmatrix} \frac13 \\ \frac13 \\ \frac13 \end{pmatrix}$ is a steady state. [3] (b) Use your GDC to find the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{T}$, and an eigenvector for each, with integer entries. [4] (c) Write down a matrix $\mathbf{P}$ and a diagonal matrix $\mathbf{D}$ such that $\mathbf{T}=\mathbf{P}\mathbf{D}\mathbf{P}^{-1}$. [2] (d) Express $\mathbf{x}_0$ as a linear combination of the three eigenvectors. [4] (e) Hence show that $f_n=\dfrac13+\dfrac{7}{60}(0.4)^n+\dfrac14(0.2)^n$. [3] (f) Find the smallest $n$ for which $f_n-\dfrac13<0.001$. [3] A promotion changes the matrix to $\mathbf{T}_p=\begin{pmatrix} 0.5 & 0.3 & \frac{1-p}{2} \\ 0.3 & 0.5 & \frac{1-p}{2} \\ 0.2 & 0.2 & p \end{pmatrix}$, where $0<p<1$ is the proportion of Premium subscribers who stay Premium. (g) (i) Show that $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$ is an eigenvector of $\mathbf{T}_p$ with eigenvalue $0.2$. [2] (ii) Show that $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}$ is an eigenvector of $\mathbf{T}_p$ with eigenvalue $p-0.2$. [2] (iii) Find the steady state of $\mathbf{T}_p$ in terms of $p$. [3] (iv) Find the value of $p$ for which the long-term proportion of Premium subscribers is $0.5$. [2] (v) For this value of $p$, state the three eigenvalues of $\mathbf{T}_p$ and comment on how the speed of convergence compares with the original matrix $\mathbf{T}$. [1]
markscheme: (a) Columns: $0.5+0.3+0.2=1$, $0.3+0.5+0.2=1$, $0.2+0.2+0.6=1$ [A1] $\mathbf{T}\begin{pmatrix} \frac13 \\ \frac13 \\ \frac13 \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} \frac{0.5+0.3+0.2}{3} \\ \frac{0.3+0.5+0.2}{3} \\ \frac{0.2+0.2+0.6}{3} \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix} \frac13 \\ \frac13 \\ \frac13 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Eigenvalues from $\det(\mathbf{T}-\lambda\mathbf{I})=0$ [M1] $\lambda=1$ with $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\lambda=0.4$ with $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\lambda=0.2$ with $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) $\mathbf{P}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & -2 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\mathbf{D}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0.4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0.2 \end{pmatrix}$ (same order as the columns of $\mathbf{P}$) [A1] [2 marks] (d) $\mathbf{x}_0=a\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}+c\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}+b\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $a+c+b=0.7$, $a+c-b=0.2$, $a-2c=0.1$ [A1] $b=\dfrac14$ [A1] $a=\dfrac13,\ c=\dfrac{7}{60}$ [A1] [4 marks] (e) $\mathbf{x}_n=\mathbf{T}^n\mathbf{x}_0=a(1)^n\mathbf{v}_1+c(0.4)^n\mathbf{v}_2+b(0.2)^n\mathbf{v}_3$ [M1] [A1] first component: $f_n=\dfrac13+\dfrac{7}{60}(0.4)^n+\dfrac14(0.2)^n$ [AG] [3 marks] (f) $\dfrac{7}{60}(0.4)^n+\dfrac14(0.2)^n<0.001$ [M1] $n=5$ gives $0.001275$ [A1] $n=6$ gives $0.000494$, so $n=6$ [A1] [3 marks] (g)(i) $\mathbf{T}_p\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 0.2 \\ -0.2 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=0.2\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (ii) $\mathbf{T}_p\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 0.8-(1-p) \\ 0.8-(1-p) \\ 0.4-2p \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=(p-0.2)\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (iii) By symmetry $f=s=x$ and $p=z$; third row of $\mathbf{T}_p\mathbf{s}=\mathbf{s}$: $0.4x+pz=z$, so $x=2.5(1-p)z$ [M1] with $2x+z=1$: $z(5(1-p)+1)=1$ [M1] $z=\dfrac{1}{6-5p}$ and $x=\dfrac{2.5(1-p)}{6-5p}$ [A1] [3 marks] (iv) $\dfrac{1}{6-5p}=0.5$ [M1] $p=0.8$ [A1] [2 marks] (v) Eigenvalues $1,\ 0.2,\ 0.6$; the second largest eigenvalue is now $0.6$ rather than $0.4$, so convergence is slower [A1] [1 mark]
tips: The key idea is that $\mathbf{T}^n$ acts on each eigenvector by multiplying it by $\lambda^n$, so every component except the one for $\lambda=1$ dies away and the second largest eigenvalue sets the speed. In part (g) test the given vectors directly rather than solving a characteristic equation.

subtopic: Two-state Markov chain and steady state by hand
statement: Each month, $20\%$ of customers of phone company $A$ switch to $B$, and $30\%$ of customers of $B$ switch to $A$. Everyone else stays. (a) Write down the transition matrix $T$, with columns giving the probabilities of moving from each state. [2] (b) Find the probability that a company A user is still a company A user after two changes (that is, the entry of $T^2$). [3] (c) Find the long-run proportion in each state by solving $T\mathbf{s}=\mathbf{s}$ with $s_1+s_2=1$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $T=\begin{pmatrix} \frac{4}{5} & \frac{3}{10} \\ \frac{1}{5} & \frac{7}{10} \end{pmatrix}$ [A1][A1] (A1 for each column) [2 marks] (b) $T^2=\begin{pmatrix} \frac{7}{10} & \frac{9}{20} \\ \frac{3}{10} & \frac{11}{20} \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1]; probability $=\frac{7}{10}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $(1-a)s_1+bs_2=s_1$ gives $as_1=bs_2$ [M1]; with $s_1+s_2=1$: $s_1=\frac{3}{5}$ [A1], $s_2=\frac{2}{5}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A steady state satisfies $T\mathbf{s}=\mathbf{s}$; the long-run proportions are in the ratio of the opposite switching probabilities.

subtopic: Determinant and inverse of a 2x2 matrix in coding
statement: Letters are given numbers $A=1$, $B=2$, $\ldots$, $Z=26$. A message is split into pairs of letters. Each pair is written as a column vector and encoded by multiplying on the left by $\mathbf{E}=\begin{pmatrix}3&2\\4&3\end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find $\det\mathbf{E}$ and write down $\mathbf{E}^{-1}$. [2] (b) Encode the message MATH, treating it as the pairs MA and TH. [2] (c) The coded vectors $\begin{pmatrix}70\\95\end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix}29\\43\end{pmatrix}$ form a four-letter word. Decode the word. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\det\mathbf{E}=9-8=1$ [A1] $\mathbf{E}^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}3&-2\\-4&3\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) MA $=\begin{pmatrix}13\\1\end{pmatrix}$ gives $\begin{pmatrix}41\\55\end{pmatrix}$ [M1] TH $=\begin{pmatrix}20\\8\end{pmatrix}$ gives $\begin{pmatrix}76\\104\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Use of $\mathbf{E}^{-1}$ [M1] $\mathbf{E}^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}70\\95\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}20\\5\end{pmatrix}$ gives TE, and $\mathbf{E}^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}29\\43\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\13\end{pmatrix}$ gives AM [A1] The word is TEAM [A1] [3 marks]
tips: To decode, multiply by the inverse matrix on the left, in the same order that you encoded. A determinant of $1$ keeps the inverse entries as integers.

subtopic: Diagonalizing a symmetric matrix
statement: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix} 5 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find the eigenvalues of $A$. [3] (b) Find an eigenvector for each eigenvalue. [3] (c) Write $A=PDP^{-1}$ and use it to find $A^{4}$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\det(A-\lambda I)=\lambda^2-(7)\lambda+(6)=0$ [M1][A1]; $\lambda=1$ or $6$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) For $\lambda=1$: $\mathbf{v}_1=\begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1]; for $\lambda=6$: $\mathbf{v}_2=\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] (any non-zero multiples) [3 marks] (c) $P=\begin{pmatrix} -1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$, $D=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 6 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; $A^{4}=PD^{4}P^{-1}$ [M1]; $A^{4}=\begin{pmatrix} 1037 & 518 \\ 518 & 260 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: For a symmetric matrix the eigenvectors for different eigenvalues are perpendicular.

subtopic: Solving a 3 by 3 system with a matrix inverse
statement: Three types of tickets (child, adult, senior) have prices $c$, $a$ and $s$ dollars. Group 1 buys $2$ child, $3$ adult and $1$ senior ticket for \$56. Group 2 buys $1$ child, $2$ adult and $2$ senior tickets for \$54. Group 3 buys $3$ child, $1$ adult and $1$ senior ticket for \$42. (a) Write the information as a matrix equation $M\mathbf{p}=\mathbf{b}$, where $\mathbf{p}=(c,\,a,\,s)^{T}$. [2] (b) Use your GDC to find $\det M$ and $M^{-1}$. [3] (c) Hence find the price of each type of ticket. [2] (d) A group buys $4$ child, $4$ adult and $2$ senior tickets. Find the total cost. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 2 \\ 3 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} c \\ a \\ s \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 56 \\ 54 \\ 42 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1][A1] [2 marks] (b) $\det M=10$ [A1]; $M^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -0.2 & 0.4 \\ 0.5 & -0.1 & -0.3 \\ -0.5 & 0.7 & 0.1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1][A1] [3 marks] (c) $\mathbf{p}=M^{-1}\mathbf{b}$ [M1]; child \$6, adult \$10, senior \$14 [A1] [2 marks] (d) $24+40+28=\$92$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Enter $M$ and $\mathbf b$ in the matrix menu, then compute $M^{-1}\mathbf b$.

subtopic: Two-state Markov chain by hand
statement: A bus is either on time (state $1$) or late (state $2$) each day. The transition matrix is $\mathbf{T}=\begin{pmatrix}0.6&0.3\\0.4&0.7\end{pmatrix}$, where the entry in row $i$ and column $j$ is the probability of moving from state $j$ to state $i$. (a) Find $\mathbf{T}^2$. [2] (b) Given that the bus is on time today, find the probability that it is late in two days' time. [2] (c) Find the steady state probability vector. [3] (d) Given that one eigenvalue of $\mathbf{T}$ is $1$, use the trace of $\mathbf{T}$ to find the other eigenvalue. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{T}^2=\begin{pmatrix}0.36+0.12&0.18+0.21\\0.24+0.28&0.12+0.49\end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix}0.48&0.39\\0.52&0.61\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Required entry is row $2$, column $1$ of $\mathbf{T}^2$ [M1] $0.52$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\mathbf{T}\mathbf{s}=\mathbf{s}$ gives $0.6a+0.3b=a$, so $0.3b=0.4a$ [M1] With $a+b=1$: $a=\frac37$ [A1] $b=\frac47$, so $\mathbf{s}=\begin{pmatrix}\frac37\\\frac47\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) Sum of eigenvalues equals the trace $=1.3$ [M1] Other eigenvalue $=0.3$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Make sure you use the convention given in the question for rows and columns. The sum of the eigenvalues of a square matrix equals its trace.

subtopic: Eigen-analysis of a pollutant exchange model
statement: The amounts of two pollutants in a lake, $x_n$ and $y_n$ in kilograms after $n$ weeks, are modeled by $x_{n+1}=3x_n+1.5y_n$ and $y_{n+1}=2x_n+4y_n$. Let $\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1.5 \\ 2 & 4 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{A}$ to 3 significant figures. [2] (b) For each eigenvalue, find an eigenvector of the form $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ m \end{pmatrix}$, with $m$ to 3 significant figures. [3] (c) Describe the long-term behavior of the ratio $\dfrac{y_n}{x_n}$ and of the total amount of pollutant. [2] (d) Initially $x_0=y_0=10$. Find $\dfrac{y_{10}}{x_{10}}$ to 3 significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\lambda^2-7\lambda+9=0$ gives $\lambda=1.70$ and $\lambda=5.30$ [A1] [A1] [2 marks] (b) $(\mathbf{A}-\lambda\mathbf{I})\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$ [M1] For $\lambda=5.30$: $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1.54 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] For $\lambda=1.70$: $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -0.869 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) The ratio $\dfrac{y_n}{x_n}$ tends to $1.54$ [A1] and the total amount is multiplied by about $5.30$ each week (growing without bound) [A1] [2 marks] (d) $\mathbf{A}^{10}\begin{pmatrix} 10 \\ 10 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $\dfrac{y_{10}}{x_{10}}=1.54$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The eigenvector of the largest-modulus eigenvalue dominates the long-term behavior, so the ratio of components settles at that eigenvector's ratio. Use the matrix power function on your GDC for part (d).

subtopic: Stage-structured population with a dominant eigenvalue
statement: A fish population has juveniles and adults. Each year, every adult produces on average $1.5$ juveniles, $60\%$ of juveniles survive to become adults, and $80\%$ of adults survive. Juveniles do not breed. Let $\mathbf{p}_n=\begin{pmatrix}j_n\\a_n\end{pmatrix}$ be the numbers of juveniles and adults after $n$ years, so that $\mathbf{p}_{n+1}=\mathbf{L}\mathbf{p}_n$, where $\mathbf{L}=\begin{pmatrix}0&1.5\\0.6&0.8\end{pmatrix}$. Initially there are $200$ juveniles and $300$ adults. (a) Find the number of juveniles and adults after $5$ years, to the nearest whole number. [3] (b) Find the largest eigenvalue of $\mathbf{L}$, and interpret its value in context. [3] (c) Find the long-term proportion of the population that are juveniles, giving your answer as a percentage to $3$ significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{L}^5\begin{pmatrix}200\\300\end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $\begin{pmatrix}1677.78\\1588.18\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $1678$ juveniles and $1588$ adults [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\lambda^2-0.8\lambda-0.9=0$ [M1] $\lambda=1.43$ [A1] In the long run the population grows by about $43\%$ each year [A1] [3 marks] (c) Eigenvector satisfies $-\lambda j+1.5a=0$, so $j:a=1.5:1.4296\ldots$ [M1] $\dfrac{j}{j+a}=\dfrac{1.5}{1.5+1.4296}$ [A1] $=51.2\%$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The dominant eigenvalue gives the long-term growth factor and its eigenvector gives the long-term proportions. Divide by the total of the eigenvector entries to get a proportion.

subtopic: General two-state Markov chain and powers of the transition matrix
statement: This question investigates the long-term behaviour of a two-state Markov chain. A system moves between states $1$ and $2$ in steps. Its transition matrix is $\mathbf{T}=\begin{pmatrix}1-a&b\\a&1-b\end{pmatrix}$, where $0<a<1$ and $0<b<1$. The entry in row $i$ and column $j$ is the probability of moving from state $j$ to state $i$. The state vector after $n$ steps is $\mathbf{s}_n=\mathbf{T}^n\mathbf{s}_0$. Let $\mu=1-a-b$. (a) Show that the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{T}$ are $1$ and $\mu$. [3] (b) Show that $\begin{pmatrix}b\\a\end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix}$ are eigenvectors of $\mathbf{T}$ corresponding to $1$ and $\mu$ respectively. [2] (c) Let $\mathbf{P}=\begin{pmatrix}b&1\\a&-1\end{pmatrix}$. Find $\mathbf{P}^{-1}$, and hence show that $$\mathbf{T}^n=\frac{1}{a+b}\begin{pmatrix}b+a\mu^n&b-b\mu^n\\a-a\mu^n&a+b\mu^n\end{pmatrix}.$$ [5] (d) Given that $|\mu|<1$, find $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbf{T}^n$, and deduce that for any initial state vector $\mathbf{s}_0=\begin{pmatrix}p\\1-p\end{pmatrix}$, the long-term state vector is $\dfrac{1}{a+b}\begin{pmatrix}b\\a\end{pmatrix}$. [3] (e) Let $a=0.3$ and $b=0.2$, and suppose the system starts in state $2$. Let $p_n$ be the probability that the system is in state $1$ after $n$ steps. Find the smallest value of $n$ for which $p_n$ is within $0.001$ of its long-term value. [3] (f) For general $a$ and $b$, let $p_n$ be the probability of being in state $1$ after $n$ steps. (i) Show that $p_{n+1}=\mu p_n+b$. (ii) Let $L=\dfrac{b}{a+b}$. Show that $L=\mu L+b$, and hence show that $p_n-L=\mu^n(p_0-L)$. [4] (g) Let $a=0.7$ and $b=0.6$, and suppose the system starts in state $1$. Find $\mu$ and an expression for $p_n-L$. Hence explain why $p_n$ alternates between values below and above $L$. [3] (h) Now let $a=b=1$. Write down $\mathbf{T}$, find $\mathbf{T}^n$ for even and odd $n$, and explain why the long-term behaviour in part (d) does not occur. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\det(\mathbf{T}-\lambda\mathbf{I})=(1-a-\lambda)(1-b-\lambda)-ab$ [M1] $=\lambda^2-(2-a-b)\lambda+(1-a-b)$ [A1] $=(\lambda-1)(\lambda-(1-a-b))$, so the eigenvalues are $1$ and $\mu=1-a-b$ [A1][AG] [3 marks] (b) $\mathbf{T}\begin{pmatrix}b\\a\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}(1-a)b+ba\\ab+(1-b)a\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}b\\a\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\mathbf{T}\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1-a-b\\a-1+b\end{pmatrix}=\mu\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\det\mathbf{P}=-(a+b)$, so $\mathbf{P}^{-1}=\dfrac{1}{a+b}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\a&-b\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\mathbf{T}^n=\mathbf{P}\mathbf{D}^n\mathbf{P}^{-1}$ with $\mathbf{D}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&\mu\end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $\mathbf{P}\mathbf{D}^n=\begin{pmatrix}b&\mu^n\\a&-\mu^n\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] Multiplication by $\mathbf{P}^{-1}$ [M1] Correct entries leading to the given result [A1][AG] [5 marks] (d) Since $|\mu|<1$, $\mu^n\to0$ [R1] $\mathbf{T}^n\to\dfrac{1}{a+b}\begin{pmatrix}b&b\\a&a\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] Then $\mathbf{s}_n\to\dfrac{1}{a+b}\begin{pmatrix}b(p+1-p)\\a(p+1-p)\end{pmatrix}=\dfrac{1}{a+b}\begin{pmatrix}b\\a\end{pmatrix}$, independent of $p$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) Here $\mu=0.5$ and the long-term value is $0.4$; starting in state $2$, $p_n$ is the entry in row $1$, column $2$ of $\mathbf{T}^n$, which is $0.4(1-0.5^n)$ [M1] $0.4\times0.5^n<0.001$ [A1] $n=8$ gives $0.00156$ and $n=9$ gives $0.00078$, so $n=9$ [A1] [3 marks] (f) (i) $p_{n+1}=(1-a)p_n+b(1-p_n)$ [M1] $=(1-a-b)p_n+b=\mu p_n+b$ [A1][AG] (ii) $\mu L+b=\dfrac{(1-a-b)b+b(a+b)}{a+b}=\dfrac{b}{a+b}=L$ [A1] Subtracting: $p_{n+1}-L=\mu(p_n-L)$, so $p_n-L=\mu^n(p_0-L)$ [R1] [4 marks] (g) $\mu=1-1.3=-0.3$ [A1] $L=\frac{6}{13}$ and $p_0=1$, so $p_n-L=\frac{7}{13}(-0.3)^n$ [A1] Since $\mu<0$, the sign of $(-0.3)^n$ alternates, so $p_n$ alternates above and below $L$ [R1] [3 marks] (h) $\mathbf{T}$ has rows $(0,\ 1)$ and $(1,\ 0)$, with $\mathbf{T}^n=\mathbf{I}$ for even $n$ and $\mathbf{T}^n=\mathbf{T}$ for odd $n$ [A1] Here $\mu=-1$, so $|\mu|=1$ and $\mu^n$ does not tend to $0$; the chain keeps alternating and has no limit [A1] [2 marks]
tips: For part (c), keep the common factor $\frac{1}{a+b}$ outside the matrices while you multiply. In parts (e) and (g), connect each numerical answer back to the general formula you proved earlier.
