tips: Rewrite every power with the same base before equating exponents.

subtopic: Laws of exponents and simplification
statement: Simplify each expression, giving answers in the form $2^p3^q$ or as an integer. (a) $\dfrac{12^3}{18^2}$ [3] (b) $\left(\dfrac{8}{27}\right)^{-2/3}$ [3]
tips: Write bases as prime factors, then subtract exponents when dividing; a negative exponent means reciprocal.

subtopic: Compounding frequency and the number e
statement: An account holds \$1000 with nominal annual rate $6\%$. When interest is compounded $n$ times per year, the balance after one year is $B_n=1000\left(1+\dfrac{0.06}{n}\right)^{n}$. (a) Use your calculator to find $B_n$ for $n=1$, $n=4$ and $n=12$. Give your answers to the nearest cent. [3] (b) Find the effective annual rate for monthly compounding, as a percentage to three significant figures. [2] (c) Explain why $B_n$ increases with $n$ but the increase becomes very small. [2] (d) The limit of $B_n$ as $n\to\infty$ is $1000e^{0.06}$. Find this value to the nearest cent, and find its difference from $B_{365}$ using the two values rounded to the nearest cent. [3] (e) With continuous compounding, $B(t)=1000e^{0.06t}$. Find the time for the balance to reach \$1500, correct to three significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) $B_1=\$1060.00$ [A1]; $B_4=\$1061.36$ [A1]; $B_{12}=\$1061.68$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\dfrac{1061.68-1000}{1000}$ [M1]; $6.17\%$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) More frequent compounding pays interest on interest sooner [R1]; the values approach a limit, so each extra increase in $n$ adds less [R1] [2 marks] (d) $1000e^{0.06}=\$1061.84$ [A1]; $B_{365}=\$1061.83$ [A1]; difference $=\$0.01$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) $e^{0.06t}=1.5$ [M1]; $t=\dfrac{\ln1.5}{0.06}$ [A1]; $6.76$ years [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Continuous compounding uses $e^{rt}$ and is the limiting case of compounding $n$ times a year as $n\to\infty$.

subtopic: Percentage error and approximation
statement: A student measures the radius of a circular pond as $7.4$ m. The true radius of the pond is $7.5$ m. (a) Use the student's measurement to calculate the area of the pond, giving your answer to three significant figures. [1] (b) Find the percentage error in the student's calculated area. [2] (c) Find the percentage error in the student's measurement of the radius. [1] (d) Explain, by referring to the formula for the area of a circle, why the percentage error in the area is approximately twice the percentage error in the radius. [2]
markscheme: (a) $A=\pi(7.4)^2=172$ m$^2$ ($172.03\ldots$) [A1] [1 mark] (b) true area $=\pi(7.5)^2=176.71\ldots$ [M1] $\dfrac{|172.03-176.71|}{176.71}\times100=2.65\%$ ($2.6489\ldots$) [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\dfrac{|7.4-7.5|}{7.5}\times100=1.33\%$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) the area is proportional to $r^{2}$ [R1] so a small relative error in $r$ is roughly doubled in $r^{2}$ ($2.65\approx2\times1.33$) [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Percentage error is $\dfrac{|v_A-v_E|}{|v_E|}\times100$, always measured relative to the exact value. Use unrounded intermediate values so your final percentage is accurate.

subtopic: Two linear equations from ticket prices
statement: At a school concert, 3 adult tickets and 2 child tickets cost \$47 in total. 2 adult tickets and 5 child tickets cost \$68 in total. Let an adult ticket cost \$$a$ and a child ticket cost \$$c$. (a) Write down two equations in $a$ and $c$. [2] (b) Solve the equations to find $a$ and $c$. [3] (c) Find the cost of 4 adult tickets and 3 child tickets. [1]
tips: Multiply the equations so that one variable has equal coefficients, then subtract. Check your answers by substituting into the second original equation.

subtopic: Inverse matrix and solving matrix equations
statement: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix} 4 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find $\det A$. [1] (b) Find $A^{-1}$. [2] (c) Hence solve $A\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 10 \\ 6 \end{pmatrix}$. [2] (d) The matrix $B$ satisfies $AB=\begin{pmatrix} 4 & 7 \\ 2 & 4 \end{pmatrix}$. Find $B$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $4(2)-3(2)=2$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $A^{-1}=\dfrac12\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -3 \\ -2 & 4 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (c) $\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix}=A^{-1}\begin{pmatrix} 10 \\ 6 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $x=1,\ y=2$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $B=A^{-1}\begin{pmatrix} 4 & 7 \\ 2 & 4 \end{pmatrix}$ (multiplying on the left) [M1] $=\dfrac12\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Matrix multiplication is not commutative: from $AB=C$ you get $B=A^{-1}C$, not $CA^{-1}$. Check by multiplying $A$ by your answer.

subtopic: Three-feed mixture using a matrix solver
statement: A gardener mixes three feeds $A$, $B$ and $C$. Each kilogram of feed $A$ contains 2 units of nitrogen, 1 unit of phosphorus and 3 units of potassium. Feed $B$ contains 3, 2 and 1 units per kilogram and feed $C$ contains 1, 4 and 2 units per kilogram, in the same order. The mixture must contain exactly 22 units of nitrogen, 30 units of phosphorus and 25 units of potassium. Let $x$, $y$ and $z$ be the masses in kilograms of feeds $A$, $B$ and $C$. (a) Write down three equations in $x$, $y$ and $z$. [2] (b) Find the values of $x$, $y$ and $z$. [2] (c) Feeds $A$, $B$ and $C$ cost \$1.20, \$0.80 and \$1.50 per kilogram respectively. Find the cost of the mixture. [2]
markscheme: (a) $2x+3y+z=22$ [A1] $x+2y+4z=30$ and $3x+y+2z=25$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) enter the coefficient matrix and use the inverse or system solver [M1] $x=4,\ y=3,\ z=5$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $1.20(4)+0.80(3)+1.50(5)$ [M1] $=\$14.70$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Each row of the system corresponds to one nutrient. Check the solution by substituting into all three equations.

subtopic: Two-state Markov chain with exact steady state
statement: A streaming service has Basic and Premium subscribers. Each month, $20\%$ of Basic subscribers upgrade to Premium and $30\%$ of Premium subscribers downgrade to Basic. Everyone else stays on the same plan. Let $T$ be the transition matrix, with the state vector written as (Basic, Premium). (a) Write down $T$. [2] (b) Initially there are 1000 subscribers, all on Basic. Find the number of subscribers on each plan after two months. [3] (c) Find the eigenvalues of $T$. [3] (d) Find the long-term number of Basic subscribers. [3]
markscheme: (a) $T=\begin{pmatrix} 0.8 & 0.3 \\ 0.2 & 0.7 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1][A1] (A1 for each correct column) [2 marks] (b) after one month $\begin{pmatrix} 800 \\ 200 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] after two months $T\begin{pmatrix} 800 \\ 200 \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 700 \\ 300 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] 700 Basic and 300 Premium [A1] [3 marks] (c) $(0.8-\lambda)(0.7-\lambda)-0.06=0$ [M1] $\lambda^{2}-1.5\lambda+0.5=0$ [A1] $\lambda=1$ or $\lambda=0.5$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) eigenvector for $\lambda=1$: $-0.2x+0.3y=0$, so $y=\dfrac23x$ [M1] $x+y=1$ gives $x=0.6$ [A1] long-term Basic $=600$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The columns of a transition matrix sum to $1$, so $1$ is always an eigenvalue. The steady state is the eigenvector for $\lambda=1$ scaled so its entries sum to the total population.

subtopic: Successive percentage changes and reverse percentages
statement: In a sale, the price of a jacket is reduced by $20\%$, and then the sale price is reduced by a further $15\%$. The final price is \$68. (a) Find the original price of the jacket. [3] (b) Find the overall percentage reduction from the original price to the final price. [2] (c) The shop wants to raise the final price back to the original price. Find the percentage increase needed, giving your answer as an exact fraction. [2]
markscheme: (a) $0.8\times0.85\times P=68$ [M1] $0.68P=68$ [A1] $P=\$100$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) final price is $68\%$ of the original [M1] reduction $=32\%$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\dfrac{100-68}{68}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{8}{17}$, that is $\dfrac{800}{17}\%$ ($\approx47.1\%$) [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Successive percentage changes multiply, they do not add. A percentage increase is always measured from the starting price of that step, here the \$68.

subtopic: Expressing logarithms in terms of given logarithms
statement: Let $p=\log_a 2$ and $q=\log_a 3$, where $a>1$. (a) Express $\log_a 18$ in terms of $p$ and $q$. [2] (b) Express $\log_a\left(\dfrac{4}{27}\right)$ in terms of $p$ and $q$. [2] (c) Find the value of $x$ such that $\log_a x=\dfrac{1}{2}(p+q)$, giving your answer as a surd. [2]
markscheme: (a) $18=2\times3^{2}$ [M1]; $\log_a 18=p+2q$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\log_a4-\log_a27$ [M1]; $=2p-3q$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\log_a x=\tfrac12\log_a 6$ [M1]; $x=\sqrt6$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Factorize the argument into powers of $2$ and $3$, then use $\log(mn)=\log m+\log n$ and $\log m^k=k\log m$.

subtopic: Upper bounds and percentage error of a tank volume
statement: The length, width and height of a rectangular tank are measured as $2.4$ m, $1.8$ m and $1.5$ m, each correct to one decimal place. (a) Calculate the volume of the tank using these measured values. [1] (b) Find the greatest possible volume of the tank, correct to three significant figures. [2] (c) Suppose the true volume is the greatest possible volume. Find the percentage error in the volume calculated in part (a). Give your answer to three significant figures. [2] (d) Find the least possible volume of the tank, correct to three significant figures. [1]
tips: A measurement given to one decimal place can be up to $0.05$ away from the true value, so use $\pm0.05$ on each dimension. Percentage error is measured relative to the true value.

subtopic: Phasor addition of alternating currents
statement: Two alternating currents in a circuit, in amperes, are modeled at time $t$ seconds by $I_1=6\cos(\omega t)$ and $I_2=4\cos\!\left(\omega t-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$, where $\omega=120\pi$. Each current is the real part of $z\,e^{i\omega t}$ for a complex number $z$. (a) Write down the complex numbers $z_1$ and $z_2$ for $I_1$ and $I_2$, giving $z_2$ in the form $a+bi$. [2] (b) The total current $I_1+I_2$ is the real part of $(z_1+z_2)e^{i\omega t}$. Find the modulus and the argument of $z_1+z_2$, to three significant figures. [3] (c) Hence find the maximum value of the total current and the smallest positive value of $t$ at which it occurs. Give $t$ to three significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) $z_1=6$ [A1] $z_2=4e^{-i\pi/3}=2-2\sqrt3\,i$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $z_1+z_2=8-2\sqrt3\,i$ [M1] modulus $=\sqrt{76}=8.72$ [A1] argument $=-0.409$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $I_1+I_2=8.72\cos(\omega t-0.409)$, so the maximum current is $8.72$ A [A1] maximum when $120\pi t-0.4086=0$ [M1] $t=0.00108$ s [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Writing each current as the real part of $z e^{i\omega t}$ turns the sum of two sinusoids into addition of complex numbers. Set the phase equal to $0$ to find where the cosine is maximal.

subtopic: Currency exchange with commission
statement: A bank exchanges currency at a rate of 1 euro $=1.0845$ US dollars (USD), charging a commission of $2.5\%$ on every transaction (deducted from the amount received). (a) Mia exchanges 2500 USD into euros. Find the amount of euros she receives, correct to the nearest cent. [3] (b) She immediately exchanges all her euros back into USD with the same rate and commission. Find how much she has, and her percentage loss. [4] (c) Explain why a customer who converts currency back and forth with the same rate always loses money. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{2500}{1.0845}=2305.21$ [M1][A1]; after commission $\times0.975=2247.58$ euros [A1] [3 marks] (b) $(2247.58)\times1.0845\times0.975$ [M1][A1]; $=\$2376.56$ [A1]; loss $=4.94\%$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) Each conversion multiplies the amount by $0.975$, a factor less than $1$, and the exchange rates cancel [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Apply the commission after the conversion each time, so two transactions lose about $5\%$ in total.

subtopic: Compound interest and effective annual rate
statement: Kavya invests \$15\,000 in an account that pays a nominal annual interest rate of $3.6\%$, compounded monthly. (a) Find the value of the investment after 8 years. Give your answer to the nearest cent. [2] (b) Find the number of complete months after which the value of the investment first exceeds \$25\,000. [3] (c) Find the effective annual interest rate, as a percentage correct to three significant figures. [2]
tips: With a TVM solver use $I\%=3.6$, $P/Y=C/Y=12$ and $N=96$. For part (b) the answer must be a whole number of months, so round up.

subtopic: Standard form with a data transfer
statement: A video file has size $4.8\times10^{9}$ bytes. It is downloaded at a constant rate of $2.4\times10^{6}$ bytes per second. (a) Find the time the download takes, in seconds. Give your answer in the form $a\times10^{k}$ where $1\le a<10$ and $k\in\mathbb Z$. [2] (b) Express this time in minutes, correct to the nearest minute. [2] (c) The rate is increased by $25\%$. Find the new download time in seconds. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{4.8\times10^{9}}{2.4\times10^{6}}$ [M1]; $2\times10^{3}$ seconds [A1] [2 marks] (b) $2000\div60$ [M1]; $33$ minutes [A1] [2 marks] (c) New rate $=3.0\times10^{6}$ [M1]; time $=1.6\times10^{3}$ seconds [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Divide the coefficients and subtract the exponents. A $25\%$ increase multiplies the rate by $1.25$.

subtopic: Rounding errors in a chain of calculations
statement: The radius of a circular pond is $r=3.847$ m. A student calculates the area $A=\pi r^{2}$ and the circumference $C=2\pi r$. (a) Find $A$ and $C$ using the exact value of $r$. Give both answers to four significant figures. [2] (b) The student first rounds $r$ to two significant figures, $3.8$ m, and recalculates $A$. Find the percentage error in $A$ caused by this rounding, to two significant figures. [3] (c) Explain why the percentage error in $A$ is roughly twice the percentage error in $r$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $A=46.49$ m$^2$ [A1]; $C=24.17$ m [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\pi(3.8)^2=45.365$ [A1]; $\dfrac{|45.365-46.494|}{46.494}\times100$ [M1]; $2.4\%$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $A\propto r^{2}$ [R1]; so a small relative change in $r$ produces about double the relative change in $A$ [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Keep full calculator values during the calculation and round only at the end.

subtopic: Successive percentage changes
statement: The price of a laptop is \$900. It is reduced by $15\%$ in a sale, and later increased by $12\%$. (a) Find the final price. [2] (b) Find the overall percentage change in the price. [2] (c) The price must be increased by a certain percentage from the sale price to return to \$900. Find this percentage. [3]
tips: Percentage changes multiply: a reduction of $15\%$ is a factor of $0.85$, and they are not reversible by the same percentage.

subtopic: Polar form products and powers
statement: Let $z=1+i\sqrt3$ and $w=-1+i$. (a) Write $z$ and $w$ in the form $r(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)$, where $r>0$ and $-\pi<\theta\le\pi$. [4] (b) Hence find $zw$ in the form $r(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)$, where $-\pi<\theta\le\pi$. [3] (c) Find $z^{6}$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $|z|=2$ [A1] $\arg z=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ [A1] $|w|=\sqrt2$ [A1] $\arg w=\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) moduli multiply, arguments add: $2\sqrt2$ and $\dfrac{\pi}{3}+\dfrac{3\pi}{4}=\dfrac{13\pi}{12}$ [M1][A1] adjust to the required range: $2\sqrt2\left(\cos\!\left(-\dfrac{11\pi}{12}\right)+i\sin\!\left(-\dfrac{11\pi}{12}\right)\right)$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $z^{6}=2^{6}\left(\cos2\pi+i\sin2\pi\right)$ [M1] $=64$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Sketch the point to choose the correct quadrant for the argument. After adding arguments, subtract $2\pi$ if the result is outside the stated range.

subtopic: Arithmetic with Cartesian complex numbers
statement: Let $z=3+4i$ and $w=1-2i$. (a) Find $zw$, giving your answer in the form $a+bi$. [2] (b) Find $\dfrac{z}{w}$, giving your answer in the form $a+bi$. [3] (c) Find the real numbers $a$ and $b$ such that $(a+bi)(2-i)=5+5i$. [3]
tips: To divide complex numbers multiply by the conjugate of the denominator. To find unknown real and imaginary parts, expand and equate real and imaginary parts.

subtopic: Laws of logarithms and logarithmic equations
statement: (a) Let $\log_2 x=a$ and $\log_2 y=b$. Express $\log_2\!\left(\dfrac{x^{3}\sqrt{y}}{8}\right)$ in terms of $a$ and $b$. [3] (b) Solve $\log_3 x+\log_3(x-6)=3$. [4] (c) Solve $5^{2x-1}=7$, giving your answer in exact form in terms of natural logarithms. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\log_2 x^{3}+\log_2\sqrt{y}-\log_2 8$ [M1] $3a+\tfrac12 b$ [A1] $-3$, so $3a+\tfrac12 b-3$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\log_3\big(x(x-6)\big)=3$ [M1] $x^{2}-6x-27=0$ [A1] $x=9$ or $x=-3$ [A1] reject $x=-3$ because $\log_3(-3)$ is undefined, so $x=9$ [R1] [4 marks] (c) $2x-1=\dfrac{\ln7}{\ln5}$ [M1] $x=\dfrac12\left(1+\dfrac{\ln7}{\ln5}\right)$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: After combining logarithms, always check each solution against the domain of the original equation. To solve $a^{u}=b$ take logarithms of both sides.

subtopic: Standard form and percentage error
statement: A rectangular solar panel measures $1.65$ m by $0.992$ m. (a) Calculate the exact area of one panel, in $\text{m}^2$. [1] (b) Write down your answer to part (a) correct to three significant figures. [1] (c) A solar farm contains $2.4\times10^{5}$ of these panels. Find the total area of the panels in $\text{km}^2$, giving your answer in the form $a\times10^{k}$, where $1\le a<10$ and $k\in\mathbb{Z}$. [2] (d) A drone survey estimates the total panel area as $0.4\ \text{km}^2$. Find the percentage error in this estimate. [2]
tips: Remember $1\ \text{km}^2=10^6\ \text{m}^2$, not $10^3$. In percentage error the exact value always goes in the denominator; use the unrounded value from earlier parts.

subtopic: Standard form with light-years
statement: Light travels at $3.00\times10^{8}$ m s$^{-1}$. One year is $3.15\times10^{7}$ seconds. A light-year is the distance light travels in one year. Give all answers in the form $a\times10^{k}$ where $1\le a<10$ and $k\in\mathbb Z$. (a) Find the length of one light-year in kilometers. [3] (b) A star is $4.2$ light-years from Earth. Find this distance in kilometers. [2] (c) A probe travels at $2.1\times10^{1}$ km s$^{-1}$. Use the unrounded distance from part (b) to find the time, in years, it takes to reach the star. [3]
markscheme: (a) $3.00\times10^{8}\times3.15\times10^{7}=9.45\times10^{15}$ m [M1][A1]; $9.45\times10^{12}$ km [A1] [3 marks] (b) $4.2\times9.45\times10^{12}$ [M1]; $3.969\times10^{13}$ km, which is $3.97\times10^{13}$ km to 3 significant figures [A1] [2 marks] (c) time in seconds $=\dfrac{3.969\times10^{13}}{21}=1.89\times10^{12}$ s [M1][A1]; $\dfrac{1.89\times10^{12}}{3.15\times10^{7}}=6.0\times10^{4}$ years [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Convert meters to kilometers by dividing by $10^{3}$. Divide coefficients and subtract exponents.

subtopic: Logarithmic scale for earthquake energy
statement: The energy $E$ joules released by an earthquake of magnitude $M$ satisfies $\log_{10}E=4.8+1.5M$. (a) Find the energy released by an earthquake of magnitude $6.3$. Give your answer in the form $a\times10^{k}$, where $1\le a<10$ and $k\in\mathbb{Z}$. [2] (b) Show that an earthquake of magnitude $7.1$ releases about $15.8$ times as much energy as one of magnitude $6.3$. [3] (c) An earthquake releases $1000$ times as much energy as one of magnitude $6.3$. Find its magnitude. [2]
tips: Subtracting two logarithms gives the logarithm of a ratio, so a change in the exponent corresponds to a multiplication of the energy. Multiplying energy by $10^{3}$ adds $3$ to $\log_{10}E$.

subtopic: Bounds and accuracy of a computed area
statement: A rectangular garden has length $14.6$ m and width $8.3$ m, each measured correct to the nearest $0.1$ m. (a) Find the lower bound and upper bound for the perimeter of the garden. [2] (b) Find the lower bound and upper bound for the area of the garden. [2] (c) Hence write down the area of the garden to the greatest degree of accuracy that is justified by the bounds, giving a reason. [2]
markscheme: (a) length in $[14.55,14.65)$, width in $[8.25,8.35)$ [M1] lower bound $2(14.55+8.25)=45.6$ m, upper bound $2(14.65+8.35)=46.0$ m [A1] [2 marks] (b) lower bound $14.55\times8.25=120.0375$ [A1] upper bound $14.65\times8.35=122.3275$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) to two significant figures both bounds round to $120$ m$^2$ [M1] to three significant figures they differ ($120$ and $122$), so the area is $120$ m$^2$ (2 s.f.) [A1] [2 marks]
tips: For a sum use the lower bounds together or the upper bounds together; for a product of positive numbers do the same. An answer is only reliable to the number of significant figures on which both bounds agree.

subtopic: Cube roots of a negative real number
statement: (a) Solve the equation $z^{3}=-8$, giving the three roots in the form $a+bi$. [5] (b) Write down the sum of the three roots. [1] (c) In the complex plane, the three roots are the vertices of a triangle. Find the exact area of this triangle. [3]
markscheme: (a) $-8=8(\cos\pi+i\sin\pi)$ [M1] $z=2\left(\cos\dfrac{\pi+2k\pi}{3}+i\sin\dfrac{\pi+2k\pi}{3}\right)$ [M1] $z=1+\sqrt3\,i$ [A1] $z=-2$ [A1] $z=1-\sqrt3\,i$ [A1] [5 marks] (b) $0$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) base between $1\pm\sqrt3 i$ has length $2\sqrt3$ [A1] perpendicular height from $-2$ to the line $x=1$ is $3$ [A1] area $=\dfrac12(2\sqrt3)(3)=3\sqrt3$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Write the right-hand side in polar form and add multiples of $2\pi$ to the argument before dividing by $3$. The $n$ roots of $z^{n}=w$ are equally spaced on a circle, which makes areas and symmetry easy to see.

subtopic: Three-state Markov chain for bike-share stations
statement: A city has three bike-share stations $A$, $B$ and $C$. Each night every bike is returned to a station, and the stations of bikes after one day are described by the transition matrix $T=\begin{pmatrix} 0.7 & 0.2 & 0.1 \\ 0.2 & 0.6 & 0.3 \\ 0.1 & 0.2 & 0.6 \end{pmatrix}$, where the columns give the probabilities of moving from $A$, $B$ and $C$ respectively. At the start of Monday there are 500 bikes at $A$, 300 at $B$ and 200 at $C$. (a) Interpret the entry $0.3$ in $T$. [1] (b) Find the expected number of bikes at each station after two days. [3] (c) Find the expected long-term number of bikes at each station, giving answers to one decimal place. [3] (d) Find the smallest number of days after which the expected number of bikes at $A$ is below $360$. [3] (e) State one reason why the model may not be realistic. [1]
markscheme: (a) the probability that a bike at $C$ is at $B$ after one day is $0.3$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $T^{2}\begin{pmatrix} 500 \\ 300 \\ 200 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $\begin{pmatrix} 392 \\ 359 \\ 249 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1][A1] (A: 392, B: 359, C: 249) [3 marks] (c) solve $T\mathbf{s}=\mathbf{s}$ with $s_A+s_B+s_C=1000$, or compute a high power of $T$ [M1] proportions $\dfrac{10}{29},\dfrac{11}{29},\dfrac{8}{29}$ [A1] $344.8,\ 379.3,\ 275.9$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) number at $A$ after $n$ days: $371.1$ ($n=3$), $359.51$ ($n=4$) [M1][A1] smallest $n=4$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) for example: bike movements may depend on the day of the week; or bikes are removed for repair; the probabilities are unlikely to be constant [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Check that every column of $T$ sums to $1$ before multiplying, and apply $T$ to a column vector on the right. For the long-term distribution use the eigenvalue $1$ eigenvector, scaled to the total of $1000$ bikes.

subtopic: Reverse percentages and successive changes
statement: A jacket is reduced by $15\%$ in a sale. A sales tax of $8\%$ is then added to the sale price, and the jacket costs $229.50$ dollars in total. (a) Find the original price of the jacket, before the sale. [3] (b) Find the single percentage change that is equivalent to the reduction followed by the tax. [2] (c) Another shop raises a price by $20\%$ and later lowers the new price by $20\%$. Find the overall percentage change in the price. [2]
markscheme: (a) Multiplier $0.85\times1.08=0.918$ [M1]; $\dfrac{229.50}{0.918}$ [M1]; original price $=250$ dollars [A1] [3 marks] (b) $0.918-1=-0.082$ [M1]; a decrease of $8.2\%$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $1.2\times0.8=0.96$ [M1]; an overall decrease of $4\%$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Percentage changes multiply; they do not add. To reverse one, divide by the multiplier.

subtopic: Currency exchange with commission
statement: A traveler exchanges $1500$ US dollars (USD) into euros (EUR) at a rate of $1$ USD $=0.9210$ EUR. A commission of $2\%$ is then deducted from the euros received. Round every money value to the nearest cent (two decimal places) and use the rounded value in later parts. (a) Find the amount in EUR that the traveler receives after the commission. [2] (b) The traveler spends $1050$ EUR and converts the rest back to USD at a rate of $1$ EUR $=1.0750$ USD with no commission. Find the amount in USD received. [3] (c) A second booth offers $1$ USD $=0.9250$ EUR with a commission of $3.5\%$ on the euros received. Find, to the nearest cent, how many more euros the first booth gives for the original $1500$ USD. [3]
tips: Apply the commission as a multiplier ($1-0.02$). Round only at the stage the question tells you to.

subtopic: Decibels and logarithms
statement: The sound level $L$, in decibels (dB), of a sound of intensity $I$ watts per square meter is given by $L=10\log_{10}\!\left(\dfrac{I}{10^{-12}}\right)$. (a) A conversation has intensity $I=10^{-5}$ W m$^{-2}$. Find its sound level. [2] (b) A rock concert has a sound level of $110$ dB. Find its intensity $I$ in W m$^{-2}$. [3] (c) The level of a sound increases by $20$ dB. Find the factor by which its intensity is multiplied. [2]
markscheme: (a) $L=10\log_{10}\!\left(10^{7}\right)$ [M1]; $L=70$ dB [A1] [2 marks] (b) $110=10\log_{10}\!\left(\dfrac{I}{10^{-12}}\right)\Rightarrow\log_{10}\!\left(\dfrac{I}{10^{-12}}\right)=11$ [M1]; $\dfrac{I}{10^{-12}}=10^{11}$ [A1]; $I=10^{-1}=0.1$ W m$^{-2}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Increase of $20$ dB means $\log_{10}\!\left(\dfrac{I_2}{I_1}\right)=2$ [M1]; the intensity is multiplied by $100$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Undo $\log_{10}$ by raising $10$ to both sides. A difference of $10$ dB multiplies the intensity by $10$.

subtopic: Currency conversion with commission
statement: Mia changes $850$ British pounds (GBP) into Canadian dollars (CAD) at an exchange rate of $1$ GBP $=1.7236$ CAD. The bank charges a commission of $2\%$ of the amount of CAD, which is deducted from the amount she receives. (a) Find the amount of CAD Mia receives. [2] (b) Mia spends $1020$ CAD during her trip and then changes the remaining CAD back into GBP at a rate of $1$ GBP $=1.7612$ CAD. The bank deducts a commission of $1.5\%$ from the GBP amount. Find the amount of GBP Mia receives, correct to two decimal places. [3] (c) The remaining CAD would have been worth $\dfrac{\text{remaining CAD}}{1.7236}$ GBP using the original exchange rate and no commission. Find the percentage by which the amount Mia actually receives is less than this value. [2]
tips: Convert in the correct direction (multiply or divide by the rate) and apply the commission to the amount received. Keep full calculator precision between steps and round only at the end.

subtopic: Laws of exponents and logarithms
statement: (a) Simplify $\left(27a^{6}b^{-3}\right)^{\frac23}$, giving your answer in the form $pa^{q}b^{r}$. [2] (b) Solve the equation $9^{x}=27^{x-1}$. [2] (c) Evaluate $\log_2 40-\log_2 5+\log_3\dfrac19$. [2]
tips: Write numbers as powers of a common base before comparing exponents. In (c) combine the first two logarithms with $\log a-\log b=\log\frac ab$ before evaluating.

subtopic: Exponential equation reducing to a quadratic
statement: Consider the equation $e^{2x}-5e^{x}+6=0$. (a) Show that the equation can be written as a quadratic in $u=e^{x}$. [1] (b) Hence find the exact solutions for $x$. [4]
tips: Substitute $u=e^{x}$; remember $u>0$, then take natural logarithms of each positive root.

subtopic: Bounds on a calculated speed
statement: A sprinter runs a distance of $100$ m, measured to the nearest meter, in a time of $12.4$ s, measured to the nearest $0.1$ s. The average speed is distance divided by time. (a) Write down the lower and upper bounds for the distance and for the time. [2] (b) Find the greatest possible value of the average speed, correct to three significant figures. [2] (c) Find the least possible value of the average speed, correct to three significant figures. [2]
tips: For a quotient, the greatest value uses the largest numerator and the smallest denominator.

subtopic: Repeated root, sign of a cubic and number of solutions
statement: Let $p(x)=x^3-3x^2-9x+27$, for $x\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Show that $p(x)=(x-3)^2(x+3)$. [3] (b) Solve the inequality $p(x)\le0$. [3] (c) Find the values of $k$ for which the equation $p(x)=k$ has exactly two distinct real solutions. [3]
markscheme: (a) $p(3)=27-27-27+27=0$, or grouping: $x^2(x-3)-9(x-3)$ [M1] $=(x-3)(x^2-9)$ [A1] $=(x-3)(x-3)(x+3)=(x-3)^2(x+3)$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Critical values $x=-3$ and $x=3$ [A1] $(x-3)^2\ge0$, so the sign of $p$ is that of $(x+3)$ except at $x=3$ where $p=0$ [M1] $x\le-3$ or $x=3$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $p'(x)=3x^2-6x-9=3(x-3)(x+1)$ [M1] local maximum $(-1,\,32)$ and local minimum $(3,\,0)$ [A1] $k=0$ or $k=32$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A repeated factor means the graph touches the axis without crossing, so the sign of the polynomial does not change there but the value zero still satisfies $\le0$. Exactly two solutions occurs when the horizontal line touches one turning point.

subtopic: Even and odd polynomial functions
statement: Let $P(x)=x^5-3x^3+x$. (a) Show that $P$ is an odd function. [2] (b) Show that $P(x)^2$ is an even function. [2] (c) Show that $R(x)=P(x)+1$ is neither even nor odd. [2]
tips: A polynomial is odd if it contains only odd powers of $x$, and even if it contains only even powers.

subtopic: Complex roots of a real quartic and sum of squares of roots
statement: The polynomial $P(z)=z^4-6z^3+az^2+bz+c$, where $a,b,c\in\mathbb{R}$, has two roots $2+i$ and $1+2i$. (a) Write down the other two roots of $P(z)=0$. [1] (b) Find the values of $a$, $b$ and $c$. [4] (c) Without finding the roots individually, use the coefficients of $P(z)$ to find the sum of the squares of the four roots. [3]
markscheme: (a) $2-i$ and $1-2i$ (complex roots of a real polynomial occur in conjugate pairs) [A1] [1 mark] (b) $(z-(2+i))(z-(2-i))=z^2-4z+5$ [M1] other factor $z^2-2z+5$ [A1] $P(z)=(z^2-4z+5)(z^2-2z+5)$ [M1] expanding: $z^4-6z^3+18z^2-30z+25$, so $a=18$, $b=-30$, $c=25$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) sum of squares $=(\text{sum of roots})^2-2(\text{sum of products in pairs})$ [M1] $=6^2-2a$ [A1] $=36-36=0$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Real coefficients force complex roots to come in conjugate pairs, so each pair gives a real quadratic factor $z^2-2\,\mathrm{Re}(w)\,z+|w|^2$. For sums of squares of roots, use $\sum\alpha^2=(\sum\alpha)^2-2\sum\alpha\beta$.

subtopic: Polynomial division and factorization
statement: Let $p(x)=x^4-3x^3-7x^2+27x-18$. (a) Show that $x=2$ and $x=3$ are roots of $p(x)=0$. [2] (b) Hence factorize $p(x)$ completely. [3] (c) Solve $p(x)>0$. [3]
tips: After finding two roots, divide by the product of the corresponding linear factors, then factorize the quotient.

subtopic: Power sums of roots of a quadratic by recurrence
statement: The roots of the equation $x^2-4x+1=0$ are $\alpha$ and $\beta$. Let $s_n=\alpha^n+\beta^n$ for $n\in\mathbb{N}$, with $s_0=2$. (a) Show that $s_{n+2}=4s_{n+1}-s_n$ for $n\geq0$. [3] (b) Find $s_0$, $s_1$ and hence find $s_4$. [3] (c) Given that the roots of the equation are $2+\sqrt3$ and $2-\sqrt3$, write down the value of $(2+\sqrt3)^4+(2-\sqrt3)^4$. [1] (d) Show that $(2+\sqrt3)^4$ differs from an integer by less than $0.01$. [3]
markscheme: (a) Since $\alpha^2=4\alpha-1$, multiply by $\alpha^n$: $\alpha^{n+2}=4\alpha^{n+1}-\alpha^n$ [M1] Similarly $\beta^{n+2}=4\beta^{n+1}-\beta^n$ [M1] Adding gives $s_{n+2}=4s_{n+1}-s_n$ [A1] [AG] [3 marks] (b) $s_0=2$, $s_1=\alpha+\beta=4$ [A1] $s_2=14$, $s_3=52$ using the recurrence [M1] $s_4=4(52)-14=194$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $(2+\sqrt3)^4+(2-\sqrt3)^4=s_4=194$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) $(2+\sqrt3)^4=194-(2-\sqrt3)^4$ [M1] $\sqrt3>1.7$ so $0<2-\sqrt3<0.3$ [A1] Hence $(2-\sqrt3)^4<0.3^4=0.0081<0.01$, so $(2+\sqrt3)^4$ is within $0.01$ of $194$ [R1] [3 marks]
tips: The recurrence comes from each root satisfying the quadratic itself. In part (d), you do not need a calculator: bound $2-\sqrt3$ using an inequality for $\sqrt3$.

subtopic: Roots of a quintic with a calculator
statement: Consider $p(x)=x^5-4x^4-3x^3+14x^2-8x+5$. (a) Use your calculator to find all the real roots of $p(x)=0$ to three significant figures. [2] (b) State the sum of all five roots (real and complex) and verify it using the roots found by the solver. [3]
markscheme: (a) polynomial solver or graph [M1] $x=3.98$, $x=-2.04$, $x=1.60$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) sum of roots $=4$ [A1] sum of the real parts of all five roots $=4.00$ [M1][A1] [3 marks]
tips: A polynomial solver returns complex roots as well; Vieta's formula gives an independent check of the sum.

subtopic: Finding an even quartic from described features, turning points and number of solutions
statement: The graph of the quartic polynomial $y=f(x)$ is symmetric about the $y$-axis and meets the $x$-axis at exactly two points, $(-3,0)$ and $(3,0)$. The graph also passes through the points $(0,-18)$ and $(1,-32)$. It is given that $f(x)=a(x^2-9)(x^2+c)$, where $a,c\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Find the values of $a$ and $c$. [4] (b) Find the coordinates of the stationary points of the graph of $f$ and determine their nature. [4] (c) Find the values of $k$ for which the equation $f(x)=k$ has exactly two distinct real solutions. [3]
markscheme: (a) $f(0)=-9ac=-18$, so $ac=2$ [M1] [A1] $f(1)=-8a(1+c)=-32$, so $a(1+c)=4$ [M1] $a+ac=4$, so $a=2$ and $c=1$ [A1] (so $f(x)=2x^4-16x^2-18$) [4 marks] (b) $f'(x)=8x^3-32x$ [A1] $=8x(x-2)(x+2)=0$, so $x=0,\ \pm2$ [A1] $f(0)=-18$ and $f(\pm 2)=-50$, giving $(0,-18)$, $(2,-50)$, $(-2,-50)$ [A1] $f''(x)=24x^2-32$: $f''(0)=-32<0$ so a local maximum at $(0,-18)$; $f''(\pm 2)=64>0$ so local minima at $(\pm2,-50)$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) consider the horizontal line $y=k$ against the turning points [M1] $k>-18$ gives two solutions [A1] $k=-50$ gives two solutions (the two minima) [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Translate each described feature into an equation in the unknown constants, using the factorized form to keep the algebra short. When counting solutions of $f(x)=k$, check the line against every turning-point height, including the special cases where it touches the curve.

subtopic: Reciprocal quartic solved with the substitution y = x + 1/x
statement: Consider the quartic equation $x^4-5x^3+8x^2-5x+1=0$. (a) Show that, with $y=x+\dfrac1x$, the equation can be written as $y^2-5y+6=0$. [4] (b) Hence find all four roots of the quartic equation, giving exact values. [4] (c) Hence solve the inequality $x^4-5x^3+8x^2-5x+1<0$. [2]
markscheme: (a) divide by $x^2$ (as $x=0$ is not a root): $x^2-5x+8-\dfrac5x+\dfrac1{x^2}=0$ [M1] $x^2+\dfrac1{x^2}=\left(x+\dfrac1x\right)^2-2=y^2-2$ [M1][A1] $y^2-2-5y+8=0$ so $y^2-5y+6=0$ [AG] [A1] [4 marks] (b) $(y-2)(y-3)=0$ so $y=2$ or $y=3$ [A1] $x+\dfrac1x=2$ gives $(x-1)^2=0$ so $x=1$ (repeated) [M1][A1] $x+\dfrac1x=3$ gives $x^2-3x+1=0$ so $x=\dfrac{3\pm\sqrt5}2$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) the quartic is $(x-1)^2\left(x^2-3x+1\right)$ [M1] it is negative when $\dfrac{3-\sqrt5}2<x<\dfrac{3+\sqrt5}2$ with $x\ne1$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The coefficients read the same forwards and backwards, so divide by $x^2$ and group the terms in $x^2+\dfrac1{x^2}$ and $x+\dfrac1x$. In part (c), note that the repeated root at $x=1$ does not change the sign of the quartic.

subtopic: Factor theorem, full factorization and cubic inequality
statement: Let $p(x)=2x^3+kx^2-13x+6$, where $k\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Given that $(x+3)$ is a factor of $p(x)$, find the value of $k$. [2] (b) Factorize $p(x)$ completely. [3] (c) Hence solve $p(x)>0$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $p(-3)=0$: $-54+9k+39+6=0$ [M1] $9k-9=0$, so $k=1$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $p(x)=2x^3+x^2-13x+6=(x+3)(2x^2-5x+2)$ [M1] [A1] $=(x+3)(2x-1)(x-2)$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) roots $-3,\ \dfrac12,\ 2$ and positive leading coefficient: sign table or sketch [M1] $-3<x<\dfrac12$ [A1] $x>2$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: After finding one factor, divide to get a quadratic and factorize it fully. For a polynomial inequality, a quick sketch (positive cubic: starts low, ends high) tells you the sign on each interval.

subtopic: Remainder on division by x squared plus one
statement: The polynomial $P(x)=x^{2023}+x^{10}+3$ is divided by $x^2+1$, with remainder $ax+b$, where $a,b\in\mathbb R$. (a) Explain why $P(\mathrm i)=a\mathrm i+b$. [2] (b) Find the remainder. [4]
markscheme: (a) $P(x)=(x^2+1)Q(x)+ax+b$ [M1] $\mathrm i^2+1=0$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\mathrm i^{2023}=\mathrm i^3=-\mathrm i$ since $2023=4\times505+3$ [M1][A1] $\mathrm i^{10}=-1$ so $P(\mathrm i)=-\mathrm i-1+3=2-\mathrm i$ [A1] $a=-1$, $b=2$, remainder $-x+2$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: The divisor vanishes at $x=\mathrm i$, so the remainder can be found from $P(\mathrm i)$. Reduce powers of $\mathrm i$ using their period 4.

subtopic: Complex roots of a real cubic
statement: The cubic equation $z^3-5z^2+pz-q=0$, where $p,q\in\mathbb{R}$, has a root $z=1+2i$. (a) Write down a second root of the equation, with a reason. [1] (b) Find the third root. [2] (c) Find the values of $p$ and $q$. [3] (d) Write the cubic polynomial as a product of three linear factors. [1]
markscheme: (a) $1-2i$, because the non-real roots of a polynomial with real coefficients occur in conjugate pairs [A1] [1 mark] (b) Sum of roots $=5$: $(1+2i)+(1-2i)+r=5$ [M1] $r=3$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $p=(1+2i)(1-2i)+3(1+2i)+3(1-2i)$ [M1] $=5+6=11$ [A1] $q=3(1+2i)(1-2i)=15$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $(z-3)(z-1-2i)(z-1+2i)$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Non-real roots of real-coefficient polynomials always come in conjugate pairs, which gives the third root from the sum of the roots. Use $z^3-(\text{sum})z^2+(\text{pair sums})z-(\text{product})$ to match coefficients.

subtopic: Roots in arithmetic progression
statement: The roots of $x^3-12x^2+kx-28=0$ are in arithmetic progression. (a) Write the roots as $a-d$, $a$ and $a+d$ and show that $a=4$. [2] (b) Use the product of the roots to find $d^2$, and hence find the roots. [3] (c) Find $k$. [2]
markscheme: (a) sum of roots $=3a=12$ [M1] $a=4$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $a\left(a^2-d^2\right)=28$ [M1] $4\left(16-d^2\right)=28$, $d^2=9$ [A1] roots $1,4,7$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $k=1\times4+4\times7+7\times1$ [M1] $=39$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Choosing the middle root $a$ as the centre simplifies the sum of the roots to $3a$.

subtopic: Roots of a cubic: symmetric functions and reciprocal roots
statement: The roots of the equation $2x^3-6x^2+3x+5=0$ are $\alpha$, $\beta$ and $\gamma$. (a) Write down the values of $\alpha+\beta+\gamma$, $\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha$ and $\alpha\beta\gamma$. [3] (b) Find the value of $\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2$. [2] (c) Find a cubic equation, with integer coefficients, that has roots $\dfrac1\alpha$, $\dfrac1\beta$ and $\dfrac1\gamma$. [5]
markscheme: (a) $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=3$ [A1] $\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha=\dfrac32$ [A1] $\alpha\beta\gamma=-\dfrac52$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2=(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)^2-2(\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha)$ [M1] $=9-3=6$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Sum of the new roots: $\dfrac{\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha}{\alpha\beta\gamma}=\dfrac{3/2}{-5/2}=-\dfrac35$ [M1] [A1] Sum of products in pairs: $\dfrac{\alpha+\beta+\gamma}{\alpha\beta\gamma}=-\dfrac65$ [A1] Product: $\dfrac1{\alpha\beta\gamma}=-\dfrac25$ [A1] Equation: $t^3+\dfrac35t^2-\dfrac65t+\dfrac25=0$, i.e. $5t^3+3t^2-6t+2=0$ [A1] [5 marks] Alternative: substitute $x=\dfrac1t$ into $2x^3-6x^2+3x+5=0$ and multiply by $t^3$ to get $2-6t+3t^2+5t^3=0$ (M1 for substitution, A1 for the equation, then A1 A1 A1 as the working shown).
tips: For a cubic $ax^3+bx^2+cx+d$, the sums of roots are $-b/a$, $c/a$ and $-d/a$. For reciprocal roots, substituting $x=1/t$ is usually the quickest method.

subtopic: Power sums of the roots of a cubic
statement: The roots of $x^3-x^2-x-1=0$ are $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$. Let $s_n=\alpha^n+\beta^n+\gamma^n$. (a) Find $s_0$, $s_1$ and $s_2$. [4] (b) Show that $s_{n+3}=s_{n+2}+s_{n+1}+s_n$ for $n\ge0$. [3] (c) Hence find $s_3,\ s_4,\ s_5$ and $s_6$. [3] (d) The equation has one real root $\alpha\approx1.84$ and two complex roots with $|\beta|<1$. Explain why $\dfrac{s_{n+1}}{s_n}\to\alpha$ as $n\to\infty$. [3] (e) Compute $\dfrac{s_6}{s_5}$ and compare it with the real root found by your calculator. [2]
markscheme: (a) $s_0=3$ [A1] $s_1=1$ [A1] $s_2=(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)^2-2\left(\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha\right)$ [M1] $=1-2(-1)=3$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) each root satisfies $x^3=x^2+x+1$ [M1] multiply by $x^n$: $x^{n+3}=x^{n+2}+x^{n+1}+x^n$ [A1] sum over the three roots [A1] [3 marks] (c) $s_3=3+1+3=7$ [A1] $s_4=7+3+1=11$ [A1] $s_5=21$, $s_6=39$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $|\beta|=|\gamma|<1$ so $\beta^n,\gamma^n\to0$ [A1] $s_n\approx\alpha^n$ for large $n$ [M1] hence $\dfrac{s_{n+1}}{s_n}\to\alpha$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) $\dfrac{39}{21}=1.857$ [A1] the real root is $1.839$, close [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Each root satisfies the cubic, so every power sum satisfies the same recurrence as the coefficients. The dominant real root controls the long-term growth.

subtopic: Quartic with a complex root and real coefficients
statement: The polynomial $p(x)=x^4-6x^3+ax^2-30x+25$ has real coefficients, and $1+2i$ is a root of $p(x)=0$. (a) Write down a second complex root of $p(x)=0$. [1] (b) Hence show that $x^2-2x+5$ is a factor of $p(x)$. [2] (c) Find the value of $a$. [3] (d) Solve $p(x)=0$ completely. [2]
markscheme: (a) $1-2i$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Sum of the two roots $=2$ and product $=1+4=5$ [M1] so $(x-(1+2i))(x-(1-2i))=x^2-2x+5$ is a factor [A1] [AG] [2 marks] (c) $p(x)=(x^2-2x+5)(x^2+qx+5)$ [M1] Coefficient of $x^3$: $q-2=-6$, so $q=-4$ [A1] Coefficient of $x^2$: $5-2q+5=a$, so $a=18$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) Other factor $x^2-4x+5=0$ [M1] $x=2\pm i$ so the roots are $1\pm2i$ and $2\pm i$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Non-real roots of a real polynomial come in conjugate pairs, and a conjugate pair always gives a real quadratic factor. Equate coefficients after writing the second quadratic factor with a constant term chosen so the constant terms match.

subtopic: Quartic: sums of roots and reciprocals
statement: The roots of the equation $x^4-x^3+2x^2+3x-5=0$ are $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$ and $\delta$. (a) Write down the values of $\alpha+\beta+\gamma+\delta$ and $\sum\alpha\beta$, the sum of the products of the roots taken two at a time. [2] (b) Find the value of $\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2+\delta^2$. [2] (c) Hence explain why the equation does not have four real roots. [2] (d) Find the value of $\dfrac1\alpha+\dfrac1\beta+\dfrac1\gamma+\dfrac1\delta$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\sum\alpha=1$ [A1] $\sum\alpha\beta=2$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\sum\alpha^2=(\sum\alpha)^2-2\sum\alpha\beta$ [M1] $=1-4=-3$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) If all roots were real, each square would be non-negative [R1] so the sum of squares could not be negative; since it equals $-3$, at least one root is non-real [R1] [2 marks] (d) $\sum\dfrac1\alpha=\dfrac{\alpha\beta\gamma+\alpha\beta\delta+\alpha\gamma\delta+\beta\gamma\delta}{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta}$ [M1] Sum of triple products $=-3$ [A1] and $\alpha\beta\gamma\delta=-5$ so the value is $\dfrac35$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: For a quartic $x^4+px^3+qx^2+rx+s$: $\sum\alpha=-p$, $\sum\alpha\beta=q$, $\sum\alpha\beta\gamma=-r$ and $\alpha\beta\gamma\delta=s$. Watch the alternating signs.

subtopic: Factorizing x to the fourth plus x squared plus one
statement: Consider $P(x)=x^4+x^2+1$. (a) Show that $P(x)=\left(x^2+x+1\right)\left(x^2-x+1\right)$. [2] (b) Hence find all roots of $P(x)=0$ in the form $a+b\mathrm i$ with $a,b$ exact. [3]
markscheme: (a) $P(x)=\left(x^2+1\right)^2-x^2$ [M1] difference of squares [A1] [2 marks] (b) $x^2+x+1=0$ gives $x=\dfrac{-1\pm\sqrt3\mathrm i}2$ [M1][A1] $x^2-x+1=0$ gives $x=\dfrac{1\pm\sqrt3\mathrm i}2$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Complete a square by adding and subtracting $x^2$.

subtopic: Cubic whose roots are the squares of the roots of a given cubic
statement: The roots of the equation $x^3-2x^2-x+3=0$ are $\alpha$, $\beta$ and $\gamma$. (a) Write down the values of $\alpha+\beta+\gamma$, $\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha$ and $\alpha\beta\gamma$. [2] (b) Find a cubic equation, with integer coefficients, whose roots are $\alpha^2$, $\beta^2$ and $\gamma^2$. [5] (c) Hence find the value of $\dfrac{1}{\alpha^2}+\dfrac{1}{\beta^2}+\dfrac{1}{\gamma^2}$. [2] (d) Find the value of $\alpha^4+\beta^4+\gamma^4$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=2$ [A1] $\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha=-1$ and $\alpha\beta\gamma=-3$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\sum\alpha^2=(\sum\alpha)^2-2\sum\alpha\beta$ [M1] $=4+2=6$ [A1] $\sum\alpha^2\beta^2=(\sum\alpha\beta)^2-2\alpha\beta\gamma(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)$ [M1] $=1-2(-3)(2)=13$ [A1] $\alpha^2\beta^2\gamma^2=(-3)^2=9$; the equation is $y^3-6y^2+13y-9=0$ [A1] [5 marks] (c) $\dfrac1{\alpha^2}+\dfrac1{\beta^2}+\dfrac1{\gamma^2}=\dfrac{\alpha^2\beta^2+\beta^2\gamma^2+\gamma^2\alpha^2}{\alpha^2\beta^2\gamma^2}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{13}{9}$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $\alpha^4+\beta^4+\gamma^4=\left(\sum\alpha^2\right)^2-2\sum\alpha^2\beta^2$ [M1] $=36-26=10$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: For the new roots $\alpha^2$ etc., apply the same symmetric-function identities a second time, with the old squares as the new roots. Keep careful track of signs: for $x^3+ax^2+bx+c=0$ the product of roots is $-c$.

subtopic: A quartic that is the square of a quadratic
statement: The polynomial $x^4+ax^3+bx^2+cx+4$ is the square of a quadratic $x^2+px+q$ with $q>0$, and $a=-6$. (a) Find $p$ and $q$, and hence $b$ and $c$. [5] (b) Factorize the polynomial fully and state the repeated roots. [2]
tips: Expand the square of a general quadratic and compare coefficients with the given polynomial.

subtopic: Cubic with roots in geometric sequence
statement: The three roots of the equation $x^3-13x^2+kx-27=0$, where $k\in\mathbb{R}$, form a geometric sequence with common ratio $r>1$. (a) Show that one of the roots is 3. [3] (b) Find the other two roots and the value of $k$. [4] (c) Hence solve the inequality $x^3-13x^2+kx-27\le 0$. [2]
markscheme: (a) let the roots be $\dfrac{a}{r},\ a,\ ar$ [M1] product of roots is $27$, so $a^3=27$ [M1] $a=3$ [A1] [AG] [3 marks] (b) sum of roots: $\dfrac3r+3+3r=13$ [M1] $3r^2-10r+3=0$ [A1] $(3r-1)(r-3)=0$, so $r=3$ as $r>1$ [A1] the roots are $1,\ 3,\ 9$ and $k=1\cdot3+1\cdot9+3\cdot9=39$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) $(x-1)(x-3)(x-9)\le 0$ [M1] $x\le 1$ or $3\le x\le 9$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Writing three terms of a geometric sequence as $a/r,\ a,\ ar$ makes the product of the roots simply $a^3$. After finding the roots, check the sum and pairwise sums against the original coefficients.

subtopic: Remainder of a high power on division by x squared minus one
statement: When the polynomial $P(x)$ is divided by $x^2-1$, the remainder has the form $ax+b$. (a) Show that $a+b=P(1)$ and $b-a=P(-1)$. [2] (b) Find the remainder when $x^{100}$ is divided by $x^2-1$, and the remainder when $x^{99}$ is divided by $x^2-1$. [3] (c) Find the remainder when $x^{99}+x^{100}+5$ is divided by $x^2-1$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $P(x)=(x^2-1)Q(x)+ax+b$ [M1] substitute $x=1$ and $x=-1$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $x^{100}$: $a+b=1$ and $b-a=1$ so $a=0$, $b=1$, remainder $1$ [M1][A1] $x^{99}$: $a+b=1$, $b-a=-1$ so $a=1$, $b=0$, remainder $x$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $x+1+5=x+6$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Evaluate the polynomial at the two roots of the divisor, $x=1$ and $x=-1$, to determine the two remainder coefficients.

subtopic: Polynomial identity and a hence factorization
statement: (a) Prove that $(x^2+x+1)(x^2-x+1)\equiv x^4+x^2+1$. [2] (b) Hence factorize $x^6-1$ completely into two linear factors and two irreducible quadratic factors. [3] (c) Hence find all real solutions of $(x^2+x+1)(x^2-x+1)=7$. [3]
tips: In a hence question, the identity from part (a) is the intended shortcut: replace the product by its expanded form before solving. Check irreducibility of a quadratic factor by its discriminant ($1-4<0$ here).

subtopic: Open box volume as a cubic
statement: A rectangular sheet of cardboard measures $30$ cm by $20$ cm. A square of side $x$ cm is cut from each corner and the sides are folded up to form an open box of volume $V\ \text{cm}^3$. (a) Show that $V=4x^3-100x^2+600x$. [2] (b) State the set of possible values of $x$. [1] (c) Find the maximum volume of the box, and the value of $x$ at which it occurs. [3] (d) The box must hold at least $900\ \text{cm}^3$. Find the possible values of $x$. [3]
markscheme: (a) Base dimensions $(30-2x)$ and $(20-2x)$, height $x$ [M1] $V=x(30-2x)(20-2x)=x(600-100x+4x^2)=4x^3-100x^2+600x$ [A1][AG] [2 marks] (b) $0<x<10$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) Maximum using the GDC (or $V'(x)=12x^2-200x+600=0$) [M1] $x=3.92$ ($3.9237\ldots$) [A1] $V=1060\ \text{cm}^3$ ($1056.3\ldots$) [A1] [3 marks] (d) Solve $4x^3-100x^2+600x=900$ [M1] $x=2.30$ and $x=5.78$ (the third root $16.9$ is outside the domain) [A1] $2.30\le x\le5.78$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: In 'show that' questions write every algebraic step. State the domain from the physical constraints: both $30-2x>0$ and $20-2x>0$, so the second condition is the binding one.

subtopic: Remainder in terms of a parameter and a unique real value
statement: Let $f(x)=x^3-kx+2$, where $k\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Find, in terms of $k$, the remainder when $f(x)$ is divided by $(x-k)$. [2] (b) Show that $(x-k)$ is a factor of $f(x)$ for exactly one real value of $k$, and state this value. [4] (c) For this value of $k$, solve $f(x)=0$, giving all roots, real and complex, in exact form. [3]
markscheme: (a) Remainder $=f(k)$ [M1] $=k^3-k^2+2$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Require $k^3-k^2+2=0$ [M1] $(k+1)(k^2-2k+2)=0$ [A1] Discriminant of $k^2-2k+2$ is $4-8=-4<0$ so no real roots [R1] Hence the only real value is $k=-1$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) $f(x)=x^3+x+2=(x+1)(x^2-x+2)$ [M1] $x=-1$ [A1] $x=\dfrac{1\pm i\sqrt7}{2}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The remainder theorem still applies when the divisor contains a parameter: substitute $x=k$. To show a cubic in $k$ has exactly one real root, factorize and check the discriminant of the remaining quadratic.

subtopic: Polynomial interpolation and the sum of squares
statement: The sum $S(n)=1^2+2^2+\cdots+n^2$ has values $S(0)=0$, $S(1)=1$, $S(2)=5$, $S(3)=14$. (a) Fit a polynomial $P(n)=an^3+bn^2+cn+d$ of degree at most $3$ through these four points, and show that $P(n)=\dfrac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}6$. [5] (b) Show that a polynomial of degree at most $3$ that takes the value $0$ at four distinct values of $n$ must be the zero polynomial, and hence that the polynomial in part (a) is unique. [3] (c) Show that $P(n)-P(n-1)=n^2$ for all $n$, and hence deduce that $P(n)=S(n)$ for all non-negative integers $n$. [4] (d) Evaluate $S(20)$. [1] (e) The formula $\left(\dfrac{n(n+1)}2\right)^2$ is proposed for $1^3+2^3+\cdots+n^3$. Show that it satisfies $T(n)-T(n-1)=n^3$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $d=0$ [A1] $a+b+c=1$, $8a+4b+2c=5$, $27a+9b+3c=14$ [M1] solve: $a=\dfrac13$, $b=\dfrac12$, $c=\dfrac16$ [A1][A1] $P(n)=\dfrac{2n^3+3n^2+n}6=\dfrac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}6$ [A1] [5 marks] (b) a non-zero polynomial of degree at most $3$ has at most $3$ roots [R1] the difference of two such interpolating polynomials vanishes at four points [M1] so the difference is $0$ [R1] [3 marks] (c) $P(n)-P(n-1)=\dfrac{n(n+1)(2n+1)-(n-1)n(2n-1)}6$ [M1] $=\dfrac{n(6n)}6=n^2$ [A1] $P(0)=S(0)=0$ and both increase by $n^2$ at each step [M1] so equal for all $n$ [R1] [4 marks] (d) $\dfrac{20\times21\times41}6=2870$ [A1] [1 mark] (e) $\dfrac{n^2\left[(n+1)^2-(n-1)^2\right]}4$ [M1] $=\dfrac{n^2\times4n}4=n^3$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Four values determine a cubic uniquely. To show the formula is correct beyond the four given values, check that it adds $n^2$ at each step.

subtopic: A sextic that is quadratic in x cubed
statement: Consider the equation $x^6-7x^3-8=0$. (a) Show that the equation can be written $(x^3-8)(x^3+1)=0$. [2] (b) Find all six solutions in the complex numbers, giving the real solutions exactly and the others in the form $a+b\mathrm i$. [5]
markscheme: (a) let $u=x^3$: $u^2-7u-8=(u-8)(u+1)$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (b) $x^3=8$: $x=2$ [A1] $x=2\operatorname{cis}\left(\pm\dfrac{2\pi}3\right)=-1\pm\sqrt3\mathrm i$ [M1][A1] $x^3=-1$: $x=-1$ [A1] $x=\operatorname{cis}\left(\pm\dfrac\pi3\right)=\dfrac12\pm\dfrac{\sqrt3}2\mathrm i$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: Treat $x^3$ as the unknown. The cube roots of a real number have one real root and a conjugate pair.

subtopic: Quartic with complex roots: building the polynomial
statement: The quartic polynomial $p(x)=x^4+ax^3+bx^2+cx+d$ has real coefficients, and two of its roots are $1-i$ and $i$. (a) Write down the other two roots. [2] (b) Find the values of $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$. [4] (c) Hence show that $p(x)>0$ for all $x\in\mathbb{R}$. [2]
tips: Pair each root with its conjugate, so each pair multiplies to a real quadratic. For positivity, complete the square on the quadratic factors.

subtopic: Cubic with roots in arithmetic progression
statement: The equation $x^3-12x^2+kx-28=0$, where $k\in\mathbb{R}$, has three real roots in arithmetic progression. (a) Show that one of the roots is $4$. [2] (b) Find the three roots and the value of $k$. [5]
markscheme: (a) Let the roots be $a-d$, $a$, $a+d$. Sum of roots $=3a=12$ [M1] so $a=4$ [A1] [AG] [2 marks] (b) Product of roots: $4(16-d^2)=28$ [M1] $d^2=9$, so $d=\pm3$ [A1] The roots are $1$, $4$, $7$ [A1] Sum of products in pairs: $k=1\times4+4\times7+1\times7$ [M1] $=39$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: Writing three terms of an arithmetic progression as $a-d$, $a$, $a+d$ makes the sum of roots collapse to $3a$ immediately. Then use the product (or pair sums) of the roots to find $d$ and the unknown coefficient.

subtopic: Odd-degree polynomials and locating a real root
statement: Let $f(x)=x^5+x^3+x-1$. (a) Explain why every polynomial of odd degree with real coefficients has at least one real root. [2] (b) Show that $f(x)=0$ has exactly one real root. [3] (c) Show that this root lies between $0.6$ and $0.7$. [2] (d) Find the root, correct to three significant figures. [1]
markscheme: (a) As $x\to\infty$ and $x\to-\infty$ an odd degree polynomial tends to values of opposite sign [R1] A polynomial is continuous, so its graph crosses the $x$-axis at least once [R1] [2 marks] (b) $f'(x)=5x^4+3x^2+1$ [M1] $f'(x)>0$ for all real $x$ [A1] so $f$ is strictly increasing and crosses the $x$-axis exactly once [R1] [3 marks] (c) $f(0.6)=-0.106<0$ [M1] $f(0.7)=0.211>0$ so there is a sign change and the root lies in $(0.6,0.7)$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $x=0.637$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: For an exactly-one-root argument, combine existence (continuity and sign change) with uniqueness (strictly monotonic). Use your GDC to find the root of $f(x)=0$ once you have bracketed it.

subtopic: Sums of powers of roots of a cubic
statement: The roots of the equation $x^3-4x^2+x+6=0$ are $\alpha$, $\beta$ and $\gamma$. (a) Write down the values of $\alpha+\beta+\gamma$, $\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha$ and $\alpha\beta\gamma$. [3] (b) Find the value of $\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2$. [2] (c) Without solving the equation, show that $\alpha^3+\beta^3+\gamma^3=34$. [3] (d) Find a cubic equation with integer coefficients whose roots are $\alpha^2$, $\beta^2$ and $\gamma^2$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=4$ [A1] $\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha=1$ [A1] $\alpha\beta\gamma=-6$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2=(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)^2-2(\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha)$ [M1] $=16-2=14$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Each root satisfies $x^3=4x^2-x-6$ [M1] Summing over the three roots: $\sum\alpha^3=4\sum\alpha^2-\sum\alpha-18$ [M1] $=4(14)-4-18=34$ [A1] [AG] [3 marks] (d) Sum of the new roots $=14$ and product $=(\alpha\beta\gamma)^2=36$ [A1] Sum of pair products $=(\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha)^2-2\alpha\beta\gamma(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)$ [M1] $=1+48=49$, so the equation is $x^3-14x^2+49x-36=0$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: For sums of squares use $(\sum\alpha)^2-2\sum\alpha\beta$. For higher powers, use the fact that each root satisfies the original equation and add the three copies. Note that the roots are rational here, so you can check your answers by solving.

subtopic: The fifth roots of unity and the exact value of cos 72 degrees
statement: Consider the equation $z^5=1$ for $z\in\mathbb C$. (a) Show that the roots other than $z=1$ satisfy $z^4+z^3+z^2+z+1=0$. [2] (b) Write down the five roots in the form $\operatorname{cis}\theta$. [2] (c) Divide the quartic by $z^2$ and let $w=z+\dfrac1z$ to show that $w^2+w-1=0$. [3] (d) For $z=\operatorname{cis}72^\circ$, show that $w=2\cos72^\circ$, and hence find $\cos72^\circ$ in exact form. [3] (e) Use $z=\operatorname{cis}144^\circ$ to find $\cos36^\circ$ in exact form. [2] (f) A regular pentagon has side $s$ and diagonal $d$. Consider the triangle formed by two adjacent sides and the diagonal joining their far ends. Using the interior angle of a regular pentagon, $108^\circ$, show that $\dfrac ds=2\cos36^\circ$ and evaluate it exactly. [3]
markscheme: (a) $z^5-1=(z-1)\left(z^4+z^3+z^2+z+1\right)$ [M1] $z\ne1$ gives the quartic [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\operatorname{cis}\dfrac{2\pi k}5$ for $k=0,1,2,3,4$ [A1][A1] [2 marks] (c) $z^2+z+1+\dfrac1z+\dfrac1{z^2}=0$ [M1] $z^2+\dfrac1{z^2}=w^2-2$ [A1] $w^2-2+w+1=0$ so $w^2+w-1=0$ [AG] [A1] [3 marks] (d) $z+\dfrac1z=2\cos72^\circ$ [A1] $w=\dfrac{-1\pm\sqrt5}2$ [M1] $w>0$, so $\cos72^\circ=\dfrac{\sqrt5-1}4$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) $2\cos144^\circ=\dfrac{-1-\sqrt5}2$ [M1] $\cos36^\circ=-\cos144^\circ=\dfrac{1+\sqrt5}4$ [A1] [2 marks] (f) the triangle has sides $s,s,d$ with apex angle $108^\circ$ [A1] base angles $\dfrac{180^\circ-108^\circ}2=36^\circ$, so $\dfrac d2=s\cos36^\circ$ [M1] $\dfrac ds=2\cos36^\circ=\dfrac{1+\sqrt5}2$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: For $z$ on the unit circle, $z+1/z=2\cos\theta$. The quartic is symmetric under $z\to1/z$, which makes the substitution possible.

subtopic: The remainder theorem and the factor theorem
statement: The polynomial $p(x)=2x^3+ax^2-7x+b$ has a factor $(x-2)$ and leaves remainder $-12$ when divided by $(x+1)$. (a) Write down two equations in $a$ and $b$. [3] (b) Find $a$ and $b$. [3] (c) Hence factorize $p(x)$ completely. [3]
tips: If $(x-k)$ is a factor then $p(k)=0$; the remainder on division by $(x-k)$ is $p(k)$.

subtopic: Factorizing x to the sixth minus one over the reals
statement: Consider $P(x)=x^6-1$. (a) Factorize $P(x)$ completely into linear and quadratic factors with real coefficients. [4] (b) Explain why the two quadratic factors have no real roots, and name the six roots of $P(x)=0$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $x^6-1=\left(x^3-1\right)\left(x^3+1\right)$ [M1] $x^3-1=(x-1)\left(x^2+x+1\right)$ [A1] $x^3+1=(x+1)\left(x^2-x+1\right)$ [A1] $(x-1)(x+1)\left(x^2+x+1\right)\left(x^2-x+1\right)$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) each has discriminant $1-4=-3<0$ [R1] the roots are the sixth roots of unity [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Use the difference and sum of cubes after writing $x^6=\left(x^3\right)^2$.

subtopic: Remainder theorem with a quadratic divisor and unknown polynomial
statement: A polynomial $p(x)$ leaves remainder 4 when divided by $(x-1)$ and remainder $-5$ when divided by $(x+2)$. (a) When $p(x)$ is divided by $(x-1)(x+2)$ the remainder is $Ax+B$. Find the values of $A$ and $B$. [4] (b) Given further that $p(x)$ is a cubic polynomial with leading coefficient 2 and that $p(0)=-7$, find $p(x)$, giving your answer in the form $ax^3+bx^2+cx+d$. [4] (c) Hence show that the equation $p(x)=0$ has a solution in the interval $0<x<1$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $p(x)=(x-1)(x+2)q(x)+Ax+B$ [M1] $p(1)=4$: $A+B=4$ [A1] $p(-2)=-5$: $-2A+B=-5$ [A1] $A=3$, $B=1$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $q(x)$ is linear with leading coefficient 2: $q(x)=2x+c$ [M1] $p(0)=(-1)(2)(c)+1=-7$ [M1] [A1] so $c=4$ $p(x)=(x^2+x-2)(2x+4)+3x+1=2x^3+6x^2+3x-7$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) $p(0)=-7<0$ and $p(1)=4>0$ [A1] $p$ is continuous, so there is a sign change and hence a root between 0 and 1 [R1] [2 marks]
tips: When the divisor is quadratic, the remainder is at most linear, so write it as $Ax+B$ and use the values at the two roots of the divisor. A sign change of a continuous function on an interval guarantees a root there.

subtopic: Cubic inequality
markscheme: critical values $-2,1,4$ [A1] sign analysis: positive for $x>4$, negative on $(1,4)$, positive on $(-2,1)$, negative for $x<-2$ [M1][A1] $x\le-2$ or $1\le x\le4$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Mark the roots on a number line and test one value in each interval.

subtopic: Criterion for a repeated root using the derivative
statement: A polynomial $P(x)$ has a repeated root at $x=a$ if $P(x)=(x-a)^2Q(x)$ for some polynomial $Q$. (a) Show that if $P$ has a repeated root at $x=a$ then $P(a)=0$ and $P'(a)=0$. [3] (b) Show that $x^3-3x^2+4$ has a repeated root, and factorize it completely. [3]
tips: Differentiate the product $(x-a)^2Q(x)$ and evaluate at $x=a$.

subtopic: Quartic with roots in arithmetic sequence
statement: The four roots of the equation $x^4-8x^3+px^2+qx+r=0$, where $p,q,r\in\mathbb{R}$, are real and form an arithmetic sequence with common difference 2. (a) Find the four roots. [3] (b) Hence find the values of $p$, $q$ and $r$. [3]
markscheme: (a) let the roots be $a-3,\ a-1,\ a+1,\ a+3$ [M1] sum of roots is 8, so $4a=8$ [M1] $a=2$; the roots are $-1,\ 1,\ 3,\ 5$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $p=$ sum of products in pairs, $q=-$(sum of products in threes), $r=$ product of all four roots [M1] $p=-1-3-5+3+5+15=14$ and $q=-(-3-5-15+15)=8$ [A1] $r=(-1)(1)(3)(5)=-15$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: For a quartic $x^4+ax^3+bx^2+cx+d$, the sum of the roots is $-a$, the sum of the pairwise products is $b$, the sum of the triple products is $-c$ and the product of all roots is $d$. Choosing a symmetric parametrization such as $a-3,a-1,a+1,a+3$ makes the sum easy.

subtopic: Polynomial identity and remainder on division by a quadratic
statement: (a) Find the values of $A$, $B$ and $C$ such that $2x^2+5x-1\equiv A(x-1)^2+B(x-1)+C$. [4] (b) Hence find the remainder when $2x^2+5x-1$ is divided by $(x-1)^2$. [2]
tips: To match an identity, expand the right-hand side and equate coefficients of each power of $x$. The remainder after division by a quadratic has degree less than $2$, so it is the leftover linear part.

subtopic: Remainder when x to the n is divided by (x - 1) squared
statement: The polynomial $x^n$, where $n\ge2$ is an integer, is divided by $(x-1)^2$ with remainder $ax+b$. (a) Write $x^n=(x-1)^2Q(x)+ax+b$. By substituting $x=1$ and differentiating, show that $a=n$ and $b=1-n$. [5] (b) Find the remainder when $x^7$ is divided by $(x-1)^2$. [1]
tips: The differentiated equation still has a factor of $(x-1)$ in each term involving $Q$, so those terms vanish at $x=1$.

subtopic: Cubic through three points and a complex equation
statement: A cubic polynomial $p(x)$ has leading coefficient $2$, and $p(1)=1$, $p(2)=2$ and $p(3)=3$. (a) Find $p(x)$, giving your answer in the form $p(x)=x+\dots$ and then expanded. [4] (b) Solve $p(x)=x+12$ over the complex numbers. [4]
markscheme: (a) $p(x)-x$ is a cubic with roots $1$, $2$, $3$ [M1] leading coefficient $2$ gives $p(x)-x=2(x-1)(x-2)(x-3)$ [A1] $p(x)=x+2(x-1)(x-2)(x-3)$ [A1] $=2x^3-12x^2+23x-12$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $2(x-1)(x-2)(x-3)=12$ so $x^3-6x^2+11x-12=0$ [M1] $x=4$ is a root [A1] $(x-4)\left(x^2-2x+3\right)=0$ [M1] $x=4$ or $x=1\pm i\sqrt2$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Consider the polynomial $p(x)-x$: its values at $1$, $2$ and $3$ are all zero. After finding one real root by inspection, use the quadratic formula for the remaining factor.

subtopic: Equations whose roots are reciprocals and multiples of given roots
statement: The roots of $x^3-2x^2-5x+6=0$ are $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$. (a) Write down $\alpha+\beta+\gamma$, $\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha$ and $\alpha\beta\gamma$. [2] (b) Find the cubic equation, with integer coefficients, whose roots are $\dfrac1\alpha$, $\dfrac1\beta$, $\dfrac1\gamma$. [4] (c) Find the cubic equation whose roots are $2\alpha$, $2\beta$, $2\gamma$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $2$, $-5$ [A1] $-6$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) sum of new roots $\dfrac{\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha}{\alpha\beta\gamma}=\dfrac56$ [M1][A1] sum of pairs $\dfrac{\alpha+\beta+\gamma}{\alpha\beta\gamma}=-\dfrac13$ and product $-\dfrac16$ [A1] $y^3-\dfrac56y^2-\dfrac13y+\dfrac16=0$, so $6y^3-5y^2-2y+1=0$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) substitute $x=\dfrac y2$: $\dfrac{y^3}8-\dfrac{y^2}2-\dfrac{5y}2+6=0$ [M1] $y^3-4y^2-20y+48=0$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Use the sums and products of the new roots in terms of the original ones. A faster check for part (b) is to substitute $x=1/y$ into the equation.

subtopic: Factorizing x to the fourth plus four
statement: Consider $P(x)=x^4+4$. (a) Show that $P(x)=\left(x^2+2\right)^2-4x^2$, and hence factorize $P(x)$ into two real quadratic factors. [3] (b) Hence solve $x^4+4=0$ for $x\in\mathbb C$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\left(x^2+2\right)^2-4x^2=x^4+4x^2+4-4x^2=x^4+4$ [A1] difference of two squares [M1] $(x^2+2x+2)(x^2-2x+2)$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $x=\dfrac{-2\pm\sqrt{4-8}}2=-1\pm\mathrm i$ [M1][A1] and $x=1\pm\mathrm i$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Add and subtract $4x^2$ to create a difference of squares.

subtopic: Quartic roots and graph features found with a GDC
statement: Let $p(x)=x^4-3x^3-4x^2+9x-3$. (a) Using your graphing calculator, find all real solutions of $p(x)=0$. Give your answers to three significant figures where they are not exact. [3] (b) Hence solve $p(x)<0$. [2] (c) The graph of $y=p(x)$ has a local maximum point. Find its coordinates. [2] (d) Find the range of values of $k$ for which the equation $p(x)=k$ has four distinct real solutions. [3]
markscheme: (a) solving $p(x)=0$ on the GDC [M1] $x=-1.93$, $x=0.448$ [A1] $x=1$ and $x=3.48$ (all four correct) [A1] [3 marks] (b) $p$ has a positive leading coefficient and four simple roots, so it is negative between the first and second, and between the third and fourth roots [M1] $-1.93<x<0.448$ or $1<x<3.48$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) local maximum at $(0.725,\ 0.556)$ [A1] [A1] [2 marks] (d) the graph has local minima at $(-1.16,\ -12.3)$ and $(2.68,\ -13.8)$ [M1] the horizontal line $y=k$ must lie above both minima and below the local maximum: $k>-12.3$ [A1] $k<0.556$, so $-12.3<k<0.556$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Graph the function in a window that shows all turning points, then use the root and extremum features of the GDC rather than guessing. For the number of solutions of $p(x)=k$, compare $k$ with every local maximum and minimum value.

subtopic: Cubic polynomial model fitted to data
statement: The number of daily users of a new app, in thousands, is modeled by $U(t)=at^3+bt^2+ct+d$ (the model allows for a small dip as the initial novelty fades, followed by growth through word of mouth), where $t$ is the number of weeks after launch and $a,b,c,d\in\mathbb{R}$. The recorded values are given in the table. $$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline t & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 \\ \hline U & 2 & 6 & 6 & 8 \\ \hline \end{array}$$ (a) Find the values of $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$. [5] (b) Find the coordinates of the local maximum of $U$ for $0\leq t\leq4$. [3] (c) Find the first time at which the model predicts that the app has $15$ thousand daily users. [2] (d) Use the model to estimate the number of daily users at $t=10$, and comment on the validity of this estimate. [2]
markscheme: (a) $U(0)=2$ gives $d=2$ [A1] $a+b+c=4$, $8a+4b+2c=4$, $27a+9b+3c=6$ [M1] Solving with GDC: $a=1$, $b=-5$, $c=8$ [A1] [A1] [A1] [5 marks] (b) $U'(t)=3t^2-10t+8=0$ [M1] $t=\dfrac43$ [A1] (or $t=2$, the local minimum) Local maximum at $(1.33,6.15)$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Solve $t^3-5t^2+8t+2=15$ [M1] $t=3.79$ weeks [A1] [2 marks] (d) $U(10)=582$ thousand users [A1] This is unlikely to be valid since a cubic model has been extrapolated far outside the data range $0\leq t\leq3$ [R1] [2 marks]
tips: With four data points and four unknown coefficients you can solve a system of linear equations, or use cubic regression on the GDC. When commenting on validity, mention extrapolation outside the data range.

subtopic: Polynomial inequality and a hence part with cosine
statement: (a) Solve the inequality $x^4-5x^2+4\le 0$. [4] (b) Hence find all solutions of $\cos^4\theta-5\cos^2\theta+4\le 0$ in the interval $0\le\theta\le 2\pi$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $(x^2-1)(x^2-4)\le 0$ [M1] [A1] $1\le x^2\le 4$ [A1] $-2\le x\le -1$ or $1\le x\le 2$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) let $x=\cos\theta$, so $-1\le x\le 1$ [M1] combining with part (a), the only possible values are $x=-1$ and $x=1$ [A1] $\theta=0,\ \pi,\ 2\pi$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Treat a quartic in $x^2$ as a quadratic in $x^2$, then convert back to intervals in $x$. In a hence part, always intersect the answer with the range of the substituted function, here $-1\le\cos\theta\le 1$.

subtopic: Writing a cubic in powers of (x-2) by repeated division
statement: Let $p(x)=2x^3-5x^2+4x-7$. (a) Find the constants $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$ such that $p(x)\equiv A(x-2)^3+B(x-2)^2+C(x-2)+D$. [4] (b) Hence show that the equation $p(x)=-3$ has exactly one real solution, and state its value. [3]
markscheme: (a) divide $p(x)$ by $(x-2)$: $p(x)=(x-2)(2x^2-x+2)-3$, so $D=-3$ [M1] [A1] divide $2x^2-x+2$ by $(x-2)$: $2x^2-x+2=(x-2)(2x+3)+8$, so $C=8$ [A1] $2x+3=2(x-2)+7$, so $A=2$, $B=7$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $p(x)=-3\Rightarrow 2u^3+7u^2+8u=0$, where $u=x-2$ [M1] $u(2u^2+7u+8)=0$ [A1] discriminant of $2u^2+7u+8$ is $49-64=-15<0$, so the only real solution is $u=0$, that is $x=2$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Repeated division by $(x-a)$ produces the successive coefficients of the expansion in powers of $(x-a)$, with the remainder at each stage being the next constant. Always test the discriminant of leftover quadratic factors to count real roots.

subtopic: Polynomial with integer coefficients and conjugate roots
statement: A quartic polynomial $Q(x)$ has integer coefficients, leading coefficient $1$, and has $1+\sqrt2$ and $3-\mathrm i$ as roots. (a) State two other roots of $Q(x)$, with a reason. [2] (b) Find $Q(x)$ in expanded form. [4]
markscheme: (a) $1-\sqrt2$ and $3+\mathrm i$ [A1] polynomial with rational coefficients has irrational and complex roots in conjugate pairs [R1] [2 marks] (b) $x^2-2x-1$ from the first pair [M1][A1] $x^2-6x+10$ from the second pair [A1] $Q(x)=x^4-8x^3+21x^2-14x-10$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: For each pair $p\pm q$, the quadratic factor is $x^2-(\text{sum})x+(\text{product})$.

subtopic: Factor and remainder theorems
statement: The polynomial $p(x)=x^3+ax^2+bx-6$, where $a,b\in\mathbb{R}$, has a factor $(x-2)$. When $p(x)$ is divided by $(x+1)$ the remainder is $-12$. (a) Find the value of $a$ and the value of $b$. [4] (b) Hence show that the equation $p(x)=0$ has exactly one real root. [2]
markscheme: (a) $p(2)=8+4a+2b-6=0 \Rightarrow 2a+b=-1$ [M1][A1] $p(-1)=-1+a-b-6=-12 \Rightarrow a-b=-5$ [A1] Solving: $a=-2,\ b=3$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $p(x)=x^3-2x^2+3x-6=(x-2)(x^2+3)$ [M1] $x^2+3>0$ for all real $x$ (discriminant $-12<0$), so the only real root is $x=2$ [R1][AG] [2 marks]
tips: Use the factor theorem ($p(2)=0$) and the remainder theorem ($p(-1)=-12$) to get two simultaneous equations. To prove there is only one real root, factorize fully and show the quadratic factor has a negative discriminant.

subtopic: Factor theorem and remainder theorem with two unknowns
statement: Let $p(x)=2x^3+ax^2-7x+b$, where $a,b\in\mathbb{Z}$. The polynomial $p(x)$ has a factor $(x-2)$, and the remainder when $p(x)$ is divided by $(x+1)$ is $12$. (a) Find the values of $a$ and $b$. [5] (b) Factorize $p(x)$ completely into linear factors over $\mathbb{R}$, and hence solve $p(x)=0$. [3]
tips: The factor theorem gives $p(c)=0$ and the remainder theorem gives $p(c)=r$ for division by $(x-c)$; each condition produces one linear equation in the unknowns. After finding a root, divide to reduce to a quadratic, then use the formula if it does not factorize.

subtopic: Division by a quadratic and remainders with unknown coefficients
statement: Let $p(x)=x^3+ax^2+bx+c$, where $a,b,c\in\mathbb{R}$. When $p(x)$ is divided by $x^2+1$ the remainder is $2x-3$, and when $p(x)$ is divided by $(x-1)$ the remainder is $5$. (a) Find the values of $a$, $b$ and $c$. [6] (b) Find the remainder when $p(x)$ is divided by $(x^2+1)(x-1)$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $p(x)=(x^2+1)(x+a)+(b-1)x+(c-a)$ [M1] Equating the remainder with $2x-3$: $b-1=2$ so $b=3$ [A1] and $c-a=-3$ [A1] $p(1)=5$: $1+a+b+c=5$ so $a+c=1$ [M1] $a=2$ [A1] $c=-1$ [A1] [6 marks] (b) $p(x)=x^3+2x^2+3x-1$ and $(x^2+1)(x-1)=x^3-x^2+x-1$, so the quotient is $1$ [M1] Remainder $=p(x)-(x^3-x^2+x-1)$ [A1] $=3x^2+2x$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: When dividing by a quadratic, write $p(x)=(x^2+1)q(x)+r(x)$ with $r$ of degree at most 1. A cubic divided by a cubic with the same leading coefficient has quotient 1.

subtopic: Sum and product of the roots of a cubic
statement: The roots of $2x^3-3x^2+4x-5=0$ are $\alpha$, $\beta$ and $\gamma$. (a) Write down $\alpha+\beta+\gamma$, $\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha$ and $\alpha\beta\gamma$. [3] (b) Find the value of $\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2$ and hence explain why the equation cannot have three real roots. [3] (c) Find the value of $\dfrac1\alpha+\dfrac1\beta+\dfrac1\gamma$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=\dfrac32$ [A1] $\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha=2$ [A1] $\alpha\beta\gamma=\dfrac52$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)^2-2\left(\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha\right)$ [M1] $=\dfrac94-4=-\dfrac74$ [A1] a sum of squares of real numbers cannot be negative, so not all roots are real [R1] [3 marks] (c) $\dfrac{\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha}{\alpha\beta\gamma}$ [M1] $=\dfrac45$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: For $ax^3+bx^2+cx+d=0$: sum of roots $-b/a$, sum of pairwise products $c/a$, product $-d/a$.

subtopic: Repeated root from tangency, using the derivative
statement: Let $p(x)=x^3+ax^2+bx+c$, where $a,b,c\in\mathbb{R}$. The graph of $y=p(x)$ touches the $x$-axis at $x=2$ and crosses the $y$-axis at $(0,-12)$. (a) Explain why $p(2)=0$ and $p'(2)=0$. [2] (b) Find the values of $a$, $b$ and $c$. [4] (c) Solve $p(x)\ge 0$. [2]
markscheme: (a) the graph meets the $x$-axis at $x=2$, so $p(2)=0$ [R1] it touches (is tangent to) the axis there, so the gradient is zero and $p'(2)=0$ [R1] [2 marks] (b) $p(0)=-12$, so $c=-12$ [A1] $p(2)=0$: $8+4a+2b-12=0$, so $4a+2b=4$ [M1] $p'(x)=3x^2+2ax+b$, so $12+4a+b=0$ [M1] solving: $a=-7$, $b=16$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) the third root satisfies $2+2+r=7$, so $p(x)=(x-2)^2(x-3)$ [A1] $(x-2)^2\ge0$, so $p(x)\ge 0$ when $x\ge 3$ or $x=2$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A graph that touches the $x$-axis indicates a repeated root, so both $p$ and $p'$ vanish there. Do not forget the isolated solution $x=2$ when solving a non-strict inequality with a squared factor.

subtopic: Symmetric functions of roots and a shifted-roots cubic
statement: The roots of the equation $x^3-2x^2+3x+4=0$ are $\alpha$, $\beta$ and $\gamma$. (a) Write down the values of $\alpha+\beta+\gamma$, $\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha$ and $\alpha\beta\gamma$. [2] (b) Show that $\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2=-2$, and explain why this shows that the equation does not have three real roots. [3] (c) Find a cubic equation, with integer coefficients, whose roots are $\alpha+1$, $\beta+1$ and $\gamma+1$. [3] (d) By using the fact that each root satisfies the original equation, find the value of $\alpha^3+\beta^3+\gamma^3$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=2$, $\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha=3$ [A1] $\alpha\beta\gamma=-4$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2=(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)^2-2(\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha)$ [M1] $=4-6=-2$ [A1] [AG] if all roots were real, the sum of their squares would be non-negative, a contradiction [R1] [3 marks] (c) let $y=x+1$, so $x=y-1$ [M1] $(y-1)^3-2(y-1)^2+3(y-1)+4=0$ [A1] $y^3-5y^2+10y-2=0$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $\alpha^3=2\alpha^2-3\alpha-4$, and similarly for $\beta$ and $\gamma$ [M1] $\alpha^3+\beta^3+\gamma^3=2(-2)-3(2)-12$ [A1] $=-22$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: To find an equation whose roots are $\alpha+k$, substitute $x=y-k$ into the original equation. A sum of squares that comes out negative proves that not all roots are real.

subtopic: Stationary points of a cubic and the number of real roots
statement: Let $f(x)=x^3-3x^2-9x$. (a) Find the coordinates of the stationary points of the graph of $y=f(x)$. [4] (b) Find the set of values of $k$ for which the equation $x^3-3x^2-9x+k=0$ has three distinct real solutions. [3] (c) Find the values of $k$ for which the equation in part (b) has exactly two distinct real solutions. [2]
markscheme: (a) $f'(x)=3x^2-6x-9$ [A1] $f'(x)=0\Rightarrow 3(x-3)(x+1)=0$ [M1] $(-1,\ 5)$ [A1] $(3,\ -27)$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) the equation is $f(x)=-k$ [M1] the cubic has a local maximum at $y=5$ and a local minimum at $y=-27$, so three distinct solutions need the horizontal line $y=-k$ to lie strictly between them: $-27<-k<5$ [M1] $-5<k<27$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) the line passes through a turning point: $-k=5$ or $-k=-27$ [A1] $k=-5$ or $k=27$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Rewrite $f(x)+k=0$ as $f(x)=-k$ and think of a horizontal line sliding across the graph; the number of roots changes only at the turning-point heights. Remember the sign: the line is at height $-k$, not $k$.

subtopic: Cubic with roots in geometric progression
statement: The equation $x^3-7x^2+kx-8=0$, where $k\in\mathbb{R}$, has three real roots that form a geometric progression. (a) Show that one of the roots is $2$. [2] (b) Find the value of $k$. [2] (c) Find the other two roots. [3]
markscheme: (a) Let the roots be $\dfrac{a}{r}$, $a$, $ar$. Product of roots $=a^3=8$ [M1] so $a=2$ [A1] [AG] [2 marks] (b) $x=2$ is a root: $8-28+2k-8=0$ [M1] $k=14$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Divide by $(x-2)$: $x^3-7x^2+14x-8=(x-2)(x^2-5x+4)$ [M1] [A1] $=(x-2)(x-1)(x-4)$ so the other roots are $1$ and $4$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Writing the roots as $a/r$, $a$, $ar$ means the product of the roots is $a^3$ regardless of $r$. Once one root is known, use the factor theorem for the unknown and polynomial division for the rest.

subtopic: Open box from a sheet: cubic volume model and GDC
statement: A rectangular sheet of cardboard measures 40 cm by 25 cm. A square of side $x$ cm is cut from each corner and the sides are folded up to form an open box with volume $V$ cm$^3$. (a) Show that $V=4x^3-130x^2+1000x$. [2] (b) Write down the set of possible values of $x$. [1] (c) Using your graphing calculator, find the maximum volume of the box and the value of $x$ for which it occurs. [3] (d) The box is required to have a volume of at least 2000 cm$^3$. Find the possible values of $x$, giving your answers to three significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) the box has length $40-2x$, width $25-2x$ and height $x$ [M1] $V=x(40-2x)(25-2x)=x(1000-130x+4x^2)=4x^3-130x^2+1000x$ [A1] [AG] [2 marks] (b) $0<x<12.5$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) graph of $V$ and maximum function on the domain [M1] $x=5$ [A1] $V=2250$ cm$^3$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) solve $4x^3-130x^2+1000x=2000$ (intersection with $y=2000$) [M1] $x=3.20$ and $x=7.01$ [A1] $3.20\le x\le 7.01$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: State the domain from the physical situation: the cut-out squares cannot use more than half of the shorter side. When solving $V\ge 2000$, a third intersection of the cubic may lie outside the domain and must be discarded.

subtopic: Complex roots of a quartic with real coefficients
statement: The polynomial $p(x)=x^4-2x^3+3x^2-2x+2$ has real coefficients, and $x=1+\mathrm i$ is a root. (a) Write down another root of $p(x)=0$ and the quadratic factor of $p(x)$ with real coefficients that they generate. [3] (b) Find the other two roots. [4]
markscheme: (a) $1-\mathrm i$ [A1] $(x-1)^2+1=x^2-2x+2$ [M1][A1] [3 marks] (b) divide: $x^4-2x^3+3x^2-2x+2=\left(x^2-2x+2\right)\left(x^2+1\right)$ [M1][A1] $x^2+1=0$ [M1] $x=\pm\mathrm i$ [A1] [4 marks]
