(a) Find the probability that none of the 3 chosen items is defective. [2] (b) Find the probability that exactly one is defective. [2] (c) Find the probability that at least two are defective. [2] (d) Find the expected number of defective items in the sample, and explain why the answer would be the same if sampling were with replacement. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{\binom{16}{3}}{\binom{20}{3}}=0.4912$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac{\binom{4}{1}\binom{16}{2}}{\binom{20}{3}}=0.4211$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (c) $1-P(0)-P(1)=0.0877$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (d) $E=n\cdot\dfrac{K}{N}=0.60$ [M1][A1]; each item is defective with marginal probability $K/N$, and expectation is additive regardless of dependence [R1] [3 marks]
tips: Counting with combinations avoids tree diagrams: favorable selections divided by all selections.

subtopic: Position of a random walker after several steps
statement: A particle starts at $0$ on a number line. At each step it moves $1$ unit right or $1$ unit left, each with probability $\tfrac12$, independently of other steps. (a) Find the probability that the particle is at $0$ after $4$ steps. [2] (b) Find the probability that the particle is at $2$ after $4$ steps. [3] (c) Find the probability that the particle is at $0$ after $6$ steps. [2]
markscheme: (a) two steps right and two left: $\binom42\left(\dfrac12\right)^4$ [M1] $=\dfrac38$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $u$ steps right: $u-(4-u)=2$ so $u=3$ [M1][A1] $\binom43\left(\dfrac12\right)^4=\dfrac14$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\binom63\left(\dfrac12\right)^6$ [M1] $=\dfrac5{16}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The number of right moves $u$ and left moves $n-u$ must give the required final position. The number of right moves is binomial.

subtopic: Selection without replacement from a box of batteries
statement: (a) A box contains $9$ batteries: $4$ new, $3$ used and $2$ faulty. Three batteries are chosen at random without replacement. Find the probability that all three batteries are of the same type. [3] (b) Find the probability that exactly two of the three batteries are new. [3] (c) Given that exactly two of the three batteries are new, find the probability that the first battery chosen is new. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\mathrm{P}(\text{3 new})=\dfrac49\times\dfrac38\times\dfrac27=\dfrac{1}{21}$ [M1] $\mathrm{P}(\text{3 used})=\dfrac39\times\dfrac28\times\dfrac17=\dfrac{1}{84}$ [A1] total $=\dfrac{4}{84}+\dfrac{1}{84}=\dfrac{5}{84}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\dfrac{\binom42\binom51}{\binom93}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{6\times5}{84}$ [A1] $=\dfrac{5}{14}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Each order (NNO, NON, ONN, where O means not new) has probability $\dfrac{4\times3\times5}{9\times8\times7}=\dfrac{60}{504}$ [M1] $\mathrm{P}(\text{first new and exactly two new})=\dfrac{120}{504}$ [A1] $\mathrm{P}=\dfrac{120/504}{180/504}=\dfrac{2}{3}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Without replacement, the denominators fall by one each draw and the numerators change with what has been removed. For 'exactly two', count all the orders in which it can happen, or use combinations.

subtopic: Probability of a matching pair among random socks
statement: A drawer contains $10$ pairs of socks, and no two pairs are alike, so there are $20$ socks. Four socks are taken from the drawer at random. (a) Show that the number of ways to choose four socks, no two of which belong to the same pair, is $\dbinom{10}4\times2^4$. [2] (b) Hence find the probability that the four socks contain at least one matching pair, giving your answer to three significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) choose which $4$ pairs the socks come from: $\binom{10}4$ [A1] one sock from each chosen pair: $2^4$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $P(\text{no pair})=\dfrac{3360}{\binom{20}4}=\dfrac{3360}{4845}$ [M1][A1] $1-0.6935=0.307$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A matching pair means two socks from the same pair, so use the complement: no pair at all.

subtopic: Union, intersection and independence
statement: The events $A$ and $B$ are such that $P(A)=0.4$, $P(B)=0.5$ and $P(A\cup B)=0.7$. (a) Find $P(A\cap B)$. [2] (b) Find $P(A\mid B)$. [2] (c) Hence state, with a reason, whether $A$ and $B$ are independent. [2] (d) Find $P(A'\cap B')$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$ [M1] $P(A\cap B)=0.4+0.5-0.7=0.2$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $P(A\mid B)=\dfrac{0.2}{0.5}$ [M1] $=0.4$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $P(A\mid B)=0.4=P(A)$ (or $P(A)P(B)=0.2=P(A\cap B)$) [M1] so $A$ and $B$ are independent [A1] [2 marks] (d) $1-P(A\cup B)=0.3$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Use the addition rule for the intersection. Independence holds exactly when $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$.

subtopic: Two-way table probabilities
statement: A survey of 200 people records their gender and their main way of traveling to work. $\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|}\hline & Bus & Bicycle & Walk \\ \hline Male & 30 & 25 & 45 \\ \hline Female & 40 & 35 & 25 \\ \hline \end{array}$ A person is chosen at random from the 200 people. (a) Find the probability that the person cycles to work. [1] (b) Given that the person walks to work, find the probability that the person is female. [2] (c) Find the probability that the person is male and does not walk to work. [2]
markscheme: (a) Total cycling $=60$, so $P=\dfrac{60}{200}=0.3$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Total walking $=70$ [M1] $P(F\mid W)=\dfrac{25}{70}=\dfrac{5}{14}=0.357$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Males not walking $=30+25=55$ [M1] $P=\dfrac{55}{200}=0.275$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Add the row and column totals first so that every probability can be read from the table. For a 'given that' question, divide by the total of the condition's row or column.

subtopic: Drawing balls without replacement
statement: A bag contains $5$ red, $4$ blue and $3$ green balls. Three balls are drawn at random, one after another, without replacement. (a) Find the probability that all three balls are red. [2] (b) Find the probability that the three balls are three different colors. [3] (c) Given that the first ball drawn is red, find the probability that at least one of the other two balls is blue. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{5}{12}\times\dfrac{4}{11}\times\dfrac{3}{10}$ [M1]; $\dfrac{1}{22}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) one color each in a given order: $\dfrac{5\times4\times3}{12\times11\times10}$ [M1]; there are $3!=6$ orders [M1]; $\dfrac{6\times60}{1320}=\dfrac{3}{11}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) after a red ball there are $4$ red, $4$ blue and $3$ green balls (11 in all) [A1]; $P(\text{no blue})=\dfrac{7\times6}{11\times10}=\dfrac{21}{55}$ [M1]; $1-\dfrac{21}{55}=\dfrac{34}{55}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: For at least one, use the complement. Remember that the pool shrinks after each draw.

subtopic: Binomial probabilities for late parcels
statement: (a) A courier company delivers $15\%$ of its parcels late, independently of each other. A random sample of $20$ parcels is taken. Let $X$ be the number delivered late. Find $\mathrm{P}(X=3)$. [2] (b) Find $\mathrm{P}(X\leq2)$. [2] (c) Find $\mathrm{P}(X\geq5)$. [2] (d) Find the expected number of late parcels in the sample. [1]
tips: State the distribution first. For 'at least' probabilities, subtract the cumulative probability of the number just below from $1$.

subtopic: Conditional probabilities when one event is contained in another
statement: Events $A$ and $B$ satisfy $P(A)=0.3$ and $P(B)=0.6$, and $A\subset B$. (a) Write down $P(A\cap B)$ and $P(A\cup B)$. [2] (b) Find $P(A\mid B)$ and $P(B\mid A)$. [2] (c) Show that $A$ and $B$ are not independent. [1]
tips: If one event is a subset of the other, the intersection is the smaller event.

subtopic: Independent events leading to a quadratic equation
statement: The independent events $A$ and $B$ satisfy $P(A)=p$, $P(B)=p+0.3$ and $P(A\cap B)=0.18$. (a) Show that $p^2+0.3p-0.18=0$. [2] (b) Find $P(A)$, justifying your choice of root. [3] (c) Find $P(A\cup B)$. [2]
tips: Form the equation from $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$ and discard any root outside $[0,1]$.

subtopic: Two counters drawn without replacement
statement: A bag contains $5$ red and $3$ blue counters. Two counters are drawn at random, one after the other, without replacement. (a) Find the probability that both counters are red. [2] (b) Find the probability that the counters are different colors. [2] (c) Given that the second counter is red, find the probability that the first counter was also red. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{5}{8}\times\dfrac{4}{7}$ [M1] $=\frac{5}{14}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $P=1-P(RR)-P(BB)$ [M1] $=\frac{15}{28}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $P(\text{2nd red})=\dfrac{5}{8}\cdot\dfrac{4}{7}+\dfrac{3}{8}\cdot\dfrac{5}{7}=0.625$ [A1]; conditional $\dfrac{P(RR)}{P(\text{2nd red})}$ [M1] $=\frac{4}{7}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Draw a tree diagram; after the first draw the numbers in the bag change.

subtopic: Poisson quiet days, binomial counts and conditional arrangements
statement: (a) A help desk receives emails at a rate that follows a Poisson distribution with mean $2.4$ per day. A day is called quiet if it receives at most one email. Find the probability that a day is quiet. [2] (b) Over a period of $7$ days (assumed independent), find the probability that at least $3$ days are quiet. [3] (c) The mean rate changes to $\lambda$ emails per day. Find the value of $\lambda$ for which the probability that a day is quiet is exactly $0.5$. [3] (d) With this value of $\lambda$, each day is quiet with probability $0.5$. Find the smallest number of days $n$ such that the probability that at least one day is quiet is at least $0.999$. [3] (e) In a particular $7$-day week, exactly $3$ days were quiet. Assuming that every day has the same probability of being quiet, find the probability that the first two days of the week were both quiet. [3]
markscheme: (a) $X\sim\mathrm{Po}(2.4)$ [M1] $\mathrm{P}(X\leq1)=0.308$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $Y\sim\mathrm{B}(7,\,0.3084)$ [M1] $\mathrm{P}(Y\geq3)=1-\mathrm{P}(Y\leq2)$ [M1] $=0.372$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $e^{-\lambda}(1+\lambda)=0.5$ [M1] solve using GDC [M1] $\lambda=1.68$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $1-0.5^n\geq0.999$ [M1] $0.5^n\leq0.001$, so $n\geq\dfrac{\ln0.001}{\ln0.5}=9.966$ [A1] $n=10$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) Each choice of $3$ quiet days out of $7$ is equally likely, giving $\binom73=35$ arrangements [M1] Arrangements with days $1$ and $2$ quiet: the third quiet day is any of the other $5$ days, so $5$ arrangements [A1] Probability $=\dfrac{5}{35}=\dfrac{1}{7}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: For part (e) the actual probability of a quiet day is irrelevant once the number of quiet days is fixed: every arrangement of the $3$ quiet days among the $7$ is equally likely. Use the GDC solver for the transcendental equation in part (c).

subtopic: Mutually exclusive and independent events with an unknown probability
statement: Events $A$ and $B$ satisfy $P(A)=0.3$, $P(B)=k$ and $P(A\cup B)=0.6$. (a) Find $k$ if $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive. [2] (b) Find $k$ if $A$ and $B$ are independent. [3] (c) Explain why $A$ and $B$ cannot be both mutually exclusive and independent here. [1]
markscheme: (a) $P(A\cap B)=0$ so $0.3+k=0.6$ [M1]; $k=0.3$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $P(A\cap B)=0.3k$ [A1]; $0.3+k-0.3k=0.6$ [M1]; $k=\dfrac37$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) If both, $P(A\cap B)=0$ and $0.3k=0$ would need $k=0$, which contradicts $k=0.3$ [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Mutually exclusive events have $P(A\cap B)=0$; independent events have $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$.

subtopic: Testing the independence of events on two dice
statement: Two fair dice are rolled. Let $B$ be the event that the first die shows $3$, $A$ the event that the sum is $7$, $C$ the event that the sum is $8$, and $E$ the event that the sum is even. (a) Show that $A$ and $B$ are independent. [3] (b) Determine whether $C$ and $B$ are independent. [3] (c) Determine whether $E$ and $B$ are independent. [2]
markscheme: (a) $P(A)=\dfrac16$, $P(B)=\dfrac16$ [A1] $P(A\cap B)=P(3,4)=\dfrac1{36}$ [A1] equals $P(A)P(B)$, so independent [R1] [3 marks] (b) $P(C)=\dfrac5{36}$ [A1] $P(B\cap C)=P(3,5)=\dfrac1{36}$ [A1] $P(B)P(C)=\dfrac5{216}\ne\dfrac1{36}$, so not independent [R1] [3 marks] (c) $P(E)=\dfrac12$ and $P(E\cap B)=\dfrac3{36}=\dfrac1{12}$ [A1] $=\dfrac12\times\dfrac16$ so independent [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Events are independent when $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$. List the outcomes of the intersection explicitly.

subtopic: Two-way table probabilities and independence
statement: A school surveyed 120 students about their diets. The numbers of people in each category are: Vegetarian and Year 12: 9; Vegetarian and Year 13: 21; Not vegetarian and Year 12: 27; Not vegetarian and Year 13: 63. One person is chosen at random. Let $A$ be the event 'Vegetarian' and $B$ the event 'Year 12'. (a) Find $P(A)$ and $P(A\cap B)$. [2] (b) Find $P(A\mid B)$. [2] (c) Determine whether $A$ and $B$ are independent, justifying your answer. [3]
markscheme: (a) $P(A)=\dfrac{30}{120}=\frac{1}{4}$ [A1] $P(A\cap B)=\dfrac{9}{120}=\frac{3}{40}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $P(A\mid B)=\dfrac{9}{36}$ [M1] $=\frac{1}{4}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $P(B)=\dfrac{36}{120}=\frac{3}{10}$ [A1] $P(A)P(B)=\frac{3}{40}$ [M1] this equals $P(A\cap B)=\frac{3}{40}$, so $A$ and $B$ are independent [R1] [3 marks]
tips: Independence means $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$, equivalently $P(A\mid B)=P(A)$. Check it with exact fractions.

subtopic: Binomial distribution in a sports context
statement: A basketball player scores on each free throw with probability $0.72$, independently of other throws. In a practice session she takes $15$ free throws. Let $X$ be the number of throws she scores. (a) Find the probability that she scores exactly $11$ throws. [2] (b) Find the probability that she scores at least $12$ throws. [2] (c) Find the probability that she scores more throws than the mean number of throws scored. [2] (d) She now takes $n$ throws. Find the smallest value of $n$ for which the probability that she misses at least once exceeds $0.99$. [3]
tips: In part (c) the mean is not an integer, so translate carefully: scoring more than $10.8$ means scoring at least $11$. In part (d) use the complement, 'at least one miss' is $1-P(\text{no misses})$.

subtopic: Poisson sums and combined distributions
statement: The number of typing errors on a page of a report written by Anya follows a Poisson distribution with mean $0.8$. The number of typing errors on a page written by Ben follows an independent Poisson distribution with mean $1.3$. A page is formed by combining a section typed by Anya with a section typed by Ben, so that the total number of errors, $T$, on the page is the sum of the two numbers of errors. (a) Write down the distribution of $T$ and find $P(T=2)$. [2] (b) Given that $T=2$, find the probability that Anya made exactly one error. [3] (c) A report has $12$ independent pages, each with the distribution of $T$. Find the probability that at most one page contains no errors. [3]
tips: The sum of independent Poisson variables is Poisson with the means added. In part (b), 'one error each' is the only way to have $A=1$ and total $2$, so the numerator is a product of two single-error probabilities.

subtopic: Conditional probability from a two-way table
statement: A gym surveys $200$ people. The numbers who are members, by age group, are given as (age group, members, non-members): Under $30$: $48$ and $32$; $30$ to $50$: $36$ and $64$; Over $50$: $8$ and $12$. One person is chosen at random. (a) Find the probability that the person is a member. [2] (b) Find the probability that the person is under $30$ given that the person is a member, as a simplified fraction. [2] (c) Find $P(\text{member}\mid\text{under }30)$ and use it to decide whether membership and being under $30$ are independent. [3]
markscheme: (a) total members $92$ [A1]; $\dfrac{92}{200}=0.46$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac{48}{92}$ [M1]; $\dfrac{12}{23}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\dfrac{48}{80}=0.6$ [A1]; $0.6\ne0.46=P(\text{member})$ [M1]; not independent [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Events $A$ and $B$ are independent when $P(A\mid B)=P(A)$.

subtopic: Conditional probability from percentages
statement: In a company, $60\%$ of employees commute by car. Of the car commuters, $25\%$ arrive late, and of the other employees, $10\%$ arrive late. (a) Find the probability that a randomly chosen employee arrives late. [3] (b) Given that an employee arrives late, find the probability that the employee commutes by car. [2] (c) Two employees are chosen at random, independently. Find the probability that exactly one of them arrives late, correct to three significant figures. [2]
tips: Use a tree diagram with the car commuters and other employees as the first branches. Divide by the total probability for the reverse conditional.

subtopic: Independent events leading to a quadratic
statement: Events $A$ and $B$ are independent, with $P(B)=p$ and $P(A)=2p$, where $0<p<\frac12$. It is given that $P(A\cup B)=0.52$. (a) Show that $2p^2-3p+0.52=0$. [2] (b) Hence find the value of $p$. [4] (c) Find $P(A'\mid B)$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)=2p^2$ [M1] $P(A\cup B)=2p+p-2p^2=0.52$, so $2p^2-3p+0.52=0$ [AG] [M1] [2 marks] (b) Attempt to solve the quadratic, e.g. using the quadratic formula [M1] $p=\dfrac{3\pm\sqrt{9-4.16}}{4}=\dfrac{3\pm2.2}{4}$ [A1] $p=0.2$ or $p=1.3$ [A1] Since $p<\tfrac12$, reject $1.3$, so $p=0.2$ [R1] [4 marks] (c) $A'$ and $B$ are independent, so $P(A'\mid B)=P(A')=1-0.4=0.6$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Independence gives $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$; substituting into the addition rule produces a quadratic in $p$. Always check each root against the stated restriction on the parameter.

subtopic: Conditional probability and Bayes' theorem
statement: A factory produces electronic components, $3\%$ of which are faulty. A test is used to detect faulty components. If a component is faulty, the test gives a positive result with probability $0.92$. If a component is not faulty, the test gives a positive result with probability $0.05$. (a) Find the probability that a randomly chosen component gives a positive result. [2] (b) Given that a component gives a positive result, find the probability that it is faulty. [2] (c) Each component that gives a positive result is tested a second time. The results of the two tests are independent for a given component. Find the probability that a component is faulty, given that it gives a positive result on both tests. [3]
markscheme: (a) $0.03\times 0.92+0.97\times 0.05$ [M1] $=0.0761$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac{0.03\times 0.92}{0.0761}$ [M1] $=0.363$ ($0.362680\ldots$) [A1] [2 marks] (c) $P(\text{both positive})=0.03\times 0.92^2+0.97\times 0.05^2=0.0278170$ [M1][A1] $P(\text{faulty}\mid\text{both positive})=\dfrac{0.03\times 0.92^2}{0.0278170}=0.913$ ($0.912823\ldots$) [A1] Alternative: use the answer to part (b) as the new prior: $\dfrac{0.36268\times 0.92}{0.36268\times 0.92+0.63732\times 0.05}=0.913$. [3 marks]
tips: A tree diagram organizes Bayes' theorem problems clearly: the denominator is the sum of all branches ending in the given event. In part (c) the independence applies only within each group (faulty or not faulty), so multiply along each branch separately.

subtopic: Two-way table probabilities and independence
statement: A company surveyed 100 employees about how they travel to work. The numbers of people in each category are: Cycle and Under 30: 30; Cycle and 30 or over: 10; Drive and Under 30: 20; Drive and 30 or over: 40. One person is chosen at random. Let $A$ be the event 'Cycle' and $B$ the event 'Under 30'. (a) Find $P(A)$ and $P(A\cap B)$. [2] (b) Find $P(A\mid B)$. [2] (c) Determine whether $A$ and $B$ are independent, justifying your answer. [3]
markscheme: (a) $P(A)=\dfrac{40}{100}=\frac{2}{5}$ [A1] $P(A\cap B)=\dfrac{30}{100}=\frac{3}{10}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $P(A\mid B)=\dfrac{30}{50}$ [M1] $=\frac{3}{5}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $P(B)=\dfrac{50}{100}=\frac{1}{2}$ [A1] $P(A)P(B)=\frac{1}{5}$ [M1] this is not equal to $P(A\cap B)=\frac{3}{10}$, so $A$ and $B$ are not independent [R1] [3 marks]
tips: Independence means $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$, equivalently $P(A\mid B)=P(A)$. Check it with exact fractions.

subtopic: Conditional probability from a two-way frequency summary
statement: (a) A swimming club has $150$ members: $90$ adults and $60$ juniors. Of the adults, $36$ compete in races, and of the juniors, $42$ compete in races. A member is chosen at random. Find the probability that the member competes in races. [2] (b) Given that the member competes in races, find the probability that the member is an adult. [2] (c) Find the probability that the member is a junior who does not compete. [1] (d) Show that being an adult and competing in races are not independent events. [2]
markscheme: (a) Number competing $=36+42=78$ [M1] $\dfrac{78}{150}=\dfrac{13}{25}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac{36}{78}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{6}{13}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\dfrac{60-42}{150}=\dfrac{18}{150}=\dfrac{3}{25}$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) $\mathrm{P}(\text{competes}\mid\text{adult})=\dfrac{36}{90}=0.4$ [M1] This differs from $\mathrm{P}(\text{competes})=\dfrac{13}{25}=0.52$, so the events are not independent [R1] [2 marks]
tips: For conditional probability from counts, restrict attention to the given group and divide by its size. Independence can be checked by comparing a conditional probability with the unconditional one.

subtopic: Sample space for three dice
statement: Three fair four-sided dice, each numbered $1$ to $4$, are rolled. Let $S$ be the sum of the three scores and $P$ their product. (a) Find $P(S=9)$. [3] (b) Find the probability that $P$ is even. [2] (c) Given that $S=9$, find the probability that $P$ is even. [3]
markscheme: (a) total outcomes $4^3=64$ [A1] number of outcomes with sum $9$ is $10$ [M1] $P(S=9)=\frac{5}{32}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $P$ is odd only if all scores are odd: $\left(\dfrac12\right)^3=\dfrac18$ [M1] $P(P\text{ even})=\dfrac78$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) outcomes with $S=9$ and $P$ odd: $1$ [M1][A1] $P=\dfrac{9}{10}=\frac{9}{10}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: With three dice it is quicker to count outcomes with a systematic list than to draw a grid. A product is odd only when every factor is odd.

subtopic: Union, intersection and independence
statement: Events $A$ and $B$ are such that $P(A)=0.4$, $P(B)=0.5$ and $P(A\cup B)=0.7$. (a) Find $P(A\cap B)$. [2] (b) Determine whether $A$ and $B$ are independent. [2] (c) Find $P(A\mid B')$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$ [M1] $0.7=0.9-P(A\cap B)$, so $P(A\cap B)=0.2$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $P(A)P(B)=0.4\times0.5=0.2$ [M1] This equals $P(A\cap B)$, so $A$ and $B$ are independent [A1] [2 marks] (c) $P(A\mid B')=\dfrac{P(A\cap B')}{P(B')}=\dfrac{0.4-0.2}{0.5}=0.4$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: To test independence, compare $P(A\cap B)$ with $P(A)P(B)$ and state the conclusion explicitly. Use $P(A\cap B')=P(A)-P(A\cap B)$ for conditional probabilities involving a complement.

subtopic: Independence implies equal conditional probabilities
statement: The events $A$ and $B$ satisfy $P(A)=0.6$, $P(B\mid A)=0.5$ and $P(B\mid A')=0.5$. (a) Find $P(B)$. [2] (b) Hence show that $A$ and $B$ are independent. [2] (c) Hence write down $P(A'\cap B')$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $P(B)=0.6\times0.5+0.4\times0.5$ [M1] $=0.5$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $P(A\cap B)=0.6\times0.5=0.3$ [M1] $P(A)P(B)=0.6\times0.5=0.3$, so independent [R1] [2 marks] (c) $A'$ and $B'$ are also independent [M1] $P(A')P(B')=0.4\times0.5=0.2$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: If $P(B\mid A)=P(B\mid A')$ then $B$ does not depend on $A$. Independence of $A$ and $B$ extends to their complements.

subtopic: Two-set Venn diagram counts
statement: In a class of 40 students, 22 study French, 18 study Spanish and 7 study both languages. A student is chosen at random from the class. (a) Find the probability that the student studies neither language. [2] (b) Given that the student studies Spanish, find the probability that the student also studies French. [2] (c) Find the probability that the student studies exactly one of the two languages. [2]
markscheme: (a) Number studying at least one language $=22+18-7=33$ [M1] $P(\text{neither})=\dfrac{7}{40}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $P(F\mid S)=\dfrac{7}{18}$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (c) Only French $=15$, only Spanish $=11$ [M1] $P=\dfrac{26}{40}=\dfrac{13}{20}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Fill in the overlap first when building a Venn diagram, then subtract it from each set total. 'Given that' restricts the sample space to one set only.

subtopic: Shared values and the complement rule
statement: Each person in a group has a birthday that is equally likely to be any of $365$ days, independently of others (ignore leap years). A group of $m$ people is chosen. (a) Find the probability that in a group of 5 people at least two share a birthday. [3] (b) Find the smallest group size for which this probability exceeds 0.5. [3]
tips: The complement of 'at least two share' is 'all different', which is a product of decreasing fractions.

subtopic: Probability with a transferred item
statement: Urn $A$ contains 3 red balls and 2 blue balls. Urn $B$ contains 2 red balls and 4 blue balls. One ball is chosen at random from urn $A$ and placed into urn $B$. A ball is then chosen at random from urn $B$. (a) Find the probability that the ball chosen from urn $B$ is red. [3] (b) Given that the ball chosen from urn $B$ is red, find the probability that the ball moved from urn $A$ was red. [3]
markscheme: (a) If a red ball is moved, urn $B$ has 3 red among 7 balls; if a blue ball is moved, urn $B$ has 2 red among 7 balls [M1] $P(\text{red from }B)=\dfrac35\times\dfrac37+\dfrac25\times\dfrac27$ [A1] $=\dfrac{9}{35}+\dfrac{4}{35}=\dfrac{13}{35}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $P(\text{moved red}\mid\text{red})=\dfrac{9/35}{13/35}$ [M1][A1] $=\dfrac{9}{13}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Condition on what was transferred, because the composition of the second urn depends on it. Then reverse the conditioning with Bayes' theorem using the same two branch products.

subtopic: Conditional probability from a two-way table
statement: A survey of 250 commuters classified each by how they travel and whether they arrive late. Frequencies: $\begin{pmatrix} 48 & 62 \\ 32 & 108 \end{pmatrix}$ (rows: bus or train, car; columns: late, on time) (a) Find the probability that a randomly chosen person is in the first row. [1] (b) Find the probability that a person is in the first row, given that they are in the first column. [2] (c) Determine whether being in the first row and being in the first column are independent events. [3] (d) Two different people are chosen at random without replacement. Find the probability that both are in the first column. [3]
tips: Conditional probability restricts the sample space to the given group; the denominator is that group's total.

subtopic: Mathematical induction for a series
statement: (a) Find the value of $\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{3} r\cdot 3^{r}$. [1] (b) Prove by mathematical induction that $$\sum_{r=1}^{n} r\cdot 3^{r}=\frac{(2n-1)3^{n+1}+3}{4}$$ for all $n\in\mathbb{Z}^+$. [6]
markscheme: (a) $3+18+81=102$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) For $n=1$: LHS $=3$, RHS $=\dfrac{1\cdot 9+3}{4}=3$, so the result is true for $n=1$ [A1] Assume true for $n=k$: $\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{k} r\cdot 3^{r}=\frac{(2k-1)3^{k+1}+3}{4}$ [M1] Then $\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{k+1} r\cdot 3^{r}=\frac{(2k-1)3^{k+1}+3}{4}+(k+1)3^{k+1}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{(2k-1)3^{k+1}+4(k+1)3^{k+1}+3}{4}=\dfrac{(6k+3)3^{k+1}+3}{4}$ [A1] $=\dfrac{(2k+1)3^{k+2}+3}{4}=\dfrac{(2(k+1)-1)3^{(k+1)+1}+3}{4}$ [A1] Since the result is true for $n=1$, and true for $n=k$ implies true for $n=k+1$, it is true for all $n\in\mathbb{Z}^+$ by mathematical induction [R1] Award [R1] only if at least three of the previous marks are earned. [6 marks]
tips: Write the target expression for $n=k+1$ before you start the algebra so you know what to aim for; here the key step is factorizing $3(2k+1)$ out of $6k+3$. Your concluding statement must mention both the base case and the inductive step.

subtopic: Proof by contradiction that root 2 is irrational
statement: (a) Prove that if $a$ is an integer and $a^2$ is even, then $a$ is even. [3] (b) Hence prove by contradiction that $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational. [5]
markscheme: (a) Prove the contrapositive: if $a$ is odd then $a^2$ is odd. Let $a=2k+1$, $k\in\mathbb{Z}$ [M1] $a^2=4k^2+4k+1=2\left(2k^2+2k\right)+1$ [A1] which is odd. So if $a^2$ is even then $a$ is even [R1] [3 marks] (b) Assume $\sqrt{2}$ is rational, so $\sqrt{2}=\frac{p}{q}$ with $p,q\in\mathbb{Z}^+$ having no common factor [M1] Then $p^2=2q^2$ [A1] So $p^2$ is even, hence $p$ is even by part (a) [R1] Let $p=2m$: $4m^2=2q^2$, so $q^2=2m^2$ [M1] So $q^2$ is even, hence $q$ is even. Then $p$ and $q$ share the factor $2$, contradicting the assumption. Hence $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational [R1] [5 marks]
tips: Begin every contradiction proof with an explicit assumption (here: lowest terms). The contradiction must be stated clearly at the end, and part (a) should be quoted by name when used.

subtopic: Direct proof of an inequality for positive reals
statement: Let $a$ and $b$ be positive real numbers. (a) Prove that $(a+b)\left(\dfrac1a+\dfrac1b\right)\ge4$. [3] (b) State when equality holds. [1]
markscheme: (a) expand: $2+\dfrac ab+\dfrac ba$ [M1] $\dfrac ab+\dfrac ba-2=\dfrac{(a-b)^2}{ab}\ge0$ [A1] so the product is at least $4$ [R1] [3 marks] (b) when $a=b$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Combine the extra terms into a single fraction with a perfect square on top.

subtopic: Proof by induction: divisibility
statement: Prove by induction that $7^n-1$ is divisible by $6$ for all $n\in\mathbb Z^+$. [6]
markscheme: $n=1$: $7-1=6$, divisible by $6$ [A1] assume $7^m-1=6M$ for some integer $M$ [M1] $7^{m+1}-1=7\cdot7^m-1=7(6M+1)-1$ [M1] $=42M+6=6(7M+1)$ [A1] divisible by $6$, so true for $n=m+1$ [R1] true for $n=1$ and $n=m\Rightarrow n=m+1$, so true for all $n\in\mathbb Z^+$ [R1] [6 marks]
tips: Write the assumption as an equation with an integer multiple and substitute it into the case $n=m+1$.

subtopic: Induction for the nth derivative of a product
statement: Let $f(x)=x\,e^{2x}$. Use mathematical induction to prove that the $n$th derivative of $f$ is $$f^{(n)}(x)=2^{\,n-1}(2x+n)\,e^{2x},\quad n\in\mathbb{Z}^+.$$ [7]
markscheme: Let $P(n)$ be the statement $f^{(n)}(x)=2^{n-1}(2x+n)e^{2x}$. Base case $n=1$: $f'(x)=e^{2x}+2xe^{2x}=(2x+1)e^{2x}$ [M1] This equals $2^{0}(2x+1)e^{2x}$, so $P(1)$ is true [A1] Assume $P(k)$ is true for some $k\in\mathbb{Z}^+$ [M1] $f^{(k+1)}(x)=\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[2^{k-1}(2x+k)e^{2x}\right]$ [M1] $=2^{k-1}\left[2e^{2x}+2(2x+k)e^{2x}\right]$ [A1] $=2^{k-1}\cdot 2\,e^{2x}\left(2x+k+1\right)=2^{k}\left(2x+(k+1)\right)e^{2x}$ [A1] So $P(k)$ true implies $P(k+1)$ true. Since $P(1)$ is true, $P(n)$ is true for all $n\in\mathbb{Z}^+$ by mathematical induction [R1] [7 marks]
tips: Use the product rule on $2^{k-1}(2x+k)e^{2x}$ and factor out $2^{k-1}\cdot 2\,e^{2x}$ to reach the target form. The target for $n=k+1$ is $2^{k}(2x+k+1)e^{2x}$, so keep it in view.

subtopic: Induction: Bernoulli's inequality
statement: (a) Prove by mathematical induction that $(1+x)^n\ge1+nx$ for all $n\in\mathbb{Z}^+$, where $x>-1$ is a fixed real number. [7] (b) Hence show that $(1.003)^{400}>2$. [2]
markscheme: (a) For $n=1$: both sides equal $1+x$, so true for $n=1$ [A1] Assume true for $n=k$: $(1+x)^k\ge1+kx$ [M1] Since $x>-1$, we have $1+x>0$, so multiplying both sides of the inequality by $1+x$ preserves it [R1] $(1+x)^{k+1}\ge(1+kx)(1+x)$ [M1] $=1+(k+1)x+kx^2$ [A1] Since $kx^2\ge0$, $1+(k+1)x+kx^2\ge1+(k+1)x$, hence $(1+x)^{k+1}\ge1+(k+1)x$, which is the statement for $n=k+1$ [R1] True for $n=1$, and true for $n=k$ implies true for $n=k+1$, so true for all $n\in\mathbb{Z}^+$ by mathematical induction [R1] [7 marks] (b) Use $x=0.003$ and $n=400$ (valid since $x>-1$) [M1] $(1.003)^{400}\ge1+400\times0.003=2.2>2$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: When an inequality is multiplied by an expression, state why that expression is positive; this is where the condition $x>-1$ is used and it earns a reasoning mark.

subtopic: Direct proof: a number minus its reversal is divisible by 99
statement: A three-digit integer has digits $a$, $b$, $c$ (hundreds, tens, units), with $a>c$. The integer $N$ is formed from these digits, and $M$ is the integer formed by reversing them. Prove that $N-M$ is divisible by $99$. [4]
markscheme: $N=100a+10b+c$ and $M=100c+10b+a$ [A1] $N-M=99a-99c$ [M1] $=99(a-c)$ [A1] $a-c$ is an integer, so divisible by $99$ [R1] [4 marks]
tips: Write each number in terms of its digits and place values.

subtopic: Completing the square to prove a strict inequality
statement: Let $x,y\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Express $x^2+y^2-6x+10y+40$ in the form $(x-a)^2+(y-b)^2+c$, where $a,b,c$ are constants to be found. [3] (b) Hence prove that $x^2+y^2-6x+10y+40>0$ for all real $x$ and $y$, and state the minimum value of the expression. [2]
markscheme: (a) $x^2-6x=(x-3)^2-9$ and $y^2+10y=(y+5)^2-25$ [M1] Expression $=(x-3)^2+(y+5)^2-9-25+40$ [A1] $=(x-3)^2+(y+5)^2+6$ so $a=3$, $b=-5$, $c=6$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Since $(x-3)^2\ge0$ and $(y+5)^2\ge0$, the expression is $\ge6>0$ for all real $x,y$ [R1] The minimum value is $6$, attained at $x=3$, $y=-5$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A sum of squares plus a positive constant is always positive. Completing the square on each variable separately is the standard route to this type of result.

subtopic: Induction on higher derivatives of ln(1+x)
statement: Let $f(x)=\ln(1+x)$ for $x>-1$. (a) Find $f'(x)$, $f''(x)$ and $f'''(x)$. [3] (b) Prove by mathematical induction that $f^{(n)}(x)=\dfrac{(-1)^{n-1}(n-1)!}{(1+x)^n}$ for all $n\in\mathbb{Z}^+$, where $f^{(n)}$ is the $n$th derivative of $f$. [6]
markscheme: (a) $f'(x)=\frac{1}{1+x}$ [A1] $f''(x)=-\frac{1}{(1+x)^2}$ [A1] $f'''(x)=\frac{2}{(1+x)^3}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) For $n=1$: $\frac{(-1)^0\,0!}{(1+x)^1}=\frac{1}{1+x}=f'(x)$, so true for $n=1$ [A1] Assume true for $n=k$: $f^{(k)}(x)=(-1)^{k-1}(k-1)!\,(1+x)^{-k}$ [M1] Differentiating: $f^{(k+1)}(x)=(-1)^{k-1}(k-1)!\cdot(-k)(1+x)^{-k-1}$ [M1] $=(-1)^{k}\,k!\,(1+x)^{-(k+1)}$ using $(-1)^{k-1}\cdot(-1)=(-1)^k$ and $(k-1)!\,k=k!$ [A1] $=\frac{(-1)^{(k+1)-1}\left((k+1)-1\right)!}{(1+x)^{k+1}}$, which is the statement for $n=k+1$ [A1] True for $n=1$, and true for $n=k$ implies true for $n=k+1$, so true for all $n\in\mathbb{Z}^+$ by mathematical induction [R1] [6 marks]
tips: Part (a) shows the pattern you are trying to prove; use it to check the formula for $n=1,2,3$ before starting the induction. Keep track of the sign factor $(-1)^{k}$ carefully when differentiating.

subtopic: Direct proof of inequalities
statement: (a) Prove that $a^2+b^2\ge2ab$ for all $a,b\in\mathbb{R}$. [2] (b) Hence prove that $\dfrac{x}{y}+\dfrac{y}{x}\ge2$ for all $x,y>0$. [2] (c) Prove that $a^2+b^2+c^2\ge ab+bc+ca$ for all $a,b,c\in\mathbb{R}$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $(a-b)^2\ge0$ for all real $a,b$ [M1] Expanding, $a^2-2ab+b^2\ge0$, so $a^2+b^2\ge2ab$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac{x}{y}+\dfrac{y}{x}=\dfrac{x^2+y^2}{xy}$ [M1] and by part (a), $x^2+y^2\ge2xy$; dividing by $xy>0$ gives $\dfrac{x}{y}+\dfrac{y}{x}\ge2$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Consider $(a-b)^2+(b-c)^2+(c-a)^2\ge0$ [M1] Expanding, $2a^2+2b^2+2c^2-2ab-2bc-2ca\ge0$ [A1] Dividing by $2$ gives $a^2+b^2+c^2\ge ab+bc+ca$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Most inequality proofs start from the fact that a square is never negative. In part (b), note why dividing by $xy$ keeps the inequality direction: it needs $xy>0$.

subtopic: Number theory: remainders of powers
statement: An integer $N$ leaves remainder $3$ when divided by $7$. (a) Show that $N^2$ leaves remainder $2$ when divided by $7$. [3] (b) Show that $N^3$ leaves remainder $6$ when divided by $7$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $N=7k+3$, $k\in\mathbb{Z}$ [M1] $N^2=49k^2+42k+9=7\left(7k^2+6k+1\right)+2$ [A1] Since $7k^2+6k+1$ is an integer, the remainder is $2$ [R1] [3 marks] (b) $N^3=(7k+3)^3=343k^3+441k^2+189k+27$ [M1] $=7\left(49k^3+63k^2+27k+3\right)+6$ [A1] Since $49k^3+63k^2+27k+3$ is an integer, the remainder is $6$ [R1] [3 marks]
tips: Write the integer as $7k+3$, expand, and split off a multiple of $7$ so the remainder is clear. In part (b) you could also use $N^3=N\cdot N^2$.

subtopic: Induction: factorial exceeds a power of two
statement: Prove by mathematical induction that $n!>2^n$ for all integers $n\ge4$. [6]
markscheme: $n=4$: $24>16$, true [A1] assume $m!>2^m$ for some $m\ge4$ [M1] $(m+1)!=(m+1)\,m!>(m+1)2^m$ [M1][A1] $m+1\ge5>2$ so $(m+1)2^m>2\times2^m=2^{m+1}$ [A1] true for $n=4$ and $n=m\Rightarrow n=m+1$, so true for all $n\ge4$ [R1] [6 marks]
tips: The base case is not $n=1$, because the inequality fails for small $n$. Use that $m+1>2$ in the inductive step.

subtopic: Induction with a second-order recurrence
statement: A sequence is defined by $u_1=1$, $u_2=5$ and $u_{n+2}=5u_{n+1}-6u_n$ for $n\in\mathbb{Z}^+$. (a) Find $u_3$. [1] (b) Prove by mathematical induction that $u_n=3^n-2^n$ for all $n\in\mathbb{Z}^+$. [6]
markscheme: (a) $u_3=5\times5-6\times1=19$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) For $n=1$: $3-2=1=u_1$ and for $n=2$: $9-4=5=u_2$, so true for $n=1$ and $n=2$ [A1] Assume true for $n=k$ and $n=k+1$: $u_k=3^k-2^k$ and $u_{k+1}=3^{k+1}-2^{k+1}$ [M1] Then $u_{k+2}=5\left(3^{k+1}-2^{k+1}\right)-6\left(3^k-2^k\right)$ [M1] $=3^k(15-6)-2^k(10-6)$ [A1] $=9\cdot3^k-4\cdot2^k=3^{k+2}-2^{k+2}$ [A1] which is the statement for $n=k+2$. True for $n=1,2$, and true for $n=k,k+1$ implies true for $n=k+2$, so true for all $n\in\mathbb{Z}^+$ by mathematical induction [R1] [6 marks]
tips: A two-term recurrence needs two base cases and an assumption for two consecutive values. Express every power in terms of $3^k$ and $2^k$ before collecting.

subtopic: Proof by induction: sum of a series
statement: Prove by mathematical induction that $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{n}2^{k} k=2^{n + 1} \left(n - 1\right) + 2$ for all $n\in\mathbb Z^+$. [7]
markscheme: for $n=1$: LHS $=2$ and RHS $=2$, equal, so true for $n=1$ [A1][A1] assume true for $n=m$: $\sum_{k=1}^m2^{k} k=2^{m + 1} \left(m - 1\right) + 2$ [M1] then $\sum_{k=1}^{m+1}=2^{m + 1} \left(m - 1\right) + 2+2^{m + 1} \left(m + 1\right)$ [M1] $=4 \cdot 2^{m} m + 2$ after simplifying, which is the formula with $n=m+1$ [A1] so true for $n=m+1$ [R1] true for $n=1$ and true for $n=m$ implies true for $n=m+1$, so true for all $n\in\mathbb Z^+$ by induction [R1] [7 marks]
tips: State the base case, the assumption, and the inductive step, and finish with the conclusion. In the step, add the next term to the assumed sum and factorize to match the target form.

subtopic: Complex numbers: proof of the parallelogram law
statement: Let $z_1,z_2\in\mathbb{C}$. (a) Show that $|z_1+z_2|^2+|z_1-z_2|^2=2|z_1|^2+2|z_2|^2$. [4] (b) Given that $|z_1|=3$, $|z_2|=5$ and $|z_1+z_2|=7$, find the exact value of $|z_1-z_2|$. [2]
tips: Replace each modulus squared by $zz^*$ and expand like ordinary brackets, remembering that $(z_1+z_2)^*=z_1^*+z_2^*$. Look for cross terms that cancel when adding.

subtopic: Induction: inequality
statement: Prove by mathematical induction that $2^n>n^2$ for all integers $n\ge5$. [7]
markscheme: For $n=5$: $2^5=32>25=5^2$, so true for $n=5$ [A1] Assume true for $n=k$ where $k\ge5$: $2^k>k^2$ [M1] Then $2^{k+1}=2\cdot2^k>2k^2$ [M1] Consider $2k^2-(k+1)^2=k^2-2k-1$ [M1] $=(k-1)^2-2\ge16-2=14>0$ for $k\ge5$ [A1] so $2k^2>(k+1)^2$ and hence $2^{k+1}>(k+1)^2$ [A1] True for $n=5$ and true for $n=k$ implies true for $n=k+1$, so true for all integers $n\ge5$ by mathematical induction [R1] [7 marks]
tips: In inequality inductions you must show the extra step that the bound you reach ($2k^2$) is at least the target ($(k+1)^2$), and this is where the condition $k\ge5$ is used.

subtopic: Proof by contradiction: rational roots
statement: Prove by contradiction that the equation $x^3+x+1=0$ has no rational roots. [6]
markscheme: Assume there is a rational root $x=\dfrac{p}{q}$, where $p,q\in\mathbb{Z}$, $q>0$, and $\dfrac pq$ is in lowest terms, so $p$ and $q$ are not both even [M1] Substituting and multiplying by $q^3$: $p^3+pq^2+q^3=0$ [M1] Case 1: $p,q$ both odd. Then $p^3$, $pq^2$, $q^3$ are all odd and their sum is odd, so cannot be $0$ [A1] Case 2: $p$ even, $q$ odd. Then $p^3$ and $pq^2$ are even and $q^3$ is odd, so the sum is odd [A1] Case 3: $p$ odd, $q$ even. Then $p^3$ is odd, while $pq^2$ and $q^3$ are even, so the sum is odd [A1] In every case the sum is odd and so is not $0$, a contradiction. Hence there are no rational roots [R1] [6 marks]
tips: Writing the fraction in lowest terms is what rules out the case where $p$ and $q$ are both even. Then check every parity case so that nothing is missed.

subtopic: Direct proof: product of two sums of two squares
statement: Let $a,b,c,d\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Show that $(a^2+b^2)(c^2+d^2)=(ac-bd)^2+(ad+bc)^2$. [3] (b) Hence write $13\times25$ as the sum of two squares of integers, by using $13=2^2+3^2$ and $25=3^2+4^2$. [2] (c) Find a way of writing $325$ as the sum of two squares of positive integers that is different from both $6^2+17^2$ and $1^2+18^2$. [2]
tips: In "show that" identities, expand each side separately and compare. Re-using an identity with a different assignment of the variables is a quick way to get a second solution in part (c).

subtopic: Direct proof: sum of four consecutive integers
statement: Let $n$ be an integer. (a) Show that the sum of the four consecutive integers $n,n+1,n+2,n+3$ is $4n+6$. [1] (b) Hence prove that the sum of four consecutive integers is never divisible by $4$. [2] (c) Given that every perfect square is of the form $4k$ or $4k+1$ for some integer $k$, prove that the sum of four consecutive integers is never a perfect square. [2]
markscheme: (a) $n+(n+1)+(n+2)+(n+3)=4n+6$ [M1] [AG] [1 mark] (b) $4n+6=4(n+1)+2$ [M1] So the sum leaves remainder $2$ when divided by $4$, hence is never divisible by $4$ [R1] [2 marks] (c) The sum is of the form $4m+2$ with $m=n+1\in\mathbb{Z}$ [M1] This is neither of the form $4k$ nor $4k+1$, so it is never a perfect square [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Rewrite the sum in the form $4m+r$ so the remainder is visible. A statement about remainders can be used to rule out whole families of values.

subtopic: Proof by induction: divisibility
statement: Prove by induction that $n^3+2n$ is divisible by $3$ for all $n\in\mathbb Z^+$. [7]
markscheme: $n=1$: $1+2=3$ [A1] assume $m^3+2m=3M$ [M1] $(m+1)^3+2(m+1)=m^3+3m^2+3m+1+2m+2$ [M1] $=\left(m^3+2m\right)+3\left(m^2+m+1\right)$ [A1] $=3M+3\left(m^2+m+1\right)=3\left(M+m^2+m+1\right)$ [A1] divisible by $3$ [R1] conclusion by induction [R1] [7 marks]
tips: Expand the cube and group the terms so that the assumed expression appears.

subtopic: Induction for a product of cosines and Viete's product
statement: (a) Prove by induction that, for all positive integers $n$ and all $\theta$ with $\sin\theta\ne0$, $\displaystyle\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}\cos\left(2^k\theta\right)=\cos\theta\cos2\theta\cos4\theta\cdots\cos\left(2^{n-1}\theta\right)=\dfrac{\sin\left(2^n\theta\right)}{2^n\sin\theta}$. [6] (b) Hence find the exact value of $\cos\dfrac\pi9\cos\dfrac{2\pi}9\cos\dfrac{4\pi}9$. [3] (c) By replacing $\theta$ with $\dfrac\theta{2^n}$ in the result of part (a), show that $\displaystyle\prod_{k=1}^{n}\cos\dfrac\theta{2^k}=\dfrac{\sin\theta}{2^n\sin\left(\theta/2^n\right)}$. [3] (d) Let $n\to\infty$ in part (c), using $\dfrac{\sin h}h\to1$ as $h\to0$, to show that $\cos\dfrac\theta2\cos\dfrac\theta4\cos\dfrac\theta8\cdots=\dfrac{\sin\theta}\theta$, and deduce the exact value of this infinite product when $\theta=\dfrac\pi2$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $n=1$: $\dfrac{\sin2\theta}{2\sin\theta}=\dfrac{2\sin\theta\cos\theta}{2\sin\theta}=\cos\theta$, so the result holds [A1] assume true for $n=m$ [M1] multiply by $\cos\left(2^m\theta\right)$: $\dfrac{\sin\left(2^m\theta\right)\cos\left(2^m\theta\right)}{2^m\sin\theta}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{\sin\left(2^{m+1}\theta\right)}{2^{m+1}\sin\theta}$ using $\sin2A=2\sin A\cos A$ [A1] [A1] true for $n=1$ and true for $n=m$ implies true for $n=m+1$, so true for all positive integers $n$ [R1] [6 marks] (b) $\theta=\dfrac\pi9$ and $n=3$ [M1] $=\dfrac{\sin\frac{8\pi}9}{8\sin\frac\pi9}$ [A1] $\sin\dfrac{8\pi}9=\sin\dfrac\pi9$, so the value is $\dfrac18$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) the product in (a) with $\theta\to\dfrac\theta{2^n}$ has factors $\cos\dfrac{2^k\theta}{2^n}=\cos\dfrac\theta{2^{n-k}}$ for $k=0,\dots,n-1$ [M1] with $j=n-k$ these are $\cos\dfrac\theta{2^j}$ for $j=1,\dots,n$ [A1] the right side becomes $\dfrac{\sin\theta}{2^n\sin\left(\theta/2^n\right)}$ [AG] [A1] [3 marks] (d) $2^n\sin\dfrac\theta{2^n}=\theta\times\dfrac{\sin h}h$ with $h=\dfrac\theta{2^n}\to0$ [M1] this tends to $\theta$, so the product tends to $\dfrac{\sin\theta}\theta$ [A1] for $\theta=\dfrac\pi2$: $\dfrac{1}{\pi/2}=\dfrac2\pi$ [A1] and the product is $\cos\dfrac\pi4\cos\dfrac\pi8\cos\dfrac\pi{16}\cdots=\dfrac2\pi$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: In the induction step multiply by the next cosine and use the double-angle formula for sine. Remember that $\sin\theta\ne0$ is needed so that you can divide by it.

subtopic: Strong induction: Fibonacci numbers are less than powers of 2
statement: The Fibonacci sequence is defined by $F_1=F_2=1$ and $F_{n+2}=F_{n+1}+F_n$ for $n\ge1$. Prove that $F_n<2^n$ for all positive integers $n$. Prove the statement by strong induction. [6]
markscheme: $F_1=1<2$ and $F_2=1<4$ [A1] assume $F_k<2^k$ for all $k\le m$, where $m\ge2$ [M1] $F_{m+1}=F_m+F_{m-1}$ [M1] $<2^m+2^{m-1}$ [A1] $<2^m+2^m=2^{m+1}$ [A1] true for $n=1,2$ and whenever true up to $m$ it is true for $m+1$, so true for all $n$ [R1] [6 marks]
tips: The recurrence uses two previous terms, so the inductive hypothesis must cover both $F_m$ and $F_{m-1}$, and two base cases are required.

subtopic: Fibonacci identities by induction
statement: The Fibonacci numbers are defined by $F_1=1$, $F_2=1$ and $F_{n+2}=F_{n+1}+F_n$ for $n\ge1$. This question proves identities involving them. (a) Write down $F_3,\dots,F_8$. [2] (b) Prove by induction that $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^nF_k=F_{n+2}-1$ for $n\ge1$. [5] (c) Prove by induction that $F_{n+1}^2-F_nF_{n+2}=(-1)^n$ for $n\ge1$. [6] (d) Use part (c) to find $F_{10}^2-F_9F_{11}$ without calculating the terms. [1] (e) Explain why consecutive Fibonacci numbers $F_n$ and $F_{n+1}$ have no common factor greater than $1$. [3]
tips: For the second identity expand $F_{m+3}$ using the recurrence and relate the result back to the assumption. The final argument is like the Euclidean algorithm.

subtopic: Induction: divisibility of 7 to the n minus 3 to the n
statement: Prove by mathematical induction that $7^n-3^n$ is divisible by $4$ for all positive integers $n$. [7]
markscheme: $n=1$: $7-3=4$, divisible by $4$ [A1] assume $7^m-3^m=4k$ for some integer $k$ [M1] $7^{m+1}-3^{m+1}=7\left(7^m-3^m\right)+4\times3^m$ [M1][A1] $=28k+4\times3^m=4\left(7k+3^m\right)$ [A1] divisible by $4$ [A1] true for $n=1$ and $n=m\Rightarrow n=m+1$, so true for all positive integers $n$ [R1] [7 marks]
tips: Write $7^{m+1}-3^{m+1}$ in terms of $7^m-3^m$ plus a leftover multiple of 4.

subtopic: Proof by contradiction: an irrational number
statement: Prove by contradiction that $\sqrt3$ is irrational. [6]
markscheme: assume $\sqrt3=\dfrac pq$ with $p,q$ integers having no common factor [M1] $3q^2=p^2$ [A1] so $p^2$ is a multiple of $3$, hence $p$ is a multiple of $3$ (since $3$ is prime) [R1] $p=3r$ gives $3q^2=9r^2$, so $q^2=3r^2$ [M1] so $q$ is a multiple of $3$ [A1] both divisible by $3$ contradicts no common factor, so $\sqrt3$ is irrational [R1] [6 marks]
tips: Assume the opposite, derive that both integers share a factor, and state the contradiction clearly.

subtopic: Direct proof of arithmetic and geometric series formulas
statement: (a) The arithmetic series with first term $a$ and common difference $d$ has $n$ terms, with sum $S_n$. By writing $S_n$ forwards and then backwards, show that $S_n=\frac{n}{2}\left(2a+(n-1)d\right)$. [3] (b) The geometric series $T_n=a+ar+ar^2+\dots+ar^{n-1}$ has common ratio $r\neq1$. By considering $T_n-rT_n$, show that $T_n=\frac{a(r^n-1)}{r-1}$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $S_n=a+(a+d)+\dots+(a+(n-1)d)$ and, reversed, $S_n=(a+(n-1)d)+(a+(n-2)d)+\dots+a$ [M1] Adding the terms in matching positions, each pair sums to $2a+(n-1)d$ [A1] There are $n$ such pairs, so $2S_n=n\left(2a+(n-1)d\right)$ [M1] $S_n=\frac{n}{2}\left(2a+(n-1)d\right)$ [AG] [3 marks] (b) $rT_n=ar+ar^2+\dots+ar^{n}$ [M1] $T_n-rT_n=a-ar^n$, since all middle terms cancel [M1][A1] So $(1-r)T_n=a(1-r^n)$ and, since $r\neq1$, $T_n=\frac{a(1-r^n)}{1-r}=\frac{a(r^n-1)}{r-1}$ [AG] [3 marks]
tips: In both derivations the idea is to line up terms so that almost everything cancels or pairs up. Write out at least three terms and the last term of each line so the cancellation is visible.

subtopic: Induction with a trigonometric sum
statement: Prove by induction that $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^n\sin\left((2k-1)x\right)=\dfrac{\sin^2(nx)}{\sin x}$ for all positive integers $n$, where $\sin x\ne0$. [7]
markscheme: $n=1$: LHS $=\sin x$, RHS $=\dfrac{\sin^2x}{\sin x}=\sin x$ [A1] assume true for $n=m$ [M1] add $\sin((2m+1)x)$ and multiply by $\sin x$: $\sin^2(mx)+\sin x\sin((2m+1)x)$ [M1] $\sin x\sin((2m+1)x)=\dfrac12\left[\cos2mx-\cos(2m+2)x\right]$ [A1] $\sin^2mx=\dfrac12(1-\cos2mx)$ [A1] total $\dfrac12-\dfrac12\cos(2m+2)x=\sin^2\left((m+1)x\right)$ [A1] true for $n=1$ and $n=m\Rightarrow n=m+1$, so true for all $n$ [R1] [7 marks]
tips: Use $2\sin A\sin B=\cos(A-B)-\cos(A+B)$ and the double-angle formula for $\cos$.

subtopic: Induction: powers of a 2 by 2 matrix
statement: Let $\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find $\mathbf{A}^2$. [1] (b) Prove by mathematical induction that $\mathbf{A}^n=\begin{pmatrix} 2^n & n\cdot2^{n-1} \\ 0 & 2^n \end{pmatrix}$ for all $n\in\mathbb{Z}^+$. [6]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{A}^2=\begin{pmatrix} 4 & 4 \\ 0 & 4 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) For $n=1$: $\begin{pmatrix} 2^1 & 1\cdot2^0 \\ 0 & 2^1 \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}=\mathbf{A}$, so true for $n=1$ [A1] Assume true for $n=k$: $\mathbf{A}^k=\begin{pmatrix} 2^k & k\cdot2^{k-1} \\ 0 & 2^k \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $\mathbf{A}^{k+1}=\mathbf{A}^k\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix} 2^k & k\cdot2^{k-1} \\ 0 & 2^k \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix} 2^{k+1} & 2^k+k\cdot2^k \\ 0 & 2^{k+1} \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $=\begin{pmatrix} 2^{k+1} & (k+1)2^k \\ 0 & 2^{k+1} \end{pmatrix}$, which is the statement for $n=k+1$ [A1] True for $n=1$, and true for $n=k$ implies true for $n=k+1$, so true for all $n\in\mathbb{Z}^+$ by mathematical induction [R1] [6 marks]
tips: Multiply the assumed form of $\mathbf{A}^k$ by $\mathbf{A}$ entry by entry and only then simplify powers of $2$. State clearly which matrix product you are using ($\mathbf{A}^k\mathbf{A}$ or $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{A}^k$).

subtopic: Induction: sum of products of consecutive integers
statement: Prove by induction that $\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^nr(r+1)=\dfrac{n(n+1)(n+2)}3$ for all positive integers $n$. [6]
markscheme: $n=1$: LHS $=2$, RHS $=\dfrac{1\times2\times3}3=2$ [A1] assume true for $n=m$ [M1] add the next term: $\dfrac{m(m+1)(m+2)}3+(m+1)(m+2)$ [M1] $=\dfrac{(m+1)(m+2)(m+3)}3$ [A1] which is the formula for $n=m+1$ [A1] true for $n=1$ and $n=m\Rightarrow n=m+1$, so true for all positive integers $n$ [R1] [6 marks]
tips: Factor out $(m+1)(m+2)$ after adding the next term.

subtopic: Direct proof: an inequality for positive numbers
statement: For positive real numbers $a$ and $b$, prove that $\dfrac{a+b}2\ge\sqrt{ab}$, and state when equality holds. [5]
markscheme: consider $\left(\sqrt a-\sqrt b\right)^2\ge0$ [M1] $a-2\sqrt{ab}+b\ge0$ [A1] $a+b\ge2\sqrt{ab}$ [A1] divide by $2$ [A1] equality iff $\sqrt a=\sqrt b$, i.e. $a=b$ [R1] [5 marks]
tips: A square is never negative: start from $\left(\sqrt a-\sqrt b\right)^2\ge0$ and rearrange.

subtopic: Direct proof: four consecutive integers
statement: Let $n\in\mathbb{Z}$. (a) Show that $n(n+1)(n+2)(n+3)=(n^2+3n)(n^2+3n+2)$. [2] (b) Hence prove that the product of four consecutive integers, plus $1$, is always a perfect square. [3] (c) Write $9\times10\times11\times12+1$ as the square of an integer. [1]
markscheme: (a) Pair the factors: $n(n+3)=n^2+3n$ [M1] and $(n+1)(n+2)=n^2+3n+2$, so the product is $(n^2+3n)(n^2+3n+2)$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Let $m=n^2+3n$ [M1] Then the product plus 1 is $m(m+2)+1=m^2+2m+1=(m+1)^2$ [A1] $=(n^2+3n+1)^2$, which is the square of an integer since $n\in\mathbb{Z}$ [R1] [3 marks] (c) With $n=9$: $n^2+3n+1=81+27+1=109$, so the value is $109^2$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: A substitution such as $m=n^2+3n$ turns a long expansion into a quick factorization. Always finish a "perfect square" proof by saying why the base is an integer.

subtopic: Proof by induction: sum of a series
statement: Prove by mathematical induction that $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{n}k^{3}=\frac{n^{2} \left(n + 1\right)^{2}}{4}$ for all $n\in\mathbb Z^+$. [7]
markscheme: for $n=1$: LHS $=1$ and RHS $=1$, equal, so true for $n=1$ [A1][A1] assume true for $n=m$: $\sum_{k=1}^mk^{3}=\frac{m^{2} \left(m + 1\right)^{2}}{4}$ [M1] then $\sum_{k=1}^{m+1}=\frac{m^{2} \left(m + 1\right)^{2}}{4}+\left(m + 1\right)^{3}$ [M1] $=\frac{\left(m + 1\right)^{2} \left(m + 2\right)^{2}}{4}$ after simplifying, which is the formula with $n=m+1$ [A1] so true for $n=m+1$ [R1] true for $n=1$ and true for $n=m$ implies true for $n=m+1$, so true for all $n\in\mathbb Z^+$ by induction [R1] [7 marks]
tips: State the base case, the assumption, and the inductive step, and finish with the conclusion. In the step, add the next term to the assumed sum and factorize to match the target form.

subtopic: Induction: sum of squares
statement: Show, using mathematical induction, that the sum of the first $n$ squares satisfies $\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{n} r^{2}=\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}$ for all $n\in\mathbb{Z}^+$. [6]
markscheme: For $n=1$: LHS $=1$ and RHS $=\frac{1\cdot2\cdot3}{6}=1$, so true for $n=1$ [A1] Assume true for $n=k$: $\sum_{r=1}^{k} r^2=\frac{k(k+1)(2k+1)}{6}$ [M1] Then $\sum_{r=1}^{k+1} r^2=\frac{k(k+1)(2k+1)}{6}+(k+1)^2$ [M1] $=\frac{(k+1)\left[k(2k+1)+6(k+1)\right]}{6}$ [A1] $=\frac{(k+1)(2k^2+7k+6)}{6}=\frac{(k+1)(k+2)(2k+3)}{6}$ [A1] which is the statement for $n=k+1$. True for $n=1$, and true for $n=k$ implies true for $n=k+1$, so true for all $n\in\mathbb{Z}^+$ by mathematical induction [R1] [6 marks]
tips: Factor out $(k+1)$ early rather than expanding everything, so the target $(k+1)(k+2)(2k+3)$ is easy to reach. Always finish with the full conclusion sentence.

subtopic: Counterexample and proof by contrapositive
statement: (a) Chloe claims that $n^2+n+41$ is a prime number for every positive integer $n$. Find a counterexample to show that her claim is false. [2] (b) Prove by contrapositive that, for $n\in\mathbb{Z}$, if $n^2$ is divisible by $3$ then $n$ is divisible by $3$. [4]
markscheme: (a) For $n=41$: $41^2+41+41=41(41+1+1)=41\times43$ [M1] which is not prime (it has factors $41$ and $43$), so the claim is false [A1] [2 marks] (Accept $n=40$ giving $1681=41^2$.) (b) The contrapositive is: if $n$ is not divisible by $3$ then $n^2$ is not divisible by $3$ [M1] If $n$ is not divisible by $3$ then $n=3k+1$ or $n=3k+2$ for some $k\in\mathbb{Z}$ [M1] $(3k+1)^2=9k^2+6k+1=3(3k^2+2k)+1$ and $(3k+2)^2=9k^2+12k+4=3(3k^2+4k+1)+1$ [A1] Each leaves remainder $1$ on division by $3$, so $n^2$ is not divisible by $3$; hence the original statement is true [R1] [4 marks]
tips: One counterexample is enough to disprove a universal claim, so show your arithmetic clearly. For a contrapositive proof, state the contrapositive in words before you start.

subtopic: Induction: sum of k times k factorial
statement: Prove by mathematical induction that $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^nk\times k!=(n+1)!-1$ for all positive integers $n$. State clearly the base case, the inductive hypothesis and the conclusion. [7]
markscheme: $n=1$: LHS $=1$, RHS $=2!-1=1$, true [A1] assume true for $n=m$: $\sum_{k=1}^mk\,k!=(m+1)!-1$ [M1] for $n=m+1$: $(m+1)!-1+(m+1)(m+1)!$ [M1][A1] $=(m+1)!\left(1+m+1\right)-1$ [A1] $=(m+2)!-1$ [A1] true for $n=1$, and true for $n=m\Rightarrow$ true for $n=m+1$, so true for all positive integers $n$ [R1] [7 marks]
tips: In the inductive step, factor out $(m+1)!$ from the two terms containing it.

subtopic: Proof by induction: an inequality
statement: Prove by induction that $2^n>n^2$ for all integers $n\ge5$. [7]
markscheme: $n=5$: $32>25$ true [A1] assume $2^m>m^2$ for some $m\ge5$ [M1] $2^{m+1}=2\cdot2^m>2m^2$ [M1] $2m^2-(m+1)^2=m^2-2m-1=(m-1)^2-2>0$ for $m\ge5$ [A1][A1] so $2^{m+1}>(m+1)^2$ [R1] conclusion by induction for all $n\ge5$ [R1] [7 marks]
tips: In an inductive inequality, show that the next bound exceeds the target by a separate algebraic inequality valid for the stated range.

subtopic: Proof by induction: sum of a series
statement: Prove by mathematical induction that $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{n}k \left(k + 1\right)=\frac{n \left(n + 1\right) \left(n + 2\right)}{3}$ for all $n\in\mathbb Z^+$. [7]
markscheme: for $n=1$: LHS $=2$ and RHS $=2$, equal, so true for $n=1$ [A1][A1] assume true for $n=m$: $\sum_{k=1}^mk \left(k + 1\right)=\frac{m \left(m + 1\right) \left(m + 2\right)}{3}$ [M1] then $\sum_{k=1}^{m+1}=\frac{m \left(m + 1\right) \left(m + 2\right)}{3}+\left(m + 1\right) \left(m + 2\right)$ [M1] $=\frac{\left(m + 1\right) \left(m + 2\right) \left(m + 3\right)}{3}$ after simplifying, which is the formula with $n=m+1$ [A1] so true for $n=m+1$ [R1] true for $n=1$ and true for $n=m$ implies true for $n=m+1$, so true for all $n\in\mathbb Z^+$ by induction [R1] [7 marks]
tips: State the base case, the assumption, and the inductive step, and finish with the conclusion. In the step, add the next term to the assumed sum and factorize to match the target form.

subtopic: Irrationality of a logarithm and a constructive existence proof
statement: (a) Prove by contradiction that $\log_23$ is irrational. [5] (b) Hence prove that $\log_212$ is irrational. [2] (c) Given that $\sqrt2$ is irrational, prove that there exist irrational numbers $a$ and $b$ such that $a^b$ is rational. [3]
markscheme: (a) suppose $\log_23=\dfrac pq$ with $p,q$ positive integers [M1] then $2^{p/q}=3$, so $2^p=3^q$ [M1] since $p\ge1$, $2^p$ is even [R1] but $3^q$ is odd [R1] this is a contradiction, so $\log_23$ is irrational [A1] [5 marks] (b) $\log_212=\log_2(4\times3)=2+\log_23$ [M1] if this were rational then $\log_23=\log_212-2$ would be rational, contradicting (a) [R1] [2 marks] (c) take $a=\sqrt2$ and $b=2\log_23$ [M1] $b$ is irrational, since otherwise $\log_23=\dfrac b2$ would be rational [R1] $a^b=2^{\frac12\times2\log_23}=2^{\log_23}=3$, which is rational [A1] [3 marks]
tips: If $\log_23=\dfrac pq$ then write the equation in exponential form and compare parities. For part (c), choose $a$ and $b$ so that the exponent simplifies to a logarithm.

subtopic: Induction: telescoping sum of fractions
statement: Prove by mathematical induction that $\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{n}\frac{1}{r(r+1)}=\frac{n}{n+1}$ for all $n\in\mathbb{Z}^+$. [5]
markscheme: For $n=1$: LHS $=\dfrac{1}{1\times2}=\dfrac12$, RHS $=\dfrac12$, so true for $n=1$ [A1] Assume true for $n=k$: $\sum_{r=1}^{k}\dfrac{1}{r(r+1)}=\dfrac{k}{k+1}$ [M1] Then $\sum_{r=1}^{k+1}\dfrac{1}{r(r+1)}=\dfrac{k}{k+1}+\dfrac{1}{(k+1)(k+2)}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{k(k+2)+1}{(k+1)(k+2)}=\dfrac{(k+1)^2}{(k+1)(k+2)}=\dfrac{k+1}{k+2}$ [A1] True for $n=1$ and true for $n=k$ implies true for $n=k+1$, so true for all $n\in\mathbb{Z}^+$ [R1] [5 marks]
tips: When the $(k+1)$th term is a fraction, put everything over a common denominator and look for a perfect square or common factor to cancel.

subtopic: Proof of de Moivre's theorem by induction
statement: (a) Prove by mathematical induction that $(\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin\theta)^n=\cos n\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin n\theta$ for all $n\in\mathbb{Z}^+$ and all $\theta\in\mathbb{R}$. [6] (b) Hence show that $(1+\mathrm{i})^8=16$. [2]
markscheme: (a) For $n=1$: both sides equal $\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin\theta$, so true for $n=1$ [A1] Assume true for $n=k$: $(\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin\theta)^k=\cos k\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin k\theta$ [M1] $(\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin\theta)^{k+1}=(\cos k\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin k\theta)(\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin\theta)$ [M1] $=(\cos k\theta\cos\theta-\sin k\theta\sin\theta)+\mathrm{i}(\sin k\theta\cos\theta+\cos k\theta\sin\theta)$ [A1] $=\cos(k+1)\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin(k+1)\theta$ [A1] which is the statement for $n=k+1$. True for $n=1$, and true for $n=k$ implies true for $n=k+1$, so true for all $n\in\mathbb{Z}^+$ by mathematical induction [R1] [6 marks] (b) $1+\mathrm{i}=\sqrt{2}\left(\cos\frac{\pi}{4}+\mathrm{i}\sin\frac{\pi}{4}\right)$ [A1] $(1+\mathrm{i})^8=(\sqrt{2})^8\left(\cos2\pi+\mathrm{i}\sin2\pi\right)$ [M1] $=16(1+0)=16$ [AG] [2 marks]
tips: The key step is recognizing the compound-angle formulas for $\cos(k+1)\theta$ and $\sin(k+1)\theta$ in the expanded product. In part (b), convert to modulus-argument form first.

subtopic: Proof by contradiction: infinitely many primes
statement: Prove by contradiction that there are infinitely many prime numbers. [6]
markscheme: Assume there are only finitely many primes, $p_1,p_2,\dots,p_n$ [M1] Let $N=p_1p_2\cdots p_n+1$ [M1] Dividing $N$ by any $p_i$ leaves remainder $1$, so no $p_i$ divides $N$ [A1] Since $N>1$, $N$ has at least one prime factor [R1] This prime factor is not in the list $p_1,\dots,p_n$, contradicting the assumption that the list contains all primes [R1] Hence there are infinitely many primes [R1] [6 marks]
tips: Be precise: the contradiction is not that $N$ is prime, but that $N$ has a prime factor missing from the list. State that every integer greater than $1$ has a prime factor.

subtopic: Direct proof: n cubed minus n is divisible by 6
statement: Let $n$ be an integer. (a) Show that $n^3-n=(n-1)n(n+1)$. [2] (b) Hence prove that $n^3-n$ is divisible by $6$. [3] (c) Hence prove that $n^3+5n$ is divisible by $6$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $n^3-n=n(n^2-1)$ [M1] $=n(n-1)(n+1)$ using the difference of two squares [A1] $=(n-1)n(n+1)$ [AG] [2 marks] (b) $(n-1)n(n+1)$ is a product of three consecutive integers [M1] Among any three consecutive integers at least one is even, so the product is divisible by $2$ [R1] Exactly one of any three consecutive integers is a multiple of $3$, so the product is divisible by $3$. As $2$ and $3$ have no common factor, the product is divisible by $6$ [R1] [3 marks] (c) $n^3+5n=(n^3-n)+6n$ [M1] Both $n^3-n$ and $6n$ are divisible by $6$, so their sum is divisible by $6$ [R1] [2 marks]
tips: For divisibility by a composite number, justify divisibility by its coprime factors separately. Look for a way to write the new expression as the old one plus an obvious multiple.

subtopic: Induction: repeated differentiation
statement: Let $f(x)=x\mathrm{e}^{x}$. (a) Find $f'(x)$ and $f''(x)$, giving each in the form $(x+a)\mathrm{e}^{x}$. [2] (b) Prove by mathematical induction that the $n$th derivative is $f^{(n)}(x)=(x+n)\mathrm{e}^{x}$ for all $n\in\mathbb{Z}^+$. [5]
markscheme: (a) $f'(x)=\mathrm{e}^x+x\mathrm{e}^x=(x+1)\mathrm{e}^x$ [A1] $f''(x)=\mathrm{e}^x+(x+1)\mathrm{e}^x=(x+2)\mathrm{e}^x$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) For $n=1$: $f'(x)=(x+1)\mathrm{e}^x$ (from part (a)), so true for $n=1$ [A1] Assume true for $n=k$: $f^{(k)}(x)=(x+k)\mathrm{e}^x$ [M1] Then $f^{(k+1)}(x)=\mathrm{e}^x+(x+k)\mathrm{e}^x$ (product rule) [M1] $=(x+k+1)\mathrm{e}^x=\big(x+(k+1)\big)\mathrm{e}^x$ [A1] True for $n=1$ and true for $n=k$ implies true for $n=k+1$, so true for all $n\in\mathbb{Z}^+$ [R1] [5 marks]
tips: Computing the first two or three derivatives suggests the pattern and also gives you the base case. In the inductive step, differentiate the assumed formula, not the original function.

subtopic: Irrationality proofs for square roots and sums of square roots
statement: You may use that if a prime $p$ divides $m^2$ then $p$ divides $m$. (a) Prove that $\sqrt3$ is irrational. [4] (b) Prove that $\sqrt6$ is irrational. [3] (c) Hence prove that $\sqrt2+\sqrt3$ is irrational. [3] (d) Prove that $2\sqrt3$ is irrational, and give an example showing that the product of two irrational numbers can be rational. [3] (e) Explain why the argument in part (a) gives no contradiction if $\sqrt3$ is replaced by $\sqrt4$. [1]
markscheme: (a) suppose $\sqrt3=\dfrac pq$ in lowest terms [M1] $p^2=3q^2$, so $3\mid p^2$, so $3\mid p$ [A1] $p=3r$ gives $9r^2=3q^2$, so $q^2=3r^2$ and $3\mid q$ [A1] contradicts lowest terms, so $\sqrt3$ is irrational [R1] [4 marks] (b) suppose $\sqrt6=\dfrac pq$ in lowest terms, so $p^2=6q^2$ [M1] $2\mid p^2$ so $2\mid p$, $p=2r$, giving $2r^2=3q^2$, so $2\mid3q^2$ and $2\mid q$ [A1] contradicts lowest terms [R1] [3 marks] (c) suppose $\sqrt2+\sqrt3=t$ rational [M1] square: $5+2\sqrt6=t^2$ so $\sqrt6=\dfrac{t^2-5}2$, rational [A1] contradicts part (b) [R1] [3 marks] (d) if $2\sqrt3$ were rational, then $\sqrt3=\dfrac{2\sqrt3}2$ would be rational, contradicting part (a) [M1][R1] $\sqrt2\times\sqrt8=4$ (both factors irrational) [A1] [3 marks] (e) $p^2=4q^2$ gives $p=2q$, so $\dfrac pq=2$ is a valid ratio of integers in lowest terms [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Assume the number is a ratio of integers in lowest terms and show that both integers must share a prime factor.

subtopic: The pigeonhole principle and subsets of consecutive integers
statement: The pigeonhole principle states that if $n+1$ or more objects are placed into $n$ boxes, then at least one box contains at least two objects. (a) Show that among any $5$ integers, two have a difference divisible by $4$. [3] (b) Seven different numbers are chosen from $\{1,2,\ldots,12\}$. Show that two of them are consecutive integers. [3] (c) Show that among any seven numbers chosen from $\{1,2,\ldots,12\}$, one divides another. [4] (d) Show that six numbers can be chosen from $\{1,2,\ldots,12\}$ so that none divides another. [2] (e) State the smallest $k$ such that any $k$ numbers chosen from $\{1,\ldots,12\}$ must contain a pair with one dividing the other, with a reason. [2]
markscheme: (a) the possible remainders on division by $4$ are $0,1,2,3$, which are the $4$ boxes [M1] $5$ integers, so two share a remainder [A1] their difference is divisible by $4$ [R1] [3 marks] (b) form the $6$ pairs $\{1,2\},\{3,4\},\ldots,\{11,12\}$ [M1] seven numbers in six pairs, so two lie in the same pair [A1] they are consecutive [R1] [3 marks] (c) write each number as $2^km$ with $m$ odd [M1] the odd parts are among $1,3,5,7,9,11$, six values [A1] two numbers share the same $m$ [A1] so one is $2^am$ and the other $2^bm$, and the smaller divides the larger [R1] [4 marks] (d) $\{7,8,9,10,11,12\}$ [A1] twice the smallest is $14>12$, so no number divides another [R1] [2 marks] (e) $k=7$ [A1] by parts (c) and (d): six numbers need not work but seven always do [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Choose boxes so that two objects in the same box must have the required property. The odd part of a number is a natural box label for divisibility.

subtopic: Proof by cases using remainders modulo 3
statement: Let $n$ be an integer. (a) By considering $n=3k$, $n=3k+1$ and $n=3k+2$, show that $n^2$ leaves a remainder of $0$ or $1$ when divided by $3$. [3] (b) Hence prove that if $a^2+b^2$ is divisible by $3$, then both $a$ and $b$ are divisible by $3$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $(3k)^2=3\left(3k^2\right)$, remainder $0$ [A1] $(3k+1)^2=3\left(3k^2+2k\right)+1$, remainder $1$ [A1] $(3k+2)^2=3\left(3k^2+4k+1\right)+1$, remainder $1$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) squares have remainder $0$ or $1$ [R1] the sum of remainders can be a multiple of $3$ only if both are $0$ ($0+0=0$; $1+1=2$ and $0+1=1$ do not work) [M1] a square with remainder $0$ means the number is a multiple of $3$ [R1] [3 marks]
tips: List the possible remainders of a square, then look at which pairs of remainders can add to a multiple of 3.

subtopic: Induction for a weighted sum with powers of 2
statement: Use mathematical induction to prove that $$\sum_{r=1}^{n} r\,2^{r-1}=(n-1)2^{n}+1$$ for all $n\in\mathbb{Z}^+$. [7]
markscheme: Let $P(n)$ be the statement $\sum_{r=1}^{n} r\,2^{r-1}=(n-1)2^{n}+1$. Base case $n=1$: LHS $=1\cdot 2^0=1$ [M1] RHS $=(0)2+1=1$, so $P(1)$ is true [A1] Assume $P(k)$ is true for some $k\in\mathbb{Z}^+$ [M1] Consider $n=k+1$: $\sum_{r=1}^{k+1} r\,2^{r-1}=(k-1)2^{k}+1+(k+1)2^{k}$ [M1] $=2k\cdot 2^{k}+1$ [A1] $=k\,2^{k+1}+1=\left((k+1)-1\right)2^{k+1}+1$ [A1] So $P(k)$ true implies $P(k+1)$ true. Since $P(1)$ is true, $P(n)$ is true for all $n\in\mathbb{Z}^+$ by mathematical induction [R1] [7 marks]
tips: State the induction hypothesis clearly and add the $(k+1)$th term to the right-hand side of the assumption. Finish with a full concluding sentence, as this earns a mark.

subtopic: Direct proof using remainders modulo 4
statement: (a) Prove that the square of any integer is of the form $4k$ or $4k+1$, where $k\in\mathbb{Z}$. [3] (b) Hence prove that $2023$ cannot be written as the sum of the squares of two integers. [3]
markscheme: (a) Let $n$ be an integer, either even or odd. If $n=2m$ then $n^2=4m^2$ [M1] If $n=2m+1$ then $n^2=4m^2+4m+1=4(m^2+m)+1$ [M1] So every square has the form $4k$ or $4k+1$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Possible values of $x^2+y^2$ are $4a+4b$, $4a+4b+1$ or $4a+1+4b+1$, i.e. remainders $0$, $1$ or $2$ when divided by $4$ [M1] [A1] $2023=4(505)+3$ has remainder $3$, so it cannot be written as $x^2+y^2$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Splitting into the two cases even and odd is the standard way to start a proof about all integers. In part (b) list every possible remainder of a sum before comparing with $2023$.

subtopic: Proof by contradiction: irrational logarithm
statement: (a) Suppose that $\log_2 3=\dfrac{p}{q}$, where $p,q\in\mathbb{Z}^+$. Show that $2^p=3^q$. [2] (b) Hence prove by contradiction that $\log_2 3$ is irrational. [3]
markscheme: (a) $2^{p/q}=3$ [M1] Raising both sides to the power $q$: $2^p=3^q$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Assume $\log_2 3$ is rational. Since $\log_2 3>0$, it can be written as $\dfrac{p}{q}$ with $p,q\in\mathbb{Z}^+$, and by part (a) $2^p=3^q$ [M1] $2^p$ is even (as $p\ge1$) but $3^q$ is odd [A1] This is a contradiction, so $\log_2 3$ is irrational [R1] [3 marks]
tips: Begin a contradiction proof by stating the assumption precisely, including any sign restrictions on $p$ and $q$. Parity (odd versus even) is a quick way to contradict an equation between integer powers.

subtopic: Proof by contrapositive of an inequality
statement: Let $a$ and $b$ be real numbers. Prove that if $a+b\ge100$, then $a\ge50$ or $b\ge50$. Prove the statement by proving its contrapositive. [4]
markscheme: contrapositive: if $a<50$ and $b<50$, then $a+b<100$ [A1][A1] adding the inequalities $a<50$ and $b<50$ gives $a+b<100$ [M1] the contrapositive is true, so the original statement is true [R1] [4 marks]
tips: The negation of 'a or b' is 'not a and not b'. A statement and its contrapositive are logically equivalent.

subtopic: Proof by contradiction that a logarithm is irrational
statement: Prove by contradiction that $\log_2 3$ is irrational. [6]
markscheme: Assume that $\log_2 3$ is rational, so $\log_2 3=\dfrac pq$ for some integers $p,q$ with $q\ne 0$ [M1] Since $\log_2 3>0$, we may take $p,q\in\mathbb{Z}^+$ [A1] Then $2^{p/q}=3$, so $2^{p}=3^{q}$ [M1] $2^{p}$ is even since $p\ge 1$ [R1] $3^{q}$ is odd since $q\ge 1$ and a product of odd numbers is odd [R1] An even number cannot equal an odd number, which is a contradiction, so $\log_2 3$ is irrational [R1] [6 marks]
tips: Start with the assumption that the number equals $p/q$ and convert the logarithm to an exponential equation. Contradictions with parity of even and odd integers are the standard route.

subtopic: Disproving claims by counterexample
statement: Two claims are made about prime numbers. (a) Claim: for every prime $p$, $2^p-1$ is prime. Give a counterexample. [2] (b) Claim: $n^2+n+41$ is prime for every positive integer $n$. Give a counterexample. [2]
tips: A single case where the claim fails is enough to disprove a statement about all numbers.

subtopic: Sums of powers and induction
statement: This question investigates formulae for the sums of powers of the first $n$ positive integers. For $k \in \mathbb{N}$ and $n \in \mathbb{Z}^+$ let $$S_k(n)=\sum_{r=1}^{n} r^k = 1^k+2^k+\cdots+n^k.$$ (a) Write down an expression for $S_0(n)$, and find the values of $S_1(4)$, $S_2(4)$ and $S_3(4)$. [2] (b) By considering $\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left[(r+1)^2-r^2\right]$ in two different ways, show that $S_1(n)=\dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}$. [3] (c) (i) Expand and simplify $(r+1)^3-r^3$. (ii) By summing both sides of your answer to part (c)(i) from $r=1$ to $r=n$, show that $3S_2(n)=(n+1)^3-1-3S_1(n)-n$. (iii) Hence show that $S_2(n)=\dfrac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}$. [6] (d) Prove by mathematical induction that $S_3(n)=\left(\dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}\right)^2$ for all $n \in \mathbb{Z}^+$. [6] (e) The results so far suggest that $S_k(n)$ is a polynomial in $n$ of degree $k+1$ with leading coefficient $\dfrac{1}{k+1}$. (i) Verify this conjecture for $k=1$, $k=2$ and $k=3$ by expanding your formulae. (ii) By considering $\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left[(r+1)^{k+1}-r^{k+1}\right]$ and the binomial theorem, explain why the conjecture is true for every $k \in \mathbb{Z}^+$. [5] (f) By writing $\dfrac{S_k(n)}{n^{k+1}}=\dfrac{1}{n}\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\dfrac{r}{n}\right)^k$, interpret this quantity as an approximation to a definite integral, and hence find $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{S_k(n)}{n^{k+1}}$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $S_0(n)=n$ [A1] $S_1(4)=10,\ S_2(4)=30,\ S_3(4)=100$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Telescoping: $\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left[(r+1)^2-r^2\right]=(n+1)^2-1$ [M1] Expanding instead: $\sum_{r=1}^{n}(2r+1)=2S_1(n)+n$ [A1] so $2S_1(n)=n^2+2n-n=n^2+n$, giving $S_1(n)=\dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}$ [A1][AG] [3 marks] (c)(i) $(r+1)^3-r^3=3r^2+3r+1$ [A1] (ii) The left-hand side telescopes to $(n+1)^3-1$ [M1]; the right-hand side sums to $3S_2(n)+3S_1(n)+n$ [A1], which rearranges to the given result [AG] (iii) $3S_2(n)=(n+1)^3-(n+1)-\dfrac{3n(n+1)}{2}$ [M1] $=n(n+1)(n+2)-\dfrac{3n(n+1)}{2}=\dfrac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{2}$ [A1] so $S_2(n)=\dfrac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}$ [A1][AG] [6 marks] (d) For $n=1$: LHS $=1$, RHS $=\left(\frac{1\cdot 2}{2}\right)^2=1$, so true for $n=1$ [A1] Assume true for $n=m$, i.e. $S_3(m)=\dfrac{m^2(m+1)^2}{4}$ [M1] Then $S_3(m+1)=\dfrac{m^2(m+1)^2}{4}+(m+1)^3$ [M1] $=\dfrac{(m+1)^2\left(m^2+4m+4\right)}{4}$ [A1] $=\left(\dfrac{(m+1)(m+2)}{2}\right)^2$, which is the statement for $n=m+1$ [A1] Since true for $n=1$, and true for $n=m$ implies true for $n=m+1$, the result holds for all $n\in\mathbb{Z}^+$ by mathematical induction [R1] [6 marks] (e)(i) $S_1=\tfrac12 n^2+\tfrac12 n$, $S_2=\tfrac13 n^3+\tfrac12 n^2+\tfrac16 n$, $S_3=\tfrac14 n^4+\tfrac12 n^3+\tfrac14 n^2$ — each has degree $k+1$ and leading coefficient $\frac{1}{k+1}$ [A2] (award [A1] for two correct) (ii) Telescoping gives $(n+1)^{k+1}-1=\sum_{r=1}^{n}\sum_{j=0}^{k}\binom{k+1}{j}r^j=(k+1)S_k(n)+\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}\binom{k+1}{j}S_j(n)$ [M1] By strong induction on $k$, each $S_j(n)$ with $j<k$ is a polynomial of degree $j+1\le k$, so $(k+1)S_k(n)=(n+1)^{k+1}-(\text{polynomial of degree}\le k)$ [R1] Hence $S_k(n)$ is a polynomial of degree $k+1$ whose leading term is $\dfrac{n^{k+1}}{k+1}$ [A1] [5 marks] (f) $\dfrac{1}{n}\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\dfrac{r}{n}\right)^k$ is a sum of $n$ rectangles of width $\frac1n$ with heights $f\left(\frac rn\right)$, $f(x)=x^k$: a Riemann sum for $\int_0^1 x^k\,dx$ [M1][R1] so the limit is $\int_0^1 x^k\,dx=\dfrac{1}{k+1}$ [A1] (consistent with (e)) [3 marks] Total [25 marks]
tips: Telescoping sums collapse to first minus last term; for the induction step, factor out (m+1)^2 before expanding.

subtopic: A difference of two squares that cannot equal 2
statement: Prove that there are no integers $x$ and $y$ such that $x^2-y^2=2$. Use a proof by contradiction. [5]
markscheme: suppose $x^2-y^2=2$, so $(x-y)(x+y)=2$ [M1] $x-y$ and $x+y$ differ by $2y$, an even number, so they have the same parity [A1] if both are even, the product is a multiple of $4$, not $2$ [A1] if both are odd, the product is odd, not $2$ [A1] contradiction, so no such integers exist [R1] [5 marks]
tips: Factor the left-hand side and look at the parity of the two factors.

subtopic: Proof by induction: sum of a series
statement: Prove by mathematical induction that $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{1}{k \left(k + 1\right)}=\frac{n}{n + 1}$ for all $n\in\mathbb Z^+$. [7]
markscheme: for $n=1$: LHS $=\frac{1}{2}$ and RHS $=\frac{1}{2}$, equal, so true for $n=1$ [A1][A1] assume true for $n=m$: $\sum_{k=1}^m\frac{1}{k \left(k + 1\right)}=\frac{m}{m + 1}$ [M1] then $\sum_{k=1}^{m+1}=\frac{m}{m + 1}+\frac{1}{\left(m + 1\right) \left(m + 2\right)}$ [M1] $=\frac{m + 1}{m + 2}$ after simplifying, which is the formula with $n=m+1$ [A1] so true for $n=m+1$ [R1] true for $n=1$ and true for $n=m$ implies true for $n=m+1$, so true for all $n\in\mathbb Z^+$ by induction [R1] [7 marks]
tips: State the base case, the assumption, and the inductive step, and finish with the conclusion. In the step, add the next term to the assumed sum and factorize to match the target form.

subtopic: Induction: sum involving powers of 2
statement: Prove by mathematical induction that $\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{n} r\cdot 2^{r}=(n-1)2^{n+1}+2$ for all $n\in\mathbb{Z}^+$. [6]
markscheme: For $n=1$: LHS $=1\cdot 2=2$ and RHS $=0\cdot 2^2+2=2$, so the result is true for $n=1$ [A1] Assume true for $n=k$: $\sum_{r=1}^{k} r\cdot 2^r=(k-1)2^{k+1}+2$ [M1] Then $\sum_{r=1}^{k+1} r\cdot 2^r=(k-1)2^{k+1}+2+(k+1)2^{k+1}$ [M1] $=\big[(k-1)+(k+1)\big]2^{k+1}+2$ [A1] $=2k\cdot 2^{k+1}+2=k\cdot 2^{k+2}+2$ [A1] $=\big((k+1)-1\big)2^{(k+1)+1}+2$, which is the statement for $n=k+1$. True for $n=1$, and true for $n=k$ implies true for $n=k+1$, so true for all $n\in\mathbb{Z}^+$ by mathematical induction [R1] [6 marks]
tips: Write out the three induction steps explicitly: base case, assumption, then the $k+1$ case reaching exactly the target form. The final conclusion sentence earns its own mark.

subtopic: Polynomials for cos(n theta), induction and exact values
statement: This question investigates how $2\cos n\theta$ can be written as a polynomial in $2\cos\theta$. Let $\theta\in\mathbb{R}$, $z=\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin\theta$ and $x=2\cos\theta$. For $n\in\mathbb{N}$ define $P_n(x)=2\cos n\theta$. (a) Use de Moivre's theorem to show that $z^n+z^{-n}=2\cos n\theta$, and deduce that $x=z+z^{-1}$. [2] (b) By expanding $\left(z+z^{-1}\right)\left(z^n+z^{-n}\right)$, show that $P_{n+1}(x)=xP_n(x)-P_{n-1}(x)$ for $n\ge1$. [4] (c) Write down $P_0(x)$ and $P_1(x)$. Hence use the recurrence in part (b) to find $P_2(x)$, $P_3(x)$, $P_4(x)$ and $P_5(x)$. [5] (d) Prove by strong induction that for all $n\ge1$, $P_n(x)$ is a polynomial of degree $n$ whose leading coefficient is $1$ and whose other coefficients are integers. [5] (e) Show that $P_5(x)-2=(x-2)\left(x^2+x-1\right)^2$. [2] (f) By setting $\theta=\dfrac{2\pi}{5}$, show that $x=2\cos\dfrac{2\pi}{5}$ satisfies $x^2+x-1=0$, and hence find the exact value of $\cos\dfrac{2\pi}{5}$. [4] (g) Use a similar argument to find the exact value of $\cos\dfrac{4\pi}{5}$. [3]
markscheme:
(a) $z^{-n}=\cos(-n	heta)+\mathrm{i}\sin(-n	heta)=\cos n	heta-\mathrm{i}\sin n	heta$ [M1] so $z^n+z^{-n}=2\cos n	heta$ [A1]; for $n=1$ this gives $x=z+z^{-1}$ [2 marks] (b) $\left(z+z^{-1}ight)\left(z^n+z^{-n}ight)=z^{n+1}+z^{-(n+1)}+z^{n-1}+z^{-(n-1)}$ [M1] [A1] $=2\cos(n+1)	heta+2\cos(n-1)	heta$ [A1] and the left-hand side is $x\cdot2\cos n	heta$.
