tips: The inverse function reverses the composition. Differentiating the identity $f(f^{-1}(x))=x$ gives its derivative.

subtopic: Composite functions and solving fg(x) = gf(x)
statement: (a) Let $f(x)=3x+2$ and $g(x)=x^2-1$. Find $(f\circ g)(x)$, giving your answer in the form $ax^2+b$. [2] (b) Find $(g\circ f)(x)$, giving your answer in the form $ax^2+bx+c$. [2] (c) Solve $(f\circ g)(x)=(g\circ f)(x)$, giving your answers in exact form. [3]
tips: Composite functions are not commutative, so $f\circ g$ and $g\circ f$ usually differ. Substitute the inner function into every $x$ of the outer function.

subtopic: Even and odd functions
statement: (a) Show that $f(x)=\dfrac{x}{x^2+1}$ is an odd function. [2] (b) Show that $g(x)=2^x+2^{-x}$ is an even function. [2] The function $p$ is odd with $p(2)=5$, and the function $q$ is even with $q(2)=3$. (c) Find (i) $r(-2)$, where $r(x)=p(x)q(x)$; (ii) $s(-2)$, where $s(x)=p(x)+q(x)$. [3]
tips: To test symmetry, always simplify $f(-x)$ and compare it with both $f(x)$ and $-f(x)$. Even means $f(-x)=f(x)$; odd means $f(-x)=-f(x)$.

subtopic: Composite functions of linear and quadratic
statement: Let $f(x)=3x-2$ and $g(x)=x^2+1$, for $x\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Find $(f\circ g)(x)$. [1] (b) Find $(g\circ f)(x)$, giving your answer in the form $ax^2+bx+c$. [2] (c) Solve the equation $(f\circ g)(x)=(g\circ f)(x)$, giving your answers in exact form. [3]
tips: $(f\circ g)(x)$ means $f(g(x))$: the inner function is applied first. In general $f\circ g\ne g\circ f$, which is why the equation in (c) is not an identity.

subtopic: Exponential model fitting
statement: The area $H$ cm$^2$ covered by a colony of algae is modeled by $H(t)=a\cdot b^t$, where $t$ is the time in days. At $t=0$ the area is $12$ cm$^2$ and at $t=3$ the area is $40.5$ cm$^2$. (a) Find the values of $a$ and $b$. [3] (b) Find the time taken for the area to double. [2] (c) Predict the area after $8$ days, to 3 significant figures. [1] (d) Give one reason why the model may be unsuitable for large values of $t$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $a=12$ [A1] $12b^3=40.5$, $b^3=3.375$ [M1] $b=1.5$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $1.5^t=2$ [M1] $t=\frac{\ln2}{\ln1.5}=1.71$ days [A1] [2 marks] (c) $12(1.5)^8=308$ cm$^2$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) The area grows without bound, but the colony is limited by its container or resources [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Substitute the known point $(0,12)$ first to find $a$, then use the second point to find $b$. Doubling time is independent of the starting value in an exponential model.

subtopic: Properties of x + 1/x
statement: Let $f(x)=x+\dfrac1x$ for $x\ne0$. (a) Show that $f$ is odd, and that $f(x)=f\left(\dfrac1x\right)$. [2] (b) Show that $f(x)\ge2$ for $x>0$, and state the range of $f$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $f(-x)=-x-\dfrac1x=-f(x)$ [A1] $f\left(\dfrac1x\right)=\dfrac1x+x=f(x)$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $f(x)-2=\dfrac{(x-1)^2}x$ [M1][A1] $\ge0$ for $x>0$, with equality at $x=1$ [R1] range $(-\infty,-2]\cup[2,\infty)$, using oddness for $x<0$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Combine $x+1/x-2$ into a single fraction with a squared numerator.

subtopic: Intersection of a linear and an exponential growth model
statement: (a) Two streaming services are modeled. The number of subscribers, in thousands, of Service A is $L(t)=10+6t$ and of Service B is $E(t)=15\times1.2^t$, where $t$ is the time in months since January, for $t\geq0$. Write down which service has more subscribers at $t=0$, and by how many thousand. [1] (b) Use your GDC to find the two times at which the services have equal numbers of subscribers. [3] (c) Find the period of time during which Service A has more subscribers than Service B. [2] (d) Find the first time at which Service B has at least twice as many subscribers as Service A. [3]
markscheme: (a) Service B, by $15-10=5$ thousand [A1] [1 mark] (b) Solve $10+6t=15(1.2)^t$ [M1] $t=1.81$ [A1] $t=6.48$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $E(t)<L(t)$ between the two intersections [M1] $1.81<t<6.48$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $15(1.2)^t=2(10+6t)$ [M1] $t=13.8$ [A1] Service B has at least twice as many subscribers from $t=13.8$ months onwards, so the first time is $13.8$ months [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Sketch both graphs on your GDC and use the intersection function. An exponential model eventually exceeds any linear model, no matter how its early values compare.

subtopic: Domain, restricted range and inverse of a logarithmic function
statement: The function $f$ is defined by $f(x)=\ln\left(x^2-2x-8\right)$. (a) Find the largest possible domain of $f$. [3] The domain of $f$ is now restricted to $x>4$. (b) Write down the range of $f$. [2] (c) Find an expression for $f^{-1}(x)$, and state its domain. [3] (d) Find $f^{-1}(2.5)$, giving your answer to three significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) Need $x^2-2x-8>0$ [M1] $(x-4)(x+2)>0$ [A1] $x<-2$ or $x>4$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) For $x>4$, $x^2-2x-8$ takes every positive value [M1] so the range is $f(x)\in\mathbb{R}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $y=\ln\left(x^2-2x-8\right)\Rightarrow e^y=(x-1)^2-9$ [M1] $x-1=\sqrt{e^y+9}$, taking the positive root since $x>4$ [A1] $f^{-1}(x)=1+\sqrt{e^x+9}$, domain $x\in\mathbb{R}$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $f^{-1}(2.5)=1+\sqrt{e^{2.5}+9}$ [M1] $=5.60$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Complete the square to invert a quadratic inside a logarithm, and use the restricted domain to choose the correct root. The domain of the inverse equals the range of $f$.

subtopic: Quartic function: roots, turning points and range
statement: (a) Consider the function $f(x)=x^4-6x^2+x+2$ for $x\in\mathbb{R}$. Use your GDC to find all solutions of $f(x)=0$, correct to 3 significant figures. [3] (b) Find the coordinates of the local minimum points and the local maximum point of the graph of $f$. [3] (c) Write down the range of $f$. [1] (d) Find the values of $k$ for which the equation $f(x)=k$ has exactly two distinct real solutions. [4]
markscheme: (a) Graph or solve $f(x)=0$ [M1] $x=-2.47,\ -0.510,\ 0.700,\ 2.27$ [A1] [A1] [3 marks] (b) Minimum at $(-1.77,\ -8.75)$ [A1] Minimum at $(1.69,\ -5.29)$ [A1] Maximum at $(0.0835,\ 2.04)$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $f(x)\geq-8.75$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) Sketch $y=f(x)$ and the horizontal line $y=k$ [M1] Two solutions between the two minimum values: $-8.75<k<-5.29$ [A1] Also two solutions above the local maximum: $k>2.04$ [A1] At $k=-5.29$ there are three solutions and at $k=2.04$ there are three solutions, so these values are excluded [R1] [4 marks]
tips: Use the GDC to find roots and turning points, and keep at least 4 significant figures until the final rounding. For the number of solutions of $f(x)=k$, imagine sliding a horizontal line up the graph and count the crossings.

subtopic: Inverse of a square root function and intersection with y = x
statement: Let $f(x)=\sqrt{2x+3}$ for $x\ge-\dfrac32$. (a) State the range of $f$. [1] (b) Find $f^{-1}(x)$ and state its domain. [3] (c) Show that the graphs of $f$ and $f^{-1}$ meet on the line $y=x$, and find the point of intersection. [4]
markscheme: (a) $y\ge0$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $y^2=2x+3$ after swapping [M1] $f^{-1}(x)=\dfrac{x^2-3}2$ [A1] domain $x\ge0$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) graphs of a function and its inverse are reflections in $y=x$ [R1] $\sqrt{2x+3}=x$ [M1] $x^2-2x-3=0$, $x=3$ (reject $-1$ since $x\ge0$) [A1] point $(3,3)$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: The domain of the inverse equals the range of the original function. Intersections on $y=x$ solve $f(x)=x$.

subtopic: Intersections of an exponential and a quadratic
statement: Let $f(x)=2^{x}$ and $g(x)=x^{2}+1$. (a) Use your GDC to find all solutions of $f(x)=g(x)$. [3] (b) Hence solve $2^{x}>x^{2}+1$. [3] (c) Explain why there is no solution with $x<0$. [1]
markscheme: (a) Sketch both graphs [M1]; $x=0$ and $x=1$ [A1]; $x=4.26$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $f$ above $g$ between the first two solutions [M1]; $0<x<1$ [A1]; and for $x>4.26$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) For $x<0$, $0<2^{x}<1\le x^{2}+1$ [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Use the intersect function and note where the exponential graph lies above the quadratic.

subtopic: Domain, range and inverse of a square root function
statement: (a) A sensor reading $R$ is related to the depth $x$ by $R=f(x)$, where $f(x)=\sqrt{2x-6}-1$. Find the largest possible domain of $f$. [2] (b) Write down the range of $f$. [1] (c) Find $f^{-1}(x)$. [3] (d) State the domain of $f^{-1}$. [1]
markscheme: (a) Require $2x-6\geq0$ [M1] so $x\geq3$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $f(x)\geq-1$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) Let $y=\sqrt{2x-6}-1$ and swap $x$ and $y$: $x+1=\sqrt{2y-6}$ [M1] $(x+1)^2=2y-6$ [M1] $f^{-1}(x)=\dfrac{(x+1)^2+6}{2}=\dfrac{x^2+2x+7}{2}$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $x\geq-1$ [A1] (the range of $f$) [1 mark]
tips: The domain of the inverse is the range of the original function, so find the range first. Square both sides carefully after swapping $x$ and $y$.

subtopic: Inverse and composite of linear and quadratic functions
statement: The functions $f$ and $g$ are defined by $f(x)=2 x + 3$ and $g(x)=x^{2} - 1$ for $x\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Find $f^{-1}(x)$. [3] (b) Find $(f\circ g)(x)$ and $(g\circ f)(x)$ in simplified form. [4] (c) Solve $(f\circ g)(x)=(g\circ f)(x)$. [3]
markscheme: (a) Let $y=f(x)$ and swap $x$ and $y$ [M1]: $x=2 y + 3$ [A1]; $f^{-1}(x)=\frac{x}{2} - \frac{3}{2}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $f(g(x))=2 x^{2} + 1$ [M1][A1]; $g(f(x))=\left(2 x + 3\right)^{2} - 1$ [M1][A1] [4 marks] (c) Set the two expressions equal [M1]: $x=-3 - \frac{\sqrt{22}}{2}$; $x=-3 + \frac{\sqrt{22}}{2}$ [A1][A1] (a repeated root counts once) [3 marks]
tips: $(f\circ g)(x)$ means apply $g$ first, then $f$; the composition is not usually commutative.

subtopic: Piecewise tariff function for electricity
statement: (a) An electricity company charges $C(x)$ dollars for $x$ kWh used in a month, where $C(x)=\begin{cases}0.18x, & 0\leq x\leq200\\ 36+0.25(x-200), & 200<x\leq500\\ 111+0.32(x-500), & x>500\end{cases}$ Find $C(150)$ and $C(350)$. [3] (b) Show that $C$ is continuous at $x=200$ and at $x=500$. [2] (c) A customer's bill is $150.60$ dollars. Find the number of kWh used. [2] (d) State the gradient of $C$ for $x>500$ and interpret it in context. [1]
tips: First decide which piece applies by comparing the input (or the bill) with the values at the boundaries. Continuity means the pieces meet with no jump.

subtopic: Quadratic profit model from roots and maximum
statement: (a) A theatre's weekly profit, $P$ thousand dollars, when a ticket costs $x$ dollars is modeled by a quadratic function. The profit is zero when $x=2$ and when $x=10$, and the maximum profit is $64$ thousand dollars. Find the ticket price that gives the maximum profit. [2] (b) Write $P(x)$ in the form $a(x-2)(x-10)$ and find the value of $a$. [3] (c) Expand $P(x)$ to the form $px^2+qx+r$. [2] (d) Write down the range of ticket prices for which the profit is positive. [1]
markscheme: (a) The axis of symmetry is halfway between the roots [M1] $x=\dfrac{2+10}{2}=6$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $P(x)=a(x-2)(x-10)$ [M1] $P(6)=a(4)(-4)=64$ [M1] $a=-4$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $-4(x^2-12x+20)$ [M1] $=-4x^2+48x-80$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $2<x<10$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: The maximum of a quadratic lies on the axis of symmetry, which is the midpoint of the roots. Use the maximum point to find the stretch factor $a$.

subtopic: Logistic population model for a deer herd
statement: (a) The number of deer, $P$, in a protected forest $t$ years after monitoring began is modeled by $P(t)=\dfrac{1200}{1+7e^{-0.35t}}$ for $t\geq0$. Find the initial number of deer. [2] (b) Write down the limiting value of $P$ as $t\to\infty$, and state what it represents in context. [2] (c) Find the time at which the population first reaches $600$. [2] (d) Find the number of deer after $10$ years, and the time at which the population first exceeds $1100$. [3] (e) Explain one reason why this model may not remain valid for large $t$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $P(0)=\dfrac{1200}{1+7}$ [M1] $=150$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $1200$ [A1] the carrying capacity of the forest (the largest population the environment can sustain) [A1] [2 marks] (c) $1+7e^{-0.35t}=2$ [M1] $t=\dfrac{\ln7}{0.35}=5.56$ years [A1] [2 marks] (d) $P(10)=990.6\approx991$ deer [A1] Solve $P(t)=1100$ [M1] $t=12.4$ years [A1] [3 marks] (e) For example, the carrying capacity may change due to disease, habitat loss or food supply, so the population would not stay near $1200$ [R1] [1 mark]
tips: At $t=0$ the exponential term equals $e^0=1$. The limiting value comes from letting $e^{-0.35t}\to0$, leaving the numerator of the fraction.

subtopic: Continuous piecewise function
statement: A function is defined by $f(x)=\begin{cases} ax+b & x\le2 \\ x^{2}-1 & x>2 \end{cases}$. The graph of $f$ is continuous (it has no break) and $f(0)=-5$. (a) Find $a$ and $b$. [3] (b) Solve $f(x)=11$. [3] (c) Use your GDC to find the range of $f$ on the domain $-1\le x\le3$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $b=-5$ [A1]; continuity at $x=2$: $2a+b=2^{2}-1=3$ [M1]; $a=4$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) For $x\le2$: $4x-5=11$ gives $x=4>2$, rejected [A1]; for $x>2$: $x^{2}=12$ [M1]; $x=\sqrt{12}=3.46$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $f(-1)=-9$ and $f(3)=8$ [A1][A1]; $f$ is increasing, so range $-9\le f(x)\le8$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: At the break point, the two pieces must give the same value.

subtopic: Restricting the domain of x e to the minus x to make an inverse
statement: Let $f(x)=xe^{-x}$ for $x\in\mathbb R$. (a) Find the coordinates of the maximum point of $f$, and state the range of $f$. [4] (b) The domain is restricted to $x\ge1$. Explain why $f$ then has an inverse, and state the domain of $f^{-1}$. [2] (c) Solve $f^{-1}(0.2)$, that is, find $x\ge1$ with $xe^{-x}=0.2$, to three significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) $f'(x)=(1-x)e^{-x}$ [M1][A1] maximum at $\left(1,e^{-1}\right)$ [A1] range $\left(-\infty,\dfrac1e\right]$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $f$ is decreasing for $x\ge1$, so one-to-one [R1] domain of $f^{-1}$ is the range of $f$: $\left(0,\dfrac1e\right]$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) solve on the calculator [M1] $x=2.54$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The inverse exists on any interval where the function is strictly monotonic. Here it cannot be written in closed form, so use the numerical solver.

subtopic: Restricted domain and inverse of a quadratic
statement: Let $f(x)=x^2-6x+11$, for $x\ge a$. (a) Find the smallest value of $a$ for which $f$ has an inverse function. [2] Let $a$ take the value found in part (a). (b) Find $f^{-1}(x)$ and state its domain. [3] (c) Solve $f(x)=f^{-1}(x)$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $f(x)=(x-3)^2+2$ [M1] smallest $a=3$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $x=(y-3)^2+2$ (interchange $x$ and $y$) [M1] $y-3=\sqrt{x-2}$ (positive root since $y\ge3$) [A1] $f^{-1}(x)=3+\sqrt{x-2}$, domain $x\ge2$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $f$ is increasing on $x\ge3$, so solutions lie on $y=x$ [R1] $x^2-6x+11=x$, so $x^2-7x+11=0$ [M1] $x=\dfrac{7\pm\sqrt5}{2}$ [A1] reject $x=\dfrac{7-\sqrt5}{2}\ (\approx2.38)$ since it is less than $3$; so $x=\dfrac{7+\sqrt5}{2}$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: The inverse of a restricted quadratic needs the correct sign for the square root: the sign is fixed by the restriction on the domain of $f$. When solving $f(x)=f^{-1}(x)$ by setting $f(x)=x$, check each root against the domain.

subtopic: Area between a function and its inverse
statement: Let $f$ be an increasing differentiable function with $f(0)=0$, and let $a>0$. (a) For $f(x)=x^2$ with $x\ge0$, find the area enclosed between the graphs of $f$ and $f^{-1}$. [4] (b) By using the substitution $y=f(x)$ and integration by parts, show that $\displaystyle\int_0^{f(a)}f^{-1}(y)\,dy=af(a)-\int_0^af(x)\,dx$. [4] (c) Interpret the identity in part (b) geometrically. [2] (d) Use $f(x)=e^x-1$ and $a=\ln2$ to show that $\displaystyle\int_0^1\ln(1+y)\,dy=2\ln2-1$. [3] (e) Use $f(x)=\sin x$ and $a=\dfrac\pi2$ to find $\displaystyle\int_0^1\arcsin y\,dy$ exactly. [2]
markscheme: (a) $f^{-1}(x)=\sqrt x$ [A1] the graphs meet at $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$ [A1] $\displaystyle\int_0^1\left(\sqrt x-x^2\right)dx$ [M1] $=\dfrac23-\dfrac13=\dfrac13$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $y=f(x)$, $dy=f'(x)\,dx$, limits $0$ to $a$ [M1] $\displaystyle\int_0^axf'(x)\,dx$ [A1] parts: $\left[xf(x)\right]_0^a-\displaystyle\int_0^af(x)\,dx$ [M1] $=af(a)-\displaystyle\int_0^af(x)\,dx$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) the two integrals are the areas of regions on either side of the curve inside the rectangle with corners $(0,0)$ and $(a,f(a))$ [A1] they add up to the area of the rectangle [R1] [2 marks] (d) $f(\ln2)=1$ and $f^{-1}(y)=\ln(1+y)$ [A1] $\displaystyle\int_0^{\ln2}(e^x-1)dx=1-\ln2$ [A1] $\displaystyle\int_0^1\ln(1+y)dy=\ln2-(1-\ln2)=2\ln2-1$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) $\dfrac\pi2\times1-\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin x\,dx$ [M1] $=\dfrac\pi2-1$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Integrating an inverse function is the same as integrating the original function and subtracting from a rectangle's area.

subtopic: Number of solutions of a quadratic depending on a parameter
statement: Let $f(x)=x^2-6x+k$, where $k$ is a constant. (a) Find the coordinates of the vertex of the graph of $f$ in terms of $k$. [2] (b) Find the values of $k$ for which the equation $f(x)=0$ has two distinct real solutions. [3] (c) Given $k=5$, use your calculator to find the zeros of $f$ and the range of $f$. [3] (d) For $k=5$, find the largest domain of the form $x\geq a$ on which $f$ has an inverse, and find $f^{-1}(x)$ for this domain. [4]
markscheme: (a) $x=\dfrac{6}{2}=3$ [A1]; $f(3)=k-9$, vertex $(3,k-9)$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\Delta=36-4k>0$ [M1][A1]; $k<9$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Zeros $x=1$ and $x=5$ [A1][A1]; range $f(x)\geq-4$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $a=3$ [A1]; $y=(x-3)^2-4$, swap and solve [M1]: $x+4=(y-3)^2$ so $f^{-1}(x)=3+\sqrt{x+4}$ [A1][A1] (positive root because $x\geq3$) [4 marks]
tips: The discriminant decides the number of real roots; to invert a quadratic, restrict the domain to one side of the vertex.

subtopic: Domain, range and a restricted inverse of a logarithm of a quadratic
statement: Let $f(x)=\ln\left(x^2-x-2\right)$. (a) Find the largest possible domain of $f$. [3] (b) Explain why $f$ is not one-to-one on its domain. [1] (c) Restrict the domain to $x>2$. Find $f^{-1}(x)$ and its domain. [4]
markscheme: (a) $x^2-x-2=(x-2)(x+1)>0$ [M1] critical values $-1$ and $2$ [A1] $x<-1$ or $x>2$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $f(x)=f(1-x)$ (symmetric about $x=\tfrac12$), for example $f(-2)=f(3)=\ln4$ [R1] [1 mark] (c) $e^y=x^2-x-2$, so $x^2-x-\left(2+e^y\right)=0$ [M1] $x=\dfrac{1+\sqrt{9+4e^y}}2$ (positive root as $x>2$) [A1][A1] $f^{-1}(x)=\dfrac{1+\sqrt{9+4e^x}}2$ for $x\in\mathbb R$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: On the restricted domain, solve $y=f(x)$ as a quadratic in $x$ and choose the root that lies in the domain.

subtopic: Logistic growth: linearization, inverse and growth rate
statement: (a) This question investigates a logistic model for the spread of a new app. The number of users, $N$ thousand, $t$ weeks after launch is modeled by $N(t)=\dfrac{800}{1+Ae^{-rt}}$, where $A$ and $r$ are positive constants. Given that $N(0)=40$, find the value of $A$. [2] (b) Write down the equations of the two horizontal asymptotes of the graph of $y=N(t)$, considering $t\to\infty$ and $t\to-\infty$. [2] (c) Given also that $N(6)=200$, find the exact value of $r$ and give it correct to 3 significant figures. [3] (d) Show that $\ln\left(\dfrac{800}{N}-1\right)=\ln A-rt$. [3] (e) The following measurements were recorded. t: 2, 4, 8, 10, 12; N: 71, 122, 305, 426, 543. Let $z=\ln\left(\dfrac{800}{N}-1\right)$. (i) Find the equation of the regression line of $z$ on $t$, to 3 significant figures. (ii) Hence estimate $r$ and $A$, and comment on the consistency with your answers to parts (a) and (c). [4] (f) Using $r=0.30764$, find an expression for $t$ in terms of $N$, and hence find the time at which the number of users reaches $600$ thousand. [3] (g) The rate of growth satisfies $\dfrac{dN}{dt}=rN\left(1-\dfrac{N}{800}\right)$. Find the maximum rate of growth, in thousands of users per week, and the time at which it occurs. [3] (h) A rival analyst suggests the exponential model $E(t)=40e^{0.3t}$. Compare the two models at $t=6$, and find when the exponential model predicts more than $800$ thousand users. [3] (i) State one reason why the logistic model is more realistic than the exponential model for the number of users. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{800}{1+A}=40$ [M1] $A=19$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $y=800$ (as $t\to\infty$) [A1] $y=0$ (as $t\to-\infty$) [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\dfrac{800}{1+19e^{-6r}}=200\Rightarrow1+19e^{-6r}=4$ [M1] $e^{-6r}=\dfrac{3}{19}$ [M1] $r=\dfrac{1}{6}\ln\dfrac{19}{3}=0.308$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $N\left(1+Ae^{-rt}\right)=800$ [M1] $\dfrac{800}{N}-1=Ae^{-rt}$ [M1] taking natural logarithms: $\ln\left(\dfrac{800}{N}-1\right)=\ln A-rt$ [AG] [3 marks] (e) (i) $z=-0.308t+2.95$ [A1] [A1] (ii) $r\approx0.308$ [A1] $A=e^{2.945}\approx19.0$, so both estimates agree with $r=0.308$ and $A=19$ [A1] [4 marks] (f) $t=\dfrac{1}{r}\left[\ln19-\ln\left(\dfrac{800}{N}-1\right)\right]$ [M1] For $N=600$: $\dfrac{800}{600}-1=\dfrac{1}{3}$ [A1] $t=\dfrac{\ln57}{0.30764}=13.1$ weeks [A1] [3 marks] (g) Maximum when $N=400$ (half the carrying capacity) [M1] $\dfrac{dN}{dt}=0.30764\times400\times\dfrac{1}{2}=61.5$ thousand users per week [A1] $400=\dfrac{800}{1+19e^{-rt}}\Rightarrow t=\dfrac{\ln19}{r}=9.57$ weeks [A1] [3 marks] (h) $N(6)=200$ and $E(6)=242$ [A1] $40e^{0.3t}=800\Rightarrow t=\dfrac{\ln20}{0.3}=9.99$ weeks [A1] The models agree early on but the exponential overestimates and then exceeds $800$ thousand [R1] [3 marks] (i) The logistic model has a finite upper limit (carrying capacity), reflecting the finite number of potential users, while the exponential grows without bound [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Part (d) is a short algebraic argument: undo the denominator, then take logarithms. In part (f) use the unrounded value of $r$ for accuracy, and remember that the maximum growth rate of a logistic curve occurs at half the carrying capacity.

subtopic: One-to-one test and restricting the domain using calculus
statement: The function $g$ is defined by $g(x)=x^4-8x^2$, for $x\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Find $g(2)$ and $g(-2)$, and hence explain why $g$ is not one-to-one. [2] (b) Find $g'(x)$ and the stationary points of $g$ for which $x\ge 0$. [3] The domain of $g$ is now restricted to $x\ge k$. (c) Find the smallest value of $k$ for which $g$ is one-to-one, giving a reason for your answer. [2] (d) For this value of $k$, write down the range of $g$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $g(2)=16-32=-16$ and $g(-2)=-16$ [M1] Two different inputs give the same output, so a horizontal line $y=-16$ meets the graph more than once and $g$ is many-to-one [R1] [2 marks] (b) $g'(x)=4x^3-16x$ [M1] $4x(x^2-4)=0$ [M1] $x=0$ or $x=2$ (with $x\ge0$) [A1] [3 marks] (c) $g'(x)<0$ for $0<x<2$ and $g'(x)>0$ for $x>2$, so $g$ decreases and then increases, and for any $k<2$ some horizontal line meets the graph twice [R1] The smallest value is $k=2$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $g(2)=-16$ and $g$ is increasing for $x\ge 2$, so the range is $g(x)\ge -16$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: A horizontal line test is a statement about outputs: if one output can come from two inputs, the function is not one-to-one. Use the derivative to find where the direction of the graph changes.

subtopic: Composite functions and their domain
statement: The functions $f$ and $g$ are defined by $f(x)=\sqrt{x-1}$ for $x\ge1$ and $g(x)=x^2+3$ for $x\in\mathbb R$. (a) Find $f\circ g(x)$ and state its domain. [3] (b) Find $g\circ f(x)$ and state its domain. [3] (c) Solve $f\circ g(x)=g\circ f(x)$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $f(g(x))=\sqrt{x^2+3-1}$ [M1] $=\sqrt{x^2+2}$ [A1] domain all real numbers, since $x^2+2>0$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $g(f(x))=\left(\sqrt{x-1}\right)^2+3$ [M1] $=x+2$ [A1] domain $x\ge1$ (inherited from $f$) [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\sqrt{x^2+2}=x+2$ with $x\ge1$ [M1] $x^2+2=x^2+4x+4$ [A1] $x=-\dfrac12$, which is outside the domain, so no solution [R1] [3 marks]
tips: The domain of $g\circ f$ is the part of the domain of $f$ for which $f(x)$ lies in the domain of $g$, but the formula may simplify and hide the restriction.

subtopic: Odd log function: domain, symmetry and inverse
statement: Let $f(x)=\ln\left(\dfrac{x+1}{x-1}\right)$, for $x$ in the largest possible real domain. (a) Find the domain of $f$. [2] (b) Show that $f$ is an odd function. [2] (c) Find $f^{-1}(x)$. [3] (d) State the domain of $f^{-1}$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{x+1}{x-1}>0$ [M1] $x<-1$ or $x>1$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $f(-x)=\ln\left(\dfrac{-x+1}{-x-1}\right)=\ln\left(\dfrac{x-1}{x+1}\right)$ [M1] $=-\ln\left(\dfrac{x+1}{x-1}\right)=-f(x)$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $x=\ln\left(\dfrac{y+1}{y-1}\right)$, so $e^x=\dfrac{y+1}{y-1}$ [M1] $ye^x-e^x=y+1$, so $y(e^x-1)=e^x+1$ [M1] $f^{-1}(x)=\dfrac{e^x+1}{e^x-1}$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $\dfrac{x+1}{x-1}=1+\dfrac{2}{x-1}$ never equals $1$, so $f(x)\ne0$; domain of $f^{-1}$ is $x\in\mathbb{R},\ x\ne0$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: For the domain of a logarithm of a fraction, solve a sign inequality for the fraction. The domain of the inverse is the range of $f$, so look for any value that $f$ can never take.

subtopic: One-to-one functions and restricting a domain
statement: Let $f(x)=x^2-4x+7$ for $x\in\mathbb R$. (a) Explain why $f$ has no inverse function on the domain $\mathbb R$. [1] (b) The domain of $f$ is restricted to $x\ge k$. Find the smallest value of $k$ for which $f$ has an inverse. [2] (c) For this restricted domain, find $f^{-1}(x)$ and state its domain. [4]
markscheme: (a) $f$ is many-to-one: it fails the horizontal line test, e.g. $f(1)=f(3)$ [R1] [1 mark] (b) vertex at $x=2$ since $f(x)=(x-2)^2+3$ [M1] $k=2$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $y=(x-2)^2+3$, swap [M1] $x-3=(y-2)^2$ [A1] $y=2+\sqrt{x-3}$ (taking the positive root since $y\ge2$) [R1] domain $x\ge3$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: A function has an inverse only if it is one-to-one. For a parabola restrict the domain to one side of the vertex.

subtopic: Quadratic: roots, axis of symmetry and vertex
statement: (a) Consider $f(x)=x^2-8x+12$. Find the roots of $f(x)=0$. [2] (b) Write down the equation of the axis of symmetry of the graph of $f$. [1] (c) Find the coordinates of the vertex. [2] (d) Write down the range of $f$. [1]
tips: The axis of symmetry is halfway between the roots, or $x=-\dfrac{b}{2a}$. The vertex gives the minimum value, which is the lower end of the range.

subtopic: Exponential function: range, solving and inverse
statement: Let $f(x)=3e^x+2$, for $x\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Write down the range of $f$. [1] (b) Solve $f(x)=17$. [2] (c) Find $f^{-1}(x)$. [3] (d) Write down the domain of $f^{-1}$. [1]
tips: The domain of an inverse function is the range of the original. Isolate the exponential before taking logarithms.

subtopic: Restricted domain and solving f(x) = f inverse (x)
statement: The function $f$ is defined by $f(x)=x^2-4x+5$, for $x\ge 2$. (a) Find an expression for $f^{-1}(x)$ and state its domain. [3] (b) Given that $f(x)=f^{-1}(x)=y$, explain why $y=x$. [2] (c) Hence solve the equation $f(x)=f^{-1}(x)$, giving your answer in exact form. [4]
markscheme: (a) $f(x)=(x-2)^2+1$ [M1] $y=(x-2)^2+1$ gives $x=2+\sqrt{y-1}$ (positive root since $x\ge 2$) [M1] $f^{-1}(x)=2+\sqrt{x-1}$, with domain $x\ge 1$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $f(x)=f^{-1}(x)=y$ implies $f(y)=x$ [R1] $f$ is increasing for $x\ge 2$, so if $y>x$ then $f(y)>f(x)$, i.e. $x>y$, a contradiction; similarly $y<x$ is impossible, so $y=x$ [R1] [2 marks] (c) $f(x)=x$ gives $x^2-5x+5=0$ [M1] $x=\dfrac{5\pm\sqrt5}{2}$ [A1] The value $\dfrac{5-\sqrt5}{2}\approx 1.38$ is less than 2, so it is rejected [R1] $x=\dfrac{5+\sqrt5}{2}$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Solutions of $f(x)=f^{-1}(x)$ for an increasing function lie on the line $y=x$, but always check each root against the restricted domain.

subtopic: Solving f(x) = g(x) and inequalities with a GDC
statement: The functions $f$ and $g$ are defined by $f(x)=e^{0.5x}$ and $g(x)=4-x^2$, for $x\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Solve the equation $f(x)=g(x)$. [3] (b) Hence solve the inequality $f(x)>g(x)$. [2]
markscheme: (a) Using a GDC to find the intersections of $y=e^{0.5x}$ and $y=4-x^2$ [M1] $x=-1.90$ [A1] $x=1.41$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) At $x=0$, $f(0)=1<g(0)=4$, so $f$ is below $g$ between the intersections [M1] $f(x)>g(x)$ for $x<-1.90$ or $x>1.41$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Sketch both graphs on your GDC and read off all intersections in the stated domain. For inequalities, test one point to decide which graph is higher between the intersections.

subtopic: Composite and inverse functions: solving equations
statement: The functions $f$ and $g$ are defined by $f(x)=2x+1$ and $g(x)=x^2-3$. (a) Find $(g\circ f)(x)$ and $(f\circ g)(x)$. [3] (b) Solve $(g\circ f)(x)=(f\circ g)(x)$. [3] (c) Find $\left(f^{-1}\circ g\right)(x)$ and its value when $x=3$. [3]
tips: $(f\circ g)(x)$ means apply $g$ first. The inverse of a linear function undoes the multiplication and the addition in reverse order.

subtopic: Inverse of a logarithmic function
statement: The function $f$ is defined by $f(x)=\ln(2x-1)+3$, for $x>\dfrac12$. (a) Find an expression for $f^{-1}(x)$ and state its domain. [4] (b) Solve $f^{-1}(x)=2$, giving your answer in exact form. [2]
tips: To invert a logarithm, isolate the log term and exponentiate both sides. The domain of the inverse is the range of the original function, which for a log function is all real numbers.

subtopic: Largest rectangle inscribed in a right-angled triangle
statement: A right-angled triangle has its two perpendicular sides along the positive $x$- and $y$-axes, with vertices at $(0,0)$, $(6,0)$ and $(0,8)$. A rectangle has one corner at the origin, two sides along the axes, and the opposite corner $(x,y)$ on the hypotenuse. (a) Show that $y=8-\dfrac43x$ and that the area of the rectangle is $A=8x-\dfrac43x^2$. [3] (b) Find the maximum area and the dimensions of the rectangle that achieves it. [3] (c) Show that the maximum area is half of the area of the triangle. [1]
markscheme: (a) hypotenuse has gradient $-\dfrac86=-\dfrac43$ [M1] $y=8-\dfrac43x$ [A1] $A=xy=8x-\dfrac43x^2$ [AG] [A1] [3 marks] (b) vertex of the parabola at $x=\dfrac{8}{2\times\frac43}=3$ [M1] $y=4$ [A1] $A=12$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) triangle area $=\dfrac12\times6\times8=24$, and $12=\dfrac12\times24$ [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Express $y$ in terms of $x$ using the equation of the hypotenuse, then maximize the quadratic area function.

subtopic: Projectile height model with a changed gravity parameter
statement: A ball is thrown upward from a height of $1.2$ m. Its height $h$ meters above the ground after $t$ seconds is modeled by $h=1.2+15t-4.9t^2$. (a) Find the maximum height of the ball and the time at which it occurs. [3] (b) Find the time at which the ball hits the ground. [2] (c) Find the length of time for which the ball is higher than $8$ m above the ground. [3] (d) On another planet, the same throw is modeled by $h=1.2+15t-kt^2$ and the ball hits the ground after exactly $6$ seconds. Find the value of $k$. [2]
tips: Reject the negative root when finding the landing time. Carry full calculator values into the subtraction in part (c) and round only at the end.

subtopic: Powers and differences of roots
statement: The roots of the equation $2x^2+6x-5=0$ are $\alpha$ and $\beta$. (a) Show that $\alpha^2+\beta^2=14$. [2] (b) Find the value of $\alpha^3+\beta^3$. [3] (c) Find the exact value of $|\alpha-\beta|$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\alpha+\beta=-3$, $\alpha\beta=-\dfrac52$ [A1] $\alpha^2+\beta^2=(\alpha+\beta)^2-2\alpha\beta=9+5$ [M1] $=14$ [AG] [2 marks] (b) $\alpha^3+\beta^3=(\alpha+\beta)^3-3\alpha\beta(\alpha+\beta)$ [M1] $=-27-3\left(-\dfrac52\right)(-3)$ [A1] $=-27-\dfrac{45}{2}=-\dfrac{99}{2}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $(\alpha-\beta)^2=(\alpha+\beta)^2-4\alpha\beta=9+10=19$ [M1] $|\alpha-\beta|=\sqrt{19}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Memorize $\alpha^3+\beta^3=(\alpha+\beta)^3-3\alpha\beta(\alpha+\beta)$ or derive it quickly by cubing $\alpha+\beta$. Part (a) is useful as a check on your signs.

subtopic: Quadratic inequality
statement: Solve $x^2-x-6\ge0$ and hence solve $\left(2^y\right)^2-2^y-6\ge0$. (a) Solve $x^2-x-6\ge0$. [3] (b) Hence solve $\left(2^y\right)^2-2^y-6\ge0$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $(x-3)(x+2)\ge0$ [M1] critical values $-2$ and $3$ [A1] $x\le-2$ or $x\ge3$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) let $x=2^y>0$ [M1] $x\ge3$ [A1] $y\ge\log_23$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A quadratic opening upward is non-negative outside its roots. For the second part, remember $2^y>0$.

subtopic: A quadratic inequality from perimeter and area
statement: A rectangle has a perimeter of $40$ cm and one side of length $x$ cm. Its area is at least $91$ cm$^2$. (a) Show that $x^2-20x+91\le0$. [2] (b) Find the possible values of $x$. [2]
markscheme: (a) the other side is $20-x$ [A1] $x(20-x)\ge91$ so $x^2-20x+91\le0$ [AG] [A1] [2 marks] (b) $(x-7)(x-13)\le0$ [M1] $7\le x\le13$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Use the perimeter to express the other side in terms of $x$.

subtopic: Roots in a given ratio
statement: The equation $2x^2-kx+9=0$, where $k\in\mathbb R$, has two real roots, one of which is twice the other. (a) Find the possible values of $k$. [6] (b) For the positive value of $k$, solve the equation. [2]
markscheme: (a) Roots $\alpha$ and $2\alpha$ [M1] Sum: $3\alpha=\dfrac k2$ [A1] Product: $2\alpha^2=\dfrac92$ [A1] $\alpha=\pm\dfrac32$ [M1] $k=6\alpha$, so $k=9$ [A1] or $k=-9$ [A1] [6 marks] (b) $2x^2-9x+9=(2x-3)(x-3)=0$ [M1] $x=\dfrac32$ or $x=3$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Let the roots be $\alpha$ and $2\alpha$ and use both the sum and product of roots. Do not forget the negative case.

subtopic: Completing the square for a concave parabola: vertex and range
statement: Let $f(x)=-x^2+6x+7$. (a) Write $f(x)$ in the form $-(x-h)^2+k$. [2] (b) Write down the coordinates of the vertex of the graph of $f$ and the range of $f$. [2] (c) Solve $f(x)=0$. [2] (d) Find the set of values of $c$ for which the equation $f(x)=c$ has two distinct real solutions. [2]
markscheme: (a) $f(x)=-(x^2-6x)+7=-\big[(x-3)^2-9\big]+7$ [M1] $=-(x-3)^2+16$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Vertex $(3,16)$ [A1] Range: $f(x)\le16$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $(x-3)^2=16$ [M1] $x=-1$ or $x=7$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) The graph opens downward with maximum value $16$ [M1] $c<16$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: For a negative leading coefficient, factor out the minus sign before completing the square. The range of a downward parabola is bounded above by the vertex $y$-value.

subtopic: Profit model: maximum profit and a range of prices
statement: A school club sells T-shirts. When the price is \$$p$ per shirt, it sells $300-8p$ shirts, where $6<p<37.5$. Each shirt costs the club \$6 to make, and there is a fixed cost of \$150. (a) Show that the profit, in dollars, is $P=-8p^2+348p-1950$. [3] (b) Find the price that maximizes the profit and find the maximum profit. [3] (c) Find the range of prices for which the profit is at least \$1000. [3]
tips: Write down revenue minus all costs, including fixed costs, before expanding. For a range of prices, solve the equation with your calculator and then choose the correct side of the parabola.

subtopic: Real roots of a family of equations, including a degenerate case
statement: Consider the equation $(k-1)x^2+4x+(k+2)=0$, where $k$ is a real number. (a) For $k\ne1$, find the set of values of $k$ for which the equation has at least one real root. [4] (b) Explain why $k=1$ must also be included, and state the complete set of values of $k$. [2]
markscheme: (a) discriminant $16-4(k-1)(k+2)\ge0$ [M1] $k^2+k-6\le0$ [A1] $(k+3)(k-2)\le0$ [A1] $-3\le k\le2$ with $k\ne1$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) when $k=1$ the equation is $4x+3=0$, which has the real root $-\dfrac34$ [R1] complete set: $-3\le k\le2$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: When the coefficient of $x^2$ is zero the equation is linear, so the discriminant test does not apply, and it must be checked separately.

subtopic: Quadratic inequality and a logarithmic substitution
statement: (a) Solve the inequality $6x^2-x-12<0$. [3] (b) Hence solve the inequality $6(\ln y)^2-\ln y-12<0$, giving your answer in exact form. [3]
markscheme: (a) $6x^2-x-12=(2x-3)(3x+4)$ [M1] Roots $x=\dfrac32$ and $x=-\dfrac43$ [A1] $-\dfrac43<x<\dfrac32$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Let $x=\ln y$ [M1] $-\dfrac43<\ln y<\dfrac32$ [A1] $e^{-4/3}<y<e^{3/2}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: For an upward parabola, the quadratic is negative between its roots. Apply the exponential function to all three parts of a double inequality.

subtopic: Inequality with a parameter and counting integer solutions
statement: Let $k$ be a real constant. Consider the inequality $x^2-(k+2)x+2k<0$. (a) Given that $k>2$, solve the inequality, giving your answer in terms of $k$. [3] (b) Given that $k>2$ and that exactly three integers satisfy the inequality, find the range of possible values of $k$. [3] (c) Show that when $k=2$ the inequality has no solution. [2]
markscheme: (a) $x^2-(k+2)x+2k=(x-2)(x-k)$ [M1] [A1] since $k>2$, the product is negative between the roots: $2<x<k$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) The integers must be $3,4,5$ [M1] so $k>5$ [A1] and $k\le 6$ [A1] giving $5<k\le 6$ [3 marks] (c) For $k=2$ the inequality is $(x-2)^2<0$ [M1] a square is never negative, so there is no solution [R1] [2 marks]
tips: In part (b) check the endpoints separately: $x=k$ itself is not included because the inequality is strict, which is why $k=6$ is allowed.

subtopic: Distinct real roots with a restricted leading coefficient
statement: Consider the equation $(k+1)x^2-6x+(k-1)=0$, where $k\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Find the set of values of $k$ for which the equation has two distinct real roots. [5] (b) Find the number of real solutions when $k=-1$ and solve the equation in this case. [2]
markscheme: (a) The equation is quadratic only if $k\ne-1$ [A1] $\Delta=(-6)^2-4(k+1)(k-1)$ [M1] $=40-4k^2$ [A1] $\Delta>0$ gives $k^2<10$ [M1] $-\sqrt{10}<k<\sqrt{10}$, $k\ne-1$ [A1] [5 marks] (b) For $k=-1$ the equation is $-6x-2=0$, which is linear [M1] One real solution, $x=-\dfrac13$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: When the coefficient of $x^2$ contains a parameter, always check the value that makes it zero separately. The discriminant only applies when the equation is truly quadratic.

subtopic: Chord of a parabola: intersection points, length and a parallel tangent
statement: The curve $C$ has equation $y=x^2-4x+1$ and the line $L$ has equation $y=x-5$. (a) Find the coordinates of the two points $A$ and $B$ where $L$ meets $C$. [4] (b) Find the exact length of $AB$. [2] (c) The line $y=x+c$ is a tangent to $C$. Find the value of $c$. [3]
tips: A tangent to a parabola corresponds to a repeated root, so set the discriminant of the combined equation to zero. Keep the exact form $\sqrt2$ in Paper 1.

subtopic: Exponential equation reduced to a quadratic, and an exponential inequality
statement: Consider the equation $2^{2x+1}-5\cdot2^x+2=0$. (a) Show that, with $y=2^x$, the equation can be written as $2y^2-5y+2=0$. [2] (b) Hence solve the equation. [3] (c) Hence solve the inequality $2^{2x+1}-5\cdot2^x+2<0$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $2^{2x+1}=2\cdot(2^x)^2=2y^2$ [M1] so the equation becomes $2y^2-5y+2=0$ [A1] [AG] [2 marks] (b) $(2y-1)(y-2)=0$ [M1] $y=\dfrac12$ or $y=2$ [A1] $2^x=\dfrac12$ or $2^x=2$ so $x=-1$ or $x=1$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) The parabola $2y^2-5y+2$ opens upward, so it is negative for $\dfrac12<y<2$ [A1] Since $2^x$ is an increasing function, the order is preserved [R1] $-1<x<1$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: After a substitution, remember to convert answers back to the original variable. When solving an inequality in $2^x$, mention that $2^x$ is increasing.

subtopic: A quadratic with a trigonometric coefficient and complex roots
statement: Consider the equation $x^2-2x\cos\theta+1=0$, where $0<\theta<\pi$. (a) Show that the equation has no real roots. [2] (b) Solve the equation for $x\in\mathbb C$, and write the roots in the form $r\operatorname{cis}\alpha$. [3] (c) Hence write down the sum and the product of the roots, and verify them against the coefficients. [2]
markscheme: (a) discriminant $4\cos^2\theta-4=-4\sin^2\theta$ [M1] $<0$ since $\sin\theta\ne0$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $x=\dfrac{2\cos\theta\pm2\mathrm i\sin\theta}2$ [M1] $=\cos\theta\pm\mathrm i\sin\theta$ [A1] $\operatorname{cis}(\pm\theta)$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) sum $2\cos\theta$ and product $\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta=1$ [A1] these equal $-(-2\cos\theta)$ and $1$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A negative discriminant gives conjugate complex roots. For these roots the modulus is 1.

subtopic: Greatest value of the reciprocal of a quadratic
statement: Let $f(x)=2x^2-12x+23$ and $g(x)=\dfrac1{f(x)}$. (a) Write $f(x)$ in the form $a(x-p)^2+q$. [3] (b) Explain why $g(x)$ is defined for all real $x$, and find its range. [3] (c) State the value of $x$ at which $g$ is greatest. [1]
markscheme: (a) $2\left(x^2-6x\right)+23$ [M1] $2(x-3)^2-18+23$ [A1] $=2(x-3)^2+5$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $f(x)\ge5>0$, so there is no division by zero [R1] $0<g(x)\le\dfrac15$ [A1][A1] [3 marks] (c) $x=3$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: The reciprocal is greatest where the original quadratic is least, provided the quadratic is positive.

subtopic: Discriminant and the number of real roots
statement: Consider the equation $kx^2-4x+k-3=0$ where $k$ is a non-zero constant. (a) Find the values of $k$ for which the equation has two distinct real roots. [5] (b) State the value of $k$ for which the equation has exactly one root, taking the positive value. [2]
markscheme: (a) discriminant $\Delta=16-4k(k-3)$ [M1] $16-4k^2+12k>0$ [A1] $k^2-3k-4<0$ [A1] $(k-4)(k+1)<0$ [M1] $-1<k<4$, $k\ne0$ [A1] [5 marks] (b) $\Delta=0$ gives $k=4$ or $k=-1$ [M1] positive value $k=4$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Two distinct real roots need $\Delta>0$. Remember that $k=0$ makes the equation linear, so exclude it.

subtopic: Projectile motion with time above a height
statement: A ball is thrown upward from the top of a building. Its height above the ground, in meters, $t$ seconds after it is thrown is modeled by $h(t)=-4.9t^2+14t+1.5$, for $t\ge0$ until the ball hits the ground. (a) Write down the height from which the ball is thrown. [1] (b) Find the maximum height reached by the ball and the time at which it occurs. [3] (c) Find the length of time for which the ball is higher than $8$ m above the ground. [3] (d) Find the time at which the ball hits the ground. [2]
markscheme: (a) $1.5$ m [A1] [1 mark] (b) $t=-\dfrac{14}{2(-4.9)}=1.43$ s [M1] [A1] maximum height $h=11.5$ m [A1] [3 marks] (c) Solve $-4.9t^2+14t+1.5=8$ [M1] $t=0.583$ and $t=2.27$ [A1] duration $=2.27-0.583=1.69$ s [A1] [3 marks] (d) Solve $h(t)=0$ [M1] $t=2.96$ s (the negative root is rejected) [A1] [2 marks]
tips: In context questions, reject roots outside the domain and use unrounded values in later steps. Use the GDC graph or the quadratic solver for the numerical roots.

subtopic: Quadratic that is always positive
statement: Let $f(x)=x^2+(k-1)x+(k+2)$, where $k\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Find the set of values of $k$ for which $f(x)>0$ for all real $x$. [5] (b) For $k=3$, find the minimum value of $f(x)$ and the value of $x$ at which it occurs. [2]
markscheme: (a) The leading coefficient is positive, so $f(x)>0$ for all $x$ exactly when $f$ has no real roots, that is $\Delta<0$ [R1] $\Delta=(k-1)^2-4(k+2)$ [M1] $=k^2-6k-7$ [A1] $(k-7)(k+1)<0$ [M1] $-1<k<7$ [A1] [5 marks] (b) $f(x)=x^2+2x+5=(x+1)^2+4$ [M1] minimum value $4$ at $x=-1$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: State the reason (positive leading coefficient and $\Delta<0$) in words, as the R mark is easily lost. The solution set of $\Delta<0$ is the region between the roots, not outside them.

subtopic: Tangent lines through a given point
statement: The curve $C$ has equation $y=x^2+2$. The line $L$ has equation $y=mx-2$, where $m\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Show that if $L$ is a tangent to $C$, then $m^2=16$. [3] (b) Write down the equations of the two tangents to $C$ that pass through the point $(0,-2)$. [1] (c) Find the coordinates of the points where these tangents touch $C$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $x^2+2=mx-2\Rightarrow x^2-mx+4=0$ [M1] A tangent meets the curve at exactly one point, so the equation has a repeated root and $\Delta=0$ [R1] $m^2-16=0$ so $m^2=16$ [A1] [AG] [3 marks] (b) $y=4x-2$ and $y=-4x-2$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) Repeated root $x=\dfrac{m}{2}$ [M1] $x=2$ for $m=4$ and $x=-2$ for $m=-4$ [A1] $y=6$ in both cases, so the points are $(2,6)$ and $(-2,6)$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Substitute the line into the curve and set the discriminant to zero. A repeated root of $x^2-mx+4=0$ is $x=\frac m2$, which saves solving again.

subtopic: Tangent line to a parabola using the discriminant
statement: The line $y=2x+c$ is a tangent to the curve $y=x^2-4x+7$. (a) Show that the $x$-coordinates of the points of intersection satisfy $x^2-6x+7-c=0$. [2] (b) Find the value of $c$ and the point of tangency. [4]
markscheme: (a) $x^2-4x+7=2x+c$ [M1] $x^2-6x+7-c=0$ [A1] [AG] [2 marks] (b) tangent means a repeated root, $\Delta=0$ [R1] $36-4(7-c)=0$ [M1] $c=-2$ [A1] repeated root $x=3$ and $y=2(3)-2=4$, point $(3,4)$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: A line is tangent to a parabola when substitution gives a quadratic with discriminant zero.

subtopic: Reflection and translation of a parabola
statement: Let $g(x)=-x^2+4x-1$. (a) Write $g(x)$ in the form $-(x-h)^2+k$. [2] (b) The graph of $y=g(x)$ can be obtained from the graph of $y=x^2$ by a reflection in the $x$-axis followed by a translation. Describe the translation fully. [3] (c) The graph of $y=g(x)$ is translated by the vector $\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}$ to give the graph of $y=h(x)$. Find $h(x)$, giving your answer in the form $-x^2+bx+c$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $g(x)=-(x^2-4x)-1=-\big[(x-2)^2-4\big]-1$ [M1] $=-(x-2)^2+3$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Reflection in the $x$-axis gives $y=-x^2$ [M1] Translation by $\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$, that is $2$ units right [A1] and $3$ units up [A1] [3 marks] (c) $h(x)=g(x-3)-2$ [M1] $=-(x-5)^2+3-2=-(x-5)^2+1$ [A1] $=-x^2+10x-24$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: State the reflection before the translation, as the order matters. A translation by $\begin{pmatrix} a \\ b \end{pmatrix}$ replaces $x$ by $x-a$ and then adds $b$.

subtopic: Integer roots and sum and product of roots with a parameter
statement: The equation $x^2-kx+12=0$, where $k>0$, has roots $\alpha$ and $\beta$. (a) Write down $\alpha+\beta$ and $\alpha\beta$ in terms of $k$. [1] (b) Given that $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are both positive integers, find all possible values of $k$. [3] (c) Find the smallest integer value of $k$ for which the equation has real roots. [3] (d) Find the value of $k$ for which $\alpha^2+\beta^2=40$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\alpha+\beta=k$ and $\alpha\beta=12$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Integer pairs with product $12$ [M1] $(1,12),\ (2,6),\ (3,4)$ [A1] $k=13,\ 8,\ 7$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\Delta=k^2-48\ge0$ [M1] $k\ge\sqrt{48}\approx6.93$ [A1] Smallest integer $k=7$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $\alpha^2+\beta^2=k^2-2(12)=k^2-24$ [M1] $k^2=64$ so $k=8$ (as $k>0$) [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Listing factor pairs of the product is faster than solving the quadratic in $k$. Check part (d) against part (b): $k=8$ gives roots $2$ and $6$.

subtopic: Quadratic model of a projectile
statement: The height $h$ meters of a ball above the ground $t$ seconds after being thrown is $h(t)=1.5+18t-4.9t^2$. (a) Find the greatest height of the ball and the time at which it occurs. [3] (b) Find the time at which the ball hits the ground. [2] (c) Find the length of time for which the ball is higher than $10$ m. [3]
tips: The maximum of $at^2+bt+c$ is at $t=-\dfrac b{2a}$. Use the quadratic formula (or solver) for times at a given height.

subtopic: Equations that reduce to quadratics
statement: (a) Solve the equation $x-5\sqrt{x}+6=0$. [3] (b) Solve the equation $(x^2-x)^2-8(x^2-x)+12=0$. [5]
tips: After finding $u$, always return to $x$ and check that each value is valid (in part (a), $u=\sqrt{x}$ must be non-negative). Substituting back into the original equation is a quick check.

subtopic: Finding a quadratic from its x-intercepts and maximum value
statement: A quadratic function $f$ has $x$-intercepts at $x=1$ and $x=5$, and its greatest value is $8$. (a) Write down the equation of the axis of symmetry of the graph of $f$. [1] (b) Find $f(x)$, giving your answer in the form $ax^2+bx+c$. [4] (c) Solve the inequality $f(x)>f(0)$. [3]
markscheme: (a) The axis of symmetry is midway between the intercepts: $x=3$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $f(x)=a(x-1)(x-5)$ [M1] $f(3)=8$ gives $a(2)(-2)=8$ [M1] $a=-2$ [A1] $f(x)=-2x^2+12x-10$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) $f(0)=-10$ so solve $-2x^2+12x-10>-10$ [M1] $-2x(x-6)>0$ [A1] $0<x<6$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The maximum occurs on the axis of symmetry, which is halfway between the $x$-intercepts. For part (c), note that $f(0)=-10$ gives a simpler inequality than expanding both sides.

subtopic: Completing the square and the vertex
statement: Let $f(x)=2x^2-12x+7$. (a) Write $f(x)$ in the form $a(x-h)^2+k$. [3] (b) Write down the coordinates of the vertex and the equation of the axis of symmetry. [2] (c) Find the exact roots of $f(x)=0$. [3]
tips: Complete the square by factoring the leading coefficient out of the $x^2$ and $x$ terms first.

subtopic: Projectile model: golf shot trajectory
statement: A golf ball is hit from the ground. Its height $y$ meters above the ground when it has traveled a horizontal distance $x$ meters is modeled by $y=-0.004x^2+0.6x$, for $x\ge0$. (a) Find the horizontal distance traveled by the ball before it hits the ground. [2] (b) Find the maximum height of the ball above the ground. [2] (c) The ball passes over a tree that is $14.4$ m tall at one horizontal position and just clears the same height again on the way down. Find the two horizontal distances at which the ball is $14.4$ m above the ground. [3] (d) A second shot is modeled by $y=ax-0.004x^2$ and lands $200$ m from the starting point. Find the value of $a$. [2]
tips: The maximum of a parabola occurs halfway between its roots, which gives a check on part (b). For part (c), a quadratic equation gives both positions at once.

subtopic: Tangents to a parabola from an external point
statement: The line through the point $P(1,-3)$ with gradient $m$ is a tangent to the curve $y=x^2$. (a) Show that $m^2-4m-12=0$, and find the two possible values of $m$. [5] (b) Find the acute angle between the two tangents, in degrees, to three significant figures. [3] (c) Find the exact area of the triangle whose vertices are $P$ and the two points where the tangents touch the curve. [3]
markscheme: (a) the line is $y=m(x-1)-3$ [M1] $x^2=mx-m-3$ so $x^2-mx+m+3=0$ [A1] tangent means the discriminant is zero: $m^2-4(m+3)=0$ [M1] $m^2-4m-12=0$ [AG] [A1] $m=6$ or $m=-2$ [A1] [5 marks] (b) $\tan\theta=\left|\dfrac{m_1-m_2}{1+m_1m_2}\right|=\left|\dfrac{8}{1-12}\right|$ [M1][A1] $\theta=36.0^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) repeated root $x=\dfrac m2$ so the points of contact are $(3,9)$ and $(-1,1)$ [A1] vectors from $P$: $\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 12 \end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix} -2 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] area $=\dfrac12|2\times4-12\times(-2)|=16$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A tangent to a parabola meets it at a repeated root, so the discriminant is zero. For the angle between the lines, use $\tan\theta=\left|\dfrac{m_1-m_2}{1+m_1m_2}\right|$.

subtopic: Equation whose roots are sums of a root and the reciprocal of the other
statement: The equation $x^2-px+q=0$, where $p,q\in\mathbb{R}$ and $q\ne0$, has roots $\alpha$ and $\beta$. A second quadratic equation has roots $\alpha+\dfrac1\beta$ and $\beta+\dfrac1\alpha$. (a) Show that the sum of the roots of the second equation is $\dfrac{p(q+1)}{q}$. [3] (b) Show that the product of the roots of the second equation is $\dfrac{(q+1)^2}{q}$. [3] (c) Given that the second equation has two equal roots, show that $(q+1)^2(p^2-4q)=0$. [3] (d) Explain what each of the two possibilities in part (c) tells you about the original roots $\alpha$ and $\beta$. [2]
markscheme: (a) Sum $=\alpha+\beta+\dfrac1\alpha+\dfrac1\beta$ [M1] $=(\alpha+\beta)+\dfrac{\alpha+\beta}{\alpha\beta}$ [A1] $=p+\dfrac pq$ [A1] $=\dfrac{p(q+1)}q$ [AG] [3 marks] (b) Product $=\alpha\beta+\alpha\cdot\dfrac1\alpha+\dfrac1\beta\cdot\beta+\dfrac1{\alpha\beta}$ [M1] $=q+1+1+\dfrac1q$ [A1] $=\dfrac{q^2+2q+1}q$ [A1] $=\dfrac{(q+1)^2}q$ [AG] [3 marks] (c) Equal roots mean $S^2-4P=0$ [M1] $\dfrac{p^2(q+1)^2}{q^2}-\dfrac{4(q+1)^2}{q}=0$ [A1] Multiply by $q^2$ and factor out $(q+1)^2$ [A1] $(q+1)^2(p^2-4q)=0$ [AG] [3 marks] (d) $p^2=4q$ means the discriminant of the original equation is zero, so $\alpha=\beta$ [R1] $q=-1$ means $\alpha\beta=-1$, so $\dfrac1\beta=-\alpha$ and both new roots equal $0$ [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Do not solve for $\alpha$ and $\beta$; keep everything in terms of $\alpha+\beta$ and $\alpha\beta$. A neat factor like $(q+1)^2$ appearing in both terms of the discriminant is the signal that it will factorize.

subtopic: Quadratics with consecutive integer roots
statement: Let $b$ and $c$ be integers, and consider the equation $x^2+bx+c=0$. (a) Show that if the roots are consecutive integers, then $b^2-4c=1$. [3] (b) Show that if $b^2-4c=1$, then the roots are consecutive integers. [3]
markscheme: (a) roots $n$ and $n+1$: $-b=2n+1$ and $c=n(n+1)$ [M1][A1] $b^2-4c=(2n+1)^2-4n(n+1)=1$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $x=\dfrac{-b\pm1}2$ [M1] $b^2=1+4c$ is odd, so $b$ is odd [R1] hence $\dfrac{-b\pm1}2$ are integers differing by $1$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Use the sum and product of roots for the first direction, and the quadratic formula with discriminant $1$ for the converse.

subtopic: Quadratic from described graph features
statement: The graph of the quadratic function $f(x)=ax^2+bx+c$ has axis of symmetry $x=-1$ and a minimum value of $-8$. The graph passes through the point $(0,-6)$. (a) Find the values of $a$, $b$ and $c$. [4] (b) Find the $x$-intercepts of the graph. [2] (c) Find the set of values of $k$ for which the equation $f(x)=k$ has two distinct real solutions. [2]
markscheme: (a) Vertex form $f(x)=a(x+1)^2-8$ [M1] [A1] $f(0)=a-8=-6$ [M1] $a=2$, so $f(x)=2x^2+4x-6$, giving $b=4$ and $c=-6$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $2(x^2+2x-3)=2(x+3)(x-1)=0$ [M1] $x=-3$ and $x=1$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) The graph opens upward with minimum $-8$, so the horizontal line $y=k$ meets it twice only above the minimum [R1] $k>-8$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Words such as "axis of symmetry" and "minimum value" translate directly into the vertex form $a(x-h)^2+k$. A horizontal line sketch helps with part (c).

subtopic: Quadratic from roots and a point; inequality
statement: The graph of the quadratic function $f$ crosses the $x$-axis at $x=-1$ and $x=4$, and passes through the point $(2,12)$. (a) Find $f(x)$, giving your answer in the form $ax^2+bx+c$. [3] (b) Find the coordinates of the vertex of the graph of $f$. [2] (c) Solve $f(x)>6$. [3]
tips: With known roots, use the factored form $a(x-p)(x-q)$. The axis of symmetry lies midway between the roots.

subtopic: Quadratic from a difference condition and a telescoping sum
statement: The quadratic function $f$ satisfies $f(x+1)-f(x)=2x+3$ for all real $x$, and $f(0)=5$. (a) Find $f(x)$. [4] (b) Hence evaluate $\displaystyle\sum_{x=0}^{9}(2x+3)$. [3]
markscheme: (a) let $f(x)=ax^2+bx+c$ so $f(x+1)-f(x)=2ax+a+b$ [M1][A1] compare with $2x+3$: $a=1$ and $b=2$ [A1] $f(0)=5$ gives $c=5$ so $f(x)=x^2+2x+5$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $\displaystyle\sum_{x=0}^{9}\left(f(x+1)-f(x)\right)$ telescopes to $f(10)-f(0)$ [M1][A1] $=125-5=120$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Substitute $x+1$ into the general quadratic and compare coefficients of $x$ and the constant terms. In part (b), the sum of differences collapses.

subtopic: Tangent lines to a parabola through a given point
statement: The curve $C$ has equation $y=x^2+3x+3$. Lines through the point $(0,-1)$ have equation $y=mx-1$. (a) Show that the $x$-coordinates of any points where such a line meets $C$ satisfy $x^2+(3-m)x+4=0$. [2] (b) Hence find the two values of $m$ for which the line is a tangent to $C$. [3] (c) Find the coordinates of the points where these two tangents touch $C$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $x^2+3x+3=mx-1$ [M1] $x^2+3x+3-mx+1=0$ [A1] so $x^2+(3-m)x+4=0$ [AG] [2 marks] (b) Tangent means a repeated root: $(3-m)^2-16=0$ [M1] $3-m=\pm4$ [A1] $m=7$ or $m=-1$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) For $m=7$: $x^2-4x+4=0$ so $x=2$, and the point is $(2,13)$ [M1] [A1] For $m=-1$: $x^2+4x+4=0$ so $x=-2$, and the point is $(-2,1)$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Substitute the line into the curve first, and keep $m$ as a parameter. A repeated root also gives the contact point directly as $x=-\dfrac b{2a}$.

subtopic: Expressions in alpha and beta and a new quadratic
statement: The roots of the equation $x^2-5x+3=0$ are $\alpha$ and $\beta$. (a) Write down the value of $\alpha+\beta$ and the value of $\alpha\beta$. [2] (b) Find the value of $\alpha^2+\beta^2$. [2] (c) Find a quadratic equation, with integer coefficients, that has roots $\alpha^2$ and $\beta^2$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\alpha+\beta=5$ [A1] $\alpha\beta=3$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\alpha^2+\beta^2=(\alpha+\beta)^2-2\alpha\beta$ [M1] $=25-6=19$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Sum of new roots $=19$, product of new roots $=(\alpha\beta)^2=9$ [M1] [A1] $x^2-19x+9=0$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Never solve for $\alpha$ and $\beta$ individually when they are irrational. Rewrite every symmetric expression using $\alpha+\beta$ and $\alpha\beta$.

subtopic: Quadratic function with a given range and intercept
statement: A quadratic function $f(x)=ax^2+bx+c$ has its vertex at $(2,-3)$ and passes through $(0,5)$. (a) Write $f(x)$ in the form $a(x-2)^2-3$ and find $a$. [3] (b) Expand to find $b$ and $c$, and find the roots of $f(x)=0$. [4]
tips: The vertex form makes the vertex explicit; use another point to find $a$.

subtopic: Completing the square and exact roots
statement: Let $f(x)=2x^2-12x+7$. (a) Write $f(x)$ in the form $a(x-h)^2+k$. [2] (b) Write down the coordinates of the vertex and the equation of the axis of symmetry of the graph of $f$. [2] (c) Solve $f(x)=0$, giving your answers in exact form. [2]
tips: When completing the square, take the factor $a$ out of the $x^2$ and $x$ terms only. Check by expanding your vertex form.

subtopic: Minimum of a quadratic on an interval that moves
statement: Let $f(x)=x^2-4x+1$ and let $m(k)$ be the least value of $f(x)$ on the interval $k\le x\le k+2$. (a) Write $f$ in the form $(x-p)^2+q$ and state the coordinates of its vertex. [2] (b) Find $m(k)$ in each of the cases $k\le0$, $0\le k\le2$ and $k\ge2$. [4] (c) Find the value of $k$ for which $m(k)=6$ and $k\ge2$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $(x-2)^2-3$ [A1] vertex $(2,-3)$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $k\le0$: the interval lies left of the vertex, $f$ decreasing, $m(k)=f(k+2)=k^2-3$ [M1][A1] $0\le k\le2$: contains the vertex, $m(k)=-3$ [A1] $k\ge2$: $f$ increasing, $m(k)=f(k)=k^2-4k+1$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) $k^2-4k+1=6$ [M1] $k^2-4k-5=0$ so $k=5$ (reject $-1$) [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The minimum on an interval is at the vertex if the vertex lies inside the interval, and otherwise at the end nearest the vertex.

subtopic: Rectangular enclosure against a wall
statement: A farmer has $80$ m of fencing to make a rectangular pen. One side of the pen is a long straight wall, so fencing is needed only for the other three sides. The two sides perpendicular to the wall each have length $x$ meters. (a) Show that the area of the pen is $A=80x-2x^2$ square meters. [2] (b) By completing the square, find the maximum area and the value of $x$ that gives it. [3] (c) The farmer needs an area of at least $750\ \text{m}^2$. Find the set of possible values of $x$. [3]
markscheme: (a) Side parallel to the wall has length $80-2x$ [M1] $A=x(80-2x)=80x-2x^2$ [A1] [AG] [2 marks] (b) $A=-2(x^2-40x)=-2(x-20)^2+800$ [M1] [A1] maximum area $800\ \text{m}^2$ when $x=20$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $80x-2x^2\ge 750\Rightarrow x^2-40x+375\le 0$ [M1] $(x-15)(x-25)\le0$ [A1] $15\le x\le 25$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Always define what the unknown represents before building the area expression. The inequality in part (c) needs the region between the two roots.

subtopic: Maximizing the minimum value of a family of parabolas
statement: For each real number $k$, let $f_k(x)=x^2-2kx+4k$. (a) Find the minimum value $m(k)$ of $f_k$ in terms of $k$. [3] (b) Find the value of $k$ for which $m(k)$ is as large as possible, and find that largest value. [3] (c) Explain what this tells you about every function $f_k$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $f_k(x)=(x-k)^2-k^2+4k$ [M1][A1] $m(k)=4k-k^2$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $m(k)=-(k-2)^2+4$ [M1] largest at $k=2$ [A1] largest value $4$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) no function $f_k$ has a least value greater than $4$, and the least value $4$ occurs only for $k=2$ [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Complete the square in $x$ to find the minimum as a function of $k$, which is itself a quadratic that can be maximized.

subtopic: Shortest distance from a point to a line using a quadratic
statement: The point $P$ is $(3,1)$ and the point $Q(x,x)$ lies on the line $y=x$. (a) Show that $PQ^2=2x^2-8x+10$. [2] (b) Find the least value of $PQ$ and the position of $Q$ at which it occurs. [3]
tips: Minimizing the squared distance is the same as minimizing the distance, and it gives a quadratic.

subtopic: Tangents to a parabola from an external point
statement: Consider the parabola $y=x^2$, and the point $P(p,q)$. (a) Show that the tangent to the parabola at the point $\left(t,t^2\right)$ has equation $y=2tx-t^2$. [2] (b) Show that the tangent passes through $P$ if and only if $t^2-2pt+q=0$, and deduce that there are two tangents from $P$ if and only if $q<p^2$. [3] (c) Show that the two tangents from $P$ are perpendicular if and only if $q=-\dfrac14$. [3] (d) The tangents from $P(3,5)$ touch the parabola at $A$ and $B$. Find $A$ and $B$. [3] (e) Show that, for general $P$, the line $AB$ joining the points of contact has equation $y=2px-q$, and verify it for $P(3,5)$. [3]
markscheme: (a) gradient $2t$ [A1] $y-t^2=2t(x-t)$, giving $y=2tx-t^2$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $q=2tp-t^2$ gives $t^2-2pt+q=0$ [M1] two distinct real values of $t$ need discriminant $4p^2-4q>0$ [A1] so $q<p^2$, that is, $P$ lies below the parabola [A1] [3 marks] (c) slopes $2t_1$ and $2t_2$ [A1] perpendicular means $4t_1t_2=-1$ [M1] $t_1t_2=q$ so $q=-\dfrac14$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $t^2-6t+5=0$ [M1] $t=1$ or $t=5$ [A1] $A=(1,1)$ and $B=(5,25)$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) $t_1+t_2=2p$ and $t_1t_2=q$ [A1] chord through $\left(t_1,t_1^2\right)$ and $\left(t_2,t_2^2\right)$ has gradient $t_1+t_2=2p$ and intercept $-t_1t_2=-q$ [M1] for $(3,5)$: $y=6x-5$, and $(1,1)$ and $(5,25)$ satisfy it [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A tangent from $P$ must satisfy the tangent equation at its point of contact. The quadratic in $t$ has the two points of contact as its roots.

subtopic: Factorization with an unknown and an inequality with integer solutions
statement: Let $p$ be a real number with $p>2$. (a) Factorize $x^2-(p+2)x+2p$. [2] (b) Solve the inequality $x^2-(p+2)x+2p\le0$, giving your answer in terms of $p$. [2] (c) Exactly five integers satisfy the inequality in part (b). Find the range of possible values of $p$. [3]
markscheme: (a) The factors need sum $-(p+2)$ and product $2p$ [M1] $(x-2)(x-p)$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Roots $2$ and $p$ with $p>2$; the parabola opens upward, so it is nonpositive between the roots [M1] $2\le x\le p$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) The integers $2,3,4,\dots$ must be included in turn; five integers means $2,3,4,5,6$ [M1] $p\ge6$ so that $6$ is included [A1] $p<7$ so that $7$ is excluded [A1] $6\le p<7$ [3 marks]
tips: Because $p>2$ is given, the order of the roots is known; without it you would need to split into cases. For integer-count questions, check both endpoints carefully.

subtopic: Projectile height model
statement: A ball is thrown upward from a point above the ground. Its height $h$ meters above the ground, $t$ seconds after it is thrown, is modeled by $h(t)=-4.9t^2+12t+1.5$ for $t\ge0$. (a) Write down the height from which the ball is thrown. [1] (b) Find the maximum height of the ball and the time at which it is reached. [3] (c) Find the time at which the ball hits the ground. [2] (d) Find the length of time for which the ball is higher than $6$ m above the ground. [3]
markscheme: (a) $1.5$ m [A1] [1 mark] (b) Use of vertex formula or GDC maximum [M1] $t=\dfrac{-12}{2(-4.9)}=1.22$ s [A1] $h=8.85$ m [A1] [3 marks] (c) Solve $h(t)=0$ [M1] $t=2.57$ s [A1] [2 marks] (d) $-4.9t^2+12t+1.5=6$ [M1] $t=0.462$ and $t=1.99$ [A1] Duration $=1.52$ s [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Reject the negative root of $h(t)=0$ because $t\ge0$. For heights above a given level, find both crossing times and subtract.

subtopic: Sum of squares of roots as a function of a parameter
statement: The roots of the equation $x^2-(k+2)x+k=0$ are $\alpha$ and $\beta$, where $k\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Show that $\alpha^2+\beta^2=k^2+2k+4$. [2] (b) Show that the roots are real and distinct for all values of $k$. [2] (c) Find the minimum value of $\alpha^2+\beta^2$ and the value of $k$ at which it occurs. [3] (d) Given that $\alpha^2+\beta^2=7$, find the possible values of $k$. [2] (e) For $k=1$, find a quadratic equation with integer coefficients whose roots are $\alpha^2$ and $\beta^2$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\alpha+\beta=k+2$ and $\alpha\beta=k$ [A1] $\alpha^2+\beta^2=(k+2)^2-2k$ [M1] $=k^2+2k+4$ [AG] [2 marks] (b) $\Delta=(k+2)^2-4k$ [M1] $=k^2+4>0$ for all $k$ since $k^2\ge0$ [R1] [2 marks] (c) $k^2+2k+4=(k+1)^2+3$ [M1] [A1] minimum value $3$ when $k=-1$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $k^2+2k+4=7\Rightarrow k^2+2k-3=0$ [M1] $k=1$ or $k=-3$ [A1] [2 marks] (e) For $k=1$: $\alpha^2+\beta^2=7$ [A1] $\alpha^2\beta^2=(\alpha\beta)^2=1$ [M1] $x^2-7x+1=0$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Parts (a) and (b) set up everything that follows, so keep them in terms of $\alpha+\beta$ and $\alpha\beta$. In (c) completing the square on a function of $k$ is the quickest route to a minimum.

subtopic: Proving an inequality by writing it as a sum of squares
statement: Let $x$, $y$ and $z$ be real numbers. (a) Show that $x^2+y^2+z^2-xy-yz-zx=\dfrac12\left[(x-y)^2+(y-z)^2+(z-x)^2\right]$. [3] (b) Hence prove that $x^2+y^2+z^2\ge xy+yz+zx$, and state when equality holds. [2]
markscheme: (a) expand the right-hand side: $\dfrac12\left[2x^2+2y^2+2z^2-2xy-2yz-2zx\right]$ [M1][A1] simplify to the left-hand side [A1] [3 marks] (b) a sum of squares is non-negative [R1] equality when $x=y=z$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Each squared bracket is non-negative, so their sum is too.

subtopic: Sum and product of roots
statement: The roots of $2x^2-5x+1=0$ are $\alpha$ and $\beta$. (a) Write down $\alpha+\beta$ and $\alpha\beta$. [2] (b) Find the value of $\alpha^2+\beta^2$. [2] (c) Find a quadratic equation with integer coefficients whose roots are $\dfrac1\alpha$ and $\dfrac1\beta$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $\alpha+\beta=\dfrac52$ [A1] $\alpha\beta=\dfrac12$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $(\alpha+\beta)^2-2\alpha\beta$ [M1] $=\dfrac{25}4-1=\dfrac{21}4$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) sum $=\dfrac{\alpha+\beta}{\alpha\beta}=5$ [M1][A1] product $=\dfrac1{\alpha\beta}=2$ [A1] $x^2-5x+2=0$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Use $x^2-(\text{sum})x+(\text{product})=0$ for the new equation; express symmetric expressions through the sum and product.

subtopic: Quadratic inequality for all x with a parameter in the leading coefficient
statement: Let $k\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Find the set of values of $k$ for which $kx^2-4x+k<0$ for all real $x$. [5] (b) For $k=1$, solve the inequality $kx^2-4x+k<0$, giving exact answers. [2]
markscheme: (a) The graph must open downward, so $k<0$ [R1] and have no real roots, so $\Delta<0$ [R1] $\Delta=16-4k^2$ [M1] $16-4k^2<0\Rightarrow k^2>4$ [A1] combining with $k<0$: $k<-2$ [A1] [5 marks] (b) $x^2-4x+1=0\Rightarrow x=2\pm\sqrt3$ [M1] $2-\sqrt3<x<2+\sqrt3$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Two conditions are needed: the sign of the leading coefficient and the sign of the discriminant. After solving $k^2>4$, discard the part that contradicts $k<0$.

subtopic: Deducing signs of coefficients from the features of a parabola
statement: The graph of $y=ax^2+bx+c$ opens upward, crosses the $y$-axis below the origin, and has its vertex to the right of the $y$-axis. (a) State, with reasons, the signs of $a$, $c$ and $b$. [4] (b) Show that the equation $ax^2+bx+c=0$ has two real roots of opposite signs, and state which root has the larger magnitude. [3]
markscheme: (a) opens upward: $a>0$ [A1] $y$-intercept is $c<0$ [A1] vertex at $x=-\dfrac b{2a}>0$ [M1] so $b<0$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $ac<0$, so the discriminant $b^2-4ac>0$ [A1] product of the roots $\dfrac ca<0$ gives opposite signs [A1] sum $-\dfrac ba>0$, so the positive root has the larger magnitude [R1] [3 marks]
tips: Use the vertex position and the sum and product of the roots to link the shape to the signs of the coefficients.

subtopic: Vertex in terms of a parameter and the greatest minimum value
statement: Let $f(x)=x^2-2kx+k+6$, where $k\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Write $f(x)$ in the form $(x-p)^2+q$, where $p$ and $q$ are expressed in terms of $k$. [2] (b) Write down the coordinates of the vertex of the graph of $f$. [1] (c) Find the set of values of $k$ for which the graph of $f$ does not meet the $x$-axis. [3] (d) The minimum value of $f$ depends on $k$. Find the value of $k$ for which this minimum value is as large as possible, and state that largest minimum. [3]
markscheme: (a) $f(x)=(x-k)^2-k^2+k+6$ [M1] $p=k$ and $q=-k^2+k+6$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Vertex $(k,\,-k^2+k+6)$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) The parabola opens upward, so no $x$-intercepts means $q>0$ [M1] $k^2-k-6<0$ so $(k-3)(k+2)<0$ [M1] $-2<k<3$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) Minimum value is $q=-k^2+k+6=-\left(k-\tfrac12\right)^2+\tfrac{25}4$ [M1] $k=\dfrac12$ [A1] Largest minimum value $=\dfrac{25}4$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: For "no real roots" with an upward parabola, it is quicker to say vertex above the axis than to use the discriminant, though both work. A second completion of the square, in $k$, answers the optimization part.

subtopic: Discriminant: tangent line and intersections
statement: Consider the curve $C:\ y=x^2-4x+7$. (a) The line $y=2x+k$ is a tangent to $C$. Find the value of $k$. [3] (b) Find the set of values of $m$ for which the line $y=mx$ intersects $C$ at two distinct points. [4]
tips: A tangent corresponds to a repeated root, that is a zero discriminant. Two distinct intersections need a positive discriminant, which for a squared expression gives two separate inequalities.

subtopic: Ratios of variables from a homogeneous quadratic
statement: The real numbers $x$ and $y$, with $y\ne0$, satisfy $6x^2+xy-2y^2=0$. (a) Factorize the left-hand side and find the possible values of $\dfrac xy$. [3] (b) Find the possible values of $\dfrac{x^2-y^2}{x^2+y^2}$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $(3x+2y)(2x-y)=0$ [M1][A1] $\dfrac xy=-\dfrac23$ or $\dfrac xy=\dfrac12$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) divide top and bottom by $y^2$: $\dfrac{r^2-1}{r^2+1}$ with $r=\dfrac xy$ [M1] $r=-\dfrac23$: $-\dfrac5{13}$ [A1] $r=\dfrac12$: $-\dfrac35$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Divide the equation by $y^2$ to turn it into a quadratic in the ratio $x/y$.

subtopic: Revenue and profit model
statement: A company sells $x$ units of a product each week. The price per unit is $\$(120-0.5x)$, and the weekly cost of producing $x$ units is $C(x)=2000+30x$ dollars. (a) Find the number of units that maximizes the weekly revenue $R(x)$, and find the maximum revenue. [3] (b) Show that the weekly profit is $P(x)=-0.5x^2+90x-2000$. [2] (c) Find the maximum weekly profit and the number of units that must be sold to achieve it. [2] (d) Find the integer values of $x$ for which the company makes a positive profit. [3]
tips: Profit is revenue minus cost, and its maximum is not at the same $x$ as the maximum revenue. For part (d) check the integer endpoints, for instance $P(26)=2>0$ but $P(25)<0$.

subtopic: Roots differing by a given amount
statement: The roots of $x^2-5x+k=0$ are $\alpha$ and $\beta$, with $\alpha>\beta$, and $\alpha-\beta=3$. (a) Use $(\alpha-\beta)^2=(\alpha+\beta)^2-4\alpha\beta$ to find $k$. [3] (b) Find the roots. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\alpha+\beta=5$ and $\alpha\beta=k$ [A1] $9=25-4k$ [M1] $k=4$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $x^2-5x+4=0$ so $\alpha=4$, $\beta=1$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: The difference of the roots is $\sqrt{(\alpha+\beta)^2-4\alpha\beta}$, which links to the discriminant.

subtopic: Range of a rational expression using the discriminant
statement: Let $y=\dfrac{x^2-x+1}{x^2+x+1}$ for $x\in\mathbb R$. (a) Show that $(y-1)x^2+(y+1)x+(y-1)=0$. [1] (b) Use the discriminant to find the range of $y$. [4] (c) State the values of $x$ at which the extreme values of $y$ occur. [2]
markscheme: (a) $y\left(x^2+x+1\right)=x^2-x+1$ and rearrange [AG] [A1] [1 mark] (b) $y=1$ is attained at $x=0$ [A1] for $y\ne1$, real $x$ requires $(y+1)^2-4(y-1)^2\ge0$ [M1] $(3-y)(3y-1)\ge0$ [A1] $\dfrac13\le y\le3$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) $y=3$: $2x^2+4x+2=0$ so $x=-1$ [A1] $y=\dfrac13$: $x=1$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A value of $y$ is attained when the quadratic in $x$ has a real solution, which needs a non-negative discriminant.

subtopic: Trigonometric equation reduced to a quadratic in cos x
statement: (a) Show that the equation $2\sin^2x+3\cos x=3$ can be written as $2\cos^2x-3\cos x+1=0$. [2] (b) Hence solve $2\sin^2x+3\cos x=3$ for $0\le x\le2\pi$. [4] (c) Hence find all solutions of $2\sin^2 2\theta+3\cos2\theta=3$ for $0\le\theta\le\pi$. [2]
markscheme: (a) Use $\sin^2x=1-\cos^2x$: $2-2\cos^2x+3\cos x=3$ [M1] $-2\cos^2x+3\cos x-1=0$ [A1] so $2\cos^2x-3\cos x+1=0$ [AG] [2 marks] (b) $(2\cos x-1)(\cos x-1)=0$ [M1] $\cos x=\dfrac12$ or $\cos x=1$ [A1] $x=\dfrac\pi3,\ \dfrac{5\pi}3$ [A1] $x=0,\ 2\pi$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) Let $x=2\theta$ with $0\le x\le2\pi$ [M1] $\theta=0,\ \dfrac\pi6,\ \dfrac{5\pi}6,\ \pi$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Do not forget the solutions where $\cos x=1$ at both ends of the interval. In part (c), the change of variable $x=2\theta$ also changes the interval.

subtopic: Optimization: minimum total area from a cut length of wire
statement: A piece of wire of length $34$ cm is cut into two pieces. The first piece, of length $x$ cm, is bent to form a square. The second piece is bent to form a rectangle whose length is twice its width. Let $A\ \text{cm}^2$ be the total area of the two shapes, where $0\le x\le34$. (a) Show that $A=\dfrac{x^2}{16}+\dfrac{(34-x)^2}{18}$. [3] (b) Show that $A=\dfrac{17}{144}(x-16)^2+34$. [3] (c) Hence write down the minimum total area and the side length of the square when this minimum occurs. [2] (d) Find the set of values of $x$ for which the total area is at most $51\ \text{cm}^2$. [3]
markscheme: (a) Square side $\dfrac x4$, area $\dfrac{x^2}{16}$ [A1] Rectangle with width $w$ and length $2w$ has perimeter $6w=34-x$ [M1] Area $=2w^2=2\left(\dfrac{34-x}6\right)^2=\dfrac{(34-x)^2}{18}$ [A1] [AG] [3 marks] (b) $A=\dfrac{9x^2+8(34-x)^2}{144}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{17x^2-544x+9248}{144}$ [A1] $=\dfrac{17(x-16)^2+4896}{144}$ [A1] $=\dfrac{17}{144}(x-16)^2+34$ [AG] [3 marks] (c) Minimum area is $34\ \text{cm}^2$ [A1] when $x=16$, so the square has side $4$ cm [A1] [2 marks] (d) $\dfrac{17}{144}(x-16)^2+34\le51$ gives $(x-16)^2\le144$ [M1] $|x-16|\le12$ [A1] $4\le x\le28$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Model each shape in terms of the single variable $x$, then complete the square to read off the optimum. In part (d), check that your interval lies within $0\le x\le34$.

subtopic: Quadratic model from three points
statement: A diver leaves a platform and her height above the water, $h$ meters, when she is a horizontal distance $x$ meters from the platform is modeled by $h=ax^2+bx+c$. She starts at a height of $10$ m, and at horizontal distances of $1$ m and $2$ m her heights are $11.5$ m and $11$ m respectively. (a) Find the values of $a$, $b$ and $c$. [3] (b) Find the maximum height reached by the diver. [2] (c) Find the horizontal distance from the platform at which the diver enters the water. [2] (d) Find the range of values of $x$ for which the diver is higher than $11$ m. [2]
tips: Substitute each data point to form simultaneous equations, or use quadratic regression on your GDC. Reject the negative root in part (c) because distances here are positive.

subtopic: Equation with roots that are the squares of the original roots
statement: The roots of the equation $x^2-5x+3=0$ are $\alpha$ and $\beta$. (a) Write down the values of $\alpha+\beta$ and $\alpha\beta$. [2] (b) Find the value of $\alpha^2+\beta^2$. [2] (c) Find a quadratic equation, with integer coefficients, whose roots are $\alpha^2$ and $\beta^2$. [3] (d) Show that $\dfrac{\alpha}{\beta}+\dfrac{\beta}{\alpha}=\dfrac{19}{3}$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\alpha+\beta=5$ [A1] $\alpha\beta=3$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\alpha^2+\beta^2=(\alpha+\beta)^2-2\alpha\beta$ [M1] $=25-6=19$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Sum of new roots $=19$ [M1] Product of new roots $=(\alpha\beta)^2=9$ [A1] Equation: $x^2-19x+9=0$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $\dfrac\alpha\beta+\dfrac\beta\alpha=\dfrac{\alpha^2+\beta^2}{\alpha\beta}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{19}{3}$ [A1] [AG] [2 marks]
tips: Express every symmetric quantity through $\alpha+\beta$ and $\alpha\beta$; never solve for the roots themselves. A new equation with sum $S$ and product $P$ is $x^2-Sx+P=0$.

subtopic: Sum and product of roots
statement: The roots of the equation $2x^2-7x+4=0$ are $\alpha$ and $\beta$. (a) Write down the values of $\alpha+\beta$ and $\alpha\beta$. [2] (b) Find the value of $\alpha^2+\beta^2$. [2] (c) Find the value of $\dfrac1\alpha+\dfrac1\beta$. [2] (d) Find a quadratic equation with integer coefficients whose roots are $\alpha^2$ and $\beta^2$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\alpha+\beta=\dfrac72$ [A1] $\alpha\beta=2$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\alpha^2+\beta^2=(\alpha+\beta)^2-2\alpha\beta$ [M1] $=\dfrac{49}{4}-4=\dfrac{33}{4}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\dfrac{\alpha+\beta}{\alpha\beta}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{7}{4}$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) Sum $\dfrac{33}{4}$ [A1] Product $(\alpha\beta)^2=4$ [A1] $x^2-\dfrac{33}{4}x+4=0$, so $4x^2-33x+16=0$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Express each required quantity in terms of $\alpha+\beta$ and $\alpha\beta$ without solving the quadratic.

subtopic: Volume of revolution of a rational curve
statement: The region under the curve $y=\dfrac1{1+x^2}$ between $x=0$ and $x=1$ is rotated through $360^\circ$ about the $x$-axis. (a) Write down an integral for the volume of the solid. [1] (b) Use the substitution $x=\tan\theta$ to show that $V=\pi\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/4}\cos^2\theta\,d\theta$. [3] (c) Hence find the exact value of $V$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $V=\pi\displaystyle\int_0^1\dfrac1{\left(1+x^2\right)^2}\,dx$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $dx=\sec^2\theta\,d\theta$ [A1] $1+x^2=\sec^2\theta$ [A1] $\dfrac{\sec^2\theta}{\sec^4\theta}=\cos^2\theta$, limits $0$ to $\dfrac\pi4$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\cos^2\theta=\dfrac{1+\cos2\theta}2$ [M1] $\left[\dfrac\theta2+\dfrac{\sin2\theta}4\right]_0^{\pi/4}=\dfrac\pi8+\dfrac14$ [A1] $V=\dfrac{\pi^2}8+\dfrac\pi4$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: For $x=\tan\theta$ use $1+\tan^2\theta=\sec^2\theta$. Then the integrand is a power of cosine, handled by a double angle formula.

subtopic: Parameter conditions for vertical asymptotes and holes
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{x+1}{x^2+kx+4}$, where $k\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Find the set of values of $k$ for which the graph of $f$ has no vertical asymptotes. [3] (b) Show that when $k=5$ the graph of $f$ has a hole, and find its coordinates. [4] (c) Find all values of $k$ for which the graph of $f$ has exactly one vertical asymptote. [4]
markscheme: (a) no real roots of the denominator, so $k^2-16<0$ [M1] [A1] $-4<k<4$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $x^2+5x+4=(x+1)(x+4)$ [M1] $f(x)=\frac{1}{x+4}$ for $x\neq-1$ [A1] the factor $x+1$ cancels, so there is a hole at $x=-1$ [R1] hole at $\left(-1,\frac13\right)$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) a repeated root: $k^2=16$ [M1] $k=\pm4$ [A1] (roots $\mp2$, neither equals $-1$, so the asymptote remains) [R1] $k=5$ also gives exactly one asymptote ($x=-4$) [A1] $k\in\{-4,4,5\}$ [4 marks]
tips: A zero of the denominator gives a vertical asymptote only if it is not also a zero of the numerator. Check for holes in every case.

subtopic: Tangents to the hyperbola y = 1/x and a triangle of constant area
statement: The tangent to the curve $y=\dfrac1x$ at the point $P\left(t,\dfrac1t\right)$, with $t>0$, meets the $x$-axis at $A$ and the $y$-axis at $B$, and $O$ is the origin. (a) Show that the tangent has equation $y=-\dfrac x{t^2}+\dfrac2t$. [3] (b) Find the coordinates of $A$ and $B$.
