[2] (c) Show that the area of triangle $OAB$ does not depend on $t$, and that $P$ is the midpoint of $AB$. [3] (d) Find the least possible length of $AB$, and the value of $t$ for which it occurs. [4] (e) Show that the tangent meets the curve at no other point. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-\dfrac1{x^2}$, gradient $-\dfrac1{t^2}$ [M1][A1] $y-\dfrac1t=-\dfrac1{t^2}(x-t)$ so $y=-\dfrac x{t^2}+\dfrac2t$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $A=(2t,0)$ [A1] $B=\left(0,\dfrac2t\right)$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) area $=\dfrac12\times2t\times\dfrac2t=2$ [M1][A1] midpoint of $AB$ is $\left(t,\dfrac1t\right)$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $AB^2=4t^2+\dfrac4{t^2}$ [M1] $=4\left(t-\dfrac1t\right)^2+8\ge8$ [M1][A1] least length $2\sqrt2$ at $t=1$ [A1] [4 marks] (e) $x\left(-\dfrac x{t^2}+\dfrac2t\right)=1$ [M1] $x^2-2tx+t^2=0$ [A1] $(x-t)^2=0$, a repeated root, so only $x=t$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The tangent line to $xy=1$ is found by differentiating. The intercepts and the area then simplify neatly.

subtopic: Drug concentration modeled by a rational function
statement: The concentration $C$ mg/L of a drug in the blood $t$ hours after an injection is modeled by $C(t)=\dfrac{20t}{t^2+4}$ for $t\ge0$. (a) Find the concentration after $1$ hour. [1] (b) Find the time at which the concentration is greatest and the maximum concentration. [4] (c) Find the times at which the concentration is $4$ mg/L. [3] (d) State what happens to the concentration in the long term. [1]
tips: Differentiate with the quotient rule and set the numerator to zero. The horizontal asymptote $y=0$ describes the long-term behavior.

subtopic: Behavior near vertical and horizontal asymptotes of an even rational function
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{x^2-1}{x^2-4}$, for $x\in\mathbb{R}$, $x\neq\pm2$. (a) Write down the equations of the vertical and horizontal asymptotes of the graph of $f$. [2] (b) For each of $x\to2^+$, $x\to2^-$, $x\to-2^+$ and $x\to-2^-$, state whether $f(x)\to+\infty$ or $f(x)\to-\infty$. [4] (c) Show that $f(x)-1=\dfrac{3}{x^2-4}$, and hence determine whether the graph approaches its horizontal asymptote from above or below as $x\to\infty$. [2] (d) Find the range of $f$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $x=2$ and $x=-2$ [A1] $y=1$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $x\to2^+$: numerator $>0$, denominator $\to0^+$, so $+\infty$ [A1] $x\to2^-$: denominator $\to0^-$, so $-\infty$ [A1] $x\to-2^+$: $x^2<4$, denominator $\to0^-$, so $-\infty$ [A1] $x\to-2^-$: denominator $\to0^+$, so $+\infty$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) $f(x)-1=\frac{x^2-1-(x^2-4)}{x^2-4}=\frac{3}{x^2-4}$ [M1] [AG] for large $|x|$ this is positive, so the graph approaches $y=1$ from above [A1] [2 marks] (d) For $|x|>2$: $f(x)-1>0$ and takes all positive values, so $f>1$ [A1] for $|x|<2$: $x^2-4\in[-4,0)$ so $\frac{3}{x^2-4}\le-\frac34$, giving $f\le\frac14$ [M1] [A1] range $(-\infty,\tfrac14]\cup(1,\infty)$ [3 marks]
tips: Write the function as a constant plus a small fraction to see on which side it approaches the asymptote. Check the sign of numerator and denominator for each one-sided limit.

subtopic: Average cost function with an oblique asymptote
statement: The total cost, in dollars, of producing $x$ items is $T(x)=0.5x^2+30x+2000$. (a) Find an expression for the average cost per item $A(x)$, in the form $px+q+\dfrac{r}{x}$. [2] (b) Treating $x$ as continuous, use your graphic display calculator to find the number of items that minimizes the average cost, and the minimum average cost. [3] (c) Find the values of $x$ for which the average cost is less than \$100. [3] (d) Write down the equation of the oblique asymptote of $y=A(x)$ and interpret it in this context. [2]
markscheme: (a) $A(x)=\frac{T(x)}{x}$ [M1] $A(x)=0.5x+30+\frac{2000}{x}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) minimum of the graph of $A$ for $x>0$ [M1] $x=63.2$ [A1] minimum average cost \$93.2 [A1] [3 marks] (c) $0.5x+30+\frac{2000}{x}=100$ gives $x=40$ or $x=100$ [M1] [A1] $40<x<100$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $y=0.5x+30$ [A1] For large $x$ the fixed cost of \$2000 is spread over many items, so $A(x)\approx0.5x+30$: the average cost is approximately \$30 plus \$0.50 for each additional item produced [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Divide each term of the total cost by x to get the average. For a minimum on the GDC, state the coordinates of the lowest point on the relevant domain.

subtopic: A rational graph crossing its own horizontal asymptote
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{3x^2-2x}{x^2+1}$. (a) Write down the equation of the horizontal asymptote. [1] (b) Show that the graph crosses its horizontal asymptote, and find the $x$-coordinate of the crossing point. [3] (c) Show that $f(x)-3=-\dfrac{2x+3}{x^2+1}$, and state on which side of the asymptote the graph lies for large positive $x$ and for large negative $x$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $y=3$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\dfrac{3x^2-2x}{x^2+1}=3$ [M1] $3x^2-2x=3x^2+3$ [A1] $x=-\dfrac32$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\dfrac{3x^2-2x-3x^2-3}{x^2+1}$ [M1] $=-\dfrac{2x+3}{x^2+1}$ [AG] [A1] large positive $x$: below; large negative $x$: above [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A horizontal asymptote describes the end behavior; the graph may still cross it at finite values of $x$.

subtopic: Sign analysis of a rational function
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{x+3}{(x-3)(x+2)}$, for $x\in\mathbb{R}$, $x\neq3,\ x\neq-2$. (a) Write down the equations of the two vertical asymptotes. [2] (b) Write down the equation of the horizontal asymptote. [1] (c) Find the coordinates of the $x$-intercept and the $y$-intercept. [2] (d) Solve the inequality $f(x)>0$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $x=3$ [A1] $x=-2$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $y=0$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $x$-intercept $(-3,\,0)$ [A1] $y$-intercept $f(0)=\dfrac{3}{(-3)(2)}$, so $\left(0,\,-\dfrac12\right)$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) Critical values $x=-3,\ -2,\ 3$; consider the sign of each factor on each interval [M1] $-3<x<-2$ [A1] $x>3$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Mark every zero and every asymptote on a number line: the sign of a rational function can only change at these points. Check one test value in each interval.

subtopic: Integral of a quadratic denominator giving a logarithm and an arctangent
statement: Consider $\displaystyle\int_0^1\dfrac{2x+3}{x^2+2x+5}\,dx$. (a) Show that $\dfrac{2x+3}{x^2+2x+5}=\dfrac{2x+2}{x^2+2x+5}+\dfrac1{(x+1)^2+4}$. [2] (b) Hence find the exact value of the integral. [4]
markscheme: (a) $2x+3=(2x+2)+1$ [M1] $x^2+2x+5=(x+1)^2+4$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\left[\ln\left(x^2+2x+5\right)\right]_0^1=\ln\dfrac85$ [M1][A1] $\left[\dfrac12\arctan\dfrac{x+1}2\right]_0^1=\dfrac12\left(\dfrac\pi4-\arctan\dfrac12\right)$ [A1] total $\ln\dfrac85+\dfrac12\left(\dfrac\pi4-\arctan\dfrac12\right)$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Split the numerator into a multiple of the derivative of the denominator plus a constant. Complete the square in the denominator for the arctangent part.

subtopic: Centre of symmetry of a hyperbola
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{2x+3}{x+1}$. (a) Show that $f(x)=2+\dfrac1{x+1}$, and write down the equations of the asymptotes. [3] (b) Show that $f(-1+t)+f(-1-t)=4$ for $t\ne0$, and explain what this shows about the graph. [3]
markscheme: (a) $2x+3=2(x+1)+1$ [M1] result [A1] asymptotes $x=-1$ and $y=2$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $f(-1+t)=2+\dfrac1t$ and $f(-1-t)=2-\dfrac1t$ [M1][A1] the graph has rotational symmetry about $(-1,2)$, the intersection of the asymptotes [R1] [3 marks]
tips: Moving the origin to the point where the asymptotes meet turns the graph into $y=1/x$, which is odd.

subtopic: Round trip with current modeled by a rational function
statement: A boat can travel at a constant speed of $x$ km/h in still water, where $x>4$. It travels 24 km upstream along a river and then 24 km back downstream to its starting point. The river current has a constant speed of 4 km/h. Let $T$ hours be the total time for the round trip, ignoring any time spent turning around. (a) Show that $T=\dfrac{48x}{x^2-16}$. [4] (b) Using your graphing calculator, find the value of $x$ for which the round trip takes exactly 3 hours. Give your answer to three significant figures. [2] (c) Write down the equation of the vertical asymptote of the graph of $T$ against $x$, and explain what this means in this context. [2] (d) The round trip must take at most 2 hours. Find the minimum possible value of $x$, to three significant figures. [3] (e) Write down the equation of the horizontal asymptote of the graph of $T$ against $x$. [1]
markscheme: (a) speed upstream $x-4$, speed downstream $x+4$ [A1] $T=\dfrac{24}{x-4}+\dfrac{24}{x+4}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{24(x+4)+24(x-4)}{(x-4)(x+4)}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{48x}{x^2-16}$ [A1] [AG] [4 marks] (b) solving $\dfrac{48x}{x^2-16}=3$ (graph intersection or equation solver) [M1] $x=16.9$ (exact value $8+4\sqrt5\approx 16.944$) [A1] [2 marks] (c) $x=4$ [A1] as $x\to 4^{+}$ the speed upstream approaches 0, so the time taken tends to infinity (the boat cannot make progress against the current) [A1] [2 marks] (d) solving $\dfrac{48x}{x^2-16}=2$ gives $x=24.649\ldots$ [M1] [A1] $T$ decreases as $x$ increases, so $T\le 2$ when $x\ge 24.649\ldots$; minimum speed $24.6$ km/h (3 s.f.) [A1] [3 marks] (e) $T=0$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: When asked to show a rational model, build it from the physical rule (time equals distance over speed) for each leg and then combine over a common denominator. For a threshold such as $T\le 2$, solve the boundary equation on the GDC and use the shape of the graph to pick the correct side.

subtopic: A family of rational functions f(x) = x/(x^2+a)
statement: This question investigates the family $f_a(x)=\dfrac{x}{x^2+a}$ where $a>0$. (a) Show that $f_a$ is an odd function and state the horizontal asymptote. [3] (b) Show that $f_a'(x)=\dfrac{a-x^2}{\left(x^2+a\right)^2}$ and find the coordinates of the stationary points in terms of $a$. [4] (c) Hence state the range of $f_a$ in terms of $a$. [2] (d) Show that the second derivative is $f_a''(x)=\dfrac{2x\left(x^2-3a\right)}{\left(x^2+a\right)^3}$ and find the $x$-coordinates of the points of inflection. [4] (e) Show that the stationary points of $f_a$ for different values of $a$ all lie on the curve $y=\dfrac1{2x}$ and that the points of inflection with $x=\sqrt{3a}$ all lie on a curve to be found. [3]
markscheme: (a) $f_a(-x)=\dfrac{-x}{x^2+a}=-f_a(x)$ [M1][A1] $y=0$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) quotient rule: $\dfrac{\left(x^2+a\right)-x(2x)}{\left(x^2+a\right)^2}$ [M1][A1] zero when $x=\pm\sqrt a$ [A1] points $\left(\sqrt a,\dfrac1{2\sqrt a}\right)$ and $\left(-\sqrt a,-\dfrac1{2\sqrt a}\right)$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) maximum value $\dfrac1{2\sqrt a}$ and minimum $-\dfrac1{2\sqrt a}$ [M1] range $\left[-\dfrac1{2\sqrt a},\dfrac1{2\sqrt a}\right]$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) differentiate the quotient [M1][A1] the numerator vanishes at $x=0$ and $x=\pm\sqrt{3a}$ [A1] $f''$ changes sign at each, so three points of inflection [A1] [4 marks] (e) for $x=\sqrt a$: $y=\dfrac1{2\sqrt a}=\dfrac1{2x}$ [A1] for $x=\sqrt{3a}$: $y=\dfrac{\sqrt{3a}}{4a}=\dfrac{3}{4x}$ [M1] curve $y=\dfrac3{4x}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Use the quotient rule twice and factorize. Eliminating the parameter $a$ between the coordinates of the special points gives a locus.

subtopic: Simplifying a rational function with a removable discontinuity
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{x^2-4}{x^2-x-2}$, for $x\in\mathbb{R}$, $x\neq-1$, $x\neq2$. (a) Show that $f(x)=\dfrac{x+2}{x+1}$ for all $x$ in the domain. [2] (b) Hence write down the equation of (i) the vertical asymptote, (ii) the horizontal asymptote. [2] (c) Find the coordinates of the $y$-intercept, and the coordinates of the point that is missing from the graph at $x=2$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $f(x)=\frac{(x-2)(x+2)}{(x-2)(x+1)}$ [M1] cancel the factor $x-2$, valid since $x\neq2$ [R1] $=\frac{x+2}{x+1}$ [AG] [2 marks] (b) (i) $x=-1$ [A1] (ii) $y=1$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $y$-intercept $(0,2)$ [A1] missing point at $x=2$: $y=\frac43$, so $\left(2,\frac43\right)$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A common factor in numerator and denominator gives a hole, not an asymptote. The hole's y-value comes from the simplified expression.

subtopic: The rational iteration for the square root of 2
statement: Define $x_{n+1}=\dfrac12\left(x_n+\dfrac2{x_n}\right)$ with $x_0=1$. (a) Calculate $x_1$, $x_2$ and $x_3$ as fractions. [3] (b) Show that $x_{n+1}^2-2=\dfrac{\left(x_n^2-2\right)^2}{4x_n^2}$. [3] (c) Deduce that $x_n>\sqrt2$ for all $n\ge1$, and that the sequence $x_1,x_2,\ldots$ is decreasing. [4] (d) Let $\varepsilon_n=x_n-\sqrt2$. Show that $\varepsilon_{n+1}=\dfrac{\varepsilon_n^2}{2x_n}$. [3] (e) Find $\varepsilon_2$ and $\varepsilon_3$ to three significant figures, and verify that $\dfrac{\varepsilon_3}{\varepsilon_2^2}$ is close to $\dfrac1{2\sqrt2}$. [3] (f) Show that if the sequence converges to $L>0$, then $L=\sqrt2$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $x_1=\dfrac32$ [A1] $x_2=\dfrac{17}{12}$ [A1] $x_3=\dfrac{577}{408}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $x_{n+1}^2=\dfrac14\left(x_n^2+4+\dfrac4{x_n^2}\right)$ [M1][A1] $x_{n+1}^2-2=\dfrac{x_n^4-4x_n^2+4}{4x_n^2}$, which is the stated result [A1] [3 marks] (c) the right side in part (b) is $\ge0$, so $x_{n+1}\ge\sqrt2$ (and is not equal to it since $x_n$ is rational) [R1][R1] $x_{n+1}-x_n=\dfrac{2-x_n^2}{2x_n}$ [M1] which is negative when $x_n>\sqrt2$ [R1] [4 marks] (d) $x_{n+1}-\sqrt2=\dfrac{x_n^2+2-2\sqrt2x_n}{2x_n}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{\left(x_n-\sqrt2\right)^2}{2x_n}$ [A1][A1] [3 marks] (e) $\varepsilon_2=2.45\times10^{-3}$ and $\varepsilon_3=2.12\times10^{-6}$ [A1][A1] $\dfrac{\varepsilon_3}{\varepsilon_2^2}=0.353\approx\dfrac1{2\sqrt2}=0.354$ [A1] [3 marks] (f) $L=\dfrac12\left(L+\dfrac2L\right)$ [M1] $L^2=2$, so $L=\sqrt2$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Complete the square in the numerator of $x_{n+1}-\sqrt2$. The new error is about the square of the old error, so the number of correct digits roughly doubles each step.

subtopic: Concentration model: inverse and horizontal asymptote
statement: A tank contains 200 liters of water with 10 kg of salt dissolved in it. Brine containing 0.8 kg of salt per liter is pumped into the tank. After $V$ liters of brine have been added (with nothing removed), the concentration of salt in the tank is $C(V)$ kg per liter, where $C(V)=\dfrac{10+0.8V}{200+V}$, for $V\ge0$. (a) Show that $C(V)=0.8-\dfrac{150}{200+V}$. [2] (b) Write down the equation of the horizontal asymptote of the graph of $C$ and interpret it in this context. [2] (c) The tank holds a total of 1000 liters. Find the concentration when the tank has been filled to capacity. [2] (d) Find an expression for $V$ in terms of $C$. [3] (e) Hence find the volume of brine that must be added for the concentration to reach 0.6 kg per liter. [2]
markscheme: (a) $0.8(200+V)-150=160+0.8V-150$ [M1] $=10+0.8V$, so $C(V)=\frac{0.8(200+V)-150}{200+V}=0.8-\frac{150}{200+V}$ [A1] [AG] [2 marks] (b) $C=0.8$ [A1] the concentration approaches 0.8 kg per liter, the concentration of the brine, as more brine is added [R1] [2 marks] (c) Filled to capacity means $200+V=1000$, so $V=800$ [M1] $C=\frac{650}{1000}=0.65$ kg per liter [A1] [2 marks] (d) $C(200+V)=10+0.8V$ [M1] $200C+CV=10+0.8V$, so $V(C-0.8)=10-200C$ [M1] $V=\frac{200C-10}{0.8-C}$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) $V=\frac{200(0.6)-10}{0.8-0.6}=\frac{110}{0.2}$ [M1] $=550$ liters (this is less than 800, so it fits in the tank) [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Writing the function as a constant minus a fraction shows the asymptote immediately. Make V the subject by collecting all V terms on one side.

subtopic: Oblique asymptotes and range
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{x^2+3x+6}{x+1}$, for $x\in\mathbb{R},\ x\neq -1$. (a) Express $f(x)$ in the form $x+a+\dfrac{b}{x+1}$, where $a,b\in\mathbb{Z}$. [2] (b) Write down the equation of (i) the vertical asymptote of the graph of $f$; (ii) the oblique asymptote of the graph of $f$. [2] (c) Find the coordinates of the stationary points of the graph of $f$. [3] (d) Hence write down the range of $f$. [1]
tips: Writing a rational function as polynomial plus remainder makes both the oblique asymptote and the derivative much easier. For the range, remember the two branches lie on opposite sides of the asymptotes, so the local maximum value is lower than the local minimum value.

subtopic: Partial fractions and integration of a rational function
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{5x+7}{(x+1)(x+2)}$. (a) Express $f(x)$ in the form $\dfrac A{x+1}+\dfrac B{x+2}$. [3] (b) Find $\displaystyle\int_0^2f(x)\,dx$, giving the answer in the form $\ln\left(\dfrac pq\right)$. [4]
tips: Use partial fractions to split the integrand into two logarithmic terms and combine the logarithms at the end.

subtopic: Sketching 1/f from a rational function
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{x-1}{x+2}$ and $g(x)=\dfrac1{f(x)}$. (a) Write down the asymptotes of $f$ and of $g$. [4] (b) Find the axis intercepts of $f$ and of $g$. [3] (c) Solve $f(x)=g(x)$. [3]
tips: The vertical asymptotes of $1/f$ are at the zeros of $f$, and the zeros of $1/f$ are at the vertical asymptotes of $f$.

subtopic: Average cost model with an oblique asymptote
statement: A company's total cost, in dollars, of producing $x$ units of a product is $C(x)=0.04x^2+8x+3200$. The average cost per unit is $A(x)=\dfrac{C(x)}{x}$, for $x>0$. (a) Find the average cost per unit when $100$ units are produced. [1] (b) Write down the equation of the oblique asymptote of the graph of $A$. [2] (c) Find the minimum average cost per unit and the number of units, to the nearest integer, at which it occurs. [3] (d) The company wants the average cost per unit to be at most $\$35$. Find the possible integer values of $x$. [3] (e) Explain, using your answer to part (b), why the average cost cannot stay below $\$35$ for all large $x$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $A(100)=\dfrac{0.04(100)^2+800+3200}{100}=44.0$ dollars [A1] [1 mark] (b) $A(x)=0.04x+8+\dfrac{3200}{x}$ [M1] oblique asymptote $y=0.04x+8$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Minimize $A$ (GDC or $A'(x)=0$) [M1] $x=283$ ($282.84\ldots$) [A1] minimum average cost $\$30.6$ ($30.627\ldots$) [A1] [3 marks] (d) Solve $0.04x^2+8x+3200=35x$ [M1] $x=153.36\ldots$ and $x=521.63\ldots$ [A1] $154\le x\le 521$ (integers) [A1] [3 marks] (e) For large $x$, $A(x)\approx0.04x+8$, which grows without bound [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Divide each term of the cost function by $x$ to expose the oblique asymptote and the shape of $A$. For an integer solution set, round the roots inward, so that the inequality is still satisfied at the end values.

subtopic: Oblique asymptote and range
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{x^2-3x+4}{x-1}$ for $x\ne1$. (a) Show that $f(x)=x-2+\dfrac2{x-1}$ and write down the equations of the asymptotes. [3] (b) Find the coordinates of the local maximum and local minimum. [4] (c) Hence state the range of $f$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $x^2-3x+4=(x-1)(x-2)+2$ [M1][A1] asymptotes $x=1$ and $y=x-2$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $f'(x)=1-\dfrac2{(x-1)^2}=0$ [M1] $(x-1)^2=2$, $x=1\pm\sqrt2$ [A1] $f(1-\sqrt2)=-1-2\sqrt2$ is a local maximum [A1] $f(1+\sqrt2)=-1+2\sqrt2$ is a local minimum [A1] [4 marks] (c) $y\le-1-2\sqrt2$ or $y\ge-1+2\sqrt2$ [A1][A1] [2 marks]
tips: Polynomial division gives the oblique asymptote. The range of a function with a gap comes from the local extrema.

subtopic: Rational inequality with a hence part on trigonometric values
statement: (a) Solve the inequality $\dfrac{2x}{x+3}>\dfrac{x}{x-1}$. [6] (b) Hence solve $\dfrac{2\sin\theta}{\sin\theta+3}>\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\sin\theta-1}$, for $0\le\theta\le 2\pi$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{2x}{x+3}-\dfrac{x}{x-1}>0$ [M1] $\dfrac{2x(x-1)-x(x+3)}{(x+3)(x-1)}=\dfrac{x(x-5)}{(x+3)(x-1)}>0$ [A1] critical values $x=-3,\ 0,\ 1,\ 5$ [A1] sign table or sketch [M1] $x<-3$ or $0<x<1$ [A1] or $x>5$ [A1] [6 marks] (b) let $x=\sin\theta$, so $-1\le x\le 1$ [M1] only $0<x<1$ is possible, so $0<\sin\theta<1$ [A1] $0<\theta<\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ or $\dfrac{\pi}{2}<\theta<\pi$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Never multiply both sides by an expression whose sign is unknown; move everything to one side and use a sign table. In a hence part, check which intervals from part (a) are actually attainable by the new expression, here $-1\le\sin\theta\le 1$ and $\sin\theta\neq 1$.

subtopic: Improper rational function: division, partial fractions and area
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{x^3+2x^2+6}{(x-1)(x+2)}$, for $x>1$. (a) Find constants $a$, $b$ and $c$ such that $f(x)\equiv x+a+\dfrac{b}{x-1}+\dfrac{c}{x+2}$. [4] (b) Hence find the exact area of the region enclosed by the graph of $y=f(x)$, the $x$-axis and the lines $x=2$ and $x=4$. Give your answer in the form $m+\ln n$, where $m,n\in\mathbb{Z}$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $(x-1)(x+2)=x^2+x-2$; dividing $x^3+2x^2+6$ by $x^2+x-2$ gives quotient $x+1$ [M1] and remainder $x+8$, so $a=1$ [A1] $\dfrac{x+8}{(x-1)(x+2)}\equiv\dfrac{b}{x-1}+\dfrac{c}{x+2}$, so $x+8\equiv b(x+2)+c(x-1)$ [M1] $b=3$, $c=-2$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $f(x)>0$ on $[2,4]$, so area $=\displaystyle\int_2^4\left(x+1+\dfrac{3}{x-1}-\dfrac{2}{x+2}\right)dx$ $=\left[\dfrac{x^2}{2}+x+3\ln(x-1)-2\ln(x+2)\right]_2^4$ [M1] [A1] $=(12+3\ln3-2\ln6)-(4+0-2\ln4)$ [M1] $=8+3\ln3-2\ln6+2\ln4=8+\ln 12$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: If the degree of the numerator is not less than the degree of the denominator, divide first and only then apply partial fractions to the remainder. Combine logarithms at the end using $a\ln b=\ln b^a$.

subtopic: Finding constants of a rational function, solving with a GDC, and an inequality
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{ax+b}{x+c}$, for $x\neq-c$. The graph of $f$ passes through the points $(0,-2)$, $(1,0)$ and $(2,1)$. (a) Find the values of $a$, $b$ and $c$. [4] (b) Write down the equations of the vertical and horizontal asymptotes of the graph of $f$. [2] (c) Use your graphic display calculator to find the coordinates of the point where the graph of $y=f(x)$ meets the graph of $y=3-x^2$, for $x>-2$. Give your answers to three significant figures. [3] (d) Solve $f(x)\le1$. [3]
tips: Substitute each point into the general form to get equations, noting that b/c = -2 comes from the y-intercept. Exclude x = -2 in the inequality.

subtopic: Solving a rational inequality by graphing
statement: Solve the inequality $\dfrac1{x-2}>x-1$. (a) Find the $x$-coordinates of the points where the graphs of $y=\dfrac1{x-2}$ and $y=x-1$ intersect, in exact form. [3] (b) Use the graphs (noting the vertical asymptote at $x=2$) to state the solution set to three significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) $1=(x-1)(x-2)$ [M1] $x^2-3x+1=0$ [A1] $x=\dfrac{3\pm\sqrt5}2$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) the hyperbola is above the line for $x<0.382$ [A1] and for $2<x<2.62$ [A1] it is below for $0.382<x<2$ and $x>2.62$, so the solution is $x<0.382$ or $2<x<2.62$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The sign of the difference can change at an intersection or at a vertical asymptote. Check each interval.

subtopic: Speed-time model with a rational function
statement: A particle moves in a straight line. Its speed, in meters per second, at time $t$ seconds is given by $v(t)=\dfrac{40t}{t^2+16}$, for $t\ge0$. (a) Find the maximum speed of the particle and the time at which it occurs. [3] (b) Find the two times at which the speed is $3\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. [3] (c) Write down the equation of the horizontal asymptote of the graph of $v$ and state what it means for the motion. [2] (d) Find the distance travelled between $t=0$ and $t=12$. [3]
markscheme: (a) maximum of the graph (or $v'(t)=0$) [M1] $t=4$ s [A1] $v=5\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\frac{40t}{t^2+16}=3$ [M1] $t=\frac43\approx1.33$ s [A1] $t=12$ s [A1] [3 marks] (c) $v=0$ [A1] the particle's speed approaches zero as time becomes large [R1] [2 marks] (d) $\int_0^{12}\frac{40t}{t^2+16}\,dt$ [M1] $=\left[20\ln(t^2+16)\right]_0^{12}$ [A1] $=20\ln10\approx46.1$ m [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A rational speed function that vanishes at t = 0 and for large t must have a single maximum in between. Distance is the integral of speed, which the GDC can evaluate.

subtopic: Odd rational function, range via derivative
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{x}{x^2+4}$, for $x\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Show that $f$ is an odd function. [2] (b) Write down the equation of the horizontal asymptote of the graph of $f$. [1] (c) Find the coordinates of the stationary points of the graph of $f$. [4] (d) Hence write down the range of $f$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $f(-x)=\dfrac{-x}{(-x)^2+4}$ [M1] $=-\dfrac{x}{x^2+4}=-f(x)$, so $f$ is odd [A1] [2 marks] (b) $y=0$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $f'(x)=\dfrac{(x^2+4)-x(2x)}{(x^2+4)^2}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{4-x^2}{(x^2+4)^2}$ [A1] $f'(x)=0\Rightarrow x=\pm2$ [A1] stationary points $\left(2,\,\dfrac14\right)$ and $\left(-2,\,-\dfrac14\right)$ [A1] [4 marks] (d) $-\dfrac14\le f(x)\le\dfrac14$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: For the range, combine the stationary values with the asymptote: the function tends to $0$ at both ends and has only these two turning points. The oddness of $f$ gives the second stationary point for free once the first is known.

subtopic: Repeated composition of a rational function and proof by induction
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{x}{x+2}$, defined wherever the expression exists. (a) Show that $(f\circ f)(x)=\dfrac{x}{3x+4}$ for all $x$ in the domain of $f\circ f$ (that is, $x\neq-2$ and $x\neq-\frac43$). [2] (b) Find $(f\circ f\circ f)(x)$ in the form $\dfrac{x}{px+q}$ where $p,q\in\mathbb{Z}$. [2] Let $f^n$ denote $f$ composed with itself $n$ times. (c) Write down a conjecture for $f^n(x)$ and prove by induction that it is true for all $n\in\mathbb{Z}^+$. [7]
markscheme: (a) $f(f(x))=\dfrac{\frac{x}{x+2}}{\frac{x}{x+2}+2}$ [M1] multiply numerator and denominator by $x+2$: $\frac{x}{x+2(x+2)}=\frac{x}{3x+4}$ [M1] [AG] (the domain excludes $x=-2$, where $f$ is undefined, and $x=-\frac43$, where $f(x)=-2$) [2 marks] (b) $f\left(\frac{x}{3x+4}\right)=\dfrac{x}{x+2(3x+4)}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{x}{7x+8}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Conjecture: $f^n(x)=\dfrac{x}{(2^n-1)x+2^n}$ [A1] For $n=1$: $\frac{x}{x+2}=f(x)$, true [A1] Assume true for $n=k$ [M1] $f^{k+1}(x)=f\left(f^k(x)\right)=\dfrac{f^k(x)}{f^k(x)+2}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{x}{x+2\left((2^k-1)x+2^k\right)}$ [A1] $=\dfrac{x}{(2^{k+1}-1)x+2^{k+1}}$ [A1] True for $n=1$, and true for $n=k$ implies true for $n=k+1$, so true for all $n\in\mathbb{Z}^+$ [R1] [7 marks]
tips: Compute two or three compositions to spot the pattern in the coefficients before conjecturing. In the induction step, use $f(u)=\frac{u}{u+2}$ with $u=f^k(x)$.

subtopic: Range of a reciprocal of a trigonometric function
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac1{2+\cos x}$ for $x\in\mathbb R$. (a) Explain why $f$ is defined for all real $x$, and find its range. [3] (b) Write down the period of $f$ and the values of $x$ in $[0,2\pi]$ at which the maximum and minimum occur. [3]
markscheme: (a) $2+\cos x\ge1>0$ [R1] $1\le2+\cos x\le3$ so $\dfrac13\le f(x)\le1$ [M1] range $\left[\dfrac13,1\right]$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) period $2\pi$ [A1] maximum $1$ when $\cos x=-1$, $x=\pi$ [A1] minimum $\dfrac13$ when $\cos x=1$, $x=0$ and $x=2\pi$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The reciprocal of a quantity between 1 and 3 lies between $1/3$ and $1$, with the order reversed.

subtopic: Higher derivatives of a rational function using partial fractions
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac1{x(x+1)}$ for $x>0$. (a) Write $f(x)$ in partial fractions. [2] (b) Find the first three derivatives of $f$, and conjecture a formula for $f^{(n)}(x)$. [3] (c) Prove your conjecture by induction. [4]
tips: Differentiate each partial fraction separately, using the power rule repeatedly.

subtopic: Two resistors in parallel as a rational function
statement: A resistor of $x$ ohms is connected in parallel with a $12$ ohm resistor. The total resistance $R$ satisfies $\dfrac1R=\dfrac1x+\dfrac1{12}$. (a) Show that $R(x)=\dfrac{12x}{x+12}$. [2] (b) Find $x$ for which $R=8$. [2] (c) State the horizontal asymptote of $R$, interpret it, and show that $R$ is always less than both $x$ and $12$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac1R=\dfrac{12+x}{12x}$ [M1] take reciprocals [A1] [2 marks] (b) $12x=8x+96$ [M1] $x=24$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $R=12$ [A1] as $x$ grows large, the first resistor carries almost no current, so $R$ tends to $12$ [R1] $\dfrac1R>\dfrac1x$ and $\dfrac1R>\dfrac1{12}$, so $R<x$ and $R<12$ [R1] [3 marks]
tips: Resistances in parallel combine by adding reciprocals.

subtopic: Partial fractions then binomial expansion of a rational function
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{5+x}{(1-x)(1+2x)}$, for $|x|<\dfrac12$. (a) Express $f(x)$ in the form $\dfrac{A}{1-x}+\dfrac{B}{1+2x}$, where $A,B\in\mathbb{Z}$. [3] (b) Hence use the binomial theorem to expand $f(x)$ in ascending powers of $x$, up to and including the term in $x^3$. [4] (c) Write down the coefficient of $x^n$ in the expansion of $f(x)$, for $n\ge 0$, and explain why the expansion is valid for $|x|<\dfrac12$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $5+x\equiv A(1+2x)+B(1-x)$ [M1] $x=1$: $6=3A$, so $A=2$ [A1] $x=-\dfrac12$: $\dfrac92=\dfrac32B$, so $B=3$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $f(x)=2(1-x)^{-1}+3(1+2x)^{-1}$ [M1] $(1-x)^{-1}=1+x+x^2+x^3+\ldots$ [A1] $(1+2x)^{-1}=1-2x+4x^2-8x^3+\ldots$ [A1] $f(x)=5-4x+14x^2-22x^3+\ldots$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) coefficient is $2+3(-2)^n$ [A1] the expansion of $(1-x)^{-1}$ needs $|x|<1$ and that of $(1+2x)^{-1}$ needs $|2x|<1$, that is $|x|<\dfrac12$ [A1] the second condition is stricter, so both are satisfied when $|x|<\dfrac12$ [R1] [3 marks]
tips: Rewrite each partial fraction as $(1+u)^{-1}$ before expanding, with $u=-x$ and $u=2x$ respectively. The expansion of a sum is valid only where all of its parts converge, so take the most restrictive condition.

subtopic: Partial fractions with an improper fraction and a repeated factor
statement: (a) Express $\dfrac{x^2+4x-6}{(x+1)(x-2)}$ in the form $1+\dfrac{A}{x+1}+\dfrac{B}{x-2}$, where $A,B\in\mathbb{Z}$. [5] (b) Express $\dfrac{3x^2-2x+2}{x(x-1)^2}$ in the form $\dfrac{P}{x}+\dfrac{Q}{x-1}+\dfrac{R}{(x-1)^2}$, where $P,Q,R\in\mathbb{Z}$. [5]
tips: If the degree of the numerator is not smaller than that of the denominator, divide first. For a repeated factor include a term for each power.

subtopic: Composite with a rational function: domain and range
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{x-3}$, for $x\neq3$, and $g(x)=x^2+1$, for $x\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Find $(f\circ g)(x)$ and state its domain. [3] (b) Find the range of $f\circ g$. [3] (c) Solve $(g\circ f)(x)=2$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $(f\circ g)(x)=\dfrac{1}{x^2+1-3}=\dfrac{1}{x^2-2}$ [A1] domain: $x\in\mathbb{R}$, $x\neq\sqrt2$, $x\neq-\sqrt2$ [A1][A1] [3 marks] (b) $x^2-2\ge-2$ [M1] so $x^2-2$ takes all values in $[-2,0)\cup(0,\infty)$ [A1] range: $y\le-\dfrac12$ or $y>0$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\dfrac{1}{(x-3)^2}+1=2$ [M1] $(x-3)^2=1$, so $x=2$ or $x=4$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: To find the range of a composite, first find the set of values of the inner expression and then apply the outer function to that set. The reciprocal reverses the order of inequalities for values of the same sign.

subtopic: Rational inequality and a hence part with exponentials
statement: (a) Solve the inequality $\dfrac{x+1}{x-3}<2$. [4] (b) Hence solve the inequality $\dfrac{e^t+1}{e^t-3}<2$, for $t\in\mathbb{R}$, giving your answer in exact form. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{x+1}{x-3}-2<0$ [M1] $\dfrac{x+1-2(x-3)}{x-3}=\dfrac{7-x}{x-3}<0$ [A1] critical values $x=3$ and $x=7$ [A1] $x<3$ or $x>7$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $e^t<3$ or $e^t>7$ [M1] since $e^t>0$, $t<\ln 3$ or $t>\ln 7$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Never multiply an inequality by $x-3$ without considering its sign; move everything to one side and combine into a single fraction, then use a sign table. In a hence part, substitute the new expression into the earlier result and remember its range.

subtopic: Fixed points of a rational function
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{x+6}{x+2}$ for $x\ne-2$. (a) Find the values of $x$ for which $f(x)=x$. [3] (b) Find $f(f(x))$ and show that its fixed points are the same as those of $f$. [4]
tips: A fixed point satisfies $f(x)=x$. Fixed points of $f$ are also fixed points of $f\circ f$.

subtopic: Rational inequality using a graph and algebra
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{2x}{x+1}$ and $g(x)=x$. (a) Solve $f(x)=g(x)$. [3] (b) Hence solve $f(x)>g(x)$. [4]
tips: Bring the inequality to one side with a common denominator and use a sign chart; the denominator's zero gives a break in the intervals.

subtopic: Partial fractions and a telescoping series sum
statement: (a) Express $\dfrac{3}{n(n+1)(n+2)}$ in the form $\dfrac{A}{n}+\dfrac{B}{n+1}+\dfrac{C}{n+2}$. [3] (b) Hence show that $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{N}\dfrac{3}{n(n+1)(n+2)}=\dfrac34-\dfrac{3}{2(N+1)(N+2)}$. [4] (c) Write down the value of $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\dfrac{3}{n(n+1)(n+2)}$. [1] (d) Find the smallest positive integer $N$ for which the sum in part (b) differs from the value in part (c) by less than $0.001$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $3\equiv A(n+1)(n+2)+Bn(n+2)+Cn(n+1)$ [M1] $n=0$: $3=2A$, $A=\dfrac32$; $n=-1$: $3=-B$, $B=-3$ [A1] $n=-2$: $3=2C$, $C=\dfrac32$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\dfrac{3}{n(n+1)(n+2)}=\dfrac32\left(\dfrac1n-\dfrac1{n+1}\right)-\dfrac32\left(\dfrac1{n+1}-\dfrac1{n+2}\right)$ [M1] writing out several terms and cancelling in pairs (method of differences) [M1] $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{N}=\dfrac32\left(1-\dfrac1{N+1}\right)-\dfrac32\left(\dfrac12-\dfrac1{N+2}\right)$ [A1] $=\dfrac34-\dfrac32\cdot\dfrac{(N+2)-(N+1)}{(N+1)(N+2)}=\dfrac34-\dfrac{3}{2(N+1)(N+2)}$ [A1] [AG] [4 marks] (c) $\dfrac34$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) $\dfrac{3}{2(N+1)(N+2)}<0.001$ [M1] $(N+1)(N+2)>1500$ [A1] $38\times 39=1482<1500$ and $39\times 40=1560>1500$, so $N+1=39$, $N=38$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: In part (b) write out the first three or four terms explicitly so you can see which terms cancel. In part (d) reduce the inequality to a product of consecutive integers and test values near $\sqrt{1500}\approx 38.7$.

subtopic: Range of a rational function using stationary points
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{x-1}{x^2+3}$ for $x\in\mathbb R$. (a) Show that $f'(x)=\dfrac{-(x-3)(x+1)}{\left(x^2+3\right)^2}$. [3] (b) Find the coordinates of the stationary points and the range of $f$. [4] (c) State the equation of the horizontal asymptote, and the $x$-coordinate where the graph crosses it. [2]
markscheme: (a) quotient rule: $\dfrac{\left(x^2+3\right)-2x(x-1)}{\left(x^2+3\right)^2}$ [M1][A1] numerator $-x^2+2x+3=-(x-3)(x+1)$ [AG] [A1] [3 marks] (b) $x=-1$ and $x=3$ [A1] $f(-1)=-\dfrac12$ minimum, $f(3)=\dfrac16$ maximum [A1] sign of $f'$: negative, positive, negative [M1] range $\left[-\dfrac12,\dfrac16\right]$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) $y=0$ [A1] $x=1$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Since $f\to0$ as $x\to\pm\infty$, the global extreme values occur at the stationary points.

subtopic: Tangent to a rational curve using the discriminant
statement: The curve $C$ has equation $y=\dfrac{4}{x-1}$, for $x\neq1$. The line $L$ has equation $y=-x+k$, where $k\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Show that the $x$-coordinates of the points where $L$ meets $C$ satisfy $x^2-(k+1)x+k+4=0$. [3] (b) Find the values of $k$ for which $L$ is a tangent to $C$. [3] (c) For each value of $k$ found in part (b), find the coordinates of the point of tangency. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{4}{x-1}=-x+k$ [M1] $4=(k-x)(x-1)=kx-k-x^2+x$ [A1] $x^2-(k+1)x+k+4=0$ [A1][AG] [3 marks] (b) Tangent when the discriminant is zero [M1] $(k+1)^2-4(k+4)=0$ [A1] $k^2-2k-15=0$, so $k=5$ or $k=-3$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) A repeated root has $x=\dfrac{k+1}{2}$. For $k=5$: $x=3$, $y=2$, so $(3,\,2)$ [A1] For $k=-3$: $x=-1$, $y=-2$, so $(-1,\,-2)$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A line is tangent to a curve when substituting it into the curve gives an equation with a repeated root. Clear the denominator carefully, remembering that $x=1$ is excluded.

subtopic: Average cost as a rational function
statement: The total cost of making $x$ items is $200+5x$ dollars, and the average cost per item is $A(x)=\dfrac{200+5x}x$. (a) Write down the equation of the horizontal asymptote of the graph of $A$, and interpret it. [2] (b) Find the least number of items for which the average cost is below $\$6.20$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $A=5$ [A1] as production grows, the average cost approaches $\$5$ but never reaches it [R1] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac{200}x+5<6.2$ [M1] $x>\dfrac{200}{1.2}=166.7$ [A1] $167$ items [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Split the average cost as $5+200/x$. The fixed cost per item shrinks as the number of items increases.

subtopic: Partial fractions with an irreducible quadratic factor and arctan integral
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{4x^2+3x+9}{(x+1)(x^2+4)}$, for $x\neq -1$. (a) Find constants $A$, $B$ and $C$ such that $f(x)\equiv\dfrac{A}{x+1}+\dfrac{Bx+C}{x^2+4}$. [5] (b) Hence show that $\displaystyle\int_0^2 f(x)\,dx=\ln 18+\dfrac{\pi}{8}$. [5]
markscheme: (a) $4x^2+3x+9\equiv A(x^2+4)+(Bx+C)(x+1)$ [M1] $x=-1$: $10=5A$, so $A=2$ [A1] equating coefficients (of $x^2$ and the constant term) [M1] $x^2$: $4=A+B$, so $B=2$ [A1] constant: $9=4A+C$, so $C=1$ [A1] [5 marks] (b) $f(x)=\dfrac{2}{x+1}+\dfrac{2x}{x^2+4}+\dfrac{1}{x^2+4}$ [M1] $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{2}{x+1}\,dx=2\ln(x+1)$ [A1] $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{2x}{x^2+4}\,dx=\ln(x^2+4)$ [A1] $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{1}{x^2+4}\,dx=\dfrac12\arctan\dfrac{x}{2}$ [A1] $\left[\,\cdot\,\right]_0^2=2\ln 3+(\ln 8-\ln 4)+\dfrac12\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{4}=2\ln 3+\ln 2+\dfrac{\pi}{8}=\ln 18+\dfrac{\pi}{8}$ [A1] [AG] [5 marks]
tips: Split $\frac{Bx+C}{x^2+4}$ into a part of the form $\frac{kx}{x^2+4}$ (a logarithm) and a part of the form $\frac{c}{x^2+4}$ (an arctangent) before integrating. Recall $\int\frac{1}{x^2+a^2}dx=\frac1a\arctan\frac xa$ is in the formula booklet.

subtopic: A rational function with a parameter and the discriminant
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{x}{x^2+1}\ (x\in\mathbb R)$. By considering the equation $f(x)=k$, find the range of $f$. [6]
markscheme: $\dfrac x{x^2+1}=k$ gives $kx^2-x+k=0$ [M1][A1] for real $x$ with $k\ne0$ need $\Delta=1-4k^2\ge0$ [M1] $-\dfrac12\le k\le\dfrac12$ [A1] $k=0$ is attained at $x=0$ [A1] range $\left[-\dfrac12,\dfrac12\right]$ [A1] [6 marks]
tips: A value $k$ is in the range exactly when $f(x)=k$ has a real solution; the discriminant of the resulting quadratic gives the allowed $k$.

subtopic: Intersection of rational and linear graphs with a GDC
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{4x+1}{x-2}$, for $x\neq2$, and $g(x)=x-3$, for $x\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Write down the equations of the vertical and the horizontal asymptotes of the graph of $f$. [2] (b) Find the $x$-coordinates of the points of intersection of the graphs of $f$ and $g$. [3] (c) Solve the inequality $f(x)\le g(x)$. [3]
markscheme: (a) Vertical asymptote $x=2$ [A1] horizontal asymptote $y=4$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Solve $\dfrac{4x+1}{x-2}=x-3$ [M1] $x=0.595$ ($0.594875\ldots$) [A1] $x=8.41$ ($8.405124\ldots$) [A1] [3 marks] (c) Use the graphs (note $f$ is undefined at $x=2$) [M1] $0.595\le x<2$ [A1] $x\ge 8.41$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: For a rational inequality, the solution set changes sides only at intersection points and at asymptotes, so list both before reading the answer from the graph. Do not forget to exclude $x=2$.

subtopic: Oblique asymptote, stationary points and range
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{x^2}{x-2}$, for $x\in\mathbb{R}$, $x\neq2$. (a) Show that $f(x)=x+2+\dfrac{4}{x-2}$. [2] (b) Write down the equations of the asymptotes of the graph of $f$. [2] (c) Find the coordinates of the stationary points of the graph of $f$, and determine their nature. [5] (d) Hence write down the range of $f$. [2]
tips: Rewriting with polynomial division makes the derivative easy. The range of a function with a vertical asymptote comes from the turning point values on each branch.

subtopic: The graph of a rational function with a calculator
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{x^2-4}{x^2+x+1}$. (a) Find the zeros of $f$ and the equation of its horizontal asymptote. [3] (b) Use your calculator to find the coordinates of the local minimum and local maximum. [3] (c) Find the point where the graph crosses its horizontal asymptote. [2]
markscheme: (a) $x^2-4=0$ so $x=\pm2$ [A1][A1] $y=1$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) graph $f$ and use the minimum and maximum functions [M1] local minimum $(-0.417,-5.06)$ [A1] local maximum $(-9.58,1.06)$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $f(x)=1$: $x^2-4=x^2+x+1$ [M1] $x=-5$, so $(-5,1)$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Graph $f$ and use the calculator's minimum and maximum functions; the denominator is always positive so there are no vertical asymptotes.

subtopic: A rational equation from combined work rates
statement: Pipe $A$ alone fills a tank in $x$ hours. Pipe $B$ alone fills it in $x+2$ hours. Together they fill the tank in $4$ hours. (a) Show that $x^2-6x-8=0$. [3] (b) Find $x$ in exact form, and the time taken by pipe $B$ alone, to one decimal place. [3]
markscheme: (a) rates $\dfrac1x+\dfrac1{x+2}=\dfrac14$ [M1][A1] $4(2x+2)=x(x+2)$, so $x^2-6x-8=0$ [AG] [A1] [3 marks] (b) $x=\dfrac{6\pm\sqrt{68}}2=3\pm\sqrt{17}$ [M1] $x=3+\sqrt{17}$ since $x>0$ [A1] $B$: $5+\sqrt{17}=9.1$ hours [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Work rates add: the combined rate is the sum of the individual rates, each being the reciprocal of the time taken.

subtopic: Asymptotes, intercepts and inverse of a Mobius function
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{2x-3}{x+4}$, for $x\in\mathbb{R},\ x\neq-4$. (a) Write down the equation of (i) the vertical asymptote; (ii) the horizontal asymptote of the graph of $f$. [2] (b) Find the coordinates of the $x$-intercept and the $y$-intercept of the graph of $f$. [2] (c) Find $f^{-1}(x)$. [3]
markscheme: (a) (i) $x=-4$ [A1] (ii) $y=2$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $x$-intercept: $2x-3=0$, so $\left(\dfrac32,\,0\right)$ [A1] $y$-intercept: $f(0)=-\dfrac34$, so $\left(0,\,-\dfrac34\right)$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $x=\dfrac{2y-3}{y+4}$ (interchange $x$ and $y$) [M1] $xy+4x=2y-3$, so $y(x-2)=-4x-3$ [M1] $f^{-1}(x)=\dfrac{4x+3}{2-x}$, $x\neq 2$ [A1] Accept $\dfrac{-4x-3}{x-2}$. [3 marks]
tips: For $\frac{ax+b}{cx+d}$, the vertical asymptote makes the denominator zero and the horizontal asymptote is $y=a/c$. When finding an inverse, collect all terms in $y$ on one side before factorizing.

subtopic: Graph of the reciprocal of a quadratic described in words
statement: Let $f(x)=x^2-2x-3$ and $g(x)=\dfrac{1}{f(x)}$, for $x\in\mathbb{R}$ where $f(x)\neq0$. (a) Write down the equations of the vertical asymptotes of the graph of $g$. [2] (b) Find the $y$-intercept of the graph of $g$ and the coordinates of its local maximum point. [3] (c) Write down the equation of the horizontal asymptote and describe the graph of $g$ on each of the intervals $x<-1$, $-1<x<3$ and $x>3$. [4] (d) Write down the range of $g$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $f(x)=(x-3)(x+1)$ [M1] $x=-1$ and $x=3$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $g(0)=-\frac13$, so $\left(0,-\frac13\right)$ [A1] the vertex of $f$ is $(1,-4)$ [M1] so $g$ has a local maximum at $\left(1,-\frac14\right)$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $y=0$ [A1] for $x<-1$: $g>0$ and increasing from near $0$ to $+\infty$ [A1] for $-1<x<3$: $g<0$, a cap shape with maximum $\left(1,-\frac14\right)$, tending to $-\infty$ at both asymptotes [A1] for $x>3$: $g>0$ and decreasing from $+\infty$ toward $0$ [A1] [4 marks] (d) $g\le-\frac14$ [A1] or $g>0$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Zeros of f become vertical asymptotes of 1/f, and a minimum of f at a negative value becomes a maximum of 1/f. Large values of f give values of 1/f near zero.

subtopic: Rational inequality and the domain of a square root function
statement: (a) Solve the inequality $\dfrac{x+4}{x-2}\le x$. [5] (b) Hence find the largest possible domain, in $\mathbb{R}$, of the function $g(x)=\sqrt{\dfrac{x^2-3x-4}{x-2}}$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $x-\dfrac{x+4}{x-2}\ge 0$ [M1] $\dfrac{x(x-2)-(x+4)}{x-2}=\dfrac{x^2-3x-4}{x-2}=\dfrac{(x-4)(x+1)}{x-2}\ge 0$ [A1] critical values $x=-1,\ 2,\ 4$ [A1] sign table or sketch [M1] $-1\le x<2$ or $x\ge 4$ [A1] [5 marks] (b) require $\dfrac{x^2-3x-4}{x-2}\ge 0$, which is the inequality found in (a) [M1] domain: $-1\le x<2$ or $x\ge 4$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The endpoints where the numerator is zero are included when the inequality is non-strict, but zeros of the denominator are never included. For a square root, the expression under the root must be greater than or equal to zero.

subtopic: Partial fractions over the complex numbers
statement: Consider $\dfrac1{x^2+1}$ for real $x$. (a) Show that $\dfrac1{x^2+1}=\dfrac1{2\mathrm i}\left(\dfrac1{x-\mathrm i}-\dfrac1{x+\mathrm i}\right)$. [3] (b) Show that $\dfrac1{x^2+1}=\operatorname{Im}\left(\dfrac1{x-\mathrm i}\right)$ for real $x$. [2] (c) The second derivative of $\dfrac1{x-\mathrm i}$ is $\dfrac2{(x-\mathrm i)^3}$. Use this to find the second derivative of $\dfrac1{1+x^2}$ at $x=0$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac1{x-\mathrm i}-\dfrac1{x+\mathrm i}=\dfrac{(x+\mathrm i)-(x-\mathrm i)}{x^2+1}$ [M1][A1] $=\dfrac{2\mathrm i}{x^2+1}$, divide by $2\mathrm i$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\dfrac1{x-\mathrm i}=\dfrac{x+\mathrm i}{x^2+1}$ [M1] imaginary part $\dfrac1{x^2+1}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\dfrac{d^2}{dx^2}\dfrac1{x^2+1}=\operatorname{Im}\left(\dfrac2{(x-\mathrm i)^3}\right)$ [M1] at $x=0$: $\dfrac2{(-\mathrm i)^3}=\dfrac2{\mathrm i}=-2\mathrm i$ [A1] so the value is $-2$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate to separate the real and imaginary parts of $1/(x-\mathrm i)$.

subtopic: Average speed as a rational function of the return speed
statement: A car travels a distance $d$ at $60$ km/h and returns the same distance at $v$ km/h. Its average speed for the round trip is $A(v)$ km/h. (a) Show that $A(v)=\dfrac{120v}{v+60}$. [3] (b) Find the value of $v$ for which the average speed is $48$ km/h, and the value for which it is $100$ km/h. [3] (c) State the equation of the horizontal asymptote of the graph of $A$ and interpret it. [2]
markscheme: (a) total time $\dfrac d{60}+\dfrac dv$ [M1] $A=\dfrac{2d}{\frac d{60}+\frac dv}=\dfrac{2}{\frac{1}{60}+\frac1v}$ [A1] $=\dfrac{120v}{v+60}$ [AG] [A1] [3 marks] (b) $120v=48(v+60)$ [M1] $v=40$ [A1] $120v=100v+6000$ gives $v=300$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $A=120$ [A1] however fast the return, the average speed can never reach $120$ km/h [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Average speed is total distance divided by total time. The distance $d$ cancels.

subtopic: Inverse of a Mobius function and the equation f(x) = f inverse of x
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{5-2x}{x+4}$, for $x\in\mathbb{R}$, $x\neq-4$. (a) Find $f^{-1}(x)$ and state its domain. [5] (b) Solve $f(x)=f^{-1}(x)$. [4]
tips: Swap the roles of x and y, collect the terms in the new subject, and factorize. Remember the domain of the inverse equals the range of f.

subtopic: Rational concentration model
statement: The concentration of a drug in a patient's blood, $C$ milligrams per liter, $t$ hours after it is injected, is modeled by $C(t)=\dfrac{24t}{t^2+16}$, for $t\ge0$. (a) Find the maximum concentration and the time at which it occurs. [2] The drug is effective while the concentration is at least $2.4$ mg per liter. (b) Find the values of $t$ for which the drug is effective. [3] (c) Find the rate of change of the concentration at $t=10$, and interpret your answer in context. [3] (d) Describe what happens to the concentration as $t$ increases without bound, giving a reason. [2]
markscheme: (a) Using the GDC: maximum concentration $3.00$ mg per liter [A1] at $t=4.00$ hours [A1] [2 marks] (b) Solve $\dfrac{24t}{t^2+16}=2.4$ [M1] $t=2$ and $t=8$ [A1] effective for $2\le t\le 8$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $C'(t)=\dfrac{24(16-t^2)}{(t^2+16)^2}$, or use the GDC derivative at $t=10$ [M1] $C'(10)=-0.150$ ($-0.14982\ldots$) [A1] At $10$ hours the concentration is decreasing at about $0.150$ mg per liter per hour [A1] [3 marks] (d) The concentration approaches $0$ [A1] because the denominator grows like $t^2$ while the numerator grows only like $t$, so $C\approx\dfrac{24}{t}\to0$ [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Write the effectiveness condition as an equation first and read the two crossing points from the graph. In a rate-of-change interpretation, state the sign, the size and the units.

subtopic: Partial fractions with a repeated factor and integration
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{5x+1}{(x-1)^2(x+2)}$, for $x\in\mathbb{R}$, $x\neq 1$, $x\neq -2$. (a) Express $f(x)$ in the form $\dfrac{A}{x-1}+\dfrac{B}{(x-1)^2}+\dfrac{C}{x+2}$, where $A,B,C\in\mathbb{Z}$. [4] (b) Hence find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_2^3 f(x)\,dx$, giving your answer in the form $p+\ln q$, where $p\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $q\in\mathbb{Q}$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $5x+1\equiv A(x-1)(x+2)+B(x+2)+C(x-1)^2$ [M1] substituting $x=1$: $6=3B$, so $B=2$ [A1] substituting $x=-2$: $-9=9C$, so $C=-1$ [A1] equating coefficients of $x^2$: $0=A+C$, so $A=1$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $\displaystyle\int\left(\dfrac{1}{x-1}+\dfrac{2}{(x-1)^2}-\dfrac{1}{x+2}\right)dx=\ln|x-1|-\dfrac{2}{x-1}-\ln|x+2|$ [M1] [A1] substituting limits: $\left(\ln 2-1-\ln 5\right)-\left(0-2-\ln 4\right)$ [M1] $=1+\ln 2+\ln 4-\ln 5=1+\ln\dfrac{8}{5}$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: For a repeated factor $(x-1)^2$ you need both $\frac{A}{x-1}$ and $\frac{B}{(x-1)^2}$. The $\frac{B}{(x-1)^2}$ term integrates to $-\frac{B}{x-1}$, not to a logarithm.

subtopic: Asymptotes and intercepts of a rational function
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{3x-6}{x^2-x-6}$ for $x\in\mathbb R$, $x\ne3$, $x\ne-2$. (a) Find the equations of all asymptotes. [3] (b) Find the coordinates of the axis intercepts. [2] (c) Determine whether the graph crosses its horizontal asymptote. [2]
markscheme: (a) $x^2-x-6=(x-3)(x+2)$ so vertical asymptotes $x=3$ and $x=-2$ [A1][A1] horizontal asymptote $y=0$ (degree of numerator is smaller) [A1] [3 marks] (b) $y$-intercept: $f(0)=\dfrac{-6}{-6}=1$, $(0,1)$ [A1] $x$-intercept: $3x-6=0$, $(2,0)$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $f(x)=0$ at $x=2$ [M1] so it crosses $y=0$ at $(2,0)$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Vertical asymptotes come from the zeros of the denominator not cancelled by the numerator. A horizontal asymptote can be crossed at finite $x$.

subtopic: Rational inequality with unlike denominators
statement: (a) Show that the inequality $\dfrac{x+4}{x-1}\le\dfrac{x}{x+2}$ is equivalent to $\dfrac{7x+8}{(x-1)(x+2)}\le0$. [2] (b) Hence solve $\dfrac{x+4}{x-1}\le\dfrac{x}{x+2}$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $\frac{x+4}{x-1}-\frac{x}{x+2}\le0$ [M1] $\frac{(x+4)(x+2)-x(x-1)}{(x-1)(x+2)}=\frac{7x+8}{(x-1)(x+2)}\le0$ [M1] [AG] [2 marks] (b) critical values $-2$, $-\frac87$, $1$ [A1] sign analysis of the fraction [M1] $x<-2$ [A1] $-\frac87\le x<1$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Never multiply by an expression whose sign is unknown. Move everything to one side, combine, and use a sign table. Check which end points are included.

subtopic: Self-inverse rational function
statement:
Let $f(x)=\dfrac{px+3}{x-4}$, for $x\in\mathbb{R},\ x
eq4$, where $p$ is a constant and $p
eq-\dfrac34$. (a) Find an expression for $f^{-1}(x)$ in terms of $p$. [4] Given that $f(x)=f^{-1}(x)$ for all $x
eq 4$, (b) find the value of $p$. [2] (c) For this value of $p$, solve $f(x)=x$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $x=\dfrac{py+3}{y-4}$ (interchange $x$ and $y$) [M1] $xy-4x=py+3$ [A1] $y(x-p)=4x+3$ [M1] $f^{-1}(x)=\dfrac{4x+3}{x-p}$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) Equate the expressions: $\dfrac{px+3}{x-4}=\dfrac{4x+3}{x-p}$ for all $x$; comparing the denominators $x-4$ and $x-p$ [M1] $p=4$ (and then the numerators agree, $4x+3$) [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\dfrac{4x+3}{x-4}=x$ [M1] $4x+3=x^2-4x$, so $x^2-8x-3=0$ [A1] $x=4\pm\sqrt{19}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A function is its own inverse exactly when its graph is symmetric in the line $y=x$. After finding the general inverse, compare coefficients, and check that your final value makes both numerator and denominator match.

subtopic: Solving a rational equation and rejecting an extraneous solution
statement: Solve the equation $\dfrac{x}{x-2}+\dfrac{3}{x+2}=\dfrac{8}{x^2-4}$. [5]
markscheme: Multiply through by $(x-2)(x+2)$ [M1] $x(x+2)+3(x-2)=8$ [A1] $x^2+5x-14=0$ [A1] $(x+7)(x-2)=0$, so $x=-7$ or $x=2$ [A1] $x=2$ is rejected because the original expressions are undefined there, so $x=-7$ [R1] [5 marks]
tips: Always substitute your solutions back, or check the domain, after clearing denominators. Values that make a denominator zero must be rejected.

subtopic: Line meeting a hyperbola-type curve and the range of a related function
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{2x+1}{x-1}$ for $x\neq1$, and $g(x)=x+f(x)$. (a) Show that the $x$-coordinates of the points of intersection of the graph of $y=f(x)$ and the line $y=k-x$ satisfy $x^2+(1-k)x+(k+1)=0$. [2] (b) Find the exact values of $k$ for which the line is a tangent to the graph of $y=f(x)$. [4] (c) Hence find the range of $g$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $2x+1=(k-x)(x-1)$ [M1] $2x+1=kx-k-x^2+x$, so $x^2+(1-k)x+(k+1)=0$ [M1] [AG] [2 marks] (b) discriminant $(1-k)^2-4(k+1)=0$ [M1] $k^2-6k-3=0$ [A1] $k=\frac{6\pm\sqrt{48}}{2}$ [M1] $k=3\pm2\sqrt3$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) $g(x)=k\iff f(x)=k-x$, so $k$ is in the range exactly when the line meets the curve [R1] this needs discriminant $\ge0$: $k^2-6k-3\ge0$ [M1] $k\le3-2\sqrt3$ or $k\ge3+2\sqrt3$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Turning "is k in the range?" into "does a line meet the curve?" lets you use the discriminant. Check the root x = 1 is not produced.

subtopic: Finding constants from a stationary point and proving the range
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{ax+b}{x^2+1}$, for $x\in\mathbb{R}$, where $a,b\in\mathbb{R}$. The graph of $f$ has a stationary point at $(2,1)$. (a) Find the values of $a$ and $b$. [5] (b) Find the coordinates of the other stationary point and determine the nature of both stationary points. [4] (c) Show that the range of $f$ is $-4\le y\le1$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $f(2)=1$: $2a+b=5$ [M1] $f'(x)=\frac{a(x^2+1)-2x(ax+b)}{(x^2+1)^2}$ [M1] $=\frac{-ax^2-2bx+a}{(x^2+1)^2}$ [A1] $f'(2)=0$: $-3a-4b=0$ [M1] $a=4$, $b=-3$ [A1] [5 marks] (b) $-4x^2+6x+4=0$, so $2x^2-3x-2=0$ [M1] $(2x+1)(x-2)=0$, $x=-\frac12$ [A1] $f\left(-\frac12\right)=-4$, so $\left(-\frac12,-4\right)$ [A1] the numerator of $f'$ is positive between the roots, so $f$ increases from $x=-\frac12$ to $x=2$: local minimum at $\left(-\frac12,-4\right)$ and local maximum at $(2,1)$ [R1] [4 marks] (c) $f(x)=k$ gives $kx^2-4x+k+3=0$ [M1] for $k\neq0$ real solutions need $16-4k(k+3)\ge0$ [M1] $k^2+3k-4\le0$, $(k+4)(k-1)\le0$ [A1] $-4\le k\le1$ (and $k=0$ gives $x=\frac34$, which is included) [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Use both the point condition and the zero-derivative condition to get two equations. For a range, treat f(x) = k as a quadratic in x and demand real roots.

subtopic: Even rational function: symmetry, asymptotes, turning point and range
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{x^2}{x^2-4}$, for $x\in\mathbb{R}$, $x\neq\pm 2$. (a) Show that $f$ is an even function and state the geometrical consequence for the graph of $y=f(x)$. [2] (b) Write down the equations of the three asymptotes of the graph of $f$. [3] (c) Find $f'(x)$ and hence find the coordinates of the stationary point of the graph of $f$. Determine its nature. [4] (d) Find the range of $f$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $f(-x)=\dfrac{(-x)^2}{(-x)^2-4}=\dfrac{x^2}{x^2-4}=f(x)$ [M1] so $f$ is even, and the graph is symmetric about the $y$-axis [A1] [2 marks] (b) $x=2$ [A1] $x=-2$ [A1] $y=1$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $f'(x)=\dfrac{2x(x^2-4)-x^2(2x)}{(x^2-4)^2}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{-8x}{(x^2-4)^2}$ [A1] $f'(x)=0\Rightarrow x=0$; stationary point $(0,0)$ [A1] $f'>0$ for $-2<x<0$ and $f'<0$ for $0<x<2$ (or $f''(0)=-\tfrac12<0$), so it is a local maximum [A1] [4 marks] (d) $f(x)=1+\dfrac{4}{x^2-4}$ [M1] for $|x|<2$: $x^2-4\in[-4,0)$, so $\dfrac{4}{x^2-4}\le -1$ and $f(x)\le 0$ (with $f\to-\infty$ near $\pm2$) [A1] for $|x|>2$: $x^2-4>0$, so $f(x)>1$; range is $f(x)\le 0$ or $f(x)>1$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Use the symmetry of an even function to halve the work: whatever happens at $x$ also happens at $-x$. For the range, write the function as a constant plus a simple reciprocal term and analyse each branch of the domain separately.

subtopic: Asymptote crossing point and turning points using a GDC
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{2x^2-3x+1}{x^2+1}$, for $x\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Write down the equation of the horizontal asymptote of the graph of $f$. [1] (b) Show that the graph of $f$ crosses its horizontal asymptote at exactly one point, and find the coordinates of that point. [3] (c) Use your graphic display calculator to find the coordinates of the local maximum and local minimum points of the graph of $f$. Give your answers to three significant figures. [3] (d) Solve $f(x)=1.5$. Give your answers to three significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) $y=2$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $2x^2-3x+1=2(x^2+1)$ [M1] $-3x=1$, $x=-\frac13$ [A1] one solution only, so one crossing point $\left(-\frac13,2\right)$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) use of GDC on the graph [M1] local maximum $(-1.39,3.08)$ [A1] local minimum $(0.721,-0.0811)$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $2x^2-3x+1=1.5x^2+1.5$ [M1] $x^2-6x-1=0$ [A1] $x=3\pm\sqrt{10}$, that is $x=6.16$ or $x=-0.162$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A curve can cross a horizontal asymptote; set f(x) equal to the asymptote value to find where. Always check which coordinate is needed when reading a GDC.

subtopic: Solving 1/x less than x
statement: Solve the inequality $\dfrac1x<x$. [5]
markscheme: $x>0$: multiply by $x$: $1<x^2$ so $x>1$ [M1][A1] $x<0$: multiplying by $x$ reverses: $1>x^2$, so $-1<x<0$ [M1][A1] solution $-1<x<0$ or $x>1$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: Never multiply an inequality by $x$ without considering its sign. Alternatively, write $x-\dfrac1x>0$ and use a sign table.

subtopic: Lens equation as a rational function and minimum object-image distance
statement: In an optics experiment, a lens of focal length 12 cm forms a real image of an object placed $u$ cm from the lens, where $u>12$. The distance $v$ cm of the image from the lens is given by $v=\dfrac{12u}{u-12}$. (a) Find $v$ when $u=20$. [1] (b) Write down the equation of the vertical asymptote of the graph of $v$ against $u$ and interpret it in this context. [2] (c) The distance between the object and its image is $D=u+v$. Show that $D=u+12+\dfrac{144}{u-12}$. [3] (d) Using your graphing calculator, find the minimum value of $D$ and the value of $u$ at which it occurs. [2] (e) Find the range of values of $u$ for which $D\le 50$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $v=\dfrac{12\times 20}{8}=30$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $u=12$ [A1] as the object approaches the focal point (from beyond it), the image distance increases without bound (the image forms infinitely far away) [A1] [2 marks] (c) $D=u+\dfrac{12u}{u-12}=\dfrac{u(u-12)+12u}{u-12}=\dfrac{u^2}{u-12}$ [M1] [A1] $u^2=(u-12)(u+12)+144$, so $D=u+12+\dfrac{144}{u-12}$ [A1] [AG] [3 marks] (d) sketch or minimum function on GDC [M1] minimum $D=48$ cm at $u=24$ [A1] [2 marks] (e) $\dfrac{u^2}{u-12}\le 50$ (graph intersection with $D=50$) [M1] $u=20$ and $u=30$ [A1] since the graph is below the line between the intersections, $20\le u\le 30$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: In a show-that part, combine into a single fraction first, then rewrite the numerator to expose the target form. For minimum or inequality questions on a GDC, sketch the graph in a window that includes the vertical asymptote and the turning point.

subtopic: Sigma notation with a linear term
statement: Let $S_n=\sum_{k=1}^{n}(2k+3)$. (a) Show that $S_n=n^{2}+4n$. [3] (b) Find the value of $n$ such that $S_n=285$. [3]
tips: Use $\sum_{k=1}^{n}k=\frac{n(n+1)}{2}$ and $\sum_{k=1}^{n}c=cn$.

subtopic: Regular deposits into a savings account
statement: Kofi opens a savings account that pays $4.8\%$ per year, compounded monthly. He deposits $200$ dollars at the end of every month, starting at the end of the first month. Round money to the nearest cent. (a) Find the balance in the account immediately after his $36$th deposit. [3] (b) Find the least number of deposits needed for the balance to exceed $10000$ dollars, immediately after a deposit. [3] (c) Kofi stops making deposits after the $36$th deposit and leaves the balance from part (a) to earn interest, with no further deposits. Find the balance $24$ months later. [2]
markscheme: (a) monthly rate $=\dfrac{4.8}{12}=0.4\%$ [M1]; GDC finance solver with $N=36$, $I\%=4.8$, $PMT=-200$, $P/Y=C/Y=12$ [M1]; $FV=7727.62$ dollars [A1] [3 marks] (b) set $FV=10000$ and solve for $N$ [M1]; $N=45.7$ [A1]; the balance first exceeds $10000$ after the $46$th deposit [A1] [3 marks] (c) $7727.62\times\left(1+0.004\right)^{24}$ [M1]; $=8504.62$ dollars [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Use $PMT=-200$ (money paid out) and $FV$ positive. Check the integer $N$ either side of the solver output.

subtopic: A geometric series with a given sum to infinity and second term
statement: A geometric series has sum to infinity $12$ and second term $3$. (a) Show that the common ratio $r$ satisfies $4r^2-4r+1=0$. [3] (b) Hence find $r$ and the first term. [2]
tips: Use the two conditions to form an equation in $r$ alone. A repeated root means there is only one geometric series satisfying both conditions.

subtopic: Logarithms of a geometric sequence
statement: A sequence has $a_n=4\times2^{3n}$. (a) Show that the sequence is geometric and find its common ratio. [2] (b) Show that $\log_2a_n$ is an arithmetic sequence and find its first term and common difference. [3] (c) Find $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{10}\log_2a_n$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}=\dfrac{4\times2^{3n+3}}{4\times2^{3n}}$ [M1] $=8$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\log_2a_n=2+3n$ [M1][A1] first term $5$, common difference $3$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $S_{10}=\dfrac{10}{2}(5+32)$ [M1] $=185$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Taking logarithms turns geometric growth into arithmetic growth: $\log(ar^n)=\log a+n\log r$.

subtopic: Recurrence relations and limits
statement: This question investigates ratios of consecutive terms in sequences defined by recurrence relations. The sequence $\{u_n\}$ is defined by $u_1 = 1$, $u_2 = 1$ and $u_{n+2} = u_{n+1} + u_n$ for $n \ge 1$. (a) Write down the values of $u_3, u_4, \ldots, u_8$. [2] (b) Let $r_n = \dfrac{u_{n+1}}{u_n}$. Calculate $r_1, r_2, \ldots, r_7$, giving non-integer answers to four significant figures, and describe the behavior of $r_n$. [3] (c) Show that $r_{n+1} = 1 + \dfrac{1}{r_n}$. [2] (d) Assuming that $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty} r_n = L$ exists, show that $L = \dfrac{1+\sqrt5}{2}$. [3] (e) Let $\varphi = \dfrac{1+\sqrt5}{2}$ and $\psi = \dfrac{1-\sqrt5}{2}$. (i) Show that $\varphi^2 = \varphi + 1$ and $\psi^2 = \psi + 1$. (ii) Prove by mathematical induction that $u_n = \dfrac{\varphi^n - \psi^n}{\sqrt5}$ for all $n \in \mathbb{Z}^+$. [7] (f) Use the result from part (e) to prove that $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty} r_n = \varphi$, without assuming that the limit exists. [4] (g) Now consider the sequence $v_1 = 1$, $v_2 = 1$, $v_{n+2} = v_{n+1} + k\,v_n$, where $k > 0$. Assuming that $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{v_{n+1}}{v_n}$ exists, find this limit in terms of $k$, and find the value of $k$ for which the limit is $2$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21$ [A2] (award [A1] for at least four correct) [2 marks] (b) $r_1=1,\ r_2=2,\ r_3=1.5,\ r_4=1.667,\ r_5=1.6,\ r_6=1.625,\ r_7=1.615$ [A2] (award [A1] for at least four correct) The ratios alternate above and below a value, with the oscillations decreasing in size: they appear to converge to approximately $1.618$ [R1] [3 marks] (c) $r_{n+1}=\dfrac{u_{n+2}}{u_{n+1}}=\dfrac{u_{n+1}+u_n}{u_{n+1}}$ [M1] $=1+\dfrac{u_n}{u_{n+1}}=1+\dfrac{1}{r_n}$ [A1][AG] [2 marks] (d) Letting $n\to\infty$: $L=1+\dfrac1L$ [M1] so $L^2-L-1=0$ and $L=\dfrac{1\pm\sqrt5}{2}$ [A1] Since $r_n>0$ for all $n$, $L\ge0$, so $L=\dfrac{1+\sqrt5}{2}$ [R1][AG] [3 marks] (e)(i) $\varphi^2=\dfrac{6+2\sqrt5}{4}=\dfrac{3+\sqrt5}{2}=\varphi+1$ [A1] and similarly $\psi^2=\dfrac{3-\sqrt5}{2}=\psi+1$ [A1] (ii) $n=1$: $\dfrac{\varphi-\psi}{\sqrt5}=\dfrac{\sqrt5}{\sqrt5}=1=u_1$; $n=2$: $\dfrac{\varphi^2-\psi^2}{\sqrt5}=\dfrac{(\varphi-\psi)(\varphi+\psi)}{\sqrt5}=1\times1=1=u_2$ [A1] Assume the formula holds for $n=m$ and $n=m+1$ [M1] Then $u_{m+2}=u_{m+1}+u_m=\dfrac{\varphi^m(\varphi+1)-\psi^m(\psi+1)}{\sqrt5}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{\varphi^m\varphi^2-\psi^m\psi^2}{\sqrt5}=\dfrac{\varphi^{m+2}-\psi^{m+2}}{\sqrt5}$ using (i) [A1] Since true for $n=1,2$, and truth for $n=m$ and $n=m+1$ implies truth for $n=m+2$, the formula holds for all $n\in\mathbb{Z}^+$ by induction [R1] [7 marks] (f) $r_n=\dfrac{\varphi^{n+1}-\psi^{n+1}}{\varphi^n-\psi^n}$ [M1] $=\varphi\cdot\dfrac{1-\left(\psi/\varphi\right)^{n+1}}{1-\left(\psi/\varphi\right)^{n}}$ [A1] $\left|\dfrac{\psi}{\varphi}\right|=\dfrac{\sqrt5-1}{\sqrt5+1}\approx0.382<1$, so $\left(\dfrac{\psi}{\varphi}\right)^n\to0$ [R1] Hence $r_n\to\varphi$ [A1] [4 marks] (g) $w_n=\dfrac{v_{n+1}}{v_n}$ satisfies $w_{n+1}=1+\dfrac{k}{w_n}$, so the limit $M$ satisfies $M=1+\dfrac{k}{M}$ [M1] $M^2-M-k=0$ [A1] $M=\dfrac{1+\sqrt{1+4k}}{2}$ (positive root since $v_n>0$) [A1] $M=2\Rightarrow 4-2-k=0\Rightarrow k=2$ [A1] [4 marks] Total [25 marks]
tips: Two base cases are needed because the recurrence uses the two previous terms.

subtopic: Compound interest with regular deposits
statement: At the start of each year a person deposits $\$500$ into an account paying $3\%$ interest per year, compounded annually. The first deposit is made at the start of year 1. (a) Show that the value of the account at the end of year 3, immediately after interest is added, is $500\left(1.03^3+1.03^2+1.03\right)$. [2] (b) Find the value of the account at the end of year $15$. [3] (c) Find the number of years needed for the account to first exceed $\$10000$. [3]
markscheme: (a) first deposit grows for 3 years: $500\times1.03^3$ [M1] second for 2 years and third for 1 year, so total $=500\left(1.03^3+1.03^2+1.03\right)$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) geometric series with first term $500\times1.03$ and ratio $1.03$ [M1] $S_{15}=\dfrac{500\times1.03\left(1.03^{15}-1\right)}{1.03-1}$ [M1] $=\$9578.44$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) solve $\dfrac{500\times1.03\left(1.03^n-1\right)}{0.03}>10000$ with a table or solver [M1][A1] $n=16$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Each deposit earns interest for a different number of years, so the amounts form a geometric series. Use $S_n=\dfrac{a(r^n-1)}{r-1}$ with $a=\text{deposit}\times(1+i)$.

subtopic: Quadratic sequence from differences
statement: The first four terms of a sequence are $4,\ 11,\ 22,\ 37$, and the $n$th term has the form $u_n=an^2+bn+c$. (a) Find the first and second differences, and hence find $a$, $b$ and $c$. [4] (b) Find $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{10}u_k$, given that $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{10}k=55$ and $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{10}k^2=385$. [3]
markscheme: (a) first differences $7,11,15$ and second differences $4,4$ [A1] $2a=4$ so $a=2$ [A1] $u_1=2+b+c=4$ and $u_2=8+2b+c=11$ give $b=1$ [M1] $c=1$, so $u_n=2n^2+n+1$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $2\times385+55+10$ [M1][A1] $=835$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A constant second difference of $2a$ indicates a quadratic sequence with leading coefficient $a$.

subtopic: Multiples in an interval as an arithmetic series
statement: Consider the positive multiples of $7$ that are greater than $100$ and less than $500$. (a) Find the number of such multiples. [3] (b) Find the sum of these multiples. [2]
tips: Use $u_n=u_1+(n-1)d$ to count, then $S_n=\frac n2(u_1+u_n)$.

subtopic: Spiral of semicircular arcs with geometric radii
statement: A spiral is built from semicircular arcs. The first arc has radius $12$ cm, and each later arc has radius $\dfrac34$ of the radius of the arc before it. (a) Find the total length of the first $8$ arcs. Give your answer to three significant figures. [3] (b) The spiral is continued indefinitely. Find the exact total length of the spiral. [2] (c) Find the least number of arcs for which the total length is at least $99\%$ of the length in part (b). [3]
markscheme: (a) the arc lengths are $12\pi,\ 9\pi,\dots$, a geometric sequence with $r=\dfrac34$ [M1] $S_8=\dfrac{12\pi\left(1-0.75^8\right)}{1-0.75}$ [A1] $=136$ cm [A1] [3 marks] (b) $S_\infty=\dfrac{12\pi}{1-0.75}$ [M1] $=48\pi$ cm [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\dfrac{12\pi\left(1-0.75^n\right)}{0.25}\ge0.99\times48\pi$ gives $1-0.75^n\ge0.99$ [M1] $0.75^n\le0.01$ so $n\ge\dfrac{\ln0.01}{\ln0.75}=16.008\dots$ [A1] $n=17$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A semicircle of radius $r$ has arc length $\pi r$, so the arc lengths form a geometric sequence. For the last part, solve the inequality with logarithms, or test $n=16$ and $n=17$ with a table.

subtopic: Geometric sequences and infinite sums
statement: A geometric sequence has $u_3=2$ and $u_6=\dfrac{2}{27}$. (a) Find the common ratio and the first term. [3] (b) Find the sum to infinity of the sequence. [2] (c) Let $S_n$ be the sum of the first $n$ terms. Find the smallest value of $n$ for which $S_n>26.99$. [3]
tips: Divide terms to isolate $r^{k}$ where $k$ is the gap between the term numbers. In part (c) check $n=7$ and $n=8$ explicitly: $S_7=26.988\ldots$ is just below $26.99$.

subtopic: Evaluating a sum in sigma notation
statement: Consider $S=\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{15}k^{2} + 2 k$. (a) Write down the first three terms of the sum and state the type of series, if it is arithmetic or geometric. [3] (b) Evaluate $S$. [2]
markscheme: (a) first terms $3,\ 8,\ 15$ [A1] differences $5,7$ are not constant and ratios are not constant [A1] neither arithmetic nor geometric [A1] [3 marks] (b) use the sum formula or the calculator's sum function [M1] $S=1480$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: When a sum is neither arithmetic nor geometric, enter the general term into the calculator's summation function.

subtopic: Arithmetic model for a training plan
statement: A runner follows a training plan. In week $1$ she runs $5$ km in total, and each week she runs $0.75$ km more than the week before. (a) Find the distance she runs in week $12$. [2] (b) Find the total distance she runs in the first $12$ weeks. [2] (c) Find the least number of weeks after which her total distance run since week $1$ exceeds $300$ km. [3]
tips: Use the sum formula with the GDC, and check the integer values either side of the crossing point.

subtopic: Sigma notation and arithmetic series
statement: (a) Evaluate $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{12}(3k+4)$. [3] (b) Given that $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{n}(3k+4)=140$, where $n\in\mathbb{Z}^{+}$, show that $3n^{2}+11n-280=0$ and hence find $n$. [4]
tips: Identify the first term and common difference from the first two values of $k$, then use $S_n=\frac{n}{2}(2u_1+(n-1)d)$. Reject any root that is not a positive integer.

subtopic: A telescoping series with factorials
statement: Consider the series $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty\dfrac k{(k+1)!}$. (a) Show that $\dfrac k{(k+1)!}=\dfrac1{k!}-\dfrac1{(k+1)!}$. [2] (b) Hence find $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^n\dfrac k{(k+1)!}$ and the sum to infinity. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac1{k!}-\dfrac1{(k+1)!}=\dfrac{(k+1)-1}{(k+1)!}$ [M1] $=\dfrac k{(k+1)!}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) the sum telescopes: $\dfrac1{1!}-\dfrac1{(n+1)!}$ [M1][A1] as $n\to\infty$ the sum tends to $1$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Write $(k+1)!=(k+1)k!$ and combine the two reciprocals over a common denominator.

subtopic: Arithmetic sequence from two terms
statement: The $p$th term of an arithmetic sequence is $u_p$. Given that $u_{3}=11$ and $u_{8}=31$: (a) Find the common difference $d$ and the first term $u_1$. [3] (b) Find the sum of the first $20$ terms. [2] (c) Which term of the sequence equals $91$? [2]
tips: Subtract two terms to find $d$, then use $u_n=u_1+(n-1)d$ and $S_n=\frac n2\left(2u_1+(n-1)d\right)$.

subtopic: Compound interest with regular deposits
statement: At the start of each year a person deposits $\$1200$ into an account paying $4.5\%$ interest per year, compounded annually. The first deposit is made at the start of year 1. (a) Show that the value of the account at the end of year 3, immediately after interest is added, is $1200\left(1.045^3+1.045^2+1.045\right)$. [2] (b) Find the value of the account at the end of year $10$. [3] (c) Find the number of years needed for the account to first exceed $\$24000$. [3]
markscheme: (a) first deposit grows for 3 years: $1200\times1.045^3$ [M1] second for 2 years and third for 1 year, so total $=1200\left(1.045^3+1.045^2+1.045\right)$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) geometric series with first term $1200\times1.045$ and ratio $1.045$ [M1] $S_{10}=\dfrac{1200\times1.045\left(1.045^{10}-1\right)}{1.045-1}$ [M1] $=\$15409.41$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) solve $\dfrac{1200\times1.045\left(1.045^n-1\right)}{0.045}>24000$ with a table or solver [M1][A1] $n=15$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Each deposit earns interest for a different number of years, so the amounts form a geometric series. Use $S_n=\dfrac{a(r^n-1)}{r-1}$ with $a=\text{deposit}\times(1+i)$.

subtopic: Geometric sequence from two terms
statement: The terms of a geometric sequence are all positive, with $u_{2}=12$ and $u_{4}=3$. (a) Find the common ratio $r$ and the first term $u_1$. [3] (b) Find the sum of the first $6$ terms. [2] (c) Find the sum to infinity. [2]
tips: From two terms of a geometric sequence, divide to get $r^{k}$ where $k$ is the gap in positions. Use $S_\infty=\dfrac{u_1}{1-r}$ only when $|r|<1$.

subtopic: Telescoping series with partial fractions
statement: (a) Show that $\dfrac1{r(r+2)}=\dfrac12\left(\dfrac1r-\dfrac1{r+2}\right)$ for $r\in\mathbb{Z}^+$. [2] (b) Hence show that $\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{n}\dfrac1{r(r+2)}=\dfrac34-\dfrac{2n+3}{2(n+1)(n+2)}$. [4] (c) Hence find $\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}\dfrac1{r(r+2)}$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac12\left(\dfrac1r-\dfrac1{r+2}\right)=\dfrac12\cdot\dfrac{(r+2)-r}{r(r+2)}$ [M1] $=\dfrac1{r(r+2)}$ [A1][AG] [2 marks] (b) Writing out terms: $\dfrac12\left[\left(1-\dfrac13\right)+\left(\dfrac12-\dfrac14\right)+\left(\dfrac13-\dfrac15\right)+\dots+\left(\dfrac1n-\dfrac1{n+2}\right)\right]$ [M1] All terms cancel except $1$, $\dfrac12$, $-\dfrac1{n+1}$, $-\dfrac1{n+2}$ [A1] Sum $=\dfrac12\left(\dfrac32-\dfrac1{n+1}-\dfrac1{n+2}\right)=\dfrac34-\dfrac12\cdot\dfrac{(n+2)+(n+1)}{(n+1)(n+2)}$ [A1] $=\dfrac34-\dfrac{2n+3}{2(n+1)(n+2)}$ [A1][AG] [4 marks] (c) As $n\to\infty$, $\dfrac{2n+3}{2(n+1)(n+2)}\to0$, so the sum is $\dfrac34$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: For telescoping sums, write out the first few and last few terms so you can see exactly which ones survive. Here the terms two steps apart cancel, so two terms remain at each end.

subtopic: Consecutive terms of a geometric sequence
statement: The numbers $k-2$, $k+2$ and $3k-2$ are the first three terms of a geometric sequence with positive common ratio. (a) Show that $k^{2}-6k=0$. [2] (b) Find the value of $k$, the common ratio and the sum of the first $8$ terms. [4]
tips: Equal ratios of consecutive terms give $u_2^{2}=u_1u_3$.

subtopic: Arithmetic sequence: terms and sums
statement: The third term of an arithmetic sequence is $11$ and the eighth term is $31$. (a) Find the first term and the common difference. [3] (b) Find the sum of the first $20$ terms. [2] (c) Find the smallest value of $n$ for which the sum of the first $n$ terms exceeds $500$. [3]
tips: Use the two given terms to form simultaneous equations in $u_1$ and $d$. For "first exceeds" questions, test consecutive values of $n$ either side of the boundary.

subtopic: Geometric series: convergence and sum to infinity
statement: Consider the infinite geometric series $5+5(x-2)+5(x-2)^2+\cdots$ (a) Find the values of $x$ for which the series converges. [2] (b) Find the sum to infinity in terms of $x$. [2] (c) Given that the sum to infinity is $8$, find the value of $x$. [2] (d) Hence, or otherwise, find the range of possible values of the sum to infinity. [2]
markscheme: (a) Common ratio $r=x-2$ [M1] Convergence requires $|x-2|<1$, so $1<x<3$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $S_\infty=\dfrac{5}{1-(x-2)}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{5}{3-x}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\dfrac5{3-x}=8$, so $3-x=\dfrac58$ [M1] $x=\dfrac{19}8$, which lies in $(1,3)$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) For $1<x<3$, $0<3-x<2$ [M1] so $S_\infty>\dfrac52$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A geometric series converges only when $|r|<1$, so always find the allowed values of $x$ first. Check that any value you find from an equation lies in that interval.

subtopic: Smallest number of terms for a geometric sum
statement: A geometric sequence has first term $6$ and common ratio $2$. (a) Write down an expression for $S_n$, the sum of the first $n$ terms. [2] (b) Find the smallest value of $n$ for which $S_n>3000$. [3]
tips: Rearrange the inequality to isolate $2^{n}$ and compare with powers of $2$.

subtopic: Arithmetic sequence from two terms
statement: The $p$th term of an arithmetic sequence is $u_p$. Given that $u_{5}=-2$ and $u_{12}=26$: (a) Find the common difference $d$ and the first term $u_1$. [3] (b) Find the sum of the first $12$ terms. [2] (c) Which term of the sequence equals $106$? [2]
tips: Subtract two terms to find $d$, then use $u_n=u_1+(n-1)d$ and $S_n=\frac n2\left(2u_1+(n-1)d\right)$.

subtopic: Arithmetic sequences and sums
statement: An arithmetic sequence has $u_5=17$ and $u_{12}=45$. (a) Find the common difference and the first term. [3] (b) Find the sum of the first $20$ terms. [2] (c) Find the smallest value of $n$ such that $u_n>200$. [2]
tips: Subtracting the two given terms gives $(12-5)d$ directly. For inequalities on $n$ always round up to the next whole number when $n$ must satisfy '$>$'.

subtopic: Convergence of a geometric series with a parameter
statement: A geometric series has first term $4$ and common ratio $\dfrac{x}{3}$, where $x$ is a real number. (a) Find the set of values of $x$ for which the series converges. [2] (b) Given that the sum to infinity is $6$, find $x$. [3] (c) Find the sum to infinity when $x=-2$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\left|\dfrac x3\right|<1$ [M1] $-3<x<3$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac{4}{1-\frac x3}=6$ [M1] $1-\dfrac x3=\dfrac23$ [A1] $x=1$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $r=-\dfrac23$ [A1] $S_\infty=\dfrac{4}{1+\frac23}=\dfrac{12}{5}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A geometric series converges exactly when $|r|<1$. Then $S_\infty=\dfrac{u_1}{1-r}$.

subtopic: Terms in geometric progression with an unknown
statement: The numbers $x-1,\ x+3,\ 4x-4$ are the first three terms of a geometric sequence. (a) Show that $3x^2-14x-5=0$. [3] (b) Find the possible values of $x$. [2] (c) For each value of $x$, find the common ratio and state whether the series converges. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{x+3}{x-1}=\dfrac{4x-4}{x+3}$ [M1] $(x+3)^2=(x-1)(4x-4)$ [A1] $x^2+6x+9=4x^2-8x+4$ gives $3x^2-14x-5=0$ [A1] [AG] [3 marks] (b) $(3x+1)(x-5)=0$ [M1] $x=5$ or $x=-\dfrac13$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $x=5$: terms $4,8,16$, $r=2$ [A1] diverges since $|r|>1$ [R1] $x=-\dfrac13$: terms $-\dfrac43,\dfrac83,-\dfrac{16}3$, $r=-2$, which also diverges [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Equate the ratios of consecutive terms and cross-multiply. Both roots must be checked, since either may give a valid sequence.

subtopic: Comparing geometric and arithmetic savings deposits
statement: Two savings plans do not earn interest; the question is about the deposits. Under Plan A, Dev deposits \$2000 in year 1 and each year deposits $5\%$ more than in the previous year. Under Plan B, Dev deposits \$2500 in year 1 and each year deposits \$80 more than in the previous year. (a) Find the deposit in year 10 under each plan, to the nearest cent. [2] (b) Find the total deposited in the first 10 years under each plan, to the nearest cent. [3] (c) Find the smallest number of years for which the total deposited under Plan A exceeds the total deposited under Plan B. [3] (d) Explain why Plan A exceeds Plan B for all larger numbers of years. [1]
markscheme: (a) A: $2000(1.05)^{9}=\$3102.66$ [A1] B: $2500+9(80)=\$3220.00$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) A: $\dfrac{2000(1.05^{10}-1)}{0.05}$ [M1] $=\$25\,155.79$ [A1] B: $\dfrac{10}{2}\left(5000+9(80)\right)=\$28\,600.00$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\dfrac{2000(1.05^{n}-1)}{0.05}>\dfrac{n}{2}\left(5000+80(n-1)\right)$ [M1] GDC graph or table: $n=19$ gives $61\,078<61\,180$ [M1] $n=20$ gives $66\,132>65\,200$, so $n=20$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) From year 12 onward the yearly deposit under Plan A exceeds that under Plan B (for example $3421>3380$) and the difference keeps growing, so after the totals cross at $n=20$ the gap keeps widening [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Plan A is geometric with $r=1.05$ and Plan B is arithmetic with $d=80$. For the crossing point use a table on your GDC and check the year just before the first time the inequality holds.

subtopic: Evaluating a sum in sigma notation
statement: Consider $S=\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{20}3 k + 1$. (a) Write down the first three terms of the sum and state the type of series, if it is arithmetic or geometric. [3] (b) Evaluate $S$. [2]
