markscheme: (a) first terms $4,\ 7,\ 10$ [A1] common difference $3$ [A1] arithmetic [A1] [3 marks] (b) use the sum formula or the calculator's sum function [M1] $S=650.0$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: For an arithmetic series use $S_n=\frac n2(u_1+u_n)$ with $u_1=4$ and $u_{20}=61$.

subtopic: Logarithms of a geometric sequence
statement: A sequence has $u_n=\ln\left(5\times3^n\right)$. (a) Show that $u_n$ is an arithmetic sequence, and state its common difference. [3] (b) Find $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{20}u_n$, giving the answer in the form $a\ln5+b\ln3$ where $a,b\in\mathbb Z$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $u_n=\ln5+n\ln3$ [M1] $u_{n+1}-u_n=\ln3$ which is constant [A1] so arithmetic with $d=\ln3$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $S_{20}=\sum(\ln5+n\ln3)$ [M1] $=20\ln5+\dfrac{20\times21}{2}\ln3$ [A1] $=20\ln5+210\ln3$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Use $\ln(ab)=\ln a+\ln b$ and $\ln a^n=n\ln a$ to separate the terms, then sum the arithmetic series.

subtopic: Infinite sequence of nested squares
statement: A square has side $10$ cm. A second square is formed by joining the midpoints of the sides of the first, a third square is formed in the same way inside the second, and so on forever. (a) Show that the side lengths form a geometric sequence with common ratio $\dfrac1{\sqrt2}$. [2] (b) Find the exact sum of the areas of all the squares. [3] (c) Find the exact sum of the perimeters of all the squares. [2]
markscheme: (a) each side of the new square is the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle with both legs $5$ cm: $\sqrt{5^2+5^2}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{10}{\sqrt2}$, so each side is $\dfrac1{\sqrt2}$ of the previous [A1] [2 marks] (b) areas $100,50,25,\ldots$ with ratio $\dfrac12$ [M1] $\dfrac{100}{1-\frac12}$ [A1] $=200\text{ cm}^2$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\dfrac{40}{1-\frac1{\sqrt2}}=40(2+\sqrt2)$ [M1][A1] [2 marks]
tips: Areas and perimeters both form geometric sequences, but with different ratios: the ratio for area is the square of the ratio for length.

subtopic: Drug dosage and the long-term level
statement: A patient takes a $200$ mg dose of a drug at the same time each day. Just before the next dose, $30\%$ of the drug in the body remains. (a) Find the amount of the drug in the body immediately after the third dose. [3] (b) Show that the amount immediately after the $n$th dose is $\dfrac{200\left(1-0.3^n\right)}{0.7}$. [3] (c) Find the limit of the amount in the body as the dosage continues indefinitely, and the least number of doses after which the amount is within $1$ mg of this limit. [4]
tips: The amount after $n$ doses is a geometric sum. The long-term level is the sum to infinity of the same series.

subtopic: Annuity due: deposits at the start of each month
statement: A saver deposits \$300 at the start of every month for $5$ years into an account paying $5\%$ nominal annual interest, compounded monthly. (a) Find the value of the account at the end of the $5$ years, to the nearest dollar. [4] (b) Find the total interest earned. [2] (c) State how much less the saver would have if the deposits were made at the end of each month, to the nearest dollar. [2]
markscheme: (a) Each deposit earns interest for one more month than an end-of-month deposit [R1]; $FV=300\times\dfrac{(1+0.05/12)^{60}-1}{0.05/12}\times\left(1+\dfrac{0.05}{12}\right)$ [M1]; or financial solver with payments at the beginning [M1]; \$20,487 [A1] [4 marks] (b) Deposits total $300\times60=18000$ [A1]; interest $=20487-18000=\$2487$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) End-of-month value $=\$20402$ [A1]; difference \$85 [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Payments at the beginning of each period earn one extra period of interest than payments at the end.

subtopic: Differentiating a geometric series to sum $k r^{k-1}$
statement: This question explores how differentiating a geometric series gives a new series. (a) Show that, for $r\ne1$, $\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{n}r^k=\dfrac{1-r^{n+1}}{1-r}$. [2] (b) By differentiating both sides of the result in part (a) with respect to $r$, show that $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{n}k\,r^{k-1}=\dfrac{1-(n+1)r^n+n\,r^{n+1}}{(1-r)^2}$. [4] (c) Hence find $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}k\,r^{k-1}$ for $|r|<1$, and find the value of $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\dfrac{k}{2^k}$. [3] (d) A biased coin lands heads with probability $p$, where $0<p<1$. The random variable $X$ is the number of tosses up to and including the first head. Show that $P(X=k)=(1-p)^{k-1}p$, and use part (c) to show that $E(X)=\dfrac1p$. [3] (e) Use part (b) to find $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{10}k\,(0.9)^{k-1}$, giving your answer to three significant figures. [2] (f) Find the least value of $n$ for which $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{n}k\,(0.9)^{k-1}$ exceeds $99$. [3]
markscheme: (a) geometric series with first term $1$, ratio $r$ and $n+1$ terms [M1] $\dfrac{1\times(1-r^{n+1})}{1-r}$ [AG] [A1] [2 marks] (b) differentiating the left side term by term gives $\sum_{k=1}^{n}kr^{k-1}$ [M1] quotient rule on the right: $\dfrac{-(n+1)r^n(1-r)+\left(1-r^{n+1}\right)}{(1-r)^2}$ [M1][A1] numerator $=-(n+1)r^n+(n+1)r^{n+1}+1-r^{n+1}=1-(n+1)r^n+nr^{n+1}$ [AG] [A1] [4 marks] (c) as $n\to\infty$ with $|r|<1$, $r^n\to0$ and $nr^{n+1}\to0$ [M1] so the sum is $\dfrac1{(1-r)^2}$ [A1] $\sum\dfrac k{2^k}=\dfrac12\sum k\left(\dfrac12\right)^{k-1}=\dfrac12\times\dfrac1{(1/2)^2}=2$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) the first $k-1$ tosses are tails and the $k$th is a head, so $P(X=k)=(1-p)^{k-1}p$ [A1] $E(X)=\sum kq^{k-1}p$ with $q=1-p$ [M1] $=p\times\dfrac1{(1-q)^2}=\dfrac p{p^2}=\dfrac1p$ [AG] [A1] [3 marks] (e) $\dfrac{1-11(0.9)^{10}+10(0.9)^{11}}{(0.1)^2}$ [M1] $=30.3$ [A1] [2 marks] (f) the sum to infinity is $\dfrac1{0.1^2}=100$ and the partial sum is $100\left(1-0.9^n(1+0.1n)\right)$ [M1] solve $0.9^n(1+0.1n)<0.01$ using a table or graph [M1] $n=62$ gives $98.95$ and $n=63$ gives $99.04$, so $n=63$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: In part (b) the derivative of the sum is a sum of derivatives of $r^k$. In part (f), compare the partial sum with its limit, which comes from part (c).

subtopic: Geometric sequence: ratio, threshold and sum
statement: A geometric sequence has second term $u_2=12$ and fifth term $u_5=40.5$. (a) Find the common ratio $r$ and the first term $u_1$. [3] (b) Find the least value of $n$ for which $u_n>1000$. [3] (c) Find $S_{10}$, the sum of the first $10$ terms, correct to 4 significant figures. [2]
tips: Divide the two given terms to isolate $r^{3}$. For the inequality, take logarithms (or use the GDC table).

subtopic: Geometric depreciation of a vehicle
statement: A van is bought for \$34,000 and loses $18\%$ of its value each year. (a) Find its value after $5$ years, to the nearest dollar. [2] (b) Find the number of complete years after which the value first falls below $30\%$ of the purchase price. [3] (c) Find the total amount of value lost in the first $5$ years, and the average value lost per year, to the nearest dollar. [3]
tips: A loss of $18\%$ each year means the multiplier is $0.82$.

subtopic: Smallest n for a sum to exceed a value
statement: An arithmetic sequence has first term $7$ and common difference $5$. (a) Write an expression for $S_n$, the sum of the first $n$ terms. [2] (b) Find the smallest value of $n$ for which $S_n>1000$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $S_n=\dfrac n2\left(2\times7+(n-1)\times5\right)$ [M1] $=\dfrac n2\left(5n+9\right)$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac n2\left(5n+9\right)>1000$ [M1] solve using a table or the quadratic [A1] $S_{19}=988.000$ and $S_{20}=1090.00$, so $n=20$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Form the quadratic inequality in $n$, or use a table of values of $S_n$ and look for the first value above the target.

subtopic: Common ratio from a sum of three terms
statement: A geometric sequence has first term $4$ and the sum of its first three terms is $28$. (a) Show that the common ratio $r$ satisfies $r^{2}+r-6=0$. [2] (b) Find the two possible values of $r$. [2] (c) For each of the two values of $r$, find the fourth term of the sequence. [2]
tips: The $n$th term of a geometric sequence is $u_1r^{n-1}$.

subtopic: Terms in arithmetic progression with an unknown
statement: The numbers $3,\ x+2,\ 3x-1$ are the first three terms of an arithmetic sequence. (a) Find the value of $x$. [3] (b) Find the 20th term and the sum of the first 20 terms. [4]
tips: Consecutive terms of an arithmetic sequence have a common difference, so equate the differences.

subtopic: Recurrence relation and its limit
statement: A sequence is defined by $u_1=5$ and $u_{n+1}=0.6u_n+8$ for $n\ge1$. (a) Find $u_2$ and $u_3$. [2] (b) Given that the sequence converges to a limit $L$, find $L$. [2] (c) Show that $u_n-20$ is a geometric sequence and hence find an expression for $u_n$. [4]
tips: At a limit $u_{n+1}$ and $u_n$ are both equal to $L$. Subtracting the limit from each term turns a first-order linear recurrence into a geometric sequence.

subtopic: Loan amortization
statement: Lina takes out a loan of USD $18\,000$ to buy a car. The loan has a nominal annual interest rate of $5.4\%$, compounded monthly, and is repaid with equal monthly payments, made at the end of each month, over $6$ years. (a) Find the amount of each monthly payment. [2] (b) Find the total interest Lina pays over the $6$ years. [2] (c) Find the amount Lina still owes immediately after her $36$th payment. [2]
markscheme: (a) using GDC TVM solver with $N=72$, $I\%=5.4$, $PV=18\,000$, $FV=0$, $P/Y=C/Y=12$ [M1] payment $=\text{USD } 293.24$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $72\times293.24-18\,000$ [M1] $=\text{USD } 3113.31$ (accept $3113$ or $3110$) [A1] [2 marks] (c) using TVM with $N=36$, $PV=18\,000$, $PMT=-293.24\ldots$, solving for $FV$ [M1] USD $9725.79$ (accept $9726$ or $9730$) [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Watch the signs in the TVM solver: money received and money paid out must have opposite signs. Use the unrounded payment when finding the outstanding balance.

subtopic: Geometric series of complex numbers and trigonometric sums
statement: This question investigates sums of the form $\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\cos k\theta$. Let $\theta\in(0,2\pi)$ and let $z=\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin\theta$. (a) Show that $1-z=-2\mathrm{i}\sin\dfrac\theta2\left(\cos\dfrac\theta2+\mathrm{i}\sin\dfrac\theta2\right)$. [3] (b) Write down an expression for $\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}z^k$ in terms of $z$ and $n$. [1] (c) Hence show that $\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}z^k=\frac{\sin\frac{n\theta}2}{\sin\frac\theta2}\left(\cos\frac{(n-1)\theta}2+\mathrm{i}\sin\frac{(n-1)\theta}2\right)$. [5] (d) Hence write down expressions for $C_n=\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\cos k\theta$ and $S_n=\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\sin k\theta$. [2] (e) Show that if $\theta=\dfrac{2\pi}n$, where $n\ge2$, then $C_n=S_n=0$, and give a geometric interpretation. [3] (f) Show that $\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{11}\cos\dfrac{k\pi}{12}=1$. [3] (g) Let $r\in\mathbb{R}$ with $|r|<1$. By considering $\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(rz)^k$, show that $\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}r^k\cos k\theta=\frac{1-r\cos\theta}{1-2r\cos\theta+r^2}$. [4] (h) Hence find the exact value of $\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{\cos\frac{k\pi}3}{2^k}$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $1-z=1-\cos\theta-\mathrm{i}\sin\theta$ [M1] $=2\sin^2\dfrac\theta2-2\mathrm{i}\sin\dfrac\theta2\cos\dfrac\theta2$ [A1] $=-2\mathrm{i}\sin\dfrac\theta2\left(\cos\dfrac\theta2+\mathrm{i}\sin\dfrac\theta2\right)$ since $-2\mathrm{i}\cdot\mathrm{i}\sin^2\frac\theta2=2\sin^2\frac\theta2$ [A1][AG] [3 marks] (b) Geometric series with ratio $z\ne1$: $\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}z^k=\dfrac{1-z^n}{1-z}$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) Apply part (a) with $\theta$ replaced by $n\theta$ (de Moivre: $z^n=\cos n\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin n\theta$): $1-z^n=-2\mathrm{i}\sin\dfrac{n\theta}2\left(\cos\dfrac{n\theta}2+\mathrm{i}\sin\dfrac{n\theta}2\right)$ [M1] [A1] Divide: $\dfrac{1-z^n}{1-z}=\dfrac{\sin\frac{n\theta}2}{\sin\frac\theta2}\cdot\dfrac{\operatorname{cis}\frac{n\theta}2}{\operatorname{cis}\frac\theta2}$ [M1] $\dfrac{\operatorname{cis}\frac{n\theta}2}{\operatorname{cis}\frac\theta2}=\operatorname{cis}\dfrac{(n-1)\theta}2$ [A1] giving the stated result [A1][AG] [5 marks] (d) Taking real and imaginary parts: $C_n=\dfrac{\sin\frac{n\theta}2\cos\frac{(n-1)\theta}2}{\sin\frac\theta2}$ [A1] $S_n=\dfrac{\sin\frac{n\theta}2\sin\frac{(n-1)\theta}2}{\sin\frac\theta2}$ [A1] [2 marks] (e) With $\theta=\dfrac{2\pi}n$: $\sin\dfrac{n\theta}2=\sin\pi=0$ [M1] and $\sin\dfrac\theta2=\sin\dfrac\pi n\ne0$ for $n\ge2$, so $C_n=S_n=0$ [A1] The terms $z^k$ are the $n$th roots of unity; they form a regular $n$-gon and their sum (the centroid, scaled) is the origin [R1] [3 marks] (f) $\theta=\dfrac\pi{12}$, $n=12$: $C_{12}=\dfrac{\sin\frac\pi2\cos\frac{11\pi}{24}}{\sin\frac\pi{24}}$ [M1] $\cos\dfrac{11\pi}{24}=\sin\left(\dfrac\pi2-\dfrac{11\pi}{24}\right)=\sin\dfrac{\pi}{24}$ [A1] so $C_{12}=\dfrac{1\times\sin\frac\pi{24}}{\sin\frac\pi{24}}=1$ [A1][AG] [3 marks] (g) $\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(rz)^k=\dfrac1{1-rz}$ since $|rz|=|r|<1$ [M1] $\dfrac1{1-rz}=\dfrac1{1-r\cos\theta-\mathrm{i}r\sin\theta}=\dfrac{1-r\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}r\sin\theta}{(1-r\cos\theta)^2+r^2\sin^2\theta}$ [M1] Denominator $=1-2r\cos\theta+r^2$ [A1] The real part of $(rz)^k$ is $r^k\cos k\theta$, so taking real parts, $\sum r^k\cos k\theta=\dfrac{1-r\cos\theta}{1-2r\cos\theta+r^2}$ [A1][AG] [4 marks] (h) $r=\dfrac12$, $\theta=\dfrac\pi3$: $\cos\dfrac\pi3=\dfrac12$ [M1] $\dfrac{1-\frac14}{1-\frac12+\frac14}=\dfrac{3/4}{3/4}=1$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The key idea is to treat $\sum\cos k\theta$ as the real part of a complex geometric series, so the standard sum formula does all the work. In part (g), a series in $rz$ converges when $|rz|<1$; multiply by the conjugate of the denominator to separate real and imaginary parts.

subtopic: Bouncing ball and total distance travelled
statement: A ball is dropped from a height of $12$ m onto a hard floor. After each bounce it rises to $\dfrac34$ of the height of the previous fall. (a) Find the height reached after the first and the second bounce. [2] (b) Show that the total distance travelled by the ball until it comes to rest is $84$ m. [5]
markscheme: (a) $12\times\dfrac34=9$ m [A1] $9\times\dfrac34=6.75$ m [A1] [2 marks] (b) distance $=12+2(9)+2(6.75)+\dots$ [M1] the rises form a geometric series with first term $9$ and ratio $\dfrac34$ [A1] $S_\infty=\dfrac{9}{1-\frac34}=36$ [M1][A1] total $=12+2\times36=84$ m [A1] [AG] [5 marks]
tips: After the initial drop, every rise is followed by an equal fall, so the distance is $12+2\times$(sum of rises).

subtopic: Mortgage repayment time and payment size
statement: A homeowner takes a mortgage of $\$150\,000$ at a nominal annual interest rate of $4.8\%$, compounded monthly. Payments are made at the end of each month. (a) Find the interest charged in the first month, and the amount by which a first payment of $\$1000$ reduces the loan balance. [2] (b) The homeowner pays $\$1000$ at the end of each month. Find the number of monthly payments needed to clear the loan (the final payment may be smaller than $\$1000$). [3] (c) Find the monthly payment, to the nearest cent, that would clear the loan in exactly $20$ years. [2]
markscheme: (a) interest $=150\,000\times0.004=\$600$ [A1] reduction in balance $=1000-600=\$400$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) TVM with $PV=150\,000$, $PMT=-1000$, $I\%=4.8$, $FV=0$, $P/Y=C/Y=12$ [M1] (or solving $150\,000(1.004)^N=1000\dfrac{1.004^N-1}{0.004}$) $N=229.5\ldots$ [A1] so $230$ payments are required [A1] [3 marks] (c) $N=240$, solve for $PMT$ [M1] $PMT=\$973.44$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The first payment first covers the month's interest, then reduces the balance. When the TVM solver returns a non-integer $N$, round up because a partial payment is still needed.

subtopic: Amortization of a loan as a geometric series
statement: This question investigates how a loan is repaid. A loan of \$20\,000 is repaid by equal payments of \$400 at the end of each month. Interest is charged at $0.5\%$ per month on the outstanding balance. Let $B_k$ be the balance immediately after the $k$th payment, with $B_0=20\,000$. (a) Show that $B_k=1.005B_{k-1}-400$. [1] (b) Hence show that $B_k=80\,000-60\,000(1.005)^k$. [4] (c) Find the number of payments needed to repay the loan, and the amount of the final payment, to the nearest cent. [4] (d) Show that the interest included in the $k$th payment is $I_k=400-300(1.005)^{k-1}$. [3] (e) Hence find the interest and the capital repaid in the first payment and in the 12th payment. [3] (f) Show that the capital repaid in successive payments forms a geometric sequence, and state its common ratio. [2] (g) Find the total interest paid over the life of the loan, to the nearest dollar. [2] (h) After the 24th payment the monthly rate drops to $\dfrac{4}{12}\%$, with payments still \$400. Find how many further payments are needed (rounding up). [4]
markscheme: (a) Interest is added to the balance then the payment is subtracted [AG] [1 mark] (b) Repeated substitution gives $B_k=20000(1.005)^k-400\left(1+1.005+\cdots+1.005^{k-1}\right)$ [M1][A1]; geometric sum $=\dfrac{1.005^k-1}{0.005}$ [M1] so $B_k=20000(1.005)^k-80000(1.005^k-1)=80000-60000(1.005)^k$ [AG] [4 marks] (c) $B_k\leq0$ gives $1.005^k\geq\dfrac{4}{3}$ [M1]; $k\geq57.68$ so 58 payments [A1]; $B_{57}=270.92$ [M1]; final payment $=1.005B_{57}=\$272.27$ [A1] [4 marks] (d) $I_k=0.005B_{k-1}$ [M1] $=0.005\left(80000-60000(1.005)^{k-1}\right)$ [A1] $=400-300(1.005)^{k-1}$ [AG] [3 marks] (e) First: interest $\$100.00$, capital $\$300.00$ [A1]; 12th: interest $\$83.08$ [A1], capital $\$316.92$ [A1] [3 marks] (f) Capital in $k$th payment $=400-I_k=300(1.005)^{k-1}$ [A1], a geometric sequence with common ratio $1.005$ [A1] [2 marks] (g) Total paid $=57(400)+272.27$ [M1], so interest $=\$3072$ [A1] [2 marks] (h) $B_{24}=\$12370.41$ [A1]; new monthly rate $i=0.00333$; solve $B_{24}(1+i)^n=400\dfrac{(1+i)^n-1}{i}$ [M1][A1]; $n=32.69$ so 33 further payments [A1] [4 marks]
tips: A loan balance obeys $B_k=(1+i)B_{k-1}-P$; its closed form comes from a geometric series. The capital repaid each month rises geometrically as the interest share falls.

subtopic: Product of the first n terms of a geometric sequence
statement: A geometric sequence has first term $2$ and common ratio $3$. Let $P_n$ be the product of its first $n$ terms. (a) Show that $P_n=2^n\times3^{n(n-1)/2}$. [3] (b) Find $P_5$. [1] (c) Show that $\ln P_n$ is a quadratic function of $n$, and state its leading coefficient. [2]
markscheme: (a) $P_n=2\times(2\times3)\times\left(2\times3^2\right)\times\cdots\times\left(2\times3^{n-1}\right)$ [M1] $=2^n\times3^{0+1+\cdots+(n-1)}$ [A1] exponent is $\dfrac{n(n-1)}2$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $32\times3^{10}=1\,889\,568$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $\ln P_n=n\ln2+\dfrac{n(n-1)}2\ln3$ [M1] leading coefficient $\dfrac12\ln3$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The exponents of $3$ form an arithmetic series.

subtopic: Annuities and perpetuities with geometric series
statement: This question investigates savings plans and endowment funds using geometric series. In all parts, interest is compounded annually at an annual rate $r$ and payments are made at the end of each year. (a) A saver deposits \$$P$ at the end of each year, starting at the end of year 1. Show that the value of the account immediately after the $n$th deposit is $\dfrac{P\left((1+r)^{n}-1\right)}{r}$. [3] (b) Anya deposits \$1200 at the end of each year at $r=0.035$. (i) Find the value of her account immediately after the 15th deposit, to the nearest dollar. [1] (ii) Find the least number of deposits needed for the account to exceed \$30\,000. [3] (c) A scholarship fund pays \$$X$ at the end of each year, forever. The present value of the payment made at the end of year $k$ is $\dfrac{X}{(1+r)^{k}}$. (i) Show that the total present value of all the payments is $\dfrac{X}{r}$. [4] (ii) Find the amount needed to fund a scholarship of \$6000 per year when $r=0.04$. [1] (d) A donor gives only \$120\,000 to a fund with $r=0.04$, which pays \$6000 at the end of each year. Let $B_n$ be the balance of the fund immediately after the $n$th payment. (i) Show that $B_n=150\,000-30\,000(1.04)^{n}$. [4] (ii) Find the number of full payments of \$6000 that the fund can make, and the balance immediately after the last full payment, to the nearest dollar. [4] (e) The scholarship now rises by $2\%$ each year, so the payment at the end of year $k$ is $6000(1.02)^{k-1}$. With $r=0.04$, show that the total present value of all the payments is \$300\,000. [3] (f) A fund of \$200\,000 pays the rising scholarship from part (e), and the balance after the $n$th payment is $B_n=300\,000(1.02)^{n}-100\,000(1.04)^{n}$. Find the number of full payments the fund can make. [3] (g) State two assumptions made in this model that may not hold in practice. [2]
markscheme: (a) value $=P(1+r)^{n-1}+P(1+r)^{n-2}+\cdots+P$ [M1] geometric series with first term $P$ and common ratio $(1+r)$, $n$ terms [A1] $S_n=\dfrac{P\left((1+r)^{n}-1\right)}{(1+r)-1}=\dfrac{P\left((1+r)^{n}-1\right)}{r}$ [AG] [3 marks] (b)(i) $\dfrac{1200\left(1.035^{15}-1\right)}{0.035}=\$23\,155$ [A1] (ii) $\dfrac{1200\left(1.035^{n}-1\right)}{0.035}>30000$ [M1] $n>18.27$ (logarithms or GDC) [A1] $n=19$ [A1] [4 marks] (c)(i) first term $\dfrac{X}{1+r}$ and common ratio $\dfrac{1}{1+r}$ [A1] $\left|\dfrac{1}{1+r}\right|<1$ so the series converges [R1] $S_\infty=\dfrac{X/(1+r)}{1-\frac{1}{1+r}}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{X}{r}$ [AG] (ii) $\dfrac{6000}{0.04}=\$150\,000$ [A1] [5 marks] (d)(i) $B_n=120000(1.04)^{n}-\dfrac{6000\left((1.04)^{n}-1\right)}{0.04}$ [M1][A1] $=120000(1.04)^{n}-150000(1.04)^{n}+150000$ [M1] $=150000-30000(1.04)^{n}$ [AG] (ii) payment $n$ can be made if $B_n\ge0$: $(1.04)^{n}\le5$ [M1] $n\le\dfrac{\ln5}{\ln1.04}=41.03$ [A1] 41 full payments [A1] $B_{41}=\$208$ [A1] [8 marks] (e) first term $\dfrac{6000}{1.04}$ and common ratio $\dfrac{1.02}{1.04}$ [A1] $S_\infty=\dfrac{6000/1.04}{1-\frac{1.02}{1.04}}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{6000}{0.02}=\$300\,000$ [AG] [3 marks] (f) $B_n\ge0$ gives $3(1.02)^{n}\ge(1.04)^{n}$ [M1] $n\ln\dfrac{1.04}{1.02}\le\ln3$, so $n\le56.58$ [M1] $56$ full payments [A1] [3 marks] (g) for example: the interest rate stays constant for decades [A1] the scholarship grows at exactly $2\%$ per year (inflation is constant) [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Parts (a) and (c) are geometric series results: identify the first term, the common ratio and the number of terms before using the formula. In part (d)(ii) a payment can only be made if the balance after it is not negative, so test $B_n\ge0$.

subtopic: Geometric series in finance: regular savings
statement: Maria deposits $\$300$ at the start of every month into a savings account that pays interest at $0.5\%$ per month, compounded monthly. Her first deposit is at the start of month $1$. Let $V_n$ be the total value of her account at the end of month $n$. (a) Find $V_2$, correct to the nearest cent. [2] (b) Show that $V_n=60\,300\left(1.005^n-1\right)$. [3] (c) Find the least number of months after which $V_n$ first exceeds $\$20\,000$. [2]
markscheme: (a) Deposit made at the start of month $1$ has grown for $2$ months and deposit of month $2$ for $1$ month: $V_2=300(1.005)^2+300(1.005)$ [M1] $=\$604.51$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $V_n=300(1.005)+300(1.005)^2+\dots+300(1.005)^n$, a geometric series with first term $300(1.005)$ and common ratio $1.005$ [M1] $V_n=\dfrac{300(1.005)\left(1.005^n-1\right)}{1.005-1}$ [A1] $=\dfrac{301.5}{0.005}\left(1.005^n-1\right)=60\,300\left(1.005^n-1\right)$ [A1][AG] [3 marks] (c) Solve $60\,300\left(1.005^n-1\right)>20\,000$ (using GDC) [M1] $V_{57}=19\,828$, $V_{58}=20\,228$, so $n=58$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Decide when each deposit starts earning interest: deposits at the start of the month earn a full month's interest in that month. Then identify the first term and common ratio of the resulting geometric series.

subtopic: Annuity: regular savings
statement: Omar saves by depositing $\$250$ at the end of every month into an account that pays a nominal annual interest rate of $4.8\%$, compounded monthly. (a) Find the value of Omar's account immediately after his deposit at the end of $5$ years ($60$ deposits). [3] (b) Find the total interest earned over the $5$ years. [1] (c) Omar wants to have $\$20\,000$ in the account after $5$ years. Find the monthly deposit that he needs to make, correct to the nearest cent. [3]
tips: Identify the type of annuity: payments at the end of each period use the ordinary-annuity form, with $N=12\times$ years. Use the GDC's TVM solver and make sure the payment sign is opposite to the future value.

subtopic: Arithmetic sequence from two terms
statement: The $p$th term of an arithmetic sequence is $u_p$. Given that $u_{4}=17$ and $u_{9}=-8$: (a) Find the common difference $d$ and the first term $u_1$. [3] (b) Find the sum of the first $15$ terms. [2] (c) Which term of the sequence equals $-98$? [2]
tips: Subtract two terms to find $d$, then use $u_n=u_1+(n-1)d$ and $S_n=\frac n2\left(2u_1+(n-1)d\right)$.

subtopic: Arithmetic sequence whose terms form a geometric sequence
statement: An arithmetic sequence has first term $5$ and common difference $d$, where $d\neq0$. The second, fifth and fourteenth terms of the arithmetic sequence are the first three terms of a geometric sequence. (a) Show that $d=10$. [4] (b) Write down the common ratio of the geometric sequence. [1] (c) Find the sum of the first 20 terms of the arithmetic sequence. [2] (d) Find the smallest value of $n$ for which the sum of the first $n$ terms of the geometric sequence exceeds $10^{6}$. [3]
tips: Three terms $a,b,c$ are geometric when $b^{2}=ac$. Remember to use the condition $d\neq0$ to discard the root $d=0$ that appears when you factorize.

subtopic: Arithmetic sequence from two terms
statement: An arithmetic sequence has fourth term $u_4=19$ and ninth term $u_9=44$. (a) Find the common difference $d$ and the first term $u_1$. [3] (b) Find $S_{20}$, the sum of the first $20$ terms. [2] (c) Given that $u_n=99$, find the value of $n$. [2]
tips: Subtract the two term formulas $u_n=u_1+(n-1)d$ to get $d$ first.

subtopic: Finding a geometric sequence from two partial sums
statement: A geometric sequence has first term $a$ and common ratio $r>0$. The sum of the first three terms is $21$ and the sum of the first six terms is $189$. (a) Show that $1+r^3=9$. [2] (b) Find $r$ and $a$. [3]
tips: The second three terms are $r^3$ times the first three terms, so $S_6=S_3\left(1+r^3\right)$.

subtopic: Simple versus compound interest
statement: Sam has $\$5000$ to invest and compares two accounts. Account $A$ pays simple interest at $4.5\%$ per year on the original amount. Account $B$ pays compound interest at $3.8\%$ per year, compounded annually. (a) Find the value of account $A$ after $6$ years. [2] (b) Find the value of account $B$ after $6$ years. [2] (c) Find the smallest number of whole years after which account $B$ is worth more than account $A$. [3]
tips: Simple interest grows linearly and compound interest grows exponentially, so the compound account eventually overtakes. Compare the two values for whole years around the crossing, not just at the GDC intersection.

subtopic: Loan amortization schedule
statement: Priya borrows $\$18\,500$ to buy a car. The loan has a nominal annual interest rate of $6.2\%$ compounded monthly and is repaid by equal payments at the end of each month for $4$ years. (a) Find the monthly payment, correct to the nearest cent. [3] (b) Find the total interest paid over the $4$ years. [2] (c) Find the balance of the loan immediately after the $24$th payment. [2] (d) Find the amount of interest included in the $25$th payment. [2]
markscheme: (a) TVM: $N=48$, $I\%=6.2$, $PV=18\,500$, $FV=0$, $P/Y=C/Y=12$ [M1][M1] $PMT=\$436.17$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) total repaid $=436.17\times48=\$20\,936.23$ (using the unrounded payment) [M1] interest $=20\,936.23-18\,500=\$2436.23$ ($2436$) [A1] [2 marks] (c) TVM with $N=24$ gives balance $\$9821.30$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (d) interest in the $25$th payment $=9821.30\times\dfrac{0.062}{12}$ [M1] $=\$50.74$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The interest in any payment is the previous balance multiplied by the monthly rate $\frac{r}{12}$; the rest of the payment reduces the balance. Use the unrounded payment for later calculations to avoid rounding drift.

subtopic: Integers in a range divisible by 3 or 5 but not both
statement: Consider the integers from $1$ to $200$ inclusive that are divisible by $3$ or by $5$ but not by both. (a) Find how many such integers there are. [3] (b) Find the sum of these integers. [5]
markscheme: (a) multiples of $3$: $66$, multiples of $5$: $40$, multiples of $15$: $13$ [A1] the multiples of $15$ are counted in both lists and must be removed twice [M1] $66+40-2\times13=80$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) multiples of $3$: $3\times\dfrac{66\times67}2=6633$ [M1][A1] multiples of $5$: $5\times\dfrac{40\times41}2=4100$ [A1] multiples of $15$: $15\times\dfrac{13\times14}2=1365$ [A1] sum $=6633+4100-2\times1365=8003$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: The multiples of each number form an arithmetic sequence. An integer divisible by both $3$ and $5$ is a multiple of $15$, and it must be excluded from both lists.

subtopic: Sigma notation with arithmetic and geometric series
statement: (a) Evaluate $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{20}(3k-2)$. [2] (b) Evaluate $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}5\left(\dfrac23\right)^{k}$. [2] (c) Find the value of $n$ for which $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{n}(2k+1)=399$. [3]
tips: Read off the first term and the common difference or ratio from the sigma expression: for a geometric series starting at $k=1$ the first term is the expression evaluated at $k=1$. Reject any negative root when $n$ counts terms.

subtopic: Smallest n for a geometric sum to exceed a value
statement: A geometric sequence has first term $3$ and common ratio $2$. (a) Write down an expression for $S_n$. [1] (b) Find the smallest $n$ such that $S_n>1000000$. [4]
tips: Isolate $r^n$ and take logarithms. Since $r>1$ the inequality direction is unchanged when dividing by $\ln r$.

subtopic: Sum to infinity of a geometric series
statement: The terms of a geometric sequence are all positive. The third term is $\dfrac{16}{9}$ and the sixth term is $\dfrac{128}{243}$. (a) Show that the common ratio is $r=\frac{2}{3}$ (given that $r>0$). [3] (b) Find the first term. [2] (c) Find the sum to infinity, stating why it exists. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{u_{6}}{u_{3}}=r^{3}$ [M1] $=\frac{8}{27}$ [A1] so $r=\frac{2}{3}$ [AG] taking the positive root [3 marks] (b) $u_{3}=u_1r^{2}$ [M1] so $u_1=4$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $|r|<1$ [R1]; $S_\infty=\dfrac{u_1}{1-r}$ [M1] $=12$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Convergence needs $|r|<1$; state this condition before using $S_\infty=u_1/(1-r)$.

subtopic: Drug accumulation modeled by a geometric series
statement: A patient takes a 200 mg dose of a drug at the start of each day. During each 24 hours, $35\%$ of the drug present in the body is eliminated. Let $A_n$ be the amount of the drug, in mg, in the body immediately after the $n$th dose. (a) Show that $A_2=330$ and find $A_3$. [2] (b) Show that $A_n=\dfrac{200\left(1-0.65^{n}\right)}{0.35}$. [3] (c) Find the smallest value of $n$ for which $A_n>500$. [2] (d) Find the value that $A_n$ approaches in the long term. Hence state whether a dose-limit of $600$ mg is ever exceeded. [2]
tips: Write $A_n$ as the sum of the doses still present, each scaled by $0.65$ for every day it has spent in the body. For the long-term value, let $0.65^{n}\to0$.

subtopic: Convergence of a geometric series with a parameter
statement: Consider the infinite geometric series $1+(2x-1)+(2x-1)^2+\dots$ (a) Find the values of $x$ for which the series converges. [3] (b) Find, in terms of $x$, the sum to infinity, simplifying your answer. [2] (c) Given that the sum to infinity is $\dfrac52$, find $x$. [2]
tips: Write down the common ratio first, then impose $|r|<1$. Check that your final $x$ lies in the interval of convergence.

subtopic: Convergence of a geometric series
statement: A geometric series has first term $5$ and common ratio $r=\dfrac{x}{2}-1$, where $x\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Find the set of values of $x$ for which the series converges. [3] (b) Given that the sum to infinity of the series is $4$, find the value of $x$. [3] (c) For the value of $x$ found in part (b), find the sum of the first three terms of the series. [2]
markscheme: (a) convergence requires $|r|<1$, so $-1<\dfrac{x}{2}-1<1$ [M1] $0<\dfrac{x}{2}<2$ [A1] $0<x<4$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\dfrac{5}{1-r}=4$ [M1] $1-r=\dfrac54$, so $r=-\dfrac14$ [A1] $\dfrac{x}{2}-1=-\dfrac14$, so $x=\dfrac32$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $S_3=5\left(1-\dfrac14+\dfrac1{16}\right)$ [M1] $=\dfrac{65}{16}=4.0625$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The sum to infinity exists only when $|r|<1$, and it is worth checking that your value of $x$ from part (b) lies inside the interval from part (a). Do not forget that a negative ratio alternates the signs of the terms.

subtopic: Koch snowflake: perimeter and area as geometric series
statement: This question investigates the Koch snowflake. Stage $0$ is an equilateral triangle with side length $1$. At each stage, every side of the previous stage is divided into three equal parts, and an equilateral triangle is built outward on the middle part, with that part then removed. Let $P_n$ be the perimeter at stage $n$ and $A_n$ the area. (a) Show that the number of sides at stage $n$ is $3\times4^n$ and the length of each side is $\left(\dfrac13\right)^n$. [3] (b) Hence show that $P_n=3\left(\dfrac43\right)^n$ and describe what happens to the perimeter as $n\to\infty$. [3] (c) At stage $n\ge1$, one new small triangle is added on each of the $3\times4^{n-1}$ sides of stage $n-1$. Show that the total area added at stage $n$ is $\dfrac{\sqrt3}{12}\left(\dfrac49\right)^{n-1}$. [4] (d) Hence find the exact limiting area $A=\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}A_n$. [4] (e) Find the ratio of the limiting area to the area of the original triangle, and comment on the result alongside part (b). [3]
markscheme: (a) each side is replaced by $4$ sides, so the number of sides is multiplied by $4$: $3\times4^n$ [M1][A1] each new side is $\dfrac13$ of the previous one: $\left(\dfrac13\right)^n$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $P_n=3\times4^n\times3^{-n}$ [M1] $=3\left(\dfrac43\right)^n$ [A1] since $\dfrac43>1$, $P_n\to\infty$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) each new triangle has side $3^{-n}$ and area $\dfrac{\sqrt3}{4}\left(3^{-n}\right)^2=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{4}\times9^{-n}$ [M1][A1] total added $=3\times4^{n-1}\times\dfrac{\sqrt3}{4}\times9^{-n}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{3\sqrt3}{36}\left(\dfrac49\right)^{n-1}=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{12}\left(\dfrac49\right)^{n-1}$ [A1] [4 marks] (d) $A=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{4}+\dfrac{\sqrt3}{12}\left[1+\dfrac49+\left(\dfrac49\right)^2+\dots\right]$ [M1] geometric series with $r=\dfrac49$, $|r|<1$ [A1] sum $=\dfrac1{1-\frac49}=\dfrac95$ [A1] $A=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{4}+\dfrac{3\sqrt3}{20}=\dfrac{2\sqrt3}{5}$ [A1] [4 marks] (e) $\dfrac{2\sqrt3/5}{\sqrt3/4}=\dfrac85$ [M1][A1] the shape has a finite area but an infinite perimeter [R1] [3 marks]
tips: Count sides and lengths stage by stage. The areas added at successive stages form a geometric series with ratio $\dfrac49$.

subtopic: Triangular numbers and the sum of triangular numbers
statement: The $n$th triangular number is $T_n=\dfrac{n(n+1)}2$. (a) Show that $T_n+T_{n+1}=(n+1)^2$. [2] (b) Using $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^nk=\dfrac{n(n+1)}2$ and $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^nk^2=\dfrac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}6$, show that $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^nT_k=\dfrac{n(n+1)(n+2)}6$. [4] (c) Find the sum of the first $10$ triangular numbers. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{n(n+1)}2+\dfrac{(n+1)(n+2)}2$ [M1] $=\dfrac{(n+1)(2n+2)}2=(n+1)^2$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac12\left(\sum k^2+\sum k\right)$ [M1] $=\dfrac12\left[\dfrac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}6+\dfrac{n(n+1)}2\right]$ [A1] $=\dfrac{n(n+1)}{12}\left(2n+1+3\right)$ [A1] $=\dfrac{n(n+1)(n+2)}6$ [AG] [A1] [4 marks] (c) $\dfrac{10\times11\times12}6=220$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Write $T_k$ as a combination of $k^2$ and $k$, then use the standard sums.

subtopic: Compound interest with monthly compounding
statement: Elena invests $\$12\,000$ at a nominal annual interest rate of $3.6\%$, compounded monthly. (a) Find the value of the investment after $7$ years. [2] (b) Find how many years it takes for the investment to double in value, giving your answer to three significant figures. [2] (c) A second bank offers the same nominal rate of $3.6\%$, but compounded quarterly. Find how much less Elena's investment would be worth after $7$ years with the second bank. [2]
tips: In compound-interest problems with $k$ compounding periods a year the number of periods is $kt$ and the rate per period is the nominal rate divided by $k$. More frequent compounding always gives a (slightly) larger value.

subtopic: Savings plan with deposits that rise each month
statement: Aroha saves \$100 in the first month and increases her deposit by \$5 each month after that. She does this for $36$ months. No interest is paid. (a) Find the deposit in the 36th month. [2] (b) Find the total saved after $36$ months. [2] (c) Her friend saves a constant \$180 every month. Find the first month at the end of which Aroha's total savings exceed her friend's total savings. [4]
tips: Compare the two partial sums as functions of $n$, or tabulate them using your GDC.

subtopic: The Sierpinski triangle: area and perimeter after n steps
statement: An equilateral triangle of side $8$ cm and area $A_0$ is modified repeatedly. At each step, the middle triangle (formed by joining the midpoints of the sides) is removed from every remaining triangle. (a) Show that the remaining area after $n$ steps is $A_0\left(\dfrac34\right)^n$. [2] (b) Find the least number of steps after which the remaining area is below $1\%$ of the original. [3] (c) After $n$ steps there are $3^n$ small triangles, each of side $8\left(\dfrac12\right)^n$. Show that the total length of the sides of all the small triangles is $24\left(\dfrac32\right)^n$ cm, and explain why it is unbounded as $n$ increases. [3]
markscheme: (a) each remaining triangle is replaced by $3$ triangles, each with $\dfrac14$ of its area [M1] area is multiplied by $\dfrac34$ at each step [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\left(\dfrac34\right)^n<0.01$ [M1] $n>\dfrac{\ln0.01}{\ln0.75}=16.01$ [A1] $n=17$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $3^n\times3\times8\left(\dfrac12\right)^n$ [M1] $=24\left(\dfrac32\right)^n$ [A1] the ratio $\dfrac32>1$, so the terms increase without bound [R1] [3 marks]
tips: The area decreases by a factor of $3/4$ and the total edge length increases by a factor of $3/2$ at each step.

subtopic: Closed form of a first-order linear recurrence
statement: A sequence satisfies $u_1=3$ and $u_{n+1}=2u_n+1$ for $n\ge1$. (a) Let $v_n=u_n+1$. Show that $v_n$ is a geometric sequence, and find $u_n$ in terms of $n$. [4] (b) Find $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^nu_k$. [3]
tips: Adding a suitable constant to $u_n$ turns the recurrence into a pure doubling pattern.

subtopic: Repaying a 25-year loan: payments, balance and extra payments
statement: A loan of \$240,000 is repaid by equal monthly payments at the end of each month for $25$ years ($300$ payments). The nominal annual interest rate is $4.8\%$, compounded monthly. In this question, round the monthly payment to the nearest cent and use that rounded payment in every later part. Give money amounts to the nearest cent. (a) Use your GDC to find the monthly payment. [2] (b) Find the total amount paid over the $25$ years and the total interest paid. [3] (c) Find the interest included in the first payment, and the amount of the first payment that reduces the debt. [3] (d) Find the outstanding balance after $5$ years ($60$ payments). [2] (e) A second loan option repays the same \$240,000 over $15$ years ($180$ payments) at the same rate. Find the monthly payment and the total interest. [3] (f) Back with the $25$-year loan, the borrower pays an extra \$200 each month, so the payment is \$1,575.19. Find the number of payments needed to clear the loan, and the number of months saved. [3]
markscheme: (a) $N=300$, $I\%=4.8$, $PV=240000$, $FV=0$, $P/Y=C/Y=12$ [M1]; payment $=\$1375.19$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Total $=300\times1375.19=\$412557.00$ [M1][A1]; interest $=\$172557.00$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $240000\times0.004=\$960.00$ [A1][M1]; principal repaid $=1375.19-960.00=\$415.19$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) Use the financial solver for $N=60$ or repeat the recurrence $B\to1.004B-1375.19$ [M1]; \$211,908.17 [A1] [2 marks] (e) Payment $=\$1872.99$ [A1]; total paid $=180\times1872.99=\$337138.20$ [M1]; interest $=\$97138.20$ [A1] [3 marks] (f) Solve for $N$ with payment $1575.19$ [M1]; $N=\dfrac{-\ln\left(1-\frac{240000\times0.004}{1575.19}\right)}{\ln1.004}=235.52$, so $236$ payments (the last one smaller) [A1]; saved $300-236=64$ months [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Interest each month is $0.004$ times the outstanding balance; extra payments go entirely to principal.

subtopic: Sum to infinity and convergence condition
statement: A geometric series has first term $8$ and sum to infinity $20$. (a) Find the common ratio. [2] (b) Find the third term. [1] A second geometric series has first term $5$ and common ratio $\dfrac{x-1}{3}$. (c) Find the set of values of $x$ for which the second series converges. [3] (d) The sum to infinity of the second series is $3$. Find the value of $x$. [2]
tips: The sum to infinity exists only when $|r|<1$. In part (d) check that your answer lies inside the interval found in part (c).

subtopic: Geometric sequence with an unknown middle term
statement: The first three terms of a geometric sequence are $4$, $x$ and $36$, where $x>0$. (a) Find the value of $x$ and the common ratio $r$. [3] (b) Find the sum of the first $6$ terms. [2] (c) Find the least value of $n$ for which $u_n>10^{4}$. [3]
tips: In a geometric sequence the ratio of consecutive terms is constant, so $\frac{u_2}{u_1}=\frac{u_3}{u_2}$.

subtopic: Smallest n for a geometric sum to exceed a value
statement: A geometric sequence has first term $3$ and common ratio $1.2$. (a) Write down an expression for $S_n$. [1] (b) Find the smallest $n$ such that $S_n>200$. [4]
tips: Isolate $r^n$ and take logarithms. Since $r>1$ the inequality direction is unchanged when dividing by $\ln r$.

subtopic: Evaluating a sum in sigma notation
statement: Consider $S=\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{10}5 \left(\frac{4}{5}\right)^{k}$. (a) Write down the first three terms of the sum and state the type of series, if it is arithmetic or geometric. [3] (b) Evaluate $S$. [2]
markscheme: (a) first terms $5,\ 4,\ 3.2$ [A1] common ratio $0.8$ [A1] geometric [A1] [3 marks] (b) use the sum formula or the calculator's sum function [M1] $S=22.85$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A geometric series has $S_n=u_1\dfrac{1-r^n}{1-r}$, here with $11$ terms starting at $k=0$.

subtopic: Geometric series in a medical context
statement: A patient takes a $200$ mg dose of a drug every morning. Over the following $24$ hours, $30\%$ of the drug in the patient's body is eliminated. Let $a_n$ be the amount of the drug in the body immediately after the $n$th dose. (a) Find $a_3$. [2] (b) Show that $a_n=\dfrac{200\left(1-0.7^{n}\right)}{0.3}$. [2] (c) Find the limiting value of $a_n$ as $n\to\infty$. [2] (d) The drug becomes ineffective if the amount in the body exceeds $650$ mg after any dose. Find the smallest number of doses after which this happens. [3]
tips: The amount just after dose $n$ is the new dose plus the surviving fraction of everything already in the body, which builds a geometric series. For the limit, note that $|0.7|<1$.

subtopic: Geometric sequence from two terms
statement: The terms of a geometric sequence are all positive, with $u_{3}=27$ and $u_{6}=1$. (a) Find the common ratio $r$ and the first term $u_1$. [3] (b) Find the sum of the first $5$ terms. [2] (c) Find the sum to infinity. [2]
tips: From two terms of a geometric sequence, divide to get $r^{k}$ where $k$ is the gap in positions. Use $S_\infty=\dfrac{u_1}{1-r}$ only when $|r|<1$.

subtopic: Smallest n for a sum to exceed a value
statement: An arithmetic sequence has first term $4$ and common difference $3$. (a) Write an expression for $S_n$, the sum of the first $n$ terms. [2] (b) Find the smallest value of $n$ for which $S_n>800$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $S_n=\dfrac n2\left(2\times4+(n-1)\times3\right)$ [M1] $=\dfrac n2\left(3n+5\right)$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac n2\left(3n+5\right)>800$ [M1] solve using a table or the quadratic [A1] $S_{22}=781.000$ and $S_{23}=851.000$, so $n=23$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Form the quadratic inequality in $n$, or use a table of values of $S_n$ and look for the first value above the target.

subtopic: Sum of multiples of an integer in a range
statement: Consider the positive integers between $100$ and $500$ that are divisible by $7$. (a) Write down the smallest and the largest of these integers. [2] (b) Find how many such integers there are. [2] (c) Find the sum of these integers. [2]
tips: The multiples form an arithmetic sequence with common difference equal to the divisor.

subtopic: Sequence from a formula for the sum
statement: The sum of the first $n$ terms of an arithmetic sequence is $S_n=3n^{2}+2n$. (a) Find $u_1$ and $u_2$, and hence the common difference $d$. [3] (b) Find $u_{20}$. [2] (c) Find the value of $n$ for which $u_n=65$. [2]
tips: The first term equals $S_1$, and the second term equals $S_2-S_1$.

subtopic: Sum of multiples of an integer in a range
statement: Consider the positive multiples of $3$ that are less than $200$ and are not multiples of $6$. (a) Explain why these numbers form an arithmetic sequence and state its first term and common difference. [2] (b) Find the number of terms. [2] (c) Find the sum of these numbers. [2]
markscheme: (a) they are the odd multiples of $3$: $3,9,15,\dots$ [A1] $u_1=3$, $d=6$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) largest term below $200$ is $195$ [A1] $3+6(n-1)=195$ gives $n=33$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $S=\dfrac{33}{2}(3+195)$ [M1] $=3267$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Multiples of $3$ that are not multiples of $6$ are the odd multiples of $3$, which step by $6$.

subtopic: Telescoping series and bounds on the sum of reciprocals of squares
statement: This question investigates series whose terms cancel in pairs. Let $S_N=\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{N}\dfrac{1}{n(n+1)}$. (a) Show that $\dfrac1{n(n+1)}=\dfrac1n-\dfrac1{n+1}$. [1] (b) Hence show that $S_N=1-\dfrac1{N+1}$. [3] (c) Write down $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\dfrac1{n(n+1)}$, and find the least $N$ for which $S_N>0.999$. [3] (d) By comparing $\dfrac1{n^2}$ with $\dfrac1{n(n-1)}$ for $n\ge2$, show that $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{N}\dfrac1{n^2}<2$ for all $N$. [4] (e) Show that $\dfrac1{n(n+1)(n+2)}=\dfrac12\left[\dfrac1{n(n+1)}-\dfrac1{(n+1)(n+2)}\right]$ and hence find the exact value of $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\dfrac1{n(n+1)(n+2)}$. [5]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac1n-\dfrac1{n+1}=\dfrac{(n+1)-n}{n(n+1)}=\dfrac1{n(n+1)}$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $S_N=\left(1-\dfrac12\right)+\left(\dfrac12-\dfrac13\right)+\dots+\left(\dfrac1N-\dfrac1{N+1}\right)$ [M1][A1] all intermediate terms cancel, leaving $1-\dfrac1{N+1}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) as $N\to\infty$, $\dfrac1{N+1}\to0$ so the sum is $1$ [A1] $1-\dfrac1{N+1}>0.999$ [M1] $N+1>1000$ so $N=1000$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) for $n\ge2$, $n^2>n(n-1)$ so $\dfrac1{n^2}<\dfrac1{n(n-1)}=\dfrac1{n-1}-\dfrac1n$ [M1][A1] $\sum_{n=2}^{N}\dfrac1{n^2}<\sum_{n=2}^N\left(\dfrac1{n-1}-\dfrac1n\right)=1-\dfrac1N<1$ [M1] adding the $n=1$ term $1$: sum $<2$ [A1] [4 marks] (e) $\dfrac1{n(n+1)}-\dfrac1{(n+1)(n+2)}=\dfrac{(n+2)-n}{n(n+1)(n+2)}=\dfrac2{n(n+1)(n+2)}$ [M1][A1] telescoping sum to $N$ terms: $\dfrac12\left[\dfrac1{1\cdot2}-\dfrac1{(N+1)(N+2)}\right]$ [M1][A1] as $N\to\infty$ the sum is $\dfrac14$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: Partial fractions turn a sum of reciprocals into a telescoping sum. To bound a sum you cannot evaluate, compare each term with a larger term that does telescope.

subtopic: Sum of an arithmetic series and its term number
statement: An arithmetic sequence has $u_{4}=2$ and $u_{10}=-16$. (a) Find the common difference and the first term. [3] (b) Find an expression for $S_k$, the sum of the first $k$ terms. [2] (c) Find the value of $k$ for which $S_k=-350$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $u_{10}-u_{4}=6d$ [M1] so $d=-3$ [A1], $u_1=2-3(-3)=11$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $S_k=\dfrac k2\left(2(11)+(k-1)(-3)\right)$ [M1] $=-\frac{3 k^{2}}{2} + \frac{25 k}{2}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $-\frac{3 k^{2}}{2} + \frac{25 k}{2}=-350$ [M1] solving the quadratic (factorizing) [A1] $k=20$ (reject the negative root) [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A negative common difference means the sum rises then falls, so a sum can be reached twice; check which root is a valid term number.

subtopic: General term from the sum of the first n terms
statement: The sum of the first $n$ terms of a sequence is $S_n=2n^2+3n$. (a) Find $u_1$ and $u_2$. [2] (b) Show that $u_n=4n+1$ for $n\ge2$ and that the formula also holds for $n=1$. [3] (c) Hence state the type of sequence, and find $n$ such that $S_n=324$. [3]
tips: For $n\ge2$, $u_n=S_n-S_{n-1}$; always check the case $n=1$ separately, where $u_1=S_1$.

subtopic: Comparing geometric and arithmetic depreciation
statement: Car $A$ is worth $\$26\,000$ when new and loses $14\%$ of its value each year, so its value after $n$ years is $V_A=26\,000(0.86)^{n}$ dollars. Car $B$ is worth $\$24\,000$ when new and loses $\$1800$ in value each year, so its value after $n$ years is $V_B=24\,000-1800n$ dollars, for $0\le n\le13$. (a) Find the value of car $A$ after $3$ years, to the nearest dollar. [2] (b) Find the number of complete years after which the value of car $A$ is first below $\$8000$. [2] (c) Find the whole-number values of $n$, with $0\le n\le13$, for which car $A$ is worth less than car $B$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $26\,000(0.86)^3$ [M1] $=\$16\,537$ ($16\,537.46$) [A1] [2 marks] (b) solve $26\,000(0.86)^n<8000$ [M1] $n>7.81\ldots$, so after $8$ years [A1] [2 marks] (c) sketch/graph $V_A$ and $V_B$ and find the intersections with GDC [M1] intersections at $n=1.10\ldots$ and $n=10.26\ldots$ [A1][A1] $V_A<V_B$ for $1.10<n<10.26$, so $n=2,3,\ldots,10$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Two models can cross twice, so check both intersection points rather than assuming one crossing. Only whole-number years lie between the two intersection values; test the integers on either side of each crossing.

subtopic: An alternating series of integers
statement: Let $S_n=1-2+3-4+5-\cdots+(-1)^{n+1}n$. (a) Find $S_{2m}$ by grouping the terms in pairs, and hence find $S_{100}$. [3] (b) Find $S_{2m+1}$ and $S_{101}$. [2] (c) Explain why the infinite series does not converge. [1]
markscheme: (a) each pair $(2k-1)-2k=-1$ [M1] $S_{2m}=-m$ [A1] $S_{100}=-50$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $S_{2m+1}=-m+(2m+1)=m+1$ [M1] $S_{101}=51$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) the partial sums alternate between values that grow in magnitude and do not approach a limit [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Pair the terms so that each pair has the same value, then deal separately with the last unpaired term when $n$ is odd.

subtopic: Arithmetic sequence model: seating
statement: A lecture hall has rows of seats. The first row has $18$ seats and each row has $3$ more seats than the row in front of it. The hall has $24$ rows. (a) Find the number of seats in the last row. [2] (b) Find the total number of seats in the hall. [2] (c) A second hall is built with the same pattern. Find the minimum number of rows needed for it to have at least $2000$ seats. [3]
tips: Write the total as a function of $n$ using $S_n=\frac n2(2u_1+(n-1)d)$, then use the GDC to solve the inequality and round up. Quote the sums for the two neighboring integers as a check.

subtopic: Loan balance defined by a recurrence relation
statement: A loan of \$200,000 is repaid by monthly payments of \$1,100. Interest of $0.48\%$ per month is added to the balance before each payment is made. Let $B_n$ be the balance immediately after the $n$th payment, so $B_0=200000$. (a) Write down a recurrence relation for $B_{n+1}$ in terms of $B_n$. [1] (b) Find $B_1$ and $B_2$, to the nearest cent. [2] (c) Use your GDC to find the balance after $10$ years (120 payments), to the nearest dollar. [2] (d) Find the amount of the first payment that goes towards reducing the loan, that is, the principal repaid in the first month, and explain why this amount grows over time. [3]
markscheme: (a) $B_{n+1}=1.0048B_n-1100$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $B_1=\$199860.00$ [A1]; $B_2=\$199719.33$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Repeated use of the recurrence, or financial solver [M1]; \$177,353 [A1] [2 marks] (d) Interest in month 1 $=0.0048\times200000=960$ [A1]; principal $=1100-960=\$140$ [A1]; as the balance falls, interest falls, so more of the fixed payment reduces the principal [R1] [3 marks]
tips: Each month: add interest to the balance, then subtract the payment.

subtopic: Comparing arithmetic and geometric growth
statement: Two runners each plan a training program. In week $1$ each runs $12\ \mathrm{km}$. Ana increases her weekly distance by $1.5\ \mathrm{km}$ each week. Ben increases his weekly distance by $8\%$ each week. (a) Find the distance Ana runs in week $10$. [2] (b) Find the total distance Ben runs in the first $10$ weeks. [2] (c) Find the first week in which Ben's weekly distance is greater than Ana's weekly distance. [3]
tips: Write the general terms of both sequences in terms of $n$ before comparing them, and use your GDC's table to check the weeks either side of the crossover. Give an integer week as the answer, not the decimal solution of the equation.

subtopic: Sum of an arithmetico-geometric series
statement: Let $S_n=x+2x^2+3x^3+\cdots+nx^n$, where $x\ne1$. (a) By considering $S_n-xS_n$, show that $S_n=\dfrac{x\left(1-x^n\right)}{(1-x)^2}-\dfrac{nx^{n+1}}{1-x}$. [5] (b) For $|x|<1$, find the limit of $S_n$ as $n\to\infty$, and evaluate it for $x=\dfrac12$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $S_n-xS_n=x+x^2+\cdots+x^n-nx^{n+1}$ [M1][A1] geometric series: $\dfrac{x(1-x^n)}{1-x}$ [A1] $(1-x)S_n=\dfrac{x(1-x^n)}{1-x}-nx^{n+1}$ [A1] divide by $1-x$ [A1] [5 marks] (b) $x^n\to0$ and $nx^{n+1}\to0$, so the limit is $\dfrac x{(1-x)^2}$ [A1] at $x=\dfrac12$ it is $2$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Subtracting $x$ times the sum from the sum leaves a geometric series and one extra term.

subtopic: Time for compound interest to reach a target
statement: An investment of \$8,000 earns $4.8\%$ nominal annual interest, compounded quarterly. The investor wants the balance to reach \$25,000. (a) Write down an equation for the number of years $t$ needed. [2] (b) Solve your equation, and state the first quarter-year end at which the balance is at least \$25,000. Give the time in years and months. [3] (c) Find the balance at that time, to the nearest dollar. [2]
tips: Use the financial solver or take logarithms; interest is only added at the end of each quarter.

subtopic: Stacked logs and partial sums of an arithmetic series
statement: Logs are stacked in rows. The bottom row has 28 logs and each row above has one log fewer than the row below it. The top row has 1 log. (a) Show that row $n$, counting from the bottom, has $29-n$ logs. [1] (b) Find the total number of logs in the complete stack. [2] (c) Only 300 logs are available. Find the number of complete rows that can be built starting from the bottom. [3] (d) Find the number of logs left over. [1]
markscheme: (a) arithmetic with $u_1=28$ and $d=-1$, so $u_n=28-(n-1)=29-n$ [AG] [1 mark] (b) $28$ rows: $S_{28}=\dfrac{28}{2}(28+1)$ [M1] $=406$ logs [A1] [2 marks] (c) $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\left(28+(29-n)\right)=\dfrac{n(57-n)}{2}\le300$ [M1] $n=13$ gives $286$ and $n=14$ gives $301>300$ [M1] $13$ complete rows [A1] [3 marks] (d) $300-286=14$ logs [A1] [1 mark]
tips: When the total is capped, test consecutive values of $n$ rather than rounding the root of the equation. A row may only be built if there are enough logs left to complete it.

subtopic: Recurring decimals as geometric series
statement: (a) Write $0.272727\ldots$ as the sum of an infinite geometric series and hence express it as a fraction in its simplest form. [3] (b) Show that $0.4363636\ldots=\dfrac{24}{55}$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $0.27+0.0027+0.000027+\cdots$ with $u_1=0.27$ and $r=0.01$ [A1] $S_\infty=\dfrac{0.27}{1-0.01}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{27}{99}=\dfrac{3}{11}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $0.4+0.036+0.00036+\cdots$ where the recurring part is geometric with $u_1=0.036$ and $r=0.01$ [M1] recurring part $=\dfrac{0.036}{0.99}=\dfrac{2}{55}$ [A1] $\dfrac25+\dfrac{2}{55}=\dfrac{22}{55}+\dfrac{2}{55}=\dfrac{24}{55}$ [AG] [3 marks]
tips: Split the decimal into the non-recurring part and a geometric series whose ratio is a power of $\tfrac{1}{10}$ matching the repeating block length. Then add the fractions over a common denominator.

subtopic: Depreciation as a geometric sequence
statement: A car is bought for $\$20000$ and loses $15\%$ of its value each year. (a) Find the value of the car after $3$ years. [2] (b) Find after how many complete years the value first falls below $\$8000$. [3] (c) Find the total depreciation (loss in value) during the first $3$ years. [1]
tips: Each year multiplies the value by $0.85$. For the smallest $n$, take logs and remember $\ln0.85<0$ reverses the inequality.

subtopic: Loan repaid by monthly payments
statement: A loan of $18000$ dollars is borrowed at $7.2\%$ per year, compounded monthly, and repaid by $36$ equal payments made at the end of each month. (a) Find the monthly payment, to the nearest cent. [3] (b) Using the rounded payment from part (a), find the total interest paid over the $36$ months. [2] (c) Use the unrounded monthly payment to find the amount still owed immediately after the $12$th payment, to the nearest cent. [3]
markscheme: (a) GDC finance solver: $N=36$, $I\%=7.2$, $PV=18000$, $FV=0$, $P/Y=C/Y=12$ [M1][M1]; $PMT=557.44$ dollars [A1] [3 marks] (b) $36\times557.44=20067.84$ [M1]; interest $=20067.84-18000=2067.84$ dollars [A1] [2 marks] (c) $N=12$ payments made, so find $FV$ of the loan [M1]; with $PMT=-557.4352\ldots$ [A1]; balance $=12425.19$ dollars [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Total interest is total repaid minus the amount borrowed. The balance owed is the future value after $12$ payments.

subtopic: Arithmetic training plan distances
statement: A runner follows a training plan. In week 1 she runs 12 km. In each following week she runs 1.5 km more than in the previous week. (a) Find the distance she runs in week 13. [2] (b) Find the total distance she runs in the first 16 weeks. [2] (c) Find the first week in which she runs more than 35 km. [2] (d) Find the first week by which her total distance since week 1 first reaches at least 500 km. [2]
tips: Use the arithmetic formulas with $u_1=12$ and $d=1.5$. For part (d) solve with a table of values on your GDC and check the weeks either side of the boundary.

subtopic: Declining oil output as a geometric sequence
statement: An oil field produces 4.2 million barrels in its first year. Each year the output is $94\%$ of the output in the previous year. (a) Find the output in year 6, in millions of barrels, to three significant figures. [2] (b) Find the total output in the first 10 years, in millions of barrels, to three significant figures. [2] (c) The field is closed in the first year in which the output is below 2.5 million barrels. Find the year in which the field is closed. [2] (d) Find the total output the field would produce if it could operate indefinitely. [2]
markscheme: (a) $4.2(0.94)^{5}$ [M1] $=3.08$ million barrels [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac{4.2\left(1-0.94^{10}\right)}{1-0.94}$ [M1] $=32.3$ million barrels [A1] [2 marks] (c) $4.2(0.94)^{n-1}<2.5$ [M1] year 9 gives $2.56$ and year 10 gives $2.41$, so year $10$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $\dfrac{4.2}{1-0.94}$ [M1] $=70$ million barrels [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The output in year $n$ is $u_n=u_1r^{n-1}$, so year 6 uses the power $5$. Check the years either side of the boundary in part (c) to avoid an off-by-one error.

subtopic: Three numbers that are in both arithmetic and geometric progression
statement: The non-zero real numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ are, in that order, consecutive terms of an arithmetic sequence and also consecutive terms of a geometric sequence. (a) Write down two equations relating $a$, $b$, $c$. [2] (b) Show that $a=b=c$. [4]
markscheme: (a) arithmetic: $2b=a+c$ [A1] geometric: $b^2=ac$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $(a-c)^2=(a+c)^2-4ac$ [M1] $=4b^2-4b^2=0$ [A1] so $a=c$ [A1] then $2b=2a$, so $b=a$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Eliminate $b$ by writing $(a-c)^2$ in terms of $a+c$ and $ac$.

subtopic: Finding the first term and sum to infinity
statement: Consider a geometric sequence with $u_2=6$ and $u_5=\dfrac{16}{9}$, where all terms are positive. (a) Show that the common ratio is $r=\frac{2}{3}$ (given that $r>0$). [3] (b) Find the first term. [2] (c) Find the sum to infinity, stating why it exists. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{u_{5}}{u_{2}}=r^{3}$ [M1] $=\frac{8}{27}$ [A1] so $r=\frac{2}{3}$ [AG] taking the positive root [3 marks] (b) $u_{2}=u_1r^{1}$ [M1] so $u_1=9$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $|r|<1$ [R1]; $S_\infty=\dfrac{u_1}{1-r}$ [M1] $=27$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: $u_5/u_2=r^3$, so the common ratio is a cube root of a fraction that is a perfect cube here.

subtopic: Present value of a stream of payments
statement: A scholarship pays $\$500$ at the end of each year, and money can be invested at $4\%$ per year compound interest. (a) Show that the present value of the first $n$ payments is $500\times\dfrac{1-1.04^{-n}}{0.04}$. [3] (b) Find the amount that must be invested now to fund the scholarship for $20$ years. [2] (c) Find the amount needed to fund the scholarship forever. [2]
markscheme: (a) present value of the payment in year $k$ is $500\times1.04^{-k}$ [A1] geometric series with first term $\dfrac{500}{1.04}$ and ratio $\dfrac1{1.04}$ [M1] sum $=\dfrac{500}{1.04}\times\dfrac{1-1.04^{-n}}{1-1/1.04}=500\times\dfrac{1-1.04^{-n}}{0.04}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $500\times\dfrac{1-1.04^{-20}}{0.04}$ [M1] $=\$6\,795$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $n\to\infty$: $1.04^{-n}\to0$ [M1] $\dfrac{500}{0.04}=\$12\,500$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Discount each payment to its present value. The discounted payments form a geometric sequence.

subtopic: Arithmetic sequence from two terms
statement: The terms of an arithmetic sequence satisfy $u_{5}=17$ and $u_{12}=45$. (a) Find the common difference and the first term. [3] (b) Find an expression for $S_k$, the sum of the first $k$ terms. [2] (c) Find the value of $k$ for which $S_k=1225$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $u_{12}-u_{5}=7d$ [M1] so $d=4$ [A1], $u_1=17-4(4)=1$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $S_k=\dfrac k2\left(2(1)+(k-1)(4)\right)$ [M1] $=2 k^{2} - k$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $2 k^{2} - k=1225$ [M1] solving the quadratic (factorizing) [A1] $k=25$ (reject the negative root) [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Use $u_q-u_p=(q-p)d$ to find $d$ first; when solving the quadratic for $k$ remember $k$ must be a positive integer.

subtopic: Sum using sigma notation
statement: Let $S_n=\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{n}(3k+2)$. (a) Find $S_{15}$. [2] (b) Show that $S_n=\dfrac{n(3n+7)}{2}$. [3] (c) Given that $S_n=948$, find the value of $n$. [3]
markscheme: (a) arithmetic series with $u_1=5$, $d=3$ [M1]; $S_{15}=\dfrac{15}{2}\left(10+14\times3\right)=390$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\left(2\times5+(n-1)\times3\right)$ [M1][A1]; $=\dfrac{n(3n+7)}{2}$ [AG] [3 marks] (c) $3n^{2}+7n-1896=0$ [M1]; $(n-24)(3n+79)=0$ [A1]; $n=24$ (since $n>0$) [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Identify the first term and common difference of $3k+2$ before using the sum formula.

subtopic: Geometric sequence from two terms
statement: The terms of a geometric sequence are all positive, with $u_{2}=12$ and $u_{5}=96$. (a) Find the common ratio $r$ and the first term $u_1$. [3] (b) Find the sum of the first $8$ terms. [2] (c) Explain why the sequence has no sum to infinity. [1]
markscheme: (a) $r^{3}=\dfrac{96}{12}$ [M1] $r=2$ [A1] $u_1=\dfrac{12}{2^{1}}=6$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $S_{8}=\dfrac{6\left(1-2^{8}\right)}{1-2}$ [M1] $=1530$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $r=2>1$, so the terms grow and the series diverges [R1] [1 mark]
tips: From two terms of a geometric sequence, divide to get $r^{k}$ where $k$ is the gap in positions. Use $S_\infty=\dfrac{u_1}{1-r}$ only when $|r|<1$.

subtopic: Loan repayment with a recurrence relation
statement: A loan of $\$20000$ is repaid by monthly payments of $\$450$. Interest of $1\%$ is added to the balance at the end of each month, before the payment is made. Let $B_n$ be the balance after the $n$th payment, with $B_0=20000$. (a) Write down a recurrence relation for $B_{n+1}$ in terms of $B_n$, and find $B_1$ and $B_2$. [3] (b) Show that $B_n=45000-25000(1.01)^n$. [3] (c) Find the number of payments needed to clear the loan. [3]
tips: Each month the balance is multiplied by $1.01$ and then reduced by the payment. The constant solution of the recurrence gives the fixed part of the closed form.

subtopic: Present value of a scholarship paid for 20 years
statement: A school wants to fund a scholarship of \$12,000 paid at the end of each year for $20$ years from a single investment made today. The investment earns $4\%$ per year, compounded annually. (a) Explain why the present value of the scholarship is the sum of a geometric series with $20$ terms, and state the first term and common ratio. [3] (b) Hence find the size of the investment needed, to the nearest dollar. [3] (c) The school invests \$250,000 instead and the payments of \$12,000 continue each year until the money runs out. Find the number of full payments that can be made. [3]
markscheme: (a) Payment $k$ years from now has present value $\dfrac{12000}{1.04^{k}}$ [M1]; first term $\dfrac{12000}{1.04}$ [A1]; common ratio $\dfrac{1}{1.04}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $S_{20}=\dfrac{12000}{1.04}\times\dfrac{1-1.04^{-20}}{1-1.04^{-1}}$ [M1][A1]; \$163,084 [A1] [3 marks] (c) $12000\times\dfrac{1-1.04^{-n}}{0.04}\le250000$ [M1]; $1.04^{-n}\ge\dfrac{1}{6}$ so $n\le\dfrac{\ln6}{\ln1.04}=45.68$ [A1]; $45$ full payments [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The present value of a payment made $k$ years from now is the payment divided by $(1+r)^{k}$.

subtopic: Mean and standard deviation of grouped heights
statement: The heights of 70 students are summarized in the table. $$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline \text{Height } h \text{ (cm)} & 140\le h<150 & 150\le h<160 & 160\le h<170 & 170\le h<180 & 180\le h<190 \\ \hline \text{Frequency} & 6 & 14 & 25 & 18 & 7 \\ \hline \end{array}$$ (a) Use midpoints of the classes to estimate the mean height. [2] (b) Estimate the population standard deviation of the heights. [2] (c) Each height is converted from centimeters to inches by dividing by 2.54. Write down the estimated mean and standard deviation of the heights in inches. [2] (d) Explain why the answers to (a) and (b) are only estimates. [1]
markscheme: (a) Midpoints 145, 155, 165, 175, 185 [M1] Mean $=\dfrac{6(145)+14(155)+25(165)+18(175)+7(185)}{70}=\dfrac{11610}{70}=165.857\ldots\approx166$ cm [A1] [2 marks] (b) Using the GDC, correct GDC list entry or sum of squares [M1] population standard deviation $\sigma=10.9$ cm [A1] [2 marks] (c) Mean $=\dfrac{165.857}{2.54}=65.3$ inches [A1] Population standard deviation $=\dfrac{10.92}{2.54}=4.30$ inches [A1] [2 marks] (d) The exact heights within each class are unknown, so the midpoint is used to represent every value in the class [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Enter midpoints and frequencies in a GDC list and read $\bar{x}$ and $\sigma$. Dividing every value by a constant divides both the mean and the standard deviation by that constant.

subtopic: Quartiles and outliers from a frequency table
statement: The following table gives the number of siblings for each of 40 students. $\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline Siblings & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 \\ \hline Frequency & 6 & 12 & 10 & 7 & 3 & 2 \\ \hline \end{array}$ (a) Find the median number of siblings. [1] (b) Find the lower quartile, the upper quartile and the interquartile range. [3] (c) Show that a student with 7 siblings would be an outlier. [2] (d) Find the mean number of siblings. [1]
markscheme: (a) Cumulative frequencies $6,18,28,35,38,40$; the median is the mean of the 20th and 21st values, both equal to $2$, so the median is $2$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Lower quartile $=1$ (10th and 11th values) [A1] Upper quartile $=3$ (30th and 31st values) [A1] $\text{IQR}=3-1=2$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Upper boundary $=3+1.5\times2=6$ [M1] $7>6$, so 7 siblings is an outlier [A1] [2 marks] (d) $\dfrac{0+12+20+21+12+10}{40}=\dfrac{75}{40}=1.875$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: For quartiles from a frequency table, build the cumulative frequency column and locate the required positions in the ordered data. Use the 1.5 IQR rule with Q3 for upper outliers.

subtopic: Unbiased estimates from summed data
statement: A random sample of 10 values $x_1,\dots,x_{10}$ is taken from a population. The sample satisfies $\sum x=120$ and $\sum x^2=1500$. (a) Find the sample mean. [1] (b) Find the variance of the sample, $\sigma_n^2$ (dividing by $n$). [2] (c) Hence find the unbiased estimate of the population variance, $s_{n-1}^2$. [2] (d) Write down the exact value of the corresponding unbiased estimate of the population standard deviation. [1]
tips: Use $\sigma_n^2=\frac{\sum x^2}{n}-\bar x^2$ and then convert with the factor $\frac{n}{n-1}$. Remember that the unbiased estimate of the standard deviation is the square root of the unbiased variance.

subtopic: Cumulative frequency, median and quartiles
statement: A cycling club recorded the distances, in km, ridden by 80 members in a month. The cumulative frequencies are (upper class boundary: cumulative frequency) $<20$: 10; $<40$: 30; $<60$: 70; $<80$: 80, and the lowest value is 0. (a) State the number of observations and the position of the median. [2] (b) Use linear interpolation to estimate the median. [3] (c) Estimate the interquartile range. [3]
markscheme: (a) $n=80$ [A1] median at the $40$th value [A1] [2 marks] (b) median lies in class $40$ to $60$ [A1] $\dfrac{40-30}{40}\times20$ [M1] median $=45$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $Q_1=30$ [A1] $Q_3=55$ [A1] $IQR=25$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: On a cumulative frequency curve, the median is the value at $n/2$, the quartiles at $n/4$ and $3n/4$. Interpolate linearly inside the class where the cumulative frequency passes the target.

subtopic: Effect of adding an observation on mean and standard deviation
statement: The masses, in kg, of fifteen parcels were recorded. A set of $15$ values has mean $3.2$ and standard deviation $0.8$. A further value $5.6$ is added to the set. (a) Find the new mean. [2] (b) Find the new standard deviation. [3] (c) State, with a reason, whether the standard deviation increases or decreases when a value equal to the mean $3.2$ is added instead. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\sum x=15\times3.2=48.000$ [M1] new mean $=\dfrac{53.600}{16}=3.350$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\sum x^2=15(0.8^2+3.2^2)=163.200$ [M1] new $\sum x^2=194.560$ [A1] $\sigma=\sqrt{\dfrac{194.560}{16}-3.350^2}=0.968$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) a value equal to the mean adds nothing to $\sum(x-\bar x)^2$ but increases $n$ [R1] so the variance, and hence the standard deviation, decreases [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Reconstruct $\sum x$ and $\sum x^2$ from the mean and standard deviation, update both sums, then recompute. A new value at the mean leaves the sum of squared deviations unchanged while $n$ grows.

subtopic: Stratified sampling
statement: A researcher surveys businesses in a region. The population has 400 members split into groups: small firms (240), medium firms (100), large firms (60). A stratified sample of size $20$ is to be taken. (a) Find the number of members that should be sampled from each group. [3] (b) State one advantage of stratified sampling over simple random sampling. [1]
markscheme: (a) small firms: $\dfrac{240}{400}\times20=12$ [A1] medium firms: $\dfrac{100}{400}\times20=5$ [A1] large firms: $\dfrac{60}{400}\times20=3$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) the sample reflects the proportions of the groups in the population, so each group is represented [R1] [1 mark]
tips: In stratified sampling the sample size from each stratum is proportional to its size in the population.

subtopic: Systematic sampling
statement: The register of a school lists its 1260 students in order, numbered from 1 to 1260. A systematic sample of 90 students is to be taken. The first student chosen is number 9. (a) Find the interval between consecutive students selected. [1] (b) Find the number of the 90th student selected. [2] (c) The register alternates between boys and girls. Explain why this sample could be biased. [1] (d) State one advantage of systematic sampling over simple random sampling. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{1260}{90}=14$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Selected numbers are $9+14(k-1)$ [M1] 90th: $9+14\times89=1255$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) With an even interval of $14$, all selected students have the same parity of number, so they would all be of the same gender [R1] [1 mark] (d) Any one of: easier or quicker to carry out; no need for random number generation; sample spread evenly across the population [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Systematic sampling picks every $k$th item after a start; the $m$th item selected is the first plus $(m-1)k$. Watch for periodic patterns in the list that line up with the interval.

subtopic: Correcting a recorded data set
statement: A teacher records the scores of $40$ students in a test. The mean is calculated as $15.5$ and the standard deviation as $2.4$. Later it is found that one score of $9$ was wrongly recorded and should have been $19$. (a) Find the correct mean. [2] (b) Find the correct standard deviation. [4]
tips: Rebuild $\sum x$ and $\sum x^2$ from the stated mean and standard deviation, fix the two sums, then recompute.

subtopic: Median and quartiles from grouped data by interpolation
statement: The frequencies of scores in a test taken by $100$ students are: $0\le s<20$: $8$; $20\le s<40$: $17$; $40\le s<60$: $35$; $60\le s<80$: $28$; $80\le s\le100$: $12$. (a) Write down the cumulative frequencies at the upper class boundaries. [1] (b) Use linear interpolation to estimate the median and the upper quartile. [4] (c) The lower quartile is $40$. Find the interquartile range. [1]
markscheme: (a) $8,\ 25,\ 60,\ 88,\ 100$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) median is the $50$th value, in the class $40$ to $60$ [M1] $40+\dfrac{25}{35}\times20=54.3$ [A1] upper quartile is the $75$th value, in the class $60$ to $80$ [M1] $60+\dfrac{15}{28}\times20=70.7$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) $70.7-40=30.7$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Locate the class containing the required value, then assume the values are evenly spread through that class.

subtopic: Correcting a recorded data set
statement: A set of 25 numbers was recorded with a mean of $14.2$ and a standard deviation of $3.1$ (the population standard deviation, $\sigma_n$). It was later discovered that a value of $12$ had been wrongly recorded as $21$. (a) Find the correct mean. [3] (b) Find the correct standard deviation. [4]
tips: To correct a data set, recover $\sum x$ and $\sum x^2$ from the stated mean and variance, subtract the incorrect value and add the correct one. Do not simply adjust the mean or standard deviation directly.

subtopic: Correcting a recorded data set
statement: A teacher records the scores of $30$ students in a test. The mean is calculated as $62$ and the standard deviation as $8$. Later it is found that one score of $45$ was wrongly recorded and should have been $54$. (a) Find the correct mean. [2] (b) Find the correct standard deviation. [4]
tips: Rebuild $\sum x$ and $\sum x^2$ from the stated mean and standard deviation, fix the two sums, then recompute.

subtopic: Frequency table with an unknown frequency
statement: A test of four questions is marked out of 4 for a class. The frequency of each value is given below (value: frequency): 1: 1; 2: k; 3: 3; 4: 2. The mean of the data is $\frac{5}{2}$. (a) Find the value of $k$. [3] (b) Find the variance of the data. [3]
markscheme: (a) total frequency $=k + 6$ [M1] $\sum fx=2 k + 18$, and $\dfrac{\sum fx}{\sum f}=\frac{5}{2}$ gives $2 k + 18=\frac{5}{2}(k + 6)$ [M1] $k=6$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\sum fx^2=84$ and $n=12$ [M1] variance $=\dfrac{\sum fx^2}{n}-\bar x^2$ [M1] $=\frac{3}{4}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Write the total frequency in terms of $k$ first, then use mean $=\sum fx/\sum f$ to form an equation. Variance is the mean of the squares minus the square of the mean.

subtopic: Outliers preserved under a positive linear transformation
statement: A data set $x$ has lower quartile $Q_1=20$ and upper quartile $Q_3=32$. A value is an outlier if it is less than $Q_1-1.5\times\text{IQR}$ or greater than $Q_3+1.5\times\text{IQR}$. (a) Find the lower and upper limits for outliers in the data set $x$. [3] A new data set $y$ is formed using $y=3x-4$. (b) Find the quartiles and interquartile range of $y$, and hence find the lower and upper limits for outliers in $y$. [3] (c) More generally, let $y=ax+b$ where $a>0$. Show that a value $x_0$ is an outlier in the data set $x$ if and only if the corresponding value $ax_0+b$ is an outlier in the data set $y$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\text{IQR}=32-20=12$ [A1] $20-1.5\times12=2$ [A1] $32+1.5\times12=50$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $Q_1=3(20)-4=56$ and $Q_3=3(32)-4=92$ [A1] $\text{IQR}=36$ [A1] Limits: $56-54=2$ and $92+54=146$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $Q_1'=aQ_1+b$, $Q_3'=aQ_3+b$ so $\text{IQR}'=a\,\text{IQR}$ [M1] Lower limit for $y$: $aQ_1+b-1.5a\,\text{IQR}=a(Q_1-1.5\,\text{IQR})+b$, and similarly the upper limit is $a(Q_3+1.5\,\text{IQR})+b$, so both limits for $y$ are the images of the limits for $x$ [A1] Since $a>0$, $x\mapsto ax+b$ preserves order, so $x_0$ is below (or above) the limit for $x$ if and only if $ax_0+b$ is below (or above) the corresponding limit for $y$ [R1] [3 marks]
tips: A positive linear transformation scales the IQR by $a$ and shifts the quartiles with the data. In part (c), use $a>0$ explicitly when preserving the direction of an inequality.

subtopic: Frequency table with an unknown frequency
statement: The following table gives the number of goals scored by a team in a number of matches. The mean number of goals per match is $3$. $\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline Goals x & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 \\ \hline Frequency & 4 & k & 7 & 5 & 2 \\ \hline \end{array}$ (a) Find the value of $k$. [3] (b) Find the median number of goals. [2] (c) Find the variance of the number of goals per match. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\sum f=18+k$ and $\sum fx=4+2k+21+20+10=55+2k$ [A1] $\dfrac{55+2k}{18+k}=3$ [M1] $55+2k=54+3k$, so $k=1$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $n=19$, so the median is the 10th value [M1] Cumulative frequencies $4,5,12,\dots$, so the 10th value is $3$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\sum fx^2=4+4+63+80+50=201$ [A1] $\sigma^2=\dfrac{201}{19}-9=\dfrac{30}{19}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Write the mean as $\frac{\sum fx}{\sum f}$ and solve the resulting linear equation for the unknown frequency. For an odd total frequency, the median is the middle value, found from cumulative frequencies.

subtopic: Frequency table with an unknown frequency
statement: A shop records the number of items per customer basket. The frequency of each value is given below (value: frequency): 2: 2; 4: k; 6: 6; 8: 1. The mean of the data is $5$. (a) Find the value of $k$. [3] (b) Find the variance of the data. [3]
markscheme: (a) total frequency $=k + 9$ [M1] $\sum fx=4 k + 48$, and $\dfrac{\sum fx}{\sum f}=5$ gives $4 k + 48=5(k + 9)$ [M1] $k=3$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\sum fx^2=336$ and $n=12$ [M1] variance $=\dfrac{\sum fx^2}{n}-\bar x^2$ [M1] $=3$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Write the total frequency in terms of $k$ first, then use mean $=\sum fx/\sum f$ to form an equation. Variance is the mean of the squares minus the square of the mean.

subtopic: Mean equal to median with an unknown value
statement: Five positive numbers are $2,\ 5,\ x,\ 9,\ 14$. Find the positive values of $x$ for which the mean of the five numbers equals their median. [6]
