markscheme: mean $=\dfrac{30+x}5$ [A1] if $x\le5$ the median is $5$, giving $x=-5$, which is rejected [M1][A1] if $5\le x\le9$ the median is $x$, so $30+x=5x$ and $x=7.5$ [A1] if $x\ge9$ the median is $9$, so $30+x=45$ and $x=15$ [M1] valid in its case, so $x=7.5$ or $x=15$ [A1] [6 marks]
tips: The median depends on where $x$ lies in the order, so solve in cases: $x$ small, $x$ in the middle and $x$ large.

subtopic: Outliers using the 1.5 x IQR rule
statement: The scores of nine competitors in a quiz were recorded. The data, in increasing order, are $1, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19$. (a) Find the median and the lower and upper quartiles. [3] (b) Find the interquartile range. [1] (c) Determine, showing your working, whether the data contain any outliers. [3]
markscheme: (a) median $=15$ [A1] $Q_1=12.5$ [A1] $Q_3=17.5$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $IQR=17.5-12.5=5$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) upper fence $=17.5+1.5\times5=25$ [M1] lower fence $=12.5-1.5\times5=5$ [A1] $1$ lies outside the fences, so it is an outlier [R1] [3 marks]
tips: An outlier is a value more than $1.5\times IQR$ below $Q_1$ or above $Q_3$. Compute both fences before comparing.

subtopic: Effect of a linear change on summary statistics
statement: The marks of a group of students in a test were recorded. The mean is $40$ and the standard deviation is $5$. (a) Each value $x$ is replaced by $y=-3x+10$. Write down the mean and the standard deviation of $y$. [2] (b) Find $\sum y^2$ given that there are $n=20$ values. [3]
markscheme: (a) mean $=-3\times40+10=-110$ [A1] standard deviation $=3\times5=15$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) variance of $y$ $=225$ [M1] $\dfrac{\sum y^2}{20}--110^2=225$ [M1] $\sum y^2=246500$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A linear change $y=ax+b$ changes the mean to $a\bar x+b$ and the standard deviation to $|a|s$; the shift $b$ does not affect the spread.

subtopic: Finding a data set from its summary statistics
statement: Five positive integers $a\le b\le c\le d\le e$ have mean $6$, median $5$, range $7$, and a unique mode of $4$. Find the five integers. [5]
markscheme: sum $=30$ and $c=5$ [A1] mode $4$ is unique and the median is $5$, so $a=b=4$ [M1][A1] range $7$ gives $e=11$ [A1] then $d=30-4-4-5-11=6$, giving $4,4,5,6,11$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: Use each condition in turn. The median fixes the middle value, and a unique mode below it forces the two smallest values.

subtopic: Mean and standard deviation from coded sums
statement: A sample of $12$ values $x$ has $\sum(x-50)=-36$ and $\sum(x-50)^2=468$. (a) Find the mean of the sample. [2] (b) Find the standard deviation of the sample, correct to three significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\sum x-12\times50=-36$ so $\sum x=564$ [M1] mean $=\dfrac{564}{12}=47$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) variance of $(x-50)$ is $\dfrac{468}{12}-\left(\dfrac{-36}{12}\right)^2$ [M1][A1] $=39-9=30$ so the standard deviation of $x$ is $\sqrt{30}=5.48$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Subtracting a constant from every value shifts the mean by that constant but leaves the standard deviation unchanged.

subtopic: Frequency table: mean, spread and values within one standard deviation
statement: The number of defects found in each of $50$ batches of a product is recorded: $0$ defects in $7$ batches, $1$ in $12$, $2$ in $18$, $3$ in $9$, $4$ in $3$ and $5$ in $1$. (a) Find the mean and the standard deviation of the number of defects. [3] (b) Find the percentage of batches whose number of defects lies within one standard deviation of the mean. [3]
markscheme: (a) using the frequency table on the calculator [M1] mean $=1.84$ [A1] standard deviation $=1.17$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) interval $1.84\pm1.17$ is $(0.67,\,3.01)$ [M1] values $1,2,3$ lie inside [A1] $\dfrac{12+18+9}{50}=78\%$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Enter the values and frequencies as two lists and read the population standard deviation. Then check which whole numbers fall in the interval.

subtopic: Outliers using the 1.5 x IQR rule
statement: The number of emails received in ten days by an office was recorded. The data, in increasing order, are $3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 30$. (a) Find the median and the lower and upper quartiles. [3] (b) Find the interquartile range. [1] (c) Determine, showing your working, whether the data contain any outliers. [3]
markscheme: (a) median $=8.5$ [A1] $Q_1=6$ [A1] $Q_3=11$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $IQR=11-6=5$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) upper fence $=11+1.5\times5=18.5$ [M1] lower fence $=6-1.5\times5=-1.5$ [A1] $30$ lies outside the fences, so it is an outlier [R1] [3 marks]
tips: An outlier is a value more than $1.5\times IQR$ below $Q_1$ or above $Q_3$. Compute both fences before comparing.

subtopic: Percentages and percentiles from a cumulative frequency table
statement: The scores of $100$ students are summarized by the cumulative frequencies: $5$ students scored at most $20$, $18$ at most $40$, $46$ at most $60$, $83$ at most $80$ and all $100$ at most $100$. (a) Use linear interpolation to estimate the percentage of students who scored more than $70$. [3] (b) Estimate the $80$th percentile. [3]
markscheme: (a) cumulative frequency at $70$: $46+\dfrac{70-60}{20}\times37$ [M1] $=64.5$ [A1] $100-64.5=35.5\%$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) the $80$th student lies in the class $60$ to $80$ [M1] $60+\dfrac{80-46}{37}\times20$ [M1] $=78.4$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Between class boundaries, assume the cumulative frequency increases at a constant rate, so you can interpolate linearly.

subtopic: Outliers using the 1.5 x IQR rule
statement: A data set has lower quartile $Q_1=34$ and upper quartile $Q_3=52$. The smallest value in the data set is $3$ and the largest is $91$. (a) Find the interquartile range. [1] (b) Find the values that separate outliers from non-outliers, using the rule that a value is an outlier if it is more than $1.5\times\text{IQR}$ below $Q_1$ or above $Q_3$. [2] (c) State which of the smallest and largest values are outliers. [1] (d) The largest value is changed to an integer $k$. Find the smallest value of $k$ for which the largest value is an outlier. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\text{IQR}=52-34=18$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $1.5\times18=27$ [M1] Lower boundary $34-27=7$ and upper boundary $52+27=79$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $3<7$ and $91>79$, so both are outliers [A1] [1 mark] (d) $k>79$, so the smallest integer is $k=80$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Calculate both boundaries of the rule, not just the one you expect to matter. For a strict inequality, the smallest integer satisfying $k>79$ is $80$, not $79$.

subtopic: Mean and standard deviation from grouped data
statement: The distances, in km, travelled to work by employees were recorded. The grouped data are (class: frequency) $0\le x<5$: 3; $5\le x<10$: 9; $10\le x<15$: 14; $15\le x<20$: 10; $20\le x<25$: 4. (a) Write down the modal class. [1] (b) Use the midpoints of the classes to estimate the mean and the standard deviation. [3] (c) Estimate the median by linear interpolation. [3]
markscheme: (a) $10\le x<15$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) midpoints $2.5, 7.5, 12.5, 17.5, 22.5$ [M1] mean $\approx12.9$ [A1] standard deviation $\approx5.41$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) total frequency $40$ so median is the $20$th value [M1] the cumulative frequency reaches this in the class containing it, interpolate within that class [M1] median $\approx12.9$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Replace each class by its midpoint and enter the midpoints and frequencies as a list on your calculator. For the median, interpolate inside the class where the cumulative frequency passes $n/2$.

subtopic: Variance of the first n positive integers
statement: For the data $1,2,3,\ldots,n$ you may use $\sum_{k=1}^{n}k=\dfrac{n(n+1)}2$ and $\sum_{k=1}^{n}k^2=\dfrac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}6$. (a) Show that the mean is $\dfrac{n+1}2$. [1] (b) Show that the variance is $\dfrac{n^2-1}{12}$. [4] (c) Find the standard deviation of the data $1,2,\ldots,20$, to three significant figures. [2] (d) The data $1,2,\ldots,10$ are transformed to $y=ax+b$ so that $y$ has mean $0$ and standard deviation $1$, with $a>0$. Find $a$ and $b$ exactly. [3] (e) Hence show that $n$ equally spaced values with common difference $d$ have variance $\dfrac{d^2(n^2-1)}{12}$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac1n\times\dfrac{n(n+1)}2=\dfrac{n+1}2$ [AG] [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\sigma^2=\dfrac{\sum k^2}n-\bar x^2$ [M1] $=\dfrac{(n+1)(2n+1)}6-\dfrac{(n+1)^2}4$ [A1] $=\dfrac{(n+1)\left[2(2n+1)-3(n+1)\right]}{12}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{(n+1)(n-1)}{12}$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) variance $=\dfrac{399}{12}=33.25$ [A1] standard deviation $=5.77$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) variance of $x$ is $\dfrac{99}{12}=\dfrac{33}4$ [A1] $a^2\times\dfrac{33}4=1$ so $a=\dfrac2{\sqrt{33}}$ [A1] mean of $x$ is $5.5$, so $5.5a+b=0$ and $b=-\dfrac{11}{\sqrt{33}}$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) the values are $d\times(1,2,\ldots,n)$ plus a constant [M1] multiplying by $d$ multiplies the variance by $d^2$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Use the computational formula for variance with the two standard sums. For the last part, think of how a linear change $y=ax+b$ affects mean and variance.

subtopic: Cumulative frequency, median and quartiles
statement: A survey recorded the time, in minutes, that 60 students spent on homework one evening. The cumulative frequencies are (upper class boundary: cumulative frequency) $<10$: 8; $<20$: 28; $<30$: 48; $<40$: 60, and the lowest value is 0. (a) State the number of observations and the position of the median. [2] (b) Use linear interpolation to estimate the median. [3] (c) Estimate the interquartile range. [3]
markscheme: (a) $n=60$ [A1] median at the $30$th value [A1] [2 marks] (b) median lies in class $20$ to $30$ [A1] $\dfrac{30-28}{20}\times10$ [M1] median $=21$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $Q_1=13.5$ [A1] $Q_3=28.5$ [A1] $IQR=15$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: On a cumulative frequency curve, the median is the value at $n/2$, the quartiles at $n/4$ and $3n/4$. Interpolate linearly inside the class where the cumulative frequency passes the target.

subtopic: Mean and variance of data taking two values
statement: A data set has $2m$ values, of which $m$ are equal to $a$ and $m$ are equal to $b$, where $a<b$. (a) Show that the mean is $\dfrac{a+b}2$. [2] (b) Show that the variance is $\left(\dfrac{b-a}2\right)^2$. [3] (c) A data set has $20$ values, with ten equal to $3$ and ten equal to $11$. Find its mean and standard deviation. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{ma+mb}{2m}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{a+b}2$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) each value is $\dfrac{b-a}2$ from the mean [M1][A1] variance is the mean of the squared deviations, which are all equal to $\left(\dfrac{b-a}2\right)^2$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) mean $=7$ [A1] standard deviation $=\dfrac{11-3}2=4$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Every value lies the same distance from the mean, so every squared deviation is identical.

subtopic: Combining the mean and standard deviation of two groups
statement: Two classes sat the same test. Group A has $10$ values with mean $5$ and variance $4$. Group B has $10$ values with mean $9$ and variance $4$. (a) Find the mean of all the values combined. [2] (b) Find the variance of all the values combined. [4]
tips: Variances cannot be averaged directly. Recover $\sum x^2$ for each group using $\sum x^2=n(\sigma^2+\bar x^2)$, add, then subtract the square of the combined mean.

subtopic: Adding a value equal to the mean
statement: A data set has $n$ values, with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$. A new value, equal to $\mu$, is added to the data set. (a) Show that the mean of the new data set is still $\mu$. [1] (b) Show that the variance of the new data set is $\dfrac{n\sigma^2}{n+1}$. [3] (c) The original data set has $24$ values with variance $50$. Find the standard deviation of the new data set. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{n\mu+\mu}{n+1}=\mu$ [AG] [A1] [1 mark] (b) sum of squared deviations from $\mu$ is $n\sigma^2+0$ [M1][A1] divide by the new number of values $n+1$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) new variance $=\dfrac{24\times50}{25}=48$ [M1] standard deviation $=\sqrt{48}=4\sqrt3$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The sum of squared deviations $\sum(x-\mu)^2$ does not change when a value equal to the mean is added, but the number of values does.

subtopic: Stratified and convenience sampling
statement: A school has 900 students: 300 in Year 9, 240 in Year 10, 210 in Year 11 and 150 in Year 12. A survey is to be given to a stratified random sample of 90 students, with strata based on year group. (a) Find the number of students from each year group in the sample. [3] A teacher suggests instead surveying the first 90 students to arrive at school on Monday. (b) State one disadvantage of this sampling method. [1] (c) State one advantage of stratified sampling over simple random sampling. [1]
markscheme: (a) Sampling fraction $=\dfrac{90}{900}=\dfrac{1}{10}$ [M1] Year 9: $30$, Year 10: $24$ [A1] Year 11: $21$, Year 12: $15$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Any one of: the sample is a convenience sample and is likely biased (e.g. early arrivals may be unrepresentative); not random; not all students have an equal chance of selection [A1] [1 mark] (c) Any one of: each year group is represented in proportion to its size; reduces sampling variability; guarantees every year group appears in the sample [A1] [1 mark]
tips: In stratified sampling each stratum is represented in proportion to its size in the population. When criticizing a sampling method, refer to bias or lack of randomness.

subtopic: Range of values giving no outliers
statement: A data set has lower quartile $14$ and upper quartile $22$. A value is an outlier if it is more than $1.5\times\text{IQR}$ above the upper quartile or below the lower quartile. (a) Calculate the interquartile range and the two boundaries beyond which values are outliers. [3] (b) The largest value in the data set is $k$ and the smallest is $5$. Find the largest integer $k$ for which neither extreme value is an outlier, and state whether $k=35$ would be an outlier. [2]
markscheme: (a) IQR $=22-14=8$ [A1] upper boundary $22+1.5\times8=34$ [M1] lower boundary $14-12=2$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) largest $k$ is $34$ [A1] $k=35$ exceeds $34$, so it is an outlier [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Compute the fences $Q_3+1.5\,\text{IQR}$ and $Q_1-1.5\,\text{IQR}$ first, then compare each extreme value with them.

subtopic: Combining the mean and standard deviation of two groups
statement: Two machines each filled bags of flour; the masses of the bags, in grams above a target, were recorded. Group A has $20$ values with mean $12$ and variance $9$. Group B has $30$ values with mean $17$ and variance $16$. (a) Find the mean of all the values combined. [2] (b) Find the variance of all the values combined. [4]
tips: Variances cannot be averaged directly. Recover $\sum x^2$ for each group using $\sum x^2=n(\sigma^2+\bar x^2)$, add, then subtract the square of the combined mean.

subtopic: Quartiles and standard deviation from a frequency table
statement: The numbers of goals scored in each of 40 matches were recorded. The frequency table is (value: frequency) 0: 4; 1: 9; 2: 12; 3: 8; 4: 5; 5: 2. (a) Find the mean and the standard deviation. [3] (b) Find the median and the interquartile range. [3]
markscheme: (a) enter values and frequencies [M1] mean $=2.175$ [A1] standard deviation $=1.32$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) median $=2$ [A1] $Q_1=1$, $Q_3=3$ [A1] $IQR=2$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Use the one-variable statistics function with a frequency list. Quartiles come from the cumulative frequencies.

subtopic: Mean and standard deviation from grouped data
statement: The ages of the customers at a café one morning were recorded. The grouped data are (class: frequency) $0\le x<10$: 5; $10\le x<20$: 12; $20\le x<30$: 18; $30\le x<40$: 5. (a) Write down the modal class. [1] (b) Use the midpoints of the classes to estimate the mean and the standard deviation. [3] (c) Estimate the median by linear interpolation. [3]
markscheme: (a) $20\le x<30$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) midpoints $5, 15, 25, 35$ [M1] mean $\approx20.8$ [A1] standard deviation $\approx8.63$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) total frequency $40$ so median is the $20$th value [M1] the cumulative frequency reaches this in the class containing it, interpolate within that class [M1] median $\approx21.7$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Replace each class by its midpoint and enter the midpoints and frequencies as a list on your calculator. For the median, interpolate inside the class where the cumulative frequency passes $n/2$.

subtopic: Effect of removing an outlier on mean and standard deviation
statement: The daily sales, in thousands of dollars, of a shop were recorded over $21$ days. The mean was $8.5$ and the standard deviation was $2.1$. The sales of $15$ thousand on one exceptional day are then excluded from the data. (a) Find the mean of the remaining sales. [2] (b) Find the standard deviation of the remaining sales. [3]
tips: Rebuild the sums from the summary statistics, subtract the excluded value (and its square), and divide by the new count.

subtopic: Effect of a linear change on summary statistics
statement: A data set $x$ has mean $14$, standard deviation $3$, median $13$ and interquartile range $5$. A new data set is defined by $y=2x-4$ for each value. (a) Write down the mean and standard deviation of $y$. [2] (b) Write down the median and interquartile range of $y$. [2] (c) Write down the variance of $y$. [1]
markscheme: (a) Mean $=2(14)-4=24$ [A1] Standard deviation $=2\times3=6$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Median $=2(13)-4=22$ [A1] Interquartile range $=2\times5=10$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $6^2=36$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Measures of location (mean, median) change with both the multiplier and the constant, but measures of spread (standard deviation, IQR) are affected only by the multiplier. Variance is the square of the standard deviation.

subtopic: Mean and standard deviation from grouped data
statement: The masses, in kg, of parcels at a depot were recorded. The grouped data are (class: frequency) $20\le x<30$: 8; $30\le x<40$: 14; $40\le x<50$: 20; $50\le x<60$: 6. (a) Write down the modal class. [1] (b) Use the midpoints of the classes to estimate the mean and the standard deviation. [3] (c) Estimate the median by linear interpolation. [3]
markscheme: (a) $40\le x<50$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) midpoints $25, 35, 45, 55$ [M1] mean $\approx40.0$ [A1] standard deviation $\approx9.13$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) total frequency $48$ so median is the $24$th value [M1] the cumulative frequency reaches this in the class containing it, interpolate within that class [M1] median $\approx41.0$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Replace each class by its midpoint and enter the midpoints and frequencies as a list on your calculator. For the median, interpolate inside the class where the cumulative frequency passes $n/2$.

subtopic: Quota sampling by age group
statement: A town has 4800 adult residents: 2000 aged 18 to 34, 1700 aged 35 to 59 and 1100 aged 60 or over. A researcher wants a sample of 240 residents, using quota sampling by age group. (a) Find the quota for each age group. [3] (b) The researcher interviews people outside a shopping center on a weekday morning until every quota is filled. State one advantage of quota sampling compared with simple random sampling, and one reason the sample may still be biased. [2]
markscheme: (a) Sampling fraction $=\dfrac{240}{4800}=\dfrac{1}{20}$ [M1] 18 to 34: $\dfrac{2000}{20}=100$ [A1] 35 to 59: $85$ and 60 or over: $55$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Advantage, for example: no sampling frame (list of all residents) is needed, so it is quicker and cheaper [A1] Bias, for example: only people at the shopping center on weekday mornings are reached, so working residents or those who rarely shop there are under-represented [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Quotas are proportional to group size. Note that quota sampling is non-random: within each quota the interviewer chooses who is asked, which can introduce bias.

subtopic: Proof of the computational formula for variance
statement: A data set $x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n$ has mean $\bar x$ and variance $\sigma^2=\dfrac1n\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2$. (a) Show that $\sum(x_i-\bar x)=0$. [2] (b) Show that $\sigma^2=\dfrac{\sum x_i^2}n-\bar x^2$. [4] (c) Hence show that $\dfrac{\sum x_i^2}n\ge\bar x^2$, with equality only when all the values are equal. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\sum x_i-n\bar x$ [M1] $=n\bar x-n\bar x=0$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2=\sum x_i^2-2\bar x\sum x_i+n\bar x^2$ [M1][A1] $=\sum x_i^2-2n\bar x^2+n\bar x^2$ [M1] $=\sum x_i^2-n\bar x^2$; dividing by $n$ gives the result [A1] [4 marks] (c) $\sigma^2\ge0$ so $\dfrac{\sum x_i^2}n-\bar x^2\ge0$ [R1] $\sigma^2=0$ only when every $x_i=\bar x$ [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Expand the square inside the sum, then use $\sum x_i=n\bar x$ to simplify. A variance can never be negative.

subtopic: Frequencies and mean from a histogram with unequal class widths
statement: A histogram has four classes. The classes and their frequency densities are: $0\le x<10$ with density $1.2$; $10\le x<20$ with density $2.5$; $20\le x<40$ with density $1.6$; $40\le x<70$ with density $0.5$. (a) Find the frequency of each class. [2] (b) Find an estimate of the mean of $x$, giving your answer as an exact fraction. [4]
markscheme: (a) frequency $=$ density $\times$ class width [M1] $12$, $25$, $32$, $15$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) total frequency $84$ [A1] midpoints $5,15,30,55$ [A1] $\dfrac{5\times12+15\times25+30\times32+55\times15}{84}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{2220}{84}=\dfrac{185}7$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: In a histogram the area, not the height, is proportional to frequency. Use midpoints of classes for the mean estimate.

subtopic: Comparing results using standardized scores
statement: In a mathematics test the class mean was $62$ and the standard deviation was $8$. In a physics test the class mean was $55$ and the standard deviation was $5$. Dara scored $74$ in mathematics and $64$ in physics. (a) Calculate Dara's standardized score $z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$ in each subject. [2] (b) State, with a reason, in which subject Dara performed better relative to the class. [1] (c) In a chemistry test the mean was $70$ and the standard deviation was $12$. Find the score that would give Dara $z=1.65$. [2]
markscheme: (a) mathematics $z=\dfrac{74-62}8=1.5$ [A1] physics $z=\dfrac{64-55}5=1.8$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) physics, since $1.8>1.5$ means her mark was further above the mean in standard deviations [R1] [1 mark] (c) $\dfrac{x-70}{12}=1.65$ [M1] $x=89.8$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A standardized score measures how many standard deviations a value is above or below the mean, so it allows comparison between different scales.

subtopic: The mean minimizes the sum of squared deviations
statement: For the data $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ with mean $\bar x$, define $f(a)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-a)^2$. (a) Show that $f(a)=na^2-2a\sum x_i+\sum x_i^2$. [2] (b) Hence show that $f$ is least when $a=\bar x$. [3] (c) For the data $3,\ 5,\ 10$, find the minimum value of $f$. [2]
markscheme: (a) expand each $(x_i-a)^2=x_i^2-2ax_i+a^2$ [M1] sum over $i$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $f'(a)=2na-2\sum x_i$ [M1] $=0$ when $a=\dfrac{\sum x_i}n=\bar x$ [A1] $f$ is an upward parabola, so this is a minimum [R1] [3 marks] (c) $\bar x=6$ [A1] $f(6)=9+1+16=26$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Treat $f$ as a quadratic in $a$. Its vertex occurs at the mean.

subtopic: Effect of changing the largest value on summary statistics
statement: A data set is $2,\ 4,\ 5,\ 7,\ 9,\ 10,\ 12$. The largest value, $12$, is replaced by $30$. Quartiles are the medians of the lower and upper halves of the data, excluding the median. (a) Find the mean before and after the change. [2] (b) State which of the median, the range and the interquartile range change, giving the new values of those that do. [4]
markscheme: (a) before: $\dfrac{49}7=7$ [A1] after: $\dfrac{67}7=9.57$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) median stays $7$ [A1] range changes from $10$ to $28$ [A1] $Q_1=4$ and $Q_3=10$ before; after the change $Q_3$ is still $10$ [M1] so the interquartile range is unchanged at $6$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: The median and quartiles depend on the positions of values, not their sizes, unless a value that defines them is changed.

subtopic: Mean and variance of two combined data sets
statement: Data set $A$ has $8$ values with mean $12$ and variance $9$. Data set $B$ has $12$ values with mean $17$ and variance $16$. The two sets are combined into one data set of $20$ values. (a) Show that for a set of $m$ values with mean $\mu$ and variance $s^2$, $\sum x^2=m(s^2+\mu^2)$. [2] (b) Find the mean of the combined data set. [2] (c) Find the variance of the combined data set. [4] (d) Show that the combined variance equals $\dfrac{8\times9+12\times16}{20}+\dfrac{8\times12}{20^2}(17-12)^2$, and interpret the two terms. [3] (e) State the condition under which the combined variance is exactly the weighted mean of the two variances. [1]
markscheme: (a) $s^2=\dfrac{\sum x^2}m-\mu^2$ [M1] rearrange [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac{8\times12+12\times17}{20}$ [M1] $=15$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\sum x^2$ for $A$ is $8(9+144)=1224$ [A1] for $B$: $12(16+289)=3660$ [A1] variance $=\dfrac{1224+3660}{20}-15^2$ [M1] $=19.2$ [A1] [4 marks] (d) first term $=\dfrac{264}{20}=13.2$ [A1] second term $=\dfrac{96\times25}{400}=6$, and $13.2+6=19.2$ [A1] the first term is the average spread within the sets, the second is the spread caused by the sets having different means [R1] [3 marks] (e) the two sets have equal means [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Use $\sum x^2=m(s^2+\mu^2)$ for each set, add, and divide by the total number of values before subtracting the square of the combined mean.

subtopic: Unbiased estimates from a sample
statement: A random sample of the masses, in kg, of eight packages is $12.1,\ 11.8,\ 12.6,\ 12.3,\ 11.9,\ 12.4,\ 12.0,\ 12.5$. (a) Find an unbiased estimate of the population mean. [1] (b) Find an unbiased estimate of the population variance. [2] (c) Explain why the sample variance obtained by dividing $\sum(x-\bar x)^2$ by $n$ is not used as an estimate of the population variance. [2] (d) Find the median mass of the eight packages. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\bar x=12.2$ kg [A1] [1 mark] (b) Use of GDC to obtain $s_{n-1}$ (sample standard deviation with $n-1$) [M1] $s_{n-1}^2=0.0857$ (or $\dfrac{0.6}{7}$) [A1] [2 marks] (c) Dividing by $n$ gives a biased estimator [R1] which on average underestimates the population variance; dividing by $n-1$ corrects this [R1] [2 marks] (d) Ordered values $11.8,11.9,12.0,12.1,12.3,12.4,12.5,12.6$; median $=\dfrac{12.1+12.3}{2}=12.2$ kg [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Make sure you read $s_{n-1}$ from the calculator, not $\sigma_n$. Square it to obtain the unbiased estimate of the variance.

subtopic: Bounds on the mean of grouped data
statement: The lengths $x$ cm of $50$ leaves are grouped: $10\le x<20$: $6$ leaves; $20\le x<30$: $14$; $30\le x<40$: $20$; $40\le x<50$: $10$. (a) Calculate an estimate of the mean length using the midpoint of each class. [2] (b) Find the least possible and the greatest possible value of the mean, if the exact data were known. [3] (c) Explain why the estimate in part (a) lies exactly halfway between these bounds. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{15\times6+25\times14+35\times20+45\times10}{50}$ [M1] $=31.8$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) least: every value equals the lower class boundary $\dfrac{10\times6+20\times14+30\times20+40\times10}{50}$ [M1] $=26.8$ [A1] greatest: add $10$ to the least (each class has width $10$) $=36.8$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) all classes have the same width, so each midpoint is exactly half a class width above its lower bound and below its upper bound [R1] [1 mark]
tips: The least possible mean uses every value at the bottom of its class, and the greatest uses the top of each class.

subtopic: Flagging outliers beyond two standard deviations
statement: The masses, in grams, of $12$ packets are: $48,\ 51,\ 52,\ 49,\ 50,\ 53,\ 47,\ 51,\ 50,\ 52,\ 49,\ 86$. A value is flagged as unusual if it is more than $2$ standard deviations from the mean. (a) Find the mean and the standard deviation of the masses. [2] (b) Identify the values that are flagged as unusual. [2] (c) The flagged value is removed. Find the new mean and standard deviation, and comment on the effect on the standard deviation. [3]
markscheme: (a) mean $=53.2$ [A1] standard deviation $=10.0$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) interval $53.2\pm2\times10.0$ is $(33.1,\ 73.2)$ [M1] only $86$ lies outside [A1] [2 marks] (c) new mean $=50.2$ [A1] new standard deviation $=1.75$ [A1] the standard deviation falls sharply because the extreme value inflated the spread [R1] [3 marks]
tips: Use the population standard deviation from the calculator. An extreme value affects the standard deviation far more than the median.

subtopic: Stratified sampling
statement: A school wants to survey students about its canteen. The population has 400 members split into groups: Year 10 (150), Year 11 (120), Year 12 (130). A stratified sample of size $40$ is to be taken. (a) Find the number of members that should be sampled from each group. [3] (b) State one advantage of stratified sampling over simple random sampling. [1]
markscheme: (a) Year 10: $\dfrac{150}{400}\times40=15$ [A1] Year 11: $\dfrac{120}{400}\times40=12$ [A1] Year 12: $\dfrac{130}{400}\times40=13$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) the sample reflects the proportions of the groups in the population, so each group is represented [R1] [1 mark]
tips: In stratified sampling the sample size from each stratum is proportional to its size in the population.

subtopic: Box plot interpretation from summary values
statement: The ages of the 120 members of a sports club are summarized by the following: minimum $12$, lower quartile $18$, median $23$, upper quartile $31$ and maximum $52$. The largest age that is not an outlier is $47$. A box-and-whisker plot of the ages is to be drawn. (a) Find the interquartile range. [1] (b) Show that the maximum age of $52$ is an outlier. [2] (c) Write down the values at the two ends of the whiskers on the box plot. [1] (d) Describe the skewness of the distribution, giving a reason. [2]
markscheme: (a) $31-18=13$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $Q_3+1.5\times\text{IQR}=31+19.5=50.5$ [M1] $52>50.5$, so $52$ is an outlier [A1] [2 marks] (c) $12$ and $47$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) Median to $Q_3$ is $8$, which is greater than $Q_1$ to median ($5$) [R1] so the distribution is positively skewed (skewed to the right) [R1] [2 marks]
tips: The upper whisker ends at the largest value that is not an outlier, and outliers are plotted separately. Compare the lengths of the two halves of the box to describe skewness.

subtopic: Combining the mean and standard deviation of two groups
statement: Group $A$ has 20 students with a mean test score of $60$ and a standard deviation of $5$. Group $B$ has 30 students with a mean test score of $70$ and a standard deviation of $4$. (The standard deviations are population standard deviations, $\sigma_n$.) (a) Find the mean score of all 50 students. [2] (b) Find the standard deviation of the scores of all 50 students. [4]
tips: You cannot average two standard deviations; instead recover $\sum x^2$ for each group, add them, and recompute the variance about the combined mean. Use unrounded values throughout.

subtopic: Choosing between the mean and the median
statement: The annual salaries, in thousands of dollars, of seven employees are $28,\ 30,\ 30,\ 32,\ 35,\ 38,\ 180$. (a) Find the mean, the median and the mode of the salaries. [3] (b) State, with a reason, which measure best describes a typical salary. [1] (c) Every salary is increased by $5\%$. State the new median and find the new standard deviation, given that the original standard deviation is $51.8$ (to three significant figures). [3]
markscheme: (a) mean $=\dfrac{373}7=53.3$ [A1] median $=32$ [A1] mode $=30$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) the median (or mode), because the value $180$ pulls the mean far above most salaries [R1] [1 mark] (c) new median $=1.05\times32=33.6$ [A1] standard deviation is multiplied by $1.05$ [M1] $1.05\times51.8=54.4$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A multiplicative change of $k$ multiplies the median, mean and standard deviation by $k$.

subtopic: Outliers using the 1.5 x IQR rule
statement: The delivery times, in minutes, of twelve orders were recorded. The data, in increasing order, are $20, 22, 23, 25, 26, 27, 28, 30, 31, 32, 33, 60$. (a) Find the median and the lower and upper quartiles. [3] (b) Find the interquartile range. [1] (c) Determine, showing your working, whether the data contain any outliers. [3]
markscheme: (a) median $=27.5$ [A1] $Q_1=24$ [A1] $Q_3=31.5$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $IQR=31.5-24=7.5$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) upper fence $=31.5+1.5\times7.5=42.75$ [M1] lower fence $=24-1.5\times7.5=12.75$ [A1] $60$ lies outside the fences, so it is an outlier [R1] [3 marks]
tips: An outlier is a value more than $1.5\times IQR$ below $Q_1$ or above $Q_3$. Compute both fences before comparing.

subtopic: Effect of a linear change on summary statistics
statement: The times, in minutes, taken by a group of runners were recorded. The mean is $12$ and the standard deviation is $3$. (a) Each value $x$ is replaced by $y=2x+5$. Write down the mean and the standard deviation of $y$. [2] (b) Find $\sum y^2$ given that there are $n=10$ values. [3]
markscheme: (a) mean $=2\times12+5=29$ [A1] standard deviation $=2\times3=6$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) variance of $y$ $=36$ [M1] $\dfrac{\sum y^2}{10}-29^2=36$ [M1] $\sum y^2=8770$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A linear change $y=ax+b$ changes the mean to $a\bar x+b$ and the standard deviation to $|a|s$; the shift $b$ does not affect the spread.

subtopic: Box plot interpretation from summary values
statement: The scores of 120 players in a game were recorded. The five-number summary of $120$ values is minimum $12$, lower quartile $35$, median $41$, upper quartile $52$, maximum $70$. (a) Find the range and the interquartile range. [2] (b) Approximately how many of the $120$ values are greater than $52$? [1] (c) Determine whether the maximum value is an outlier. [3]
markscheme: (a) range $=70-12=58$ [A1] $IQR=52-35=17$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) about a quarter of the values, so about $30$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) upper fence $=52+1.5\times17=77.5$ [M1][A1] 70 is not greater than the fence, so it is not an outlier [R1] [3 marks]
tips: A quarter of the data lies above the upper quartile. The outlier test compares the extreme value with $Q_3+1.5\times IQR$.

subtopic: Describing skewness from summary statistics
statement: The summary statistics for a data set are minimum $12$, lower quartile $20$, median $26$, upper quartile $40$, maximum $75$ and mean $31$. (a) State, with two reasons, whether the distribution is skewed to the right or to the left. [3] (b) Determine whether the maximum value is an outlier, according to the $1.5\times\text{IQR}$ rule. [3]
markscheme: (a) positive (right) skew [A1] $Q_3-Q_2=14>Q_2-Q_1=6$ [R1] mean $31>$ median $26$ [R1] [3 marks] (b) IQR $=20$ [A1] upper boundary $40+1.5\times20=70$ [M1] $75>70$ so it is an outlier [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Compare the distances from the median to each quartile, and compare mean with median. A long tail pulls the mean towards it.

subtopic: Weighted mean of course components
statement: A course grade is a weighted mean: coursework counts $30\%$, a project $25\%$ and the final exam $45\%$. Sam scored $72$ in coursework and $64$ in the project. (a) Find Sam's course grade if the final exam score is $60$. [2] (b) Find the lowest exam score that gives a course grade of at least $70$. [3]
tips: Multiply each score by its weight (as a decimal) and add. For the second part, form an inequality in the exam score.

subtopic: Box plot interpretation from summary values
statement: The times, in minutes, taken by 80 commuters to reach work were recorded. The five-number summary of $80$ values is minimum $4$, lower quartile $10$, median $14$, upper quartile $19$, maximum $40$. (a) Find the range and the interquartile range. [2] (b) Approximately how many of the $80$ values are greater than $19$? [1] (c) Determine whether the maximum value is an outlier. [3]
markscheme: (a) range $=40-4=36$ [A1] $IQR=19-10=9$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) about a quarter of the values, so about $20$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) upper fence $=19+1.5\times9=32.5$ [M1][A1] 40 is greater than the fence, so it is an outlier [R1] [3 marks]
tips: A quarter of the data lies above the upper quartile. The outlier test compares the extreme value with $Q_3+1.5\times IQR$.

subtopic: Effect of adding an observation on mean and standard deviation
statement: The ages of members of a book club were recorded. A set of $24$ values has mean $52$ and standard deviation $6$. A further value $70$ is added to the set. (a) Find the new mean. [2] (b) Find the new standard deviation. [3] (c) State, with a reason, whether the standard deviation increases or decreases when a value equal to the mean $52$ is added instead. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\sum x=24\times52=1248.0$ [M1] new mean $=\dfrac{1318.0}{25}=52.72$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\sum x^2=24(6^2+52^2)=65760.0$ [M1] new $\sum x^2=70660.0$ [A1] $\sigma=\sqrt{\dfrac{70660.0}{25}-52.72^2}=6.86$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) a value equal to the mean adds nothing to $\sum(x-\bar x)^2$ but increases $n$ [R1] so the variance, and hence the standard deviation, decreases [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Reconstruct $\sum x$ and $\sum x^2$ from the mean and standard deviation, update both sums, then recompute. A new value at the mean leaves the sum of squared deviations unchanged while $n$ grows.

subtopic: Frequency table with an unknown frequency
statement: Students in a school club recorded the number of books they read in a month. The frequency of each value is given below (value: frequency): 0: 3; 1: k; 2: 5; 3: 3. The mean of the data is $\frac{3}{2}$. (a) Find the value of $k$. [3] (b) Find the variance of the data. [3]
markscheme: (a) total frequency $=k + 11$ [M1] $\sum fx=k + 19$, and $\dfrac{\sum fx}{\sum f}=\frac{3}{2}$ gives $k + 19=\frac{3}{2}(k + 11)$ [M1] $k=5$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\sum fx^2=52$ and $n=16$ [M1] variance $=\dfrac{\sum fx^2}{n}-\bar x^2$ [M1] $=1$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Write the total frequency in terms of $k$ first, then use mean $=\sum fx/\sum f$ to form an equation. Variance is the mean of the squares minus the square of the mean.

subtopic: Mean and standard deviation from grouped data
statement: The times, in minutes, taken by 40 students to complete a puzzle are summarized in the table. $\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline Time t & 0\le t<10 & 10\le t<20 & 20\le t<30 & 30\le t<40 & 40\le t<50 \\ \hline Frequency & 4 & 9 & 15 & 8 & 4 \\ \hline \end{array}$ (a) Estimate the mean time taken. [2] (b) Estimate the standard deviation of the times. [2] (c) Write down the modal class. [1] (d) Find the percentage of students who took less than 20 minutes. [1]
markscheme: (a) Use of midpoints $5,15,25,35,45$ [M1] $\bar t=\dfrac{990}{40}=24.75$ minutes [A1] [2 marks] (b) Use of GDC (or formula) with midpoints [M1] $\sigma=11.1$ minutes [A1] [2 marks] (c) $20\le t<30$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) $\dfrac{4+9}{40}=32.5\%$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: For grouped data always use the class midpoints and state that the results are estimates. Enter the midpoints and frequencies as two lists in your calculator and read off $\bar x$ and $\sigma_x$.

subtopic: Effect of a linear change on summary statistics
statement: The lengths, in cm, of some seedlings were measured. The mean is $8$ and the standard deviation is $1.5$. (a) Each value $x$ is replaced by $y=4x-6$. Write down the mean and the standard deviation of $y$. [2] (b) Find $\sum y^2$ given that there are $n=15$ values. [3]
markscheme: (a) mean $=4\times8-6=26$ [A1] standard deviation $=4\times1.5=6.0$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) variance of $y$ $=36.0$ [M1] $\dfrac{\sum y^2}{15}-26^2=36.0$ [M1] $\sum y^2=10680.0$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A linear change $y=ax+b$ changes the mean to $a\bar x+b$ and the standard deviation to $|a|s$; the shift $b$ does not affect the spread.

subtopic: Five-number summary after a decreasing linear transformation
statement: A data set $x$ has minimum $4$, lower quartile $9$, median $12$, upper quartile $18$ and maximum $30$. A new data set is defined by $y=10-2x$. (a) Find the median and the range of $y$. [3] (b) Find the lower and upper quartiles of $y$, and the interquartile range of $y$. [3]
markscheme: (a) median of $y=10-2\times12=-14$ [A1] range of $x=26$ [A1] range of $y=2\times26=52$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) the order reverses, so $Q_1(y)=10-2\times18=-26$ [M1][A1] $Q_3(y)=10-2\times9=-8$, so $\text{IQR}=18$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A negative multiplier reverses the order of the data, so the lower quartile of $y$ comes from the upper quartile of $x$.

subtopic: Modelling with a 3x3 linear system
statement: A florist makes three types of bouquet, $A$, $B$ and $C$. Each bouquet $A$ uses 5 roses, 3 lilies and 4 tulips. Each bouquet $B$ uses 3 roses, 6 lilies and 2 tulips. Each bouquet $C$ uses 2 roses, 4 lilies and 7 tulips. The florist has exactly 123 roses, 162 lilies and 141 tulips, and uses all of them. Let $a$, $b$ and $c$ be the numbers of bouquets of types $A$, $B$ and $C$ made. (a) Write down a system of three linear equations in $a$, $b$ and $c$. [3] (b) Hence find the number of bouquets of each type. [3]
markscheme: (a) Roses: $5a+3b+2c=123$ [A1] Lilies: $3a+6b+4c=162$ [A1] Tulips: $4a+2b+7c=141$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Attempt to solve the system using a GDC (e.g. matrix inverse or polynomial/simultaneous solver) [M1] $a=12$ [A1] $b=15$ and $c=9$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Define your variables clearly and set up one equation per resource. On Paper 2, solving a $3\times3$ system with the GDC is expected, so write down the equations carefully, then use the solver.

subtopic: Consistency conditions for a system with two parameters
statement: Consider the system of equations $$\begin{aligned} x+y+2z&=1\\ 2x+3y+z&=3\\ 3x+4y+az&=b \end{aligned}$$ where $a,b\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Show that if $a\neq3$ the system has a unique solution, and find $x$, $y$ and $z$ in terms of $a$ and $b$. [5] (b) Show that when $a=3$ the system is consistent if and only if $b=4$. [2] (c) Given that $a=3$ and $b=4$, find the general solution in terms of a parameter $\lambda$ where $z=\lambda$. [2] (d) Given that $a=3$ and $b\neq4$, describe the geometrical arrangement of the three planes. [1]
markscheme: (a) Add the first two equations: $3x+4y+3z=4$; subtract this from the third equation [M1] $(a-3)z=b-4$ [A1] Since $a\neq3$, $z=\dfrac{b-4}{a-3}$, which gives a unique solution [R1] Substitute in the first two equations: $x+y=1-2z$ and $2x+3y=3-z$ [M1] $y=1+3z$ and $x=-5z$, so $x=\dfrac{-5(b-4)}{a-3}$, $y=1+\dfrac{3(b-4)}{a-3}$ [A1] [5 marks] (b) With $a=3$ the elimination gives $0=b-4$ [M1] so the equations are consistent only if $b=4$; otherwise they contradict [R1] [2 marks] (c) Set $z=\lambda$ and use the first two equations [M1] $x=-5\lambda$, $y=1+3\lambda$, $z=\lambda$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) The third equation's left side is the sum of the other two but its right side differs, so no two planes are parallel and there is no common point; the planes form a triangular prism [A1] [1 mark]
tips: When the left side of one equation is a combination of the others, add the equations first: the result shows immediately which parameter values make the system degenerate. Check your general solution by substituting into all three equations.

subtopic: Consistency of a 3x3 system with parameters on the right-hand side
statement: Consider the system $$\begin{cases} x+y+z=a \\ x-y+2z=b \\ 3x+y+4z=c \end{cases}$$ where $a,b,c\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Show that the system has a solution only if $c=2a+b$. [4] (b) Given that $a=1$, $b=3$ and $c=5$, find the general solution of the system. [4] (c) Given that $c\neq 2a+b$, describe the geometrical arrangement of the three planes. [2]
markscheme: (a) $2(x+y+z)+(x-y+2z)=3x+y+4z$ [M1] so any solution of the first two equations satisfies $3x+y+4z=2a+b$ [R1] hence a solution requires $c=2a+b$ [A1] if $c=2a+b$ the third equation is redundant, and the first two planes (not parallel) meet in a line, so solutions exist [R1] [4 marks] (b) $x+y+z=1$ and $x-y+2z=3$; adding: $2x+3z=4$ [M1] let $z=t$: $x=2-\frac32 t$ [A1] $y=1-z-x=-1+\frac12 t$ [M1] so $(x,y,z)=\left(2-\frac32 t,\,-1+\frac12 t,\,t\right)$, $t\in\mathbb{R}$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) The normal vectors are pairwise non-parallel, so no two planes are parallel [R1] there is no common point, so the planes form a triangular prism [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Look for a linear combination of the equations: the left-hand side relationship forces the same relationship on the right. For no solution with no parallel planes, think prism.

subtopic: Tangent lines to an ellipse using a discriminant
statement: Consider the ellipse $x^2+4y^2=16$ and the line $y=mx+c$. (a) Show that the $x$-coordinates of the intersection points satisfy $(1+4m^2)x^2+8mcx+4c^2-16=0$. [2] (b) Show that the line is a tangent to the ellipse if and only if $c^2=4+16m^2$. [4] (c) Find the equations of the two tangents to the ellipse with gradient $\dfrac12$. [2]
markscheme: (a) substitute: $x^2+4(mx+c)^2=16$ [M1] expand and collect [A1] [2 marks] (b) tangent means one repeated solution, discriminant $=0$ [R1] $64m^2c^2-4(1+4m^2)(4c^2-16)=0$ [M1] simplify: $-16c^2+64+256m^2=0$ [A1] $c^2=4+16m^2$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) $c^2=4+4=8$ [M1] $y=\dfrac12x\pm2\sqrt2$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A line is tangent when the quadratic obtained from substitution has a repeated root.

subtopic: Intersection of a line and a rectangular hyperbola
statement: The curve $C$ has equation $xy=12$, for $x>0$, and the line $L$ has equation $x+y=7$. (a) Find the coordinates of the two points $A$ and $B$ where $L$ meets $C$. [4] (b) Find the distance $AB$. [2] (c) The line $x+y=k$, with $k>0$, is a tangent to $C$. Find the exact value of $k$. [3]
markscheme: (a) Substitute $y=7-x$: $x(7-x)=12$ [M1] $x^2-7x+12=0$ [A1] $x=3$ or $x=4$ [A1] $A(3,4)$ and $B(4,3)$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $AB=\sqrt{(4-3)^2+(3-4)^2}$ [M1] $=\sqrt2$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Substituting $y=k-x$: $x^2-kx+12=0$; tangent means a repeated root [M1] discriminant $k^2-48=0$ [A1] $k=4\sqrt3$ (since $k>0$) [A1] [3 marks]
tips: To intersect a line with a curve, eliminate one variable and solve the resulting equation. A tangent corresponds to a repeated root, so set the discriminant to zero.

subtopic: Quadratic through three points and its x-intercepts
statement: A quadratic function is defined by $f(x)=ax^2+bx+c$. Its graph passes through the points $(1,-1)$, $(2,-2)$ and $(-1,13)$. (a) Write down three equations in $a$, $b$ and $c$. [2] (b) Solve the system to find $a$, $b$ and $c$. [5] (c) Hence find, in exact form, the $x$-intercepts of the graph. [2]
markscheme: (a) $a+b+c=-1$ [A1] $4a+2b+c=-2$ and $a-b+c=13$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) First minus third: $2b=-14$ [M1] $b=-7$ [A1] Second minus first: $3a+b=-1$ [M1] $a=2$ [A1] $c=-1-2+7=4$ [A1] [5 marks] (c) $2x^2-7x+4=0$ gives $x=\dfrac{7\pm\sqrt{49-32}}{4}$ [M1] $x=\dfrac{7\pm\sqrt{17}}{4}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Substitute each point into the general form to get one linear equation per point. Subtracting pairs of equations removes $c$ quickly.

subtopic: Entries of a magic square from linear equations
statement: In a $3\times3$ magic square the three rows, three columns and two diagonals all have the same sum $S$. The entries are $\begin{pmatrix}a & b & c\\ d & e & f\\ g & h & i\end{pmatrix}$. (a) By adding the middle row, the middle column and the two diagonals, show that $e=\dfrac S3$. [3] (b) Given $a=2$, $c=6$, $g=4$ and $e=5$, find all the other entries and the value of $S$. [4]
markscheme: (a) the four lines sum to $4S$ [A1] they contain every entry once, plus the centre $e$ three extra times [M1] the total of all entries is $3S$, so $4S=3S+3e$, giving $e=\dfrac S3$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $S=3e=15$ [A1] $i=15-2-5=8$ [A1] $b=15-2-6=7$, $d=15-2-4=9$ [A1] $f=15-6-8=1$, $h=15-4-8=3$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Each entry other than $e$ lies on one or two of the lines through the centre. Count how many times each appears.

subtopic: Simultaneous equations with logarithms
statement: Solve the system of equations, where $x>0$ and $y>0$, $$\begin{aligned} \log_3 x+\log_3 y&=3\\ x-2y&=3 \end{aligned}$$ [6]
tips: Combine logs into a single log, then undo it. Always check solutions against the stated domain: log arguments must be positive.

subtopic: A word problem leading to a linear system
statement: A theater sells adult, child and senior tickets. On one day $120$ tickets were sold for a total of $\$1080$. Adult tickets cost $\$12$, child tickets $\$7$ and senior tickets $\$9$. The number of adult tickets sold was twice the number of senior tickets. (a) Let $a$, $c$ and $s$ be the numbers of adult, child and senior tickets. Write down three equations. [3] (b) Solve the system. [3]
tips: Define variables, translate each sentence into an equation, then eliminate.

subtopic: Unique, no or infinitely many solutions for a symmetric parametric system
statement: Consider the system of equations $$\begin{aligned} kx+y+z&=1\\ x+ky+z&=k\\ x+y+kz&=k^2 \end{aligned}$$ where $k\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Show that the determinant of the coefficient matrix is $(k-1)^2(k+2)$. [3] (b) Determine the number of solutions of the system when (i) $k=1$ (ii) $k=-2$. [5] (c) Solve the system when $k=0$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\det=k(k^2-1)-1(k-1)+1(1-k)$ [M1] $=k^3-k-2k+2=k^3-3k+2$ [A1] $=(k-1)^2(k+2)$ [A1] [AG] [3 marks] (b) (i) With $k=1$ all three equations become $x+y+z=1$ [A1] the planes coincide, so there are infinitely many solutions [A1] (ii) With $k=-2$ add the three equations: $(k+2)(x+y+z)=1+k+k^2$, i.e. $0=3$ [M1] [A1] a contradiction, so there is no solution [A1] [5 marks] (c) With $k=0$: $y+z=1$, $x+z=0$, $x+y=0$ [M1] From the last two, $x=-z$ and $y=z$, so $2z=1$ [A1] $z=\frac12$, $y=\frac12$, $x=-\frac12$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Adding all three equations of a symmetric system gives a quick consistency test. For each critical parameter value, substitute it and compare the equations before claiming none or infinite.

subtopic: Exponential equations reduced to a linear system
statement: Solve the simultaneous equations $$2^x+3^y=17,\qquad 2^{x+1}-3^{y-1}=13,$$ where $x,y\in\mathbb{R}$. [6]
markscheme: Let $u=2^x$ and $v=3^y$ [M1] Then $u+v=17$ [A1] and $2u-\dfrac v3=13$, i.e. $6u-v=39$ [A1] Adding: $7u=56$, so $u=8$ [M1] and $v=9$ [A1] $2^x=8$ gives $x=3$ and $3^y=9$ gives $y=2$ [A1] [6 marks]
tips: Spot the hidden linear system by substituting $u=2^x$ and $v=3^y$. Use index laws such as $2^{x+1}=2\cdot2^x$ and $3^{y-1}=\tfrac13\cdot3^y$ before substituting.

subtopic: Fitting a quadratic through three points
statement: A parabola $y=ax^2+bx+c$ passes through the points $(1,2)$, $(2,5)$ and $(3,12)$. (a) Write down three equations for $a$, $b$ and $c$. [2] (b) Solve the system using your calculator, and write down the equation of the parabola. [2] (c) Find the coordinates of the vertex. [2]
tips: Substitute each point to form a linear system in $a$, $b$, $c$.

subtopic: Parameter in coefficients, consistency and geometry of planes
statement: Consider the system of equations $$\begin{aligned} x+y+z&=2\\ 2x+3y+az&=5\\ x+2y+3z&=b \end{aligned}$$ where $a,b\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Show that the system does not have a unique solution when $a=4$, and for no other value of $a$. [3] (b) Given that $a=4$, show that the system is consistent if and only if $b=3$. [3] (c) Given that $a=4$ and $b=3$, find the general solution, in terms of a parameter $\lambda$ where $z=\lambda$. [3] (d) Given that $a=4$ and $b\ne3$, describe the geometrical arrangement of the three planes represented by the equations. [1]
markscheme: (a) Determinant of the coefficient matrix: $1(9-2a)-1(6-a)+1(4-3)$ [M1] $=4-a$ [A1] No unique solution when determinant is $0$, i.e. $a=4$ only [A1] [3 marks] (b) With $a=4$, equation 2 minus equation 1 gives $x+2y+3z=3$ [M1] [A1] Comparing with equation 3, $x+2y+3z=b$: consistent if and only if $b=3$; otherwise the equations contradict [R1] [3 marks] (c) Let $z=\lambda$; then $x+y=2-\lambda$ and $x+2y=3-3\lambda$ [M1] Subtracting: $y=1-2\lambda$ [A1] $x=1+\lambda$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) The planes form a triangular prism: no two are parallel, but there is no common point, so they intersect pairwise in three parallel lines [A1] [1 mark]
tips: In a parametric problem, a zero determinant only says that the solution is not unique; decide between no solution and infinitely many by checking consistency. For three planes with no solution, check whether any are parallel before choosing the geometry.

subtopic: Ticket sales modelled with three equations
statement: A theater sells adult tickets at \$12, child tickets at \$7 and senior tickets at \$9. On one evening a total of 200 tickets were sold and the total revenue was \$1880. The number of adult tickets sold was twice the number of senior tickets sold. Let $a$, $c$ and $s$ be the numbers of adult, child and senior tickets sold. (a) Write down three equations in $a$, $c$ and $s$. [3] (b) Use your GDC to find the number of tickets of each type sold. [3]
markscheme: (a) $a+c+s=200$ [A1] $12a+7c+9s=1880$ [A1] $a=2s$ (or $a-2s=0$) [A1] [3 marks] (b) Use the GDC simultaneous equation solver [M1] $a=80$ [A1] $c=80$ and $s=40$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Define the variables clearly and translate each sentence into exactly one equation. Check that your answers are whole numbers and that they satisfy the revenue equation.

subtopic: Solving a system of three linear equations
statement: A shop sells three products with prices $x$, $y$, $z$ dollars. Consider the system $\begin{cases} 3x+2y+z=11 \\ x-y+2z=7 \\ 2x+3y-2z=1 \end{cases}$ (a) Solve the system using your calculator. [3] (b) State the determinant of the coefficient matrix and explain what it tells you about the solution. [2]
markscheme: (a) enter the augmented matrix or use the system solver [M1] $x=2.000$ [A1] $y=1.000$, $z=3.000$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\det=5\ne0$ [A1] so there is a unique solution (the three planes meet at a single point) [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Use the system solver and check the solution in one of the equations.

subtopic: Intersections of an exponential and a line
statement: Consider the curve $y=e^x$ and the line $y=x+2$. (a) Use your calculator to find the $x$-coordinates of the points where they intersect, to three significant figures. [3] (b) Hence solve $e^x<x+2$. [2]
markscheme: (a) graph both [M1] $x=-1.84$ [A1] $x=1.15$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) the curve lies below the line between the intersection points [M1] $-1.84<x<1.15$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A solver or intersection tool gives both intersection points. Check the graph to see which function is larger between them.

subtopic: Classifying the solutions of a system with a parameter
statement:
This question investigates the system $x+y+z=1$, $x+2y+3z=4$, $x+4y+az=b$, where $a$ and $b$ are constants. (a) Eliminate $x$ to obtain two equations in $y$ and $z$. [3] (b) Show that the system has a unique solution if and only if $a
e7$. [3] (c) For $a
e7$, find $x$, $y$, $z$ in terms of $a$ and $b$. [4] (d) Describe the solution set when $a=7$ for $b=10$ and for $b
e10$. [3] (e) Find the solution when $a=3$ and $b=2$ and check it in all three equations. [2]
markscheme:
(a) second minus first: $y+2z=3$ [M1][A1] third minus first: $3y+(a-1)z=b-1$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) substitute $y=3-2z$: $9-6z+(a-1)z=b-1$ [M1] $(a-7)z=b-10$ [A1] a unique $z$ exists iff $a
e7$ [R1] [3 marks] (c) $z=\dfrac{b-10}{a-7}$ [A1] $y=3-2z=\dfrac{3a-21-2b+20}{a-7}=\dfrac{3a-2b-1}{a-7}$ [A1] $x=1-y-z=\dfrac{a-7-3a+2b+1-b+10}{a-7}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{-2a+b+4}{a-7}$ [A1] [4 marks] (d) $b=10$: $0z=0$, infinitely many solutions on a line [A1] $b
e10$: $0=b-10
e0$, no solutions [A1] geometrically: three planes meeting in a line, or forming a triangular prism [A1] [3 marks] (e) $z=\dfrac{-8}{-4}=2$, $y=\dfrac{9-4-1}{-4}=-1$, $x=\dfrac{-6+2+4}{-4}=0$ [A1] check: $0-1+2=1$, $0-2+6=4$, $0-4+6=2$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Eliminate one variable at a time; the coefficient $(a-7)$ of $z$ in the reduced equation decides between unique, none or infinitely many solutions.

subtopic: Partial fractions via a linear system
statement: The expression $\dfrac{4x^2+5x-21}{(x-1)(x+2)(x-3)}$ can be written as $\dfrac{A}{x-1}+\dfrac{B}{x+2}+\dfrac{C}{x-3}$, where $A,B,C\in\mathbb{Z}$. (a) By equating coefficients of $x^2$, $x$ and the constant term, form a system of three linear equations in $A$, $B$ and $C$. [3] (b) Solve the system to find $A$, $B$ and $C$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $4x^2+5x-21=A(x+2)(x-3)+B(x-1)(x-3)+C(x-1)(x+2)$ [M1] Expanding: $A(x^2-x-6)+B(x^2-4x+3)+C(x^2+x-2)$ [A1] $x^2$: $A+B+C=4$; $x$: $-A-4B+C=5$; constant: $-6A+3B-2C=-21$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Attempt to eliminate a variable to reach two equations in two unknowns [M1] E.g. (first)$-$(second) gives $2A+5B=-1$; $2\times$(first)$+$(third) gives $-4A+5B=-13$ [A1] Hence $6A=12$, $A=2$, $B=-1$, $C=3$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Equating coefficients always produces a linear system, even when a shortcut such as the cover-up method exists. Check your final values by substituting a convenient value of $x$.

subtopic: Positive integer solutions of a reciprocal equation
statement: Find all pairs of positive integers $(x,y)$ with $x\le y$ such that $\dfrac1x+\dfrac1y=\dfrac16$. (a) Show that $(x-6)(y-6)=36$. [2] (b) Hence list all pairs $(x,y)$ with $x\le y$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $6y+6x=xy$ [M1] $xy-6x-6y+36=36$, so $(x-6)(y-6)=36$ [AG] [A1] [2 marks] (b) $x>6$ and $y>6$, since $x,y>6$ is needed for $\dfrac1x<\dfrac16$ [R1] factor pairs of $36$ with $x-6\le y-6$: $1\times36$, $2\times18$, $3\times12$, $4\times9$, $6\times6$ [M1] $(7,42),(8,24),(9,18),(10,15),(12,12)$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Rearranging gives a product of two factors equal to a constant. List the factor pairs of that constant.

subtopic: Cubic model from four data points
statement: The temperature, $T$ degrees Celsius, in a greenhouse is modelled by $T(t)=at^3+bt^2+ct+d$, where $t$ is the time in hours after 08:00, for $0\le t\le4$. The temperature was measured as $2$ at $t=0$, $6$ at $t=1$, $4$ at $t=2$ and $6$ at $t=4$. (a) Write down a system of four linear equations in $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$. [2] (b) Hence find the values of $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$. [2] (c) Find the values of $t$, in the interval $0\le t\le4$, for which the model gives a temperature of $5$ degrees Celsius. [2]
tips: With four unknowns, each data point gives one equation; the GDC's simultaneous-equation solver or a matrix inverse handles it. Check that all your answers lie in the stated domain.

subtopic: Common tangents to two parabolas
statement: Consider the parabolas $y=x^2$ and $y=-(x-3)^2$. (a) The tangent to $y=x^2$ at $x=a$ has equation $y=2ax-a^2$. Find the equation of the tangent to $y=-(x-3)^2$ at $x=b$. [3] (b) The two tangents coincide. Show that $b=3-a$, and that $a^2=3a$. [3] (c) Hence find the equations of the two common tangents. [2]
tips: For a line to be tangent to both parabolas, the gradient and the intercept must agree in both tangent equations.

subtopic: Three linear equations with parameters
statement: Consider the system of equations $$\begin{aligned} x+2y-z&=3\\ 2x-y+kz&=1\\ 3x+y+2z&=m \end{aligned}$$ where $k,m\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Find the value of $k$ for which the system does not have a unique solution. [3] (b) Given that $k$ takes the value found in part (a), find the value of $m$ for which the system has infinitely many solutions. [2] (c) For the values of $k$ and $m$ found in parts (a) and (b), find the general solution of the system, giving your answer in terms of a parameter $\lambda$, where $z=\lambda$. [3]
markscheme: (a) Attempt to find the determinant of the coefficient matrix (or to row reduce) [M1] $\det=1(-2-k)-2(4-3k)-1(2+3)=5k-15$ [A1] No unique solution when $5k-15=0$, so $k=3$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) With $k=3$, adding the first two equations gives $3x+y+2z=4$ [M1] Comparing with the third equation, the system is consistent (infinitely many solutions) when $m=4$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Let $z=\lambda$: $x+2y=3+\lambda$ and $2x-y=1-3\lambda$ [M1] Attempt to solve, e.g. $5x=5-5\lambda$ [M1] $x=1-\lambda,\ y=1+\lambda,\ z=\lambda$ [A1] Accept equivalent forms, e.g. a vector equation $\mathbf{r}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}-1\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}$. [3 marks]
tips: A zero determinant only tells you the solution is not unique; you must then check consistency to decide between no solutions and infinitely many. Always substitute your general solution back into the third equation as a check.

subtopic: Solving a 2x2 linear system by elimination
statement: Solve the system of equations $$\begin{aligned} 3x+2y&=7\\ 5x-4y&=-3 \end{aligned}$$ [4]
markscheme: Multiply the first equation by $2$: $6x+4y=14$ [M1] Add to the second equation: $11x=11$, so $x=1$ [A1] Substitute: $3+2y=7$ [M1] $y=2$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Match coefficients so that one variable cancels when you add or subtract. Check the answer in the equation you did not use for substitution.

subtopic: Nonlinear symmetric system solved by adding the equations
statement: Consider the system of equations $$x^2+xy=12,\qquad y^2+xy=4.$$ (a) By adding the equations, show that $(x+y)^2=16$. [2] (b) Hence solve the system. [5]
markscheme: (a) Adding: $x^2+2xy+y^2=16$ [M1] $(x+y)^2=16$ [A1] [AG] [2 marks] (b) $x+y=\pm4$ [A1] the equations factorize as $x(x+y)=12$ [M1] and $y(x+y)=4$ [M1] if $x+y=4$: $x=3$, $y=1$ [A1] if $x+y=-4$: $x=-3$, $y=-1$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: Look for a factorization or symmetry before resorting to substitution. Check both sign cases of the square root.

subtopic: Geometric sequence from a term and a sum, with sum to infinity
statement: In a geometric sequence, $u_2=6$ and $u_1+u_2+u_3=21$. Let the common ratio be $r$. (a) Show that $2r^2-5r+2=0$. [3] (b) Find the two possible values of $r$ and the corresponding values of $u_1$. [3] (c) For the sequence whose sum to infinity exists, find that sum. [2]
markscheme: (a) $u_1=\dfrac6r$ and $u_3=6r$ [A1] $\dfrac6r+6+6r=21$ [M1] Multiply by $r$: $6r^2-15r+6=0$, so $2r^2-5r+2=0$ [A1] [AG] [3 marks] (b) $(2r-1)(r-2)=0$ [M1] $r=2$ or $r=\frac12$ [A1] $u_1=3$ (for $r=2$) or $u_1=12$ (for $r=\frac12$) [A1] [3 marks] (c) The sum to infinity exists only if $|r|<1$, so $r=\frac12$ [R1] $S_\infty=\dfrac{12}{1-\frac12}=24$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Express the other terms in terms of $u_2$ and $r$ to avoid a messy cubic. State the condition $|r|<1$ explicitly before using the sum to infinity.

subtopic: Solving a system of three linear equations
statement: Consider the system $\begin{cases} x+2y+3z=14 \\ 2x-y+z=3 \\ 4x+y-2z=0 \end{cases}$ (a) Solve the system using your calculator. [3] (b) State the determinant of the coefficient matrix and explain what it tells you about the solution. [2]
markscheme: (a) enter the augmented matrix or use the system solver [M1] $x=1.000$ [A1] $y=2.000$, $z=3.000$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\det=35\ne0$ [A1] so there is a unique solution (the three planes meet at a single point) [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Use the simultaneous equation solver on your calculator.

subtopic: Simultaneous equations with exponents
statement: Solve the system of equations $$\begin{aligned} 2^x\cdot 4^y&=32\\ \frac{3^x}{9^y}&=27 \end{aligned}$$ [5]
tips: Rewrite every power with the same base within each equation so you can equate exponents. This turns the system into a linear one.

subtopic: Three numbers in arithmetic sequence that become geometric
statement: Three numbers form an increasing arithmetic sequence with sum 18. When 1 is added to the largest number, the three numbers form a geometric sequence. (a) Show that the middle number is 6. [2] (b) Find the three original numbers. [5]
markscheme: (a) Let the numbers be $m-d$, $m$, $m+d$ with sum $3m=18$ [M1] $m=6$ [A1] [AG] [2 marks] (b) Numbers: $6-d$, $6$, $6+d$, with $d>0$; after the change: $6-d$, $6$, $7+d$ [M1] $6^2=(6-d)(7+d)$ [M1] $d^2+d-6=0$ [A1] $d=2$ or $d=-3$ [A1] $d>0$ since the sequence is increasing, so $d=2$ and the numbers are $4$, $6$, $8$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: Using $m-d$, $m$, $m+d$ for three terms in arithmetic sequence makes the sum trivial. In a geometric sequence the middle term squared equals the product of its neighbors.

subtopic: Solving a system of three linear equations
statement: Consider the system $\begin{cases} x+y+z=6 \\ 2x-y+z=3 \\ x+2y-z=2 \end{cases}$ (a) Solve the system by elimination. [4] (b) State the determinant of the coefficient matrix and explain what it tells you about the solution. [2]
markscheme: (a) eliminate one variable from two pairs of equations [M1] obtain a $2\times2$ system [A1] $x=1$ [A1] $y=2$ and $z=3$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $\det=7\ne0$ [A1] so there is a unique solution (the three planes meet at a single point) [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Eliminate the same variable from two different pairs of equations to reduce to two equations in two unknowns.

subtopic: Using an inverse matrix on a 3x3 system
statement: The matrix $A$ is given by $$A=\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 3 \\ 1 & -1 & 2 \\ 3 & 2 & -1 \end{pmatrix}.$$ (a) Find $\det A$ and explain what this tells you about the system $A\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{B}$ for any vector $\mathbf{B}$. [2] (b) Use your GDC to find $A^{-1}$. [1] (c) Hence solve $$\begin{aligned} 2x+y+3z&=10\\ x-y+2z&=4\\ 3x+2y-z&=7 \end{aligned}$$ giving your answers to 3 significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\det A=16$ [A1] Since $\det A\neq0$, $A$ is invertible, so there is a unique solution for every $\mathbf{B}$ [R1] [2 marks] (b) $A^{-1}=\dfrac1{16}\begin{pmatrix} -3 & 7 & 5 \\ 7 & -11 & -1 \\ 5 & -1 & -3 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $\mathbf{X}=A^{-1}\begin{pmatrix} 10 \\ 4 \\ 7 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $x=2.06$, $y=1.19$, $z=1.56$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The system's coefficient matrix is $A$, so the inverse from part (b) can be reused directly. Keep full precision in your GDC and round only at the end.

subtopic: Solving a system of three linear equations
statement: Consider the system $\begin{cases} 2x+y-z=1 \\ x-2y+3z=9 \\ 3x+y+2z=13 \end{cases}$ (a) Solve the system by elimination. [4] (b) State the determinant of the coefficient matrix and explain what it tells you about the solution. [2]
markscheme: (a) eliminate one variable from two pairs of equations [M1] obtain a $2\times2$ system [A1] $x=\frac{3}{2}$ [A1] $y=\frac{3}{2}$ and $z=\frac{7}{2}$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $\det=-14\ne0$ [A1] so there is a unique solution (the three planes meet at a single point) [R1] [2 marks]
tips: A non-zero determinant guarantees a unique solution.

subtopic: Solving three linear equations by elimination
statement: Solve the system of equations $$\begin{aligned} x+y+z&=6\\ 2x-y+z&=3\\ x+2y-z&=2 \end{aligned}$$ [6]
markscheme: Eliminate $z$: (1)$-$(2) gives $-x+2y=3$ [M1] [A1] (1)$+$(3) gives $2x+3y=8$ [A1] Solve the pair: from the first, $x=2y-3$, so $2(2y-3)+3y=8$ [M1] $7y=14$, so $y=2$ [A1] $x=1$ and $z=3$ [A1] [6 marks]
tips: Choose the variable that is easiest to eliminate (here $z$ has coefficients $\pm1$), eliminate it twice, and then solve the resulting $2\times2$ system. Substitute your answer back into all three equations.

subtopic: Arithmetic sequence from two terms and a partial sum condition
statement: An arithmetic sequence has first term $u_1=a$ and common difference $d$. It is given that $u_5=17$ and $u_{12}=45$. (a) Write down two equations in $a$ and $d$ and hence find $a$ and $d$. [3] (b) Let $S_n$ be the sum of the first $n$ terms. Find the smallest value of $n$ for which $S_n>1000$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $a+4d=17$ and $a+11d=45$ [A1] Subtract: $7d=28$ [M1] $d=4$, $a=1$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $S_n=\frac n2\left(2+4(n-1)\right)=n(2n-1)$ [M1] [A1] Using the GDC (table or solver): $S_{22}=946$ and $S_{23}=1035$, so $n=23$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Use $u_n=a+(n-1)d$ to turn each given term into a linear equation. For a threshold on $S_n$, compare the two consecutive values either side of $1000$ to justify the smallest $n$.

subtopic: Symmetric systems and the cubic whose roots are the unknowns
statement: Consider the system $x+y+z=6$, $x^2+y^2+z^2=14$ and $xyz=6$. (a) Show that $xy+yz+zx=11$. [2] (b) Show that $x$, $y$ and $z$ are the roots of $t^3-6t^2+11t-6=0$, and solve the system. [4] (c) State the number of solutions $(x,y,z)$ of the system. [1] (d) Show that $x^3+y^3+z^3-3xyz=(x+y+z)\left(x^2+y^2+z^2-xy-yz-zx\right)$. [2] (e) Solve the system $x+y+z=0$, $x^2+y^2+z^2=6$ and $x^3+y^3+z^3=6$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $(x+y+z)^2=x^2+y^2+z^2+2(xy+yz+zx)$ [M1] $36=14+2(xy+yz+zx)$, so $xy+yz+zx=11$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) sum, pairwise sum and product of the roots are $6$, $11$, $6$ [M1] $t^3-6t^2+11t-6=0$ [A1] $(t-1)(t-2)(t-3)=0$ [A1] $(x,y,z)$ is any ordering of $1,2,3$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) $3!=6$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) expand the right-hand side: $x^3+y^3+z^3-3xyz$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (e) $xy+yz+zx=\dfrac{0-6}2=-3$ [A1] identity gives $x^3+y^3+z^3=3xyz$, so $xyz=2$ [M1] $t^3-3t-2=(t-2)(t+1)^2=0$ [A1] solutions are the $3$ orderings of $(2,-1,-1)$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: The sum, sum of pairs and product of $x,y,z$ are the coefficients of a cubic, so the unknowns are its roots.

subtopic: Intersection of two lines in 3D with an unknown constant
statement: Two lines have equations $$L_1:\ \mathbf{r}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}+s\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix},\qquad L_2:\ \mathbf{r}=\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 3 \\ k \end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix},$$ where $k\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Given that $L_1$ and $L_2$ intersect, find the value of $k$ and the coordinates of the point of intersection. [6] (b) Find the exact value of the acute angle between $L_1$ and $L_2$. [3] (c) Show that if $k\neq2$, the lines are skew. [2]
markscheme: (a) $1+s=2t$, $2s=3-t$, $2-s=k-t$ [M1] from the first two, $s=2t-1$ so $4t-2=3-t$ [A1] $t=1$, $s=1$ [M1] substitute into the third: $1=k-1$ [A1] $k=2$ [A1] point $(2,2,1)$ [A1] [6 marks] (b) $\mathbf{d}_1\cdot\mathbf{d}_2=2-2+1=1$ [M1] $|\mathbf{d}_1|=|\mathbf{d}_2|=\sqrt6$ [A1] $\theta=\arccos\frac16$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) The direction vectors are not parallel [R1] the first two equations force $s=t=1$ uniquely, and the third then fails when $k\neq2$, so no intersection; not parallel and not intersecting means skew [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Equate components and solve two of the three equations, then use the third as the check that fixes the unknown. The angle uses the direction vectors only.

subtopic: Number of solutions of a cubic and horizontal line system
statement: Consider the system of equations $$y=x^3-3x,\qquad y=k,$$ where $k\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Find the coordinates of the stationary points of the curve $y=x^3-3x$. [3] (b) Hence determine the values of $k$ for which the system has (i) exactly one solution, (ii) exactly two solutions, (iii) exactly three solutions. [4] (c) Use your graphic display calculator to solve the system when $k=1$. Give your answers to three significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\frac{dy}{dx}=3x^2-3$ [M1] $=0$ gives $x=\pm1$ [A1] stationary points $(-1,2)$ and $(1,-2)$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) The cubic has positive leading coefficient with local maximum $2$ and local minimum $-2$ [R1] (i) one solution when $|k|>2$ [A1] (ii) two solutions when $k=2$ or $k=-2$ [A1] (iii) three solutions when $-2<k<2$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) $x^3-3x-1=0$ [M1] $(x,y)=(-1.53,1)$ and $(-0.347,1)$ [A1] $(1.88,1)$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Intersections with a horizontal line count the number of times the curve takes a value, so use the turning point values as the boundaries.

subtopic: Mixing solutions of different concentrations
statement: A chemist mixes $x$ liters of a 10\% acid solution with $y$ liters of a 25\% acid solution to make 30 liters of a 16\% acid solution. (a) Write down two equations in $x$ and $y$. [2] (b) Hence find $x$ and $y$. [3] (c) The 10\% solution costs \$4 per liter and the 25\% solution costs \$9 per liter. Find the cost of the 30 liters of mixture. [1]
tips: Write one equation for total volume and one for the amount of pure acid. Convert percentages to decimals before forming the second equation.

subtopic: Three planes with a linear dependence
statement: Three planes have equations $x+y+z=3$, $x-y+2z=2$ and $2x+3z=k$, where $k$ is a constant. (a) Show that the three planes have no common point unless $k$ takes one particular value, and find that value. [3] (b) For this value of $k$, find a vector equation of the line of intersection of the three planes. [3]
markscheme: (a) adding the first two equations gives $2x+3z=5$ [M1][A1] this contradicts the third equation unless $k=5$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) let $z=t$: $x=\dfrac{5-3t}2$ [M1] $y=3-x-t=\dfrac{1+t}2$ [A1] $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix} 5/2 \\ 1/2 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix} -3/2 \\ 1/2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Look for a linear dependence between the equations: if the third is a combination of the first two, the planes share a line when consistent and have no common point otherwise.

subtopic: Homogeneous system and determinant
statement: Consider the system of equations $$\begin{aligned} kx+y+z&=0\\ x+ky+z&=0\\ x+y+kz&=0 \end{aligned}$$ where $k\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Show that the determinant of the coefficient matrix is $(k-1)^2(k+2)$. [3] (b) Hence find the values of $k$ for which the system has non-trivial solutions (solutions other than $x=y=z=0$). [1] (c) For the smaller of these two values of $k$, find all solutions. [2] (d) For the larger of these two values of $k$, describe the set of solutions. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\det=k(k^2-1)-1(k-1)+1(1-k)$ [M1] $=k^3-3k+2$ [A1] $=(k-1)^2(k+2)$ [A1][AG] [3 marks] (b) Non-trivial solutions exist when the determinant is $0$: $k=1$ or $k=-2$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $k=-2$: $-2x+y+z=0$ and $x-2y+z=0$. Subtracting gives $-3x+3y=0$, so $x=y$, and then $z=x$ [M1] Solutions: $(x,y,z)=(\lambda,\lambda,\lambda)$, $\lambda\in\mathbb{R}$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $k=1$: all three equations reduce to $x+y+z=0$ [A1] The solutions are $x=s$, $y=t$, $z=-s-t$ for $s,t\in\mathbb{R}$ (a plane through the origin) [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A homogeneous system always has the trivial solution; non-trivial solutions appear exactly when the determinant is zero. The number of free parameters in the solution depends on how many independent equations remain.

subtopic: A nonlinear system made linear by using reciprocals
statement: Solve the system $\dfrac2x+\dfrac3y=7$ and $\dfrac1x-\dfrac1y=1$. [5]
markscheme: let $u=\dfrac1x$, $v=\dfrac1y$: $2u+3v=7$ and $u-v=1$ [M1] $u=v+1$ gives $5v+2=7$ [M1] $v=1$ [A1] $u=2$ [A1] $x=\dfrac12$, $y=1$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: Replace $1/x$ and $1/y$ by new variables to get a linear system.

subtopic: Number of solutions of a 2x2 system with a parameter
statement: Consider the system of equations $$\begin{aligned} x+ky&=3\\ kx+4y&=6 \end{aligned}$$ where $k\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Show that the system does not have a unique solution if and only if $k=2$ or $k=-2$. [3] (b) For each of these two values of $k$, determine whether the system has no solution or infinitely many solutions. [3] (c) For $k=2$, write down the general solution in terms of a parameter $\lambda$ where $y=\lambda$. [1]
markscheme: (a) The determinant of the coefficient matrix is $1\cdot4-k\cdot k$ [M1] $=4-k^2$ [A1] No unique solution when $4-k^2=0$, i.e. $k=\pm2$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $k=2$: the equations are $x+2y=3$ and $2x+4y=6$; the second is twice the first, so they describe the same line [M1] infinitely many solutions [A1] $k=-2$: $x-2y=3$ and $-2x+4y=6$, i.e. $x-2y=-3$; these are parallel and distinct (contradiction), so no solution [A1] [3 marks] (c) $y=\lambda$, $x=3-2\lambda$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: A zero determinant only tells you the solution is not unique. To decide between none and infinitely many, substitute the value of the parameter and compare the equations, including their right-hand sides.

subtopic: Symmetric nonlinear system
statement: Find all real solutions of the system $$x^2+y^2=13,\qquad xy=6.$$ [6]
tips: For symmetric equations in $x$ and $y$, work with $x+y$ and $x-y$ rather than substituting. List all four solutions, since each sign choice gives a pair.

subtopic: Conditions for no solution or infinitely many solutions
statement: Consider the system $\begin{cases} x+2y-z=1 \\ 2x+5y-3z=3 \\ x+3y+kz=m \end{cases}$ where $k$ and $m$ are constants. (a) Show that eliminating $x$ from the first two equations gives $y-z=1$. [2] (b) Eliminate $x$ from the first and third equations, and hence find the value of $k$ for which the system does not have a unique solution. [4] (c) For $k=-2$, find the value of $m$ for which the system has infinitely many solutions, and the value of $m$ for which it has no solution. [3] (d) Describe the geometrical arrangement of the three planes when $k=-2$ and $m=2$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $(2x+5y-3z)-2(x+2y-z)=3-2$ [M1] $y-z=1$ [A1] [AG] [2 marks] (b) $(x+3y+kz)-(x+2y-z)=m-1$ gives $y+(k+1)z=m-1$ [M1][A1] subtract $y-z=1$: $(k+2)z=m-2$ [M1] no unique solution when $k+2=0$, $k=-2$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) $0\cdot z=m-2$ [M1] infinitely many solutions when $m=2$ [A1] no solution when $m\ne2$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) the planes share a common line [A1] forming a sheaf (they meet along a line) [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Reduce to a single equation in $z$; a zero coefficient on the left with a non-zero right side means inconsistency.

subtopic: A symmetric nonlinear system
statement: Solve the system $x^2+y^2=25$ and $xy=12$. [6]
tips: Expanding $(x+y)^2$ and $(x-y)^2$ uses $x^2+y^2$ and $xy$ directly.

subtopic: Row reduction of an augmented matrix and the determinant
statement: A linear system is given by $$\begin{aligned} x+y+z&=2\\ 2x+3y+z&=1\\ 3x+y-z&=0 \end{aligned}$$ (a) Write down the augmented matrix for this system. [1] (b) Use row operations to reduce the augmented matrix to upper triangular form. [3] (c) Hence solve the system. [2] (d) Use your answer to (b) to find the determinant of the coefficient matrix. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\left(\begin{array}{ccc|c} 1 & 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 3 & 1 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 & -1 & 0 \end{array}\right)$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $R_2\to R_2-2R_1$ gives $(0,1,-1\mid-3)$ [M1] $R_3\to R_3-3R_1$ gives $(0,-2,-4\mid-6)$ [A1] $R_3\to R_3+2R_2$ gives $(0,0,-6\mid-12)$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $z=2$ [A1] $y=z-3=-1$ and $x=2-y-z=1$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) The operations $R_i\to R_i+cR_j$ do not change the determinant [M1] $\det=1\times1\times(-6)=-6$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Clearly label each row operation so a marker can follow it. Row operations that add a multiple of one row to another leave the determinant unchanged; swapping rows or scaling a row does not.

subtopic: Balancing a chemical equation with a linear system
statement: A chemical reaction is $a\,\mathrm{C_2H_6}+b\,\mathrm{O_2}\to c\,\mathrm{CO_2}+d\,\mathrm{H_2O}$, where $a,b,c,d$ are positive integers with no common factor. (a) Write down equations for the numbers of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen atoms. [3] (b) Solve the system to find the smallest positive integer values of $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$. [4]
markscheme: (a) carbon: $2a=c$ [A1] hydrogen: $6a=2d$ [A1] oxygen: $2b=2c+d$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) let $a=1$: $c=2$ and $d=3$ [M1][A1] $2b=4+3=7$, so $b=\dfrac72$ [A1] multiply by $2$: $a=2$, $b=7$, $c=4$, $d=6$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: The system has more unknowns than independent equations, so set one unknown to a convenient value and scale to clear fractions.

subtopic: Line and plane intersection with parameters
statement: The line $L$ has equation $\dfrac{x-1}{2}=\dfrac{y+1}{3}=\dfrac{z-2}{-1}$ and the plane $\Pi$ has equation $x+ay+2z=b$, where $a,b\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Given that $a=1$ and $b=7$, find the coordinates of the point where $L$ meets $\Pi$. [3] (b) Show that if $a\neq0$, then $L$ meets $\Pi$ at exactly one point for every value of $b$. [3] (c) Given that $a=0$, find the value of $b$ for which $L$ lies in $\Pi$, and describe the relationship between $L$ and $\Pi$ for all other values of $b$. [3] (d) Given that $b=7$, find the value of $a$ for which the point of intersection lies in the plane $z=0$. [3]
