markscheme: (a) $L$: $(x,y,z)=(1+2\lambda,\,-1+3\lambda,\,2-\lambda)$ [M1] $(1+2\lambda)+(-1+3\lambda)+2(2-\lambda)=7$ so $3\lambda=3$, $\lambda=1$ [M1] point $(3,2,1)$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $(1+2\lambda)+a(-1+3\lambda)+2(2-\lambda)=b$ [M1] $3a\lambda=a+b-5$ [A1] since $a\neq0$, $\lambda=\frac{a+b-5}{3a}$ is unique, so exactly one point [R1] [3 marks] (c) With $a=0$: $0\cdot\lambda=b-5$ [M1] if $b=5$ it holds for all $\lambda$, so $L$ lies in $\Pi$ [A1] if $b\neq5$ there is no solution, so $L$ is parallel to $\Pi$ and does not meet it [R1] [3 marks] (d) $z=0$ gives $\lambda=2$ [M1] $6a=a+7-5$ [M1] $a=\frac25$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Substituting the parametric form of the line into the plane gives a linear equation in the parameter. Whether its coefficient is zero decides between one point, none, or the whole line.

subtopic: A symmetric linear system solved by adding the equations
statement: Solve the system $x+y=5$, $y+z=7$, $z+x=8$. [4]
tips: Adding the equations gives the total, from which each variable follows by subtracting one equation.

subtopic: Simultaneous equations with complex numbers
statement: Let $z,w\in\mathbb{C}$ satisfy the simultaneous equations $$z+w=3-2\mathrm{i},\qquad z-\mathrm{i}w=-1.$$ (a) Find $z$ and $w$, giving each in the form $a+b\mathrm{i}$. [6] (b) Find $\dfrac zw$ in the form $a+b\mathrm{i}$. [2]
markscheme: (a) From the first equation $w=3-2\mathrm{i}-z$. Substituting: $z-\mathrm{i}(3-2\mathrm{i}-z)=-1$ [M1] $z-3\mathrm{i}-2+\mathrm{i}z=-1$, so $(1+\mathrm{i})z=1+3\mathrm{i}$ [A1] $z=\dfrac{1+3\mathrm{i}}{1+\mathrm{i}}$, multiply numerator and denominator by $1-\mathrm{i}$ [M1] $z=\dfrac{(1+3\mathrm{i})(1-\mathrm{i})}{2}=\dfrac{4+2\mathrm{i}}{2}$ [A1] $z=2+\mathrm{i}$ [A1] $w=3-2\mathrm{i}-(2+\mathrm{i})=1-3\mathrm{i}$ [A1] [6 marks] (b) $\dfrac{2+\mathrm{i}}{1-3\mathrm{i}}\times\dfrac{1+3\mathrm{i}}{1+3\mathrm{i}}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{2+6\mathrm{i}+\mathrm{i}+3\mathrm{i}^2}{10}=-\dfrac{1}{10}+\dfrac{7}{10}\mathrm{i}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Treat $z$ and $w$ as unknowns exactly as in a real linear system; the only new step is dividing by a complex number by multiplying by the conjugate of the denominator.

subtopic: Simultaneous equations with logarithms
statement: Solve the simultaneous equations $$\log_2x+\log_2y=5,\qquad x-2y=4,$$ where $x,y>0$. Give your answers in exact form. [7]
tips: Combine logarithms first so that the system becomes algebraic. Remember the domain condition: logarithms need positive arguments, which rules out one root.

subtopic: Three planes with a Vandermonde-type coefficient matrix
statement: The following system has real parameters $a$ and $b$: $$\begin{aligned} x+y+z&=2\\ x+ay+a^2z&=b\\ x+2y+4z&=5 \end{aligned}$$ (a) Show that the system has a unique solution unless $a=1$ or $a=2$. [3] (b) Given that $a=2$, find the value of $b$ for which the system is consistent, and for this value of $b$ find the general solution in terms of a parameter $\lambda$ where $z=\lambda$. [4] (c) Given that $a=2$ and $b$ takes any other value, describe the geometrical arrangement of the three planes. [1]
markscheme: (a) Determinant: $1(4a-2a^2)-1(4-a^2)+1(2-a)$ [M1] $=-a^2+3a-2$ [A1] $=(a-1)(2-a)$, which is zero only for $a=1$ or $a=2$, so a unique solution exists otherwise [A1] [3 marks] (b) With $a=2$ the second and third equations have the same left-hand side $x+2y+4z$, so they are consistent only if $b=5$ [R1] Subtract the first equation from the third: $y+3z=3$ [M1] [A1] With $z=\lambda$: $y=3-3\lambda$ and $x=2-y-z=-1+2\lambda$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) The second and third planes are parallel and distinct; the first plane is not parallel to them, so it cuts them in two parallel lines and there is no common point [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Expanding a $3\times3$ determinant along the first row is quicker here because all its entries are $1$. When two equations share the same left-hand side, compare the right-hand sides immediately.

subtopic: Quadratic through three points and tangent line
statement: The graph of $y=f(x)$, where $f(x)=ax^2+bx+c$, passes through the points $(1,6)$, $(2,11)$ and $(-1,2)$. (a) Find the values of $a$, $b$ and $c$. [5] (b) Show that the graph of $f$ does not intersect the $x$-axis. [2] (c) The line $y=mx$ is a tangent to the graph of $f$. Find the possible values of $m$, giving your answers in exact form. [3]
markscheme: (a) Substituting the points: $a+b+c=6$, $4a+2b+c=11$, $a-b+c=2$ [M1] [A1] Subtracting the first and third: $2b=4$, so $b=2$ [M1] [A1] Then $a+c=4$ and $4a+c=7$, giving $3a=3$, so $a=1$, $c=3$ [A1] [5 marks] (b) $f(x)=x^2+2x+3$, discriminant $=2^2-4(1)(3)$ [M1] $=-8<0$, so there are no real roots and the graph does not meet the $x$-axis [A1] [2 marks] (c) $x^2+2x+3=mx$ gives $x^2+(2-m)x+3=0$ [M1] Tangent means discriminant is zero: $(2-m)^2-12=0$ [M1] $m=2\pm2\sqrt3$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Writing each point as an equation gives a linear system; look for the pair of equations that eliminates a variable most easily. In part (c), a tangent line corresponds to a repeated root, i.e. discriminant zero.

subtopic: Circle through three points using a linear system
statement: A circle has equation $x^2+y^2+Dx+Ey+F=0$ and passes through the points $(1,2)$, $(4,-1)$ and $(-2,-1)$. (a) Write down a system of three linear equations in $D$, $E$ and $F$. [2] (b) Solve the system to find $D$, $E$ and $F$. [4] (c) Find the center and radius of the circle. [2]
markscheme: (a) $(1,2)$: $5+D+2E+F=0$ [A1] $(4,-1)$: $17+4D-E+F=0$ and $(-2,-1)$: $5-2D-E+F=0$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) The equations are $D+2E+F=-5$, $4D-E+F=-17$, $-2D-E+F=-5$. Subtract the third from the second: $6D=-12$ so $D=-2$ [M1] [A1] The first and third give $2E+F=-3$ and $F-E=-9$, so $3E=6$ [M1] $E=2$ and $F=-7$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) Completing the square: $(x-1)^2+(y+1)^2=9$ [M1] center $(1,-1)$ and radius $3$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Substituting each point into the general circle equation gives a linear system in $D$, $E$, $F$. Complete the square at the end to read off the center and radius.

subtopic: Matrix form of a 3x3 system and solving with a GDC
statement: Consider the system of equations $$\begin{aligned} 2x+3y-z&=-2.5\\ x+y+2z&=7\\ 4x-2y+z&=16 \end{aligned}$$ (a) Write the system in the form $A\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{B}$, stating $A$, $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{B}$. [2] (b) Use your GDC to find the values of $x$, $y$ and $z$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $A=\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 3 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 4 & -2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\mathbf{X}=\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{pmatrix}$, $\mathbf{B}=\begin{pmatrix} -2.5 \\ 7 \\ 16 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Use the GDC simultaneous equation solver (or $\mathbf{X}=A^{-1}\mathbf{B}$) [M1] $x=2.5$, $y=-1.5$, $z=3$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Enter the coefficient matrix row by row and double-check each sign before using the GDC. Substitute the result into one equation as a quick check.

subtopic: Integer solutions of an underdetermined system
statement: A theater sells $20$ tickets for a total of $\$190$. Adult tickets cost $\$12$, child tickets cost $\$7$ and senior tickets cost $\$9$. Let $a$, $c$ and $s$ be the numbers of adult, child and senior tickets sold. (a) Write down two equations for $a$, $c$ and $s$, and show that $5a+2s=50$. [3] (b) Find all possible solutions where $a$, $c$, $s$ are non-negative integers. [4]
markscheme: (a) $a+c+s=20$ [A1] $12a+7c+9s=190$ [A1] subtract $7\times$ the first: $5a+2s=50$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $a=\dfrac{50-2s}5$, so $s$ is a multiple of $5$ [M1][A1] $(a,c,s)=(10,10,0),(8,7,5),(6,4,10),(4,1,15)$ [A1] $s=20$ gives $c<0$, rejected [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Eliminate one variable to get a single equation in two unknowns, then use the requirement that quantities are whole numbers.

subtopic: A system with a linear and a quadratic equation
statement: Solve the system $y=2x-1$ and $x^2+y^2=13$. [6]
tips: Substitute the linear equation into the quadratic one and solve; do not forget the corresponding $y$-values.

subtopic: A system with a modulus
statement: Solve the system $|x-y|=2$ and $x+y=6$. [4]
tips: A modulus equation splits into two linear equations: $x-y=2$ and $x-y=-2$.

subtopic: Triangle formed by three lines
statement: The lines $y=x$, $y=-x+4$ and $y=0$ form a triangle. (a) Find the coordinates of the three vertices. [3] (b) Find the area of the triangle. [2]
markscheme: (a) $y=x$ and $y=0$: $(0,0)$ [A1] $y=-x+4$ and $y=0$: $(4,0)$ [A1] $y=x$ and $y=-x+4$: $(2,2)$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) base $4$ and height $2$ [M1] area $=\dfrac12\times4\times2=4$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Each pair of lines gives one vertex. Use the base along the $x$-axis and the vertical height of the third vertex.

subtopic: Matrix form and inverse of a 3x3 system
statement: Consider the system of equations $$\begin{aligned} 2x+y+3z&=9\\ x-y+2z&=9\\ 3x+2y+z&=2 \end{aligned}$$ which can be written as $A\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{B}$, where $\mathbf{X}=\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\\z\end{pmatrix}$. (a) Write down the matrices $A$ and $\mathbf{B}$. [2] (b) Use your GDC to find $\det A$ and $A^{-1}$, giving the entries of $A^{-1}$ as decimals. [2] (c) Hence solve the system. [2] (d) The third row of $A$ is changed to $\begin{pmatrix}3&2&k\end{pmatrix}$. Find the value of $k$ for which the new matrix has no inverse. [2]
tips: Use the GDC for the inverse and the product $A^{-1}\mathbf{B}$, but state the matrix equation first so that the method mark is secure. A matrix has no inverse exactly when its determinant is zero.

subtopic: Traffic flow through a network
statement: In a one-way road network, $500$ cars per hour enter at junction $A$, which has roads to $B$ (flow $x_1$) and to $C$ (flow $x_2$). From $B$ there are roads to $D$ (flow $x_3$) and to $C$ (flow $x_5$). From $C$ there is a road to $D$ (flow $x_4$), and $500$ cars per hour leave at $D$. The flow into each junction equals the flow out. (a) Write down four equations for the flows, one for each junction. [2] (b) Express $x_2$, $x_3$ and $x_4$ in terms of $x_1=s$ and $x_5=t$. [3] (c) Given $x_1=350$, find the range of possible values of $x_5$, if every flow must be non-negative. [3]
tips: There are five unknowns and only three independent equations, so two of the flows can be chosen freely.

subtopic: A direct-current circuit as a linear system
statement: A $12$ V battery is connected in series to a $2$ ohm resistor. This is followed by two branches in parallel: one with a $4$ ohm resistor carrying current $I_2$ and one with a resistor of $r$ ohms carrying current $I_3$. The current in the battery is $I_1$ (amps). By Kirchhoff's laws, $I_1=I_2+I_3$, $12=2I_1+4I_2$, and $4I_2=rI_3$ (the parallel branches have equal voltage). (a) For $r=6$, write the system in matrix form $A\mathbf I=\mathbf b$ and solve it using your calculator. [4] (b) For general $r$, show that $I_3=\dfrac{24}{3r+4}$ and $I_2=\dfrac{6r}{3r+4}$. [4] (c) Find the limits of $I_2$ as $r\to\infty$ and as $r\to0$, and explain each in terms of the circuit. [3] (d) The power dissipated in the resistor of $r$ ohms is $P=rI_3^2$. Show that $P=\dfrac{576r}{(3r+4)^2}$, and find the value of $r$ at which $P$ is greatest, and the greatest power. [5]
markscheme: (a) $\begin{pmatrix}1 & -1 & -1\\ 2 & 4 & 0\\ 0 & 4 & -6\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}I_1\\ I_2\\ I_3\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\ 12\\ 0\end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1] $I_1=\dfrac{30}{11}$ [A1] $I_2=\dfrac{18}{11}$ and $I_3=\dfrac{12}{11}$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $I_3=\dfrac{4I_2}r$ and $I_1=I_2\left(1+\dfrac4r\right)$ [M1][A1] $12=2I_2\left(1+\dfrac4r\right)+4I_2=I_2\,\dfrac{6r+8}r$ [M1] $I_2=\dfrac{6r}{3r+4}$ and then $I_3=\dfrac{24}{3r+4}$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) $r\to\infty$: $I_2\to2$ [A1] the second branch carries no current, so the $4$ ohm resistor is in series with the $2$ ohm resistor: $\dfrac{12}6=2$ [R1] $r\to0$: $I_2\to0$, since the short circuit takes all the current [R1] [3 marks] (d) $P=r\times\dfrac{576}{(3r+4)^2}$ [A1] $\dfrac{dP}{dr}=576\times\dfrac{(3r+4)-6r}{(3r+4)^3}$ [M1][A1] $=0$ at $r=\dfrac43$ [A1] $P_{\max}=\dfrac{576\times\frac43}{64}=12$ W [A1] [5 marks]
tips: Express each current in terms of $I_2$ using the equations, then substitute into the voltage equation for the battery loop.

subtopic: Line meeting a cubic: intersections and tangency
statement: The curve $C$ has equation $y=x^3-4x$. (a) The line $y=2x-3$ meets $C$ at three points. Find the $x$-coordinates of these points, correct to 3 significant figures. [3] (b) The line $y=2x+k$ meets $C$ at exactly two distinct points. Find the possible values of $k$, giving your answers to 3 significant figures. [4]
markscheme: (a) $x^3-4x=2x-3$, so $x^3-6x+3=0$ [M1] Using the GDC: [A1] $x=-2.67$, $x=0.524$, $x=2.15$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $x^3-4x=2x+k$ gives $k=x^3-6x$; define $g(x)=x^3-6x$ [M1] Exactly two intersections occur when $k$ equals a local maximum or minimum value of $g$: $g'(x)=3x^2-6=0$ so $x=\pm\sqrt2$ [A1] $g(\sqrt2)=-4\sqrt2$ and $g(-\sqrt2)=4\sqrt2$ [M1] $k=\pm4\sqrt2=\pm5.66$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Rearrange to make the parameter the subject, then use the turning points of the resulting cubic to count solutions. A horizontal line meets a cubic in exactly two points when it touches a turning point.

subtopic: Diet plan with three foods and a 3x3 system
statement: Three foods, $X$, $Y$ and $Z$, contain protein, carbohydrate and fat. Each 100 g of $X$ contains 10 g of protein, 20 g of carbohydrate and 5 g of fat. Each 100 g of $Y$ contains 5 g of protein, 30 g of carbohydrate and 2 g of fat. Each 100 g of $Z$ contains 20 g of protein, 10 g of carbohydrate and 15 g of fat. A meal plan must provide exactly 45 g of protein, 100 g of carbohydrate and 26.5 g of fat. Let $x$, $y$ and $z$ be the numbers of 100 g portions of $X$, $Y$ and $Z$ used. (a) Write down a system of three equations for $x$, $y$ and $z$. [2] (b) Use your GDC to find $x$, $y$ and $z$. [2] (c) Find the total mass of food, in grams, in the meal plan. [2]
markscheme: (a) Protein: $10x+5y+20z=45$ [A1] Carbohydrate: $20x+30y+10z=100$ and fat: $5x+2y+15z=26.5$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Solve with the GDC [M1] $x=1.5$, $y=2$, $z=1$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Total mass $=100(x+y+z)$ [M1] $=100(4.5)=450$ g [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Set up one equation per nutrient, keeping every food in the same order. The unknowns are numbers of 100 g portions, so convert to grams at the end.

subtopic: Geometry of three planes with a parallel pair and their line of intersection
statement: Three planes have equations $$\begin{aligned} \Pi_1&:\ 2x-y+3z=4\\ \Pi_2&:\ 4x-2y+6z=c\\ \Pi_3&:\ x+y-z=1 \end{aligned}$$ where $c\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Find the value of $c$ for which $\Pi_1$ and $\Pi_2$ are the same plane. [1] (b) For this value of $c$, find a vector equation of the line of intersection of the three planes. [4] (c) Given that $c=5$, describe the arrangement of the three planes, justifying your answer. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\Pi_2$ is $2\times\Pi_1$ on the left, so $c=8$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Adding $\Pi_1$ and $\Pi_3$: $3x+2z=5$ [M1] [A1] Let $x=1-2s$: then $z=1+3s$ and from $\Pi_3$, $y=1-x+z=1+5s$ [M1] $\mathbf{r}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}+s\begin{pmatrix} -2 \\ 5 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) The normal to $\Pi_2$ is $(4,-2,6)=2(2,-1,3)$, parallel to the normal of $\Pi_1$, and $5\neq 2\times4$ so these planes are parallel and distinct [R1] The normal to $\Pi_3$, $(1,1,-1)$, is not parallel to $(2,-1,3)$ [R1] So $\Pi_3$ meets each of the parallel planes in a line; the two lines are parallel and there is no common point of all three planes [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Compare normal vectors first: proportional normals mean parallel or coincident planes, and the right-hand sides then decide which. Check any line you find by substituting its general point into every plane.

subtopic: Hyperbola and line: intersection and tangency
statement: (a) Solve the simultaneous equations $xy=6$ and $2x+y=7$. [4] (b) The line $2x+y=c$ is a tangent to the curve $xy=6$. Find the possible values of $c$, giving your answers in exact form. [4]
markscheme: (a) $y=7-2x$, so $x(7-2x)=6$ [M1] $2x^2-7x+6=0$ [A1] $(2x-3)(x-2)=0$ [M1] $x=\frac32,\ y=4$ and $x=2,\ y=3$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $y=c-2x$, so $x(c-2x)=6$, giving $2x^2-cx+6=0$ [M1] A tangent meets the curve at exactly one point, so the discriminant is zero [R1] $c^2-48=0$ [M1] $c=\pm4\sqrt3$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Substitute the linear equation into the nonlinear one to get a quadratic. Tangency means a repeated root, so set the discriminant to zero.

subtopic: Concurrent lines and an unknown coefficient
statement: The lines $x+2y=3$, $2x-y=1$ and $3x+ky=5$ meet at a single point. (a) Find the point where the first two lines meet. [3] (b) Hence find $k$. [2]
tips: Three lines are concurrent when the intersection of two of them lies on the third.

subtopic: Quadratic from a point values and an area
statement: A quadratic function $f(x)=ax^{2}+bx+c$ satisfies $f(0)=3$, $f(1)=2$ and $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{3}f(x)\,dx=9$. (a) Show that $9a+\dfrac{9}{2}b+3c=9$. [2] (b) Find $a$, $b$ and $c$. [3] (c) Find the coordinates of the minimum point of the graph of $y=f(x)$. [2]
tips: Each condition on $f$ gives one linear equation in the three unknown coefficients.

subtopic: Mixing fertilisers
statement: A farmer mixes three fertilisers $F_1$, $F_2$ and $F_3$. The percentages by mass of nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P) and potassium (K) in each fertiliser are shown below. $$\begin{array}{c|ccc} & \text{N} & \text{P} & \text{K}\\ \hline F_1 & 10\% & 5\% & 20\%\\ F_2 & 20\% & 10\% & 5\%\\ F_3 & 5\% & 20\% & 10\% \end{array}$$ The farmer uses $a$ kg of $F_1$, $b$ kg of $F_2$ and $c$ kg of $F_3$ to supply exactly $33$ kg of nitrogen, $34$ kg of phosphorus and $38$ kg of potassium. (a) Write down three equations for $a$, $b$ and $c$. [3] (b) Solve the equations. [2] The fertilisers cost $\$0.45$, $\$0.60$ and $\$0.50$ per kilogram respectively. (c) Find the total cost of the fertiliser used. [2]
tips: Convert each percentage to a decimal and write one equation for each nutrient, not for each fertiliser. Check your solution against all three nutrient totals.

subtopic: Solving a 3x3 system by elimination
statement: Consider the system $\begin{aligned} x + 2y - z&=-3 \\ 2x + y + z&=6 \\ 3x - y + 2z&=13 \end{aligned}$ Solve the system of equations. [5]
markscheme: Label the equations (1), (2), (3). (2)$-2\times$(1): $-3y + 3z=12$ [M1]; (3)$-3\times$(1): $-7y + 5z=22$ [A1]. Solving these two equations simultaneously gives $y=-1$ [M1] and $z=3$ [A1]. Substituting into (1) gives $x=2$ [A1]. [5 marks]
tips: Use the equation with coefficient $1$ on $x$ to eliminate $x$ from the other two equations, then solve the resulting $2\times2$ system. Always substitute back to check one equation you did not use.

subtopic: Quadratic through three points
statement: A parabola with equation $y=ax^{2}+bx+c$ passes through the points $(0, -2)$, $(2, -2)$ and $(3, 4)$. (a) Find the values of $a$, $b$ and $c$. [4] (b) Find the coordinates of the vertex. [2] (c) Find the exact values of the $x$-intercepts. [2]
tips: Use the point on the $y$-axis first to find $c$, then form two equations in $a$ and $b$.

subtopic: Solving a 3x3 system by elimination
statement: Solve the system of equations $$\begin{aligned}x+y+z&=6\\2x-y+z&=3\\x+2y-z&=2\end{aligned}$$ [6]
markscheme: Attempt to eliminate one variable [M1] Adding the first and third equations: $2x+3y=8$ [A1] Subtracting the first equation from the second: $x-2y=-3$ [A1] Attempt to solve the two equations in $x$ and $y$ [M1] $x=1$, $y=2$ [A1] $z=3$ [A1] [6 marks]
tips: Eliminate the same variable from two different pairs of equations so that you get two equations in two unknowns. Substitute your solution into all three original equations to check.

subtopic: Three unknown prices by elimination
statement: In a stationery shop a pen costs $p$ dollars, a notebook costs $n$ dollars and a folder costs $f$ dollars. Three orders are made: $3p+2n+f=19$, $2p+n+2f=15$ and $p+3n+2f=23$. (a) Solve the system of equations to find $p$, $n$ and $f$, showing your elimination steps. [6] (b) Find the total cost of two pens, two notebooks and two folders. [1]
markscheme: (a) eliminate $f$: eq2 $-$ eq3 gives $p-2n=-8$ [M1][A1]; $2\times$eq1 $-$ eq2 gives $4p+3n=23$ [M1][A1]; solving, $p=2$, $n=5$ [A1]; $f=19-6-10=3$ [A1] [6 marks] (b) $2(2+5+3)=20$ dollars [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Eliminate the same variable from two different pairs of equations to get a $2\times2$ system.

subtopic: Reading solutions from an augmented matrix
statement: A system of linear equations has the following augmented matrix after Gaussian elimination. $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & k^2-1 & 4(k+1) \end{pmatrix}$ where $k$ is a constant. The variables are $x$, $y$, $z$ and the last column holds the constants. (a) Find the values of $k$ for which the system has a unique solution. [2] (b) Find the value of $k$ for which there are infinitely many solutions, and write the general solution in terms of $\lambda$ where $z=\lambda$. [4] (c) Explain why there is no solution when $k=1$. [2] (d) Find the solution when $k=3$. [3]
markscheme: (a) Unique solution when the third row is not all zeros in the coefficients: $k^2-1\neq0$ [M1] so $k\neq\pm1$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $k=-1$ gives the third row $(0\ 0\ 0\mid 0)$ [M1][A1]; $y=3 - 2 \lambda$ [A1], $x=3 \lambda - 1$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) With $k=1$ the third row is $(0\ 0\ 0\mid 8)$ [A1] which states $0=8$, a contradiction [R1] [2 marks] (d) $z=\dfrac{4(3+1)}{3^2-1}=2$ [A1], then back-substitute: $y=-1$ [A1], $x=5$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Back-substitution from the row-echelon form is quick once the parameter is fixed; keep $\lambda$ for the free variable.

subtopic: Monthly sales modeled by a cubic
statement: The monthly sales $S$ (in hundreds of units) of a seasonal product are recorded in four months, where $m$ is the month number ($m=1$ for January). The model is $S=am^3+bm^2+cm+d$ and it passes through $(1, 67.5)$, $(4, 84)$, $(7, 64.5)$, $(11, 122.5)$. (a) Write the conditions on $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ as a matrix equation $M\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{w}$. [3] (b) Solve the matrix equation using your calculator. [2] (c) Find the coordinates of the local maximum and the local minimum of the graph for $1\leq m\leq 11$. [3] (d) Use the model to predict $S$ when $m=13$ and comment on the reliability of the prediction. [2]
markscheme: (a) $M=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 64 & 16 & 4 & 1 \\ 343 & 49 & 7 & 1 \\ 1331 & 121 & 11 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1], $\mathbf{v}=\begin{pmatrix} a \\ b \\ c \\ d \end{pmatrix}$ [A1], $\mathbf{w}=\begin{pmatrix} 67.5 \\ 84 \\ 64.5 \\ 122.5 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\mathbf{v}=M^{-1}\mathbf{w}$ or system solver [M1]: $a=0.5$, $b=-8$, $c=35$, $d=40$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Setting $1.5m^2+(-16)m+(35)=0$ [M1] (or GDC turning points) gives $m=3.07$ and $m=7.59$ [A1]; the corresponding values are $S=86.5$ and $S=63.4$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $S=242$ [A1]; $m=13$ lies outside the data range $1\leq m\leq 11$, so this is extrapolation and may be unreliable [R1] [2 marks]
tips: The inverse-matrix route and the system solver give the same coefficients; keep full calculator precision until the final answers.

subtopic: Balancing the combustion of propane
statement: The combustion of propane is represented by $a\,\mathrm{C_3H_8} + b\,\mathrm{O_2} \to c\,\mathrm{CO_2} + d\,\mathrm{H_2O}$ where $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ are positive integers that balance the numbers of atoms of each element. (a) Write down a system of linear equations, one for each element, that the integers must satisfy. [3] (b) Show that the system has infinitely many solutions and find the general solution, in terms of $\lambda$ where $a=\lambda$. [3] (c) Hence write the balanced equation using the smallest positive integers. [2]
markscheme: (a) Balance each element: $3a=c$ (for C), $8a=2d$ (for H), $2b=2c + d$ (for O) [A1][A1][A1] (any three correct equations) [3 marks] (b) The rank of the coefficient matrix is 3 (fewer than 4 unknowns) so there are infinitely many solutions [R1]; solving gives $a=\lambda$, $b=5 \lambda$, $c=3 \lambda$, $d=4 \lambda$ [M1][A1] [3 marks] (c) Choose $\lambda$ so all values are the smallest positive integers [M1]: $\mathrm{C_3H_8} + 5\mathrm{O_2} \to 3\mathrm{CO_2} + 4\mathrm{H_2O}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Use the GDC to find the null space or set one variable to $\lambda$ and back-substitute; clear fractions to get smallest integers.

subtopic: Free variable with a parameter in the x column
statement: Consider the equations $\begin{aligned} x + 2z&=3 \\ y - z&=1 \\ kx + y + z&=c \end{aligned}$ where $k$ and $c$ are constants. (a) By considering (3)$-$(1)$-$(2), find the value of $k$ for which the system does not have a unique solution. [3] (b) Given that $k=1$, find the value of $c$ for which the system has infinitely many solutions, and give the general solution in terms of $\lambda$, where $x=\lambda$. [4] (c) Explain why there is no solution when $k=1$ and $c\neq4$. [1]
markscheme: (a) (3)$-$(1)$-$(2) gives $(k-1)x=c-4$ [M1][A1] so a unique solution exists unless $k=1$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Need $0=c-4$, so $c=4$ [A1]; solve (1) and (2) for the other two variables [M1] giving $x=\lambda$, $y=\frac{5}{2} - \frac{\lambda}{2}$, $z=\frac{3}{2} - \frac{\lambda}{2}$ [A1][A1] [4 marks] (c) The third equation reduces to $0=c-4\neq0$, a contradiction [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Whichever variable carries the parameter in the dependent equation becomes the free variable $\lambda$.

subtopic: Inconsistent system and its meaning
statement: Consider the system $\begin{aligned} x + y + z&=6 \\ x + 2y + 3z&=14 \\ 2x + 3y + 4z&=19 \end{aligned}$ (a) Show that the system has no solution. [3] (b) Write down the number of solutions if the right-hand side of the third equation is changed to $20$, and justify your answer. [2]
markscheme: (a) Equation (1)+(2): $2x+3y+4z=20$ [M1]; compare with equation (3), $2x+3y+4z=19$ [A1]; contradiction so no solution [R1] [3 marks] (b) The third equation becomes dependent on the first two [M1]; infinitely many solutions [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Add or subtract equations and look for a pair of left-hand sides that agree while the right-hand sides do not.

subtopic: Solving in terms of a free parameter
statement: The system $\begin{aligned} x + 2y + z&=4 \\ 2x + y - z&=5 \\ 3x + ky&=c \end{aligned}$ where $k$ and $c$ are constants. (a) By considering (3)$-$(1)$-$(2), find the value of $k$ for which the system does not have a unique solution. [3] (b) Given that $k=3$, find the value of $c$ for which the system has infinitely many solutions, and give the general solution in terms of $\lambda$, where $y=\lambda$. [4] (c) Explain why there is no solution when $k=3$ and $c\neq9$. [1]
markscheme: (a) (3)$-$(1)$-$(2) gives $(k-3)y=c-9$ [M1][A1] so a unique solution exists unless $k=3$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Need $0=c-9$, so $c=9$ [A1]; solve (1) and (2) for the other two variables [M1] giving $x=3 - \lambda$, $y=\lambda$, $z=1 - \lambda$ [A1][A1] [4 marks] (c) The third equation reduces to $0=c-9\neq0$, a contradiction [R1] [1 mark]
tips: When the parameter makes the equations dependent, one variable is free; write it as $\lambda$ and solve the other two in terms of it.

subtopic: Parameters, infinitely many solutions and no solution
statement: Consider the system of equations $$\begin{aligned}x+y+z&=2\\2x+3y+4z&=5\\x+2y+kz&=m\end{aligned}$$ where $k,m\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Find the value of $k$ for which the system does not have a unique solution. [3] (b) For this value of $k$, find the value of $m$ for which the system has infinitely many solutions. [3] (c) For these values of $k$ and $m$, find the general solution of the system, using the parameter $t$ where $z=t$. [2] (d) State what happens when $k$ takes the value found in part (a) and $m$ takes any other value. [1]
markscheme: (a) Attempt to find the determinant or to row reduce [M1] $\det=1(3k-8)-1(2k-4)+1(4-3)=k-3$ [A1] $k=3$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Subtract $2\times$ equation $1$ from equation $2$: $y+2z=1$; subtract equation $1$ from equation $3$: $y+2z=m-2$ [M1] Both are expressions for $y+2z$, so we need $m-2=1$ [A1] $m=3$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $z=t$, $y=1-2t$ [M1] $x=1+t$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) The system has no solution (it is inconsistent) [A1] [1 mark]
tips: A zero determinant means the system has either no solution or infinitely many, and the right-hand sides decide which. Row reduce and compare the two equations that become parallel.

subtopic: Interpolating through equally spaced points
statement: This question investigates how a quadratic $y=px^2+qx+r$ is determined by its values at $x=1$, $x=2$ and $x=3$. Let the values be $y_1$, $y_2$, $y_3$ respectively. (a) Show that $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 4 & 2 & 1 \\ 9 & 3 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} p \\ q \\ r \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} y_1 \\ y_2 \\ y_3 \end{pmatrix}$. [2] (b) Find the determinant of the $3\times3$ matrix $M$, and use your calculator to find $M^{-1}$. [3] (c) Hence express $p$, $q$ and $r$ in terms of $y_1$, $y_2$ and $y_3$. [3] (d) A quadratic passes through $(1,5)$, $(2,8)$ and $(3,15)$. Find $p$, $q$ and $r$. [2] (e) Show that $p$ is half of the second difference $y_3-2y_2+y_1$, and state the geometric meaning of the sign of $p$. [2] (f) A fourth point $(4,y_4)$ lies on the same parabola. Show that $y_4=y_1-3y_2+3y_3$. [3] (g) The measured values are $y_1=5$, $y_2=8$, $y_3=15$ and $y_4=27$. Show that a quadratic does not fit all four points. [2] (h) Find the cubic $y=ax^3+bx^2+cx+d$ through all four points, and use it to estimate $y$ when $x=5$. [5] (i) Explain why the estimate of $y$ at $x=5$ is less reliable than an estimate at $x=2.5$. [2]
markscheme: (a) Substitute $x=1,2,3$: $p+q+r=y_1$ [A1], $4p+2q+r=y_2$, $9p+3q+r=y_3$ [A1] which is the stated matrix equation [2 marks] (b) $\det M=-2$ [A1]; $M^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{1}{2} & -1 & \dfrac{1}{2} \\ -\dfrac{5}{2} & 4 & -\dfrac{3}{2} \\ 3 & -3 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1][A1] [3 marks] (c) $\mathbf{v}=M^{-1}\mathbf{y}$ [M1]; $p=\dfrac{y_1-2y_2+y_3}{2}$ [A1]; $q=-\frac{5 y_{1}}{2} + 4 y_{2} - \frac{3 y_{3}}{2}$ and $r=3 y_{1} - 3 y_{2} + y_{3}$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $p=2$, $q=-3$, $r=6$ [A1][A1] [2 marks] (e) From part (c), $p=\tfrac12(y_1-2y_2+y_3)$ [AG]; $p>0$ means the parabola opens upward (the data are convex) [R1] [2 marks] (f) $y_4=16p+4q+r$ [M1]; substituting $p,q,r$ from (c) [M1]; simplifying to $y_1-3y_2+3y_3$ [AG] [3 marks] (g) A quadratic through the first three gives $y_4=26$ [A1], not 27, so no quadratic fits [R1] [2 marks] (h) Set up the $4\times4$ system and solve [M1][A1]: $a=\frac{1}{6}$, $b=1$, $c=-\frac{7}{6}$, $d=5$ [A1]; at $x=5$: $y=45$ [M1][A1] [5 marks] (i) $x=5$ lies outside the interval of the data (extrapolation) [R1] whereas $2.5$ is between known points (interpolation) [R1] [2 marks]
tips: In an interpolation problem, each data point supplies one linear equation; a unique polynomial of degree $n-1$ passes through $n$ points whose $x$-values are distinct.

subtopic: Piecewise quadratic path joined smoothly
statement: This question models the path of a stunt cyclist over a ramp. The height $y$ meters at horizontal distance $x$ meters is given by $y=f(x)=ax^{2}+bx+c$ for $0\le x\le3$ and by $y=g(x)=px^{2}+qx+r$ for $3\le x\le8$. The first piece passes through $(0, 0)$ and $(3, 3.6)$, and its gradient at $x=3$ is $2.4$. (a) Write down three equations for $a$, $b$ and $c$ and solve them to find $f(x)$. [4] (b) The second piece joins the first at $(3, 3.6)$ with the same gradient there, and passes through $(8, 0.6)$. Write down three equations for $p$, $q$ and $r$. [3] (c) Solve these equations to find $g(x)$. [2] (d) Find the greatest height of the cyclist and the value of $x$ where it occurs. [3] (e) Find the values of $x$, between $3$ and $8$, for which the height is at least $5$ m, to 3 significant figures. [3] (f) State one way in which the model would be unrealistic if the two pieces met at $x=3$ with different gradients. [1]
tips: Continuity gives the point equation and smoothness gives equal gradients, so both pieces share the derivative value at $x=3$.

subtopic: Sensitivity of a nearly singular system
statement: This question investigates how small changes in the data affect the solution of two nearly parallel lines. Consider the system $x+y=2$ and $x+1.001y=2.001$. (a) Solve the system. [3] (b) The second right-hand side is changed to $2.002$ (a change in the third decimal place). Solve the new system. [2] (c) Write the original system as $A\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{b}$. Show that $\det A=0.001$ and find $A^{-1}$. [3] (d) The right-hand side is now $\mathbf{b}=\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 2.001+\delta \end{pmatrix}$. Use $A^{-1}$ to show that $x=1-1000\delta$ and $y=1+1000\delta$. [4] (e) Each coefficient and constant in the data is rounded to 3 decimal places, so $|\delta|$ can be as large as $0.0005$. Find the largest possible error in $y$, and comment on the reliability of the solution. [3] (f) The two lines have gradients $-1$ and $-\dfrac{1}{1.001}$. Find the acute angle between them in degrees, correct to 3 significant figures. [3] (g) Explain, using the angle between the lines, why the intersection point is so sensitive to small changes in the equations. [2] (h) The second equation is replaced by $x-y=0$, and its right-hand side is changed by $\delta$. Show that the solution changes by only $\dfrac{\delta}{2}$ in each variable. [3]
markscheme: (a) Subtract the first equation from the second: $0.001y=0.001$ [M1] so $y=1$ [A1] and $x=1$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $0.001y=0.002$ so $y=2$ [A1] and $x=0$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\det A=1(1.001)-1(1)=0.001$ [AG]; $A^{-1}=\dfrac{1}{0.001}\begin{pmatrix} 1.001 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 1001 & -1000 \\ -1000 & 1000 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1] [3 marks] (d) $\mathbf{v}=A^{-1}\mathbf{b}$ [M1]; $x=1001(2)-1000(2.001+\delta)$ [M1] $=2002-2001-1000\delta=1-1000\delta$ [A1]; $y=-1000(2)+1000(2.001+\delta)=1+1000\delta$ [A1] [4 marks] (e) $\max|1000\delta|=0.5$ [A1][M1]; an input error of $0.0005$ can produce an error of $0.5$ in $y$ (1000 times larger), so the solution is unreliable [R1] [3 marks] (f) $\left|\tan^{-1}(1)-\tan^{-1}\left(\tfrac{1}{1.001}\right)\right|$ [M1][A1] $=0.0286^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks] (g) The lines are almost parallel [R1], so a small vertical shift of one line moves the intersection a long way along the lines [R1] [2 marks] (h) $x+y=2$, $x-y=\delta$ [M1] so $x=1+\dfrac{\delta}{2}$ and $y=1-\dfrac{\delta}{2}$ [A1][A1] [3 marks]
tips: A system is sensitive when its coefficient matrix has a determinant that is small compared with the size of its entries. Compare the effect of the same small change $\delta$ in two different systems.

subtopic: Parameter k in a three-variable system
statement: Consider the system $x+2y+z=4$, $2x+3y+kz=9$ and $x+y+2z=5$, where $k$ is a constant. (a) Find the value of $k$ for which the system does not have a unique solution. [3] (b) For this value of $k$, show that the system is consistent and find the general solution in terms of a parameter $t=z$. [4] (c) For $k=2$, use your GDC to solve the system. [2]
markscheme: (a) coefficient matrix $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 & k \\ 1 & 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ has determinant $k-3$ [M1][A1]; $k=3$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) subtract eq3 from eq1: $y-z=-1$ so $y=t-1$ [M1][A1]; $x=4-2(t-1)-t=6-3t$ [A1]; sum of eq1 and eq3 gives eq2 (LHS and RHS), so the equations are consistent with infinitely many solutions $(6-3t,\ t-1,\ t)$ [R1] [4 marks] (c) unique solution since $k\ne3$ [M1]; $x=6$, $y=-1$, $z=0$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A zero determinant means no unique solution. Check consistency by seeing whether the dependent equation's right-hand side matches.

subtopic: Fitting a quadratic model through three points
statement: The height $h$ metres of a drone above the ground, $t$ seconds after it is launched, is modelled by $h=at^2+bt+c$. The drone is at a height of $2$ m when $t=0$, $12$ m when $t=2$, and $18$ m when $t=4$. (a) Write down a system of three equations for $a$, $b$ and $c$. [2] (b) Solve the system to find $a$, $b$ and $c$. [2] (c) Find the maximum height reached by the drone, and the time at which this occurs. [3] (d) Find the time at which the drone lands, giving your answer to three significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) $c=2$ [A1] $4a+2b+c=12$ and $16a+4b+c=18$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Use of GDC or elimination [M1] $a=-0.5$, $b=6$, $c=2$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $t=-\dfrac{b}{2a}=6$ [M1] Maximum height $=-0.5(36)+36+2=20$ m [A1] at $t=6$ seconds [A1] [3 marks] (d) $-0.5t^2+6t+2=0$ [M1] $t=12.3$ seconds (reject the negative root) [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Each data point gives one equation in the unknown coefficients. Once you have the model, use your GDC to find the maximum and the zeros, and reject any root that is not physically sensible.

subtopic: Dependent third equation with parameter in the first column
statement: The system $\begin{aligned} 2x + y&=5 \\ x - y + z&=1 \\ kx + z&=c \end{aligned}$ where $k$ and $c$ are constants. (a) By considering (3)$-$(1)$-$(2), find the value of $k$ for which the system does not have a unique solution. [3] (b) Given that $k=3$, find the value of $c$ for which the system has infinitely many solutions, and give the general solution in terms of $\lambda$, where $x=\lambda$. [4] (c) Explain why there is no solution when $k=3$ and $c\neq6$. [1]
markscheme: (a) (3)$-$(1)$-$(2) gives $(k-3)x=c-6$ [M1][A1] so a unique solution exists unless $k=3$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Need $0=c-6$, so $c=6$ [A1]; solve (1) and (2) for the other two variables [M1] giving $x=\lambda$, $y=5 - 2 \lambda$, $z=6 - 3 \lambda$ [A1][A1] [4 marks] (c) The third equation reduces to $0=c-6\neq0$, a contradiction [R1] [1 mark]
tips: The third row is built from the first two, so subtracting them isolates the parameter; check the consistency condition on the right-hand side.

subtopic: Ticket prices from two simultaneous equations
statement: At a school play, an adult ticket costs $a$ dollars and a student ticket costs $s$ dollars. Three adult tickets and two student tickets cost $41$ dollars in total. Two adult tickets and five student tickets cost $53$ dollars in total. (a) Write down two equations in $a$ and $s$ and solve them to find $a$ and $s$. [4] (b) Find the cost of four adult tickets and three student tickets. [1] (c) A group of $12$ people, each with an adult or a student ticket, pays $102$ dollars in total. Find how many of them hold adult tickets. [3]
markscheme: (a) $3a+2s=41$ and $2a+5s=53$ [A1]; eliminate, e.g. $15a+10s=205$ and $4a+10s=106$ [M1]; $11a=99$ so $a=9$ [A1]; $s=7$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $4\times9+3\times7=57$ dollars [A1] [1 mark] (c) let $x$ adult and $y$ student tickets: $x+y=12$ and $9x+7y=102$ [M1]; $9x+7(12-x)=102$ so $2x=18$ [A1]; $x=9$ adult tickets [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Multiply one or both equations so that a variable has equal coefficients, then add or subtract.

subtopic: Balancing a chemical equation
statement: Butane burns in oxygen according to the reaction $$a\,\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}+b\,\text{O}_2\to c\,\text{CO}_2+d\,\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ where $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ are positive integers. The number of atoms of each element must be the same on both sides. (a) Write down three equations connecting $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$, one for each of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. [3] (b) Show that the equations have infinitely many solutions, and express $b$, $c$ and $d$ in terms of $a$. [3] (c) Find the smallest positive integers $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ that balance the equation. [2]
markscheme: (a) Carbon: $4a=c$ [A1] Hydrogen: $10a=2d$ [A1] Oxygen: $2b=2c+d$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Three equations in four unknowns, so there is a free parameter [R1] $c=4a$ and $d=5a$ [A1] $2b=8a+5a$, so $b=\frac{13}{2}a$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $b=\frac{13a}{2}$ must be an integer, so $a$ must be even [M1] Smallest values: $a=2$, $b=13$, $c=8$, $d=10$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Count atoms of each element separately, then express every unknown in terms of one parameter. Remember to impose the integer condition at the end, which may require scaling the solution.

subtopic: Non-negative integer solutions of an underdetermined system
statement: A craft shop makes $20$ items in a day, of three kinds: mugs ($x$), plates ($y$) and bowls ($z$). The materials cost \$5, \$8 and \$12 per item respectively and the total materials cost is \$150. (a) Write down two linear equations for $x$, $y$ and $z$. [2] (b) Show that $3y+7z=50$. [2] (c) Find all solutions in which $x$, $y$ and $z$ are non-negative integers. [4] (d) The shop needs at least $8$ plates. State the number of each item made. [1]
markscheme: (a) $x+y+z=20$ [A1]; $5x+8y+12z=150$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Substitute $x=20-y-z$ into the cost equation [M1]; $100+3y+7z=150$ so $3y+7z=50$ [AG] [2 marks] (c) $z\le7$ since $7z\le50$ [M1]; $y=\dfrac{50-7z}{3}$ must be a non-negative integer [M1]; $z=2$ gives $y=12$, $x=6$ [A1]; $z=5$ gives $y=5$, $x=10$ [A1] [4 marks] (d) $6$ mugs, $12$ plates, $2$ bowls [A1] [1 mark]
tips: With three unknowns and two equations, express two unknowns in terms of a third and then test integer values.

subtopic: Three lines meeting at a point
statement: The lines $l_1$, $l_2$ and $l_3$ have equations $l_1$: $x + 2y=7$, $l_2$: $3x - y=7$, $l_3$: $2x - 3y=k$. (a) Find the coordinates of the point where $l_1$ and $l_2$ intersect. [3] (b) Hence find the value of $k$ for which the three lines are concurrent (meet at a single point). [2] (c) When $k$ takes any other value, the three lines form a triangle. State, with a reason, whether the system of three equations has a solution in that case. [2]
markscheme: (a) Eliminate one variable, e.g. multiply to match coefficients [M1], giving $x=3$ [A1] and $y=2$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) The point must lie on $l_3$ [R1]: $k=2(3)+(-3)(2)=0$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) The system has no solution [A1] since no point lies on all three lines [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Solve any two lines first, then substitute the intersection point into the third equation to find the constant.

subtopic: Row-reduced matrix with a parameter
statement: After row operations, the augmented matrix of a system of three equations is $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & k^2-4 & 3(k+2) \end{pmatrix}$ where $k$ is a constant. The variables are $x$, $y$, $z$ and the last column holds the constants. (a) Find the values of $k$ for which the system has a unique solution. [2] (b) Find the value of $k$ for which there are infinitely many solutions, and write the general solution in terms of $\lambda$ where $z=\lambda$. [4] (c) Explain why there is no solution when $k=2$. [2] (d) Find the solution when $k=6$. [3]
markscheme: (a) Unique solution when the third row is not all zeros in the coefficients: $k^2-4\neq0$ [M1] so $k\neq\pm2$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $k=-2$ gives the third row $(0\ 0\ 0\mid 0)$ [M1][A1]; $y=1 - \lambda$ [A1], $x=\lambda + 2$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) With $k=2$ the third row is $(0\ 0\ 0\mid 12)$ [A1] which states $0=12$, a contradiction [R1] [2 marks] (d) $z=\dfrac{3(6+2)}{6^2-4}=\frac{3}{4}$ [A1], then back-substitute: $y=\frac{1}{4}$ [A1], $x=\frac{11}{4}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Read the last row first: a zero coefficient with a zero constant means infinitely many solutions, with a non-zero constant it means no solutions.

subtopic: Finding the constant for concurrent lines
statement: Consider the lines $l_1$: $4x - y=3$, $l_2$: $2x + 3y=19$ and $l_3$: $3x + 4y=k$. (a) Find the coordinates of the point where $l_1$ and $l_2$ intersect. [3] (b) Hence find the value of $k$ for which the three lines are concurrent (meet at a single point). [2] (c) When $k$ takes any other value, the three lines form a triangle. State, with a reason, whether the system of three equations has a solution in that case. [2]
markscheme: (a) Eliminate one variable, e.g. multiply to match coefficients [M1], giving $x=2$ [A1] and $y=5$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) The point must lie on $l_3$ [R1]: $k=3(2)+(4)(5)=26$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) The system has no solution [A1] since no point lies on all three lines [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Use elimination to find the intersection point and check it in both original equations before substituting into the third line.

subtopic: Number of solutions depending on a parameter
statement: Consider the system $\begin{aligned} x+y+z&=3 \\ x+2y+3z&=5 \\ x+3y+kz&=8 \end{aligned}$ where $k$ is a real constant. (a) Eliminate $x$ to show that the system reduces to $y+2z=2$ and $2y+(k-1)z=5$. [2] (b) Find the value of $k$ for which the system has no solution. [3] (c) Given that $k=2$, find the solution of the system. [3]
tips: After eliminating $x$ you have two equations in $y$ and $z$; the system is inconsistent when their left-hand sides are proportional but the right-hand sides are not.

subtopic: Matrix methods and fitting a quadratic model
statement: A theater sells adult, student and child tickets at prices of USD $a$, USD $s$ and USD $c$ respectively. Three groups bought tickets for the same show: Group 1 bought $2$ adult, $3$ student and $4$ child tickets for USD $105$; Group 2 bought $4$ adult, $1$ student and $2$ child tickets for USD $102$; Group 3 bought $3$ adult, $2$ student and $5$ child tickets for USD $119.50$. (a) Write this information as a matrix equation $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$. [2] (b) Find $\det A$ and explain why the system has a unique solution. [2] (c) Find the price of each type of ticket. [2] The theater manager models the revenue $R$, in USD, from a show as a quadratic function of the adult ticket price $p$, in USD, $R(p)=\alpha p^2+\beta p+\gamma$. Past shows gave revenues of USD $4200$ when $p=10$, USD $5100$ when $p=15$ and USD $5300$ when $p=20$. (d) Write down three equations in $\alpha$, $\beta$ and $\gamma$. [2] (e) Find the values of $\alpha$, $\beta$ and $\gamma$. [2] (f) Find the adult ticket price that maximizes the revenue according to this model, and the maximum revenue. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\begin{pmatrix}2&3&4\\4&1&2\\3&2&5\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}a\\s\\c\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}105\\102\\119.5\end{pmatrix}$ [A1][A1] [2 marks] (b) $\det A=-20$ [A1] $\det A\ne0$ so $A^{-1}$ exists and there is a unique solution [R1] [2 marks] (c) $\mathbf{x}=A^{-1}\mathbf{b}$ using GDC [M1] adult USD $18.50$, student USD $12$, child USD $8$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $100\alpha+10\beta+\gamma=4200$, $225\alpha+15\beta+\gamma=5100$, $400\alpha+20\beta+\gamma=5300$ [A2] Note: award [A1] for two correct equations [2 marks] (e) using GDC [M1] $\alpha=-14$, $\beta=530$, $\gamma=300$ [A1] [2 marks] (f) $p=-\dfrac{530}{2(-14)}=18.9$ ($18.928\ldots$), i.e. USD $18.93$ [A1] maximum revenue USD $5316$ ($5316.07\ldots$) [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A non-zero determinant is the standard justification for a unique solution. When fitting a curve through points, substitute each point to create one linear equation, then let the GDC solve the system.

subtopic: Three investment accounts
statement: A client invests a total of \$30,000 in three accounts paying $3\%$, $4.5\%$ and $6\%$ simple interest per year. The amounts in the accounts are $x$, $y$ and $z$ respectively. The total interest after one year is \$1,290 and the amount in the $6\%$ account is \$2,000 less than the amount in the $4.5\%$ account. (a) Write down a system of three linear equations for $x$, $y$ and $z$. [3] (b) Solve the system to find the amount in each account. [2] (c) Find the overall interest rate on the total investment, as a percentage. [2]
tips: Interest on each account is the amount multiplied by its rate.

subtopic: Break-even between two printers
statement: Printer A charges a set-up fee of $80$ dollars plus $0.45$ dollars per copy. Printer B charges a set-up fee of $150$ dollars plus $0.30$ dollars per copy. For $n$ copies, the costs are $C_A$ and $C_B$ dollars. (a) Write down expressions for $C_A$ and $C_B$ in terms of $n$. [2] (b) Find the number of copies for which both printers charge the same, giving your answer to 1 decimal place. [2] (c) Find the least whole number of copies for which printer B is cheaper, and find how much cheaper B is than A for $600$ copies. [3]
tips: The costs are equal where the two lines intersect. Beyond that point the line with the smaller gradient is cheaper.

subtopic: Market equilibrium and a tax
statement: In a market, the price $p$ dollars of a product when $q$ units are demanded is $p=150-0.5q$. The price at which $q$ units are supplied is $p=20+0.8q$. (a) Find the equilibrium quantity and the equilibrium price. [3] (b) A tax of $13$ dollars per unit is introduced, so that the supply equation becomes $p=33+0.8q$. Find the new equilibrium quantity and price. [3] (c) Find the total tax revenue collected, and the increase in the price paid by consumers per unit. [2]
markscheme: (a) $150-0.5q=20+0.8q$ [M1]; $q=100$ [A1]; $p=100$ dollars [A1] [3 marks] (b) $150-0.5q=33+0.8q$ [M1]; $q=90$ [A1]; $p=105$ dollars [A1] [3 marks] (c) tax revenue $=13\times90=1170$ dollars [A1]; price rise $=105-100=5$ dollars per unit [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Equilibrium is where the demand and supply prices are equal. A per-unit tax shifts the supply line up by the tax.

subtopic: Planning a diet with three or four foods
statement: This question investigates how a dietician combines foods to meet exact nutrient targets. The table gives the grams of each nutrient in 100 g of foods $A$, $B$ and $C$: food $A$ has protein 20, carbohydrate 5, fat 10; food $B$ has protein 6, carbohydrate 25, fat 2; food $C$ has protein 4, carbohydrate 8, fat 30. Let $x$, $y$ and $z$ be the amounts, in units of 100 g, of foods $A$, $B$ and $C$ in a meal. The meal must supply exactly 57 g of protein, 63.5 g of carbohydrate and 83 g of fat. (a) Write down the matrix equation $N\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{t}$ that $x$, $y$ and $z$ must satisfy. [2] (b) Solve for $x$, $y$ and $z$, and state the mass in grams of each food. [3] (c) A second target is $80$ g of protein, $30$ g of carbohydrate and $20$ g of fat. Show that this target cannot be met using only foods $A$, $B$ and $C$. [3] (d) A fourth food $D$ contains protein 10, carbohydrate 10 and fat 10 per 100 g. The first meal target is kept, and the meal now contains $\lambda$ units of $D$. Show that $N\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{pmatrix}=\mathbf{t}-\lambda\begin{pmatrix} 10 \\ 10 \\ 10 \end{pmatrix}$ and find $x$, $y$ and $z$ in terms of $\lambda$. [4] (e) Find the range of values of $\lambda$ for which all four amounts are non-negative. [3] (f) The costs per 100 g are $2.50$ for $A$, $1.20$ for $B$, $1.80$ for $C$ and $0.90$ for $D$. Show that the cost of the meal is a linear function of $\lambda$ and find the cheapest meal. [5] (g) State one practical reason why a dietician might prefer the meal with $\lambda=0$ even though it costs more. [2]
markscheme: (a) $N=\begin{pmatrix} 20 & 6 & 4 \\ 5 & 25 & 8 \\ 10 & 2 & 30 \end{pmatrix}$, $\mathbf{v}=(x,y,z)^T$ [A1], $\mathbf{t}=\begin{pmatrix} 57 \\ 63.5 \\ 83 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\mathbf{v}=N^{-1}\mathbf{t}$ or system solver [M1]; $x=2$, $y=1.5$, $z=2$ [A1]; masses $200$ g, $150$ g and $200$ g [A1] [3 marks] (c) Solving gives $x=3.95$, $y=0.632$, $z=-0.692$ [M1][A1]; $z<0$ is impossible because a negative amount cannot be eaten [R1] [3 marks] (d) The nutrients from $D$ are $10\lambda$ of each, so the other foods supply the remainder [R1]; multiply by $N^{-1}$ [M1]: $x=2 - \frac{51 \lambda}{133}$ [A1], $y=\frac{3}{2} - \frac{5 \lambda}{19}$ and $z=2 - \frac{25 \lambda}{133}$ [A1] [4 marks] (e) Each of $x,y,z\geq0$ gives an upper limit on $\lambda$ [M1]; the smallest is $\lambda\leq5.216$ [A1] together with $\lambda\geq0$ gives $0\leq\lambda\leq5.216$ [A1] [3 marks] (f) Cost $=2.5x+1.2y+1.8z+0.9\lambda$ [M1]; substituting gives cost $=10.40-0.7128\lambda$, linear [A1][A1]; the gradient is negative so the cost is least at the largest allowed $\lambda=5.216$ [R1]; minimum cost $=6.68$ [A1] [5 marks] (g) Any reasonable reason, e.g. simpler to prepare with three foods [R1]; the cheapest meal uses a large amount of food $D$ and so may be less palatable or varied [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Four unknown amounts with three nutrient conditions give a one-parameter family; the non-negativity of every amount restricts the parameter to an interval, and a linear cost is optimized at an endpoint of that interval.

subtopic: Intersecting lines and parameters
statement: Consider the system of equations $x+ky=3$ and $2x+8y=m$, where $k$ and $m$ are constants. (a) Find the value of $k$ for which the system does not have a unique solution. [2] (b) With this value of $k$, find the value of $m$ for which the system has infinitely many solutions. [2] (c) With this value of $k$ and $m=10$, state, with a reason, the number of solutions. [2]
markscheme: (a) unique solution fails when the lines are parallel [M1]; $\dfrac{1}{2}=\dfrac{k}{8}$ so $k=4$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $2x+8y=m$ must be $2\times(x+4y=3)$ [M1]; $m=6$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) the equations give $x+4y=3$ and $x+4y=5$ [M1]; these are contradictory, so there is no solution (parallel distinct lines) [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Two lines in a plane have no unique intersection when they are parallel: equal gradients.

subtopic: Balancing the reduction of iron ore
statement: The reaction of iron(III) oxide with carbon monoxide is represented by $a\,\mathrm{Fe_2O_3} + b\,\mathrm{CO} \to c\,\mathrm{Fe} + d\,\mathrm{CO_2}$ where $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ are positive integers that balance the numbers of atoms of each element. (a) Write down a system of linear equations, one for each element, that the integers must satisfy. [3] (b) Show that the system has infinitely many solutions and find the general solution, in terms of $\lambda$ where $a=\lambda$. [3] (c) Hence write the balanced equation using the smallest positive integers. [2]
markscheme: (a) Balance each element: $b=d$ (for C), $2a=c$ (for Fe), $3a + b=2d$ (for O) [A1][A1][A1] (any three correct equations) [3 marks] (b) The rank of the coefficient matrix is 3 (fewer than 4 unknowns) so there are infinitely many solutions [R1]; solving gives $a=\lambda$, $b=3 \lambda$, $c=2 \lambda$, $d=3 \lambda$ [M1][A1] [3 marks] (c) Choose $\lambda$ so all values are the smallest positive integers [M1]: $\mathrm{Fe_2O_3} + 3\mathrm{CO} \to 2\mathrm{Fe} + 3\mathrm{CO_2}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The number of independent equations is one fewer than the number of unknowns, which is why a one-parameter family of solutions appears.

subtopic: Fitting a cubic to water depth readings
statement: The depth $D$ metres of water in a tidal basin is recorded at four times $t$ hours after midnight. The model is $D=at^3+bt^2+ct+d$ and it passes through $(0, 3)$, $(3, 1.74)$, $(6, 3.72)$, $(9, 2.46)$. (a) Write the conditions on $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ as a matrix equation $M\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{w}$. [3] (b) Solve the matrix equation using your calculator. [2] (c) Find the coordinates of the local maximum and the local minimum of the graph for $0\leq t\leq 9$. [3] (d) Use the model to predict $D$ when $t=12$ and comment on the model's validity. [2]
markscheme: (a) $M=\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 27 & 9 & 3 & 1 \\ 216 & 36 & 6 & 1 \\ 729 & 81 & 9 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1], $\mathbf{v}=\begin{pmatrix} a \\ b \\ c \\ d \end{pmatrix}$ [A1], $\mathbf{w}=\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 1.74 \\ 3.72 \\ 2.46 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\mathbf{v}=M^{-1}\mathbf{w}$ or system solver [M1]: $a=-0.04$, $b=0.54$, $c=-1.68$, $d=3$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Setting $-0.12t^2+(1.08)t+(-1.68)=0$ [M1] (or GDC turning points) gives $t=2.00$ and $t=7.00$ [A1]; the corresponding values are $D=1.48$ and $D=3.98$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $D=-8.52$ [A1]; the model gives a negative depth, which is impossible, so it is not valid at this time [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Because the leading coefficient is negative the cubic eventually decreases without bound, which is unphysical for a depth.

subtopic: Circle through three points
statement: A circle has equation $x^{2}+y^{2}+Dx+Ey+F=0$ and passes through the points $(0,\,0)$, $(4,\,0)$ and $(0,\,6)$. (a) Find $D$, $E$ and $F$. [4] (b) Find the coordinates of the centre and the radius of the circle. [3]
tips: Substitute each point to get one linear equation in $D$, $E$, $F$; complete the square to read off the centre.

subtopic: Digits of a three-digit number
statement: A three-digit number has digits $a$ (hundreds), $b$ (tens) and $c$ (units). The sum of the digits is $12$. Reversing the digits gives a number $198$ less than the original. The tens digit is the mean of the other two digits. (a) Write down three linear equations for $a$, $b$ and $c$. [3] (b) Solve the system and write down the original number. [3]
tips: Write the place values as $100a+10b+c$ and the reversed number as $100c+10b+a$.

subtopic: Cubic curve from a point and two stationary points
statement: The curve $y=ax^{3}+bx^{2}+cx$ passes through the point $(1,\,4)$ and has stationary points at $x=1$ and $x=3$. (a) Write down three linear equations for $a$, $b$ and $c$. [3] (b) Solve the system to find $a$, $b$ and $c$. [3] (c) Hence find the coordinates of the stationary point at $x=3$ and classify it. [3]
tips: Each condition on the curve gives one linear equation in $a$, $b$, $c$; a stationary point means $\frac{dy}{dx}=0$.

subtopic: Production planning with three resources
statement: A factory makes three products P, Q and R. One unit of P, Q and R uses respectively $2$, $1$ and $1$ hours of machine time, $1$, $2$ and $1$ hours of labor, and $1$, $1$ and $2$ units of material. In one week, $110$ hours of machine time and $90$ hours of labor are available, and $t$ units of material are available. Let $x$, $y$ and $z$ be the numbers of P, Q and R made, using all resources. (a) Write the conditions as a matrix equation $M\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{b}$, giving $M$, $\mathbf{v}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ in terms of $t$. [3] (b) Find $\det M$ and explain what this tells you about the solutions for any value of $t$. [2] (c) For $t=100$, find $x$, $y$ and $z$. [2] (d) The profits are $40$, $55$ and $60$ dollars per unit of P, Q and R. Find the total profit for $t=100$. [2] (e) Use $M^{-1}$ to find $x$, $y$ and $z$ in terms of $t$. [3] (f) Find the range of values of $t$ for which $x$, $y$ and $z$ are all non-negative, giving the bounds to 3 significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) $M=\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; $\mathbf{v}=\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; $\mathbf{b}=\begin{pmatrix} 110 \\ 90 \\ t \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\det M=4$ [A1]; $\det M\neq0$ so $M^{-1}$ exists and there is exactly one solution for every $t$ [R1] [2 marks] (c) $\mathbf{v}=M^{-1}\mathbf{b}$ [M1]; $x=35$, $y=15$, $z=25$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $35\times40+15\times55+25\times60$ [M1]; $3725$ dollars [A1] [2 marks] (e) $\mathbf{v}=\dfrac{1}{4}\begin{pmatrix} 3 & -1 & -1 \\ -1 & 3 & -1 \\ -1 & -1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 110 \\ 90 \\ t \end{pmatrix}$ [M1]; $x=\dfrac{240-t}{4}$ [A1]; $y=\dfrac{160-t}{4}$ and $z=\dfrac{3t-200}{4}$ [A1] [3 marks] (f) $x\ge0\Rightarrow t\le240$ and $y\ge0\Rightarrow t\le160$ [M1]; $z\ge0\Rightarrow t\ge\dfrac{200}{3}$ [A1]; $66.7\le t\le160$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Write the system as $M\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{b}$, find $M^{-1}$ with the GDC, and keep $t$ symbolic in the last column of $\mathbf{b}$.

subtopic: Investment portfolio
statement: A trust invests $80000$ dollars in bonds, stocks and property. Let $b$, $s$ and $p$ be the amounts, in dollars, invested in bonds, stocks and property. The yearly returns are $3\%$ on bonds, $7\%$ on stocks and $10\%$ on property, and the total return for the year is $4200$ dollars. The amount invested in stocks is twice the amount invested in property. (a) Write down three equations for $b$, $s$ and $p$. [3] (b) Solve the equations to find $b$, $s$ and $p$. [2] (c) The next year the rates fall to $2\%$, $6\%$ and $9\%$ respectively, with the same amounts invested. Find the total return. [2]
tips: Percentages become decimal multipliers in the return equation; the third condition is $s-2p=0$.

subtopic: A parametrized system and its determinant
statement: Consider the system $M\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{b}$ where $M=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & k \\ 1 & 4 & k^{2} \end{pmatrix}$, $\mathbf{v}=\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{b}=\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 4 \\ m \end{pmatrix}$, and $k$, $m$ are real constants. (a) Show that $\det M=(k-1)(k-2)$. [3] (b) State the values of $k$ for which the system does not have a unique solution, and explain why. [2] (c) Given that $k=3$ and $m=9$, find $\mathbf{v}$. [3] (d) For $k=1$, show that the system has infinitely many solutions only when $m=6$, and find the general solution when $m=6$ in terms of a parameter $t$ where $z=t$. [5] (e) For $k=2$ and $m=7$, determine whether the system has a solution, and justify your answer. [3] (f) For $k=2$, find the value of $m$ for which the system has infinitely many solutions. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\det M=1(2k^{2}-4k)-1(k^{2}-k)+1(4-2)$ [M1][A1]; $=k^{2}-3k+2=(k-1)(k-2)$ [AG] [3 marks] (b) $k=1$ or $k=2$ [A1]; because $M$ is singular (no inverse) there [R1] [2 marks] (c) $\det M=2$, so $M^{-1}$ exists [R1]; GDC: $\mathbf{v}=M^{-1}\mathbf{b}$ [M1]; $x=\dfrac{7}{2}$, $y=-2$, $z=\dfrac{3}{2}$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) Equations: $x+y+z=3$, $x+2y+z=4$, $x+4y+z=m$ [A1]; (2)$-$(1): $y=1$ [A1]; (3)$-$(2): $2y=m-4$ so $m=6$ for consistency [M1][A1]; $y=1$, $x=2-t$, $z=t$ [A1] [5 marks] (e) Equations: $x+y+z=3$, $x+2y+2z=4$, $x+4y+4z=7$ [A1]; (2)$-$(1): $y+z=1$ and (3)$-$(2): $2y+2z=3$ [M1]; these contradict each other, so there is no solution [R1] [3 marks] (f) (3)$-$(2): $2(y+z)=m-4$ with $y+z=1$ [M1]; $m=6$ [A1]; the equations are then dependent [R1] [3 marks]
tips: A $3\times3$ system has a unique solution exactly when $\det M\ne0$; when $\det M=0$ it has either no solution or infinitely many.

subtopic: Parameter makes the third equation dependent
statement: Consider the system $\begin{aligned} x + y + z&=1 \\ x + 2y + 3z&=2 \\ 2x + 3y + kz&=c \end{aligned}$ where $k$ and $c$ are constants. (a) By considering (3)$-$(1)$-$(2), find the value of $k$ for which the system does not have a unique solution. [3] (b) Given that $k=4$, find the value of $c$ for which the system has infinitely many solutions, and give the general solution in terms of $\lambda$, where $z=\lambda$. [4] (c) Explain why there is no solution when $k=4$ and $c\neq3$. [1]
markscheme: (a) (3)$-$(1)$-$(2) gives $(k-4)z=c-3$ [M1][A1] so a unique solution exists unless $k=4$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Need $0=c-3$, so $c=3$ [A1]; solve (1) and (2) for the other two variables [M1] giving $x=\lambda$, $y=1 - 2 \lambda$, $z=\lambda$ [A1][A1] [4 marks] (c) The third equation reduces to $0=c-3\neq0$, a contradiction [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Combine the equations so that one variable survives with coefficient $k-$constant; a zero coefficient decides between no solution and infinitely many.

subtopic: Elimination with a fractional solution
statement: Consider the system $\begin{aligned} x + y + z&=-1/2 \\ 2x - y + 3z&=-10 \\ 4x + 2y - z&=9 \end{aligned}$ Solve the system of equations. [5]
markscheme: Label the equations (1), (2), (3). (2)$-2\times$(1): $-3y + z=-9$ [M1]; (3)$-4\times$(1): $-2y - 5z=11$ [A1]. Solving these two equations simultaneously gives $y=2$ [M1] and $z=-3$ [A1]. Substituting into (1) gives $x=\frac{1}{2}$ [A1]. [5 marks]
tips: A non-integer value can appear for the variable eliminated first; keep exact fractions and check by substitution.

subtopic: Traffic flow with a free parameter
statement: Four one-way roads form a ring through junctions $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$. The numbers of vehicles per hour on the roads are $x$ ($A$ to $B$), $y$ ($B$ to $C$), $z$ ($C$ to $D$) and $w$ ($D$ to $A$). Vehicles also enter and leave the ring at each junction, as given in the table. $$\begin{array}{c|cccc} & A & B & C & D\\ \hline \text{Enter from outside} & 300 & 150 & 50 & 250\\ \text{Leave to outside} & 100 & 250 & 200 & 200 \end{array}$$ At each junction, the number of vehicles arriving equals the number leaving. (a) Write down four equations that $x$, $y$, $z$ and $w$ must satisfy. [4] (b) Solve the equations, giving $x$, $y$ and $z$ in terms of $w$. [3] (c) Each road can carry at most $400$ vehicles per hour, and no flow can be negative. Find the possible values of $w$. [3]
markscheme: (a) Junction $A$: $300+w=x+100$ [A1] Junction $B$: $x+150=y+250$ [A1] Junction $C$: $y+50=z+200$ [A1] Junction $D$: $z+250=w+200$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $x-w=200$, $x-y=100$, $y-z=150$, $z-w=-50$ (the fourth is not independent of the others) [M1] $x=w+200$ [A1] $y=w+100$ and $z=w-50$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $z\ge0$ gives $w\ge50$ [M1] $x\le400$ gives $w\le200$ (and $y\le400$ gives $w\le300$, $w\le400$) [A1] $50\le w\le200$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: At each junction write 'flow in $=$ flow out' including the outside traffic. A consistent system with fewer independent equations than unknowns has a free parameter, and the constraints on flows restrict its range.

subtopic: Balancing a neutralization reaction
statement: The reaction of calcium hydroxide with phosphoric acid is represented by $a\,\mathrm{Ca(OH)_2} + b\,\mathrm{H_3PO_4} \to c\,\mathrm{Ca_3(PO_4)_2} + d\,\mathrm{H_2O}$ where $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ are positive integers that balance the numbers of atoms of each element. (a) Write down a system of linear equations, one for each element, that the integers must satisfy. [3] (b) Show that the system has infinitely many solutions and find the general solution, in terms of $\lambda$ where $a=\lambda$. [3] (c) Hence write the balanced equation using the smallest positive integers. [2]
markscheme: (a) Balance each element: $a=3c$ (for Ca), $2a + 3b=2d$ (for H), $2a + 4b=8c + d$ (for O), $b=2c$ (for P) [A1][A1][A1] (any three correct equations) [3 marks] (b) The rank of the coefficient matrix is 3 (fewer than 4 unknowns) so there are infinitely many solutions [R1]; solving gives $a=\lambda$, $b=\frac{2 \lambda}{3}$, $c=\frac{\lambda}{3}$, $d=2 \lambda$ [M1][A1] [3 marks] (c) Choose $\lambda$ so all values are the smallest positive integers [M1]: $3\mathrm{Ca(OH)_2} + 2\mathrm{H_3PO_4} \to \mathrm{Ca_3(PO_4)_2} + 6\mathrm{H_2O}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Count hydrogen and oxygen atoms carefully when a polyatomic group appears in brackets; each bracket multiplies every atom inside it.

subtopic: Fuel consumption against speed
statement: A car's fuel consumption $C$ in litres per 100 km is measured at three speeds $v$ km/h. The model is $C=av^2+bv+c$ and it passes through $(40, 4.2)$, $(60, 3.2)$, $(100, 6)$. (a) Write down three equations that $a$, $b$ and $c$ must satisfy. [2] (b) Use your calculator to find $a$, $b$ and $c$. [2] (c) Find the minimum value of $C$ predicted by the model, and the value of $v$ at which it occurs. [2] (d) Find the range of speeds at which the consumption is at most $4$ litres per 100 km (3 significant figures). [3]
markscheme: (a) Substituting the three points: $1600a+40b+c=4.2$, $3600a+60b+c=3.2$, $10000a+100b+c=6$ [A1][A1] [2 marks] (b) Solving the system on the GDC [M1]: $a=0.002$, $b=-0.25$, $c=11$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $v=-\dfrac{b}{2a}=62.5$ [M1], $C=3.1875$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) Solve $0.002v^2+(-0.25)v+11=4$ [M1] giving $v=42.3$ and $v=82.7$ [A1]; the model gives $C\leq4$ for $42.3\leq v\leq 82.7$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Here $a>0$, so the vertex is a minimum and the consumption is below the target between the roots.

subtopic: Mixing three alloys to a target composition
statement: Three alloys are made of copper, zinc and tin. By mass, alloy $A$ is $50\%$ copper, $30\%$ zinc and $20\%$ tin; alloy $B$ is $20\%$ copper, $60\%$ zinc and $20\%$ tin; alloy $C$ is $10\%$ copper, $30\%$ zinc and $60\%$ tin. A foundry melts $a$ kg of $A$, $b$ kg of $B$ and $c$ kg of $C$ to make $100$ kg of a new alloy containing $29$ kg of copper and $39$ kg of zinc. (a) Write down three equations in $a$, $b$ and $c$. [3] (b) Solve the system to find $a$, $b$ and $c$. [2] (c) Find the mass of tin in the new alloy, and its percentage by mass. [2] (d) The foundry instead wants $100$ kg containing $10$ kg of copper and $50$ kg of zinc. Solve this new system and explain why the requirement cannot be met. [3]
tips: The mass of each metal in the mixture is the sum of its masses from each alloy.

subtopic: Concurrency of three lines
statement: Three lines are given by $l_1$: $2x + 3y=12$, $l_2$: $x - y=1$ and $l_3$: $5x + 2y=k$, where $k$ is a constant. (a) Find the coordinates of the point where $l_1$ and $l_2$ intersect. [3] (b) Hence find the value of $k$ for which the three lines are concurrent (meet at a single point). [2] (c) When $k$ takes any other value, the three lines form a triangle. State, with a reason, whether the system of three equations has a solution in that case. [2]
markscheme: (a) Eliminate one variable, e.g. multiply to match coefficients [M1], giving $x=3$ [A1] and $y=2$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) The point must lie on $l_3$ [R1]: $k=5(3)+(2)(2)=19$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) The system has no solution [A1] since no point lies on all three lines [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Concurrent means that all three lines share one point, so the solution of the first two must satisfy the third.

subtopic: Mixing three acid solutions
statement: A chemist mixes three solutions containing $10\%$, $20\%$ and $40\%$ acid by volume. Let $x$, $y$ and $z$ be the numbers of liters of the $10\%$, $20\%$ and $40\%$ solutions used. The mixture has a total volume of $60$ L and contains $11$ L of pure acid. The volume of the $10\%$ solution is three times the volume of the $40\%$ solution. (a) Write down three linear equations for $x$, $y$ and $z$. [3] (b) Solve the system to find $x$, $y$ and $z$. [2] (c) Find the percentage concentration of acid in the final mixture, correct to 3 significant figures. [2]
tips: Each equation comes from a different fact: total volume, total acid, and the stated ratio.

subtopic: Suspension arch modeled by a quadratic
statement: The height $y$ metres of a footbridge arch above the water at horizontal distance $x$ metres from the left bank is measured at three places. The model is $y=ax^2+bx+c$ and it passes through $(0, 1.5)$, $(10, 7.25)$, $(30, 11.25)$. (a) Write down three equations that $a$, $b$ and $c$ must satisfy. [2] (b) Use your calculator to find $a$, $b$ and $c$. [2] (c) Find the maximum value of $y$ predicted by the model, and the value of $x$ at which it occurs. [2] (d) A boat needs a clearance of at least $8$ m. Find the horizontal distances between which the arch is at least this high (3 significant figures). [3]
markscheme: (a) Substituting the three points: $0a+0b+c=1.5$, $100a+10b+c=7.25$, $900a+30b+c=11.25$ [A1][A1] [2 marks] (b) Solving the system on the GDC [M1]: $a=-0.0125$, $b=0.7$, $c=1.5$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $x=-\dfrac{b}{2a}=28$ [M1], $y=11.3$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) Solve $-0.0125x^2+(0.7)x+1.5=8$ [M1] giving $x=11.8$ and $x=44.2$ [A1]; the model gives $y\geq8$ for $11.8\leq x\leq 44.2$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Roots of the quadratic equation give the ends of the interval where the arch is high enough.

subtopic: Rectangle from perimeter and length condition
statement: A rectangle has perimeter $54$ cm. Its length is $3$ cm more than twice its width. (a) Let $w$ be the width and $l$ the length, in cm. Find $w$ and $l$. [3] (b) Find the area of the rectangle. [1] (c) Find the length of a diagonal, giving your answer as a surd in simplest form. [2]
tips: Substitute the length condition into the perimeter equation to get one equation in $w$.

subtopic: Diet plan with a matrix equation
statement: Three foods X, Y and Z are mixed in portions of $100$ g. Each $100$ g of X, Y and Z contains respectively $20$ g, $8$ g and $2$ g of protein, $5$ g, $30$ g and $60$ g of carbohydrate, and $3$ g, $1$ g and $10$ g of fat. A diet requires $63.6$ g of protein, $105.5$ g of carbohydrate and $17$ g of fat. Let $x$, $y$ and $z$ be the numbers of $100$ g portions of X, Y and Z. (a) Write the requirements as a matrix equation $A\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{b}$, stating $A$, $\mathbf{v}$ and $\mathbf{b}$. [3] (b) Use your GDC to solve the matrix equation and state the mass in grams of each food needed. [3]
markscheme: (a) $A=\begin{pmatrix} 20 & 8 & 2 \\ 5 & 30 & 60 \\ 3 & 1 & 10 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; $\mathbf{v}=\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; $\mathbf{b}=\begin{pmatrix} 63.6 \\ 105.5 \\ 17 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\mathbf{v}=A^{-1}\mathbf{b}$ [M1]; $x=2.5$, $y=1.5$, $z=0.8$ [A1]; $250$ g of X, $150$ g of Y, $80$ g of Z [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Each row of $A$ is one nutrient and each column is one food. Then $\mathbf{v}=A^{-1}\mathbf{b}$ on the GDC.

subtopic: Coins problem with three unknowns
statement: A jar contains $24$ coins, each a dime (\$0.10), a quarter (\$0.25) or a half-dollar (\$0.50). The total value is \$5.75 and there are twice as many dimes as half-dollars. Let $d$, $q$ and $h$ be the numbers of dimes, quarters and half-dollars. (a) Write down three equations connecting $d$, $q$ and $h$. [3] (b) Hence find the number of each type of coin. [3]
tips: Work in cents to avoid decimals, and substitute $d=2h$ to reduce to two unknowns.

subtopic: Fitting a cubic model through four points
statement: The monthly running cost, $C$ thousand dollars, of a machine in month $x$ is modelled by $C=px^3+qx^2+rx+s$. The costs recorded are $6$ when $x=0$, $5$ when $x=1$, $2$ when $x=2$ and $3$ when $x=3$. (a) Write down a system of four linear equations for $p$, $q$, $r$ and $s$. [2] (b) Solve the system. [2] (c) For $0\le x\le4$, treating $x$ as continuous, find the minimum cost predicted by the model and the value of $x$ at which it occurs. [4]
markscheme: (a) $s=6$ [A1] $p+q+r+s=5$, $8p+4q+2r+s=2$ and $27p+9q+3r+s=3$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Use of GDC [M1] $p=1$, $q=-4$, $r=2$, $s=6$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $C'(x)=3x^2-8x+2=0$ [M1] $x=2.39$ (the other stationary point at $x=0.279$ is a local maximum) [A1] $C(2.387)=1.58$ [A1] Comparison with the end values $C(0)=6$ and $C(4)=14$ shows this is the minimum on the interval [R1] [4 marks]
tips: A cubic has four unknown coefficients, so you need four data points and four equations. When asked for an extreme value on an interval, compare the stationary value with the values at the endpoints.

subtopic: Quadratic model of a ball's height
statement: The height $h$ meters of a ball above the ground $t$ seconds after it is thrown is modeled by $h=at^{2}+bt+c$. The height is $10.25$ m when $t=0.5$, $16.5$ m when $t=1$ and $20.25$ m when $t=2.5$. (a) Write down three linear equations in $a$, $b$ and $c$. [2] (b) Solve the equations using your GDC to find $a$, $b$ and $c$. [2] (c) Find the greatest height of the ball and the time at which it occurs. [3] (d) Find the time at which the ball lands on the ground, correct to 3 significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) $0.25a+0.5b+c=10.25$ [A1]; $a+b+c=16.5$ and $6.25a+2.5b+c=20.25$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) GDC simultaneous equation solver [M1]; $a=-5$, $b=20$, $c=1.5$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $t=-\dfrac{b}{2a}=2$ s [M1][A1]; greatest height $h(2)=21.5$ m [A1] [3 marks] (d) solve $-5t^{2}+20t+1.5=0$ [M1]; $t=4.07$ s (reject the negative root) [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Substitute each data point into the model to get three equations, then use the GDC. The vertex of a quadratic is at $t=-\frac{b}{2a}$.

subtopic: Solving a system using a given inverse matrix
statement: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$. It is given that $A^{-1}=\dfrac{1}{3}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -2 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Verify that the second row of $A$ multiplied by the first column of $A^{-1}$ gives the correct entry of $AA^{-1}=I$. [2] (b) Hence solve $\begin{aligned} x+2y&=7 \\ y+z&=2 \\ x+z&=5 \end{aligned}$. [4]
markscheme: (a) Row $(0,1,1)$ times column $\frac13(1,1,-1)^{T}$ [M1]; $\frac13(0+1-1)=0$, as required for an off-diagonal entry of $I$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{pmatrix}=A^{-1}\begin{pmatrix} 7 \\ 2 \\ 5 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1]; $x=\frac13(7-4+10)=\frac{13}{3}$ [A1]; $y=\frac13(7+2-5)=\frac43$ [A1]; $z=\frac13(-7+4+5)=\frac23$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: For $A\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{b}$, multiply both sides on the left by $A^{-1}$.

subtopic: Roller coaster profile from four height readings
statement: The height $h$ metres of a roller coaster track above the ground is measured at horizontal distances $x$ metres from the start. The model is $h=ax^3+bx^2+cx+d$ and it passes through $(0, 5)$, $(10, 85)$, $(20, 45)$, $(40, 85)$. (a) Write the conditions on $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ as a matrix equation $M\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{w}$. [3] (b) Solve the matrix equation using your calculator. [2] (c) Find the coordinates of the local maximum and the local minimum of the graph for $0\leq x\leq 40$. [3] (d) Use the model to predict $h$ when $x=50$ and comment on whether the model is reasonable for this value. [2]
markscheme: (a) $M=\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 1000 & 100 & 10 & 1 \\ 8000 & 400 & 20 & 1 \\ 64000 & 1600 & 40 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1], $\mathbf{v}=\begin{pmatrix} a \\ b \\ c \\ d \end{pmatrix}$ [A1], $\mathbf{w}=\begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ 85 \\ 45 \\ 85 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\mathbf{v}=M^{-1}\mathbf{w}$ or system solver [M1]: $a=0.02$, $b=-1.2$, $c=18$, $d=5$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Setting $0.06x^2+(-2.4)x+(18)=0$ [M1] (or GDC turning points) gives $x=10.0$ and $x=30.0$ [A1]; the corresponding values are $h=85.0$ and $h=5.00$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $h=405$ [A1]; for large $x$ the cubic term dominates and $h$ keeps growing without limit, so the model should not be extrapolated beyond the track [R1] [2 marks]
tips: A cubic has up to two turning points; check the endpoints of the interval before calling a value the greatest or least height.

subtopic: Matrix inverse and solving several systems
statement: Let $\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix}2&1&3\\1&4&2\\3&2&5\end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find $\det\mathbf{A}$. [1] (b) Find $\mathbf{A}^{-1}$, giving your answer with exact fractions. [2] (c) Use your answer to part (b) to solve (i) $\mathbf{A}\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\\z\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}13\\11\\21\end{pmatrix}$ and (ii) $\mathbf{A}\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\\z\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}16\\17\\27\end{pmatrix}$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $\det\mathbf{A}=3$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Use of GDC [M1] $\mathbf{A}^{-1}=\dfrac13\begin{pmatrix}16&1&-10\\1&1&-1\\-10&-1&7\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{B}$ [M1] (i) $\begin{pmatrix}3\\1\\2\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] (ii) $\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\4\end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1] [4 marks]
tips: Once you have the inverse, each new right-hand side needs only a single matrix multiplication, with the inverse on the left. Check one answer by substituting into the original matrix equation.

subtopic: Fitting a quadratic to a ball's flight
statement: A ball is thrown upward from a balcony. Its height $h$ metres above the ground $t$ seconds after the throw was recorded at three times. The model is $h=at^2+bt+c$ and it passes through $(0, 1.2)$, $(1, 12.3)$, $(3, 5.1)$. (a) Write down three equations that $a$, $b$ and $c$ must satisfy. [2] (b) Use your calculator to find $a$, $b$ and $c$. [2] (c) Find the maximum value of $h$ predicted by the model, and the value of $t$ at which it occurs. [2] (d) Find the values of $t$ for which the ball is at least $10$ m above the ground (give answers to 3 significant figures). [3]
markscheme: (a) Substituting the three points: $0a+0b+c=1.2$, $1a+1b+c=12.3$, $9a+3b+c=5.1$ [A1][A1] [2 marks] (b) Solving the system on the GDC [M1]: $a=-4.9$, $b=16$, $c=1.2$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $t=-\dfrac{b}{2a}=\frac{80}{49}$ [M1], $h=\frac{3494}{245}$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) Solve $-4.9t^2+(16)t+1.2=10$ [M1] giving $t=0.700$ and $t=2.57$ [A1]; the model gives $h\geq10$ for $0.700\leq t\leq 2.57$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Each data point gives one linear equation in $a$, $b$, $c$; enter them as a $3\times3$ system. For the last part solve the equality first, then decide which side of the roots the inequality holds.

subtopic: Systems with a parameter: unique, none or infinite solutions
