tips: The amplitude is half the difference between the maximum and minimum, and the midline value is their mean. Convert the interval for $x$ to the interval for $3x$.

subtopic: Reciprocal trigonometric ratios
statement: The angle $\theta$ satisfies $\sec\theta=-3$ and $\dfrac\pi2<\theta<\pi$. (a) Find the exact value of $\sin\theta$. [3] (b) Find the exact value of $\cot\theta$. [2] (c) Solve $\operatorname{cosec}x=2$ for $0\le x\le2\pi$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\cos\theta=-\dfrac13$ [A1] $\sin^2\theta=1-\dfrac19=\dfrac89$ [M1] $\sin\theta=\dfrac{2\sqrt2}{3}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\cot\theta=\dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{-1/3}{2\sqrt2/3}=-\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt2}=-\dfrac{\sqrt2}{4}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\sin x=\dfrac12$ [M1] $x=\dfrac\pi6$ [A1] $x=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Rewrite every reciprocal function in terms of $\sin$ and $\cos$ first. In the second quadrant sine is positive and cosine is negative.

subtopic: Solving a trigonometric equation graphically
statement: Let $f(x)=3\sin2x+1$ and $g(x)=0.5\cos x$, for $0\leq x\leq2\pi$. (a) Write down the range of $f$ and the period of $f$. [2] (b) Use your calculator to solve $f(x)=g(x)$. [3] (c) Hence solve $f(x)>g(x)$ for $0\leq x\leq2\pi$. [3] (d) Find the greatest value of $f(x)-g(x)$ on the interval and the value of $x$ at which it occurs. [2]
markscheme: (a) Range $[-2,4]$ [A1]; period $\pi$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Solve on the GDC (radians) [M1]: $x=1.757$, $x=2.883$, $x=4.869$, $x=6.199$ [A2] (award A1 for at least three correct) [3 marks] (c) Graph of $f$ above that of $g$ [M1]: $0\leq x<1.757$; $2.883<x<4.869$; $6.199<x\leq2\pi$ [A1][A1] [3 marks] (d) Maximum of the difference [M1]: $4.359$ at $x=3.898$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: List all solutions in $[0,2\pi]$ by examining the intersections on a sketch; solve inequalities from the graph.

subtopic: Modeling tides with a sinusoidal function
statement: The depth $d$ meters of water at the entrance to a harbor $t$ hours after midnight is modeled by $d(t)=6+2.5\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi(t-1)}{6}\right)$ for $0\le t\le24$. (a) Write down the maximum depth, the minimum depth and the period of the model. [3] (b) Find the depth at $t=0$. [2] (c) A ship needs a depth of at least $7.5$ m. Find the times in the first $12$ hours when the depth is exactly $7.5$ m, and the length of time the ship can enter. [4]
markscheme: (a) maximum $8.5$ m [A1] minimum $3.5$ m [A1] period $=\dfrac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=12$ hours [A1] [3 marks] (b) $d(0)=6+2.5\sin\left(-\dfrac\pi6\right)$ [M1] $=4.75$ m [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi(t-1)}6\right)=0.6$ [M1] $\dfrac{\pi(t-1)}6=0.6435$ or $\pi-0.6435$ [A1] $t=2.23$ and $t=5.77$ [A1] duration $=3.54$ hours [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Read amplitude, midline and period from the formula. To solve for a threshold depth, isolate the sine and use both solutions in one period.

subtopic: Finding sine and tangent from cosine in the third quadrant
statement: The angle $\theta$ satisfies $\cos\theta=-\dfrac{5}{13}$ and $\pi<\theta<\dfrac{3\pi}{2}$. (a) Find the exact value of $\sin\theta$. [3] (b) Find the exact value of $\tan\theta$. [1] (c) Write down the exact values of $\sin(\pi-\theta)$ and $\cos(\pi-\theta)$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\sin^2\theta=1-\dfrac{25}{169}=\dfrac{144}{169}$ [M1] $\sin\theta=\pm\dfrac{12}{13}$ [A1] $\theta$ is in the third quadrant so $\sin\theta=-\dfrac{12}{13}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\tan\theta=\dfrac{-12/13}{-5/13}=\dfrac{12}{5}$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $\sin(\pi-\theta)=\sin\theta=-\dfrac{12}{13}$ [A1] $\cos(\pi-\theta)=-\cos\theta=\dfrac{5}{13}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Use $\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1$, then pick the sign from the quadrant. Angles such as $\pi-\theta$ are reflections on the unit circle, so only the sign of cosine changes.

subtopic: Sequence of transformations from the basic sine curve
statement: The graph of $y=\sin x$ is transformed to the graph of $y=g(x)$, where $g(x)=3\sin\left(2\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\right)+1$. (a) Describe fully the sequence of transformations that maps $y=\sin x$ onto $y=g(x)$. [4] (b) The point $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2},1\right)$ lies on $y=\sin x$. Find the coordinates of its image on the graph of $y=g(x)$. [2]
markscheme: (a) A horizontal stretch with scale factor $\dfrac12$ (parallel to the $x$-axis) [A1] A vertical stretch with scale factor $3$ (parallel to the $y$-axis) [A1] A horizontal translation of $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ to the right [A1] A vertical translation of $1$ up [A1] [4 marks] (b) The $x$-coordinate becomes $\dfrac12\times\dfrac{\pi}{2}+\dfrac{\pi}{4}=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ [M1] The $y$-coordinate becomes $3(1)+1=4$ so the image is $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2},4\right)$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Read the transformations in the order they act on the input and output: the factor inside the bracket stretches horizontally by its reciprocal, and a translation inside is $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ to the right when it is written $x-\dfrac{\pi}{4}$. Check by working one point through the whole formula.

subtopic: Solving a shifted cosine equation using the full range
statement: Solve the equation $2\cos\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)=1$ for $0\le x\le2\pi$, giving exact answers. [5]
markscheme: $\cos\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)=\dfrac12$ [M1] For $0\le x\le2\pi$, the angle $u=x-\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ satisfies $-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\le u\le\dfrac{5\pi}{3}$ [M1] $u=-\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ gives $x=0$ [A1] $u=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ gives $x=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ [A1] $u=\dfrac{5\pi}{3}$ gives $x=2\pi$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: Substitute $u=x-\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ and write down the interval for $u$ before solving; the shift changes which angles are allowed, so you can miss solutions at the ends if you skip this step.

subtopic: Proving an identity and using it
statement: (a) Show that $\dfrac{1-\cos2x}{\sin2x}\equiv\tan x$. [3] (b) Hence solve $\dfrac{1-\cos2x}{\sin2x}=\sqrt3$ for $0<x<\pi$. [2] (c) Hence find the exact value of $\tan\dfrac\pi8$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $1-\cos2x=2\sin^2x$ [M1] $\sin2x=2\sin x\cos x$ [M1] $\dfrac{2\sin^2x}{2\sin x\cos x}=\tan x$ [AG] [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\tan x=\sqrt3$ [M1] $x=\dfrac\pi3$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Let $x=\dfrac\pi8$: $\tan\dfrac\pi8=\dfrac{1-\cos\frac\pi4}{\sin\frac\pi4}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{1-\frac{\sqrt2}{2}}{\frac{\sqrt2}{2}}=\dfrac{2-\sqrt2}{\sqrt2}$ [M1] $=\sqrt2-1$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Start from the more complicated side and use $1-\cos2x=2\sin^2x$. For part (c) choose $x$ so that $2x$ is a standard angle.

subtopic: Water level and the passing times of a canal boat
statement: The water level $L$ metres at a canal bridge, $t$ hours after midnight, is modeled by $L(t)=3.2+1.4\cos\left(\dfrac{2\pi t}{12.4}\right)$, for $0\le t\le24$. A canal boat can pass under the bridge only when the water level is at most $2.4$ m. (a) Write down the maximum and minimum water levels. [2] (b) Write down the time between two consecutive high tides. [1] (c) Use your GDC to find the times during the $24$ hours when the water level equals $2.4$ m, correct to three significant figures. [3] (d) Find the total time during the $24$ hours for which the boat can pass under the bridge, correct to three significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) Maximum $=3.2+1.4=4.6$ m [A1] minimum $=3.2-1.4=1.8$ m [A1] [2 marks] (b) The period is $12.4$ hours [A1] [1 mark] (c) Solve $3.2+1.4\cos\left(\dfrac{2\pi t}{12.4}\right)=2.4$ [M1] $t=4.30$ and $t=8.10$ [A1] $t=16.7$ and $t=20.5$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) The boat can pass when $4.30\le t\le8.10$ and $16.7\le t\le20.5$ [M1] total time $=2\times(3.799)=7.60$ hours [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The model has period $12.4$ hours, so in $24$ hours there are almost two complete cycles; make sure your graph window shows both. A boat can pass when the water is low, so you need the intervals where the graph is below the line $L=2.4$.

subtopic: Segment area using radians
statement: A circle has centre $O$ and radius $8$ cm. Chord $AB$ subtends an angle $\dfrac\pi2$ at the centre. (a) Find the exact length of the arc $AB$. [2] (b) Find the exact area of the sector $OAB$. [2] (c) Find the exact perimeter of the sector. [1] (d) Find the exact area of the segment formed by the chord $AB$ and the arc $AB$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $s=r\theta=8\times\frac{\pi}{2}$ [M1] $=4 \pi$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $A=\dfrac12r^2\theta=\dfrac12(8)^2\frac{\pi}{2}$ [M1] $=16 \pi$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $2r+s=2(8)+4 \pi=4 \pi + 16$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) Triangle area $=\dfrac12r^2\sin\theta=\dfrac12(8)^2\sin\frac{\pi}{2}=32$ [M1][A1]; segment $=$ sector $-$ triangle $=-32 + 16 \pi$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: For a right angle at the centre the triangle area is $\frac12r^2$.

subtopic: Proving trigonometric identities
statement: Prove each identity. (a) $\cot x+\tan x\equiv2\operatorname{cosec}2x$ for $0<x<\dfrac\pi2$. [4] (b) $\cos4x\equiv8\cos^4x-8\cos^2x+1$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}+\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}=\dfrac{\cos^2x+\sin^2x}{\sin x\cos x}$ [M1][A1] $=\dfrac1{\sin x\cos x}$ [A1] $=\dfrac2{\sin2x}=2\operatorname{cosec}2x$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $\cos4x=2\cos^22x-1$ [M1] $=2(2\cos^2x-1)^2-1$ [A1] $=2\left(4\cos^4x-4\cos^2x+1\right)-1$ [M1] $=8\cos^4x-8\cos^2x+1$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Write in terms of sine and cosine. For multiple angles, apply the double angle identity repeatedly.

subtopic: Inverse trigonometric functions
statement: (a) Find the exact value of $\arccos\left(\cos\dfrac{7\pi}{6}\right)$. [2] (b) Solve the equation $\arcsin x=\arccos(2x)$. [5]
markscheme: (a) $\cos\dfrac{7\pi}{6}=-\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ [M1] $\arccos\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$ (the principal value lies in $[0,\pi]$) [A1] [2 marks] (b) Let $\theta=\arcsin x=\arccos2x$, so $\sin\theta=x$, $\cos\theta=2x$ [M1] $\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1$: $5x^2=1$ [M1] $x=\pm\dfrac{1}{\sqrt5}$ [A1] $\theta=\arcsin x\in\left[-\dfrac\pi2,\dfrac\pi2\right]$ and $\theta=\arccos2x\in[0,\pi]$, so $\theta\in\left[0,\dfrac\pi2\right]$ and $x\ge0$ [R1] $x=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt5}$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: Remember the ranges: $\arcsin\in[-\pi/2,\pi/2]$ and $\arccos\in[0,\pi]$. Squaring can introduce extra solutions, so always check the sign against the ranges.

subtopic: Approximating pi with inscribed and circumscribed polygons
statement: This question uses trigonometry to bound $\pi$. A regular polygon with $n$ sides is inscribed in a circle of radius $1$ (perimeter $P_n$) and another is circumscribed about the same circle (perimeter $Q_n$). (a) Show that $P_n=2n\sin\dfrac\pi n$ and $Q_n=2n\tan\dfrac\pi n$. [3] (b) Find $P_6$ and $Q_6$ exactly. [2] (c) Show that $\sin\dfrac\pi{12}=\dfrac{\sqrt6-\sqrt2}4$, and hence find $P_{12}$ exactly. [4] (d) Using $\sin x<x<\tan x$ for $0<x<\dfrac\pi2$, show that $P_n<2\pi<Q_n$ for $n\ge3$. [3] (e) For $n=96$, find $\dfrac{P_{96}}2$ and $\dfrac{Q_{96}}2$ and state the bounds for $\pi$ that result. [3] (f) Using $\sin x\approx x-\dfrac{x^3}6$ and $\tan x\approx x+\dfrac{x^3}3$ for small $x$, show that $Q_n-P_n\approx\dfrac{\pi^3}{n^2}$, and estimate the least $n$ for which the gap $Q_n-P_n$ is less than $0.001$. [3]
markscheme: (a) each side of the inscribed polygon subtends angle $\dfrac{2\pi}n$ at the centre, so has length $2\sin\dfrac\pi n$ [M1][A1] each side of the circumscribed polygon is $2\tan\dfrac\pi n$ (tangent length $\tan\dfrac\pi n$ on each side of the contact point) [A1] [3 marks] (b) $P_6=12\sin\dfrac\pi6=6$ [A1] $Q_6=12\tan\dfrac\pi6=\dfrac{12}{\sqrt3}=4\sqrt3$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\sin(45^\circ-30^\circ)=\sin45^\circ\cos30^\circ-\cos45^\circ\sin30^\circ$ [M1] $=\dfrac{\sqrt6-\sqrt2}4$ [A1] $P_{12}=24\times\dfrac{\sqrt6-\sqrt2}4$ [M1] $=6(\sqrt6-\sqrt2)=3.106$ [A1] [4 marks] (d) put $x=\dfrac\pi n$ [M1] $\sin\dfrac\pi n<\dfrac\pi n<\tan\dfrac\pi n$ [A1] multiply by $2n$: $P_n<2\pi<Q_n$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) $\dfrac{P_{96}}2=96\sin\dfrac\pi{96}=3.14103$ [A1] $\dfrac{Q_{96}}2=3.14271$ [A1] $3.14103<\pi<3.14271$ [A1] [3 marks] (f) $Q_n-P_n\approx2n\left(\dfrac{x^3}3+\dfrac{x^3}6\right)$ with $x=\dfrac\pi n$ [M1] $=n x^3=\dfrac{\pi^3}{n^2}$ [A1] $\dfrac{\pi^3}{n^2}<0.001$ gives $n>176.1$ so $n=177$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Each part of the polygon is described by a right triangle with an angle $\dfrac\pi n$. Use the small-angle inequalities for the bounds and the cubic approximations for the gap.

subtopic: Pendulum displacement and angular velocity
statement: The angular displacement, $\theta$ radians, of a pendulum from the vertical is modeled by $\theta(t)=0.3\cos(4\pi t)$, where $t$ is the time in seconds after release and the argument of cosine is in radians. (a) Write down the amplitude of the motion and find its period. [2] (b) Find the first time at which $\theta=0.1$, correct to three significant figures. [3] (c) Find the angular velocity $\theta'(t)$ at the time found in part (b), correct to three significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) Amplitude $=0.3$ radians [A1] Period $=\dfrac{2\pi}{4\pi}=0.5$ seconds [A1] [2 marks] (b) $0.3\cos(4\pi t)=0.1$ gives $\cos(4\pi t)=\dfrac13$ [M1] $4\pi t=1.2310\ldots$ [M1] $t=0.0980$ seconds [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\theta'(t)=-1.2\pi\sin(4\pi t)$ [A1] At $4\pi t=\arccos\dfrac13$, $\sin(4\pi t)=\dfrac{\sqrt8}{3}$ [M1] $\theta'=-1.2\pi\times0.9428=-3.55$ radians per second [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The first positive solution of $\cos u=\tfrac13$ is $u=\arccos\tfrac13$ in radian mode. For part (c), use the identity $\sin^2u+\cos^2u=1$, or the GDC, to evaluate the sine.

subtopic: Beats from the sum of two sound waves
statement: Two tuning forks of frequencies $440$ Hz and $444$ Hz sound together, giving a pressure variation $p(t)=\sin(880\pi t)+\sin(888\pi t)$, where $t$ is in seconds. (a) Show that $p(t)=2\sin(884\pi t)\cos(4\pi t)$. [3] (b) The amplitude of the rapid oscillation is $2|\cos(4\pi t)|$. Find the greatest amplitude and the first time after $t=0$ at which the amplitude is zero. [3] (c) The loudness peaks each time $|\cos4\pi t|=1$. Find the number of loudness peaks per second. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\sin P+\sin Q=2\sin\dfrac{P+Q}2\cos\dfrac{P-Q}2$ [M1] $\dfrac{P+Q}2=884\pi t$ [A1] $\dfrac{P-Q}2=-4\pi t$, and cosine is even [A1] [3 marks] (b) greatest amplitude $2$ [A1] $\cos4\pi t=0$ [M1] $4\pi t=\dfrac\pi2$, $t=\dfrac18$ s [A1] [3 marks] (c) $|\cos4\pi t|$ has period $\dfrac14$ s [M1] $4$ peaks per second, equal to the difference of the frequencies [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A sum of two sinusoids with close frequencies is a fast oscillation multiplied by a slowly varying amplitude.

subtopic: Ferris wheel height and time above 35 m
statement: A Ferris wheel has diameter $40$ m. Its centre is $22$ m above the ground, and it completes one full revolution every $8$ minutes. A passenger boards at the lowest point of the wheel when $t=0$, where $t$ is the time in minutes. The height $h$ meters of the passenger above the ground is modeled by $h(t)=22-20\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\right)$, where the argument of cosine is in radians. (a) Find the height of the passenger when $t=3$. [2] (b) Find the times in the first revolution when the passenger is exactly $35$ m above the ground, correct to three significant figures. [3] (c) Find the percentage of each revolution for which the passenger is above $35$ m, correct to three significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) $h(3)=22-20\cos\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\right)$ [M1] $=36.1$ m [A1] [2 marks] (b) $22-20\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\right)=35$ [M1] $t=2.90$ minutes [A1] and $t=5.10$ minutes [A1] [3 marks] (c) Time above $35$ m $=5.0991-2.9009=2.198$ minutes [M1] Fraction $=\dfrac{2.198}{8}$ [M1] $=27.5\%$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Make sure your GDC is in radian mode because the argument of the cosine contains $\pi$. The second intersection can be found by symmetry about $t=4$.

subtopic: Mixed trigonometric equation solved on a calculator
statement: (a) Solve $3\cos x=2\sin2x+1$ for $0\le x\le2\pi$. [4] (b) Hence write down the solutions of the equation in the interval $2\pi\le x\le4\pi$. [2]
markscheme: (a) Attempt to solve graphically or with GDC, e.g. intersection of $y=3\cos x$ and $y=2\sin2x+1$ [M1] Both intersections found in the interval [A1] $x=0.486$ [A1] $x=4.86$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) Add $2\pi$ to each solution [M1] $x=6.77$, $x=11.1$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Sketch both sides on your GDC over the whole interval so that no intersections are missed. Solutions repeat every period of $2\pi$.

subtopic: Blood pressure over a heartbeat
statement: The blood pressure $P$ (mmHg) of a patient with a heart rate of $72$ beats per minute is modeled by $P(t)=100+20\cos(2.4\pi t)$, where $t$ is time in seconds. (a) Find the period of the function and confirm that it matches a heart rate of $72$ beats per minute. [2] (b) Write down the maximum and minimum pressures. [2] (c) Use your GDC to find the fraction of each heartbeat for which the pressure is above $110$ mmHg, as a percentage to three significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{2\pi}{2.4\pi}=0.833$ s [A1]; $60\div0.8333=72$ beats per minute [A1] [2 marks] (b) $120$ mmHg [A1]; $80$ mmHg [A1] [2 marks] (c) $100+20\cos(2.4\pi t)=110$ gives $t=0.139$ s in the first half-period [M1]; above $110$ for $t$ in $(0,0.139)$ and $(0.694,0.833)$ [A1]; $33.3\%$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Within one period the pressure is above $110$ for two symmetric intervals around the maximum.

subtopic: A mass on a spring with a phase shift
statement: A mass on a spring has displacement $x$ centimeters from its rest position given by $x=12\cos\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{1.6}t+0.9\right)$, where $t$ is the time in seconds. (a) State the amplitude and the period of the motion. [2] (b) Find the initial displacement, to 3 significant figures. [2] (c) Find the first time at which the mass is at its greatest positive displacement. [3] (d) Find all times in the first two periods ($0\leq t\leq3.2$) at which the displacement is $6$ cm. [3] (e) Find the speed of the mass when $t=0.5$ s. [2]
markscheme: (a) Amplitude $12$ cm [A1]; period $1.6$ s [A1] [2 marks] (b) $x(0)=12\cos0.9=7.459$ cm [M1][A1] [2 marks] (c) Maximum when $\dfrac{2\pi}{1.6}t+0.9=2\pi$ [M1]; $t=\dfrac{(2\pi-0.9)(1.6)}{2\pi}=1.371$ s [A1][A1] [3 marks] (d) Solve $x=6$ on the GDC [M1]: $t=0.037$, $t=1.104$, $t=1.637$, $t=2.704$ [A1][A1] [3 marks] (e) $x'=-12\cdot\dfrac{2\pi}{1.6}\sin\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{1.6}t+0.9\right)$ [M1]; speed $=12.937$ cm/s [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A phase shift is written inside the bracket; set $\dfrac{2\pi}{1.6}t+0.9$ equal to $2\pi$ for the first maximum, and differentiate with the chain rule for speeds.

subtopic: Tidal depth model and time above a threshold
statement: The depth of water, $D$ metres, in a harbor $t$ hours after midnight is modeled by $D(t)=4.7-2.8\cos(bt)$, for $t\ge0$, where $b>0$ and the argument of cosine is in radians. The time between consecutive high tides is $12.4$ hours. (a) Find the minimum and maximum depths predicted by the model. [2] (b) Show that $b=0.507$, correct to three significant figures. [2] (c) A ship can enter the harbor only when the depth is at least $6$ m. Find the times, in the first $12.4$ hours, between which the ship can enter, giving each time to the nearest minute. [3] (d) Find the total time in each $12.4$ hour cycle during which the depth is at least $6$ m, in hours correct to three significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) Minimum $=4.7-2.8=1.9$ m [A1] Maximum $=4.7+2.8=7.5$ m [A1] [2 marks] (b) Period $=\dfrac{2\pi}{b}=12.4$ [M1] $b=\dfrac{2\pi}{12.4}=0.507$ (0.50670...) [A1] [2 marks] (c) Solve $4.7-2.8\cos(bt)=6$ using $b=\dfrac{2\pi}{12.4}$ [M1] $t=4.05$ hours [A1] and $t=8.35$ hours [A1] i.e. between about 04:03 and 08:21 (accept 4 h 3 min to 4 h 4 min and 8 h 21 min; accept 4.05 h and 8.35 h) [3 marks] (d) Duration $=8.347-4.053$ (using unrounded values, or $12.4-2(4.053)$) [M1] $=4.29$ hours [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Use the unrounded value of $b$ in your GDC and sketch the graph to see which intersections you need. For the duration, subtract the two unrounded times instead of the rounded ones.

subtopic: Intersection and enclosed area of a sine curve and its translation
statement: Let $f(x)=2\sin x+1$ and let $g(x)=f\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$, for $0\le x\le2\pi$. (a) Describe the transformation that maps the graph of $f$ onto the graph of $g$. [1] (b) Use your GDC to find the $x$-coordinates of the points where the graphs of $f$ and $g$ intersect, correct to three significant figures. [2] (c) Show that the exact $x$-coordinates of these points are $\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ and $\dfrac{5\pi}{3}$ by considering the symmetry of the sine curve, or by substituting into the equation $f(x)=g(x)$. [2] (d) Find the area of the region enclosed between the graphs of $f$ and $g$ for $\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\le x\le\dfrac{5\pi}{3}$. [3]
markscheme: (a) A horizontal translation of $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ to the right [A1] [1 mark] (b) Graph $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$ [M1] $x=2.09$ and $x=5.24$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) At $x=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$: $f=2\sin\dfrac{2\pi}{3}+1=\sqrt3+1$ and $g=2\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}+1=\sqrt3+1$ [M1] At $x=\dfrac{5\pi}{3}$: $f=-\sqrt3+1$ and $g=2\sin\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{3}\right)+1=-\sqrt3+1$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) Area $=\displaystyle\int_{2\pi/3}^{5\pi/3}\left|f(x)-g(x)\right|dx$ [M1] where $g>f$ on this interval [R1] Area $=4$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Two sine curves of equal amplitude cross where they have the same value, which happens at points symmetric about the maximum of the shifted function, so check the exact values to confirm your GDC answers. For the area, use the numerical integration function and enter the absolute difference of the two functions.

subtopic: Sinusoidal model of daylight hours
statement: The number of hours of daylight $y$ in a northern city is modeled by a cosine function of the day number $t$ ($t=0$ is January 1). The longest day has $15.8$ hours and occurs on day $172$. The shortest has $8.2$ hours. (a) Show that the model $y=d+a\cos(b(t-c))$ can have $a=3.8$, $d=12$. [2] (b) Find the values of $b$ and $c$, given that the period is 365 days and the maximum occurs at $t=172$. [2] (c) Find the predicted daylight (hours) at $t=100$. [2] (d) Find the times in one period ($0\leq t\leq365$) when the daylight (hours) is 10. [3]
tips: The midline is the mean of the maximum and minimum; the amplitude is half their difference. Check radians mode.

subtopic: Showing that cos 36 degrees times cos 72 degrees equals one quarter
statement: Let $P=\cos36^\circ\cos72^\circ$. (a) By multiplying $P$ by $\sin36^\circ$ and using the double angle formula twice, show that $4\sin36^\circ P=\sin144^\circ$. [4] (b) Hence show that $P=\dfrac14$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\sin36^\circ\cos36^\circ=\dfrac12\sin72^\circ$ [M1][A1] $\dfrac12\sin72^\circ\cos72^\circ=\dfrac14\sin144^\circ$ [M1] so $\sin36^\circ P=\dfrac14\sin144^\circ$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $\sin144^\circ=\sin36^\circ$ [M1] divide by $\sin36^\circ\ne0$: $P=\dfrac14$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Multiplying by a sine lets you apply $\sin2\theta=2\sin\theta\cos\theta$ repeatedly, doubling the angle each time.

subtopic: Sum-to-product from compound angles and an equation
statement: Use the compound angle formulae for $\sin(A+B)$ and $\sin(A-B)$ in the parts below. (a) Show that $\sin P+\sin Q=2\sin\dfrac{P+Q}2\cos\dfrac{P-Q}2$. [3] (b) Hence solve $\sin3x+\sin x=0$ for $0\le x\le\pi$. [4]
markscheme: (a) let $A=\dfrac{P+Q}2$ and $B=\dfrac{P-Q}2$, so $P=A+B$ and $Q=A-B$ [M1] $\sin(A+B)+\sin(A-B)=2\sin A\cos B$ [A1] substitute back [A1] [3 marks] (b) $2\sin2x\cos x=0$ [M1] $\sin2x=0$ gives $x=0,\dfrac\pi2,\pi$ [A1][A1] $\cos x=0$ gives $x=\dfrac\pi2$, already found; solutions $0,\ \dfrac\pi2,\ \pi$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Adding the expansions of $\sin(A+B)$ and $\sin(A-B)$ leaves $2\sin A\cos B$.

subtopic: Reading amplitude, period and phase shift
statement: Consider the function $f(x)=3\sin\left(2x-\dfrac\pi3\right)+1$. (a) Write down the amplitude, the period and the midline. [3] (b) Find the maximum and minimum values of $f$ and the smallest positive $x$ at which the maximum occurs. [3] (c) Describe the horizontal shift of the graph of $y=3\sin2x+1$ that gives the graph of $f$. [2]
markscheme: (a) Amplitude $3$ [A1]; period $\dfrac{2\pi}{2}=\pi$ [A1]; midline $y=1$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Maximum $4$, minimum $-2$ [A1]; $2x-\dfrac\pi3=\dfrac\pi2$ [M1]; $x=\dfrac{5\pi}{12}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $f(x)=3\sin2\left(x-\dfrac\pi6\right)+1$ [M1]; shift right by $\dfrac\pi6$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Rewrite $2x-\pi/3$ as $2(x-\pi/6)$ to read the horizontal shift correctly.

subtopic: Solving equations using the double angle identity
statement: Let $f(x)=\cos2x+5\cos x+3$. (a) Show that $f(x)=2\cos^2x+5\cos x+2$. [2] (b) Hence solve $f(x)=0$ for $0\le x\le2\pi$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $\cos2x=2\cos^2x-1$ [M1] $f(x)=2\cos^2x-1+5\cos x+3=2\cos^2x+5\cos x+2$ [A1] [AG] [2 marks] (b) $(2\cos x+1)(\cos x+2)=0$ [M1] $\cos x=-\dfrac12$ or $\cos x=-2$ [A1] reject $\cos x=-2$ since $|\cos x|\le1$ [R1] $x=\dfrac{2\pi}3,\ \dfrac{4\pi}3$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Choose the form of $\cos2x$ that leaves a single trigonometric function. Always reject roots outside $[-1,1]$.

subtopic: Using a double angle identity with a given sine
statement: The angle $\theta$ is acute with $\sin\theta=\dfrac{3}{5}$. (a) Find $\cos\theta$. [1] (b) Find the exact values of $\sin2\theta$ and $\cos2\theta$. [3] (c) Hence find $\tan2\theta$ and the value of $\tan\left(2\theta+\dfrac\pi4\right)$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\cos\theta=\dfrac45$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\sin2\theta=2\times\dfrac35\times\dfrac45=\dfrac{24}{25}$ [M1][A1] $\cos2\theta=1-2\times\dfrac9{25}=\dfrac7{25}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\tan2\theta=\dfrac{24}7$ [A1] $\tan\left(2\theta+\dfrac\pi4\right)=\dfrac{\frac{24}7+1}{1-\frac{24}7}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{31/7}{-17/7}=-\dfrac{31}{17}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Draw a right triangle to find the missing ratio. Use $\sin2\theta=2\sin\theta\cos\theta$ and $\cos2\theta=1-2\sin^2\theta$.

subtopic: Tangent identity for the angles of a triangle
statement: The angles $A$, $B$, $C$ of a triangle satisfy $A+B+C=\pi$, and none of them is a right angle. (a) Show that $\tan A+\tan B+\tan C=\tan A\tan B\tan C$. [4] (b) In a triangle, $\tan A=1$ and $\tan B=2$. Find $\tan C$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\tan(A+B)=\tan(\pi-C)=-\tan C$ [M1] $\dfrac{\tan A+\tan B}{1-\tan A\tan B}=-\tan C$ [A1] $\tan A+\tan B=-\tan C+\tan A\tan B\tan C$ [M1] rearrange [A1] [4 marks] (b) $1+2+\tan C=2\tan C$ [M1] $\tan C=3$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Write $C=\pi-(A+B)$ and use the compound angle formula for tangent.

subtopic: Proving a tangent double angle identity
statement: (a) Use the compound angle formula for $\tan(A+B)$ to show that $\tan2x\equiv\dfrac{2\tan x}{1-\tan^2x}$. [3] (b) Hence solve $\tan2x=3\tan x$ for $-\dfrac\pi2<x<\dfrac\pi2$, $x\ne\pm\dfrac\pi4$. [5]
markscheme: (a) $\tan2x=\tan(x+x)$ [M1] $=\dfrac{\tan x+\tan x}{1-\tan x\tan x}$ [A1] $=\dfrac{2\tan x}{1-\tan^2x}$ [A1] [AG] [3 marks] (b) $\dfrac{2t}{1-t^2}=3t$ where $t=\tan x$ [M1] $t\left(2-3+3t^2\right)=0$ [A1] $t=0$ or $t^2=\dfrac13$ [A1] $x=0$ [A1] $x=\pm\dfrac\pi6$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: Put $t=\tan x$ and factorize; do not cancel $t$ since $t=0$ is a solution.

subtopic: Range, period and solutions of a cosine function
statement: Let $f(x)=3\cos(2x)+1$, for $0\le x\le2\pi$. (a) Solve $f(x)=2.5$. [4] (b) Write down the range of $f$. [2] (c) Write down the period of $f$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $3\cos2x+1=2.5$ gives $\cos2x=\dfrac12$ [M1] $2x=\dfrac\pi3,\ \dfrac{5\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{3}$ (all solutions in $0\le2x\le4\pi$) [M1] $x=\dfrac\pi6,\ \dfrac{5\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{6}$ [A1] [A1] [4 marks] (b) $-3+1\le f(x)\le3+1$ [M1] $-2\le f(x)\le4$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Period $=\dfrac{2\pi}{2}=\pi$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: When the angle is $2x$, the interval for $2x$ doubles to $[0,4\pi]$, so look for twice as many solutions. Award yourself the A marks only when every solution in the interval is listed.

subtopic: Area of an isosceles triangular flowerbed
statement: A triangular flowerbed has two sides of length $10$ m, with an angle of $\theta$ radians between them, where $0<\theta<\pi$. (a) Show that the area of the flowerbed is $50\sin\theta\ \text{m}^2$. [1] (b) The area of the flowerbed is $30\ \text{m}^2$. Find the two possible values of $\theta$, correct to three significant figures. [3] (c) Find the maximum possible area of the flowerbed, and the value of $\theta$ at which it occurs. [2] (d) Find the perimeter of the flowerbed when its area is a maximum, correct to three significant figures. [1]
markscheme: (a) Area $=\tfrac12(10)(10)\sin\theta=50\sin\theta$ [AG] [1 mark] (b) $50\sin\theta=30$ so $\sin\theta=0.6$ [M1] $\theta=0.644$ [A1] $\theta=\pi-0.6435=2.50$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Maximum area $=50\ \text{m}^2$ [A1] when $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) Third side $=\sqrt{10^2+10^2}=10\sqrt2$ so perimeter $=20+10\sqrt2=34.1$ m [A1] [1 mark]
tips: When $\sin\theta$ is known, there are two angles in $0<\theta<\pi$: the acute one and its supplement $\pi-\theta$. The largest value of $\sin\theta$ is $1$, which occurs at a right angle between the two equal sides.

subtopic: Writing a sin x + b cos x in the form R sin(x + alpha)
statement: Let $f(x)=5\sin x+12\cos x$. (a) Write $f(x)$ in the form $R\sin(x+\alpha)$ where $R>0$ and $0<\alpha<\dfrac\pi2$. [3] (b) Write down the maximum and minimum values of $f$ and the smallest positive value of $x$ at which the maximum occurs. [3] (c) Solve $f(x)=6$ for $0\le x\le2\pi$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $R=\sqrt{5^2+12^2}=13.00$ [A1] $\cos\alpha=\dfrac{5}{R}$, $\sin\alpha=\dfrac{12}{R}$ [M1] $\alpha=\arctan\dfrac{12}{5}=1.176$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) maximum $=13.00$ and minimum $=-13.00$ [A1] maximum when $x+\alpha=\dfrac\pi2$ [M1] $x=0.3948$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\sin(x+1.176)=\dfrac{6}{13.00}$ [M1] $x+1.176=0.4797$ or $\pi-0.4797$ [A1] $x=1.486$ or $x=5.587$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Expand $R\sin(x+\alpha)=R\sin x\cos\alpha+R\cos x\sin\alpha$ and match coefficients. The maximum of $R\sin(\cdot)$ is $R$.

subtopic: Solving a trigonometric equation graphically
statement: Consider the equation $\sin x=0.25x$ where $x$ is in radians. (a) Use your GDC to find all solutions in the interval $-5\le x\le5$, to three significant figures. [3] (b) Explain why there are no solutions with $x>4$. [2] (c) Hence solve $\sin x>0.25x$ for $x\ge0$. [2]
markscheme: (a) Intersect the graphs of $y=\sin x$ and $y=0.25x$ [M1]; $x=0$ [A1]; $x=\pm2.47$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) For $x>4$, $0.25x>1$ [A1]; but $\sin x\le1$ [R1] [2 marks] (c) The sine curve is above the line between the intersections [M1]; $0<x<2.47$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A line of gradient $0.25$ through the origin crosses the sine curve until its height exceeds $1$.

subtopic: Pedal height as a negative sine function
statement: The height $h$ cm of a bicycle pedal above the ground, $t$ seconds after the pedal is at its mean height and moving downward, is modeled by $h(t)=30-12\sin(\pi t)$, for $t\ge0$. (a) Write down the amplitude and the period of the motion. [2] (b) Find $h(0)$. [1] (c) Find the maximum height of the pedal and the smallest positive value of $t$ at which it occurs. [3]
markscheme: (a) Amplitude $=12$ cm [A1] period $=\dfrac{2\pi}{\pi}=2$ s [A1] [2 marks] (b) $h(0)=30-12\sin0=30$ cm [A1] [1 mark] (c) Maximum $=30+12=42$ cm [A1] when $\sin(\pi t)=-1$ [M1] $\pi t=\dfrac{3\pi}{2}$ so $t=1.5$ s [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The minus sign turns the sine wave upside down: it starts at the mean value but first moves down. The maximum of $-\sin(\pi t)$ occurs where $\sin(\pi t)=-1$.

subtopic: Angle between the curves y = sin x and y = cos x
statement: The curves $y=\sin x$ and $y=\cos x$ intersect at the point $P$ where $x=\dfrac\pi4$. (a) Find the gradient of each curve at $P$. [3] (b) Find the acute angle between the two curves at $P$, to the nearest tenth of a degree. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{d}{dx}\sin x=\cos x$ and $\dfrac d{dx}\cos x=-\sin x$ [M1] $m_1=\dfrac{\sqrt2}2$ [A1] $m_2=-\dfrac{\sqrt2}2$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\tan\theta=\left|\dfrac{m_1-m_2}{1+m_1m_2}\right|$ [M1] $=\dfrac{\sqrt2}{1-\frac12}=2\sqrt2$ [A1] $\theta=70.5^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The angle between two curves at a point is the angle between their tangent lines there.

subtopic: Identities between inverse trigonometric functions
statement: Consider the inverse trigonometric functions $\arcsin$, $\arccos$ and $\arctan$. (a) Show that $\arcsin x+\arccos x=\dfrac\pi2$ for $-1\le x\le1$. [3] (b) Show that $\arctan x+\arctan\dfrac1x=\dfrac\pi2$ for $x>0$. [3]
markscheme: (a) let $\theta=\arcsin x$ so $\sin\theta=x$ [M1] $\cos\left(\dfrac\pi2-\theta\right)=x$ [A1] and $\dfrac\pi2-\theta\in[0,\pi]$, so $\arccos x=\dfrac\pi2-\theta$ [R1] [3 marks] (b) let $\theta=\arctan x$ so $\tan\theta=x$ [M1] $\tan\left(\dfrac\pi2-\theta\right)=\dfrac1x$ [A1] $\dfrac\pi2-\theta\in\left(0,\dfrac\pi2\right)$ so it equals $\arctan\dfrac1x$ [R1] [3 marks]
tips: Use the complementary angle identities $\cos(\pi/2-\theta)=\sin\theta$ and $\tan(\pi/2-\theta)=1/\tan\theta$.

subtopic: Solving basic sine and tangent equations exactly
statement: Solve each equation for $0\le x\le2\pi$, giving exact answers. (a) $2\sin x=-1$. [3] (b) $\tan x=-\sqrt3$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\sin x=-\dfrac12$, reference angle $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ [M1] $x=\dfrac{7\pi}{6}$ [A1] $x=\dfrac{11\pi}{6}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Reference angle $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ [M1] tangent is negative in the second and fourth quadrants so $x=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ [A1] $x=\dfrac{5\pi}{3}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Find the reference angle from the positive value first, then use the quadrant rule ("CAST") for the sign. Give exactly the number of solutions in the domain, no more and no fewer.

subtopic: Loudspeaker diaphragm moving sinusoidally
statement: The displacement $x$ millimeters of the diaphragm of a loudspeaker from its rest position, $t$ seconds after it starts moving, is modeled by $x(t)=0.4\sin(660\pi t)$. (a) Write down the amplitude and find the exact period of the motion. [2] (b) Find the frequency, in hertz (cycles per second), of the sound. [1] (c) Find the displacement when $t=0.001$ s, correct to three significant figures. [1] (d) Find an expression for the velocity $v=\dfrac{dx}{dt}$, and hence find the maximum speed of the diaphragm, correct to three significant figures. [3] (e) Find the first time after $t=0$ at which the displacement equals $0.3$ mm, correct to three significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) Amplitude $=0.4$ mm [A1] period $=\dfrac{2\pi}{660\pi}=\dfrac{1}{330}$ s [A1] [2 marks] (b) Frequency $=330$ Hz [A1] [1 mark] (c) $x(0.001)=0.4\sin(0.66\pi)=0.351\ \text{mm}$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) $v=0.4\times660\pi\cos(660\pi t)$ [M1] $=264\pi\cos(660\pi t)$ [A1] maximum speed $=264\pi=829\ \text{mm/s}$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) $0.4\sin(660\pi t)=0.3$ so $\sin(660\pi t)=0.75$ [M1] $t=\dfrac{\sin^{-1}0.75}{660\pi}=4.09\times10^{-4}\ \text{s}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The period of $\sin(kt)$ is $\dfrac{2\pi}{k}$, and the frequency is the reciprocal of the period. The maximum speed is the amplitude of the velocity function, which is the displacement amplitude multiplied by $k$.

subtopic: Energy demand over a day from a sinusoidal model
statement: The electricity demand $D$ megawatts (MW) in a town, $t$ hours after midnight, is modeled by $D(t)=420+130\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{12}(t-9)\right)$, for $0\le t\le24$. (a) Find the maximum demand, and the time of day at which it occurs. [3] (b) The total energy used between $t=6$ and $t=18$, in megawatt-hours (MWh), is given by $\displaystyle\int_6^{18}D(t)\,dt$. Find this energy, correct to three significant figures. [2] (c) Without integrating, explain why the mean demand over $0\le t\le24$ is $420$ MW, and hence write down the total energy used in the whole day. [2] (d) Use your GDC to find, correct to the nearest minute, the length of time in the day for which the demand exceeds $500$ MW. [2]
markscheme: (a) Maximum demand $=420+130=550$ MW [A1] $\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{12}(t-9)\right)=1$ when $\dfrac{\pi}{12}(t-9)=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ [M1] $t=15$, that is $15{:}00$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\displaystyle\int_6^{18}D(t)\,dt$ [M1] $=5740$ MWh [A1] [2 marks] (c) $24$ hours is exactly one period, so the sine term averages to zero over the day [R1] total energy $=420\times24=10\,080$ MWh [A1] [2 marks] (d) Solve $D(t)=500$: $t=11.53$ and $t=18.47$ [M1] Time $=6.936$ hours $\approx6$ h $56$ min [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Integration of a sinusoid over a whole number of periods leaves only the contribution of the midline, which is a quick check on a GDC answer. Convert decimal hours to minutes at the end only.

subtopic: Solving an equation for a cosine transformation
statement: Let $f(x)=3\cos(2x)-1$ for $0\le x\le\pi$. (a) Write down the amplitude, the period and the range of $f$. [3] (b) Find the exact solutions of $f(x)=\dfrac12$. [4]
markscheme: (a) amplitude $3$ [A1]; period $\pi$ [A1]; range $-4\le f(x)\le2$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $3\cos2x=\dfrac32$ so $\cos2x=\dfrac12$ [M1]; $2x=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ or $\dfrac{5\pi}{3}$ [A1][A1]; $x=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ and $x=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Solve for $\cos2x$ first, then list every value of $2x$ in $[0, 2\pi]$ before halving.

subtopic: Quadratic equation in sine using the Pythagorean identity
statement: Solve the equation $2\cos^2x+3\sin x=3$ for $0\le x\le2\pi$. [6]
markscheme: Use $\cos^2x=1-\sin^2x$: $2(1-\sin^2x)+3\sin x=3$ [M1] $2\sin^2x-3\sin x+1=0$ [A1] $(2\sin x-1)(\sin x-1)=0$ [M1] $\sin x=\dfrac12$ or $\sin x=1$ [A1] $x=\dfrac\pi6,\ \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$ [A1] $x=\dfrac\pi2$ [A1] [6 marks]
tips: Convert to a single trigonometric function, treat the result as a quadratic and factorize. Remember that sine takes each positive value twice in $[0,2\pi]$.

subtopic: Solving equations using the double angle identity
statement: Solve each equation for $0\le x\le2\pi$, giving exact answers. (a) $\cos2x+3\sin x-2=0$. [5] (b) $\sin2x=\sin x$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $\cos2x=1-2\sin^2x$ [M1] $-2\sin^2x+3\sin x-1=0$ [A1] $(2\sin x-1)(\sin x-1)=0$ [M1] $\sin x=\dfrac12$ or $1$ [A1] $x=\dfrac\pi6,\ \dfrac{5\pi}6,\ \dfrac\pi2$ [A1] [5 marks] (b) $2\sin x\cos x-\sin x=0$ [M1] $\sin x(2\cos x-1)=0$ [A1] $\sin x=0$ gives $x=0,\pi,2\pi$ [A1] $\cos x=\dfrac12$ gives $x=\dfrac\pi3,\dfrac{5\pi}3$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Rewrite every term in terms of one trigonometric function, or factorize, rather than dividing by $\sin x$ (which loses solutions).

subtopic: An equation in cosine of a double angle
statement: Solve $2\cos(2x)=-1$ for $0\le x\le\pi$, giving exact answers. (a) Find $\cos(2x)$ and the possible values of $2x$ in the interval $0\le 2x\le2\pi$. [3] (b) Hence write down all the solutions for $x$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\cos2x=-\dfrac12$ [A1]; $2x=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ [A1]; $2x=\dfrac{4\pi}{3}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $x=\dfrac\pi3$ [A1]; $x=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: First solve for the whole argument $2x$ over a doubled interval, then divide by $2$.

subtopic: Where sine and cosine curves meet
statement: The graphs of $y=\sin x$ and $y=\cos x$ intersect for $0\le x\le2\pi$. (a) Find the exact values of $x$ at the points of intersection. [3] (b) Find the exact $y$-coordinates of these two points. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\sin x=\cos x$ so $\tan x=1$ [M1]; $x=\dfrac\pi4$ [A1]; $x=\dfrac{5\pi}{4}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$ [A1]; $-\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Dividing both sides by $\cos x$ gives $\tan x=1$.

subtopic: Rate of growth of a cyclical fox population
statement: The number of foxes $P$ in a nature reserve, $t$ years after the start of a study, is modeled by $P(t)=800+300\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{5}\right)$, for $0\le t\le10$. (a) Find the maximum and minimum populations predicted by the model. [2] (b) Find an expression for $\dfrac{dP}{dt}$. [2] (c) Find the maximum rate of increase of the population, correct to three significant figures. [2] (d) Use your GDC to find the values of $t$ in $0\le t\le10$ for which the population is increasing at a rate of at least $100$ foxes per year, correct to three significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) Maximum $=800+300=1100$ [A1] minimum $=800-300=500$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=300\times\dfrac{\pi}{5}\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{5}\right)$ [M1] $=60\pi\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{5}\right)$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) The maximum of $\cos$ is $1$ [M1] so the maximum rate is $60\pi=188$ foxes per year [A1] [2 marks] (d) Solve $60\pi\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{5}\right)\ge100$ [M1] $0\le t\le1.61$ [A1] and $8.39\le t\le10$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The derivative of $a\sin(bt)+d$ is $ab\cos(bt)$, so the largest rate of change is $ab$. For part (d) sketch the derivative and find where it is above the line $y=100$, remembering the whole domain, including both ends.

subtopic: Tangent graph with a horizontal stretch
statement: Consider $f(x)=\tan\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)$ for $0\le x<4\pi$. (a) Write down the period of $f$ and the equations of its vertical asymptotes in the given interval. [3] (b) Solve $f(x)=\sqrt3$ in the interval $0\le x<4\pi$. [3]
markscheme: (a) period $2\pi$ [A1]; asymptotes where $\dfrac{x}{2}=\dfrac\pi2+k\pi$ [M1]; $x=\pi$ and $x=3\pi$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\dfrac{x}{2}=\dfrac\pi3+k\pi$ [M1]; $x=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ [A1]; $x=\dfrac{8\pi}{3}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: For $\tan(bx)$, the period is $\frac{\pi}{b}$.

subtopic: Sum of three inverse tangents
statement: Show that $\arctan\dfrac12+\arctan\dfrac15+\arctan\dfrac18=\dfrac\pi4$. (a) Find $\tan\left(\arctan\dfrac12+\arctan\dfrac15\right)$. [2] (b) Hence show that the sum of the three inverse tangents is $\dfrac\pi4$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{\frac12+\frac15}{1-\frac1{10}}$ [M1] $=\dfrac79$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\tan\left(\arctan\dfrac79+\arctan\dfrac18\right)=\dfrac{\frac79+\frac18}{1-\frac7{72}}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{65/72}{65/72}=1$ [A1] each term is positive and the sum is less than $\dfrac\pi2$, so the sum is $\dfrac\pi4$ [R1] [3 marks]
tips: Combine two terms at a time with the tangent addition formula. Check the quadrant of the final angle.

subtopic: The triple angle formula and the roots of a cubic
statement: This question uses trigonometry to find the roots of a cubic equation. (a) Use the compound angle formulas to show that $\cos3\theta=4\cos^3\theta-3\cos\theta$. [4] (b) Hence show that $x=\cos\dfrac\pi9$ is a root of $8x^3-6x-1=0$. [3] (c) By solving $\cos3\theta=\dfrac12$ for $0<\theta<\pi$, find the other two roots of the cubic in terms of cosines of rational multiples of $\pi$. [4] (d) Use the sum and product of the roots to show that $\cos\dfrac\pi9+\cos\dfrac{5\pi}9+\cos\dfrac{7\pi}9=0$ and $\cos\dfrac\pi9\cos\dfrac{5\pi}9\cos\dfrac{7\pi}9=\dfrac18$. [3] (e) Find the value of $\cos\dfrac\pi9\cos\dfrac{5\pi}9+\cos\dfrac\pi9\cos\dfrac{7\pi}9+\cos\dfrac{5\pi}9\cos\dfrac{7\pi}9$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\cos3\theta=\cos(2\theta+\theta)=\cos2\theta\cos\theta-\sin2\theta\sin\theta$ [M1] $=\left(2\cos^2\theta-1\right)\cos\theta-2\sin^2\theta\cos\theta$ [A1] $\sin^2\theta=1-\cos^2\theta$ [M1] $=2\cos^3\theta-\cos\theta-2\cos\theta+2\cos^3\theta=4\cos^3\theta-3\cos\theta$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $2\cos3\theta=8\cos^3\theta-6\cos\theta$ [M1] with $\theta=\dfrac\pi9$: $2\cos\dfrac\pi3=1$ [A1] so $8x^3-6x-1=0$ for $x=\cos\dfrac\pi9$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $3\theta=\dfrac\pi3,\ \dfrac{5\pi}3,\ \dfrac{7\pi}3$ [M1][A1] $\theta=\dfrac\pi9,\ \dfrac{5\pi}9,\ \dfrac{7\pi}9$ [A1] roots $\cos\dfrac{5\pi}9$ and $\cos\dfrac{7\pi}9$ [A1] [4 marks] (d) the cubic $8x^3-6x-1=0$ has no $x^2$ term, so the sum of the roots is $0$ [A1] product of roots $=-\dfrac{-1}{8}$ [M1] $=\dfrac18$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) sum of pairwise products $=\dfrac{-6}{8}$ [M1] $=-\dfrac34$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Use $\cos3\theta$ to turn a cubic in $x=\cos\theta$ into a trigonometric equation. Vieta's formulas then give the symmetric functions of the roots without calculating them.

subtopic: Closest approach of a ship to a lighthouse
statement: A lighthouse $L$ is $14$ km from a ship at $A$, on a bearing of $070^\circ$ from the ship. The ship sails in a straight line on a bearing of $110^\circ$. (a) Find the angle between the ship's course and the line $AL$. [1] (b) Find the shortest distance between the ship and the lighthouse during the journey, correct to three significant figures. [2] (c) Find the distance the ship has sailed from $A$ when it is closest to the lighthouse, correct to three significant figures. [2] (d) The light of the lighthouse is visible up to a distance of $10$ km. Find the distance sailed from $A$ when the ship first comes within sight of the light, and the distance sailed when it goes out of sight again, each correct to three significant figures. [4]
markscheme: (a) $110^\circ-70^\circ=40^\circ$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) The shortest distance is perpendicular to the course: $14\sin40^\circ$ [M1] $=9.00\ \text{km}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $14\cos40^\circ$ [M1] $=10.7\ \text{km}$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) With $x$ the distance sailed, $10^2=x^2+14^2-2(14)x\cos40^\circ$ [M1] [A1] $x^2-21.45x+96=0$ so $x=6.36\ \text{km}$ or $x=15.1\ \text{km}$ [A1] [A1] [4 marks]
tips: The closest approach to a point is where the line from the point meets the course at a right angle. For the visibility limit, a cosine rule equation in the unknown side gives a quadratic whose two roots are entering and leaving the visible range.

subtopic: Approximating pi with inscribed and circumscribed polygons
statement: This question investigates how regular polygons can be used to approximate the circumference and area of a unit circle. A regular polygon with $n$ sides is inscribed in a circle of radius $1$ (all its vertices lie on the circle). Let $P_n$ be its perimeter. A second regular polygon with $n$ sides is circumscribed about the same circle (all its sides touch the circle). Let $Q_n$ be its perimeter. (a) Show that $P_n=2n\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{n}\right)$. [2] (b) Find $P_6$ and $P_{12}$, giving $P_{12}$ correct to four significant figures. [2] (c) Show that $Q_n=2n\tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{n}\right)$. The circle has circumference $2\pi$, and $P_n<2\pi<Q_n$. Use $n=12$ to find lower and upper bounds for $\pi$, each correct to four significant figures. [5] (d) Find the smallest value of $n$ for which $Q_n-P_n<0.01$. [3] (e) The area of the inscribed polygon is $A_n$. Show that $A_n=\dfrac n2\sin\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{n}\right)$. Hence find the smallest $n$ for which $A_n$ is within $0.1\%$ of $\pi$, that is $\dfrac{\pi-A_n}{\pi}<0.001$. [5] For small values of $x$ (in radians), $\sin x\approx x-\dfrac{x^3}{6}$ and $\tan x\approx x+\dfrac{x^3}{3}$. (f) Use the first approximation to show that, for large $n$, $P_n\approx2\pi-\dfrac{\pi^3}{3n^2}$. [3] (g) Find a similar approximation for $Q_n$. Hence show that $\dfrac{2P_n+Q_n}{6}\approx\pi$, with the terms in $\dfrac{1}{n^2}$ cancelling. [4] (h) For $n=12$, find $\dfrac{2P_{12}+Q_{12}}{6}$ and the percentage error of this estimate of $\pi$. Compare it with the percentage error of the estimate $\dfrac{P_{12}}{2}$. [3]
markscheme: (a) Each side subtends an angle $\dfrac{2\pi}{n}$ at the centre; splitting the isosceles triangle in half gives side length $2\sin\dfrac{\pi}{n}$ [M1] $P_n=n\times2\sin\dfrac{\pi}{n}$ [AG] [2 marks] (b) $P_6=6.000$ [A1] $P_{12}=6.212$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Each side of the circumscribed polygon has length $2\tan\dfrac{\pi}{n}$ (half-side is $\tan\dfrac{\pi}{n}$ in the right-angled triangle with the radius) [M1] so $Q_n=2n\tan\dfrac{\pi}{n}$ [AG] For $n=12$: $P_{12}<2\pi<Q_{12}$ gives $6.212<2\pi<6.431$ [M1] $3.106<\pi<3.215$ [A1] [A1] [5 marks] (d) $Q_n-P_n=2n\left(\tan\dfrac{\pi}{n}-\sin\dfrac{\pi}{n}\right)$ evaluated for increasing $n$ [M1] $n=55$ gives $0.0103\ge0.01$ [A1] $n=56$ gives $0.00989<0.01$ so $n=56$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) The polygon is made of $n$ triangles each with area $\tfrac12(1)(1)\sin\dfrac{2\pi}{n}$ [M1] $A_n=\dfrac n2\sin\dfrac{2\pi}{n}$ [AG] Solve $\dfrac{\pi-A_n}{\pi}<0.001$ by table or graph [M1] $n=81$ gives $A_{81}=3.1384$ with relative error $0.100\%$ so not enough [A1] $n=82$ gives $A_{82}=3.1385$ with relative error $0.0978\%$ so $n=82$ [A1] [5 marks] (f) $P_n\approx2n\left(\dfrac{\pi}{n}-\dfrac{1}{6}\dfrac{\pi^3}{n^3}\right)$ [M1] $=2\pi-\dfrac{2\pi^3}{6n^2}$ [A1] $=2\pi-\dfrac{\pi^3}{3n^2}$ [AG] [3 marks] (g) $Q_n\approx2n\left(\dfrac{\pi}{n}+\dfrac13\dfrac{\pi^3}{n^3}\right)=2\pi+\dfrac{2\pi^3}{3n^2}$ [M1] [A1] $2P_n+Q_n\approx4\pi-\dfrac{2\pi^3}{3n^2}+2\pi+\dfrac{2\pi^3}{3n^2}$ [M1] $=6\pi$ so $\dfrac{2P_n+Q_n}{6}\approx\pi$ [A1] [4 marks] (h) $\dfrac{2(6.2117)+6.4308}{6}=3.1423$ [A1] Percentage error $=\dfrac{\pi-3.1423}{\pi}\times100\approx0.024\%$ [A1] For $\dfrac{P_{12}}{2}=3.1058$ the percentage error is $1.14\%$, about $47$ times larger [A1] [3 marks]
tips: In the approximation parts, replace sine and tangent by the given polynomials and simplify the powers of $n$ carefully: $2n\times\dfrac{\pi^3}{n^3}=\dfrac{2\pi^3}{n^2}$. Use a table or the solver on your GDC for the search questions, and always check the neighbouring integer to justify that your $n$ is the smallest.

subtopic: Two triangles from a given area
statement: In triangle $ABC$, $AB=10$ cm, $AC=14$ cm and the area of the triangle is $56\ \text{cm}^2$. Angle $BAC$ is $\theta$. (a) Find the two possible values of $\theta$, in degrees, correct to three significant figures. [3] (b) Find the two possible lengths of $BC$, correct to three significant figures. [4]
markscheme: (a) $\tfrac12(10)(14)\sin\theta=56$ [M1] $\sin\theta=0.8$ [A1] so $\theta=53.1^\circ$ or $\theta=127^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $BC^2=10^2+14^2-2(10)(14)\cos\theta$ [M1] For $\theta=53.13^\circ$, $\cos\theta=0.6$: $BC^2=128$, $BC=11.3\ \text{cm}$ [A1] For $\theta=126.87^\circ$, $\cos\theta=-0.6$: $BC^2=464$ [M1] $BC=21.5\ \text{cm}$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: An area equation $\tfrac12ab\sin\theta=A$ gives two angles between $0^\circ$ and $180^\circ$, one acute and one obtuse. Remember that $\cos$ changes sign for the obtuse angle.

subtopic: Arc length and chord length from a central angle
statement: A circle has centre $O$ and radius $r$. A chord $AB$ subtends an angle of $\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ at $O$ and the length of the minor arc $AB$ is $4\pi$ cm. (a) Find $r$. [2] (b) Find the exact length of the chord $AB$. [3] (c) Find the exact area of the sector $AOB$. [2]
tips: Arc length is $r\theta$ with $\theta$ in radians.

subtopic: Cosine rule, angles and area from three sides
statement: A triangle has sides of length $7$ cm, $9$ cm and $12$ cm. (a) Find the size of the largest angle, correct to the nearest tenth of a degree. [3] (b) Find the area of the triangle, correct to three significant figures. [3] (c) Find the size of the smallest angle, correct to the nearest tenth of a degree. [2]
markscheme: (a) The largest angle $\theta$ is opposite the side of length $12$: $\cos\theta=\dfrac{7^2+9^2-12^2}{2(7)(9)}$ [M1] [A1] $\theta=96.4^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Area $=\tfrac12(7)(9)\sin96.38^\circ$ [M1] [A1] $=31.3\ \text{cm}^2$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) The smallest angle $\phi$ is opposite the side $7$: $\cos\phi=\dfrac{9^2+12^2-7^2}{2(9)(12)}$ [M1] $\phi=35.3^\circ$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The largest angle is always opposite the longest side, and a negative cosine tells you it is obtuse. Use the area formula $\tfrac12ab\sin C$ with the unrounded angle from your calculator.

subtopic: Circular segment in a lawn with chord and radius
statement: A circular lawn has centre $O$ and radius $7.5$ m. A straight path $AB$ of length $10$ m joins two points on the edge of the lawn. (a) Find angle $AOB$ in radians, correct to three significant figures. [3] (b) Find the length of the minor arc $AB$, correct to three significant figures. [2] (c) Find the area of the segment between the path $AB$ and the minor arc $AB$, correct to three significant figures. [3] (d) Find the perimeter of this segment, correct to three significant figures. [2]
tips: When the angle is not given, a chord and two radii form an isosceles triangle: use the cosine rule. Keep your GDC in radian mode for sector formulas and use unrounded values in later parts.

subtopic: Sine rule with exact values in a roof truss
statement: A triangular roof truss $ABC$ has angle $BAC=45^\circ$, angle $ABC=60^\circ$ and $BC=6\sqrt2$ m. (a) Find the exact length of $AC$. [3] (b) Find the size of angle $ACB$, and state, with a reason, which side of the truss is longest. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{AC}{\sin60^\circ}=\dfrac{6\sqrt2}{\sin45^\circ}$ [M1] $AC=\dfrac{6\sqrt2\times\frac{\sqrt3}{2}}{\frac{\sqrt2}{2}}$ [M1] $=6\sqrt3$ m [A1] [3 marks] (b) Angle $ACB=180^\circ-45^\circ-60^\circ=75^\circ$ [A1] $AB$ is the longest side because it is opposite the largest angle [R1] [2 marks]
tips: The sine rule is easiest when a pair of known quantities is written as one ratio, here $\dfrac{BC}{\sin A}$. The longest side is always opposite the largest angle.

subtopic: A ski lift on a slope
statement: A ski lift runs in a straight line from a base station at an altitude of $1480$ m to a top station at an altitude of $1900$ m. The horizontal distance between the stations is $1250$ m. (a) Find the length of the lift cable, to the nearest meter. [2] (b) Find the angle the cable makes with the horizontal, to one decimal place. [2] (c) A gondola travels along the cable at $4.5$ m/s. Find the time of the ride, in minutes and seconds, to the nearest second. [2]
tips: The cable, the horizontal distance and the vertical rise form a right-angled triangle.

subtopic: Regular nonagon park inside a circle
statement: A park is in the shape of a regular polygon with $9$ equal sides. All nine vertices lie on a circle of radius $20$ m with centre $O$. (a) Write down the angle at $O$ subtended by one side of the park. [1] (b) Find the length of one side, correct to three significant figures. [2] (c) Find the area of the park, correct to three significant figures. [2] (d) Find the percentage of the area of the circle that is covered by the park, correct to the nearest percent. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{360^\circ}{9}=40^\circ$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $s^2=20^2+20^2-2(20)(20)\cos40^\circ$ or $s=2(20)\sin20^\circ$ [M1] $s=13.7\ \text{m}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Area $=9\times\tfrac12(20)^2\sin40^\circ$ [M1] $=1160\ \text{m}^2$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) Circle area $=\pi(20)^2=1257\ \text{m}^2$ and percentage $=\dfrac{1157}{1257}\times100$ [M1] $=92\%$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A regular $n$-sided polygon splits into $n$ identical isosceles triangles at the centre, each with apex angle $\dfrac{360^\circ}{n}$. Multiply one triangle's area by $n$ for the whole polygon.

subtopic: Swing of a pendulum
statement: A pendulum has a string of length $1.2$ m and swings through a total angle of $40^{\circ}$ (from one extreme to the other), with the string always straight. (a) Find the length of the arc traveled by the bob in one swing from one extreme to the other, to three significant figures. [2] (b) Find the area of the sector swept out by the string, to three significant figures. [2] (c) Find how much higher the bob is at an extreme than at its lowest point, in centimeters to three significant figures. [3]
tips: The lowest point is directly below the pivot, so each extreme is $20^{\circ}$ from the vertical.

subtopic: Isosceles triangle with an obtuse apex angle
statement: In triangle $ABC$, $AB=AC=10$ cm and angle $BAC=120^{\circ}$. (a) Use the cosine rule to find $BC$ in the form $k\sqrt3$. [3] (b) Find the exact area of the triangle. [2] (c) Find the perpendicular distance from $A$ to $BC$. [2]
tips: Use $\cos120^{\circ}=-\frac12$ and $\sin120^{\circ}=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$.

subtopic: Cosine rule to find an obtuse angle
statement: Triangle $PQR$ has sides $PQ=3$ cm, $QR=5$ cm and $PR=7$ cm. (a) Use the cosine rule to find the exact value of $\cos\angle PQR$, and hence the size of the angle $PQR$. [3] (b) Find the exact area of triangle $PQR$. [2] (c) Find the exact length of the perpendicular from $P$ to the line $QR$ (the height of the triangle with base $QR$). [2]
tips: The largest angle is opposite the longest side; a cosine of $-\tfrac12$ corresponds to $120^\circ$.

subtopic: Arc length, sector and segment
statement: A circle has centre $O$ and radius $8$ cm. Chord $AB$ subtends an angle of $1.2$ radians at $O$. (a) Find the length of the minor arc $AB$ and the area of the minor sector $OAB$. [2] (b) Find the area of the segment bounded by the chord $AB$ and the minor arc $AB$, correct to three significant figures. [3] (c) Find the perimeter of this segment, correct to three significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) Arc length $=8\times1.2=9.6$ cm [A1] Sector area $=\tfrac12(8)^2(1.2)=38.4\ \text{cm}^2$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Triangle $OAB$ has area $\tfrac12(8)^2\sin1.2$ [M1] $=29.8$ [A1] Segment area $=38.4-29.8=8.57\ \text{cm}^2$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Chord $AB=2(8)\sin0.6$ or $\sqrt{8^2+8^2-2(8)(8)\cos1.2}$ [M1] $=9.03$ [A1] Perimeter $=9.6+9.03=18.6\ \text{cm}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Switch your calculator to radian mode for $\sin1.2$. A segment is a sector minus a triangle, and its perimeter is the arc plus the chord.

subtopic: Width of a river by triangulation
statement: To find the width of a river, a surveyor marks two points $A$ and $B$ on one bank, $80$ m apart. A tree $T$ is on the opposite bank. The angles are $\angle TAB=52^\circ$ and $\angle TBA=71^\circ$. (a) Find angle $ATB$. [1] (b) Find the distance $AT$. [3] (c) Find the shortest distance from the tree to the line $AB$, which is the width of the river. [3]
markscheme: (a) $180-52-71=57^\circ$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\dfrac{AT}{\sin71^\circ}=\dfrac{80}{\sin57^\circ}$ [M1][A1]; $AT=90.19$ m [A1] [3 marks] (c) Width $=AT\sin52^\circ$ [M1][A1]; $=71.07$ m [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The shortest distance from a point to a line is the perpendicular distance; use the sine of the angle at $A$ in the right-angled triangle.

subtopic: Sine and cosine rule with exact values
statement: In triangle $ABC$, $AB=6$ cm, angle $A=45^\circ$ and angle $B=60^\circ$. (a) Find angle $C$. [1] (b) Use the sine rule to show that $BC=\dfrac{6\sin45^\circ}{\sin75^\circ}$, and find the exact value of $BC$ given that $\sin75^\circ=\dfrac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}{4}$. [3] (c) Find the exact area of triangle $ABC$ using $\dfrac12\,AB\cdot BC\sin B$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $C=180-45-60=75^\circ$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\dfrac{BC}{\sin45^\circ}=\dfrac{6}{\sin75^\circ}$ [M1][A1]; $BC=\dfrac{6\cdot\frac{\sqrt2}{2}}{\frac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}{4}}=\dfrac{12\sqrt2}{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}=\dfrac{12\sqrt2(\sqrt6-\sqrt2)}{4}=3\sqrt{12}-3\cdot2=6\sqrt3-6$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Area $=\dfrac12(6)(6\sqrt3-6)\sin60^\circ$ [M1]; $=3(6\sqrt3-6)\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ [A1]; $=27-9\sqrt3$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: When angles such as $75^\circ$ appear, the question will supply the sine value; rationalize denominators at the end.

subtopic: Surveying the width of a river with the sine rule
statement: A surveyor wants to find the width of a river. She marks two points $A$ and $B$, $80$ m apart on one bank, and a tree $C$ on the opposite bank. She measures angle $CAB=62^\circ$ and angle $CBA=71^\circ$. (a) Find angle $ACB$. [1] (b) Find the distance $AC$, correct to three significant figures. [3] (c) Find the width of the river, which is the shortest distance from $C$ to the line $AB$, correct to three significant figures. [2] (d) Find the distance along the bank from $A$ to the point opposite $C$, correct to three significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) Angle $ACB=180^\circ-62^\circ-71^\circ=47^\circ$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\dfrac{AC}{\sin71^\circ}=\dfrac{80}{\sin47^\circ}$ [M1] [A1] $AC=103\ \text{m}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Width $=AC\sin62^\circ$ [M1] $=91.3\ \text{m}$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) Distance $=AC\cos62^\circ$ [M1] $=48.6\ \text{m}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Label the triangle and match each side with its opposite angle before using the sine rule. The shortest distance to a line is perpendicular, so the width is a right-angled triangle calculation using the unrounded value of $AC$.

subtopic: Triangle with an angle of 120 degrees
statement: In triangle $ABC$, $AB=3$ cm, $AC=5$ cm and $BC=7$ cm. (a) Use the cosine rule to find angle $BAC$. [3] (b) Find the exact area of the triangle. [2] (c) Find the exact shortest distance from $A$ to the line $BC$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\cos A=\dfrac{3^{2}+5^{2}-7^{2}}{2\times3\times5}$ [M1]; $=-\dfrac12$ [A1]; $A=120^{\circ}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\dfrac12\times3\times5\times\sin120^{\circ}$ [M1]; $\dfrac{15\sqrt3}{4}$ cm$^{2}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) area $=\dfrac12\times7\times h$ [M1]; $h=\dfrac{15\sqrt3}{14}$ cm [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Area equals half base times height, so equate the two expressions for the area to find the perpendicular height.

subtopic: Height of a tower from two angles of elevation
statement: A vertical tower $TB$ stands on level ground, with $B$ at the base. From a point $P$ on the ground, the angle of elevation of the top $T$ is $25^{\circ}$. From a point $Q$, $40$ m closer to the tower on the same straight line through $B$, the angle of elevation of $T$ is $38^{\circ}$. (a) Write expressions for $PB$ and $QB$ in terms of the height $h$ of the tower. [2] (b) Find $h$, correct to 3 significant figures. [3] (c) Find the distance $PB$, correct to 3 significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) $PB=\dfrac{h}{\tan25^{\circ}}$ [A1]; $QB=\dfrac{h}{\tan38^{\circ}}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $PB-QB=40$ [M1]; $h\left(\dfrac{1}{\tan25^{\circ}}-\dfrac{1}{\tan38^{\circ}}\right)=40$ [A1]; $h=46.3$ m [A1] [3 marks] (c) $PB=\dfrac{46.27}{\tan25^{\circ}}$ [M1]; $99.2$ m [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Both distances to the base involve the same height, and their difference is $40$ m.

subtopic: Bearings and a right-angled triangle with exact values
statement: A hiker walks $4$ km from $A$ to $B$ on a bearing of $090^\circ$, then $4\sqrt3$ km from $B$ to $C$ on a bearing of $000^\circ$. (a) Find the exact distance $AC$. [2] (b) Find the bearing of $C$ from $A$. [3] (c) Find the bearing of $A$ from $C$. [1] (d) The hiker walks directly from $C$ back to $A$ at $4$ km/h. Find the time taken. [1]
markscheme: (a) $AC^2=4^2+(4\sqrt3)^2=16+48=64$ [M1] so $AC=8$ km [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\tan\angle CAB=\dfrac{4\sqrt3}{4}=\sqrt3$ [M1] so the angle between $AC$ and east is $60^\circ$ [A1]; bearing $=090^\circ-60^\circ=030^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $030^\circ+180^\circ=210^\circ$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) $\dfrac84=2$ hours [A1] [1 mark]
tips: A bearing is measured clockwise from north; the bearing of $A$ from $C$ is the back-bearing, differing by $180^\circ$.

subtopic: Roof rafters and pitch
statement: A symmetrical roof has a horizontal span of $9.6$ m and each side slopes at $32^{\circ}$ to the horizontal. The roof is $12$ m long. Rafters run along each sloping side from the eave to the ridge. (a) Find the length of one rafter, to three significant figures. [3] (b) Find the height of the ridge above the eaves, to three significant figures. [2] (c) Find the total area of the two sloping rectangular faces, to three significant figures. [2]
tips: Use the right-angled triangle formed by half the span, the height and the rafter.

subtopic: Ships leaving a port: cosine rule and bearing
statement: Two ships leave a port $P$ at the same time. Ship $A$ sails on a bearing of $040^{\circ}$ at $15$ km h$^{-1}$ and ship $B$ sails on a bearing of $100^{\circ}$ at $12$ km h$^{-1}$. Both sail in straight lines for $3$ hours. (a) Find the distance $AB$ between the ships after $3$ hours, correct to 3 significant figures. [4] (b) Find the size of angle $PAB$, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (c) Find the bearing of ship $B$ from ship $A$, correct to the nearest degree. [2]
markscheme: (a) $PA=45$ and $PB=36$ [A1]; angle $APB=60^{\circ}$ [A1]; $AB^{2}=45^{2}+36^{2}-2(45)(36)\cos60^{\circ}$ [M1]; $AB=41.2$ km [A1] [4 marks] (b) $\dfrac{\sin PAB}{36}=\dfrac{\sin60^{\circ}}{41.243}$ [M1]; $PAB=49.1^{\circ}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) bearing of $P$ from $A$ is $220^{\circ}$ [A1]; bearing of $B$ from $A$ is $220-49.1=171^{\circ}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Draw a diagram with north lines at $P$ and $A$. Angle $APB$ is the difference of the two bearings from $P$.

subtopic: Angles and canvas area of a pyramid tent
statement: A tent is a right pyramid with a horizontal square base of side $6$ m and a vertex $V$ directly above the centre of the base at a height of $4$ m. (a) Find the length of a sloping edge of the tent, correct to three significant figures. [3] (b) Find the angle between a sloping edge and the base, correct to the nearest tenth of a degree. [2] (c) Find the angle between a triangular face and the base, correct to the nearest tenth of a degree. [2] (d) Find the total area of canvas needed for the four triangular faces. [2]
markscheme: (a) Half the base diagonal $=\dfrac{\sqrt{6^2+6^2}}{2}=3\sqrt2$ m [M1] edge $=\sqrt{(3\sqrt2)^2+4^2}$ [M1] $=\sqrt{34}=5.83\ \text{m}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\tan\alpha=\dfrac{4}{3\sqrt2}$ [M1] $\alpha=43.3^\circ$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) The midpoint of a base edge is $3$ m from the centre, so $\tan\beta=\dfrac43$ [M1] $\beta=53.1^\circ$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) Slant height $=\sqrt{3^2+4^2}=5$ m, so area $=4\times\tfrac12(6)(5)$ [M1] $=60\ \text{m}^2$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Pick the right right-angled triangle: edge-to-base uses half the diagonal of the base, but face-to-base uses the perpendicular from the centre to a base edge. Sketching each triangle separately avoids mixing them up.

subtopic: Radius and angle from arc length and sector area
statement: A curved window is in the shape of a sector of a circle. The arc length of the sector is $4\pi$ cm and its area is $12\pi\ \text{cm}^2$. (a) Find the radius of the circle. [3] (b) Find the angle of the sector in radians. [2] (c) Write your answer to part (b) in degrees. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\tfrac12r^2\theta=12\pi$ and $r\theta=4\pi$ [M1] Hence $\tfrac12r(4\pi)=12\pi$ [M1] $r=6$ cm [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\theta=\dfrac{4\pi}{6}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ rad [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\times\dfrac{180}{\pi}=120^\circ$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Sector area can be written as $\tfrac12 r s$ where $s$ is the arc length, which is useful when you know $s$ but not $\theta$. Radian measure is the ratio of arc length to radius.

subtopic: Angles of elevation from two points
statement: A vertical tower $TP$ stands on level ground with $T$ the top and $P$ the foot. From a point $A$ on the ground the angle of elevation of $T$ is $30^\circ$. Walking $40$ m directly toward the tower to a point $B$, the angle of elevation of $T$ is $60^\circ$. Let the height of the tower be $h$ m. (a) Show that $PA=h\sqrt3$ and $PB=\dfrac{h}{\sqrt3}$. [2] (b) Write down an equation for $h$ using $AB=40$ and hence find the exact value of $h$. [3] (c) Find the exact distance $PB$. [1] (d) Find the exact distance $TB$ from $B$ to the top of the tower. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\tan30^\circ=\dfrac h{PA}$ so $PA=\dfrac{h}{1/\sqrt3}=h\sqrt3$ [A1]; $\tan60^\circ=\dfrac h{PB}=\sqrt3$ so $PB=\dfrac{h}{\sqrt3}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $PA-PB=40$: $h\sqrt3-\dfrac h{\sqrt3}=40$ [M1]; $h\left(\dfrac{3-1}{\sqrt3}\right)=40$ [A1]; $h=20\sqrt3$ m [A1] [3 marks] (c) $PB=\dfrac{20\sqrt3}{\sqrt3}=20$ m [A1] [1 mark] (d) $TB^2=20^2+(20\sqrt3)^2=400+1200=1600$ [M1] so $TB=40$ m [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Draw two right-angled triangles sharing the vertical side; the two ground distances differ by the distance walked.

subtopic: Area of a triangle and the cosine rule with unknown angle
statement: In triangle $ABC$, $AB=8$, $AC=5$ and angle $A=60^\circ$. (a) Find the exact length of $BC$. [3] (b) Find the exact area of the triangle. [2] (c) Find the exact value of $\sin B$, and explain why angle $B$ must be acute. [3]
markscheme: (a) $BC^2=64+25-2(8)(5)\cos60^\circ$ [M1] $=89-40=49$ [A1]; $BC=7$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\dfrac12(8)(5)\sin60^\circ$ [M1] $=10\sqrt3$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Sine rule: $\dfrac{\sin B}{5}=\dfrac{\sin60^\circ}{7}$ [M1]; $\sin B=\dfrac{5\sqrt3}{14}$ [A1]; $B$ is opposite the shortest side $AC=5$, so it is the smallest angle and therefore acute [R1] [3 marks]
tips: The cosine rule finds the third side when two sides and the included angle are known; the sine rule then gives the remaining angles.

subtopic: Cone formed from a sector of paper
statement: A paper cone is made by cutting a sector from a circular sheet of radius $20$ cm. The sector has centre $O$ and angle $1.4\pi$ radians. The straight edges of the sector are joined together, without overlap, to make a cone with slant height $20$ cm. (a) Find the arc length of the sector, correct to three significant figures. [2] (b) Hence show that the base radius of the cone is $14$ cm. [2] (c) Find the vertical height of the cone, correct to three significant figures. [2] (d) Find the volume of the cone, correct to three significant figures. [2] (e) Find the curved surface area of the cone, correct to three significant figures. [1]
markscheme: (a) $s=20\times1.4\pi$ [M1] $=28\pi=88.0\ \text{cm}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) The arc becomes the circumference of the base: $2\pi r=28\pi$ [M1] $r=14$ cm [AG] [2 marks] (c) $h=\sqrt{20^2-14^2}$ [M1] $=\sqrt{204}=14.3\ \text{cm}$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $V=\tfrac13\pi(14)^2(14.283)$ [M1] $=2930\ \text{cm}^3$ [A1] [2 marks] (e) The curved surface has the area of the sector: $\tfrac12(20)^2(1.4\pi)=280\pi=880\ \text{cm}^2$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: When a sector is rolled into a cone, its arc length becomes the circumference of the base and its radius becomes the slant height. The curved surface area equals the area of the sector.

subtopic: Two ships leaving port, distance and bearing
statement: Two ships leave a port $P$ at the same time. Ship $A$ sails at $18$ km/h on a bearing of $040^\circ$ and ship $B$ sails at $24$ km/h on a bearing of $125^\circ$. Both ships keep a constant speed and direction. After $2.5$ hours the ships are at $A$ and $B$ respectively. (a) Show that angle $APB=85^\circ$. [1] (b) Find the distance $AB$, correct to three significant figures. [3] (c) Find the bearing of $B$ from $A$, correct to the nearest degree. [4] (d) Find the time, in hours, after leaving port when the ships are first $100$ km apart, correct to three significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) $125^\circ-40^\circ=85^\circ$ [AG] [1 mark] (b) $PA=18\times2.5=45$ km and $PB=24\times2.5=60$ km; $AB^2=45^2+60^2-2(45)(60)\cos85^\circ$ [M1] [A1] $AB=71.8\ \text{km}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\dfrac{\sin\angle PAB}{60}=\dfrac{\sin85^\circ}{71.79}$ [M1] $\angle PAB=56.4^\circ$ [A1] The bearing of $P$ from $A$ is $040^\circ+180^\circ=220^\circ$ [M1] Bearing of $B$ from $A$ $=220^\circ-56.4^\circ=164^\circ$ [A1] [4 marks] (d) The distance between the ships is proportional to time, so $AB=\dfrac{71.79}{2.5}t$ [M1] $t=\dfrac{100\times2.5}{71.79}=3.48$ hours [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Compute both distances from speed times time before applying the cosine rule. In part (c) draw a north line at $A$ and decide whether to subtract or add the interior angle to $220^\circ$ by checking where $B$ lies relative to the line $AP$.

subtopic: Two triangles from a given area and two sides
statement: A triangular sail has two sides of length $8$ m and $6$ m, with an angle $\theta$ between them, and its area is $12\sqrt3\ \text{m}^2$. (a) Find the two possible values of $\theta$ for which $0^\circ<\theta<180^\circ$. [3] (b) For each value of $\theta$, find the exact length of the third side of the sail. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\tfrac12(8)(6)\sin\theta=12\sqrt3$ [M1] $\sin\theta=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ [A1] $\theta=60^\circ$ or $120^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\theta=60^\circ$: $c^2=64+36-2(8)(6)\cos60^\circ=52$ so $c=2\sqrt{13}\ \text{m}$ [M1] [A1] $\theta=120^\circ$: $c^2=64+36+48=148$ so $c=2\sqrt{37}\ \text{m}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Because $\sin\theta=\sin(180^\circ-\theta)$, an area condition gives an acute and an obtuse possibility. Remember $\cos120^\circ=-\tfrac12$, so the cosine rule adds the product term.

subtopic: Length of a median using two cosine rules
statement: In triangle $ABC$, $AB=9$ cm, $AC=14$ cm and angle $BAC=52^\circ$. The point $D$ is the midpoint of $[BC]$. (a) Find the length of $BC$, correct to three significant figures. [3] (b) Find the size of angle $ABC$, correct to the nearest tenth of a degree. [3] (c) Find the length of $AD$, correct to three significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) $BC^2=9^2+14^2-2(9)(14)\cos52^\circ$ [M1] [A1] $BC=11.0\ \text{cm}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\cos\angle ABC=\dfrac{9^2+BC^2-14^2}{2(9)(BC)}$ [M1] [A1] $\angle ABC=88.0^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $BD=\dfrac{BC}{2}=5.519\ \text{cm}$ [A1] $AD^2=9^2+BD^2-2(9)(BD)\cos\angle ABC$ [M1] $AD=10.4\ \text{cm}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The midpoint splits $BC$ in half, so you can apply the cosine rule in the smaller triangle $ABD$ once you know angle $B$. Store $BC$ and angle $B$ unrounded in your GDC.

subtopic: Height of a mast supported from opposite sides
statement: A vertical mast $FT$ stands on level ground with its foot $F$ between two points $A$ and $B$ on the ground, where $A$, $F$ and $B$ lie on a straight line and $AB=90$ m. The angle of elevation of the top $T$ of the mast from $A$ is $38^\circ$ and from $B$ is $52^\circ$. Let the height of the mast be $h$ metres. (a) Show that $h\left(\dfrac{1}{\tan38^\circ}+\dfrac{1}{\tan52^\circ}\right)=90$. [2] (b) Find $h$, correct to three significant figures. [2] (c) Find the distance $AF$, correct to three significant figures. [1] (d) A support cable runs from $A$ to $T$. Find its length, correct to three significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) $AF=\dfrac{h}{\tan38^\circ}$ and $BF=\dfrac{h}{\tan52^\circ}$ [M1] $AF+BF=90$ gives the required equation [AG] [2 marks] (b) $h=\dfrac{90}{\frac{1}{\tan38^\circ}+\frac{1}{\tan52^\circ}}$ [M1] $=43.7\ \text{m}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $AF=\dfrac{43.663}{\tan38^\circ}=55.9\ \text{m}$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) $AT=\dfrac{h}{\sin38^\circ}$ [M1] $=70.9\ \text{m}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: When the unknown height is shared by two right-angled triangles, write both horizontal distances in terms of $h$ and use the fact that they add to the known total. Use the unrounded height in parts (c) and (d).

subtopic: Area of a quadrilateral field and a cyclic test
statement: A field is in the shape of a quadrilateral $ABCD$ with $AB=9$ m, $BC=7$ m, $CD=8$ m and $DA=10$ m. Angle $ABC=70^\circ$. (a) Find the length of the diagonal $AC$, correct to three significant figures. [3] (b) Find angle $ADC$, correct to the nearest tenth of a degree. [3] (c) Find the area of the field, correct to three significant figures. [4] (d) A surveyor claims that $ABCD$ is a cyclic quadrilateral. Use your answers to justify that she is incorrect. [2]
markscheme: (a) $AC^2=9^2+7^2-2(9)(7)\cos70^\circ$ [M1] [A1] $AC=9.32\ \text{m}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\cos D=\dfrac{10^2+8^2-AC^2}{2(10)(8)}$ [M1] [A1] $\angle ADC=61.2^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Area of $ABC=\tfrac12(9)(7)\sin70^\circ=29.60\ \text{m}^2$ [M1] [A1] Area of $ACD=\tfrac12(10)(8)\sin61.2^\circ=35.05\ \text{m}^2$ [M1] Total area $=64.7\ \text{m}^2$ [A1] [4 marks] (d) In a cyclic quadrilateral opposite angles sum to $180^\circ$ [R1] but $70^\circ+61.2^\circ=131.2^\circ\neq180^\circ$, so it is not cyclic [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Split a quadrilateral into two triangles with a diagonal, and keep the diagonal unrounded for later parts. For the cyclic test use a necessary condition: if opposite angles do not sum to $180^\circ$ the quadrilateral cannot be cyclic.

subtopic: Space diagonal and angle with the base of a tall crate
statement: A tall cuboid-shaped display case has a rectangular base measuring $4$ m by $3$ m and a height of $12$ m. (a) Find the length of the longest diagonal of the case, from a bottom corner to the opposite top corner. [2] (b) Find $\cos\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between this diagonal and the base. [2] (c) Hence find the exact values of $\sin\theta$ and $\tan\theta$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\sqrt{4^2+3^2+12^2}=\sqrt{169}$ [M1] $=13$ m [A1] [2 marks] (b) The diagonal of the base is $\sqrt{4^2+3^2}=5$ m, so $\cos\theta=\dfrac{5}{13}$ [M1] [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\sin\theta=\sqrt{1-\dfrac{25}{169}}=\dfrac{12}{13}$ [A1] $\tan\theta=\dfrac{12/13}{5/13}=\dfrac{12}{5}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Angles in 3D are found in a right-angled triangle: identify the diagonal of the base first. Since $\theta$ is acute, take the positive root when using $\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1$.

subtopic: Cosine rule and exact area of a garden bed
statement: A triangular garden bed $ABC$ has $AB=8$ m, $AC=5$ m and angle $BAC=60^\circ$. (a) Find the length of $BC$. [3] (b) Find the exact area of the garden bed. [2]
tips: Learn the exact values of sine and cosine for $30^\circ$, $45^\circ$ and $60^\circ$; they make non-calculator trigonometry quick. Write the cosine rule with the given angle between the two known sides.

subtopic: Two boats leaving the same port
statement: Boat $A$ leaves a port $O$ on a bearing of $040^{\circ}$ at $18$ km/h. Boat $B$ leaves $O$ at the same time on a bearing of $110^{\circ}$ at $24$ km/h. Both travel in straight lines at constant speed. (a) Find the distance $AB$ between the boats after $2.5$ hours, to three significant figures. [4] (b) Find the bearing of $B$ from $A$, to the nearest degree. [4]
tips: Draw a sketch with north lines at $O$ and $A$; the bearing of $O$ from $A$ is $40^{\circ}+180^{\circ}$.

subtopic: Arc and sector swept by a clock hand
statement: The minute hand of a tower clock has length $1.2$ m. (a) Find the angle, in radians, through which the minute hand turns in $20$ minutes. [2] (b) Find the exact distance travelled by the tip of the minute hand in $20$ minutes. [1] (c) Find the exact area swept out by the minute hand in $20$ minutes. [2]
markscheme: (a) $20$ minutes is $\dfrac13$ of a revolution [M1] angle $=\dfrac13\times2\pi=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ rad [A1] [2 marks] (b) $s=1.2\times\dfrac{2\pi}{3}=0.8\pi$ m [A1] [1 mark] (c) $A=\tfrac12(1.2)^2\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ [M1] $=0.48\pi\ \text{m}^2$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A full turn is $2\pi$ radians, so work with fractions of a revolution. With radians, the arc formula $r\theta$ and area formula $\tfrac12r^2\theta$ need no conversion.

subtopic: Ambiguous case for a drone within radar range
statement: A radar station is at a point $B$. A drone flies in a straight line away from a point $A$, which is $500$ m from $B$. The line of flight makes an angle of $35^\circ$ with $AB$. The radar can detect the drone only while it is within $340$ m of $B$. Let $D$ be a point on the flight path at which the drone is exactly $340$ m from $B$. (a) Find the two possible sizes of angle $ADB$, correct to the nearest tenth of a degree. [3] (b) Find the two possible distances $AD$, correct to the nearest metre. [3] (c) Hence find the distance the drone travels while it is detectable. [2] (d) Find the smallest distance from $B$ to the flight path. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{\sin\angle ADB}{500}=\dfrac{\sin35^\circ}{340}$ [M1] $\angle ADB=57.5^\circ$ [A1] or $180^\circ-57.5^\circ=122.5^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) The angle at $B$ is $180^\circ-35^\circ-\angle ADB$, giving $22.5^\circ$ and $87.5^\circ$ [M1] $\dfrac{AD}{\sin\angle ABD}=\dfrac{340}{\sin35^\circ}$ so $AD=227\ \text{m}$ [A1] and $AD=592\ \text{m}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Distance detectable $=592-227$ [M1] $=365\ \text{m}$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) Perpendicular distance $=500\sin35^\circ=287\ \text{m}$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: When two sides and a non-included angle are given, the sine rule gives an acute and an obtuse angle; check that each leaves a positive third angle. The drone is detectable between the two positions where it is exactly $340$ m away, so subtract the two lengths from $A$.

subtopic: Arc, sector and segment in radians
statement: A sector $OAB$ of a circle with centre $O$ and radius $10$ cm has angle $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ radians. (a) Find the exact arc length $AB$ and the exact area of the sector. [3] (b) Show that triangle $OAB$ is equilateral and find the exact length of the chord $AB$. [2] (c) Find the exact area of the segment bounded by the chord $AB$ and the arc $AB$. [3]
markscheme: (a) arc $=10\times\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\dfrac{10\pi}{3}$ cm [A1]; area $=\dfrac12(10)^{2}\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ [M1]; $\dfrac{50\pi}{3}$ cm$^{2}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $OA=OB$ and angle $AOB=60^{\circ}$ [R1]; $AB=10$ cm [A1] [2 marks] (c) triangle area $=\dfrac12(10)(10)\sin\dfrac\pi3=25\sqrt3$ [M1][A1]; segment $=\dfrac{50\pi}{3}-25\sqrt3$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Segment area $=$ sector area $-$ area of triangle $OAB$.
