subtopic: Sector watered by a rotating lawn sprinkler
statement: A lawn sprinkler at the centre $O$ of a sector waters a sector of a circle of radius $8.5$ m. The angle of the sector is $140^\circ$. (a) Write $140^\circ$ in radians, correct to four significant figures. [1] (b) Find the area of the lawn watered, correct to three significant figures. [2] (c) Find the perimeter of the watered region, correct to three significant figures. [2] (d) The sprinkler is adjusted so that it waters a sector of the same radius with area $60\ \text{m}^2$. Find the new angle of the sector in degrees, correct to the nearest degree. [3]
tips: Remember that the perimeter of a sector includes both straight radii as well as the arc. Rearranging $A=\tfrac12r^2\theta$ for $\theta$ gives radians, so convert at the end if degrees are requested.

subtopic: Bearings and the cosine rule
statement: A ship leaves port $P$ and sails $12$ km on a bearing of $065^\circ$ to a buoy $B$. It then sails $9$ km on a bearing of $150^\circ$ to a point $Q$. (a) Show that angle $PBQ=95^\circ$. [2] (b) Find the distance $PQ$, correct to three significant figures. [3] (c) Find the bearing of $P$ from $Q$, correct to the nearest degree. [3]
markscheme: (a) The bearing of $P$ from $B$ is $065^\circ+180^\circ=245^\circ$ [M1] Angle $PBQ=245^\circ-150^\circ=95^\circ$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $PQ^2=12^2+9^2-2(12)(9)\cos95^\circ$ [M1] [A1] $PQ=15.6\ \text{km}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\dfrac{\sin\angle BQP}{12}=\dfrac{\sin95^\circ}{15.61}$ so $\angle BQP=49.9^\circ$ [M1] The bearing of $B$ from $Q$ is $150^\circ+180^\circ=330^\circ$ [A1] The bearing of $P$ from $Q$ is $330^\circ-49.9^\circ=280^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Draw a north line at each point and mark the interior angle using alternate angles: bearings differing by $180^\circ$ describe the return direction. Keep the unrounded value of $PQ$ for the sine rule in part (c).

subtopic: Sector and segment of a circle
statement: A sector $OAB$ of a circle with center $O$ and radius $9$ cm has angle $AOB=1.4$ radians. (a) Find the length of arc $AB$ and the area of the sector. [3] (b) Find the area of triangle $OAB$ and hence the area of the segment cut off by chord $AB$, correct to 3 significant figures. [3] (c) Find the perimeter of the segment, correct to 3 significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) arc $=9\times1.4=12.6$ cm [A1]; area $=\dfrac12\times81\times1.4$ [M1]; $56.7$ cm$^{2}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\dfrac12\times81\sin1.4=39.9$ cm$^{2}$ [A1]; segment $=56.7-39.9$ [M1]; $16.8$ cm$^{2}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) chord $AB=2\times9\sin0.7=11.6$ cm [M1]; perimeter $=12.6+11.6=24.2$ cm [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Calculators must be in radian mode. Segment area is sector area minus triangle area.

subtopic: The ambiguous case of the sine rule
statement: In triangle $ABC$, $a=9$ cm, $b=12$ cm and angle $A=40^\circ$ (the angle opposite side $a$). (a) Show that there are two possible triangles. [3] (b) Find the possible lengths of the third side $c$. [3] (c) Find the area of each triangle. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{\sin B}{12}=\dfrac{\sin40^\circ}{9}$ [M1]; $\sin B=0.8571$ so $B=59.0^\circ$ or $B=121.0^\circ$ [A1]; both give $A+B<180^\circ$ so both triangles exist [R1] [3 marks] (b) $c=\dfrac{9\sin C}{\sin40^\circ}$ [M1]; $C=81.0^\circ$ gives $c=13.83$ [A1]; $C=19.0^\circ$ gives $c=4.56$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\dfrac12ab\sin C$: $53.34$ and $17.57$ [A1][A1] [2 marks]
tips: The ambiguous case occurs when the given angle is opposite the shorter of the two given sides.

subtopic: Height of a cliff from two angles of elevation
statement: From a point $A$ at sea level, the angle of elevation of the top $T$ of a vertical cliff is $24^\circ$. A boat sails $150$ m directly towards the cliff to a point $B$, where the angle of elevation of $T$ is $38^\circ$. (a) Find angle $ATB$. [2] (b) Find the distance $BT$, correct to three significant figures. [3] (c) Find the height of the cliff, correct to three significant figures. [2] (d) Find the horizontal distance from $B$ to the foot of the cliff, correct to three significant figures. [1]
markscheme: (a) The exterior angle at $B$ equals the sum of the interior angles at $A$ and $T$ [M1] $\angle ATB=38^\circ-24^\circ=14^\circ$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac{BT}{\sin24^\circ}=\dfrac{150}{\sin14^\circ}$ [M1] [A1] $BT=252\ \text{m}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Height $=BT\sin38^\circ$ [M1] $=155\ \text{m}$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $BT\cos38^\circ=199\ \text{m}$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Elevation problems with two observation points need the sine rule in a non-right-angled triangle first. The angle at the top comes from the exterior angle theorem, so state it.

subtopic: Cosine rule with exact values
statement: In triangle $PQR$, $PQ=5$, $PR=8$ and angle $QPR=60^{\circ}$. (a) Find $QR$. [3] (b) Find the exact area of the triangle. [2] (c) Use the sine rule to find the exact value of $\sin(\text{angle }PRQ)$. [2]
tips: The side $QR$ is opposite the $60^{\circ}$ angle; the side $PQ$ is opposite angle $R$.

subtopic: Exact distance and bearing after two legs
statement: A boat sails from a harbor $H$ on a bearing of $090^{\circ}$ for $8$ km and then on a bearing of $180^{\circ}$ for $8\sqrt3$ km, reaching point $B$. (a) Find the exact distance $HB$. [3] (b) Find the bearing of $B$ from $H$. [3] (c) Find the bearing of $H$ from $B$. [1]
markscheme: (a) The two legs are perpendicular [R1]; $HB^{2}=64+192=256$ [M1]; $HB=16$ km [A1] [3 marks] (b) angle at $H$ below east: $\tan\alpha=\dfrac{8\sqrt3}{8}=\sqrt3$ so $\alpha=60^{\circ}$ [M1][A1]; bearing $=90^{\circ}+60^{\circ}=150^{\circ}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $150^{\circ}+180^{\circ}=330^{\circ}$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Bearings are measured clockwise from north; a back-bearing differs by $180^{\circ}$.

subtopic: Two ships leaving a harbor
statement: Two ships leave port $P$ at the same time. Ship $A$ sails at $20$ km/h on a bearing of $060^\circ$; ship $B$ sails at $26$ km/h on a bearing of $140^\circ$. Both keep constant velocity. (a) Find the angle between the two directions of travel. [1] (b) Find the distance between the ships after 3 hours. [3] (c) Find the angle $PAB$ and hence the bearing of $B$ from $A$, to the nearest degree. [4]
markscheme: (a) $140^\circ-60^\circ=80^\circ$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $AB^2=60^2+78^2-2(60)(78)\cos80^\circ$ [M1][A1]; $AB=89.8$ km [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\dfrac{\sin PAB}{78}=\dfrac{\sin80^\circ}{89.77}$ [M1]; $PAB=58.8^\circ$ [A1]; bearing of $P$ from $A$ is $240^\circ$ [M1]; bearing of $B$ from $A$ $=181^\circ$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Draw the triangle $PAB$; the bearing of $B$ from $A$ needs the back-bearing of $P$ from $A$.

subtopic: Height of a tower using two angles of elevation
statement: Points $A$ and $B$ lie on level ground in a straight line with the base of a vertical tower, with $B$ between $A$ and the tower. $AB=50$ m. The angles of elevation of the top $T$ of the tower from $A$ and from $B$ are $25^\circ$ and $40^\circ$ respectively. (a) Find the size of angle $ATB$. [2] (b) Find the distance $AT$, correct to three significant figures. [3] (c) Find the height of the tower, correct to three significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) Angle $ABT=180^\circ-40^\circ=140^\circ$ [M1] Angle $ATB=180^\circ-25^\circ-140^\circ=15^\circ$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac{AT}{\sin140^\circ}=\dfrac{50}{\sin15^\circ}$ [M1] [A1] $AT=124\ \text{m}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Height $=AT\sin25^\circ$ [M1] $=52.5\ \text{m}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: When the two observation points are in line with the tower, the exterior angle at $B$ gives an oblique triangle: use the sine rule there, then a right-angled triangle for the height. Check your answer with $h=50/(\cot25^\circ-\cot40^\circ)$.

subtopic: Maximum area of a sector with fixed perimeter
statement: A piece of wire of length $40$ cm is bent to form the boundary of a sector of a circle with radius $r$ cm and angle $\theta$ radians, where $0<\theta<2\pi$. (a) Show that $\theta=\dfrac{40-2r}{r}$. [2] (b) Hence show that the area $A$ of the sector is given by $A=20r-r^2$. [2] (c) Find the value of $r$ for which $A$ is a maximum, and find this maximum area. [3] (d) Find the value of $\theta$ that gives the maximum area. [1] (e) Find the two values of $r$ for which the area of the sector is $75\ \text{cm}^2$, and show that both give a valid sector. [3]
markscheme: (a) Perimeter $=2r+r\theta=40$ [M1] $\theta=\dfrac{40-2r}{r}$ [AG] [2 marks] (b) $A=\tfrac12r^2\theta=\tfrac12r^2\left(\dfrac{40-2r}{r}\right)$ [M1] $=20r-r^2$ [AG] [2 marks] (c) $\dfrac{dA}{dr}=20-2r=0$ [M1] $r=10$ cm [A1] $A_{\max}=20(10)-10^2=100\ \text{cm}^2$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $\theta=\dfrac{40-20}{10}=2$ rad [A1] [1 mark] (e) $20r-r^2=75$ so $r^2-20r+75=0$ [M1] $r=5$ or $r=15$ [A1] For $r=5$: $\theta=6$ rad and for $r=15$: $\theta=\dfrac{10}{15}=0.667$ rad; both lie between $0$ and $2\pi$ so both are valid [R1] [3 marks]
tips: Eliminate $\theta$ using the perimeter condition before maximizing, so that the area is a function of $r$ alone. A quadratic area function has a symmetric maximum, so two different radii can give the same area.

subtopic: Sector and segment of a glass panel in radians
statement: A decorative glass panel is a sector $OAB$ of a circle with centre $O$ and radius $6$ dm. The angle $AOB$ is $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ radians. (a) Find the exact length of the arc $AB$. [2] (b) Find the exact area of the sector $OAB$. [2] (c) A segment is the region between the chord $AB$ and the arc $AB$. Show that the area of the segment is $6\pi-9\sqrt3\ \text{dm}^2$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $s=r\theta=6\times\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ [M1] $=2\pi$ dm [A1] [2 marks] (b) $A=\tfrac12r^2\theta=\tfrac12(36)\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ [M1] $=6\pi\ \text{dm}^2$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Area of triangle $OAB=\tfrac12(6)(6)\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ [M1] $=18\times\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}=9\sqrt3$ [A1] Segment area $=6\pi-9\sqrt3\ \text{dm}^2$ [AG] [3 marks]
tips: Segment area is always sector area minus triangle area. Keep $\pi$ and surds exact when the question says exact, and do not switch to decimals part way through.

subtopic: Triangle from two sides and the area
statement: In triangle $ABC$, $AB=7$ cm, $BC=10$ cm and the area of the triangle is $28$ cm$^{2}$. Angle $ABC$ is $\theta$. (a) Find $\sin\theta$. [2] (b) Find the two possible sizes of $\theta$ in degrees, correct to 1 decimal place. [2] (c) For each value of $\theta$, find the length of $AC$, correct to 3 significant figures. [4]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac12\times7\times10\sin\theta=28$ [M1]; $\sin\theta=0.8$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\theta=53.1^{\circ}$ [A1]; $\theta=180-53.1=126.9^{\circ}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $AC^{2}=49+100-140\cos\theta$ [M1]; for $\theta=53.1^{\circ}$, $\cos\theta=0.6$ and $AC^{2}=65$ [A1]; $AC=8.06$ cm [A1]; for $\theta=126.9^{\circ}$, $AC^{2}=233$ so $AC=15.3$ cm [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Two sides and the area give $\sin\theta$; both an acute and an obtuse angle have that sine.

subtopic: Exact sector, triangle and segment
statement: A sector $OAB$ of a circle with center $O$ and radius $6$ cm has angle $AOB=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$. (a) Find the exact length of arc $AB$ and the exact area of the sector. [3] (b) Find the exact area of triangle $OAB$. [2] (c) Hence write down the exact area of the segment cut off by chord $AB$. [1]
markscheme: (a) arc $=6\times\dfrac{2\pi}{3}=4\pi$ cm [A1]; area $=\dfrac12\times36\times\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ [M1]; $12\pi$ cm$^{2}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\dfrac12\times36\times\sin\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ [M1]; $9\sqrt3$ cm$^{2}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $12\pi-9\sqrt3$ cm$^{2}$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Use $\sin\frac{2\pi}{3}=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$ from the special triangle.

subtopic: Two triangles from given area and two sides
statement: Triangle $ABC$ has $AB=6$, $AC=10$ and area $15\sqrt3$, and angle $BAC=\theta$ is not known. (a) Find the two possible values of $\theta$ for $0^{\circ}<\theta<180^{\circ}$. [3] (b) Find the two possible exact values of $BC$. [4]
tips: Both an acute and an obtuse angle have the same sine.

subtopic: Ambiguous case of the sine rule
statement: In triangle $ABC$, $BC=9$ cm, $AC=12$ cm and angle $BAC=40^\circ$. (a) Find the two possible values of angle $ABC$, correct to the nearest tenth of a degree. [3] (b) Find the two possible values of $AB$, correct to three significant figures. [3] (c) Find the area of the larger of the two possible triangles, correct to three significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{\sin B}{12}=\dfrac{\sin40^\circ}{9}$ [M1] $B=59.0^\circ$ [A1] or $B=180^\circ-59.0^\circ=121.0^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) For $B=59.0^\circ$: $C=81.0^\circ$ and $AB=\dfrac{9\sin81.0^\circ}{\sin40^\circ}=13.8\ \text{cm}$ [M1] [A1] For $B=121.0^\circ$: $C=19.0^\circ$ and $AB=\dfrac{9\sin19.0^\circ}{\sin40^\circ}=4.56\ \text{cm}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Larger triangle has $AB=13.83$: area $=\tfrac12(12)(13.83)\sin40^\circ$ [M1] $=53.3\ \text{cm}^2$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: When you are given two sides and a non-included angle, the sine rule can give two angles; always check whether $180^\circ-\theta$ also fits. The two triangles are different, so compute each third side and area separately.

subtopic: Land plot split by a diagonal
statement: A four-sided plot of land $ABCD$ has $AB=45$ m, $BC=60$ m, $CD=50$ m and $DA=70$ m. Angle $ABC=80^\circ$. The vertices $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ are in order around the boundary and the plot is convex. (a) Find the length of the diagonal $AC$, correct to three significant figures. [3] (b) Find the size of angle $ADC$, correct to the nearest tenth of a degree. [3] (c) Find the total area of the plot, correct to three significant figures. [4]
tips: Split any quadrilateral along a diagonal into two triangles, then alternate cosine rule and area formula. Do not round the diagonal until the final answer.

subtopic: Radians turned by a rolling bicycle wheel
statement: A bicycle wheel has radius $0.35$ m and rolls along a straight road without slipping. (a) The bicycle travels $50$ m. Find the angle, in radians, through which the wheel turns, correct to three significant figures. [2] (b) Find the number of complete revolutions the wheel makes. [1] (c) The bicycle travels at a constant speed of $6$ m/s. Find the angular speed of the wheel in radians per second, correct to three significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) Distance $=r\theta$ so $\theta=\dfrac{50}{0.35}$ [M1] $=143\ \text{rad}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac{142.86}{2\pi}=22.74$ so $22$ complete revolutions [A1] [1 mark] (c) $\omega=\dfrac{6}{0.35}$ [M1] $=17.1\ \text{rad/s}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: When a wheel rolls without slipping, the distance travelled equals the arc length $r\theta$. Divide the total angle by $2\pi$ to count revolutions, and give only the complete ones when asked.

subtopic: Area of a quadrilateral using a diagonal
statement: A field $ABCD$ has $AB=7$ m, $BC=9$ m, $CD=8$ m, $DA=6$ m and the diagonal $AC=10$ m. (a) Find angle $ABC$. [3] (b) Find angle $ADC$. [3] (c) Find the area of the field. [3]
tips: Split the quadrilateral into two triangles along the diagonal; each angle needs the cosine rule.

subtopic: Exact bearings of a drone flight
statement: A drone flies from $P$ a distance of $12$ km on a bearing of $030^\circ$ to a point $Q$. It then flies $12$ km on a bearing of $150^\circ$ to a point $R$. (a) Show that angle $PQR=60^\circ$. [2] (b) Find the distance $PR$. [2] (c) Find the bearing of $R$ from $P$. [2]
markscheme: (a) The bearing of $P$ from $Q$ is $030^\circ+180^\circ=210^\circ$ [M1] Angle $PQR=210^\circ-150^\circ=60^\circ$ [AG] [2 marks] (b) $PR^2=12^2+12^2-2(12)(12)\cos60^\circ$ [M1] $=144$ so $PR=12$ km [A1] [2 marks] (c) Triangle $PQR$ is isosceles with apex angle $60^\circ$, so it is equilateral and angle $QPR=60^\circ$ [M1] The bearing of $R$ from $P$ is $030^\circ+60^\circ=090^\circ$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: To find the angle inside the triangle at a turning point, reverse the first bearing by adding or subtracting $180^\circ$. Check your final bearing against a quick sketch with a north line at each vertex.

subtopic: Triangle in three dimensions: angle and area
statement: The points $A(2, -1, 3)$, $B(4, 1, 3)$ and $C(4, -1, 5)$ are the vertices of a triangle. (a) Find $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}$. [2] (b) Find the size of angle $BAC$. [3] (c) Find the exact area of the triangle. [2] (d) Find the coordinates of the point $D$ such that $ABDC$ is a parallelogram. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; $\overrightarrow{AC}=\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 0 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot\overrightarrow{AC}=4$ [A1]; $\cos A=\dfrac{4}{\sqrt8\sqrt8}=\dfrac12$ [M1]; $A=60^{\circ}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\dfrac12\sqrt8\sqrt8\sin60^{\circ}$ [M1]; $2\sqrt3$ square units [A1] [2 marks] (d) $D=B+\overrightarrow{AC}=(6, 1, 5)$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Angle at $A$ uses the two vectors that start at $A$.

subtopic: Shortest distance between two skew lines
statement: This question finds the shortest distance between two skew lines $l_1:\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ and $l_2:\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 4 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}+\mu\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Show that the lines are not parallel and do not intersect. [3] (b) Find $\mathbf d_1\times\mathbf d_2$ and explain its geometric significance. [2] (c) Hence find the shortest distance between the lines using $\dfrac{|(\mathbf a_2-\mathbf a_1)\cdot\mathbf n|}{|\mathbf n|}$. [3] (d) Find the points $P_1$ on $l_1$ and $P_2$ on $l_2$ such that $P_1P_2$ is perpendicular to both lines, and verify that $|P_1P_2|=\sqrt3$. [5] (e) Find the Cartesian equation of the plane containing $l_1$ and parallel to $l_2$, and verify that the point $(3,4,1)$ of $l_2$ is at distance $\sqrt3$ from it. [3]
markscheme: (a) direction vectors are not scalar multiples [R1] first two components: $1+\lambda=3+2\mu$, $2\lambda=4+\mu$ give $\lambda=2$, $\mu=0$ [M1] third component: $2+2=4\ne1$, so no intersection [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\mathbf d_1\times\mathbf d_2=\begin{pmatrix} -3 \\ 3 \\ -3 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] it is perpendicular to both lines [R1] [2 marks] (c) $\mathbf a_2-\mathbf a_1=\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 4 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] with $\mathbf n=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$: $|2-4-1|=3$ [M1] distance $=\dfrac3{\sqrt3}=\sqrt3$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $\overrightarrow{P_1P_2}=\begin{pmatrix} 2+2\mu-\lambda \\ 4+\mu-2\lambda \\ -1-\mu-\lambda \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] perpendicular to $\mathbf d_1$: $3+\mu-2\lambda=0$ [M1][A1] perpendicular to $\mathbf d_2$: $3+2\mu-\lambda=0$ [A1] $\lambda=1$, $\mu=-1$ so $P_1(2,2,3)$, $P_2(1,3,2)$ and $|P_1P_2|=\sqrt{1+1+1}=\sqrt3$ [A1] [5 marks] (e) normal $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ through $(1,0,2)$: $x-y+z=3$ [M1][A1] distance of $(3,4,1)$: $\dfrac{|3-4+1-3|}{\sqrt3}=\sqrt3$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The common perpendicular is parallel to $\mathbf d_1\times\mathbf d_2$. Two methods (the formula and the perpendicularity conditions) should agree; the plane method is a third check.

subtopic: Boat course relative to a buoy with a keep-out zone
statement: A boat leaves a harbor at the origin and travels at a constant speed of $18$ km h$^{-1}$ on a bearing of $065^\circ$. The $x$ and $y$ directions are east and north. A marker buoy is at the point $B(20,12)$, with distances in kilometers. The boat is not allowed to come within $3$ km of the buoy. (a) Show that the velocity of the boat is $\begin{pmatrix} 16.3 \\ 7.61 \end{pmatrix}$ km h$^{-1}$, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (b) Find the bearing of the buoy from the harbor, to the nearest degree. [2] (c) Find the minimum distance between the boat and the buoy, and the time at which it occurs. Give both answers to 3 significant figures. [3] (d) Show that the boat breaks the keep-out rule, and find for how many minutes, to the nearest minute, it is within $3$ km of the buoy. [3]
markscheme: (a) $x$: $18\sin65^\circ=16.3$ [A1] $y$: $18\cos65^\circ=7.61$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\tan^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{20}{12}\right)$ [M1] $=59^\circ$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) distance at time $t$: $\left|t\begin{pmatrix} 16.3 \\ 7.61 \end{pmatrix}-\begin{pmatrix} 20 \\ 12 \end{pmatrix}\right|$ [M1] $t=1.29$ hours [A1] $d=2.42$ km [A1] [3 marks] (d) $d_{\min}=2.42<3$, so the rule is broken [R1] solve $d=3$: $t=1.19$ and $t=1.39$ [M1] $(1.39-1.19)\times60=12$ minutes [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A bearing is measured clockwise from north, so the components are $\sin$ for east and $\cos$ for north. To find when the boat is within a given distance, solve an equation for the distance function on your GDC.

subtopic: Testing whether four points are coplanar
statement: The points are $A(1,0,0)$, $B(0,2,0)$ and $C(0,0,3)$. (a) Find the equation of the plane through $A$, $B$ and $C$ in the form $ax+by+cz=d$. [4] (b) Determine whether each of $D(2,2,-6)$ and $E(1,1,1)$ lies in the plane $ABC$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\ 2\\ 0\end{pmatrix}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\ 0\\ 3\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] normal $\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}=\begin{pmatrix}6\\ 3\\ 2\end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1] $6x+3y+2z=6$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $D$: $12+6-12=6$, so $D$ is in the plane [A1] $E$: $6+3+2=11\ne6$, so $E$ is not [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Four points are coplanar when the fourth lies on the plane through the other three.

subtopic: Line meets plane; angle between line and plane
statement: The line $l$ has equation $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\3\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\-1\end{pmatrix}$ and the plane $\Pi$ has equation $x+2y+2z=11$. (a) Find the coordinates of the point where $l$ meets $\Pi$. [3] (b) Find the exact value of the sine of the acute angle between $l$ and $\Pi$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $(1+2t)+2(-2+t)+2(3-t)=11$ [M1] $3+2t=11$, $t=4$ [A1] Point $(9,2,-1)$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\mathbf d\cdot\mathbf n=2+2-2=2$ [A1] $\sin\theta=\dfrac{|\mathbf d\cdot\mathbf n|}{|\mathbf d||\mathbf n|}$ with $|\mathbf d|=\sqrt6$, $|\mathbf n|=3$ [M1] $\sin\theta=\dfrac{2}{3\sqrt6}=\dfrac{\sqrt6}{9}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The angle between a line and a plane uses $\sin$ with the normal vector (the angle with the normal is the complement). Substitute the line's parametric coordinates into the plane equation.

subtopic: Plane containing a line and a point
statement: The line $L$ has equation $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 0\\ 2\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 1\\ 0\end{pmatrix}$, and $Q$ is the point $(0,1,1)$. Find the equation of the plane that contains $L$ and $Q$, in the form $ax+by+cz=d$. [5]
markscheme: $A(1,0,2)$ is on $L$, $\overrightarrow{AQ}=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\ 1\\ -1\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] normal $=\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 1\\ 0\end{pmatrix}\times\begin{pmatrix}-1\\ 1\\ -1\end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\ 1\\ 2\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $-x+y+2z=3$ using $A$ [M1] check with $Q$: $0+1+2=3$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: The plane contains the direction of the line and the vector from a point on the line to $Q$, so the cross product of these gives its normal.

subtopic: Diagonals of a parallelogram and a rhombus
statement: The vectors $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf c$ are the adjacent sides of a parallelogram, so its diagonals are along $\mathbf a+\mathbf c$ and $\mathbf a-\mathbf c$. (a) Prove that the diagonals are perpendicular if and only if $|\mathbf a|=|\mathbf c|$. [4] (b) Given that $\mathbf a=\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf c=\begin{pmatrix} k \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$, where $k>0$, and that the diagonals are perpendicular, find the value of $k$. [2] (c) For this value of $k$, find the exact area of the parallelogram. [2]
markscheme: (a) the diagonals are perpendicular when $(\mathbf a+\mathbf c)\cdot(\mathbf a-\mathbf c)=0$ [M1] $\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf a-\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf c+\mathbf c\cdot\mathbf a-\mathbf c\cdot\mathbf c$ [A1] $=|\mathbf a|^2-|\mathbf c|^2$ [A1] this is zero if and only if $|\mathbf a|=|\mathbf c|$ (both lengths being positive) [R1] [4 marks] (b) $|\mathbf a|=3$ and $|\mathbf c|^2=k^2+5=9$ [M1] $k=2$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\mathbf a\times\mathbf c=\begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ -6 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] area $=\sqrt{25+36+4}=\sqrt{65}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Perpendicular vectors have a scalar product of zero. Expand the scalar product of the two diagonals using the distributive law.

subtopic: Cartesian form and perpendicular direction of a 2D line
statement: A straight road is modeled by the line $L:\ \mathbf{r}=\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -3 \end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 6 \end{pmatrix}$, where distances are in kilometers. (a) Write down the gradient of $L$. [1] (b) Find the equation of $L$ in the form $y=mx+c$. [2] (c) Find the value of $\lambda$ at the point where the road crosses the $x$-axis. [2] (d) A second road passes through the point $(2,-3)$ and is perpendicular to $L$. Write down a direction vector of the second road. [2]
markscheme: (a) gradient $=\dfrac{6}{4}=\dfrac32$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $y+3=\dfrac32(x-2)$ [M1] $y=\dfrac32x-6$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $-3+6\lambda=0$ [M1] $\lambda=\dfrac12$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) Scalar product with $\begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 6 \end{pmatrix}$ equals zero [M1] e.g. $\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}$ (or any multiple) [A1] [2 marks]
tips: To get a perpendicular direction in 2D, swap the components and change one sign. Check by taking the scalar product.

subtopic: Line of intersection of two planes
statement: Two planes have equations $\Pi_1:\ x+2y-z=4$ and $\Pi_2:\ 2x-y+3z=3$. (a) Find a direction vector for the line of intersection of $\Pi_1$ and $\Pi_2$. [3] (b) Show that the point $(2,1,0)$ lies on both planes, and hence write down a vector equation of the line of intersection. [3] (c) Find the exact value of the cosine of the acute angle between the planes. [3]
markscheme: (a) Normals $\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\-1\end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\3\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] Cross product [M1] $\begin{pmatrix}5\\-5\\-5\end{pmatrix}$, so direction $\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\-1\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\Pi_1$: $2+2-0=4$ [A1] $\Pi_2$: $4-1+0=3$ [A1] $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\-1\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\mathbf n_1\cdot\mathbf n_2=2-2-3=-3$ [A1] $\cos\theta=\dfrac{|\mathbf n_1\cdot\mathbf n_2|}{|\mathbf n_1||\mathbf n_2|}=\dfrac{3}{\sqrt6\sqrt{14}}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{3}{2\sqrt{21}}=\dfrac{\sqrt{21}}{14}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The line of intersection is perpendicular to both normals. Any direction vector can be scaled, so simplify it before writing the line.

subtopic: Cartesian equation of a plane through three points
statement: The points $A(2, 1, 1)$, $B(0, 3, 1)$ and $C(1, 1, 4)$ lie in a plane $\Pi$. (a) Find $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}$. [2] (b) Find a vector normal to $\Pi$. [2] (c) Find the Cartesian equation of $\Pi$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\begin{pmatrix} -2 \\ 2 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 0 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}=\begin{pmatrix} 6 \\ 6 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (c) $\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf r=\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf a$ [M1] $3x+3y+1z=10$ [A1] check with $B$ and $C$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Take the cross product of two vectors in the plane to get the normal, then use $\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf r=\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf a$ with any point of the plane.

subtopic: Work done by a force using the scalar product
statement: A constant force $\mathbf{F}=\begin{pmatrix} 12 \\ 5 \\ 8 \end{pmatrix}$ newtons moves a crate through the displacement $\mathbf{s}=\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 4 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}$ meters. The work done, in joules, is $\mathbf{F}\cdot\mathbf{s}$. (a) Calculate the work done by the force. [2] (b) Find the angle between the force and the displacement, correct to 3 significant figures. [3] (c) Find the component of $\mathbf{F}$ in the direction of $\mathbf{s}$, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (d) A second force $\mathbf{G}=\begin{pmatrix} q \\ 5 \\ 8 \end{pmatrix}$ N moves the crate through the same displacement and does no work. Find the value of $q$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $12(3)+5(4)+8(-2)$ [M1] $=40$ J [A1] [2 marks] (b) $|\mathbf{F}|=\sqrt{233}$, $|\mathbf{s}|=\sqrt{29}$ [A1] $\cos\theta=\dfrac{40}{\sqrt{233}\sqrt{29}}$ [M1] $\theta=60.9^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) component $=\dfrac{\mathbf{F}\cdot\mathbf{s}}{|\mathbf{s}|}$ [M1] $=7.43$ N [A1] [2 marks] (d) $3q+20-16=0$ [M1] $q=-\dfrac43$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Work is a scalar product, so it is zero when the force is perpendicular to the displacement. The component of a vector in a given direction is the scalar product divided by the length of that direction vector.

subtopic: Intersection and angle between two lines
statement: Two lines have equations $L_1:\ \mathbf{r}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}+s\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$ and $L_2:\ \mathbf{r}=\begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ 3 \\ -4 \end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix} -2 \\ 1 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Show that $L_1$ and $L_2$ intersect and find the coordinates of the point of intersection. [4] (b) Find the acute angle between the lines, correct to 1 decimal place. [4]
markscheme: (a) $1+s=5-2t$ and $2s=3+t$ [M1]; solving, $s=2$, $t=1$ [A1]; third coordinate: $2-2=0$ and $-4+4=0$, so consistent [R1]; point $(3, 4, 0)$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) direction scalar product $=-2+2-4=-4$ [A1]; $|d_1|=\sqrt6$ and $|d_2|=\sqrt{21}$ [A1]; $\cos\theta=\dfrac{4}{\sqrt{126}}$ (acute angle uses the absolute value) [M1]; $\theta=69.1^{\circ}$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: If the two parameter values from two coordinates also satisfy the third coordinate, the lines meet. Use $|\cos\theta|$ for the acute angle.

subtopic: Skew lines in three dimensions
statement: Consider the lines $l_1:\ \mathbf{r}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$ and $l_2:\ \mathbf{r}=\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}+s\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Show that the lines are not parallel. [1] (b) Show that the lines do not intersect, and state what this means about their relationship. [4]
markscheme: (a) The direction vectors are not scalar multiples of each other [R1] [1 mark] (b) $1+t=0$ gives $t=-1$ [A1]; $y$: $t=1+s$ gives $s=-2$ [A1]; $z$: $2=s=-2$ is false [M1]; no intersection, so the lines are skew [R1] [4 marks]
tips: Use the first two coordinates to find $t$ and $s$, then test the third coordinate.

subtopic: Closest approach of moving objects
statement: Two drones move so that, $t$ seconds after take-off, their position vectors (in metres) relative to an origin $O$ are $\mathbf r_A=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\4\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}3\\1\\-2\end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf r_B=\begin{pmatrix}14\\5\\-6\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}-2\\1\\4\end{pmatrix}$ for $t\ge0$. (a) Find the distance between the drones when $t=0$. [2] (b) Show that the square of the distance between the drones at time $t$ is $D(t)=61t^2-240t+280$. [3] (c) Find the minimum distance between the drones, and the time at which it occurs. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\overrightarrow{BA}=\begin{pmatrix}-12\\-6\\10\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\sqrt{144+36+100}=\sqrt{280}=16.7$ m [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\mathbf r_A-\mathbf r_B=\begin{pmatrix}-12+5t\\-6\\10-6t\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $D=(5t-12)^2+36+(10-6t)^2$ [M1] $=25t^2-120t+144+36+100-120t+36t^2=61t^2-240t+280$ [AG] [A1] [3 marks] (c) Use of $D'(t)=0$ or GDC minimum [M1] $t=1.97$ s [A1] Minimum distance $=\sqrt{43.93}=6.63$ m [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Minimising the squared distance is easier than the distance itself and gives the same time. Keep unrounded values until the final square root.

subtopic: Resultant of two forces and equilibrium
statement: Two forces act on a particle: $\mathbf{F}_1=\begin{pmatrix}12\\5\end{pmatrix}$ newtons and $\mathbf{F}_2=\begin{pmatrix}-4\\9\end{pmatrix}$ newtons, where the components are horizontal and vertical respectively. (a) Find the resultant force $\mathbf{F}$. [1] (b) Find the magnitude of $\mathbf{F}$, correct to three significant figures. [2] (c) Find the acute angle that $\mathbf{F}$ makes with the horizontal, correct to the nearest tenth of a degree. [2] (d) A third force $\mathbf{F}_3$ is added so that the particle is in equilibrium. Write down $\mathbf{F}_3$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{F}=\begin{pmatrix}12-4\\5+9\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}8\\14\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $|\mathbf{F}|=\sqrt{8^2+14^2}$ [M1] $=\sqrt{260}=16.1\ \text{N}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\tan\theta=\dfrac{14}{8}$ [M1] $\theta=60.3^\circ$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $\mathbf{F}_3=-\mathbf{F}=\begin{pmatrix}-8\\-14\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Add the components separately to find a resultant, and use the right-angled triangle of its components for magnitude and direction. In equilibrium, the forces sum to the zero vector.

subtopic: Intersection of two lines and the angle between them
statement: Two lines are given by $l_1:\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ and $l_2:\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 4 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}+\mu\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Use the first two components to find $\lambda$ and $\mu$ at a possible intersection. [3] (b) Show that the lines do not intersect (they are skew). [2] (c) Find the acute angle between the lines. [3]
markscheme: (a) equate components [M1] $\lambda=2$ [A1] $\mu=0$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) third component gives $4$ for $l_1$ and $1$ for $l_2$, which differ [M1] the lines are not parallel and do not meet, so are skew [R1] [2 marks] (c) $\cos\theta=\dfrac{|\mathbf d_1\cdot\mathbf d_2|}{|\mathbf d_1||\mathbf d_2|}$ [M1] $=\frac{1}{2}$ [A1] $\theta=60.0^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Solve two component equations, then test the third. Lines that are neither parallel nor intersecting are skew. The angle between lines uses the direction vectors only.

subtopic: Ships on intersecting paths: do they collide?
statement: Two boats move with constant velocities. At time $t$ hours after noon, the position vector in kilometers of boat $A$ is $\mathbf{r}_A=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\end{pmatrix}$ and the position vector of boat $B$ is $\mathbf{r}_B=\begin{pmatrix}15\\0\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}-3\\3\end{pmatrix}$. (a) Show that the paths of the two boats cross at the point $(9,6)$. [3] (b) Show that the boats do not collide. [2] (c) After noon, find the minimum distance between the boats, correct to three significant figures, and the time at which it occurs. [4]
markscheme: (a) For boat $A$: $1+2t=9$ gives $t=4$ and $2+t=6$ is consistent, so $A$ passes $(9,6)$ [M1] For boat $B$ (using parameter $s$): $15-3s=9$ gives $s=2$ and $3s=6$ is consistent [M1] Both paths contain $(9,6)$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $A$ is at $(9,6)$ when $t=4$, but $B$ is at $(9,6)$ when $t=2$ [M1] At $t=4$, $B$ is at $(3,12)\neq(9,6)$, so they are not at the same place at the same time [R1] [2 marks] (c) Displacement $\mathbf{r}_B-\mathbf{r}_A=\begin{pmatrix}14-5t\\-2+2t\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $d^2=(14-5t)^2+(2t-2)^2=29t^2-148t+200$ [M1] Minimum at $t=\dfrac{148}{58}=2.55$ hours [A1] $d=\sqrt{29(2.5517)^2-148(2.5517)+200}=3.34$ km [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Intersecting paths do not guarantee a collision: the boats must be at the intersection at the same time. Use a different parameter for each path when finding where the paths cross.

subtopic: Intersection and angle between two lines in 3D
statement: Two lines are given by $L_1:\ \mathbf{r}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\-1\end{pmatrix}+s\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}$ and $L_2:\ \mathbf{r}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\6\\-6\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\2\end{pmatrix}$. (a) Show that $L_1$ and $L_2$ intersect, and find the coordinates of the point of intersection. [4] (b) Find the acute angle between $L_1$ and $L_2$. [4]
markscheme: (a) Equating $x$ and $y$: $1+2s=t$ and $2+s=6-t$ [M1] Substituting: $2+s=6-1-2s$, so $s=1$ and $t=3$ [A1] Check $z$: $-1+s=0$ and $-6+2t=0$, equal, so the lines intersect [R1] Point of intersection $(3,3,0)$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}\cdot\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\2\end{pmatrix}=2-1+2=3$ [A1] $\left|\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}\right|=\left|\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\2\end{pmatrix}\right|=\sqrt6$ [A1] $\cos\theta=\dfrac{3}{\sqrt6\sqrt6}=\dfrac12$ [M1] $\theta=60^\circ$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Solve two of the three coordinate equations for the parameters and then test the third; if it fails, the lines are skew. The angle between lines uses only the direction vectors.

subtopic: Exact cosine of the angle between two vectors
statement: A beam is modeled by the vector $\mathbf{u}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$ and a support strut by $\mathbf{w}=\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 3 \\ 6 \end{pmatrix}$. Let $\theta$ be the angle between $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{w}$. (a) Find $|\mathbf{u}|$ and $|\mathbf{w}|$. [2] (b) Find $\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{w}$. [1] (c) Hence show that $\cos\theta=\dfrac{20}{21}$. [2] (d) State, with a reason, whether $\theta$ is acute or obtuse. [1]
markscheme: (a) $|\mathbf{u}|=\sqrt{1+4+4}=3$ [A1] $|\mathbf{w}|=\sqrt{4+9+36}=7$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $2+6+12=20$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $\cos\theta=\dfrac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{w}}{|\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{w}|}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{20}{3\times7}=\dfrac{20}{21}$ [AG] [2 marks] (d) Acute, because $\cos\theta>0$ [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Use $\cos\theta=\dfrac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{w}}{|\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{w}|}$ and keep exact values when a calculator is not allowed. The sign of the scalar product tells you whether the angle is acute or obtuse.

subtopic: Distance, foot and reflection in a plane
statement: The plane $\Pi$ has equation $2x-3y+6z=5$ and the point $P$ has coordinates $(3,-1,4)$. (a) Find the perpendicular distance from $P$ to $\Pi$. [3] (b) Find the coordinates of the foot $F$ of the perpendicular from $P$ to $\Pi$. [3] (c) Find the coordinates of the reflection of $P$ in $\Pi$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $d=\dfrac{|2(3)-3(-1)+6(4)-5|}{\sqrt{2^2+3^2+6^2}}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{28}{7}$ [A1] $=4$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Line through $P$ perpendicular to $\Pi$: $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}3\\-1\\4\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}2\\-3\\6\end{pmatrix}$ [M1] Substituting: $33+49\lambda=5$, $\lambda=-\dfrac47$ [A1] $F=\left(\dfrac{13}{7},\dfrac57,\dfrac47\right)$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\overrightarrow{OP'}=2\overrightarrow{OF}-\overrightarrow{OP}$ [M1] $P'=\left(\dfrac57,\dfrac{17}{7},-\dfrac{20}{7}\right)$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The foot of the perpendicular is the intersection of $\Pi$ with the line through $P$ parallel to the normal. The reflection lies the same distance beyond the plane, so use the midpoint relation.

subtopic: Drone separation: closest approach, collision course and avoidance
statement: This question investigates the motion of two drones, $A$ and $B$, flying in a large open field. Positions are measured in meters relative to a fixed origin, with the $z$-axis vertical, and $t$ is the time in seconds after $t=0$. The drones move with constant velocities. The position of $A$ is $\mathbf{r}_A=\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 30 \end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix} 6 \\ 4 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ and the position of $B$ is $\mathbf{r}_B=\begin{pmatrix} 120 \\ -10 \\ 70 \end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix} -6 \\ 6 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}$. The drones must remain at least $25$ m apart at all times. (a) Find the speed of each drone, and the distance between the drones at $t=0$. Give your answers to 3 significant figures. [4] (b) Show that the distance $d$ between the drones at time $t$ satisfies $d^2=157t^2-3160t+16100$. [4] (c) Use differentiation to find the time at which the drones are closest, and hence find the minimum distance between them. Give your answers to 3 significant figures. [5] (d) Show that the drones breach the safety rule, and find the length of time, to the nearest tenth of a second, for which they are less than $25$ m apart. [4] (e) The velocity of $B$ is changed to $\begin{pmatrix} -6 \\ k \\ m \end{pmatrix}$ from $t=0$ so that the drones would collide. Find the values of $k$ and $m$, and the time and point of collision. [4] (f) Instead, the velocity of $B$ stays as originally stated and drone $A$ changes its velocity to $s\begin{pmatrix} 6 \\ 4 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ where $0<s\le1$ is a scale factor (so $A$ can only slow down). Show that the relative velocity is $\begin{pmatrix} -6-6s \\ 6-4s \\ -2-s \end{pmatrix}$, and use your graphic display calculator to find the largest value of $s$, to 3 significant figures, for which the minimum distance between the drones is at least $25$ m. [5] (g) State one assumption of this model that may not hold in practice, and describe the effect it could have on the safety conclusion. [2]
markscheme: (a) speed of $A$: $\sqrt{36+16+1}=7.28$ m s$^{-1}$ [M1][A1] speed of $B$: $\sqrt{36+36+4}=8.72$ m s$^{-1}$ [A1] distance at $t=0$: $\sqrt{120^2+10^2+40^2}=127$ m [A1] [4 marks] (b) $\overrightarrow{AB}=\mathbf{r}_B-\mathbf{r}_A=\begin{pmatrix} 120-12t \\ -10+2t \\ 40-3t \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1] $d^2=(120-12t)^2+(-10+2t)^2+(40-3t)^2$ [M1] expanding: $144t^2+4t^2+9t^2=157t^2$, etc. giving $157t^2-3160t+16100$ [AG] [4 marks] (c) $\dfrac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}(d^2)=314t-3160$ [M1][A1] set to zero: $t=\dfrac{3160}{314}=10.1$ s [A1] $d^2=157t^2-3160t+16100$ evaluated at the unrounded $t=\dfrac{3160}{314}$ [M1] $d=14.1$ m [A1] [5 marks] (d) $14.1<25$, so the rule is breached [R1] solve $157t^2-3160t+16100=625$ [M1] $t=8.42$ and $t=11.7$ [A1] duration $=3.3$ s [A1] [4 marks] (e) $x$: $120-6t=6t$ so $t=10$ [M1][A1] $y$: $-10+10k=4(10)$ so $k=5$; $z$: $70+10m=30+10$ so $m=-3$ [A1] collision point $(60,40,40)$ [A1] [4 marks] (f) relative velocity $=\mathbf{v}_B-s\mathbf{v}_A=\begin{pmatrix} -6-6s \\ 6-4s \\ -2-s \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] minimum distance $d_{\min}(s)=\left|\mathbf{p}+t\mathbf{w}\right|$ with $t=-\dfrac{\mathbf{p}\cdot\mathbf{w}}{|\mathbf{w}|^2}$ [M1] (graph $d_{\min}$ against $s$ or tabulate) [M1] set $d_{\min}(s)=25$ [M1] $s=0.757$ [A1] [5 marks] (g) e.g. constant velocity / drones are points / no wind or position error [R1] a deviation could bring the drones closer than predicted, so a larger safety margin is needed [R1] [2 marks]
tips: In part (c) use the derivative of $d^2$, which is a quadratic and much easier than differentiating $d$. For the final calculation, think of the minimum distance as a function of the scale factor and use the table or graph on your GDC.

subtopic: Intersection of two lines in the plane
statement: Two lines have equations $\mathbf{r}_1=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}+s\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{r}_2=\begin{pmatrix} 7 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Write the equations of the lines in the form $y=mx+c$. [3] (b) Find the point of intersection. [3] (c) Find the acute angle between the lines. [2]
markscheme: (a) Line 1: $x=1+2s$, $y=s$ so $y=\dfrac{x-1}{2}$ [A1]; line 2: $x=7-t$, $y=-2+t$ so $y=-x+5$ [A1][A1] [3 marks] (b) $\dfrac{x-1}2=-x+5$ [M1]; $x=\dfrac{11}{3}$ [A1]; $y=\dfrac43$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\cos\theta=\dfrac{|(2)(-1)+(1)(1)|}{\sqrt5\sqrt2}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}}$ [M1]; $\theta=71.6^\circ$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Eliminate the parameter, or equate components and solve for the two parameters.

subtopic: Intersection of lines and angle between lines
statement: Two lines have equations $l_1:\ \mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\3\end{pmatrix}+s\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix}$ and $l_2:\ \mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}4\\0\\-1\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}-1\\1\\5\end{pmatrix}$. (a) Show that the lines intersect and find the coordinates of the point of intersection. [4] (b) Find the cosine of the acute angle between the lines. [3]
markscheme: (a) Equating components: $1+2s=4-t$, $2-s=t$, $3+s=-1+5t$ [M1] From the first two: $1+2s=4-(2-s)\Rightarrow s=1,\ t=1$ [A1] Third equation: $3+1=4$ and $-1+5=4$, so consistent [R1] Intersection $(3,1,4)$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $\mathbf d_1\cdot\mathbf d_2=-2-1+5=2$ [A1] Use of $\cos\theta=\dfrac{|\mathbf d_1\cdot\mathbf d_2|}{|\mathbf d_1||\mathbf d_2|}$ with $|\mathbf d_1|=\sqrt6$, $|\mathbf d_2|=\sqrt{27}$ [M1] $\cos\theta=\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{162}}=\dfrac{\sqrt2}{9}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Solve two of the three component equations and then test the third; a failed check means the lines are skew. Use the direction vectors, not the position vectors, for the angle.

subtopic: The orthocentre and the Euler line using position vectors
statement: Triangle $ABC$ has circumcentre at the origin $O$, so $|\mathbf a|=|\mathbf b|=|\mathbf c|=R$. The point $H$ has position vector $\mathbf h=\mathbf a+\mathbf b+\mathbf c$. (a) Show that $\overrightarrow{AH}\cdot\overrightarrow{BC}=0$. [3] (b) Explain, by the same argument, why $H$ is the orthocentre of the triangle. [2] (c) The centroid $G$ has position vector $\dfrac13(\mathbf a+\mathbf b+\mathbf c)$. Show that $O$, $G$, $H$ are collinear and find the ratio $OG:GH$. [3] (d) A triangle has vertices $A(5,0)$, $B(-3,4)$, $C(-3,-4)$, all on a circle of radius $5$ centered at the origin. Find $H$, and verify that $BH$ is perpendicular to $CA$. [4] (e) Find the position of $H$ for an equilateral triangle with circumcentre at $O$, and explain. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\overrightarrow{AH}=\mathbf b+\mathbf c$ [A1] $(\mathbf b+\mathbf c)\cdot(\mathbf c-\mathbf b)=|\mathbf c|^2-|\mathbf b|^2$ [M1] $=0$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) similarly $\overrightarrow{BH}\cdot\overrightarrow{CA}=0$ and $\overrightarrow{CH}\cdot\overrightarrow{AB}=0$ [R1] $H$ lies on all three altitudes [R1] [2 marks] (c) $\mathbf h=3\mathbf g$ [A1] so $H$ lies on the line $OG$ [R1] $OG:GH=1:2$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $\mathbf h=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\ 0\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\overrightarrow{BH}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\ -4\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\overrightarrow{CA}=\begin{pmatrix}8\\ 4\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] dot product $16-16=0$ [A1] [4 marks] (e) $\mathbf a+\mathbf b+\mathbf c=\mathbf0$ by symmetry, so $H=O$, the centroid, circumcentre and orthocentre coincide [R1] [1 mark]
tips: With the circumcentre at the origin, the equal lengths of the position vectors make the dot products in the altitude condition cancel.

subtopic: Distance between two parallel lines
statement: The lines $L_1$ and $L_2$ have equations $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 2\\ 0\end{pmatrix}+s\begin{pmatrix}2\\ 1\\ 2\end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}3\\ 0\\ 1\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}2\\ 1\\ 2\end{pmatrix}$. (a) Explain why the lines are parallel, and find a vector joining a point of $L_1$ to a point of $L_2$. [2] (b) Find the distance between the lines, in exact form. [4]
markscheme: (a) the direction vectors are equal [R1] $\begin{pmatrix}2\\ -2\\ 1\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) distance $=\dfrac{|\mathbf w\times\mathbf d|}{|\mathbf d|}$ with $\mathbf w=\begin{pmatrix}2\\ -2\\ 1\end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf d=\begin{pmatrix}2\\ 1\\ 2\end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $\mathbf w\times\mathbf d=\begin{pmatrix}-5\\ -2\\ 6\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] magnitude $\sqrt{65}$ [A1] distance $=\dfrac{\sqrt{65}}3$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: The distance between parallel lines is the length of the component of the joining vector that is perpendicular to the common direction. The cross product with a unit direction vector gives it.

subtopic: Shortest distance from a point to a line using the scalar product
statement: The line $l$ has equation $\mathbf{r}=(2,-1,3)+\lambda(1,2,2)$ and the point $P$ has coordinates $(5,4,1)$. (a) Find the vector $\overrightarrow{AP}$ where $A(2,-1,3)$ is on $l$. [1] (b) Let $F$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to $l$. Show that $\overrightarrow{AF}=\lambda(1,2,2)$ and find $\lambda$. [3] (c) Find the coordinates of $F$ and the shortest distance from $P$ to $l$. [3] (d) Find the acute angle between $l$ and the line $OP$ where $O$ is the origin. [3]
tips: The shortest distance is along the perpendicular, which means the scalar product of $\overrightarrow{PF}$ with the direction vector is zero.

subtopic: Parallelogram in 3D: fourth vertex, diagonals and area
statement: The points $A(1,2,3)$, $B(4,3,5)$ and $C(6,7,3)$ are three vertices of a parallelogram $ABCD$ in that order, with coordinates in centimeters. (a) Find the coordinates of $D$. [3] (b) Find the lengths of the diagonals $AC$ and $BD$, correct to 3 significant figures. [3] (c) Find the acute angle between the diagonals, correct to the nearest degree. [3] (d) Find the area of the parallelogram, correct to 3 significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\overrightarrow{AD}=\overrightarrow{BC}$ [M1] $\overrightarrow{BC}=\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 4 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $D(3,6,1)$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\overrightarrow{AC}=\begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ 5 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\overrightarrow{BD}=\begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 3 \\ -4 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $AC=7.07$ cm and $BD=5.10$ cm [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\overrightarrow{AC}\cdot\overrightarrow{BD}=10$ [A1] $\cos\theta=\dfrac{10}{7.07\times5.10}$ [M1] $\theta=74^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$, $\overrightarrow{AD}=\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 4 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] angle $BAD=70.9^\circ$ [M1] area $=|AB||AD|\sin(BAD)=17.3$ cm$^2$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: In a parallelogram $ABCD$, $\overrightarrow{AD}=\overrightarrow{BC}$. The angle between the diagonals can be found from either pair of directions; give the acute value when asked.

subtopic: Intersection of a line and a plane, and the angle between them
statement: The line $l$ has equation $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$ and the plane $\Pi$ has equation $2x-1y+1z=7$. (a) Find the coordinates of the point where $l$ meets $\Pi$. [4] (b) Find the acute angle between $l$ and $\Pi$. [3]
markscheme: (a) substitute $x,y,z$ in terms of $\lambda$ [M1] $3\lambda+0=7$ [A1] $\lambda=\frac{7}{3}$ [A1] point $(\frac{10}{3}, \frac{13}{3}, \frac{14}{3})$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $\sin\theta=\dfrac{|\mathbf d\cdot\mathbf n|}{|\mathbf d||\mathbf n|}$ [M1] $=0.5000$ [A1] $\theta=30.0^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The angle between a line and a plane is $90^\circ$ minus the angle between the line and the normal, so use sine with $|\mathbf d\cdot\mathbf n|$.

subtopic: Aircraft velocity relative to the ground in a wind
statement: In still air an aircraft would fly with velocity $\begin{pmatrix} 240 \\ 70 \end{pmatrix}$ km h$^{-1}$, where the components are in the east and north directions. There is a steady wind with velocity $\begin{pmatrix} -35 \\ 25 \end{pmatrix}$ km h$^{-1}$. (a) Find the velocity of the aircraft relative to the ground. [2] (b) Find the ground speed of the aircraft, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (c) Find the bearing of the aircraft's path over the ground, to the nearest degree. [3] (d) The aircraft must cover a ground distance of $600$ km along this path. Find the time this takes, in minutes, to the nearest minute. [2]
markscheme: (a) ground velocity $=\begin{pmatrix} 240 \\ 70 \end{pmatrix}$ $+$ $\begin{pmatrix} -35 \\ 25 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix} 205 \\ 95 \end{pmatrix}$ km h$^{-1}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\sqrt{205^2+95^2}$ [M1] $=226$ km h$^{-1}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) angle from north: $\tan^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{205}{95}\right)$ [M1] $=65.1^\circ$ [A1] bearing $=65^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $\dfrac{600}{226}$ [M1] $=2.66$ hours $=159$ minutes [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Ground velocity is the sum of the air velocity and the wind velocity. Speeds use magnitudes and bearings are measured from north.

subtopic: Dividing a line segment externally
statement: The points $A(1,2,3)$ and $B(2,0,5)$ are given. The point $C$ lies on the line $AB$ beyond $B$, with $AC=3AB$. (a) Find the position vector of $C$. [3] (b) Find the ratio $AB:BC$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\overrightarrow{AC}=3\overrightarrow{AB}=3\begin{pmatrix}1\\ -2\\ 2\end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1] $\overrightarrow{OC}=\overrightarrow{OA}+\overrightarrow{AC}$, so $C=(4,-4,9)$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $BC=2AB$, so $AB:BC=1:2$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Because $C$ is beyond $B$, the vectors $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}$ point in the same direction.

subtopic: Shortest distance between skew lines
statement: Consider the lines $l_1:\ \mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\2\end{pmatrix}+s\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}$ and $l_2:\ \mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\2\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}2\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}$. (a) Show that $l_1$ and $l_2$ are skew. [3] (b) Find a vector perpendicular to both lines. [2] (c) Hence find the shortest distance between the two lines. [3]
markscheme: (a) Directions are not parallel, since $(1,1,0)$ is not a multiple of $(2,0,1)$ [R1] Equating: $1+s=2t$, $s=1$, $2=2+t$ [M1] gives $s=1$, $t=0$, but then $1+s=2\neq 2t=0$, so no intersection [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}\times\begin{pmatrix}2\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\-2\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\overrightarrow{A_1A_2}=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $d=\dfrac{|\overrightarrow{A_1A_2}\cdot\mathbf n|}{|\mathbf n|}=\dfrac{|-1-1+0|}{\sqrt6}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{2}{\sqrt6}=\dfrac{\sqrt6}{3}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: To show lines are skew you need both non-parallel directions and no common point. The shortest distance is the projection of the vector between the lines onto the common perpendicular.

subtopic: Plane from vector form to Cartesian equation
statement: The plane $\Pi$ has equation $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\2\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}+\mu\begin{pmatrix}0\\2\\-1\end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find a vector normal to $\Pi$. [2] (b) Find the Cartesian equation of $\Pi$ in the form $ax+by+cz=d$. [2] (c) Determine whether each of the points $A(4,5,1)$ and $B(2,1,3)$ lies on $\Pi$. [2] (d) Find the distance from the origin to $\Pi$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}\times\begin{pmatrix}0\\2\\-1\end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\1\\2\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $-x+y+2z=-1+0+4$ [M1] $-x+y+2z=3$ (accept $x-y-2z=-3$) [A1] [2 marks] (c) $A$: $-4+5+2=3$, so $A$ lies on $\Pi$ [A1] $B$: $-2+1+6=5\neq3$, so $B$ does not lie on $\Pi$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $d=\dfrac{|3|}{\sqrt{(-1)^2+1^2+2^2}}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{3}{\sqrt6}=1.22$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A normal vector comes from the cross product of the two direction vectors. Always test points by substituting into the Cartesian equation.

subtopic: Two particles with constant velocity: showing a collision
statement: Two small particles move in a plane. After $t$ seconds, the position of particle $A$ is $\mathbf{r}_A=\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$ and the position of particle $B$ is $\mathbf{r}_B=\begin{pmatrix} 10 \\ -3 \end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix} -2 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}$, with distances in centimeters. (a) Find the exact speed of particle $A$. [1] (b) Show that the particles collide, and find the time of the collision. [4] (c) Find the coordinates of the collision point. [1] (d) Find the exact distance between the particles at $t=0$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\sqrt{9+4}=\sqrt{13}$ cm s$^{-1}$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $3t=10-2t$ so $t=2$ [M1][A1] $1+2t=-3+4t$ gives $t=2$ [A1] the same $t$ satisfies both components so they collide at $t=2$ [R1] [4 marks] (c) $(6,5)$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) $\mathbf{r}_B-\mathbf{r}_A=\begin{pmatrix} 10 \\ -4 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] distance $=\sqrt{116}=2\sqrt{29}$ cm [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A collision needs both components to agree at the same value of $t$. If the times differ the paths cross but the particles do not meet.

subtopic: Cross product and the area of a triangle
statement: The points $A$, $B$ and $C$ have coordinates $A(0,0,0)$, $B(2,1,3)$ and $C(1,-1,2)$. (a) Find $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}$. [2] (b) Find $\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}$. [3] (c) Hence find the exact area of triangle $ABC$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\overrightarrow{AC}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) cross product [M1] components [A1] $\begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ -1 \\ -3 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) area $=\dfrac12\left|\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}\right|$ [M1] $=\dfrac12\sqrt{35}=\frac{\sqrt{35}}{2}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Area of a triangle $=\frac12|\mathbf a\times\mathbf b|$. The cross product is perpendicular to both $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}$.

subtopic: Intersection of two lines in the plane and angle between them
statement: Two straight paths on a flat field are modeled by the lines $L_1:\ \mathbf{r}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}+s\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ and $L_2:\ \mathbf{r}=\begin{pmatrix} 7 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Write down two equations in $s$ and $t$ that must be satisfied at a point of intersection. [2] (b) Solve these equations to find $s$ and $t$. [2] (c) Hence find the coordinates of the point of intersection. [1] (d) Find the exact value of the cosine of the acute angle between the paths. [3]
markscheme: (a) $1+2s=7-t$ [A1] $2+s=-1+t$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Eliminating, e.g. $t=3+s$ and $3s=3$ [M1] $s=1,\ t=4$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $(3,3)$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) Direction vectors scalar product $=-2+1=-1$ [M1] magnitudes $\sqrt5$ and $\sqrt2$ [A1] $\cos\theta=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}}$ (taking the absolute value for the acute angle) [A1] [3 marks]
tips: For the acute angle between two lines, take the absolute value of the scalar product of the direction vectors. Always check an intersection by substituting both parameters back.

subtopic: Vector equation of a line through two points
statement: The points $A(0, 1, 4)$ and $B(2, 3, 2)$ lie on a line $l$. (a) Find a vector equation of $l$. [3] (b) Determine whether the point $Q(3, 4, 1)$ lies on $l$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1] [3 marks] (b) set $\mathbf r=\overrightarrow{OQ}$ and solve for $\lambda$ from each component [M1] $\lambda$ values: 1.5, 1.5, 1.5 [A1] consistent, so $Q$ lies on $l$ [R1] [3 marks]
tips: A line needs a point and a direction vector. A point lies on the line only if the same value of the parameter works in all three components.

subtopic: Plane through three points
statement: The points $A(1,0,2)$, $B(2,1,0)$ and $C(0,3,1)$ lie in the plane $\Pi$. (a) Find a vector normal to $\Pi$. [3] (b) Find the Cartesian equation of $\Pi$. [2] (c) Find the coordinates of the point where $\Pi$ meets the $z$-axis. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\-2\end{pmatrix}$, $\overrightarrow{AC}=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\3\\-1\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] Cross product [M1] $\mathbf n=\begin{pmatrix}5\\3\\4\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $5x+3y+4z=5(1)+3(0)+4(2)$ [M1] $5x+3y+4z=13$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Set $x=y=0$: $4z=13$ [M1] $\left(0,0,\dfrac{13}{4}\right)$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Verify your Cartesian equation by substituting all three given points. Points on a coordinate axis have the other two coordinates equal to zero.

subtopic: Vector equation of a line through two points
statement: The points $A(1,2,3)$ and $B(4,0,6)$ lie on the line $l$. (a) Find a vector equation of $l$. [2] (b) Determine whether the points $C(7,-2,9)$ and $D(5,-1,7)$ lie on $l$. [3] (c) Find the exact distance $AB$. [1]
markscheme: (a) direction $\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ -2 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; $\mathbf{r}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ -2 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $C$: $\lambda=2$ gives $(7,-2,9)$, so on $l$ [M1][A1]; $D$: $1+3\lambda=5$ gives $\lambda=\frac43$ but then $y=2-\frac83\ne-1$, so not on $l$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\sqrt{9+4+9}=\sqrt{22}$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: A point lies on the line if one value of $\lambda$ satisfies all three components.

subtopic: Drone descending along a straight line to the ground
statement: A delivery drone is at the point $(10,25,120)$ at time $t=0$, where distances are in meters and the ground is the plane $z=0$. It descends in a straight line with constant velocity $\begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ -3 \\ -8 \end{pmatrix}$ m s$^{-1}$, where $t$ is in seconds. (a) Write down a vector equation for the position of the drone at time $t$. [2] (b) Find the speed of the drone, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (c) Find the time at which the drone lands, and the coordinates of the landing point. [3] (d) Find the angle between the path of the drone and the horizontal ground, in degrees to 3 significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{r}=\begin{pmatrix} 10 \\ 25 \\ 120 \end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ -3 \\ -8 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (b) $\sqrt{16+9+64}$ [M1] $=9.43$ m s$^{-1}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $120-8t=0$ [M1] $t=15$ s [A1] $(70,\,-20,\,0)$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) horizontal speed $=\sqrt{16+9}=5$ [A1] $\tan\phi=\dfrac85$ [M1] or $\sin\phi=\dfrac{8}{\sqrt{89}}$ $\phi=58.0^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The ground is the plane $z=0$, so set the third component to zero to find the landing time. The angle to the horizontal uses the vertical component against the horizontal speed.

subtopic: Cross product and the area of a triangle
statement: The points $A$, $B$ and $C$ have coordinates $A(1,1,1)$, $B(2,3,5)$ and $C(4,2,3)$. (a) Find $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}$. [2] (b) Find $\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}$. [3] (c) Hence find the exact area of triangle $ABC$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\overrightarrow{AC}=\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) cross product [M1] components [A1] $\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 10 \\ -5 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) area $=\dfrac12\left|\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}\right|$ [M1] $=\dfrac12\sqrt{125}=\frac{5 \sqrt{5}}{2}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Area of a triangle $=\frac12|\mathbf a\times\mathbf b|$. The cross product is perpendicular to both $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}$.

subtopic: Ship velocity, speed, position and bearing of travel
statement: A ship leaves a port at the origin $O$ at time $t=0$. Relative to $O$, east is the positive $x$-direction and north is the positive $y$-direction, with distances in kilometers and $t$ in hours. The ship moves with constant velocity $\begin{pmatrix} 14.5 \\ 8.2 \end{pmatrix}$ km h$^{-1}$. (a) Find the speed of the ship, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (b) Find the position of the ship after $2.5$ hours. [2] (c) Find how far the ship is from the port after $2.5$ hours, correct to 3 significant figures. [1] (d) A lighthouse is at a point with $x$-coordinate $60$. Find the time at which the ship has the same $x$-coordinate as the lighthouse, and the $y$-coordinate of the ship at that time. Give both answers to 3 significant figures. [3] (e) Find the bearing on which the ship is traveling, to the nearest degree. [2]
tips: Bearings are measured clockwise from north, so use the angle from the $y$-axis. A sketch with east and north axes helps you avoid mixing up the angle.

subtopic: Showing that two lines in 3D are skew
statement: Two cables in a stadium roof are modeled by the lines $L_1:\ \mathbf{r}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$ and $L_2:\ \mathbf{r}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}+\mu\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Show that $L_1$ and $L_2$ are not parallel. [1] (b) Show that $L_1$ and $L_2$ do not intersect. [4] (c) Find the exact acute angle between $L_1$ and $L_2$. [3]
markscheme: (a) The direction vectors are not scalar multiples of each other [R1] [1 mark] (b) $x$: $1+\lambda=1+\mu$ so $\lambda=\mu$ [A1] $y$: $2\lambda=3-\mu$ so $3\lambda=3$, $\lambda=\mu=1$ [M1][A1] $z$: $3-1=2$ but $1+2(1)=3$, which are not equal [R1] so the lines do not intersect [4 marks] (c) $\cos\theta=\dfrac{|1-2-2|}{\sqrt6\sqrt6}$ [M1][A1] $=\dfrac12$ so $\theta=60^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Lines in 3D that are neither parallel nor intersecting are skew. Solve using two coordinates, then test the third.

subtopic: A tetrahedron: volume, face area, height and dihedral angle
statement: The points $O(0,0,0)$, $A(2,0,0)$, $B(0,3,0)$ and $C(0,0,6)$ are the vertices of a tetrahedron. (a) Find the volume of the tetrahedron using $V=\dfrac16\left|\overrightarrow{OA}\cdot\left(\overrightarrow{OB}\times\overrightarrow{OC}\right)\right|$. [3] (b) Show that the plane $ABC$ has equation $3x+2y+z=6$. [3] (c) Find the exact area of triangle $ABC$. [2] (d) Find the distance from $O$ to the plane $ABC$, and verify that it is consistent with $V=\dfrac13\times\text{area}\times\text{height}$. [3] (e) Find the acute angle between the faces $ABC$ and $OAB$. [3] (f) Find the coordinates of the foot $F$ of the perpendicular from $O$ to the plane $ABC$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\overrightarrow{OB}\times\overrightarrow{OC}=\begin{pmatrix} 18 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1] $V=\dfrac16\times36=6$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix} -2 \\ 3 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$, $\overrightarrow{AC}=\begin{pmatrix} -2 \\ 0 \\ 6 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] normal $\begin{pmatrix} 18 \\ 12 \\ 6 \end{pmatrix}\parallel\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] through $A$: $3x+2y+z=6$ [A1] [AG] [3 marks] (c) $\dfrac12\left|\begin{pmatrix} 18 \\ 12 \\ 6 \end{pmatrix}\right|=\dfrac12\sqrt{504}$ [M1] $=3\sqrt{14}$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $\dfrac{6}{\sqrt{14}}$ [A1] $\dfrac13\times3\sqrt{14}\times\dfrac6{\sqrt{14}}$ [M1] $=6$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) $OAB$ lies in $z=0$ with normal $\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\cos\theta=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{14}}$ [M1] $\theta=74.5^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks] (f) $F=t\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $14t=6$, $t=\dfrac37$ [A1] $F=\left(\dfrac97,\dfrac67,\dfrac37\right)$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Use scalar triple products for volumes and cross products for areas and normals. The same volume can be found two ways, which checks the work.

subtopic: Closest approach of two moving particles
statement: Two drones have position vectors (in meters) $\mathbf r_A=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf r_B=\begin{pmatrix} 9 \\ 0 \\ 6 \end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 2 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$ at time $t$ seconds, $t\ge0$. (a) Show that the vector from $A$ to $B$ at time $t$ is $\begin{pmatrix} 8-3t \\ -2+t \\ 6-2t \end{pmatrix}$. [2] (b) Show that the square of the distance between the drones is $14t^2-76t+104$. [3] (c) Find the time at which the drones are closest together and the minimum distance between them. [4]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf r_B-\mathbf r_A$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix} 9-t-1-2t \\ 2t-2-t \\ 6-t-t \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 8-3t \\ t-2 \\ 6-2t \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [AG] [2 marks] (b) $(8-3t)^2+(t-2)^2+(6-2t)^2$ [M1] $=64-48t+9t^2+t^2-4t+4+36-24t+4t^2$ [A1] $=14t^2-76t+104$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(14t^2-76t+104\right)=28t-76$ [M1] $t=\dfrac{19}7=2.71$ s [A1] $D^2=104-\dfrac{76^2}{4\times14}=\dfrac67$ [M1] minimum distance $=\sqrt{\dfrac67}=0.926$ m [A1] [4 marks]
tips: The squared distance is a quadratic in $t$; its minimum is at the vertex $t=-\dfrac b{2a}$.

subtopic: Reflection of a point in a line in three dimensions
statement: The line $L$ passes through the origin with direction vector $\mathbf d=\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 1\\ 0\end{pmatrix}$, and $P$ is the point $(1,2,3)$. (a) Find the coordinates of the point $F$ on $L$ that is closest to $P$. [4] (b) Find the reflection $P'$ of $P$ in the line $L$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $F=t\mathbf d$ and $(\overrightarrow{OP}-F)\cdot\mathbf d=0$ [M1] $(1-t)+(2-t)=0$ [A1] $t=\dfrac32$ [A1] $F=\left(\dfrac32,\dfrac32,0\right)$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $\overrightarrow{OP'}=2\overrightarrow{OF}-\overrightarrow{OP}$ [M1] $P'=(2,1,-3)$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The foot of the perpendicular is the midpoint of $PP'$, so double its position vector and subtract that of $P$.

subtopic: Scalar product and the angle between vectors
statement: The vectors $\mathbf a=\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf b=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}$ are given. (a) Find $\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b$. [2] (b) Find $|\mathbf a|$ and $|\mathbf b|$. [2] (c) Find the angle between $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$, giving your answer to the nearest degree. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b=\sum a_ib_i$ [M1] $=-4$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $|\mathbf a|=3$ [A1] $|\mathbf b|=3$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\cos\theta=\dfrac{\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b}{|\mathbf a||\mathbf b|}$ [M1] $=-\frac{4}{9}$ [A1] $\theta=116^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Use $\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b=|\mathbf a||\mathbf b|\cos\theta$ and take the inverse cosine; a negative scalar product means an obtuse angle.

subtopic: Magnitude and unit vector of a 2D displacement
statement: A warehouse robot makes two moves. The first move is the displacement $\mathbf{p}=\begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ 12 \end{pmatrix}$ and the second is $\mathbf{q}=\begin{pmatrix} -8 \\ 6 \end{pmatrix}$, both in meters. (a) Find $|\mathbf{p}|$. [1] (b) Find the single displacement $\mathbf{p}+\mathbf{q}$. [1] (c) Find a unit vector in the direction of $\mathbf{q}$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $|\mathbf{p}|=\sqrt{25+144}=13$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\mathbf{p}+\mathbf{q}=\begin{pmatrix} -3 \\ 18 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $|\mathbf{q}|=\sqrt{64+36}=10$ [M1] unit vector $=\dfrac{1}{10}\begin{pmatrix} -8 \\ 6 \end{pmatrix}$ $=\begin{pmatrix} -0.8 \\ 0.6 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A unit vector is the vector divided by its own magnitude. Check your answer by confirming that its magnitude is 1.

subtopic: Magnitude of a cross product and the identity with the dot product
statement: Let $\mathbf a=\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 2\\ 3\end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf b=\begin{pmatrix}2\\ -1\\ 1\end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find $\mathbf a\times\mathbf b$ and verify that it is perpendicular to both $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$. [4] (b) Verify that $|\mathbf a\times\mathbf b|^2=|\mathbf a|^2|\mathbf b|^2-(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b)^2$, and deduce the angle between $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf a\times\mathbf b=\begin{pmatrix}5\\ 5\\ -5\end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1] $\mathbf a\cdot(\mathbf a\times\mathbf b)=5+10-15=0$ [A1] $\mathbf b\cdot(\mathbf a\times\mathbf b)=10-5-5=0$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) left side $=75$; $|\mathbf a|^2=14$, $|\mathbf b|^2=6$, $\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b=3$, right side $84-9=75$ [A1] $|\mathbf a\times\mathbf b|=|\mathbf a||\mathbf b|\sin\theta$ gives $\sin\theta=\dfrac{\sqrt{75}}{\sqrt{84}}$ [M1] $\theta=70.9^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The identity follows from $\sin^2\theta=1-\cos^2\theta$ with the dot product and cross product formulas.

subtopic: Intersection point and angle between two straight pipes
statement: Two straight pipes meet at a junction. Their centre lines are modeled by $L_1:\ \mathbf{r}=\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$ and $L_2:\ \mathbf{r}=\begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 0 \\ 6 \end{pmatrix}+\mu\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$, with distances in meters. (a) Show that the pipes meet, and find the coordinates of the junction. [4] (b) Find the acute angle between the pipes, correct to 3 significant figures. [3] (c) A third straight pipe from the junction has direction $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \\ k_0 \end{pmatrix}$. Find the value of $k_0$ so that it is perpendicular to the first pipe. [2]
markscheme: (a) $x$: $2+\lambda=-1+2\mu$ and $y$: $2\lambda=\mu$ [A1] solve: $\lambda=1$, $\mu=2$ [M1] check $z$: $1+3(1)=4$ and $6-2=4$, so the pipes meet [R1] junction $(3,2,4)$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $\mathbf{d}_1\cdot\mathbf{d}_2=2+2-3=1$ [A1] $\cos\theta=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{14}\sqrt6}$ [M1] $\theta=83.7^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $1-2+3k_0=0$ [M1] $k_0=\dfrac13$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Solve for the parameters using two coordinates and then check the third. Use the absolute value of the scalar product when an acute angle is required.

subtopic: Intersection of a line and a plane, and the angle between them
statement: The line $l$ has equation $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ and the plane $\Pi$ has equation $1x+1y+3z=10$. (a) Find the coordinates of the point where $l$ meets $\Pi$. [4] (b) Find the acute angle between $l$ and $\Pi$. [3]
markscheme: (a) substitute $x,y,z$ in terms of $\lambda$ [M1] $4\lambda+6=10$ [A1] $\lambda=1$ [A1] point $(2, 2, 2)$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $\sin\theta=\dfrac{|\mathbf d\cdot\mathbf n|}{|\mathbf d||\mathbf n|}$ [M1] $=0.4924$ [A1] $\theta=29.5^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The angle between a line and a plane is $90^\circ$ minus the angle between the line and the normal, so use sine with $|\mathbf d\cdot\mathbf n|$.

subtopic: Boat with constant velocity
statement: A boat moves with constant velocity $\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}$ km h$^{-1}$. At noon its position vector relative to a harbor $H$ is $\begin{pmatrix} -6 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}$ km, where the unit vectors point east and north. (a) Find the speed of the boat. [2] (b) Write down the position vector of the boat $t$ hours after noon, and find its position at $t=3$. [3] (c) Find the time after noon when the boat is due north of the harbor, and its distance from $H$ then. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\sqrt{3^{2}+4^{2}}$ [M1]; $5$ km h$^{-1}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\mathbf{r}=\begin{pmatrix} -6 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; at $t=3$: $\begin{pmatrix} -6+9 \\ -2+12 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1]; $(3, 10)$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) east coordinate $=0$: $-6+3t=0$ [M1]; $t=2$ hours after noon [A1]; north coordinate $-2+8=6$, so the distance from $H$ is $6$ km [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Due north or south of $H$ means the east coordinate is zero.

subtopic: Dividing a line segment in a given ratio
statement: The points $A(-1,4,2)$ and $B(9,-1,7)$ are given. The point $P$ lies on $AB$ so that $AP:PB=2:3$. (a) Find $\overrightarrow{AB}$. [1] (b) Find the position vector of $P$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\begin{pmatrix} 10 \\ -5 \\ 5 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\overrightarrow{AP}=\dfrac25\overrightarrow{AB}$ [A1]; $\overrightarrow{OP}=\begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 4 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}+\begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ -2 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1]; $\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: If $AP:PB=m:n$ then $\overrightarrow{AP}=\frac{m}{m+n}\overrightarrow{AB}$.

subtopic: Crossing a river with a current
statement: A river is $120$ m wide and flows east at $1.5$ m/s. A boat can travel at $3$ m/s relative to the water. The boat starts on the south bank and wants to reach the north bank. (a) The boat is steered directly north (relative to the water). Find the distance it is carried downstream when it reaches the north bank. [3] (b) The boat is steered so that it travels directly north relative to the ground. Find the angle, to the nearest degree, that the heading makes with north, and the direction (east or west of north). [3] (c) Find the time needed to cross in the second case, to three significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) time $=\dfrac{120}{3}=40$ s [A1]; drift $=1.5\times40$ [M1]; $60$ m [A1] [3 marks] (b) the east component of the boat's velocity must cancel $1.5$: $3\sin\alpha=1.5$ [M1]; $\alpha=30^{\circ}$ [A1]; heading $30^{\circ}$ west of north [A1] [3 marks] (c) northward speed $3\cos30^{\circ}=2.598$ m/s [A1]; $\dfrac{120}{2.598}=46.2$ s [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Resolve the boat's velocity relative to the water into components east and north, then add the river's velocity.

subtopic: Scalar product and perpendicular vectors in 3D
statement: The vectors $\mathbf{a}=\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{b}=\begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 5 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$ are given. (a) Find $\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}$. [2] (b) Write down what your answer to part (a) tells you about the angle between $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$. [1] (c) The vector $\mathbf{c}=\begin{pmatrix} k \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ is perpendicular to $\mathbf{a}$. Find the value of $k$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=2(4)+(-1)(5)+3(-1)$ [M1] $=0$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) The vectors are perpendicular, so the angle is $90^\circ$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $2k-2+3=0$ [M1] $k=-\dfrac{1}{2}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Two non-zero vectors are perpendicular exactly when their scalar product is zero. Set the scalar product equal to zero to find an unknown component.

subtopic: Closest approach of two ships moving at constant velocity
statement: Two ships, $A$ and $B$, are observed from a coastguard station at the origin. Distances are in kilometers and $t$ is the time in hours after observations begin. The position vectors are $\mathbf{r}_A=\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix} 15 \\ 8 \end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{r}_B=\begin{pmatrix} 80 \\ 20 \end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix} -12 \\ -5 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find the position vector of $B$ relative to $A$, $\overrightarrow{AB}$, at time $t$. [2] (b) Hence show that the distance $d$ between the ships satisfies $d^2=898t^2-4840t+6800$. [2] (c) Use your graphic display calculator to find the minimum distance between the ships and the time at which it occurs. Give your answers to 3 significant figures. [3] (d) Safety rules require ships to stay at least $20$ km apart. Find the length of time, in minutes, for which the ships are less than $20$ km apart. Give your answer to the nearest minute. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\overrightarrow{AB}=\mathbf{r}_B-\mathbf{r}_A$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix} 80-27t \\ 20-13t \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $d^2=(80-27t)^2+(20-13t)^2$ [M1] $=898t^2-4840t+6800$ [AG] [2 marks] (c) Minimum of $d=\sqrt{898t^2-4840t+6800}$ (or of $d^2$) [M1] $t=2.69$ hours [A1] $d=16.7$ km [A1] [3 marks] (d) Solve $d^2=400$ [M1] $t=2.33$ and $t=3.06$ [A1] $(3.06-2.33)\times60=44$ minutes [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Write $d^2$ as a quadratic in $t$; the minimum of $d$ occurs at the same time as the minimum of $d^2$. For part (d), solve an equation with your GDC and convert hours to minutes at the end.

subtopic: Scalar product and the angle between vectors
statement: The vectors $\mathbf a=\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 0 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf b=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ are given. (a) Find $\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b$. [2] (b) Find $|\mathbf a|$ and $|\mathbf b|$. [2] (c) Find the angle between $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$, giving your answer to the nearest degree. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b=\sum a_ib_i$ [M1] $=7$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $|\mathbf a|=5$ [A1] $|\mathbf b|=\sqrt{3}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\cos\theta=\dfrac{\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b}{|\mathbf a||\mathbf b|}$ [M1] $=\frac{7 \sqrt{3}}{15}$ [A1] $\theta=36^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Use $\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b=|\mathbf a||\mathbf b|\cos\theta$ and take the inverse cosine; a negative scalar product means an obtuse angle.

subtopic: Cable car line: length, point at a given height and elevation angle
statement: A cable car runs in a straight line from a base station $A(0,0,0)$ to a summit station $B(1200,500,650)$, where coordinates are in meters and $z$ is the height above the base. (a) Find the length of the cable, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (b) Write down a vector equation of the line $AB$ using a parameter $\lambda$ such that $\lambda=1$ at $B$. [1] (c) A midway pylon is at height $300$ m. Find the $x$ and $y$ coordinates of the point on the cable at this height, correct to 3 significant figures. [3] (d) Find the angle of elevation of the cable above the horizontal, correct to the nearest degree. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\sqrt{1200^2+500^2+650^2}$ [M1] $=1450$ m [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\mathbf{r}=\lambda\begin{pmatrix} 1200 \\ 500 \\ 650 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $650\lambda=300$ so $\lambda=\dfrac{6}{13}$ [M1] $x=1200\lambda=554$ [A1] $y=500\lambda=231$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) horizontal distance $=\sqrt{1200^2+500^2}=1300$ [A1] $\tan\phi=\dfrac{650}{1300}$ [M1] $\phi=27^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Choosing a parameter that equals 1 at the far end makes it easy to locate any fraction along the line. For elevation use the vertical rise against the horizontal distance, not the total length.
