subtopic: Vector proof: diagonals of a parallelogram
statement: $OABC$ is a parallelogram with $\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf a$ and $\overrightarrow{OC}=\mathbf c$. The diagonals are $OB$ and $AC$. (a) Express $\overrightarrow{OB}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}$ in terms of $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf c$. [2] (b) Show that the midpoint of $OB$ and the midpoint of $AC$ are the same point, and state what this shows about the diagonals. [3] (c) Given that $|\mathbf a|=|\mathbf c|$, show that the diagonals are perpendicular. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\overrightarrow{OB}=\mathbf a+\mathbf c$ [A1] $\overrightarrow{AC}=\mathbf c-\mathbf a$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) midpoint of $OB$: $\dfrac12(\mathbf a+\mathbf c)$ [A1] midpoint of $AC$: $\mathbf a+\dfrac12(\mathbf c-\mathbf a)=\dfrac12(\mathbf a+\mathbf c)$ [M1] the same, so the diagonals bisect each other [R1] [3 marks] (c) $\overrightarrow{OB}\cdot\overrightarrow{AC}=(\mathbf a+\mathbf c)\cdot(\mathbf c-\mathbf a)$ [M1] $=|\mathbf c|^2-|\mathbf a|^2$ [A1] $=0$ since $|\mathbf a|=|\mathbf c|$ [R1] [3 marks]
tips: Write every vector in terms of two position vectors from $O$. Perpendicular vectors have zero scalar product.

subtopic: A particle moving in a straight line towards a plane
statement: A bird flies so that its position (in meters) at time $t$ seconds is $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 5 \end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}$, where the $z$-coordinate is the height above flat ground (the plane $z=0$). (a) Find the speed of the bird. [2] (b) Find the time at which the bird reaches the ground and its position then. [3] (c) Find the distance travelled by the bird before it reaches the ground. [1]
markscheme: (a) speed $=\left|\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}\right|$ [M1] $=\sqrt{1+4+4}=3\text{ m s}^{-1}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $5-2t=0$ [M1] $t=2.5$ s [A1] position $(4.5,\ 6,\ 0)$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $3\times2.5=7.5$ m [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Speed is the magnitude of the velocity vector. The ground is where the vertical coordinate is zero.

subtopic: Resolving a force into components along and perpendicular to a direction
statement: A force $\mathbf F=\begin{pmatrix}6\\ -3\\ 2\end{pmatrix}$ N acts on a particle. The particle can move only in the direction $\mathbf d=\begin{pmatrix}2\\ 1\\ 2\end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find the component of $\mathbf F$ parallel to $\mathbf d$, as a vector. [3] (b) Find the component of $\mathbf F$ perpendicular to $\mathbf d$, and verify that it is perpendicular. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf d}{|\mathbf d|^2}\mathbf d$ [M1] $\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf d=12-3+4=13$ and $|\mathbf d|^2=9$ [A1] $\dfrac{13}9\begin{pmatrix}2\\ 1\\ 2\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\mathbf F-\dfrac{13}9\mathbf d=\dfrac19\begin{pmatrix}28\\ -40\\ -8\end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1] dot product with $\mathbf d$: $56-40-16=0$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The parallel component is the projection of the force onto the direction. The remainder is perpendicular to the direction.

subtopic: Shortest distance from a point to a line
statement: The line $l$ has equation $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$ and the point $P$ has coordinates $(3, 0, 2)$. (a) Find the value of $\lambda$ at the foot $F$ of the perpendicular from $P$ to $l$. [2] (b) Find the coordinates of $F$ and the shortest distance from $P$ to $l$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\overrightarrow{PF}\cdot\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}=0$ with $F$ on $l$ [M1] $\lambda=\frac{1}{3}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $F=(\frac{1}{3}, \frac{5}{3}, \frac{5}{3})$ [A1] $PF=\sqrt{10}$ [M1] $=3.162$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: At the foot of the perpendicular, $\overrightarrow{PF}$ is perpendicular to the direction of the line. Alternatively the distance is $\dfrac{|\overrightarrow{AP}\times\mathbf d|}{|\mathbf d|}$.

subtopic: Perpendicular vectors and the angle between vectors
statement: Let $\mathbf{a}=\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ k \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{b}=\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 4 \\ k \end{pmatrix}$, where $k$ is a real constant. (a) Find the value of $k$ for which $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ are perpendicular. [3] (b) For $k=1$, find the angle between $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$, to the nearest degree. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=6+4k-k$ [M1]; $6+3k=0$ [A1]; $k=-2$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=9$, $|\mathbf{a}|=\sqrt6$, $|\mathbf{b}|=\sqrt{26}$ [A1]; $\cos\theta=\dfrac{9}{\sqrt{156}}$ [M1]; $44^{\circ}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Two vectors are perpendicular exactly when their scalar product is zero.

subtopic: Scalar product and the angle between vectors
statement: The vectors $\mathbf a=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf b=\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$ are given. (a) Find $\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b$. [2] (b) Find $|\mathbf a|$ and $|\mathbf b|$. [2] (c) Find the angle between $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$, giving your answer to the nearest degree. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b=\sum a_ib_i$ [M1] $=0$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $|\mathbf a|=\sqrt{14}$ [A1] $|\mathbf b|=\sqrt{5}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\cos\theta=\dfrac{\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b}{|\mathbf a||\mathbf b|}$ [M1] $=0$ [A1] $\theta=90^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Use $\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b=|\mathbf a||\mathbf b|\cos\theta$ and take the inverse cosine; a negative scalar product means an obtuse angle.

subtopic: Two aircraft in 3D: near miss and separation rule
statement: Two aircraft are tracked by an air traffic control center at the origin. Distances are in kilometers and $t$ is the time in minutes after tracking begins. Aircraft $P$ has position $\mathbf{r}_P=\begin{pmatrix} -20 \\ 35 \\ 8 \end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix} 7 \\ -5 \\ 0.2 \end{pmatrix}$ and aircraft $Q$ has position $\mathbf{r}_Q=\begin{pmatrix} 60 \\ -15 \\ 9.5 \end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix} -8 \\ 4 \\ -0.3 \end{pmatrix}$, where the third component is the altitude. (a) Show that $\overrightarrow{PQ}=\begin{pmatrix} 80-15t \\ -50+9t \\ 1.5-0.5t \end{pmatrix}$. [2] (b) Show that the aircraft do not collide. [3] (c) Find the minimum distance between the aircraft and the time at which it occurs. Give both answers to 3 significant figures. [3] (d) Regulations require a separation of at least $5$ km. Find the length of time, in seconds to the nearest second, for which the separation is less than $5$ km. [3] (e) Find the vertical separation of the aircraft at the time of closest approach, correct to 3 significant figures, and state which aircraft is higher. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\overrightarrow{PQ}=\mathbf{r}_Q-\mathbf{r}_P$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix} 80-15t \\ -50+9t \\ 1.5-0.5t \end{pmatrix}$ [AG] [2 marks] (b) A collision needs $\overrightarrow{PQ}=\mathbf{0}$ [M1] $80-15t=0$ gives $t=\dfrac{16}{3}$ [A1] but $-50+9t=0$ gives $t=\dfrac{50}{9}$, a different time, so no collision [R1] [3 marks] (c) $|\overrightarrow{PQ}|^2=306.25t^2-3301.5t+8902.25$ (or use of GDC on $|\overrightarrow{PQ}|$) [M1] $t=5.39$ minutes [A1] $d=2.09$ km [A1] [3 marks] (d) Solve $|\overrightarrow{PQ}|^2=25$ [M1] $t=5.13$ and $t=5.65$ [A1] $(5.65-5.13)\times60=31$ seconds [A1] [3 marks] (e) $1.5-0.5(5.39)$ [M1] $=-1.20$ so the vertical separation is $1.20$ km, and $P$ is higher [A1] [2 marks]
tips: To show that two aircraft collide you need all three components of their separation to vanish at the same time. For the minimum distance, a quadratic in $t$ for the squared distance is easy to explore on your GDC.

subtopic: A light ray hitting the floor
statement: A ray of light passes through the point $A(1,2,5)$ with direction $\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \\ -4 \end{pmatrix}$ and hits the floor, which is the plane $z=0$, at the point $F$. (a) Write down a vector equation of the ray and find the coordinates of $F$. [3] (b) Find the distance $AF$, to three significant figures. [2] (c) Find the angle between the ray and the floor, to the nearest tenth of a degree. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{r}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 5 \end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \\ -4 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; $5-4\lambda=0$ gives $\lambda=1.25$ [M1]; $F=(3.5,\,0.75,\,0)$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $1.25\sqrt{4+1+16}$ [M1]; $5.73$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) the vertical component is $4$ and $|d|=\sqrt{21}$ [A1]; $\sin\theta=\dfrac{4}{\sqrt{21}}$ [M1]; $60.8^{\circ}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The angle between a line and a horizontal plane is found from the vertical component of the direction vector.

subtopic: Cartesian equation of a plane through three points
statement: The points $A(1, 0, 0)$, $B(0, 2, 0)$ and $C(0, 0, 3)$ lie in a plane $\Pi$. (a) Find $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}$. [2] (b) Find a vector normal to $\Pi$. [2] (c) Find the Cartesian equation of $\Pi$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 2 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 0 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}=\begin{pmatrix} 6 \\ 3 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (c) $\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf r=\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf a$ [M1] $6x+3y+2z=6$ [A1] check with $B$ and $C$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Take the cross product of two vectors in the plane to get the normal, then use $\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf r=\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf a$ with any point of the plane.

subtopic: Intercepting a moving target
statement: A drone moves in a horizontal plane with position $\begin{pmatrix}10-2t\\ t\end{pmatrix}$ km at time $t$ hours. An interceptor leaves the origin at $t=0$ and travels in a straight line at a constant speed of $5$ km/h. (a) Show that the interceptor meets the drone at time $t$ where $t^2+2t-5=0$. [3] (b) Find the time of the interception and the position of the drone at that time. [3] (c) Find the angle above the positive $x$-axis at which the interceptor should be launched, to the nearest tenth of a degree. [2]
markscheme: (a) distance from the origin to the drone is $\sqrt{(10-2t)^2+t^2}$ [A1] this equals $5t$ at the meeting time [M1] $100-40t+5t^2=25t^2$, so $20t^2+40t-100=0$, that is $t^2+2t-5=0$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $t=-1+\sqrt6=1.45$ hours [A1] position $(10-2t,\ t)$ [M1] $=(7.10,\ 1.45)$ km [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\tan\theta=\dfrac{1.449}{7.101}$ [M1] $\theta=11.5^\circ$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: At the interception time, the distance travelled by the interceptor equals the distance from the origin to the drone's position.

subtopic: Intercepting a moving target
statement: A coast-guard boat leaves the origin $O$ at time $t=0$ and travels in a straight line at a constant speed of $20$ km/h to intercept a target vessel. At $t=0$ the target is at $(30,40)$ km and moves with constant velocity $(-6,2)$ km/h. (a) Write down the position of the target at time $t$ hours. [1] (b) Show that interception at time $t$ requires $(30-6t)^2+(40+2t)^2=400t^2$, and simplify. [3] (c) Solve for $t$ and find the position of the interception point. [3] (d) Find the velocity of the boat, and check that its speed is $20$ km/h. [3]
tips: Equate the boat's distance traveled with the target's distance from the start at the interception time, then solve the quadratic in $t$ and take the positive root.

subtopic: Intersection of two lines and the angle between them
statement: Two lines are given by $l_1:\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$ and $l_2:\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 4 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}+\mu\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Use the first two components to find $\lambda$ and $\mu$ at a possible intersection. [3] (b) Show that the lines intersect and find the coordinates of the point of intersection. [3] (c) Find the acute angle between the lines. [3]
markscheme: (a) equate components [M1] $\lambda=1$ [A1] $\mu=1$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) check the third component [M1] both give the same value so the lines intersect [R1] point of intersection $=(3, 3, 2)$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\cos\theta=\dfrac{|\mathbf d_1\cdot\mathbf d_2|}{|\mathbf d_1||\mathbf d_2|}$ [M1] $=\frac{1}{6}$ [A1] $\theta=80.4^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Solve two component equations, then test the third. Lines that are neither parallel nor intersecting are skew. The angle between lines uses the direction vectors only.

subtopic: Time an aircraft spends within radar range
statement: A radar station at the origin detects aircraft within $50$ km. An aircraft flies at constant altitude with position vector $\mathbf{r}=\begin{pmatrix} -90 \\ 40 \end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix} 110 \\ -30 \end{pmatrix}$ relative to the station, where distances are in kilometers and $t$ is in hours after $12{:}00$. (a) Find the speed of the aircraft, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (b) Show that the distance $d$ of the aircraft from the station satisfies $d^2=13000t^2-22200t+9700$. [2] (c) Find the two values of $t$ for which the aircraft is exactly $50$ km from the station. [3] (d) Find the length of time, to the nearest minute, for which the aircraft is within range of the radar. [2] (e) Find the minimum distance between the aircraft and the station, correct to 3 significant figures. [2]
tips: Turn the problem into a quadratic equation by squaring the distance. The time inside the range is the difference between the two roots, converted to minutes.

subtopic: Dividing a line segment in a given ratio
statement: The points $A$ and $B$ have position vectors $\overrightarrow{OA}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\3\end{pmatrix}$ and $\overrightarrow{OB}=\begin{pmatrix}7\\-4\\9\end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find $\overrightarrow{AB}$. [1] (b) Find the exact value of $|\overrightarrow{AB}|$. [2] (c) The point $P$ lies on $AB$ such that $AP:PB=1:2$. Find the position vector of $P$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix}6\\-6\\6\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $|\overrightarrow{AB}|=\sqrt{36+36+36}$ [M1] $=\sqrt{108}=6\sqrt3$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\overrightarrow{AP}=\tfrac13\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-2\\2\end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $\overrightarrow{OP}=\overrightarrow{OA}+\overrightarrow{AP}$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix}3\\0\\5\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: For a ratio $AP:PB=1:2$, the point is one-third of the way from $A$ to $B$, not one-half. Write $\overrightarrow{AB}=\overrightarrow{OB}-\overrightarrow{OA}$ before doing anything else.

subtopic: Vector equation of a line through two points
statement: The points $A(1, 2, -1)$ and $B(3, 1, 2)$ lie on a line $l$. (a) Find a vector equation of $l$. [3] (b) Determine whether the point $Q(7, -1, 8)$ lies on $l$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1] [3 marks] (b) set $\mathbf r=\overrightarrow{OQ}$ and solve for $\lambda$ from each component [M1] $\lambda$ values: 3.0, 3.0, 3.0 [A1] consistent, so $Q$ lies on $l$ [R1] [3 marks]
tips: A line needs a point and a direction vector. A point lies on the line only if the same value of the parameter works in all three components.

subtopic: Intercepting a moving vessel at a given speed
statement: A patrol boat leaves a harbor at the origin $O$ at $t=0$ and travels in a straight line at a constant speed of $15$ km h$^{-1}$. A suspect vessel is at the point $(30,40)$ at $t=0$ and moves with constant velocity $\begin{pmatrix} 6 \\ -8 \end{pmatrix}$ km h$^{-1}$. The $x$ and $y$ directions are east and north, distances are in kilometers, and $t$ is in hours. The patrol boat intercepts the vessel at time $t=T$. (a) Write down the position vector of the vessel at time $t$. [1] (b) Show that $T$ satisfies the equation $125T^2+280T-2500=0$. [3] (c) Solve the equation to find $T$, correct to 3 significant figures, and justify your choice of root. [3] (d) Find the coordinates of the interception point, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (e) Find the bearing on which the patrol boat should sail, to the nearest degree. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\begin{pmatrix} 30+6t \\ 40-8t \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Distance traveled by the patrol boat $=15T$ [A1] $(30+6T)^2+(40-8T)^2=(15T)^2$ [M1] $2500-280T+100T^2=225T^2$ so $125T^2+280T-2500=0$ [AG] [3 marks] (c) $T=3.49$ [A1] the other root is $-5.73$, which is negative, and time must be positive [R1] (use of GDC solver or quadratic formula) [M1] [3 marks] (d) $(30+6\times3.49,\ 40-8\times3.49)$ [M1] $(50.9,\ 12.1)$ [A1] [2 marks] (e) $\tan^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{50.9}{12.1}\right)$ [M1] bearing $=77^\circ$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Interception problems are solved by equating the distance the pursuer travels with the distance from the origin to the target at that time. Reject any root that gives a negative time.

subtopic: Collinearity and ratio; line meets coordinate plane
statement: The points $A(2,1,-1)$ and $B(5,4,2)$ lie on a line $L$. The point $C$ has coordinates $(11,p,q)$ and also lies on $L$. (a) Find the values of $p$ and $q$. [3] (b) Find the ratio $AB:BC$. [2] (c) Find the coordinates of the point where $L$ meets the $xy$-plane. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix}3\\3\\3\end{pmatrix}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}=\begin{pmatrix}9\\p-1\\q+1\end{pmatrix}=\lambda\overrightarrow{AB}$ [M1] $\lambda=3$ [A1] $p=10$, $q=8$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\overrightarrow{BC}=\begin{pmatrix}6\\6\\6\end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $AB:BC=1:2$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\-1\end{pmatrix}+\mu\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $z=0\Rightarrow\mu=1$ [M1] $(3,2,0)$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Three points are collinear when one displacement vector is a scalar multiple of another. The $xy$-plane is $z=0$.

subtopic: Scalar product: perpendicular vectors and angle
statement: Let $\mathbf{a}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\3\end{pmatrix}$, $\mathbf{b}=\begin{pmatrix}k\\4\\1\end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{c}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\2\end{pmatrix}$. (a) Given that $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ are perpendicular, find the value of $k$. [3] (b) Find the angle between $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{c}$, correct to the nearest tenth of a degree. [4]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=0$ [M1] $2k-4+3=0$ [A1] $k=\dfrac12$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{c}=2-2+6=6$ [A1] $|\mathbf{a}|=\sqrt{14}$ and $|\mathbf{c}|=3$ [A1] $\cos\theta=\dfrac{6}{3\sqrt{14}}$ [M1] $\theta=57.7^\circ$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Perpendicular vectors have a zero scalar product. Compute the dot product and both magnitudes separately before substituting into $\cos\theta=\dfrac{\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{c}}{|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{c}|}$.

subtopic: A right angle in a triangle and its area
statement: The points $A(1,2,3)$, $B(3,4,2)$ and $C(2,1,3)$ form a triangle. (a) Find $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}$. [2] (b) Show that angle $BAC=90^{\circ}$. [2] (c) Find the exact area of the triangle. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; $\overrightarrow{AC}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot\overrightarrow{AC}=2-2+0=0$ [M1]; so the vectors are perpendicular [A1] [2 marks] (c) $|AB|=3$, $|AC|=\sqrt2$ [A1]; area $=\dfrac12\times3\times\sqrt2=\dfrac{3\sqrt2}{2}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A zero scalar product means the angle between the two vectors is $90^{\circ}$.

subtopic: Lines that intersect: finding an unknown constant
statement: Two lines are $l_1:\ \mathbf{r}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}+s\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$ and $l_2:\ \mathbf{r}=\begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ -1 \\ k \end{pmatrix}+u\begin{pmatrix} -2 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$, where $k$ is a constant. The lines intersect. (a) Use the $x$ and $y$ components to find $s$ and $u$. [3] (b) Find $k$ and the coordinates of the point of intersection. [3] (c) Find the acute angle between the lines, to the nearest tenth of a degree. [3]
tips: Use two components to find the parameters, then use the third component to find $k$.

subtopic: Laser beam reflecting from a wall and reaching the floor
statement: In a science demonstration, a laser beam starts at the point $S(0,1,8)$ and travels in the direction $\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$, where coordinates are in meters. The floor is the plane $z=0$ and a vertical mirror is on the plane $x=10$. (a) Write down a vector equation for the beam before it reaches the mirror. [1] (b) Find the coordinates of the point $H$ where the beam hits the mirror. [3] (c) After reflection in the mirror, the $x$-component of the direction reverses and the other components are unchanged. Write down a vector equation for the reflected beam. [2] (d) Find the coordinates of the point where the reflected beam hits the floor. [2] (e) Find the total length of the beam's path from $S$ to the floor, correct to 3 significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{r}=\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 8 \end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $2\lambda=10$ so $\lambda=5$ [M1][A1] $H(10,6,3)$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) new direction $\begin{pmatrix} -2 \\ 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\mathbf{r}=\begin{pmatrix} 10 \\ 6 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}+\mu\begin{pmatrix} -2 \\ 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $3-\mu=0$ so $\mu=3$ [M1] $(4,9,0)$ [A1] [2 marks] (e) $|\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}|=\sqrt6$ [A1] $5\sqrt6+3\sqrt6$ [M1] $=8\sqrt6=19.6$ m [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Reflection in a plane perpendicular to the $x$-axis reverses only the $x$-component of the direction. Because the speed along the parameter is the same, path length is parameter multiplied by the length of the direction vector.

subtopic: Line through two points and where it meets the ground
statement: A zip line is strung from the point $A(1,-2,4)$ to the point $B(3,0,3)$, where coordinates are in meters and the $z$-axis points upward from the ground $z=0$. The line $L$ passes through $A$ and $B$. (a) Find $\overrightarrow{AB}$. [1] (b) Write down a vector equation of $L$. [2] (c) Show that the point $C(7,4,1)$ lies on $L$. [2] (d) Find the coordinates of the point where the line meets the ground. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\mathbf{r}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (c) $1+2\lambda=7$ gives $\lambda=3$ [M1] $-2+2(3)=4$ and $4-3=1$, so $C$ lies on $L$ [R1] [2 marks] (d) $4-\lambda=0$ so $\lambda=4$ [M1] point $(9,6,0)$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A point lies on a line if one value of the parameter gives all three coordinates. For the ground, set the $z$-component equal to zero first.

subtopic: Reflection of a ray in a plane
statement: A light ray leaves the origin in the direction $\mathbf d=\begin{pmatrix}2\\ 2\\ 1\end{pmatrix}$ and hits the plane $\Pi$ with equation $x+2y+2z=9$. A ray with direction $\mathbf d$ reflects from a plane with normal $\mathbf n$ with new direction $\mathbf d'=\mathbf d-\dfrac{2(\mathbf d\cdot\mathbf n)}{|\mathbf n|^2}\mathbf n$. (a) Find the coordinates of the point $P$ where the ray meets $\Pi$. [3] (b) Find the direction of the reflected ray. [3] (c) Find the angle between the incoming ray and the normal to the plane, and show that $\mathbf d'$ has the same length as $\mathbf d$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $(2t,2t,t)$ in the plane: $2t+4t+2t=9$ [M1] $t=\dfrac98$ [A1] $P=\left(\dfrac94,\dfrac94,\dfrac98\right)$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\mathbf n=\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 2\\ 2\end{pmatrix}$, $\mathbf d\cdot\mathbf n=8$ and $|\mathbf n|^2=9$ [A1] $\mathbf d'=\begin{pmatrix}2\\ 2\\ 1\end{pmatrix}-\dfrac{16}9\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 2\\ 2\end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=\dfrac19\begin{pmatrix}2\\ -14\\ -23\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\cos\phi=\dfrac{8}{3\times3}$ [M1] $\phi=27.3^\circ$ [A1] $|\mathbf d'|^2=\dfrac{4+196+529}{81}=9=|\mathbf d|^2$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A reflection reverses the component of the direction along the normal and keeps the component in the plane.

subtopic: Line of intersection of two planes
statement: Two planes have equations $\Pi_1:1x+1y+1z=6$ and $\Pi_2:1x-1y+2z=3$. (a) Find a direction vector of the line of intersection of the two planes. [3] (b) Find a point on the line, and write down a vector equation of the line. [3] (c) Find the acute angle between the planes. [2]
markscheme: (a) the direction is perpendicular to both normals [R1] $\mathbf n_1\times\mathbf n_2=\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ -1 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1] [3 marks] (b) set $z=0$ and solve [M1] point $(9/2, 3/2, 0)$ [A1] $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix} \frac{9}{2} \\ \frac{3}{2} \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ -1 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\cos\theta=\dfrac{|\mathbf n_1\cdot\mathbf n_2|}{|\mathbf n_1||\mathbf n_2|}=0.4714$ [M1] $\theta=61.9^\circ$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The line of intersection lies in both planes so its direction is perpendicular to both normals. The angle between two planes equals the angle between their normals.

subtopic: Cross product and the area of a triangle
statement: The points $A$, $B$ and $C$ have coordinates $A(1,0,2)$, $B(3,1,0)$ and $C(2,4,1)$. (a) Find $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}$. [2] (b) Find $\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}$. [3] (c) Hence find the exact area of triangle $ABC$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\overrightarrow{AC}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 4 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) cross product [M1] components [A1] $\begin{pmatrix} 7 \\ 0 \\ 7 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) area $=\dfrac12\left|\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}\right|$ [M1] $=\dfrac12\sqrt{98}=\frac{7 \sqrt{2}}{2}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Area of a triangle $=\frac12|\mathbf a\times\mathbf b|$. The cross product is perpendicular to both $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}$.

subtopic: Line of intersection of two planes
statement: Two planes have equations $\Pi_1:2x+1y-1z=5$ and $\Pi_2:1x+3y+1z=10$. (a) Find a direction vector of the line of intersection of the two planes. [3] (b) Find a point on the line, and write down a vector equation of the line. [3] (c) Find the acute angle between the planes. [2]
markscheme: (a) the direction is perpendicular to both normals [R1] $\mathbf n_1\times\mathbf n_2=\begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ -3 \\ 5 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1] [3 marks] (b) set $z=0$ and solve [M1] point $(1, 3, 0)$ [A1] $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ -3 \\ 5 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\cos\theta=\dfrac{|\mathbf n_1\cdot\mathbf n_2|}{|\mathbf n_1||\mathbf n_2|}=0.4924$ [M1] $\theta=60.5^\circ$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The line of intersection lies in both planes so its direction is perpendicular to both normals. The angle between two planes equals the angle between their normals.

subtopic: Angle, area and perimeter of a triangle from 3D coordinates
statement: Three beacons are located at $A(2,1,-3)$, $B(5,-2,4)$ and $C(-1,3,6)$, with coordinates in kilometers. (a) Find $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}$. [2] (b) Find angle $BAC$, correct to the nearest tenth of a degree. [3] (c) Find the area of triangle $ABC$, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (d) Find the perimeter of the triangle, correct to 3 significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ -3 \\ 7 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\overrightarrow{AC}=\begin{pmatrix} -3 \\ 2 \\ 9 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot\overrightarrow{AC}=48$ [A1] $\cos BAC=\dfrac{48}{\sqrt{67}\sqrt{94}}$ [M1] $BAC=52.8^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\dfrac12\sqrt{67}\sqrt{94}\sin(52.8^\circ)$ [M1] $=31.6$ km$^2$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $|\overrightarrow{AB}|=8.19$, $|\overrightarrow{AC}|=9.70$ [A1] $\overrightarrow{BC}=\begin{pmatrix} -6 \\ 5 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$, $|\overrightarrow{BC}|=8.06$ [A1] perimeter $=25.9$ km [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Form both vectors from the same vertex before using the scalar product formula. Keep the unrounded angle in your calculator for the area calculation.

subtopic: A regular tetrahedron inscribed in a cube
statement: The points $A(1,1,1)$, $B(1,-1,-1)$, $C(-1,1,-1)$ and $D(-1,-1,1)$ are four vertices of a cube with vertices $(\pm1,\pm1,\pm1)$, and $O$ is the origin. (a) Show that all six edges of $ABCD$ have length $2\sqrt2$. [2] (b) Find the angle $AOB$ between two vertices seen from the centre. [3] (c) Show that the plane through $A$, $B$, $C$ has equation $x+y-z=1$, and find the equation of the plane through $A$, $B$, $D$. [4] (d) The outward normals to the faces $ABC$ and $ABD$ are $\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 1\\ -1\end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix}1\\ -1\\ 1\end{pmatrix}$. Find the angle between these faces, explaining how it relates to the angle between the normals. [3] (e) The tetrahedron is obtained from the cube by removing four corner tetrahedra. Find its volume, and check it against the formula $V=\dfrac{\sqrt2}{12}s^3$ for a regular tetrahedron with edge $s$. [3]
markscheme: (a) e.g. $\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\ -2\\ -2\end{pmatrix}$ has length $\sqrt8=2\sqrt2$ [A1] the other five edge vectors are $\begin{pmatrix}-2\\ 0\\ -2\end{pmatrix}$, $\begin{pmatrix}-2\\ -2\\ 0\end{pmatrix}$, $\begin{pmatrix}-2\\ 2\\ 0\end{pmatrix}$, $\begin{pmatrix}-2\\ 0\\ 2\end{pmatrix}$, $\begin{pmatrix}0\\ -2\\ 2\end{pmatrix}$, each with length $2\sqrt2$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\overrightarrow{OA}\cdot\overrightarrow{OB}=1-1-1=-1$ [A1] $|\overrightarrow{OA}|^2=3$ [A1] $\cos AOB=-\dfrac13$, so $AOB=109.5^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\ -2\\ -2\end{pmatrix}\times\begin{pmatrix}-2\\ 0\\ -2\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}4\\ 4\\ -4\end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1] $x+y-z=1$ using $A$ [AG] plane $ABD$: $\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AD}=\begin{pmatrix}-4\\ 4\\ -4\end{pmatrix}$, giving $-x+y-z=-1$ [A1][A1] [4 marks] (d) $\cos\alpha=\dfrac{1-1-1}{3}=-\dfrac13$ for the outward normals [A1] the angle between the faces is $180^\circ-\alpha$ [R1] $=\arccos\dfrac13=70.5^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) cube volume $2^3=8$ [A1] each corner tetrahedron has volume $\dfrac13\times\dfrac12\times2\times2\times2=\dfrac43$, so $V=8-4\times\dfrac43=\dfrac83$ [A1] $\dfrac{\sqrt2}{12}\left(2\sqrt2\right)^3=\dfrac{\sqrt2}{12}\times16\sqrt2=\dfrac83$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Alternating vertices of a cube form a regular tetrahedron. The angle between faces is the angle between the normals when the normals point outward, subtracted from $180^\circ$.

subtopic: Ratios in which two cevians of a triangle divide each other
statement: In triangle $ABC$, let $\overrightarrow{AB}=\mathbf b$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}=\mathbf c$. The point $D$ lies on $BC$ with $BD:DC=1:2$, and $E$ is the midpoint of $AC$. The lines $AD$ and $BE$ meet at $P$. (a) Show that $\overrightarrow{AD}=\dfrac13(2\mathbf b+\mathbf c)$, and write down $\overrightarrow{AE}$. [3] (b) Write $\overrightarrow{AP}$ in two ways, using $\overrightarrow{AP}=\lambda\overrightarrow{AD}$ and $\overrightarrow{AP}=\overrightarrow{AB}+\mu\overrightarrow{BE}$, and find $\lambda$ and $\mu$. [5] (c) State the ratios $AP:PD$ and $BP:PE$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\overrightarrow{AD}=\mathbf b+\dfrac13(\mathbf c-\mathbf b)$ [M1] $=\dfrac13(2\mathbf b+\mathbf c)$ [AG] [A1] $\overrightarrow{AE}=\dfrac12\mathbf c$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\overrightarrow{AP}=\dfrac\lambda3(2\mathbf b+\mathbf c)$ [A1] $\overrightarrow{AP}=\mathbf b+\mu\left(\dfrac12\mathbf c-\mathbf b\right)=(1-\mu)\mathbf b+\dfrac\mu2\mathbf c$ [A1] $\mathbf b$ and $\mathbf c$ are not parallel, so compare coefficients: $\dfrac{2\lambda}3=1-\mu$ and $\dfrac\lambda3=\dfrac\mu2$ [M1] solve: $\lambda=\dfrac34$ [A1] $\mu=\dfrac12$ [A1] [5 marks] (c) $AP:PD=3:1$ and $BP:PE=1:1$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Take $A$ as the origin so that the two non-parallel vectors $\mathbf b$ and $\mathbf c$ serve as a basis. Equate coefficients.

subtopic: Closest point on a line and area of triangle
statement: The line $l$ has equation $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\0\end{pmatrix}+s\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\-2\end{pmatrix}$ and the point $P$ has coordinates $(5,4,3)$. (a) Find the coordinates of the point $Q$ on $l$ that is closest to $P$. [4] (b) Find the shortest distance from $P$ to $l$. [2] (c) The points $R$ and $S$ lie on $l$ with $s=-1$ and $s=2$ respectively. Find the area of triangle $PRS$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\overrightarrow{PQ}=\begin{pmatrix}2s-4\\s-2\\-2s-3\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\overrightarrow{PQ}\cdot\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\-2\end{pmatrix}=0$ [M1] $4s-8+s-2+4s+6=9s-4=0$ [A1] $s=\dfrac49$, $Q=\left(\dfrac{17}{9},\dfrac{22}{9},-\dfrac89\right)=(1.89,\,2.44,\,-0.889)$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $|\overrightarrow{PQ}|$ [M1] $=\dfrac{7\sqrt5}{3}=5.22$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $RS=3\left|\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\-2\end{pmatrix}\right|=9$ [A1] Area $=\tfrac12\times9\times5.217$ [M1] $=23.5$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The shortest distance from a point to a line is along the perpendicular, so set the scalar product of $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ with the direction vector to zero. The perpendicular distance is also the height of the triangle.

subtopic: Vector proof that the midpoints of a quadrilateral form a parallelogram
statement: $ABCD$ is any quadrilateral with position vectors $\mathbf a$, $\mathbf b$, $\mathbf c$, $\mathbf d$. The points $P$, $Q$, $R$, $S$ are the midpoints of $AB$, $BC$, $CD$, $DA$ respectively. (a) Write down the position vectors of $P$, $Q$, $R$, $S$. [2] (b) Show that $\overrightarrow{PQ}=\overrightarrow{SR}$, and deduce that $PQRS$ is a parallelogram. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf p=\dfrac{\mathbf a+\mathbf b}2$, $\mathbf q=\dfrac{\mathbf b+\mathbf c}2$ [A1] $\mathbf r=\dfrac{\mathbf c+\mathbf d}2$, $\mathbf s=\dfrac{\mathbf d+\mathbf a}2$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\overrightarrow{PQ}=\mathbf q-\mathbf p=\dfrac{\mathbf c-\mathbf a}2$ [M1] $\overrightarrow{SR}=\mathbf r-\mathbf s=\dfrac{\mathbf c-\mathbf a}2$ [A1] equal vectors give a pair of opposite sides that are equal and parallel, so $PQRS$ is a parallelogram [R1] [3 marks]
tips: The vector joining two midpoints is half of the vector between the corresponding vertices.

subtopic: Two aircraft on constant velocities in three dimensions
statement: This question investigates the safety of two aircraft. Position is measured in kilometers from a radar station at the origin $O$, with $x$ east, $y$ north and $z$ the altitude. At time $t=0$ (hours) aircraft $A$ is at $(0,0,9)$ with velocity $(240,120,0)$ km/h, and aircraft $B$ is at $(150,10,6)$ with velocity $(-180,60,40)$ km/h. (a) Find the speed of each aircraft. [2] (b) Write down the position vector of each aircraft at time $t$ and the vector $\overrightarrow{BA}$ at time $t$. [3] (c) Show that the square of the distance between the aircraft is $d^2=181600 t^2-127440 t+22609$. [3] (d) Find the time at which the aircraft are closest and the least distance between them. [3] (e) The minimum safe separation is $20$ km. Find the times (in minutes after $t=0$) between which the separation is less than $20$ km. [3] (f) Find the acute angle between the flight directions of the two aircraft. [3] (g) At $t=0.5$ hours, find the distance of $B$ from the radar and the angle of elevation of $B$ as seen from the radar. [3] (h) Air traffic control instructs $B$ to climb at a different rate so that its altitude at time $t$ is $6+kt$, with the horizontal velocity unchanged. Find the value of $k$ for which the aircraft are at the same altitude at the time of closest horizontal approach. [3]
markscheme: (a) $|\mathbf{v}_A|=\sqrt{240^2+120^2}=268.3$ km/h [A1]; $|\mathbf{v}_B|=\sqrt{180^2+60^2+40^2}=193.9$ km/h [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\mathbf{r}_A=(240t,120t,9)$ [A1]; $\mathbf{r}_B=(150-180t,10+60t,6+40t)$ [A1]; $\overrightarrow{BA}=(-150+420t,-10+60t,3-40t)$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $d^2=(-150+420t)^2+(-10+60t)^2+(3-40t)^2$ [M1]; coefficients of $t^2$: $176400+3600+1600=181600$ [A1]; $t$: $-127440$, constant: $22609$ [AG] [3 marks] (d) Minimum at $t=-\dfrac{b}{2a}=0.3509$ h [M1][A1]; $d_{min}=15.839$ km [A1] [3 marks] (e) Solve $d^2=400$ [M1]: $t=0.3222$ and $t=0.3795$ h [A1]; i.e. between $19.33$ and $22.77$ minutes [A1] [3 marks] (f) $\cos\theta=\dfrac{|\mathbf{v}_A\cdot\mathbf{v}_B|}{|\mathbf{v}_A||\mathbf{v}_B|}$ [M1]; $\mathbf{v}_A\cdot\mathbf{v}_B=-36000$ [A1]; $\theta=46.2^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks] (g) $\mathbf{r}_B(0.5)=(60,40,26)$ [A1]; distance $=76.66$ km [A1]; elevation $\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{26}{\sqrt{5200}}\right)=19.83^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks] (h) Horizontal separation squared $=(-150+420t)^2+(-10+60t)^2$ [M1]; minimum at $t_h=\dfrac{150\cdot420+10\cdot60}{420^2+60^2}=0.3533$ h [A1]; $9=6+kt_h$ gives $k=8.49$ km/h [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The squared distance between two objects moving with constant velocities is a quadratic in $t$ with leading coefficient $|\mathbf{v}_A-\mathbf{v}_B|^2$; its vertex gives the closest approach.

subtopic: The direction that bisects the angle between two vectors
statement: Let $\mathbf a=\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 2\\ 2\end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf b=\begin{pmatrix}2\\ 3\\ 6\end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find $|\mathbf a|$ and $|\mathbf b|$. [2] (b) The vector $\mathbf d=\dfrac{\mathbf a}{|\mathbf a|}+\dfrac{\mathbf b}{|\mathbf b|}$ bisects the angle between $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$. Show that $\mathbf d$ is parallel to $\begin{pmatrix}13\\ 23\\ 32\end{pmatrix}$. [2] (c) Verify that $\mathbf d$ makes equal angles with $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $|\mathbf a|=3$ [A1] $|\mathbf b|=7$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac13\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 2\\ 2\end{pmatrix}+\dfrac17\begin{pmatrix}2\\ 3\\ 6\end{pmatrix}=\dfrac1{21}\begin{pmatrix}13\\ 23\\ 32\end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (c) $\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf d'=13+46+64=123$ and $\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf d'=26+69+192=287$ for $\mathbf d'=\begin{pmatrix}13\\ 23\\ 32\end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $\cos$ of the angle with $\mathbf a$ is $\dfrac{123}{3|\mathbf d'|}=\dfrac{41}{|\mathbf d'|}$ [A1] with $\mathbf b$: $\dfrac{287}{7|\mathbf d'|}=\dfrac{41}{|\mathbf d'|}$, so the angles are equal [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Two unit vectors of equal length form a rhombus with their sum, and the diagonal of a rhombus bisects its angle.

subtopic: Are two lines in space intersecting or skew?
statement: Line $l_1$ has equation $\mathbf{r}=(1,2,0)+s(2,1,-1)$ and line $l_2$ has equation $\mathbf{r}=(4,1,5)+t(1,-1,2)$. (a) Show that the lines are not parallel. [1] (b) Write down three equations for $s$ and $t$ if the lines intersect, and solve two of them. [3] (c) Check the third equation and state whether the lines intersect. [2]
markscheme: (a) $(2,1,-1)$ is not a multiple of $(1,-1,2)$ [R1] [1 mark] (b) $1+2s=4+t$, $2+s=1-t$, $-s=5+2t$ [A1]; the first two give $t=2s-3$ and $t=-1-s$ [M1]; so $3s=2$, $s=\dfrac23$ and $t=-\dfrac53$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Third equation: left side $-\dfrac23$, right side $5+2\left(-\dfrac53\right)=\dfrac53$ [M1]; not equal, so the lines are skew (they do not intersect) [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Two lines in three dimensions can be parallel, intersecting or skew; check the third equation after solving two.

subtopic: Closest approach of two aircraft
statement: Two aircraft $A$ and $B$ have position vectors, in kilometers relative to an airport, $\mathbf{r}_A=\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 3 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ -1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{r}_B=\begin{pmatrix} 20 \\ 1 \\ 9 \end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix} -3 \\ 2 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$, where $t$ is the time in hours after noon. (a) Find the vector $\overrightarrow{AB}$ at time $t$, and show that the square of the distance between the aircraft is $d^{2}=67t^{2}-312t+392$. [3] (b) Find the time at which the aircraft are closest and the minimum distance between them, in kilometers to 3 significant figures. [3] (c) Safety rules require a separation of at least $6.5$ km. Find the time interval, in hours to 3 significant figures, during which the aircraft are closer than $6.5$ km. [3]
tips: Work with $d^{2}$ rather than $d$ to avoid the square root, then take the square root of the minimum.

subtopic: Lines and planes
statement: The plane $\Pi_1$ has equation $2x-y+2z=7$. The line $L$ has vector equation $$\mathbf{r}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\3\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\-1\end{pmatrix},\quad \lambda\in\mathbb{R}.$$ The point $C(1,-2,3)$ lies on $L$. (a) Show that the point $A(3,1,1)$ lies on $\Pi_1$. [1] (b) Find the coordinates of the point $B$ where $L$ meets $\Pi_1$. [3] (c) Find the acute angle between $L$ and $\Pi_1$. [4] (d) Find the shortest distance from $C$ to $\Pi_1$. [2] (e) The plane $\Pi_2$ contains $L$ and the point $A$. Find the Cartesian equation of $\Pi_2$. [4] (f) Find a vector equation of the line of intersection of $\Pi_1$ and $\Pi_2$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $2(3)-1+2(1)=7$, so $A$ lies on $\Pi_1$ [A1][AG] [1 mark] (b) $2(1+\lambda)-(-2+\lambda)+2(3-\lambda)=7$ [M1] $10-\lambda=7 \Rightarrow \lambda=3$ [A1] $B(4,\,1,\,0)$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\mathbf{n}\cdot\mathbf{d}=2-1-2=-1$ [A1] $\sin\theta=\dfrac{|-1|}{3\times\sqrt{3}}$ [M1][A1] $\theta=11.1^\circ$ ($11.0958\ldots$) or $0.194$ radians [A1] Award [M1] for use of $\sin\theta$, or for $90^\circ$ minus the angle between $\mathbf{n}$ and $\mathbf{d}$. [4 marks] (d) $\dfrac{|2(1)-(-2)+2(3)-7|}{\sqrt{4+1+4}}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{3}{3}=1$ [A1] [2 marks] (e) $\overrightarrow{CA}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\3\\-2\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] Normal $=\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\-1\end{pmatrix}\times\begin{pmatrix}2\\3\\-2\end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}$ (or any multiple) [A1] $x+z=4$ [A1] [4 marks] (f) $A$ and $B$ lie on both planes (or the direction is $\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\2\end{pmatrix}\times\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}$) [M1] $\mathbf{r}=\begin{pmatrix}3\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}+\mu\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\-1\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] Accept any correct point and direction. [2 marks]
tips: The angle between a line and a plane uses $\sin$, not $\cos$, because the normal is perpendicular to the plane. In part (f), look for points already known to lie on both planes before computing a cross product.

subtopic: Three planes: parameter and geometry
statement: Consider the planes $\Pi_1:\ x+y+z=3$, $\Pi_2:\ 2x+y-z=1$ and $\Pi_3:\ 3x+2y+kz=m$, where $k,m\in\mathbb R$. (a) Find the value of $k$ for which the three planes do not meet at a single point. [3] (b) For this value of $k$, find the value of $m$ for which the three planes intersect in a line. [2] (c) For this value of $k$ and $m\neq4$, describe the geometrical arrangement of the three planes. [2] (d) For $m=4$, find a vector equation of the line of intersection. [3]
markscheme: (a) Determinant of coefficient matrix [M1] $\begin{vmatrix}1&1&1\\2&1&-1\\3&2&k\end{vmatrix}=1(k+2)-1(2k+3)+1(4-3)=-k$ [A1] No unique intersection when $k=0$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) With $k=0$ the left side of $\Pi_3$ is $\Pi_1+\Pi_2$ [M1] Consistent when $m=3+1=4$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) No common point, but no two planes are parallel (normals not multiples) [R1] The planes form a triangular prism [A1] [2 marks] (d) Let $z=\lambda$: $x+y=3-\lambda$, $2x+y=1+\lambda$ [M1] $x=-2+2\lambda$, $y=5-3\lambda$ [A1] $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\5\\0\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}2\\-3\\1\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: For three planes, zero determinant means either a common line or a triangular prism (or parallel planes); consistency decides which. Check that no two normal vectors are parallel before naming the arrangement.

subtopic: Distance from a point to a plane and the reflection of a point
statement: The plane $\Pi$ has equation $2x-2y+1z=3$ and the point $P$ is $(1, 2, 3)$. (a) Find the shortest distance from $P$ to $\Pi$. [3] (b) Find the coordinates of the foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to $\Pi$. [3] (c) Hence find the reflection of $P$ in $\Pi$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{|2(1)-2(2)+1(3)-3|}{\sqrt{9}}$ [M1][A1] $=\frac{2}{3}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) line through $P$ with direction $\mathbf n$: $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}+s\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $s=\frac{2}{9}$ [A1] foot $(\frac{13}{9}, \frac{14}{9}, \frac{29}{9})$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) reflection $=2F-P$ [M1] $(\frac{17}{9}, \frac{10}{9}, \frac{31}{9})$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The shortest distance from a point to a plane is along the normal. The reflection is the same distance beyond the plane.

subtopic: Centroid of a triangle using position vectors
statement: A triangle has vertices $A(1,2)$, $B(7,4)$ and $C(4,9)$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$ and $G$ the point on $AM$ with $AG:GM=2:1$. (a) Find the coordinates of $M$ and $G$. [3] (b) Show that $\overrightarrow{OG}=\dfrac13\left(\overrightarrow{OA}+\overrightarrow{OB}+\overrightarrow{OC}\right)$ for these points. [2] (c) Find the area of triangle $ABC$ using $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $M=(5.5,\,6.5)$ [A1]; $\overrightarrow{AM}=\begin{pmatrix} 4.5 \\ 4.5 \end{pmatrix}$, $\overrightarrow{OG}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}+\dfrac23\begin{pmatrix} 4.5 \\ 4.5 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1]; $G=(4,5)$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\dfrac13\begin{pmatrix} 1+7+4 \\ 2+4+9 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1]; $=\begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 5 \end{pmatrix}$ [AG] [2 marks] (c) $\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix} 6 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$, $\overrightarrow{AC}=\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 7 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; area $=\dfrac12|6\times7-2\times3|$ [M1]; $18$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The three medians of a triangle meet at the centroid, which divides each median in the ratio $2:1$.

subtopic: Line parallel to a plane and distance
statement: The line $l$ has equation $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\-1\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}2\\a\\1\end{pmatrix}$ and the plane $\Pi$ has equation $3x-y+2z=b$, where $a,b\in\mathbb R$. (a) Given that $l$ is parallel to $\Pi$, find $a$. [3] (b) Given also that $l$ lies in $\Pi$, find $b$. [2] (c) Given instead that $b=6$, find the distance between $l$ and $\Pi$. [3]
markscheme: (a) Direction vector perpendicular to normal [M1] $\begin{pmatrix}2\\a\\1\end{pmatrix}\cdot\begin{pmatrix}3\\-1\\2\end{pmatrix}=6-a+2=0$ [A1] $a=8$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Substitute a point of $l$, e.g. $(1,2,-1)$ [M1] $b=3-2-2=-1$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) The distance is that of any point of $l$ to $\Pi$, e.g. $(1,2,-1)$ [M1] $\dfrac{|3-2-2-6|}{\sqrt{14}}=\dfrac{7}{\sqrt{14}}$ [A1] $=\dfrac{\sqrt{14}}{2}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A line parallel to a plane has a direction vector perpendicular to the plane's normal, and every point on it is the same distance from the plane.

subtopic: Right angle in a 3D triangle and its area
statement: The triangle $ABC$ has vertices $A(0,1,2)$, $B(3,3,1)$ and $C(k,5,2k)$, where $k$ is a constant. Angle $ABC$ is $90^\circ$. (a) Write down $\overrightarrow{BA}$ and $\overrightarrow{BC}$, the latter in terms of $k$. [2] (b) Find the value of $k$. [3] (c) Find the exact area of triangle $ABC$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\overrightarrow{BA}=\begin{pmatrix} -3 \\ -2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\overrightarrow{BC}=\begin{pmatrix} k-3 \\ 2 \\ 2k-1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\overrightarrow{BA}\cdot\overrightarrow{BC}=0$ [M1] $-3(k-3)-4+(2k-1)=0$ [A1] $k=4$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\overrightarrow{BC}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 7 \end{pmatrix}$, $|\overrightarrow{BA}|=\sqrt{14}$, $|\overrightarrow{BC}|=\sqrt{54}$ [A1] area $=\dfrac12\sqrt{14}\sqrt{54}$ [M1] $=\dfrac12\sqrt{756}=3\sqrt{21}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A right angle at $B$ means $\overrightarrow{BA}\cdot\overrightarrow{BC}=0$. In a right-angled triangle the area is half the product of the two perpendicular sides.

subtopic: Cartesian equation of a plane through three points
statement: The points $A(1, 2, 0)$, $B(3, 1, 2)$ and $C(2, 0, 1)$ lie in a plane $\Pi$. (a) Find $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}$. [2] (b) Find a vector normal to $\Pi$. [2] (c) Find the Cartesian equation of $\Pi$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}=\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 0 \\ -3 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (c) $\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf r=\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf a$ [M1] $1x+0y-1z=1$ [A1] check with $B$ and $C$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Take the cross product of two vectors in the plane to get the normal, then use $\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf r=\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf a$ with any point of the plane.

subtopic: Cartesian form of a line in three dimensions
statement: A line has equation $\dfrac{x-1}2=\dfrac{y+2}3=\dfrac{z-4}{-1}$. (a) Write down a point on the line and a direction vector. [2] (b) Find the coordinates of the point where the line meets the plane $z=0$. [3] (c) Show that the point $(3,1,3)$ lies on the line. [2]
markscheme: (a) $(1,-2,4)$ [A1] $\begin{pmatrix}2\\ 3\\ -1\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) let the common value be $\lambda$, so $x=1+2\lambda$, $y=-2+3\lambda$, $z=4-\lambda$ [M1] $z=0$ gives $\lambda=4$ [A1] $(9,10,0)$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\dfrac{3-1}2=1$, $\dfrac{1+2}3=1$ [M1] $\dfrac{3-4}{-1}=1$, all equal [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Set each ratio equal to a parameter to turn the Cartesian form into a vector equation.

subtopic: Crossing paths and collision of two particles
statement: Two particles move in the plane. At time $t$ seconds, the position of $P$ is $\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$ and the position of $Q$ is $\begin{pmatrix} -9 \\ -8 \end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$, with distances in meters. (a) Show that the paths of $P$ and $Q$ cross at the point $(11,7)$. [3] (b) Explain why the particles do not collide. [1] (c) Find the vector $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ in terms of $t$, and use your GDC to find the minimum distance between the particles and the time at which it occurs. [3]
markscheme: (a) $P$: $2+3t=11$ and $1+2t=7$ give $t=3$ [A1]; $Q$: $-9+4s=11$ and $-8+3s=7$ give $s=5$ [A1]; both pass through $(11,7)$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $P$ reaches $(11,7)$ at $t=3$ but $Q$ reaches it at $t=5$ [R1] [1 mark] (c) $\overrightarrow{PQ}=\begin{pmatrix} t-11 \\ t-9 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; $|PQ|^{2}=2t^{2}-40t+202$ [M1]; minimum $\sqrt2=1.41$ m at $t=10$ s [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Particles collide only if they are at the same position at the same time.

subtopic: Scalar product: angle, perpendicularity, unit vector
statement: Let $\mathbf u=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\2\end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf v=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\2\end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find the cosine of the angle between $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf v$. [3] (b) The vector $\mathbf w=\begin{pmatrix}3\\k\\-1\end{pmatrix}$ is perpendicular to $\mathbf u$. Find $k$. [2] (c) Find a unit vector in the direction opposite to $\mathbf u$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v=2-2+4=4$ [M1] $|\mathbf u|=|\mathbf v|=3$ [A1] $\cos\theta=\dfrac49$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf w=0$: $6-k-2=0$ [M1] $k=4$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $-\dfrac{1}{3}\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\2\end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix}-\frac23\\ \frac13\\ -\frac23\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Two vectors are perpendicular exactly when their scalar product is zero. A unit vector is a vector divided by its own magnitude.

subtopic: Cross product and area of a triangle
statement: The points $A(1,2,0)$, $B(3,-1,2)$ and $C(0,4,5)$ form a triangle. (a) Find $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}$. [2] (b) Find $\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}$. [3] (c) Hence find the exact area of triangle $ABC$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-3\\2\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\overrightarrow{AC}=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\2\\5\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Attempt at cross product [M1] $\begin{pmatrix}(-3)(5)-(2)(2)\\(2)(-1)-(2)(5)\\(2)(2)-(-3)(-1)\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $=\begin{pmatrix}-19\\-12\\1\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Area $=\tfrac12\left|\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}\right|$ [M1] $=\tfrac12\sqrt{361+144+1}=\dfrac{\sqrt{506}}{2}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Check your cross product by taking its scalar product with each original vector; both must give zero. The area of the triangle is half the magnitude of the cross product.

subtopic: Shortest distance between two skew lines
statement: Two straight cables are modeled by the lines $L_1:\ \mathbf{r}=\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$ and $L_2:\ \mathbf{r}=\begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 0 \\ 5 \end{pmatrix}+\mu\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$, where distances are in meters. (a) Show that $L_1$ and $L_2$ are skew. [3] (b) Let $P$ be the point on $L_1$ with parameter $\lambda$ and $Q$ the point on $L_2$ with parameter $\mu$. Find $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ in terms of $\lambda$ and $\mu$. [2] (c) The distance $PQ$ is a minimum when $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ is perpendicular to both lines. Write down two equations in $\lambda$ and $\mu$ that express this, and solve them. [4] (d) Hence find the shortest distance between the cables, correct to 3 significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) Directions are not parallel [R1] $x$ and $y$: $\lambda=4+2\mu$ and $2+\lambda=-\mu$ give $\mu=-2$, $\lambda=0$ [M1] $z$: $1\neq5$, so there is no intersection and the lines are skew [R1] [3 marks] (b) $\overrightarrow{PQ}=\overrightarrow{OQ}-\overrightarrow{OP}$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix} 4+2\mu-\lambda \\ -2-\mu-\lambda \\ 4-2\lambda \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\overrightarrow{PQ}\cdot\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$ $=0$ gives $(4+2\mu-\lambda)+(-2-\mu-\lambda)+2(4-2\lambda)=0$, i.e. $10+\mu-6\lambda=0$ [A1] $\overrightarrow{PQ}\cdot\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$ $=0$ gives $2(4+2\mu-\lambda)-(-2-\mu-\lambda)=0$, i.e. $10+5\mu-\lambda=0$ [A1] solve simultaneously [M1] $\lambda=1.38$, $\mu=-1.72$ [A1] [4 marks] (d) $\overrightarrow{PQ}=\begin{pmatrix} -0.828 \\ -1.66 \\ 1.24 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $|\overrightarrow{PQ}|=2.23$ m [A1] [2 marks]
tips: For skew lines, the shortest distance occurs along a segment perpendicular to both direction vectors. This gives two linear equations that you can solve on your GDC.

subtopic: Robot with a change of velocity: position and distance traveled
statement: A robot starts at the origin and moves with constant velocity $\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}$ m s$^{-1}$ for $10$ seconds. It then changes direction and moves with constant velocity $\begin{pmatrix} -2 \\ 5 \end{pmatrix}$ m s$^{-1}$ for a further $10$ seconds. (a) Find the position of the robot when $t=10$. [1] (b) Write down an expression for the position vector of the robot at time $t$ for $10\le t\le20$. [2] (c) Find the distance of the robot from its starting point when $t=20$, correct to 3 significant figures. [3] (d) Find the total distance the robot has traveled in the $20$ seconds, correct to 3 significant figures. [3] (e) Explain why the total distance traveled is greater than the answer to part (c). [1]
markscheme: (a) $10\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}$ $=\begin{pmatrix} 30 \\ 40 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\begin{pmatrix} 30 \\ 40 \end{pmatrix}+(t-10)\begin{pmatrix} -2 \\ 5 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (c) position $=\begin{pmatrix} 10 \\ 90 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\sqrt{10^2+90^2}$ [M1] $=90.6$ m [A1] [3 marks] (d) speeds $5$ and $\sqrt{29}$ [A1] $10(5)+10\sqrt{29}$ [M1] $=104$ m [A1] [3 marks] (e) The robot did not travel in a straight line from start to finish, so the path is longer than the straight-line distance [R1] [1 mark]
tips: When velocity changes, build the position in stages: the start of the second stage is the end of the first. Distance traveled adds the length of each stage, which is different from displacement.

subtopic: Closest approach of a drone to an antenna
statement: A drone flies along a straight path with position vector $\mathbf{r}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}3\\2\\1\end{pmatrix}$, where the components are in meters and $t$ is the time in seconds, $t\ge0$. An antenna is at the point $Q(10,9,2)$. (a) Find the speed of the drone, correct to three significant figures. [2] (b) Find the value of $t$ for which the drone is closest to the antenna. [4] (c) Find the shortest distance between the drone and the antenna, correct to three significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) Speed $=\left|\begin{pmatrix}3\\2\\1\end{pmatrix}\right|=\sqrt{3^2+2^2+1^2}$ [M1] $=\sqrt{14}=3.74\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Vector from the drone to $Q$: $\begin{pmatrix}8-3t\\8-2t\\2-t\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $d^2=(8-3t)^2+(8-2t)^2+(2-t)^2=14t^2-84t+132$ [M1] Minimise, e.g. $\dfrac{d(d^2)}{dt}=28t-84=0$ (or use the GDC, or perpendicularity to the direction vector) [M1] $t=3$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) $d^2=14(9)-84(3)+132=6$ [M1] $d=\sqrt6=2.45\ \text{m}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Minimising the squared distance avoids a square root and gives the same $t$. Alternatively the closest point occurs when the vector from the drone to the antenna is perpendicular to the direction of travel.

subtopic: Reflection of a point in a line using vectors
statement: A line has equation $\mathbf{r}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ and $P$ is the point $(6,3)$. Let $F$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to the line. (a) Write down the position vector of a general point on the line and the vector from this point to $P$. [2] (b) Find $t$ and the coordinates of $F$. [3] (c) Find the coordinates of the reflection of $P$ in the line, and the distance from $P$ to the line, to three significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\begin{pmatrix} 1+2t \\ 2+t \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; $\begin{pmatrix} 5-2t \\ 1-t \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) perpendicular: $2(5-2t)+(1-t)=0$ [M1]; $t=2.2$ [A1]; $F=(5.4,\,4.2)$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\overrightarrow{OP'}=2\overrightarrow{OF}-\overrightarrow{OP}$ [M1]; $P'=(4.8,\,5.4)$ [A1]; distance $PF=\sqrt{0.36+1.44}=1.34$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: At the foot of the perpendicular, the vector from $F$ to $P$ is perpendicular to the direction of the line.

subtopic: Parameter making two 3D lines intersect
statement: The lines $L_1$ and $L_2$ are given by $L_1:\ \mathbf{r}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$ and $L_2:\ \mathbf{r}=\begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ k \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}+\mu\begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$, where $k$ is a constant. The lines intersect at a single point. (a) Use the $x$ and $z$ components to find $\lambda$ and $\mu$. [4] (b) Hence find the value of $k$. [2] (c) Find the coordinates of the point of intersection. [1]
markscheme: (a) $1+\lambda=5-\mu$ [A1] $3+2\lambda=2+\mu$ [A1] from the $x$ equation $\mu=4-\lambda$, so $3+2\lambda=2+(4-\lambda)$ [M1] $\lambda=1,\ \mu=3$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $y$: $2+1=k-3$ [M1] $k=6$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $(2,3,5)$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Use two of the three equations to find the parameters, then use the third equation to determine the unknown constant.

subtopic: Shortest distance from a point to a line
statement: The line $l$ has equation $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}$ and the point $P$ has coordinates $(4, 3, 5)$. (a) Find the value of $\lambda$ at the foot $F$ of the perpendicular from $P$ to $l$. [2] (b) Find the coordinates of $F$ and the shortest distance from $P$ to $l$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\overrightarrow{PF}\cdot\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}=0$ with $F$ on $l$ [M1] $\lambda=\frac{1}{3}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $F=(\frac{5}{3}, \frac{1}{3}, \frac{4}{3})$ [A1] $PF=\sqrt{26}$ [M1] $=5.099$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: At the foot of the perpendicular, $\overrightarrow{PF}$ is perpendicular to the direction of the line. Alternatively the distance is $\dfrac{|\overrightarrow{AP}\times\mathbf d|}{|\mathbf d|}$.

subtopic: Vectors in a square-based pyramid
statement: A pyramid has a square base with vertices $A(0,0,0)$, $B(6,0,0)$, $C(6,6,0)$ and $D(0,6,0)$, and apex $V(3,3,8)$. (a) Find $\overrightarrow{VA}$ and $\overrightarrow{VC}$ and the angle $AVC$, to the nearest tenth of a degree. [4] (b) Find the angle between the edge $VA$ and the base, to the nearest tenth of a degree. [3] (c) Let $M$ be the midpoint of $VB$. Find the coordinates of $M$ and the length $AM$, to three significant figures. [3] (d) Find the area of triangle $VAB$ to three significant figures, using the angle between $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{AV}$. [3] (e) The point $P$ lies on $VC$ with $\overrightarrow{OP}=\overrightarrow{OV}+s\overrightarrow{VC}$, and $AP$ is perpendicular to $VC$. Find $s$ and the length $AP$, to three significant figures. [4] (f) Let $N$ be the midpoint of $VC$. Show that the lines $AM$ and $DN$ meet, and find the point where they meet. [4]
markscheme: (a) $\overrightarrow{VA}=\begin{pmatrix} -3 \\ -3 \\ -8 \end{pmatrix}$, $\overrightarrow{VC}=\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 3 \\ -8 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1][A1]; $\cos\theta=\dfrac{-9-9+64}{82}$ [M1]; $55.9^{\circ}$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) the foot of $V$ is on $AC$, so the angle is $VAC$ [R1]; $\cos=\dfrac{\overrightarrow{AV}\cdot\overrightarrow{AC}}{|AV||AC|}=\dfrac{36}{\sqrt{82}\sqrt{72}}$ [M1]; $62.1^{\circ}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $M=(4.5,\,1.5,\,4)$ [A1]; $AM=\sqrt{20.25+2.25+16}$ [M1]; $6.20$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $\cos\angle VAB=\dfrac{18}{6\sqrt{82}}$ so angle $=70.7^{\circ}$ [A1]; area $=\dfrac12\times6\times\sqrt{82}\times\sin70.7^{\circ}$ [M1]; $25.6$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) $\overrightarrow{AP}=\begin{pmatrix} 3+3s \\ 3+3s \\ 8-8s \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; $\overrightarrow{AP}\cdot\overrightarrow{VC}=0$ gives $18+18s-64+64s=0$ [M1]; $s=\dfrac{23}{41}=0.561$ [A1]; $AP=7.50$ [A1] [4 marks] (f) $N=(4.5,\,4.5,\,4)$; $AM:\ \lambda(4.5,\,1.5,\,4)$ [A1]; $DN:\ (0,6,0)+\mu(4.5,\,-1.5,\,4)$ [A1]; equate: $\lambda=\mu=2$ satisfies all three components [M1]; meeting point $(9,\,3,\,8)$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Use position vectors and the scalar product; a perpendicularity condition gives an equation for the parameter.

subtopic: Vector equation of a line and a point on it
statement: A line $l$ passes through $A(1,2,-1)$ and $B(4,-1,5)$. (a) Find the vector $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and the vector equation of $l$. [3] (b) Determine whether the point $C(7,-4,11)$ lies on $l$. [3] (c) Find the coordinates of the point on $l$ where $z=2$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ -3 \\ 6 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; $\mathbf{r}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ -3 \\ 6 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1] [3 marks] (b) $1+3\lambda=7$ gives $\lambda=2$ [M1]; $2-3(2)=-4$ (satisfied) and $-1+6(2)=11$ (satisfied) [A1]; so $C$ lies on $l$ [R1] [3 marks] (c) $-1+6\lambda=2$ gives $\lambda=\dfrac12$ [M1]; point $\left(\dfrac52,\dfrac12,2\right)$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A point lies on a line if one value of the parameter satisfies all three coordinate equations.

subtopic: Intersection of a line and a plane, and the angle between them
statement: The line $l$ has equation $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ and the plane $\Pi$ has equation $1x+2y-1z=4$. (a) Find the coordinates of the point where $l$ meets $\Pi$. [4] (b) Find the acute angle between $l$ and $\Pi$. [3]
markscheme: (a) substitute $x,y,z$ in terms of $\lambda$ [M1] $-1\lambda-1=4$ [A1] $\lambda=-5$ [A1] point $(-10, 6, -2)$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $\sin\theta=\dfrac{|\mathbf d\cdot\mathbf n|}{|\mathbf d||\mathbf n|}$ [M1] $=0.1667$ [A1] $\theta=9.59^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The angle between a line and a plane is $90^\circ$ minus the angle between the line and the normal, so use sine with $|\mathbf d\cdot\mathbf n|$.

subtopic: Intersection of two lines in the plane and the angle between them
statement: Two lines are $l_1:\ \mathbf{r}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ and $l_2:\ \mathbf{r}=\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}+s\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find the coordinates of the point of intersection. [4] (b) Find the acute angle between the lines, to the nearest tenth of a degree. [3]
markscheme: (a) $1+3t=2s$ and $2+t=-1+2s$ [M1][A1]; eliminating $s$: $1+3t=3+t$ so $t=1$ [A1]; intersection $(4,3)$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $\cos\theta=\dfrac{|3\times2+1\times2|}{\sqrt{10}\sqrt{8}}$ [M1][A1]; $26.6^{\circ}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: At the intersection, both lines give the same position, so equate the components.

subtopic: Line in three dimensions: points and perpendicular direction
statement: A line $L$ has equation $\mathbf{r}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find the coordinates of the point on $L$ where $t=3$. [1] (b) Determine whether the point $Q(9, -2, 11)$ lies on $L$. [3] (c) Find the value of $k$ such that $\begin{pmatrix} k \\ 2 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$ is perpendicular to the direction of $L$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $(7, -1, 8)$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $1+2t=9$ gives $t=4$ [M1]; $2-t=-2$ gives $t=4$ and $-1+3t=11$ gives $t=4$ [A1]; the same $t$ works, so $Q$ lies on $L$ [R1] [3 marks] (c) scalar product $=0$ [M1]; $2k-2-3=0$ [A1]; $k=\dfrac{5}{2}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Equate each coordinate to the same parameter value; perpendicular vectors have scalar product zero.

subtopic: Dividing a line segment in a given ratio
statement: Two radio masts are located at $A(2,-1,5)$ and $B(8,5,-4)$, with distances in kilometers. (a) Find $\overrightarrow{AB}$. [1] (b) Show that $|\overrightarrow{AB}|=3\sqrt{17}$. [2] (c) Find the position vector of the midpoint $M$ of $AB$. [1] (d) The point $P$ lies on $AB$ so that $AP:PB=2:1$. Find the coordinates of $P$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix} 6 \\ 6 \\ -9 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $|\overrightarrow{AB}|=\sqrt{36+36+81}=\sqrt{153}$ [M1] $=\sqrt{9\times17}=3\sqrt{17}$ [AG] [2 marks] (c) $\overrightarrow{OM}=\begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ 2 \\ \frac12 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) $\overrightarrow{OP}=\overrightarrow{OA}+\dfrac23\overrightarrow{AB}$ [M1] $P(6,3,-1)$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: For a ratio $m:n$, the point is $\dfrac{m}{m+n}$ of the way along the vector from the first point. Midpoints are the special case 1:1.

subtopic: An aircraft climbing at constant velocity
statement: An aircraft takes off from the origin $O$ and then flies with constant velocity $\begin{pmatrix} 120 \\ 90 \\ 12 \end{pmatrix}$ km/h, where the first two components are east and north and the third is vertical (up). Time $t$ is in hours after take-off. (a) Write down the position vector at time $t$, and the speed of the aircraft to three significant figures. [3] (b) Find the time at which the aircraft reaches an altitude of $9$ km, and the horizontal distance from $O$ at that time. [3] (c) Find the angle of climb, the angle between the velocity and the horizontal, to the nearest tenth of a degree. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{r}=t\begin{pmatrix} 120 \\ 90 \\ 12 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; speed $=\sqrt{120^{2}+90^{2}+12^{2}}$ [M1]; $150$ km/h [A1] [3 marks] (b) $12t=9$ so $t=0.75$ h [A1]; horizontal position $(90,\,67.5)$ [A1]; distance $\sqrt{90^{2}+67.5^{2}}=112.5$ km [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\tan\theta=\dfrac{12}{150}$ [M1]; $4.6^{\circ}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The horizontal speed is the length of the east-north components.

subtopic: Vector proof: the centroid divides each median in the ratio 2:1
statement: The position vectors of the vertices of a triangle $ABC$ are $\mathbf a$, $\mathbf b$, $\mathbf c$. The point $M$ is the midpoint of $BC$. (a) Write down the position vector of $M$. [1] (b) The point $G$ lies on $AM$ with $AG:GM=2:1$. Show that $\mathbf g=\dfrac13(\mathbf a+\mathbf b+\mathbf c)$. [3] (c) Explain why $G$ also lies on the median from $B$, and so the three medians are concurrent. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf m=\dfrac12(\mathbf b+\mathbf c)$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\mathbf g=\mathbf a+\dfrac23(\mathbf m-\mathbf a)$ [M1] $=\dfrac13\mathbf a+\dfrac23\times\dfrac12(\mathbf b+\mathbf c)$ [A1] $=\dfrac13(\mathbf a+\mathbf b+\mathbf c)$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) the expression for $\mathbf g$ is symmetric in $\mathbf a$, $\mathbf b$, $\mathbf c$ [R1] so the same calculation from $B$ (or $C$) gives the same point [R1] [2 marks]
tips: A point dividing $AM$ in the ratio $2:1$ is two-thirds of the way from $A$ to $M$.

subtopic: Common perpendicular of two skew lines
statement: The lines $l_1$ and $l_2$ have equations $l_1:\ \mathbf r=s\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$ and $l_2:\ \mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ -2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Show that $l_1$ and $l_2$ are skew. [3] (b) Find the shortest distance between $l_1$ and $l_2$. [3] (c) Find the coordinates of the point $A$ on $l_1$ and the point $B$ on $l_2$ for which $AB$ is perpendicular to both lines, and write down an equation of the line $AB$. [4]
markscheme: (a) the direction vectors are not parallel [R1] $s=3$, $s=-2+t$, $0=1+t$ gives $t=-1$ and then $s=-3$, which contradicts $s=3$ [M1] so the lines do not intersect and are skew [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}\times\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] distance $=\dfrac{\left|\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ -2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}\cdot\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}\right|}{\sqrt3}$ [M1] $=\dfrac6{\sqrt3}=2\sqrt3$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $A=(s,s,0)$ and $B=(3,-2+t,1+t)$ so $\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix} 3-s \\ t-2-s \\ 1+t \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}=0$ gives $1+t-2s=0$ and $\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}=0$ gives $2t-s-1=0$ [M1] solving: $s=1$, $t=1$ [A1] $A=(1,1,0)$ and $B=(3,-1,2)$, and a line through them is $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Two lines are skew if they are not parallel and do not meet. The shortest distance is the length of the projection of a vector joining the lines onto the common normal direction.

subtopic: Shortest distance from a point to a line using the scalar product
statement: A straight underground pipeline is modeled by the line $L:\ \mathbf{r}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$, where distances are in meters. A house is located at the point $H(7,8,5)$. (a) Let $F$ be the point on $L$ closest to $H$. Write down $\overrightarrow{FH}$ in terms of $\lambda$. [2] (b) Use the fact that $\overrightarrow{FH}$ is perpendicular to the direction of $L$ to show that $\lambda=\dfrac{28}{9}$. [3] (c) Find the coordinates of $F$, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (d) Find the shortest distance from the house to the pipeline, correct to 3 significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\overrightarrow{OF}=\begin{pmatrix} 1+2\lambda \\ 2+\lambda \\ 2\lambda \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\overrightarrow{FH}=\begin{pmatrix} 6-2\lambda \\ 6-\lambda \\ 5-2\lambda \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\overrightarrow{FH}\cdot\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$ $=0$ [M1] $2(6-2\lambda)+(6-\lambda)+2(5-2\lambda)=0$ [A1] $28-9\lambda=0$ so $\lambda=\dfrac{28}{9}$ [AG] [3 marks] (c) $\overrightarrow{OF}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}+\dfrac{28}{9}\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $F(7.22,\ 5.11,\ 6.22)$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $|\overrightarrow{FH}|=\sqrt{(-0.222)^2+(2.89)^2+(-1.22)^2}$ [M1] $=3.14$ m [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The shortest distance from a point to a line is along the perpendicular, so the scalar product of the connecting vector with the direction vector is zero. Use unrounded values when computing the final distance.

subtopic: Perpendicular vectors and parallel vectors with unknowns
statement: Let $\mathbf u=\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ k \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$, $\mathbf v=\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 4 \\ k \end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf w=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Given that $\mathbf u$ is perpendicular to $\mathbf v$, find $k$. [3] (b) Find the values of $\lambda$ and $\mu$ such that $\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ \lambda \\ \mu \end{pmatrix}$ is parallel to $\mathbf w$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v=0$ [M1] $6+4k-k=0$ [A1] $k=-2$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) parallel means a scalar multiple: $2\mathbf w=\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -4 \\ 6 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1] $\lambda=-4$, $\mu=6$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Perpendicular vectors have zero scalar product. Parallel vectors are scalar multiples of each other.

subtopic: Lines with an unknown component: perpendicular and 60 degree cases
statement: Two straight support rods are modeled by the lines $L_1:\ \mathbf{r}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix} p \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$ and $L_2:\ \mathbf{r}=\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 4 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}+\mu\begin{pmatrix} p \\ -5 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}$, where $p$ is a constant. (a) Find the two values of $p$ for which the rods are perpendicular. [3] (b) For $p=1$, find the acute angle between the rods, correct to 3 significant figures. [3] (c) Find the two positive values of $p$ for which the acute angle between the rods is exactly $60^\circ$. Give your answers to 3 significant figures. [4]
markscheme: (a) direction vectors have scalar product zero [M1] $p^2-10-6=0$ [A1] $p=4$ or $p=-4$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\mathbf{d}_1\cdot\mathbf{d}_2=1-10-6=-15$ [A1] $\cos\theta=\dfrac{15}{\sqrt{14}\sqrt{30}}$ [M1] $\theta=43.0^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\cos60^\circ=\dfrac{|p^2-16|}{\sqrt{p^2+13}\sqrt{p^2+29}}$ [M1][A1] solve using GDC (graph intersection or solver) [M1] $p=2.03$ and $p=7.25$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: The direction vectors decide the angle between lines, not the points they pass through. For the last part, enter both sides as functions of $p$ and find the intersections on your GDC.

subtopic: Cyclist on a straight road: where the nearest station changes
statement: Two charging stations are at $A(2,6)$ and $B(10,2)$, where each unit represents $1$ km. A straight road follows the line $y=0.4x+2$, for $0\leq x\leq12$. A cyclist rides along the road from the point with $x=0$ to the point with $x=12$ and always uses the nearer station. (a) Show that the perpendicular bisector of $A$ and $B$ has equation $y=2x-8$. [3] (b) Find the coordinates of the point $P$ where the road crosses the perpendicular bisector. [2] (c) Find the distance $PA$, correct to three significant figures, and state the distance $PB$. [2] (d) State which station the cyclist uses at the start of the road and which station at the end, giving a reason for each. [3]
markscheme: (a) Midpoint of $AB=(6,4)$ [A1] Gradient of $AB=-\dfrac12$, so bisector gradient $=2$ [A1] $y-4=2(x-6)\Rightarrow y=2x-8$ [AG] [3 marks] (b) $0.4x+2=2x-8$ [M1] $1.6x=10$, so $P=(6.25,4.5)$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $PA=\sqrt{(6.25-2)^2+(4.5-6)^2}=4.51$ km [A1] $PB=PA=4.51$ km because $P$ is on the bisector [A1] [2 marks] (d) At $(0,2)$: distance to $A=\sqrt{4+16}=4.47$ and to $B=\sqrt{100+0}=10$, so station $A$ [A1] At $(12,6.8)$: distance to $A=\sqrt{100+0.64}=10.0$ and to $B=\sqrt{4+23.04}=5.20$, so station $B$ [A1] The nearest station changes at $P$, where the road crosses the cell boundary [R1] [3 marks]
tips: The place where a path crosses a Voronoi boundary is where the nearest site changes. Solve the equation of the path together with the equation of the bisector.

subtopic: Finding an unknown site from a vertex
statement: Sites $P(0,0)$ and $Q(6,0)$ are given. A third site $R$ lies on the $y$-axis with positive $y$-coordinate, and the Voronoi vertex of $P$, $Q$ and $R$ is at $(3,4)$. (a) Find the distance from the vertex $(3,4)$ to $P$. [1] (b) Find the coordinates of $R$. [4]
tips: The vertex is equidistant from all three sites.

subtopic: Voronoi vertex of an isosceles triangle with exact fractions
statement: Three sensors are placed at $A(-4,0)$, $B(4,0)$ and $C(0,6)$. Their Voronoi cells meet at a single vertex $V$. (a) Write down the equation of the perpendicular bisector of $AB$. [1] (b) Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of $AC$, in the form $y=mx+c$. [3] (c) Hence find the coordinates of $V$. [2] (d) Find the exact distance from $V$ to each of the three sensors. [2]
markscheme: (a) $x=0$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Midpoint of $AC=(-2,3)$ [A1] Gradient of $AC=\dfrac{6}{4}=\dfrac32$, so bisector gradient $=-\dfrac23$ [A1] $y-3=-\dfrac23(x+2)$, i.e. $y=-\dfrac23x+\dfrac53$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Substitute $x=0$ [M1] $V=\left(0,\dfrac53\right)$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $VA=\sqrt{16+\dfrac{25}{9}}$ [M1] $=\sqrt{\dfrac{169}{9}}=\dfrac{13}{3}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Because $A$ and $B$ are symmetric about the $y$-axis, the vertex lies on the $y$-axis, so only one more bisector is needed. Keep fractions exact.

subtopic: Nearest neighbor interpolation of temperature from three stations
statement: Three weather stations are located at $S_1(1,2)$, $S_2(5,6)$ and $S_3(7,1)$, where each unit is $1$ km. They record temperatures of $14^\circ\mathrm{C}$, $18^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $11^\circ\mathrm{C}$ respectively. The temperature at any other location is estimated by using the temperature at the nearest station. (a) Find the squared distance from the point $P(3,3)$ to each of the three stations. [3] (b) Hence write down the estimated temperature at $P$. [1] (c) Estimate the temperature at $Q(6,4)$, showing your working. [2] (d) A point lies exactly on the boundary between the cells of $S_1$ and $S_2$. State what is true about its distances from $S_1$ and $S_2$. [1]
tips: In nearest neighbor interpolation each point takes the value of the closest site. Compare squared distances; the smallest one gives the nearest station.

subtopic: Bisector with unknown coordinate and a third site
statement: Two sites in a Voronoi diagram are $A(1,2)$ and $B(7,k)$, where $k\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Given that the perpendicular bisector of $[AB]$ has gradient $-3$, find the value of $k$. [2] Use the value of $k$ from part (a) in the remaining parts. (b) Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of $[AB]$. [3] A third site $C$ is added at $(1,8)$. (c) Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of $[AC]$. [2] (d) Find the coordinates of the Voronoi vertex of $A$, $B$ and $C$. [2]
markscheme: (a) Gradient of $AB=\frac{k-2}{6}$ [M1] $\frac{k-2}{6}=\frac13$, so $k=4$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $B=(7,4)$, midpoint $(4,3)$ [A1] Use of perpendicular gradient $-3$ through the midpoint [M1] $y-3=-3(x-4)$, so $y=-3x+15$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $AC$ is vertical, so the bisector is horizontal [M1] Passes through the midpoint $(1,5)$, so $y=5$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $5=-3x+15$ [M1] $x=\frac{10}3$, so the vertex is $\left(\frac{10}3,5\right)$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The gradients of a segment and its perpendicular bisector multiply to $-1$, which lets you find an unknown coordinate from a given gradient. A vertical segment always has a horizontal bisector.

subtopic: Voronoi vertices and the toxic waste location
statement: A region is modelled by the rectangle $0\le x\le12$, $0\le y\le10$, with units in kilometres. Four fire stations are located at $A(2,3)$, $B(8,2)$, $C(5,8)$ and $D(10,9)$. The Voronoi diagram for the four stations has two vertices inside the rectangle: $V_1$, equidistant from $A$, $B$ and $C$, and $V_2$, equidistant from $B$, $C$ and $D$. (a) Find the coordinates of $V_1$. [4] (b) Find the coordinates of $V_2$. [3] (c) A storage depot for hazardous chemicals is to be placed at one of the two Voronoi vertices so that its distance from the nearest fire station is as large as possible. Determine which vertex should be used, and find this distance. [3]
markscheme: (a) Perpendicular bisector of $[AB]$: midpoint $(5,2.5)$, gradient of $AB=-\frac16$, so perpendicular gradient is $6$, giving $y=6x-27.5$ [A1] Perpendicular bisector of $[BC]$: midpoint $(6.5,5)$, gradient of $BC=-2$, so perpendicular gradient $\frac12$, giving $y=0.5x+1.75$ [A1] Attempt to solve simultaneously [M1] $V_1=(5.32,4.41)$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) Perpendicular bisector of $[CD]$: midpoint $(7.5,8.5)$, gradient of $CD=\frac15$, perpendicular gradient $-5$ [M1] $y=-5x+46$ [A1] Solve with $y=0.5x+1.75$: $V_2=(8.05,5.77)$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Distance from $V_1$ to $A$: $\sqrt{(5.318-2)^2+(4.409-3)^2}=3.60$ and from $V_2$ to $B$: $\sqrt{(8.045-8)^2+(5.773-2)^2}=3.77$ [M1] Both distances correct [A1] Use $V_2$, at a distance of $3.77$ km from the nearest station [A1] [3 marks]
